Widening gap between aid, development needs threatens global security: Stockholm Peace Institute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:42:46 UTC
22:42:46 KST

Efe Ozkan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A widening gap between official development assistance and global development and humanitarian needs could have serious consequences for human security and political stability, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) said in a report released Tuesday.
The report said the gap could be closed with only a small fraction of the resources being directed toward increased military spending.
Global military expenditures reached a record $2.9 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 2.5% of global gross domestic product, according to SIPRI data.
At the same time, official development assistance (ODA) has declined since 2024, based on figures from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
SIPRI said core official development assistance spending began to stagnate in 2021, a trend temporarily obscured by increased aid to Ukraine following the start of the war in 2022 and higher spending by donor countries on hosting refugees.
The largest declines in core official development assistance spending have been seen in economic infrastructure and health, according to the report.
“Wealthy states in Europe and beyond have sharply increased their military spending in response to rising military threats,” said Xiao Liang, a researcher with SIPRI's Military Expenditure and Arms Production Program.
“But this has coincided with deep cuts in other budget lines, including development and humanitarian aid. This can create widespread insecurity for people and states that rely on aid.”
'Sustained withdrawal of vital humanitarian and development assistance' even as needs 'are growing'
SIPRI researchers estimate that official development assistance funding needs could reach as much as $326 billion in 2028, depending on developments related to armed conflicts, natural disasters, and other factors.
That would leave a potential funding gap of $179 billion, exceeding the total amount of official development assistance expected to be committed in 2028.
“We are in the middle of a sustained withdrawal of vital humanitarian and development assistance at a time when needs for it are growing,” said Nan Tian, the director of SIPRI's Military Expenditure and Arms Production Program.
He added that the projected funding gap represents only a fraction of the additional resources being allocated to military spending and that meeting future official development assistance needs remains affordable.
The report examined recent development aid and military spending policies in Germany and the UK, finding that governments had cited the need to finance higher military spending when justifying cuts to official development assistance.
However, SIPRI said the reductions in aid made only a marginal contribution to planned increases in military expenditure.
“With the weakening of international cooperation and rising geopolitical tensions and militarization, it is understandable that states are seeking to invest in their security,” Liang said.
“But military capabilities alone do not guarantee security. Development aid can address long-term drivers of insecurity and should therefore be seen as complementing military spending, not competing with it.”

Voter turnout in Israeli elections reaches 44.9% after 7 hours, highest since 1973
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:41:37 UTC
22:41:37 KST

Rania Abushamala
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Voter turnout in Israel’s legislative elections reached 44.9% by 2 pm (1200GMT) on Tuesday, the highest figure recorded for that hour since 1973, according to the Central Elections Committee.
More than 3.29 million voters had cast their ballots nationwide, Din Livneh, the commission’s acting director general, said in statements carried by the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.
“We have broken all records registered by the Elections Committee since 1973,” Livneh said. “There has been no such data.”
Earlier, the Elections Committee said a total of 2.39 million Israelis had cast their ballots by noon local time (1000GMT), an increase of more than 3 percentage points compared with the previous election.
Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich attributed the high turnout to exceptionally strong participation among Arab voters and in left-wing strongholds.
More than 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote in Tuesday’s elections to choose members of the 120-seat Knesset.
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500 GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 pm (2000 GMT).
The elections are Israel’s first general polls since the start of its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

Bird flu detected at Dutch farm, 45,000 laying hens to be culled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:41:35 UTC
22:41:35 KST

Aysu Bicer
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Bird flu has been detected at a poultry farm in Lutjegast, a village in the northern Dutch province of Groningen, prompting authorities to cull 45,000 laying hens, the Dutch Agriculture Ministry said.
The outbreak is the first reported in the Netherlands since July, according to the ministry.
The affected farm keeps laying hens, regional broadcaster RTV NOF reported.
Authorities immediately imposed a transport ban within a 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) radius of the farm to prevent the virus from spreading.
The ban prohibits the transport of birds, eggs, manure and used bedding within the designated zone, which extends across parts of the provinces of Groningen and Friesland.
The restricted area includes 21 other agricultural businesses, according to the report.
The ministry said the outbreak does not currently warrant a nationwide or regional confinement requirement for poultry.

Kryvyi Rih HOAs can receive backup power equipment grants from URCS
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:40:06 EET
22:40:06 KST

Homeowners associations (HOAs) in Kryvyi Rih will be able to receive grant support to purchase backup power equipment from the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS).
"The Ukrainian Red Cross, with the support of the Norwegian Red Cross, is launching a grant support program for HOAs in Kryvyi Rih. The funding will help acquire backup power equipment to ensure the operation of basic in-house systems during prolonged power outages," the URCS reported on Facebook.
The application period began on October 26 and will last through November 15, 2026.
HOAs registered as legal entities that manage apartment buildings in one of the three districts of Kryvyi Rih - Pokrovskyi, Metalurgijnyi, and Saksahanskyi - are eligible to participate in the program.
A single HOA may submit several applications if it manages multiple buildings. A separate application and a corresponding packet of documents must be prepared for each building.
Participation in the program is competitive: applications will be checked for compliance with the terms, and winners will be determined based on the selection results. Submitting an application does not guarantee funding.
The grant amount depends on the height of the building: UAH 100,000 for up to 6 floors inclusive; UAH 200,000 for 7 to 16 floors; UAH 300,000 for 17 floors and above, or for buildings from 4 to 16 floors inclusive with three or more entrances.
Grant funds can be used to purchase gasoline, diesel, or gas generators, inverters, batteries, solar panels, and high-voltage battery control units.
Equipment installation costs, related materials, and other additional expenses are not covered by grant funds. If necessary, HOAs and/or building residents may cover them through their own co-financing.

Decoupling ‘would be a big mistake’, says Germany’s Merz as he seeks balanced ties with China
- Germany’s Merz said a balanced China policy needs a united, strong and competitive Europe. He warned that decoupling would be “a big mistake” and backed “de-risking and diversification” instead.
- He spoke in Singapore during a five-day Asia tour, amid rising EU-China trade strains. He cited China’s “€360 billion” trade surplus and called for more dialogue on trade, security and world order.
- Merz linked China to wider security issues, urging Beijing to help end Russia’s war in Ukraine. He also backed stronger EU-ASEAN trade ties and said any peace deal must include Ukraine.
AI generated
SINGAPORE - Building a balanced relationship with China requires Germany and Europe to be united, innovative and competitive, said German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“Wise China policy begins at home,” he said on Oct 27 in a lecture in Singapore where he is on a two-day official visit, amid trade tensions between Europe and China that has threatened to escalate into an all-out trade war.
“We will be better equipped to build balanced relations with China if we ourselves are united, strong, resilient, innovative and competitive.
“We are working systematically towards that goal, both in Germany and at the European level,” he said, as he delivered the 49th Singapore Lecture organised by the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.
Europe-China talks earlier in October resulted in China agreeing to cap hybrid electric vehicle exports to the European Union over a four-year period. Brussels is alarmed at a ballooning trade deficit that reached €360 billion (S$515 billion) in 2025 - or about €1 billion a day.
China’s manufacturing might is causing frictions with European industries, in sectors from electric vehicles to chemicals, pharmaceuticals and industrial machinery.
Germany has advocated stronger defensive trade tools against what it views as unfair trade practices by other countries. Merz visited Beijing in February to address issues such as Germany’s growing trade deficit and Chinese industrial overcapacity.
Speaking at the Singapore Marriott Tang Plaza Hotel in Orchard Road, Merz said that it is imperative to continue dialogue with great powers, “even where our interests and values only align in part”.
“This also applies to China. Our view of Beijing has become more nuanced. China’s pivotal role in world politics raises deep questions regarding trade, security and international order,” he said, adding that dealing with these challenges is a major long-term strategic task for Europe.
But decoupling “would be a big mistake”, he said, as doing so would make Germany neither safe nor more prosperous. “Instead, we are pursuing de-risking and diversification.”
How Germany intends to manage its growing strains with China was a key theme of Merz’s lecture, alongside the existential nature of the Russia-Ukraine war for Europe, and advancing cooperation in research, technology and people-to-people exchanges.
His 20-minute speech was titled Germany and the Indo-Pacific: Partnership, Competitiveness and Resilience in a Changing World.
‘New geopolitical era’
He described a “new geopolitical era” shaped by new dynamics among great powers, technological revolutions and by the erosion of an international order. This erosion is “at odds with our fundamental values and interests”, he added.
Nowhere was this more evident than in Ukraine, he said, as Russia – “a great power pursuing a militant, revisionist agenda” – invaded Ukraine, its neighbour, unprovoked.
He reiterated European calls for China to play a greater role in restraining Moscow.
“As a permanent member of the Security Council, China bears a particular responsibility for upholding international law. China’s voice carries weight in Moscow. We encourage China to use her power to help bring about a just peace in Ukraine, rather than enabling Moscow’s war of aggression.”
Merz said that Germany intends to play its part for order, peace and security in the Indo-Pacific, with the German government’s “continued adherence to its One-China policy” with regard to Taiwan.
“We know as well as our partners in the region: Any escalation or violent change to the status quo in the Indo-Pacific would have grave consequences for global security and prosperity.”
Merz is on five-day tour of Singapore, Japan and South Korea, which he described as “three of our most important partners in the region”. Germany is also forging closer ties with India, Indonesia and Vietnam, he added.
His lecture was chaired by Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo, who said that Germany is one of the most important trading partners with ASEAN within the EU, as well as the largest exporter of goods to the region.
With the international rules-based order and globalisation coming under great strain, Germany is a trusted and reliable partner for the region in cooperation to support international law, free trade and economic resilience, said Teo.
In a question-and-answer session following his speech, Jens Ruebbert, chairman of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, asked the German leader if the German government could do more to advance a bloc-to-bloc free trade agreement (FTA).
He cited the initial FTA deal between the Philippines and the EU reached in September, which could pave the way for an eventual ASEAN-EU FTA.
Merz said he was in favour of such an FTA, “provided we have enough in common to do it fast”.
“If not, I would like to see as a step in between to have preliminary FTAs with those who are in this area and willing to move forward. But the best way to move forward would be a bloc-to-bloc agreement.”
Ian Storey, a researcher at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, asked about speculation that US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin may meet at the APEC summit in November to discuss the Russia-Ukraine war.
What steps are Germany and its European partners taking to ensure that Europe plays a central role in this peace process, Storey asked.
Merz said Europe was trying to find ways which they can engage Russia, not just involving the so-called E3 grouping of the United Kingdom, France and Germany, but also others such as Poland, Italy and Norway.
While the US and Russia might negotiate, “they can never find solutions without Ukraine”, he added.
“This is absolutely not acceptable - that one day Russia, perhaps China and the United States of America, find a way to bring this war to an end without having Ukraine at the table.”
“I want to make no doubt that this is in our European interest to defend this country, because we’re not just defending the territorial integrity of this country, we’re defending the entire political order of the European continent, and that’s the reason why we’re still engaged.”

Eurovision in crisis: Netherlands make U-turn and pull out of Eurovision 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:38:08 UTC
22:38:08 KST

The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to participate.
The Netherlands will not participate in 2027's Eurovision Song Contest after all.
NPO, the umbrella organization for public broadcasters in the country, has reversed its earlier decision to return to the contest, after Dutch public broadcaster AVROTROS had announced in August that it would not take part because of Israel's presence in the line-up.
The decision to return to the competition was met with widespread criticism and around 400 NPO employees signed a letter urging the organisation to reconsider its participation.
In a statement, NPO's director Jet de Ranitz said that NPO was unable to secure a broadcaster who would send a Dutch artist.
“In our coordinating role, we held discussions with the broadcasters to investigate whether there are any broadcasters willing to facilitate the participation of a Dutch artist. In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return,” De Ranitz said.
"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027." He added: "Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."
NPO will still broadcast the event.
Eurovision director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".
He said in a statement: "We recognise that opinions about the Contest are deeply and sincerely held at the moment, and that they differ widely, both within countries and between them. We do not dismiss any of those views. Public service media exist to serve their audiences, and it is right that our Members weigh these questions carefully, in dialogue with their own communities."
He added: "At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience. That spirit of unity is what the Contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."
"We are very happy that the 2027 Contest will still be broadcast in the Netherlands and look forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again whenever NPO, its members and audiences feel the time is right."
Ireland has already announced it will not take part in Eurovision 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.
The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.
Last year, five countries - Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia - boycotted Eurovision after organizers declined to exclude Israel over its military actions in Gaza and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
The Spanish broadcaster RTVE said at the time that it would not broadcast the contest or the semi-finals and criticised the decision-making process as “insufficient”. They said that the EBU’s decision to keep Israel as a competitor “increases RTVE’s distrust of the festival’s organisation and confirms the political pressure surrounding it.”
Irish broadcaster RTÉ stated: “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation remains unconscionable given the appalling loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there, which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk.” As for Slovenian broadcaster RTVSLO, they said last year that taking part “would conflict with its values of peace, equality and respect” and that it was pulling out of the competition "on behalf of the 20,000 children who died in Gaza".
The 2026 competition drew 131 million viewers, down 35 million from the year before.
Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year.

EU Commission proposes expanding powers of border police force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:36:04 UTC
22:36:04 KST

EU Commission proposes expanding powers of border police force
BRUSSELS, Oct 27 - The European Commission proposed a major expansion of the powers of the EU border agency Frontex on Tuesday, including giving it the capacity to act beyond EU territory, in the aftermath of the massive rush to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta last summer.
The proposal would significantly expand Frontex's mandate, providing additional resources and empowering the agency to support non-EU countries to return migrants to the countries of origin.
The proposed legislation is an attempt to make Frontex more reactive to large-scale arrivals at the EU's borders, such as in Ceuta on the North African coast, as European governments push for tougher migration policies despite concerns from rights advocates over accountability.
"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs and migration, told reporters.
"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can deploy within 24 hours and spot risks early, before an event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.
OVERSIGHT CONCERNS
But while the proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's role, it would also narrow the scope of its internal rights watchdog, with complaints referred to national authorities to handle.
The proposal comes as member states increasingly focus on returns, arguing that too many migrants ordered to leave the bloc ultimately remain.
Although irregular arrivals have decreased, the arrival of more than 72,000 people in Ceuta from Morocco in late July, most of whom later left, reignited debate over the EU's migration rules and was cited by several member states as evidence for stronger tools.
The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers, who would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.
The proposal would create a new EU Return Coordination Centre within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process, from voluntary return counselling to organising returns and reintegration support, the statement said.
The proposal would also create a new online monitoring centre to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.
The proposal was met with criticism from rights groups and lawmakers.
"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.
"We need a human rights-based approach to border management and Frontex plays a key role. But instead the Commission risks turning Frontex into a European version of ICE," she said. REUTERS

Ukraine Develops Ground Robots That Launch Interceptor Drones

Unknown Publisher

22:34:58 KST

A Ukrainian company is beginning to assemble interceptor drones designed to launch from unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), with specialized launch boxes being developed for their deployment.
Taras Ostapchuk, founder of Ratel Robotics, announced the plans in an interview with Forbes, as cited by RBC-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The company has previously demonstrated the launch of strike FPV drones from its ground robots. It now plans to adapt the concept to counter aerial threats.
Ratel will initially focus on multi-rotor interceptor drones before moving on to fixed-wing, airplane-type models.
The company is also developing launch boxes for deployment from UGVs and integrated software to enable data exchange between ground and aerial platforms.
Under the concept, a UGV would carry interceptor drones to a designated position and launch them to engage enemy aerial targets.
Ostapchuk told Forbes that integrating different types of unmanned platforms was a key direction in robotics development. By combining their capabilities, the systems could enable operators to perform a wider range of tasks remotely.
Vsviti, which also cited the interview, reported that Ratel is currently focusing on multi-rotor interceptors that do not use jet engines. Fixed-wing drones are planned for a later stage.
The company is also working on unified software for ground, aerial and, eventually, maritime unmanned systems. The software is intended to improve data exchange and interoperability between different platforms.
Russian Commander Complains NATO Testing Drones on Ukraine’s Front Line
As part of this effort, the company is testing an autopilot system for ground robots that it plans to adapt for aerial drones.
According to Ostapchuk, Ratel has already invested approximately $200,000 in developing its aerial division. Developing fixed-wing drones could require several million dollars.
Ukrainian troops have completed their first logistics mission using a domestically developed amphibious UGV, traveling more than 40 kilometers (nearly 25 miles) across land and water to deliver supplies to frontline positions, Ukraine’s defense ministry said.
The vehicle can cross rivers, canals, and marshes without switching platforms, allowing it to continue operating where conventional ground robots might be unable to pass.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps has begun using unmanned ground vehicles for assaults on Russian positions. Its NC13 unit equipped kamikaze robots with Bullspike grenade launchers and deployed them against Russian troops, including positions inside shelters.
The corps has also tested dropping UGVs from Gryphon heavy bombers and used robotic platforms to strike Russian positions and logistics targets up to 15 kilometers (about 9 miles) from the front line.

Russia's return to global sports gathers momentum as EU mulls response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:34:30 UTC
22:34:30 KST

BRUSSELS, Belgium — The EU is working on how to stop Russia from laundering its reputation through international sporting events, but as it talks, Moscow creates new facts on the ground.
"Sports and culture must not become vehicles for whitewashing Russian aggression," the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas told journalists on Oct. 13.
But since then, there have been at least two instances in which Russia has been able to advance its sports agenda.
Lithuania was stripped of its right to host an April 2027 international pentathlon tournament on Oct. 19 after it refused to grant visas to Russian and Belarusian athletes for the event.
And on Oct. 25, the International Weightlifting Federation announced that its 2030 championship would take place in Moscow, the first time such a high-level contest has been awarded to Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In both cases, the condemnations and expressions of disappointment have come thick and fast.
Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys called the pentathlon decision "shameful" and said the EU "must tighten restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes competing under national colors, expand visa bans and sanctions, and cut support for those enabling state-sponsored propaganda."
And Ukraine's Sports Minister Matvii Bidnyi told public broadcaster Suspilne that Kyiv would boycott the weightlifting tournament in Moscow.
The minister added that he considers the choice of host "an alarming and unacceptable signal," which "suggests that the influence of Russians in some international federations is extremely strong."
Likewise, European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova told the Kyiv Independent that the EU's executive arm "regrets" both of those decisions.
"In line with the autonomy of sport, international federations are responsible for decision-making on where to host international competitions. However, both federations and member states should act in line with EU sanctions and values," Hrncirova said.
Beyond criticism, the EU is also preparing measures in a bid to tackle the issue.
Kallas said on Oct. 13 that the EU's diplomatic arm, the European External Action Service, "together with the Commission, will put forward proposals on how to sustain Russia's isolation in global sports."
And Hrncirova said that "the Commission is facilitating and supporting coordinated action among member states and with like-minded international partners to resist the instrumentalization of sport by Russia and Belarus."
However, it remains unknown when the new measures will be announced. In the meantime, Russia's lobbying to return to sports continues unabated.
Russia's all-out war has taken a heavy toll on Ukraine, with hundreds of Ukrainian athletes and coaches killed and hundreds of sports facilities destroyed by Russian missile and drone attacks.

LNG accounts for half of global gas trade now — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:32:38 UTC
22:32:38 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. LNG, which currently accounts for half of global trade, could help resolve the issue of disruptions in worldwide gas supplies, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit.
The key problem now is the disruption of gas supplies to global markets, he said. "Large volumes of supply have been removed from the market in a short period, with demand remaining unchanged. This means we need to work on optimizing transport routes, taking into account the geographical locations of the Forum’s member countries, through mutual operations among them, that is among us," Putin explained.
The growing flexibility of the gas market driven by the widespread use of liquefied natural gas makes this possible, he noted. "After all, LNG supplies do not depend on international pipelines, and LNG already accounts for about half of global gas trade. I would like to emphasize that replacing lost volumes and revising logistics is no simple task: it is essential to strike a balance between the interests of gas suppliers and consumers, while also fulfilling existing contractual obligations," the Russian leader said.

NSDC enlists Weatherman Foundation to help identify fallen Ukrainian defenders
Ukraine

2026-10-27
15:31:41 EET

Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine Ihor Klymenko and Megan Mobbs, head of the R.T. Weatherman Foundation, have discussed future cooperation on identifying the remains of fallen Ukrainian defenders.
"I recently met with Megan Mobbs, head of the R.T. Weatherman Foundation, which implements important humanitarian projects in Ukraine. One of the main topics of our discussion was the identification of the remains of fallen Ukrainian defenders," Klymenko wrote on Telegram on Tuesday.
"The NSDC coordinates work in this area, involving state institutions and experts," Klymenko said. According to him, Mobbs confirmed the foundation's readiness to assist, and the two sides discussed opportunities for future cooperation.
"We also discussed cybersecurity and information security. Against the backdrop of growing Russian threats, these areas require increasingly close cooperation between Ukraine and its international partners. It is important to pool experience and resources to counter challenges that extend far beyond our country's borders," Klymenko said.
"I thank Megan Mobbs and the entire team for their sustained assistance," he added.
The R.T. Weatherman Foundation is a US nonprofit organization founded in 2022 by Elizabeth Weatherman and Andrew Duncan. It has operated in Ukraine since March 2022, focusing on the consequences of the war in three areas: body, including medical care; mind, including PTSD treatment and recovery; and spirit, including the search for and repatriation and identification of war victims, as well as support for the families of the fallen.

Gold smuggling funds Islamic State-linked insurgency in eastern Congo, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Gold smuggling funds Islamic State-linked insurgency in eastern Congo, report says
DAKAR, Oct 27 - An Islamic State-aligned insurgency in eastern Congo generates most of its revenue from gold production and smuggling, allowing it to finance its own operations, a report said on Tuesday.
The Allied Democratic Forces, or ADF, which has killed thousands in attacks on civilians and security forces in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo over the last decade, generates between $1 million-$1.6 million a year from gold mining sites in one area of North Kivu province alone.
The gold is trafficked through trading hubs in eastern Congo and onwards to refiners and export networks in neighbouring Uganda, according to a report by The Sentry, a US-based investigative organisation that tracks violent conflict and illicit financial networks.
Uganda has deployed thousands of troops to Congo to help local forces fight the ADF, but the group has proved itself to be resilient, embedding itself deeply in local economic networks.
Revenue from gold has allowed the group to rely less on financial support from Islamic State since late 2024, when US sanctions targeted key facilitators in its networks, according to The Sentry.
Fighters also generate money from cocoa production, extortion and kidnapping, it said.
“The ADF has adapted to military pressure and sanctions by finding new ways to fund its operations, particularly through gold and other resource trafficking,” said Justyna Gudzowska, executive director of The Sentry, calling for governments to disrupt the ADF’s sources of funding.
“That means going after the financiers, gold traders, and facilitators,” she said.
Spokespersons for Uganda's army, Uganda's government and Congo's government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
ADF RESILIENT TO YEARS OF UGANDAN OPERATIONS IN CONGO
Established as an Islamist group in Uganda in the 1990s, the ADF had shifted most of its operations to eastern Congo by 2000. It then pledged allegiance to Islamic State in 2019 and has received support from IS central.
Since doing so, the ADF has combined a local insurgency rooted in the Uganda-Congo borderlands with transnational jihadist ambitions.
The group has carried out a number of bomb attacks in Uganda and has attracted a number of fighters from across the region.
Joint Congolese-Ugandan operations launched in late 2021 helped secure major cities and trade routes but the ADF has been fragmented, not defeated, and moved deeper into remote mining areas of North Kivu, Ituri and Tshopo provinces, the report said.
A representative of a Congolese mining cooperative said the ADF moved into the area in mid-2024, establishing bases near mining sites.
The representative, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told Reuters the group abducted miners and prospectors to extract, transport and sell gold on its behalf. Some residents cooperated in return for payment, he said, creating a system sustained by a mix of coercion and economic incentives.
The ADF continues to operate while most international attention remains largely focused on the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 rebellion, now known as FRN, which seized large swathes of eastern Congo last year. REUTERS

Will Israel elections change its Iran approach?

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

Will Israel elections change its Iran approach?
October 27, 2026
Israel's vote this Tuesday is the first general election for the country since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 — an assault which led to one of the deepest security crises in Israel's history.
As incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to retain power, the question is not merely who will lead Israel's next government, but also how that government will navigate the region-wide security crisis that was triggered by the attack and the Israeli reaction, which included launching a war against Iran.
US President Donald Trump recently issued a full-throated endorsement of the incumbent Israeli leader as a "warrior prime minister" and warned that any other choice would affect Israel's alliance with Washington.
"If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi (Benjamin Netanyahu), America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said in an online post, referring to the Iran conflict.
Behind the scenes, however, media reports indicated a rift between the Israeli government and the Trump administration. According to The Financial Times, the Israeli military intended to launch a new round of attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities, government centers, and energy infrastructure around October 10. However, Trump opposed the new escalation before the US midterm elections on November 3.
The Jerusalem Post later questioned the narrative, reporting that the army had no specific directive for such an operation.
Israel's moves hinge on Trump's decision
The Israeli race has turned into a tight duel between Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot — former IDF (Israel Defense Forces) chief of staff and leader of the front-running centrist party "Yashar."
But Raz Zimmt, the head of the Iran program at the Tel Aviv-based Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), warns political divisions between the two options are not deep enough to speak of a "fundamental change in Tel Aviv's approach toward Tehran" after the election.
"In the perception of Israel's left, right, and center factions regarding the Iranian threat, especially its nuclear threat, there are minor differences," Zimmt told DW.
Moreover, according to Zimmt, any military escalation against Iran depends "on the decision of the US president" far more than on the identity of Israel's prime minister.
"Overall, I do not expect Israel's policy toward Iran and its proxies to undergo dramatic changes, regardless of the future government's composition," he said.
INSS senior fellow Danny Citrinovitch agrees that one should not expect "fundamental changes" in Israel's Iran policy depending on the election outcome.
"Even if Netanyahu personally steps down from power, his influence and the policies shaped over recent years will not simply vanish," Citrinovitch told DW.
Hamas attack as a turning point for Israel and Iran
The current consensus on Iran can be traced to the Hamas terror attack three years ago. Before the assault, according to Navid Toobian from the US-based Middle East Media Research Institute, many believed Israel should deal with the Islamic Republic "in a limited and managed way" and confront only the arms of the so-called "Axis of Resistance." But October 7 completely changed the rules of the game.
While Israel had been aware of Iran's slogans calling for its destruction, it was believed that such calls had an "internal aspect" to rally the base of hardcore Islamists in Iran, Toobian says.
The terror strike by the Iran-allied Hamas, however, showed that Tehran "spares no effort to strike Israel."
What are US and Israel hoping to achieve in the Iran war?
Damon Golriz, a researcher at the Hague Institute for Geopolitics, also points to October 7 as the trigger of the "largest historical trauma of the Jewish nation" caused by the Holocaust.
"Preserving Iran's nuclear ambitions and continuous threats against Israel has intensified this fear that for a large portion of Israeli society, today's rulers in Iran have become a symbol of a historical threat," he told DW.
With that in mind, the current US and Israeli policy towards Iran follows three vectors, according to Golriz.
"First, the removal of the regime's leaders; second, industrial and infrastructural collapse," and third, orchestrating a civil war and what he calls "geographic scissors" to dismember Iran, with the help of armed Kurdish and Baluch separatists, he said.
The US and Israel, however, are not the only players in the conflict. In a recent report, the Reuters news agency cited senior Iranian security officials as saying that Tehran has prepared detailed operational plans for retaliatory strikes. Tehran warned that their retaliatory tools include destroying undersea fiber-optic communication cables in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, alongside targeting US-dependent data centers and AI infrastructure in the region.
Diplomacy: A missed opportunity?
Commenting on possible alternatives to military escalation, Golriz highlights a diplomatic opportunity that opened six months ago in Islamabad, when Tehran agreed to never initiate war or military operations against Israel.
"For the first time in the history of the Islamic Republic, the fundamental national security interests of Israel were signed by the presidents of Iran and the United States," according to Gorliz.
The first article of the Islamabad framework could have been "the beginning of the end for 'Death to America' slogans and anti-Jewish threats, including 'Death to Israel," Golriz said.
This diplomatic window was quickly closed, but "with political will, the provisions and spirit of the Islamabad Memorandum will be the first strategic step toward lasting peace," he said.
But INSS senior fellow Citrinovitch was less optimistic when assessing the willingness of Israeli elites to return to diplomacy.
"Currently, returning to the nuclear deal has no place in Israel's political arena," he told DW.

Iraq PM sacks spy chief as provincial leader faces legal action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:30:27 UTC
22:30:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq PM sacks intelligence chief as provincial leader released after arrest warrant over civil disobedience threats
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has removed the head of the country’s National Intelligence Service, while a Baghdad court has issued an arrest warrant for the chairman of a southern provincial council over threats to start civil disobedience in protest against the closure of a border crossing with Iran.
The state news agency INA reported on Monday that al-Zaidi had ordered the termination of Hamid al-Shatri’s appointment as head of the National Intelligence Service. Al-Shatri had held the post since December 2024.
The agency did not provide a reason for the decision or name a successor.
Separately, the Third Karkh Investigative Court issued an arrest warrant for Maysan Provincial Council chairman Mustafa al-Muhammadawi, following a complaint submitted by the prime minister’s office over his threat to declare civil disobedience and block roads unless the government reopened Al-Sheeb border crossing with Iran.
Al-Muhammadawi was later released by the court on Tuesday after complying with the relevant legal procedures, his office said, according to the privately-owned National Iraqi News Agency (NINA).
The legal action followed remarks al-Muhammadawi made during a news conference at the crossing on Sunday, when he gave the federal government until 29 October to reopen it. He threatened to declare civil disobedience and block major roads if the government failed to meet his demand and used language that al-Zaidi’s media office described as inappropriate.
Al-Zaidi ordered an investigation into the remarks on Monday. His office said the move was intended to ensure compliance with the law and constitutional and administrative procedures when dealing with public service and administrative matters. It added that the relevant authorities would determine any legal responsibility arising from the statements.
Dozens of protesters also blocked the nearby Bazargan road, a key route used by oil companies in Maysan, in protest against the continued closure of the crossing. Security forces were deployed around the demonstrations.
Members of Maysan Provincial Council have warned that the closure could have serious consequences for the province’s economy and residents’ livelihoods and called on the government to reopen the crossing.
The Iraqi government ordered the closure of Al-Sheeb crossing on 20 October, with the suspension taking effect the following morning and remaining in place until further notice. Baghdad said the move was intended to improve the crossing’s technical and logistical readiness. An Iraqi border official separately told Reuters that security measures at the crossing were weak and inadequate.
The decision prompted criticism from Iran’s Interior Ministry, which said Tehran had not received prior notification from Baghdad.
Iraq also ordered the temporary closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing with Iran in September as a precaution following drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, according to Iraqi security sources. Riyadh said the drones had been launched from Iraqi territory.
On 28 July, joint US-Saudi airstrikes targeted Iran-backed militias in Iraq, which they said were reportedly responsible for attacks on US forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.
Wider government shake-up
Separately, al-Zaidi has ended the contracts of 69 advisers, experts and other staff working in his office, as part of a wider government shake-up that has also included a change at the top of the prime minister’s office.
INA reported on Monday that the decision was set out in an administrative order dated 22 October, which cited the “public interest” but did not provide specific reasons for ending the appointments.
Records reviewed by 964media news site showed that the affected positions covered areas including security, foreign affairs, economic policy, health, education and public administration. Paid posts carried salaries of between one million and five million Iraqi dinars, while several contracts were unpaid.
Some of those dismissed had worked in the office for several years, while others had contracts due to run until 2027.
The list also included political figures, former ministers and judges, The New Arab had learned. The appointments had generated additional costs, including allowances for protection, accommodation and transport.
The prime minister’s office director, Ihsan al-Awadi, was also replaced by Rashad Khalaf Hashim, who took over at a handover ceremony on Monday.
Bloated public sector
The changes come amid expectations of further dismissals and retirements across Iraqi ministries and state institutions.
An unnamed official at the prime minister’s office told The New Arab that the government would begin a campaign to address excessive employment in the public sector, using performance assessments to determine whether officials should remain in their positions or leave public service.
The official said there was broad political agreement on the measures, which would extend beyond Baghdad to include ministries, security institutions and provincial administrations. A recent government review had identified dozens of surplus positions draining the state’s operating budget, some of which had been created under previous governments as political or personal favours rather than to meet administrative needs.
Iraqi political affairs expert Ahmed Ali al-Hamdani told The New Arab that at least 30 other advisers had been retained because they performed actual duties within the government office.
He said some of those whose contracts were terminated had remained in government for as long as 19 years without producing research, policy proposals or ideas, adding that many of the appointments had been made for political reasons.
Al-Hamdani also said the list included the daughter of a former president, the son of a minister, former lawmakers and ministers, and politicians who had lost elections but were subsequently appointed as advisers.

The Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision 2027 due to Israel ‘sensitivities’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision 2027 due to Israel ‘sensitivities’
Dutch withdrawal is the latest in a number of boycotts by countries unhappy about Israel’s inclusion.
The Netherlands has withdrawn from next year’s Eurovision Song Contest, its public broadcaster NPO has confirmed, citing “sensitivities” over Israel’s participation.
“We have known for some time that Israel’s participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division,” the NPO’s media director Jurre Bosman said in a statement.
“Therefore, after consultation with the board of broadcasters, the NPO has decided to forgo participation in 2027.”
The announcement follows a decision in August by Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS to boycott the competition. AVROTROS, which usually selects the Netherlands’ entry and broadcasts the show, said the event could “no longer be considered neutral”.
NPO stepped in last month, saying it would take responsibility for the Dutch entry to the competition, before reversing course on Tuesday.
Jet de Ranitz, NPO’s executive chairman, acknowledged that the decision would disappoint fans but stressed that the contest would still be aired on public channels.
“Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being,” De Ranitz said.
The announcement follows the Netherlands’ boycott of the 2026 edition. Iceland, Spain, Ireland, and Slovenia all pulled out, with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all.
More withdrawals
In August, the organisers announced that countries would be unable to host the competition if “an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region.”
But that has not prevented withdrawals, with Ireland already having announced that it will not be participating in next year’s contest for the second year in a row.
Earlier this month, the Czech broadcaster also pulled out of next year’s event, but cited spending cuts as the reason.
Bulgaria will host next year’s edition of Eurovision for the first time in the Black Sea city of Burgas, after Bulgarian singer Darina Yotova, known as Dara, won this year’s contest in Vienna, Austria, with her catchy floor-filler ‘Bangaranga’.
Since its first edition in 1956, Eurovision has become the world’s biggest live televised music event. It catapulted Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame, as well as boosting artists such as Celine Dion and Olivia Newton-John.

UK Politician Jess Asato Got Deepfaked. Now She’s Taking xAI to Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:29:41 UTC
22:29:41 KST

Few people understand the current deepfake epidemic better than Jess Asato. The British Labour MP has spent years campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent.
Disturbing and degrading deepfake images of the MP circulated widely. One appeared to depict a sexual assault. When Asato reported them to X, the platform repeatedly dismissed her complaints. So she decided to take the fight somewhere else: the courts. She is now pursuing legal action against Musk’s xAI, arguing that it unlawfully used her image without her consent. The case could help establish a precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm.
For Asato, this is personal, but it is hardly new territory. Before entering Parliament, she spent years working with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children. That experience has shaped her political career, informing her push for stronger protections for women and children online. Now, she is confronting more troubling questions: What happens when the technology enabling abuse becomes ubiquitous, the platforms hosting it refuse to intervene, and the people targeted are left to fight back on their own?
At stake for Asato is more than the misuse of a single image. It is whether consent still means anything when AI can manufacture almost anything, and whether the companies building these tools can be made to answer for what they do. Asato is betting that the law can catch up with the technology. And she is prepared to take on Musk to find out. (xAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
Also, before you read on, be aware that this interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
ROSIE SWASH: Jess, I just want to have a couple of warm-up questions before we get into it. Tell us a bit about your background, how did you end up becoming MP for Lowestoft?
JESS ASATO: Sure. So, I grew up in East Anglia in Norfolk and Suffolk, and in a not very political family. I got the politics bug in 1997 when Tony Blair was talking about education, education, education. Having experienced it, I felt that we could be doing a lot better in our education system. So I joined the Labour Party and got involved with my local groups.
Before Parliament, I worked for the largest children's charity in the UK for three years on their policy and public affairs, trying to change legislation on behalf of the most vulnerable children in the country. Six years prior to that I worked for a domestic abuse charity called SafeLives where we did huge amounts of work to try and improve the situation for survivors of domestic abuse, particularly through the Domestic Abuse Act.
Those twin issues of women and children have become my focus in Parliament, and I’ve been very clear that my reason for being here, my mission really, is to be a voice for women and children.
Well, that’s a good entry point for us to start talking about this year. So in early 2026, there was widespread reporting on Grok, xAI’s chatbot, being used to create sexualized images of children and women, and those images being circulated on X. How aware were you at this point of the phenomenon of deepfakes being used in this way?
Very aware, and actually had been working with survivors who had experienced deepfakes for quite a number of years. Ever since the advent of AI this has been happening to women, and there’s also been developing risks of children both being put into child sexual abuse material and also children using nudification tools on other children, thereby criminalizing themselves because these tools are so easy to access and often free.
So I was already very alive to the huge harms being created by AI deepfakes of both women and children before Grok ever happened. It was a known harm, which is why many of the tools from other companies had already taken steps to stop them from being used to create this kind of content.
There are a number of tools where, if you type in “nudify,” or “take the clothes off this person,” the tool will refuse to do that. So into that environment came Grok.
Was there a particularly egregious example or incident prior to Grok when you became aware of deepfakes that really stuck with you?
There is a brilliant campaigner who goes by the name of Jodie. I think it was probably listening to the experiences of Jodie, who was deepfaked, and it was such an affront to her that somebody would do this, and then she found out it was actually a friend. Such a betrayal of trust.
These things destroy not just the individual involved, but often families and everyone around them too.
For people who don’t know, who exactly was Jodie? Is this a constituent of yours or someone who came forward to you specifically?
No, no, no. She's a very well-known campaigner on this issue. That’s not her real name.
I know it sounds obvious, but what exactly is nudification?
It is where you ask an AI tool to take the image or video of a real person and use generative AI to make that person either nude, partially nude, or engaging in pornographic acts. This is something that, because of the photorealistic nature of AI images, it has become increasingly hard to see what is a fake image.
It can often look incredibly, incredibly real.
So what was it particularly about the Grok scandal earlier this year that made you want to raise this in the House of Commons?
It was the fact that we already knew that you could stop this from happening by designing the AI tool to reject the ability to do this.
This was completely avoidable. That’s why I spoke out, but also because I’d just spent a year and a half campaigning to get a ban on nudification apps, and here was an all-purpose AI tool becoming a nudification app.
It just felt to me as though we were making strides in the UK, and then the world’s richest man and his product decided to turn the clock back.
So what exactly did you stand up and say?
What I did was I talked about the need for the government to accelerate its ban on nudification apps, which it did. So the then secretary of state for science, innovation and technology, Liz Kendall, said that she was going to bring that ban into law through the Crime and Policing Act, which she did.
But I also said that it was very important that we went further than that, because, of course, Grok itself is not a sole-purpose nudification tool. It has a general use, and therefore we needed to bring all AI chatbots under the auspices of the Online Safety Act. That is also what eventually happened in the Crime and Policing Act, and we’re now waiting until that legislation comes into effect. There’s got to be a consultation, I understand, before it does.
So technically another Grok could happen in this period, but in the future there would be much stronger measures that we could take against tools like Grok creating nudification content.
So that’s a really positive outcome of your interjection in Parliament, but what else happened as a result of you standing up?
Well, one of the things that happened was that I posted on social media saying that Elon Musk should stop Grok from being able to do this.
And then, of course, I became a victim of the same trend. So Grok put this woman in a bikini. And most of the images were sort of pornified, I would say. They weren’t nude images, but they were me with inflated boobs in a bikini.
Then people tried to make it funny, I guess, by putting a swastika on me or hammer and sickles. Or making me pregnant with quintuplets and putting me in a kitchen. Because of course that’s the only use for women—birthing and making dinner. But the really disturbing one was a video of me being surrounded by a group of men, chloroformed over my mouth, and then I fall backwards onto a chair. Then my skirts are lifted up. So no nudity, but clearly the next frame is meant to be a sexual assault. So it was really distressing and disturbing.
That was the point at which a friend said, “You probably need to reach out to a lawyer.” Because each of these things we reported to X, and none of them contravened their terms and conditions. We just kept getting those sort of repeat emails coming back. “We’ve looked into this, and there’s nothing to see here.” So I did engage a lawyer, who sent a letter to X to ask for these to be removed, and they were.
But it was at that point that he said, “I think you might actually have a case. We think that xAI have broken the law.”
It’s impressive how you handled it, but it must have been really awful.
It was; it was awful. This is done to demean, to degrade, and to push women out of online spaces. From my perspective, I tend to use bad or difficult things that happen as a way of thinking about how we change this for the future.
My old boss was an amazing woman called Tessa Jowell. She used to say to me, “How do we change this negative energy into something positive?” “How do we work our way out of this into a place where we actually feel that we’ve learnt from it?”
So I guess she instilled in me that sense that when something bad happens you’ve got a choice. You can wallow in it, you can try and forget about it, or you can use it as a catalyst for change.
So I was quite trepidatious about the idea of taking on a legal action. Not least because of the person who is at the top of xAI, now SpaceXAI. [Eds. note: The company recently rebranded itself as SpaceXSI.] He’s the world’s richest man. But also because I didn’t want myself to necessarily be the story. Many, many women had things that were created of them through both Grok and other nudification tools that are much, much worse.
Having said that, I knew that if there was the opportunity to say that actually they’d broken the law, there was an important point of principle on behalf of all of the women and the children whose images were manipulated and misused by Grok, who would never, ever be able to bring a legal case. So I decided that I wanted to do this, because I wanted to be able to show that no one is bigger than the law.
Doesn’t matter how rich you are or how powerful you are or how big a reach you have in terms of your social media presence or who your friends might be at the top of various governments. If you break the law in our country, you need to feel the force of that. As an ex-lawyer and now as a legislator, it is important that we uphold our law where it has been broken.
So it’s also about giving control back, I think, to us as individuals, but also as a society. So many of these digital changes have been done without our consent or say, and I think there’s a feeling that there’s a sort of runaway train that we’re all on, whether we want to be or not, because we all need to use online spaces for our work, for connection.
And so my view is that we should be expecting companies to respect our law or at least make new laws to bring them more into line with what society really needs.
You said that you gave it some thought. In that moment of trying to decide how to respond, what are you weighing up? Who are you talking to? Are you going back and talking to your team or your family to work out how you should respond, knowing that it may invite further speculation and further attention?
My family mostly, my husband in particular. It’s one thing being a politician and arguing your case to change the law on behalf of women and children; it’s another having your own legal case.
So I was worried about the impact that that might have on my family, my children. I also know that this can bring danger to politicians. So I worried about the fact that I am obviously engaging and making the defendant somebody who has got this very wide reach on social media. However, I don’t like bullies. I very strongly believe that it’s important to fight on the field that you’ve got, and this was an opportunity I felt to make a difference.
So I weighed that up and thought that it was worth having that kind of attention and potential danger, because there is a bigger issue here that we need to get right.
When you say you don’t like bullies, are you talking about, let’s face it, men who used Grok in this way in the first place, or are you talking about Elon Musk?
I’m talking about the men who use this as a form of trying to push women out of the online space. Actually it was quite clear in quite a lot of the comments that they were saying, “Well, if you don’t like this, then get off the platform.”
Either that or, “If this is too hot for you, get out the kitchen,” which I always find quite funny because they put me in a kitchen. I think it’s really interesting when you look at X in terms of its demographics in the UK, it’s highly weighted toward men. I think some of that’s down to the fact that there is just so much misogyny and abuse on it. So I’m assuming, and correct me if I’m wrong, that the other side of the response to going public is that other women have come forward to you.
Absolutely. Actually, one of the heartening things has been people coming forward and saying, “Thank you, because this has now given me the license to actually accept that what happened to me wasn’t my fault. It’s not my shame.” So, in a way, what I’m hoping is that this has helped some victims to process what has happened to them and understand that this was not right.
I’ve also had emails from parents where they’ve said that this has happened to their daughter. It’s been done by boys at school. I’ve had teachers saying that boys have made pornographic AI imagery of them. And it’s something where we’ve just sort of let it happen and wash over us and accept that somehow this is now a part of the society we live in.
So yes quite a number of people have come forward. Obviously not all of their experiences have been through Grok, and I think one of the things is that often, when you see these films or images, you don’t know what platform they’ve been created on. I mean, the only reason why I knew it was Grok was because it was integrated with X, and you could see the commands that had been given by the users.
But much of the time, when this content is created, most victims don’t know by whom or on what platform. And so there’s really very little they can do about it. And I think it’s that sort of sense of helplessness that you have been violated, and that is the word that comes up so frequently from victims of this particular issue.
It’s not just that it’s nudified. Of course, much of my content wasn’t. It’s the lack of consent. And lots of people say, “Oh, but it’s fake. It’s just a laugh.” But what people don’t understand is that it is hyperrealistic, and it’s your face.
It’s a piece of your soul. It’s not just pixels on the internet. It is a person. And because obviously I’ve worked for a long time in violence against women and girls and spoken to many victims of sexual assault and to children who’ve been victims of child sexual abuse, it is the lack of consent that is so disturbing.
It can leave people with PTSD and quite deep trauma. And there have been a number of people I’ve met who have said that the world seems less safe to them because this has happened to them.
I think you’ve already touched on it, but what is the biggest myth around deepfakes that you would wish to dispel?
That it comes without any harm.
That it’s just a laugh.
There is clear harm, even when it’s not done to demean or degrade. So even if it’s done sometimes by friends, the fact is that you haven’t consented to that. There is something about the human psyche which is that when you see yourself so realistically created in a different situation or scenario, something that’s not something you would have done, I think it’s quite discombobulating.
I think your brain can’t quite process it because your brain knows it’s not true, but it looks very true. And I think psychologically we still don’t really understand how this content is going to change the way we think about our world, how we know what is true and what isn’t true.
Right.
Now, of course, you can do fantastic things with generative AI. All I’m calling for is that we respect people’s consent, and that’s why one of the things I’ve been working on since this happened is to look at whether we could create a system of consent to be manipulated by AI.
Could we create a greater right over our likeness online so that there’s a new social norm, which is that no, you can’t copy and paste that picture into an AI chatbot and do whatever you want with it. That’s not yours. It’s not your data. It’s their data, and you’re breaching the law if you do that.
I think if we were to do that, we could have a wide range of applications. It wouldn’t just be in this space of the sexualization of women and children. But also with political disinformation. We are so close to a moment where somebody produces a hyperrealistic video of a politician saying something that they didn’t, and then that leads to real-world harm. And so we’ve got to find a new social norm that says unless for public figures it’s parody or satire—and absolutely you’ve got to protect that—but in all other instances your picture, your voice, and your moving image is your personal data, and it’s not for anyone else to use.
So that’s interesting because you’re touching on new social norms and the possibility of new laws to keep up with this technology. But your lawsuit is specifically under a data law. Talk to me about that versus a law around consensual imagery or deepfakes specifically.
So, my case is brought under existing law, the GDPR, the data protection law, and it contends that Grok misused my data without my consent. It didn’t have consent to process my data, the data being my face and my likeness. But also under privacy laws that I had a reasonable expectation of privacy and that particularly the video of me being prepared for sexual assault reaches a criminal threshold and that nobody should be expected to be on the receiving end of.
Let’s remember, this is actually a product that has been designed by software engineers and developers, and that actually products should not lead to an invasion of privacy and the harm that I then experienced as a result of that, including distress and a sense that I was being harassed by this particular creation of this particular video.
So, it rests on good solid legal grounds, and we await the defense from SpaceX AI.
I don’t know how much you can say, legally, but what part of the process are you in? What happens next? What’s the timeline for a resolution to this case?
So like with a lot of legal cases, it’s very, very hard to pin down a timeline. But my understanding is that we should be receiving the response and the defense from SpaceXAI in the near future. But we don’t have a deadline or a particular time that I can put on it.
After that, my understanding is that the case will then be looked at, and if there is a case to answer, then it will go to a court hearing. But once again, no idea when that might be. And I think there’s lots of legal things that I don’t understand that need to be worked out in the meantime as well between my lawyers and their lawyers.
Have you ever had any acknowledgment on X itself from Elon Musk or anyone at xAI about this case? Has he ever spoken publicly about it?
No.
Would you expect him to?
I don’t think so. They clearly want to challenge this case, and so the best place to do that, I think, is in the courts and to leave it to see whether the merits of the case come through.
You were in New York recently to address the city council about your case. You didn’t get to speak to anyone directly at the company, is that right?
No. I mean, despite being subpoenaed, they didn’t turn up. Four of the other frontier AI companies did attend under subpoena. SpaceXAI didn’t, but they eventually did get their hearing with SpaceX in the city council. So, they have now had their opportunity to put questions and indeed did raise my case with them, I understand.
Was it a little enraging to attend a hearing like that where a company that you’re suing doesn't bother turning up?
I think it’s quite rude to the elected members of the New York City Council when you are a business that operates in New York. Indeed, I was told that they were just a few subway stops from City Hall. So I had traveled quite a long way from England to be there. And they couldn’t be bothered to turn up, which yeah, it felt arrogant and a bit of a snub, but they’ve now got there, so that’s a good thing.
Since you made the decision to take this to the courts, there have been a number of proposals in Parliament, notably there was a proposal for a kill switch bill at one point. Now I believe it’s dead or it’s not going very well. Is that right?
So, yes, there have been proposals put forward for a kill switch. And my understanding is the government rejected that. There continues to be strong calls for regulation of particularly superintelligent AI. We’ve heard various theories, whether it’s 2 percent, 10 percent, 20 percent risk of human extinction from this sort of race to superintelligence, a recursive AI, and we wouldn’t allow those margins of risk in any other sphere.
We would not allow it in bridge building or airplane making. They didn’t even allow it when they were testing the nuclear bomb and the Trinity test. It feels to me as though so much of this decision-taking is outside of democratic structures. It’s not with the public. It is being done by some incredibly, exceptionally wealthy companies and organizations who say they have the interests of the planet at heart.
But each time, actually, they’re asked about whether that is the future of humanity or whether they think that these risks could kill humanity, there’s a sort of shrugging of the shoulders and, “We’ll just keep going because we want to make money,” I guess.
It has been reported in the British press that there are members of Parliament, some of whom are working on committees to do with technology, who still don’t really understand what AI is. And clearly you’re not one of them because you’re aware of the dangers of this issue. But do you feel working across parties that you’re still having to explain technology and its dangers and possibilities to people who are making laws, or should be making laws, to protect the public from AI?
Well, look, I don’t think that’s only the case about AI. We are humans after all, and we have to deal with every single subject that exists under the sun. We have to get our heads around things that we’ve never heard of before.
A bit like being a journalist actually.
That’s true. But you have to then make laws and decisions. So, I don’t want to be unfair to my colleagues.
You may be a specialist in housing policy and you then need to get your head around AI. But I would say that this is the most important issue in front of anybody in parliament or politics at the moment, and therefore, everyone needs to get their head around AI.
My background is in social policy for women and children. But because we did quite a lot of work on the Online Safety Act when I was working for a children’s charity, we campaigned to get the age verification ban for children in pornography into the OSA. And indeed, created quite a strong piece of legislation in respect of that.
We had to get our heads around online safety on the online space. The problem was, of course, that act didn’t include AI chatbots. There were a number of amendments that tried to get it in and we would’ve been in a much better place had we actually succeeded.
But you know, I’m still not a tech expert even though I had quite a while to try to understand these things. But my view is that this is definitely the new front line of where harms are occurring. We can see that hugely in the increase in AI-generated child sexual abuse material, which is absolutely exploding.
In the end it comes down to the people who create the products. And that’s why we should be seeing digital product regulation in the same way as we would any other product regulation.
I’m very, very hopeful that the government is going to look at it really, really closely because there are always design choices that you can make and that can help to prevent these harms, these harms that are completely knowable. We can predict these harms, and so it should be easy to design them out from the start.
Companies can put in more safeguards. Why don’t they?
Profit. But also, let’s be honest, these are global tools and companies. So unless you have international agreement it is a bit like playing whack-a-mole, isn’t it?
The person who made that horrible video of me being chloroformed lives in the US, so the police aren’t gonna follow it up because they’re out of the country.
Do you know who did it?
I don’t know who they are, but the police did find who they were because it’s a criminal offense what they did. They just weren’t able to bring the charge.
We’ve spoken in the last 40 minutes about the full spectrum of human awfulness. I don’t think there’s any area of it that we haven’t …
Oh, sorry. Welcome to my life.
I’m really struck by how cheerful you are despite this. How do you remain so upbeat and hopeful while dealing with all of this?
Because you’ve always got to have hope for the future. I do have a really strong conviction that with the right group of people pushing toward a goal, you can achieve that. You don’t have to accept that things will always be like this. When people come together, when communities come together, you can act for change.
We’re just about to introduce our ban on strangulation in pornography, which is another thing that I’ve been campaigning for and introduced an amendment last year, which the government accepted.
There are always things that we can do to change. You just need to keep going. And also I would say that when you work with these terribly dark areas, yes, it can be quite vicariously traumatizing. But actually the people who work within the sectors are some of the most hopeful people, partly because if you lose hope, then it’s really bad. And we can’t because we’re talking about protecting vulnerable children, and we are fighting for women and our rights to be free of this harm.

Iran’s official IRNA news agency said the two leaders reviewed the latest state of relations between Tehran and Doha and stressed the importance of expanding political and economic ties and using existing potential to deepen bilateral cooperation.

This comes as Qatar continues mediating between Iran and the US, with negotiations between the two sides still ongoing.
Separately, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry Director of Media and Communication Ibrahim al-Hashmi said it was “unacceptable” for the region to normalise the current state of “no war and no peace.”
Addressing a news briefing in Doha, Hashmi warned that escalating tensions were draining the region’s resources and economies and having repercussions beyond the region.
“Qatar is working intensively with regional and international partners, including China, to revive diplomacy and dialogue and put forward practical proposals addressing the concerns of all parties,” he said.
Hashmi stressed, however, that political will from both Iran and the US was essential to resume dialogue and resolve the crisis peacefully.
He also described the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz as an “absolute priority” for Qatar and other countries in the region because of its importance to regional and global economies.
“Using it as a pressure card in this way is rejected and unacceptable to the international community,” he said.

Tallinn mulling 1+1 and 2+1 lane options for Tulika tänav renovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Tallinn mulling 1+1 and 2+1 lane options for Tulika tänav renovation
Preliminary designs have been released for the renovation of Tulika tänav and the section of Paldiski maantee that intersects with it in Tallinn's Kristiine district, and the street will be rebuilt with either 1+1 or 2+1 traffic lanes.
Ahead of the renovation of Tulika tänav, which connects the Kristiine traffic junction and the Sõle intersection, Tallinn is considering two options: rebuilding the street with either 1+1 or 2+1 traffic lanes.
Both solutions will include new sidewalks, cycle paths and street greenery. A traffic study has been carried out to find a suitable solution, and the final choice will be made after assessing spatial possibilities and the needs of different modes of transport.
Tallinn Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) said that he and Tallinn Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse (Center) prefer the 2+1 option.
"Our clear view is that this location cannot accommodate a 1+1 solution, and our firm preference is 1+2," he noted.
However, no decision has yet been made. "When making the final decision, we will naturally take residents' feedback into account," Järvan said.
The reconstruction will also include the renovation of water supply and sewerage facilities, the construction of a separate stormwater drainage system and improvements to street lighting.
Feedback on both options can be submitted until November 10.
