Just a few minutes of speech may offer a window into brain health and aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:00:02 UTC
22:00:02 KST

An automated analysis of short voice recordings can produce an estimate of “speech age” that runs older in people with dementia than in cognitively healthy adults, according to a study of nearly 3,000 adults across Latin America published in Science Advances. The gap between this speech-based estimate and a person’s actual age was also linked to brain-scan and DNA-based measures of aging, a blood marker of Alzheimer’s disease, and lifetime social hardship.
To estimate whether a person’s body appears older or younger than their calendar age, scientists use tools known as biological aging clocks. A biological aging clock is a statistical model that analyzes physical or behavioral data to predict a person’s age. The difference between this predicted age and the person’s actual chronological age is called an age gap, where a positive gap is typically interpreted as accelerated aging and a negative gap as healthier, delayed aging.
Most established aging clocks rely on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure brain tissue volume and activity, or blood draws to examine chemical modifications to DNA known as epigenetic methylation. While a study covered by PsyPost in early 2026 showed that blood tests can detect dementia-linked proteins in Latin American populations, both neuroimaging and molecular blood analyses remain expensive and logistically difficult to deploy in lower-income regions. Behavioral age clocks based on questionnaires and cognitive exams also require trained specialists and can be skewed by a patient’s literacy level.
Natural speech may offer an accessible, non-invasive alternative for tracking how the brain and body age. Speaking requires the rapid coordination of multiple cognitive and physical systems, which shift during normal aging and break down more rapidly in neurodegenerative diseases. A slower speaking rate and longer pauses between words or syllables are thought to reflect declines in mental processing speed and word retrieval.
Changes in vocal pitch and the emotional tone of words can capture the flattened emotional expression often seen in dementia. Shifts in vocabulary, such as relying on words for physical objects rather than abstract ideas or using less precise terms, point to the erosion of semantic memory, which is the brain’s system for storing general knowledge and facts.
The research was led by Hernan Hernandez of the Latin American Brain Health Institute at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, with senior authors Agustin Ibanez and Adolfo M. García. Ibanez is a professor of global brain health at the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin, scientific director of the Latin American Brain Health Institute, and strategic scientific director at the Barcelonaβeta Brain Research Center. García directs the Cognitive Neuroscience Center at Universidad de San Andrés in Argentina and is affiliated with the Global Brain Health Institute at the University of California, San Francisco, and the Universidad de Santiago de Chile.
They sought to test whether discrepancies between a person’s chronological age and their speech-predicted age could distinguish between different types of dementia and mirror internal biological aging.
“This study grew from two related goals,” Ibanez told PsyPost. “First, our group has been developing multiple aging clocks to capture the cumulative burden of biological, brain, behavioral, and exposome processes across aging and dementia. Second, many established biomarkers are expensive and difficult to scale, particularly in low-resource settings. We therefore wanted to test whether natural speech could provide a low-cost, non-invasive measure that captures several dimensions of aging simultaneously.”
“We wanted to establish whether speech recordings (an affordable, naturalistic, scalable data source) could offer reliable predictions of aging, considering multiple sociobiological factors in both healthy older adults and individuals with dementia,” García added.
The researchers analyzed data from 2,928 native Spanish speakers across five Latin American countries: Colombia, Peru, Mexico, Chile, and Argentina. The participants were recruited through a multi-country research network and had an average age of about 65 years, with women making up 67 percent of the sample. The cohort included 1,504 cognitively healthy individuals and 1,424 patients diagnosed with various neurodegenerative conditions.
Among the patient group, 24 had mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a transitional stage between normal aging and dementia, and 1,068 had Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the most common form of dementia characterized by progressive memory loss. Another 332 patients had frontotemporal dementia, a group of disorders caused by damage to the brain’s frontal and temporal lobes. The team divided the frontotemporal dementia patients into 255 individuals with variants that primarily affect behavior and movement, and 77 individuals with variants that primarily impair language production and comprehension.
Every participant completed seven brief speaking tasks in a quiet room, including describing an animated video, retelling a short story immediately and after a 20- to 30-minute delay, and naming as many words as possible starting with a specific letter or belonging to a category like animals within 60 seconds. The researchers processed the audio recordings using TELL, an automated speech-analysis app for which García serves as founder and chief scientific officer. Its pipeline removed background noise, isolated the participant’s voice from the examiner’s, and generated text transcripts.
From these recordings and transcripts, the team extracted over 700 distinct acoustic and language measurements and grouped them into seven composite categories: speech timing, vocal pitch, emotional content, word frequency, verbosity, semantic concreteness, and semantic granularity (how specific a word is, such as saying “robin” instead of “bird”).
The scientists trained a machine learning model on these seven speech categories to predict chronological age, and then subtracted each person’s actual age from their predicted age to calculate their speech age gap. On average, the model’s age estimates missed participants’ actual ages by about nine years and accounted for roughly 44 percent of the variation in age across the sample; after a statistical correction commonly applied to age-prediction models, predicted and actual ages correlated at 0.74. Verbosity and speech timing were the most influential features indicating preserved or younger-sounding speech, while vocal pitch variations and negative emotional word content were the strongest indicators of accelerated speech aging.
When comparing the diagnostic groups, cognitively healthy adults had the lowest speech age gaps, whereas every patient group showed larger gaps, reflecting older-sounding speech. Patients with language-dominant frontotemporal dementia displayed the largest speech age gaps, followed by those with behavioral or motor frontotemporal dementia, and then those with Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment.
These group differences held up in sensitivity analyses that controlled for chronological age, sex, years of education, country of origin, medical comorbidities, and the number of languages a participant spoke. The researchers also examined whether speaking multiple languages was linked to lower speech age gaps in a subset of participants, finding a slight trend toward younger-sounding speech among multilingual speakers that did not reach statistical significance.
In additional comparisons, the full speech clock separated the diagnostic groups more effectively than any isolated acoustic or language category on its own. “Aging leaves a distributed signature across multiple dimensions of speech—timing, lexical choice, semantic properties, prosody, and verbal output,” García explained. “No single feature tells the whole story; the informative signal emerges from their combination.”
“All too often, brain disorders are conceived as primarily affecting or broadly sparing language,” García said. “This usually reflects a poor operationalization of language. When rich characterizations of speech and discourse are used, ensuing signals can improve the detection, differentiation, and characterization of disorders which are traditionally not associated with language anomalies as a defining feature.”
The researchers next examined how these speech age gaps related to cognitive test scores, blood biomarkers, and lifetime social environment. Across the cohort, larger speech age gaps were associated with worse performance on clinical tests of memory, executive function, everyday functional ability, and both verbal and non-verbal tasks. The link was stronger for tests with a verbal component, such as retelling a story, than for tests the authors classified as nonverbal, such as copying and later redrawing a complex figure. In a subset of participants who underwent blood testing, higher speech age gaps correlated with elevated blood plasma levels of phosphorylated tau-217, a protein that accumulates in the brain during Alzheimer’s disease, specifically among the Alzheimer’s patients.
The team also evaluated each participant’s social exposome, a comprehensive measure combining 319 survey items covering lifetime socioeconomic factors such as education, food insecurity, financial stress, healthcare access, and childhood adversity. Higher speech age gaps were linked to a more adverse social exposome among healthy controls and Alzheimer’s patients, suggesting that cumulative social hardship may be reflected in how old a person sounds. This aligns with earlier research covered by PsyPost in 2025, conducted by several members of the same research network, which found that a heavier lifetime burden of social adversity was associated with poorer cognition and disrupted brain connectivity in Latin American cohorts.
“I was particularly struck that speech reflected not only brain and molecular aging but also the social exposome,” Ibanez said. “It suggests that the cumulative environments people live in (their socioeconomic circumstances, education, access to resources, and other life-course exposures) may leave measurable traces in something as everyday as speech.”
To verify whether the speech clock reflected internal biological aging, the authors compared the speech age gaps against established brain and epigenetic clocks in subsets of participants with available neuroimaging and blood DNA data. The speech age gaps showed moderate-to-strong positive correlations with brain age gaps derived from structural MRI scans measuring gray matter volume (correlation of 0.42), functional MRI scans measuring how brain regions communicate at rest (correlation of 0.49), and a combined brain clock (correlation of 0.53) across healthy controls and all dementia groups. In addition, larger speech age gaps were positively associated with accelerated biological aging across three independent epigenetic clocks that measure DNA methylation patterns in white blood cells, particularly among healthy adults and patients with Alzheimer’s disease, though these links were weaker (correlations of about 0.2) than those with the brain clocks.
When the team examined specific brain networks, they found that the speech clock tracked whole-brain aging more closely than the aging of isolated brain circuits, including the brain’s dedicated language network. Only the language network and the salience network, which helps the brain monitor speech and allocate attention, showed small links to the speech clock, while other individual brain networks showed no statistically significant relationship.
“One striking finding was how strongly the speech clock aligned with brain-age measures across several dementia syndromes, despite being derived solely from speech,” García told PsyPost. “We were also intrigued that whole-brain aging measures related more strongly to speech aging than most individual functional networks did. That suggests speech may reflect the coordinated state of distributed brain systems rather than the condition of a single language circuit.”
“Speech appears to contain much more information about aging than we usually assume,” Ibanez noted. “Our speech-derived aging measure was associated not only with cognitive and clinical impairment, but also with brain aging, epigenetic aging, p-tau217, and social exposures. This suggests that a few minutes of speech may eventually provide an accessible window into broader brain and biological health.”
One independent researcher’s assessment highlighted both the scale of the multi-country effort and the nuances of interpreting speech-based aging markers across neurodegenerative conditions. The cohort’s language-dominant frontotemporal dementia group included patients with non-fluent and semantic variants of primary progressive aphasia, which are neurological syndromes that gradually erode a person’s ability to speak or understand word meanings.
“Hernandez et al. have derived a novel marker of aging by analyzing acoustic and linguistic features of speech samples using a machine-learning algorithm to predict age and by subsequently computing deviations of predicted age from actual age,” Mai-Carmen Requena-Komuro, a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Systems Neuroscience at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf in Germany who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “They show that these ‘speech age gaps’ (SAGs) enable us to distinguish healthy elderly people from people diagnosed with dementia in a large-scale Spanish-speaking cohort living across several countries in Latin America.”
“Speech deficits are known characteristics of language variants of frontotemporal dementia (non-fluent variant primary progressive aphasia and semantic variant primary progressive aphasia, both included in the current cohort), although the specific speech domains targeted differ,” Requena-Komuro said. “Speech deficits have recently caught more attention in patients diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease (there is in fact a language variant of AD known as logopenic primary progressive aphasia).”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider, including how participants were screened. To qualify as cognitively healthy in the study, participants had to demonstrate functional independence and score above 25 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), a standard 30-point questionnaire used to screen for cognitive impairment. In addition, the sample sizes for certain subgroups, particularly the 24 patients with mild cognitive impairment and the 77 patients with language-dominant frontotemporal dementia, were relatively small, and not all participants had blood, brain scan, or epigenetic data available. Because the study relied on cross-sectional data collected at a single point in time, it cannot establish whether an older-sounding voice actually predicts future cognitive decline or tracks the speed of aging over the years.
“I do find it admirable that the authors managed to recruit such a diverse and large cohort of people living with dementia across so many countries,” Requena-Komuro noted. “However, there are a couple of points that made me slightly skeptical: (i) the cut-off score of the MMSE for the healthy controls is set at 25, but the questions are relatively easy so I would not expect elderly adults to score anything below 28 (the maximum is 30). Some of these healthy controls may therefore have belonged to the MCI group instead; (ii) it is unclear whether the regression models aimed at predicting the age of participants included both healthy elderly and elderly with dementia; I would expect an initial model focusing on healthy elderly only to then better understand where and by how much elderly with dementia deviate.”
“Not all speech features go in the same direction, yet they all contribute to the ‘speech age gap’ (SAG),” Requena-Komuro added. “I would therefore caution readers not to overinterpret the SAG as an overall marker of degraded speech. Overall, this study is rich in correlation plots, but correlation does not mean causation. The fact that the SAG correlates with many different factors does not provide much more explanation than these individual factors considered individually.”
Another consideration involves how different neurodegenerative conditions progress across the lifespan and how much speech patterns vary from person to person within the same diagnostic category. Frontotemporal dementia often begins at an earlier age than typical Alzheimer’s disease.
“Generally, a more hypothesis-driven study would have been more insightful,” Requena-Komuro explained. “Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is an early-onset dementia; it is therefore not surprising that the SAG scores for these subgroups are significantly higher than that of the AD group (if the signs of dementia start earlier for FTD patients, when we compare them at the same age of AD patients, their symptoms are likely to be more severe). Perhaps this is one way of validating the SAG, but given the substantial variability in individual trajectories even within the same clinical group, the SAG could not be used as a standalone measurement to establish diagnosis or characterize disease progression. Unlike what the authors claim, I would therefore say that we are not ready to replace standard cognitive and neuropsychological tests for dementia.”
The study’s authors also describe the speech clock as a complement to existing evaluations rather than a stand-alone diagnostic test. “The speech clock captured clear differences between groups and showed especially strong links with brain-age measures, but it is best viewed as a signal that becomes informative when combined with other evidence, not as a stand-alone test of a person’s health or prognosis,” García said. “A positive speech-age gap should not be interpreted as a diagnosis or as proof that someone is literally ‘aging faster.'”
Because the study was conducted entirely among Spanish speakers in five Latin American nations using structured speaking tasks, the speech clock cannot be applied directly to other languages or casual everyday conversations without further testing. Different languages have unique grammatical rules and acoustic rhythms, meaning that the specific features that signal Alzheimer’s or frontotemporal dementia in Spanish may behave differently in other languages, particularly word-based features, which have carried over less well than timing features in earlier cross-language work. Future longitudinal studies tracking diverse, multilingual populations over time will be needed to determine whether automated voice analysis can serve as a routine screening tool in clinics and public health programs.
“Some associations were moderate rather than large, so this should be viewed as a complementary biomarker rather than a replacement for established clinical tools,” Ibanez said. “Aging clocks are estimations, not diagnoses or deterministic measures of how fast a specific person is aging. Importantly, this study was primarily cross-sectional, so we cannot yet infer individual aging trajectories or say that someone whose speech appears ‘older’ is necessarily aging faster over time.”
“A valuable next step is to determine whether speech-age gaps predict longitudinal cognitive and clinical change, especially across different languages,” García added. “Prediction of future states is a fundamental but rarely hit milestone in speech biomarker research.”
Moving forward, the team plans to explore how lifestyle and clinical interventions might influence vocal aging markers and how these tools can expand dementia research in regions with limited medical infrastructure.
“We also want to test whether interventions that improve brain health shift speech aging toward a healthier trajectory, and to validate these models across languages, cultures, and more naturalistic speech,” Ibanez said. “One important aspect of the study is that it included nearly 3,000 participants across five Latin American countries, which are populations that remain underrepresented in dementia research. Speech-based approaches could be particularly valuable in settings where MRI, PET, or sophisticated molecular biomarkers are difficult to access at scale.”
The study, “Speech clocks decode dementia phenotypes, social exposome, and biological aging,” was authored by Hernan Hernandez, Lizeth Katherine Pedraza, Hernando Santamaria-Garcia, Sebastian Moguilner, Agustina Legaz, Pavel Prado, Jhosmary Cuadros, Lucía Amoruso, Liset Gonzalez, Damián Dellavale, Juan Pablo Espinoza–Puelles, Javier Palma Espinosa, Cecilia Jarne, Fabio Mattiussi, Matías Caccia, Alejandro Sosa Welford, Nicolás Pelella, Jeremías Inchauspe, Franco J. Ferrante, Gonzalo Pérez, Marcelo Adrián Maito, Guido Rocatti, Maria Eugenia Godoy, Joaquin Migeot, Paulina Orellana, Ariel Caviedes, Martin Bruno, Leonel Takada, Andrea Slachevsky, Maria I Behrens, Bárbara Bruna, David Aguillon, Lina Zapata, Jose Alberto Avila-Funes, Nilton Custodio, Bruce Miller, Maria Luisa Gorno-Tempini, Stefanie Pina Escudero, Pablo Reyes, Kun Hu, Maira Okada de Oliveira, Carlos Coronel-Oliveros, Josephine Cruzat, Juan Felipe Cardona, Michael Corley, Irene B. Meier, Vaibhav A. Narayan, Enzo Tagliazucchi, Sandra Baez, Claudia Duran-Aniotz, Adolfo M. García, and Agustin Ibanez.

After the dinosaurs died, the massive ‘D. rex’ fungus ruled the woods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

A pineapple-sized fungus has quietly grown undetected in the forests of southwestern China – until now. The massive mushroom may set a size record for a major branch of the fungal family tree.
The fungus — named Dianjunus rex — may also represent a previously unknown family, researchers report September 28 in Frontiers in Fungal Biology. Fittingly, D. rex is part of a lineage that split off from other fungi right after the dinosaurs — like T. rex — went extinct.
In 2024, researchers in China were conducting a survey of fungal diversity in a tropical rainforest in Yunnan Province when local farmers tipped them off to an unusual fungus in the area. The farmers included photos, says Indunil Chinthani Senanayake, a mycologist at the Kunming Institute of Botany in China. Some of the farmers who’d made the discovery took a bite of the mystery fungus, Senanayake says, and the tipster “wanted to confirm whether it was edible or not.”
When Senanayake and her colleagues went to the location, they found strange, yellowish, tentacle-like and spatula-like mushrooms growing out of decaying tree roots. These were some kind of ascomycete, or “sac fungi”. Sac fungi like morels, truffles and molds make their spores in microscopic bladderlike receptacles, unlike the bowling pin-shaped reproductive structures in club fungi, the group that includes most culinary mushrooms.
The mushrooms we see growing out of the ground are called fruiting bodies and make the spore-producing cells for the often hidden or subterranean fungus. Most sac fungi have relatively small fruiting bodies. But the mushrooms growing off these mysterious Yunnan fungi were enormous, with some reaching 50 centimeters tall. The team took samples of the fungi back to the lab for further study and found that they weighed up to 2.2 kilograms. By their estimates, these are the largest spore-making fruiting bodies among all sac fungi.
Torda Varga — a mycologist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in Richmond, England who was not involved with the research — notes that some truffle species are known to get close to the bulk. D. rex appears to be the largest sac fungal fruiting body he’s aware of. “What I find particularly remarkable is that a fungus with such an enormous fruiting body appears to have remained scientifically undocumented until now,” says Varga, though he adds his experience has mostly been within Europe.
The researchers compared samples of the fungus’s DNA with those from other fungi to determine its evolutionary relationships. They found that it was a relative of species like candlesnuff fungus and dead-man’s-fingers, which make fruiting bodies only a few centimeters tall, but that it was probably in its own, unique family. The team gave the new species the name Dianjunus rex, referencing both the Latin “rex” for “king” and the ancient Dian kingdom of the region.
The team’s genetic analysis suggests D. rex’s family first evolved in the aftermath of the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous Period that wiped out the dinosaurs, some 65 million years ago. “During the dark, cold, postimpact years after the mass extinction, fungi that decompose dead organic matter could keep functioning better than light-dependent photosynthesizers,” Senanayake says.
Varga wonders if searching databases for bits of DNA shed into the environment could help uncover other members of D. rex’s royal family in the absence of physical specimens.
“Some of these [genetic] sequences might belong to previously undocumented relatives of Dianjunus rex,” he says. Finding these hidden species could tell researchers more about the biology and evolutionary history of this king of the sac fungi.

Estonia has run out of asphalt, says Tallinn deputy mayor

Estonia has run out of asphalt, says Tallinn deputy mayor
Estonia is experiencing a shortage of asphalt as factories in Sweden and Lithuania are currently not supplying it to the country, Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) has said
"I have to start with some sad news. Namely, Estonia has run out of asphalt," Järvan said at a Tallinn city government press conference on Tuesday.
The official said Estonia usually imports bitumen from two sources in Sweden and Lithuania.
"And for reasons still unknown, the Swedish company decided not to bring any more. It said that the ship that arrived three weeks ago would be the last this year. The next one will come in the spring. The Lithuanian company was delighted, immediately raised its prices, and then its factory broke down. This means that asphalt plants in Estonia can no longer obtain bitumen," the deputy mayor said.
"What this means nationally is that those construction companies that have their own asphalt plants probably have their own contracts covered and, as usual, any surplus asphalt is put on the open market," he added.
Tallinn is affected by the issue as the second supplementary budget set aside money for roadworks this autumn.
"Now both of the City of Tallinn's partners have said that, unfortunately, the market situation is such that asphalt is simply unavailable. And this means that we are in a situation where we can happily announce that we have asphalt for resurfacing Liivalaia. We have to take a positive view of what we have," Järvan said.
Asphalting work on Liivalaia began on Monday, and Tallinn will grant an additional two weeks for this work, the deputy mayor added.
"But this also means that we will not take the risk of milling up Viljandi maantee and Vabaõhumuuseumi tee to lay new asphalt there. We will still avoid a situation where we have streets dug up for the winter and no asphalt to put down in their place," Järvan said.

What сomes after the war: Bosnia's lesson for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:00:00 EET
22:00:00 KST

What сomes after the war: Bosnia's lesson for Ukraine
This op-ed was co-authored with Kateryna Kyrychenko, a Ukrainian international lawyer and Head of Ukraine Legal Affairs and Programme Management at the Public International Law & Policy Group (PILPG). Her work covers international criminal law, accountability for Russian war crimes, peace negotiations and transitional justice. She is pursuing a PhD in international criminal law at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.
On a sunny September afternoon, Kyiv almost seemed at peace. People sat outside the Food Market, talking and eating. Between meetings, we discussed Bosnia's and Ukraine's shared experience. For one of us, war is a memory shaping life three decades later; for the other, an immediate reality of air-raid alerts, sleepless nights and uncertainty about the next Russian attack. We returned to one question: what does it mean for war to end?
A month earlier in Sarajevo, a meeting with Ukrainian officials and civil-society representatives had focused on how Bosnia and Herzegovina handled post-war return and reconstruction. Families crossed former front lines to reclaim homes; property disputes took years, and people returned to areas governed by forces that had driven them out. These challenges are familiar to Bosnians. For Ukrainians still at war, the question was not simply how people had managed to return, but what it had taken to rebuild their lives in places from which they had once been driven.
Pressure to negotiate is mounting in Kyiv, yet little attention goes to a peace framework with credible guarantees. After more than 12 years of Russian aggression, including nearly five of full-scale invasion, Ukraine's weariness is understandable. Millions have lost homes, loved ones or livelihoods; families have been separated for years, and communities live between air-raid alerts and the next attack. They want the war to end, but exhaustion is not willingness to accept peace at any price. Distant negotiators may see this desire for relief as a chance for a quick deal. What seems a breakthrough in Washington or a European capital can have different consequences for those living with its terms. Bosnia shows the gap between signing an agreement and the reality that follows.
Ending the war is only the beginning
Dayton, Ohio, is remembered for producing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the Bosnian war. Its annexes covered the constitution, military arrangements, elections, human rights and refugee return. Unlike an archived document, it had force behind it: some 60,000 NATO-led Implementation Force (IFOR) troops separated armies, oversaw territorial transfers and enforced military provisions. Peace required troops on the ground, and the money and governments willing to keep them involved after Bosnia left the front pages.
Ukraine knows the limits of a mission without enforcement powers. From March 2014, the OSCE Special Monitoring Mission monitored the security situation, established facts and reported violations, while also facilitating dialogue and supporting local ceasefire arrangements; it had no power to enforce compliance. Its mandate expired on 31 March 2022 because OSCE consensus on an extension could not be reached owing to Russia's position. The Minsk agreements, meant to end hostilities in eastern Ukraine, proved vulnerable to manipulation: repeated ceasefire violations, unresolved security questions and incompatible readings of political provisions. They neither secured peace nor prevented Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. For Ukraine, the question is not whether another agreement can be signed but what would make it different from arrangements Russia has already violated: who would verify compliance, respond to renewed attacks and impose consequences?
Dayton was possible under different conditions: the parties accepted IFOR's deployment and undertook to facilitate its operations, while the UN Security Council authorised the force. Russia, by contrast, is Ukraine's aggressor and holds a UN Security Council veto. A guarantee it can veto offers little protection. Ukraine's security cannot rest on monitoring or diplomatic assurances: its ability to defend itself, maintain military capabilities and choose security partnerships must be central to any settlement. Restricting its self-defence while Russia can rearm risks another war.
Civilian implementation was equally demanding. Dayton created the Office of the High Representative, but implementation soon exposed serious obstacles. In December 1997, the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn supported the exercise of what became known as the Bonn Powers: the High Representative could impose binding decisions on specified implementation issues and remove officials who obstructed Dayton commitments.
Ukraine faces a less favourable international environment. Beyond Russia's veto, other major powers' interests may not align with its security needs. Those conditions cannot simply be recreated. Proposals for Ukraine must start from this reality, not assume guarantees will enforce themselves.
The unfinished business of peace
Property return showed that work went beyond the text. Annex 7 gave refugees and displaced people the right to return home and have their property restored, or to receive compensation where restoration was impossible. Laws and administrative procedures were developed and enforced, with municipalities monitored and pressed to comply. People could receive house keys yet find the hardest part of return ahead. For some returnees, especially those returning as an ethnic minority, the label "returnee" can be a reminder that the return of property does not necessarily restore their place in society.
Much will be familiar in Ukraine: destroyed or occupied homes, separated families and repeated displacement. The scale of destruction, mines and unexploded ordnance, displacement of millions and Russia's systematic efforts to alter the demographic, legal and cultural realities of occupied territories will compound Ukraine's challenges. Restoring Ukrainian governance requires more than replacing flags or reopening offices. It must address documented pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, property expropriation, the replacement of Ukrainian education and the suppression of Ukrainian identity, forcible transfers or deportations of civilians, including children, to the Russian Federation, arbitrary detention by Russian forces or occupation authorities, and the consequences of occupation.
War's end brings difficulties beyond rebuilding homes and institutions: disputes over education, integration, national symbols, history, heroes and victims. Who decides what schools teach, whose suffering is recognised and whose history becomes official? Bosnia has grappled with these issues since 1995; many remain unresolved. Survivors and victims' families still face denial of the Srebrenica genocide, historical revisionism and glorification of convicted war criminals, according to the Srebrenica Memorial. Reconciliation efforts have sometimes emphasised moving forward rather than confronting the past. Ukraine should heed the warning: ending a war and reconciling societies are different things.
Despite its achievements, Dayton left unresolved questions, notably the struggle over the Bosnian state. Its two entities and political system enabled obstruction and challenged state authority. Bosnia's experience is not a warning against decentralisation or minority rights. Nevertheless, trouble begins when arrangements protecting communities let a neighbouring government prevent a country from deciding for itself. For Ukraine, a Russian veto over defence or European integration would be especially dangerous. Russia has sought to use the status of occupied territories to influence Ukraine's internal affairs. A settlement must not institutionalise that interference as political compromise or minority protection.
What happens after the diplomats leave?
We sought no Ukrainian version of Dayton. and Dayton's unfinished business in Bosnia makes it no blueprint. But it stopped the war, and some people returned and homes were rebuilt because outsiders stayed to enforce commitments local politicians resisted.
Ukraine's partners should ask what they will do on the first day after the war, not just what they will sign, propose or pressure others to accept. Bosnians understand Ukraine's reluctance to accept promises without guarantees: they have been down that road and, in many ways, still are.
These answers will matter years later, when another crisis dominates headlines and Ukraine leaves the global spotlight. Who will remain engaged, provide assistance or step in when agreements are violated or institutions fail?
"At least nobody's shooting" was common in post-war Bosnia. It is a painfully modest definition of peace, hardly a foundation for the future, especially for those living with unresolved consequences.
Nedim Jahić and Kateryna Kyrychenko

Saab Announces Key Partners for Gripen Canada
Saab plans to work with CAE, IMP and Magellan Aerospace as its principal Canadian industry partners if Gripen E is selected by the Government of Canada.
Saab today confirms its intention to collaborate with several of Canada’s major international aerospace firms in a first step to establish a broad, national ecosystem that will build, deliver and support the Gripen E advanced multi-role fighter, should the Government of Canada proceed with a Gripen acquisition.
If selected, Saab and its Canadian partners will establish a comprehensive, in-country capability for the production, final assembly, support and further development of airpower capabilities. The collaboration would also include in-service support (ISS), training and long-term sustainment capabilities.
“Canada's fighter capability is a long-term national investment. Together with CAE, IMP and Magellan Aerospace we are prepared to establish a strong Canadian industrial ecosystem around Gripen that delivers operational effect, national sovereignty and lasting industrial and technological benefits," says Micael Johansson, President and CEO of Saab.
Saab has signed a new Teaming Agreement with IMP to establish a new final assembly line, for the Gripen fighter in Canada, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft. IMP will also be responsible for electrical assembly production and ISS for Canada’s Gripens.
Saab has signed a new Memorandum of Understanding with Magellan Aerospace to provide local manufacturing of advanced aerostructures, composite structures and structural assemblies in Canada, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft.
Saab has previously signed a Memorandum of Understanding with CAE to deliver advanced fighter pilot and technician training, mission systems engineering and support/sustainment capabilities in Canada, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft.
“We are proud to be selected by Saab to establish a Canadian capability for the production and long-term support of Gripen. While that capability would be established to meet Canada’s requirements, its potential reaches well beyond Canada. We see a real opportunity for IMP to produce and support aircraft for Gripen customers internationally, positioning Canadian industry as an enduring part of the global Gripen program,” says David Gossen, President, IMP Aerospace & Defence.
“As a proud Canadian manufacturer, Magellan Aerospace is well-positioned to bring decades of advanced aerospace manufacturing expertise to the Gripen program, supporting the creation of high-tech jobs and sovereign defence capability right here in Canada," says Haydn Martin, Vice President Business Development, Magellan Aerospace.
“CAE has decades of experience contributing to the mission readiness of fighter pilots around the world,” says Pascal Grenier, President, CAE Defense & Security. “We have a longstanding commitment to the Royal Canadian Air Force and its training needs. Should the Government of Canada select the Gripen, CAE is prepared to work with Saab to support Canada’s future fighter force.”
These partnerships are designed to strengthen Canada’s sovereign defence capability while contributing to the development of advanced aerospace and defence expertise across the country. When activated, they will add significant new jobs and skills in areas such as high-technology manufacturing, advanced materials, and model-based systems engineering. They will also provide Canada with a self-reliant and sovereign capability to deploy, sustain and enhance a critical national asset for decades to come.
Additionally, Saab is engaged with a broad range of Canadian companies, academic institutions and research organizations to further develop a future defence industrial ecosystem in Canada.

Russia’s internet regulator proposes limiting screen time for children under 14 and requiring social media platforms to verify users’ ages
Roskomnadzor, Russia’s federal media regulator, has sent a bill to the information policy committee of the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, proposing mandatory identification of children on social networks, the Russian business daily Vedomosti reported, citing a statement by a regulator representative at the committee meeting.
The agency also proposed limiting the amount of time children under 14 are allowed online. A Roskomnadzor representative said the measure is meant to restrict children’s access to banned content.
The Internal Affairs Ministry announced it is concerned about children and teenagers being drawn into offenses and crimes through social networks, messaging apps, forums, and gaming chats.
According to the ministry, the most common crimes children are drawn into are acting as “droppers” and giving third parties access to their own accounts.
The Digital Development Ministry announced as far back as June that it is considering introducing age verification mechanisms for users of online platforms. Its head, Maksut Shadayev, said the ministry is studying how other countries have approached the issue.
Various restrictions on children and teenagers’ access to social media are being discussed worldwide. Since late 2025, a law banning social media for children under 16 has been in effect in Australia. Similar restrictions are being discussed in the UK and EU countries, including France and Spain.

Nationwide, Russia’s 2026 budget deficit is expected to reach a record 7.345 trillion rubles (88 billion), nearly twice the previous forecast of 3.785 trillion rubles (45 billion). That new projection represents 3.2% of GDP compared to the previous target of 1.6%.
President Vladimir Putin said last month that the size of Russia’s budget deficit poses no “critical” risk for the economy and that officials will do everything to keep it under control.

Court orders Egyptian website closed in case seen as test for independent media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Court orders Egyptian website closed in case seen as test for independent media
CAIRO, Oct 27 - A court ordered a leading independent Egyptian news site closed on Tuesday after its editor-in-chief was convicted of running the site without a licence and taken into custody pending bail, her lawyers and the outlet said.
Lina Attalah of the news site Mada Masr, which has won numerous international awards for its reporting, was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds ($53,400), her lawyers told Reuters.
The court gave her the maximum penalty, ordering the website to be shut down and its equipment confiscated, Mada Masr said in a statement.
After prosecutors referred Attalah to trial last Thursday, a group of 119 rights groups and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, called the case an "unprecedented attack on press freedom".
US Senator Chris Van Hollen said in a statement on the social media platform X on Friday that the charges were baseless and that "journalism is not a crime".
Egyptian authorities say the state is committed to upholding freedom of expression but that the media must operate within the law, respect national security and counter misinformation.
Founded in 2013, Mada Masr is the most internationally prominent independent outlet in a landscape mostly dominated by media owned by or closely affiliated with the state, and it regularly publishes on politically sensitive topics.
It has been blocked inside the country since 2017. Mada Masr says six cases have been brought against it and its journalists over the last six years, though rights groups say this is the first of its kind to be referred to trial.
The case against Attalah — named one of the world's 100 most influential people by Time magazine in 2020 — follows the arrest last month of the entire newsroom of the fact-checking outlet Matsaddash.
The CPJ said the arrests risked "deepening a climate of fear that threatens independent journalism".
Mada Masr says it has asked for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation repeatedly since 2018 but heard nothing back and only learned of a rejection when prosecutors raised the issue during an earlier case in 2022.
The outlet contested that decision in court, and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.
The council has not commented on the case but has said that it facilitates procedures for outlets which meet official requirements and is keen to promote freedom of expression. State authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In September, the US waived rights conditions, which include protecting media freedoms, on a portion of the roughly $1.3 billion of military aid it sends Egypt each year. REUTERS

The Netherlands is boycotting Eurovision again due to Israel's participation
Kyiv • UNN
The Dutch broadcaster NPO has withdrawn from Eurovision 2027 due to public sensitivity surrounding Israel's participation. The contest will be broadcast.
The Netherlands will not participate in the next Eurovision Song Contest, its broadcaster NPO said on Tuesday, citing the "sensitivity" surrounding Israel's participation. UNN reports this with reference to AFP.
Details
"We have known for some time that Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and leads to discussions and divisions... therefore, after consultations with the Broadcasters' Council, NPO has decided to withdraw from participation in 2027," NPO Director of Media Jurre Bosman said in a statement.
NPO Executive Chair Jet de Ranitz acknowledged that this would disappoint many Dutch Eurovision fans and stressed that the contest would still be broadcast on public broadcasters.
However, he said: "We must conclude that it is still too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027."
"Because of the sensitivity surrounding the issues currently being discussed, we have decided to take a step back for now," De Ranitz added.
The contest was recently hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel's participation, in protest against the country's deadly offensive in Gaza, which was triggered by Hamas militants' attacks in 2023.
Earlier this month, the Czech public broadcaster also withdrew from participation, but cited cost-cutting as the reason.
Ireland has already announced that it will not participate, while the head of Spain's public broadcaster spoke in support of a boycott.
This is only the second time that the Dutch broadcaster has withdrawn from the competition.

Denmark criticizes Finnish and Norwegian call with Putin on Ukraine
October 27, 2026
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized Finland's and Norway's leaders Tuesday after they held a joint phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.
The call came ahead of planned US-led peace talks, which European leaders are seeking to join.
Why did Denmark criticize the call?
Frederiksen said that Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store had gone "solo.”
"I'm very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn't been coordinated with any of the rest of us," she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordics leaders.
"I honestly don't know what those two countries think they can achieve with this."
"I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone," Frederiksen said.
Stubb and Store said they had consulted Ukraine before initiating the call.
They stressed that they represented their own countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe.
What did the leaders discuss with Putin?
Stubb described the conversation as "frank and substantive." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the call, the first between the three leaders.
"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.
Finland and Norway both border Russia and have supported Ukraine throughout the war.
Store said the leaders had emphasized de-escalation.
"The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations," he said.
How was Ukraine involved?
The call followed an October 20 meeting in Oslo involving Stubb, Store, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US envoy Steve Witkoff. US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner joined remotely.
Zelenskyy also spoke with the Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin.
"Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace," Stubb wrote on social media.
A US-mediated ceasefire in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky is set to last until November 1,
Ukraine's top negotiator Davyd Arakhamia said on Tuesday.
"This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," he said on Telegram, adding that every such step brings peace closer.

Israeli election: A referendum on 'Bibi' Netanyahu?

Issued on: Modified:
PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, October 27: The Israeli, Palestinian and Lebanese papers break down what's at stake on election day for Israel and its neighbours. Also, the French government announces its first major concessions to protesting high school students, hoping to calm the movement. Finally, Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or means Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappé will have to wait their turn.
The Times of Israel reports from Kibbutz Be'eri, where one in 10 residents was slaughtered on October 7, 2023, and where "hearts and minds will be broken if Netanyahu retains power". Meanwhile, a Jerusalem Post commentator says "form a government, you can hate each other on your own time", arguing that what Israel needs now above all is stability from a broad coalition of Zionists. Haaretz, though, says the Palestinians are the real crux: with 2 million displaced Gazans living in camps, and a policy of "settler terror" forcing Palestinians into ever smaller corners of their territory, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ready to continue the latter policy at the risk of sweeping international sanctions. Centrist leader Gadi Eisenkot, however, according to the left-leaning paper, understands that the West expects a policy shift on the West Bank.
Palestinian paper Al Quds, meanwhile, reports that an attempt to ban weapons inside polling stations in majority-Arab towns has been refused by the Israeli supreme court, raising fears of armed right-wing groups intimidating voters. Lebanese paper Al Akhbar is covering the hundreds of fixed and mobile polling stations which have been set up in southern Lebanon, Gaza and Syria for occupying Israeli soldiers to cast their votes. A message, according to Al-Diyar, that there is no current intention to withdraw. "The occupier is voting for its own occupation," says the newspaper. L'Orient-Le Jour has published a letter to an Israeli voter by a Lebanese journalist who says these elections will probably affect his life more than any in his own country. He recognises that Israel's options are politically similar in many ways, but says the election is essentially about one thing: finishing with "Bibi" in power, once and for all.
Meanwhile in France, the government "backs down", in the words of Libération, by promising to reform and replace Parcoursup, the platform by which high schoolers are offered options for higher education; to limit class sizes to 28 in the third-last year; to create 15,000 new spots in higher education courses; and to make €4 billion available for renovations of school buildings. But the calls to protest remain in place for both this coming Saturday and November 5. For journalists at L'Humanité, the government has "timidly taken out the chequ ebook": they point out that the €4 billion for renovations are in fact loans, and that the new places on university courses were announced after 10,000 spots were done away with last year. L'Opinion, meanwhile, has the headline "long live selectivity at universities," saying the prime minister has lied to the French youth twice: once by pretending the country could afford these measures, and again by pretending that higher education could exist without selectivity.
Finally, The Times vaunts Harry Kane's 73 goals across 65 games for club and country in the 2025-26 season, which have won the 33-year-old striker his first ever Ballon d'Or. French sporting newspaper L'Equipe hails "King Harry" on its website's front page, which is rather gracious given that another favourite for the title was Les Bleus' Kylian Mbappé. Spanish Marca discusses why the winner wasn't Lamine Yamal, as the jury focused this year on individual performance, rather than team successes. For Goal.com, Kane "isn't the world's best footballer...but deserved the 2026 Ballon d'Or", adding that "Yamal and Mbappe's time will surely come. But in 2026, they must bow to Harry Kane".

‘Children first and competitors second’: Esports industry failing young players’ wellbeing, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:50:58 UTC
21:50:58 KST

Sleep disruption, mental health pressures and online abuse are among the risks young esports players face, as a lack of common standards leaves their protection fragmented, Save the Children says.
Children’s health and wellbeing are not adequately protected in competitive gaming, according to a new report, “Protecting Child Rights in Esports,” by Save the Children, published on Tuesday.
The report calls on the fast-growing esports industry to put children’s rights, enshrined in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), ahead of competitive ambitions.
Young esports players — up to 300 million children worldwide — can face disrupted sleep, musculoskeletal problems, sexism, anxiety, online harassment and depression, while intensive training can leave less time for education, family and friends.
"Esports offers exciting opportunities for children, but participation should never come at the expense of their rights, wellbeing or development,” Theo Toresson, a psychologist at Save the Children and gaming expert, said in a press release.
"As the industry continues to grow, children must be recognised as children first and competitors second,” he added, calling for children's involvement in decision-making and ensuring a future where “every child can participate safely, develop their talents and enjoy the benefits of gaming without being exposed to harm.”
The concern is that children entering structured competitive environments may face expectations associated with professional sport without equivalent safeguards designed around their age and development.
No common standards for healthy competition
Long periods of sitting, inadequate breaks and training schedules that encroach on sleep, physical activity or schoolwork are among the concerns facing young players.
Long sessions and poor posture can also contribute to neck, shoulder and wrist pain, highlighting the need for ergonomic guidance and better-structured training.
Sleep is another concern. Late-night gaming schedules and the demands of competition can disrupt rest, affecting cognitive performance, mood regulation and overall wellbeing, the report says.
A representative of a national esports federation, quoted anonymously in the report, said there were no established guidelines on playing hours or training methods.
“We do talk about screen breaks, healthy diets, sleep, and hydration. But these are practices we've found best from different researchers and brought together ourselves. There isn't yet a centralized body trying to bring this together,” the representative said.
The absence of common standards raises questions about who is responsible for ensuring that competitive gaming remains compatible with children’s physical and psychological development.
The picture is not uniformly negative, however. The report notes that many professional esports players report satisfactory levels of physical activity, with higher-ranking players often placing greater emphasis on fitness. Players may also adopt healthy habits around diet and other aspects of their lifestyles.
Mental health under pressure
The psychological demands of competition are another concern.
“The demanding nature of esports, coupled with online toxicity, can create significant mental health challenges” for Youth Esports Athletes, the report says.
Stress, anxiety and depression can be compounded by intense competition and limited access to appropriate support. This can be further fueled by, for example, sexism and online harassment, as many interact with audiences through in-game chats, Discord communities, livestreaming platforms such as Twitch and YouTube and social media.
These channels can help young players build communities and develop public profiles, but they also expose them to cyberbullying and privacy violations. The report cited an analysis of chatrooms during 302 gameplay segments from the top 20 streamers on Twitch, one of the most popular platforms for esports
and gaming-related streaming, which revealed that 62% of streams included sexist language, 37% included racist language, 84% included ableist language, and 97% included violent language.
Some esports federations and teams require staff to obtain mental health first-aid training, according to the report, but such practices are not widespread across the industry.
The report warns that young players can be thrust into public-facing roles before they have the experience or support needed to navigate online scrutiny, interviews and livestreams.
The report also exposes challenges such as ensuring equal participation, with persisting large disparities based on access, gender, race, LGBTQIA+and disability; children's involvement in decision-making; economic exploitation, as teams, agents, and even parents sometimes exploit young players, taking advantage of non-transparent contracts and unequal power dynamics; and risks at live events without an adequate supervision.

Israel votes on Netanyahu’s future
Voter turnout is at a five-decade high in Israel’s closely-contested parliamentary election, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a referendum on his handling of political scandals, corruption allegations, and wars with Hamas and Iran.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who heads the centrist Yashar party, has emerged as Netanyahu’s strongest challenger. Eisenkot is unlikely to soften Israel’s military or foreign policies. Instead, he has portrayed himself as a patriotic centrist, free of the self-interest that characterized Netanyahu prior to Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.
Before the attack, Netanyahu faced corruption probes and was sinking in the polls as protesters took to the streets to oppose his controversial judicial reforms. Although the attack and subsequent war on Gaza bought Netanyahu some political breathing space, his opponents are now questioning how the prime minister could have left Israel undefended on October 7, and whether he ignored forewarnings about the attack.
Netanyahu has also been condemned for putting his interests before Israel’s by attempting to push Israel Defense Forces (IDF) Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir into a new military operation on the eve of the election, according to a Channel 12 report. Former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman has demanded that the prime minister be investigated on suspicion of treason over the allegation.
Rising defense spending, higher living costs, and wartime tax hikes have further eroded Netanyahu’s popularity. An October 21 Jerusalem Post analysis of four major surveys put Eisenkot’s Yashar party at an average of 22.5 seats, compared with 19.75 for Netanyahu’s Likud.
However, neither Netanyahu’s allies nor the opposition appear assured of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-member Knesset. ‘We bear the consequences’: Diaspora Jews fear fallout from Israel’s election - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:46:39 UTC
21:46:39 KST

As Israelis head to the polls, Diaspora Jews are watching with a stake in an election they cannot vote in, fearing its consequences will follow them home.
From Norway to Mexico to the US, Diaspora Jews told The Jerusalem Post they are “terrified” that the outcome could deepen the conflation of Israel’s government with Jews worldwide, leaving them to bear the fallout of decisions they did not make.
Robert Hercz, the head of B'nai B'rith Norway, told the Post that he has been closely following the elections and is "terrified: not only for the future of Israel, but also for how the election will affect Jewry worldwide."
"The world - and especially the European countries - are disproportionately occupied with Israeli politics - and much of what we get served in the media is oversimplified and polarized. And governments and politicians need to fodder their Israel-bashing voter bases."
This means that if Netanyahu wins, Hercz continued, "the politicians and the media in our parts of the world will go crazy, which in turn will have extremely negative consequences for us Jews living outside Israel."
Israel-Norway relations will not improve while Netanyahu in office
Regarding Norway, Hercz opined that Israel-Norway relations will not improve as long as Netanyahu is in office.
"Not necessarily because of the politics in Israel, but because the Norwegian government and institutions are so over-invested in anti-Netanyahu rhetoric that they will not be able to move over to a different relationship and policy until Netanyahu is no longer in office," he added.
Mark Freedman has spent 43 years working as a Jewish communal professional. He has also served as North American board chair of the Pardes Institute of Jewish Studies, and chairs the board of Amiti, a US-based nonprofit that works primarily in Israel to help CEOs of Israeli NGOs.
He told the Post that "The sands have shifted beneath our feet."
"In the past, lay leadership primarily took a neutral role in how it viewed the Israeli government and the elections that created that government."
"I think the main change now is the emergence of an old form of antisemitism that has renewed itself, the one that deems Jews in North America to somehow have collective responsibility for the actions of the Israeli government."
"So that naturally makes one feel that [Diaspora Jews] have more of a stake in the outcome of the elections."
He gave examples of how Israeli domestic politics filters are felt in the diaspora.
"A lot of it plays out in local elections, where you see discussions about Israel that you've never seen before. Local municipalities are now adopting resolutions that are criticizing Israel as racist and genocidal. That would have been unheard of 15, 20 years ago."
"So naturally this filters down to the local level."
Freedman does believe that the outcome of the elections could have an impact on global antisemitism, and that a new government could lead to an "incremental shift" in a positive direction.
"If there's a government in Israel that is willing to align itself with what we view as traditional values in terms of law enforcement, in terms equal participation in society, that would have an impact certainly on American views."
He added that, on a personal level, "it's really heartbreaking," to see the divisions and issues inside Israel.
"There is so much positive about Israel, as a Jewish state and beyond that as a democratic state, and that's at risk right now," Freedman told the Post.
"I think that people in the United States who follow Israeli politics and who care about Israel as a Jewish homeland are just deeply concerned. So tomorrow's election will have a great deal of impact on the way that the that perception will be formed going forward."
Netanyahu's international image is 'permanent flashpoint'
Arielle Shturman Waiss is a physician from Mexico City and the founder of ConCiencia Project, a science-based sexual and reproductive health education initiative. She leads health programming in the humanitarian aid sector and is active in Jewish communal life in Mexico and the international Jewish world.
She told the Post that Netanyahu's international image is a "permanent flashpoint" and that "regardless of context, he ends up embodying everything perceived as wrong with Israeli political leadership."
This perception, by immediate extension, attaches to Jews in the diaspora, Shturman Waiss added, "because the ability to distinguish between what is Israeli, what is Jewish, and what is legitimate criticism of a government keeps eroding in public debate."
"For those of us living in the diaspora, the problem is more specific: his electoral victory imposes a presumption of consensus on us. It is assumed that we endorse his actions and his radical style of leadership, and that we do so by choice. Because he reached power through a democratic process, that presumption becomes nearly impossible to dismantle any nuance we try to introduce reads as an excuse."
"But a citizenry's vote of a complex parliamentary structure is not a mandate over the identity of an entire people," she stressed.
Israel events affect Diaspora Jews more since October 7
"Whatever happens in Israel reaches us in Jewish communities worldwide," Venezuelan national and founder of Tikun Talks, Deborah Apeloig, told the Post.
"That has always been true, but since October 8, 2023, we have seen it and felt it with a different intensity."
Apeloig spoke of October 8 deliberately, as she says this day marked the moment the narrative "began shifting against Israel, even as we were still trying to comprehend the massacre."
She added that, as a Venezuelan Jew working across Latin America, she has felt "how quickly events in Israel become judgments about Jews everywhere."
"Too often, the Israel presented to the world is reduced to black and white. Its complexity, humanity and diversity disappear behind headlines, political statements and social media narratives better known as 'TikTok University.' Through Tikun Talks, I work to reach beyond our echo chamber, build bridges and repair the world, one conversation at a time."
Apeloig told the Post she has received hundreds of thousands of meaningful messages from non-Jewish people whose perspectives have shifted, alongside comments "demonizing Netanyahu or using inflammatory statements by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to condemn an entire country and Jews collectively."
Echoing the words of Shturman Waiss, she said it can feel like we take one step forward in building bridges, and a "radical politician’s words send us ten steps backward."
"Those politicians are responsible for their words; the people spreading antisemitism are responsible for theirs. But we in the Diaspora live with the consequences of both."
Because of this, she said the elections are of great importance to her, even though she cannot vote.
"The decisions belong to Israeli citizens, but their impact reaches far beyond Israel’s borders."
"I’m hopeful as I watch Israeli democracy unfold, and I hope the outcome brings leadership that strengthens Israel, helps heal its divisions and builds a brighter future for the Jewish people worldwide," she concluded.

A 4-watt video link passed Ukraine’s state tests, its maker says, and could stretch STING interceptors’ radius from 20 km to 30 km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:46:13 UTC
21:46:13 KST

A new video transmitter for Wild Hornets’ drones, including its STING interceptors, has passed state tests, the Ukrainian drone maker told Militarnyi. The module sends a drone’s camera feed to its pilot. The company expects it to widen its interceptors’ operating radius.
Russia launched 140 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on 26 October and 280 the next night, when its main target was Kyiv, Air Force figures as of the morning show. Interceptor drones, which cost dozens of times less than the Shaheds they hunt, are one of Ukraine’s answers. The STING alone downed more than 3,000 drones in its first seven months of use, Wild Hornets says. If the company’s estimate holds, a 30 km radius would let each ground station cover more than twice the area it covers at 20 km.
What the testers checked
Specialists from the State Research Institute for Testing and Certification of Arms and Military Equipment and the Defense Ministry’s State Quality Assurance Directorate confirmed the module’s declared characteristics on three drone types, the company said. The three were the STING interceptor, the Queen of Hornets cargo platform, and the 10-inch Wild Hornets Digital anti-aircraft drone.
Some of the drones’ figures exceeded the values the company had set for them, Wild Hornets told Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka, without saying which ones. Those figures will enter the official specifications after further field tests, it said.
More than double the power
The module, called HV VTX Pro, is part of an upgrade to Wild Hornets’ Hornet Vision digital video system. It more than doubles the transmitter’s maximum power, to 4 W. That sends a clear picture farther and makes the feed steadier in crowded airwaves and under electronic jamming, the company said.
Wild Hornets first described the module in August, when it was already in serial production. Its interceptors’ operating radius would grow from around 20 km to 30 km, the company said at the time. That estimate assumed good line of sight and the 360-degree antenna on its ground stations, according to a company statement Interfax-Ukraine quoted. Interception could also become at least 20% more effective against targets flying extremely low, the statement said.
Wild Hornets is a Ukrainian company that designs and builds drones, from strike FPV drones and cargo platforms to the STING, which the company says flies at up to 280 km/h to hunt Shaheds. Its drones serve with more than 100 units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, from the army and the National Guard to military intelligence, the Air Force, and the border guard, according to Interfax-Ukraine.

'What are they hiding?': SNP MP describes Israeli 'psychological aggression' after West Bank entry ban

Bird said Israel was deliberately preventing international observers from witnessing its actions against Palestinians, questioning what the authorities were trying to conceal as settler violence and military raids intensify across the occupied Palestinian territory.
"What is abundantly clear is that there is still a very systematic and intentional effort to stop people from coming into the West Bank to witness what is going on in the illegally occupied West Bank," Bird told The New Arab.
"And that’s the thing that needs to be discussed – not our experiences of being denied entry, but what it is that they are so terrified of people seeing."
The Progressive International delegation had travelled to the region to meet Palestinian farmers, students, academics and civil society organisations, and to participate in the annual olive harvest, which has been targeted by escalating Israeli settler attacks.

Bird said the group attempted to enter the West Bank through the Allenby Bridge crossing from Jordan but were detained, interrogated and refused entry "with no justification".

Israeli authorities took delegates to a separate section of the crossing and confiscated their passports.

The delegation's exclusion comes as Israeli military restrictions and escalating settler attacks deprive thousands of Palestinian farmers of access to their land during the annual olive harvest, a vital source of income and a longstanding symbol of Palestinian attachment to their land.
Palestinian communities have reported attacks involving live ammunition, arson, the destruction of centuries-old olive trees and the theft of harvested olives and agricultural equipment.
Israeli settlers have carried out attacks under the protection of, and in some cases alongside, Israeli forces, as Palestinians face mounting pressure on their land and livelihoods.
The United Nations has described attacks on the olive harvest as "yet another tool of displacement and dispossession".
"We know that violence and demolitions and crackdowns are happening more and more in the West Bank, and that experiences of Palestinians in the West Bank are getting more and more horrific," Bird said.

"This is an attempt to isolate Palestinians and intimidate those who stand with them. It will fail," he said. "European governments must stop supplying the weapons and diplomatic protection that allow this violence to continue."

Months-old US startup accessed Anthropic’s sensitive data in under 12 hours: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:41:58 UTC
21:41:58 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A cybersecurity startup gained access to sensitive internal data at artificial intelligence company Anthropic in less than 12 hours, according to a report by The Washington Post .
Cathedral, a months-old startup founded by former members of the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), identified vulnerabilities in third-party business software used by Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, according to a draft report reviewed by the newspaper.
The researchers used AI agents to find pathways into Anthropic’s internal systems, gaining access to meeting transcripts, salary and job offer details, and Slack messages discussing advanced AI models, the report said.
The testing was conducted under a program that allows outside cybersecurity researchers to probe Anthropic’s systems for vulnerabilities.
Anthropic confirmed that Cathedral accessed a “limited set” of its sales, human resources and IT systems. 
The company said it had closed the exposed pathways and briefed federal officials about the incident.
An Anthropic spokesperson said Cathedral had spent several days attempting to breach the company’s own software before turning to third-party business tools.
A senior Trump administration official reportedly said the report had circulated within the government and prompted concern over the speed with which the startup accessed sensitive systems.
The official warned that the findings raised questions about whether foreign intelligence agencies could exploit similar weaknesses.

What’s your comment?

This photo exhibition brings together a large number of photographs and archives of the Tokyo Trials depicting the true history of Japan’s militarist aggression and the wartime crimes to the international community. The United Nations was born out of humanity’s reflection on the devastation of war, therefore it fully serves the international community’s common pursuit of remembering history and cherishing peace to hold the exhibition in the UN.
The Tokyo Trials constitute a historic trial in which peace subdued violence and justice prevailed over evil. The Trials are an integral part of the postwar international order. Recognizing and accepting the judgement of the Tokyo Trials is the prerequisite for Japan’s postwar return to the international community. Eighty years on, however, it is alarming that Japan’s right-wing forces still defy the historic verdict of the Tokyo Trials and try every possible means to deny and whitewash the crimes of aggression, promote a distorted view of history, and brazenly worship war criminals as “gods.” The international community should jointly push back against these trends. The lessons of history are still fresh in memory. Anyone who undermines peace and challenges righteousness and conscience is bound to be brought once again before the court of history and justice.

TikTok parent company founder tops China's rich list amid AI boom

Zhang Yiming has reclaimed his position as China's richest person, with a €89.4 billion fortune driven by AI, as the country's technology sector booms while traditional industries struggle.
TikTok parent company ByteDance's founder Zhang Yiming has reclaimed his position as China's richest person, fuelled by the company's expansion into artificial intelligence.
Zhang topped the Hurun Report's rich list with a fortune of $100 billion (€89.4bn), up 43%, “almost all of it on the back of AI,” according to its chairman, Rupert Hoogewerf.
“AI is the biggest single wealth engine on this list: 160 Hurun rich listers — 1 in 10 — now make their money from AI,” he added.
The Hurun Research Institute, which has published the ranking annually since 1999, identified a record 1,529 individuals with fortunes exceeding 5 billion yuan (€645mn), up 6.6% from last year.
China now has 1,176 billionaires, up 155 from last year and 176 more than the US, although still below its 2021 peak of 1,185.
The ranking comes as China's economy grew 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, supported by strong exports, while weak domestic demand and a prolonged property downturn continued to weigh on growth.
“This year’s gains were polarised — entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink — a two-speed economy,” Hoogewerf said.
The property sector's struggles were also reflected in the ranking. For the first time, no mainland Chinese property developer featured among the 100 richest people, with only Hong Kong property-owning families remaining at the top.
