On US social media platform X, Zelenskyy said his call with Stubb and Store additionally took place as a continuation of their discussions in the Norwegian capital Oslo last Tuesday, which also involved representatives of the US, Europe, and NATO, and thanked the two for their briefing and active support for Kyiv’s diplomacy and peace efforts.
“Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said, noting they also discussed preparations for US-mediated trilateral peace talks planned for next month.
Saying that Finland and Norway, as countries bordering Russia, have a particular interest in “sound and reliable” security arrangements, Zelenskyy said they also discussed various formats for their engagement with partners in Europe that “could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security.”
“There must be peace, de-escalation is needed, and Russia must stop dragging out the war,” Zelenskyy added.
His statement came soon after Stubb and Store's phone call with Putin, which the Nordic leaders initiated to discuss the ongoing war, as well as diplomatic efforts to end it and promote peace and stability in Europe.
“The aim of the call was to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin. The call was related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi,” said a corresponding statement by the Finnish presidency.
Separately, a Kremlin statement said that the three leaders welcomed an agreement to resume trilateral peace talks in early November, noting that Putin had said that reaching a “just and lasting” settlement is only possible with “full and unconditional consideration” of Russia’s interests.
“At the same time, attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are leading to a prolongation of hostilities,” the statement said, adding that issues of ensuring security and stability in the Baltic Sea and Northern Europe were also discussed.
Moscow and Kyiv last held US-mediated peace negotiations earlier this year, with three rounds of talks this January and February, in Abu Dhabi and Geneva.

The Verkhovna Rada has changed the rules governing the stay of foreign military personnel in Ukraine: what the new law provides
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:57:35 EET
20:57:35 KST

The Verkhovna Rada has changed the rules governing the stay of foreign military personnel in Ukraine: what the new law provides
Kyiv • UNN
Foreign military personnel have been given until May 10, 2027, to apply for a residence permit. A three-month period will apply after the conclusion or termination of a contract.
The Ukrainian parliament extended the deadlines for processing residence permits for foreign military personnel. UNN reports this, citing the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine.
The new law adopted by the lawmakers establishes the rules for the lawful stay of military personnel after signing a contract and being discharged from service.
Details
On Tuesday, October 27, Parliament adopted as a basis and as a whole Draft Law No. 16094, "On Amendments to Certain Laws of Ukraine Concerning the Grounds for the Stay in Ukraine of Military Personnel Who Are Foreigners and Stateless Persons." The decision was supported by 282 members of parliament. No parliamentarian voted against it, while 26 more MPs did not vote.
The document concerns foreigners and stateless persons serving under contract in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the National Guard, and the State Special Transport Service. According to the bill’s authors, the main purpose of the legislative changes is to eliminate the risk that service members could lose lawful grounds for staying in Ukraine because they were unable to complete the necessary documents in time due to combat missions or other circumstances.
What changes the adopted law provides for
One of the main innovations is the extension—from six months to one year—of the transitional period for applying for a temporary residence permit for the relevant categories of foreign military personnel. Under the bill’s provisions, for military personnel covered by the transitional rules, the deadline for applying for a residence permit is extended until May 10, 2027.
In addition, the document provides for a separate three-month period of lawful stay in Ukraine for foreigners and stateless persons after signing a contract for military service. During this period, the service member will be able to submit documents to obtain a temporary residence permit.
At the same time, the one-year transitional period and the three-month period after signing a contract apply to different legal situations. This does not mean that every foreigner who joins the military will be able to refrain from applying for a residence permit for one year.
Certain provisions also concern foreigners who have been discharged from service. For specified categories of such persons, an additional period of lawful stay in Ukraine is established, during which they will be able to regulate their migration status. In particular, this includes the possibility of staying for three months after termination of the contract in cases provided for by law, including for certain former service members who hold passport documents that have expired.
Why the deadlines needed to be extended
The issue of the legal status of foreign defenders of Ukraine became especially relevant ahead of November 10, 2026. On that date, the six-month period was to expire during which foreigners and stateless persons already serving in the military were required to apply for temporary residence permits. However, some service members were unable to meet this requirement on time.
As explained by the relevant parliamentary committee, the reasons were primarily related to the specifics of military service. Foreign military personnel take part in combat operations, carry out tasks to protect Ukraine’s territorial integrity, and do not always have the physical opportunity to personally apply to units of the State Migration Service.
Without legislative changes, such circumstances could have created legal uncertainty regarding their continued stay in the country. In particular, service members who continue to perform their duties could have faced difficulties when confirming the legality of their stay in Ukraine, processing documents, and receiving administrative services. That is why, on October 15, the Parliamentary Committee on Human Rights, the De-occupation and Reintegration of Temporarily Occupied Territories of Ukraine, National Minorities, and International Relations recommended that the Verkhovna Rada adopt the bill both as a basis and as a whole.
How residence permits are currently issued to foreign military personnel
The updated procedure for processing documents for foreigners serving in Ukraine’s Defence Forces came into effect on May 10, 2026. It was introduced pursuant to Law No. 4730-IX of December 17, 2025, and Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 573 of May 6, 2026. Under these rules, a temporary residence permit is issued for the entire duration of the military contract, as well as for six months after its termination or cancellation.
This additional period allows former service members to resolve issues related to their further residence in Ukraine, obtain other documents, or travel abroad.
To obtain a residence permit, applicants must contact a territorial office of the State Migration Service, the state-owned enterprise "Document," or the relevant Administrative Services Center.
The documents to be submitted by foreign military personnel include a military registration document or service ID, a military service contract, and an undertaking by the military unit to notify the migration service of the early termination of the contract.
At the same time, certain administrative procedures have already been simplified for this category of foreigners. In particular, when processing a residence permit, the migration service does not verify the residential address. In some cases, legislation also permits the use of passport documents whose validity has expired.
What rights does a temporary residence permit provide?
A temporary residence permit is a document confirming the legal grounds for a foreign citizen’s stay in Ukraine. In particular, the document makes it possible to confirm legal status when dealing with government institutions, opening bank accounts, and obtaining financial, notarial, and medical services.
The absence of properly оформed documents can complicate such procedures even for foreigners who are officially serving in the military under contract.
The Ministry of Defence previously emphasized that the changes to the documentation procedure are intended to reduce the bureaucratic burden on foreign defenders who have to resolve migration issues while simultaneously performing their service duties.
What will change after a foreign national is discharged from military service?
The authors of the new law devoted particular attention to the legal status of foreigners who have completed their military service.
The problem is that after the termination of a contract, a person may need time to determine the further grounds for staying in Ukraine. This may concern service members undergoing treatment or rehabilitation, planning to obtain another legal status, or preparing to return to their homeland.
The draft law provides additional transitional mechanisms for certain categories of discharged service members so that they do not lose their legal grounds for staying in Ukraine immediately after completing their service. At the same time, it is necessary to distinguish between the three-month transitional period for cases specified by law and the six-month validity period of an already issued residence permit after the termination of the contract. These provisions regulate different situations and do not replace one another.
Reminder
At present, around 16,000 foreign volunteers from 72 countries are defending Ukraine.

Turkish communications chief highlights COP31 as opportunity to advance climate diplomacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:56:51 UTC
20:56:51 KST

Türkiye's upcoming hosting of the UN climate summit COP31 will provide an important opportunity to share the country's vision for climate diplomacy with the international community, Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said Tuesday. 
"COP31, to be held in Antalya on Nov. 9-20, is an important opportunity for our country to share its vision in the field of climate diplomacy with the international community," Duran said at a panel titled From Zero Waste to COP31: Türkiye's Climate Diplomacy, held at the Communications Directorate. 
Duran said that climate challenges, including biodiversity loss, ocean pollution, desertification, water-related problems, global warming and waste management, had long exceeded the capacity of individual countries to address them using national resources alone. 
"Climate diplomacy is a concept we use precisely for this reason," he said, adding that government policies could become meaningful only through international negotiations, cooperation, and shared commitments. 
Duran said a climate diplomacy book prepared by the Communications Directorate aims to bring together Türkiye's experience, efforts, and vision in the field and contribute to policymaking and further work. 
- Scientific knowledge 'must also be reflected positively in political decision-making processes' 
Emphasizing that the consequences of the climate crisis were already being felt, Duran said international policies must balance countries' sovereign rights with their global responsibilities. 
He said countries with greater responsibility for climate change were expected to build greater capacity for technology transfer and climate finance, while a fair negotiation framework was needed to reconcile national interests. 
"Scientific knowledge is not enough. It must also be reflected positively in political decision-making processes," he said. 
Duran cited political scientist Joseph Nye's description of climate change as a "threat multiplier" rather than merely an ecological crisis, saying the issue was directly linked to global justice and equity. 
He also argued that conflicts in different parts of the world had serious environmental and climate consequences. 
"Israel's unlawful attacks on Gaza not only threaten human life but also deepen the climate crisis through the intensive greenhouse gas emissions they release into the atmosphere," Duran said. 
He added that carbon emissions caused by Israel's attacks since October 2023 had exceeded the annual emissions of hundreds of countries and the consequences extended beyond regional peace and security to the global climate.  
Türkiye's climate policies and Zero Waste initiative 
Duran said that Türkiye had adopted a comprehensive approach to combating climate change, ratifying the Paris Agreement in 2021 and setting a 2053 net-zero emissions target under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. 
Priority areas include improving energy efficiency, expanding renewable energy, reducing industry's carbon footprint, developing sustainable agricultural practices, and protecting natural areas, he said. 
He also highlighted the Zero Waste initiative led by first lady Emine Erdogan, saying the UN General Assembly's designation of March 30 as International Zero Waste Day, with support from 105 countries under Türkiye's leadership, reflected the country's efforts. 
Duran said the initiative had given Türkiye a distinctive form of soft power in climate diplomacy by helping turn the Zero Waste approach into a global norm. 
He stressed the need to support climate efforts with legal frameworks and warned that inadequate public communication could leave them vulnerable to disinformation and social resistance. 
"My personal view is that conducting politics through social vulnerabilities will not carry us into the future," he said. 
Duran said the Communications Directorate's Center for Combating Disinformation monitored misleading campaigns on climate issues and other subjects, adding that authorities needed to build a bridge of communication between legislation and society. 
He also urged the media to focus not only on the risks of climate change but also on solutions, warning that repetitive negative messaging could increase public anxiety and lead to "green fatigue." 
Long-term communication strategy 
Duran said climate change was a long-term issue that would affect future generations even more than the present one, calling for hopeful messaging across communication platforms. 
He said Türkiye envisioned a multifaceted, long-term climate communication strategy, including age-appropriate environmental education for children through experiments, trips, books and stories. 
He stressed the role of Turkish public broadcaster TRT in promoting environmental awareness through children's programs. 
Duran also cited Anadolu's "Green Line" project, launched in 2022, to provide accessible coverage of environmental and climate issues, and a joint statement on Mediterranean forest fires signed by news agencies from Italy, Spain, and Greece. 
He said environmental awareness needed to become part of everyday life, including home heating, transport, consumption habits, packaging and waste management, rather than remaining limited to expert opinions. 
COP31 to promote shared solutions 
Duran said Türkiye's vision for COP31 was based on restoring trust through dialogue and translating commitments into concrete results on the ground.  
"Our goal is to help turn climate pledges into measurable and lasting action," he said, adding that Türkiye aimed to accelerate the implementation of international commitments, strengthen cooperation among countries, and support tangible results in climate action. 
The Communications Directorate was organizing environmental and climate media tours, accrediting national and international journalists for COP31 and helping plan and establish the media center at the conference venue, he said. 
"Of approximately 3,000 members of the press, the procedures for 1,400 have been completed," Duran said. 
He expressed confidence that the summit, to be hosted by Türkiye, would bring countries with different circumstances and priorities together around shared solutions, and wished the conference success.

Greenhouse gas levels set records again in 2025, U.N. says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:55:59 UTC
20:55:59 KST

Greenhouse gas levels set records in 2025, U.N. says, expressing alarm
Geneva — Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases -- the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide -- all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the U.N.'s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO's 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.
"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO2) has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries."
El Nino's impact
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations -- the amount of those gases in the atmosphere -- rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm); methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them, respectively, to 153%, 267% and 126% of the pre-industrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO2 accounts for about 66% of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm -- smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.
WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the "recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino," the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
"However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning."
It is also above the average growth rate for the past decade of 2.6 ppm -- a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.
"We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Nino which will impact land carbon sinks, as it did in 2023/2024," Tarasova warned.
Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.
The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems toward decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
SF6 has been rising steadily over the past three decades. It is used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution.
Why hydrogen levels have increased over the past decade is unknown but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

1st 4 participants vaccinated in DRC trial testing Ebola jab's effectiveness against Bundibugyo virus: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:55:07 UTC
20:55:07 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The first four participants in a clinical trial launched in the Democratic Republic of Congo have been vaccinated to assess whether an existing Ebola vaccine can reduce severe illness and deaths caused by the Bundibugyo virus, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Tuesday.
WHO Director of Science for Health Meg Doherty told reporters in Geneva that the trial, named TUMAINI, meaning "hope" in Swahili, began Friday.
The first vaccine being evaluated is Ervebo, which is known to be safe and effective against Ebola caused by the Zaire virus. Its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus disease remains unknown.
Doherty clarified that researchers are examining whether the vaccine reduces severe disease or death, rather than whether it prevents infection.
The trial uses a ring-vaccination approach involving people who have been in close contact with confirmed Ebola patients or otherwise exposed to the virus.
Two vaccination rings have already been established, with several more being prepared. Eligible participants can be vaccinated between one and 21 days after exposure, although researchers do not yet know whether the timing affects outcomes.
"We do not yet know for certain when results will begin to emerge. We expect it will take several months," Doherty said.
The trial is led by Congolese researchers and managed by the country's National Institute for Biomedical Research, with support from WHO and international partners.
Designed as a platform trial, TUMAINI can evaluate multiple vaccine candidates within a single research framework.
WHO advisory groups also reviewed two vaccines developed specifically against the Bundibugyo virus last week: ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469.
Recommendations on those vaccines are expected this week, according to the science director.
Doherty said community members were already approaching the trial site seeking to enroll, underscoring the urgent need for an effective vaccine.
The trial builds on the ring-vaccination strategy used during the West African Ebola outbreak a decade ago, which helped establish Ervebo's effectiveness against the Zaire virus.

A parliamentary panel has approved the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement that paves the way for the establishment of the Türkiye-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia Mecca Alliance.
The Turkish parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee was convened on Oct. 27 under the leadership of the committee leader, ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) deputy Fuat Oktay and with the participation of Deputy Foreign Minister Levent Gümrükçü.
The leaders from three founding members signed the agreement on Aug. 7 in Riyadh. Türkiye is mulling over providing defensive support to Saudi Arabia after the parliament ratifies it and authorizes the government to send troops abroad.
The commission approved the agreement with the votes of the People’s Alliance, composed by the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP).
The agreement will later be brought to the General Assembly as part of the ratification process.
Deputy Foreign Minister Gümrükçü, in his explanations about the agreement, stressed that this is purely defensive. “This agreement is not an alternative to NATO but complementary to it,” he said.
“The Mecca Agreement, which is entirely defense-oriented, does not target any country. It is open to the participation of all regional countries that respect international law, particularly the principles of respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, refraining from the use of force except for self-defense, and non-interference in internal affairs, while pursuing the goal of ensuring regional peace and security,” he stated.
In his opening statement, Oktay also recalled that the trilateral agreement is aiming to establish peace and stability in the region through boosting collective security and deterrence. He stressed that this agreement is purely defensive and not against any third party.
“On the contrary, our country is a party to defense agreements aimed at peace and stability that will increase deterrence and fortify our geography,” he stated.
The opposition lawmakers from the New Party, Democracy and Equality Party (DEM) and the Good Party, however, questioned the motives of the Mecca Alliance, especially at a moment when Saudi
Arabia is in an armed conflict with Yemen-based Iran-backed Houthi groups.
Yeni Party Deputy Utku Çakırözer explained that the main opposition will vote against the Mecca Alliance and the defense agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia saying, “We are of the opinion that this agreement will add additional risks to our country’s security.”
“We don’t want to see that our soldiers are deployed to Yemen,” he stated.
The agreement is expected to be brought to the parliament’s General Assembly in the first week of November.

Parties barred from using voter-tracking apps inside polling stations found other ways on Tuesday to track which of their supporters turned out to vote.
Under this election's rules, parties may not use voter-management apps such as Elector inside polling stations. The restriction aims to stop party systems from collecting voter information inside polling stations and to protect voters’ privacy and the integrity of the vote.
Parties, including Likud and United Torah Judaism, have apparently found a workaround. Representatives and activists stationed outside polling stations are reportedly asking voters to identify themselves, then logging in to party systems to record that those voters have cast their ballots. Voters can choose to do this freely, within the limits of the law.
WhatsApp allegedly being used to track vote
WhatsApp is also allegedly being used to track the vote. When contacted, Likud’s Elector operation said its system was working normally and that it was encouraging supporters of the “national camp,” as the right-wing bloc calls itself, to vote.
The instructions sent over WhatsApp were detailed: open the app, go to the “Contacts” tab and mark supporters. A follow-up message asked recipients to use the app to message all their supporters.
So while the app has been kept out of polling stations, parties are still running a digital operation just outside them, updating voter information, reaching supporters, and managing their Election Day effort.

One of the Ukrainian negotiators at the peace talks, Member of Parliament Davyd Arakhamia, named the timeframe for the ceasefire regime as part of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky, in the temporarily occupied territory of Kherson region, UNN writes.
As part of an initiative by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump to unblock Oleshky, the largest-scale ceasefire regime on the largest section of the front in southern Ukraine began today at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time. This is the largest de-escalation since 2022. The ceasefire regime will last from October 27 until 10:59 p.m. on November 1. Each such de-escalation effort brings the long-awaited peace in Ukraine closer
What is known about the humanitarian mission in Oleshky
Ukraine announced a ceasefire regime in a designated area of temporarily occupied Oleshky in Kherson region, effective from 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time on October 27. This is necessary to carry out a humanitarian operation, deliver aid to the city's residents, and prepare for the safe evacuation of civilians.
Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov announced the start of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky on the morning of October 27.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets went to the site and will be responsible for coordinating the process.
Lubinets said overnight: "Oleshky: the ceasefire regime has begun; the Ukrainian side is fulfilling its commitments."
Ukrainian Navy Marine Corps spokesman Pavlo Drohal stated later that, as of 9:00 a.m. on October 27, the enemy was observing the ceasefire regime as part of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky.
Meanwhile, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine urged citizens to rely exclusively on official statements regarding the humanitarian operation.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday said that it would examine all aspects of the Election Commission of India's (ECI) decision-making process amid allegations that key decisions, including those related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls were taken without the unanimous consent."We know everything. We will examine," Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said while hearing a batch of petitions challenging the functioning of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the poll panel, Live Law reported.The three-judge bench, comprising CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, adjourned the hearing to November 17.The top court granted the petitioners 10 days to file rejoinders to the ECI’s counter-affidavit, which was submitted on Monday and asserted that the decisions in question were unanimous.The CJI's remark came after senior advocate Abhishek Manu Singhvi, appearing for leader of opposition on Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders, urged the court to direct the ECI to preserve file notings and internal communications related to its decisions.Singhvi argued that the records were crucial to determining whether the decisions concerning the SIR were taken unanimously or unilaterally."This whole issue depends on the decision-making process, consultation, and whether the decision was unanimous or not unanimous.
Let file notings, etc be preserved," Singhvi added.The petitions challenge the functioning of Gyanesh Kumar alleged that several ECI decisions, including those related to the SIR, were issued without the concurrence of the other two Election Commissioners.The bench also issued notices to the ECI and other respondents on a fresh petition filed by Rajya Sabha MP Dola Sen. The plea alleges that changes were made to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR without the Supreme Court’s approval.Senior advocate and MP Maneka Guruswamy, appearing for Sen, told the court that the poll panel had wrongly claimed that the changes to Form 6 were approved by the top court.The CJI said the court would examine all the issues and asked senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the first petitioner, Rakesh Kumar Singh to file a rejoinder within 10 days to the ECI’s reply affidavit.Earlier on Monday, in its 248-page affidavit, the ECI strongly defended the SIR and rejected allegations that Form 6, the statutory form used for voter registration, had been amended."The attempt to make aspersions against the Election Commission is unfortunate," the affidavit, filed by Deputy Election Commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu on behalf of the ECI said, PTI reported.The poll panel also maintained that no changes had been made to the statutory Form 6. It said the affidavit itself had been approved for filing through a unanimous decision of all three Election Commissioners.
The petitions followed a report published by The Indian Express on September 25, which said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the preceding 10 months to decisions and orders concerning the SIR.According to the report, the two commissioners had objected that the decisions were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.The allegations triggered protests by opposition parties and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which demanded the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.The Supreme Court will take up the matter again on November 17, after the petitioners file their rejoinders to the ECI's affidavit.

Australia’s ABC to demand One Nation remove violent Bluey cartoon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:53:15 UTC
20:53:15 KST

Dilara Hamit
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Australia's national broadcaster ABC said Tuesday it would demand that the right-wing populist One Nation party remove a violent political cartoon featuring the popular children's character Bluey.
ABC Managing Director Hugh Marks described the animation as "a shocking use of Australia's most loved character" and "disrespectful to the children of Australia."
Speaking at a Senate estimates hearing, Marks said the broadcaster had sought legal advice after learning of the video last week and would send a cease-and-desist letter.
“We will be taking further action, I can assure you,” Marks said.
The three-minute cartoon, titled The State of Melbourne, was released in 2024 as part of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's animated Please Explain series.
It depicts caricatures of former Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in an SUV that hits Bluey and Australian conservationist and television presenter Robert Irwin.
The politicians then put the victims' bodies in the trunk. Later, Bluey takes the wheel and drives into cartoon versions of Andrews, Albanese and Irwin in revenge.
Marks said One Nation had not sought permission to use Bluey and argued that the video did not qualify as a parody of the original program.
"It's not a parody of any Bluey work," he said. "It's not a minor use of the intellectual property. In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property."
The ABC has contacted Bluey's international distributor, BBC Studios, and Brisbane-based production company Ludo Studio about the video.
Marks said the letter would demand the video's removal and that the broadcaster could also seek damages.
The controversy comes amid scrutiny of political violence following an alleged attack on independent lawmaker Helen Haines, who was struck by a vehicle outside her electoral office on Oct. 19 and lost both legs.
Labor Senator Varun Ghosh called One Nation's use of Bluey "heinous" in light of the incident.
One Nation lawmaker Barnaby Joyce defended the cartoons as satire and warned against excessive restrictions on political expression.
“You get to a point where you are sanitizing beyond satire,” he said.
The video, which has received more than 1.3 million views, remained available on YouTube as of Tuesday.

EU Commission presents climate resilience framework amid rising costs of climate damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:50:47 UTC
20:50:47 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The European Commission on Tuesday presented a framework to strengthen the EU’s ability to anticipate, prepare for and manage climate risks, citing rising economic losses and the impact of extreme weather events.
The Commission said estimated economic losses from climate damage between 2022 and 2025 totaled approximately €200 billion ($232 billion), or around €50 billion ($58 billion) annually.
“Europe is warming at double the global rate,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, adding that climate resilience should be integrated into policies across the continent to support investment, innovation and long-term growth.
The framework proposes integrating climate resilience into major domestic and international policy areas and supporting local and regional authorities through pilot projects and advisory services.
The Commission said adapting Europe’s infrastructure and economy to future climate conditions is expected to require investment of around €70 billion ($81 billion) annually.
It added that investment in climate adaptation could generate returns exceeding 10 times initial amounts through avoided losses and damage.
The global market for climate adaptation solutions is projected to reach €3.5 trillion ($4.1 trillion) by 2050, the Commission said, presenting opportunities for European businesses developing resilience technologies.
Alongside the framework, the Commission proposed a Climate Resilience Law intended to establish a common reference trajectory for global warming and simplify national planning requirements through a single strategic plan for each member state.
The proposal cites scientific projections that global temperatures could rise to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels by 2030, 2C (3.6F) by 2050 and 3C (5.4F) by 2100.
The framework also envisages new digital tools to help public authorities, businesses and communities assess climate risks.
These include an interactive European Climate Viewer showing projected climate hazards and a platform to help users identify adaptation tools and solutions.
The Commission said it would begin implementing the framework immediately. It is also developing a European Heatwave Plan, a Climate Insurance Alliance and a European Water initiative, alongside measures to strengthen disaster preparedness.
The Commission plans to propose an EU strategic plan on climate resilience in 2028.

emma sicher grows biomaterials from wild berries and microorganisms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:50:35 UTC
20:50:35 KST

emma sicher grows biomaterials from wild berries and microorganisms
with bacteria and locally sourced plants, biodesigner emma sicher grows microbial cellulose into edible prototypes and packaging.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
emma sicher grows materials with microbes
Berlin-based biodesigner Emma Sicher is experimenting with materials grown by bacteria and yeast, turning microbial cellulose into everything from translucent packaging to edible food prototypes. Some of her samples resemble crinkled pieces of pink glass, while others form glossy, gelatinous spheres. Their unusual colors and textures emerge through fermentation, a process in which microorganisms help produce the material itself.
At the center of her practice is SCOBY, a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast commonly associated with kombucha. As the microorganisms grow in a nutrient-rich liquid, cellulose-producing bacteria form a gelatinous membrane at the surface. This can be harvested and processed into flexible sheets, or developed into different forms for food and material applications.
when microbial cellulose becomes food
Emma Sicher’s EATING SCOBY project explores the culinary possibilities of this cellulose-rich membrane. Developed during her MA in Eco-Social Design, the research involved food microbiologists and consultation with chefs. Among the prototypes are SCOBY chips that begin crunchy before becoming chewy and slightly gelatinous in the mouth. An experimental ice cream cone offers another application, with the possibility of an inner coating of melted chocolate.
A double-flavor popsicle takes the material in a different direction, with a consistency the designer compares to blended aloe vera. These familiar food formats make the unusual ingredient easier to imagine on a plate, while introducing new possibilities for its texture and presentation. The prototypes remain experimental, exploring how microbial cellulose might become part of future food systems.
packaging grown from food waste
Sicher first explored bacterial cellulose in her 2017 project From Peel to Peel, which proposed biodegradable food packaging grown from discarded fruit and vegetables. Apple peels and beetroot scraps became nutrients for microbial cultures, producing thin sheets that could be dried into wrappers and small containers. The packaging took on different colors depending on the ingredients, ranging from pale yellow to deep pink.
The dried material can resemble paper or leather, with its finish influenced by the surface on which it dries. Its tendency to absorb moisture presents limitations for conventional packaging, particularly for wet foods. Still, the project established an approach that continues throughout Sicher’s work: allowing biological processes to influence the properties of a material from the beginning.
growing materials from local ecosystems
More recently, Sicher has begun investigating how materials can be grown using microorganisms already present in the surrounding environment. In research published in 2026, she describes experiments with rowan berries foraged around Berlin and mirabelle plums collected in Brandenburg. Both successfully produced cellulose membranes through fermentation using naturally occurring microbial communities, without conventional kombucha starter cultures.
Other experiments combined elderberries with a fermentation starter made from wild mirabelle plums, producing an intensely colored membrane. Sicher’s research also draws on fermentation practices she studied with local practitioners in Thailand. Together, these investigations explore how the plants and microbial populations of a particular region might influence the materials cultivated there, introducing biological variations that would be difficult to achieve through standardized production.
designing alongside living organisms
Sicher also brings microbial experimentation into educational workshops, where participants learn to prepare plant infusions and cultivate their own SCOBY membranes. During a workshop at Elisava School of Design and Engineering in Barcelona, students worked with wet and dried cellulose, exploring how its texture and behavior change through processing. Her research with alternative plant infusions has similarly examined how botanical ingredients can influence the density and physical properties of the grown material.
Across these experiments, Sicher works with processes that depend on the behavior of other living organisms. She can select the plants and prepare the growing environment, but the microorganisms play their own part in forming the material. What emerges is shaped by those biological interactions, suggesting a way of making in which the surrounding ecology participates in the design process.
project info:
designer: Emma Sicher | @seeker_biodesign

27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Deaths from dengue infections rose to 400 in Bangladesh on Tuesday with the addition of 11 more fatalities registered in the past 24 hours.
The Health Services Directorate under the Health and Family Welfare Ministry also reported 2,071 new cases of hospitalizations in the same period, bringing the caseload since this January to 128,237.
Of the total hospitalized patients, 6,415 patients remained in hospitals across the country while the rest returned home after recovery.
Bangladesh this year has started reporting a growing number of deaths from an increased number of hospitals.
There were 269 deaths and 66,423 dengue cases recorded in the corresponding period of 2025, according to directorate data.
Bangladesh usually experiences its dengue season between June and September. The mosquito-borne disease has shown a sharp rise in infections and related deaths compared with the corresponding period last year.
Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes. There is no specific treatment for the viral infection.
The South Asian nation of 175 million saw its highest-ever annual number of dengue deaths in 2022, when 281 people died.
 
7 more children die from measles and suspected cases
Meanwhile, health authorities also reported seven more deaths of children involving confirmed measles and measles-like symptoms.
The total number of child deaths linked to measles infections rose to 1,240 since mid-March. Of these, 105 have been confirmed as definitely due to measles.
The directorate also registered 1,232 new suspected cases and 63 new confirmed infections nationwide. With this, the number of symptomatic measles cases reached 223,784, while confirmed cases stood at 23,541.
The Health Ministry has immunized around 20 million children in response to the outbreak, in addition to routine vaccinations and a catch-up campaign launched late last month.
Bangladesh historically had herd immunity against measles but has lost it in recent years due to declining vaccination coverage.

Nearly 40,000 flee Ethiopia clashes into Kenya as rights commission urges urgent action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:48:36 UTC
20:48:36 KST

Andrew Wasike 
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Nearly 40,000 Ethiopians have sought refuge in Kenya after fleeing deadly clashes in their country, Kenya’s independent human rights commission said Tuesday, urging authorities to provide emergency assistance and protect civilians escaping the violence.
“The protection of life and human dignity cannot be postponed. KNCHR urges all responsible authorities and partners to act urgently, in coordination and with compassion, so that everyone seeking safety in Moyale is protected by the law and can access essential humanitarian assistance,” Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) Chairperson Claris Ogangah said in a statement.
The latest figure represents a sharp increase from the more than 14,000 displaced Ethiopians reported by the Kenya Red Cross over the weekend, as fighting between regional security forces and armed civilians from Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional states continues near the shared border.
The commission said it was concerned by reports that “approximately 40,000 people have sought refuge in Moyale after fleeing unrest in Ethiopia.”
More than 15,000 were reportedly staying in eight temporary shelters, including churches and schools, while over 20,000 others were being accommodated by relatives and friends.
The influx has placed considerable pressure on host communities, with shortages of food, clean water, shelter, sanitation and healthcare raising concerns about deteriorating humanitarian conditions.
KNCHR warned that overcrowding and inadequate sanitation could increase the risk of communicable disease outbreaks.
It also reported that two women had given birth at Manyatta Burji and another two at Bitiye, highlighting the urgent need for maternal healthcare, emergency treatment and postnatal services.
The commission called on the Kenyan and Ethiopian governments to coordinate efforts to address the violence and ensure the safe and humane movement of civilians across the border.
KNCHR emphasized that Kenya’s constitutional protections apply to everyone within its borders, regardless of nationality or immigration status.
It also reminded authorities of their obligations under international refugee law, including the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they face persecution or serious threats to their safety. 
Flag dispute triggers deadly fighting
The humanitarian crisis follows clashes involving security forces and armed civilians from Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional states, particularly among the Oromo Borana and Somali Garre communities.
Both groups inhabit areas around Moyale, where longstanding disputes over administrative boundaries and territorial control have repeatedly fueled tensions.
The latest violence was preceded by a dispute over the raising of the Somali Regional State flag and the opening of a new administrative office in an area of Moyale claimed by Oromia authorities.
Tensions intensified following the killing of a 13-year-old girl on Oct. 18, triggering protests, business closures and further confrontations between the communities.
Heavy fighting erupted on Oct. 22, with regional security forces and armed civilians exchanging gunfire as violence spread to several settlements in southern Ethiopia.
Representatives of the rival communities have accused each other of provoking the clashes, while residents have reported deaths, injuries and the destruction of homes and businesses.
The fighting has also disrupted transport and commercial activities along the Kenya-Ethiopia border, an important trade corridor connecting the two East African countries.
Kenyan lawmakers from Marsabit County earlier appealed to President William Ruto to engage Ethiopian authorities diplomatically and help restore calm.
KNCHR warned that humanitarian assistance must also take into account the needs of Kenyan communities hosting displaced families, saying coordinated intervention was essential to prevent conditions from deteriorating further.

French MPs will vote on Sánchez-style amnesty plan for undocumented workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:46:57 UTC

French MPs will vote on Sánchez-style amnesty plan for undocumented workers
Presidential candidate Raphaël Glucksmann is expected to endorse the measure, which would grant amnesty to hundreds of thousands of unauthorized immigrants.
Lawmakers attend a session of questions to the government at the National Assembly in Paris on June 19, 2018. | Christophe Archambault/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Lawmakers in the French National Assembly will vote on a Socialist Party proposal to grant amnesty to an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 unauthorized immigrants employed in France.
The measure is expected to be supported by center-left presidential candidate Raphaël Glucksmann, whose campaign is eager to find some breathing space between centrist candidates like Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, his rival on the radical left. Glucksmann has previously expressed support for such a step in multiple interviews.
The proposal, introduced by Socialist lawmaker Paul Christophle, hails Spain’s Pedro Sánchez for having “chosen to provide foreign nationals with the legal means to settle and work” instead of “trying — in vain — to control migration flows.”
Advertisement
Earlier this year, Spain moved to grant legal status to half a million unauthorized immigrants who could prove they had been living in Spain for at least five months, could provide proof of employment or a familial link to the country and did not have a criminal record.
Christophle wants to grant legal status to an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 people who have been employed in France for over six months but without proper documentation.
The bill is likely to unite left-leaning MPs in the French National Assembly, but opposition from center-right and far-right groups means it will probably fail.
However, Glucksmann’s campaign hopes the proposal will highlight a rift between lawmakers backing French President Emmanuel Macron and voters who elected him in 2022 — some of whom are more progressive on issues like immigration.
The debate on immigration will be an effective way to differentiate Glucksmann from his center-right rival Édouard Philippe, who believes that amnesty plans should be contingent on a European agreement, said an official who is backing the center-left MEP. It might also help poach Macron voters “who are completely opposed to a closed society,” he added.
Among those who voted for Macron in 2022, 29% plan to vote for Raphaël Glucksmann next year, according to a Cluster17 poll commissioned by POLITICO, against 49% for Édouard Philippe.
Glucksmann is currently projected to receive 13% of the overall vote, according to the poll, against 16% for Philippe. They both trail far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen (33%) and Mélenchon (18.5%). The top two candidates will advance to a runoff if no one wins a majority in the first round.

Estonian media association: Meta is planning the largest theft of content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:46:00 UTC
20:46:00 KST

Estonian media association: Meta is planning the largest theft of content
Estonian media companies have warned US tech giant Meta's new business terms would let it use news content without consent or payment.
The companies are urging the European Commission to intervene over the terms, due originally to take effect October 30.
The Commission says Meta has postponed them to 20 November, following discussions, but the Estonian Association of Media Companies (Eesti meediaettevõtete liit) says the delay changes little.
The Estonian Association of Media Companies has appealed to policymakers and regulators over Meta's new business terms, which would require business users — including news publishers — to grant Meta permission to access their web content by automated software. Meta could then index, store, search and update that content for its business purposes, without separate permission or payment.
Meta initially sought the right to use content for AI training. After publisher protests, it removed the word "training," but the association says the remaining terms are broad enough to permit AI-related use anyway.
In the association's view the terms threaten media business models, as Meta could build competing products from journalistic content without paying for it. Publishers now face a choice: allow the use of their content, or lose a key channel for reaching readers.
Media association board member Väino Koorberg called the development potentially the largest theft of content, while in the U.S., the News/Media Alliance, representing nearly 2,000 American publishers, has written Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, demanding the terms be withdrawn. A further four European publishers' organizations have approached the Commission with similar concerns.
"In European Union terms, Meta is a so-called major gatekeeper, on whose activities the visibility of others hinges, hence why stricter rules have been established for them," Koorberg said.
He added that Meta is also testing restrictions on link sharing on Facebook. "Only two links can be shared free of charge during a month," he said, which serves to limit the platform as a marketing channel.
The association says the situation threatens access to reliable information: more than half of people get daily news from social media, and reduced visibility for journalism could increase vulnerability to disinformation.
Koorberg said Estonia should send a clear message. "For example, state institutions can end cooperation with Meta and leave those platforms, because the change in terms also affects them," he said.
Elis Paemurd, deputy head of the European Commission Representation in Estonia, said Meta had postponed the terms to November 20 following discussions, adding that the Commission is ensuring Meta complies with EU law, including the prohibition on abuse of a dominant position.
Koorberg said the delay does not mean media have escaped. "Meta itself explains that it wants to specify and clarify how the terms should be interpreted," he said, adding that it may be a step toward neutralizing possible legal action. The association has told members to follow developments closely, and that the most extreme step would be to end all cooperation with Meta's products.
Estonian media companies have warned US tech giant Meta's new business terms would let it use news content without consent or payment.

====================================================================================================

What’s next for Brazil after Lula’s victory and Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:44:37 UTC
20:44:37 KST

Brazil’s election dispute has entered a new phase, with presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro yet to formally concede defeat, despite his Liberal Party (PL) recognizing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s victory.
Bolsonaro initially threatened to seek annulment of Sunday’s election, which Lula won by more than 4.4 million votes.
He later said he would seek to have Lula’s electoral ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of political and economic power.
Bolsonaro also said he had been ordered to surrender his passports and barred from leaving Brazil under a separate investigation.
The dispute comes as Lula prepares for a fourth, non-consecutive presidential term, which is due to begin in January. He faces a strengthened conservative opposition in Congress, economic concerns and strained relations with US President Donald Trump.
Trump also questioned the election on Monday, saying it “looked like another rigged election” without presenting evidence of fraud.
Meanwhile, Brazil’s real recorded its steepest daily fall against the US dollar since 2002, according to media reports, following Lula’s victory.
Bolsonaro initially threatened to seek annulment of the election over a two-hour extension of voting hours but later shifted to seeking the disqualification of Lula’s electoral ticket.
The extension followed requests from both campaigns. About 34,330 votes were cast after the original closing time, far below Lula’s winning margin of approximately 4.4 million votes.
Mahrukh Doctor, a professor of comparative political economy at the University of Hull, said the circumstances gave Bolsonaro grounds to challenge the result but that annulment was highly unlikely.
“Bolsonaro rejecting the result (when he lost) is not surprising – some would say ‘like father like son’,” she said.
Consuela Thiers, a lecturer in international relations at the University of Edinburgh, warned that rejecting election results could erode public trust, undermine democratic institutions and deepen political divisions.
She noted that former President Jair Bolsonaro also did not publicly concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022. His party’s subsequent challenge over electronic voting machines was rejected by the electoral court.
“The margin between Bolsonaro and Lula is quite large to be attributed to the extension of voting time (about 4 million votes), which makes Bolsonaro's attempts to contest the results less credible,” Thiers said.
Analysts say that Lula’s victory does not necessarily signal a broader revival of left-wing politics across Latin America, where right-wing forces have gained ground in several countries.
Thiers said Lula benefited from the mobilization of voters who had not participated in the first round, an effective media campaign and his political experience.
But she cautioned against interpreting the result as a renewed left-wing surge.
“I think we should be cautious about presenting Lula’s victory as a signal of a renewed rise of the left, since other factors are at play,” she said.
Many voters, she added, may have supported Lula primarily to prevent another Bolsonaro presidency rather than out of strong personal loyalty to the incumbent.
Thiers, however, said Lula's victory is particularly "significant" for a region that has recently seen a marked turn toward far-right leaders, such as Keiko Fujimori in Peru, Jose Antonio Kast in Chile, and Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia.
"Brazil now remains one of the few countries in the region led by a left-wing president.
"Lula’s victory in the last elections in Brazil came as a surprise in several ways. It was the first time since Brazil’s return to democracy that a candidate who lost the first round went on to win the run-off. It also ran counter to the broader anti-incumbency trend in which governing parties tend to lose elections."
Elizabeth Dickinson, deputy director for Latin America at International Crisis Group, said the election had produced a divided government, with the presidency remaining in left-wing hands while right-wing parties gained ground in the legislature.
“What we see is that really Brazil will have an essentially divided government because the parties on the right, did advance and did gain representation in the legislature and Lulas holds on to the presidency,” she said.
Dickinson warned that the arrangement would complicate efforts to build consensus.
“What that likely means is that it will be a few difficult years, in terms of governing, in terms of passing legislation, finding consensus, and that is really the political challenge that stands ahead for Lula as he enters his next term,” she said.
Lula’s priorities include managing public finances, addressing social and economic concerns and reducing political polarization. Negotiations with a more conservative Congress will determine how much of his program he can implement.
Meanwhile, Doctor called the result a rejection of ‘Bolsonarism’ and what the populist far-right stood for in terms of inclusion, human rights and progressive societal values.
The election also has implications for Brazil’s relations with Washington, where Trump has questioned Lula’s victory despite the absence of evidence of electoral fraud.
Doctor said the US could initially increase trade pressure on Brazil but would eventually have incentives to adopt a more pragmatic approach.
“It is likely to switch to resolving trade issues on more technical rather than ideological grounds,” she said.
She pointed to US interest in Brazil’s critical minerals and rare earth resources as a reason for continued engagement between the two countries.
Lula is expected to pursue a foreign policy centred on multilateralism and balanced relations with partners including the European Union, China, India and others.
Dickinson said Brazil’s position in global supply chains and the future of the Amazon would remain important issues for the incoming administration.
“The Amazon, we know, is home to many of the minerals that are needed and in high tech and defense industries and the sort of rapid interest in these minerals, I think has placed Brazil really at the center of the geopolitical debate,” she said.
Thiers said that the Trump administration was probably expecting to gain another ally in the region, as they would have benefited from having the largest country and economy in Latin America within the US sphere of influence.
"In this sense, Lula’s victory is a setback for US plans in the region and the expansion of the Donroe doctrine."
“This victory comes at a time when the US is attempting to increase its influence through initiatives such as the Shield of the Americas, a US-led security coalition that has already attracted support from several conservative and far-right governments," she said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) on Tuesday defended the government’s decision to deny entry to Chinese actor Zhang Linghe, citing the sensitive timing ahead of the November elections.
Zhang, who stars in the Chinese television series “Pursuit of Jade,” was reportedly scheduled to visit Taiwan later this month, but MAC formally rejected his application Wednesday.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office criticized the move as “undermining cross-strait cultural exchanges,” saying it was “against the wishes of Taiwanese youth.”

At the Legislative Yuan, Chiu told reporters Tuesday that Taiwan welcomes cultural exchanges based on “mutual respect, parity and dignity,” but the agency had doubts about the true purpose of Zhang’s visit.
With the elections approaching, his visit could cause social unrest, and it would be better for him to consider arranging a cultural exchange event at another time, Chiu added.
Zhang’s planned visit has been in the public eye since late April, when KMT Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) asked at a Legislative Yuan session how the Ministry of Culture would respond if the Chinese actor came to Taiwan for a fan meeting. Culture Minister Li Yuan (李遠) did not answer directly, saying Zhang had not applied for a visit.

Hozier, Kneecap join Macklemore at sold-out launch of Free Palestine tour

Irish artists Hozier, Kneecap and Beoga joined US rapper Macklemore as surprise guests Monday at the sold-out opening of his Free Palestine tour in Dublin.
The concert at the 13,000-capacity 3Arena marked the first European date of the benefit tour Macklemore organized after being removed from Ed Sheeran’s US tour over his public support for Palestine.
“I am proud to stand here on stage in solidarity with the Palestinian people,” Macklemore told the audience. “We will continue to fight for collective liberation until our last breath.”
Palestinian flags and keffiyehs were visible throughout the arena as the audience repeatedly chanted “Free Palestine.”
“Six weeks ago, two words is all that it took,” Macklemore said, referring to the declaration that led to his removal from Sheeran’s remaining concerts.
“Those two words are so threatening to some people that we’d rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean,” he said. “Somehow those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary.”

The Dublin concert was the first of three announced European performances, followed by shows in Paris on Thursday and London on Friday. All three dates sold out.
Proceeds will support organizations providing Palestinians with medical care, humanitarian assistance, education and community services.
Macklemore was removed from Sheeran’s tour after declaring “Free Palestine” and criticizing Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank during performances at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium in September.
Several other performers subsequently withdrew from Sheeran’s tour in solidarity. Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was made after promoters were told venues would not permit further concerts with the rapper on the bill.

====================================================================================================

The AI social paradox: Better at communicating, worse at connecting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:40:59 UTC
20:40:59 KST

A text from a family member. An email from the boss. A friend seeking advice after an argument. These are ordinary moments that are part of everyday interactions. Yet, increasingly, there is another participant in these conversations, one that neither feels emotions nor has any personal stake in the relationship - artificial intelligence.For generations, people learnt social etiquette, understood different perspectives and navigated relationships through actual interactions. They often said the wrong things, misunderstood intentions and learnt from those experiences.Now, with AI offering an instant answer to every social dilemma, some of that effort can be outsourced.So, why has replying to an ordinary message become something we might need assistance with? Also while AI may make us more articulate, polite and confident, does that necessarily make us better at connecting?A 'social animal' with AI?Humans have long been described as social animals. Relationships are shaped not merely by what one says, but by how they listen, react, disagree and adapt to one another.AI, however, offers something human relationships rarely can: immediate attention, endless patience and responses tailored to specific concerns. There is no awkward silence, no raised eyebrow and seemingly no fear of embarrassment.This was highlighted by Shailesh K Nevatia, founder director of Grandeavour Communication, having spent nearly 25 years in the communication industry but described himself as shy when it comes to open communication concerning himself.
He said AI helps him navigate differences of opinion, offering perspectives he might otherwise overlook. "With humans we may have certain opinions, views, or thoughts, while with AI, the most valuable thing it offers is not the right answer but a different perspective than us," he said.
"AI can be a guide"
Nevertheless, he maintained that the emotional depth, vulnerability and shared experiences of human relationships cannot be replicated by a chatbot.When the robot does the talkingThe concern with AI-assisted communication is not just that people are using it to find the right words, but that repeated reliance on it could weaken their confidence in finding those words themselves.For instance, Riddhi turns to ChatGPT almost instinctively when responding at times. Whether she needs to sound polite yet firm in a professional email or find a way to decline plans with friends, AI helps her navigate the interaction. "It's not like I can't reply without AI, but having someone to proofread the convos is better than just listening to how they sound in my head," she said.Yet, the reassurance comes with a trade-off for her. "AI has such a grasp on my writing that I am not very confident even while writing this, and that is, without being said, one of the biggest disadvantages." She also called to embrace AI but be careful.
Now that AI has become a new normal, its not possible to go back to the non-AI era, but its also important to not let it become the master of ourselves.
Riddhi
Her experience pointed to a potential paradox: a tool intended to make communication easier can also leave users less confident about communicating independently.The stakes may be higher when AI is used not just to frame a response, but to interpret another person's intentions. Consider someone who turns to a chatbot after an argument and asks who was at fault. The response can sound considered and convincing, but it is based on the account presented to the system, which may omit details or reflect the user's own biases.In that context, Reshmithaa Nair, counselling psychologist at SPARSH Hospital, Hennur Road, warned that such interactions can reinforce confirmation bias, making people more convinced of their existing interpretation rather than open to another perspective.That matters because disagreements are also opportunities to develop social skills. Understanding another person's point of view, managing uncomfortable emotions and responding to unexpected reactions require practice, not simply a well-worded reply."Social skills are learned in actual situations that involve emotions, misunderstanding, conflict, and sometimes rejection," Nair explained.Repeatedly delegating these situations to AI could reduce opportunities to develop empathy, emotional intelligence and the ability to navigate uncertainty. A person may learn to phrase a difficult message more effectively without necessarily becoming better at handling the conversation that follows.The missing human touchA message is not simply a collection of sentences. Its meaning can change with the relationship between the people involved, their shared experiences and even the pauses between words.Ritu Mehrotra, Founder and CEO of Shunya Labs, a voice AI company, pointed out that natural communication involves much more than language."Communication is not only about words, it’s also about tone, pauses, context, emotion and all the things we communicate without explicitly saying them."Advances in voice AI are making it possible for technology to interpret language, intent and context with greater sophistication, including across different accents and communication styles. Yet, recognising emotional signals is not the same as experiencing emotions."And as AI is becoming a part of more and more personal conversations, we have to realise that understanding emotion is not feeling it. Trust, privacy, and transparency must be fundamental," she said.
AI should help people connect with one another, not replicate human empathy or replace human relationships.
Ritu Mehrotra, Founder & CEO, Shunya Labs
A chatbot may recognise expressions of sadness or affection and produce an empathetic-sounding response. But recognising emotional patterns is different from sharing the emotional responsibility of a human relationship. For ex, an AI chatbot was asked to give advice to reply on a (hypothetical) "text to a friend who was laid off"
Response of AI
While the response was considerate, it was also generic. It offered comfort without knowing the friend's emotional state, personality or the nature of the relationship. Even a seemingly caring question like “Are you OK?” may fall flat when the person is looking for encouragement rather than a question whose answer seems obvious. A more personal response might acknowledge the setback while affirming the friend's abilities: “OMG, that's awful. I know the job market is tough, but you're talented. You'll land on your feet.”The difference is not simply about choosing warmer words. It is about understanding what a particular person might need in that moment, something a chatbot may struggle to judge without sufficient context.There is also the question of authenticity. When a message is carefully constructed by AI, it may communicate the intended information effectively. But does it still sound like the person sending it?In this example, of AI removing the human touch, another chatbot was asked "Someone close to me is grieving. I don't know what to say, and I'm afraid of making things worse. What should I tell them?". It gave a response, which is not wrong but is too robotic. "I am here with you. I care about your pain. Speak if you wish; silence is acceptable." Perfect words but not someone who is comforting says in such "rigid tone"The little hesitations, imperfect expressions and familiar phrases that characterise someone's communication can disappear beneath polished language. A message can become more grammatically correct while feeling less personal.
What aI can't do when comes to social interactions
Not all badDismissing AI as a threat to social skills, however, would overlook how it can help people who struggle to express themselves.For Pooja, a college student who hesitates to speak up in front of the entire class or repeatedly ask friends to explain something, AI offers a space where she can ask questions without worrying about others' reactions.She uses it to understand complicated topics and brainstorm ideas, sometimes asking ChatGPT to explain something as though she were a 10-year-old.
What I love most is that I can ask the dumbest questions without feeling embarrassed. But I also feel it's very easy to become too dependent on it.
Pooja
Yet, she recognises the possibility of becoming overly reliant on it. "AI can give you answers in seconds, but actually understanding and learning something is still on us."For others, AI serves as a sounding board before difficult conversations. It can also help people become more mindful of how their words might affect others. It can suggest more inclusive language, flag potentially insensitive phrasing and help users consider perspectives they might otherwise overlook. For someone unsure how to communicate across differences, this can offer a starting point for more thoughtful interactions.But knowing which words are considered appropriate is not necessarily the same as understanding why they matter. Genuine inclusivity requires empathy and a willingness to understand experiences different from one's own, qualities that must extend beyond the words suggested by a chatbot.Also, in such cases, might not give you the perfect answer, but may help you think in the right direction and give you options that you may not have thought about. In another hypothetical test, a chatbot was asked how to support a family member struggling with their mental health without pushing them away. While its response was not fully correct, it offered different approaches to consider, giving the person a starting point for thinking about how to respond.
AI bot's advice giving suggestions on comforting a family member
Thus, the value, then, may not lie in AI providing the perfect answer, but in helping someone see possibilities they had not considered. The important distinction is whether people use these suggestions to develop their own judgement or simply follow them without question.As Shruti Rajan Kappil, clinical lead, excellence and quality at a mental health care platform Amaha, explained, that while the need to feel heard and supported is fundamental to human relationships, not every concern feels safe to share. Shame, embarrassment and fear of judgement often prevent people from opening up, particularly where stigma remains prevalent.
"AI offers space"
AI offers an alternative, but Kappil pointed to an important distinction. "Good support often needs honest disagreement or gentle challenge with a different point of view. AI tends to be agreeable more often than not, and being agreed with is easily mistaken for being helped."She also noted that repeatedly seeking AI's approval before sending a message can become a form of reassurance seeking. While it offers immediate relief, constantly checking whether one's words are "correct" may gradually undermine confidence in one's own judgement.Shristi Chaudhari, senior executive, regulatory intelligence and market research at Bureau Veritas, uses AI almost daily to condense regulatory updates. Increasingly, she also turns to it for interpersonal communication.From identifying emotional undertones to making messages warmer and more polite for colleagues and professional contacts, AI has become a useful sounding board.
While AI can refine written communication, help us anticipate reactions and interpret conversational nuances, it cannot replace the soft skills, verbal cues and lived experiences that shape genuine human connections.
Shristi Chaudhari
These experiences suggest AI can help people prepare for conversations, overcome language barriers and articulate thoughts they might otherwise struggle to express.Perfect talks, weaker bonds?Communication is one of the ways human beings establish connection. But effective communication and meaningful connection are not necessarily the same thing.
What AI can and can't do
One involves expressing something clearly. The other requires understanding, trust, emotional involvement and vulnerability.Tanvi Mankodi, assistant professor at SPJIMR, believes the deeper concern is not whether AI will replace human relationships, but what excessive dependence might do to our ability to participate in them."For me, the essence of human relationships is about our vulnerabilities, about our imperfections, and about how we try to relate with each other with our discomforts and uncertainties," she said.Misunderstandings, difficult conversations and moments when people struggle to find the right words are also experiences through which patience, compassion and empathy develop."Rather than worrying about AI replacing human relations, I am more worried about how if we use AI in a way that we are dependent on it, it might reduce our ability to be vulnerable and to be human," she added.
Impact of AI-dictated communications
Her concern captures the paradox: in trying to eliminate the discomfort of human interaction, we may also remove experiences that make relationships meaningful.
Of course, not every AI-generated message weakens a relationship, and the long-term effects of outsourcing everyday communication are still being understood. AI may help some people overcome barriers to social participation while encouraging others to avoid interactions through which confidence develops. But, the concern is can it address the individuality and complexity of human behaviour?However, using AI to prepare for a difficult discussion is one thing. Allowing it to decide how we interpret another person's intentions and what we say in every interaction is another.The point is not whether AI can offer thoughtful, nuanced or well-structured answers to human dilemmas. It is whether those answers can replicate the emotional understanding, vulnerability and lived experiences through which we learn to navigate relationships and grow socially. After all, relationships are not assignments to be completed with perfectly structured answers. They evolve through disagreement, compromise and sometimes saying something imperfectly but sincerely.Perhaps the real challenge is not learning how to communicate better with AI, but ensuring that, in the process, we do not forget how to connect without it.
Trisha Mahajan is a journalist with The Times of India digital, with keen interest in covering business and corporate affairs. She also reports on key national and world developments and global news trends. A keen reader with a strong interest in storytelling that adds context, clarity, and depth to complex issues.
