Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion.
The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections.
Do sześciu razy sztuka. Grzegorz Braun dostał zarzuty, w tym za uwięzienie ginekolożki Gizeli Jagielskiej
Wcześniej europoseł Grzegorz Braun pięć razy unikał przedstawienia zarzutów w Prokuraturze Okręgowej we Wrocławiu. Zainterweniował Prokurator Generalny Waldemar Żurek.…
— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026
As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges.
Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read.
In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges.
Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hannukah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”.
Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups.
Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison.
In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month.
The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher.
Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”.
For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term.
Finally, Braun has been charged with destruction of property for an incident during his presidential campaign in March this year when he vandalised an exhibition about the local LGBT+ community in the city of Opole, spray-painting “stop the propaganda of perversion” on it.
Police are investigating far-right presidential candidate and MEP Grzegorz Braun after he vandalised an LGBT+ exhibition.
The city where it took place immediately cancelled a meeting he was due to hold there and is seeking compensation for the damage https://t.co/EbDpMzmpFw
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 20, 2025
Braun has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him, as he has done with a string of other charges for various offences relating to his antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT rhetoric and actions.
In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”.
Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%.
If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition.

Tit-for-tat Sudan drone strikes kill 21, cause mass power outages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Retaliatory drone strikes between Sudan's warring factions killed at least 21 people in Darfur and caused widespread power outages in the east, witnesses and medics said Tuesday.
A drone strike on a market in Nyala, the de facto capital of Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Darfur, killed 21 people and wounded at least 40 others, a medical source and witnesses said.
One Nyala resident said a market in the city's north was struck by a drone on Monday around 8:00 p.m. (6 p.m. GMT).
Another said the market was frequented by young men, particularly Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters.
"Twenty-one people were killed in last night's bombing, and more than 40 others injured," a medic at Nyala Hospital said, though he was unable to identify how many were RSF fighters.
Sudan's military, at war with the RSF since April 2023, regularly strikes Nyala, where the RSF has declared an administration rivaling the army-backed internationally recognized government in Khartoum.
The RSF has in turn launched repeated strikes targeting Khartoum's airport, as well as dams and power stations across the country's east.
On Tuesday, "RSF militia drones targeted the Al-Markhiyat transformer station, disrupting the power supply across large parts of Khartoum and Al-Jazira states," a source in the national electricity company said on condition of anonymity.
The strike comes a day after a coordinated RSF drone attack on six power stations left millions without power in Al-Jazira, White Nile, Sennar and Gedaref states.
The war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks from across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October alone, drone strikes killed over 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a U.N. tally.
Since it began, the war has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate and has triggered the world's largest humanitarian crises.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people.
Close to 3 million people have returned to Khartoum state since it was recaptured by the army last year, but many have struggled to rebuild their lives in a scarred city.
Power and water supplies remain unreliable, much of the capital remains unsafe from unexploded bombs and many struggle to put food on the table in a collapsed economy.
On Monday, 30 countries including the United States, France and the United Kingdom warned that urgent action was needed to prevent famine expanding across the country.
Sudan is facing "an alarming deterioration" of food security, they said, citing the war, a currency in freefall, higher fuel prices due to the Middle East war and a drought induced by the El Nino climate phenomenon.
Sudan's Foreign Ministry Monday insisted the country's food security was "reassuring," in an attempt to "refute claims of famine."
It accused "some countries and organizations" of "politically exploiting the humanitarian situation."
The army has for years denied claims of documented famine and has been accused of blocking access to humanitarian aid.

Saab announces new Sea Giraffe AMB D radar
Saab introduces Sea Giraffe Agile Multi Beam D (AMB D), the latest evolution of its Giraffe AMB radar family, providing naval forces with enhanced 3D surveillance and tracking of air and surface targets in increasingly complex maritime environments.
Sea Giraffe AMB D can detect, track and classify aircraft, drones, missiles and crewed or uncrewed surface vessels, with a range of up to 250 km for air targets and 50 km for surface targets. It provides early warning and accurate target information to support decision-making in distributed, multi-domain operations, where reliable sensors are the foundation of operational advantage.
Designed for demanding maritime environments, the radar combines advanced Electronic Counter-Countermeasures (ECCM) capabilities against jamming attempts, with a modular architecture that enables integration with other naval systems. Its software-defined architecture also enables continuous upgrades as operational requirements evolve.
“Sea Giraffe AMB D takes a proven naval radar capability to the next level, combining increased performance with a low footprint and an architecture built for continuous development. It is designed to meet the demands of today’s naval forces while giving customers the flexibility to evolve with future threats,” says Carl-Johan Bergholm, head of Saab’s business area Surveillance.
Building on more than 70 years of radar innovation and over two decades of ongoing operational success with Sea Giraffe AMB radars, the new Sea Giraffe AMB D leverages Active Electronically Scanned Array radar hardware with a new software architecture and modern processing capabilities to provide enhanced air surveillance performance.

- The move angered German workers and union leaders, who called it “highly embarrassing” and “politically unacceptable”, and warned it could affect approval of the factory.
- The plant plan comes as parent Volkswagen cuts costs, reshapes its workforce, and faces weak demand, Chinese competition, and tariff pressure in the US.
AI generated
Audi chief executive officer Gernot Dollner said he acted in the interest of the carmaker when he took part in US President Donald Trump’s campaign rally that announced the company would build a US$4 billion (S$5.1 billion) plant in the country.
The two men shared the stage in Georgia over the weekend, days before the US midterm elections. The appearance triggered a wave of criticism in Germany as taking sides in the upcoming vote.
The Audi executive, who had travelled to the US for talks about the project, said the company was asked to announce the go-ahead for the facility together with Trump, Dollner said in a letter to workers seen by Bloomberg News. The decision to appear “was taken solely in the interest of the company”, it said.
“At the same time, we realise that the announcement was taken as signalling a political stance,” Dollner wrote. “We take this very seriously.”
The planned site in Georgia still needs to be greenlighted at Audi parent Volkswagen’s supervisory board level, where worker representatives hold half the seats. The furore about the Trump rally could complicate this step, and push the company into making concessions elsewhere.
VW as well as Audi are in the midst of tense talks on wages and tough savings measures with workers in Germany.
On Oct 26, Christiane Benner, the head of IG Metall union and VW’s deputy supervisory board chairwoman, called Dollner’s appearance “highly embarrassing” and pointed to labour’s leverage over whether the factory goes ahead. As part of the broad restructuring talks, VW is looking into alternative uses for its large Audi factory in Neckarsulm after earlier saying the plant could be shut.
“The way Gernot Dollner presented himself and Audi in the US is highly embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company and, above all, its employees,” she said.
VW’s works council chief Daniela Cavallo separately accused Dollner of providing “active campaign assistance”. She said Audi’s internal guidelines prohibit public-facing appearances with politicians standing for election during the final three months before a vote, and that he had signed those principles only months ago.
The plan to spend US$4 billion on a facility in the US lands in the middle of VW’s attempt to radically reshape its industrial footprint and shrink its domestic workforce in Europe.
VW CEO Oliver Blume is pushing to cut jobs and factory costs while investing more heavily in growth markets including the US. Europe’s largest carmaker is struggling with weak demand, fierce Chinese competition and the costly shift to electric and software-defined vehicles.
Audi is particularly exposed to the US trade shift because it still imports most of the vehicles it sells there, leaving the brand vulnerable to tariffs that have already raised costs across VW’s North American business. Media groups challenge India’s privacy law at top court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:56:22 UTC
19:56:22 KST

Media groups challenge India’s privacy law at top court
News organisations are challenging the law, arguing it could hamper investigative journalism and endanger sources.
The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounts to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups have told the Supreme Court.
A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s law on Tuesday, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow the government to identify journalists’ sources, according to The Indian Express newspaper.
“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), told judges.
“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission … it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”
The Supreme Court said it would hear the case next month.
Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written exemption for journalists as in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.
The DNPA’s members include Ambani’s Network18, which has seven digital news platforms, Adani’s NDTV and other high-profile media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.
Fear of putting sources at risk
A key concern in the law is the requirement of consent, says the group’s filing, cited by the Reuters news agency.
A social media platform or online retailer can seek consent from users when they sign up, but the DNPA has argued that requiring a journalist to notify the subject of an investigation and seek consent “would allow that subject to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses”.
The law also lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand that their data be erased, without any public-interest safeguard, which the DNPA says could force its members to unpublish or heavily redact a factual news report.
News publishers are concerned that a federal authority created under the law can impose fines for noncompliance, and grants powers to New Delhi to block access to any information in the “interests of the general public”, which would curtail press freedom, the DNPA said.
From next year, the law will also let New Delhi order any organisation handling personal data “to furnish such information as it may call for”, putting newsrooms at risk of having to divulge sources, the filing said.
It can also deter whistleblowers from sharing information on corruption, corporate wrongdoing or electoral malpractice with reporters, the DNPA argued.
The “nakedly unguided” provision must be quashed, the DNPA said, adding that the power “can extend to privileged communications in possession of a reporter or the informant.”

Is Jagan Reddy's 'regret' message a calculated alliance pitch for Congress?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:55:55 UTC
19:55:55 KST

A successful alliance with the INDIA bloc hinges on the YSRCP and Congress aligning, which could be Jagan Mohan Reddy’s biggest challenge
NEW DELHI: Is YSRCP supremo YS Jagan Mohan Reddy signalling a drift towards the Congress-led INDIA bloc? Or is he trying to break free from the image of being soft on the BJP?The former Andhra Pradesh chief minister has provided issue-based support to the BJP-led NDA government on several key legislations in Parliament while he was in power in the state. However, he has stayed away from joining any alliance till now. So, when Jagan Reddy recently regretted his “mistake” of supporting the 2023 NDA legislation for selecting the Chief Election Commissioner, it fuelled speculation about his future political moves."We regret supporting the process under which the ruling party nominates the Chief Election Commissioner at the Centre. Neither the CEC nor the SEC should be appointed by the ruling party. The selection committee should comprise the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition and the Chief Justice of India (CJI), with all three exercising their voting rights," the YSRCP chief said recently, calling the current selection system "flawed."The timing and context of Jagan’s remarks are significant. So, is he rethinking his “solo” politics? And if yes, will the Congress be ready to tango with him in Andhra Pradesh? After all, alliances with regional parties have been the Congress’s biggest Achilles heel across states.
Jagan’s support for NDA’s key Bills
Jagan Mohan Reddy’s MPs backed the Modi government several times between 2019 and 2024, both in Lok Sabha and in Rajya Sabha, on many important legislations. However, when it came to stitching an alliance for the 2024 elections, the BJP ignored Jagan’s help and joined hands with his arch-rival Chandrababu Naidu. Together, TDP and BJP swept the polls in Andhra Pradesh, winning 164 out of 175 seats in the assembly and 21 out of 25 seats in Lok Sabha. The YSRCP was reduced to 11 seats in the assembly and 4 in Lok Sabha.Despite being spurned by the BJP and his party’s shock defeat, Jagan Mohan Reddy remained confident about his BJP ties. After all, he still had 15 MPs (4 in Lok Sabha and 11 in Rajya Sabha) to provide the much-needed support to the BJP’s minority government at the Centre. Jagan even announced that his MPs would extend issue-based support to the NDA government in matters concerning national and state interest.But with the BJP heavily dependent on Chandrababu Naidu’s support for survival of its government at the Centre, there was little room for the saffron party to accommodate Jagan Reddy. Nearly two and a half years down the line, Reddy seems to have accepted this harsh reality and is perhaps gearing up to chart a new path for the next political challenge in 2029.
Jagan vs Congress
However, for any successful alliance with the INDIA bloc - the YSRCP and the Congress will have to be on the same page. And that perhaps would be the biggest challenge for Jagan Mohan Reddy.Jagan Mohan Reddy had a bitter parting from the Congress in 2010, a year after the death of his father YS Rajasekhara Reddy. YSR Reddy was in his second term as the chief minister of Andhra Pradesh when he died in a helicopter crash on September 2, 2009. Jagan’s supporters, who were many in number, lobbied hard with the Congress high command for the top post, but Sonia Gandhi did not budge and made K Rosaiah the chief minister. The Congress leadership did not approve of Jagan’s Odarpu Yatra, which was part of his announced plan to meet the families of many people who had sacrificed their lives after his father’s death.That set the stage for his eventual exit from the Congress, which he announced on November 29, 2010 in an open letter to Sonia Gandhi carefully written to ensure there was enough public sympathy for his second phase of political career.In the 2014 assembly elections, the YSRCP made an impressive debut and won 67 out of the 175 seats with a vote share of 44.46%, while the Congress could manage only a vote share of 2.8%. The Congress decision to bifurcate the state and create Telangana played a huge role in the party’s declining political fortunes in the state.On November 6, 2017, Jagan embarked on the Praja Sankalpa Yatra and covered 3,648 km in 341 days, crossing 134 assembly constituencies. The Yatra, from YSR Ghat at Idupulapaya to the northeastern tip of Ichchapuram, powered Jagan Mohan Reddy to a historic mandate of 151 seats in the 175-member assembly in the 2019 elections. The Congress’s vote share was reduced to less than 1%.The Congress, since then, has been making efforts to reclaim its lost political space in the state. It roped in Jagan Reddy’s sister Y S Sharmila as part of the party’s revival plan. Sharmila, who started her political career with her brother Jagan Mohan Reddy eventually drifted towards the Congress and was appointed president of Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee in January 2024.However, both Jagan Mohan Reddy and his sister Y S Sharmila failed to make an impact in the 2024 elections. The 2024 elections saw a dramatic collapse of Jagan’s electoral fortunes, and his party was reduced to only 11 seats. The Congress once again failed to make its presence felt.
The 2029 challenge
And that brings us to the 2029 elections - a do-or-die challenge for both Jagan Mohan Reddy and the Congress. Jagan’s remark on backing the CEC appointment Bill is his first open “regret” for backing the BJP.But does this “open regret” mean an olive branch for the Congress?Former Congress leader and senior political commentator Sanjay Jha strongly feels that Jagan and Congress should come together, though he admits that this may not be easy.“Politics is the art of the possible and I'm sure Jaganmohan Reddy is aware that Chandrababu Naidu has been an extremely close alliance partner of the Modi government. While the Congress doesn't have a base in Andhra like it used to have once upon a time. The support base of Jaganmohan Reddy is basically the Congress vote which moved away from the traditional Congress to the Congress that Jaganmohan Reddy, branded as the Congress of his father. So, if the merger were to happen, it would, frankly speaking, give them a huge advantage because then both the Central Congress and the Jaganmohan Congress could be on the same page,” Sanjay Jha says.However, he accepts that merger of the two parties could be a difficult process while stitching an alliance may be easier. “Once a political party becomes independent and has power, they don't like to give it up in a hurry. The TMC or the NCP are good examples. In which case it could be an alliance,” Sanjay Jha adds.The third option, according to Sanjay Jha, is for the Congress to resurrect itself on its own strongly in Andhra by capturing both the anti-incumbent votes against Chandrababu Naidu and winning back the loyalist voters of the Congress who had moved over to Jaganmohan Reddy.
This is easier said than done. The Congress has a poor track record when it comes to winning back states it has lost. We have seen several states across the country where the Congress has lost its government and eventually its support base but does little to reclaim it.In Andhra Pradesh, Chandrababu Naidu and the BJP are going all out to consolidate their position. Naidu’s call for greater cooperation and coordination among southern states at a recent conference is perhaps an effort to keep his importance and relevance intact. We saw DMK’s MK Stalin make similar moves before he lost power to Vijay’s TVK in the last assembly elections.Jagan Mohan Reddy and the Congress face an uphill electoral battle in 2029. It will be interesting to see if they can agree to an alliance to take on Chandrababu Naidu and the BJP.

A Kuwaiti court has sentenced three individuals to death and eight others to five years in prison in a case involving an alleged plot to assassinate Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad Al-Yousef and accusations of collusion with Iran and the Lebanese group Hezbollah.
The verdict was issued by Kuwait’s State Security and Terrorism Crimes Court, presided over by Judge Nasser Al-Bader, alongside judges Omar Al-Mulaifi, Abdullah Al-Faleh and Salem Al-Zayed.
According to the prosecution, the defendants faced charges of collaborating with foreign entities, planning hostile acts against Kuwait, targeting senior government officials, joining a banned organization and engaging in activities deemed harmful to national interests.
The charges also included plans to use explosives in the assassination attempt and create panic among the population.
Investigators accused one defendant of attempting to obtain explosives to facilitate the planned operation.
READ: Egypt moves to address Kuwait teachers’ job losses
In its ruling, the court stated that the defendants had sought to undermine Kuwait’s national security, provoke social unrest and weaken public confidence in the authorities’ ability to protect lives, property and state institutions.
The case comes amid heightened security measures in Kuwait aimed at countering what authorities describe as threats to national stability, including foreign interference and activities involving prohibited organizations.
The proceedings have attracted particular attention because of the alleged involvement of Iran and Hezbollah and the reported targeting of a senior member of the Kuwaiti government.
Sheikh Fahad Al-Yousef serves as Kuwait’s Minister of Interior, overseeing internal security, policing, crime prevention and the protection of public order.
The report did not provide details of the defendants’ identities or indicate whether the verdicts would be appealed.

Shadow from Trump's Washington arch would land on Arlington Cemetery, Washington Post finds
Since President Trump first proposed the installation of a monumental new arch in Washington, critics have argued it would detract from another important site nearby: Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest military cemetery, which sits just across a nearby bridge.
But a new analysis by The Washington Post has found that the arch would, quite literally, cast a shadow over the hallowed burial ground.
On 284 days out of the year, the arch would block sunlight from portions of the cemetery, its shadow passing over the graves of more than 75,000 people, as well as several notable memorial sites. Those include the eternal flame honoring former president John F. Kennedy and the Military Women’s Memorial.
The shadow would also pass over the grave sites of several Supreme Court Justices, including Thurgood Marshall and Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the Post found.

As tens of millions of Americans prepare to cast their vote, social media companies have scaled back their efforts to protect voters from lies meant to manipulate elections.
While the backlash against Facebook after the Cambridge Analytica scandal prompted social media giants to bolster their trust and safety operations, a counter-backlash from the right over fears of speech restrictions – which intensified after Elon Musk’s takeover of X, formerly Twitter, and the election of Donald Trump in 2024 – has led to significant layoffs from relevant teams.
Artificial intelligence has made it easier than ever to launch a disinformation campaign. And platforms are increasingly relying on AI, rather than human intervention, to respond.
“You can run an information operation now with quality that was impossible in 2016 for super, super cheap,” said Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower and advocate for transparency and accountability in Big Tech. Norwegian confirms job cuts at Copenhagen Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:53:12 UTC
19:53:12 KST

Norwegian will lay off 123 employees at Copenhagen Airport following discussions with unions, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
The layoffs will affect 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members and will take place in stages.
Most employees will leave at the end of January 2027, while the remaining dismissals are scheduled for approximately 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, Norwegian’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The dismissals are happening out of necessity.”
Last week, aviation news outlet Check-in.dk reported that 125 employees at Norwegian’s Copenhagen base were at risk of losing their jobs.
The airline plans to reduce the number of aircraft based in Copenhagen during the summer season from 16 to 14.
According to Norwegian, the decision reflects significant seasonal differences in passenger demand.
The airline currently needs 16 aircraft during the busy summer months but only 10 during winter.
Despite the reduction in Copenhagen-based aircraft, Norwegian says it will maintain its existing number of summer departures from the Danish capital.
Some routes will instead be operated using aircraft based in Spain.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline last year, accounting for 15 percent of passengers, according to the airport’s latest financial statements.
SAS held the largest share at 38 percent, followed by Ryanair in third place with nine percent.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest operating base after Oslo.
Last year, the airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen Airport.

Danish Minister steps down as minister due to stress
A change in the government happened overnight, with a member of the government stepping down from her role for health reasons.
Signe Munk is stepping down as Denmark’s minister for cities, rural areas and transport after becoming ill with stress, the Prime Minister’s Office announced.
Munk, 36, a member of the Socialist People’s Party, known as SF, said she needed time to recover and find a better balance between work and family life. “I have become ill with stress. And I have decided to step down as minister,” she wrote on Facebook, adding that she intended to remain in politics.
Munk became a minister when the government was formed this summer, after years of working alongside SF leader Pia Olsen Dyhr to rebuild the party following its crisis in 2014. Fellow SF politician Karina Lorentzen Dehnhardt, who has served as the party’s justice spokesperson, will replace her.
Lorentzen Dehnhardt first entered Denmark’s parliament in 2007, though she was out of office from 2015 to 2019. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen praised Munk’s contribution to the government negotiations, while Olsen Dyhr expressed full support for her decision to step down.
Nils Brøgger, an SF senior adviser and former campaign manager, will take Munk’s parliamentary seat during her sick leave. Having served less than a year as minister, Munk will not qualify for a ministerial pension but will receive six months of post-service pay.
Three senior doctors leave Rigshospitalet after being sent home following patient safety warnings
Three senior doctors who raised concerns about patient safety at Rigshospitalet’s transplant department are leaving the Copenhagen hospital after management sent them home, according to Danish broadcaster DR.
They were among five senior doctors who wrote to hospital management and the Capital Region, which oversees the hospital, expressing concern after two surgeons left the department earlier this year.
Nurses and doctors have also raised questions about professional standards at the Department of Transplantation and Diseases of the Digestive System, Denmark’s only unit performing liver transplants.
At a meeting Monday, hospital managers assured regional politicians that the department still had the quality and capacity needed to treat patients properly.
Regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt welcomed that assurance but said the departing doctors’ expertise would be difficult to replace. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj said it was too early to determine whether guidelines for experimental surgery had been breached. Those guidelines cover how procedures are documented and how patients are informed and involved.
An external investigation will review previous treatments to assess whether the department followed the guidelines and met professional standards.
Bank deposits in Denmark fall for two consecutive months
Danes’ bank deposits fell for a second consecutive month in September, reaching 1,309.3 billion kroner, according to figures from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank.
That was down from 1,317.7 billion kroner in August and 1,323.2 billion kroner in July. Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension provider Sampension, said the last decline lasting two consecutive months occurred in January 2023, but cautioned against treating the latest figures as evidence of a broader trend.
Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, said September declines were common, occurring in 16 of the past 20 years. He suggested loan payments and spending on autumn and winter clothing could help explain the fall, while noting that September does not bring large child benefit payments or tax refunds.
Despite the recent declines, deposits remained above the 1,283.1 billion kroner recorded at the beginning of the year. Dalsgaard expects savings to grow again, saying uncertainty about personal finances could encourage Danes to put more money aside.

The University of Copenhagen (KU) shut down several administrative systems Monday after another cyberattack, just days after hackers gained access to personal information belonging to approximately 525,000 people.
The university confirmed the latest attack on its website, reporting disruptions to several administrative systems and difficulties accessing university websites on Monday evening.
The previous breach exposed personal information including full names, CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers, work and private telephone numbers, and private email addresses.
The university has not provided further details about Monday’s attack.
Denmark’s Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization, Christina Egelund of Moderaterne (the Moderates), expressed serious concern about the repeated incidents.
“It is the second time in a short period, and it does not become less serious that it comes in the wake of several attacks on our universities,” she told Ritzau.
Several Danish universities, including the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and Aarhus University, have also experienced cyberattacks in recent weeks.
Egelund said the incidents highlighted the seriousness of the security situation.
“It is an attack on our knowledge institutions, which are an absolutely crucial pillar of society in Denmark,” she said.
The minister summoned leaders from Denmark’s eight universities to a meeting Monday to discuss cybersecurity.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, explained that universities hold large amounts of personal and research data, making them attractive targets.
Their public visibility also increases their exposure to cyber threats.
“That makes us potential targets for both cybercriminals, foreign states, and activist groups,” he said in an Aarhus University press release.
New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.
Human editors select stories, determine their angles, review AI-generated drafts, make revisions and choose images before publication.
“We could have made it so that AI did everything. But it doesn’t,” Dyrby said.
AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.
Dyrby, who graduated from the Danish School of Journalism in 1989, previously helped launch TV 2 News in the mid-2000s.
Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.
Danish publisher bans AI tools for work on manuscripts
Danish publisher Lindhardt og Ringhof has prohibited employees and external partners from using artificial intelligence to complete work for the company.
The ban applies to proofreaders, editors, manuscript readers and consultants, according to a letter distributed by the publisher.
“It is not permitted for any purpose to use AI tools for tasks that one as an external partner solves for Lindhardt og Ringhof,” the letter states.
Manuscripts and other documents provided by the publisher must not be uploaded to AI systems under any circumstances.
The company said even apparently harmless uses, such as asking AI to summarize a manuscript, could create legal and copyright risks.
“Texts that are uploaded into AI tools can subsequently be copied and data mined, even if the provider claims otherwise,” the publisher said.
Literary director Sune de Souza Schmidt-Madsen told Danish public broadcaster DR that Lindhardt og Ringhof was not aware of external partners already using AI for its assignments.
However, he said the publisher expected the issue to emerge eventually and wanted to establish its rules in advance.
The restrictions also apply to the publisher’s own employees, Schmidt-Madsen said.
Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak
The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.

Some areas continued to experience storm-force gusts, although the wind was expected to weaken during the day.
DMI maintained warnings for elevated water levels around the Wadden Sea, the central western coast of Jutland and parts of the Limfjord.

Western Denmark will experience the most clouds Monday, while eastern areas will have clearer conditions. Showers are expected in several places before conditions improve later in the day.
Temperatures will range from 9 to 13 degrees Celsius.
A new front will bring clouds, rain and stronger southerly winds overnight into Tuesday. Winds could reach gale force along the west coast, although less rain is expected than during the weekend.
Wednesday will bring a mixture of rain, showers and sunshine.
A high-pressure system is expected to stabilize the weather from Thursday, bringing less wind, drier conditions and more sunshine.

Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.
Danish Crown confirms slaughter without stunning at Polish subsidiary
Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.

“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.

“It is therefore extra important at this time of year that everyone who keeps poultry or other birds does everything to prevent contact between their animals and wild birds,” agency veterinarian Mette Kirkeskov Sie said.

The agency said avian influenza only very rarely spreads to humans.
However, people should avoid touching sick, weakened or dead wild birds.
Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

RITZAU
Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.

Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.

Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.
During the debate, opposition party Naleraq proposed putting the agreement to a referendum.
The Greenlandic government holds a majority in Inatsisartut. In Denmark, the government must secure support from other parties to obtain a parliamentary majority for the agreement.
Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.

Danish military to fund four bus routes to attract and retain staff
Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.
The initiative is outlined in a funding document approved by the Folketing’s Finance Committee, a parliamentary body that approves certain government spending outside the annual Finance Act.
The Armed Forces will receive 2 million kroner in 2026 to establish the routes. The initiative is planned to run for three years, with a total budget of 17 million kroner.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said the routes would help make military employment more attractive at garrisons in remote parts of Denmark, where public transport services are inadequate.
“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.

Strong winds, heavy rain and potentially elevated sea levels are forecast across parts of Denmark on Sunday, with the west coast of Jutland expected to experience the worst conditions.
According to Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, wind gusts could locally reach storm force, particularly along the North Sea coast.
“One should consider whether it is worth going outside when the wind is blowing the most,” DMI meteorologist Hans Ole Wanner told Ritzau.
Southerly winds are expected to strengthen overnight into Sunday as a warm front brings widespread rain.

Higher water levels are also possible along Jutland’s west coast, particularly around the Wadden Sea.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a storm system moving toward Denmark from the British Isles over the weekend.
DMI advises residents to secure loose outdoor items, including garden furniture and trampolines, before the strongest winds arrive.
The institute also recommends clearing leaves from gutters and drains to help prevent problems during heavy rainfall.
Wind gusts are expected to weaken Monday, although breezy conditions will continue.

Denmark to end mink farming by August 2029 under EU ban
Denmark’s remaining seven mink farms will have to close by August 7, 2029, after the government decided not to seek an exemption from an upcoming European Union ban.
The Ministry for Nature and Animal Welfare announced the decision, citing animal welfare concerns and the industry’s limited economic contribution.
“An industry should not continue solely because it has existed for a long time. It must also make sense for society, for the economy, and for the animals,” said Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats).
The EU added mink to its list of invasive species last summer, introducing a ban on breeding and production that takes effect August 7, 2027. Existing farms will have a two-year transition period.

Carl Valentin, animal welfare spokesperson for Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, welcomed the government’s decision.
“As we see it, it is not good animal welfare to have mink in tiny cages,” he told Ritzau.
Denmark’s mink industry was severely affected in 2020 when authorities ordered approximately 15 million animals culled over concerns about coronavirus mutations.
A temporary farming ban followed, lasting until January 2023, when some producers resumed operations.
The total estimated cost of pandemic-related compensation, farm demolition and administrative work reached 29.1 billion DKK in early 2026.
The government has yet to determine compensation costs for closing the remaining farms.
Valentin said an earlier estimate was around 14 million DKK, although the final amount could be higher.
Politicians push to change rules for dogs suspected of being banned breeds
Several Danish opposition politicians are calling for changes to the country’s dog laws after reports of legally owned dogs being kept in kennels for months while authorities investigate their breeds.
Under Denmark’s Dog Act, 13 breeds are banned from ownership, breeding and importation, including pit bull terriers and American bulldogs. Crossbreeds containing any of the prohibited breeds are also illegal.
When police suspect a dog belongs to a banned breed, its owner must provide documentation proving otherwise. During the investigation, the animal may be placed in a boarding kennel.
Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten has reported cases involving dogs that were eventually found to be legal but had spent months in kennels.
Danmarksdemokraterne (the Denmark Democrats), an opposition party, has proposed allowing dogs to remain with their owners while investigations take place, potentially using electronic tracking devices instead.
Borgernes Parti (the Citizens’ Party) and independent lawmakers Nadja Natalie Isaksen, Cecilie Liv Hansen and Emilie Schytte have also criticized police powers to order euthanasia based on visual assessments of a dog’s breed.
The law requires police to euthanize dogs found to belong to prohibited breeds.
The restrictions were introduced in 2010 following incidents involving dog attacks on people and other animals.
Christian Rabjerg Madsen, Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare from Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats), told Jyllands-Posten he was open to discussing changes to the law and its enforcement.
He said the challenge was balancing public safety with fair treatment of owners who struggle to document their dogs’ breeds.
Danske Bank announces third round of layoffs this year
Danske Bank is cutting 106 jobs, around half of them in Denmark, in its third round of layoffs this year.
The bank announced the cuts in a press release on Thursday, saying they are intended to help create a “more efficient and competitive bank”.
The remaining positions are in the bank’s operations in Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Poland and Sweden.
“We continue to develop Danske Bank to meet our customers’ expectations, strengthen our competitiveness, and realize the ambitions in our Forward ’28 strategy,” Karsten Breum, the bank’s head of human resources, said in the release.
“This means that we continuously simplify the organization, invest in new competencies, and move resources to the areas where we create the greatest value for our customers.
“It is a natural part of running and developing a large company.”
The latest cuts follow two previous rounds of job reductions in 2026.
In February, Danske Bank announced that it would cut 420 positions across the organization. At the time, the bank said it wanted to adapt to customer needs, invest in technology and advisory services, and become more digital.
Three months later, a further 262 positions were affected. The bank gave broadly similar reasons for those cuts.
Both earlier rounds primarily affected employees in Denmark.
Breum acknowledged the impact of the latest decision on employees.
“Decisions like these affect people,” he said in Thursday’s press release.
“For the colleagues who are affected, it is a difficult situation. Therefore, it is important that we implement the changes responsibly and give our affected colleagues the support and respect they deserve throughout the entire process.”
All employees affected by the latest cuts have been notified.
Danske Bank says on its website that it has more than 20,000 employees across its international operations.
Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.
Denmark to get 51 emergency supermarkets stocked for major crises
Shoppers across Denmark will be able to buy essential groceries and household supplies during power outages, cyberattacks and other emergencies under a new initiative by Salling Group.
The Danish retail giant, which operates Bilka, Føtex and Netto, plans to establish 51 emergency-ready supermarkets nationwide by 2027.
The stores will be equipped to operate for at least 48 hours without electricity or external communication systems, ensuring access to basic necessities during major disruptions.
According to Salling Group, the network will include 17 Bilka stores, 32 Føtex stores and two Netto locations.
The stores will be distributed so that up to 80 percent of Denmark’s population lives within 50 kilometers of one.
Each location will maintain emergency stocks of 50 essential products, selected according to Danish authorities’ recommendations for household preparedness.
These include oatmeal, protein bars, canned meatballs in curry, rice cakes, tuna, beans, chickpeas and other foods with long shelf lives.
Nonfood essentials such as batteries, wet wipes and diapers will also be available.
Customers will be able to pay offline using almost all physical payment cards and digital cards stored on smartphones.
Salling Group recently partnered with payment provider Nets to help maintain card transactions during system failures.
CEO Anders Hagh said establishing the emergency stores remains a top priority, with preparations progressing toward the 2027 target.
Meanwhile, competing retailer Coop, which operates Brugsen, SuperBrugsen, 365discount and Kvickly, has not decided whether to establish similar stores.
Coop’s chief risk officer, Ulrik Mester, said the company was discussing crisis preparedness with authorities, including Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed (SAMSIK), Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security.
Politicians across Danish political spectrum condemn MP’s meeting with Russian ambassador
Politicians from both left and right have criticized independent Danish MP Jacob Harris for planning to meet Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, on 10 November.
Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen, Denmark’s former defense minister, expressed strong opposition to the meeting in a post on X.
“I actually thought it was a bad joke when I read it,” he wrote, adding that “we must fight Putin. Not drink coffee with his ambassador”.
“It is completely, completely the wrong way to go, and it actually makes me furious. While Russian missiles rain down on Ukrainian cities, while innocent civilians are being killed, and while Russia is waging hybrid warfare against Denmark and our allies, a Danish member of parliament apparently believes that the time has come to sit down at the table with Putin’s representative,” Lund Poulsen wrote.
Mohammad Rona, political spokesperson for the Moderates, and Mette Abildgaard, parliamentary group leader for the Conservatives, also criticized Harris.
“Why is Harris turning his back on Denmark? Harris’ loyalty apparently lies somewhere else. Sad that a Danish parliamentarian can sink so low,” Rona wrote on X.
Abildgaard wrote: “He becomes a useful idiot in the Russians’ propaganda machine. If he wants to be a great diplomat so badly, then apply for a job in the Foreign Service instead.”
Sigurd Agersnap, political spokesperson for the Socialist People’s Party (SF), described the planned meeting as “deeply naive”.
Harris risks giving the Russian ambassador exactly what he needs: “An image that Danish politicians are softening toward Russia while the attacks on Ukraine continue,” Agersnap said in a written comment to Ritzau.
“Of course we must have diplomacy. But a lasting peace requires that we stand firm on the Ukrainians’ right to freedom and self-determination. Harris does not help that by showing up for this meeting,” he added.
Trine Pertou Mach, the Red-Green Alliance’s foreign affairs spokesperson, told DR that the meeting was “decidedly stupid”.
Harris announced the planned meeting with Barbin in a Facebook post on Thursday. He also said he expected criticism from fellow politicians.
He has defended the decision, arguing that meeting a foreign ambassador is not an act of disloyalty.
“Speaking with a foreign ambassador is not treason. Seeking diplomatic solutions is not treason. And working to ensure that Denmark is not dragged into a war is certainly not treason either,” Harris wrote on Facebook.
Harris is an independent member of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. He was elected in March as a member of Borgernes Parti, or the Citizens’ Party, but was expelled a few days later.
He has since established a “working partnership” in parliament with fellow independent Cecilie Liv Hansen, who supports his decision to meet the Russian ambassador.
“I think it is reasonable to meet with ambassadors, regardless of where they come from. Jacob Harris has also tried to reach out to several, including the Ukrainian one,” Hansen told DR.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four and a half years ago. Denmark and several other countries have supported Ukraine since then, including through financial assistance and weapons deliveries.
Danish People’s Party seeks to strike Pakistani man from citizenship bill
Dansk Folkeparti (DF), the Danish People’s Party, wants a Pakistani man removed from a bill that would grant Danish citizenship to 2,055 foreign nationals next year.
The party’s citizenship spokesperson, Mikkel Bjørn, cited a Facebook post from 2016 that DF claims showed the man supporting an execution carried out under Islamic law.
Bjørn told public broadcaster DR that the government should remove the applicant from the bill or, at minimum, arrange for him to appear before Parliament’s Naturalisation Committee for questioning.
DR contacted the man, who said he could not explain why he had shared the post but denied supporting violence or murder.
“I respect people of all religions, from all backgrounds, and of all genders. I support freedom of speech, mutual respect, and peaceful coexistence,” he wrote in an email.
The dispute follows a similar demand from Liberal Alliance concerning a female citizenship applicant.
The party claims she repeatedly praised Hamas and its former leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh. It wants her questioned by the parliamentary committee.
The cases have intensified debate over whether citizenship applicants are adequately screened for attitudes considered incompatible with democratic values.
Denmark typically introduces citizenship bills every six months, following an extensive application process.
The current bill was first debated in Parliament, known as the Folketing, on February 5 but was postponed after Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a general election later that month.
Earlier in October, the government announced plans to introduce a screening system to identify potentially anti-democratic attitudes among citizenship applicants.
However, it has decided to proceed with the citizenship bill before the new screening system is ready.

Denmark’s national police commissioner, Lasse Boje, will meet representatives of two journalism organizations on Friday following incidents in which police officers struck two press photographers with batons during demonstrations in Copenhagen.
The meeting will bring together the leadership of the Danish Union of Journalists and the Danish Association of Press Photographers to discuss guidelines governing interactions between police and journalists.

He plans to propose changes to police training, including more extensive instruction at the Police Academy on how officers should interact with journalists covering demonstrations.
