“It will obviously not resolve the fact that trained officers would not receive that training, so it may be that there needs to be some form of continuing education or further training,” he said.
Copenhagen Police announced Monday that it had requested an investigation by Den Uafhængige Politiklagemyndighed (DUP), Denmark’s Independent Police Complaints Authority.
The independent watchdog confirmed Tuesday that it had opened investigations into both incidents.
According to DUP, its investigations typically involve interviewing witnesses and collecting video footage to establish what happened.
The findings of the investigations have not yet been announced.
Hacker attempts to compromise 1,700 accounts at Aarhus University
A hacker gained access to a server at Aarhus University and attempted to access and change passwords belonging to approximately 1,700 users, the university has confirmed.
The attempted password changes were unsuccessful after the intrusion was detected Monday, according to a statement published on the university’s internal website.
There is currently no indication that sensitive or confidential information was leaked during the attack. However, the university said further investigations would be carried out in the coming days to establish the full extent of the incident.
The university also clarified that the attack was unrelated to the security vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, a widely used programming language, which prompted temporary shutdowns of several Danish websites Wednesday.
Despite the breach, Aarhus University said students and employees could continue their normal activities without disruption.
However, it urged everyone to remain particularly vigilant about suspicious online activity, including phishing attempts, in which criminals use fraudulent messages to obtain passwords or other personal information.
Anyone noticing unusual activity has been advised to contact the university’s IT support team.
Minister for Societal Security and Emergency Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, confirmed that authorities were aware of the incident.
In a written statement, she said the Agency for Societal Security was closely monitoring developments and maintaining contact with the university.
“There is dialogue with Aarhus University, and relevant higher education institutions have already been gathered for a briefing where the Agency for Civil Security has advised,” the minister said.
Aula reopens as Danish authorities restore websites following security scare
Aula, Denmark’s widely used school communication platform, reopened Thursday morning after being taken offline Wednesday afternoon because of a global cybersecurity vulnerability.
Aalborg Municipality confirmed the reopening in a press release, saying the necessary security measures had been implemented.
The platform connects schools, daycare facilities and families across Denmark. It has approximately two million active users, with more than 600,000 logging in on a typical weekday.
The disruption followed the discovery of security flaws in PHP, a programming language widely used to operate websites, online shops and digital services.
The vulnerabilities left websites worldwide potentially exposed to cyberattacks, prompting authorities and public institutions in several countries to temporarily shut down services as a precaution.
In Denmark, affected websites included those belonging to Copenhagen Municipality, Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, and Vejdirektoratet, the Danish Road Directorate.
All affected Danish websites have since reopened.
Minister for Societal Security and Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen of Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, stressed Wednesday that the incident was not a cyberattack.
Speaking to TV 2, she explained that the vulnerabilities could nevertheless have serious consequences if left unaddressed.
The situation also prompted Denmark’s National Operational Staff, known as NOST, to activate its lowest crisis preparedness level, according to TV 2.
NOST brings together several public authorities to coordinate responses to major emergencies and crises.
The activation, known as information readiness, is the lowest of three preparedness levels and allows authorities to share information and coordinate their response to developing threats.
The measure was introduced Wednesday evening as authorities monitored the global security situation.
Security flaw in widely used software forces Danish websites offline
Several Danish public websites were shut down Wednesday after security vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used by websites and online services worldwide.
Minister for Societal Security and Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen described the situation as a “global incident” but stressed that it was not a cyberattack.
Speaking to TV 2, she warned that websites could face serious risks unless their operators installed the necessary security updates.
“It can potentially be really serious if system owners do not get a security update done. If that is not possible right here and now, then one must consider going offline,” she said.
The vulnerabilities affect PHP, which powers many websites, online shops and digital portals.
According to Reuters, PHP’s developers identified the flaws Tuesday but released an update to fix them Wednesday at 1:45 p.m.
Bech-Nielsen told Denmark’s public broadcaster, DR, that websites without the update could be exposed to attacks.
“It is in a way positive that we have found these vulnerabilities. But because it is publicly known, there are some who will exploit it,” she said.
Authorities and public institutions in several countries temporarily shut down websites as a precaution.
In Denmark, affected services included websites belonging to Copenhagen Municipality, the Danish Road Directorate and the Danish Meteorological Institute, known as DMI.
Kombit, an organization that manages shared IT solutions for Danish municipalities, also confirmed that Aula, the digital communication platform used by schools and parents, had been taken offline.
The ministry said authorities were closely monitoring developments but did not clarify whether further political action would be necessary.
Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.
Danish bishops consider moving Great Prayer Day to autumn when holiday returns
Great Prayer Day could return to Denmark’s calendar in a different season, with most bishops of the Church of Denmark open to moving the public holiday from spring to autumn.
The discussion follows the government’s announcement that Store Bededag, or Great Prayer Day, will be reinstated as a public holiday in 2030, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
The holiday was abolished by the previous Social Democrat, Venstre and Moderates coalition government, with the change taking effect in 2024.
The Ministry of Ecclesiastical Affairs has confirmed that the Church of Denmark will be involved in the reinstatement process. A bill is expected in spring 2027.
Thomas Reinholdt Rasmussen, bishop of Aalborg, suggested that late October might be a suitable alternative.
“Liturgically, it does not really fit into the period from Easter to Pentecost, so perhaps it would be good to place it at the end of October,” he told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Marianne Gaarden, bishop of Lolland-Falster, also expressed openness to changing the date, noting that spring already has several public holidays.
“I like the idea of a prayer day where the focus is on spiritual reflection, and that focus must be preserved. But of course it is possible to consider that it can be moved,” she said.
Bishops in Funen, Aarhus and Viborg are similarly open to discussions, while Helsingør’s bishop, Peter Birch, has not taken a position.
However, the bishops of Ribe and Roskilde favor restoring the holiday to its original spring date.
The bishop of Copenhagen has not commented, while Haderslev’s bishop, Marianne Christiansen, will wait until the government presents its proposal.
Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey
Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey with Danish minister
Denmark’s Queen Mary will travel to Antalya, Turkey, from November 8 to 10 to participate in the United Nations climate summit COP31, the Danish Royal House has announced.
She will be accompanied by Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party.
Turkey is co-hosting this year’s summit with Australia, which is responsible for leading the negotiations.
The annual UN climate conferences bring countries together to discuss international efforts to address climate change and reach agreements on reducing its impact.
During her visit, Queen Mary will meet representatives of Danish companies showcasing environmentally friendly technologies and solutions at the Danish pavilion.
She will also focus on the challenges facing Pacific island nations, including Vanuatu and Fiji, which are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels and other consequences of climate change.
Another part of her program involves meeting young delegates from around the world to hear about their experiences with climate change and efforts to support the green transition.
Queen Mary also attended last year’s UN climate summit in Brazil, where her program included visits to a cocoa production facility and a research institute working on sustainability.
Her upcoming visit follows a new report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), published Wednesday, warning that global warming will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.
The report attributes this to decades of insufficient climate action.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries committed to keeping global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius compared with temperatures between 1850 and 1900, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees.
Severed network cable disrupts departure screens and train information apps across Denmark
A severed network cable at Banedanmark disrupted departure and arrival information at many train stations across Denmark on Wednesday.

Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, said information about train times was being provided through station loudspeakers wherever possible.

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.

“Speaking with a foreign ambassador is not treason. Seeking diplomatic solutions is not treason. And working to ensure that Denmark is not dragged into a war is certainly not treason either,” Harris wrote on Facebook.
Harris is an independent member of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. He was elected in March as a member of Borgernes Parti, or the Citizens’ Party, but was expelled a few days later.
He has since established a “working partnership” in parliament with fellow independent Cecilie Liv Hansen, who supports his decision to meet the Russian ambassador.
“I think it is reasonable to meet with ambassadors, regardless of where they come from. Jacob Harris has also tried to reach out to several, including the Ukrainian one,” Hansen told DR.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four and a half years ago. Denmark and several other countries have supported Ukraine since then, including through financial assistance and weapons deliveries.

U.K. charges 2 men arrested over alleged Iran-linked terror plot against RAF Fairford air base used by U.S.
London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.
Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."
The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford air base in England.
Abdulkarim was arrested by Counter Terror Police under the National Security Act last week, along with another 25-year-old man — a British-Iranian dual national who was released on bail pending further investigation.
Police are still investigating a suspected terror plot against Fairford after five men were initially detained on Sept. 27 near the base in western England. All five of those men were also released on bail, but police said they remained under investigation and would be monitored.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the base, which prompted the U.S. Air Force to remove all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford. The base had been home to U.S. long-range bombers for many years, and it was used during the war with Iran to launch strikes on the Islamic Republic.
Residents of a nearby town were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police and bomb-disposal experts searched the area on Sept. 27. They found gasoline in three vans that had been driven by the five initial suspects, parked close to an entrance to the base, but no explosives.
Iranian officials have said repeatedly that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. The Iranian Embassy in London, however, said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Police said Tuesday that six men remain free on bail in relation to the incident, four of whom were arrested on Sept. 27 — all U.K. nationals and London residents in their 20s — and two others who were detained subsequently, including the 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national who was detained on Oct. 1.

Taiwan receiving 6 MS-110 reconnaissance pods for F-16Vs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:36 UTC
19:50:36 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is scheduled to receive six US-made MS-110 Multispectral Airborne Reconnaissance System pods by the end of December, enhancing its F-16V fighter fleet's surveillance capabilities and speeding access to battlefield intelligence.
The defense ministry confirmed the updated delivery schedule in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan, per Liberty Times. The procurement program has a budget of NT$9.63 billion (US$302 million), with two pods already delivered and the remaining four expected by the end of the year.
The Air Force began installation testing and personnel conversion training in June. In August, F-16Vs operating from Hualien's Chiashan Air Force Base carried the first two pods on flights that completed the initial phase of flight-performance evaluations.
The MS-110 is expected to double the imaging capabilities of the Air Force's existing tactical reconnaissance pods, commonly known as the Phoenix Eye system, Liberty Times reported. Its seven spectral bands — blue, green, red, near-infrared, shortwave infrared, and two midwave infrared bands — enable multispectral imaging for target identification and surveillance.
Military sources said the system has an effective imaging range exceeding 148 kilometers and can capture high-resolution imagery at a rate of up to 26,000 square kilometers per hour. This would allow F-16Vs operating east of the Taiwan Strait median line to monitor Chinese coastal military deployments and troop movements without flying deep into contested airspace.
The system also lets the Air Force receive reconnaissance imagery in real time, rather than waiting for aircraft to land and retrieve recorded images, according to Liberty Times. Its digital data link transmits high-resolution imagery to ground stations while airborne.
If terrain or low-altitude flight disrupts the signal, the pod stores imagery internally and automatically transmits it when connectivity is restored. The Air Force has established four ground receiving stations that relay imagery through military data networks and fiber-optic connections to the Heng Shan Military Command Center and operational theater commands.

Underwater data centers may be coming to the U.S.—smack in the middle of endangered whale habitat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:19 UTC
19:50:19 KST

The battle over where to put data centers is heading below the waves: the Trump administration is considering proposals to build two massive underwater data centers off the country’s coast. The sites selected for the projects—one in Cook Inlet, Alaska, and one in the Gulf of Maine—are smack in the middle of two endangered whale populations’ habitats.
Whales are “skittish animals,” says Arial Brewer, a beluga researcher at the University of Washington and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “A massive-scale project like this could really stress them out in a lot of different ways.”
Data centers, with their thousands of servers, generate considerable heat that can damage equipment if not offset in some way. Land-based facilities use massive amounts of fresh water to cool down. By putting a data center underwater, the ocean can easily dispel that heat. “Cooling is a large part of what a data center costs to run, and seawater is a free sink,” says Vishal Misra, a computer scientist and professor at Columbia University.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Microsoft showed that the concept could work with a pilot project off California in 2015 and another off Scotland a few years later. Currently, there are only two operational underwater data centers in the world, one off the Chinese island of Hainan and another off the coast of Shanghai, and they’re a fraction of the size of the proposed centers at the two U.S. sites.
In the Maine project, a cluster of what official documents call “subsea-compute hives” or “data center pods” would rest on the seabed, powered by up to 50 tidal turbines across 27 acres. In Cook Inlet, the data center would be made up of 66 pods and more than 300 tidal turbines. Its footprint would span 1,650 acres—more than 1,000 football fields.
The locations were chosen by DeepGreen Holdings LLC—a U.S.-based developer—because of their potential for tidal power, which works by harnessing the movement of water.
But each spot is also home to beleaguered groups of whales. A distinct population of around 300 critically endangered beluga whales lives in Cook Inlet. And the Gulf of Maine hosts feeding grounds for the North Atlantic right whale, a species whose numbers have dropped below 400 individuals.
The primary concern over data centers underwater is the same as for those on land: they are exceedingly noisy. “Pumps, fans and especially turbine arrays make continuous low-frequency sound, and pile-driving during construction is louder still,” Misra says.
Shipping noise has doubled every decade since the 1960s, and there’s evidence to suggest that when the volume goes down, marine mammals are less stressed. One study found that when ship noise decreased immediately after 9/11, right whales in the Gulf of Maine had lower levels of stress hormones. As for the belugas in Cook Inlet, they are particularly sensitive to noise, Brewer says. Because of glacial runoff, the bay is very turbid. “It literally looks like chocolate milk,” she says, so the belugas there rely almost entirely on echolocation to feed, mate and move around.
The purpose for putting the data centers underwater—heat shedding—also threatens the whales. When a pattern of warming waters hit the Gulf of Maine in the early 2010s, right whales started to abandon their feeding grounds. “Ocean warming is a big, big deal to them,” says Philip Hamilton, a senior scientist at the New England Aquarium.
In Alaska, salmon are one of the main prey sources for belugas—and the fish need cold water to develop their eggs, keep their metabolism stable and prevent energy depletion during long migratory journeys. “All that hot energy, what’s that going to do to very delicate salmon populations that rely on cold water?” Brewer says.
Community backlash has been fervent: The city of Eastport, Maine, issued a moratorium halting all permits and applications for all industrial data centers. The local Passamaquoddy tribe has also publicly expressed that it has no interest in any sort of collaboration with DeepGreen. Several groups have filed motions to intervene with the proposal for Cook Inlet.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which oversees such energy projects, notes that these proposals are just that: proposals. “A preliminary permit does not authorize construction of any kind,” says Celeste Miller, a FERC representative.
Indeed, FERC found the original proposals for both projects “deficient,” citing a lack of details and insufficient identification of Indigenous tribes who have historic ties to the local areas. But the agency has accepted amended versions; the Maine project, which originally called for 170 turbines on 400 acres of seafloor, now has a smaller proposed footprint. The public comment period for Maine closed on October 19, but the one for Cook Inlet is open until November 2. After that, FERC will review the applications and comments and issue preliminary permit decisions.
“We have no intent to build at this stage,” Louis Wolfson, the luxury real estate developer behind DeepGreen, says. “If equipment cannot operate safely well within federal marine mammal thresholds, it will never be licensed or deployed.”
But over the past two years, the federal government has sought to strip back those very thresholds. For example, the Senate is considering a bill that would delay new protections for right whales against entanglements in fishing gear. And though belugas and right whales have historically been protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, proposed amendments to it would drastically draw back protections.
“It feels like every day they’re chopping at another protection,” Hamilton says.

Why we’ll never have another Black Death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:10 UTC
19:50:10 KST

Scientists disagree over how scared we should be by the mysterious death of a worker at a Russian plague lab. A young laboratory technician died earlier this month of an undisclosed illness after working on research at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East. Although officials have not released details about the cause of death, scientists agree that if it was caused by ordinary plague, the wider world has little to worry about. This bacterial illness is infamous for the explosive killing spree known as the Black Death, which wiped out between a third and half of the population of Europe between 1347 and 1353. Today, however, plague is curable and extremely unlikely to blow up into a new pandemic, experts say. That’s thanks to a combination of antibiotic development, scientific understanding and luck.
Experts who study plague are reluctant to say it’s been completely conquered. The World Health Organization (WHO) recently reported approximately 3,800 infections and 423 deaths from plague between 2019 and 2025. And scientists haven’t cracked all the mysteries behind the plague bacterium, known as Yersinia pestis—one of the biggest being how it hides for years in cryptic reservoirs only to spring out in unpredictable new waves of infection in humans or other animals.
The disease is endemic in rodents living in the Americas, Central Asia and Africa, says David Wagner, a plague expert who directs the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “It’s constantly cycling between rodents via fleas, and it just does that in perpetuity in a manner we poorly understand, despite 100 years of research.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Studies of ancient DNA show plague-infected prehistoric hunter-gatherers in Siberia 5,500 years ago. Plague is known for causing three major pandemics: in addition to the one that started with the Black Death, which peaked between 1347 and 1351 and was followed by outbreaks into the 18th century, there was the plague of Justinian from C.E. 541 to 549 and a third pandemic that started in the 1800s and spread to every inhabited continent by 1900. That last pandemic was accelerated by a boom in rail and steamship travel but was eventually quashed by advances in science.
In 1894 French-Swiss bacteriologist Alexandre Yersin isolated the plague bacterium and connected rat infestations to the disease. Rat eradication campaigns followed around the world, drastically slowing the spread of plague, Wagner says. Though it was really the fleas that spread the disease to people, rat control worked because fleas are very specific about hosts. Different animal species have their own flea species, so rats and plague-carrying fleas traveled together.
Quarantines also helped, Wagner adds, because doctors started to recognize that the bacteria could sometimes spread from person to person through respiratory droplets. In the 1940s, when antibiotics had become widely available, doctors started curing plague cases with the drugs. Several vaccines have been developed over the years and deployed in severe outbreaks, in which they offered partial protection. No vaccine has been deemed effective enough to gain approval from the WHO or the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but labs in Russia and the U.S. continue to work on them.
Today most plague cases occur in Madagascar. Because food can be scarce there and people fear theft, individuals will store rice in their dirt-floor homes, Wagner says, allowing close contact with the rats that infest the island.
Though fleas are picky about their hosts, plague-carrying fleas in the U.S. are commonly found on prairie dogs, thanks to the animals having some functional similarities to rats. The plague bacterium now infects all five known species of prairie dogs and is one of the factors that contributed to a population decline in these social, burrowing rodents of about 98 percent from their historical levels. Because prairie dogs are a food source for other animals, including the critically endangered black-footed ferret, plague has been wreaking ecological havoc.
Even now it’s not clear where Y. pestis hides out between detectable outbreaks, Wagner says, and it’s surprising that it can be transmitted both by respiratory droplets and through fleas. But important clues about how the sickness operates are emerging from the latest studies of bacterial DNA in ancient bones and teeth.
The plague bacterium appears to have emerged as a human pathogen more than 5,700 years ago, evolving from a soil bacterium called Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, says Hendrick Poinar, a biologist at McMaster University, who works with ancient DNA. For the next 3,000 years, it infected Late Stone Age hunter-gathers and Bronze Age herders. Scientists suspect it was transmitted from human to human via respiratory droplets or via contaminated food because it hadn’t yet acquired the genes needed to travel through fleas.
Despite the versatility of Y. pestis, we’re lucky it can’t spread between humans unless an infected person is very sick and the contact is very close. Because of this limitation, even the emergence of an antibiotic-resistant strain won’t necessarily spark a new pandemic, Wagner says, noting that such strains have already shown up in Madagascar.
Though most scientists aren’t too alarmed about the situation in Russia, some are speculating that the death was caused by some highly genetically modified version of the plague bacterium or a different germ entirely. There’s no evidence for this, though the lack of transparency from Russia is unnerving. Regardless of the cause, the death of the worker is tragic. But if it was caused by the plague we know, the rest of us need not worry.

Jordan says it killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on Syria

19:49:32 KST

Oct 27 (Reuters) - Jordan said on Tuesday its forces had killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on southern Syria the previous evening, following a deadly church attack in Jordan that authorities linked to militants operating across the border.
The strikes, which followed a rare attack in Jordan, have inflamed tensions between the two US allies.
Jordan has been a longtime partner to the US in its fight against extremism, while the Islamist-led government of Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who wants to restore the country’s relations with the West after overthrowing longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, said it was seeking to curb extremism.
Syria said the strikes killed seven people, including three children and a woman. Jordan regrets the civilian casualties, Government Communication Minister Mohammed al-Momani said in a post on X.
Jordan said on Monday its air force had struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week’s church attack were linked to “terrorist groups” based there. Jordanian security officials said separately that security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law following a shootout linked to the church attack, which killed nine people.
Local resident Salah Mahwash, speaking to Reuters during the funeral of four people including three children in Al-Mismiyah in southern Syria, said:
“At around 10 p.m., there was an explosion and the sound of aircraft overhead. We went to the site, and it was a poor family whose father had gone missing during the events and was in Sednaya prison.
“Today, as you can see, these are people just trying to make a living, tending to their sheep and goats and doing manual labour. We condemn what happened in the Jordanian state, of course.”
Attacks such as the church shooting are rare in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East. No group has claimed responsibility for the shooting, although Jordan said the militants it targeted in Syria were members of Islamic State.
Monday’s strikes have nevertheless sparked anger in Syria. While the Jordanian military said they were conducted in coordination with Damascus, Syria’s government said they were carried out without prior coordination. It also said it would hold an investigation.
Statements in recent days by Jordanian authorities that there appeared to have been no prior planning of the church attack have added to the confusion, seemingly at odds with Jordan’s justification for Monday’s cross-border strikes.
Syria’s Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as a violation of the country’s sovereignty.
It said, however, that Damascus was coordinating with Amman and would establish a joint security committee to strengthen border security and prevent similar incidents.
Last year, Jordan and Syria agreed to form such a committee to secure their border, combat arms and drug smuggling and work to prevent any resurgence of Islamic State militancy.

Leaders of Norway, Finland hold calls with Putin then Zelenskiy
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:49:25 CET
19:49:25 KST

By Essi Lehto
HELSINKI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The leaders of Finland and Norway called Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine, breaking with a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin.
The phone call by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was a bid to influence the diplomatic process at a time when US President Donald Trump has shifted his position in favour of Russia and US ties with Ukraine have hit their lowest point in 18 months.
The Nordic leaders spoke by phone to Putin and afterwards to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, according to a Zelenskiy aide.
“The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” Stubb said in a joint statement with Stoere.
The Norwegian added: “The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation.”
Both leaders stressed their strong support for Ukraine, which they said would continue.
NO SIGN OF COMPROMISE FROM THE KREMLIN
The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not suggest that Putin had signalled any compromise from previously stated positions.
“It was emphasized that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account,” the Kremlin said.
“At the same time, attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities.”
Western European leaders have mostly shunned contact with Putin, while piling up sanctions on Moscow, since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022.
But that stance has left them sidelined as efforts to end the war have been led by Trump, who is seen in many EU capitals as unpredictable, erratic and prone to side with Putin at the expense of Ukraine.
That perception has been reinforced by deals this month in which Putin agreed to supply Russian diesel to the US and Trump eased sanctions on Russia while saying it was time for Ukrainians to replace Zelenskiy as their leader. Ukraine has also complained of disruption to intelligence-sharing by the US and to satellite internet services on which its military relies.
DANISH LEADER CRITICISES NORDIC PEERS FOR MAKING THE CALL
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticised the Finnish-Norwegian decision to talk to Putin, adding that she saw no signs that Russia wants peace.
“I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo,” Frederiksen told public broadcaster DR.
Stubb and Stoere participated in the call as leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole, they said, adding that the two Nordic nations will continue their longstanding support for Ukraine.
Russia has frequently accused European governments of stoking the war by arming Ukraine and refusing direct talks.
It has contrasted the stance of Western European leaders with that of Trump, who has engaged with Putin and tried — so far without success — to broker a peace agreement.
A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that French President Emmanuel Macron was the last EU leader to speak with Putin by phone. The call, which took place in July this year, was not made public and did not yield any results, according to the source.
The source said Putin told Stubb and Stoere that Russia would not compromise over its aim to capture the whole of Ukraine’s Donbas region. The Europeans responded by saying that a “just” peace is needed, this person said.
(Reporting by Essi Lehto; additional reporting by Darya Korsunskaya in London, writing by Mark Trevelyan; editing by Andrew Heavens)

Ukraine improves jet-powered drone interception rates, but Starlink disruptions threaten progress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:49:20 UTC
19:49:20 KST

Ukraine made significant progress in countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some air defence units reporting interception rates around 80%. But recent restrictions on US satellite services exposed Kyiv's reliance on US technology as it races to develop cheaper, more effective interceptors.
Ukraine's improved interceptor drone technology has helped it counter Russia's jet-powered drones, but disruptions to US Starshield satellite services threaten those gains.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Ukraine's interception rate fell slightly from 77% to around 74% during disruptions to the military-grade satellite service between 14 and 24 October.
The figures nevertheless represent a marked improvement on early September, when Ukrainian officials reported intercepting around 60% of Russia's jet-powered drones.
Some Ukrainian air defence units have reported interception rates exceeding 80%, although these figures reflect individual units' performance rather than nationwide results.
The Starshield restrictions, which affected high-speed drone operations, were lifted on 24 October, according to Ukrainian officials. However, the disruption highlighted the country's dependence on US satellite communications to sustain its air defences.
ISW warned that maintaining and improving interception rates would require Ukraine to develop and deploy affordable, high-speed interceptor drones on a much larger scale.
Russia has increasingly turned to jet-powered versions of its Shahed-type attack drones, which travel considerably faster than conventional propeller-driven models, leaving Ukrainian air defence crews with significantly less time to detect and intercept them.
Ukraine relies on a combination of interceptor drones, fighter aircraft and ground-based systems to counter the threat.
Interceptor drones have proved particularly effective, according to ISW, but many depend on Starshield connectivity to operate at the speeds required to engage faster Russian targets.
Ukrainian forces also use F-16 fighter jets, either firing air-to-air missiles or engaging targets with onboard guns. Both approaches have drawbacks: missiles are expensive and scarce, while gun engagements demand considerable pilot skill and expose aircraft and crews to additional risks.
Using fighter jets against drones also increases maintenance requirements and diverts aircraft from other missions.
Ukraine has installed ground-based gun turrets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, although expanding these systems nationwide would require considerable time and resources.
The race for cheaper interceptors
The growing threat has accelerated efforts by Ukrainian manufacturers to develop faster, more affordable interception systems.
One such project is the F-Jet 80, a jet-powered interceptor being developed by Ukrainian company F-Drones, which plans to incorporate artificial intelligence into its guidance system.
The company aims to keep the unit cost at approximately $7,000, compared with an estimated $20,000 to $70,000 for other high-speed interceptor drones and around $1 million for an air-to-air missile launched from an F-16.
Although the F-Jet 80 remains under development, its manufacturer says it has already successfully intercepted several Russian drones.
For Ukraine, the challenge extends beyond developing effective technology to producing it in sufficient numbers to counter Russia's expanding use of jet-powered drones.
ISW argues that integrating affordable interceptor drones into Ukraine's existing air defence network offers the strongest prospect of sustaining high interception rates as the country approaches another winter of Russian aerial attacks.

Pope Leo to return to his adopted home on South America tour
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:48:56 CET
19:48:56 KST

By Marco Aquino
ZAÑA, Peru Oct 27 (Reuters) - As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America next week, many Peruvians remember him as the priest who helped feed hungry families, delivered aid after floods and walked alongside migrants in the country he would eventually call his own.
When the pandemic emptied the streets of northern Peru and one of the world’s longest quarantines left many struggling to eat, Bishop Robert Prevost, as Leo was known, helped launch a soup kitchen in 2020 in the small town of Zaña.
“He gave us an example of human charity, and we prepared the ‘aguadito con fe’,” recalled former cook Betty Burga Campos, referring to the traditional soup of rice, meat and vegetables that volunteers served.
Prevost left Peru for Rome three years later after Pope Francis tapped him to lead the Vatican office that recommends candidates for bishop appointments worldwide.
After rising from missionary and bishop in Peru’s far north to cardinal and ultimately pope, Leo, 71, is set to revisit the country where he became a citizen and built some of the relationships that defined his ministry, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer. The Vatican confirmed on Monday that his November 6 to 17 South America tour remained on schedule.
Across northern Peru, regional governments are refurbishing churches and residents are preparing celebrations for his visit, which also includes earlier stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
For many Peruvians, memories of the Chicago-born head of the Catholic Church are less about Vatican titles than muddy boots, long drives across the country’s rugged north and a hands-on approach to helping people.
“He had become Peruvian, even in the way he spoke. He no longer had much of that American accent,” said José Manuel Zamora Romero, a priest in Lambayeque who knew him for years.
The share of adults in Peru who identify as Catholic has fallen from 76% to 67% over the decade to 2024, according to Pew Research Center. The decline is often linked to social changes and distrust of institutions, following years of political instability that have caused Peru to cycle through nine presidents in a decade.
A BISHOP ON THE MOVE
Prevost arrived in Peru in 1985 at age 30. After years based in the United States and Rome with his Augustinian order, he returned in 2014 and became bishop of the Peruvian city of Chiclayo in 2015. In 2023, Pope Francis brought Prevost to the Vatican. Francis named him a cardinal later that year and he was elected pope in 2025.
Across northern Peru’s sun-baked farm belt, residents and priests recall a churchman constantly on the move.
For the future pontiff, “the distances were not limits, the distances were opportunities,” said David Farfán, a priest in Zaña, one of the towns on the pope’s upcoming itinerary.
Many remember Prevost riding horseback to isolated Andean communities. Others recall him driving hundreds of kilometers himself across Peru’s rugged north.
“His hobby was driving,” Zamora Romero said. “And I know he taught some priests to drive so they could get their licenses … and they all passed the test.”
That practical approach became evident during emergencies.
When severe flooding linked to the El Niño climate phenomenon inundated northern Peru in 2023, photos circulated on social media of Prevost wading through knee-deep water in rubber boots as he helped deliver aid.
When natural disasters occurred, “he was on the front lines to bring the help that the population needed,” said Rev. Jorge Villegas of Chiclayo, where the pope will spend two full days.
Residents pointed to moments like those as evidence of a bishop who preferred action over visibility.
“He wasn’t very focused on being with the press; he was more with the poor and in social conflicts,” said Verónica Castillo, a journalist in Chiclayo who witnessed his intervention during a 2015 labor conflict.
“He was a bishop who intervened, who took action, and people remember that,” she added, recalling how Prevost helped mediate the prolonged protest by workers against a sugar company, which turned violent.
‘PUT HIMSELF IN SHOES OF A MIGRANT’
Migration has reshaped much of Latin America over the past decade, as millions of Venezuelans fled economic collapse and political turmoil. Peru hosts the world’s second-largest Venezuelan diaspora community, with more than 1.5 million migrants. Many arrived without proper documentation and live with inadequate access to healthcare and basic services.
Prevost founded a Catholic organization in Chiclayo in 2018 to assist newcomers.
“He put himself in the shoes of a migrant first and foremost and knew what the situation was like,” said Augusto Martínez, who leads the organization.
The group has assisted thousands of Venezuelans.
As pope, Leo has called for migrants to be treated with dignity, condemned human trafficking and warned traffickers to repent or face divine judgment. He has criticized anti-immigration policies, including measures pursued by US President Donald Trump.
“He supported migrants on how to have a dignified life here in Peru,” said Lisbeth Coromoto Díaz, who received help through the Chiclayo organization and said he held Masses in honor of migrants.
Leo’s planned return to Peru has revived hopes among Catholics in Eten, near Chiclayo, that he could advance a long-running campaign to secure Vatican recognition of the town’s reported Eucharistic miracle. As bishop, he supported the cause, presenting historical records and thousands of testimonies of faith in Rome, linked to a 1649 apparition in which devotees say the image of the Christ Child appeared in a consecrated host.
Tourism officials are promoting routes tied to the places Leo lived and worked. Souvenir shops are stocking shelves with pope-inspired hats, key chains and pins.
In a shop window in the capital Lima’s Gamarra textile district, an image of Leo on a T-shirt depicts him smiling while enjoying a plate of Peruvian food.
“We’ve got the pope looking spirited; we’ve got the pope as a foodie, enjoying delicious ceviche and rotisserie chicken. We even have the play on words: ‘The Pope and the papa (potato) are Peruvian’,” said clothing maker Victoria Quiñones.
Quiñones predicted a 200% increase in her workload and was running low on fabric for the T-shirts.
Nearby, Maria Rodriguez, 70, was shopping for pope T-shirts.
“I’m buying several,” Rodriguez said.
“I’ll be wearing them all through November because I am Catholic: Roman and Peruvian,” she added.
(Reporting by Marco Aquino; additional reporting by Alfredo Galarza, Carlos Valdez and Joshua McElwee; Writing by Cassandra Garrison in Mexico City; Editing by Lucinda Elliott and Rod Nickel)

Exclusive-Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:48:45 CET
19:48:45 KST

By Raphael Satter
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink’s satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.
Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro, concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX’s Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people.
The researchers, who drew on digital advertising data in TrendAI’s telemetry for their conclusions, found that Discover-Tech had become one of the world’s leading bidders for ads aimed at Starlink users and that it was the No. 1 bidder on Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink itself was banned or restricted. Bidding refers to the complex auction system by which advertisers secure space inside people’s browsers and apps.
SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. Discover-Tech and its chief executive did not respond to requests for comment over the past two weeks.
TrendAI released a report on October 15 about the targeting of Starlink users but did not name Discover-Tech, instead saying the party responsible was “an ad tech entity” which it called “Shadow-Earth-79.” The six sources said Shadow-Earth-79 is TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech.
TrendAI did not directly address questions about why its report did not identify Shadow-Earth-79 by name, saying in a statement that its approach to attribution was aimed at reducing the risk of mistakes and avoiding “hype-driven labels” or “unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort risk prioritization, and trigger inappropriate response actions.”
Finding ways to track Starlink users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals. Because they route data through SpaceX-operated satellites rather than nationally regulated telecommunications firms, the terminals can sidestep local internet restrictions, communicate in hostile areas or coordinate action across battlefields. Starlink has become a particularly important resource in Ukraine, whose military relies on the service for frontline communications and directing drone strikes.
In May, Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and track Starlink users. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role in the process.
DISCOVER-TECH ACCUSED OF WIDER SPY EFFORT
The same day that TrendAI published its report on Shadow-Earth-79, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York advertising technology firm Confiant outed Discover-Tech by name.
Both groups said the Israeli company abused the ad bidding process, which can leak data about internet users back to the bidder.
Over time, bidders can collect that leaked data, collate it and merge it with other information to de-anonymize users, follow them around the web and, in some cases, set them up for targeting with surveillance software.
Citizen Lab and Confiant said the ads had been shown inside dozens of sensitive networks belonging to media organizations, governments and tech firms.
In response to the investigations, Google, Comcast and other companies said they had removed Discover-Tech from their ad platforms.
At least one big US tech company and one international organization recently launched internal inquiries into whether Discover-Tech’s ads targeted their employees, according to one of the people and a seventh person familiar with the matter.
TOP ADVERTISER IN YEMEN, SOUTH SUDAN
TrendAI’s report cited suspicious bidding patterns that suggested Shadow-Earth-79 was running “targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation.”
In addition to noting the “obvious skew” towards buying ads aimed at Starlink users, the report said that Shadow-Earth-79 was the top buyer of ads in Syria, Libya, Yemen and South Sudan and was the No. 2 ad buyer in Afghanistan even though “the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero.” It said the entity won “an implausibly dominant share” of bids in several countries including Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan and Venezuela.
TrendAI researchers were convinced Discover-Tech was behind the suspicious bidding activity and discussed naming the company in TrendAI’s report, according to the six people familiar with the matter. But they eventually dropped the idea of publicly attributing the activity to a named company after TrendAI executives raised legal concerns, five of the sources said.
Self-censorship is common in the cybersecurity industry, especially when executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, industry experts say.
Earlier this year, US cybersecurity company Palo Alto stripped explicit references to China from a report on a global cyberespionage campaign even though its researchers were confident the hacking could be pinned on Beijing, Reuters reported at the time. Reuters said the report was watered down over fears that calling out China would cause problems for Palo Alto’s operations there, which were already under scrutiny following a Beijing directive ordering domestic companies not to use its products. Palo Alto said the lack of attribution in its report was not correlated with “procurement regulations in China” and that any suggestion otherwise was “speculative and false.”
(Reporting by Raphael Satter; editing by Chris Sanders and Rod Nickel)

Swiss house prices continued to rise over summer
House prices in Switzerland have continued to rise unabated. The upward trend continued in the third quarter of 2026 for both detached houses and flats.
From July to September, the Swiss Residential Property Price Index (IMPI) rose by 1.7% compared with the previous quarter to 129.8 points, as announced by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) on Tuesday. Year-on-year, prices have climbed by as much as 4.4%.
At national level, prices for detached houses have risen by 2.1%. Prices for flats have also increased by 1.3% compared with the previous quarter.
The sharpest rises in property prices were seen in urban municipalities within a small conurbation or outside a conurbation (+3.4%). The smallest price increase, at 0.6%, was recorded in so-called intermediate municipalities, which exhibit both urban and rural characteristics.
More
Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
Significant year-on-year increase
In the longer term, the upward trend in the property market is continuing despite prices already being high. Compared with the previous year, both detached houses (+3.3%) and flats (+5.4%) have risen significantly in price.
The IMPI is a relatively new indicator: it has only been published quarterly since the third quarter of 2020. According to the FSO, it is calculated based on an average of around 7,000 transactions from all regions of Switzerland. The FSO obtains data from the 28 largest mortgage lenders in Switzerland. These cover a very large market share, as the vast majority of property purchases are financed by a mortgage.

Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan's Mecca Agreement aims to strengthen regional security, Turkish official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:47:48 UTC
19:47:48 KST

Busranur Keskinkilic, Gokhan Celiker and Fatma Zehra Solmaz
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan aims to strengthen regional security through cooperation and collective defense, the Turkish deputy foreign minister said Tuesday.
“The Mecca agreement is not only an extension of the special friendly relations between the three countries, but also a concrete product of the regional ownership increasingly needed in our region,” Ambassador Levent Gumrukcu told the Turkish Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee.
Gumrukcu submitted the agreement for approval by the committee and the Turkish parliament, as lawmakers continued their deliberations on the proposed legislation.
He recalled that the agreement was signed in Mecca on Aug. 7 by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
He said Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had completed their domestic ratification procedures and submitted the required official notifications.
Gumrukcu said the agreement marked an initial step toward establishing a regional security framework based on cooperation and collective defense, adding that the three countries aimed to take responsibility for addressing regional challenges rather than waiting for solutions from outside the region.
He said the framework was intended to contribute not only to the security of the three signatories but also to that of the wider region by strengthening dialogue and cooperation based on mutual trust and promoting lasting stability.
 
Deal 'envisions integration rather than bloc-building in region'
Gumrukcu stressed that the agreement was entirely defensive in nature and did not target any country.
He said it was open to all regional countries that respect international law, including the principles of state sovereignty and territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force except in self-defense, the peaceful settlement of disputes and non-interference in internal affairs.
"The agreement envisions integration rather than bloc-building in the region, embracing an inclusive rather than divisive vision," he added.
 
Defense cooperation and NATO commitments
Gumrukcu said the agreement envisaged strengthening collective deterrence, holding regular consultations on international security issues, and improving interoperability between the countries' armed forces through personnel exchanges, joint training programs, and military exercises.
It also provides for closer defense industry cooperation, including joint production and technology sharing, stronger joint counterterrorism efforts, and logistical support between the parties in implementing the agreement, he said.
The deputy foreign minister emphasized that the agreement would neither replace nor undermine Türkiye's obligations under its existing alliances and agreements.
He said the initiative was expected to complement Türkiye's participation in multilateral platforms, particularly NATO, by contributing to security and stability across the broader Middle East and supporting European security in light of the interconnected nature of the two regions.

Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:46:21 UTC
19:46:21 KST

Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.
- Share:
Medications are designed to treat diseases and relieve symptoms, but some can also produce unintended effects that put patients at risk. While side effects are common with many treatments, researchers have identified a particularly concerning possibility involving drugs used to control inflammation.
Scientists at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) have discovered that a widely used class of anti-inflammatory medications may make it easier for certain viruses to infect cells and spread throughout the body.
"We have found a surprising and potentially serious side effect of a class of anti-inflammatory drugs. They can help viruses spread more easily in the body," says Denis Kainov, a professor at the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
Common Anti-Inflammatory Drugs May Help Viruses Spread
The medications at the center of the findings belong to a class called Janus kinase inhibitors, or JAKs. These drugs are widely prescribed to control inflammation, but their effects on the immune system may also leave the body more vulnerable to viral infections.
"Among the viruses that more easily affect the body with the help of these drugs are Rift Valley fever virus, influenza A, adenovirus and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19," Kainov says.
These viruses can cause significant illness, making any treatment that potentially increases their ability to spread a serious concern.
Why Arthritis Drugs Can Weaken Antiviral Defenses
In a new study published in NAR Molecular Medicine, Kainov and his colleagues investigated how JAK inhibitors influence the body's ability to defend itself against viruses.
"JAK inhibitors are often prescribed for autoimmune diseases and inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis," says Erlend Ravlo, a PhD research fellow at NTNU and first author of the article.
Although these medications can be highly effective at reducing inflammation, their benefits come with an important trade-off. By suppressing certain immune responses, they can also interfere with the mechanisms that normally protect the body from viral infections.
"In particular, the drugs suppress an important immune signalling pathway that helps protect healthy cells from viral attacks," Ravlo said.
This pathway plays a central role in coordinating the body's response when viruses attempt to infect healthy tissue.
Scientists Discover How JAK Inhibitors Disrupt Immune Protection
The research team found that JAK inhibitors, including the medication baricitinib, can reduce the activity of genes involved in fighting viral infections.
"These genes play a crucial role in the body's response to viral infections," said Aleksandr Ianevski, an NTNU researcher and coauthor of the new paper.
When JAK inhibitors interfere with this immune signaling system, they weaken an important layer of antiviral protection. Without the usual defensive response, viruses may find it easier to establish an infection and spread between cells.
To investigate these effects, the scientists combined advanced virology methods with gene expression analysis and organoid technology. Their experiments included cells from the lungs, eyes and brain, along with miniature organ models grown in the laboratory.
These approaches allowed the team to examine how the drugs affect antiviral defenses across different types of human tissue.
"Although JAK inhibitors are effective in the treatment of inflammation, this shows that they can pose a hidden risk for patients who have latent or active viral infections," says Ravlo.
What the Findings Mean for Patients and Future Treatments
The results highlight the importance of carefully considering the risks associated with JAK inhibitors, particularly when patients may already have a viral infection or when outbreaks are occurring.
Researchers suggest that healthcare professionals should exercise caution when prescribing these medications during periods of increased viral transmission.
However, the same immune-suppressing properties that create potential risks for patients could also offer advantages in certain research settings. Under controlled laboratory conditions, these effects may help scientists develop vaccines or evaluate potential antiviral medications.
The researchers hope their findings will encourage greater awareness of how JAK inhibitors influence the immune system and support further investigations into their safest and most effective uses.
"We recommend further studies to better understand how the drugs can be used optimally, especially during virus outbreaks or pandemics," says Ianevski.
Professor Magnar Bjørås of the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine provided significant scientific expertise and secured most of the funding for the research. Additional financial support came from the Central Norway Regional Health Authority, the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority, the Research Council of Norway and the Swedish Research Council.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Erlend Ravlo, Aleksandr Ianevski, Marius Nårstad Skipperstøen, Hilde Lysvand, Jørn-Ove Schjølberg, Ole Solheim, Wei Wang, Miroslava Kissova, Marthe Vestvik, Olli Vapalahti, Teemu Smura, Hanna Vauhkonen, Valentyn Oksenych, Friedemann Weber, Mårten Strand, Magnus Evander, Janne Fossum Malmring, Jan Egil Afset, Magnar Bjørås, Denis E Kainov. JAK inhibitors remove innate immune barriers facilitating viral propagation. NAR Molecular Medicine, 2025; 2 (2) DOI: 10.1093/narmme/ugaf017

Verkhovna Rada approved budget conclusions for 2027 State Budget - what this means and when the final vote will take place
Kyiv • UNN
A total of 232 deputies voted for the budget conclusions. The document contains 90 proposals concerning 5,236 amendments ahead of the first reading of the budget.
On October 27, the Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis a draft resolution on the Budget Conclusions (No. 16000/P) as part of the consideration of the draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027. This was reported by Parliament, UNN writes.
Details
The motion was supported by 232 members of parliament. This is the first stage in adopting the draft state budget in the first reading.
The document contains 90 proposals, which the Verkhovna Rada Budget Committee formulated on the basis of 5,236 amendments submitted by members of parliament, committee chair Roksolana Pidlasa said while presenting the document in the session hall.
"According to a preliminary estimate, taking the submitted amendments into account would require an additional UAH 13.5 trillion — that is almost two more budgets for next year. Many proposals do not meet the regulatory requirements: they are unbalanced, or the proposed sources are not supported by calculations and are unrealistic. Therefore, we rejected such amendments," Pidlasa explained.
After their adoption by the Verkhovna Rada, the Budget Conclusions become a list of changes that the government must take into account or consider when revising the draft budget for the second reading.
"The committee recommends that the Verkhovna Rada adopt the resolution on the Budget Conclusions as a basis and send the budget draft to the government for preparation for the second reading. Together with the government, we will eliminate the main shortcomings of this budget," Pidlasa said during the consideration.
As reported by the Verkhovna Rada, the committee's main proposals include:
-  increasing military personnel's financial support and doubling state guarantees for defense-industry enterprises, to UAH 60 billion;  
-  additional funds for medicines for patients with rare diseases, on top of the UAH 21 billion already allocated;  
-  allocating 4% of personal income tax to community budgets;  
-  increasing funding for housing for internally displaced persons;  
-  expanding the program for insuring war risks and supporting farmers, as well as banning the payment of the "National Cashback" from the UAH 9.4 billion production and entrepreneurship support program. 
What happens next
As explained by MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak of the Finance Committee, the Rada adopted the proposals and conclusions on the Budget as a basis — "not to be confused with the first reading of the Budget, which is tomorrow (October 28)."
"Now the Rada is moving on to consider the 5,236 amendments from MPs. Forty-seven MPs have signed up to speak on them. Tomorrow there will be a vote on the remaining amendments taken into account and the first reading of the 2027 Budget. It will then be sent to the government, and the second reading and final adoption are planned for November 23–26," Zhelezniak reported on social media.
Reminder
The 2027 Budget draft envisages a deficit of 15% of GDP and debt exceeding 110% of GDP. UAH 4.885 trillion is planned to be allocated for security and defense.

Climber dies in 5,000-foot fall after reaching mountain's summit

Climber falls nearly 5,000 feet to his death on Nepal mountain after reaching summit
A German climber fell about 1,500 meters (nearly 5,000 feet) to his death on Monday, a day after reaching the summit of Ama Dablam mountain, according to a trekking company operator.
Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, was reported missing from Camp 3, which lies at around 6,200 meters. He had been resting after reaching the 6,812-meter summit on Sunday, before his planned descent.
"After a successful summit, he spent a night at Camp 3 on Sunday, and on Monday morning, his guide found him missing," Gokul Thapa, head of the trekking company Real Himalaya, told AFP.
Thapa said Waschiczek's personal trekking guide, Sonam Lama, had left him in the tent for a few minutes to return borrowed equipment, telling him to stay inside. When he returned, Waschiczek was missing.
Waschiczek's body was spotted by another Sherpa at Camp 2 at around 8 am on Monday at an altitude of about 4,600 metres, Thapa said.
The body was retrieved by helicopter during the afternoon and taken to Lukla, a town known as a gateway for mountaineers and trekkers heading to the Everest region.
It was then flown to the capital, Kathmandu, where a postmortem will be performed at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.
"Once the postmortem is done, the body will be handed over to his family members through the embassy," Thapa told AFP.
He said this was Waschiczek's second visit to Nepal.
"He had come to Nepal in 2024 for a trek, and his passing saddened us," he added.
Two Japanese climbers died last week on another peak in west Nepal, the Reuters news agency reported.
Ama Dablam lies in Nepal's Khumbu region and is considered a technically challenging mountain with steep faces.
This is the first fatality on the mountain this year.
Last October, two climbers, one French, aged 65, and the other South Korean, aged 66, died during expeditions there.
This climbing season, more than 300 climbers are attempting to scale Ama Dablam.
Mountaineers have died on other peaks this year.
In July, famed British Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers were killed after being swept away by an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak.
In May, two Indian climbers died on Mount Everest during a record-breaking period of ascents via Nepal's southern route.
In May, American climber Shelley Johannesen died in an avalanche on Nepal's Mount Makalu. Johannesen, co-founder of U.S.-based outfitter Dash Adventures, had successfully reached the 27,838-foot summit before she was struck by an avalanche at around 23,600 feet while coming down.
