Russian President Vladimir Putin held telephone talks Tuesday with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre as part of renewed diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, Russian state news agency TASS reported, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky subsequently spoke with the Finnish and Norwegian leaders following their conversation with Putin, an aide to the Ukrainian president told Reuters. No immediate details were provided about the substance or outcome of the discussions.
The conversations follow a renewed diplomatic push led by U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff, who met Putin in St. Petersburg last week. Before traveling to Russia, Witkoff held discussions in Oslo with Zelensky and the leaders of Finland and Norway.
The calls represent a rare direct exchange between Putin and senior European leaders aligned with Ukraine. Bloomberg reported earlier Tuesday that the conversations were being prepared, citing people familiar with the matter. The last comparable contact occurred in July 2025, when French President Emmanuel Macron spoke with the Russian president.
Both Finland and Norway share borders with Russia, a geographic reality their leaders have cited in arguing that they should be involved in negotiations affecting Europe's security. European governments have increasingly sought a direct role in diplomatic discussions over Ukraine, concerned that decisions affecting the continent's security could otherwise be made without their participation.
Following Witkoff's meeting with Putin last week, Peskov acknowledged that Moscow regarded Finland and Norway as new participants in efforts to resolve the conflict, now in its fifth year. However, he questioned whether they would be capable of making a meaningful contribution to the negotiations.
The diplomatic developments come amid growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington. According to Bloomberg, relations have deteriorated following a diesel agreement between Trump and Putin earlier this month, alongside disputes over slowing Starlink internet connectivity, which Ukraine relies on for critical military communications and defense operations.
Ukraine is also facing mounting financial pressures and shortages of air defense systems as Russia prepares for another winter military campaign. Tuesday's conversations mark a new stage in efforts to involve European leaders directly in negotiations with Moscow, while Zelensky's subsequent contacts underscore Kyiv's continued engagement with the diplomatic process.

Shotgun-armed drone gets Pentagon green light
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:36:05 UTC
18:36:05 KST

- Skyborne Technologies’ Cerberus MI armed drone was added to the U.S. Department of War’s Blue UAS Cleared List on Oct. 26, 2026.
- The reusable drone carries 40 mm grenade or 12-gauge shotgun payloads and flies about 35 minutes with a weapon fitted.
An armed, reusable drone that fires 40 mm grenades and 12-gauge shotgun rounds and then flies back to be reloaded has been cleared for purchase and use across the U.S. military, after Skyborne Technologies’ Cerberus MI was added to the U.S. Department of War’s Blue UAS Cleared List, the company announced on Oct. 26, 2026.
The listing means U.S. military units can buy and fly the Cerberus MI without an exception to policy, after an independent assessment found that the platform meets the Blue UAS standard for cybersecurity, supply chain and foreign ownership, control or influence, as well as the National Defense Authorization Act requirements that bar certain foreign-made components, and the list itself is managed by the Defense Contract Management Agency.
Cerberus MI is a Group 2 small unmanned aircraft that weighs 18 kg (39.7 pounds), can be carried by troops, and flies for roughly 35 minutes with a weapon fitted, and Skyborne says the airframe was designed from the start to absorb the recoil of direct-fire weapons rather than adapted from a commercial drone.
It carries two interchangeable weapon payloads, the HAVOC 40 mm low-velocity grenade launcher and the CHAOS 12-gauge shotgun, both of which use standard ammunition, while Skyborne’s onboard EXITUS AI targeting software combines electro-optical, infrared and laser rangefinder data to calculate firing solutions and support engagements from more than 300 meters (984 feet) away, with a human operator making the decision to fire.
The company is pitching the drone as an alternative to the one-way attack and FPV strike drones already on the Blue UAS list, which are destroyed when they hit a target, saying Cerberus MI can return from a mission, reload and fly again, giving units more shots from the same aircraft at a lower cost per shot.
“We’ve always believed that affordable mass isn’t just about building cheaper drones. It’s about delivering more effects from the same platform,” said Adrian Dudok, chief executive of Skyborne Technologies USA.
Skyborne, which was founded in 2014 and operates in Virginia and in Brisbane, Australia, has been working on armed drones for years, and an earlier version of the aircraft, the Cerberus GL, live-fired five 40 mm grenade rounds in front of U.S. Army personnel during the Army Expeditionary Warrior Experiment in late 2019.
The company has since expanded into ground robots, and in October 2025 it unveiled the CODiAQ, a four-legged robot armed with the same HAVOC 40 mm launcher, which Skyborne said is meant to work together with the Cerberus MI and was being evaluated by U.S. government partners.
“Cerberus MI was engineered as a reusable platform with a modular architecture that allows the capability to evolve over time. From expanding direct-fire weapon integrations to advancing autonomy and AI through our EXITUS software, our focus has been on building a system that can adapt to emerging operational requirements without continually replacing the underlying hardware,” said Michael Creagh, chief executive of Skyborne Technologies APAC.

TikTok parent ByteDance's founder is China's richest person again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:35:37 UTC
18:35:37 KST

TikTok parent ByteDance's founder Zhang Yiming reclaims spot as China's richest person, thanks to firm's AI push
Beijing — ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into artificial intelligence.
The rankings released by The Hurun Research Institute on Tuesday reflected that the country's high-tech sectors were rising while others, like the consumer sector and real estate, were under pressure.
The institute, which has published the list annually since 1999, found a record 1,529 people with more than 5 billion yuan (about $750 million), up 6.6% from last year.
The number of billionaires based on their net worth in U.S. dollars rose to 1,176, up 155 people - 176 more than in the U.S. That was slightly below the 1,185 people in 2021.
Zhang topped the list with $100 billion, up 43%, "almost all of it on the back of AI," and the amount was a record high for China's richest person, Rupert Hoogewerf, Hurun Report chairman, said in a statement. Hoogewerf noted that ByteDance's Doubao is China's most used AI assistant.
AI is the biggest single wealth engine on the list: 160 people - one in 10 - now make their money from AI, he said.
ByteDance is the parent company of popular short-video platforms TikTok and Douyin.
TikTok's U.S.-based operations were shifted to a new joint venture in January made up mostly of American investors due to years of national security-related concerns that almost got TikTok banned in the U.S. ByteDance still holds a minority stake in TikTok's U.S. arm.
One of the investors in TikTok's U.S. venture is Oracle, a tech company chaired by Larry Ellison. His son David Ellison is co-CEO of Skydance Corp., the parent company of CBS News.
Bottled water magnate Zhong Shanshan fell to second place on the list with $61 billion, down 23%, while Robin Zeng, chairman of CATL, the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, came in third, Hurun said.
Hurun cross-checked its information with entrepreneurs, regulators, industry experts and others to compile the list, while acknowledging limitations.
Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng, a new face on the list, ranked seventh. AI chipmaker Cambricon chair Chen Tianshi was 10th.
Trends in China's economy are reflected on the list
"This year's gains were polarised - entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink - a two-speed economy," Hoogewerf said.
China last week said its economy grew 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year ago, fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target for 2026. For the entire year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5%, down from last year's 5% expansion.
While some industries were thriving thanks to government support for technologies such as AI and electric vehicles, owners of small businesses reported tough times as their customers cut back on spending.
China's domestic demand has been weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market.
The Hurun list reflected that, as well.
Hoogewerf said Lei Jun, chairman of Chinese smart consumer electronics maker Xiaomi, was this year's "biggest faller," with his wealth halved to $25.1 billion. Consumer fortunes also fell across the board, Hoogewerf said.
"Today, for the first time ever, not a single mainland property developer remains in the Top 100 - the only property names left at the top are the Hong Kong landlord families," he said.

Is an Under-Sink Reverse Osmosis System Worth It? Benefits, Costs, and Drawbacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:35:00 UTC
18:35:00 KST

That funny taste in your tap water may be a harmless nuisance—or it may be cause for serious concern. Either way, you can do something about it by installing a reverse osmosis (RO) water filtration system in your home.
Stand-alone RO systems and pitchers sit on your countertop and generally require manual refilling from the tap. You’ll save space and avoid the hassle of constantly refilling the unit by installing an under-sink or under-counter model that connects directly to your plumbing lines. Either way, RO systems aren’t cheap. But for some homeowners, they may be an invaluable investment.
Featured in this Article
What Is Reverse Osmosis?
Osmosis is the movement of molecules—usually water—through a semipermeable membrane that blocks larger particles like salts and sugars from passing through. After osmosis, the concentration of particles on both sides of the membrane ends up in equilibrium. It’s how plants get water from the soil, and it’s how your kidneys filter junk out of your blood.
While osmosis is a spontaneous phenomenon that happens naturally, reverse osmosis requires pressure to force water through a membrane in the other direction, effectively removing all of those compounds from the water to render it pure. It’s how salt is removed from seawater to make it drinkable, and it’s one way tap water can be purified in your home.
RO differs considerably from traditional filtration systems, which rely on physical barriers, typically activated carbon, to manually capture particles that pass through. Eventually, these filters become saturated with sediments and other matter and have to be replaced. While carbon filters are fairly blunt, able to capture larger particles of at least 0.1 microns in size, RO systems have a much finer-grained membrane that captures contaminants on a microscopic level (typically down to 0.0001 microns).
Carbon filters can make your water taste and smell better, but with RO you are getting much, much cleaner water than what that inexpensive Brita filter can muster. (That said, RO can’t capture everything, and carbon filters are still useful for capturing certain volatile organic compounds through adsorption. Most RO systems also have an additional carbon filtration system included.)
Note that two types of RO systems are available: Tanked RO systems filter water slowly (albeit passively, without electricity) and sequester it in a (rather large) tank under your sink. Today, tankless RO systems are more popular, processing water on demand but requiring electricity to keep things flowing expeditiously. Tankless systems are considerably more expensive due to their inherent complexity.
What Are the Real Risks of Contaminants in Water Today?
“US tap water is safe for most people most of the time,” says John Voll, an industrial water treatment veteran and the founder of Tap & Air, a website that monitors water and air quality for hundreds of municipalities. “The problems are local, not universal.”
The first step to understanding your personal risk is to gauge whether your own water is up to snuff by simply looking up its most recent data report online. The Safe Drinking Water Act requires community water systems to publish an annual report on the quality of water they’re delivering, due by July 1 each year.
These are heady documents, so to keep things simple, Voll says to keep your eye on three key pollutant metrics: lead, nitrate or arsenic, and PFAS (so-called forever chemicals popular in nonstick cookware and other products). While the first two are serious issues, they’re fairly rare today. PFAS, however, are a particularly significant problem across the country. Voll says that 98 of the 200 largest US cities have at least one PFAS compound detected in their water supply. Reverse osmosis systems can handle them—as well as lead and other compounds. Carbon filters usually can’t.
“Most people don't need RO,” Voll says, “but some households clearly do, and the way to tell is to read your own water report first.”
What Are the Drawbacks of Using an RO System?
RO systems come with a host of downsides, but most are related in some fashion to cost.
- RO wastes water: The particulars of RO technology have historically meant it requires a large amount of unprocessed tap water to create a small amount of purified water, sometimes up to 4 gallons or more of tap to 1 gallon of clean water (called the pure-to-drain ratio). In recent years that number has dramatically shifted, with 4 gallons of tap water producing up to 3 gallons of clean water, or a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio.
- Filters are costly: RO systems can require up to six different filtration cartridges that must be replaced every year or two, depending on use. Much like printer ink, these costs can be easily overlooked when making your initial purchase. Plan to spend $50 to $200 annually on replacement cartridges, but check prices before you buy.
- RO can strip “good” minerals from your water: Calcium, magnesium, and potassium are all unable to pass through the RO membrane. RO systems also remove fluoride from your water, which many users may not desire and which dentists abhor. Some RO systems can remineralize water and/or raise the pH level of the processed water thanks to additional cartridges—but these, of course, mean further expense on replaceables.
- Plan for professional installation (and additional financial outlays): I try not to DIY too much when there’s even a remote potential for a water leak, so I get a plumber involved for installations like these. And since most RO systems require their own faucet, you’ll need to prepare to have a new hole drilled into your countertop for your tap if you don’t already have one available.
Do You Need an Under-Sink RO System?
Based on my analysis of my city’s water report, no I don’t really need an RO system, as there’s nothing hazardous to worry about. However, as the linked report notes, our water supplier uses chloramine as a disinfectant, and drinking that chloramine-treated water straight from the tap has a slight but noticeable, off-putting taste. This is exacerbated by the extreme hardness of the water; this part of Texas is basically built on top of nothing but limestone, and the resulting amount of calcium carbonate in the water can add a slightly bitter flavor, as well.
For me, RO is all about the way the water tastes. Any lingering contaminants that are removed along the way are just a bonus.
I tested the Waterdrop X12 for this story, hiring a plumber to remove a well-aged unit under the sink and replace it with this more capable one. The job was done in less than an hour.
Under-sink RO filters are separate from your existing plumbing, and most use three color-coded lengths of tubing to tie into it. One connects to your incoming water supply through an adapter valve, one clips into your wastewater drainpipe via an included fitting, and one connects to the faucet. I am confident I could have made these connections on my own—especially since I was replacing an existing system—but I’ve seen how even a small water leak can lead to devastating problems and was happy for the peace of mind that professional oversight supplied.
Once installed and powered up, the X12 launches a 35-minute priming process designed to flush the filters before first use. It seems like an awfully long time for the sink to run, and it is. If you have some way to capture and use all this extra water, plan ahead to collect it. After the session completed (it stops automatically), I was ready to start sipping from the tap.
The X12 is exceedingly simple to use. Tap the LED-equipped button on top of the faucet to start or stop the flow of water, or twist the same button to dial in the number of ounces you want to dispense (up to 999) before depressing it. This way, you can drop your 64-ounce Stanley Quencher in the sink and walk away without having to wait around or worry about an overflow, with a digital timer first offering a measurement of your water’s current TDS (total dissolved solids), then counting down the ounces as they’re dispensed. The good news is that you won’t have to wait long: The X12 blasts water out of its spigot faster than my kitchen sink does—a far cry from the sad dribble of H2O my old RO system provided.
The unit can also be switched into one of two alternate operating modes, including an energy-saving mode (which quiets the device) and “flow mode,” which is designed for high-use households. Both require pressing certain button combinations on the filtration unit. I have used the device in all three modes, and (contrary to other reviews I’ve seen) I’ve never found it to be noisy at all, even though it’s located just 20 feet from my bed.
As for the water, it tastes great. The remineralization feature and pH adjustment (to about 7.5, which I confirmed with a pH test strip) give the water a pleasant tang while avoiding any harshness or chemical flavors. Unfortunately it doesn’t come out particularly cold, which means having to add non-RO ice to the glass to chill it down. First-world problem, I know.
I was especially pleased to discover that the X12 has one of the best water efficiency rates in the business, with a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio (3 gallons of pure water production to 1 gallon lost). Replacement filters (three are needed in total) are sold à la carte for $30 to $160 each.
For an even more powerful version—ideal for larger households—consider the Waterdrop X16, which uses the same cartridges and offers the same features as the X12. WIRED editor Kat Merck, whose municipal water supply does contain PFAS, has had one installed for a year and a half without any maintenance or reliability issues.

Battlefield in Kherson Region’s island area is now “transparent”,  military says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:34:37 UTC
18:34:37 KST

Battlefield in Kherson Region’s island area is now “transparent”, military says
Pavlo Drohal, spokesperson for Ukraine’s 30th Marine Corps, told Ukrinform about the situation.
“As for the island area in the Dnipro River delta, the enemy continues to make systematic attempts to advance onto the islands. They try to reach them in small boats, using small assault groups, and attempt to establish positions there so they can infiltrate closer to the right bank. Given the challenging geography and the large number of islands — this is not just the Dnipro River proper, but also its tributaries, forming an extensive island zone with a complex network of waterways — they continue these attempts systematically. The difference is that we can see them because technology makes the battlefield ‘transparent,’ and the airspace is under constant surveillance,” Drohal said.
According to him, Ukrainian defenders spot and destroy Russian troops, in most cases as soon as they begin moving. In autumn, the enemy is trying to use fog and rain as cover, but the outcome remains the same: these groups are destroyed.
“Regarding the attempt to land in Kherson’s Korabel neighborhood, yes, such an attempt was made last week. It was unsuccessful because the enemy was spotted, targeted with weapons, and destroyed,” the spokesperson said.
He added that rumors suggesting an enemy sabotage and reconnaissance group might nevertheless have landed and hidden in the neighborhood were unfounded.
“That is impossible. Those who attempted to land were destroyed. Our defenders are monitoring the area very closely and keeping track of everything happening there,” Drohal emphasized.
He also noted that Russian forces had conducted intensive assaults in the island area in spring and early summer, operating “nonstop.” At the time, there could be as many as 50 assaults a month. The number of attacks subsequently declined: there were no such attempts in July, but they resumed in August and continue to this day.
“In other words, the enemy is experiencing something of a seasonal surge. It is once again imagining that it can advance toward the islands, establish a foothold, and set up positions there. But doing so is extremely difficult in practical terms, and given our countermeasures and constant surveillance, it is virtually impossible,” the spokesperson stressed.
However, Drohal said these failed attempts had not deterred the Russian military command, which continued to send assault groups on missions that amounted to a death sentence, showing little regard for its personnel. Russian servicemen receive some training for combat in these conditions, he added, but the enemy’s assault groups “are not particularly well supplied.”
As for Kherson city, Drohal stressed that Ukrainian forces were doing everything possible to protect it. Although Russian forces launch a huge number of drones, Ukrainian defenders destroy or suppress 90–93% of them.
“We are equally successful in targeting enemy artillery along the Dnipro River axis. Since the beginning of summer, we have destroyed or damaged around 150 enemy artillery systems. Once a gun starts operating in our area, it is tracked almost immediately and survives for only two to three days. The Russian command shows little regard for its artillery either,” the spokesperson said.
The number of artillery attacks in autumn has fallen by a factor of 2.5 compared with spring. While there were around 2,000–2,500 attacks in spring, the current figure is approximately 1,000–1,200, Drohal said.
As reported, Russian artillery shelling along the Dnipro River axis has decreased significantly as Ukrainian Defense Forces successfully destroy Russian artillery systems.
Photo provided by Pavlo Drohal, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Navy’s Marine Corps

The Crown Prosecution Service charged Mohmed A., 24, of London, with engaging in conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Counterterrorism police chief Laurence Taylor said investigators believed the country involved was Iran.
Nouman E., 24, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on August 22. Both men were due to appear in court later Tuesday.
Nouman E. was initially arrested near the Gloucestershire base on September 27 and rearrested on October 20.
A separate suspect, a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national also arrested on October 20, was released without charge over the suspected intelligence offense. He remains on bail following an October 1 arrest on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five other men also remain on police bail.
How did the Fairford investigation begin?
Armed police responded to reports of three suspicious vehicles near the base on September 27 and arrested five men. Scores of residents were evacuated as police and military bomb-disposal experts searched the area for explosives.
Police have said they consider Iranian state involvement "highly likely."
"We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state," said Laurence Taylor, head of UK counterterrorism policing.
He said police were working with MI5, Britain's domestic intelligence service, to counter the threat and urged the public to report concerns.
Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said it considers bases used to attack its territory legitimate targets.

A decade after liquor ban, Bihar faces a new drug question: What the numbers reveal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

NCB destroyed 1,170.15 kg of seized narcotics worth Rs 4.54 crore in Patna, Bihar, across four cases to prevent their recirculation in September (Credit: NCB's X)
Punjab is set to go to polls in 2027, and the BJP, seeking to form its first government in the state, has made the drug menace a major election issue. The party has been targeting the ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) over its handling of the problem. Union home minister Amit Shah has even promised to make Punjab "drug-free" by December 2029 if the BJP comes to power.But AAP has hit back. Its national convener Arvind Kejriwal questioned the BJP over the drug problem in states where it is in power, including Bihar, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Goa, asking why the same deadline had not been set for them.The political exchange has also put the focus on Bihar, where alcohol has been banned for a decade but recent drug seizures have raised fresh concerns. More than 4.13 lakh intoxicating injections were seized in Patna in the first eight months of 2026, while investigations have uncovered heroin consignments, codeine-based cough syrup and networks involved in preparing and distributing narcotics.But what do these seizures actually reveal? Is Bihar witnessing a rise in drug consumption, or is the state increasingly becoming a transit route for narcotics headed elsewhere? And has a decade of prohibition had any bearing on the availability and use of other intoxicants? Here's what the data reveals
Does Bihar have a new drug problem?
More than 4.13 lakh intoxicating injections seized in Patna in the first eight months of 2026.
A sharp rise in smack seizures. Growing quantities of codeine-based cough syrup being intercepted. Across Bihar, recent drug seizures and investigations point to a changing narcotics landscape, raising questions about what is entering the state, where it is going and who is using it.But do these seizures signal a growing drug problem within Bihar, or are they exposing the scale of a trafficking network that uses the state as a transit route? Police have traced consignments from the Northeast and Nepal-linked routes, while investigations in Patna have uncovered alleged local networks involved in preparing and distributing narcotics.The answers are not straightforward. Five years of seizure data show sharp fluctuations rather than a consistent rise across substances. Meanwhile, a debate over Bihar’s liquor prohibition has raised another question about whether the use of alternative intoxicants has changed since the ban came into force in 2016.What do the numbers reveal?Bihar’s drug seizure data over five years shows that ganja accounted for the largest quantities seized among the major narcotics listed, while seizures of heroin fluctuated sharply. Ganja seizures rose from 16,607 kg in 2020 to 33,603 kg in 2021, before falling to 23,023 kg in 2022 and 13,129 kg in 2023. They increased again to 18,356 kg in 2024.Heroin seizures fell from 363.77 kg in 2020 to 9.62 kg in 2021, before rising to 31.13 kg in 2022, 27.37 kg in 2023 and 53.35 kg in 2024. Hashish seizures also varied, peaking at 395.12 kg in 2021 before declining to 195 kg in 2024.A person whose circle consumes drugs said, on the condition of anonymity, that marijuana remained the most widely consumed substance in their social circle and that they had not noticed a significant shift in preferences towards other drugs.“In most circles, marijuana is most widely consumed, and I don't think synthetic drugs have made their way to Bihar,” the person said.The data records smaller seizures of other substances, including ATS, cocaine and LSD in certain years. While these figures show fluctuations in the quantities of narcotics seized, they do not establish a steady year-on-year rise in drug trafficking or consumption. Seizure figures reflect what enforcement agencies intercept and, on their own, cannot establish how many people use drugs or whether drug abuse is increasing in Bihar.
Where are the drugs coming from?
Police say a significant share of narcotics reaching Patna comes from the Northeast. The routes and methods of transportation vary according to the size of a consignment.Investigations have also pointed to supply chains passing through multiple states. In September, four people were arrested near JP Setu in Patna with 274 gm of heroin. Police traced the consignment to Assam, from where it allegedly travelled to Tamkuhi in Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh, before being sent towards Patna.Bihar’s location along the Nepal border adds another dimension to the problem. On October 25, Motihari Police, in a joint operation with the Bihar Special Task Force, seized smack valued at Rs 4 crore near Raxaul, close to the India-Nepal border.
Cops suggest that drugs in Bihar enters from multiple states
In a separate operation, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence’s Muzaffarpur unit and the Bihar STF busted a suspected network involved in smuggling Nepal-origin charas into India. Two people were arrested and 5.14 kg of charas, valued by officials at Rs 5.14 crore, was seized. Investigators said the consignment was intended for onward transportation to Indore in Madhya Pradesh.The cases point to Bihar’s role as a route for narcotics moving between regions. However, seizures along transport corridors do not establish how much of the intercepted supply is consumed within the state.
Is the trade limited to transportation?
Police investigations suggest that local networks are also involved in storage, preparation and distribution.In March, police found a rented room in Patna’s Ramakrishna Nagar area allegedly being used to prepare smack. A flat in Alamganj was allegedly used for distribution. Police recovered 1.68 kg of brown sugar and cash, along with cheques worth around Rs 70 lakh issued in the name of a police officer.The trade is not confined to substances traditionally associated with narcotics smuggling. Pharmaceutical products have also featured in investigations. In May, the DRI seized 7,500 bottles of codeine-based cough syrup from a pickup van outside Patna’s Rajendra Nagar Terminal. Investigators found that the consignee’s drug licence had been cancelled and that the firm did not exist at its stated address.Such cases raise questions about how pharmaceutical products enter illicit supply chains, how they are distributed and whether existing monitoring systems are able to detect diversion from legitimate channels.A Patna high court order has raised questions about how narcotics can travel long distances before being intercepted.In an order dated September 15, the court expressed concern over two minor boys who had travelled from Assam to Bihar in a car without a registration certificate. The vehicle was intercepted near Patna, and the directorate of revenue intelligence recovered more than 60 kg of cannabis from a concealed compartment.The court questioned how the vehicle had travelled uninterrupted from Assam to Bihar while carrying a commercial quantity of cannabis.Has prohibition changed pattern of substance use?Bihar banned the sale and consumption of alcohol in April 2016 under a policy introduced by the Nitish Kumar government. The prohibition was intended, among other objectives, to reduce domestic violence and encourage households to spend money on more productive needs.A research paper by the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), titled Macro Perspective of Bihar's Development Achievements, Unfinished Agenda, and the Way Forward, has questioned whether the ban achieved its intended outcomes.The paper said reported crimes against women had not declined following prohibition and that total reported crimes against women increased over the post-2016 period. It also pointed to concerns about the expansion of illicit liquor trade, enforcement challenges, corruption and the use of alternative intoxicants, including illicit drugs."In tandem, there was a significant rise in illegal liquor trade leading to higher alcohol consumption, increased crime and corruption, and an increase in the use of alternative additive substances, such as illicit drugs," the paper said.The authors argued that Bihar should reconsider prohibition and restore alcohol excise duty to historical levels. They estimated that doing so could increase the state’s own revenues by 14-15%.Some residents also believe prohibition may be one factor behind the availability of other intoxicants, although personal accounts cannot establish a direct link between the ban and drug consumption.“I would argue that it is a byproduct of the prohibition in the state, but that isn't the full picture,” another person who spoke on condition of anonymity said, referring to the perceived increase in drug availability.The person said their observations were based on the experiences of people in their social circle who use drugs, adding that young people and those in their 30s appeared to be among the users they had noticed.“In a state like Bihar, with a large chunk of youth population that haven't so far been backed with job opportunities, [this] has also contributed to the rise of drug consumption in the state,” the person said.They also flagged a lack of awareness about addiction and the support available to people who use drugs.“I feel like there is a lack of awareness against remedial methods, like what to do if someone you know has become addicted to drugs, what are you supposed to do then. I feel like there is a lack of rehabilitation system and awareness among the people needed to curb the drug menace,” the person said.
Is Bihar seeing a rise in consumption or a rise in detection?
The distinction matters because seizures measure what enforcement agencies intercept, not the total volume of drugs entering the market or being consumed.Bihar’s prohibition and narcotics enforcement policies also form part of a wider debate over how the state measures the effectiveness of its policing. A rise in seizures can reflect an increase in trafficking, improved detection or a combination of both.Bihar minister Madan Sahni has rejected the charge that rising seizures indicate a failure of prohibition. He said the increase was not confined to Bihar but was a phenomenon seen in other states as well."I must say that due to the alertness of the officials concerned, the quantity of the seizure of substances prohibited under the NDPS Act has increased in the state, but at the same time, people should know that the majority of the prohibited substances seized in Bihar are meant for supply to other states," he said.Sahni added that intercepting consignments within Bihar could create the impression that the drugs were intended for local consumption, even when they were being transported elsewhere. He also defended prohibition, saying it had been successful.The minister’s argument points to an important gap in the available figures. Without comparable data on drug use, treatment demand, drug-related health emergencies and the destinations of intercepted consignments, it is difficult to determine how much of the rise reflects local consumption.
RJD MP Manoj Kumar Jha, meanwhile, cited a media report and said the situation was out of control."An entire generation has been ruined. This is what happens when the government has no control. The situation here is completely out of control..." he said.
Does Bihar have a new drug problem?
Bihar’s recent seizure figures and investigations point to a changing narcotics landscape. Police have reported sharp increases in some categories, identified supply routes running through several states and uncovered alleged local networks involved in preparation and distribution. Seizures near the Nepal border have also highlighted the state’s role in cross-border trafficking.But the central question remains unresolved. Is Bihar facing a growing drug-consumption problem, a trafficking problem that extends beyond its borders, or both?

Trump's son spent two days hunting in Mongolia with a Russian oligarch
The eldest son of US President Donald Trump, Donald Trump Jr, went hunting in Mongolia at the end of August, where he may have spent several days in a camp with Kremlin-linked oligarch Umar Kremlev. The Financial Times established the circumstances of the trip on the basis of testimony from local guides and officials, flight data, social media posts and public documents.
Source: The Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The meeting took place at the end of August. The FT notes that Kremlev flew to the Mongolian capital of Ulaanbaatar by charter plane from Kazakhstan, after which he travelled to Donald Trump Jr's hunting camp in the western part of the country.
Travelling alongside Kremlev was Russian businessman Arthur Martirosov, a partner in the US-sanctioned venture fund Voskhod. According to the FT, Trump Jr and Kremlev spent two days together, after which the Russian returned to Ulaanbaatar.
One of the local participants in the trip said that Trump Jr and Kremlev were careful not to be photographed together during their stay at Trump Jr's camp.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr stated that the men developed a personal friendship through a shared passion for hunting, fishing and outdoor recreation. According to him, they were introduced by a mutual acquaintance from the hunting community, and there are no business relations between them.
Quote from spokesperson for Trump Jr: "Don has made clear that he has a personal friendship, not a business relationship, with Umar. Their friendship is largely based on their shared love for hunting, fishing and the outdoors. It shouldn't be a surprise to anyone that they went hunting together earlier this year."
Details: Meanwhile, counterintelligence experts warn that contacts between members of the US president's family and individuals with ties to the Russian authorities could pose national security risks.
"It really doesn't matter if people have the most above board intentions. The moment the Russian security and intelligence services figure out someone has a relationship with anyone of high value, they will try to weaponise that," said Holden Triplette, who served as director of counterintelligence on the US National Security Council during Trump's first term.

Russia’s Strikes on Ukraine’s Energy Grid Amount to Crimes Against Humanity, UN Inquiry Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:30:52 UTC
18:30:52 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Strikes on Ukraine’s Energy Grid Amount to Crimes Against Humanity, UN Inquiry Finds
A UN-mandated commission of inquiry has found that Russia’s systematic strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid amount to crimes against humanity, in addition to war crimes committed through deliberate attacks on civilian targets.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, created by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022, set out its findings in a report published by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The investigation assessed the impact of these strikes during the 2025–2026 winter, noting that hundreds of drones and missiles damaged Ukraine’s energy grid in increasingly frequent attacks starting in autumn 2022.
The report drew on testimony from 255 individuals across nine regions—Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr—as well as input from Ukrainian authorities, medical professionals, and non-governmental organizations.
The commission concluded that Russian commanders issuing the strike orders knew the targeted heating facilities in major population centers were essential for civilian survival, particularly during winter conditions.
Russian authorities had also publicly announced plans for upcoming strikes. Investigators established that the energy grid was targeted deliberately as part of a state policy intended to cut off electricity and essential services, deliberately causing civilian suffering.
While the panel also reviewed Ukrainian strikes against energy infrastructure in Russia and occupied territories, it was unable to analyze their effects further because Russia refused access and failed to respond to requests for information.
The commission emphasized that international law prohibits attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, demanding an immediate end to such strikes.
Regarding the recruitment of foreign citizens into the Russian military, the commission gathered evidence linking Russian authorities to human trafficking operations spanning 29 countries. Recruits were obtained through deception or coercion, with operations coordinated through international agents and agencies.
Intermediaries operating under the guise of legal, government-approved companies processed visas and travel documentation. Upon arrival, foreign nationals were forced to sign military contracts written in Russian before being deployed to frontline positions for hazardous assignments, resulting in numerous casualties, disappearances, and surrenders into Ukrainian captivity as prisoners of war.
Similar cases have also been reported in other countries. The Peruvian government, for example, has confirmed that 11 of its citizens who joined Russian forces have been killed, while 114 remain missing and three have been captured by Ukrainian forces.
According to Spanish news agency EFE, Peruvian authorities said that among Peruvians recruited into the Russian military were people who are now missing or being held captive by Ukraine.
Overall, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate has identified more than 28,000 foreign nationals serving in the Russian Armed Forces under military contracts, with the number continuing to rise.

OHLAB experiments with colour-blocking and cork in old and new buildings of Terreno Barrio Hotel in Mallorca

OHLAB experiments with colour-blocking and cork in old and new buildings of Terreno Barrio Hotel in Mallorca
Mallorca-based architecture and interiors studio OHLAB has overseen the design of a hotel in Palma, including a renovated heritage building from 1935 and a new structure built from cross-laminated timber and cork.
The 41-room Terreno Barrio Hotel was envisioned as “a catalyst for the neighbourhood” of El Terreno, in the west of the Mallorcan city, serving as a community hub as well as a destination for tourists.
“Terreno is not conceived as a tourist object imposed on its context, but as a device for exchange – a hotel that, before being a hotel, aims to be an extension of the barrio,” said OHLAB founders Paloma Hernaiz and Jaime Oliver.
“This is not a slogan; it is the principle that orders programme, thresholds, atmospheres and materiality.”
The hotel’s reception is in the renovated 1935 building, a five-storey apartment block designed by local architect Francesc Casas, along with the restaurant and bar, a club, and a roof bar.
OHLAB refers to this building as “the stage”, the eye-catching focal point of the complex, while the new structure is described as “the bazaar”, its civic heart.
Wrapping a new public plaza, this second block houses the community-led spaces, including a cafe, coworking areas, a bookshop and gallery, pop-up retail, a gym, a spa and a cinema.
OHLAB adopted different strategies for the architecture and interior design of the two structures, creatively exploring the themes of building and material reuse in various ways.
“Here, circularity was understood not only as an environmental or material strategy, but also as an economic, social and territorial one, a way of keeping value within the local ecosystem by activating residents, culture, crafts, suppliers and everyday life,” they said.
In the renovated building, interior design revives the existing structure rather than covering it.
Communal spaces have a theatrical character, with patterned floor tiles and heavy curtains. Highlights include a golden mirror bar and a wool curtain installation by artist Sylvia Sanchez Montoya.
In the bedrooms, colourblocking creates a horizontal divide between top and bottom.
Floors and furniture feature matching terrazzo, produced by local tile manufacturer Huguet using the project’s demolition waste.
Materials are even more prominent in the seven-storey new building, thanks to the choice of materials. Cork clads the courtyard-facing north facade, while the other exterior walls feature timber louvres that shade the windows from direct sunlight.
Inside, the exposed CLT structure is brought to life through more playful use of colour and materials. The cafe and shop is a key example, with shades of brown and lime green extending across to the terrazzo floors and wooden furniture.
The bedrooms in this block have a different character, with murals by Mallorcan artist Albert Pinya, bathrooms housed inside mirrored boxes, and timber flooring that merges with joinery.
OHLAB was appointed by José Taltavull, who developed the concept for the hotel after being brought on board by hotelier Lydia Piñero.
Taltavull appointed graphic design office StudioRoses to oversee the hotel’s visual identity, which fed into OHLAB’s scheme.
Various elements were picked out in the same red as the hotel logo, including the ramped floor between the bar and reception, the stage in the club, and the sculptural stools located in the bar.
Most of the furniture was either designed by OHLAB or sourced from Mallorca-based manufacturers. A DJ table was made from cork leftover from the construction, while Mallorcan artist Pedro Óliver contributed the neon lighting pieces that feature throughout.
Terreno Barrio Hotel is the latest in a series of major openings in Palma in recent years, with the city in the midst of a cultural renaissance.
El Terreno is a major part of that story, particularly since Mallorca-based shoe brand Camper completed its 15,000-square-metre Project Gomila in 2023, which includes the new Jasper Morrison-designed Can Pa bakery.
OHLAB’s other projects in the city include the Can Santacilia residential development and the Paral·lel apartment complex.

I Tested Every Major AI Agent for a Day. Here’s the Best One
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Last year, I remember sitting in WIRED’s office, complaining to my colleagues nonstop about how much AI agents suck. They were just bad at everything.
As a software reporter, I sat through meeting after meeting where tech bros—mostly men—demonstrated how their new agent would revolutionize my everyday life and automate away the tedium. The catch was that none of these so-called “agents” actually worked.
Fast-forward to today, and always-on AI agents are booming, with major players racing to release their own versions to attract early adopters. The key reason these personal agents are hitting the larger zeitgeist, beyond Silicon Valley nerds, is that they work. Well, at least more reliably than last year. AI agents still make mistakes, but I also see significant improvements in following through on tasks and controlling a browser. These little guys got their glow-up.
It can be hard to know where to start with AI agents and which one best fits your automation needs. So I spent a day experimenting with every major AI agent to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Before going to bed on Wednesday last week, I set up six always-on agents on my iPhone: Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Instinct, Anthropic’s Claude Duet, Google’s Gemini Spark, and xAI’s Grok Bot.
Each agent differs slightly in price and function. Muse is free to use and has dominated the smartphone app download charts since its September release. Instinct is also free, but you need an invite code from a user; it’s operated through your texts rather than an app. OpenAI’s Dots are behind a $100-a-month paywall, the most expensive I tested, and built inside of ChatGPT. Google’s Gemini Spark is a beta inside the Gemini app and costs $20 a month. xAI’s Grok Bot costs $30 a month and is in its own app. Lastly, Anthropic’s Claude Duet costs $20 a month and is the newest of the bunch—released as a wait-listed research preview the night before my tests.
OpenClaw isn't on my list. Despite the AI agent sparking much of this innovation earlier this year, it’s too clunky for the average person to set up. Maybe it will be in a future ranking, where I could also include smaller players like Hermes by Nous Research and Poke.
What Exactly Is an AI Agent?
If you’ve never used an AI agent—I have zero judgment for the holdouts—it's like texting a digital assistant to complete tasks: scan your email for important missed messages, track vacation flight deals, and help with daily shopping decisions.
Compared to a chatbot’s turn-based experience, these tools are more proactive and will nudge you first when they detect an opportunity to be helpful. All of your messages with these agents are often stored in a single thread that feels like a group text. The AI agents complete many of these tasks by controlling a virtual browser, essentially their own computer for internet access.
The Rubric
I’ve tested AI software from a nontechnical perspective for the last few years, so I feel especially qualified to help guide you through this moment. I designed five basic tests to run each agent through, enacting all this chaos over 24 hours to gauge their proactivity, direction following, and browsing abilities. (Somehow, my iPhone didn’t melt into a puddle.) I scored each attempt on a scale of 1 to 5, and tallied the results at the end to crown a winner—and hand out an award for most annoying.
This is not an endorsement of any of these AI agents. The software remains nascent and often fraught with privacy and security concerns. These agents work best when connected to your personal data, like email and calendars, but require a level of trust that could ward off some users. For example, an X user claimed he recently connected AI agents to his bank account and work Slack, and then was mortified when an agent posted how much money he had for his colleagues to see.
Additionally, these tests are a limited sliver of what the tools can do. All of the agents will improve over time, as you share more data about yourself and how you like to complete tasks. I only shared my personal Google Calendar and Gmail with the tools, so I didn’t fully expose the AI agents, Billy Evans–style, to everything.
Morning Briefing
On Thursday mornings, WIRED’s Gear desk meets to chat about current coverage plans and sometimes pitch ideas for the next week. So, I wanted to see which AI agent put together the best tech news briefing and could use that information to generate a compelling headline. Companies often tout these tools as being great for compiling morning dossiers that keep you up-to-date on important events and breaking news.
I sent each AI agent an extensive prompt detailing my areas of coverage at WIRED, along with context about how this pitch would be used. Even though I asked the AI agents to take 30 minutes and really do deep research before answering, only Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots actually kept researching for most of the allotted time. The other AI agents either instantaneously spit out a pitch or sent me the headline after a couple of minutes of searching. While not a major mistake, it suggests that in this instance Muse and Dots were a bit better at following my instructions—a critical function of an AI agent.
The content of these six AI-generated pitches was a different beast. As you might have already guessed, the pitches didn’t exactly go over well in the editorial meeting. I could see my colleague’s eyes starting to glaze over as I read each headline and description. Gemini Spark generated the best angle, contrasting how Walmart created ways for third-party agents to use its shopping platform while Amazon recently gave Muse the boot. My colleagues, when they stopped yawning, didn’t seem too concerned about getting scooped by an agent.
Walmart Wants Your AI Agent to Buy Your Groceries. Amazon Is Calling the Cops. As retail giants clash over autonomous checkout, giving an AI companion like Meta’s Muse a weekly spending allowance reveals what happens when we stop clicking “Add to Cart” and outsource our domestic appetites to software.
ChatGPT's Locked Chats Hide Your Secrets From Everyone but OpenAI. OpenAI's new PIN-protected chats treat ChatGPT like the diary a lot of people already use it as, but they guard what you say from roommates and coworkers, not from the company itself.
I Let Claude Duet Text Me First—and It Spent My Claude Plan While I Wasn’t Looking. Anthropic’s new proactive agent promises to watch your inbox, calendar, and invoices so you don’t have to, but every time it checks in on you, drafts a reply you never asked for, or builds a dashboard overnight, it quietly bills that work to the same usage limit you pay for to chat.
This Anti-Doomscrolling App Wants to Be Your Phone’s Boss. I’d test SHIFT, whose developers decide which apps stay available during focus sessions, to explore whether escaping doomscrolling is worth outsourcing control of your phone.
Meta's Muse Has Basic Taste—by Design. A leaked set of instructions tells Meta's AI agent to fill its top picks with well-known stores and to check only three websites per request, just as millions of people start handing it their holiday shopping lists.
I Spent a Week Steering My Feeds. The Algorithm Barely Noticed. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube are all rolling out "tell the algorithm what you want" controls—I'd test whether they actually change what you see, or just make you feel in charge.
Lunch Time
Next, I wanted to test how these tools help for small, daily purchases. So I outsourced my lunch decisions to my team of AI agents, committing to order from whichever bot did the best.
I added another person, my wonderful boss, to the takeout order, to complicate the task a bit further. He’s vegan and was craving Vietnamese. I wanted something meaty and a hefty dose of caffeine. I needed to order from somewhere close to the WIRED office so I could stretch my legs, pick it up, then immediately keep working on this article.
They all picked similar places: DragonEats or Freshroll. Those Vietnamese restaurants make sense as reasonable, nearby lunch spots. DragonEats is a bit tastier and cheaper, so we went with that one. Instinct and Claude Duet built carts that were a bit too pricey compared to the other options. The only AI agent that truly failed at this task was Gemini Spark. The agent just added a single $5 roll for my boss. More of a snack than anything, I’d say!
You: Roast pork bánh mì + Vietnamese iced coffee. Your boss: teriyaki tofu fresh rolls with soy sauce instead of fish sauce. Subtotal: $30.57 before tax/fees.
For you: Roast Pork BM—$13.19, Vietnamese Iced Coffee—$5.29. For your boss (all vegan): Teriyaki Tofu Roll—$12.09—the fresh spring roll, kept with the default peanut sauce, not fish sauce; Teriyaki Tofu BM—$12.09. Item total is $42.66. DoorDash doesn't show tax or any fees until the checkout screen, so that final total will be a bit higher.
For you: Power Hour vermicelli bowl with garlic-ginger-honey pork and NamNam sauce, $15.85. Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee, $5.85. For your boss (vegan): Rainbow Bowl, vermicelli with sesame-lime tofu and citrus ginger sauce, $15.85. Freshroll tofu spring roll with peanut sauce, no fried piece, $5.85. That's $43.40 before tax and fees.

For you, there's a regular bánh mì sandwich loaded with garlic-, ginger-, and honey-roasted pork ($10.85), paired with a Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee ($5.85) for an afternoon caffeine boost—bringing the pickup subtotal to $22.55.
Schedule Conflicts
Another major selling point of these tools is their ability to be proactive, compared to chatbots that essentially only react to your prompts. Before I started the test, I created a Google Calendar event for 2 pm, labeling it as an important source meeting that can’t be moved. I also sent an email from my work account to my personal account, with the made-up scenario that my mom was getting out of the hospital today, and I needed to call her at 2 pm to send love and support from afar.
Which AI agents would read the email and calendar event, identify the conflict, and message me before the overlap to suggest alternatives? Only two of the bots succeeded here, which was fewer than I expected.
A possible clash this afternoon: your note to call Mom says 2 pm, and your important source meeting is 2-3 pm, Pacific. Would calling her before the meeting or after 3 work with her discharge timing?
Reece, good morning. Your 2 pm source meeting runs until 3, right when your own reminder says to call your mom.
I should have caught it, and from now on I'll check your self-reminder emails along with your calendars.
I had nothing cross-checking your inbox against your calendar. Want me to run that check every morning and flag collisions before they hit?
My mistake was treating your calendar as the only source — I never cross-checked that email reminder against it, even though Gmail was right there.
Because the reminder arrived as an email message rather than a calendar entry or scheduled task, the cross-app overlap wasn't surfaced before 2:00 pm.
Vacation Itinerary
I rarely go on vacation, so when I do, I spend an obscene number of hours researching, and I relish it. I love watching YouTube street food tours and aimlessly scrolling through flights trying to find the best deal. So I don't want to automate this task fully. Even so, I’m open to the idea that these AI agents could help with some of the logistical planning.
As with any AI-generated output, I still recommend checking multiple, non-AI sources before trusting these itineraries or revolving your whole trip around what agents recommend. When travelers in California recently trusted a chatbot to plan everything for a strenuous hiking excursion, the group had to be rescued because they lacked critical supplies (and maybe some critical thinking).
For this test, I sent all the AI agents a long paragraph explaining that my partner and I are considering exploring China late next year during a two-week-long adventure. I asked for a first draft of a potential itinerary that included: flight, hotel, nightlife, and food recommendations. Also, I asked the AI agents to chart a course that blends historical moments with big-city vibes. I can’t stand constantly changing locations, so I told the agents I want to stay in four different hotels max.
Notably, all of them chose identical routes through China—potentially ushering a new era of the Lonely Planet effect, where groups of travelers are nudged to visit similar locations, shops, and restaurants.
Fly out of SFO the week after Golden Week, on a nonstop to Beijing, home nonstop from Shanghai. Four hotels, no backtracking — imperial history first, Sichuan food and pandas in the middle, Shanghai nightlife to finish.
AI agent snippet: My recommendation: fly into Beijing, take high-speed trains to Xi’an and Chengdu, then fly to Shanghai and home. You get imperial history, the Terracotta Army, Sichuan food and a big-city finale without an overnight train or an extra hotel move.
A first-draft 13-night trip for two: Beijing, Xi'an, Chengdu and Shanghai, departing SFO on Oct 13 and returning Oct 27, after Golden Week.
A First-Time Traveler's Route Blending Imperial History, Sichuan Gastronomy, Vibrant Nightlife & 4-Hotel Hub Comfort.
Beijing in, Shanghai home, with Xi'an and Chengdu between: four bases, no backtracking, history up front and the food and bars getting better every stop.
Fly into Beijing on Saturday, Oct 9, 2027, then go Beijing → Xi'an → Chengdu → Shanghai, and fly home from Shanghai on Saturday, Oct 23. That's 13 nights in four hotels, two bullet trains and one short flight.
Insomnia Check
I was having trouble sleeping after all this AI agent chaos, though the Vietnamese coffee probably didn’t help. What happens when you give these tools a broad, open-ended task? Sometimes when I need the most help is when I don’t even know where to start.
If I had a human assistant, I would never message them in the middle of the night, so maybe that’s a plus for these digital helpers. The two agents that really flopped at this task, Gemini Spark and Claude Duet, responded to me without the soft touch or situational context a real person might.
I can set a reminder for later this morning to check in on your mom and see how her leg's doing, so it's off your mind for now.
Send me the three things taking up space in your head; messy is fine, and I’ll turn them into a short checklist with one clear first step. Then you can put the phone down.
Here's one you can do from bed: skim the China draft and tell me the one thing you'd change. I'll have a v2 ready when you wake up.
I'll cross-check today's calendar and your self-sent email reminders for any conflicts or can't-miss items—the check I should've done properly yesterday—and only surface it at a sane hour, unless something's urgent early.
The best quick task right now is a mental download to get whatever is looping in your head onto paper so your brain can let go of it—especially since your calendar is completely clear today, with no morning commitments waiting for you.
Let's close out yesterday's two loose ends. Your Thursday pitch is delivered, and your lunch cart got covered by the DragonEats order. Say the word, and I'll mark both done, then you can get back to sleep.
Best Overall: OpenAI Dots
Yes, it’s still behind an expensive paywall, so I would suggest most people wait until OpenAI launches this agent for free, or at least on the $20-a-month plan, before trying it out. Even so, Dots performed the best overall in these tests and failed at a task that’s fairly specific to my niche.
In the month since its release, Dots already feels more polished. I prefer a separate app over the current ChatGPT integration, though the smartphone widget option is a decent compromise. Dots for the win.
Most Accessible: Meta Muse
Muse is for the normies! And that’s fine. It did well in tests, coming in a close second on the scorecard, and was the easiest to set up. Oh, and it's free. Despite Meta’s assurances that it responsibly processes user info in secure virtual machines, I still have concerns given the company’s past mishandling of user data.
Best Interface: Anthropic Claude Duet
I tested this AI agent just one day after it officially launched as a research preview, so a few rough edges were expected. Despite Claude Duet scoring in the middle of the pack on most tests, its dedicated app was extremely user-friendly to navigate and follow up on ongoing tasks. I could see users obsessed with productivity and streamlined software experiences really latching onto Claude Duet in the next couple of months. Though you currently have to sign up for Anthropic’s waiting list to access Duet, and it’s behind a $20-a-month paywall.
Most Annoying: Instinct
You might like the sparse design fully integrated into your messenger; I did not. While other WIRED writers have lauded Instinct, calling it so good that they didn’t care what happened to their privacy, the texting-only aspect felt like a deal-breaker for me. I left the experience feeling too removed from what my agent was doing on my behalf and annoyed at its emoji reactions, like a grimace face when I told the agent it missed my scheduling conflict.

Two weeks after a Russian supply base burned in Luhansk’s Khrustalnyi, Ukrainian drones came back for an ammo depot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Ukrainian drones blew up a Russian ammunition depot near Khrustalnyi in occupied Luhansk Oblast overnight on 27 October, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported. Drones also hit the oblast’s capital, Luhansk, for hours, and part of the city lost power. Russia’s occupation authorities have not commented.
Russia keeps pushing toward the last big Ukrainian-held cities in Donetsk Oblast. Its artillery there runs on shells kept in rear depots across occupied territory, and those depots sit within reach of Ukraine’s mid-range drones. Each depot lost behind the front pushes Russia to store and move its shells from farther back. That lengthens the supply runs Ukraine’s drones already hunt on the roads of occupied Ukraine.
Secondary detonations near Khrustalnyi lasted over an hour
The drone attack on occupied Luhansk Oblast went on for several hours, Exilenova+ said. Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the depot near Khrustalnyi, and secondary detonations continued for more than an hour, the channel added. It posted night footage of a large fire glowing on the horizon.
Russia has occupied Khrustalnyi, formerly called Krasnyi Luch, since 2014. The city lies about 65 km southwest of Luhansk. It serves Russian troops as a rear and logistics hub.
Luhansk lost power as drones hit its former airfield
The attack on the city of Luhansk lasted more than four hours, Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of Occupation, said. Residents reported many explosions and fires in several districts, and the power went out. The main strike hit the city’s former airfield, he added. In October 2023, Ukraine’s ATACMS missiles destroyed Russian helicopters at air bases in occupied Luhansk and Berdiansk.
On Yandex Maps, the Russian online mapping service, the struck area near Luhansk airport is blurred, Andriushchenko noted. Yandex blurs military and critical infrastructure sites this way, he wrote.
Exilenova+ also reported a series of explosions in Luhansk. The oblast had been under a mass drone attack for an hour, with dozens of hits in different towns, Ukrainian Telegram channel DroneBomber wrote late on 26 October.
Neither side’s military has mentioned the attack on Luhansk Oblast. Ukraine’s General Staff left it out of its morning report. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it downed 222 drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea, without listing Luhansk Oblast.
Pro-Russian local channels confirmed the attack from their side. A channel covering occupied Luhansk Oblast wrote that eyewitnesses saw a large fire and secondary detonations in Khrustalnyi. LIC, the news agency of Russia’s occupation administration in Luhansk Oblast, reported a series of powerful explosions over Luhansk and a visible glow.
The third drone night over occupied Luhansk Oblast in a week
Drones have now hit occupied Luhansk Oblast on three nights in seven days. On 21 October, they struck the seized telecom building in the city of Luhansk that houses the occupation’s mobile operator. Two nights later, strikes cut communications and power in part of the city.
Ukrainian drones just lit up Russian-occupied Crimea, Donetsk, and Luhansk — here’s how (video)
Khrustalnyi itself burned on 12 October, when strikes hit a former motor depot housing Russian troops. Ukraine also hit an ammunition depot there in June 2022. Back then, the site supplied Russia’s offensive on Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk.
Blasts in Mariupol, Berdiansk, and Melitopol, and Russian claims from Bryansk
Occupied Mariupol heard two waves of explosions overnight, and the power went out after the attack, Andriushchenko also said. In occupied Berdiansk, several blasts near the Ekvator shopping center preceded a large fire, he added.
On the evening of 26 October, strike drones attacked occupied Melitopol in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Exilenova+ said. Locals also reported FPV drones hitting targets in the city.
In Russia’s city of Bryansk, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk claimed a night drone attack injured six people and damaged three apartment blocks. He said a man also died when a drone-dropped explosive went off. Yevhen Balytskyi, the Russian-installed head of occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, claimed a drone hit a Simferopol–Moscow bus near Prymorsk, killing one passenger.
As the attacks began, Russian monitoring resources tracked up to 350 Ukrainian drones in the air, DroneBomber said. Most flew over Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, with more groups near Crimea, Novorossiysk, and occupied Luhansk Oblast.
Ukraine’s drones also weigh on Russia’s road to occupied Crimea. Truck traffic on the R-280 highway from Rostov Oblast has halved to about 1,000 a day because of drone attacks. Anatolii Tsurkin, who heads a carriers’ association set up in occupied Crimea, said so.
Kyiv set aside $113 million for the first phase of a program of middle-strike drones aimed at Russia’s rear. That makes nights like this one likely to keep coming for depots, airfields, and roads across occupied Ukraine.

German troops test Auterion’s Talon drone interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:29:41 UTC
18:29:41 KST

- Auterion showed its Talon interceptor drone on a test range with the Bundeswehr, launched from a rifle-style launcher and guided by a second soldier.
- The company says Talon can engage single drones and swarms but did not disclose its performance or any German purchase plans.
Auterion, the drone software company best known for the autonomy systems inside thousands of Ukrainian strike drones, has shown its Talon interceptor on a test range with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, saying the system is built to take on both single drones and swarms.
Footage released by the company this week shows several German soldiers in Flecktarn camouflage working with the system on an open airfield, with one soldier firing the Talon interceptor drone into the air from a special rifle-style launcher fitted with an optical sight, while another soldier standing nearby guides the drone onto its target after launch.
Auterion did not say where or when the trials took place, which Bundeswehr unit was involved, or whether Talon destroyed any targets during the tests, and the company has given few technical details about the interceptor itself.
In the way it is used, Talon resembles Russia’s Yolka, a small interceptor drone that Russian troops fire from a handheld launcher at an aerial target that has already been spotted, and which uses an optical seeker and an onboard AI module to track its target out to about 3 km (1.9 miles) at speeds of up to 200 km/h (124 mph), although Yolka is described as a largely fire-and-forget weapon, while the Talon footage shows a second soldier steering the drone after launch.
Auterion’s chief executive, Lorenz Meier, described the company’s approach to interceptors in July, saying the first version would be simple enough for a soldier to point the interceptor at an identified target and launch it, with later versions moving into vehicle launchers, deeper integration with air defense networks and fixed installations to protect sites such as airports, stadiums and government buildings.
The company, which has a major hub in Munich, has been growing its business in Germany through a joint venture with Ukrainian drone maker Airlogix that was formed in February 2026 with backing from the German and Ukrainian governments, and the venture began serial production in September of more than 5,000 Seth X and Anubis strike drones under a German government-funded contract, using Auterion software for AI-guided terminal navigation and flight without satellite navigation.
Germany is buying several layers of counter-drone defense at once, and in November 2025 the Bundestag’s budget committee approved about €490 million (about $546 million) for MBDA’s DefendAir short-range anti-drone missile, while the Bundeswehr has also signed contracts for interceptor drones with other companies, such as TYTAN Technologies.

British prosecutors charged two men Tuesday with national security offenses linked to an investigation into suspicious activity near RAF Fairford, a military airbase in southwestern England used by U.S. bombers to launch strikes against Iran. Police said they suspect Iranian involvement in the incident.

U.S. bombers stationed at the base were withdrawn shortly afterward amid security concerns.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Britain's Counter Terrorism Policing, previously said investigators considered Iranian state involvement highly likely, although the precise nature and objective of any suspected operation remained under investigation.
Five other men arrested during the investigation remain on police bail. Prosecutors emphasized that the proceedings are ongoing and that the defendants have not been found guilty of any offense.

Online casino tax cut brings no extra revenue, but culture picks up the bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:26:00 UTC
18:26:00 KST

Online casino tax cut brings no extra revenue, but culture picks up the bill
The promised extra revenue from Estonia's online casino tax cut has not materialized for this year, making next year's culture budget €6–7 million smaller than hoped.
The Finance Ministry says only two new license applications have appeared following the cut, which was a pledge of the coalition Eesti 200 party, and one of those applications has been declined.
The tax cut, to apply to online casinos licensed in Estonia, was meant to make everyone happy. A lower rate would, it was argued, make Estonia a casino mecca; the state would have amassed more revenues, and culture – gambling tax revenues are a major source of funding for the sector — would finally stop struggling,
"This law isn't built on dreams. Together with the Foresight Center we modeled the entire potential tax take — how much market share would move to Estonia if the tax fell, how much tax revenue would come from that share, what the growth in receipts would be and how we could use it for extra funding for culture and sport," Eesti 200 leader Kristina Kallas had said last December.
A scenario accompanying the cut illustrated these hopes: online casino tax revenues rising to €95 million by 2029. Advocates turned a blind eye warnings at the time which found that not enough new companies might arrive to offset the lower rate. Yet this is what has materialized, though a finance ministry spokesperson rejected claims this had come as a surprise.
"Only two new license applications have come in. One is in process, one has been refused — so there hasn't been a great rush for Estonian licenses. Nor did we expect there to be one. So it went more or less as we thought," said Evelyn Liivamägi, deputy secretary general with the Ministry of Finance.
The Cultural Endowment (Eesti Kultuurikapital) which disburses culture funding to major projects is preparing to tighten its belt, with next year's budget must be made €6–7 million smaller than was projected just a couple of years ago, directly as a result of the tax break.
"The lion's share of that reduction will come from the gambling tax cut, and a very large part of the gambling tax cut comes from the fact that the gambling tax rates have been lowered," said Margus Allikmaa, head of the Cultural Endowment.
The under-construction new ERR TV house, the "Siuru" Tartu Downtown Cultural Center, and the Tallinn Film Wonderland development are among the projects receiving Cultural Endowment money; should tax revenues come in lower than expected, however, the funding payment schedule stretches out. This in turn will mean a greater reliance on loans, and consequently higher interest payments. In the case of the new TV house, this could translate into less funding for new equipment.
"Indeed, if money has to be spent on loan interest instead, it could mean a couple of million less for new television equipment, and we would have to bring equipment over from the old TV house — which we are anyway trying to do as much as possible — but which isn't really very high quality or particularly viable any more," said Erik Roose, ERR board chair.
Current law provides for the online casino tax cut to go ahead in increments, however, reaching 4 percent by 2029.
Allikmaa, Roose's predecessor as ERR chief, said he wants the cuts stopped. "I have proposed that the sensible thing is to end the gambling tax cut as a matter of urgency. The worst thing would be to do nothing," he said.
Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi (Reform) too considers the online casino tax cut bad policy, yet despite this, the government is not planning reverse the tax decision, noting it passed a Riigikogu vote.
"We didn't initiate it and we won't reverse the Riigikogu's choice. But if the Riigikogu does so itself, we'll take an understanding view," Ligi said.
Tax policy must be predictable. Tax rises, or abandoning tax cuts, must be announced at least six months in advance, Ligi added.
The current Reform-Eesti 200 administration is now a minority government, and a general election is taking place in March 2027.

Last week, Rinwa had explained that the software was designed to transliterate names entered in English into Hindi.However, in some cases, instead of transliterating names, it translated the words, resulting in incorrect entries. For instance, if "Ramhit Yadav" was mistakenly typed as "Ram Hit Yadav", the software translated it into Hindi as "Ram ne Yadav ko Maara" (Ram hit Yadav). He said the errors could have been corrected using the editing feature, but some remained in the final list.Another instance, in which "B.Com" was entered in place of the father's name in the electoral roll for the legislative council polls, appeared to be a case of human error or negligence, the CEO had said.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.
