Greenhouse gas levels hit record highs in 2025, driving further global warming: WMO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:25:17 UTC
18:25:17 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Concentrations of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane, and nitrous oxide in the atmosphere reached record highs in 2025, committing the planet to further warming for decades and centuries to come, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned Monday.
In its latest Greenhouse Gas Bulletin, the UN weather agency said globally averaged CO2 concentrations reached 426.8 parts per million, equivalent to 153% of pre-industrial levels seen in 1750, the baseline year.
"Another year, another new record. Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies," said Ko Barrett, the WMO’s deputy secretary-general.
She warned that the past 11 years had been "the warmest on record" and that the warming trend is expected to continue.
"CO2 has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries," she said.
The report found that annual CO2 growth rates have tripled since the 1960s, rising from 0.8 to 2.4 parts per million annually during 2011-2020.
Between 2024 and 2025, concentrations rose by another 2.8 parts per million, driven partly by continued fossil fuel combustion.
Methane concentrations reached 1,948 parts per billion, or 267% of pre-industrial levels, while nitrous oxide climbed to 339.1 parts per billion, equivalent to 126% of the baseline from 1750.
The WMO also warned that sulfur hexafluoride, widely used in electricity distribution, saw its largest annual increase in 2025 despite having a warming potential approximately over 24,000 times greater than CO2.
The findings come on the eve of the COP31 UN Climate Change Conference hosted by Türkiye, set to start on Nov. 9, where governments are expected to discuss translating climate commitments into concrete action.

How do I vote? All you need to know before casting your ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:24:18 UTC
18:24:18 KST

Elections are being held Tuesday, with 7,331,981 Israeli citizens eligible to vote. Beyond practical questions about polling hours, voting station locations and how to avoid invalidating a ballot, this year's election has also raised questions about election integrity and the limits on the information political parties are permitted to collect about voters.
What are polling station committee members allowed to ask as you cast your vote? Can you be photographed at the polling station? The following guide answers these questions and more.
Where do I vote?
A total of 12,018 polling stations have been set up across Israel, with another 102 at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad. Each eligible voter should receive a notice by mail specifying their assigned polling station.
Those who have not received a notice can find their polling station on the Interior Ministry's website, call the multilingual voter information hotline at (+972) 1-800-1011975 or (+972) 073-2458358, or send a text to (+972) 53-3801464.
Who is eligible to vote?
Every Israeli registered as a resident in the Population Registry who is at least 18 years old on Election Day is eligible. This means anyone born on or before October 27, 2008, or on or before 16 Cheshvan 5769, according to the Hebrew calendar. In the case of a discrepancy between the Hebrew and Gregorian birth dates, the earlier of the two is valid.
What should I bring with me to the polling station?
A valid identity card, driver's license or Israeli passport. IDF soldiers can present a military I.D. card, and police officers can identify themselves with police credentials.
What are the voting hours?
Polling stations are open from 7 A.M. to 10 P.M. In communities with fewer than 350 eligible voters, as well as in prisons, hospitals and nursing homes, voting takes place from 8 A.M. to 8 P.M.
Is public transportation free?
Travel on Israel Railways and intercity bus routes covering distances of more than 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) will be free of charge until midnight, with no identification required.
How exactly do I cast my vote?
Upon arriving at the polling station, you must identify yourself to the committee secretary. You will then receive a ballot envelope and proceed behind the voting screen, where ballot slips for all competing lists, blank slips and a blue pen will be available.
Place only one ballot slip in the envelope. If the slip for your preferred list is unavailable, you may write its letter or letters on a blank slip using a blue pen only. The envelope does not need to be sealed. Then exit the booth and place the envelope in the ballot box in front of the committee members.
What invalidates a vote?
A blank white slip is invalid, as is a slip bearing anything other than the list's letters or designation, or its designation without the letters. Blank slips must be completed in blue ink.
An envelope is invalid if it bears any mark that could identify the voter, if it contains slips for different slates, more than three identical slips or anything other than a ballot slip. Two or three identical slips count as one vote; four invalidate the ballot. Envelopes not supplied by the Central Elections Committee are also invalid.
What if a ballot slip is torn?
Elections Committee guidelines do not address this explicitly, but slips that differ from official ones in size, shape, color or printing are invalid. A distinctive tear or perforation that could identify the voter may also lead to disqualification.
Can anyone enter behind the screen with me?
Generally, no, as voting is secret. The exception is voters who are physically unable to cast their ballots on their own, who may be assisted by a companion with their consent.
Are photos allowed at the polling station or taking a selfie?
No. Photography is prohibited inside polling station compounds, including by committee members. The exception is trained election-integrity supervisors, who may use dedicated cameras supplied by the election committee, but may not photograph voters casting their ballots behind the screen.
Committee members and observers are also prohibited from sharing information about a person's presence at the polling station, whether they voted or the circumstances of their vote.
Violations may lead to criminal prosecution, prison sentences of up to five years for privacy violations or four years for violating a legal instruction, and civil lawsuits seeking up to 50,000 shekels ($16,000) without proof of damages.
I have a disability. Can I change polling station?
Yes. More than 3,600 specially accessible polling stations will be available across Israel, allowing voters with mobility disabilities to cast their ballots there even if they are not assigned to those stations.
I'm a soldier. Where can I vote?
Active-duty soldiers and reservists can vote at a military polling station on their base or at the polling station assigned to them based on their registered address in the Population Registry.
I was evacuated due to the war. Where can I vote?
Evacuees can vote at any accessible polling station across the country, regardless of their registered address, after signing a declaration confirming that they were evacuated from their homes due to the security situation.

Deindustrialization of Ukraine can be considered complete — political scientist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:24:03 UTC
18:24:03 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The catastrophic state of Ukraine’s metallurgical industry is a consequence of the Kiev regime’s anti-Russian policies, and the country’s deindustrialization is now effectively complete, Ukrainian political scientist Taras Sidorets told TASS in an interview.
"Today, the state of Ukraine’s metallurgical industry is not merely depressing; it is catastrophic. The process of decommunization and deindustrialization is, in effect, complete. There are no longer any major metallurgical plants operating in Ukraine. For the first time in many years of independence, the country has been unable to produce a single ton of steel. In principle, this is the natural outcome of an anti-Russian policy," he said.
However, Sidorets clarified that Ukraine’s deindustrialization began in 1991. At the time of independence, the country’s metallurgical sector comprised more than 130 enterprises, 14 of which formed the backbone of its steelmaking capacity.
"Much has changed since then. Privatization took place: some factories were acquired by private owners and continued operating under new management, while others were privatized and subsequently sold off," the political scientist noted.
The metallurgical industry in the 2010s
"Throughout the entire period of Ukraine’s independence, only one major steel plant was built: Interpipe Steel, whose construction was completed in 2012. Most notably, despite the launch of this facility, Ukraine’s share of global steel production did not increase," Sidorets said.
He noted that between 1991 and 2012, Ukraine’s share of global steel production fell from 6% to just over 2%.
According to figures cited by Sidorets, Ukraine produced approximately 32 million tons of steel in 2012, compared with 21 million tons in 2021. Pig iron production fell from 28 million tons in 2012 to slightly more than 21 million tons in 2021, a decline of around 7 million tons. Finished steel production also decreased, from 26 million tons to 19 million tons over the same period.
In October, Alexander Kalenkov, president of the Ukrmetallurgprom association, told Ukrainian Radio that Ukraine had not produced a single ton of steel in September 2026.
On September 5, ArcelorMittal announced that it would be unable to resume operations at ArcelorMittal Krivoi Rog, Ukraine’s largest metallurgical plant. It was the country’s last major steelworks that had not previously announced a shutdown.
On September 22, the Interpipe Steel plant halted operations. Earlier, on September 18, Zaporozhstal and Kametstal had also suspended production. Another major enterprise, the Dnieper Metallurgical Plant, had effectively ceased operations earlier because of financial difficulties.
Before their shutdowns, ArcelorMittal Krivoi Rog and Zaporozhstal each contributed approximately $90 million annually to the state budget, while Kametstal paid around $56 million.

Researchers in Australia develop simpler design for quantum sensors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:23:39 CST
18:23:39 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Quantum engineers in Australia have developed a simpler design for highly sensitive electromagnetic sensors, potentially advancing brain imaging, medical diagnostics and communications technology.
The research solves a long-standing problem that has limited the performance of superconducting quantum interference devices, known as SQUIDs, which are among the most sensitive magnetic field detectors but have struggled to accurately identify when a magnetic field is exactly zero, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's Adelaide University.
Until now, engineers have addressed this problem by building complex circuits containing hundreds or even thousands of differently sized superconducting loops, reducing overall sensor sensitivity, the statement said.
The Adelaide team discovered a simpler solution by keeping the loops the same size but replacing selected loops with "bare loops" containing no Josephson junctions, a key component of traditional SQUIDs. This creates a "synthetic area spread," allowing the sensor to behave as though it contains loops of many different sizes without requiring them.
Lead researcher Giuseppe Tettamanzi, an associate professor at Adelaide University, said the approach could achieve the same result while preserving the conditions needed for maximum sensitivity.
The researchers developed the theory and experimentally confirmed the effect using fabricated superconducting circuits operating at very low temperatures. The discovery could also make future devices easier and less costly to manufacture because the new approach removes the need to fabricate large arrays containing many different loop sizes.
Potential future applications include improved brain monitoring systems, more sensitive radio-frequency receivers, low-noise communication technologies and advanced electromagnetic sensing platforms, according to the study published in Physical Review Applied. ■

Pic story: inheritor of Huining paper-cutting uses traditional art form to tell stories of Long March
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:23:36 CST
18:23:36 KST

Wang Xinsheng makes a Long March-themed paper-cutting work in Huining County, northwest China's Gansu Province, Oct. 17, 2026. Wang Xinsheng, 56, a representative inheritor of Huining paper-cutting, has spent years using the traditional art form to tell stories of the Long March. Known for its vivid designs and diverse themes, Huining paper-cutting was listed as a national intangible cultural heritage in 2011.
Wang learned paper-cutting from his mother at an early age, developing his skills through works featuring flowers, animals and traditional opera characters. After he began working, he gradually shifted his focus from traditional subjects to real-life themes, particularly stories of the Long March associated with Huining.
In 2025, Wang spent several months creating a 15-meter-long paper-cutting scroll titled "The Long March." The artwork combines major events of the historic journey with poetry and traditional floral and bird patterns. It is now in the collection of the cultural center of Huining County, and has been exhibited to mark the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
Today, Wang is passing the craft to his children and grandchildren. "As paper-cutting artisans, we have a responsibility to keep this tradition alive," he said. (Xinhua/Lang Bingbing)

Voting begins in Israel's closely contested parliamentary election

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (R) casts his ballot at a polling station in Jerusalem on Oct. 27, 2026. JERUSALEM, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Voting in Israel's parliamentary election began at 7 a.m. local time (0500 GMT) on Tuesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political future in focus.
Netanyahu has campaigned on his security record and close ties with U.S. President Donald Trump, while his opponents accuse him of failing to take responsibility for the Oct. 7 attack and of deepening the country's political divisions, including by promoting a highly controversial judicial reform.
The latest opinion polls showed a tight race between Netanyahu's right-wing bloc and opposition parties led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Neither camp is expected to secure the 61 seats needed for an outright majority in the 120-member Knesset, potentially leading to weeks of coalition negotiations after the election.
A total of 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote at 12,018 polling stations across the country, according to the Central Elections Committee, which oversees the election. Thirty-six party lists are competing.
The election, Israel's first since the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership, with voters divided over his handling of the wars, security failures, and the country's future direction.
"I think this is one of the most important elections the country has ever had," said Roy Azulai, 30, a computer engineering student who arrived at a polling station in Tel Aviv early Tuesday morning.
"We definitely need a change of direction. We've had enough of wars and corruption," he said.
Ahia Yedia, 51, a flower shop owner, said he had voted for Netanyahu's Likud party in most elections since turning 18 and planned to do so again.
"For me, the decisive issue is security. I know Bibi puts our security first," he said, using Netanyahu's nickname. ■

Over 3,000 Australians died by suicide in 2025: statistics bureau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:48 CST
18:22:48 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Over 3,000 Australians died by suicide in 2025, according to official data published on Tuesday, with males accounting for a significant majority.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said that 3,283 of the 188,421 deaths registered nationally in 2025 were classified as being due to suicide, making it the 15th most common cause of death.
The figure was a slight decrease from the 3,326 suicide deaths reported in 2024, but the ABS noted that the number is expected to rise as ongoing coronial investigations progress.
It said that 73.9 percent of all people who died by suicide in 2025 were males.
The median age at death for those who died by suicide was 45.0 years. For males, it was 45.5 years, and for females it was 43.8 years.
By comparison, no other cause of death that ranked in the top 20 nationally in 2025 had a median age at death lower than 65.5 years.
The ABS said that suicide was the leading cause of death for Australians aged 15-44 in 2025 and was the overall leading cause of premature mortality, with suicide victims accounting for 108,674 combined years of potential life lost. ■

Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:22:45 UTC
18:22:45 KST

Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
Exit polls are expected soon after voting closes late on Tuesday, but a final verdict might take days.
Israelis are voting in a closely watched election to decide on the direction of the country, three years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on southern Israel that set off the genocidal war on Gaza.
The first election since those attacks comes at a time when Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of its neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.
But the vote also comes amid growing domestic questions that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces over alleged failures that allowed the October 7 attack, his government’s handling of efforts to retrieve captives taken to Gaza, alleged corruption and disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service.
In final polls published Friday, Netanyahu’s coalition is expected to be neck and neck with – or trail slightly behind – the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
According to Israeli news outlet Haaretz, which has collated polls from Israeli news channels, as of Friday, an average of Channels 11, 12 and 13 predicts Netanyahu’s bloc will win 50 seats while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc will take 54 seats. The Israeli parliament, known as the Knesset, has 120 seats in all, so 61 is the mark that a grouping needs to reach a majority.
Here’s what you need to know about the election.
When do polls close in Israel?
On Tuesday, polls opened at 7am local time (05:00 GMT) and will end at 10pm (20:00 GMT).
About 7.3 million Israelis will be eligible to vote, including 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel. Israelis living abroad cannot vote because the country does not have a general absentee ballot, requiring voters to be physically present on election day.
Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception and cast their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.
When will Israel’s election results be announced?
News channels will broadcast exit poll results once the election ends, with the first indications likely within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or weeks to get a clear result.
Results will also be live on the Central Elections Committee website once polls close.
While a clear picture of the election results may come out quickly, if no party or coalition secures a majority, it could take much longer.
The final vote tally is expected by Friday, and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.
How does the electoral system work?
Under a proportional representation system, Israelis vote for a single party, not individual candidates.
The number of seats the party gains in the Knesset is linked to the proportion of the vote it receives. For example, if Netanyahu’s Likud party secures 50 percent of the national vote, it would take 50 percent of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats.
For a party to enter the Knesset, it must secure at least 3.25 percent of the national vote.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
How is Israel’s next prime minister chosen?
Once the final count is in, President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
The person nominated then has up to 42 days to form a government. As it stands, no single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks.
What happens if Netanyahu or his rivals cannot form a government?
If no government emerges, the current cabinet, Netanyahu’s government, will remain as a caretaker government.
But before that point, whoever gains the most votes will have different options to assemble support from smaller parties, including forming a minority government or working with another political leader to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.
If all negotiations fail, and no grouping is able to cobble together a workable government, new elections will have to be called.

Scientists uncover how living cells in human milk use nutrients
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:43 CST
18:22:43 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Advanced nanoscale imaging has revealed the diversity of living cells in human milk, how these cells are structured, what they contain, and how they use nutrients, according to an Australian study.
The study provides a new view of the cellular and metabolic complexity of human milk by combining correlative imaging, stable isotope tracing and single-cell analysis to examine major cell populations, including milk-producing cells and immune cells, according to a statement released Tuesday by the University of Western Australia (UWA).
Lead author UWA PhD candidate Lin Qiongxiang said human milk is an incredibly complex biological system containing many different types of living cells, and stable isotope tracing showed that cells in human milk use nutrients in very different ways.
"When we tracked where sugar (glucose) ended up, we found it was being turned into fat droplets inside macrophages in milk, and those cells were switching on genes involved in handling fat," Lin said.
The findings, published in ACS Nano, showed that human milk cells have distinct functions to enable optimal milk composition and volume. The study also identified high levels of sulfur and iron in neutrophils, a type of immune cell that contributes to the killing of bacteria and helps protect infants from infection.
The researchers said the platform could help investigate how human milk cells vary between individuals, throughout lactation and under different maternal health conditions, including gestational diabetes. The findings could improve understanding of the biological roles of living cells in human milk and their potential importance for maternal and infant health. ■

The latest deterioration in relations between Ukraine and the United States is forcing Europe to consider how to help Ukraine without American support, Bloomberg said. Pistorius said the E5 countries are also working with Ukraine on their own air defense system meant to supplement the U.S. Patriot systems.

What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:21:33 UTC
18:21:33 KST

When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

Is it too early for kūčiukai?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:21:00 UTC
18:21:00 KST

With two months to go until Christmas, Lithuanian bakeries and supermarkets are already starting to sell kūčiukai, traditional pastries eaten on Christmas Eve. Some businesses say early sales have proved successful and others planning to wait until after All Saints’ Day.
The small, crunchy pastries made from leavened dough and poppy seeds are a staple of the Lithuanian Christmas Eve – Kūčios – as even the name suggests. Granted, most of us indulge in them throughout the holiday season.
Lina, a resident of Panevėžys, tells LRT TV she buys kūčiukai as soon as they hit supermarket shelves because she misses their taste and enjoys the festive mood they bring.
“It’s really nice that kūčiukai are already available and we can enjoy them and taste them until then. Is it too early? Definitely not. Nothing is ever too early; sometimes it’s just too late,” she says.
The Velželio duona bakery in Panevėžys is among the first to begin production each year. Its production manager, Marius Sarapas, said starting early helps attract customers eager for the traditional treat.
“People have been looking forward to them. There’s that initial purchase, when they’re not available anywhere else yet, but we already have them,” Sarapas said.
He added that early sales also allow the bakery to build up its seasonal business and give customers a chance to compare its products with those of competitors entering the market in the following weeks.
The first kūčiukai have also appeared in some supermarket chains.
Rimi Lietuva communications director Luka Lesauskaitė-Remeikė said the retailer was gradually bringing forward the start of sales to see whether customers would buy the pastries earlier.
“We can see that kūčiukai could be part of our assortment all year round. People like them as a snack, almost like sunflower seeds. We sometimes joke that you can watch a movie while eating them,” she said.
Last year, the pastries appeared in Rimi stores much later than this year, she added. This year, they arrived last week as the retailer experiments with earlier sales to gauge customer interest.
However, shoppers will not find kūčiukai in all major supermarket chains just yet. Lidl, Iki and Maxima plan to start selling them in November, after All Saints’ Day.
Consumers are divided over whether the early appearance of Christmas treats is welcome.
Some say selling them in October is premature and risks overshadowing the holiday season. One woman interviewed by LRT TV said Christmas preparations should begin after Halloween or the early November period of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day.
Others are indifferent because they make the pastries themselves rather than buying them in stores.
“I’m 96, and I’ve always made everything for the holidays myself,” one woman said when asked whether she baked kūčiukai at home. “When you buy them, they’re made by someone else.”
Meanwhile, the price of kūčiukai in supermarkets is expected to rise by about 7% this year, according to estimates by retailers.

Two men charged in Britain with helping Iran over RAF Fairford incident
- Two men were charged under Britain’s National Security Act after the RAF Fairford incident, which drew international attention and raised security concerns linked to Iran.
- Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, is accused of helping a foreign intelligence service, believed to be Iran, while Nouman Essghir, 24, is charged with entering a prohibited place for a harmful purpose.
- Police said six others remain on bail, and Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the earlier decision helped secure “swifter progress” and “better evidence”.
AI generated
LONDON – Two men were charged on Oct 27 under Britain’s National Security Act following September’s security incident at the RAF Fairford military base, with prosecutors accusing one of them of trying to assist Iranian intelligence operations in Britain.
RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five British men were arrested outside the military base in south-west England in the early hours of Sept 27.
The circumstances of the incident, which remain largely unexplained, attracted huge international attention, coming at a time of heightened concern about the security implications for Western states of the war between the United States and Iran.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier in October that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Tehran’s ambassador to Britain has denied.
British national Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, was charged with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service between Aug 31 and Sept 28, with police saying the country is believed to be Iran.
Nouman Essghir, a 24-year-old dual British-Iranian national who was first arrested outside RAF Fairford on Sept 27, was charged with one offence of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on Aug 22.
The pair will appear at London’s Westminster Magistrates’ Court later on Oct 27.
Police said that six other people, four of whom are British nationals who were arrested outside RAF Fairford on Sept 27, remain on police bail.
The decision to bail suspects after an apparent major incident had drawn scrutiny, but on Oct 27 police said that decision had helped secure charges against the two men.
“We know the decisions made during our investigations can sometimes appear illogical to those on the outside, but I want to make it very clear that there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them,” said Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in Britain.
“In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I have announced today.” REUTERS

Nova Poshta has implemented a private air defense project and has downed Russian strike drones, co-owner of the Nova group of companies Viacheslav Klymov said, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
"We are one of the few companies that implemented this project. I don't want to disclose numbers to you, but we have Shahed shootdowns," Klymov said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF), 'People. Business. Economy. What Next?', in Kyiv on Monday.
He stressed the importance of further developing private air defense projects and said business can take on functions that were considered the exclusive responsibility of the state before the full-scale invasion.

"Now big businesses are looking in Europe for fire trucks to create their own services. It is our property, what is the problem, who can forbid me to put out a fire on my own territory?" Klymov said.
Nova Poshta's main business remains express delivery of documents, parcels and palletized oversized cargo. It is the leader in express delivery in Ukraine. Its ultimate beneficial owners are Volodymyr Popereshniuk and Viacheslav Klymov.
The company's consolidated net profit rose 24.3% year-on-year to UAH 2.195 billion in the first half of 2026, and its revenue rose 31.8% to UAH 39.127 billion.
As of July 13, 2026, Nova Poshta's network had 54,700 service points: 16,800 branches and 37,900 parcel lockers across Ukraine.

Aeon unveils 140,000-square-foot missile plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:19:26 UTC
18:19:26 KST

- Aeon Industrial unveiled the Armory, a 140,000-square-foot factory for missile systems, interceptors, fuzes and seekers, targeting initial production in the coming months.
- The Texas company says its high-voltage fuzes are in volume production and were demonstrated at the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program.
Aeon Industrial, a Texas company that already makes low-cost drone fuzes in volume, has unveiled the Armory, a planned 140,000-square-foot (13,000-square-meter) factory for missile systems, interceptors, high-voltage fuzes, seekers and other critical components, saying it wants to add production capacity where the U.S. munitions supply chain depends on too few suppliers.
The company said the Armory is its first manufacturing site and is targeting initial production in the coming months, and that it is already developing a second site, Armory-2, to expand production further, though it did not say where either facility is located or how many missiles or interceptors it expects to build there.
Aeon is based in Austin, Texas, with offices in Oklahoma and Alabama, and it says its plans rest on proven hardware and contracts worth “eight figures,” meaning at least $10 million, although it did not name the customers or programs behind those contracts.
The company’s most mature product is MERC, a low-cost, high-voltage electronic safe-and-arm fuze that decides when a warhead detonates and keeps it safe until then, and Aeon says it is in volume production with 10,000 units on the line, after Aeon and warhead maker Mountain Horse Solutions said in September that their combined warhead and fuze package had flown on drones from several top-performing companies at the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance Gauntlet at Fort Carson, Colorado, where one-way attack drones were put through competitive testing.
The Drone Dominance program is the U.S. Department of War’s effort to buy large numbers of cheap attack drones quickly, and in October it led to orders for 60,000 attack drones from nine companies, after earlier rounds in which five companies led the scoring in the $1 billion program, while fuzes like MERC are designed to work across quadcopters, fixed-wing drones, missiles and interceptors, which lets one component supply several of these weapons at once.
The company is also pushing into air defense, and its joint low-cost interceptor proposal with European missile maker Destinus was selected on Sept. 30, 2026, as one of 10 finalists in the U.S. Army’s xTech Apex Intercept competition, which is looking for cheaper weapons to supplement the Patriot air and missile defense system against cruise missiles, short-range ballistic missiles and other aerial threats, with the U.S. Army planning to pick up to three winners in that category by Dec. 31, 2026.
Christopher “Gus” Jennings, Aeon’s director of growth and a former U.S. Army Special Forces soldier, said the company is building “next-generation weapon systems,” but Aeon has not identified which missile or interceptor designs will be built at the Armory first.

AI chip boom tripled South Korea's economic growth in the third quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:19:18 UTC
18:19:18 KST

South Korea's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter. However, analysts warned that its heavy reliance on the chip industry leaves the country vulnerable to a slowdown in global AI spending.
South Korea's economy grew more than three times faster than expected in the third quarter, fuelled by strong demand for semiconductors, according to central bank data released on Tuesday.
GDP rose by 1.0% in the July-to-September period compared with the previous quarter, preliminary figures from the Bank of Korea (BOK) showed.
The figure surpassed the central bank's August forecast of 0.3% growth.
The reading was boosted by a 2.3% rise in exports, "led by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment", the BOK said.
Investment in facilities rose by 4.1%, largely driven by spending on machinery used in semiconductor production.
The data validates the "BOK's upbeat assessment...that booming demand for chips is keeping exports and investment strong", said Kwon Hyo-sung of Bloomberg Economics.
Semiconductor exports soared by 218.7% year-on-year to $148 billion (€127bn) in the third quarter, according to government figures.
On an annual basis, the economy grew by 3.4%, slightly below the 3.7% recorded in the previous quarter.
Real gross domestic income (GDI), which measures purchasing power, surged by 18.8% year-on-year, marking its fastest increase in nearly 49 years, supported by rising semiconductor prices.
South Korea's economy had already recorded its fastest growth in more than five years in the first quarter, expanding by 1.7% quarter-on-quarter amid strong demand for semiconductors.
Growth remains 'heavily concentrated' in chip sector
However, analysts cautioned that South Korea's economic growth remained heavily reliant on the semiconductor industry.
"The risk is that growth stays heavily concentrated in the semiconductor sector, leaving South Korea exposed to a slowdown in global AI spending," said John Bromhead, a senior economist at Moody's Analytics.
The surge in semiconductor demand has also helped push the country's current account surplus to record highs.
South Korea posted a current account surplus of $116.6 billion (€100bn) in the second quarter.
Meanwhile, semiconductor exports soared by 218.7% year-on-year to $148 billion (€127bn) in the third quarter, according to government figures.

Russia and Ukraine have begun a local ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, both sides said Tuesday, but strikes continued elsewhere across Ukrainian and Russian territory, with several people being reported killed.
The ceasefire, which the Trump administration announced last week, should enable deliveries of humanitarian aid as well as evacuations from the frontline town as its residents grapple with acute shortages of food and medicine.
“As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments,” Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said in a Facebook post confirming Russia’s timing of its halt.
On Telegram, Russia’s Defense Ministry said it stopped shelling in the area of Kherson as it prepared for the ceasefire around Oleshky, which is located nearby.
Despite the local ceasefire, Ukraine and Russia continued to trade strikes elsewhere overnight.
In western Russia’s Bryansk region, Ukrainian drone attacks killed two people and wounded at least six others, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said Tuesday.
The first victim was killed when an explosive was dropped from a drone, Kovalchuk said. He later confirmed the death of a 67-year-old man in the same area.
Elsewhere, authorities in the Belgorod region said one woman was killed and seven people were injured over the past 24 hours.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 222 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Monday night and Tuesday morning.
In Ukraine, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one and wounded 15 others, including students in a dormitory. Overnight Russian attacks also killed and injured people in the cities of Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
Meanwhile, in the partially occupied Zaporizhzhia region, Kremlin-installed authorities said one person was killed and 30 others were injured when a Ukrainian drone struck an inter-regional passenger bus.

President Isaac Herzog cast his ballot in the elections for the 26th Knesset on Tuesday at a polling station in Jerusalem. After submitting his vote, the president called on all Israeli citizens to go out and vote too.
“Michal and I are very proud to be here today as millions of Israelis will go to the ballot box to vote and take their fate into their hands in a true, proud, and dignified democracy,” Herzog said. “This is the story of Israel, an incredible nation going to vote and deciding on our future.”
“I call upon all citizens of the state: we are all equal; this is our day to go out, make an impact, and vote,” he said. “Tomorrow, we will all continue here together; we have no other country.”
Herzog said he met a group of wounded IDF soldiers participating in a rehabilitation program the night before. “I told them that, among other reasons, they went out to fight so that we could experience this day, so that we could exercise Israeli democracy,” he said, calling voting “a tremendous privilege.”
The president also thanked the Central Elections Committee and said he hoped for “a true celebration of democracy,” adding, “We will not let anyone spoil or sabotage this.”
According to the Central Elections Committee, there are over 7.3 million eligible voters, 12,018 polling stations, about 100,000 workers and 450 million ballots printed, on a budget of NIS 690 million ($223.3 million).

====================================================================================================

Africa is more than its crises, but the West won’t let you see it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:16:02 UTC
18:16:02 KST

Africa is more than its crises, but the West won’t let you see it
When it comes to media in all its formats, Africa does not lack voices. It has thousands of newspapers, radio stations, television channels and digital platforms. What it often lacks is equal power to shape international conversations about its own affairs, and the resources to ensure that African perspectives reach audiences beyond the continent. The real challenge is who sets the agenda, the background and chooses the frames through which events are understood, breaking out of the stereotypes. And above all, who decides which voices deserve to be heard.
There is an important distinction between challenging an unequal international media landscape and achieving genuine media independence. The real test of the emerging Russia–Africa media cooperation will be whether it strengthens African media institutions’ ability to investigate, hold power to account and tell stories on their own terms.
Research published by the European Council on Foreign Relations in October 2025 reported that more than 1,000 African journalists had completed RT Africa training courses across 35 countries. Although the report presents this as part of Russia’s expanding media influence on the continent, the figure illustrates the reach of RT’s professional engagement with African journalists. It does not, however, establish that the journalists share Moscow’s political objectives or are becoming Russian mouthpieces. Far from it.
Separately, BBC Monitoring reported, citing the South African Institute of International Affairs, that as many as 4,000 African news websites republish content from RT and Sputnik, a Russian news agency. This is an estimate of the network’s potential reach, not a measure of audience size or editorial allegiance.
However, the underlying issue is not simply whether Russian media are gaining a foothold in Africa, but whether greater access to international content and training can strengthen African journalism’s independence. Research by Africa No Filter, analyzing 60 African news outlets across 15 countries in 2020, found that approximately one-third of stories in the surveyed outlets about Africa were sourced from non-African news services. The findings point to a structural problem: African newsrooms often rely on external sources to cover the continent itself simply because they lack the means to do the field work themselves.
A 2024 Global Media Index for Africa, produced by the University of Cape Town, South Africa, in partnership with Africa No Filter and The Africa Center, analyzed more than 1,000 articles published by 20 international news organizations over six months.
Its findings offer grounds for questioning how major Western outlets portray the continent. Africa is covered through a narrow set of crises, while the lives, ideas and achievements of its people receive less international attention.
The Washington Post, for example, scored just 29% for diversity of topics, while the Wall Street Journal covered the fewest African countries among the outlets assessed, with a score of 31%. The study also found that reporting across the sample privileged political and business elites over ordinary Africans.
The relationship between media and power has a long history that predates today’s digital platforms and geopolitical competition. During the era of slavery and European colonial expansion, newspapers helped shape how readers understood Africa, its people and the economic systems, built around their exploitation. Their positions were not uniform: some publications campaigned against slavery, while others defended the interests of enslavers or opposed more radical demands for emancipation. The Manchester Guardian, for example, supported abolition but also argued that enslavers should be compensated for losing “their property.”
This reveals a wider contradiction: abolition was championed even as the interests of slaveholders and traders were protected. The historical question, therefore, is not whether all Western media defended slavery or colonialism, but how economic and political power shaped the stories told about Africa – and whose voices were given authority. Literal slavery is here being minimized as a human issue in the first place.
The same question of whose perspective shapes the story is relevant to contemporary demands for reparative justice. African and Caribbean governments and campaigners have long argued that slavery and colonial rule were systems whose consequences continue to shape economic and social inequalities. Yet these demands can be presented in international coverage primarily as disputes over money, political controversy or diplomatic embarrassment, rather than as challenges to the historical and legal foundations of the present order.
Jamaica’s September 2026 petition to King Charles III offers a concrete example. It asked the King to refer questions about the legality of the enslavement of Africans, possible breaches of international law and Britain’s obligation to provide a remedy to the Privy Council; it did not demand a specified payment. Nevertheless, some coverage framed the issue around the prospect of a multibillion-dollar bill, prompting Jamaica’s culture minister to stress that the petition was about legal questions, not a monetary claim.
This is where Russia-Africa media cooperation can be assessed by more than the number of journalists trained or alternative outlets made available. Challenging Western dominance of international news is not, by itself, the same as securing media independence. Russian media can offer African audiences and journalists perspectives that differ from those of Western outlets, but the same scrutiny must apply to their ownership, funding, editorial priorities and relationship with political power. The meaningful measure of cooperation is whether it helps African newsrooms develop the professional freedom to investigate their own governments, question foreign partners and report beyond the narratives promoted by either side.
Maybe what should be ask is this: not whether Africa should choose between Western and Russian narratives, but whether African journalists have the freedom to develop their own narratives, bring home know-how and strengthen their media institutions at home. That requires investment in African-owned media, stronger local news networks and editorial independence from both foreign powers and domestic authorities.
Africa’s media landscape should no longer be viewed through the prism of Cold War rivalries, in which facts risk being distorted to serve one side at the expense of the truth. Nor should Western media dominance, with its persistent stereotypes and narrow framing of the continent, remain the norm. Africa does not need another outside power to speak for it; it needs the conditions in which its own journalists can be heard, taken seriously and trusted to hold power to account.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

In short:
Olympic gold medallist Tom Slingsby says Tribeca Loyal could break the Sydney to Hobart race record "by a lot" if it gets the right conditions in this year's race.
Tribeca Loyal, owned and skippered by Anthony Bell, is a renamed version of last year's line honours winner and race record-holder, Comanche.
What's next?
The Sydney to Hobart will begin in Sydney Harbour on Boxing Day.
A decade after his last appearance in the Sydney to Hobart Yacht Race, Anthony Bell has unveiled a new Loyal boat to challenge for line honours in this year's race.
But it's not a new boat — it's an old one.
Bell was first to Hobart in 2011 with Investec Loyal and in 2016 with Perpetual Loyal, setting a then-race record in the latter race of one day 13 hours, 31 minutes and 20 seconds.
On Tuesday in Sydney, Bell revealed his boat for this year's edition of the bluewater classic — the race record-holder and last year's winner, Comanche.
Bell spent up big to buy the five-time line honours-winning boat, which will race on Boxing Day as Tribeca Loyal.
Bell, the owner and skipper of the supermaxi, is aiming to lift the J.H. Illingworth Challenge Cup for a third time.
He has again recruited America's Cup and Olympic gold medallist Tom Slingsby to serve as the crew's sailing master.
The three-time world sailor of the year is delighted to be working on a yacht with the quality and power of Comanche.
"It's the most powerful supermaxi there is in the world," Slingsby said in Sydney.
"There's times there where we actually try to slow the boat down because it's got so much power and the waves could be too big that you're flying off the waves too fast.
"It averages really high speeds, it loves it when it's windy, so it's an exciting boat. You wouldn't want to choose any other boats to do the home run on.
"This boat already owns the Sydney Hobart race record, but … if we get the right conditions, we can break that record by a lot."
Despite his past success with Loyal, the 2012 Olympic gold medallist admits sailing on the open seas is a long way from his comfort zone.
"I'm not an ocean racer," Slingsby declared.
"I'm more of the short-course stuff.
"It's not something that I'm good at and really want to do, but I love coming back."
A major motivation for Slingsby and the crew is the continuing partnership with the Humpty Dumpty Foundation, which raises money for life-saving infant medical equipment for Australian hospitals.
The worthy cause is why Loyal will once again take on some celebrity deckhands to boost its fundraising profile.
Former Wallaby turned Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh and Sydney Roosters great Anthony Minichello are among the famous names heading south.
"I certainly don't miss the contact of playing rugby league, but the camaraderie, and everyone being laser-focused on achieving a goal, that's the stuff you do miss when you retire from professional sport," Minichello said.
This year's star-studded crew continues the tradition for Loyal to rely on some unconventional athletes taking up a new sport.
"We've had 21 people who represented Australia, won world surfing titles, gold medals, played for the Wallabies, played rugby league, and we have two TV Week Gold Logie winners as well," Bell said.

Australia’s national broadcaster will send a cease and desist letter to the rightwing populist party One Nation for using Bluey in a “shocking and disrespectful” cartoon which sees the beloved character repeatedly ramming politicians with an SUV.
The ABC’s managing director, Hugh Marks, told Senate estimates on Tuesday he became aware of One Nation’s potential breach of intellectual property last week and sought legal advice. “We will be taking further action, I can assure you,” he said.
The legal dispute came to light after the Western Australian Labor senator Varun Ghosh asked the ABC if it had sought legal advice over the 2024 political cartoon, called State of Melbourne, which has had 1.3m views on YouTube so far.
“I appreciate it was published two years ago, but has a particular poignancy in the last week,” Ghosh, the communications committee chair, said.
Estimates was held a week after the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines outside the politician’s northern Victorian electorate office, which led to her losing both legs.
Marks said he believed the use is a clear breach of intellectual property and “a cease and desist letter should be issued”.
He revealed the ABC had been in contact with Bluey’s international distributor, BBC Studios, and the Brisbane-based creators Ludo. He said Pauline Hanson’s party had not sought permission to use the children’s character in the hit show. The BBC, Ludo and One Nation have been approached for comment.
“It’s not a parody of any Bluey work,” Marks said. “It’s not a minor use of the [intellectual property]. In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property, number one. But it’s also a shocking use of Australia’s most loved character.”
“In fact, probably the globally most loved character in a video. That is both shocking and disrespectful to the children of Australia who love that character so much.”
The animation shows Bluey behind the wheel striking a depiction of the former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, with an SUV, as well as TV host and conservationist Robert Irwin. Before he is run over, the Albanese character says to Bluey: “You’ve got that crazy look in your eyes”.
In one scene in the three-minute video, Andrews is at the wheel, Albanese is his passenger and the car deliberately runs over Bluey and Irwin. The politicians are then shown putting the bodies of Bluey and Irwin in the boot of the SUV.
In the hearing of the environment and communications committee, senators also heard evidence on other matters concerning the ABC.
Marks told them the ABC’s former news director Justin Stevens received a termination payout of $353,230 because he did not want him to work out his notice.
“Following Mr Stevens’s resignation, we had the option to ask Mr Stevens to continue to work through his notice period, or for me to ask him not to work out his notice period,” Marks said.
“I felt it was important, given what had happened, that I asked him not to work out his period, and to pay him his contractual entitlement to do so.
“I felt it was important that we move forward with new leadership. So I didn’t want to continue Mr Stevens in that role.”
Stevens, whose total remuneration for the financial year was $864,394, was replaced by Reuters executive Simon Robinson last month after a 19-year career at the public broadcaster. His base salary was $529,202, according to the annual report.
Marks told senators “mistakes” were made in the production of programs by former Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal but the entire leadership of Four Corners had now been replaced.
The ABC has removed several programs made by the sacked bikie turned journalist because of concerns over his use of anonymous interviewees.
“We did a review of Mr Fazal’s work and found substantial flaws in much of that work,” he said.
“I think we can take confidence that there are many great people who do work for Four Corners. And with new editorial leadership, we are obviously very confident as to its future.”
The ABC said it was reviewing its editorial guidance about the use of anonymous sources in light of the Fazal incident.
Sally Neighbour, a former Four Corners executive producer, alleged in the Monthly that “an associate of Fazal played different roles in different stories, disguised behind a mask”.
Fazal has previously said he stands by his reporting. In July, he said he was “shocked” by the removal of the two Four Corners episodes and that he believed the ABC’s process and decisions “set a worrying precedent for the organisation’s independence and commitment to public-interest journalism”.

UK prosecutors charge two after RAF Fairford incident
British Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir charged under the National Security Act.
British prosecutors say they have charged two men with offences under the National Security Act following an incident in September at RAF Fairford, an airbase in England used by the United States.
British Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir, both aged 24, were charged under the National Security Act, the Crown Prosecution Service said. They are due to appear in court later on Tuesday.
Abdulkarim is charged with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of the United Kingdom’s Counter Terrorism Policing, said police believed the country Abdulkarim was assisting was Iran.
Essghir was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
Both men live in Westminster, a district in London.
The airbase in Gloucestershire, southwestern England, had been used by US bombers to carry out attacks on Iran this year.
Essghir was arrested outside the base on September 27, when armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Dozens of residents were evacuated from their homes as police and experts searched for explosives.
Abdulkarim was arrested in the past week. Six other men remain on bail, all living in London and aged between 23 and 25, as investigations continue.
Shortly after the incident at the base, US B-1 bombers were withdrawn from the site.
“We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state and, as the Director General of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat,” Taylor said in a statement.
Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec, reporting from London, said police initially commented that they were considering all avenues and that they were not ruling out a state actor.
“But at the time, they didn’t go so far as to point towards Iran – although US President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were fairly quick to say they believed that there was credible evidence to suggest Iran was involved,” she said.
“It’s only in the past few days that police who have been in charge of this investigation have increasingly said they believe there is evidence that Iran is involved,” she added.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last week said the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Iran’s ambassador to the UK has denied.
Last year, the UK said there had been 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK.
In July, Britain used new powers to ban support for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and a linked group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which had claimed responsibility for seven attacks earlier this year at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities and Persian-language media.

Actual Swiss wages increase by 0.5% in 2026

Actual Swiss wages increase by 0.5% in 2026
Actual and minimum wages in Switzerland are set to rise by an average of 0.5% and 0.8% respectively in 2026. This was announced on Monday by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), based on the provisions of the main collective labour agreements (CLAs).
The average increase of 0.5% in actual wages, agreed by the social partners in the main collective labour agreements, was broken down into 0.3% at individual level and 0.2% at collective level. According to inflation forecasts for 2026 (+0.6%), real wages in sectors covered by collective agreements are not expected to rise this year. The agreements on actual wages cover just under 700,000 people.
In detail, the increase in actual wages was 0.2% in the secondary sector and 0.8% in the tertiary sector. Among the economic sectors, the largest increases were recorded in transport and storage (+1.2%), Financial and insurance activities (+1%) and professional, scientific and technical activities (+0.8%). Manufacturing and construction saw more modest increases, of 0.3% and 0.2% respectively.
More
Median annual salary in Switzerland rose to CHF87,000 in 2025
As regards minimum wages, the average increase of 0.8% in 2026 follows rises of 1% in 2025 and 2% in 2024. More than 1.85 million people are covered by a collective labour agreement (CLA) that includes statutory provisions on minimum wages and for whom agreements have been concluded.
Minimum wage increases varied by sector: +0.3% in the secondary sector and +0.8% in the tertiary sector. Among the sectors, ‘unclassified activities’ (commercial employees and sales staff) stood out with +2.3%, followed by ‘financial and insurance activities’ (+1.8%) and ‘other service activities’ (+1.5%). The lowest increases were recorded in manufacturing (+0.1%) and accommodation and food service activities (+0.2%).

Putin to host 22 African leaders in Moscow

The accompanying Economic and Humanitarian Forum will cover agriculture, energy, mining, finance, and technology, with around 4,000 Russian and African entrepreneurs invited.
The gathering follows the 2019 Sochi summit, attended by 43 African heads of state or government, and the 2023 St. Petersburg summit, which drew delegations from 48 African countries, including 17 heads of state. He noted that the number of people injured in a Russian strike on a university campus and the surrounding area the previous evening had risen to 12, five of them students or university staff.
“While emergency services were helping people and dealing with the aftermath of the first strike, the Russians launched another ballistic missile attack. A total of 16 ballistic missiles were launched overnight, along with more than 280 drones. Unfortunately, there have been casualties, and targets in Kyiv were hit, including the Southern Bridge. This is a serious escalation in Russia’s campaign targeting our logistics,” the President said.
He added that strikes had also targeted the Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, and Kherson regions, as well as Chernivtsi region. In almost every region, Zelensky said, Russia’s targets were energy facilities, logistics, and civilian urban infrastructure.
As Ukrinform previously reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky said the previous day that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on the supply of missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

18:10:57 KST

Ukraine’s Ambassador to the United Kingdom and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), Valeriy Zaluzhny, believes that the war in Ukraine persists due to the weakness of the Western world and its security system—a system that requires a new military doctrine reflecting the realities of modern warfare.
"The West needs to step out of its comfort zone and into the reality of what war looks like in 2026; it must shed the illusion that outdated guarantees and doctrines can truly protect it and its children," Zaluzhny wrote in a Facebook post.
According to him, the Western security system remains rooted in a World War II-era doctrine, merely supplemented by expensive, high-precision weaponry whereas modern conditions demand a comprehensive overhaul of approaches to combat operations.
Zaluzhny emphasized that for the West to ensure its own security, it is not enough to simply procure new weapons or adjust tactics to account for the use of drones.
"The West needs a new doctrine to defend itself. For us in the military, a doctrine is a 'Bible of war'—it integrates all components of the armed forces—weaponry, tactics, structure, training, and funding—into a unified system," he noted.
Zaluzhny stated that such a doctrine would enable the assessment of the impact of new technologies, adaptation to change, and the planning of joint operations. "A relevant, up-to-date doctrine means security for your children and for your state. No other commitments will save you," he wrote.
He added that the West still possesses sophisticated and costly technologies that could help build a new security system; however, the key factor remains the willingness to step out of one’s comfort zone and take collective action. According to Zaluzhny, only by working together can the war for the future of our children be won.
Zaluzhny also mentioned that he addressed officers from various nations at the Joint Services Command and Staff College of the UK Defence Academy, where they are preparing for senior command roles, and noted the participation of Ukrainian military personnel with firsthand combat experience in the training program. Among them is a Hero of Ukraine, Lieutenant Colonel Serhiy Roschin, a squadron commander who has been defending the Ukrainian skies since 2022.

Migrant workers urge Taiwan to strengthen protections for pregnant caregivers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:10:55 UTC
18:10:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Migrant worker groups protested outside the health ministry Tuesday, calling for stronger labor protections and better home care services amid concerns over pregnant caregivers, CNA reported.
Taiwan relies too heavily on families hiring migrant caregivers directly, worker groups said, leaving both workers and employers with too much responsibility. They urged the government to provide more affordable and flexible home care services.
The Taiwan Care Workers' Union said many migrant caregivers work long hours without clear limits. It urged the government to gradually replace direct household employment with a system in which professional care organizations hire caregivers and provide services to families.
Taiwan prohibits employers from firing migrant caregivers because they become pregnant. However, household caregivers are not covered by the Labor Standards Act, and their maternity leave is unpaid, per the labor ministry.
At a separate protest outside the labor ministry, employers and families raised concerns about finding replacement caregivers. They said families caring for people with severe disabilities could be left without enough support for months when their regular caregivers cannot work.
The Taiwan Association of Families with Disabilities and Migrant Caregiver Employers called for a government agency to oversee recruitment, insurance, training, and job placement to help families maintain care.
The labor ministry said that if a caregiver cannot perform the required work, both sides may agree to end the contract, allowing the employer to apply for a replacement under existing rules.
The health ministry said it would work with the labor ministry to improve care services and support for families. Since September 2025, households employing migrant caregivers have had greater access to government-supported services, including care provided outside the home.
The labor ministry said the government has allocated about NT$2 billion (US$63 million) for respite and short-term care services. Eligible households can receive a combined total of up to 52 days of support annually when regular caregivers are unavailable, per Liberty Times.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taitung District Court ruled Tuesday that bail for former Taitung County Magistrate Wu Chun-li (吳俊立) would be raised to NT$7 million (US$215,500) after prosecutors appealed the previous NT$5 million bail decision.
The court reasoned that although evidence not yet secured by prosecutors remained at risk of destruction, Wu’s hospitalization for heart treatment, along with the completion of relevant searches and the seizure of his cellphone, had significantly reduced that risk, per Liberty Times. The court said NT$7 million in bail and travel restrictions would be sufficient to deter him from fleeing or interfering with the investigation.
Prosecutors suspect Wu of pressuring the county government to undertake public works projects that benefited his family, including road-widening projects near resort development sites owned by his family. The investigation has also led to the detention of Chiu Chia-ping (邱嘉平), an aide to Wu’s sister, Taitung County Council Speaker Wu Hsiu-hua (吳秀華), as well as two Taitung County Government officials, Hsu Chia-hao (許家豪) and Tsai Ming-han (蔡明翰), per CNA.
Prosecutors detained Wu at a Kaohsiung hospital on Monday after he failed to physically appear at a detention hearing that morning. Asked by the media about the incident, Wu said he had applied for two days of leave to prepare for heart surgery scheduled for Wednesday, per China Times.
Wu accused prosecutors of overstepping their authority, describing the incident as an erosion of human rights protections. After the presiding judge granted bail, Wu’s family posted the NT$7 million bond and took him back to the family residence, per ETtoday.
Wu’s defense team objected to his treatment, questioning whether prosecutors had obtained a medical assessment to determine if he was fit to leave the hospital, per SETN. The team emphasized that the court had approved his leave, adding that Wu had agreed to attend the evening hearing in person after prosecutors objected to his absence.
Wu’s lawyers questioned whether prosecutors’ insistence on detaining him at the hospital was intended to create what they described as the false impression that he was evading court proceedings.
The Taitung District Prosecutors Office responded by highlighting its efforts to verify whether Wu needed to remain hospitalized for further treatment, per Tai Sounds. It said the detention decision took both Wu’s health and the ongoing investigation into account.
Prosecutors also noted that the subsequent court proceedings would determine the legality of the detention.
Wu Chun-li manages Wu Hsiu-hua's Taitung County magistrate campaign.

Congo's Ebola cases surpass 10,000 as fears grow of wider African spread
Oct 27 - The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo has risen above 10,000, government data showed on Tuesday, a milestone that coincides with growing fears the epidemic could spread to more African countries.
The latest situation report from Congo's public health institute put the number of cases at 10,060, with those killed by the virus reaching 4,887.
The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, was announced in mid-May and has since become the largest and deadliest in Congo, surpassing a 2018-2020 epidemic.
It is now the second-largest and second-deadliest on record behind only the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first case and went on to announce nine cases in total, after a man who had travelled from Congo via Uganda died in Nairobi.
Last week, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case.
Health officials have been seeking to work out how and where the patient — the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who had not travelled to Congo — contracted the disease. The Swiss government said she was believed to have contracted it in Uganda.
The woman and her husband were flown to hospitals in Switzerland on Monday.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Ugandan officials say the country does not have any Ebola cases.
Uganda's health minister said on Sunday that Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Congo would be quarantined for 21 days. REUTERS
