Bunun people’s farming practices featured in COP17 report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:10:31 UTC
18:10:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The traditional farming practices of the Bunun people have been highlighted in the latest edition of Local Biodiversity Outlooks, a report presented at the COP17 biodiversity conference in Yerevan, Armenia.
The report, presented last week, examines 56 cases of how Indigenous and local communities around the world preserve and sustain biodiversity. One features a collective of Bunun farmers in Zhuoqing Village, Hualien County.
Tse-Xin Organic Agriculture Foundation, which has collaborated with the farmers for more than a decade to revive traditional agricultural practices, said the case study from Taiwan underscores “the key value of Indigenous agricultural wisdom in conservation and sustainable development,” per CNA.
Zhuoqing Village sits at the edge of Yushan National Park, and according to recent government data, the vast majority of its 1,235 residents are Bunun.
Research shows the Bunun’s relationship with the land has gone through a profound change over the past century due to colonization and forced resettlement, with farming shifting from diversified cultivation to rice monoculture.
The revival of traditional farming practices began in 2013, when a young man who had returned to the village took over his family’s rice paddies and persuaded fellow farmers to pursue organic cultivation, according to the report.
The farmers began working with the foundation in 2014, focusing on documenting traditional practices and preserving local crop seeds, especially legumes.
One way the farmers and the foundation preserve Indigenous knowledge is through a mentorship program that pairs six elders with six young participants. Each month, the young participants visit their mentors’ gardens to record crop types, planting arrangements, plant growth, and surrounding wildlife.
Over 12 years, 20 hectares of farmland in the village have been converted to organic production, conserving local varieties of beans and grains, the foundation said.
“Indigenous peoples and local communities are by no means passive aid recipients,” the foundation added. “They are the most important rights-holders and guardians in achieving global biodiversity goals.”

French consumer confidence hits a 2013 low in October amid protests

French consumer confidence hits a 2013 low in October amid protests
- French consumer confidence fell to 80 in October, its lowest since June 2013, as protests, political unrest and austerity fears hit sentiment, INSEE said.
- Households grew more worried about prices, jobs and finances. Views on saving weakened, and Bloomberg Economics warned weak sentiment could hurt spending and fourth-quarter growth.
- The government announced school and university reforms to calm unrest, but protests and strikes are set to continue. Inflation may rise to 3.6%, with growth near 0.1%.
AI generated
French consumer confidence fell by five points to 80 in October, its lowest level since June 2013, amid widespread protests in the country, official statistics agency INSEE said on Oct 27.
The country is being hit by a wave of protests, which began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris in September to denounce school conditions and swiftly broadened into a wider demonstration against the government’s economic policies.
Economists surveyed by Reuters and Bloomberg had expected confidence to be around 85, the same as the revised September number and the latest figure is below any economist forecast.
The latest consumer confidence level is well below a long-term average of 100 between January 1987 and December 2025. The reading has been below 100 for five years amid bouts of inflation and political and budget instability and consumers are gloomy over a host of indicators.
The backdrop has worsened significantly in recent weeks with the minority government entering another showdown over austerity measures, a surge in borrowing costs as investors dump French bonds and an escalation of student protests.
The tensions boiled over on Oct 17 with violence breaking out around cost-of-living demonstrations, looting across the country and thousands of arrests.
INSEE’s latest consumer confidence measure does not reflect the full impact of the upheaval: while the cut-off was Oct 19, most of the responses are collected at the start of the three-week survey period.
“Weak sentiment is likely to weigh on spending as political uncertainty increases. This brings further downside risks to our fourth-quarter growth forecast,” said Jean Dalbard, economist at Bloomberg Economics.
In an attempt to calm the unrest that began with students blocking high schools, the French government announced on Oct 26 that it will overhaul the system for allocating university places, limit some class sizes and provide loans for building renovations.
But protests are set to continue on Saturdays as well as a day of demonstrations and strikes on Nov 5 that is backed by the country’s biggest trade unions.
The proportion of consumers who believe that prices have risen sharply over the past 12 months has risen by eight points, having already gained six points in September.
Data on Oct 30 is expected to show inflation accelerated further to 3.6% this month. A reading of gross domestic product, also due that day, will likely reveal that the economy expanded only 0.1% in the third quarter after stagnating in the previous three months and contracting at the start of 2026.
The INSEE survey found that households’ sentiment towards their past and future personal financial situations has dropped by nine and six points, respectively.
Fears over the trend in unemployment are on the rise again, up by five points following a fall in September.
The proportion of households considering this a good time for savings has fallen by six points, while views on their current ability to save remain stable. REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

The Israeli army continued a large-scale offensive in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron for a fifth consecutive day on Tuesday, forcing nearly 5,000 Palestinians from their homes.
Hebron municipality said 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families had been forcibly displaced from the Deir Bahha and Al Jilda areas since the campaign began on Friday.
Among those displaced are 336 infants, 441 elderly people, 216 pregnant and nursing women, 44 people with disabilities and 312 people with chronic illnesses, the municipality said, warning of growing humanitarian consequences.
The army has shut entrances to Hebron and surrounding villages since Friday, following a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.
Anadolu footage showed Palestinians being stopped, searched and mistreated by Israeli forces at military checkpoints near Al Jilda Roundabout. Witnesses said reinforcements arrived in Ein Deir Baha, where troops took over Palestinian buildings and turned them into military posts.
The Palestinian Prisoner Society said the army had arrested 85 Palestinians across Hebron governorate since Friday.
Raids and closures across the West Bank
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces arrested at least nine Palestinians during raids and closed all main entrances to Ramallah.
In the northern West Bank, troops raided Jenin’s eastern neighbourhood and the towns of Meithalun, Jaba and Qabatiya, arresting at least six Palestinians, according to local sources.
In the central West Bank, Israeli forces closed Ramallah’s main entrances, including the Ein Sinya and Atara checkpoints, the Rawabi gate and the Nabi Saleh and Aboud gates, and set up additional checkpoints on alternative roads.
In Al Bireh, troops turned a Palestinian home into a military post, held four residents inside and confiscated their phones, local sources said.
Farmers were also expelled from their land in Turmus Ayya, while troops raided Tuqu, southeast of Bethlehem, with tracked military vehicles.
In Hebron governorate, troops repeatedly raided Taffuh and searched the homes of former prisoners. Israeli forces also assaulted and arrested a Palestinian man and his son in the Hawara area south of Hebron, according to local sources.
Illegal settler attacks and outposts
Separately, Israeli occupiers set fire to three Palestinian vehicles early Tuesday in Umm Safa, west of Ramallah.
Village municipal chief Marwan Sabah told Anadolu that attackers entered around midnight and set the vehicles ablaze. Residents confronted the group, forcing it to withdraw, he said.
Sabah said Umm Safa had repeatedly faced attacks involving assaults, vehicle arson, intimidation and harassment, adding that occupiers had seized large areas of village land.
Israeli occupiers also established a settlement outpost at Al Bireh’s northern entrance, overlooking the Al Balou neighbourhood, the Bedouin rights group Al-Baidar said.
According to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, occupiers attempted to establish 21 new settlement outposts across the West Bank in September, including 10 in Ramallah and Al Bireh governorate.
The incidents come amid intensified Israeli army raids and attacks by Israeli occupiers across the occupied West Bank since Israel launched its war on Gaza in October 2023.

Israel election turnout hits 45-year high at 16.68% by 10 a.m.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:07:25 UTC
18:07:25 KST

Voter turnout in Israel's parliamentary election reached 44.9% by 2 p.m. Tuesday, surpassing the 38.9% recorded at the same hour in the previous election, the Central Elections Committee announced. According to official figures, 3,290,480 Israelis had cast their ballots by that time. "We've broken all records," said attorney Din Livne, the committee's acting director-general, as long lines formed at polling stations across the country.
Turnout was also high among military personnel. The IDF Spokesperson's Unit reported that 48% of service members had voted by 1 p.m., compared with 44.4% at the same hour during the election for the 25th Knesset.
A breakdown of turnout by city revealed significant differences across the country. By noon, 28.8% of eligible voters in Tel Aviv had cast their ballots, compared with 27.1% in Jerusalem, 27.3% in Haifa, 29% in Rishon LeZion and 27.4% in Be'er Sheva.
Among the municipalities included in the committee's figures, Modi'in-Maccabim-Re'ut recorded particularly high participation at 36.7%, followed by Modi'in Illit at 33.2%. Turnout reached 31.4% in Kiryat Ata, 30.4% in Ashdod and 30.3% in Sderot. Lower figures were recorded in Netanya at 23.8%, Nazareth at 24.9% and Eilat at 22.2%.
The midday figures followed an already strong start to voting. By 10 a.m., turnout had reached 16.68%, the highest recorded at that hour since 1981. More than 1.2 million Israelis had cast their ballots during the opening hours, an increase of 0.78 percentage points compared with the same stage of the previous election, when turnout stood at 15.9%.
Voting was also significantly higher among military personnel. According to the IDF, 48% of eligible service members had voted by 1 p.m., compared with 44.4% at the same hour during the previous election.
A total of 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote in the election for the 26th Knesset, with 36 parties competing for seats in the 120-member parliament. Some 12,018 polling stations are operating nationwide, with most remaining open until 10 p.m.
Early reports indicated considerable voter interest, with long lines forming at polling stations in Ra'anana, Ramat Gan and other cities. At a school in Ra'anana, one voter expressed surprise at the unusually large morning crowds, saying she had never encountered such a long line so early on election day.
Livne acknowledged the lengthy queues, saying the high turnout had inevitably led to delays as election officials carefully verified each voter's identity. He urged citizens to remain patient and promised that everyone who arrived before the deadline would be able to vote.
"We promise that everyone will get to vote," Livne said, explaining that polling stations would remain open beyond 10 p.m. if necessary to accommodate voters already waiting in line by that time.
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg acknowledged the inconvenience caused by the queues, noting that voters were waiting between 15 and 20 minutes at some polling stations. However, he said the strong participation demonstrated that Israelis were determined to exercise their democratic rights despite the country's political divisions.
President Isaac Herzog, who voted in Jerusalem alongside his wife Michal, urged Israelis to participate in the democratic process. He described election day as a celebration of democracy and called on citizens not to allow political divisions to undermine the vote.
"This is our day to go out, make a difference and vote," Herzog said, emphasizing that all citizens have an equal voice at the ballot box.
Shin Bet Director David Zini also addressed the Central Elections Committee's control center, saying the election was being conducted safely and under close supervision despite attempts by some individuals to disrupt the process.
The committee separately dismissed reports of systematic damage to ballot slips belonging to political parties, saying it had found no evidence of widespread tampering. Officials stressed that individual complaints were being examined immediately and urged voters to rely on official information.
Voting is taking place under unsettled weather conditions. The Israel Meteorological Service issued a yellow warning for thunderstorms and lightning between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., with rain, strong winds and possible hail forecast across parts of the country. Flash floods are also possible in southern Israel.
Although most polling stations will close at 10 p.m., when television networks release their exit polls, the final outcome may remain uncertain for several days. Between 600,000 and 650,000 Israelis are expected to cast special double-envelope ballots, primarily soldiers, reservists and displaced residents voting away from their registered polling stations.
Those ballots could affect the distribution of approximately 15 parliamentary seats and potentially change the balance between competing political blocs. Election officials expect to complete the full count by Thursday afternoon, meaning the final allocation of seats may remain unresolved beyond election night.

EU readying for major Australian resources investment, ambassador says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:07:16 CET
18:07:16 KST

By Melanie Burton
SYDNEY, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The European Union expects a wave of investment into the Australian critical minerals sector as it pushes to diversify its supply chain away from China, the bloc’s ambassador to Australia Lawrence Meredith said on Tuesday.
Australia and the European Union struck a free trade agreement in March after eight years of negotiations, removing tariffs on almost all goods and easing EU access to Australian critical minerals.
Once both parties sign and ratify that agreement, expected early next year, a 5.5% EU tariff on critical minerals will be removed.
“It is going to be a game changer,” Meredith said.
In parallel, talks are “very close” for Australia to sign a memorandum of understanding with the European Investment Bank, which would act as the bloc’s funding vehicle, Meredith added.
“The European Union will be massively investing in critical minerals. Since we wish to diversify away from China, then one of the most likely partners has to be Australia,” he said.
EU policy proposals have laid out as much as €10 billion ($11.2 billion) for critical raw materials within the larger €409 billion competitiveness fund, as the EU debates its budget from 2028 to 2034.
Australia is one of several critical minerals “superpowers” in which the EU is looking to invest, including Brazil, South Africa and Canada. The EU also expects to invest along the supply chain, including in processing, Meredith said.
Australia said on Tuesday it would refresh its critical minerals strategy to place greater emphasis on refining and processing, as competition for investment intensifies and supply-chain concerns persist.
The bloc is looking initially at the minerals that Australia will prioritise for its strategic reserve: gallium, antimony and rare earths.
Australian companies going faster through the early project development would speed the investment process, he said.
“(The FTA) is a signal that Europe wants to do far more with Australia. We also have a security and defence partnership. A lot of that is dual technology, and it requires precisely these critical minerals,” he said.
The European Union plans to mobilise €800 billion into defence under ReArm Europe by 2030.
Australia is also on track to join the EU’s flagship funding program for research and innovation, Horizon Europe, next year.
Meredith said 2026 had been a “transformational” year for Australian-EU relations.
“You’ve seen a big surge in EU-Australia in 2026, and I’m very confident we will go to the next level in 2027.”
($1 = 0.8961 euros)

Tories dismiss PM’s budget ‘everyday fixes’ as little more than ‘cheaper gherkins’, and ‘an insult to families’ – UK politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:07:05 UTC
18:07:05 KST

Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – UK politics live
Greens say Labour has ‘no respect for young people’ amid reports chancellor will pause equalisation of minimum wage for under-21s with that paid to older workers
Greens accuse Labour of breaking manifesto pledge, after minister signals minimum wage age equalisation being paused
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has not contested reports saying that, in the budget tomorrow, John Healey, the chancellor, will pause the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage paid to people under the age of 21 with the more generous national living wage that applies to older workers.
In an interview on the BBC this morning, Reynolds was asked to respond to a story suggesting the equalisation process has been put on hold because of concerns about youth unemployment.
John Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for young people after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs.
The Times has been told that the national living wage, which applies to those aged 21 and over, is expected to rise from £12.71 to around £13.20 – an increase of 3.9%.
However, Healey has decided not to repeat the big rises of the past two budgets in the national minimum wage, which applies to those aged 18 to 21. It will rise broadly in line with the rate for older workers – from £10.85 to around £11.27, an increase of 3.9%.
In its manifesto, Labour said it would raise the level of the national minimum wage to the level of the national living wage to “so all adults are entitled to the same minimum wage, delivering a pay rise to hundreds of thousands of workers across the UK”. The manifesto implied this would happen during this parliament, but in May Torsten Bell, the pensions minister, said implementation of this commitment could be delayed until after the general election – implying the government is worried equalisation now could increase youth unemployment.
Asked about the Times story on the Today programme, Reynolds insisted the new national living wage and national minimum wage rates would be announced tomorrow.
But he went on:
The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies, but it was always clear it would happen over time and we would take into account, as the minimum wage uprating each year always does, the relative strength of the labour market and other pressures …
Of course, you want not just good wages, but good work. And the way this has always been done – it is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account. That is the approach you will see confirmed [in the budget].
The Green party has accused Labour of breaking a manifesto promise. Responding to the Times’ story, and Reynolds’ comments in effect confirming it, Mothin Ali, the Greens’ co-deputy leader, said:
Anyone doing a day’s work, needs to be paid the same rate for the same job. A young person’s rent and food bill is no less because they are young, so they need to receive the same wage.
Healey and Burnham are now breaking a manifesto pledge to young people that even Starmer managed to keep. Labour have no respect for young people, who appear to just be there for cheap labour for the wealthy and their corporate donors.
Ali said the Greens would introduce a £15 minimum wage for workers of all ages.
Streeting signs defence agreement with Poland, describing it as 'one of UK's closest allies'
Britain and Poland have agreed to work together to build a new generation of air defence missiles, as the west gears up its defence efforts against Russia, the Press Association reports. PA says:
A new agreement, the Warsaw Defence Plan, will also see the two nations work together to build new drones and anti-drone measures, as well as collaborate closely on more traditional land, sea and air defence.
Defence secretary Wes Streeting signed the pact in Warsaw today, where he met his Polish counterpart Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Streeting said: “Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century.
“The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger Nato.
“From collaborating on Nato exercises that deter our adversaries to working together to support Ukraine in its fight for freedom, we are committed to standing together for European security whilst boosting our economies with stronger defence industries.”
Under the pact, the two nations will share their experiences of developing new warships. Britain’s Type 31 frigate and Poland’s Miecznik are based on a common design.
The allies have also agreed to increase shared patrols in the Baltic Sea, to protect vital communications cables on the seabed.
The agreement comes ahead of a major coalition of the willing exercise next month, which will see British, French and German forces join Warsaw’s soldiers in Poland for training to prepare for a peacekeeping mission in Ukraine once the war is over.
No 10 says Burnham to set out 'next steps' for long-term relations with EU around time of 20 November summit
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said this morning that British government officials would be talking to their EU counterparts about possible changes to the UK-EU relationship. Possible options include the UK joining the single market, and so free movement would be part of that discussion.
The government seems to be nervous about suggestions it is already in talks about the UK signing up for free movement rules and, at the Downing Street lobby briefing this morning, a No 10 spokesperson insisted free movement was not part of the current talks with the EU.
Those talks are “focused solely on next month’s summit, and the practical agreements that we hope to make there that will add billions to the economy and cut the red tape that holds back British business,” the spokesperson said.
She added:
Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements, on what is realistic for both sides, and, crucially, on what the British public supports. And the prime minister will set out the next steps when it comes to our longer term relationship around the time of the summit.
The summit will take place in Brussels on Friday 20 November.

Farage says Reform UK candidates would not be banned for liking Tommy Robinson
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, has suggested that someone would not be banned from standing as a candidate for his party just for liking a social media post from the far-right activist and provocateur Tommy Robinson.
In his Today programme interview, Nick Robinson, the presenter, asked about the recent ITV News undercover exposé of Reform UK, which included footage of a potential candidate who flagged up pro-Robinson social media posts as a potential problem being told he should just delete his social media account.
Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is currently on trial for harassment charges.
Asked if the ITV report showed that Reform UK’s vetting procedures were too lax, Farage said he “wouldn’t ban anybody for liking someone like Tommy Robinson”.
He went on:
[It] wouldn’t be my cup of tea, but I wouldn’t ban anybody from doing so … I don’t want us to get into a world of cancel culture.
When Nick Robinson asked if Farage was saying it would be OK for a Reform UK candidate to approve any post by Tommy Robinson, Farage said that would depend what the post said. But he went on:
I’m not going to have run a party where we say you can’t talk about that person or that person. We have to be sensible about vetting. And we are.
Farage also claimed that the BBC’s own experience with staff subsequently accused of paedophilia showed that all big organisations ran the risk of having rogue members or employees. And he claimed that Reform UK candidates were subject to a “much higher level” of scrutiny than candidates from other parties.
Referring to another person filmed in the exposé, a councillor with extreme racist views, Farage said that he was a former Conservative. When Nick Robinson put it to him that the ITV film suggested he had joined Reform UK because he realised he would be “among friends” there because other Reform UK members shared his views, Farage said that was “absolute cobblers”.
Back to “everyday fixes” (see 9.07am), and groups representing men have welcomed the news that self-employed men will be able to qualify for parental pay.
The Labour MP Amanda Martin, who co-chairs the Labour Men and Boys group, said:
I’ve long believed that self-employed dads deserve the same chance as everyone else to be there for their families when a new baby arrives, so I’m delighted that this is becoming a reality. It’s about time self-employed fathers got the support they deserve.
Self-employed tradies build our homes, fix our heating and keep our lights on, so ensuring they can access paternity leave is a proper mark of respect for the people who keep our country going. This will make a real difference to tens of thousands of dads each year, giving them the chance to welcome their children into the world and be present fathers without facing financial ruin. I’m especially pleased that self-employed dads in my home city of Portsmouth will benefit.
And George Gabriel, co-founder of the Dad Shift, which campaigns for better paternity leave rights, said:
Paternity leave is a cost of living lifeline for new families. This decision gives self-employed dads breathing space and a chance to show up for their loved ones when they’re needed the most.
The Women’s Budget Group, a feminist economic thinktank, has also welcomed the announcement. Eva Neitzert, its head of research and policy, said:
We’re pleased to see the chancellor recognise cost of living pressures on families and carers in his package of pre-announced measures. The lack of statutory paternity pay for self-employed fathers was a massive gap in parental leave …
We hope the chancellor will go further in his cost of living budget and increase statutory maternity pay as well. State support for new mum’s still sits at less than half of minimum wage beyond the first six weeks. Our cost benefit analysis of extending this to 12 weeks and raising pay to the national living wage found it was a net positive to the exchequer and would make the world of difference to families in the first nine months of their children’s lives.
Streeting says on visit to Poland that UK and Nato need to be ready for war with Russia
Jakub Krupa
Jakub Krupa writes the Guardian’s Europe live blog.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has warned that Russia’s Vladimir Putin is “testing us and testing Nato’s resolve” as he condemned hybrid threats and “state-sponsored terrorism” from Russia.
Streeting repeated his recent warnings that “we have to be ready for a scenario in which the United Kingdom and the Nato alliance finds itself at war with Russia”. He went on:
Not because we want war – we have no quarrel with the Russian people, and we have no desire for war with Russia; Nato is a defensive alliance – but when Putin gives assurances that he has no intentions to provoke a war with Nato, we are reminded of what he said about Ukraine only days before the invasion.
Speaking in Warsaw alongside Poland’s defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Streeting stressed Nato is ready “to defend every inch of Nato territory” and will continue its support for Ukraine.
The defence secretary added:
The more ready we are to face against Russia, to defend every inch of Nato territory, the less likely we are to find ourselves in that scenario.
Poland is one of our greatest and certainly our most reliable friend in Europe, and we value and treasure this friendship very much.
The partnership is “not simply about our shared history,” but also “our shared determination that in that contest between freedom and tyranny, the United Kingdom and Poland will not be bystanders.”
He said that UK forces will next month take part in major exercises as part of the multinational force for Ukraine.
An astonishing 80% of donations to Reform UK in the past 12 months have come from donors or companies recently based overseas, The Independent can reveal.
An analysis of data from the Electoral Commission shows the amount received from donors who were based abroad in the past two years by Nigel Farage’s party dwarfs that of other parties amid growing concern about overseas influence in British politics.
In comparison, Labour and the Conservatives received just 0.15% and 3.57% of their donations from people or companies based abroad respectively during the same period.
Asked about the Independent’s analysis in his Today programme interview, Farage said the conclusions were “completely wrong”.
He told the programme:
Whoever’s done this research doesn’t understand where people domicile, how they operate, where they live, and where they vote …
I can assure you, these people vote here, live here, some of them are international businessmen who travelled the world constantly. In the old days, we used to be proud of British pioneers that went out there and made a great success of their lives.
Asked why Reform UK was so reliant on donors who spent a lot of time abroad, Farage said it would be a lot easier for him if he could just “sell some peerages” like other parties.
(Of course, parties aren’t allowed to sell peerages. But Farage is right to say that donating large sums to a mainstream political party does seem to have a remarkably positive effect on one’s chance of getting a seat in the House of Lords.)
Treasury claims its food tariff cuts, combined with Rachel Reeves' tariff cuts, will cut consumer costs by up to £595m
It is not just gherkins where the Treasury is cutting import tariffs. (See 9.07am.) Here is the lists from the Treasury of mostly food imports where tariffs are being cut.
Garlic (8% + £100 per 100 kg)
Gherkins (12%)
Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes (20% + £19 per 100 kg)
Throat pastilles and cough drops (8%)
Boiled sweets, filled or unfilled (8%)

The Treasury also cut tariffs on some food imports in the summer. It says “together, the two packages are expected to reduce consumer costs by approximately £245m to £595m a year”.
When Andy Burnham opened a debate on revising the Brexit settlement in his Labour conference speech, he did so on the basis of a simple proposition. He declared: “I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good.”
The Conservatives have strongly attacked Burnham’s move – but mostly on the basis that the 2016 referendum decision should be honoured, that a new debate would be divisive and that Burnham’s initiative went against assurances he made during the Makerfield byelection. Very few Tories have challenged the proposition that “Brexit has done more harm than good”, and Kemi Badenoch has not seriously tried to take on this argument.

But, in an interview this morning on the Today programme, Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, did argue that Brexit had worked.
Asked if he regarded Brexit as a success, he replied:
Yes, I do. We certainly stand taller in the world. The terrible projections of doom as to what would happen to our financial sector etc haven’t happened. Our growth rates are higher than our European competitors. Our exports, particularly of services to the European Union, have actually rocketed. And we’ve now got more trade deals and more options around the rest of the world.
But Farage also accepted that Brexit had failed to cut immigration numbers in the way that people who voted for leave were expecting. “So yes, in the eyes of many, the delivery of Brexit has been a failure.”
Farage also claimed Burnham had no mandate to reopen the Brexit debate. He said:
Five months ago, Andy Burnham says … I’m not going to reopen these arguments.
Two-and-a-half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up a debate on the free movement of people.
What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.
Unison says focus on cost of living, including tax-free mileage, 'commendable', but 'bolder' policies needed
Unison has particularly welcomed the announcement today about higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent. (See 9.07am.) The union has been campaigning for this, and some of its members will benefit.
But, in her response, Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary illustrated how there is a limit to how much goodwill a government can generate from small “everyday fixes”. She said:
These are welcome measures, especially making the uplift to mileage rates permanent, something Unison has campaigned hard for. The government’s relentless focus on the cost of living is commendable.
But the cost of essentials, including food and fuel, is going to keep soaring, meaning breathing space will quickly be closed down. The Treasury says three million people are expected to benefit from the mileage changes. It says:

Tories dismiss PM’s budget ‘everyday fixes’ as little more than ‘cheaper gherkins’, and ‘an insult to families
Good morning. Prime ministers tend to get judged by posterity by the decisions they take on the big issues of the day. But little things matter too in the here and now, often disproportionately, and Andy Burnham, more than his predecessors, has decided that what he calls “everyday fixes” are worth focusing on too. Alexandra Topping wrote a good analysis about the pluses and minuses of this approach last week. But she filed too soon, because this morning Burnham has announced another five.
These are all changes contained in tomorrow’s budget but being announced today – presumably because John Healey will have bigger surprises for MPs tomorrow, and the Treasury wants these measures to get some media attention today because tomorrow they will be overshadowed by another story.
One of the measures is of particular interest to the Guardian because we have highlighted the scandal that led to hundreds of thousands of people getting the carer’s allowance being ordered to pay back huge sums of money because inadvertently their weekly earnings went slightly above the threshold allowed. In other parts of the welfare system, people just have to return the overpayment, but the rules for carer’s allowance were draconian, and a tiny breach of the weekly earnings allowance could lead to people being ordered to pay back thousands of pounds.
As Patrick Butler and Pippa Crerar report in our splash, this rule is being scrapped.
But this is one of just five “everyday fixes” announced this morning. Here is what the Treasury says about them.
• Making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent and increasing support for nurses, care workers, self employed builders and others who drive for work. The chancellor is locking in the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles from 25p to 35p per mile, supporting around 3 million employees and self-employed people who use their own vehicle for work.
• Extending parental pay to more than 150,000 additional parents per year, including self-employed dads and partners who have previously missed out, giving eligible parents two weeks of support currently worth up to £194 a week so they can spend more time with their child.
• Ending the Carer’s Allowance cliff edge, so unpaid carers no longer lose their entire allowance simply for earning a penny over the Weekly Earnings Limit, equivalent to 16 hours of the National Living Wage. Instead, only £1 of support will taper away for every additional £1 earned.
• Removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, helping lower import costs on family favourites including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on kerosene heating oil. Together with tariff suspensions already introduced, households could save up to £21 on their food shop each year.
• Rolling out hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, making it easier and more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue at a Post Office counter, helping take some of the hassle out of everyday errands in the run-up to Christmas. This comes alongside upgrades to 600 Post Office branches by the end of the financial year, improving services for customers across the country.
There is more detail in the Treasury news release here.
It is always easy to mock, and the Conservatives could not resist. Here is their response, from Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor.
Rampant borrowing, soaring taxes and an utter inability to cut spending mean inflation has already wiped out the benefits of Burnham’s ‘everyday fixes’.
Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham’s plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour’s tax rises.
The mention of gherkins in the Treasury press release did come as a surprise, given that they are not a key feature of the national diet, but maybe someone in Whitehall read the reports earlier this year about their importance for Pret a Manger sandwiches.
The problem with the Tory response is that, even though “everyday fixes” might not make a big difference, people tend to welcome them anyway. This is from Novara Media’s Aaron Bastani.
Part of the genius with this stuff is the negative polarisation, when people start attacking perfectly sensible and helpful – albeit small – changes.
Actually I want longer Post Office queues please!
Here is the agenda for the day.
10.30am: Sarah Sackman, the courts minister, gives evidence to the Lords justice committee on support for jurors.
Morning:Andy Burnham hosts a meeting with Muslim leaders in No 10.
11.30am: Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: Dan Jarvis, the security minister, is expected to give a statement to MPs about the government’s ‘Be Ready’ resilience advice about stockpiling essentials.

Jailed Tanzanian opposition leader begins hunger strike
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:06:43 CET
18:06:43 KST

NAIROBI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu, who was charged with treason last year, has started a hunger strike to protest his inability to access his lawyers, his party said.
Lissu, who leads the CHADEMA opposition party and came second in the 2020 presidential election, began refusing food on Monday after his lawyers were denied entry to the prison where he is being held, party spokesperson Brenda Rupia wrote on X.
Tanzania Prisons Service spokesperson Elizabeth Mbezi said it would give an update on Lissu soon. Government spokesperson Gerson Msigwa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Lissu was charged with treason over what prosecutors said was a speech calling on the public to rebel and disrupt last year’s general election. He pleaded not guilty to the charges, which his lawyer has said are politically motivated.
Tanzania’s electoral commission had barred CHADEMA from participating in the polls after it failed to sign a code of conduct document.
The election was marred by protests and unrest, with a government-appointed commission of inquiry saying the violence that broke out afterwards killed at least 518 people and blaming the protesters for the violence.
CHADEMA’s chief legal counsel, Rugemeleza Nshala, told journalists on Saturday that Lissu had planned the strike because he was denied privacy during talks with his lawyers in violation of a court order.
The court is due to deliver its judgement in Lissu’s case on November 6.
Lissu’s detention, along with the alleged abductions of government critics, has shone a spotlight on the human rights record of President Samia Suluhu Hassan, who won the 2025 election.
The government has rejected accusations of widespread rights abuses and said it is committed to respecting human rights. It ordered an investigation into reports of abductions in 2024, though no official findings have been made public.

Finnish drone electronics maker raises $2.8M in five days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:06:27 UTC
18:06:27 KST

- Finnish drone electronics maker Arctic RAVN secured €2.5 million in convertible loan commitments in five days, exceeding its €2 million target.
- The company aims to build tens of thousands of speed controllers by the end of 2026 and eventually up to two million circuit boards a year.
Finnish drone electronics maker Arctic RAVN has secured €2.5 million (about $2.8 million) in convertible loan commitments in five days, passing its €2 million (about $2.2 million) target before it has officially launched a single product, and it plans to use the money to scale up production of the circuit boards that power and steer military drones.
The company said on Oct. 27, 2026, that it opened the round in October and that the financing will go toward ramping up manufacturing and product development, as it already holds follow-up orders and is in talks with several leading European defense manufacturers.
Arctic RAVN builds electronic speed controllers, the boards that regulate power to a drone’s motors, and flight controllers, the onboard computers that keep the aircraft stable and carry out its pilot’s commands, and it says every product is designed and manufactured in Finland with components sourced entirely from Europe and NATO-allied countries.
“Investors committed to the round within days, even though we have not yet officially launched a single product. Follow-up orders and discussions with several leading defence manufacturers indicate a need for high-performance European drone electronics. We are now scaling our manufacturing capabilities for industrial-level output and strengthening Europe’s ability to produce critical drone electronics,” said Matti Vansén, chief executive of Arctic RAVN.
The company has already put more than €1 million (about $1.1 million) into scaling up production of its speed controllers and aims to build tens of thousands of units by the end of 2026, with a significant share already reserved by customers, before shifting its next production ramp-up to flight controllers and, over the longer term, expanding capacity to as many as two million circuit boards a year.
Its current lineup includes the AR41ESC, a four-in-one speed controller that runs on 6S to 12S lithium-polymer batteries and handles at least 60 amps of continuous current per channel, with 90-amp bursts, and the AR32FC flight controller, which accepts 4S to 14S battery input, carries two inertial measurement units and runs custom firmware.
Arctic RAVN is one of the studio companies of Finnish Defence House, a defense technology venture studio that finds, funds and builds new companies, and it joins a growing number of Finnish firms working on military drones, including Summa Defence, which delivered its first batch of Zeus FPV drones to the Armed Forces of Ukraine in December 2025.

Brussels Army Museum stages exhibition on Lukas Dhont’s film ‘Coward’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:05:56 UTC
18:05:56 KST

Flemish film director Lukas Dhont and the Brussels Army Museum are joining forces for a temporary exhibition. From 7 November, visitors will be able to discover which historical sources and museum collections form the basis of ‘Coward’, Dhont’s latest film about the First World War.
‘Coward’ premiered in Belgian cinemas on 21 October and has already attracted considerable international attention. The film won awards and was enthusiastically received at Cannes, received rave reviews in both domestic and international media, and was selected as Belgium’s entry for the Oscars.
In the film, Dhont approaches the First World War in a unique way. Alongside the violence and destruction, he emphasises beauty, art and the love between two soldiers at the front. He also highlights aspects of ‘the Great War’ that have been forgotten over the years.
For the film, Dhont worked closely with experts and historians, including staff from the Brussels Army Museum. This collaboration continues in the ‘14–’18’ gallery at the museum in the Jubel Park.
From 7 November onwards, a pop-up exhibition will showcase costumes, props, archive footage and clips from the film. This will give visitors an insight into how historical sources and museum collections were brought to life on the silver screen. The exhibition also places the film within a broader historical context.

Israel Heads to the Polls as Netanyahu Battles to Stay in Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Israelis headed to polling stations Tuesday to decide the political fate of Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving Prime Minister who faces one of the most consequential tests of his decadeslong political career.
Netanyahu was joined by his wife Sara as he cast his ballot just after midday, local time, at a polling station in a Jerusalem school. “This is a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are truly overwhelmed,” Netanyahu told reporters after voting. “We know what is at stake, and since I am not allowed to say things explicitly, I will say: Vote correctly.”
From 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time (1 a.m. to 4 p.m. EDT), Israelis can cast votes for representatives in the Knesset. Early numbers from the Central Elections Committee suggest turnout is strong, with 44.9% of eligible voters reported to have cast their ballots by 2 p.m., local time.
This is the first election in the country since the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks by Palestinian militant group Hamas and the subsequent Israeli war in the Gaza Strip. Since then, Israel under Netanyahu has pursued an aggressive military campaign across the Middle East—going to war with Iran, backing settler attacks and displacement in the West Bank, and carrying out strikes against militant groups in Lebanon and Yemen.
Tuesday’s election is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and Israelis’ willingness to change course amid uncertainty. According to polls, the outcome is far from certain, with a tight race expected as Israel decides upon its future.
Read More: Israel's Choice
“I hope this will be a true holiday for democracy,” Isaac Herzog, the Israeli head of state, told reporters from a polling station in Rehavia, where he and his wife voted. “No one can be allowed to spoil or undermine it.”
Here’s what to know.
Who’s running?
Two main political blocs are contending to form Israel’s next government. The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition led by Netanyahu’s Likud party. The coalition includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, such as Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) led by national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Religious Zionism-Zehut led by finance minister Bezalel Smotrich. Their ultranationalist policies have found an audience in younger right-wing Israelis.
On the other side are the Jewish-led opposition movements—with former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot and the centrist Yashar (Straight) party at the forefront. Eisenkot, who entered politics in 2022, joined Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet after the Oct. 7 attack on Israel. But after having lost a son in combat in Israel’s wars, Eisenkot left his post in 2024. Two of his nephews also died fighting in Gaza, a prominent campaign talking point.
The opposition also includes a joint ticket led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid, the secular nationalist party Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) led by former finance minister Avigdor Lieberman, and the Democrats led by former IDF deputy chief of staff Yair Golan.
Some polls suggest that Eisenkot’s Yashar party may garner slightly more support than Netanyahu’s Likud, but they also project that neither the Prime Minister’s right-wing bloc nor the opposition may win the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government.
Including Arab parties such as United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List, or fringe parties, could be necessary to form a government. Both pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu coalitions have so far ruled out teaming up with the Arab-led parties. Arab citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the population, though they receive fewer government services and endure higher poverty and unemployment rates. Discrimination and disappointment have historically depressed Arab-Israeli voter turnout.
Hours after the polls opened Tuesday, Netanyahu told his supporters that "buses are heading to the polling stations and huge lines are being reported in the Arab settlements." Complaining that "the right-wing strongholds are not waking up," he urged people to go out and vote.
Netanyahu touts Trump endorsement
Netanyahu hopes to maintain his premiership with the help of his longstanding ally, U.S. President Donald Trump, who only announced his endorsement days before the election as conflict in the Middle East has tested their friendship.
In a late-night TV appearance on Oct. 25, Netanyahu boasted of Trump’s endorsement and said that Trump was willing to take action “that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat” so long as Netanyahu stayed in power. Netanyahu added that he has already instructed Israel’s national intelligence agency Mossad as well as the IDF to “bring down” the Iranian regime. Trump remains very popular in Israel.
By contrast, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance declined to endorse Netanyahu for re-election, just a day after Trump put his “complete and total” support behind the Israeli leader.
“The President has the most effective endorsement in American, or international, political history,” said Vance, when asked in an interview if he would also be extending an endorsement of his own. “I endorse American candidates and that’s where I'm focused on, is the midterms, so I'm not getting involved in the Israeli elections.”
When pushed for an answer, Vance added: “I'm not anti-endorsing [Netanyahu], I'm not pro-endorsing him.”
A high-stakes election for Netanyahu
At stake for Netanyahu could be more than his continued leadership. The premier faces an international arrest warrant for alleged crimes related to the Israeli military campaign in Gaza. And even domestically, critics have demanded an inquiry into Netanyahu’s decision-making around Oct. 7. The attack, which resulted in over 1,200 people in Israel killed and around 250 hostages taken, is considered by many to be indicative of a major security failure.
The Gaza health ministry reports that since Oct. 7, 2023, more than 74,000 individuals have been killed. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, Gaza’s health ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME.
Another issue driving the election is public fury over ultra-Orthodox communities’ exemption from military conscription for men engaged in religious studies. Despite a shortage of soldiers, less than 10% of eligible ultra-Orthodox men enlist, amid demands from Netanyahu’s allies to exempt them. Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, has promised to end the de facto exemptions.
Netanyahu’s repeated attempts to reform the judiciary also factor into this election, with critics slamming his undermining of democratic institutions and connecting it to his legal interests. Netanyahu is in the middle of a yearslong corruption trial, which he and his allies—including Trump—have claimed is politically motivated. He sought but didn’t receive a presidential pardon from Herzog.
When will we know the results?
About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote on Tuesday. The election fills the Knesset’s 120 seats through proportional representation—which means parties, not personalities, are on these voters’ ballots.
After polling stations close at 10 p.m. (4 p.m. EDT), local media are expected to broadcast exit polls. The final vote tally is expected by Oct. 30, with official results published on Nov. 4.
But getting a clear picture of the Israeli government is likely to take longer. No single party has ever claimed 61 seats to form a government, meaning Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Such alliances can take weeks or months to form. What those coalitions may look like will depend on the election outcomes for smaller parties, which each need 3.25% of the votes to secure a seat in the Knesset.
Once the election winners are determined, President Herzog will refer to party leaders to choose a preferred Prime Minister and will ask the strongest candidate to form a government within 42 days. If a coalition cannot be formed after multiple attempts, the current Likud-led coalition government will continue to serve as caretaker before another round of elections is held in the coming months.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said restoring full diplomatic representation between Lithuania and China should not be directly linked to changing the name of Taiwan’s representative office in Vilnius, stressing that normalising relations is a pragmatic goal.
“Such efforts are fully justified, and I do not think they should be linked very directly to the name of the Taiwanese Representative Office. We simply want neither more nor less – we want to restore relations with China to a normal level,” Nausėda told the radio Žinių Radijas on Tuesday.
He said Lithuania could initially accept a lower level of diplomatic representation, with the interests of either country represented by a deputy head of mission rather than an ambassador.
“This is a completely pragmatic goal to normalise diplomatic relations. That is something we should do in any case,” the president said.

Lithuania’s ruling majority aims to normalise relations with China and restore diplomatic representation to the level maintained by other European Union member states. The goal is also included in the government’s program.
Relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in the autumn of 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representative office under the name “Taiwanese”. Similar offices in other countries generally operate under the name Taipei, which Beijing prefers because it does not imply recognition of Taiwan as a separate state.
China responded by unilaterally downgrading its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassador to chargé d’affaires. Lithuania subsequently stopped issuing new accreditations to Chinese diplomats, leaving China without accredited diplomats in the country since May last year.

Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:01:07 UTC
18:01:07 KST

The number of UK businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, as pressure grows on the chancellor to provide more support to the private sector in Wednesday’s budget.
There were 738,144 businesses in “significant” financial distress in the third quarter of this year, up 1.6% compared with the same period last year, according to BTG. That is the highest level since the administrator’s closely watched “red flag” report began in 2004.
The UK’s support services, construction and real estate sectors were among the most vulnerable, with the highest numbers of businesses in significant distress – at 118,695, 108,340 and 99,908 respectively.
The hospitality industry was hardest hit this year, with a 5% rise in the number of bars and restaurants in distress to 18,866. Struggling food and drug retailers rose by more than 7% to 19,269, according to BTG, which is one of the UK’s biggest insolvency practitioners and changed its name from Begbies Traynor in February.
The growing strain on UK companies comes as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to give his first budget on Wednesday, against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East disrupts the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis.
The chancellor has vowed to use the budget to provide households and businesses with more “breathing space”.
Mark Fry, the chief executive of BTG, said British businesses were “battling a combination of rising employment costs, inflationary pressures, higher energy prices and elevated borrowing costs.
“Crucially, these pressures are not only affecting small businesses’ ability to operate, but also larger businesses’ ability to compete on a global stage,” he said.
A freedom of information request by BTG also found that British businesses still owed £27.3bn in arrears to HMRC in VAT, corporation tax and PAYE at the end of August.
About £24bn has been recovered since arrears reached a peak of £51.3bn during the Covid pandemic, compared with a pre-pandemic total of £11.4bn.
“With £27.3bn owed to HMRC, high levels of recovery activity and record financial distress across the economy, many companies are approaching this budget from a position of financial weakness rather than strength,” Fry said.
“We hear from businesses that structural hurdles, weight of red tape, employment legislation and the tax burden alongside high interest and energy costs will need to be tackled if this is to be a budget for business.”
Last week the prime minister, Andy Burnham, promised that his government would “slash red tape” for businesses, with plans to make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses.

Türkiye completes EU machinery safety harmonization to boost $10 bln in exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:59:51 UTC
17:59:51 KST

The Turkish Trade Ministry has announced the signing of a declaration confirming Türkiye’s alignment with EU machinery safety legislation, fulfilling customs union requirements.
The regulatory harmonization “paves the way for the Turkish machinery sector to benefit from the free movement of goods across European markets.”
Ankara can now designate accredited notified bodies within Türkiye, enabling Turkish machinery exporters to conduct their conformity assessment and certification procedures at home instead of relying on foreign institutions.
The local assessments will be recognized under the same conditions as those performed by EU manufacturers.
The deal marks a major milestone in simplifying technical and administrative processes that Turkish exporters deal with when accessing the European single market.
The financial costs and administrative burdens associated with these regulatory procedures will be significantly reduced.
The alignment will reportedly benefit more than $10 billion worth of Turkish machinery exports to the EU per year.
Machinery sales make up 10 percent of Türkiye’s total export volume to the EU, according to the ministry.

GDELS and ARMMO team up on mobile anti-drone system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:58:47 UTC
17:58:47 KST

- ARMMO and Santa Bárbara Sistemas launched and flew the Bandit-X interceptor drone from an ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier during Spain’s ATLAS 26 exercise.
- ARMMO says Bandit-X exceeds 360 km/h, flies for 20 to 25 minutes and has an estimated range of 40 to 50 km.
Spanish drone maker ARMMO Defense Technologies and General Dynamics European Land Systems’ Spanish unit, Santa Bárbara Sistemas, launched and flew ARMMO’s Bandit-X interceptor drone from an ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier tracked armored vehicle during the ATLAS 26 counter-drone exercise in Huelva, Spain, turning the heavy vehicle into a mobile launcher for drones that hunt down other drones.
The two companies announced the demonstration on Oct. 27, 2026, along with a cooperation agreement to develop and integrate autonomous systems on armored vehicles and other ground platforms, and they said the launch was carried out in front of senior Spanish and NATO officers, including Spain’s Chief of the Defence Staff, Adm. Gen. Manuel Teodoro López Calderón, and Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation.
The launcher had already been spotted at the exercise, when Defence Blog reported that a tracked ASCOD carrier was seen with box-shaped launch containers marked with ARMMO’s logo on its open rear deck at the Médano del Loro training range, where ATLAS 26 ran from Oct. 19 to Oct. 23 under the direction of the Spanish Army’s Anti-Aircraft Artillery Command.
Bandit-X is a high-speed interceptor built to find and destroy hostile unmanned aircraft, and ARMMO says it flies at more than 360 km/h (224 mph), with plans to push that to 420 km/h (261 mph), stays in the air for 20 to 25 minutes and has an estimated operational range of 40 to 50 km (25 to 31 miles), depending on conditions and mission profile.
The company says the drone can navigate on its own when satellite navigation is jammed or denied, resists electronic interference and guides itself autonomously in the final phase of an intercept, and that it was validated during NATO experimental activities in Slovakia in 2026 and has been assigned a NATO Stock Number, which lets allied militaries identify and order it through their common logistics catalog.
The ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier is a modular tracked platform from Santa Bárbara Sistemas that can be fitted for ground-based air defense, artillery, fire support, heavy recovery, logistics, electronic warfare, medical evacuation and counter-drone missions, and it uses the NEVA open digital architecture, built to NATO’s Generic Vehicle Architecture standard, so that systems from other companies can be added to the vehicle.
ARMMO, which operates an industrial site of more than 30,000 square meters (323,000 square feet) in Zafra, in Spain’s Badajoz province, also builds unmanned ground and surface vehicles and electronic warfare systems, and the agreement with Santa Bárbara Sistemas sets up a framework for putting its autonomous technologies on a range of ground vehicles.

Natural History Museum launches new tender for permanent exhibition project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:58:00 UTC
17:58:00 KST

Natural History Museum launches new tender for permanent exhibition project
The Natural History Museum has launched a new €3 million tender to find a contractor for one of the largest projects in Estonia's museum sector in the past decade.
The museum is seeking a contractor to design the new permanent exhibition and to implement it based on that design at the newly built wooden Nature House in Põhja-Tallinn. The two-part tender has a total value of €2,812,950.
Egle Hecht, acting director of the Estonian Museum of Natural History, said she hopes to see companies from both Estonia and abroad that have previously carried out similar museum projects among the bidders for the permanent exhibition tender.
"This is a very large international tender for Estonia's museum sector, the likes of which was last carried out more than 10 years ago when the Estonian National Museum was established," she said.
The previous tender failed.
"A total of three bids were submitted for the first tender for the core exhibition, but unfortunately none of them qualified. As these were predominantly some of the world's leading creative agencies specializing in exhibition construction, which often do not participate in public procurement tenders, it turned out that they misunderstood the tender conditions and made mistakes when submitting their bids. With the new tender, we hope to avoid similar situations," Hecht said.
The acting director said the museum's new core exhibition will tell the story of the coexistence of nature and humans through Estonia's natural environment. It is hoped it will be "more ambitious and exceptional than before in terms of its concept, size and execution."
"In every chapter, humans are one of the characters, equal among others. Alongside well-known and visible species, we emphasize the richness of microscopic life and its coexistence with other living organisms. We talk about different relationships in nature, also touching on, for example, how rich biodiversity influences culture and language, and vice versa. The new permanent exhibition offers something for all age groups, being accessible and taking different visitors into account," Hecht said.
The museum is also planning a separate children's exhibition, where they can learn about nature in a way that supports their natural curiosity.
Natural History Museum to fully open in 2028
The tender consists of two parts: the permanent exhibition and the exhibition for young children.
"We will open the children's exhibition together with the museum's first temporary exhibition in 2027, meaning there is less time to complete it, while the permanent exhibition will open in 2028. That is why the tender has been divided into two parts," Hecht said.
The acting director said the museum will open its doors with its first exhibition in 2027, as planned from the outset, although the exact date is not yet clear.
"Once the Taru Nature House is completed, the museum will only then begin moving into the building and constructing and setting up the exhibitions. The completion of the building will allow us to begin creating the exhibition," Hecht said.
The expected final deadline for the design and exhibition construction work under the procurement contract is April 6, 2028.
The deadline for submitting bids is in one month's time, on November 23. The work will be financed from external funds (the Cohesion Policy Funds Implementation Programme 2021–2027) and the Environmental Investment Center's environmental program.

====================================================================================================

EXPLAINER - Israel election: What to expect after polls close
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:56:58 UTC
17:56:58 KST

Polling stations in Israel’s closely contested general election will close Tuesday at 10 pm local time (2000GMT), beginning a counting and coalition-building process that could determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power.
Around 7.3 million voters are eligible to elect the 120 members of the Knesset in Israel’s first general election since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and its first held on schedule since 1988.
Final opinion polls placed former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud, but projected neither political bloc securing the 61 seats normally required to form a government.
Here is what to expect after voting ends.
Israeli broadcasters Kan 11, Channel 12, and Channel 13 are expected to release separate exit polls immediately after polling stations close.
The surveys will provide the first estimates of how many seats each party may receive and whether Netanyahu or Eisenkot has a possible route to a governing majority.
Exit polls, however, are projections rather than counted votes. Small differences between the surveys could prove significant because several parties are polling close to the 3.25% electoral threshold.
A party falling slightly below the threshold would receive no representation, potentially shifting several seats between the rival blocs.
Final pre-election surveys projected Yashar winning 22 or 23 seats and Likud receiving between 19 and 21.
Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious alliance was projected to secure around 50 seats, while the main opposition parties were forecast to receive between 52 and 56. Palestinian-led parties were expected to win a combined 14 to 16 seats.
Votes cast at ordinary polling stations will be counted locally after voting ends, with results transmitted to regional counting centers and the Central Elections Committee.
The first official figures are expected to emerge during the night, gradually replacing the television projections.
A clearer picture should be available Wednesday morning, but closely contested seats may remain unresolved.
Israel allocates parliamentary seats nationally through proportional representation. Votes cast for parties that fail to reach the electoral threshold are excluded before seats are distributed among the qualifying lists.
This means the balance of power may change sharply as the count reveals which smaller parties have entered parliament.
The initial count will not include all ballots.
Soldiers, diplomats, hospital patients and staff, prisoners, election workers and voters using specially accessible polling stations cast their votes through a double-envelope system.
Officials first verify the voter’s identity and ensure that the person has not also voted at an ordinary polling station. The identifying outer envelope is then separated from the anonymous ballot before counting.
Approximately 650,000 such ballots are expected, representing enough votes to affect around 14 parliamentary seats.
Their counting is expected to take between 24 and 36 hours and could move parties above or below the electoral threshold, change individual seat allocations and alter the coalition arithmetic.
The final tally is expected by Friday, while the official results are scheduled to be published on Nov. 4.
Finishing first does not guarantee that a party leader will become prime minister.
Once the results are official, President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of every party elected to the Knesset. Each faction will recommend the lawmaker it believes should be asked to form a government.
Herzog will then assign the task to the member of parliament considered most capable of assembling a coalition, regardless of whether that person leads the largest party.
The first nominee will receive 28 days to form a government and may request an extension of up to 14 days.
If the attempt fails, Herzog may give another lawmaker 28 days to try. If that candidate is also unsuccessful, 61 lawmakers can propose a third candidate, who would have 14 days to build a government.
Failure at every stage would dissolve the Knesset and trigger another election. Netanyahu’s current government would remain in office in a caretaker capacity throughout the process.
Government formation in Israel has taken between 20 and 100 days, and no new government has been sworn in less than 50 days after an election during the past two decades.
Netanyahu’s established alliance consists of Likud, the far-right Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism parties, and the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties.
Final polls consistently projected the bloc at around 50 seats, leaving it 11 short of a majority.
To remain in power, Netanyahu would need his alliance to outperform the polls or persuade lawmakers from outside the bloc to support him.
He could seek an agreement with a right-wing opposition party, encourage defections or pursue a broader unity government.
However, most opposition leaders have pledged not to join a Netanyahu-led coalition.
Eisenkot’s potential alliance includes Yashar, the Bennett-Lapid-led B’Yachad party, Yair Golan’s Democrats and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu.
Although projected to finish ahead of Netanyahu’s bloc, these parties are also expected to fall short of 61 seats.
Support from the Palestinian-led Joint List or Ra’am could provide Eisenkot with the necessary parliamentary numbers, either through formal coalition participation or outside backing.
But such an arrangement faces major political obstacles.
Lieberman has ruled out serving in a government dependent on Palestinian-led parties, while Eisenkot has avoided committing himself to such a coalition. Netanyahu has also sought to mobilize right-wing voters by portraying Palestinian parties as potential kingmakers.
A minority government could theoretically take office if it received more votes in favor than against during the Knesset confidence vote, but it would face immediate questions about stability.
If neither bloc can assemble a workable majority, pressure could grow for a national unity government involving Likud and one or more opposition parties.
Such an agreement could involve Netanyahu leaving office, a rotating premiership or a limited-term government focused on security and constitutional issues.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have rejected serving under Netanyahu, making a unity arrangement difficult unless Likud changes its leadership or accepts a power-sharing formula.
The remaining possibility is another election.
Israel held five general elections between 2019 and 2022 after repeated coalition deadlocks. A similarly fragmented result could return the country to political paralysis, with negotiations rather than Tuesday’s vote determining who ultimately governs.

Kazakhstan completes over 820 gasification projects in 7 years

Kazakhstan completes over 820 gasification projects in 7 years
Kazakhstan has expanded access to natural gas to 772 settlements over the past seven years, increasing the number of people with access from 9.5 million to 13.1 million, Qazinform News Agency reports.
During this period, Kazakhstan invested 612.3 billion tenge from the national budget and Samruk-Kazyna funds in gasification, completing 821 projects and building more than 31,500 kilometers of gas networks.
These efforts increased the share of the population with access to natural gas from 51.47% to 64.2%, an increase of 12.73 percentage points.
Kazakhstan continues to expand its gas infrastructure by building main and distribution pipelines to ensure a reliable supply of natural gas to more settlements, homes, and businesses.
In 2025 alone, more than 354,000 people in 94 settlements gained access to natural gas, with approximately 2,000 kilometers of distribution networks built across the country.
Work is continuing in 2026, with 40 gasification projects underway, including seven carried over from previous years and 33 new projects. Once completed, they are expected to provide natural gas access to another 36,000 people.
To reach its target of providing natural gas access to 80% of the population by 2035, Kazakhstan's Ministry of Energy plans to expand major pipelines, regional gas networks, and the country's natural gas resource base.
A key project is the Ishim–Astana gas pipeline, backed by a memorandum signed between the Kazakh Government and Russia's Gazprom. The pipeline is expected to supply natural gas to Astana, Kokshetau, and Petropavlovsk, while also diversifying supply routes to northern Kazakhstan.
Another major project involves the construction of a second line of the Beineu–Bozoy–Shymkent main gas pipeline. The expansion aims to increase the capacity of Kazakhstan's gas transportation system, improve supply reliability, and meet growing demand for natural gas in the country's southern and central regions.
In Zhetysu region, the 302-kilometer Taldykorgan–Usharal gas pipeline was completed and commissioned in 2025, paving the way for up to 84 settlements to be connected to the gas network.
Kazakhstan also plans to expand gas supply and distribution networks in Almaty, Turkistan, Kyzylorda, Zhambyl, Kostanay, Karaganda, and other regions.
These projects are expected to extend natural gas coverage across the country, giving more people and businesses access to natural gas.
Earlier, Qazinform reported KazMunayGas and Belorusneft discussed prospects for expanding cooperation.

Russia and Ukraine began a regional cease-fire Tuesday to launch a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, though fighting persisted elsewhere, including the capital of Kyiv.
The cease-fire is intended to enable aid deliveries and evacuations from the frontline southern Ukrainian town, which faces acute shortages of food and medicine.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said on Facebook, confirming the halt's timing.
On Telegram, Russia's Defense Ministry said it stopped shelling toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson starting at 4 a.m. Moscow time (1 a.m. GMT) to prepare for the Oleshky effort; Oleshky faces Kherson across the Dnipro River.
Lubinets added the deal was reached in coordination with U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Russia's commissioner for human rights, Yana Lantratova.
New strikes Tuesday hit the Southern Bridge and subway infrastructure in Kyiv, forcing traffic suspension, city officials said. A Reuters witness heard explosions.
Oleshky lies on the Dnipro's eastern bank in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, opposite Kherson, held by Ukrainian forces.
Russian troops have controlled the town since seizing it in the early days of their February 2022 invasion.
White House envoys talked with both sides in recent days to find a solution as the U.S. seeks to mediate a peace deal to end the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II.
Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said peace negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States agreed to meet at a technical level in early November in Abu Dhabi to continue the talks.
Since Monday evening, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 15, including students in a dormitory. The attacks also killed and injured people in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
On Telegram, the Russian Defense Ministry said it hit transport infrastructure in Kyiv, a logistics hub in Kharkiv region, as well as industrial facilities and cargo vessels elsewhere it said were being put to military use.
A drone attack killed one man and wounded six others in the western Russian city of Bryansk, near the Ukrainian border.
A drone hit a bus, killing another person and injuring 30 in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, local officials said.
Reuters could not immediately verify the reports. Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.

reclaimed timber frames shape skroget coastal sauna and community hub in norway

Unknown Publisher
