reclaimed timber frames shape skroget coastal sauna and community hub in norway
rare collectiv constructs skroget, a 40-meter-long arctic sauna and gathering pavilion in båtsfjord built from nineteen reclaimed timber portal frames resembling a ship-like hull.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
RARE COLLECTIV BUILDS HARBOR PAVILION and sauna IN BÅTSFJORD
Located nearly 500 kilometers above the Arctic Circle in Båtsfjord, Norway, Skroget is a coastal sauna and community pavilion conceived by Rare Collectiv, a group of fifteen international architecture students from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) under the Design in Context course. Commissioned by the local municipality to establish an accessible public harbor hub, the project was designed in two days and constructed in ten days, translating reclaimed materials and site-specific environmental conditions into a functional community infrastructure.
RECLAIMED LUMBER FORMS THE SKELETON AND INTEGRATED FURNITURE
Extending nearly 40 meters along the shoreline, the pavilion’s structural system references the skeletal frame of a ship’s hull. The volume is organized around nineteen identical timber portal frames that establish a clear programmatic and climatic orientation: sloping downward toward the water to frame sea views, while opening toward the south to create wind-sheltered outdoor seating that maximizes solar gain. The structural grid organizes a linear progression of amenities, linking an open-air fire pit, communal seating areas, changing facilities, and showers to a central sauna. The entire structure by Rare Collectiv design group, along with its integrated benches and tables, is fabricated from reused 3×7-inch municipal timber, employing uniform member dimensions and angled joinery to maintain structural continuity across the harsh coastal terrain.
project info:
name: Skroget
designer: Rare Collectiv
location: Båtsfjord, Norway

Norway's Støre defends Putin call, but acknowledges 'significant' differences in opinions
Jakub Krupa
Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre has offered a bit more colour on his and Stubb’s call with Russia’s Putin in a huddle with journalists in Helsinki just now.
He and Stubb had been initially given only 20 minutes to talk to Putin, but ended up speaking for 90 minutes, in a conversation he described as “substantive, focused on the issues at hand, and professional.”
“Much of what he said was already known – he [Putin] recalled his views on how the conflict evolved since 2014 – and we stated our positions. These are well-known views, which we were able to acknowledge and respond to,” he said.
The talks touched on what can be done to tackle most pressing issues, including attacks on energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea.
But Støre conceded “there remain significant differences in our respective positions,” reiterating Norway’s continued support for Ukraine.
“We stand with Ukraine, defend its right to self-defence, and emphasise the need for a diplomatic path to end this war in a lasting and just manner,” he said.
Støre also stressed that he and Finland’s Stubb spoke on behalf of their two countries only, “and no one else.”
Responding to criticism of their call from Denmark’s Frederiksen(11:26), he said that “all our partners and allies were informed in advance and received a detailed account afterwards.”
Pushing back further, he added:
“If one assumes that the current situation – where communication from the American administration to Moscow serves as the sole channel for discussing Ukraine outside of Ukraine – is the only way, then one is entitled to that view. I believe it is important that other voices are heard as well.”
Støre also stressed that the importance of the meeting in Abu Dhabi, first agreed as a result of the Oslo consultations that he and Stubb hosted.
In a brief section of the briefing in English, Støre again focused on pushing back against Frederiksen’s criticism:
“I believe that talking, having the right messages, is not wrong. Today these messages [are] coming out of the American administration; that is the only thing reaching Moscow. So [now] there are [also] voices from two neighbouring states, speaking on behalf of Finland and Norway, not speaking on behalf of others, but … in full compliance with the coalition of the willing who share view on the nature of this war and how with has to end.”
Sweden's Kristersson insists any peace deal must be achieved on Ukraine's terms
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has insisted that any peace “must be achieved on Ukraine’s terms,” joining a growing chorus of sceptical voices after an earlier call between Finland and Norway’s leaders and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Talking to reporters, Kristersson said that any peace settlement “must be brought about through strength, and not through appeasement towards Russia.”
“If talks lead to that, then talks are good. But my experience so far – based on the reports we received from German and French attempts at dialogue [with Moscow] – is that the results have been very, very modest.”
Kristersson added that given Russia’s continued aggression against Ukraine, “I see nothing to suggest that they are seeking peace.”
“But we will surely receive an update on those discussions later today, and I am interested in that,” he said.
No solution to end the war can be found without Ukraine's involvement, Merz says
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday that attempts by the US and Russia to end the war in Ukraine “can never find solutions without Ukraine” and said any talks must also include European countries.
Merz was speaking at the Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore as he described diplomatic efforts to build a negotiating format with Moscow.
He said the end of the war depended “only on one person” and framed continued backing for Kyiv as a defence of Europe’s political order.
He said “as long as he [Putin] does not want to end the war, we will support Ukraine” and that Europe was not just defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity but also “the entire political order of the European continent”.
Merz added that Russia, Ukraine, the United States and European countries should be at the negotiating table and warned against a scenario where “Russia, perhaps China and the United States of America” end the war without Ukraine.
Stubb talked of 'very restrained optimism' about constructive peace talks in Abu Dhabi, Tusk says
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk has also responded to Stubb and Støre’s engagement with Putin, giving a detailed account on the European consultations ahead of and after the call.
Speaking before the cabinet meeting in Warsaw, Tusk said the call followed “consultations with me, among others, but primarily with president Zelenskyy and the US side … that it would be good for European politicians to have a working contact given the planned ceasefire talks that may take place in Abu Dhabi.”
He said the UAE talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US are provisionally planned for 4 November.
Tusk confirmed he had been briefed on plans for the call beforehand, with Norway’s Støre assuring him that he and Stubb were ready to take political responsibility for this rare engagement with Putin, and would stick to the agreed position of the coalition of the willing.
He said Finland’s Stubb then briefed him after the call, saying “both sides maintained their positions,” and that “the European side’s impression during the call was one of very restrained optimism” about the chances of making progress in Abu Dhabi.
Tusk said he was “very cautions” about engaging with Russia and urged Stubb and Store to be “vigilant” in their talks with Putin, as “Russia’s agenda and interests are quite precisely defined, and that one should harbour any illusions about getting an agreement.”
He said Stubb and Støre also told Putin that the security of Nato’s northern and eastern flanks were “non-negotiable”.
Poland’s PM also stressed that despite the resumed dialogue, “nothing changes” in Europe’s “full support for Ukraine,” or collective views on “the [broader] security architecture and security guarantees for Ukraine.”
Summing up the talks, he said:
“We should not have any illussions; it is clear what the Russian side is playing at, but I will remain in constant contact with all those who possess the good will and the belief that an agreement is possible – or at the very least, a ceasefire before winter.”
Without specifying the source of his claim, Tusk said that “three, four nights ago,” “Russia lost 2,500 men” during one night. “This gives us an idea of just how dire the further consequences of this war could be.”

Russia says three tankers with diesel en route to US
Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are en route to the United States, with a fourth expected to depart Wednesday, Moscow said, part of a deal that triggered a fierce Ukrainian and European backlash.
US president Donald Trump this month struck an agreement with Russia’s president Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions in exchange for Moscow releasing diesel onto global markets.

"We attach particular importance to the close cooperation supported within the Commonwealth in the fields of trade, investment, and high technology. The annual [trade] turnover between Russia and the CIS countries is significant - it is above $110 bln and is growing at double-digit percentage rates," he said.
Trade within the CIS is stable and mutually beneficial, the ambassador said. "Up to 90% of settlements are carried out in national currencies. Large industrial projects are being implemented, and the transcontinental logistics corridors North-South and East-West are being modernized and developed," Grigoryev stressed.
The CIS countries have established mechanisms of multilateral cooperation that are reliable, flexible, and adaptive to current realities, which cover an increasing number of relevant fields of activity, the Russian diplomat added.

Rogue AI, cyberattacks and weapons: the risks Anthropic is warning investors about ahead of its IPO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:52:25 UTC
17:52:25 KST

The AI company’s IPO paperwork warns of potential harms from increasingly autonomous systems, alongside financial and regulatory challenges.
Rogue AI systems, cyberattacks and the potential use of artificial intelligence to develop dangerous weapons feature among the risks Anthropic has disclosed to investors as it prepares for a stock market debut.
Of the 335 pages outlining Anthropic’s finances, executive compensation, dividend policy and the like, 93 pages are devoted to “risk factors” — things that could hurt potential shareholders’ investments. Rival SpaceX’s listed risk factors, in comparison, took up 38 out of more than 250 pages.
The disclosures are required as part of the IPO process, giving potential investors a clearer picture of the risks they face by buying into the company.
In pitching itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” write the company’s founders in a letter to prospective shareholders in the IPO filing. “Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organisation, founded in large part to help the world realise AI’s benefits and avoid its dangers.”
Still, the risks are many. They range from the mundane — the possibility it won’t be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation.
Here is a look at some of the risks Anthropic details:
The technology’s rapid development
Anthropic said it’s possible its models could develop so quickly the company won’t be able to implement adequate safety measures, “which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in September that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet.The warning, and now Anthropic’s move to sell shares, comes amid growing concern inside and outside the industry about increasingly powerful systems that can solve problems beyond human capacity but could also act on their own to carry out harmful tasks.
As AI systems “become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the SEC filing said, there’s a risk that such systems could “take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.”
“Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business,” Anthropic said.
Now that the AI models are themselves contributing to Anthropic’s own research and development, it’s possible that AI could progress “beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models,” according to the filing. This, the document said, could adversely affect Anthropic’s business.
Malicious actors could cause mayhem with the technology
The filing discussed concerns that advanced AI systems, if not developed and operated with enough safeguards and oversight, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”
The company said it would be harmed if use by bad actors causes damage, “or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse.”
Anthropic sketched out the prospect of bad actors using AI models to build chemical weapons or authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens. In September, the company disclosed that it had blocked efforts to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapon development.
The company could run up against limits on processing power
Compute — the computing power or resources needed to build, test and improve AI models — is expensive and in high demand. Anthropic notes that if it’s unable to secure adequate compute, or if “we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.”
Anthropic mentioned community opposition to data centres as a risk to its business. Data centre development “has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources,” the filing said, adding that if regulators impose new requirements or charges as a result, its ability to do business could suffer.
In addition, the company relies on a small number of customers, including SpaceX and Microsoft, and distribution channels for a large portion of its revenue. This means that even if just one of its big customers decides to scale back — or drop the company altogether — Anthropic said it could see its prospects and finances suffer.
Mitigating the risks
In some ways, AI’s enormous risk, combined with its enormous potential, is Anthropic’s main selling point. The company has tried to position itself as a responsible AI company, and courts business customers by emphasising safety-mindedness.
“We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology,” the filing said.
Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Research, said IPO deals have to display “very clearly” what risks people face when they invest their money in a newly public stock.
“That’s one of the things that’s great about our capital markets here domestically is the level of transparency that you must commit to, to be a publicly traded corporation on a U.S. exchange requires you to outline those risks in a very clear way, so that people understand if they want to participate by offering their hard-earned money and help finance this type of a deal,” he said.

Number of millionaires in NL skyrockets as house prices rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

17:52:15 KST

Number of millionaires in NL skyrockets as house prices rise
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Over 81,000 households achieved millionaire status last year without needing to do anything to earn it – the rise in house prices has quietly boosted their wealth.
The figures come from national statistics bureau CBS, which counted 547,000 households with net assets of at least €1 million at the start of 2025 – 6.6% of all Dutch households.
A year earlier the number stood at 466,000. In 2011 it was 170,000. The main driver is the rise in asset valuations – namely house prices.
Two-thirds of millionaire households have between €1 million and €2 million, and 3% have over €10 million.
Those who got rich this way tend to be older – the average millionaire is 61, and fewer than 3% are under 35. For younger people, entrepreneurship and ownership in company shares is the more common way to millionaire status. CBS does not say what role inheritance plays here.
Where you live, of course, makes a big difference. In Bloemendaal and Laren, close to two in five households are now millionaires. In Kerkrade, Zuid-Limburg, it’s closer to 1 in 100. Groningen, Flevoland and Friesland are all below 5%.

NATO simulates war with a million troops on each side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:51:22 UTC
17:51:22 KST

- NATO and U.S. Army commanders ran the Avenger Triad 26 simulation from Wiesbaden, Germany, from Oct. 6 to Oct. 15, 2026, with one million simulated soldiers on each side.
- Palantir’s Maven Smart System was the central system tested to give commanders a full operational picture within seconds.
NATO commanders spent 10 days in October rehearsing how they would fight a war against an enemy army of one million soldiers, running the alliance’s Avenger Triad 26 computer-assisted exercise from a command center in Wiesbaden, Germany, where about 150 officers from several countries tracked a simulated attack on alliance territory around the clock on a live map of Europe.
The exercise ran from Oct. 6 through Oct. 15, 2026, at headquarters in Germany, France, Poland and the Netherlands, with Wiesbaden, home of U.S. Army Europe and Africa, coordinating the effort, and the simulated scenario pitted one million soldiers on each side against each other, local news outlet Merkurist reported after a press tour that gave it rare access to the command center.
Merkurist reported that about 20,000 troops took part in the field, including 4,000 U.S. soldiers, although Avenger Triad 26 was mainly a simulation for command staffs and not a traditional field training exercise, with headquarters from NATO’s 32 member countries practicing how to run joint operations in a crisis, share information and make decisions quickly.
U.S. Army Europe and Africa and NATO’s Allied Land Command worked as a single integrated headquarters during the exercise, which brought in U.S. Army V Corps, the 2nd Polish Corps, the 1st French Corps and the 1st German-Netherlands Corps under an Article 5 collective defense scenario, in which an attack on one ally is treated as an attack on all.
All incoming information was pulled together in Wiesbaden, where a map of Europe showed NATO bases and enemy positions in real time, and one of the main goals of the exercise was to cut the time it takes commanders to react to an attack, partly by using artificial intelligence, so that in a real emergency they could see a complete picture of the battlefield within seconds.
“We must connect the information technology of the 21st century with the military capabilities of the 20th century,” said British Army Lt. Gen. Jez Bennett, acting commander of NATO’s Allied Land Command.
The central system tested in Wiesbaden was the Maven Smart System, the data and targeting platform built by U.S. company Palantir, which uses artificial intelligence to sort through large amounts of data quickly, and the plan is to eventually feed information from reconnaissance drones, ground sensors, radars and cameras into one common network. The U.S. military is also building new tools on the same platform, with U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps developers demonstrating a Maven-based air-defense dashboard at Marine Corps Air Station Yuma, Arizona, in October.
“In the past, a military commander had to wait for a messenger on horseback. Now information reaches us at lightning speed,” said German Army Maj. Gen. Björn Schulz.
Lessons from the war in Ukraine were also built into the exercise, and U.S. Army Maj. Ben Schiff said that Ukraine, which was invaded by Russia, has advanced military drone technology faster than any other country.
During a preliminary exercise in Wiesbaden the week before Avenger Triad 26 began, soldiers were shown several new systems, including unmanned vehicles built to search for mines and drones meant to defend against enemy aerial weapons, and some of that technology is being researched and developed in laboratories at the Wiesbaden-Erbenheim installation.

“Fifteen Tulips” and countless hits: Mimi Ivanova celebrates 80 with a concert

News
“Fifteen Tulips” and countless hits: Mimi Ivanova celebrates 80 with a concert
Tuesday 27 October 2026 10:15
Tuesday, 27 October 2026, 10:15
Mimi Ivanova
PHOTO Facebook/ Mimi Ivanova and Razvigor Popov
Font size
One of Bulgaria’s most popular singers over the past six decades, Mimi Ivanova, is celebrating her 80th birthday with an anniversary concert entitled “When I Was a Girl – Mimi at 80.” On October 28, the festive evening at Hall No 1 of the National Palace of Culture in Sofia will feature golden hits, new songs and special musical collaborations.
Mimi Ivanova and Razvigor Popov
PHOTO Facebook/ Mimi Ivanova and Razvigor Popov
Joining Mimi Ivanova on stage will be much-loved Bulgarian performers, who will perform songs from her repertoire as well as works by her longtime creative partner and husband, composer Razvigor Popov. Among the special guest performers are Veselin Marinov, Margarita Hranova, Elvira Georgieva, and DesiSlava. The concert will also feature appearances by Yordanka Hristova, Vasil Naydenov, Georgi Hristov, Orlin Goranov, the Argirov Brothers, Toni Dimitrova and Stefan Diomov.
Born on December 28, 1946, Mimi Ivanova began singing at a very young age. Her musical journey started at a music school in her hometown of Hisarya. She later graduated from the Music School in Plovdiv and went on to study in the estrada department of the Music Academy in Sofia, where she was taught by the renowned singer Irina Chmihova.
While still a student, Mimi became a soloist with the Sofia Orchestra, performing alongside fellow singers Pasha Hristova, Maria Neykova and Boris Gudjunov. The artists later recorded songs together that won prestigious awards, including the Golden Orpheus and Spring music festivals. Throughout her career, Mimi Ivanova has received numerous awards in Bulgaria and across Europe, released a number of albums, and won the hearts of many fans.
PHOTO Facebook/ Mimi Ivanova and Razvigor Popov
Mimi Ivanova’s partnership with the Bulgarian National Radio began in the early 1970s, when she worked extensively with the Radio’s Big Band, led by conductor Vili Kazasyan. This longstanding partnership has continued throughout her career. Songs performed by Ivanova have won awards six times at BNR’s Spring music contest.
Among the award-winning entries is “Fifteen Tulips” (1978), with music and arrangement by Razvigor Popov and lyrics by Yordan Yankov. The song has since become one of Mimi Ivanova’s signature hits.

U.S. Marine Corps tests kamikaze drones in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:47:17 UTC
17:47:17 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps tested Neros Archer kamikaze drones with live warheads at Camp Fuji, Japan, for the first time on Oct. 20, 2026.
- Junior enlisted Marines from Battalion Landing Team 1/1 destroyed targets in two scenarios, including an anti-armor ambush, with no unexploded drones left behind.
The U.S. Marine Corps has tested kamikaze drones in Japan, flying Neros Archer one-way attack drones armed with live explosive warheads at Combined Arms Training Center Camp Fuji, at the foot of Mount Fuji, on Oct. 20, 2026, the first time the drone has been used in its live kinetic form at the range.
Marines from Battalion Landing Team 1/1 of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit flew the drones into targets in two separate training scenarios, one of them an anti-armor ambush, and both flights ended with the targets destroyed and no unexploded drones left on the range for the Explosive Ordnance Disposal team to recover.
“This week is the first time, here at CATC Camp Fuji, that we’ve deployed the Neros Archer in a live kinetic variant,” said Chief Warrant Officer 2 Stephen Bilbo, Camp Fuji’s Gunner and Range Control Officer. “Neros Archer is the current Marine Corps’ program of record for one-way attack drones flown by a first-person view pilot.”
The Archer is a small first-person-view strike drone built by Neros Technologies of El Segundo, California, and flown by a pilot wearing a video headset who steers it directly into the target, and the Camp Fuji flights follow the U.S. Marine Corps’ first live-fire FPV attack drone training, held in South Korea on July 30 and Aug. 5, when Marines from the 3rd Marine Division struck armored and personnel targets with Archers at ranges of up to about 20 km (12.4 miles).
The Marines in Japan are testing how the drone fits into small ground units, and the battalion described the exercise as a different kind of training from what 1st Battalion, 1st Marines had previously done at its home station at Camp Pendleton, California.
“This scenario is going to be a little bit different than we’ve done in the past, this is going to be a proof of concept tied to our hunter-killer teams. The goal of this is to be an extension of our hunter-killers’ capabilities with defeating armor and a means of ground line communication within our adversary force,” said Master Sgt. Glenn Dayton, company operations chief of Weapons Company, Battalion Landing Team 1/1.
The pilots are junior enlisted Marines, from lance corporal to sergeant, who are hand-picked by their unit leadership for a three-week operator course, and the only prerequisite is that they have no previous drone experience, which the U.S. Marine Corps says lets them learn the Archer’s flying skills without old habits to unlearn.
“All this is handled by noncommissioned officers and non-NCOs,” said Dayton. “You’re looking at the heart and soul of our ground force. This is not executed by staff NCO or officers, I think that’s a huge aspect. Our lower enlisted are the ones we rely on to master this craft.”
A few dozen observers watched the two flights, and the Camp Fuji EOD technicians were there because an armed drone that fails to detonate is treated as live ordnance lying on the range.
“The drone carries an explosive payload, if for any reason it’s not able to function as designed with the controller and it goes down [without exploding] it counts as unexploded ordnance or UXO and then that falls under our bread and butter,” said Staff Sgt. Francisco Melandez, a CATC Camp Fuji explosive ordnance technician.
The U.S. Marine Corps signed a $17 million contract for 8,000 Archer Strike drones, while the U.S. Army has turned to the same company for its own FPV needs, awarding Neros a contract worth up to $500 million in 2026 after selecting it in November 2025 as one of three primary manufacturers for its Purpose-Built Attritable Systems program.

Norwegian media companies take Meta to court over new commercial terms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:42:06 UTC
17:42:06 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Major Norwegian media companies have taken Meta to court over its proposed new commercial terms, raising concerns about the potential use of news content to train artificial intelligence models, broadcaster NRK reported Tuesday.
Members of the Norwegian Media Association (MBL) argue that the new terms would grant Meta the right to scrape every article, photo and video published by editorially controlled media outlets.
Major media organizations, including NRK, TV 2, Schibsted, Amedia, Polaris, Aller, DN, Mentor Medier, NTB and Hordaland Folkeblad, have asked the Oslo District Court to suspend Meta’s new terms pending a judicial review of their legality.
“We believe that this should be legally assessed to see if this is actually in line with Norwegian law,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, chairwoman of the MBL.
NRK’s legal director Olav Nyhus also said they “in no way” want Meta to be able to use their content to further strengthen platforms such as Facebook and Instagram.
Nyhus added that it would not be easy to terminate agreements with Instagram and Facebook, as the platforms have become important channels for disseminating information.
“What Meta is doing is destroying the entire financial basis for journalism,” he said, adding: “We believe that Meta’s conduct and terms are a clear violation of competition law.”
Meta recently revised its commercial terms to remove language that raised concerns about the potential use of news websites to train artificial intelligence models.
The revised terms specify that automated website crawling is intended to develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products.
The provisions still allow Meta to use automated tools, including web scrapers, bots and crawlers, to access and collect content from websites associated with businesses using its platforms.
An earlier version of the proposed terms included language about using collected material to “train” Meta products, prompting concerns among publishers and legal experts over the potential use of copyrighted news content for AI development.
Meta subsequently removed the reference and clarified that the crawling provisions apply to advertising and business products.

EU readying for major Australian resources investment, ambassador says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:40:59 UTC
17:40:59 KST

EU readying for major Australian resources investment, ambassador says
SYDNEY, Oct 27 - The European Union expects a wave of investment into the Australian critical minerals sector as it pushes to diversify its supply chain away from China, the bloc's ambassador to Australia Lawrence Meredith said on Tuesday.
Australia and the European Union struck a free trade agreement in March after eight years of negotiations, removing tariffs on almost all goods and easing EU access to Australian critical minerals.
Once both parties sign and ratify that agreement, expected early next year, a 5.5% EU tariff on critical minerals will be removed.
"It is going to be a game changer," Meredith said.
In parallel, talks are "very close" for Australia to sign a memorandum of understanding with the European Investment Bank, which would act as the bloc's funding vehicle, Meredith added.
"The European Union will be massively investing in critical minerals. Since we wish to diversify away from China, then one of the most likely partners has to be Australia," he said.
EU policy proposals have laid out as much as €10 billion ($11.2 billion) for critical raw materials within the larger €409 billion competitiveness fund, as the EU debates its budget from 2028 to 2034.
Australia is one of several critical minerals "superpowers" in which the EU is looking to invest, including Brazil, South Africa and Canada. The EU also expects to invest along the supply chain, including in processing, Meredith said.
Australia said on Tuesday it would refresh its critical minerals strategy to place greater emphasis on refining and processing, as competition for investment intensifies and supply-chain concerns persist.
The bloc is looking initially at the minerals that Australia will prioritise for its strategic reserve: gallium, antimony and rare earths.
Australian companies going faster through the early project development would speed the investment process, he said.
"(The FTA) is a signal that Europe wants to do far more with Australia. We also have a security and defence partnership. A lot of that is dual technology, and it requires precisely these critical minerals," he said.
The European Union plans to mobilise €800 billion into defence under ReArm Europe by 2030.
Australia is also on track to join the EU's flagship funding program for research and innovation, Horizon Europe, next year.
Meredith said 2026 had been a "transformational" year for Australian-EU relations.
"You've seen a big surge in EU-Australia in 2026, and I'm very confident we will go to the next level in 2027." REUTERS

India ramps up oil imports from Middle East – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:40:20 UTC
17:40:20 KST

India ramps up oil imports from Middle East – media
India’s imports of Middle Eastern crude have surged to more than half of its total oil purchases, as steep Gulf discounts and soaring freight costs make Russian supplies less competitive for Indian refiners.
Middle Eastern crude accounted for 54% of India’s oil imports in September, up from 32% in August, while Russia’s share fell to 33.5% from 46.6%, according to ship-tracking data reported by Reuters. Russia nevertheless remained India’s largest individual oil supplier.
The shift is reflected in purchases by state-owned Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), which expects Russian crude volumes to decline significantly in November. Russian oil accounted for around 37% of BPCL’s crude sourcing during July-September.
India increased Russian oil purchases when the US-Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern supplies. However, Gulf shipments have since recovered to prewar levels, with producers offering steep discounts to attract buyers.
The conflict has driven up global tanker rates, making the longer voyages from Russian ports increasingly expensive. Average crude freight costs have risen nearly sevenfold over the past year, from around $3 per barrel to more than $20, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank cited war-risk premiums, higher fuel expenses, and costly ship-to-ship transfers.
Freight costs for Russian Urals crude shipped to Asia reached around $30 per barrel or more in early October. Transporting a tanker shipment from Russia’s Black Sea ports to India currently costs $27 million-$30 million, compared with approximately $19 million in September, Reuters reported.
Meanwhile, some Iraqi cargoes are being offered at discounts exceeding $25 per barrel against the Dubai benchmark before shipping, while selected Saudi shipments have been discounted by as much as $10, Bloomberg reported, citing traders. Russian crude, which previously sold at steep discounts, was being offered at around a $2 premium to the separate Dated Brent benchmark.
“Due to the increase in freight, we are not getting good offers from Russia,” BPCL finance director Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta told analysts on Monday.
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL), another state-owned oil company, is also adjusting its procurement strategy, increasingly buying crude on a delivered-price basis to manage shipping costs. HPCL Chairman Vikas Kaushal also confirmed that Gulf producers are offering discounts to offset the elevated freight rates.
Indian Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday that Middle Eastern supplies are increasing, and noted that Russian oil purchases depend on pricing and discounts compared with other grades.
Asked whether Washington had pressured India to reduce Russian oil imports, Puri said, “I never felt anything.”

U.S. Navy nuclear submarine arrives in Australia for maintenance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:40:18 UTC
17:40:18 KST

- USS Colorado (SSN 788) arrived at HMAS Stirling for a monthlong maintenance period involving more than 30 Australian civilian technicians from ASC.
- Colorado has been named the first U.S. Navy Virginia-class submarine assigned to Submarine Squadron 3 and will return in late 2027.
The U.S. Navy attack submarine USS Colorado (SSN 788) arrived at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia on Oct. 27 to begin a scheduled monthlong maintenance period. For the first time, Australian civilian technicians will carry out routine maintenance on a Virginia-class submarine in Western Australia, working alongside American shipyard specialists, with the U.K. Royal Navy also taking part in the work.
More than 30 trained and certified technicians from Australian shipbuilder ASC Pty Ltd. will work on the boat alongside specialists from Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility, the U.S. Navy yard in Hawaii where the Australian workers were trained.
The visit comes one day after Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and his Australian and British counterparts issued a joint statement on Oct. 26 naming Colorado as the first U.S. Navy Virginia-class submarine assigned to Submarine Squadron 3, the American squadron reactivated at HMAS Stirling in June. When Colorado returns in late 2027, it is set to help formally establish Submarine Rotational Force-West, the arrangement under which up to four U.S. submarines and one British submarine will operate on rotation from the base south of Perth.
“This maintenance period brings us closer to establishing SRF-West,” said U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Doug Adams, director of AUKUS, International & Systems. “Our Lead Maintenance Activity, Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility, is doing a great job ensuring the Australian personnel trained in Hawaii are ready and able to support our submarines.”
Colorado’s visit is the fourth submarine maintenance period in Western Australia since the AUKUS partnership was formed and the third in the past 12 months, and each one has handed Australia a larger share of the work. USS Hawaii (SSN 776) was serviced at Stirling in 2024 with help from the submarine tender USS Emory S. Land (AS 39), while USS Vermont (SSN 792) arrived in October 2025 for a larger and more complex maintenance package that was carried out without a tender. The British submarine HMS Anson followed with its own maintenance period in February 2026, and Colorado is the sixth nuclear-powered attack submarine to visit Stirling since the AUKUS partners announced Australia’s path to a nuclear-powered fleet.
The latest period will also be the first to use several new pieces of Australian-built infrastructure together, including a custom-made metal safety walkway around the submarine’s sail known as a “racetrack,” nuclear submarine upgrades to the base’s Diamantina Pier, a pure water plant, a high-pressure air compressor and a dehumidifier.
“During last year’s maintenance period, we successfully delivered pure water from an Australian-designed and built plant and validated the sail racetrack was fit for purpose. During the U.K.’s maintenance period in February, we validated the high-pressure air compressor and dehumidifier systems. Now, with the racetrack, we’re using it to conduct maintenance, utilizing the pier upgrades, and leveraging a workforce of about three dozen fully qualified and certified Australian civilian nuclear-powered submarine maintenance workers,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Jason Pittman, commander of Submarine Squadron 3.
Australian officials said the visits are building the country’s ability to keep allied submarines in port longer and return them to sea on time, which it will need before the rotational force begins operating.
“These maintenance periods have been critical to Australia being on track to start SRF-West in 2027,” said Royal Australian Navy Rear Adm. David Mann, head of the Australian Submarine Agency’s Virginia Division.
The British side will be directly involved in the work on the American boat, which officials presented as a way to bring all three navies closer to common maintenance practices.
“The more the three nations work together to maintain submarines – whether American or British – the faster we’ll be able to uplift our Australian partner’s knowledge and skills and increase commonality across our submarine forces,” said Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the U.K. Prime Minister’s Special Representative for AUKUS.
Under the first pillar of AUKUS, Australia plans to buy three in-service Virginia-class submarines from the United States before moving to the new SSN-AUKUS design, and the port visits are intended to prepare its workforce and facilities to maintain and operate a conventionally armed, nuclear-powered fleet of its own. Ahead of Colorado’s arrival, about 20 Australian civilian maintainers and 25 Royal Australian Navy divers, Fleet Support Unit officers and sailors had completed training at Pearl Harbor, and more than 230 others were still training in Hawaii, USNI News reported in June.
“The success of any maintenance period comes down to the people on the deckplates, and the Australian personnel stepping aboard our ship are true professionals,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Justin Reeves, commanding officer of USS Colorado.

Israeli defense tech M&A surges to $3.26 billion in first half of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:38:58 UTC
17:38:58 KST

Merger and acquisition activity in Israel's defense technology sector jumped to $3.26 billion in the first half of 2026, an 8.5-fold increase from $384 million in 2025, according to a report by the American consulting giant Frost & Sullivan exclusively seen by Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post.
The report, presented this week at an industry event in Tel Aviv hosted by law firm Gornitzky in collaboration with defense-focused investment fund Aurelius, found a growing demand for Israeli military technologies, particularly in autonomous systems, sensors, robotics and counter-drone technologies.
It examined 44 announced mergers and acquisitions in Israel's aviation and defense sectors between 2023 and 2026, excluding cyber and cyber intelligence transactions. Deal values were publicly disclosed in 22 of those transactions, totaling about $4.1b. The median disclosed deal size was approximately $37.8m.
While, in part, a small number of large acquisitions drove the dramatic increase in the 2026 deal value, Frost & Sullivan said the data also point to a broader trend of defense companies seeking to acquire technologies rather than develop them internally.
"The market is increasingly focused on buying capabilities that can close operational gaps, accelerate time to market and respond quickly to evolving defense requirements," the report said.
US-based acquirers accounted for roughly 45% of the transactions reviewed, making them the largest buyer group. Israeli purchasers represented about 30% of acquisitions, while European companies accounted for approximately 11%.
More than half of the deals were concentrated in three sectors: defense electronics and sensors, unmanned aerial vehicles and autonomous systems, and ground systems and robotics.
According to the report, the wars in Ukraine, the Persian Gulf, Lebanon, and Gaza are not the only reason why the growth of the Israeli defense tech industry has accelerated; the technology has proven its effectiveness and ability to adapt on the battlefield; Israeli defense technologies have attracted increased interest from international buyers for this reason as well.
Not slowing down
Ariel Sagee, a partner at Gornitzky GNY who also leads the firm's defense and defense regulation practices, linked the sector’s growth to recent conflict and tense global geopolitics.
“The war in Ukraine highlights the need for stable international alliances to ensure the supply chain. Israel cannot be isolated. Ukraine is under two-way pressure - Chinese drone components on the one hand and SpaceX's satellite technology on the other. These two forces pull at it and illustrate the importance of international alliances in building stable defense solutions,” he said.
Irit Nudelman, vice president and head of defense consulting for Israel and Europe at Frost & Sullivan, said she expects deal activity to remain strong.
"We will continue to see significant deals in the coming years, primarily in the fields of anti-drone systems, robotics, underwater systems, space and autonomy," she said, adding that the defense sector is becoming more receptive to technologies developed by start-ups and that maturation of the defense innovation market is likely to continue.
Although US and Israeli strategic buyers remain the dominant acquirers, Nudelman said European and Asian firms are more often pursuing partnerships, joint ventures and targeted investments rather than full acquisitions.
‘The Democratization of lethality’
The event also featured a discussion between retired Maj.-Gen. Amir Eshel, a partner at Aurelius and a former commander of the Israel Air Force, and Sagee.
Eshel noted that technological advances have expanded access to military capabilities once limited to nation-states.
"You can call it the democratization of lethality," Eshel said. "Once, states were the sole sovereign that controlled war capabilities; today, organizations and individuals also have state capabilities."
He also warned against weakening Israel's domestic defense innovation ecosystem by relocating early-stage companies abroad. He stressed the importance of strengthening supply-chain partnerships rather than pursuing complete self-sufficiency.
"Full Israeli defense production independence is not possible," Eshel said. "We do not have the raw materials, and there is also a lack of workforce. Nevertheless, Israeli capability can be strengthened, and additionally it is right to create partnerships for the supply chains required by Israel."

Drone strike in Sudan’s Nyala kills at least 21, injures 40

A Nyala resident said the attack took place at about 8pm (18:00 GMT) on Monday at a market in the north of the city, which serves as the de facto capital of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
“Twenty-one people were killed in last night’s bombing, and more than 40 others injured,” a medic at Nyala Hospital said on Tuesday.
Another Nyala resident told AFP that the market was frequented by armed men, particularly RSF fighters.
The Sudanese military, which has been at war with the RSF since April 2023, regularly strikes Nyala, where the RSF has declared an administration rivalling the military-backed, internationally recognised government in Khartoum.
The attack comes as the warring sides are increasingly turning to drone warfare.
Earlier this month, the RSF launched strikes targeting Khartoum’s airport, as well as dams and power stations in the government-controlled east.
An RSF drone attack on Tuesday “targeted the al-Markhiyat transformer station, disrupting power supplies for millions across large parts of Khartoum and Gezira state”, a national electricity company told AFP on condition of anonymity.
It followed Monday’s coordinated RSF drone strikes on six power stations, which cut off electricity to millions in the states of Gezira, White Nile, Sennar and Gadarif.
A government drone attack in a disputed border region between Sudan and South Sudan earlier this month killed more than 150 people.
The war began in 2023 when a dispute over how to integrate the two forces erupted into clashes in the capital, Khartoum. The fighting has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 13 million, and created the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises.
On Monday, the United States, the European Union and 30 other countries warned of an “alarming deterioration” in food access in Sudan and called for “urgent action” to prevent famine.
In a joint statement released by the US State Department on Monday, the signatories called on the groups fighting Sudan’s civil war “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance”.

He said passengers who did not need hospital treatment were provided with meals and accommodation.
"I am in direct contact with the emergency services," he added.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said one person was killed and 15 others were injured in Russian attacks on the capital Kyiv.
Russia’s Defense Ministry separately said its forces carried out a massive overnight strike with ground-launched precision weapons and drones on Ukrainian defense industry enterprises and transport infrastructure in Kyiv, a logistics center in the Kharkiv region, and vessels used in the interests of Ukrainian forces.
According to the ministry, the targets in Kyiv included an industrial enterprise producing and storing long- and medium-range drones, and a drone assembly shop of the company Oakline, which it said produces and stores the FP-1 and FP-2 long- and medium-range drones of the company Fire Point.
It also said it hit a drone assembly workshop and the Yuzhny road-rail bridge, which it claimed was used for transit of military cargo by road and rail.
In the Kharkiv region, the ministry said it struck an unloading and customs terminal of the company Regional Logistics Center, which it said is used to store and distribute supplies and dual-use goods for Ukrainian forces, as well as reconnaissance and strike drones.
The ministry also claimed that a dry cargo vessel carrying supplies for Ukrainian forces to the port of Chornomorsk in Ukraine’s Odesa region was hit at sea.
Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 222 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over 15 Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.
The claims from both sides could not be independently verified.

Lithuania Urges Stronger Controls Against Stolen Ukrainian Grain Transit
Lithuania is pushing for practical implementation of a verification mechanism to trace the origin of grain and prevent European Union ports and transport infrastructure from being used to move Ukrainian grain stolen by Russia from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Lithuanian Vice Minister of Agriculture Rolandas Taraškevičius made the statement on the sidelines of the EU Agriculture and Fisheries Council meeting in Luxembourg, according to European Pravda.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
EU agricultural ministers met in Luxembourg on October 26 to discuss implementing grain origin inspection mechanisms to detect agricultural products originating from occupied regions of Ukraine.
“We need more concrete and practical steps to implement the grain origin verification mechanism,” Taraškevičius stated.
The official noted that he discussed the practical application of the mechanism last week with representatives of the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.
Work on implementing the controls is ongoing, and Taraškevičius planned to update EU counterparts on progress during the meeting.
The Lithuanian official made a clear distinction between the transit of Russian grain in general and the transport of grain stolen from temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories. He explained that the main task is to prevent EU ports and logistics infrastructure from being utilized for moving stolen grain.
Previously, an Israeli official announced that a shipment of Ukrainian grain, which had been taken by Russia from temporarily occupied territories, was blocked from unloading in Israel. The decision to reject the wheat and barley cargo carried by the Panama-flagged vessel Panormitis was made directly by the country’s largest grain importer, Cenziper, rather than by government authorities.
This outcome followed intensive diplomatic and legal efforts by Ukraine, prompting Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha to warn other global operators against participating in the trade of stolen agricultural goods.

Russian sabotage network was exposed in Romania following a fire at an arms factory
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

Russian sabotage network was exposed in Romania following a fire at an arms factory
Kyiv • UNN
The network is linked to the fire at the Carfil factory in Brașov on September 14. Its coordinators may have been planning acts of sabotage in Romania and neighboring countries.
A Russian sabotage network has been uncovered in Romania, one that was involved in the fire at the Carfil arms factory in the city of Brașov. They may have had other targets in Romania and neighboring countries as well. This was reported by Romania’s intelligence service, according to UNN.
Details
"The Romanian Intelligence Service, in cooperation with domestic and foreign partners, uncovered a coordinated sabotage network from the Russian Federation that was involved in causing the fire on September 14, 2026, at the Carfil industrial site in Brașov, near CARFIL SA, a subsidiary of CN ROMARM. The investigation confirmed the involvement of several citizens of former Soviet states residing in European Union countries. Judicial investigations into their activities in Romania, conducted in cooperation with the authorities of several European states, are ongoing," the post said.
According to the intelligence service, the data it obtained indicate that the network’s missions were not limited to Romania alone.
"Coordinators in the Russian Federation identified a wide range of targets for it in the region: state-owned and private weapons production facilities, as well as other sites of military and industrial interest. This case is part of a broader campaign of sabotage operations coordinated by the Russian Federation in Europe. Investigations conducted this year also uncovered other attempts targeting sites in Romania, including international military facilities or those used to train the armed forces of Ukraine. These actions are aimed at intimidation, undermining defense capabilities, and weakening the contribution of target states to European and regional security," the intelligence service said in its post.
According to the available data, recruitment often begins on social media with offers of money for tasks that appear harmless, such as observing facilities or photographing them. The tasks may later become more complex and involve arson, destruction, or murder.
"In the event of refusal, coordinators may resort to pressure and blackmail. These networks exploit, in particular, financial vulnerability, addictions, or a criminal past. To conceal their identities and movements, their members often use vehicles, accommodation, and means of payment registered in other people’s names, as well as communication via cards from third countries and encrypted messengers. These elements must be assessed together and in context; individually, they do not indicate a person’s involvement in sabotage activities," the post said.
Reminder
A fire broke out at an arms factory in Cugir, Romania, causing damage of more than €400,000. Some 150,000 machine-gun rounds were destroyed, and the authorities are considering sabotage as a possible cause.

U.S. Marine Corps tests new Maven air-defense dashboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:33:57 UTC
17:33:57 KST

- U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps teams demonstrated a prototype air-defense dashboard built inside the Maven Smart System at Marine Corps Air Station Yuma on Oct. 5.
- Developers built the tool in under two months and plan to beta test it during upcoming large-scale simulation exercises.
U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps teams have shown Marine air-defense operators a prototype dashboard that brings threat and resource data into one screen. It is meant to help a regional commander see what is in the air and what defenses are available to respond, and it was first demonstrated on Oct. 5 during the Weapons and Tactics Instructor course 1-27 at Marine Corps Air Station Yuma, Arizona.
The tool is officially named the Maven Smart System Regional Air Defense Commander Dashboard C2 Tool. It runs inside the Maven Smart System, the Palantir-built data and targeting platform that the U.S. Department of War has spread across its commands, and it pulls together information from multiple sources to give commanders a clearer picture of regional air-defense operations.
Development moved quickly for a military software project. The Overmatch Rapid Capability Cell, part of the Department of the Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Mission Systems, led development and engineering, and its developers worked directly with Marine air-defense operators to build the prototype inside the existing Maven environment in less than two months after coordination began.
On the Marine Corps side, Project Dynamis and Task Force Maven led the effort, with the 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing acting as the Fleet Marine Force sponsor and the Aviation Expeditionary Enablers team under the Deputy Commandant for Aviation providing support.
“Ready-to-use C2 tools are critical as 3d MAW continues to experiment with the various methods of supporting joint air defense command and control. The collaboration among Project Overmatch, Project Dynamis, and Fleet operators at WTI drives us forward,” said Brig. Gen. Dolberry Jr., assistant wing commander of 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing.
WTI is the Marine Corps’ advanced aviation tactics course, run by Marine Aviation Weapons and Tactics Squadron One (MAWTS-1) at Yuma, which made it a useful place to put the prototype in front of experienced operators. Representatives from all four Marine Aircraft Wings, MAWTS-1 instructors and personnel from Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron One (VMX-1) gave feedback during the course, and that input is now shaping which data the dashboard needs to combine to support integrated air and missile defense.
The team is also looking at how to add what the Marine Corps release calls Maven Smart System’s “super intelligence features,” so that commanders can better assess adversary activity. The release did not say what those features are or how they would work in the air-defense tool.
The dashboard arrives as the Marine Corps opens Maven to far more of its personnel. DefenseScoop reported on Oct. 20 that an administrative message, effective Oct. 1, directs units at every echelon to give authorized personnel their own accounts on the system, and that it names Project Dynamis and Task Force Maven as the coordinating offices for the rollout. The Department of War raised the ceiling on its Palantir contract for the Maven Smart System to nearly $1.3 billion through 2029 in 2025, DefenseScoop also reported.
The platform is already in wide use elsewhere in the U.S. military. Defense One reported in September that all U.S. combatant commands use Maven for intelligence and operations data analysis, and that the system drew attention early in the war with Iran for helping to facilitate strikes on thousands of targets.
The next step for the air-defense dashboard is a beta test during upcoming large-scale simulation exercises, where operators will use it during exercise operations to judge how easy it is to navigate, how quickly it responds and whether its features give them the information they need to make air-defense decisions. The Marine Corps did not say when those exercises will take place, which units will take part, or whether the tool is expected to move beyond the prototype stage.

The court is due to deliver its judgement in Lissu's case on November 6.

EU-China hybrid car deal won’t really help European carmakers

The View
EU-China hybrid car deal won’t really help European carmakers
The quota helps neither consumers nor companies in the long run. EU carmakers should up their game by leveraging China’s supply chain
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Winston Mok, a private investor, was previously a private equity investor. 
Earlier this month, simmering trade tensions between the EU and China ease as the two sides reached an agreement in Beijing limiting hybrid car exports from China to an annual quota of 350,000 units. After the European Union imposed tariffs on fully electric cars from China in 2024, hybrid imports surged. The quota would result in more than a halving of the 800,000 hybrid cars expected to be sold this year, a figure which may soon exceed a million if unchecked.
The quota would likely shift China’s product mix towards the premium segment to maximise the value of the 350,000 hybrid cars allowed per year, a cap which can rise by only 6 per cent a year during the four-year agreement.
Europe’s challenge goes beyond hybrids to all electric vehicles. Unlike the earlier mass-market Japanese and Korean imports which largely complemented the premium German brands, Europe can expect high-end EVs from China offered at a fraction of the price of their European counterparts, while potentially delivering superior features and performance.

Richest 0.1% produce more carbon pollution than poorest half of humanity: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:29:10 UTC
17:29:10 KST

İlayda Çakırtekin
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A new Oxfam analysis released Tuesday revealed that the world’s richest 0.1%, comprising around 8 million people, produce more carbon pollution than the world’s poorest 3.5 billion people combined.
The report found that a person in the richest 0.1% contributed nearly 400 times more to today’s extreme heat waves than someone in the poorest 50% of the global population, while the richest 0.1% collectively produce more than three times as much carbon pollution as the entire population of sub-Saharan Africa.
The report also found that the world’s richest 1% have been responsible for 20% of global warming since 1990, with per capita emissions 100 times higher than those of the poorest half of humanity.
It estimated that a single year of emissions from the richest 1% could cause 1.9 million excess heat-related deaths, with 78% of these deaths projected to occur in low- and lower-middle-income countries, which account for just 8% of global emissions.
The report further projected that emissions from the richest 1% would cause nearly $53 trillion in economic damage by 2050.
The report also highlighted private aviation as a stark example of carbon inequality, finding that private jets collectively emit more carbon pollution in two seconds than a person in the poorest half of the global population produces in a year.
“While the super-rich are responsible for a disproportionate share of carbon pollution, it is ordinary people who bear the brunt of the resulting floods, fires and famine,” the report noted.
The report also warned that climate change could displace up to 1 billion people, around 10% of the global population, by 2050, with most expected to be in the Global South.
“The climate crisis is often described as a shared human challenge. It is not. Those who have done the least to cause it are losing their homes, their harvests and, increasingly, their lives. Meanwhile, the super-rich can buy their way out of danger,” said Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar.
Behar noted that the super-rich also actively profit from the consequences of their pollution.
“This is not a tragedy of shared fate; it is a crime of extreme inequality,” Behar added.
The report also cautioned that climate disasters are increasingly being used to advance policies that deepen inequality, including privatization, land grabs, deregulation and tax breaks for the super-rich.
“The ultra-rich are setting the planet on fire and then charging the rest of us for the extinguishers,” Behar said, adding: “They profit from the pollution. They profit from the disaster. And they profit again from the clean-up.”
Oxfam called on governments attending COP31 to make wealthy polluters pay through higher taxes, significantly increase public climate finance for the Global South and triple adaptation funding by 2035.
It also urged governments to reduce inequality through climate-resilient public infrastructure and services, and curb corporate profiteering from climate disasters.

Nitin Gadkari says E20 criticism has faded, backs ethanol push to cut oil imports
NEW DELHI: Union road transport minister Nitin Gadkari on Tuesday described the backlash against petrol blended with 20% ethanol (E20) as a “paid campaign”. His remarks came a day after the government notified changes to motor vehicle rules allowing flex-fuel vehicles to run on blends containing up to 100% ethanol.Speaking at an event organised by industry body CII, Gadkari said the opposition to E20 had intensified about three months ago but had since subsided.“Three months ago, huge noise (khub halla) was made against the E20 (20 per cent ethanol-blended petrol) fuel; now rage against E20 fuel is over...It was a paid campaign,” news agency PTI quoted Gadkari as saying.The government on Monday notified amendments to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, permitting flex-fuel vehicles capable of running on fuel containing up to E100, or nearly pure ethanol.Gadkari has repeatedly advocated greater use of ethanol as part of efforts to reduce the country's dependence on imported fossil fuels. He said expanding the use of alternative fuels could help the country save valuable foreign exchange by cutting fossil fuel imports.
The Centre’s nationwide rollout of petrol blended with 20% ethanol (E20) had triggered protests and political criticism earlier this year, with motorists raising concerns over reduced mileage and the compatibility of the fuel with older vehicles.
Opposition leaders questioned the government’s decision to make E20 the standard fuel at petrol pumps across India in April 2025.The row escalated after attorney general R Venkataramani referred to E20 as an “experiment” during a Supreme Court hearing, saying its results would be known next year. The remark went viral, prompting renewed criticism of the policy.The Centre subsequently clarified that the attorney general was referring to ethanol supply volumes, not describing the E20 policy itself as an experiment. Venkataramani also told Reuters that his comments had been misunderstood.The government and automobile industry cited studies indicating that E20 does not significantly damage metallic engine components, while acknowledging that fuel efficiency and compatibility can vary across vehicles.

China calls for efforts to solve issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
16:27:09 CST
17:27:09 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy on Monday called for efforts to properly solve the issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property from the Gulf War.
The issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property, a legacy of the Gulf War, has remained unresolved for 35 years and continues to tug at the heartstrings of the Kuwaiti people, said Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations.
"Properly addressing this historical legacy issue is of great significance for soothing the emotional wounds caused by the war, improving relations between Kuwait and Iraq, and promoting friendly cooperation among countries in the region," he said.
Achieving this goal requires not only the joint efforts of the parties concerned, but also the political support of the Security Council, said Sun.
In September 2025, the council unanimously adopted Resolution 2792, which decides to establish the position of senior representative of the UN secretary-general to advance the resolution of the issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property.
Since her appointment, Senior Representative Mari Yamashita has maintained close communication with both Kuwait and Iraq. Kuwait, Iraq, and the International Committee of the Red Cross have made great efforts in this regard, Sun noted.
"We hope that Kuwait and Iraq will further demonstrate sincerity, patience, and determination, build on the prior work, and, in keeping with the principle of mutual respect and friendly consultation, intensify their efforts and work in the same direction, so as to create favorable conditions for substantive progress on the issue," Sun told a Security Council briefing on the issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property.
As a good friend and good partner of both Kuwait and Iraq, China will continue to play a constructive role in promoting a proper settlement of the issue, he said. ■

Defense Minister Martin Herem hires air defense expert Mati Tikerpuu as adviser
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:27:00 UTC
17:27:00 KST

Defense Minister Martin Herem hires air defense expert Mati Tikerpuu as adviser
Reservist Colonel Mati Tikerpuu, an air defense specialist, starts work as an adviser to Defense Minister Martin Herem (Reform) next month.
Herem told ERR that Tikerpuu's two main tasks will relate to air alerts and public threats notification, as well as improving society's awareness of threats and how to reduce and mitigate them — whether by finding an alternative location, creating a shelter, or strengthening infrastructure by engineering means.
"Air alerts and public notification need to be at a better level; all providers of vital services, and society as a whole, need to be better informed about both the threats and the possibilities for reducing and mitigating them," Herem said.
Herem described Tikerpuu as a "very high level" air defense specialist, noting he has also served as a brigade commander. "He understands general military questions very well and will help move this issue forward quickly over the next six months," the minister, a former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF), added.
Tikerpuu, who will be a full-time hire, himself told ERR he has served in the defense forces for more than 30 years, over half of that working on air defense.
"I'm being hired to help the minister make informed decisions. But Herem himself also has a very clear ambition about where he wants to get to with these developments in the near future. We've had conversations about where to go and what to do. But as for various development ideas or proposals, I couldn't comment on them publicly right now," Tikerpuu said.
Tikerpuu is the former commander of the EDF's 2nd Infantry Brigade (South). He worked for nearly a year at the Center for Defense Investment (RKIK) as category manager for communications and radars, finishing in that role last December. Since then he has been working as development director for the drone sector with the volunteer Defense League (Kaitseliit).
He has served in the EDF since 1997. He starts in his new role in November.
A recent drone threat warning drill was assessed to have gone better than the previous two earlier this year, but improvements still need to be made, authorities say.
Herem has said improvements need to be made in air and also maritime defense more generally, and the option of purchasing light fighter jets for Estonia's Air Force (Õhuvägi), part of the EDF, is being weighed up. Their role would include countering drones.

====================================================================================================

Jordan strikes 'terrorists' inside Syria over church attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:27:00 UTC
17:27:00 KST

Jordan said Tuesday its airstrikes in southern Syria killed more than 20 Daesh militants and destroyed a weapons depot, while Damascus condemned the operation as a violation of sovereignty and reported several casualties.
Jordanian government spokesperson Mohammad al-Momani said the strikes were conducted after Amman had "run out of patience" with the movements of terrorist groups and threats to its national security.
"The operation was based on field intelligence aimed at neutralizing confirmed threats and planned terrorist attacks against Jordan," he said.
"Initial results of this operation indicate significant losses among ISIS (Daesh), estimated at more than 20 members, as well as the destruction of a major weapons depot belonging to the group," Momani said.
He expressed regret over civilian casualties, saying Jordan refrained from striking locations where intelligence indicated civilians were present.
"Jordan takes precautions to avoid harming civilians and attaches the same importance to the lives of innocent civilians outside its borders as it does to the lives of Jordanians," he said.
Al-Momani said Jordanian authorities were following up on the matter with their Syrian counterparts.
He said the two countries would establish a joint committee to examine the consequences of the operation and strengthen coordination in combating Daesh while protecting civilians.
The spokesperson stressed that Jordan values its relations with Syria and remains committed to developing cooperation in confronting common challenges.
"Jordan's security and Syria's security are one," he said, adding that combating terrorism remains a shared objective.
Momani also linked the security threats to a recent attack on a church in Jordan's Karak governorate that killed nine people.
He reiterated Jordan's support for Syria's security, unity and stability, particularly in the country's south.
Syria's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, strongly condemned Jordanian airstrikes targeting several locations in the southern Daraa province a day earlier, saying they were carried out without prior coordination with Damascus.
In a Tuesday statement, the ministry said the attacks killed and injured several people, describing the operation as an "unacceptable violation" of Syrian airspace and national sovereignty.
Syrian authorities had earlier reported that seven people were killed in the strikes.
Damascus also condemned Friday's attack targeting St. George Greek Orthodox Church in Jordan, offering condolences to the victims' families and wishing the injured a speedy recovery.
However, the ministry stressed that the Jordanian military operation inside Syrian territory was unacceptable and violated the principles of good neighborliness and bilateral coordination.
It warned that certain parties were seeking to undermine relations between the two countries and fuel tensions, without elaborating.
The ministry said coordination was underway with Jordan to establish an urgent joint civilian and security committee to investigate the incidents, prevent their recurrence and strengthen security cooperation along their shared border.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's Energy Market Authority (EMA) and the French Energy Regulatory Commission have signed a memorandum of understanding to strengthen cooperation on energy market regulation, regional interconnectivity and low-carbon technologies.
Signed on the sidelines of the Singapore International Energy Week, the agreement will facilitate cooperation on electricity and gas market regulation, drawing on France's experience in cross-border electricity interconnections and integrated European power markets, the duo said in a joint statement on Tuesday.

Finnish fast food chain Hesburger has opened its first ever outlet in Italy.
The restaurant in the city of Matera, in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, officially began welcoming customers on Friday 23 October.
With the opening of the outlet in Matera coming in the wake of similar recent expansions into the Romanian and Polish markets, Hesburger now operates in 10 different countries across Europe.
In a press release, the firm said that the move will create 20 new jobs in the city.
The statement also noted the influential role Italian entrepreneur Venanzia Rizzi, who is originally from Matera but has lived in Finland for a long time, had in bringing the Finnish chain to Italy.
"Matera is my hometown and Finland is my second home country. That's why it's especially wonderful to connect these two important places to me through entrepreneurship," Rizzi said.
Hesburger's statement further added that its arrival in Matera — a city known for its strong food culture — has drawn both "positive and cautious reactions".
"The feedback we've received directly has been positive, and we're happy that our brand is generating interest. Above all, we want to earn the trust of local customers through quality products, friendly service, and a positive customer experience," noted Ieva Salmela, Hesburger's Director of Communications and International Marketing.
When Hesburger's plans were first revealed in September, Italian newspaper La Repubblica reported that some locals were not pleased by the arrival of another fast food chain in their city, coming just months after a similar expansion by McDonald's.
Yle News reporter Ronan Browne explains the cultural and historical context behind Hesburger's expansion into Italy.

General Dynamics gets $136M to upgrade Stryker power system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:25:23 UTC
17:25:23 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded General Dynamics Land Systems a $135.9 million modification to price Stryker Enhanced Power Distribution Unit Version 2 retrofit kits.
- The modification raises the contract’s total value to $162.4 million, with work expected to be completed by Aug. 8, 2030.
The U.S. Army has awarded General Dynamics Land Systems a $135.9 million contract modification that sets prices for buying complete retrofit kits for the Stryker armored vehicle’s Enhanced Power Distribution Unit Version 2, raising the total value of the contract to $162.4 million, the Department of War announced on Oct. 26.
The kits are designed to be installed on Strykers already in service, but the contract announcement did not say how many kits the Army will buy, which Stryker variants or units will receive them, or when installation will begin. Work locations and funding will be set with each individual order under the contract, which runs until Aug. 8, 2030.
A power distribution unit manages how electrical power from the vehicle’s generator and batteries is routed to its systems, from radios and computers to sensors and weapon stations, and the demand for that power has grown as the U.S. Army has added new equipment to the eight-wheeled Stryker. Neither the Army nor General Dynamics has published details of what the Version 2 unit changes compared with earlier designs.
Only one company was asked to bid, and General Dynamics, the Stryker’s manufacturer, submitted the only offer. Army Contracting Command at Detroit Arsenal in Michigan is managing the contract.
The award adds to a steady flow of Stryker work for the Sterling Heights, Michigan-based company. In August, the U.S. Army awarded General Dynamics a $54.3 million contract for field-level maintenance and sustainment support for the Stryker fleet running through 2031. The service received its first Strykers with new or upgraded double-V hulls, which deflect mine and roadside bomb blasts away from the crew, in March 2025, and in December 2025 it tested an upgraded Stryker armed with a 30 mm autocannon at Yakima Training Center in Washington.
The Stryker serves as the main combat and combat-support vehicle of the U.S. Army’s Stryker Brigade Combat Teams and comes in variants for carrying infantry, reconnaissance, command and control, medical evacuation, engineering, mortar fire and anti-tank missions.
