"Things start in really simple gestures" says Es Devlin of her Design Museum retrospective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

British artist and designer Es Devlin explains how ambitious creative projects begin with simple ideas in this exclusive video interview with Dezeen, filmed at Es Devlin: Other Worlds, her first European retrospective at London’s Design Museum.
“This is literally my favourite project. A book which took me seven years to make and it contains everything I’ve ever made,” Devlin told Dezeen, referring to a companion book created to coincide with the exhibition.
The book, as well as the exhibition, brings together three decades of Devlin’s work across theatre, opera, concert stage design and large-scale public installations.
The exhibition explores how Devlin’s projects develop, from early drawings and models to monumental installations experienced by audiences around the world.
In the interview, she explains how she hopes the presentation will demystify the creative process and encourage visitors to pursue their own ideas.
“I really hope that when people leave this exhibition, they’ll see objects and traces of things which make them say, ‘Oh, I could do that’,” she said.
“It’s not a mystery. It doesn’t come by magic. It comes step by step, with attention, curiosity, work and collaboration.”
The exhibition begins with a replica of Devlin’s studio in Peckham, complete with her books, objects, models, drawings, tools and paints.
“I love visiting other artists and designers’ studios,” she said. “I think it’ll make people feel something about what these rooms feel like, where creativity is allowed to happen at all times.”
From the studio, visitors encounter Come Home Again, Devlin’s installation originally presented outside Tate Modern in 2022.
The original work featured illuminated cut-outs of endangered wildlife arranged within a cross-section of the dome of St Paul’s Cathedral.
Reconfigured beneath a mirrored ceiling for the Design Museum exhibition, it is followed by A 30-Year Desk, a series of concentric circular desks displaying archival objects, drawings and models from across her career.
The archive includes material relating to her designs for the 2018 theatre production The Lehman Trilogy, the Forest of Us installation in Miami and the closing ceremony of the London 2012 Olympic Games, alongside more than 30 models of projects that have previously been exhibited in Britain.
The exhibition culminates in An Infinite Library, an eight-metre-wide rotating sculpture containing more than 2,000 books that have shaped Devlin’s worldview.
The artwork was originally installed on the beachfront of the Faena Beach hotel in Miami Beach and has been reimagined for the Design Museum retrospective.
Arranged in bands of colour above a circular mirror, the books are illuminated by projections and accompanied by recordings of Devlin reading selected passages.
Devlin began her career designing sets for small-scale theatre productions in 1996 before moving into opera, dance and concert stage design. Over the past decade, she has increasingly focused on large-scale public artworks and installations.
For Es Devlin: Other Worlds, she brought together material spanning her career, including childhood experiments and paintings made shortly before the exhibition opened, to reveal the ideas and processes behind her finished projects.
“I began to develop an attitude on how to take things that are amassed in piles and are somewhat overwhelming, to spread them out along a timeline and make them digestible and legible to an audience,” she said.
“Actually, these things that seem huge and overwhelming and complicated, they start in really simple gestures.”
Es Devlin: Other Worlds runs at the Design Museum in London until 4 April 2027.

‘Unacceptable’: condemning writers over AI detector scores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

‘Unacceptable’: condemning writers over AI detector scores
When a detector flagged a bestselling novel as AI-generated, it sparked a controversy that had serious consequences for the author. Swiss experts and artists examine how much these tools can really prove and what their verdicts mean for creative work.
Haitian-Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien had a promising career ahead of him. His novel C’était ça ou mourir (It was either that or die), a critical and commercial success, was in the running for some of France’s most prestigious literary prizes, including the Goncourt. That was until an anonymous account on X accused him of writing almost the entire book using artificial intelligence (AI).
Orélien denied using AI to write the novel. But to his accusers, the evidence seemed unequivocal: Pangram, one of the most popular tools for detecting AI content, had classified more than 95% of the book as AI-generated.
From there, things took a turn for the worse for Orélien. His novel was removed from the Goncourt selection, also amid revelations by the press of plagiarism in earlier works, for which he apologised. His Canadian publisher cut ties with him after an external analysis uncovered further evidence of AI use. Orélien continued to deny having written the book with AI, while acknowledging that he had turned to it for historical research during the creative process.
From the beginning, the controversy divided the literary world between those who defended the author and questioned the reliability of AI detectors, and those who criticised him.
Beyond Orélien’s case, Swiss filmmaker, screenwriter and lecturer Manuel Flurin Hendry believes it’s unfair to damage a writer’s reputation based on a software-generated score. “The idea that you feed a text into Pangram and then socially execute a writer feels unacceptable,” Hendry told Swissinfo in an interview at the AI+X Summit in early October. Hendry defends artists’ freedom to choose their own tools.
Other Swiss writers and artists have openly experimented with AI. Author Charles Lewinsky incorporated entire passages generated by ChatGPT into his novel Täuschend echt. Photographer Matthieu Gafsou has used image-generation tools such as DALL·E in his artistic work.
These are just a few transparent examples of how AI has entered creative work in Switzerland. But deciding how to respond to undisclosed and potentially extensive use of AI is far more difficult. As is determining how much AI-generated material is acceptable in a work of art, and whether tools like Pangram can really be trusted as a definitive proof of fraud.
How reliable is Pangram?
For Hendrik Strobelt, a senior researcher at IBM in the United States, the question of Pangram’s reliability is complex. In 2019, Strobelt and his colleagues developed GLTR, one of the first experimental tools designed to help identify text potentially generated by language models.
At the time, OpenAI had just released GPT-2, the model on which GLTR was based. AI models tended to produce rather dull texts that were very similar in style, because this type of content was the most common, Strobelt explains.
Identifying whether a text might have been produced with the help of AI was therefore relatively straightforward: it was enough to look for the most likely words.
Then language models became more sophisticated. Strobelt believes that, with today’s advanced AI systems, it has become extremely difficult to establish clear rules to distinguish AI-generated text from human writing.
“Now these models are significantly larger. They can imitate styles if you prompt them accordingly,” the IBM researcher says.
Software such as Pangram uses a method known as “supervised classification”. It compares and classifies texts written before generative AI became widespread – which is presumed to be human-written – with “mirror” versions on the same topic, generated by different commercially available language models. During training the software learns to identify the differences between them.
The logic is that if a system can distinguish between texts that are very similar in subject matter, its predictions will become more accurate.
“You want to train on things that are very close to each other, to be sure that you get the hard tasks trained first,” Strobelt explains.
Pangram claimsExternal link an accuracy rate of 99.98% and a false-positive rate of 0.01%. Its high performance has also been supported by independent researchExternal link, including a studyExternal link published this year.
According to Paolo Italiani, an AI and machine-learning researcher at the Università della Svizzera italiana (USI), the longer a text is, the more reliable a detector’s assessment tends to be.
“It’s quite probable that at least a portion of [the text] is AI-generated,” he says.
The limits of AI detectors
Yet it remains difficult to understand exactly which features of a text these tools rely on to make their classifications, says Lonneke van der Plas, professor of natural language processing at USI.
Interpretability studies would be needed to gain more understanding, she explains. But because commercial tools such as Pangram are largely black boxes whose internal workings are not accessible to independent researchers, it is challenging to study how they reach their conclusions.
In theory, certain clues such as an overly linear argumentative structure could help determine whether a text was more likely written by AI or by a human, researchExternal link co-authored by Van der Plas highlights. But such features, she cautions, are not sufficient to establish a text’s origin with certainty.
Van der Plas also points out that detection tools tend to perform less reliably in languages other than English and in more specialised genres that may have been less well represented in their training data.
The problem becomes even more complicated when a text is the product of collaboration between humans and AI. Some tests showExternal link, detectors’ accuracy drops by around 20 percentage points in such cases. Pangram’s own technical reportExternal link also indicates that the software loses accuracy when faced with content that alternates between human-written and AI-generated sentences.
“This software has been mostly trained on either completely human-generated or machine-generated texts. As soon as they get something that it’s in between, they get into trouble,” van der Plas says.
A score is not sufficient proof
From a legal perspective, results produced by tools such as Pangram do not constitute proof that an author has committed fraud.
“A legal decision cannot simply rely on those technologies because they can be inaccurate” says Jacques de Werra, professor of intellectual property law at the University of Geneva.
If a case like Orélien’s were brought before a court, de Werra explains, other evidence alongside detector scores should be considered, including original manuscripts, successive drafts and even exchanges with AI systems. De Werra also points out that AI involvement in creative work does not automatically invalidate an author’s copyright claims.
“If a person can demonstrate that there is a sufficiently close creative link between the input, creative prompting, and the output, it could be possible to claim human creativity,” he says.
The key is whether the author’s creative contribution is sufficient. De Werra stresses, however, that there is no fixed numerical threshold that determines how much of a text must be written by a person for a work to be considered their own.
If a book moves you, does it matter if AI helped write it?
For Manuel Flurin Hendry, however, the issue goes beyond legal protection.
Hendry openly uses AI-based technologies, some of which he has developed himself, for various aspects of his work, from analysing screenplays to assisting his academic research.
Technology, he explains, opens new channels of inspiration, sometimes suggesting approaches he had not previously considered. It also frees up more time for the creative process.
“True human writing is thinking in action. It requires friction and to enter a state where one can just concentrate on their flow of thoughts,” he says.
And he poses a provocative question: why should it matter how much AI contributed to a work? “If it moves you. If you find it interesting. If it makes you think, what is the argument?” he asks.
What’s important, Hendry argues, is learning which tasks to delegate to AI and which are better done personally. Rather than rejecting technology, artists should be transparent about how they use it.
“If I pretend this is mine, but it’s totally AI generated, then it’s fake,” Hendry says.
What is at stake is not only an artist’s reputation, but above all the relationship of trust with their audience.

At this stage, the operation does not involve evacuating residents of Nablus or surrounding villages, as was done in Hebron following last week's terrorist attack that killed Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem. However, the operation is expected to continue for several days.
Meanwhile, Palestinians report that IDF forces have already demolished 10 memorials commemorating terrorists, including in the villages of Rujeib, Azmut, Madama and Iraq Burin, as well as the town of Beit Furik.
The operation was launched as troops from the Paratroopers Brigade and the Maglan commando unit continue their operations in Hebron. The IDF aims to maintain a presence on the ground and prevent terrorist infrastructure from becoming established. Ahead of the election, security officials are concerned about attempts to carry out additional attacks.
ynet military analyst Ron Ben-Yishai reported that a disagreement between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir over the continuation of the Hebron operation is among the factors behind the tensions between the two in recent days.

Qatar’s path to defence autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:55:01 UTC
16:55:01 KST

Qatar’s path to defence autonomy
Qatar and other Gulf states need to strengthen their defence capabilities and diversify security partnerships to reduce reliance on external protection.
Developments in the Gulf since the beginning of this year have raised fundamental questions about the security of the region in general and Qatar in particular. How can Qatar and other Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states become effective, independent military powers that do not rely on external security guarantees to ensure their safety?
The question for Qatar is how it can build, over the next five years, a national defence capability that would enable it to protect the state and its vital interests even in the absence of Gulf or regional support, or if the United States provides only limited assistance. The aim is to explore whether Qatar can achieve what might be described as defence autonomy, rather than isolation. In other words, Qatar should remain open to alliances and partnerships without making its security dependent on the decisions of another state.
Qatar is a small country in terms of geography and population, but it enjoys numerous advantages. It has highly valuable critical infrastructure, a sensitive geographical location and an economy that depends heavily on the uninterrupted flow of energy exports, trade and shipping to almost every part of the world. At the same time, it possesses substantial financial resources, extensive international relationships, a major military base hosting US forces, advanced air defence capabilities and a network of political relationships that give it influence beyond its physical size.
These advantages, however, do not amount to “strategic autonomy”. In a major crisis such as the one the region has been experiencing for several months, Qatar’s protection remains heavily dependent on the US. Nor does reliance on the collective capabilities of the GCC provide sufficient assurance that its member states would be able, or willing, to take risks in defence of another member.
Against this backdrop, Qatar’s policy objective over the next five years should be to design and build an independent national strategy based on the capacity to prevent threats, withstand attacks and maintain continuity. The goal should be to achieve defence autonomy, rather than to build an army capable of confronting a major regional power on its own.
Such a strategy would rest on six pillars:
- Air and missile defence
- Early warning capabilities and information sovereignty
- Protection of critical infrastructure
- Air and naval power
- Cybersecurity and electronic warfare
- Restructuring security and military policy around the principle of multiple security guarantees rather than dependence on a single guarantor
Defence autonomy
Qatar does not need to exhaust its resources building the capabilities required to fight an all-out war alone against a major regional power, regardless of which power that might be. Such an ambition would be unrealistic for a country with limited territory and population.
A more realistic objective is to achieve a degree of defence autonomy appropriate for a small state such as Qatar. This means being able to perform a number of essential tasks without waiting for assistance from others.
These include, but are not limited to:
- Detecting threats and identifying their nature before they reach Qatari territory
- Delaying or absorbing an initial strike
- Protecting the country’s leadership and strategic centres
- Maintaining energy and water supplies, electricity, communications, ports and airports
- Keeping political and economic activities functioning during a crisis
- Imposing sufficiently high costs on an aggressor to force it to reconsider its calculations
- Withstanding a prolonged crisis without making the state’s continued functioning conditional on the arrival of external forces
To carry out these tasks effectively, the strategy should focus on the following priorities:
First: Building an integrated Qatari air defence shield
This is the most important gap that needs to be addressed. Possessing advanced fighter aircraft and air defence systems is not enough to make Qatar militarily autonomous. What is needed is an integrated national air and missile defence system.
The objective by 2031 should not be to possess the best defence system, but one that continues to function even in the absence of US forces or any other external security guarantor.
Such a system should include:
- A multilayered Qatari radar network
- Integration of civilian and military radar systems
- A unified national command and control centre
- Integration of short, medium and long-range air defences
- Expanded counter-drone capabilities
- Stronger electronic warfare capabilities and equipment
- Low-cost interception systems for small targets
- Enhanced mobile protection for radar installations and command centres
- Large national stockpiles of ammunition and spare parts
Second: An air force designed for independence
Qatar currently possesses an advanced air fleet. But the independence of an air force cannot be measured by the number of aircraft it operates. The crucial question is whether the Qatari air force can sustain operations for several consecutive weeks if external supply lines are disrupted.
For the answer to be yes, Qatar must develop the capacity to continue air operations even without direct US or other foreign support, albeit at a reduced level.
This requires policymakers and those responsible for developing the national defence strategy to focus on the following priorities over the next five years:
- Increasing ammunition stockpiles, whether through domestic production or imports
- Expanding domestic defence manufacturing capabilities and strengthening maintenance capacity
- Training more Qatari personnel to carry out a range of functions, including maintenance
- Building up dispersed ammunition stockpiles rather than concentrating them in a single location
- Increasing stocks of drones and other unmanned aircraft
- Developing ground and aerial refuelling capabilities and strengthening logistical support
Third: The sea as a second line of defence
For Qatar, a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides, protecting its maritime domain is not merely a military concern. It is also an economic necessity of the highest importance.
Liquefied natural gas, oil exports and imports all depend on the security of the surrounding waters. Qatar should therefore develop a naval force suited to its needs, equipped with advanced technology and capabilities.
The objective is not to build a large fleet, but to make attacks on Qatar’s maritime infrastructure both difficult and costly.
This requires a focus on several important priorities:
- Continuously improving and expanding maritime surveillance capabilities to protect Qatar’s waters and offshore installations
- Strengthening and developing capabilities to counter maritime drones
- Enhancing the protection of ports and securing shipping routes
Fourth: A national resilience programme
The most serious vulnerability of a country with limited territory and population lies in its infrastructure. A successful attack on a small number of critical facilities could have severe and far-reaching consequences for the entire country.
Given the importance of this threat, the national defence strategy should include the establishment of what might be called a “national resilience and protection programme”.
Such a programme would aim to protect critical infrastructure, including gas and energy facilities, water desalination plants, power stations, telecommunications centres and towers, civilian and military airports, ports and fuel networks, hospitals, government institutions and data centres.
One aspect of this protection is ensuring that every sector has adequate backup capacity. If a major desalination plant were to stop operating for any reason, for example, an alternative source of supply should be available to prevent a water supply problem from escalating into a national crisis. The same principle should apply to every other sector.
Fifth: Qatar must know what is happening around it before the US does
Military independence begins with information. Qatar therefore needs to develop its own national capabilities in the following areas:
- Space-based reconnaissance
- Unmanned aerial vehicles
- Radar systems
- Electronic intelligence
- Artificial intelligence-driven data analysis
This does not mean that Qatar needs to launch large satellites for every mission. Instead, it should work towards building an integrated system combining commercial and military satellites, international partnerships and national capabilities for collecting and analysing data.
The underlying principle is that Qatar should not depend on an external party to inform it of a threat approaching its territory.
Qatar will undoubtedly continue to need intelligence from the US, France, the United Kingdom and other countries. Nevertheless, it must possess the independent capacity to produce its own national intelligence picture, assess the nature of threats and determine how to prepare for them at an early stage, before requesting assistance from allies or partners.
Sixth: Diversifying security guarantees
The events of this year have demonstrated to all GCC states the importance of diversifying their alliances and security guarantees rather than relying on a single external power, particularly the US.
That power could become involved in future international crises, decide for one reason or another to limit its direct involvement in regional crises, or even reduce its military presence.
This makes it necessary to adopt a forward-looking approach based on diversifying alliances and making the security of the Gulf a matter of global interest requiring international cooperation.
In this context, GCC states could benefit from partnerships with South Korea, Turkiye and certain European powers, as well as regional powers such as Pakistan and China in specific fields, without hastily abandoning cooperation with the US.
The objective is to reduce the risks associated with dependence on a single supplier or ally. Such diversification does not mean building an alliance against the US.
Achieving defence and political autonomy for Qatar by 2031 does not mean isolating the country from its partners or dispensing with existing alliances. Rather, it means developing national capabilities that can ensure the protection of the state and its vital interests under all circumstances.
This strategic objective requires the development of an integrated air defence system, stronger intelligence and cyber capabilities, and better protection of critical infrastructure. It also requires improving the effectiveness of Qatar’s air and naval forces to ensure resilience and allow state institutions to continue functioning during a crisis.
Defence autonomy also requires diversifying international partnerships and establishing multiple security guarantees to reduce dependence on any single external power.
The foundation of this strategy is a transition from dependence on external protection towards the ability to deter threats, withstand crises and make independent national decisions at the appropriate time, while remaining open to international cooperation and partnerships.
A version of this piece in Arabic was originally published by Al Jazeera Arabic here.

Dr Stamen Grigorov and the bacterium that made Bulgarian yoghurt a legend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:52:45 UTC
16:52:45 KST

News
148 years since the birth of the distinguished scientist
Dr Stamen Grigorov and the bacterium that made Bulgarian yoghurt a legend
A 1905 discovery captures the scientific community’s attention and puts Bulgaria on the map of global microbiology
Tuesday 27 October 2026 09:10
Tuesday, 27 October 2026, 09:10
Dr Stamen Grigorov (1878–1945)
PHOTO nauka.bg
Font size
Bulgarian yoghurt is more than just a food; it is a symbol of tradition, health and distinctive flavour. It is popular worldwide for its exceptional nutritional value and health benefits, attributed to the specific lactic acid bacteria Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus.
Authentic Bulgarian yoghurt has a thick, uniform and creamy texture, with a delicate, fresh aroma. Its taste is well-balanced, tangy and refreshing, without any bitterness or artificial notes. The quality of Bulgarian yoghurt is guaranteed by a national standard known as “Bulgarian State Standard Yoghurt” (BDS). It sets out the requirements for the product: it must be made from cow’s, sheep’s, buffalo’s or goat’s milk, or a mixture of these, and fermented with the symbiotic cultures Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus, isolated in Bulgaria and free from genetic modification. Since the summer of 2023, Bulgarian yoghurt has been registered in the EU register of Protected Designations of Origin (PDO).
PHOTO nivabg.com
The history of Bulgarian yoghurt is inextricably linked to the name of the distinguished Bulgarian scientist Dr Stamen Grigorov (27 October 1878 – 27 October 1945), a microbiologist who left a lasting mark on science by discovering the bacterium characteristic of Bulgarian yoghurt and conducting research into a vaccine against tuberculosis.
In 1905, at just 27 years of age, Dr. Stamen Grigorov described the lactic acid microorganism Lactobacillus bulgaricus which causes milk to ferment.
Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus
PHOTO gbif.org
Born and raised in the country, the ninth of twelve children in the family – who would have thought that the little boy from Studen Izvor village would end up in Montpellier and graduate science at the university there with honours? With the support of patriotically-minded Bulgarians he went to study in Geneva where his perspicacity was noticed by foremost bacteriologist Prof. Léon Massol. It was he who assigned Stamen Grigorov the task of studying the flora of Bulgarian yoghurt. At that same time, Nobel prize winner Prof. Ilya Mechnikov was looking into the causes of ageing and ascertained that the greatest number of centenarians were to be found in Bulgaria. Regrettably, this is no longer so. But can one of the reasons for this phenomenon be found in Bulgarian yoghurt?
“Many manufacturers prefer to use cheaper starter cultures of lower quality“, says Yulia Grigorova, the scientist’s granddaughterin an interview preserved in Radio Bulgaria’s archives. Of course it tastes different, because they have to make it marketable, more durable and give it a certain thickness. Whereas homemade yoghurt does not have the same density or consistency but it is this kind of yoghurt that has an excellent effect on the body’s microflora. As to longevity, the drop in consumption of real yoghurt is not the only reason. Many Bulgarians opt to live in the country when they retire and with good reason – the air there is very different.”
PHOTO culinarytourism.bg
And one interesting fact from Dr. Grigorov’s biography – by an odd confluence of events, his name has not gone down in history as the father of the tuberculosis vaccine. So, it was Albert Calmette and Camille Guerin who put their names down as the men who discovered it.
“Before his return to Bulgaria, Dr. Grigorov started work on tubercular cells and continued his research as head physician of the hospital in Trun”, his relative Yulia Grigorova told Radio Bulgaria reporter Diana Tsankova in an interview more than a decade ago. “In 1906 - three months before the two Frenchmen made their discovery – he created the vaccine but there was no institution in Bulgaria powerful enough to back him, so it was the other vaccine that gained popularity. What is more, senior medical staff in this country paid no heed to his research or the excellent results he obtained. That is the reason why he left for Milan where he hoped to have the vaccine approved. As a matter of fact, his vaccine is not just for prevention but also for treatment. Nowadays, researchers base their work on it.”
The Yoghurt Museum in the village of Studen Izvor
PHOTO transkotd.org
Today, a dedicated Yoghurt Museum stands in Studen Izvor, the birthplace of Dr Stamen Grigorov, located 7.5 km southwest of the town of Tran in western Bulgaria. A central place in the museum is devoted to the scientist’s contribution. Visitors learn about the fermentation process and the origins of the distinctive flavour of Bulgarian yoghurt.
PHOTO bulgariatravel.org
The exhibits include household utensils once used to prepare and store yoghurt and other dairy products, as well as models and objects illustrating industrial yoghurt production, from preparation to the delivery of the finished product to consumers. And those consumers are found all over the world: the name bulgaricus appears on yoghurt packaging everywhere from Europe and the United States to Japan.
Edited by Elena Karkalanova
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

Netanyahu, Eisenkot or another election? Five scenarios for Israel's next government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:52:14 UTC
16:52:14 KST

A shift of just one or two parliamentary seats could determine whether Benjamin Netanyahu remains Israel's prime minister, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot replaces him or the country finds itself heading toward yet another election. As Israelis vote Tuesday, the outcome remains deeply uncertain, with several possible paths to forming a government and no guarantee that either political camp will secure a majority.
Most opinion polls suggest neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious allies nor the parties seeking to replace him will win the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-member Knesset. But even without a clear winner, negotiations could produce a new government, a fragile minority administration or an unexpected agreement between political rivals. Here are the five main scenarios and the timetable for what happens after the votes are counted.
Scenario 1: opposition government led by Eisenkot
Most polls suggest neither political bloc will win 61 seats, making an outright opposition victory an unexpected outcome. But if the parties seeking to replace Netanyahu secure a majority, they could form a coalition comprising Gadi Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party, former prime minister Naftali Bennett's Together party, Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan's left-wing Democrats.
Despite disagreements within the opposition, particularly Bennett's and Liberman's reluctance to accept Eisenkot as prime minister, Eisenkot would be the likely candidate to lead such a government if his party emerges as the largest in the bloc. The challenge would then be translating an electoral majority into a functioning coalition despite the parties' political and ideological differences.
Scenario 2: Netanyahu wins another term
The alternative is a victory for Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc, which would have to secure at least 61 seats despite polls suggesting that outcome is even less likely than an outright opposition majority. Such a result would allow Netanyahu to rebuild his current coalition, bringing together Likud, the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties, Itamar Ben-Gvir's far-right Otzma Yehudit and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism party.
The coalition could also include the People of Israel party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, provided it wins enough votes to enter parliament. If Winter's party fails to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold, Netanyahu's prospects of securing a majority could become even more difficult.
Scenario 3: minority government that depends on Arab parties
If the opposition wins more seats among Jewish-led parties than Netanyahu's bloc but falls short of an outright majority, Eisenkot could attempt to form a minority government. Under Israel's parliamentary system, a new government does not necessarily need the support of 61 lawmakers to take office. It needs to win a parliamentary confidence vote, which can pass with a simple majority of those voting, even by a single vote.
Eisenkot has said he will not negotiate with Arab or ultra-Orthodox parties, offer them political concessions or enter agreements with them. His calculation is that Arab lawmakers would abstain from a confidence vote rather than help Netanyahu remain in office. But even if such a government were formed, its survival could depend on outside parliamentary support from Arab parties or Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox factions willing to negotiate over government funding and military conscription. Without that support, it could quickly collapse.
The biggest obstacle, however, is Liberman, who has ruled out supporting a minority government. He argues that such an arrangement would be short-lived and could ultimately strengthen Netanyahu in another election. Unless Liberman reverses his position, this scenario appears unlikely, even though some opposition figures would prefer replacing Netanyahu for a limited period to leaving him in office.
Scenario 4: Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government
Another possibility is a broad coalition bringing together Netanyahu and Eisenkot, particularly if strong results for Arab parties leave both rival blocs well short of a majority. Such an agreement could include a power-sharing arrangement under which the two leaders alternate as prime minister during the government's term.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have publicly rejected such a partnership, making it politically difficult. Nevertheless, President Isaac Herzog could attempt to encourage a compromise if the election produces an extended deadlock and neither side can assemble a viable coalition.
Scenario 5: another election, with Netanyahu remaining in office
If Netanyahu's bloc wins more seats among Jewish-led parties than the opposition but falls short of 61, and neither side is willing to cooperate with parties outside its camp, Israel could face another election.
Under such circumstances, Netanyahu would remain in office as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed, potentially extending his time in power by several months without securing a fresh parliamentary majority. This outcome would prolong the political uncertainty and could send Israelis back to the polls without any assurance that another vote would produce a different result.
What happens next? The timetable for forming a government
Even if the election delivers a clear winner, the process of forming a government could take weeks. Israel's Central Elections Committee has eight days to publish the official results, making Wednesday, November 4, the legal deadline. Election officials expect to complete the vote count by Thursday afternoon, October 29, potentially allowing the new 26th Knesset to be sworn in on Tuesday, November 10, two weeks after election day.
Once the official results are submitted, President Herzog will consult representatives of the parties elected to parliament and ask whom they recommend to form the next government. Within seven days of the publication of the official results, he must assign that task to the lawmaker he believes has the best chance of assembling a coalition. This is usually the candidate with the most support from other parties, although the leader of the largest party does not automatically receive the first opportunity.
The first candidate has 28 days to form a government, with the president authorized to grant extensions totaling up to 14 additional days. If that effort fails, Herzog can either select another lawmaker, who would receive 28 days without an extension, or formally announce that he sees no prospect of a government being formed.
If the president makes that announcement, or if a second candidate also fails, a final 21-day period begins during which at least 61 lawmakers can submit a written request asking the president to appoint a particular member of parliament. That candidate would then have 14 days to establish a government.
If no government emerges from these procedures, the Knesset is automatically dissolved and another election must be held. Until a new government takes office, the outgoing administration remains in power.
For now, the crucial question is not simply which party wins the most seats on Tuesday, but whether any combination of parties can overcome their differences and command enough parliamentary support to govern. Based on Israel's recent political history, another election would offer no guarantee of breaking the deadlock.

“I believe we should retake wartime OPCON as soon as possible,” Cho said. “The two countries’ military authorities were continuing discussions on the timing of the transfer, and the talks were proceeding well.”

SIR row: Supreme Court defers hearing, grants petitioner 10 days to reply to EC's counter-affidavit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:45:45 UTC
16:45:45 KST

SC granted petitioner 10 days to respond to the EC’s defence of its functioning and the SIR exercise, deferring the hearing until after Diwali
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has deferred hearing on a batch of petitions challenging the functioning of the Election Commission (EC), including allegations that Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar took unilateral decisions on matters that required unanimous approval, particularly in connection with the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant granted petitioner Rakesh Kumar Singh 10 days to file a rejoinder to the EC’s counter-affidavit, which was submitted on Monday night. Senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the petitioner, sought time to respond to the poll body's submissions.
The matter is likely to be listed on November 17, after the Diwali vacation and completion of the 10-day period.The petitions challenge the EC’s decision-making process and seek to invalidate the SIR exercise and related actions. Singh’s plea also sought the suspension of the CEC over allegations of unilateral decision-making.
What the EC told SC
In its counter-affidavit, the EC defended its functioning and the conduct of the SIR exercise, rejecting allegations of irregularities and questioning the basis of the petition.The affidavit was unanimously approved by Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi. The EC said all three SIR orders issued in June 2025, October 2025 and May 2026 were unanimous decisions of the Commission.
The poll body also maintained that notes, queries or suggestions made by individual commissioners while files are being processed do not constitute decisions of the Commission. It said files are routed through one Election Commissioner, then the other, and finally the CEC, while urgent approvals may be obtained electronically and recorded on file later.On allegations concerning changes to voter enrolment forms, the EC said Form 6 had not been amended and that only the Centre could make such changes. However, it acknowledged that the online display could be interpreted as an amendment and said that, from October 21, the online application would be split into Form 6 and a separate SIR declaration, in line with the physical form.The Commission also said voters whose records could not be mapped during the SIR need not attend hearings as a rule, with booth-level officers (BLOs) collecting documents from their homes.
Hearings would be held only in exceptional cases, preferably online.On the ECINet electoral database, the poll body said no name could be added or deleted without an order from the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO). It added that a committee involving experts from IIT and IISc had been set up to examine compliance.The EC further argued that a plea seeking to restrain the CEC was not maintainable, stating that the CEC could be removed only through the process applicable to a Supreme Court judge.

Antwerp police have already arrested 432 known troublemakers since start of crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:45:37 UTC
16:45:37 KST

Since the beginning of the month, Antwerp police have arrested 432 people, who were already known for causing a public nuisance, on one or more occasions. 615 arrests were made in all. The arrests are the result of a controversial measure introduced by the city council cabinet comprising Flemish nationalist N-VA and socialist Vooruit – in collaboration with the police. Just over half of the arrests took place in the Antwerp North District. Opposition parties Communist PVDA, ecologist Groen and Christian democrat CD&V have levelled fierce criticism at the measure.
Antwerp police have already arrested 432 known troublemakers since start of crackdown
At the beginning of this month, at the mayor’s request, Antwerp police tightened their approach to known troublemakers. Officers can now arrest them more quickly and hold them in custody for up to 12 hours, even if they are not causing a disturbance at that moment.
The measure applies primarily to Antwerp North, which had previously been designated by the city as a ‘neighbourhood requiring special attention’. When it was launched, the city and police’s approach faced fierce criticism from academics, opposition parties and the Human Rights League, even triggering for street protests.
At the city council meeting on Monday evening, Antwerp’s city cabinet presented the initial figures and assessment. In the core area of Antwerp North, the police carried out 336 administrative arrests of people whom the city and the police refer to as ‘claimers’ in Dutch.
Several people were arrested multiple times, the mayor’s office added. In Antwerp North alone, 56 people have been arrested more than five times in the past year. Seven of them have even been arrested at least 15 times.
Across the city as a whole, there were a total of 615 arrests involving 432 different individuals. Around a quarter of them are residing in our country illegally.
Locals welcome approach
At the city council meeting, Mayor Els van Doesburg (N-VA) defended the approach. She quoted from messages from grateful local residents.
“As a child, I was never able to play outside without a care or walk to school on my own. I’ll never get that time back. Since the measures were introduced, however, my three-year-old nephew has been able to experience that freedom,” Van Doesburg quoted.
“What’s more, I haven’t had to miss a single morning’s lesson because of fights, and this week I was even able to have a cup of coffee with my neighbour on my own doorstep for the first time.”
More figures
Nathalie van Baren (N-VA), the alderwoman for Social Affairs, also presented figures. According to her, there has been no decline in the number of visitors to reception centres. She counters criticism from the left that people in need are slipping through the cracks of the support system as a result of the strict approach.
Condemned by most opposition parties
According to the largest opposition party, the Communist PVDA, the roundups of those causing a nuisance are unlawful and too little is being done to help them.
“All you want to do is sweep the problems under the carpet rather than solve them,” says Jos D’Haese (PVDA). “But you know full well that those people will simply go somewhere else, and that the 12 hours you lock them up will not have solved a single thing. Your approach is as unlawful as it gets.”
Criticism was also levelled at socialist Vooruit, Flemish nationalist N-VA’s coalition partner. “How much longer are you going to put up with this? You say: we’re pleased that there’s been a change of course. And then the mayor comes along with a straight face and says: There’s been no change of course.”
Ecologist Groen and Christian democrat CD&V were also critical of the temporary arrests of those causing a nuisance. The measure did, however, receive the support of the other opposition party, far right Vlaams Belang.

Oil companies will be "held accountable" if they import any barrels of Russian diesel fuel under the deal reached by U.S. President Donald Trump with the Kremlin. Jamie Raskin, a member of the U.S. House Judiciary Committee, said this in a letter to industry leaders on Monday, October 26, UNN reports, citing Politico.
Details
Democratic Congressman Raskin, who is expected to chair the influential Judiciary Committee if Democrats take control of the House of Representatives in next week’s elections, is the latest lawmaker to warn the industry against importing or processing any Russian fuel subject to U.S. sanctions. Trump has faced a wave of criticism from both parties over his statement earlier this month that the United States would buy Russian diesel fuel in an attempt to lower fuel prices, which are currently $2.70 per gallon higher (approximately $0.71 per liter higher) than a year ago.
Raskin sent the letter to the heads of the industry trade groups the American Petroleum Institute and the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers. Another copy was sent to the head of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
Your members are now warned that participating in any efforts to help President Putin sell Russian diesel fuel in the United States is an obvious and dangerous violation of federal law. Those who choose to act in this manner do so at their own peril and will undoubtedly be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law, whether under this administration or the next one
A White House representative said that the deal "complies with all applicable laws".
"Democrats are already making clear that once again they have no plans to improve the lives of Americans, and instead they will continue their decade-long obsession with investigating President Trump," said White House Press Secretary Taylor Rogers.
At least one shipment of Russian diesel fuel is headed to the United States and is expected to arrive next week, Reuters reported, citing vessel-tracking data. As Axios reported earlier on Monday, Democratic lawmakers have already sent letters to port authorities and banks asking them to preserve all records concerning the receipt of Russian diesel shipments.
Anyone who imports Russian diesel fuel into the United States "is violating federal law and therefore may be subject to both civil and criminal penalties, including imprisonment for up to 20 years," Raskin noted in the letter.

====================================================================================================

European natural gas prices soar: What it means for your winter bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:43:20 UTC
16:43:20 KST

Gas prices have tripled in 2026 and EU storage is at a record low. Analysts explain what it means for winter bills and how long it could last.
After 2022, Europe made itself a promise: never again would its winter depend on a country at war.
Four years later, it does. Only the country has changed.
While public attention has been mostly focused on oil and diesel, a potentially more serious squeeze has been building through natural gas.
Analysts now warn that Europe may have to cut its gas consumption to get through to the end of March, as storage levels head into winter at their lowest for the time of year on record.
“Wind output and temperatures will determine how tight Europe’s gas supply becomes this winter and how high prices go,” Ana Maria Jaller-Makarewicz, lead energy analyst for Europe at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), told Euronews.
“Demand reduction remains the biggest lever within Europe’s control,” she added.
How high have European gas prices climbed?
The Dutch TTF contract, Europe’s benchmark gas price, traded at around €28 per megawatt hour at the start of January.
On Monday, it hovered near €96, after briefly touching €97.64, its highest level since December 2022. That is a rise of about 234% since the start of the year.
Prices remain far from the August 2022 peak above €340.
Yet, the worry now is less the level than the direction.
Where has Europe’s gas gone?
The war with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have cut Europe off from one of its key suppliers: Qatar.
Middle Eastern liquefied natural gas (LNG) made up roughly 8% of the EU’s LNG imports last year, according to Brussels-based think tank Bruegel.
Since May, none has arrived.
The share may sound small. But in a tight global market, every missing cargo has to be replaced by one that Asian buyers are also bidding for.
There is also a second gap on the horizon. Russian LNG still made up about a fifth of the EU’s LNG imports in the second quarter, according to Bruegel.
From January 2027, the EU will ban it completely.
“In the report, the Russian LNG ban starting in January 2027 is included in the calculation showing that the EU may need to use about 7% less gas than it did last winter,” Jaller-Makarewicz said, referring to IEEFA’s study published earlier this month.
Why are Europe's gas storage levels so worrying?
Without Qatari gas, Europe could not rebuild its reserves this summer.
EU storage was 74.6% full on 24 October, according to Bruegel. A year earlier, it stood at 82.9%. In 2023, it was almost full, at 98.5%.
IEEFA says it is the lowest for this time of year since records began in 2011.
What stands out most is that reserves have stopped growing. In the week to 24 October, daily changes hovered around zero, and some countries have already started drawing on winter stocks before November.
Austria’s storage, for example, has slipped from 69.3% in mid-October to 67.2%, against 84% a year ago.
Wood Mackenzie, the energy research firm, now expects European storage to be only around 17% to 20% full by the end of March, a few points lower than its previous forecast.
That view assumes a normal winter, and that the Middle East conflict ends this year with Qatar and the United Arab Emirates returning to usual LNG output in early 2027, according to Tom Marzec-Manser, the firm’s director for Europe gas and LNG.
“If it’s a cold winter – which is not the consensus because of El Niño – storage levels could be even lower,” Tom Marzec-Manser, director for Europe Gas & LNG at Wood Mackenzie, told Euronews.
Prices would then climb further, he said, as Europe outbids Asia for spare cargoes.
For Europe, finishing winter with near-empty stocks would then force a bigger refill next summer, pushing prices up once again.
How long could high prices last?
Even a quick end to the war would not bring immediate relief.
“Even assuming the conflict ends by the end of the year and the Middle Eastern producers do begin returning their LNG operations at the start of next year, we still hold the view it will take to the autumn of 2028 to bring the global LNG market back to balance,” Marzec-Manser said.
“This does mean wholesale gas prices will remain high in Europe during much of this time,” he added.
So, how much could your bill rise?
TTF futures for the coming winter months trade at about €95 per megawatt hour, nearly three times last winter’s average of about €36.
That gap works out to roughly six euro cents for every kilowatt hour of gas.
For a typical home that heats with gas, using around 10,000 kilowatt hours between November and March, that would add about €600 to the energy cost alone.
With an average VAT rate of 20%, the figure rises to around €715.
Household prices had already started to climb. Residential gas cost an average of 11.9 euro cents per kilowatt hour across EU capitals in early September, 12% more than in February, according to the Household Energy Price Index (HEPI) compiled by Energie-Control Austria, MEKH and VaasaETT.
How much of the wholesale surge reaches each family will depend on where they live and what contract they have. Fixed-price contracts, regulated tariffs and government support can delay or soften the hit.
Can Europe cut its way through the winter?
Part of the demand reduction may happen anyway, Jaller-Makarewicz said, because high prices push some users to consume less.
For households, the measures are simple.
Turning thermostats down by one degree could save up to 10% on energy bills, according to Jaller-Makarewicz. Lowering hot water temperatures and draught-proofing homes also help.
On whether Brussels should coordinate demand cuts now, rather than wait for a price spike, she suggested a shared approach with national flexibility.
“Brussels could provide a framework to achieve this target, allowing individual member states to implement measures tailored to their specific domestic gas markets.”
The longer-term answer, in her view, is to keep reducing how much gas Europe needs.
“Each new renewable energy project, battery storage system and grid upgrade helps to reduce Europe’s reliance on gas,” she said. EU gas demand fell by 17.7% between 2021 and 2025, which she called a crucial buffer against supply shortages.
That buffer is now being tested.
Europe changed its suppliers after 2022. It did not change how much it depends on them. And this winter, whether that becomes a crisis may come down less to Brussels than to how cold January gets, and how hard the wind blows.

Israel faces four possible scenarios for forming next government after elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:43:16 UTC
16:43:16 KST

Israel could face four possible scenarios for forming its next government if neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot secures enough support to build a governing coalition after Tuesday’s general elections, an expert on Israeli politics said.
Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party, nor Eisenkot, leader of Yashar party, is expected to reach the 61-seat threshold required to form a government with their respective blocs.
Israel is treated as a single electoral district, with voters electing members of the 120-seat Knesset by voting for party lists.
The prime minister is not directly elected but must be a member of parliament capable of securing the confidence of at least 61 lawmakers.
Since no single Israeli party typically wins a parliamentary majority, governments are generally formed through coalitions of parties with broadly compatible political positions.
Speaking to Anadolu, Wadie Abu Nassar outlined four possible scenarios following the elections.
“The first scenario is that Netanyahu or Eisenkot manages to form a regular government through a coalition with parties that win seats in the polls,” Abu Nassar said.
He described that scenario as “difficult” in light of polls showing neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition camp reaching 61 seats.
“Still, this scenario cannot be completely ruled out, particularly amid reports that Eisenkot is trying to win over lawmakers from the Haredi parties to support a government he would form,” he added.
Minority government
“The second scenario would involve Eisenkot forming a minority government that relies on Arab votes in the Knesset without those parties joining the government,” Abu Nassar said.
Arab parties in Israel have said they could provide Eisenkot with a parliamentary “safety net” in exchange for guarantees for Arab citizens, aimed at preventing the current government — which includes far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich — from remaining in office as a caretaker administration.
The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, headed by Mansour Abbas, have expressed willingness to support an Eisenkot-led government from outside the coalition.
In return, they have sought measures including halting home demolitions, combating crime in Arab communities and opening a political horizon with Palestinians.
Eisenkot has not taken a definitive position on the proposal, though he has previously ruled out including Arab parties in a coalition he seeks to form.
Polls suggest that 13 electoral lists could enter the Knesset, including two representing Arab citizens, who make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
The Arab parties are projected to win a combined 14 to 15 seats, according to opinion polls.
National unity government
Abu Nassar said the third scenario would be the formation of a national unity government bringing together Netanyahu, Eisenkot and other Israeli parties.
“There are discussions in Israeli circles that if the elections reach a deadlock, meaning neither bloc obtains the required majority to form a government, a national unity government could be formed,” he said.
He said Israeli President Isaac Herzog has been pushing such an option to avoid another election, while reports indicate that figures close to US President Donald Trump also favour the scenario.
“Under such an arrangement, the government would include Likud under Netanyahu and Yashar under Eisenkot, along with other parties, while excluding Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power party and Smotrich’s far-right Religious Zionism party,” Abu Nassar said.
The main obstacle, he added, is that opposition parties reject joining a government with Netanyahu or one led by him, even though he appears open to a unity government in which he and Eisenkot would rotate as prime minister, provided Netanyahu serves first.
“Opposition parties do not necessarily reject joining Likud in a unity government but object to Netanyahu personally,” Abu Nassar said.
“Some Israeli circles have raised the possibility of Herzog granting Netanyahu a pardon in corruption cases against him in return for his withdrawal from political life,” he added.
Netanyahu has said that he would not leave politics even if he loses the elections.
Netanyahu faces charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate corruption cases, known as Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000.
Separately, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on Nov. 21, 2024, accusing him of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, where more than 74,000 people have been killed in a brutal offensive since October 2023.
Ben-Gvir has also claimed that Netanyahu has avoided appearing in photographs with him because he is seeking a possible unity government with Eisenkot.
New elections
The fourth scenario would see neither Netanyahu nor the opposition succeeding in forming a government, leaving the current Cabinet in place as a caretaker government until another election is held several months later.
“In the fourth scenario, elections would be repeated after several months, and until then the current government would remain as a caretaker government until a new one is formed,” Abu Nassar said.
“This is the scenario Netanyahu would prefer and work toward if he fails to form a government,” he added.
Under Israeli law, Knesset elections are normally held every four years.
The elections are widely seen as crucial for the political future of Netanyahu, 76, who is standing trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which could result in imprisonment if convicted.
Netanyahu has also been wanted by the International Criminal Court since 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed against Palestinians during Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, where more than 74,000 people have been killed since October 2023.

PPA to change mobile speed camera tactics following new warning sign rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:43:00 UTC
16:43:00 KST

PPA to change mobile speed camera tactics following new warning sign rules
Mobile speed cameras may only be used in cities in the future as the police (PPA) look for ways to make the devices more efficient following new warning sign rules.
Since August, the law has required a warning sign to be placed several hundred meters before a mobile speed camera. Due to the new rule, using the cameras in the same way as before no longer works.
"We see that in the specific location where the cameras are operating, these signs reduce the risk of speeding, but once the signs are gone and the camera's work at that location is finished, speeds increase again," said Taavi Kirss, head of traffic supervision at the Police and Border Guard Board.
Following the increase in the enforcement threshold from 3 km/h to 6 km/h and the installation of warning signs, revenue from traffic fines has fallen by more than 90 percent.
The police now plan to change their tactics. While mobile speed cameras have so far been used mainly on multilane roads and roads with heavy traffic, Kirss said it might make more sense to use them near schools or dangerous pedestrian crossings to calm traffic.
The Transport Administration said speeding occurs most frequently on roads between cities, and the number of fatal traffic accidents on these roads has also increased this year.
"If the cameras are removed from highways, it must still be clear what measures we will use to replace their existing safety impact. The greater the speed enforcement, or the greater the perceived likelihood of enforcement, the less speeding there is, the lower vehicle speeds are, and that is where the safety effect comes from," said Maria Paschkevich.
Minister of Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said it is too early to say what impact the warning signs have had. Although revenue from fines has decreased, this is more likely due to the increase in the enforcement threshold.
"But the fact that we have fewer fines does not mean that there are fewer traffic violations. If we have a violation that we do not fine, that does not mean it is not a violation, and let's be honest, these rules have been put in place so that people survive on our roads, not specifically to fine anyone," he said.
Sweden has abandoned the use of mobile speed cameras. However, patrol cars do record speeding violations. Kirss said this option is also under consideration in Estonia.

Rising costs and difficulties in securing land are pushing hotel investors in Türkiye to acquire existing properties rather than build new ones, according to industry representatives.
International hotel chains looking to expand in Türkiye or enter the market are increasingly approaching owners of existing hotels as acquisition opportunities gain prominence.
Despite expectations of increased activity through new hotel openings and renovation projects in 2027, investment momentum has slowed compared with previous years. According to research by Tourism Databank, as of Oct. 22,, a total of 280 new hotels are expected to open in Türkiye by the end of 2027, with total investment spending projected to exceed $3 billion.
Çiğdem Türkyılmaz, chairman of international tourism investment consultancy Servus International, said acquisitions have become a key component of investors’ growth strategies.
Türkyılmaz noted that finding suitable land for new hotel developments has become increasingly difficult, particularly in major cities and leading tourism destinations.
“Approximately 7,000 new beds are expected to be added in Istanbul alone in 2027. However, there is a slowdown in investments, and the previous momentum is no longer there,” she said.
According to Türkyılmaz, many investors are choosing to sell their hotels, creating opportunities for market entrants to acquire operating properties instead of developing new projects.
“Brands want to establish hotels in prime destinations, but especially in Istanbul, there is virtually no space left for new hotel construction, so they are pursuing available properties for sale,” she said.
Türkyılmaz said foreign investors have not abandoned their interest in Türkiye but are acting more cautiously. She also noted that Turkish investors have increasingly turned their attention to Europe.
“We observe that 30 percent to 40 percent of investors in Türkiye have investments in Europe. Investments in the range of 20 million to 30 million euros are being made, and on average at least 10 to 15 hotels are developed each year,” she said.

Israel elections: High Arab turnout seeks to punish Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:40:51 UTC

Breadcrumb
As Israel's elections get underway, high Arab turnout seeks to punish Netanyahu's government
Palestinian towns and villages across Israel saw significant voter turnout on Tuesday morning as polls opened for the 26th Knesset elections. Voters began arriving at polling stations as early as 7am, with a heavy presence of Jewish observers, including representatives from far-right parties.
Despite reported delays in opening several polling stations due to administrative procedures, activists from both the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra'am) mobilised to urge Arab citizens to cast their ballots early in the day to avoid anticipated congestion during the afternoon and evening.
The elections come three years into Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, with widespread expectations of strong mobilisation by Palestinian citizens of Israel seeking to punish the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court, and his far-right coalition partners.
According to the Central Elections Committee, the total number of eligible voters stands at 7,331,981, an increase of 543,177 compared to the previous election. Arab citizens account for roughly 18% of the eligible electorate, numbering approximately 1.172 million voters.
Most opinion polls project an increase in Arab voter participation.
Data from the Midgam Research Institute indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in the previous elections.
Meanwhile, Yousef Makladeh, director of the Stat-Net research institute, which specialises in polling within the Arab community, projected that turnout could reach around 68% if current campaign momentum is sustained.
Polling analysts further suggest that if turnout exceeds 70% on election day, Arab parliamentary representation could climb to 16 seats.
Writer and researcher Marzouq Halabi told The New Arab that the anticipated mobilisation reflected a defensive response to the policies of Netanyahu's government, including the genocide in Gaza, forced displacement, home demolitions and growing anti-Palestinian incitement.
"This is purely defensive voting, more than anything else," he said, arguing that Palestinian citizens of Israel increasingly view the election as an opportunity to resist the far right rather than simply choose between competing political programmes," he said.
"They are not asking about party platforms; rather, they are asking how the fascist right can be repelled and its agendas obstructed," Halabi said.
He added that the vote was also about asserting Palestinian presence and identity in the face of attempts to marginalise and silence the community.
Maha Karkabi, a candidate representing the Joint List, similarly argued that higher Arab turnout could prevent some far-right parties from crossing the electoral threshold and potentially deny Netanyahu the parliamentary support needed to form another government.
"Most opinion polls indicate that a high Arab turnout will prevent extremist and racist right-wing parties from crossing the electoral threshold, and could, to a certain extent, prevent Netanyahu from forming a government with the far right," she told The New Arab.
Karkabi said the Joint List would nevertheless remain in opposition, ruling out participation in Israeli governments because of their policies towards Palestinians, including occupation, ethnic cleansing and home demolitions.
However, analysts cautioned that Netanyahu's defeat would not necessarily bring an immediate end to Israel's policies in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Muhanad Mustafa, a researcher at the Haifa-based Mada al-Carmel Center, told The New Arab that much would depend on the election results, but that even a victory for the opposition would be unlikely to produce an immediate change.
Instead, he suggested that an alternative government could gradually shift towards political arrangements centred on Israeli security interests, rather than the religious ideology that has shaped the current coalition's approach.
"An alternative government would not bear the burden of the 7 October failure, and its approach would be primarily security-driven rather than rooted in messianic religious ideology," Mustafa said.
He added that a more ideologically diverse coalition could be more inclined towards internal compromises when addressing Gaza and the West Bank, although this would not necessarily translate into a fundamental change in Israeli policy.
Discussing the broader political and psychological shifts within Israeli society since 7 October, Mustafa said that the war had intensified anti-Palestinian sentiment and normalised increasingly extreme attitudes towards Palestinians.
"The fundamental shift is the desire for revenge against the Palestinians and treating them as a dehumanised population that can be annihilated, with a sense of relief following such actions," he said.
Mustafa also argued that religious narratives portraying the war as part of a broader struggle for salvation had gained influence, while much of Israeli society continued to view the events of 7 October in isolation from decades of occupation, siege and settlement expansion.
He said this had reinforced a widespread denial of Palestinian humanity and obscured the broader political context of the conflict.
Beyond domestic political shifts, the vote has drawn intense international scrutiny amid concerns over a potential resumption of war on Iran and its geopolitical and economic consequences.
Meanwhile, many Israelis, including expatriates who travelled back specifically to vote, hope the election outcome could help restore Israel's international standing, which has suffered significant damage in global public opinion following the war on Gaza.
Honida Ghanim, director of the Palestinian Forum for Israeli Studies (MADAR), told The New Arab that Israel's international reputation had deteriorated sharply, particularly among Western publics, even as governments continued to provide political support.
"Israel's international standing has declined sharply, to the point that it is closer to a rogue state, at least at the level of public opinion, and the United States is the clearest illustration of this," she said.
Ghanim argued that the Trump administration had given Israel's far-right leadership considerable freedom to pursue its policies despite mounting international criticism and concerns over violations of international law.
She warned that one of the most dangerous election outcomes for Palestinians would be a political deadlock that left Netanyahu in power as caretaker prime minister for an extended period.
"The most dangerous possible outcome of the elections is therefore a stalemate, with Netanyahu's government remaining in office as a caretaker government for what could be two years under Trump," she said.
Ghanim warned that such a scenario could allow the Israeli right to intensify its policies of forced displacement and territorial control while enjoying continued backing from Washington.
Even a victory for former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, she argued, would be unlikely to reverse Israel's international isolation or produce a fundamental shift in its policies towards Palestinians.
She suggested that Western governments might seek to rehabilitate Israel's image by presenting a new leadership as a departure from Netanyahu's far-right coalition, but questioned whether such a distinction would be credible.
Ghanim pointed to changing attitudes towards Israel in the United States, the difficulty of forming a stable alternative coalition and the continued support among mainstream Israeli politicians for policies that violate international law.
She also cited UN Security Council Resolution 2334 of 2016 and the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion on Israel's occupation, arguing that settlement expansion had become so deeply embedded in the Israeli political system that a change of government alone could not resolve the underlying issues.
"Israel has moved beyond the stage of repair: the settlement, which the world has regarded as a violation of international law, most notably in UN Security Council Resolution 2334 of 2016 and the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion, is today Israel itself," Ghanim concluded.

this fictional beverage comes with a real warning about fake news
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:37:43 UTC
16:37:43 KST

this fictional beverage comes with a real warning about fake news
dysturb’s fake drink campaign arrives in paris and NYC to encourage media literacy and critical thinking in an age of misinformation.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
dysturb launches a beverage with 0% fake news
Paris-based nonprofit Dysturb has launched Source.s, a fictional beverage advertised across the streets of Paris and New York in October 2026. The campaign gives its imaginary drink a convincing product launch, with large-scale murals, posters, and promotional cans handed out to passersby.
At first glance, Source.s could easily pass for another new drink brand. Its aluminum can comes in pale blue with oversized navy lettering, while its advertising borrows the familiar promises of refreshment and well-being. While the brand is invented, the promotional cans themselves are real.
The packaging begins to give the idea away upon closer look. An ‘informational value’ label replaces conventional nutrition facts, listing 0% fake news and 100% critical thinking. Even the language of hydration gets a rewrite. The American campaign reads ‘hydrate your mind, filter your feed,‘ to turn a familiar wellness slogan into a reminder to question the information we consume. It’s a playful piece of packaging design, with an underlying concern about how readily we trust something that looks convincing.
between paris and new york
The campaign for Dysturb’s fake beverage Source.s takes two different forms depending on where it appears. In Paris, it borrows the visual language of a classic bistro drink. Its posters use oversized yellow typography against photographic backgrounds, while the cans themselves have the polished appearance of a commercial beverage. A monumental mural on the Quai de Valmy extends the campaign into the city, accompanied by smaller posters across several neighborhoods. The team also distributed cans along the canal and around nearby métro entrances.
In New York, the American version takes its cues from contemporary wellness branding. The same pale-blue can appears against bright skies and sunlit architecture, with a model holding it in the kind of lifestyle imagery associated with functional drinks. Large murals were erected near the Navy Yard in Brooklyn and in Manhattan.
Dysturb credits AI-generated imagery in the campaign, an interesting detail for a project concerned with the credibility of visual information. Both versions use recognizable advertising conventions to lend an invented product the appearance of legitimacy.
a health warning disguised as a drink campaign
The message becomes more direct in the posters’ smaller print, where Source.s borrows the language of consumer health warnings. One reads, ‘Excessive consumption of fake news is hazardous to democracy.’ Another compares questionable information to a contaminated source, extending the drink metaphor into the way misleading stories circulate online. QR codes appear alongside the advertising, giving passersby a way to follow the campaign beyond the posters.
For Dysturb, the fictional beverage offers a way to introduce a familiar problem through an unexpected format. The organization has spent more than a decade bringing photojournalism and public information into urban spaces, often through large photographic installations. With Source.s, it has adopted the techniques of commercial advertising itself. The campaign asks people to consider why professional graphics and familiar branding can make a message seem credible, even before its source has been examined.
free guides bring the campaign beyond the street
Source.s is part of Dysturb’s Anti Fake News Club, an educational initiative that also offers five free media-literacy guides in English, French, and Spanish. The downloadable materials address the mechanics of misinformation and the habits that shape how people encounter the news. Their practical exercises encourage readers to look beyond a headline, compare independent sources, and examine the origins of photographs.
One guide explains how cropping or a misleading caption can change the meaning of an image, while another examines the influence of algorithms on the information appearing in social feeds. The resources have been used in educational programs across schools and other institutions.
The organization is also developing JustCheck, a verification platform intended to help users evaluate questionable content. According to Dysturb, the proposed tool will accept everything from screenshots to videos and return a credibility assessment supported by evidence and sources.
For now, Source.s puts the same questions into a more immediate, physical setting. A fake drink appears on a café table or a neighborhood wall, complete with all the visual cues of a genuine product. Its real purpose becomes clear once someone stops to read the label.

"AI is helping researchers identify promising new materials faster, but turning these into materials that can be synthesized, validated and manufactured at scale remains a challenge," the statement said. ■

Gap narrows between National, Labor in New Zealand poll ahead of general election
