In the years since October 7, Netanyahu led multiple wars that have seen Israeli forces reduce Gaza to rubble, occupy southern Lebanon and for the first time pummel arch-foe Iran with US help.
At home, Israelis have faced bombardment from Iran, Hamas, Lebanese militant group Hezbollah, and Yemen’s Houthi rebels.
-‘Not afraid to take action’ -
Zipporah Bennett, an 85-year-old retiree, said she was voting for Netanyahu “because he has had the experience of navigating the country through a lot of difficult seasons”, praising his support from the US and adding: “He’s a man who’s not afraid to take action.”
Netanyahu returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket.
Wearing his trademark noose-shaped lapel pin, far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir cast his ballot in the West Bank settlement of Kiryat Arba, where his supporters had set up banners and speakers.
The opposition has scorned Netanyahu for his backing of ultra-Orthodox parties fighting to keep exemptions for religious Jewish students from drafting into the military, which faces personnel shortages.
But one of the biggest criticisms levelled at the premier is his failure to take responsibility for the October 7 attack, the deadliest day in the country’s history.
Eisenkot, 66, has pledged to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the attack, something Netanyahu’s government has resisted.
Seeking to unseat the premier is an informal bloc of parties led by Eisenkot’s Yashar and spanning from the right to the centre-left.
Eisenkot has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state and expressed support for Israeli settlements, but has promised to crack down on violent settlers.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu has publicly said they would partner with the predominantly Arab lists, which represent some 21 percent of Israel’s population and who could become kingmakers if the results are as close as expected.
Yousef Jabareen, who heads one of the Arab-majority lists, told AFP he hoped for a high turnout among his community to help topple Netanyahu’s coalition, after voting in the northern town of Umm al Fahm.
Most polling stations will close at 10 pm (2000 GMT).
Final results could take days to trickle in and it is highly unlikely that any single party will come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member parliament.
Cobbling together any coalition could take weeks or months, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.

UN recognized Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as war crimes and crimes against humanity
Kyiv • UNN
The UN Commission reported Russia’s war crimes against civilian objects and crimes against humanity. It also addressed human trafficking.
The Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately directing attacks against civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts by carrying out attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, and also engaged in human trafficking to recruit foreign nationals into their armed forces for subsequent participation in hostilities in Ukraine, the UN Commission of Inquiry stated. This is stated in a UN statement, reports UNN.
The Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately directing attacks against civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts by carrying out continuous attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
The Commission reportedly "also concluded that the Russian authorities recruited into their armed forces men who had become victims of human trafficking in various countries, in violation of international human rights law".
The Commission investigated the impact of the large-scale attacks by the Russian armed forces on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure on the civilian population, including during the difficult winter period of 2025–2026, as well as the cumulative consequences of these attacks since autumn 2022. Over the years, it notes, systematic waves of attacks, during which hundreds of drones and missiles were used simultaneously, became increasingly frequent and intense and covered an ever-wider area, causing significant damage to Ukraine’s energy sector.
According to the Commission’s assessment, "the Russian commanders who ordered the attacks were aware that the heating facilities they selected as targets in large population centers were vital to the civilian population, especially in winter. The Russian authorities officially stated their intention to continue the attacks and referred to plans to carry them out. The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately directing attacks against civilian objects".
"The evidence collected indicates that the attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure were carried out deliberately, in accordance with a state policy aimed at depriving the civilian population of electricity and other essential services dependent on energy supplies and causing them suffering. The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts," the statement said.
The Commission relied on testimony from 255 people who endured the winter under the conditions described above in the Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr regions, as well as on information provided by Ukrainian authorities, doctors and non-governmental organizations.

Who named Cyclone Arnab and why? Where it will hit, states on alert and preparedness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:16:13 UTC
16:16:13 KST

Rough sea conditions prevail ahead of the expected landfall, in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh
India is bracing for Cyclone Arnab as it moves towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, with landfall expected by Wednesday forenoon as authorities expect strong winds, heavy rainfall and possible flooding across several states.Cyclone Arnab is drawing attention not only for its projected impact along the Andhra Pradesh coast but also for its name.Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast maximum sustained wind speeds of 115-125 kmph, with gusts reaching 140 kmph, when the storm crosses the coast near Yanam, between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam. Its effects are expected in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh, prompting weather alerts and precautionary measures.
Why is it named Arnab? How storm naming works
The name Arnab was contributed by Bangladesh to the list of names used for tropical cyclones over the North Indian Ocean. It is pronounced “Ornab”.Cyclone names in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea are assigned by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO)/United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) Panel on Tropical Cyclones. The naming system began in 2004, with the list subsequently expanded as more countries joined the panel.
The current list contains 52 names contributed by 13 countries: Bangladesh, India, Iran, Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen. The list was adopted in April 2020.Names are used sequentially, column-wise, according to the established list. Each name is used only once and is not repeated in subsequent lists. The Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre in New Delhi, operated by the IMD, is responsible for naming cyclones that form over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea once they reach the prescribed intensity.Naming storms helps meteorological agencies, governments, disaster management authorities and the public identify and communicate warnings about individual weather systems more easily.
Andhra Pradesh braces for landfall
The cyclone was centred over the west-central Bay of Bengal on Tuesday morning, moving west-northwestwards before its expected turn towards the coast. The Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) has warned of heavy rainfall in northern coastal districts, including Srikakulam, with strong winds already affecting parts of the coast.Authorities have identified 16 districts, covering 2,460 revenue villages and 92 urban areas, as potentially vulnerable. According to the state disaster management authorities, 1,763 cyclone shelters have been readied, 2,907 control rooms established and 3,185 nodal officers deployed. National and state disaster response teams have also been positioned in 11 high-risk districts.Authorities have banned public access to beaches and announced restrictions on coastal road movement. Fishing vessels have been secured at harbours, with the APSDMA saying 30,043 fishing vessels have been anchored.Air India has warned that adverse weather could affect flights to and from Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada on October 27. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status and allow additional time for travel to airports.Ashwini Vaishnaw said safety protocols and rapid restoration measures were in place across the Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam divisions ahead of Cyclone Arnab’s expected landfall on October 28. In a post on X, he said war rooms were active at zonal, divisional and Railway Board levels, with around 600 km of track under close watch. “Passenger safety is the top priority,” Vaishnaw said, adding that relief wagons, diesel locomotives, ambulances and restoration equipment had been stationed at key locations, while wind speeds and water levels were being monitored hourly. He also said coordination with the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and state disaster authorities was under way.
Odisha, Jharkhand face heavy rain, strong winds
Odisha has already experienced heavy rain and strong winds in parts of the state. The IMD has issued an orange warning for heavy to very heavy rainfall, ranging from 12 cm to 20 cm, in Puri, Gajapati, Ganjam, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri. A yellow warning has been issued for several other districts.Tourist boat and ferry operations at Chilika Lake have been suspended from October 26 to 29 as a precaution. Authorities have moved boats to safer locations, while Paradip Port has provided shelter to 305 fishermen at its Eastern Quay-1 berth.In Jharkhand, the state government has directed district administrations to remain vigilant. A yellow alert for heavy rain has been issued for several districts on October 28, followed by orange alerts for parts of the state through October 30. Thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds are also expected.The Ranchi district administration has warned of waterlogging, overflowing drains and water bodies, damage to weak structures and possible flood-like conditions in low-lying areas. Standing crops could also be affected by water accumulation.
West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh also likely to see unseasonal rain
The cyclone's influence is expected to extend to West Bengal between October 28 and 30. In south Bengal, heavy rainfall is forecast in South 24 Parganas, Purba Medinipur, Paschim Medinipur, Jhargram, Purulia, Bankura and Paschim Bardhaman on October 28 and 29. Kolkata is likely to receive light to moderate rain over the next 48 hours.
In the sub-Himalayan region, Darjeeling, Kalimpong, Alipurduar and Jalpaiguri are likely to experience heavy rain on October 29 and 30. The IMD has also advised fishermen not to venture into the sea until October 29, warning of rough to very rough conditions and squally winds of 40-50 kmph, gusting up to 60 kmph, along and off the West Bengal coast.Uttar Pradesh is forecast to receive unseasonal rain, thunderstorms and strong winds between October 28 and 31. The IMD has issued alerts for several districts, with heavy rain possible in parts of eastern Uttar Pradesh, Awadh and the Terai region. Daytime temperatures could fall by 5-8 degrees Celsius in some areas on October 30.Authorities have advised residents to follow official weather bulletins, avoid unnecessary travel during storms and stay away from trees, electricity poles, weak structures and open fields during lightning.

Kyrgyzstan keeps key interest rate at 12% as inflation slows
The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic has kept its key interest rate at 12% amid ongoing inflationary pressures and global economic uncertainty. The decision was made on October 26 and took effect on October 27, 2026, Qazinform News Agency cites the bank’s press service.
Annual inflation slowed to 10.8% in October, down from 12.2% in September, while cumulative inflation since the beginning of the year reached 8.5%, according to the central bank.
The regulator attributed inflationary pressures to fluctuations in global food and raw material prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. However, tight monetary policy and government measures to ensure sufficient supplies of essential goods have helped slow price growth.
Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan’s economy expanded by 10.8% in real terms during the first nine months of 2026. Growth was driven by strong investment, particularly in construction, rising domestic consumption, tourism, and major international events.
The central bank said maintaining the key rate would help limit inflationary pressures and support its medium-term target of bringing inflation within the 5-7% range. It added that monetary policy could be adjusted if risks to price stability increase.
The next scheduled meeting to review the key interest rate will take place on November 30, 2026.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kyrgyzstan’s foreign trade rose 13.3% to 12 billion US dollars in the first eight months of 2026.

Mbappé dropped by major Chinese brands drop as backlash grows over Mao joke

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
- Published
Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands.
Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.
The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement.
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."
Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.
A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.
Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé.
The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".
The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".
Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.
But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".
Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".
Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.
What is the reaction in China?
Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another comment on Weibo.
As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".
Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."
According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.
China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with Mbappé, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry.
By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on Mbappé, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with Mbappé" topping the list.
"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo.
Why is Mao a sensitive topic?
Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s.
His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.
His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.
So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past.
It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online.
Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business.
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname.
France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.
In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people".
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said.
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."

Kazakhstan begins construction of 272-meter skyscraper in new city of Alatau

Kazakhstan begins construction of 272-meter skyscraper in new city of Alatau
Construction of Iconic Complex, a landmark multifunctional development set to become the first skyscraper in the city of Alatau, has officially begun, Qazinform News Agency cites the press service of the Kazakh Government.
A groundbreaking ceremony was held with the participation of Kazakhstan’s Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev.
The new complex is expected to become one of the key developments in Alatau’s emerging business district. With an investment of more than 800 million US dollars, the project provides for the construction of two towers measuring 272 and 78 meters in height. The development will accommodate office spaces, residential units, a hotel, retail outlets, and public areas.
Bozumbayev noted that the development of Alatau remains under the close supervision of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. At the Head of State’s initiative, a special legal regime is being introduced in stages to create favorable conditions for investors and establish a modern governance system.
These measures are contributing to increased investment activity. In the first nine months of 2026, investment in fixed capital in Alatau rose 1.6 times to reach 70.3 billion tenge. Overall, the city’s investment portfolio includes 67 projects worth nearly 6.9 billion US dollars, with the potential to create around 55,000 jobs.
Urban infrastructure is also being developed to support the implementation of investment projects. Work is currently underway on 28 projects, with 35.3 billion tenge allocated from the reserve fund. Key initiatives include the reconstruction of the Kokpa-1 substation, the construction of water supply facilities, and road repairs. These improvements are expected to provide the necessary conditions for launching new businesses and supporting further construction.
The deputy prime minister placed particular emphasis on the quality and safety of Iconic Complex. He stressed the importance of meeting construction deadlines, complying with seismic safety and energy efficiency requirements, and involving Kazakhstani companies and specialists in the project.
As part of the special legal regime, a mechanism for independent technical review of project documentation has also been introduced, involving international experts. The initiative is intended to bring international best practices into the assessment of complex construction projects.
We expect Iconic Complex to set a new standard for design and construction quality and contribute to Alatau’s development as a modern city. The project must be completed on schedule while meeting stringent quality and safety requirements, said Bozumbayev.
China State Construction Engineering Corporation (CSCEC) is serving as the project’s general contractor, while the architectural concept was developed by the US-based firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM).
Construction of Iconic Complex is scheduled for completion by the end of 2029.
Earlier, Qazinform reported the KAIST branch would open in Alatau.

Kazakhstan to open official consular office in Houston
Kazakhstan celebrated its Republic Day in Houston, bringing together members of the Kazakhstani community, local officials and representatives of business and cultural organizations. The evening opened with the national anthems of Kazakhstan and the United States, setting a solemn and friendly tone for the event, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
During the celebration, representatives of the Houston city administration, on behalf of Mayor John Whitmire, presented the organizers, Texas Qazaq Foundation, with a proclamation recognizing Kazakhstan’s national holiday.
One of the evening’s key announcements came from Kazakhstan’s Consul General in Houston, Gabidulla Ospankulov, who said that an official consular office of Kazakhstan would open in the city in the near future.
On the instructions of President of the Republic of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, an official consular office of Kazakhstan will be opened in Houston. Its opening and the commencement of operations are expected in the near future, said Ospankulov.
The new office is expected to strengthen ties between Kazakhstani citizens living in the United States and their homeland while creating additional opportunities for cooperation.
Jason Wilson, director at the U.S. Commercial Service Office in Houston, noted that bilateral trade in goods and services between the United States and Kazakhstan exceeded $7 billion for the first time in 2025.
The celebration also highlighted efforts to preserve the Kazakh language, culture and national traditions abroad.
Children from Houston Qazaq School, described as the first Kazakh school in the United States, performed traditional Kazakh dances and songs and played the dombra.
The school, which has been operating for nearly 15 years, began with just 10 students and now brings together around 80 children. Young members of the community are also developing initiatives to strengthen connections among Kazakh Americans and preserve their cultural heritage.
Twelve Kazakhstani entrepreneurs played an important role in supporting and organizing the celebration.

Among the foundation’s long-term plans is the establishment of its own Kazakh community center to host cultural events and support future generations.
The evening culminated in a concert by Kazakhstani singer Miras Zhugunusov, which attracted a large audience.
The celebration served as an occasion to reaffirm national identity, pride in Kazakhstan and the friendship between Kazakhstan and the United States. The official recognition of Republic Day and the announcement of the forthcoming consular office opening marked significant milestones for the Kazakhstani community in Houston, which continues to preserve its roots and introduce American society to Kazakhstan’s rich cultural heritage.

SC seeks Centre’s response to media body’s plea challenging data protection act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:13:53 UTC
16:13:53 KST

SC asks for Centre's reply against Data Protection Act
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday issued notice to the Centre on a petition filed by the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) challenging provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and its accompanying rules. The association had alleged that the act infringe press freedom and the right to information.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued the notice after hearing senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the DNPA. The matter will be heard next on November 17 along with pending petitions.The plea seeks to strike down several provisions of the law, arguing that the absence of an exemption for journalistic activities could impede reporting, undermine investigative journalism and compromise the confidentiality of sources.Describing the petition as a comprehensive challenge by traditional news organisations, Divan told the bench, “This is perhaps the first comprehensive petition by what we call legacy media. There has been some debate over citizen journalists. We are the traditional, conventional legacy media.”She sought an interim stay on the challenged provisions, arguing that consent requirements could make routine and time-sensitive reporting difficult.
“If I am left to the mercy of the data principal as to whether he or she will give consent, how will news be reported?” she asked.Divan also warned that the provisions could affect live television coverage and restrict newsrooms from reporting without prior permission.
“What is the point if I have to ask for permission and consent,” she asked.According to Reuters, media groups told the court that the law amounted to pre-censorship and could force newsrooms to shut down. The challenge involves 21 news publishers.
RTI amendment also challenged
The DNPA has also challenged the amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, arguing that it restricts access to information and limits public scrutiny.“Section 8(1)(j), the deletion, is changing the whole concept of news,” Divan submitted according to news agency PTI.The petition further questions the Centre’s powers to requisition information under the DPDP Act, claiming they could affect news organisations’ ability to report on matters of public interest.The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear the matter on November 17 alongside pending cases.
Subhadra Srivastava is a journalist with The Times of India, covering geopolitics, international and national affairs. With over three years of experience, she focuses on national and global developments, conflict, diplomacy and their impact on India. Her work combines breaking news with in-depth analysis, offering readers context and clarity on the stories shaping the world.

Sahin Demir

Israeli opposition leaders on Tuesday urged voters to turn out in large numbers in the country’s parliamentary elections to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rule.
Voting began at 7 am local time (0500GMT) and is scheduled to continue until 10 pm (2000GMT).
Opposition Yisrael Beiteinu party leader and former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman called on Israelis to vote to bring an end to Netanyahu’s political era.
“Vote. Let’s put an end to the Netanyahu era and the rule of the Haredim,” Lieberman wrote on US social media company X, referring to ultra-Orthodox religious groups.
Netanyahu has headed Israel’s current right-wing government since late December 2022, which has been described as the most far-right in the country’s history.
Meanwhile, opposition Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief, said replacing Netanyahu depends on his party emerging as the largest political force.
“There is only one path to achieving change and replacing Netanyahu, and that is the Yashar path,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
He stressed that his party must become the largest in Israel to bring about political change.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state despite UN resolutions supporting a two-state solution.
Separately, Gilad Kariv, a lawmaker from the opposition Democrats party, urged voters to participate in the elections, describing the vote as an opportunity for political change.
“Today, we are taking the struggle we have waged over the past four years to the ballot box,” Kariv wrote on X.
He said Election Day marked “the beginning of four years of hope.”
Kariv also warned that Netanyahu and his allies would attempt to undermine the electoral process by spreading misinformation.
“In the coming hours, Netanyahu and his associates will flood you with fake news and misleading messages in an attempt to undermine the elections by spreading lies and illusions,” he said.
“Our response must be a massive turnout at the polls,” he added.
The elections are widely seen as crucial for the political future of Netanyahu, 76, who is standing trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which could result in imprisonment if convicted.
Netanyahu has also been wanted by the International Criminal Court since 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed against Palestinians during Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, where more than 74,000 people have been killed since October 2023.

Britain issues costliest five-year debt since 2008
Britain has successfully sold more government debt this morning, but at the highest price since the financial crisis almost two decades ago.
The Debt Management Office sold £4.5bn of 5-year debt at an average yield of 5.036%, the highest since 2008, Reuters reports.
There was plenty of interest in the gilts – perhaps not surprising, given the lucrative yields the DMO was prepared to pay. Investors bid for 3.51 times as much debt as was available, allowing the DMO to pick the best offers (ie, the investors offering to accept lower yields).
If Chancellor Healey can deliver the dull budget the market expects on Wednesday then the UK will be rewarded with lower gilt yields, says Matthew Amis, investment director, rates management at Aberdeen Investments:
“It’s been a year of negative gilt headlines. The rise in oil and gas has put pressure on gilt yields, which has impacted everything from Government borrowing to mortgages. In all this negativity what hasn’t been reported is that gilt yields have surprisingly held up okay. When we look at gilt yield moves we don’t simply view them in isolation. We have to view them vs our US and European peers. If UK yields move in isolation, the UK has a problem. If yields move in line, yes the yield move is a negative but it’s a global story.
Since the political volatility of May, gilt yields have been relatively well behaved. Against both Germany and US, gilts have remained in recent historic ranges. The big move has been against France. If Chancellor Healey needs any reminder of what can happen to gilt yields if you lose control of the fiscal message then the French OAT move is exactly that. In May, UK 10 year yields were approximately 1.30% higher than French yields, going into the budget they now trade only 0.30% higher; a huge move.
London’s stock market has been marking the 40th anniversary of the Big Bang – the sweeping, Thatcherite deregulation of the London Stock Exchange.
The Big Bang brought several fundamental changes to the City, including the end of fixed fees for share trading, allowing firms to operates as both brokers and market-makers, and bringing in electronic trading.
It also allowed foreign firms to buy UK stockbrokers, paving the way for the takeover of UK banks by (largely) American rivals.
To mark the occasion, this morning’s opening ceremony at the London Stock Exchange rang its new bell for the first time. This bell, the LSE says, is “a symbol of its heritage, ambition and the market community.”
This morning’s expensive sale of five-year UK bonds underlines how little room for error the Chancellor has, says Ion Jauregui, analyst at ActivTrades.
“I think the market will want a relatively dull budget with credible fiscal control, sensible spending commitments and greater breathing space. There is very little room for error here. With gilts yielding 5.35% 10-year, inflation proving sticky and the Bank of England remaining concerned about inflation, the market will not look kindly at any sign of slippage. I don’t think we should get too excited by the yield fall recently. It appears to be being done more as a precaution.
“Investors will want crystal-clear transparency. The extra £20.4 billion of funding proposal for the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank could help to boost long-term growth, but as borrowing is not expected to begin until 2028-29, this should not cause any issues for gilts. Investors will still want to know what borrowing needs are going forward, the credit risk and if the investments actually give value for money. As long as this is properly accounted for and is financially credible, then the markets should be comfortable. However, if it is seen as an exploit or abuse of accounting rules to disguise fiscal risks, gild yields may rise high again.”
UK borrowing costs could come under more pressure if bond investors are unimpressed by tomorrow’s budget.
The City is expecting a “low-key, low-vol event”, to quote MorganStanley analysts this morning.
Investors are expecting a drop in the UK’s fiscal headroom (the margin to keep within the borrowing targets), to around £15bn to £20bn, down from £23.6bn in March.
To achieve that, Healey will have to demonstrate spending restraint kicking in towards the end of this parliament, but the big questions about government spending will probably have to wait until next year’s Spending Review.
Berenberg say investors expect this Wednesday’s budget to keep the government’s fiscal consolidation plans on course, warning there is “a risk of a jump in yields if Chancellor Healey announces more borrowing than investors expect on 28 October.”
The monthly consumer morale gauge produced by statistics body INSEE fell from 85 points to 80 this morning, below forecasts.
INSEE said “household confidence has strongly worsened” this month, with people more pessimistic about their personal financial situation
The proportion of households believing it is a good time, in the current economic situation, to make major purchases fell, as did gouseholds’ opinion on their future ability to save.
Accountancy firm EY UK has lifted the pay of its partners by over 10% to £870,000.
The increase is twice as large as the 5.2% average pay rise for EY employees last year.
EY’s partners are paid from its distributable profits, which rose to £702m before tax in the last financial year, up from £679m.
The firm has also boosted its staff bonus pot by 25%, and reported reported that its UK fee income rose by 2% to £3.86bn in the financial year ending on 3 July 2026.
Anna Anthony, EY UK & Ireland regional managing partner says:
“These are a solid set of results in a challenging market. We’ve continued to grow the business, while making significant investments in talent and technology to support our future growth and deliver high quality and innovative services to our clients.
“In FY26 alone, we hired 2,300 people across all parts of the UK, made over 3,700 internal promotions and progressions and announced a significant evolution of our global Alliance with Microsoft.
“We also recognised the contribution and performance of our people with our largest variable pay pool to date, whilst continuing to invest in training and development, with over 1.2m learning hours completed.
“With economic uncertainty, technological transformation and shifting expectations of business reshaping every sector, I’m proud of the steps we’ve taken to position our firm for the future while continuing to deliver for our clients, people and the communities we operate in.”
Britain issues costliest five-year debt since 2008
Britain has successfully sold more government debt this morning, but at the highest price since the financial crisis almost two decades ago.
The Debt Management Office sold £4.5bn of 5-year debt at an average yield of 5.036%, the highest since 2008, Reuters reports.
There was plenty of interest in the gilts – perhaps not surprising, given the lucrative yields the DMO was prepared to pay. Investors bid for 3.51 times as much debt as was available, allowing the DMO to pick the best offers (ie, the investors offering to accept lower yields).
The jump in interst rates which has boosted bank profits is also weighing on the housing market.
Zoopla has reported this morning that 35% of UK homes are in postcode areas where house prices are falling, up from 12% a year ago.
These price falls are “concentrated in London and the South East”, it says, where 85% of homes are in local markets with price falls.
This trend is due to higher mortgage rates which have increased the cost of buying and made buyers more selective – the number of sales agreed over the last four weeks is seven per cent lower than a year ago across the UK.
Richard Donnell, executive director at Zoopla, says,
“The extra cost of mortgages has made home buyers more selective while greater choice of homes for sale has increased the scope to negotiate on price. The impact is being felt by sellers in southern England where house price falls are most concentrated as average prices continue to rise across the rest of the country.
“There is still demand to buy homes, and those that are well priced and presented are selling just as quickly as last year. Getting the price right from the start is essential. Overpricing significantly reduces the chances of selling, so sellers should seek advice from local agents on buyer demand and the right asking price for their home.”
Record 738,000 UK businesses in ‘significant’ financial distress ahead of the Budget
Although HSBC has been raking in the profits, smaller businesses are finding life rather tougher.
The number of UK businesses in ‘significant’ financial distress has hit a record high of 738,144, according to the latest Red Flag Alert research from financial group BTG. That’s the highest level since the report began in 2004.
BTG found that the highest volumes of firms strugging operate in support services, construction and real estate and property services.
Julie Palmer, managing partner at BTG, says its a worrying sign ahead of the budget:
“Record levels of ‘significant’ financial distress underline just how many businesses are approaching the Autumn Budget with limited financial headroom. While firms will naturally be looking for clarity on taxation and economic policy, many of the pressures they face extend well beyond any single Budget announcement.
“My real concern is for consumer-facing sectors such as leisure and hospitality, particularly as we enter the run up to the vital Christmas trading period. Higher employment costs, rising inflation and interest rates will add real-world pressure to many domestic budgets. Add into that a forecast 26% rise in the January 2027 energy price cap and households are likely to concentrate on the essentials.
We’ll find out in around 28 hours what new taxes the chancellor has decided to impose on the UK banking sector.
These pictures from the Treasury show John Healey preparing for the budget in his flat in Downing Street in recent days:
You’ll note there appears to be a bottle of HP sauce behind Healey’s left ear, as the chancellor moves between his kitchen island and the dining table.
Frankly I’m surprised it’s not closer. The chancellor is rather fond of a dob of brown sauce, and even carries a bottle with him.
The Times reported that last week he bought a sausage roll from Greggs, pulled a bottle of HP Sauce from his briefcase and “permitted himself a moment’s indulgence” after announcing the approval of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
HSBC CFO’s, Pam Kaur, was asked by reporters why the bank’s shares were down today (they fell in Hong Kong first, and then in London).
Kaur suggested some reasons:
“I think in a high interest rate environment, there’s sometimes a market expectation that we upgrade guidances or we change our targets, and particularly from a banking NII perspective. So that’s all I can think of.”
Here’s Will Howlett, financials analyst at QuilterCheviot, on the drop in HSBC’s shares this morning:
“HSBC’s third-quarter results have fallen a little short of market expectations. Revenue was weaker than anticipated, with pressure on net interest income and a slowdown in wealth, and that disappointment has translated into a slide in the share price.
“The numbers themselves are not disastrous. Profitability remains strong, with an 18.2% return on tangible equity, while loan losses were better than expected and HSBC has reiterated its target of delivering returns above 17% over the next three years. The bank is also returning another $1bn to shareholders through a buyback.
“The issue is that HSBC has set a high bar for itself. Following a strong run for the shares, investors have become accustomed to robust results, so even relatively modest misses can prompt a sharper reaction. Today’s fall therefore looks more like disappointment against high expectations than a significant deterioration in the underlying business.”

Book of Wills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:09:55 UTC
16:09:55 KST

“In Gaza, where the world wavers between silence and forgetting, the written word becomes a final sanctuary – a fragile, luminous act of survival,” Reem Ghanayem writes in the Editor’s Note to the bilingual edition of Book of Wills (Akoya Publishing, 2026). Both erasure and preservation are recorded in this collection of brief writings from Gaza during the genocide. As the writers in this anthology address various people, including the readers themselves, there is no escaping the importance of language.
“Language is a feeble tool,” Alberto Manguel writes in the foreword. “And yet, despite the impossibility of finding language adequate to address a victim’s suffering, when confronted with that suffering, our human condition impels us to speak.”
The book opens with a strong denunciation by Saleem al-Naffar, killed in December 2023 by an Israeli airstrike. Al-Naffar’s contribution is written just 25 days into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and his words are directed at the Arabs who failed to stand with Palestinians: “They and their leaders are part of the conspiracy that aims to exterminate us.”
In most of the writings in this anthology, extermination becomes a personal reckoning imparted to various audiences. Several contributions impart the final wishes of a person expecting death, because death became an inescapable reality during Israel’s genocide in Gaza, rather than a natural termination of life. However, the book also forces the world outside Gaza to a reckoning with its own oblivion, as Amal Abu Assi al-Yazji writes of the aftermath of genocide: “Tear Palestine out of the notebook of your memory, since you’ll have no need for it.” The reader cannot help but contemplate the various levels of oblivion, and al-Yazji’s use of language is particularly striking when she writes, “That worry of yours is gone for good.” How much did all the people outside Gaza worry about Gaza, and what form did that worry take from a sheltered distance? This is perhaps one of the book’s deepest moments, as no one outside of Gaza can truly comprehend the imminent threat of erasure Palestinians have experienced. What would the Palestinian people’s erasure mean, from a distance?
What significance does a will have when military power supports erasure? As the writers in this anthology ponder their last wishes, some create ambivalence through imaginings of survival, even as forced displacement and airstrikes limit areas of safety. Others ponder a will and testament from the hypocritical lens of the humanitarian paradigm, such as Hussein Hazrallah who writes, “I’m nearly certain that the world has seen nothing but a tiny fraction of what’s happening in Gaza, less than the trickle of crumbs that have reached the people here under the label of ‘humanitarian aid’.” The same humanitarian aid also carries death with it, as the author remembers “the death we carried away in sacks marked with United Nations logos, or with the propaganda of the Arab and Islamic nations.”
BOOK REVIEW: Every Moment Is a Life: Gaza in the Time of Genocide
Hazrallah also connects the past to the present when he notes of Palestinians’ ancestors, “They died after escaping death previously, and we were born to them in an attempt to restore the rights that are now slipping through our fingers.” Colonialism, however, made sure that rights and Palestinians are separated by the coloniser’s violence.
Layan Osama Abu al-Qumsan narrates the story of her family’s death by an Israeli airstrike, reflecting upon the fact that her father, a doctor, was unable to live up to his promises of keeping her safe: “I realise that the doctor, with his medicine and medical knowledge, couldn’t avert the disaster that had come upon us.”
Ni’mah Hassan also reflects on her inability to keep her children safe from Israel’s genocide. “I keep trying to put off writing my will,” she writes, while she imagines futures in Gaza despite the absence of futures. Turning to the present scenario, she writes of looking at her children’s fingers: “I never thought of writing their names on them, to prevent death from noticing them. May death leave their limbs intact.”
Other writings take a completely opposite direction – the normalcy in the abnormal life during genocide also speak of having abandoned the fear of death. “Death no longer concerns us as much as the question of how to get a bag of flour or a gas cylinder the next morning,” Nasser Rabah writes. Yet death also occurred during the search for necessities such as flour or gas. The mind filters out the fear of death to accommodate the human instinct to survive.
Writing provides testimony in the face of annihilation. The imagined audiences for each testament in this book vary – from loved ones to the global population away from Gaza. It is through reading from the point of view of the latter that the pain sears through in a different way. Language testifies not only to the lived experiences of the writers, but also as to how much all those not living in Gaza do not know. Under the threat of erasure, language is a tool of preservation.
BOOK REVIEW: Resisting Erasure: Libraries in Palestine and Palestine in Libraries

Scientists uncover new clues to the actual night sky behind Van Gogh’s The Starry Night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:07:52 UTC
16:07:52 KST

Researchers led by South Korean scientist Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim argue that Vincent van Gogh's painting may show the Taurus constellation rather than Aries, challenging the accepted timeline of the impressionist masterpiece.
More than a century after Vincent van Gogh painted one of the most recognisable night skies in art history, scientists believe they may have pinpointed the real celestial scene that inspired it - and the answer could change the accepted date of his masterpiece.
Their findings indicate that rather than being a product of Van Gogh’s imagination, The Starry Night may have been inspired by what he saw as he gazed heavenward from his French asylum 137 years ago.
A South Korean team recently reported that after years of forensic astronomy and research into the Dutch artist, they have matched his masterpiece to a predawn sky over France’s Saint-Remy de Provence right around 22 July 1889.
That’s a month later than the long-accepted time frame for the post-impressionist painting which depicts a sky with swirling ribbons of blue, blazing stars and luminous crescent moon, with a village nestled below and cypress trees looming on one side.
Art historians have long dated the painting to June 1889, soon after Van Gogh checked into the asylum. He'd cut off his left ear several months earlier during an argument with painter Paul Gauguin.
A team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of a Seoul telescope maker, is now disputing that date in a study appearing in the journal Scientific Reports.
"No two skies are the same. Something always changes. I believe Vincent noticed those changes and put them into the painting," Kim said in an email. He added: "I am confident that July 22 is the better date. I will bet on this date."
The latest study addresses "a real puzzle" that in mid-June 1889, the moon was not the thin crescent painted by van Gogh, said Jose Luis Aragon at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. He has studied The Starry Night as a physicist, but did not take part in the new research.
"Still, I would see the July date as an intriguing hypothesis rather than a settled answer," Aragon said in an email to AP.
Kim and his team discovered that around 22 July 1889, the shape of the moon before dawn appeared like the one in the painting, with the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus rising in the east alongside Venus. The sky should have been clear enough for Van Gogh to see all this, based on their weather analyses.
The researchers tested and verified their methods on night skies in other paintings, making for what Aragon considers "a careful and genuinely interdisciplinary study."
There is another important complication: Van Gogh did not simply stand at his window and reproduce the sky exactly as he saw it. He worked on The Starry Night in a studio at the asylum, drawing on sketches and memory to construct its extraordinary landscape.
That means the painting’s celestial elements may not correspond to a single night at all, and that "the sky is likely a composite of many nights as the authors themselves acknowledge," Aragon said.

King Charles heads to Caribbean as calls for slavery reparations grow

AI generated
LONDON – King Charles heads to the Caribbean this week on a tour that comes against the backdrop of increasingly vocal demands from the region that Britain pays reparations for its role in the slave trade.
Charles and his wife, Queen Camilla, will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana before heading to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), the biennial get-together of the international organisation the king heads. The tour runs from Oct 27 to Nov 4.
At a previous meeting in 2022 of the leaders of the Commonwealth – a group of 56 nations that were mainly former British colonies – Charles expressed deep personal sorrow over slavery, and the issue is certain to be prominent once again.
In September, the Caribbean Community (Caricom), a group of 23 member and associate member states that includes the Bahamas, Barbados and Jamaica, said it would push for reparations to be on the CHOGM agenda.
“The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” Caricom’s secretary-general Carla Barnett said in a speech in September.
“It is about recognition, accountability and transformation, and about building a just and equitable future for the descendants of those who, as the chattel of colonial owners, endured untold suffering, loss of life and freedom,” she said.
While Buckingham Palace has said the monarch would not shy away from Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade during his tour, he would not formally apologise for it as some have wanted, in keeping with British government policy that also excludes making any financial reparations.
“It is important to note here the work his majesty himself has done over many years both to acknowledge the wrongs of the past and to find creative ways to right inequalities that endure,” a palace spokesman said.
Shirley Botchwey, secretary-general of the Commonwealth that encompasses some 2.7 billion people, said last week the time has come for discussions about reparations, be they financial or in some other form such as the return of artefacts.
As for an apology from the king, who remains the head of state of a number of Caribbean nations, including both the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, she told Sky News: “It wouldn’t hurt to have that.”
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants, with Britain responsible for transporting an estimated 3.2 million people, making it the second most active European nation after Portugal. REUTERS

Mice in folklore beliefs and traditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:04:43 UTC
16:04:43 KST

Author
Albena Bezovska
Tuesday 27 October 2026 08:25
Tuesday, 27 October 2026, 08:25
PHOTO Pixabay
Font size
It is an established fact that before converting to Christianity, proto-Bulgarians used a 12-year East Asian calendar cycle in which every year was named after a given animal. Studies of the so-called Nominalia of the Bulgarian khans have found that the calendar of the proto-Bulgarians coincides fully with the Chinese calendar we know today. The months are even named after the same animals – the first year is samor (mouse), the second – shegor (ox) and so on. The Bulgarian folk calendar includes special days dedicated to appeasing this cunning and troublesome little creature. One of them falls on October 27, a day traditionally known by our ancestors as Mouse Day (Mishinden).
In the folklore of our ancestors, the mouse was seen as a symbol of impure chthonic forces. There is even a legend that mice can be inhabited by unclean spirits and demonic creatures. This applied to both house mice and field mice, which damaged crops, roamed through barns and cupboards, ate stored food, and gnawed on fabrics and clothing.
PHOTO Pixabay
Not being able to find any way to fight this mischievous animal, peasants turned their attention to the spiritual sphere, writes renowned Bulgarian ethnographer Dimitar Marinov and adds that it was believed the mouse was a “tiny spirit which cannot be vanquished except by supplication and appeasement”. In honour of mice, people once organized so-called Mouse Days, lasting one, three or, more rarely, seven days. Most often the Mouse Days are around 27 October, the day of St. Nestor, or in some parts of the country the 24 November, the day of St. Catherine, who is, according to popular belief, the patron saint of rats.
Saint Martyr Nestor of Thessalonica
PHOTO pronewsdobrich.bg
For the ruptsi ethnographic group in Strandzha and the Rhodopes, as well as the migrants coming to Dobroudzha, the mouse days fall on Trifuntsi (1,2 and 3 February), in some towns and villages of the same regions – on Dog Monday (the first day of Lent and St. Todor’s day week). The rituals performed on these days are intended to ward off and drive away harmful rodents. With their eyes closed, women smear mud over the floor around the hearth, the mice’s holes, and the four corners of the room, symbolically “sealing the mice’s eyes.”
To “sew up” the lips of the vermin, people in Eastern Thrace would make stitches on a piece of cloth and then throw it into the fire. On Mouse Days no animal names should be said out loud, people would call them “lads”, “grouse” etc. There are other prohibitions as well – working with wool or sharp objects is not allowed, nor is opening chests of clothes, the lard keg or the flour box. “Mouse weddings” were once put on during Mouse Days or at another time of the year. Two women with the same name would catch a male and a female mouse, “dress them up” as bride and groom, tie them to one another and put them inside a basket or wooden bowl. The whole village would follow the “newlyweds” to the sound of wedding music. They would go to the forest, next to a river or up a hill and would let the mice loose. It was believed all other mice would follow and the homes and the village would be rid of them. After that the villagers would all sit down to a festive dinner.
PHOTO Pixabay
It was once said that mice would never infest a home where Mouse Days were observed. If mice did appear, it was taken as a sign that someone in the family was stealing or secretly taking things out of the house, that daughters-in-law were disobeying their mothers-in-law, sons were defying their fathers, or that there was discord among family members.
In folk tales, the mouse is often brave and cunning, but also overconfident. The expression "as poor as a church mouse" refers to someone who is extremely poor. We use the phrase "blinking like a mouse in bran" to describe a person who has been unpleasantly surprised and does not know how to react.
According to the folklore dream book if you dream of a mouse you shall have worries, friends will leave you… If you dream you are chasing a mouse – good things shall enter your life, and if you catch it – some kind of gain awaits you.
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

Business confidence improves, but Estonian consumers turn more pessimistic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:02:00 UTC
16:02:00 KST

Business confidence improves, but Estonian consumers turn more pessimistic
Consumer confidence in Estonia fell sharply in October to -32.4 from -23.5 in September, even as business confidence improved slightly, Statistics Estonia reported.
Trade confidence was highest at +23, services +2.7 and industry +3.5, all up on September. Construction stayed at -3.8, with firms citing insufficient demand as the main limit, the agency reported.
In October, the confidence indicator was still highest in trade (+23, up from +21.1 in September). Compared with the previous month, trade enterprises' assessments of sales in the last three months and expected sales in the next three months improved, while their assessment of the current volume of stock was somewhat more negative.
The confidence indicator for the services sector was +2.7 (+1.2 in September). Service enterprises were considerably more optimistic about expected demand in the next three months, but their assessments of turnover and demand in the last three months declined slightly. The industrial confidence indicator was +3.5 in October (+1.4 in September). Industrial enterprises took a more positive view of current demand and stocks of finished products, while their assessment of expected production volume in the next three months remained at September's level.
The construction sector's confidence indicator was unchanged from September at -3.8, and remains the lowest of all sectors. As in previous months, construction enterprises cited insufficient demand as the main factor limiting their activity.
The consumer confidence indicator was -32.4 in October, significantly lower than in September (-23.5). Consumers' assessments of their household's financial situation and the country's general economic situation deteriorated, both currently and for the next 12 months, as did their forecast for major purchases.
The business and consumer surveys measure economic confidence across four business sectors and among private consumers. A confidence indicator is calculated for each sector based on the responses, and is used as a basis for economic forecasts and Europe-wide comparisons.
Statistics Estonia surveys four sectors and consumers monthly; the indicators feed forecasting and international comparisons. The next round begins on 2 November.
More detailed information is available from Statistics Estonia here, here and here.

The One About Matthew Perry Is More Than the Typical Saga of Fame and Addiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:01:02 UTC
16:01:02 KST

When it comes to representing the famous and addicted, Hollywood seems to know only two stories. Both begin with a passionate talent who longs to make an impact on the world. Then, as no less an expert on this subject than Courtney Love memorably put it, they get what they want and they never want it again. Afflicted by affluenza or impostor syndrome or the newfound knowledge that success can’t heal their internal wounds, they escape into substance abuse. It’s only in their final chapters that the two narratives diverge. Some lucky souls hit rock bottom, get clean, and live happily ever after. The rest die young.
It would be easy to slot Matthew Perry, the Friends star who died from ketamine and drowning in October 2023, into the latter category. But in the intimate three-part Netflix documentary The One About Matthew Perry, director Mary Robertson (Quiet on the Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV) honors his memory by resisting that simplistic binary. Yes, addiction (and a cadre of enablers who are now serving time for their roles in his death) killed Perry at 54. It’s also true that he spent more than 25 years surviving it, fighting to act and write and enjoy his friendships and make his family proud and fall in love. Instead of hiding that struggle, he used his fortune to aid others in their recoveries and his platform to advocate for a broader understanding of addiction as the illness that it is.
Robertson captures all of this in straightforward, chronological order, through emotional interviews with family and longtime friends, as well as Perry’s own startlingly frank reflections in media appearances and his 2022 memoir, Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing. The absence of major celebrities, whether by design or otherwise, limits the fond platitudes. In their place are vivid behind-the-scenes anecdotes and candid memories of who he was offscreen—the ambition, charm, humor, and magnanimity, but also the pain he was capable of inflicting on those who loved and needed him. His sister Mia Perry Bowick, a psychotherapist, is the most insightful presence, embracing grief and ambivalence as she ties her big brother’s highs and lows to early family dynamics.
With all due respect to Chandler Bing, Perry’s greatest contribution was his vulnerability, even when the image of him it exposed wasn’t flattering. In its honesty, this documentary continues that work.
Correction, Oct. 27
The original version of this story misstated the last name of the series' director. She is Mary Robertson, not Mary Robinson.

Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:00:06 UTC
16:00:06 KST

Andy Burnham will “sleepwalk” into climate disaster if he fails to get a grip on a series of important policies whose combined impact could scupper plans to reach net zero, campaigners have said.
Big decisions on North Sea drilling, the expansion of Heathrow airport, electric vehicles (EVs) and grants for heat pumps are awaiting decisions from ministers.
But they should be considered in the context of their cumulative impacts rather than be taken separately by different government departments, according to Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth (FoE) in a letter to the prime minister.
Taken together, the emissions resulting from approving drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, expanding Heathrow airport, watering down the UK’s EV targets and cutting heat pump grants would be 402m tonnes of CO2 over the next 25 years, the letter says.
The emissions would be greater than those of 106 coal plants running for a year, more than enough to prevent the UK meeting its carbon budgets and net zero.
Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace, said: “The Burnham government is facing a series of big decisions over the next few months that could define its legacy on climate. This administration seems to get the urgency of cutting the emissions causing deadly heatwaves and droughts, but there’s a real risk they could still sleepwalk into reversing the strong progress the UK has made so far.”
Last week, the government gave the go-ahead to drill the Jackdaw gasfield, despite warnings that it would create only 27 new jobs, fail to cut the cost of living, and add little to UK tax revenues. Now, the North Sea fossil fuel industry is pressing for a green light to the more controversial Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, which would produce higher emissions.
Car manufacturers have lobbied hard for the government to water down its mandate to ensure all new car and van sales are electric by 2035, by allowing as many as half of sales to be petrol or diesel in 2030, which would mean falling far short of the current target of 80% electric by then. Given the long life of vehicles, this could produce future emissions equal to about 60% of the emissions from Rosebank, according to analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank.
Airlines are also pressing for an expansion of Heathrow, which the chancellor, John Healey, strongly favours in the belief that it could increase economic growth. Campaigners challenge this analysis, arguing the UK is already embarking on airport expansion at Gatwick.
In his budget on Wednesday, Healey is also likely to cut the boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants to households installing heat pumps in place of gas boilers, despite the savings on gas use that it represents and the slow speed of the transition to electric heating so far.
Parr said: “Decisions about Rosebank, Heathrow expansion, electric vehicle targets or heat pump funding should not be rushed through or made in isolation – ministers need to be far-sighted and keep track of their cumulative impact on our climate. The carbon bill may take a while to turn up, but there’s hell to pay when it does.”
If Burnham were to reject these high-carbon plans, the UK could build a cleaner, more equal and more prosperous society, added Imogen Dow, climate lead at FoE. Renewable energy could bring down bills, particularly amid soaring oil and gas prices, and the net zero economy has grown faster than the rest of the economy, according to the CBI.
Dow said: “Delivering on our climate goals is not solely a win for the planet – it will also strengthen the economy, lower household bills, improve public health and protect the places we call home.
“At a time when powerful vested interests are pushing the world towards climate catastrophe, it’s more important than ever that governments like the UK stand strong.”
A government spokesperson said: “Reindustrialisation will never mean reneging on our climate obligations and net zero. Over the past two years, clean power has secured £110bn in announced investment and supported thousands of jobs through our record renewable energy auctions.”

UK government met 137 businesses over AI datacentres – but no environmental groups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:00:04 UTC
16:00:04 KST

The UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without any meetings with environmental groups, an investigation has found.
The nonprofit organisation Spotlight on Corruption said a “considerable revolving door” shaped the government’s development of “AI growth zones”, a central plank of the former prime minister Keir Starmer’s AI and economic policy, with 38 ministers, senior civil servants and special advisers hired to positions in AI companies between July 2024 and September 2026.
Meanwhile, even as top officials left government for jobs at OpenAI and Anthropic, government departments largely failed to engage meaningfully with stakeholders outside the technology industry.
Kamila Kingstone, a campaign lead at the NGO, said: “The government totally failed at the most senior level to speak to environmental NGOs or community groups when developing its flagship policy on AI datacentres. This is despite the serious environmental implications of its plans.”
Over 12 months, Spotlight on Corruption filed 40 freedom of information requests to 18 government agencies, seeking details of meetings and investment figures relating to the government’s policymaking on the growth zones, covering the period between July 2024 and June 2026.
The investigation found that ministers, permanent secretaries and directors general involved in developing the policy met 137 businesses – some several times – to discuss Britain’s datacentre policy. By contrast, senior officials met only two community groups and no environmental organisations.
Of the 38 senior officials who left government, nine were from the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, which has played a central role in shaping Britain’s AI strategy. These included a former minister for AI and intellectual property, a former AI adviser to the prime minister, a former director of AI opportunities, a deputy director of AI international policy and a head of AI engineering.
AI growth zones were a groundbreaking policy under which the government promised to “turbocharge the economy” and create jobs by building massive datacentres across five regions – in Starmer’s words, “mainlining AI into the veins” of the country.
The policy aimed to pave the way for Britain to build big datacentres, some of them larger than any datacentre that has been built in the country so far. These developments, often partnered with US tech companies, would supposedly bring in thousands of jobs.
Investigations by the Guardian have called the policy into question, suggesting that it rests on assumptions that do not hold up, financial figures that were not audited and exaggerated projections for job creation.
In particular, the Guardian has shown there is little realism behind announced plans to power these developments, and claims that they will use purpose-built renewables. In fact, different government departments appear to diverge on how much electricity the UK’s datacentre plans will actually require – and what their environmental cost will therefore be.
Meanwhile, there has been growing opposition to datacentres in Britain, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging from Auchtertool, a rural village north of Edinburgh, to Brick Lane in east London.
Chi Onwurah, the MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the growing backlash – and the far larger opposition in the US – was a warning that the government needed to seek greater community input.
“It is critically important that AI benefits communities and is also shaped by them,” she said. “I’ve been concerned about what we’ve seen in the US, where there’s a strong feeling that datacentres are being imposed without adequate consultation. We can see the backlash influencing the midterms. It’s really important that communities are involved in datacentres and AI growth zones and see the benefits.”
Spotlight on Corruption’s investigation suggests that previous policy was largely shaped by conversations with business, and that the government “failed to take the environmental and social impacts [of datacentres] seriously”.
While the government met a handful of civil society groups, these meetings were “held a few days before the launch of the policy, meaning they had no meaningful input”, according to the report.
Finally, many further meetings between businesses and Starmer’s administration would not have been disclosed, said Spotlight on Corruption. This is largely because Starmer’s policy was led by a special adviser, Jade Leung, whose role was subject to far less stringent transparency requirements.
Spotlight on Corruption also looked at how other countries – including Canada, Germany and Australia – developed policy. It found these countries consulted far more widely on introducing datacentres and had more stringent environmental criteria. It said the UK had “fallen behind equivalent jurisdictions” in developing an equitable strategy.
A government spokesperson said: “We are clear that datacentres should create British jobs, strengthen supply chains and deliver benefits for the communities that host them, while prioritising clean power and using water responsibly – and meet with these companies to make sure that happens. We want to work closely with industry, local authorities, environmental groups and communities, and welcome opportunities to hear their views.
“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes. We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”

Likud sources also indicated that footage collected outside polling stations could be circulated as purported evidence of electoral fraud, despite the teams having no legal authority to verify voters’ identities.
Separately, party observers across Israel are expected to report unusual incidents to a dedicated election fraud monitoring centre.
The allegations come as Israelis vote in the country’s first general election since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

London’s most famous shopping street is now pedestrianised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:57:37 UTC
15:57:37 KST

Ahead of the holiday season, cars, buses and bikes are banned from nearly a kilometre of Oxford Street.
For first-time visitors to London, there are certain addresses you need to tick off, like Leicester Square, Brick Lane, or Abbey Road.
And while the latter is most famous for its zebra crossing – thanks to The Beatles, whose album cover of the same name was shot here – one popular tourist location is making sure marked crosswalks are no longer necessary: Oxford Street.
That’s because the world-famous shopping street is now closed to cars, buses and bicycles as of 26 October.
Nearly a kilometre of Oxford Street, between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street, is now traffic-free, with vehicles diverted onto surrounding roads.
The move is the first step in a makeover of the storied shopping precinct, with plans to plant trees, install seating and add two new public squares.
Oxford Street still sees about half a million visitors a day, with shoppers bustling between retailers such as Selfridges, Zara and John Lewis.
But city officials say pedestrianising the street will put it back into the league of top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla.
“This is a momentous day for London, a momentous day for Oxford Street,” London Mayor Sadiq Khan told the BBC. “It’s a new era.”
Why now?
While local officials began discussing the idea of pedestrianising Oxford Street more than a decade ago, momentum began to build over the last two years when the mayor’s office created the Oxford Street Development Corporation to shepherd the project.
That helped overcome opposition from local residents who complained that diverting vehicles from Oxford Street would clog their neighbourhoods with traffic.
A public consultation later determined that removing traffic would attract new shops and visitors to Oxford Street, making it “an iconic destination”.
The project also got a boost from the new Elizabeth Line, which runs through the heart of the city, with a stop on Oxford Street.
Further work on the makeover will begin in the new year, with city officials refining their plans based on feedback from visitors, Khan told reporters.
“In advance of Christmas, you know, I want people to come here and shop and enjoy the experience,” he added.
Oxford Street’s famed lights
As hinted at by Khan, one of the best times to visit (or worst, if you hate crowds) is during the holiday season when lights line Oxford Street, a tradition first started in 1959.
According to the official website, this year the Christmas lights will be Harry Potter themed to mark the opening of the UK’s largest official Harry Potter store as well as the launch of the controversial new HBO series.
Previous years have seen the street lit up with 5,000 stars glowing thanks to the help of 300,000 LED bulbs.
