US, EU and 30 countries warn of famine risk in Sudan, call for aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:56:30 UTC
15:56:30 KST

US, EU and 30 countries warn of famine risk in Sudan, call for aid
Countries also urge Sudan’s warring parties to ‘lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance’.
The United States, the European Union and 30 countries have warned of an “alarming deterioration” in food security in Sudan, calling for “urgent action” to prevent famine in the African country.
In a joint statement released by the US State Department on Monday, the signatories called on the groups fighting Sudan’s civil war “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance”.
The signatories included Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and the European Commissioner for equality, preparedness and crisis management.
“Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action,” the statement said. “The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people.”
Sudan’s army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when a dispute over how to integrate the two forces erupted into clashes in the capital, Khartoum. The war has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 13 million, and created the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises.
In June, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a United Nations-backed hunger monitor known as the IPC, said 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.
Farmers have struggled to harvest crops since the war began, and the IPC said a drought linked to El Nino had driven up food prices and reduced supplies this year.
Without immediate action, the joint statement warned, “the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000.”
The signatories urged the warring parties to allow humanitarian operations through all routes across front lines and borders, including air access to the region of Darfur. They also called on the parties to “sustain presence and protection of humanitarian personnel” throughout Sudan and to refrain from hitting civilian infrastructure.
“In the face of a potential famine, we call on all members of the international community to urgently scale up funding in response to increased needs and support efforts to ensure assistance reaches those most in need,” the statement said.
Besides the US, Australia and Canada, the statement was signed by 28 European countries.
Last month, the State Department said that neither the Sudanese army nor the RSF “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan”.

New fee added to packages sent from outside EU from November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:55:00 UTC
15:55:00 KST

New fee added to packages sent from outside EU from November
From November 1, a handling fee of €2 will be added for each item of goods contained in a shipment ordered from online stores outside the European Union, regardless of the shipment's value.
"The calculation logic for the handling fee is indeed the same or similar to that of the customs duty on small consignments. The amount of the fee depends on the number of goods lines listed on the declaration. If we take the example of 100 pairs of jeans, which are identical goods, they can be entered on a single goods line on the customs declaration," Kaari Lainevool, service manager at the Tax and Customs Board's customs administration department, explained to ERR.
A customs duty of €3 applies to shipments worth up to €150. If the contents of a package has to be declared on three goods lines, for example, the total customs duty is €9 and the new handling fee is €6.
Customs duty on more expensive shipments depends on the goods, but the €2 handling fee will also be added for each goods line in these shipments.
Tõnu Väät, executive director of the Estonian E-Commerce Association, said the additional cost may discourage buyers from ordering cheap goods: "The same product that I used to order and that cost, for example, €6 – if I add €3 to that and another €2 from November, then it is no longer worth ordering."
He added that some Estonian retailers have already noticed an increase in sales figures following the introduction of the customs duty in July.
"For example, several electronics retailers selling phone chargers, headphones, phone cases, screen protectors and other similar products have said that their sales have increased by 10-20 percent in recent months," Väät explained.
However, customs statistics do not show how much people in Estonia have reduced their orders from outside the European Union.
The Tax and Customs Board said the volume of small consignments declared in Estonia fell by 80 percent in July and August. However, some packages are cleared through customs in other European Union member states and arrive in Estonia as intra-EU shipments. As a result, they are not reflected in Estonian customs statistics.
The new handling fee will cover the costs of checking shipments, including risk analysis and package inspections.
Depending on the online store, buyers may pay the handling fee either when completing their purchase or only when importing the goods. The decisive factor is the date of declaration: the fee will also apply to packages ordered or arriving in Estonia before November if the customs declaration is submitted on November 1 or later.

Olpha introduce a new diabetes medicine in the Baltics in partnership with international pharmaceutical company Adalvo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:52:23 UTC
15:52:23 KST

Latvian pharmaceutical manufacturer Olpha has signed a cooperation agreement with Switzerland-based international pharmaceutical company Adalvo to introduce a new medicine for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and weight management in the Baltic markets. The partnership will expand Olpha’s diabetes treatment portfolio.
The agreement was signed at the CPHI Milan pharmaceutical industry exhibition in early October this year, and the new medicine is expected to become available to patients soon. The partnership combines Adalvo’s expertise in pharmaceutical product development and supply with Olpha’s sales infrastructure, market knowledge and presence in all three Baltic countries.
New treatment options are particularly important in Latvia, where more than 100,000 people are registered as living with diabetes. According to the Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 105,608 people in Latvia were registered as having diabetes at the end of 2025, an increase of 2.1% compared with the previous year. Approximately 7,000 people were newly diagnosed with diabetes during the year.[1]
Timely diagnosis, appropriate treatment and regular health monitoring can help prevent or delay the development of complications. Broader treatment options, alongside a healthy diet and physical activity, therefore, play an essential role in patient care.
“This agreement is a significant strategic step in the company’s development as we actively expand both our presence in Europe and our product portfolio. Our partnership with Adalvo strengthens our offering in the strategically important field of diabetes and obesity treatment and lays the foundation for long-term growth in the Baltic countries. By combining our regional expertise and sales infrastructure with Adalvo’s product development capabilities, we aim to improve access to treatment options and deliver long-term benefits for patients and healthcare professionals in Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia,” says Juris Hmeļņickis, Chairman of the Management Board of JSC Olpha.
The partnership aligns with both companies’ growth strategies. For Latvian pharmaceutical manufacturer Olpha, it offers an opportunity to expand its product portfolio and strengthen its position in the Baltics while pursuing broader development plans in Europe. For Adalvo, the partnership strengthens its position in the GLP-1 receptor agonist segment and supports the strategic objectives of its dedicated GLP-1 business unit. GLP-1 receptor agonists are prescription medicines that mimic the action of the naturally occurring hormone GLP-1 and help regulate blood glucose levels.
“Adalvo is committed to building strong partnerships to accelerate access to innovative treatment options in key markets. Olpha’s well-established presence in the Baltics makes it an ideal partner, and we are pleased to begin working together to realise the full potential of this collaboration,” says Anil Okay, CEO of Adalvo.
This is not the first collaboration between the two companies. In March 2025, a generic antibacterial medicine for the treatment of urinary tract infections, jointly developed by Olpha and Adalvo, was launched in the Baltic markets.
The companies will announce the trade name and availability of the new diabetes medicine in the Baltic countries separately.

Ukraine has waited nearly a month for Patriot missiles
Ukraine will again raise the issue of delayed air defense missile deliveries with the US, as Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, Zelensky said on Monday.
Zelensky added that he had instructed his team to raise the issue with Washington again. Ukraine is also seeking PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors from EU countries and other partners holding existing stocks.
The shortage comes as Ukraine struggles to secure enough ammunition to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelensky previously said Ukraine had received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite requiring around 350 per month.
He has also asked European partners to provide 300 interceptors for the winter, but efforts to obtain missiles from existing stockpiles have faced resistance, including from Greece.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian Air Force official Yuriy Ihnat said that missiles expended in the Middle East could have sustained Ukraine’s Patriot systems for several years.
He said Ukrainian crews had developed more efficient tactics, typically using one interceptor per target and employing ambushes before quickly relocating systems. By contrast, air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight interceptors at a single target, including relatively cheap Shahed drones.
Zelensky also called for faster implementation of decisions expected to support Ukraine’s air defense, as officials prepare for the next Ramstein-format meeting in November. “Every support package is an opportunity to protect people’s lives,” he said.

Creepy Cat in the Hat videos reach Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:51:19 EET
15:51:19 KST

Viral images that purport to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character roaming the streets after dark are sparking fear and confusion among children.
The so-called Cat in the Hat phenomenon is spreading on social media. In frightening videos, the black-and-white feline, familiar from 1950s children's books, turns up in various towns and cities.
Over the past few days, the phenomenon has also reached Finland. Police in Oulu told Yle that they have been contacted about it. They said they have searched the streets but have not found anyone sneaking around in a cat costume.
Jyrki Mikkonen, principal of Koivuhaka School in Kokkola, says he is aware that content featuring the hat-wearing feline is circulating on social media. The school learned about it from parents.
"There were posts on social media warning that the figure would show up in this area. According to messages from guardians, this is worrying kids," he says.
The phenomenon centres on videos, shared especially on TikTok, that portray the cat character as menacing and claim it has been 'spotted' in various places or is 'on its way' to a particular town or school.
Kaisa Rissanen, of Someturva, a Finnish service that helps victims of online harassment and bullying, says the pattern is familiar. About ten years ago, people dressed up as clowns sparked similar worry.
"The threat is specific to videos created with AI, not to real dangerous situations," she notes.
But even if the threat isn't real, Rissanen says children's fear is genuine.
She also points out that digital security skills are becoming increasingly important as AI-generated content on social media keeps growing.
"This is a good wake-up call that we need to address these topics more broadly," she says.

South Korea’s GDP growth beats forecasts amid AI boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:50:53 UTC
15:50:53 KST

South Korea’s GDP growth beats forecasts amid AI boom
Asia’s fourth-largest economy grows 3.4 percent year-on-year amid strong semiconductor demand.
South Korea’s economy grew much faster than expected in the July-September quarter amid booming demand for chips used in artificial intelligence (AI).
Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 1 percent on a quarterly basis, or 3.4 percent year-on-year, advance estimates released by the Bank of Korea showed on Tuesday.
The Bank of Korea forecast in August that GDP would grow 0.3 percent in the third quarter.
Exports, which account for about 45 percent of South Korea’s GDP, rose 2.3 percent quarter-on-quarter, driven by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment, according to the central bank.
Investment in facilities and intellectual property rose 4.1 percent and 2.3 percent, respectively, while investment in construction edged up 0.7 percent.
Despite the robust growth in exports and investment, private consumption fell 0.2 percent.
The latest results put the South Korean economy well on track to achieve its biggest economic expansion in more than a decade.
South Korean Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said earlier this month that he expected growth to reach 3.4-3.6 percent in 2026, which would be the strongest performance since 2011, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic.
South Korea’s economy grew 1 percent in 2025, its slowest expansion since the pandemic.
Asia’s fourth-largest economy has capitalised on the AI boom amid a global shortage of memory chips.
South Korea is home to two of the three largest memory chip makers, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, which together control roughly 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory.
South Korea’s exports in September surged 83.5 percent year-on-year to $120.9bn, with chips accounting for nearly half of all shipments, according to the Korea Customs Service.

Several injured in car ramming in northern Germany; suspects at large
BERLIN - Several people were injured after a car drove into a group of people in a northern German town close to Hanover shortly before midnight on Oct 26, a police spokesperson said on Oct 27.
A BMW was driven deliberately into a group of people in Neustadt am Ruebenberge, leaving four to five of them with injuries ranging from minor to severe, the spokesperson said.
A police patrol that was nearby carrying out a routine traffic check intervened and prevented further harm.
Officers fired shots at the vehicle during the incident, the spokesperson said.
Initial information suggests those involved were known to each other. The occupants of the BMW fled and remain at large, the spokesperson added. REUTERS

China brings legacy of Tokyo Trial to UN Headquarters with exhibition marking 80th anniversary
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:50:18 CST
15:50:18 KST

People view exhibits at an exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial at the UN Headquarters in New York, Oct. 26, 2026. An exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial opened at UN Headquarters in New York on Monday. Titled "Justice and Peace for All Humanity," the exhibition features historical photographs, archival documents and publications on the investigation and prosecution of Japanese war crimes during World War II. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- An exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial opened at UN Headquarters in New York on Monday.
Titled "Justice and Peace for All Humanity," the exhibition features historical photographs, archival documents and publications on the investigation and prosecution of Japanese war crimes during World War II.
"The Tokyo Trial cements the post-war world order, upholds fairness and justice, and advances international rule of law. It is a landmark victory of peace over war, civilization over barbarism, and justice over evil, with far-reaching political and historical significance," said Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations, at the opening ceremony.
"The Tokyo Trial put Japanese militarism in the dock. It's essential for Japan to bear in mind what is at the core of the trial, make a clean break with militarism, and commit itself to peace once and for all," he said.
"Regrettably, right-wing forces in Japan keep questioning the legitimacy of the Tokyo Trial under various pretexts, and try to gloss over Japan's history of aggression. From worshiping Class-A war criminals to hollowing out the pacifist Constitution, from easing controls on arms exports to lifting the ban on the right to collective self-defense, Japan is going further away from the Tokyo Trial and tearing up its 'pacifist' rulebook."
"History, if not forgotten, can serve as a guide for the future," said Fu. "We need to guard against rising neo-militarism, and together uphold the post-war order and international peace and security."
Qi Dahai, director-general of the Department of Treaty and Law of China's Foreign Ministry, Zhou Feng, curator of the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, and officials from Russia and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea addressed the opening ceremony. Permanent representatives to the United Nations from Spain, Nicaragua and other countries attended the ceremony.
Speakers highlighted the Tokyo Trial's role in upholding peace through the rule of law and bringing Japan's wartime aggression to justice. They stressed the need to learn from history, remember the suffering caused by war, and work together to prevent the resurgence of militarism and aggression.
Organized by China's Permanent Mission to the United Nations, the exhibition is being held during the UN International Law Week. ■

World Insights: Japanese firm under fire over Mongolia wildfire, ecological damage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:50:13 CST
15:50:13 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A subsidiary of a Japanese telecom firm is under fire and facing legal consequences after its executives' activities sparked a massive wildfire in Mongolia near the Chinese border, which burned an area more than twice the size of Tokyo.
The fire broke out on Oct. 8 in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area, one of eastern Mongolia's best-preserved natural ecosystems and a habitat for a wide range of wildlife, including rare and endangered species. It was extinguished on Oct. 16, according to Mongolian media reports.
The wildfire burned for more than eight days, sweeping across approximately 530,000 hectares, destroying about 80 percent of the protected nature reserve, according to the country's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change.
Some wild animals, among them rare and endangered species, fled across the border into China. More than 2,000 personnel were deployed in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region to contain a grassland fire spreading from Mongolia. As Chinese firefighters worked to contain the blaze, they also left a passage open for the fleeing animals to escape.
OUTRAGE AND UNANSWERED QUESTIONS
Japanese telecommunications operator KDDI did not admit until Oct. 20, almost two weeks after the fire broke out, that the disaster was linked to the activities of its subsidiary, Mobicom.
According to Mongolian media, a five-vehicle Mobicom convoy led by senior Japanese executives and carrying 13 people entered the restricted area. Dry grass beneath one vehicle caught fire, and strong winds quickly spread the flames across the grassland.
Mobicom claimed the trip was an official survey for telecom infrastructure construction, describing the fire as an operational accident.
However, Mongolian government officials and local media have strongly questioned the explanation, pointing out that the proposed fibre-optic project lacked technical and economic justification.
Local media reports said the convoy may have entered the area for illegal hunting and fishing involving critically endangered species. Such activities are prohibited under Mongolian criminal law in specially protected areas, where starting a forest or steppe fire can also carry criminal penalties.
Although the company apologized for the fire, it did not directly address the allegations.
The incident has sparked widespread public outrage in Mongolia, with questions raised over whether the convoy had obtained the necessary permits to enter the ecologically sensitive reserve during the high-risk fire season.
Amid mounting public anger over the delayed apology from the Japanese side and the lack of a plan and compensation to address the damage, Mongolia's Deputy Prime Minister Nyamtaishiryn Nomtoibayar said, "Strictly protected areas are not places that anyone can simply enter at will ... Mobicom's empty 'apology' means nothing to me."
Temuulen Ganzorig, Mongolia's minister of justice and internal affairs, said those involved, along with personnel from relevant border-port administrations, would be held accountable and ordered to compensate for the losses.
The incident was "not merely a private matter for one company," Kazuya Shimba, secretary-general of Japan's Democratic Party for the People, told a press conference, noting that "Japan as a nation must take it seriously."
"No one should be allowed to escape accountability for the damage. The investigation must establish who authorized entry into the protected area, for what purpose, who was responsible for ensuring fire safety, and what measures were taken after the fire broke out," said Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osor Uchral.
"Any issues related to Mobicom's operations must also be investigated in accordance with the law and based on evidence," he stressed.
ECOLOGICAL DAMAGE
Beyond the immediate damage, the fire's long-term ecological consequences could be far more difficult to assess.
A Mongolian government working group is assessing damage to the Numrug Strictly Protected Area. The country's environment ministry said the assessment should examine the fire's impacts on soil, water, air, vegetation, wildlife and ecosystem functions, as well as its long-term ecological consequences.
The grasslands in eastern Mongolia form a vital ecological barrier in Northeast Asia, Liu Zhiyan, a senior research fellow at the Research Institute for Eco-civilization of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told the media.
The fire may have affected not only grasslands but also riverbanks, wetlands and other ecosystems, said Wang Qinxue, a researcher at Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies who has long studied the region's ecological environment.
Even if vegetation regrows the following year, plant species composition and soil conditions may not recover at the same pace, said Wang, stressing that further assessment is needed to determine whether wildlife can safely survive the winter and whether ash, sediment or smoke from the fire has crossed national borders.
The wildfire also released smoke and particulate matter that could be carried across borders by air currents, said Liu.
The fire's potential transboundary ecological effects warrant further investigation, including whether ash and sediment could enter rivers and wetlands through surface runoff and whether smoke had crossed national borders, Wang said.
Citing research in Mongolia's Dornod Province, Wang said fires occurring from autumn through the following spring were associated with the number of dust storm days in spring. Reduced vegetation cover leaves soil more vulnerable to wind erosion, making surface materials more susceptible to being carried away by the wind, he said.
Regular international cooperation on fire warnings, emergency response and ecological restoration is essential to containing cross-border disasters and reducing environmental risks, Liu said.
Kazuo Yawata, a former senior official at Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry and a history writer, reiterated that Mobicom should offer a sincere apology for the disaster, stressing that the fire had caused "a significant impact on the local ecosystem." ■

A missing link to Australia's newest airport comes with a $55 sting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:50:12 UTC
15:50:12 KST

in brief
- Western Sydney International Airport travellers face public transport stopgaps.
- The promised metro line to the airport may not be operational until mid 2028.
Western Sydney International Airport (WSI)'s opening marks Australia's first major new aviation gateway in over half a century, yet it will be a long time before visitors will be able to take a train to or from the terminal.
From its outset, state and transit authorities had promised that WSI would come complete with a high-speed, driverless metro line to connect passengers to the wider Sydney rail network.
However, disputes with contractors, corruption allegations, and deadline blowouts have left staff and travellers forced to use stop-gap methods to reach the airport, with alternative arrangements unlikely to materialise for well over a year.
In June, the NSW government was forced to concede that the delays to the metro line opening could continue until mid-2028 — some 18 months after the grand opening of WSI.
While construction delays continue, travellers and staff face limited public transport options, with private firms' alternatives costing up to $55 per person.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Temporary transport measures
While the NSW government and Sydney Metro maintained that the metro line connecting Badgerys Creek to Bradfield and St Marys would open on schedule, planning for an emergency alternative began in early 2025, internal policy documents later revealed.
After spending $11 billion on an incomplete metro line, the NSW government announced earlier this month that the WSI Link free shuttle service would ferry passengers the 20km shortfall between the terminal and St Marys railway station on the T1 Western Line.
Five suburban bus routes have also been re-routed to the airport precinct to deliver travellers to Mount Druitt, Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown and Leppington at standard rates.
Other travel options to the city
Private operator Super Shuttle WSI offers an express coach service to Parramatta, the Sydney CBD and Sydney Airport (Kingsford Smith). A single adult ticket to Parramatta costs $25 and a return $45, the single/return adult fares to the Sydney CBD are $55/$80 and for Sydney Airport they are $65/$90.
One of the primary advantages of WSI over Sydney's original Kingsford Smith Airport is its lack of curfew, allowing passengers to arrive and depart 24 hours a day. However, current public transport services keep to standard operational hours, potentially leaving some passengers and staff with limited early-morning options.
Transport for NSW defended the interim transit arrangements, stating operating hours reflect current scheduling.
"There are currently no passenger flights operating or at this moment planned between 1 and 4.30am through Western Sydney International Airport," a Transport for NSW spokesperson told SBS News. "Transport for NSW continues to monitor service demand as the airport grows."
The department said travellers arriving during the overnight window have access to private shuttles, rideshares, and vehicle parking.
While current schedules favour daytime hours, international and budget carriers are scheduled to scale up through early 2027.
Western Sydney International's limitations 'understood'
Adam Leto, CEO of the Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue, told SBS News that the airport ought to be seen in its broader context and that initial concerns over transport pale in comparison to the benefit it brings.
"Rome wasn't built in a day," Leto said. "We've understood what the airport was going to look like when it opened, and it's not going to be the full picture. I think most people in western Sydney understood that and accepted that."
Leto noted that the surrounding road network, including the newly opened M12 motorway, was always expected to carry the bulk of early passenger movements but that it will need to adapt as passenger numbers swell.
"This is about what's happening over the next 20 — 30 years, not what happens over the next 20 — 30 days," he said. "I think there's going to be more infrastructure that will be required to support the growth of the airport."
Round-the-clock transport will take time to mature, Leto said.
"We've never had a 24-hour airport, so it's a new thing for Sydney to grapple with and understand and learn how to leverage."
However, local government leaders have warned that interim solutions must not displace long-term public transport commitments.
Penrith mayor Todd Carney said the completed metro line to St Marys would eventually be a "gamechanger", but called on the state government to fund the full north-south rail link. The route linking St Marys to Tallawong and Bradfield to Macarthur remains in the early planning stages.
"Ours is one of the fastest-growing regions in the country and with that growth comes enormous opportunity," Carney said. "However, communities can only benefit from opportunity if they can access it.''
The rail delivery timeline blew out after lead contractor Webuild lodged claims for around $2.2 billion in contract variations, slowing station works.
The dispute was compounded when an independent probity investigation uncovered invoicing and payroll irregularities among subcontractors, triggering referrals to the police, the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, and the National Anti-Corruption Commission.
Commercial passenger services on the airport metro line are now not expected to run until late 2027 at the earliest, with Premier Chris Minns revealing in June that services may not open until mid 2028.

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Commentary: Washington's proposed new China curbs could deal costly blow for U.S. businesses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:49:46 CST
15:49:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. government's latest proposed rules on outbound investment in China are set to tighten the screws on American businesses yet again. Far from protecting U.S. interests, this move politicizes normal business activity, undermines market principles and fuels uncertainty in China-U.S. economic relations.
The U.S. Treasury's proposal to add biotechnology to its outbound investment restrictions on China, alongside curbs on supercomputing and hypersonic technologies, marks another potential expansion of Washington's sweeping investment controls.
Fundamentally, the proposed rules run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state. Since the 2023 executive order targeting semiconductors, quantum computing and AI, Washington's approach has remained consistent: impeding China's technological advance.
Ironically, biotechnology is where both sides share huge mutual benefits. One-third of the world's innovative drugs in development come from China. In 2025, overseas licensing deals for Chinese innovative drugs reached a historic high of more than 130 billion U.S. dollars, according to China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.
Major U.S. drugmakers, including Pfizer and Bristol Myers Squibb, have struck multibillion-dollar deals with Chinese biotech firms in 2026, while the U.S. pharmaceutical industry has repeatedly lobbied against stringent investment restrictions. According to the U.S.-China Business Council, 95 percent of respondents to the council consider China "somewhat to very important" for them to stay competitive globally. Washington's restrictions risk undermining the commercial partnerships that American companies see as vital to their competitiveness and depriving them of access to one of the world's most dynamic markets.
China remains a magnet for foreign investors. The Ministry of Commerce revealed that China had registered 33.8-percent growth in foreign direct investment (FDI) in high-tech industries during the first nine months of this year. As capital flows into China, U.S. investors constrained by Washington's red tape risk watching valuable opportunities slip away.
Biotechnology sits at the heart of global public health. Combating pandemics, advancing breakthroughs in oncology and developing vaccines against infectious diseases all demand pooled scientific data, shared clinical trial networks and cross-border talent flows. By lumping biotech into its national security basket, Washington conflates life-saving medical innovation with the so-called strategic competition. As the world's two largest economies and permanent members of the UN Security Council, China and the United States bear shared global responsibilities to advance health security for all. Unilateral restrictive measures go against the trend of the times and run counter to the due responsibilities of major countries.
Time and again, history has shown that the China-U.S. economic relationship is rooted in mutual benefit and win-win cooperation. It must not be derailed by the politicization of economic ties or overstretching of national security concerns. Pressure from Washington will not stop China from moving forward and delivering its opening-up commitment.
China will closely follow further developments in the issue and reserves the right to take corresponding measures. It is time for Washington to listen to its own business community and recalibrate its approach along rational and market-oriented lines. Pressure from Washington will only serve to make it very hard for American firms to advance in collaboration with their Chinese peers. ■

However, it was not until Monday, more than two weeks after the fire broke out, that the Japanese government responded for the first time, with Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara saying the government takes the matter seriously and will maintain close communication with Mongolia and cooperate in efforts to restore the damaged area.
"Only now?! The government should've said it two weeks ago. Where were they back then?" one Japanese netizen wrote in the comments under a news post on X about Kihara's remarks. Meanwhile, not only the government but also Japan's mainstream media were slow to report, initially giving the fire little coverage and only stepping it up after public discussion and outrage gained traction on social media.

Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osor Uchral said on Monday that the damage caused by the fire is not simply a matter of land being burned but a serious loss of Mongolia's pristine natural environment, rare wildlife and plant species, and natural heritage that must be preserved for future generations.
"No one should be allowed to escape accountability for the damage. The investigation must establish who authorized entry into the protected area, for what purpose, who was responsible for ensuring fire safety, and what measures were taken after the fire broke out. Any issues related to Mobicom's operations must also be investigated in accordance with the law and based on evidence," he stressed. ■

Xinhua Commentary: China and Germany should deepen cooperation amid economic uncertainty
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
14:49:36 CST
15:49:36 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- As two major economies with close business ties and complementary strengths, China and Germany have much to gain from deeper engagement and collaboration.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's state visit to China, the first in nearly eight years, offers an opportunity to strengthen the foundation of China-Germany economic cooperation and explore new avenues for mutually beneficial development.
For Germany, China is seen as a partner in addressing global challenges and a competitor in economic and trade affairs. Concerns over industrial competition and trade imbalances have fueled calls for a tougher approach toward China. Yet these challenges should not overshadow the broader benefits of bilateral economic ties.
Trade between the two countries reflects their respective strengths, market demands and business choices. Rather than letting competition undermine cooperation, both sides stand to gain by addressing the concerns through dialogue.
Investment figures offer a telling illustration. According to an analysis published by the German Economic Institute, German companies invested around 5.6 billion euros (about 6.5 billion U.S. dollars) in China in the first half of 2026, roughly one-third more than that in the same period a year earlier. A survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China, cited in the analysis, found that more than 85 percent of German companies operating in China intended to maintain or expand their presence, while more than half planned to increase investment.
For German companies, investing in China offers more than access to a large market. China's fast-evolving industrial landscape and strong innovation capabilities also offer opportunities to test new technologies, improve products and respond more quickly to changing market demands. The expertise gained in China can, in turn, help German companies strengthen competitiveness at home and in global markets. This makes a continued presence in China a strategic business choice, not simply a means of expanding sales.
Steinmeier's planned visit to Volkswagen's technology center in Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, offers a concrete example of this cooperation. The center integrates vehicle development, component R&D, procurement and testing, enabling Volkswagen to develop and validate vehicles locally and shorten time to market by around 30 percent, according to the German carmaker.
These business realities also offer a practical lesson for policymakers: competition need not come at the expense of cooperation. Siemens CEO Roland Busch told German newspaper Welt am Sonntag in August that Chinese companies had become highly capable competitors, citing strong engineering teams, innovative products and rapid adoption of new technologies, including AI. He cautioned against using tariffs to shield industries from competition.
BMW CEO Milan Nedeljkovic likewise opposed heightening trade tensions in an interview published by Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung last month, saying, "Nobody is interested in an escalation," and calling for dialogue to resolve trade disputes.
The interests of German companies in China reflect a broader reality: China and Germany's economic ties are deeply embedded in each other's industrial development. China has been Germany's largest trading partner in nine of the past 10 years, and the relationship extends well beyond the exchange of finished goods to manufacturing, research and investment.
For many businesses in both countries, cooperation across these areas helps them innovate, compete and reach global markets. Preserving and deepening these links is therefore not just about sustaining trade flows, but also about creating new opportunities for both economies to grow.
The stakes extend beyond bilateral trade. As the world's second- and third-largest economies, China and Germany, which are all-around strategic partners, share an interest in global economic stability, climate mitigation and multilateral cooperation.
As protectionism and uncertainty rattle global supply chains, the two countries can ease the strain by keeping economic channels open, addressing trade concerns through dialogue and working under the auspices of the World Trade Organization. A more stable and balanced economic relationship would benefit businesses and consumers in both nations while supporting broader global growth.
Steinmeier's visit offers an opportunity to consolidate mutual trust, strengthen mutual understanding and maintain the momentum of practical cooperation. In a world of growing uncertainty, a stable and constructive China-German relationship can bolster global economic growth and help create a more predictable international environment. ■

A choice between debt and inflation: As protests rage, the French government has no good option for solving its financial problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:46:47 UTC
15:46:47 KST

Protests in France have brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets demanding higher wages, lower inflation, and more funding for hostpitals and schools. The government, meanwhile, is trying to cut spending on benefits, pensions, and public-sector salaries as part of an effort to curb the growth of a record-high public debt that has already reached 119% of GDP. Borrowing costs are rising, with investors now demanding higher yields on French debt than on Italian or Greek bonds. And although France’s social spending is indeed burdensome — the highest among OECD countries — the problem lies less in the spending itself than in the near-stagnation of the economy. France appears to be stuck in a vicious circle: the more aggressively Paris cuts spending, the more the economy will slow, making it even harder to reduce the debt. Before long, the problem could spread throughout the eurozone — after all, France is too big to bail out.
After a demonstration in Paris on Oct. 17, the statue of Marianne in the Place de la République was left bearing the inscription “Those who sow poverty reap anger.” According to the Interior Ministry, 550,000 people took to the streets across the country that day, though the protest organizers put the figure at 800,000.
The public discontent began in late September with a blockade of a high school near Paris, where students complained of teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and crumbling buildings. A month later, trade unions and the Yellow Vests joined the students, expanding the list of demands to include more funding for hospitals, higher wages, lower fuel prices, and wealth redistribution. In Limoges, the historic city hall was set on fire; in Marseille, protesters stormed a government building; and in Paris, stores were looted.
President Emmanuel Macron addressed the nation on television, speaking of “anger and shame” and insisting that the protesters’ demands had been heard. However, he said nothing about money — after all, parliament is debating the 2027 budget, which must convince France's creditors that Paris can rein in its growing debt.
Debt is growing, but the economy is not
France’s public debt stands at nearly €3.6 trillion — or 119% of GDP, an all-time high — and it is rising rapidly. A year ago, it stood at 115%, and the government expects it to reach 122% by the end of 2027.
Servicing the debt is becoming increasingly expensive. Next year the public sector will pay €91.2 billion in interest, up from €79.2 billion this year. Debt-servicing costs in the central government budget will rise by €10.3 billion. No other spending item is growing as fast. Excluding civil-service pensions, interest payments are becoming the government’s largest expenditure item, surpassing both defense (€64 billion) and education (€62.2 billion).
Excluding civil-service pensions, which are allocated across ministries, interest payments are becoming the government’s largest spending item
The average yield for French bonds sold in 2025 was 3.4%, Fitch notes, but earlier this month yields on French 10-year bonds topped 5% — the first time since 2002. The difference between the interest rate investors demand from France is now more than 1.4% higher than that demanded of Germany — wider than at any point since 2012, when the eurozone was in the midst of a debt crisis.
By mid-October, markets had calmed somewhat, but France was still paying more to borrow than countries that had been at the heart of that previous crisis: 4.8%, compared with 4.5% for Italy and 4.05% for Spain. (During the 2011 debt crisis, Italy paid as much as 7% — a rate that ultimately cost Silvio Berlusconi his job.)
Even with its new measures, the government projects a budget deficit of 5% of GDP in 2027. Without them, it estimates, the deficit would have reachd 6.4%. To keep public debt from rising relative to GDP, France needs to cut its deficit by around 3.5 percentage points of GDP, Fitch estimates.
A comparison with other countries shows how unusual France’s situation is. Sweden demonstrates that a generous welfare state can coexist with low public debt. The United States has a similar debt-to-GDP ratio to France’s, but it borrows in its own currency and controls its monetary policy. As a member of a currency union, France has no such option.
France spends more on healthcare as a share of GDP than any of the other countries in the comparison, and almost as much as Italy on pensions. It also spends a larger share of GDP on education than Germany, Italy, or Spain, though considerably less than Sweden.
Sweden shows that generous social spending does not necessarily lead to high public debt. It spends more than the EU average on old-age benefits and more than any of the other countries on education, yet its debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly one-third of France’s. France, by contrast, spends heavily on pensions without standing out for its education spending.
The growth picture is more complicated. In 2025, the French economy grew more slowly than those of Spain, Sweden, and the United States, but faster than Germany’s and Italy’s. However, Germany’s public debt is just 63% of GDP.
Spain presents the opposite picture. In the first half of 2026, its public debt rose by 4.3% in nominal terms, but its debt-to-GDP ratio fell by 1.8 percentage points, to 101.4%, as the economy grew faster than the debt. In the second quarter, Spanish GDP rose by 0.7%, while French GDP stagnated.
France may be much harder to rescue than the countries bailed out during the debt crisis, and experts like Nobel laureate Paul Krugman believe a bailout may no longer even be feasible. “France may have crossed the line between ‘too big to fail’ and ‘too big to save,’” he wrote earlier this month. France’s economy is far larger than those of Greece or Portugal, making a bailout much more expensive. Eurozone countries would also be likely to argue far more bitterly over who should foot the bill.
How France got to this point
The French economy is hovering on the brink of stagnation. Growth is being held back by weak consumer spending, rising borrowing costs, a decline in construction, the the hesitancy of businesses to commit to investment.
The main source of uncertainty is energy prices driven by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The Bank of France expects the purchasing power of wages to fall by 0.7% in 2026 and unemployment to rise to 8.4% by the end of the year.
The weak economy is putting pressure on public finances. The projected 2026 budget deficit has risen to 5.4% of GDP — already in excess of its 5% target. Fitch attributes this to two factors: the economic and labor-market slowdown is weighing on tax revenues, while interest payments on the debt are rising. In effect, the economy itself is contributing to the budget problem.
There are two familiar explanations for France’s troubles. The first is that the state spends too much. The second is that it allocates money, failing to turn government outlays into effective public services.
Two familiar explanations for France’s troubles: excessive public spending and poor allocation of funds
According to the IMF, France's public spending will reach a whopping 57.6% of GDP in 2026, and social spending exceeds 30% of GDP, one of the highest levels among OECD members. It is important to note that this OECD measure excludes schools and universities, covering only childcare and care for children under six. France’s exceptionally generous social spending is therefore not inconsistent with high school students’ complaints about teacher shortages.
A special OECD study put France’s social spending at 31.6% of GDP in 2022, compared with 26.7% in Germany. Pensions alone account for 24.3% of all public spending. France does collect significant amounts of tax revenue — but this fact means that there is little room to raise them further, as government revenue is already among the highest in the eurozone, the IMF notes.
Public money is also poorly allocated — at least, that's what citizens themselves say. In a 2022 survey conducted by the OECD, respondents in France were, on average, less satisfied with access to high-quality, affordable public services than respondents in Germany and the UK.
Where the government plans to make savings
On Oct. 1, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s government presented its 2027 budget. New measures are expected to directly save €43 billion, and the government puts the total expected impact at €54 billion once the lingering effects of past measures are factored in. Overall, the plan calls for cuts to spending and in increase in tax revenues.
The main puzzle with this budget is the arithmetic. The €43 billion in new measures amounts to roughly 1.4% of GDP, yet the deficit is expected to fall by just 0.4 percentage points, from 5.4% to 5% of GDP. Without the new measures, however, the deficit would have been expected to rise to 6.4%.
Two possible scenarios: both are worse
France faces a choice between two strategies: continuing to borrow or rapidly cutting the deficit. Neither guarantees the desired outcome.
Continuing to pile up debt is the least painful option for those in power. Pensions, benefits, and public-sector salaries would continue to be indexed, consumption would hold up, and the protest wave would likely subside. However, every year of deficit spending adds to public debt, and each new loan becomes more expensive.
Debt accumulated when interest rates were near zero now has to be refinanced at significantly higher rates. Eventually, interest payments will crowd out other spending, including on education and healthcare. Fitch estimates that debt-servicing costs as a share of GDP are rising by 0.2–0.3 percentage points a year.
France could face another problem even sooner: a loss of investor confidence that sees them demand higher interest rates that in turn widen the deficit and thereby further reduce the market's faith in the French government. Unlike the United States, France cannot unilaterally devalue its currency or print money. In the event of a true debt criis, Paris would simply have to impose much harsher spending cuts.
For now, however, this remains a theoretical risk, and the eurozone also has a safety net in place in the event that creditors panic. Since 2022, the European Central Bank has been able to buy a country’s bonds when their yields rise unjustifiably, with no predetermined limit on purchases. The instrument is intended to counter market panic unrelated to a country’s economic fundamentals, and before using it, the ECB assesses whether the country complies with EU fiscal rules and whether its debt is sustainable.
“The first and foremost solution lies within France itself — in its fiscal policy,” as ECB President Christine Lagarde said on Oct. 14.
The alternative — radically cutting spending to reduce the deficit — would be painful. Sharp austerity would mean reductions in pensions, public-sector salaries, and government procurement. Such a move would increase the likelihood of even larger protests and greater instability while also weakening demand. As an IMF review of fiscal consolidation programs shows, spending cuts have a particularly severe impact during economic downturns, with low-income people hit hardest due to the fact that they have little access to credit to help them weather a loss of income.
If GDP contracts sharply enough, the debt-to-GDP ratio can even rise despite the presence of a smaller deficit. According to the IMF, austerity programs have frequently relied on overly optimistic growth forecasts, with debt ultimately rising rather than falling. The French Pensions Advisory Council illustrated this mechanism using economic models: cutting pension spending by 0.2% of GDP in the short term reduces economic activity by about 0.1 percentage points.
In practice, Paris is unlikely to choose either extreme, instead gradually reducing the deficit by reviewing spending and phasing out tax breaks. This is the approach the IMF recommends: bring the deficit below 3% of GDP by 2029 while protecting the most vulnerable members of society.
France will take a middle path, gradually reducing the deficit by reviewing spending and phasing out tax breaks
In May, IMF staff recommended scrapping ineffective tax breaks, eliminating duplicate spending, and developing a “credible pension reform strategy.” Still, even if the plan goes ahead, the IMF forecasts that public debt will continue to rise in 2028, reaching 121% of GDP.
The current budget, however, may pass more easily than its predecessor, as the approaching presidential election in April 2027 gives parties an incentive to leave the next government with the current budget, which it will then have to revise.
“We inherit the mistakes of our leaders, and they fall on our children’s shoulders,” read one placard in Place de la République captured by Euronews. The central question for France now is how to distribute the inevitable costs among generations and social groups.

What is Modified Wood? How Technology Is Expanding What Wood Can Do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

Wood has been used in buildings for thousands of years. It is natural, renewable and versatile, but its response to moisture requires consideration in design and specification. Changing moisture conditions can cause it to swell and shrink, while prolonged moisture exposure can create conditions for fungal decay. Historically, using wood outdoors has therefore meant choosing naturally durable species, protecting the material or designing around the way wood behaves. Wood modification offers another approach: changing certain properties of the material itself.
What Is Modified Wood?
Modified wood is real wood that has undergone a process designed to alter certain properties of the material itself. The goal is to improve characteristics such as durability and dimensional stability while retaining the qualities that make wood desirable in the first place.
Several technologies are used commercially, including thermal modification, furfurylation and acetylation. Each works differently and can produce different performance characteristics. This article focuses on acetylation and its implications for architectural applications.
Unlike conventional preservative treatments, which typically introduce substances to protect wood against biological threats, modification changes properties of the wood itself. Depending on the process, that can change not only durability but also how wood responds to moisture and changing environmental conditions.
What Is Acetylated Wood?
Acetylation is a modification process that changes wood at the molecular level. Acetyl groups already occur naturally within wood. During acetylation, moisture-attracting hydroxyl groups are converted into acetylated groups, substantially reducing the wood's ability to absorb bound water.
In practical terms, the wood swells and shrinks less, becomes more dimensionally stable and is more resistant to fungal decay. Accoya is a commercial example of acetylated wood. Through acetylation, fast-growing radiata pine is transformed into a highly durable and dimensionally stable material.
Consider a deck exposed to rain followed by intense sun, or cladding moving through seasons of heat, cold and humidity. Windows and doors need to maintain tight tolerances despite constant weather exposure. Around pools and in coastal environments, repeated moisture exposure can place even greater demands on the material.
When wood absorbs less bound water and moves less, its behavior becomes more predictable. Deck boards can maintain more consistent gaps. Cladding can remain more stable. For windows and doors, reduced movement can help preserve the fit between components. Reduced movement can also place less stress on coatings.
Greater durability also means wood can be considered for applications where long-term exposure might otherwise make unmodified wood more challenging.
Accoya is now used across decking, siding, windows and doors, landscape structures, bridges and other infrastructure, with performance backed by a 50-year warranty above ground and 25 years in ground or freshwater.
For centuries, choosing wood largely meant finding a species whose natural properties suited the application. Wood modification adds another consideration to material selection. Today, acetylated wood with its improved properties of enhanced dimensional stability and decay resistance allows architects to expand their consideration of where and how real wood can perform in a wider range of exterior applications.

Deadly parasite: how fox tapeworm warns of pandemic X
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:41:31 UTC
15:41:31 KST

The WHO has developed an early warning system to spot looming pandemics. Tropical medicine expert Dr Carsten Köhler from Tübingen explains the background to Euronews.
The warning about fox tapeworm is something almost everyone in Germany has heard if they have ever wanted to pick berries or collect mushrooms in the forest. The concern is that the tapeworm eggs could be stuck to them - a parasite that attacks the liver and can cause a potentially life-threatening disease.
This disease is one of 21 illnesses that the World Health Organization WHO has placed on its list of NTDs. These so-called "Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs)", known in German as "vernachlässigte Tropenkrankheiten", are regarded as a global early-warning system.
"Wherever NTDs occur, they mark the weak points in the global health system, precisely because there is no system in place there," explains Dr. Dr. Carsten Köhler from the University of Tübingen in an interview with Euronews. He heads, among other things, the Institute of Tropical Medicine, Travel Medicine and Human Parasitology and is president of the German Society for Tropical Medicine, travel medicine and global health.
NTDs can therefore show where medical care, disease surveillance and reliable data are lacking. Precisely in such places, infectious diseases may remain undetected for a long time - with consequences that can reach far beyond the regions directly affected.
Fox tapeworm: Is it still a threat?
The parasite measures only two to six millimetres but can cause severe liver disease in humans. The medical term is alveolar echinococcosis. Adult tapeworms live in the small intestine of foxes and occasionally also in the intestines of dogs and cats.
These animals are then the so-called "definitive hosts" of the tapeworms.
To explain: in biology and medicine, a definitive host is the organism in which a parasite reaches sexual maturity and reproduces. Many parasites have a complex life cycle and change their host - their "home" - during their lifetime. Example: a mouse (intermediate host) ingests the tapeworm eggs. Larvae develop inside the mouse. A fox (definitive host) eats the mouse. In the fox's intestine, the larvae develop into adult tapeworms, which then mate and produce new eggs. The fox is therefore the definitive host.
According to the Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL), the most important definitive host in central Europe is the red fox. Infection in humans is very rare but, if it occurs, can be life-threatening.
In 2024, 52 infections were recorded at the Robert Koch Institute (RKI); in previous years the number in humans mostly lay between 40 and 45 cases. According to the German Liver Aid, the majority of cases come from the southern federal states of Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria. Depending on the region, between 33 and 50 percent of foxes are infected with the parasite.
Echinococcosis is one of the neglected tropical diseases that occur in Germany. But according to Köhler, leishmaniases are now also knocking at the door. This infectious disease can present in different ways and is transmitted by tiny sandflies.
"Many Germans like to travel to the Mediterranean region on holiday and can then bring it back with them," Köhler explains in the interview with Euronews. According to the health magazine of the AOK health insurer, the disease is often curable if it is detected and treated early. The WHO estimates that around 700,000 to one million people worldwide fall ill with leishmaniases every year.
However, most of the 21 neglected tropical diseases occur above all in parts of the world whose health systems are less developed than Germany's.
New neglected disease identified
For example, in 2026 the state of Gabon in Central Africa submitted an application to the World Health Organization WHO to have another disease added to the list of NTDs. "Only endemic countries are allowed to submit applications," Köhler explains. In this case it concerns Loa loa disease, a so-called eye worm. According to Köhler, the WHO will deliberate on the request.
The parasite is transmitted by horseflies. The worms can move through the subcutaneous tissue and sometimes become visible under the conjunctiva of the eye. Infection may be accompanied by itching, swelling and other complaints.
In Köhler's view, the WHO should consider the application. However, in October 2026 the responsible WHO advisory committee recommended a temporary pause in adding new diseases. First, the criteria and procedures for inclusion on the list are to be fundamentally reviewed.
"NTDs occur in regions where the health system does not exist or is only rudimentary," Köhler continues. The diseases themselves are not automatically a danger to the global population. What matters far more is what they reveal about the conditions under which infections can spread: lack of medical care, inadequate monitoring and gaps in the recording of disease cases. There is also a risk that illnesses with pandemic potential may emerge and spread there.
NTDs as an early-warning system for potential endemics
So-called community health workers operate in such regions. They go from community to community, inform the population and observe the local health situation. "A community health worker who is looking out for a worm infection that itself has no pandemic potential would still notice if, all of a sudden, an entire family had died and could report that immediately," says tropical medicine specialist Köhler.
They can recognise illnesses, refer people to medical facilities and report unusual developments to the responsible authorities. "That is why we say these structures can be used as an early-warning system if such basic services have already been set up for NTDs," he explains in his interview with Euronews at the World Health Summit.
The advantage is that helpers are already present in the communities. If NTD programmes are already running in these regions, diseases with pandemic potential are likely to be detected earlier.
Emergency structures do not have to be created from scratch when a new infectious disease appears. If staff are already supporting people with neglected tropical diseases, they can at the same time observe changes that point to other health threats. The work of health workers is also about collecting data as comprehensively as possible.
For this reason, in its strategy to combat neglected tropical diseases up to 2030 the WHO is also relying on integrated approaches: measures are to be more firmly embedded in existing health systems and linked with other areas of public health.
Ebola outbreak: data gap noticed too late
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo showed exactly how problematic missing data can be, says Köhler. "In fact we had expected an outbreak in other hotspots," explains the director of the Centre for Tropical Medicine. "Then we had to realise that the data for the Democratic Republic of Congo were out of date."
When up-to-date information from a region is lacking, health authorities may misjudge the risk. Contact tracing and the targeted deployment of medical staff and supplies also become more difficult.
Local health workers are therefore not only vital for the treatment of individual diseases; they also help to detect outbreaks earlier and to coordinate the response more effectively.
In some cases, the withdrawal of the USA from health promotion has also made data collection in affected areas more difficult. "Because funding from the USA has fallen so sharply, the community health worker structures that were built up over recent decades have collapsed dramatically," Köhler explains.
The missing funds meant, among other things, that former health workers had to give up their jobs. According to UNAIDS, as a result of US funding cuts, thousands of community health workers in Malawi were affected by contract terminations in 2025. The organisation also reported restrictions in the electronic recording of health data.
A study published in 2026 from Zambia likewise describes how cuts in international development aid undermined the work of health facilities. Staff reported lay-offs, a lack of diagnostic tests and difficulties in using electronic patient records. The result: less comprehensive health data.
The next pandemic: Disease X
A new pandemic triggered by Ebola is not considered likely, as the risk varies greatly from disease to disease. While in the case of coronavirus, for example, droplet infection was enough, Ebola mainly threatens people who come into contact with the body fluids of infected patients.
Neglected tropical diseases likewise do not automatically have pandemic potential. A high number of NTD cases is rather a possible indication that medical care and surveillance in a region need to be strengthened.
"We should prepare for the next pandemic, which the WHO calls Disease X, whatever it turns out to be," warns Köhler. It is assumed that Covid-19 will not have been the last pandemic; only the timing cannot be predicted.
Preparation therefore means not only developing vaccines and medicines. It also includes having laboratories, specialist staff, data infrastructures and international networks in place that can work together quickly in an emergency. Köhler points to the importance of European and international cooperation.
"That is why I very much hope that programmes such as the European Vaccine Hub for Pandemic Preparedness (EvH) or the European & Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership (EDCTP) continue to receive support," Köhler says in his Euronews interview. These programmes bring together research structures, laboratory capacity and experts.
"It is important to create a platform now that enables very rapid action and to have functioning cooperative structures in place when this Disease X arrives," Köhler stresses. "For that you need a network. Health has no borders, and neither do pathogens."

10L people, 20k vehicles, Rs 10k cr loss: Why traders' body want Rahul's Nov 1 rally postponed

Delhi traders have urged Rahul Gandhi to postpone the November 1 rally, warning of potential losses of Rs 10,000 crore
The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) has urged Congress leader Rahul Gandhi to postpone the party’s proposed November 1 rally at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan, warning that it could disrupt business across 21 major wholesale and retail markets during the peak festive shopping season and cause losses of up to Rs 10,000 crore.The traders’ body has asked Congress to defer the rally until November 10, after Bhai Dooj, or shift it to an alternative venue away from commercial areas. The Congress has claimed that the rally could draw 10 lakh people.
In a letter to Rahul Gandhi, a copy of which was also sent to Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, CTI chairman Brijesh Goyal raised concerns about possible barricading and road closures on October 31 and November 1. He said traders were worried about whether customers would be able to reach shops during the crucial festive period, news agency PTI reported.
10 lakh people, up to 20,000 vehicles
According to the CTI, a gathering of 10 lakh people could bring between 15,000 and 20,000 vehicles into Delhi. These could include 10,000 to 12,000 buses and 5,000 to 7,000 smaller vehicles, such as cars, minibuses and tempo travellers.The organisation questioned where these vehicles would be parked, claiming there was no authorised parking facility for even 200 vehicles in the immediate vicinity of Ramlila Maidan.
It also warned that congestion could spill into the narrow lanes of Old Delhi, many of which are only 10 to 12 feet wide. A single truck getting stuck in these lanes could trigger traffic jams lasting several hours, it said.
21 markets at risk
The CTI identified 21 markets that could be affected by the rally, including Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar, Khari Baoli, Bhagirath Palace, Chawri Bazaar, Kashmere Gate, Karol Bagh, Daryaganj, Paharganj, Jama Masjid and Lajpat Rai Market.The body cited the October 10 event at Jantar Mantar, claiming that a gathering of around 3,000 to 4,000 people had disrupted movement across central Delhi and caused traders losses of Rs 3,000 crore.It projected that the November 1 rally could bring commercial activity across Old Delhi to a standstill, with losses potentially reaching Rs 10,000 crore.The CTI has proposed Burari Ground or Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium as alternative venues if the rally cannot be postponed. It has urged the Congress leadership to consider the concerns of traders and minimise disruption to business during the festive season.
'We hear you': Rahul Gandhi
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi expressed solidarity with Delhi’s traders, alleging that government restrictions had disrupted business by shutting metro services, sealing roads and locking down the capital.Linking the disruption to his allegations of “vote chori”, Rahul demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi sack Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, whom he referred to as “Accused No. 4”.“To every trader in Delhi: We love you and hear you. The Govt shut the metro, sealed our roads and locked down our capital. With a stolen vote nothing is safe - your shop, your savings, your children’s future. Tell Modi to sack accused no. 4, Gyanesh Kumar and the protests will stop in 30 seconds,” Rahul said.
Traders reported losses after Oct 10 protest
Delhi traders sought Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s intervention over losses allegedly caused by the October 10 protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), demanding compensation from those responsible for the disruption.The Automotive Parts Merchants Association (Regd.), Delhi, said customers stayed away from markets for four to five days before and after the protest call, resulting in heavy business losses.The association had said October, November and December were crucial for traders because of the festive season, including Navratri, Dhanteras and Diwali. It warned that repeated disruptions during this period could threaten the livelihoods of shopkeepers and their employees.
The trade body called for a transparent assessment of the losses and sought full compensation from the principal organisers and participants responsible for the disruption, arguing that traders should not bear the financial burden.It said shop earnings were used to support traders’ families and employees, pay rent, fund children’s education and cover medical expenses for elderly parents.The association also flagged the absence of basic emergency arrangements, including ambulances, fire services and first aid, at protests, warning that such gaps could lead to serious accidents.

The BOVESPA stock index is displayed on an electronic board at the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange (B3) in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 26, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The reelection of Brazilian leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva rattled markets as investors, who had expected a win for his conservative rival, worried about fiscal discipline.
Sao Paulo's stock exchange, which had soared to new highs after Flavio Bolsonaro received the most first-round votes earlier this month, plunged 17 percent on Oct. 26 before slightly recovering to end the session down almost 14 percent.
The sharp decline in the benchmark Ibovespa index at one point triggered the first 30-minute halt to trading since the COVID pandemic in 2020.
"No one had this result on their radar," Leandro Gabiati, of the political consultancy firm Dominium in Brasilia, told AFP.
Against a backdrop of mounting fiscal pressures, Bolsonaro had promised to slash government spending and shrink the state.
However, he never gave details on where the cuts would come from, and vowed to maintain social programs.
The Brazilian state spends more than it collects, public debt exceeds 80 percent of GDP.
In the final stretch of his campaign, Lula rolled out costly measures, such as increasing the value of cash transfers to the poor or debt forgiveness for micro-entrepreneurs.
"Lula made several spending promises, and those need to be priced in," said Andre Perfeito, chief economist at the financial firm Garantia Capital.
"Sound fiscal reform is the price Lula 4.0 must pay to regain market confidence," said Mariano Machado, Americas Principal Analyst at global risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft.

Former US official says Taiwan’s value goes beyond strategic location
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:31:27 UTC
15:31:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Thomas J. Christensen warned that emphasizing Taiwan's strategic location could weaken efforts to deter a Chinese attack.
In an essay published Wednesday by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Christensen said Washington should focus on Taiwan's democracy, economic importance, and regional security rather than geography alone. He argued that focusing on Taiwan's location could imply unconditional US support for its defense, increasing tensions with China.
Taiwan sits at the center of the first island chain, which stretches from Japan to the Philippines. Christensen acknowledged its military importance but said preventing a Chinese attack matters more than denying Beijing control of a strategic location.
He said an attack on Taiwan would damage US credibility among Asian allies, regardless of any military advantage China might gain. A successful invasion could also encourage Beijing to use force in future disputes with neighboring countries.
Christensen noted that the Trump administration's 2025 National Security Strategy highlighted Taiwan's location as a key US defense concern. However, citing US Naval War College scholar Jonathan Caverley, he questioned how much additional military advantage China would gain from controlling Taiwan, given its growing military capabilities.
He warned that placing too much emphasis on geography could undermine Washington's policy of strategic ambiguity. Under this policy, the US does not explicitly state the circumstances under which it would intervene militarily to defend Taiwan.
Christensen argued that an unconditional US defense commitment could weaken support for peaceful unification within Chinese policy circles, increasing the risk of conflict. He also warned that stronger US guarantees could encourage Taiwanese politicians to pursue formal independence, further raising tensions with China.
Taiwanese officials have emphasized the country's strategic position as they seek stronger regional security cooperation. Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) has warned about China's expanding military reach, while National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) has said Beijing's military activities threaten countries beyond Taiwan.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) has also called for closer security cooperation with Japan and the Philippines to counter Chinese threats. Christensen said Taiwan's emphasis on the first island chain reflects efforts to secure stronger defense support from Washington and Tokyo.
Christensen said strategic ambiguity has helped prevent major conflict in the Taiwan Strait for decades. He cited the Taiwan Relations Act and the Six Assurances as key parts of US policy that support Taiwan's security without guaranteeing military intervention.
He urged Washington to maintain its current approach and continue helping Taiwan deter a Chinese attack. He argued that protecting Taiwan's democracy and preserving regional peace offer stronger reasons for US support than geography alone.

NEW DELHI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounted to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups told the Supreme Court on Tuesday, starting the most high-profile challenge against the legislation.
The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Prime Minister Narendra Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have not done enough to scrutinise Modi’s government, which has denied such allegations and says it respects press freedom.
A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged the privacy law, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow New Delhi to identify journalists’ sources, Reuters reported on Monday.
“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) told the judges.
“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission…it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”
The lawsuit is the most high-profile challenge to Modi’s privacy law. Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had challenged it.
The Supreme Court posted the case for next month.
BIG MEDIA GROUPS VS MODI
Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.
The publishers are demanding that most of the law’s contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, should be quashed. They say the law could also force publishers to erase stories and give powers to government to demand information from publishers that could expose reporters’ sources.
DNPA, the group which has challenged Modi’s government, counts as members Ambani’s Network18, Adani’s NDTV and other marquee media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.
Divan said during the hearing that earlier versions of the law excluded journalists, but the final one did not.

North Korean artillery pointed south stirs concern at border observatory
