‘Learning the language is hard’: Adewuyi on life in Lithuania, racism and missing Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

When Olugbenga Adewuyi decided to move from Nigeria to Lithuania, he did not speak Lithuanian and knew almost nothing about the country. Over the past seven years, he has reached A2 level in the language, obtained a permanent residence permit and grown accustomed to life there. But when discussing integration, he says language is not the only challenge.
For a non-white foreigner trying to become part of Lithuanian society, avoiding racism can be difficult – from offensive comments online to situations in which you feel unwelcome.
First shock: the weather
Adewuyi was given the opportunity to take part in an EU project for IT specialists and arrived in Kaunas in October 2019. At the time, he did not know he would settle in the country for the long term.
“I had lived in Nigeria all my life and really wanted to try something new. Many of my colleagues had found jobs in various European countries, so I started looking for an opportunity to do the same,” Adewuyi told LRT.lt.
His first impressions of Lithuania had less to do with a new city or a different culture than with the weather. On the day he arrived, the temperature was just 4C.
“Where I come from, the temperature almost never drops below 20C. I went outside wearing just a T-shirt because I wanted to find out what a Lithuanian autumn was like. I quickly realised it was not a good idea,” he says with a laugh.
Today, he works as a software developer and says he is satisfied with his standard of living in Lithuania.
“IT specialists are paid well here. Of course, I considered opportunities to move to another country, but for now, things have worked out in such a way that I am staying in Lithuania,” he says.
After living in the country for several years, Adewuyi has obtained a permanent residence permit. However, he admits that he is seriously considering spending part of his time in Africa.
“I miss Africa. Here, I always stand out from the crowd. Sometimes you just want to be among people who look like you,” he says.
‘I thought I would never learn Lithuanian’
One of the biggest challenges Adewuyi has faced in Lithuania is the language. His native languages are English and Yoruba, spoken by one of Nigeria’s largest ethnic groups.
Lithuanian seemed completely unlike any language he knew.
“When I first heard Lithuanian, I thought I would never learn it. The hardest part is the grammatical cases. In English, everything is much simpler: we use prepositions, whereas here you have to change word endings. For someone who speaks English, that is very unusual,” he says.
He began learning Lithuanian almost as soon as he arrived. His employer paid for his first language courses.
Adewuyi says his progress really took off when he began studying independently in preparation for the state Lithuanian language examination.
“I passed the A2-level exam. That is enough for everyday life – I can find my way around the city and deal with daily practical matters. But, for example, visiting a doctor and communicating in Lithuanian is still a difficult task,” he admits.
Adewuyi’s circle of friends now includes Lithuanians, Belarusians and people from other countries. One Lithuanian friend helped him prepare for the exam by speaking to him exclusively in Lithuanian and correcting his mistakes.
“Even now, when I write to him in English, he replies in Lithuanian. I still find grammatical cases particularly difficult to understand,” Adewuyi says.
He has noticed that many migrants are in no hurry to learn Lithuanian because they are unsure whether they will stay in the country for long.
“Most foreigners think they will live here for a while and then leave. So they are not always motivated to learn the language. But when they need to obtain a permanent residence permit, their attitude changes,” he says.
Adewuyi identifies the changing seasons, the way public institutions operate and the sense of security as the main advantages of living in Lithuania.
He says that when you approach a government institution, you generally get what you need “without unnecessary formalities or having to know the right people”. He has also grown quite fond of Lithuanian cuisine.
“I like variety. I often visit different cafes and restaurants and try new dishes. The food here suits me perfectly,” he says.
Nevertheless, Adewuyi believes cultural differences are one of the most challenging aspects of living abroad.
“Where I come from, people are generally very open and welcoming. Lithuanians are more reserved, so it takes time to make friends. Being a foreigner is probably difficult in any country, but here you feel it particularly strongly,” he says.
Racism and difficulties finding accommodation
Speaking about attitudes towards people with a different skin colour, Adewuyi acknowledges that during his seven years in Lithuania, he has experienced both positive encounters and unpleasant situations.
He says discrimination is far from always being obvious.
“The thing about discrimination is that it is often impossible to say for certain whether it has taken place. You cannot always prove that you were treated differently specifically because of your skin colour,” he says.
The most painful experience for Adewuyi has been looking for accommodation. This year, while searching for a new flat, he became acutely aware that, in his view, foreign nationals with a different skin colour have to make considerably more effort than local residents.
“If your skin colour is different from that of the majority of the population, you automatically find yourself at the bottom of the list of potential tenants. That was probably the most unpleasant experience I have had recently,” he says.
Nevertheless, Adewuyi says he has experienced few instances of overt aggression during his years in Lithuania. He recalls hearing racist insults on several occasions, but says such incidents have been rare.
“Yes, I have been called the N-word, but those incidents were very rare. In general, I cannot say that I constantly encounter this kind of attitude,” he says.
According to Adewuyi, he feels safe in everyday life. In public places, at events and in clubs, people tend to show curiosity and friendliness rather than hostility.
“When I go out, people are usually friendly and interested in where I come from. I do not feel that I am in danger, and I am not afraid to walk around the city,” he says.
Online comments cause concern
Speaking about religion, Adewuyi says he grew up in a religious family but now describes himself as an agnostic.
“I grew up first in a Muslim environment and later in a Christian one. But I am not religious now. I am an agnostic,” he says.
He says that over the past year or two, he has found some public debates in Lithuania particularly difficult to watch, especially those concerning religion and attitudes towards people from different cultural and religious backgrounds.
In particular, he is referring to the debate surrounding the burning of the Quran. Online comments and public discussions about migrants have had a significant impact on his emotional wellbeing.
Further reading
“The past year or two have been quite difficult. Sometimes you open the news or social media and see a huge number of negative comments. This is especially true when the discussion concerns events attended by Black people. Posts like these almost always trigger a wave of hatred,” he says.
He believes such rhetoric also influences how people perceive others in real life.
“After reading comments like these, you start wondering: if someone looks at you in the street, what are they really thinking? Perhaps the person is simply looking at you, but you have already started to doubt yourself. It really does have an impact,” he says.
One incident at a city fair has stayed in Adewuyi’s memory. He says he was standing in a queue at a market stall when the vendor, having served other customers, simply walked to the back of the stall without acknowledging him.
“To this day, I cannot explain it any other way. After that incident, I found it much harder to attend similar events. Perhaps someone will say it was a trivial matter, but when you live far from home and do not have the support of your family nearby, such seemingly small things hurt much more,” the Nigerian says candidly.
Despite these experiences, Adewuyi stresses that he does not consider Lithuania a dangerous country for foreign nationals.
However, he admits that he sometimes feels tired of standing out.
“Sometimes you just want to be among people who are similar to you. There are many foreigners, Ukrainians and Belarusians living in Vilnius, but I still stand out very clearly. Over time, you begin to understand how important it is sometimes to feel like part of the majority rather than an exception,” he says.

AFL abandons Opening Round for season 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:59:59 UTC
14:59:59 KST

The AFL has abandoned Opening Round for 2027 with all 18 teams now drawn to play in Round One.
Opening Round was played in the prior two seasons but was widely criticised for compromising the competition.
The AFL's first game in 2027 will be delayed by one week due to the 150th anniversary Test cricket match.
The AFL has abandoned the Opening Round fixture from the past two seasons, with all 18 clubs now set to play in Round One in 2027.
The previous seasons saw the four teams based in New South Wales and Queensland play home games, while this year's draw also included one game at the MCG.
The split fixture meant each of the teams that played in the Opening Round — also referred to as round zero — subsequently had an early season bye.
Critics say the fixturing caused distortions in the draw, giving an advantage to the teams that played in Opening Round.
"We have listened to feedback and are pleased to be able to deliver a Round One for all our 18 clubs and fans as we bring back a traditional nine-game opening weekend across the country," AFL chief Andrew Dillon said in a statement.
Former premiership coach with West Coast and Collingwood and now ABC analyst, Mick Malthouse, said Opening Round compromised the fixture.
"We don't need it and it's a blessing now that we don't have it," he told ABC Sport.
"Let me say that 'zero round' was appropriately named.
"It had zero impact on the public; in fact, I'll go in the reverse and say it had a completely negative impact."
Malthouse said the early season byes caused by the Opening Round meant the ladder was not meaningful until all teams had played the same number of games, which in the season just passed did not happen until the end of Round 4.
"All round zero did was compromise the ability of sides to be ready for the next game," Malthouse said.
"If you've got a game tucked under your belt, you're ready; you're miles in front of the next side.
"And don't worry about the results of those games; it's more important about the long-term effect on players.
The president of the AFL Fans' Association, Ron Issko, welcomed the move to reinstate a full Round One.
"Credit to the AFL for listening," he told ABC Sport.
"When you start a season after waiting six months for the season to start and not all teams are playing, it's sort of like a soft launch.
"It just didn't have that energy.
"We're a national competition and what's better than having all teams playing on Round One."
The AFL's move to highlight games in NSW and Queensland was seen as a response to the National Rugby League's move to stage that competition's opening games in Las Vegas.
"We've looked over the border and so seeing that there's games played in Las Vegas, [said] 'Wow, if that's the way they operate, let us do something similar,'" Malthouse said.
"Forget about what's happening over the border and in fact embrace what's over the border and applaud them," he said.
Round One of the 2027 season will be played from March 17-21, with matches in NSW, Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria.
It has been delayed one week from the usual season start time by the test cricket 150th anniversary match between Australia and England at the MCG.
The season will kick off with a match between the Sydney Swans and Geelong at the SCG on Wednesday, March 17.
The following night, losing grand finalist Fremantle will play the Western Bulldogs at home.
Three-time reigning premiers Brisbane will play on the Friday night against Hawthorn at the MCG.

UN experts disappointed shackling and strip-searching bills blocked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:59:39 UTC
14:59:39 KST

UN experts criticise parliament for blocking shackling and strip-searching bills
In short:
United Nations experts have rebuked the Australian parliament for failing to vote on bills banning the shackling of incarcerated women during childbirth and strip-searching children.
Advocates say the shackling of women during and immediately after childbirth can harm a mother and child.
What's next?
The UN experts are urging the federal government to ensure the treatment of women and children in custody is consistent with international human rights law.
United Nations special rapporteurs have expressed disappointment that the Australian parliament failed to vote on two bills banning the shackling of prisoners during childbirth and the strip-searching of children.
It comes after reports this month of a WA teen girl being shackled in hospital after being detained, and an Indigenous woman in a Queensland hospital allegedly shackled after giving birth.
In a statement, special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, Reem Alsalem, and special rapporteur on contemporary forms of racism, Ashwini K.P., said the bills were in line with international standards.
"It is disappointing that parliament was not given the opportunity to formally decide on reforms aimed at protecting the dignity, bodily integrity and rights of women and children deprived of liberty," they said.
"We encourage Australian authorities and parliamentarians to continue pursuing reforms that prohibit shackling during childbirth and protect children from invasive strip-searching practices."
The two bills were brought by senator Lidia Thorpe and debated in the Senate earlier this month.
They had support from the Senate crossbench, but the government and the opposition joined forces to block a vote on the legislation.
Senator Thorpe said she had thought the legislation would be an "easy win" after consulting senators on it.
"I thought that the Labor government would want to end shackling of women giving birth and strip searching of children," she said.
"Every senator I spoke to was horrified, so I thought we could have a chance here. But no, the political will is not there."
Shackling 'psychological and physical abuse'
The shackling bill would have banned restraints at "at any time" during the child birthing process, including immediately after giving birth.
The ABC last week reported Queensland Corrective Services officers allegedly restrained a prisoner at Townsville hospital after she gave birth via C-section earlier this month.
A spokesperson says the woman's care is under review and restraints on pregnant prisoners are only used as a last resort.
Chief executive of advocacy organisation Sisters Inside, Debbie Kilroy, said the woman was giving birth while debate on the bills was underway in the Senate.
"This was an opportunity for them to make a stance against violence against women, which is shackling women during birth [and] after birth, and they actually let us down," she said.
As a UN member state, Australia has endorsed the Bangkok rules, a UN resolution that sets out minimum standards for the treatment of women in prison.
They specifically outlaw the use of restraints on women during labour, birth or immediately after birth.
Ms Kilroy, who was part of initial meetings to develop the Bangkok rules, said Australia's failure to ensure those standards were met was an "embarrassment".
"It's psychological abuse and also physical abuse that not only harms mum, but can harm the child medically," she said.
"When they know that they were born in shackles, it can cause harm for them psychologically as well as the child grows older."
The bills remain in the Senate, but it could be months before they can come up for a vote again.
"Sadly, it means that they [women and children] will continue to be violated," Senator Thorpe said.
"I'll continue to ramp up a campaign to put a vote to the Senate once again to get the support and end the harm against women and children in this country."
A Labor-led Senate inquiry this month recommended the federal government "engage with states and territories" on shackling practices, which Ms Kilroy said was just pushing the issue back on the states.
"We're going to see more people die, more black deaths in custody, more women shackled, more babies harmed, unless the federal government intervenes. They have an opportunity and they can intervene, but they choose not to," she said.
"They need some courage and to step up and intervene into what's happening in states and territories."
The federal government and WA Department of Justice have been contacted for comment.

Israel election: Israelis vote for 1st time since October 7 terror attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

Israel election: Israelis vote for 1st time since October 7 attack
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026
What you need to know
- Israelis voting to elect Knesset
- Israel election committee reports highest voter turnout in decades
- Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces a staunch challenge to his grip on power
- His chief rival is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot
- Eisenkot's Yashar party has polled higher than Netanyahu's Likud party
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:
Eisenkot promises 'change' after casting his vote
Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, urged voters on Tuesday to oust what he called the "worst government" in Israel's history and promised a more responsible style of leadership.
"There is a wind of change blowing in Israel, and this change will come into effect tonight at 10 p.m.," at which point polls close, he said after casting his own vote at a polling station in Holon, just south of Tel-Aviv.
"We will not lead Israel through division and scaremongering, but through unity and true love," he said. "We will win!"
Ahead of election day, Israeli pollsters had predicted a close race between Netanyahu's right-wing conservatives and Eisenkot's opposition bloc, with neither expected to win an outright majority.
"I call on all citizens of Israel to vote, not to buckle under the heat or the disruptions, to stick to the mission," said Eisenkot. "To replace tonight the worst government since the state was established."
WATCH: How Israel's PM Netanyahu holds on to power
Three years after the Hamas-led October 7 attacks exposed major flaws in Israeli security, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains the dominant figure in Israel's political landscape. DW examines how many Israeli voters judge him more on his response to the crisis than on the failures that preceded it.
Experts point to security concerns, fear, Israel's conflicts on multiple fronts, and the absence of a clear challenger as key factors behind Netanyahu's resilience. The report also explores why international criticism can strengthen his support ahead of Israel's upcoming Knesset election.
Netanyahu casts ballot, while accusing Arab-Israeli parties of fraud
Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday that "there are currently no indications of systematic tampering with ballot slips" after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arab-Israeli parties of "trying to steal the election."
Netanyahu made the allegation after casting his own ballot in Jerusalem while urging voters to choose his Likud party.
"We know what is at stake ... We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," he said.
Netanyahu has used Arab-Israeli parties throughout the election to stoke fears of a Palestinian state and mobilize voters for Likud.
"So no barbecues, don't go to the beach — go to the polling station and vote Likud."
Netanyahu had said that three senior officials from the opposition Ra'am party, which has an Arab Muslim voter base, had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes full of cash.
The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, referred to the "unusual" incident with the envelopes in a press conference Tuesday morning but said that "police, even before people arrived at the polling stations, caught individuals who tried to bribe voters."
He said the unidentified suspects were not actually at polling stations and were caught near their homes, adding the matter was under investigation.
"There are no similar incidents of this kind across the country," he concluded. "This was a localized case."
Opposition parties, including that of Netanyahu's main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, have also complained that ballot papers were being defaced and stolen at polling stations.
Early Israel election turnout highest in decades
Voter turnout in the first three hours of the Israeli general election was the highest in decades, Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday.
According to the committee, nationwide turnout by mid-morning was already at 16.68%, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981 and up from 15.9% at the same time in the 2022 election.
"By 10 a.m., more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted," said the committee's acting director general, Dean Livne.
Total voter turnout in Israeli general elections approached 80% the 1990s but hasn't been higher than 72.3% since the turn of the century. Turnout at the last general election in 2022 was 70.6%.
Turnout among Arab Israelis is expected to be particularly important given the role Arab parties could play as potential kingmakers in coalition talks.
"Our vote will change the government," predicted Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party as he cast his vote, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.
Arabs in Israel make up about 18% of the electorate, and pre-election surveys have suggested a sharp increase in voter participation.
Data from the Midgam Research Institute cited by the Qatar-owned The New Arab indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in previous elections. The National, based in the United Arab Emirates, said its sources were predicting an "astronomical" Arab turnout.
How does Israel's election work?
Who is eligible to vote?
Around 7.3 million Israelis (including around 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel) are eligible to vote on Tuesday.
More than 640,000 young Israelis will be eligible to vote in a general election for the first time.
Around 3.1 million Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank do not have the right to vote in Israeli elections, but 500,000 illegal settlers in those territories do.
A further 350,000 Palestinians live in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and also cannot vote, whereas around 230,000 Israelis living there can.
The US-based non-profit America-Israel Democracy Coalition (AID Coalition) has organized a "Fly&Vote" initiative, with as many as 67,000 voters returning to Israel to participate in the election, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data.
The coalition said half are coming from the US, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Israel does not have postal voting.
How does the voting system work?
Israel is a parliamentary democracy and voters elect a legislature rather than choosing their prime minister directly. Voters choose a party "list."
Israel uses a proportional representation system under which 120 parliamentary seats are distributed roughly in proportion to a party's share of the vote.
To enter parliament (known as the Knesset), parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes, which is equivalent to roughly four seats.
The party which can command a majority of at least 61 seats is called upon to form a government. No single party has ever won an outright majority, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Polls suggest this year will be no different.
Unlike many other democracies around the world, Israel is not divided up into geographic electoral districts.
Rather than electing individual lawmakers to represent local areas, voters in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and Haifa all choose from the same party lists in one, single, nationwide constituency.
When polling stations close at 10 p.m. local time (9 p.m. CET), broadcasters will publish their first exit polls, offering an initial indication of the results. Official results are scheduled to be published on November 4.
Arab-Israeli parties: Potential kingmakers in Israel's future ruling coalition?
While the main competition for the largest number of seats is between Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the Arab parties are projected to play a key role in determining Israel's next ruling coalition.
For a party or coalition to rule, it needs to secure 61 seats in the Knesset.
As per a recent Channel 12 poll, Eisenkot's bloc is hovering around 55 seats, while Netanyahu's bloc is trailing behind with some 51 seats. This means that either bloc would need to form coalitions in order to rule, should the election results come out similar to the polls.
The most likely parties to tip the scales are the Joint List (projected to win around 9 seats) and the Ra'am (projected to win around 5 seats). The Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by nationality, make up around a fifth of Israel's eligible voters. Polls suggest a higher turnout rate for the Arab voters than seen in previous elections.
Netanyahu's Likud and Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudi parties attempted last month to ban the Joint List and Ra'am from running in the race, but Israel's Supreme Court reversed the parties' disqualification earlier in October.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties. But analysts suggest such stances are not set in stone and can shift amid coalition talks, a move Netanyahu himself has resorted to in the past.
Gadi Eisenkot: Who is Netanyahu's main opponent?
The Israeli general election is considered by many to be a verdict on the country's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
But who is the opposition, and what do they stand for?
The main opposition force is a so-called "change bloc," a mixed group of center-right and some left-wing parties led by the newly formed Yashar (honesty) party and its leader Gadi Eisenkot.
A relative political newcomer, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to become the chief of the staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) between 2015 and 2019.
Eisenkot has positioned himself squarely in opposition to Netanyahu in terms of his personality — an unpolished man of the people in contrast to the highly stylized and controlling prime minister.
Campaigning on accountability, political reform, and national unity, Eisenkot has sharply criticized Netanyahu's leadership before and after the October 7 Hamas attacks.
But his politics don't differ massively and, although he has emphasized equal rights for all Israeli citizens, he has been ambiguous on the idea of a two-state solution since October 7.
While backing Israel's military operations, he argues the government lacks a clear strategy and has called for an independent inquiry into the failures surrounding the attacks. His military record and the death of his son in the Gaza war have strengthened his standing among many voters
The parties in Eisenkot's bloc all have ideological differences but are united by their goal of removing Netanyahu from power.
Polls open in Israel election
Voting began in Israel at 7 a.m. local time (6 a.m. CET) on Tuesday in the first general election since the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the devastating war in Gaza unleashed by Israel in response.
Some 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote, with polls showing a bloc led by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving premier, neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot's centrist opposition alliance.
Most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. local time (8 p.m. UTC).
WATCH: Netanyahu's final campaign? — Israel heads to the polls
There's a lot at stake in this election: The fallout and questions of political accountability for the attacks of October 7, 2023; mandatory military service for ultra-Orthodox men and sharing the burden of national defense; along with Israel's standing in the international community.
Nowhere can the division within Israeli society be more felt than in debate over Benjamin Netanyahu.
For the past four years, Israel's long-standing prime minister has led what has been described as the most right-wing government in the country's history. He broke with political convention by forming an alliance with ultranationalist politician Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Many Israelis want to see an end to this government. They blame it for the failures surrounding Hamas' terror attack and for the country's growing isolation internationally. Many are placing their hopes in Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as a leading opposition figure to challenge Netanyahu.
Security fears and domestic divides define Israel's election battle
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his top challenger Gadi Eisenkot are both against the creation of an independent Palestinian state, meaning the election is not expected to lead to major policy changes that could revive the long-stalled peace process.
Here are some of the other major campaign issues:
- Security and the War: Voters are focused on the management of the Israel-Hamas war, the future of Gaza, and handling threats from Iran and Hezbollah.
- Military Service: There is an intense debate over whether the exemption for ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) men should be extended or whether they should be required to serve in the military like other Jewish citizens.
- The Justice System: There are deep disagreements over proposed judicial reforms that would change the balance of power between elected politicians and the Supreme Court.
- The Economy: Voters are highly concerned about the cost of living, housing prices, inflation, and war-related spending, although these are not the primary campaign issues.

Israelis head to the polls today to elect a new Knesset in what is expected to be a tightly contested race.
Incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, is fighting to stay in power, with several court cases awaiting him if he loses office.
Polls suggest his opponent, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is in the lead.

What are double envelopes and how might they affect the election results?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:57:49 UTC
14:57:49 KST

While millions of Israelis vote in Tuesday’s elections for the 26th Knesset, hundreds of thousands of ballots are expected to be counted only after preliminary results are published, potentially changing the distribution of seats in the coming days.
According to a report by ynet, Israel’s Central Elections Committee expects between 600,000 and 650,000 people to vote using double envelopes, an unprecedented number in the country’s election history.
By comparison, around 463,000 voters used the method in the 2022 elections.
The expected increase is mainly attributed to the large number of reservists and residents evacuated from their homes due to the war, many of whom are unable to vote at the polling stations where they are registered.
The Elections Committee estimates that these ballots could amount to the equivalent of roughly 15 Knesset seats, potentially affecting the final allocation after the regular vote count.
The double-envelope method allows citizens who cannot reach their registered polling station to vote while preventing double voting and preserving ballot secrecy.
Under the system, voters place their ballot slips in regular envelopes, which are then inserted into outer envelopes bearing their personal details.
The envelopes are sent to the Central Elections Committee, which checks whether the voter has also cast a ballot at their registered polling station. Once verification is complete, the inner envelopes are separated from identifying details and sent for counting.
The method is also used by hospital inpatients, prisoners, police officers, foreign service personnel and people with disabilities who meet the legal requirements, in addition to soldiers and reservists.

Israel votes: 10 factors that could decide Netanyahu's political future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:52:03 UTC
14:52:03 KST

Israelis headed to the polls Tuesday in one of the country's most consequential elections in recent years, with the political future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the balance of power between his allies and opponents at stake. 
But even after polling stations close, the outcome may remain uncertain, with an unprecedented number of special ballots expected to delay the final count. From voter turnout and shifting political loyalties to the weather, these are the 10 factors that could determine who emerges victorious and whether either side can form the next government.
1. Voter turnout
Overall turnout is one of the most important figures to watch throughout election day. Approximately 70% of eligible voters cast ballots in the previous election, while estimates for this election suggest participation could reach 75%. Higher turnout could significantly affect smaller parties struggling to enter the Knesset, Israel's 120-seat parliament. Although the electoral threshold remains fixed at 3.25% of valid votes, a larger number of ballots means parties must secure more votes to win seats, potentially determining whether they gain parliamentary representation or are left out altogether.
2. Which side gets its supporters to vote?
The national turnout figure will tell only part of the story. Equally important is where participation is highest and which political parties manage to mobilize their supporters. Southern towns such as Ofakim, Yeruham and Sderot, along with the northern city of Kiryat Shmona, have traditionally been strongholds of Netanyahu's Likud party. More liberal cities, including Tel Aviv, Herzliya, Ramat Hasharon and Kfar Saba, generally favor parties seeking to unseat him. Turnout figures in these communities will offer an early indication of which side has succeeded in getting its supporters to the polls and where voter apathy may be affecting the results.
3. A record 650,000 special ballots
An estimated 650,000 votes are expected to be cast through Israel's special double-envelope voting system, a record number that could complicate efforts to determine the election outcome on Tuesday night. The system allows eligible voters who cannot vote at their designated polling stations to cast ballots elsewhere. It is used by soldiers, diplomats, Foreign Ministry personnel, voters with disabilities and residents displaced from their homes. Each ballot is placed inside two envelopes, allowing election officials to verify voter eligibility and prevent duplicate voting while preserving ballot secrecy.
Counting these ballots takes longer than processing ordinary votes, meaning a more accurate picture of the results may not emerge until Wednesday afternoon. With so many votes outstanding, the final count could push smaller parties above the electoral threshold and potentially alter the balance of power between Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition.
4. Turnout among Arab voters
Participation among Israel's Arab citizens could prove decisive for both Netanyahu's allies and his political opponents. The Joint List, an alliance of Arab-majority parties, and Ra'am, also known as the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, have conducted separate campaigns to encourage voting in Arab communities. Both political blocs are closely monitoring turnout, recognizing that the number of seats won by Arab parties could significantly affect the prospects of forming a governing coalition. Political observers believe a combined result of more than 14 seats would represent a major achievement for the Arab parties, but could also leave both competing blocs short of a parliamentary majority, depending on the final distribution of seats and potential coalition partners.
5. The impact of young voters
The campaign's heavy emphasis on social media has led political parties to anticipate greater participation among younger Israelis, including many who previously showed little interest in politics. Celebrities, online personalities and social media influencers have played an unusually prominent role, publicly declaring which parties they support and generating political debate among their followers.
Campaign strategists across the political spectrum believe young voters may turn out in greater numbers than usual, potentially giving them greater influence over the outcome and challenging traditional assumptions about the strength of individual parties.
6. The unpredictable ultra-Orthodox vote
Israel's ultra-Orthodox Jewish community has traditionally voted in large numbers, often following the guidance of influential rabbis and religious leaders. This time, however, even prominent figures within the community acknowledge that predicting voting patterns is unusually difficult. Several developments have unsettled the political landscape, including the failure to pass legislation addressing military service for ultra-Orthodox men, the emergence of new parties challenging established religious factions and significant leadership changes within United Torah Judaism, one of the main ultra-Orthodox political alliances.
Veteran lawmaker Moshe Gafni has been replaced at the party's helm by Yaakov Asher, marking a significant shift in a political movement known for its longstanding leadership. Both Netanyahu's allies and his opponents are uncertain whether ultra-Orthodox voters will maintain their traditional party loyalties or express their dissatisfaction by supporting alternative parties. The outcome could affect Netanyahu's ability to rely on his longstanding ultra-Orthodox coalition partners.
7. Does winning the most seats guarantee victory?
One of the campaign's recurring debates has centered on whether finishing as the largest party actually matters when the votes are counted. Under Israel's parliamentary system, the party winning the most seats does not automatically get to form the next government. Instead, President Isaac Herzog consults with the newly elected parties and chooses the lawmaker he believes has the best chance of assembling a governing coalition. The president has considerable discretion in making that decision, meaning the leader of a smaller party could be given the first opportunity to form a government if that candidate appears more likely to secure sufficient parliamentary support.
8. Why getting the first chance to form a government matters
The decision over who gets the first opportunity to form a government could have consequences extending well beyond coalition negotiations. Under Israeli law, the candidate selected by the president initially receives 28 days to assemble a coalition, with the possibility of extensions totaling another 14 days. That period can provide significant political leverage even if the candidate ultimately fails to form a government.
The party whose leader receives the first opportunity to form a government also generally chairs the Knesset's temporary Arrangements Committee, which helps manage parliamentary business until permanent committees are established. The committee can influence parliamentary procedures, committee appointments and the early legislative agenda. Control of these mechanisms could help a political bloc advance legislation or pursue the replacement of the Knesset speaker before a new government takes office, although such moves still depend on securing sufficient parliamentary support.
9. The technology tracking voter turnout
Behind the scenes, political parties are relying on sophisticated technology to monitor voter participation and maximize support. Among their most important tools is Elector, an application valued at hundreds of thousands of shekels that allows campaign teams to manage information collected about potential supporters. The system contains personal details and voting preferences gathered during the campaign, enabling party activists to track which identified supporters have cast their ballots and focus efforts on those who have yet to vote.
The technology has also raised privacy concerns and questions about the legality of political parties collecting and using voters' personal information. Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg expressed reservations about its use, but the application was ultimately permitted. For parties competing over every seat, the ability to identify supporters who have not voted and encourage them to reach polling stations could prove crucial.
10. Could the weather affect the outcome?
One final factor may have little to do with politics but could still influence the result: the weather. With rain and thunderstorms forecast across much of Israel on election day, political parties are closely monitoring conditions and assessing whether they could discourage less motivated voters from leaving home. Campaign strategists are particularly concerned about undecided voters and supporters who are not enthusiastic about participating. Heavy rain could make mobilizing those voters more difficult, increasing the importance of organized transportation and personal outreach. In an election potentially decided by narrow margins, even a small change in turnout could affect the distribution of seats and ultimately determine which political camp gets the first chance to form Israel's next government.

First Olympic flame legend attracts tourists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:49:53 UTC
14:49:53 KST

The origin of the gas feeding Yanartaş is the subject of scientific research.
Nestled within Beydağları Coastal National Park in the Mediterranean province of Antalya’s Çıralı village, the legendary natural flames of Yanartaş attract groups of domestic and international hikers along the Lycian Way to admire ancient historical remains and roast marshmallows over the eternal fires.
Recent observations at Yanartaş have revealed that flames are no longer visible at some spots where they previously burned, while combustion continues in other rock crevices. Flames rising from separate points across the rocky surface remain the main attraction for hikers visiting the site.
The reason some of the flames have gone out, and whether the change is temporary, has not yet been established.
Tour groups hiking this section of the Lycian Way include Yanartaş in their itineraries. Visitors carrying backpacks and trekking poles take breaks around the flames emerging from the rocks and photograph the natural phenomenon. Most of the visitors at the site are foreign tourists.
Fuzuli Yağmurlu, a professor at Süleyman Demirel University’s Faculty of Engineering who previously studied the area, told the Demiroren News Agency (DHA) in 2017 that the flames were caused by natural gas leaks.
Yağmurlu said the gas may have been ignited in ancient times by lightning or human activity.
“These flames indicate that there is a significant natural gas leak in this area,” he said, offering assessments of the source of the gas rising from underground.
The origin of the gas feeding Yanartaş has also been the subject of international scientific research. A study by Giuseppe Etiope and Artur Ionescu demonstrated experimentally that methane can form at low temperatures without a biological source, with the catalytic effect of the element ruthenium.
The findings are among the scientific explanations for how methane may form in rock environments containing gas emissions, such as those found at Yanartaş.
The flames of Yanartaş are associated with the mythological monster Chimera. According to the legend recounted on the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Culture Portal, Chimera had the head of a lion, the body of a goat and the tail of a snake, and breathed fire.
According to the same account, athletic competitions were held on Mount Olympos to celebrate Bellerophon’s victory. Athletes lit their torches using the sacred fire of Yanartaş and ran to Olympos.
The Culture Portal describes these competitions as the earliest examples of the Olympic Games in Anatolia.

Cats’ well-being linked to owners’ emotional states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:49:43 UTC
14:49:43 KST

Cats’ bonding hormone levels are linked to those of their owners.
Cats’ emotional well-being may be linked to their owners’ emotional states through the hormone oxytocin, according to a study published in the journal “iScience.”
Researchers from Kyoto University and Azabu University in Japan tracked 29 cats and 19 owners over one month, measuring levels of oxytocin, associated with social bonding, and cortisol, a stress hormone.
The study found that higher oxytocin levels in cats were associated with higher levels in their owners and fewer negative mood states, including anxiety and tension. Higher stress levels in owners were also linked to lower oxytocin levels in their cats.
Spending more time in close physical proximity to cats was associated with greater energy and vitality among owners, while the length of time they had owned their pets showed no similar link.
Researchers said further studies are needed to establish whether owners’ emotional states affect their cats or whether affectionate cats improve their owners’ moods.

Digital database preserves centuries-old mansions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:49:32 UTC
14:49:32 KST

The inventory includes stone mansions, churches, mosques, madrasas and fountains. (AA Photo)
Centuries-old stone mansions and historic buildings in Mustafapaşa, a town in the central province of Nevşehir’s Ürgüp district, are being preserved for future generations through a digital database documenting the area’s cultural heritage.
The project, led by Cappadocia University, aims to make Mustafapaşa an open-air museum through QR codes installed at 55 locations, providing visitors with information about historic buildings and supporting the accurate restoration of the structures in the future.
Mustafapaşa, named one of the United Nations World Tourism Organization’s “Best Tourism Villages” in 2021, is installing signs featuring QR codes at the entrances of historic buildings to help visitors discover the town’s cultural heritage.
Visitors can scan the codes to access a website available in Turkish and English, offering information about the history and architectural features of each building.
Şükran Ünser, head of the Cappadocia Cultural Studies Center at Cappadocia University, told Anadolu Agency that research into Mustafapaşa’s historic buildings intensified in 2020, leading to the creation of a digital database.
The inventory, developed to support tourism, includes not only stone mansions but also churches, mosques, madrasas and fountains. The work is ongoing, she said.
Emphasizing Mustafapaşa’s importance for its civil architectural heritage, Ünser said the town was particularly valuable because it had preserved so many historic residential buildings.
“Historic buildings have always been valuable, but religious structures are often treated with greater respect and better protected because of their sacred character. The mansions and other residential buildings in Mustafapaşa, however, hold a particularly important place,” she said.
“Because they are intertwined with everyday life, they change as daily life changes and evolves, and unfortunately, many do not survive. We do not see this happening in Mustafapaşa.”
The buildings were catalogued not merely as an inventory but also in a way that would serve tourism and help visitors identify and explore sites worth seeing, she added, describing the database as a documentary heritage archive.
‘I compare Mustafapaşa’s mansions to portraits’
Ünser said the database would also prove valuable when restoration projects are undertaken, allowing architects to consult historical photographs and restore buildings accordingly.
“I compare Mustafapaşa’s mansions to portraits. Each has its own distinctive character, shaped by the possibilities offered by nature and adapted to the topography. They form portraits that are remarkably respectful of and harmonious with their natural surroundings,” she said.
She also highlighted photographs and notes kept by Serafim Rizos, who moved to Greece during the population exchange between Türkiye and Greece, as valuable sources for documenting the town’s historic buildings. The research team is working to bring these records together, she said.
The center also organizes activities to raise local residents’ awareness of the town’s cultural heritage. Following Mustafapaşa’s selection as one of the world’s best tourism villages, the team launched an awareness campaign and established a platform, while continuing educational seminars for different audiences.
The digital project has long been a goal for the team, Ünser said, noting that QR codes at 55 locations now allow visitors to access the website and explore the town’s heritage.
“We wanted Mustafapaşa to become a small open-air museum,” she said.
Mustafapaşa Mayor Mustafa Özer said the town has approximately 400 stone mansions, 140 of which are officially registered as historic buildings. The area also offers several tourist attractions, including Manastır Valley, a popular destination for visitors.
Fifty-five of the town’s historic mansions currently offer accommodation to tourists, Özer said.
“Although some mansions have been restored and converted into hotels, many are still homes where local people live. Together, we will pass these buildings on to future generations,” he said.
He added that bringing neglected and dilapidated buildings back into use as hotels, restaurants or residences was a source of satisfaction.
Comparing historic photographs with the buildings’ present-day condition has strengthened the town’s architectural inventory, Özer said, adding that the municipality aims to preserve Mustafapaşa’s heritage through cooperation with the university, nongovernmental organizations and investors.

Hattusha archives shed light on 120 years of archaeological discoveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:49:12 UTC
14:49:12 KST

Historical photographs from the archives of the German Archaeological Institute and the excavation team document the evolution of archaeological research at the Hittite capital. (İHA Photo)
Historical photographs from archaeological excavations at Hattusha, the capital of the Hittite Empire, are bringing the past into focus as the ancient city marks the 40th anniversary of its inclusion on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.
Compiled from the archives of the German Archaeological Institute and the Hattusha excavation team, the photographs shed light on scientific efforts to uncover the remains of a civilization that flourished thousands of years ago and highlight Anatolia’s rich cultural heritage.
Located in the Boğazkale district of Çorum province, Hattusa played a central political, administrative and religious role in the Hittite Empire during the second millennium B.C.
Added to UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 1986, the ancient city is known for its advanced urban planning, monumental fortifications, palaces, temples and impressive stonework.
The city’s fortifications extend for more than 8 kilometers. The Lion Gate and King’s Gate reflect the architectural and artistic achievements of the Hittites, while the Great Temple in the Lower City provides important clues about religious life at the time.
At the nearby Yazılıkaya open-air rock sanctuary, reliefs of gods and goddesses carved into the rock offer insights into Hittite beliefs. Together, these structures provide a comprehensive picture of the civilization’s urban life, religious practices and worldview.
Preserving the visual memory of history
Excavations at Hattusha began in 1906 and have continued for more than a century, bringing to light remains that had lain buried for thousands of years. Historical photographs taken during different phases of the excavations document this long scientific undertaking.
Images of excavation teams, work sites and the process of uncovering archaeological structures show the effort and research behind the remains visitors see today.
By documenting structures before and during their excavation, the photographs provide a visual record of how the site has changed over the decades. They also connect earlier archaeological work with current research, turning archival material into a record that links the past with the present.
The photographs preserved in the archives of the German Archaeological Institute and the Hattusha excavation team illustrate the development of archaeological research and the importance of documenting cultural heritage. They also demonstrate that protecting the past involves not only preserving historic structures but also safeguarding the scientific records that explain how they were discovered and studied.
Çorum Governor Ali Çalgan said Hattusha was an important part of humanity’s shared civilizational heritage, extending beyond Anatolia.
“Hattusha holds a distinguished place in the collective memory of humanity with its historical heritage, which has survived for thousands of years,” Çalgan said.
He noted that the Hittite civilization’s achievements in state administration, law, architecture and diplomacy demonstrated Anatolia’s importance in world history.
The historical excavation photographs, he added, documented not only the past but also the process of uncovering the heritage, the work of scientists and the recording of history for future generations.
“Every photograph is a valuable part of the connection between the past and the present and of our responsibility to protect our cultural heritage,” he said.
Çalgan also highlighted Çorum’s other important archaeological sites, including Şapinuva and Alacahöyük, saying the province was home to a wealth of remains that illuminate the region’s ancient civilizations.
Every artifact from Hattusha, he said, helps researchers understand the knowledge, art and way of life of the civilizations that developed in the region.
The 40th anniversary of Hattusha’s inclusion on UNESCO’s World Heritage List provides an opportunity to renew public attention to the site and strengthen efforts to preserve and promote its heritage internationally, Çalgan added.

Speaking to ISNA, Sabzevari said the Khorasan Razavi Chamber of Commerce had placed a range of initiatives on its agenda following the festival’s registration and the establishment of its permanent secretariat.
The initiatives aim to preserve saffron’s standing in domestic and international markets while strengthening links among producers, processors, traders and exporters, she said.
Over the past two years, the National Saffron Day festival has featured exhibitions, conferences, urban advertising campaigns and plans for promotional caravans and tourism tours in different counties across the province.
This year’s program takes an integrated approach to the saffron value chain, covering all its stages and related industries, she added.
Also, an international saffron exhibition was inaugurated in the presence of officials and featured traditional and cultural programs intended to celebrate the local heritage associated with saffron cultivation.
Sabzevari said the festival’s registration as an international event on Iran’s tourism calendar had been secured through follow-up with the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts.
Known as “red gold,” saffron is a valuable agricultural product widely used in Persian cuisine, where it lends distinctive aroma and color to dishes and desserts. It also has a long-standing place in traditional Iranian medicine and cultural practices.
Iran is one of the world’s major saffron-producing countries, with much of its cultivation concentrated in the country’s eastern and northeastern regions. The annual harvest generally begins in early November, when saffron’s vivid purple flowers emerge across fields in otherwise dry landscapes.
Beyond its economic value, the harvest season offers opportunities for rural tourism, allowing visitors to experience saffron picking and learn about the cultivation and processing of the spice. Organizers’ plans for promotional caravans and tourism tours reflect efforts to connect the product more closely with the region’s cultural heritage and travel industry.

Permanent handicrafts exhibition planned at Shams Tabrizi shrine in northwest Iran
TEHRAN - A permanent handicrafts exhibition themed around the spiritual and literary traditions of Shams Tabrizi and Jalal al-Din Rumi is planned at the shrine of Shams Tabrizi in Khoy, West Azarbaijan province, as part of efforts to promote local artisans and strengthen cultural tourism.
Rita Khazrzadeh, deputy director of handicrafts at the West Azarbaijan Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Department, announced the plan during a meeting with handicrafts producers and artists in Khoy on Tuesday.
Khazrzadeh outlined the department’s plans for the county and discussed artisans’ concerns, calling on them to produce competitively priced handicrafts inspired by the shrine and the life and legacy of Shams Tabrizi.
The products would be marketed to tourists and visitors interested in Shams and Rumi, the renowned Persian mystic and poet whose spiritual outlook was profoundly influenced by his encounter with Shams.
Khazrzadeh said the permanent exhibition would provide an opportunity to showcase the skills and creative potential of Khoy’s artisans to pilgrims and tourists visiting the cultural and religious complex.
The initiative also aims to create a dedicated space for presenting locally made products and connecting the region’s handicrafts with its rich spiritual and cultural heritage.
Ali-Akbar Chitsaz, cultural and artistic affairs director at Khoy Municipality, welcomed the proposals and pledged municipal support for developing the handicrafts sector.
He said the municipality was prepared to cooperate in organizing specialized handicrafts exhibitions and setting up regular open-air markets at suitable locations, with careful planning.
Chitsaz stressed the need to implement the initiatives promptly to provide artisans with better opportunities to sell their work and contribute to the local economy.
During the meeting, participating artists and craftspeople also raised concerns and shared their views on the challenges facing the development of handicrafts in Khoy.
The proposed exhibition comes amid broader efforts to develop the Shams Tabrizi shrine as a destination for cultural and spiritual tourism.
Earlier this month, a vast extension to the original mausoleum was officially inaugurated after two decades of anticipation, marking another step in efforts to promote the legacy of the Persian mystic.
The shrine complex covers 7,000 square meters and includes a domed chamber, a library housing 8,000 volumes and research facilities. The site was inscribed on Iran’s National Heritage List on October 3, 2026.
Shams Tabrizi, a Persian mystic who lived in the 13th century, is widely known for his transformative spiritual relationship with Rumi, whose mystical poetry became a major contribution to Persian literature and Sufi tradition. Rumi’s Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi bears the mystic’s name and reflects the significance of their relationship.

Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL) formally recognised the results of Sunday’s presidential runoff, which confirmed President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s reelection over its candidate, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who continues to dispute the vote count.
In a statement posted on Monday on social media, PL President Valdemar Costa Neto said that while the party accepts the official tallies certified by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), it will demand answers regarding pre-election social spending implemented by the ruling Workers' Party (PT).
“We acknowledge the presidential election results, as announced by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), but we believe that the concerns raised need to be properly addressed within a balanced and democratic political debate,” Costa Neto wrote. “We will continue to monitor the facts and seek answers with responsibility, transparency, and respect for our institutions.”
The PL statement came shortly after TSE President Justice Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Federal Court (STF) by former President Jair Bolsonaro, confirmed the final election results. Nunes Marques expressed "absolute confidence in the entire electoral process," effectively shutting down speculation regarding electronic ballot integrity.
Lula secured a historic fourth non-consecutive term with 51.76% of valid votes (over 60 million ballots), defeating Flavio Bolsonaro, who garnered 48.24%. The result sealed a dramatic comeback from the Oct. 4 first round, in which Bolsonaro led by nearly two percentage points.
Despite his party's official acknowledgement, Flavio Bolsonaro doubled down on his refusal to concede, insisting on Monday that he will push forward with legal petitions to annul the election.
“It is impossible to recognise the elections under these conditions. I am going to request that these elections be annulled,” Bolsonaro said in a statement, alleging "unprecedented abuses of political and economic power.”
In a video message addressed to his supporters on Monday, the senator announced plans to leverage conservative gains in the National Congress.
He vowed to mobilise the right-wing bloc to transform the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate into a "fortress against the barbarism" he claims will define Lula's upcoming term.
Costa Neto highlighted the PL-led coalition's substantial congressional footprint, which includes 121 federal deputies, 29 senators and six state governorships.
While the PL leadership indicated that it will pursue grievance mechanisms regarding government spending through formal institutional channels, it stopped short of endorsing Bolsonaro’s demand for a complete annulment of the vote.

Could US midterms reshape Pakistan’s relationship with Washington?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:47:36 UTC
14:47:36 KST

Could US midterms reshape Pakistan’s relationship with Washington?
Pakistan has gained diplomatic visibility under Trump, but analysts question how much the relationship has delivered.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Addressing a mixed crowd of the diaspora and policy experts in New York late in September, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar was asked about challenges in New Delhi’s relationship with the United States under President Donald Trump.
“Well, I think if I stand back and look at the relationship … I note that much of the world has had a more difficult relationship with the US,” Jaishankar responded.
Pakistan – perhaps uncomfortably for rival India – is an exception.
Trump’s tumultuous second term has seen him rock the global economy with tariffs and the Iran war, upend decades of trust with traditional US allies, and attempt to shred international law and the institutions that govern it. From Europe to the Middle East to East Asia, allies that counted on a US security umbrella are scrambling to build alternative partnerships, unable to rely on Washington for help if they are attacked. Leaders of nations that have been staunch US supporters have instead found themselves targeted – often personally – by Trump.
Yet amid this churn, Pakistan has managed to turn what was a deeply troubled relationship with the US into a partnership that Trump repeatedly touts, even as the government in Islamabad has faced mounting criticism domestically over allegations that it is crushing political opposition and entrenching military rule in all but name.
As the US holds its midterm elections on November 3, with the power in the House of Representatives and Senate at stake, Pakistan is one country that will prefer success for Trump and his Republican Party, which at present is expected to lose critical seats in both chambers.
“The prime minister of Pakistan – terrific man – said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives and probably many more than that,” the US president said, addressing the United Nations General Assembly in September, referring to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif – and to a war that appears to have endeared Islamabad to Trump.
A closer relationship
After decades of strong ties, US-Pakistan relations had plummeted in recent years, as successive US presidents built close ties with rival India, and Islamabad was seen in Washington as duplicitous over its role in supporting both the US and, at the time, the Afghan Taliban.
As presidents, Trump in his first term and then Joe Biden used harsh words to describe Pakistan.
But two months into his second term, in March 2025, Trump thanked Pakistan in his address to Congress for helping arrest a suspect in the 2021 Abbey Gate bombing at Kabul airport.
Then, in May, came a major turning point. India and Pakistan fought an intense, four-day war after armed fighters killed 26 tourists in Indian-administered Kashmir. The war ended in a ceasefire on May 10. Trump announced it first, and Pakistan thanked him for mediating it, but India rejects his account, insisting that the war was ended through bilateral talks.
Since then, Pakistan’s top leadership has been welcomed at the White House, tariffs on its exports have been cut, and Islamabad has mediated between Washington and Tehran in their ongoing war.
Trump hosted Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, for lunch at the White House – the first time for a Pakistani army chief who is not the country’s president. Trump has described Munir as his “favourite field marshal”.
Pakistan also nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize. On October 9, the day the Nobel Peace Prize was announced for South African jurist Navi Pillay, Sharif posted on X: “President Donald Trump played a historic role in advancing peace in South Asia. His timely intervention helped bring Pakistan and India back from the brink and secure a ceasefire, that is holding till today.”
Analysts say Islamabad’s relevance to Washington extends beyond South Asia.
“Pakistan is now an important player that must be seen within the Middle East security framework,” Qamar Cheema, executive director of the Islamabad-based Sanober Institute, told Al Jazeera.
A trade deal in July 2025 cut US tariffs on Pakistani goods from 29 to 19 percent. Memorandums of understanding with US firms on minerals, cryptocurrency and drones have followed.
Imran Khan, a geopolitical analyst and former Pakistan country director at the United States Institute of Peace, said Islamabad’s closeness to Trump had significantly raised its diplomatic profile.
“But at the same time, you could say that Pakistan has not gained anything directly from the Americans, apart from some intangibles: Its diplomatic profile and its geopolitical relevance,” he told Al Jazeera.
Mediation and the Gulf
Following the US-Israel attacks on Iran in February, Pakistan brokered a ceasefire between Washington and Tehran on April 8 and hosted the highest-level direct talks between the two sides since 1979.
In June, the US and Iran agreed to the 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding. “Pakistan was able to bring the United States and Iran under one roof after 47 years,” Cheema said.
But the 60-day period for further talks expired in mid-August without an extension.
Munir returned to Tehran on October 20, his fifth visit since the war began. Iranian officials said they had nothing new to offer Washington. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said threats and military manoeuvres would not influence Iran’s decisions. No breakthrough was announced.
“The Iran war continues to loom large in the Gulf, especially as there are increased indications that the US, possibly again with Israel, will relaunch attacks after their respective elections,” Grace Wermenbol, a former US national security official and senior visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund, told Al Jazeera. Israel’s elections are scheduled for October 27.
The congressional test
Trump goes into the midterms with historically low popularity numbers. His approval rating stood at 30 percent in a Pew Research Center survey conducted between September 28 and October 4, down from 37 percent in January.
Khan, the analyst, said Democrats would prioritise treaty alliances such as NATO if they won both chambers.
“[In that case], the Senate and the House of Representatives, where the Democrats would have a majority, would lean more towards India than Pakistan,” he said.
Wermenbol, who is also an executive director of the Paris-based advisory firm Boussole Mondiale, said allies and partners were asking whether the midterms could shape US foreign policy in the short term.
In the longer term, she said, the result could foreshadow a change in the White House in 2028 or 2029.
For Pakistan, the question is how to position itself.
Cheema said Pakistan should not shape its approach around whether Trump’s influence grows or weakens. Its strength, he said, lay in its Middle East relevance and role in protecting US interests.
“It is not just a question of Trump’s weakening influence. It is a question of how Pakistan can stay relevant,” he said.
Khan said a weaker Trump might change little in the short term but warned that it could mark the beginning of the end of Pakistan’s current importance.
“But what it does not change is Pakistan’s amplified geopolitical profile globally, and its increasing national security and defence relevance in West Asia,” Khan told Al Jazeera. “That is not going to change whether the Trump administration is strong or weak, or whether Trump is around or not.”

Spanish language learning surges in China but teachers are in short supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:45:43 UTC
14:45:43 KST

Spanish language teaching is booming in China, with enrolments up 12.6% between 2023 and 2025. But the Cervantes Institute says there's a shortage of teachers to meet rising demand.
The number of children choosing to learn Spanish in China is growing at an incredible rate, according to new figures from the Cervantes Institute.
Enrolments in Philology degrees, optional subjects and Spanish as a foreign language courses have soared by 12.6% between 2023 and 2025. However, this post-pandemic surge has coincided with a shortage of staff.
In a speech in Beijing to launch the "Spanish in the World 2026" yearbook, Luis García Montero, director of the Cervantes Institute said: "Teachers tell us that demand for Spanish keeps rising in the wake of the pandemic, which is why we are prioritising teacher training: quite simply, more teachers are needed."
The document was presented at the symposium 'Spanish in China: Evolution and new dynamics', organised to mark the 20th anniversary of the institution in Beijing. The second part of the yearbook pays tribute to this milestone with several analyses of the impact, evolution and reach of the language in the education system of the Asian giant.
Between the market and the humanities
China is approaching 98,000 potential Spanish speakers, a group made up of more than 18,000 native residents and some 66,000 students of the language. This boom in Spanish is reflected in data from the Global Spanish Observatory: the language is now offered in 31 Chinese cities and up to 98% of universities in the country already teach a degree in Hispanic Philology.
García Montero spoke of the "essential dialogue between China and the Spanish-speaking world", driven decisively by Latin America, but he did not hide his misgivings about teaching that is increasingly geared towards the market. Although the language is gaining ground in business, engineering and science, he warned that philology is losing weight: "In the current dynamic of commercialisation, the humanities are in decline, and that is something that worries us."
The map of Spanish in China counts 55,000 university graduates after "an expansion at extraordinary speed", as explained at the event by SISU vice-dean Yang Ming. However, the professor highlighted the new demands of the business sector: the market no longer looks only for translators, but for multidisciplinary professionals able to master the language alongside law, accounting or business management.
The world’s third native language
Globally, Spanish now has 640 million users with some degree of proficiency, after growing by 1.5% in the last year, which means 10 million more Spanish speakers. The "Spanish in the World" yearbook also underlines the weight of the language in migration flows: one in ten native speakers already lives in non-Spanish-speaking countries.
In its 27th edition, the report explores the role of the language in strategic areas such as machine translation, digital media and the presence of Spanish in Europe. With more than 520 million native speakers (second only to Mandarin Chinese and Hindi) and 95 million speakers with limited skills (+3.3%), Spanish is consolidating its position among the most widely spoken languages in the world. Within the Spanish-speaking sphere, the report counts around 460 million native speakers and more than 20 million people with partial knowledge.
Without including students, Spanish has more than 137 million potential users in countries where it is not an official language. The United States leads this group with the largest pool of speakers outside the Spanish-speaking world, driven largely by its native community.
From AI to challenges in the classroom
With almost 50 million potential speakers in the EU, the yearbook also points to the fragile state of creole and contact varieties, which together do not reach one million people (0.2% of the global total).
Among the more than 24 million students of Spanish worldwide (+7% in two years), the contrast between continents is striking: while Brazil has suffered a 46% decline due to changes in legislation affecting public schools, Africa is seeing vigorous growth, driven by formal teaching in countries such as Cameroon, Ivory Coast, Benin, Morocco and Tunisia.
In the digital environment, Spanish stands out as the second language with the strongest presence on websites and has 72 million learners on Duolingo (two thirds of them English speakers). Digital reading leads in Spain (31.7%), Mexico (21%) and Argentina (20%), while audiobooks are gaining ground.
In artificial intelligence, Ibero-America accounts for 14% of global traffic for AI solutions, above its share of total internet users (11%). This growing demand, according to the yearbook, is reshaping the consumption of information and securing the language’s weight in the new era of virtual assistants.
Two decades of the Cervantes Institute in Beijing
The programme opened with a debate around the exhibition 'Truths and Lies. The power of fiction', with the participation of journalists, curators and renowned local artists such as Xu Bing and Zhang Peili. Several round tables focused on methods for teaching Spanish, updating textbooks and the pedagogical application of artificial intelligence.
Following the presentation of the yearbook, Inmaculada González Puy, director of the Cervantes Institute in Beijing, and Hispanist Lu Jingsheng held a discussion titled 'Spanish in China'. The sessions were rounded off with contributions from ambassador Marta Betanzos Roig, Chinese education official Chang Fuliang and prestigious academics such as Carme Riera and Darío Villanueva.

14:38:49 KST

Türkiye’s Capital Markets Board (SPK) raised financial thresholds for qualified investors on Oct. 26 and extended the deadline for investment funds to comply with portfolio and investment limits to Jan. 31, 2027.
For clients applying for professional status, the total financial asset threshold rose from 10 million Turkish Liras to 50 million liras.
The trading volume threshold increased from 5 million liras to 25 million liras.
The changes also apply to qualified investor requirements linked to professional client rules.
An exemption for investors buying units in real estate and venture capital investment funds was abolished, making them subject to the general thresholds.
Existing investors who obtained their status through financial criteria must provide written or electronic evidence to their investment firm that they meet the requirements.
Those who fail to do so will be limited to selling their holdings in instruments reserved for qualified investors.
Citing recent market developments, the SPK also scrapped interim compliance deadlines of Oct. 31 and Nov. 30 for funds’ portfolio and investment limits.
Full compliance, previously required by Dec. 31, is now due a month later.
The board removed a provision in its fund guide covering exemptions for financial instruments of public institutions and their affiliates, while preserving corresponding provisions in the underlying regulations.
Separately, the SPK temporarily suspended the capital market activities of Tera Portföy and Pusula Portföy and expanded the liquidation of their funds.
The decision covers investment funds, including real estate and venture capital funds, outside the liquidation orders issued on Sept. 17.
Türkiye İş Bankası will handle the liquidation of Tera’s funds, while Ziraat Bank will oversee Pusula’s.

Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing, with at least 61 seats needed to form a governing coalition.
The main contenders include Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party and the Together alliance led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett.
Other prominent parties include the Democrats, led by Yair Golan; Yisrael Beiteinu, headed by Avigdor Lieberman; and Jewish Power, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Palestinian-led parties include the Joint List, headed by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas.
First general vote since October 7
The elections are Israel’s first general vote since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 7 2023.
Vote counting will begin after polling stations close at 10 pm local time (2000 GMT), when Israeli television channels are expected to release exit polls.
Initial results are expected overnight, while the official results are scheduled to be published by November 4, according to the Central Elections Committee.
Separately, 4,218 Israelis cast ballots during early voting at 101 polling stations across 99 diplomatic missions abroad on October 15–16.
The turnout represented 86.7 percent of the 4,863 eligible overseas voters, according to the Central Elections Committee.
