The cases have intensified debate over whether citizenship applicants are adequately screened for attitudes considered incompatible with democratic values.
Denmark typically introduces citizenship bills every six months, following an extensive application process.
The current bill was first debated in Parliament, known as the Folketing, on February 5 but was postponed after Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a general election later that month.
Earlier in October, the government announced plans to introduce a screening system to identify potentially anti-democratic attitudes among citizenship applicants.
However, it has decided to proceed with the citizenship bill before the new screening system is ready.
Police treatment of press at Copenhagen demonstrations prompts high-level talks
Denmark’s national police commissioner, Lasse Boje, will meet representatives of two journalism organizations on Friday following incidents in which police officers struck two press photographers with batons during demonstrations in Copenhagen.
The meeting will bring together the leadership of the Danish Union of Journalists and the Danish Association of Press Photographers to discuss guidelines governing interactions between police and journalists.
The incidents occurred Saturday when photographers from Danish newspapers Ekstra Bladet and Politiken were covering demonstrations for and against remigration, a term referring to the return of immigrants to their countries of origin.
Both photographers were struck by police officers at separate locations a short distance apart.
Allan Boye Thulstrup, chair of the Danish Union of Journalists, described the incidents as completely unacceptable.
He plans to propose changes to police training, including more extensive instruction at the Police Academy on how officers should interact with journalists covering demonstrations.
However, Thulstrup acknowledged that changes to basic training would not address the needs of officers already serving in the police force.
“It will obviously not resolve the fact that trained officers would not receive that training, so it may be that there needs to be some form of continuing education or further training,” he said.
Copenhagen Police announced Monday that it had requested an investigation by Den Uafhængige Politiklagemyndighed (DUP), Denmark’s Independent Police Complaints Authority.
The independent watchdog confirmed Tuesday that it had opened investigations into both incidents.
According to DUP, its investigations typically involve interviewing witnesses and collecting video footage to establish what happened.
The findings of the investigations have not yet been announced.
Hacker attempts to compromise 1,700 accounts at Aarhus University
A hacker gained access to a server at Aarhus University and attempted to access and change passwords belonging to approximately 1,700 users, the university has confirmed.
The attempted password changes were unsuccessful after the intrusion was detected Monday, according to a statement published on the university’s internal website.
There is currently no indication that sensitive or confidential information was leaked during the attack. However, the university said further investigations would be carried out in the coming days to establish the full extent of the incident.
The university also clarified that the attack was unrelated to the security vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, a widely used programming language, which prompted temporary shutdowns of several Danish websites Wednesday.
Despite the breach, Aarhus University said students and employees could continue their normal activities without disruption.
However, it urged everyone to remain particularly vigilant about suspicious online activity, including phishing attempts, in which criminals use fraudulent messages to obtain passwords or other personal information.
Anyone noticing unusual activity has been advised to contact the university’s IT support team.
Minister for Societal Security and Emergency Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, confirmed that authorities were aware of the incident.
In a written statement, she said the Agency for Societal Security was closely monitoring developments and maintaining contact with the university.
“There is dialogue with Aarhus University, and relevant higher education institutions have already been gathered for a briefing where the Agency for Civil Security has advised,” the minister said.
Aula reopens as Danish authorities restore websites following security scare
Aula, Denmark’s widely used school communication platform, reopened Thursday morning after being taken offline Wednesday afternoon because of a global cybersecurity vulnerability.
Aalborg Municipality confirmed the reopening in a press release, saying the necessary security measures had been implemented.
The platform connects schools, daycare facilities and families across Denmark. It has approximately two million active users, with more than 600,000 logging in on a typical weekday.
The disruption followed the discovery of security flaws in PHP, a programming language widely used to operate websites, online shops and digital services.
The vulnerabilities left websites worldwide potentially exposed to cyberattacks, prompting authorities and public institutions in several countries to temporarily shut down services as a precaution.
In Denmark, affected websites included those belonging to Copenhagen Municipality, Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, and Vejdirektoratet, the Danish Road Directorate.
All affected Danish websites have since reopened.
Minister for Societal Security and Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen of Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, stressed Wednesday that the incident was not a cyberattack.
Speaking to TV 2, she explained that the vulnerabilities could nevertheless have serious consequences if left unaddressed.
The situation also prompted Denmark’s National Operational Staff, known as NOST, to activate its lowest crisis preparedness level, according to TV 2.
NOST brings together several public authorities to coordinate responses to major emergencies and crises.
The activation, known as information readiness, is the lowest of three preparedness levels and allows authorities to share information and coordinate their response to developing threats.
The measure was introduced Wednesday evening as authorities monitored the global security situation.
Security flaw in widely used software forces Danish websites offline
Several Danish public websites were shut down Wednesday after security vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used by websites and online services worldwide.
Minister for Societal Security and Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen described the situation as a “global incident” but stressed that it was not a cyberattack.
Speaking to TV 2, she warned that websites could face serious risks unless their operators installed the necessary security updates.
“It can potentially be really serious if system owners do not get a security update done. If that is not possible right here and now, then one must consider going offline,” she said.
The vulnerabilities affect PHP, which powers many websites, online shops and digital portals.
According to Reuters, PHP’s developers identified the flaws Tuesday but released an update to fix them Wednesday at 1:45 p.m.
Bech-Nielsen told Denmark’s public broadcaster, DR, that websites without the update could be exposed to attacks.
“It is in a way positive that we have found these vulnerabilities. But because it is publicly known, there are some who will exploit it,” she said.
Authorities and public institutions in several countries temporarily shut down websites as a precaution.
In Denmark, affected services included websites belonging to Copenhagen Municipality, the Danish Road Directorate and the Danish Meteorological Institute, known as DMI.
Kombit, an organization that manages shared IT solutions for Danish municipalities, also confirmed that Aula, the digital communication platform used by schools and parents, had been taken offline.
The ministry said authorities were closely monitoring developments but did not clarify whether further political action would be necessary.
Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.
Danish bishops consider moving Great Prayer Day to autumn when holiday returns
Great Prayer Day could return to Denmark’s calendar in a different season, with most bishops of the Church of Denmark open to moving the public holiday from spring to autumn.
The discussion follows the government’s announcement that Store Bededag, or Great Prayer Day, will be reinstated as a public holiday in 2030, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
The holiday was abolished by the previous Social Democrat, Venstre and Moderates coalition government, with the change taking effect in 2024.
The Ministry of Ecclesiastical Affairs has confirmed that the Church of Denmark will be involved in the reinstatement process. A bill is expected in spring 2027.
Thomas Reinholdt Rasmussen, bishop of Aalborg, suggested that late October might be a suitable alternative.
“Liturgically, it does not really fit into the period from Easter to Pentecost, so perhaps it would be good to place it at the end of October,” he told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Marianne Gaarden, bishop of Lolland-Falster, also expressed openness to changing the date, noting that spring already has several public holidays.
“I like the idea of a prayer day where the focus is on spiritual reflection, and that focus must be preserved. But of course it is possible to consider that it can be moved,” she said.
Bishops in Funen, Aarhus and Viborg are similarly open to discussions, while Helsingør’s bishop, Peter Birch, has not taken a position.
However, the bishops of Ribe and Roskilde favor restoring the holiday to its original spring date.
The bishop of Copenhagen has not commented, while Haderslev’s bishop, Marianne Christiansen, will wait until the government presents its proposal.
Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey
Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey with Danish minister
Denmark’s Queen Mary will travel to Antalya, Turkey, from November 8 to 10 to participate in the United Nations climate summit COP31, the Danish Royal House has announced.
She will be accompanied by Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party.
Turkey is co-hosting this year’s summit with Australia, which is responsible for leading the negotiations.
The annual UN climate conferences bring countries together to discuss international efforts to address climate change and reach agreements on reducing its impact.
During her visit, Queen Mary will meet representatives of Danish companies showcasing environmentally friendly technologies and solutions at the Danish pavilion.
She will also focus on the challenges facing Pacific island nations, including Vanuatu and Fiji, which are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels and other consequences of climate change.
Another part of her program involves meeting young delegates from around the world to hear about their experiences with climate change and efforts to support the green transition.
Queen Mary also attended last year’s UN climate summit in Brazil, where her program included visits to a cocoa production facility and a research institute working on sustainability.
Her upcoming visit follows a new report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), published Wednesday, warning that global warming will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.
The report attributes this to decades of insufficient climate action.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries committed to keeping global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius compared with temperatures between 1850 and 1900, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees.
Severed network cable disrupts departure screens and train information apps across Denmark
A severed network cable at Banedanmark disrupted departure and arrival information at many train stations across Denmark on Wednesday.
The problem also affected the MitTog app, while users experienced difficulties getting updated information on Rejseplanen, Denmark’s journey planning service.
Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, said information about train times was being provided through station loudspeakers wherever possible.
The disruption did not affect information screens for the S-trains, Copenhagen’s suburban rail network, according to railway operator DSB.

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.

In Kyiv, a Russian missile struck the Southern Bridge—metro service was partially suspended and bus routes were changed
Kyiv • UNN
Due to damage to the Southern Bridge, the metro is not running between Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir stations. Buses have been added to the routes.
As a result of the Russian missile attack on Kyiv, a strike on the Southern Bridge was recorded. Metro infrastructure was damaged, causing part of the train service on the green line to be temporarily suspended. This was reported by Mayor Vitali Klitschko, while the Kyiv City Military Administration clarified changes to public transport operations, UNN writes.
Details
According to the mayor, due to damage to the metro infrastructure on the Southern Bridge, trains are temporarily not running between the Osokorky and Chervonyi Khutir stations.
At the same time, all stations on the red metro line are open to passengers. Trains are running between Akademmistechko and Lisova stations, despite the damage sustained the previous day by the section between Darnytsia and Chernihivska stations, as well as the exits from Lisova station.
How public transport is operating after the attack
Because of the closure of the Southern Bridge and restrictions on metro operations, the city authorities are increasing surface public transport services.
Fifteen buses will operate on temporary bus route No. 1-M to reduce pressure on the red metro line.
Bus routes No. 22 and No. 91 are also being changed. Because of the closure of the Southern Bridge, they will run via the Darnytskyi Bridge.
The number of buses on route No. 22 will be increased to 14. Another 5 buses will operate on a shortened route between Trostianetska Street and Lybidska metro station.
Four buses will be added to route No. 91, bringing the total number of vehicles transporting passengers to 7.
The Kyiv City Military Administration urged Kyiv residents to plan their trips in advance and follow official announcements about changes to public transport operations.

US Senator Chris Van Hollen renewed his call for accountability for nine American citizens killed by Israel in the occupied West Bank since 2022.
“I want to take a few minutes to tell my colleagues about these nine American citizens who’ve been killed by Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces in just over the last four years,” Van Hollen said in a Senate floor speech shared in a video on his X account.
He named the dead as Omar Assad, 78; Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, 51; Tawfic Abdel Jabbar, 17; Mohammad Khdour, 17; Turkish-American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, 26; Amer Rabee, 14; Saif Musallet, 20; Khamis Ayyad, 40; and Nasrallah Abu Siyam, 19.
He said Israeli soldiers stopped Assad at a checkpoint in January 2022 and “dragged him from his car. They bound his hands behind his back. They gagged him. They blindfolded him, and they left him lying on the ground outside.” Assad “died of a stress-induced heart attack,” he said.
Abu Akleh was shot in the head and killed by Israeli security forces near the Jenin refugee camp in May 2022. “When she was killed, she was wearing a bright blue vest, clearly identifying her as a journalist,” Van Hollen said.
Eygi, who was raised in Seattle, was “shot in the head by an Israeli soldier from approximately 200 meters” in September 2024, he said. He added that Rabee was “shot 11 times by two different weapons.”
Van Hollen also cited US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who called Musallet’s killing “a criminal and terrorist act.”
“He even said there must be accountability. So why has there been no accountability?” Van Hollen said.
After each case, he repeated: “No one has been held accountable.”
“Nine American citizens dead. No accountability,” he said.
Last month, the Senate voted 47-51 to block a resolution led by Van Hollen. It would have required the secretary of state to submit a report on Israel’s human rights practices within 30 days, including the killings of US citizens by Israeli forces or occupiers since January 2022 and the status of any investigations.

Israelis head to polls as voting begins in pivotal Knesset election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:05:50 UTC
14:05:50 KST

Polls opened across Israel on Tuesday morning as eligible voters head to the polls to elect the country's next Knesset in a pivotal race pitting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his sitting coalition against the opposition bloc seeking to replace him.
Within the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has taken the lead ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud in the majority of recent polling, though neither bloc still appears able to secure a 61-seat Knesset majority.
Polling stations opened at 7:00 a.m., and exit polls are expected at 10:00 p.m., offering preliminary projections of the election results. The official results will be finalized in the coming days, following the completion of the vote count.
Voting at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad concluded on October 16, while voting at some military bases began last week.
The fateful elections will be the first to take place since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, with the political landscape and the issues at the forefront of voters’ minds having shifted significantly since the previous vote in 2022.
IDF manpower crisis, haredi draft, Oct. 7 commission central issues for Israeli voters
Some of the central issues include the IDF’s severe manpower crisis after three years of war, contentious haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription legislation, and calls for a state commission of inquiry into the government’s failures surrounding the attack.
Meanwhile, traditional election issues, such as the establishment of a Palestinian state, have moved further to the background as Israel’s security outlook has changed, and most parties stand in agreement against Palestinian statehood.
Another major issue is the fate of long-serving Netanyahu, who has led Israel for 19 non-consecutive years.
Following the October 7 massacre and the ensuing war, the opposition bloc has called for Netanyahu to be held accountable for the attacks, arguing that he should no longer serve as prime minister.
There appears to be no clear outcome for the elections, as neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc has been projected as being able to secure a 61-seat majority without the support of the Arab parties.
According to the final Channel 12 poll released on Friday before the election, Netanyahu’s bloc stood at 50 seats, while the opposition bloc was projected to win 56 seats.
The Arab parties, meanwhile, were projected to win a combined 16 seats. Most opposition party leaders have pledged not to form a government with the Arab parties, arguing that such a coalition would not be viable following the October 7 attacks.
Netanyahu’s Likud party was projected to win 19 seats in the poll, down from the 32 seats it currently holds in the outgoing Knesset.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party projected to win greatest number of Knesset seats
Meanwhile, Eisenkot’s Yashar party was projected to win 22 seats, ahead of both Likud and B’Yachad, led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett, which was projected to receive 14 seats.
Voter turnout throughout the day will have a significant impact on the results of the elections. With the electoral threshold set at 3.25% of valid votes, the number of votes a party needs depends on how many people turn out on election day.
The Taub Center's updated calculations, prepared by Prof. Alex Weinreb, head of its Demography Area and research director, estimate that at a 70% turnout rate, similar to the 2022 election, a party would need 165,635 votes to cross the threshold.
The required vote count rises as turnout increases, meaning smaller parties could face a tougher challenge if more Israelis head to the polls.
Several parties are fighting to secure enough votes to enter the Knesset and clear the threshold, including Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel’s the Reservists-Economics party.
Whether these parties cross the threshold is expected to significantly affect both blocs' ability to form a coalition.
For these small parties, even a slight shift in voter support could determine whether they enter the next Knesset or leave their supporters without representation.
Meanwhile, police have prepared for the possibility of clashes and public order disruptions on Election Day, particularly in the hours following the release of exit polls.
Police announced on Monday that as part of special preparations, approximately 20,000 police officers, Border Police officers, and volunteers would carry out a range of actions throughout the country on Election Day.
Forces are expected to be deployed at thousands of polling stations nationwide and in surrounding areas to maintain public order and protect public safety and security, the police stated.
This will be done to “safeguard the integrity of the elections, and ensure that the democratic process is conducted properly and in accordance with the law,” the police added.
Alex Winston contributed to this report.

Election Day: A complete guide to Israel’s political parties and what they stand for
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:05:36 UTC
14:05:36 KST

Israelis head to the polls today to elect the country's next Knesset, with parties competing for votes and a chance to shape the country's future.
But what does each party stand for, who leads it, and what are its key policies and priorities?
The Jerusalem Post has prepared a series of explainers breaking down the platforms, leaders, and main positions of all the main parties running in the election.
Explore our guides below to learn what each party stands for before casting your vote.
What does Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar stand for?
Led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, Yashar is a centrist party focused on national security, government reform, and replacing Benjamin Netanyahu. Yashar is part of the opposition bloc.
Ballot letters: דרך | Explore Yashar’s policies and platform
What does Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud stand for?
Led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Likud is a right-wing party that emphasizes national security, Jewish nationalism, and a strong stance against Palestinian statehood. The Likud heads the right-wing bloc and Netanyahu's sitting coalition.
Ballot letters: מחל | Explore Likud’s policies and platform
What does Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad stand for?
Led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett, B’Yachad is a centrist party focused on government reform, economic growth, and the enlistment of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men into the IDF. B'Yachad is part of the opposition bloc.
Ballot letters: רק | Explore B’Yachad’s policies and platform
What does Yair Golan’s Democrats stand for?
Led by Yair Golan, the Democrats is a left-wing, Zionist party that emphasizes liberal democracy, civil rights, education reform, and a greater equality in military service. The Democrats is part of the opposition bloc.
Ballot letters: אמת | Explore the Democrats’ policies and platform
What does Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu stand for?
Led by Avigdor Liberman, Yisrael Beytenu is a right-wing, secular nationalist party focused on national security, a tougher stance against Hamas, and reducing the influence of religious parties in government. Yisrael Beytenu is part of the opposition bloc.
Ballot letter: ל | Explore Yisrael Beytenu’s policies and platform
What does Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit stand for?
Led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Otzma Yehudit is a far-right nationalist party that advocates a hardline approach to security threats, expanded Jewish settlement, and tougher law enforcement. Otzma Yehudit is part of the Netanyahu bloc and the sitting coalition.
Ballot letter: ב | Explore Otzma Yehudit’s policies and platform
What do the Joint List and Ra’am stand for?
The Joint List and Ra’am represent different strands of Arab Israeli politics. The Joint List is generally left-wing and emphasizes equality, civil rights, and Palestinian national rights, while Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am takes a more pragmatic approach focused on tackling crime, securing funding, and improving living conditions in Arab communities.
Ballot letters: ודם (Joint List); עמ (Ra'am) | Explore the Joint List and Ra’am’s policies and platform
What do Shas and United Torah Judaism stand for?
Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) are ultra-Orthodox (haredi) parties that prioritize protecting the status of religious institutions in Israel and maintaining broad exemptions from IDF service for yeshiva students.
Shas primarily represents Sephardi and Mizrahi haredi and religious Jews, while UTJ represents Ashkenazi haredi communities. Both parties are part of the Netanyahu bloc and were part of the sitting coalition.
Ballot letters: שס (Shas); ג (UTJ) | Explore Shas and United Torah Judaism’s policies and platform
What does Bezalel Smotrich’s RZP-Zehut stand for?
Led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Zehut leader Moshe Feiglin, Religious Zionist Party-Zehut is a far-right, religious-nationalist party that supports expanding West Bank settlements, applying Israeli sovereignty over the territory, and advancing judicial reform. RZP is part of the Netanyahu bloc and the sitting coalition.
Ballot letter: ט | Explore Religious Zionist Party’s policies and platform
What about the parties hovering above - or below - the electoral threshold?
Several parties are fighting to secure enough votes to enter the Knesset, with the 3.25% electoral threshold determining which lists win parliamentary representation. For these parties, even a small shift in voter support could determine whether they enter the next Knesset or leave their supporters without representation.
Recent polls have placed the People of Israel party and the Reservists-Economic Party near the threshold, with their standings varying between surveys. Their results could have a significant impact on the balance between the political blocs.
Led by former IDF general Ofer Winter, People of Israel is a right-wing party that supports Benjamin Netanyahu for prime minister and calls for new leadership outside the political establishment.
It makes haredi enlistment a condition for joining a government, rejects blanket exemptions for yeshiva students, and advocates a hardline security policy, including voluntary emigration from Gaza.
The Reservists-Economic Party, led by former minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha, combines a right-leaning Zionist and security agenda with an emphasis on economic reform. The party says it will join only a Zionist government and demands that a universal conscription law be passed before a government is formed.
Led by Moti Leitner, the Haredi Public Party seeks to offer an alternative to the established ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism. It supports broader haredi military or national service, core-curriculum studies including math and English, and greater accountability from haredi political leadership.
Ballot letters: ך (People of Israel); די (Reservists-Economic Party); זך (Haredi Public) | Explore these parties’ policies and platforms

Russian sabotage network behind Romanian arson attack, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:03:02 UTC
14:03:02 KST

A fire that broke out on Sept. 14 near a state-owned arms company in Romania was coordinated by a Russian network, Romanian officials said on Oct. 26.
The fire erupted in Brasov, in central Romania, near CARFIL SA, a subsidiary of the national company ROMARM.
The arson attack is "part of a larger campaign of sabotage operations attributed to the Russian Federation in Europe," according to a news release from Romania's Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, known as DIICOT, and the Romanian Intelligence Service.
Romanian officials identified three perpetrators who they said were coerced by Russian operatives into carrying out the attack. Two suspects are said to be from Belarus and one from Ukraine.
Two have been arrested, allegedly while preparing to carry out similar attacks in Germany, according to DIICOT.
The third suspect remains at large and is believed to be in Poland. European authorities issued a warrant for his arrest on Monday.
Romanian investigators believe that prior to the Brasov fire, the suspects instigated similar incidents which were also coordinated by Russia.
According to the Romanian Intelligence Service, the sabotage operations aim to intimidate and undermine the defense capabilities of affected states, and weaken their contributions to European and regional security.
The attacks join a string of similar incidents across Europe that authorities believe were instigated by Russian operatives.
Lithuanian forces thwarted Russian attempts to burn down Starlink satellite communications equipment on Oct. 18. A similar incident happened in Poland less than a month prior. In August, an arson attack against a defense contractor in Tallinn was likely caused by Russian sabotage operations, Estonian officials said.
Experts warn that the increase in Russian hybrid attacks is a way for Russia to test how far it can push NATO and Europe — probing the limits of NATO security and sowing chaos without triggering all-out war.
Romania, which borders Ukraine, has also been affected directly by Russia's full-scale invasion, particularly by drone activity in the Black Sea. A civilian cargo ship sank on Oct. 23 after a series of Russian strikes.

The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine expected next month aimed at ending the war after more than 4½ years of fighting.
Up to 2,000 people are stranded in Oleshky with dwindling food and medicine. They are unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the UN.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators as well as the militaries of the two countries confirmed in separate statements that the ceasefire had begun.
Announcing last Friday that she had brokered the ceasefire, Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and "determine the level of assistance they require".
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," she said.
Newsmax, a right-wing US cable network, has said it had been granted "exclusive television access" to accompany observers entering the city on Thursday.
Kyiv struck by wave of Russian strikes
Minutes after 3 am, multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.
A Russian strike damaged a major bridge spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv, the city's mayor said.
"A strike hit the Southern Bridge. Metro infrastructure on the bridge was also damaged," Mayor Vitaly Klitschko wrote on Telegram, with city officials adding that train services across the bridge had been suspended.
Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said.
Moscow's latest pummelling has damaged medical facilities in the capital, Klitschko said, adding that a "blast wave shattered the windows in (an) intensive care unit".
"At another medical facility in the same district, windows were also shattered in two wards. Neither patients nor medical staff were wounded," he said on social media.
In another attack, "a building in a non-residential area was also hit. According to preliminary reports, there is one fatality near one of the supermarkets in the area," Klitschko said.
A strike near a dormitory belonging to one of Kyiv's universities has shattered windows in the building, wounding a 20-year-old woman, Klitschko said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said "Russian ballistic missiles struck the grounds of a university in Kyiv and the area around it –- effectively the campus, Kyoto Park, the area near a metro station, and residential buildings."
"The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure," he said on social media.
In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.
“It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.

Netanyahu resorting to racist scare tactics in last-ditch effort
Emma Graham-Harrison
Amid the highest voter turnout in decades, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies resorted to racist scare tactics, including unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud, to urge their own voters to the polls.
“We’re in a war for our home,” Netanyahu said in a social media post in the early afternoon, with unsourced claims of low voter turnouts in strongholds of his Likud party. “Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections. Go out and vote, recover it!”
In 2015, Netanyahu claimed that “Arab voters are coming out in droves to the polls” in a bid to motivate his party’s base. The comments drew a rebuke from then-US President Barack Obama and Netanyahu apologised for them soon after winning another mandate.
A decade later he is doubling down on that political tactic. A robo-call to voters purporting to come from the prime minister made groundless accusations that Palestinian citizens of Israel were trying to “steal the election”. A spokesman for Netanyahu did not respond to questions about the call.
In a recording shared with the Guardian, a man who sounds like the prime minister falsely claims that three leaders of the Ra’am party had been caught with envelopes full of cash. He also says that left wing women were driving Palestinian women to polling stations, which is not illegal under Israeli law.
He finishes by urging his own voters to turn out. Polling day is a holiday for most Israelis, who often use it to go to the beach, hiking or other activities with their family.
“You need to go to the polling stations. Everyone needs to vote. There is no beach. No barbecue, there is nothing (else) now,” it says. “Everyone must go out to vote to ensure the victory of the right against the left.”
Earlier he shared photos that purported to show empty polling stations in Likud-supporting areas, and long lines in opposition strongholds. The Guardian saw long queues on Tuesday morning in areas with high support for Netanyahu and his allies, including parts of Jerusalem and the settlement of Efrat.

Don’t let them win”, he posted above a social media video filmed on the outskirts of the town, the site of a notorious massacre by Israeli border police in 1956.

US ambassador clarifies 'Arabs vote same as Israelis' post

Today is election day in Israel, which is a national holiday. All voting is in person, ID required. No mail-in or absentee ballots. Arabs vote same as Israelis. Contentious process, but it’s a democracy-not many of those in this region!
The “Arabs vote same as Israelis” phrasing was perceived by some as appearing to imply that Arab voters in Israel aren’t Israeli or due the same vote.
Huckabee’s since posted a follow-up, agreeing with Axios journalist Barak Ravid who pointed out “Mr Ambassador, the Arabs who vote are Israelis…”.
"Correct and I should have stated it that way!” said Huckabee.
10 million ppl in 8m Jews, 2m Arabs. ALL are Israeli citizens-Jew, Muslim, or Christian. All vote, serve in IDF, in Knesset, & proudly have Israeli passports. Women equal to men. All have free speech.
As we reported earlier though, there are serious concerns about voter intimidation of Palestinian citizens in Israel - who represent about 21% of the population – and suppression of Arab parties.

Of the 15 million people who live in areas under Israeli control, more than 5.5 million Palestinians have no vote including 3.1 million Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, 350,000 Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem and 2 million Palestinians in Gaza.

It has just gone past 3pm in Tel Aviv and 1pm in London, where we are currently blogging from. Here is a summary of where things stand:
Turnout is at its highest so far in decades as Israelis vote in what is widely considered to be one of the most consequential elections in the country’s history.
Polls have opened in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, Israel’s subsequent destruction of Gaza, and the launch of its war with the US against Iran.
Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad have flown in for the elections, according to Aid Coalition.
Exit polls are released at 10pm Israeli time (8pm GMT), and the first indication of actual voting counts usually emerges in the early hours of the morning.
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israeli military and relative political newcomer.
A consistent majority of Israeli polls show Netanyahu’s coalition bloc with the ultra-Orthodox and the far right will fall below the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government.
But even though there is a clear anti-Netanyahu majority, polls indicate that the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc will also fall short of the required seats, meaning weeks or even months of political wrangling may be in store as parties make deals and trade concessions.
There was a suspected attempted stabbing of the leader of the Democrats party, Yair Golan, at HaMesila park in Tel Aviv, earlier today, the party said. The security guards “subdued” the suspect before he could do anything, the party said in a statement. The suspect was subsequently arrested.
The Central Elections Committee told reporters earlier that there had been no indication of widespread irregularities.
Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has continued to urge right-wing voters to go out and vote, claiming that if they don’t then a new government will be formed with parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel.
“Buses are heading to the polling stations, and huge lines are being reported in the Arab settlements,” he wrote in a social media post that appears as if it is part of a scare campaign.
“If we don’t go out to vote now, we’ll find ourselves with a government of the Arab parties. We must not stay home. Every vote counts!”
The Central Elections Committee told journalists earlier today that there had been no indication of widespread irregularities.
In an earlier post, we mentioned that, as of 10am local time, turnout in the Israeli general election was at its highest point at that stage of voting since 1981.
We now have some more figures from the Central Elections Committee, which appear to confirm the trend, with the new data showing that 31.5% of Israelis voted by noon, the highest voter turnout by midday since 1977.
In the settlement of Efrat near Jerusalem, Shani, 19, had come to the polling station with her parents, to cast her vote for the far-right party of finance minister Bezalel Smotrich.
She is part of a large cohort of first-time voters who are more rightwing than older generations, and may help bolster support for Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners.
More than 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the last election in 2022, and three-quarters of first-time Jewish voters define themselves as right or centre-right, a recent poll for Channel 12 television found (it did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel).
Shani said she chose Smotrich, a settler himself, for his promises to expand Israel’s footprint in occupied Palestine. “Smotrich is pushing forward with settlement expansion and improving security,” she said.
Her mother, kindergarten teacher Rivka, also voted for Smotrich, and said her priority was to return Netanyahu’s coalition to office.
“The right must win, because otherwise there is a chance of a Palestinian state, which will be very bad for Jews,” she said. Her husband Motti, who runs a healthcare standup had voted directly for Netanyahu. “He’s a diplomat, he’s strong. He’s got whatever leadership should have.”
Software engineer, Yitzchak Schwarz, 36 is an activist for far-right libertarian Moshe Feiglin, running on a joint slate with Smotrich for this election. “If there are sanctions, it’s going to hurt a bit, but we have to think about our own survival and our own national rights,” he said.
Sue and Tom Rosenfelt, who have lived in Efrat for over 30 years and have three sons in the reserves, said national unity and the unequal burden of military service are their main concerns. “I think that at this point getting another foothold and another hilltop isn’t the thing that’s going to strengthen the country as a whole,” Tom said. “We need to work more on unity.”
In an election which many Israelis describe as critical, turnout was so high at their polling station at a school in Efrat that they had left the long lines, and planned to come back later.
Both plan to vote for the party of Naftali Bennett, a rightwing settler and tech multimillionaire, who joined forces with centrist Yair Lapid. “I feel like this is a time when we need to come together,” Sue Rosenfeld said. “You know, Bennett and Lapid are on different sides of the spectrum, but they’ve come together and that’s something I want to support.”

Golan fought a long legal battle to get security protection from the Shin Bet security service. They only resumed responsibility for his security on Monday, the day before the elections.
While the media attention has been focusing on the country’s parliamentary elections, Israel’s assault on Gaza has continued, a year after the signing of a so-called ‘ceasefire’ with Hamas.
A UN commission said yesterday that Israel was continuing to commit genocide in Gaza despite the signing of the US-brokered ceasefire last October.
The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, rejected a claim in May by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace that the truce had “largely held”.
It said Israeli authorities had kept committing “genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza”. The report said:
The perception of Palestinians and a possible Palestinian state as a threat to Israel and the desire to reduce the Palestinian population contribute to a permissive military culture where Israeli soldiers, with or without directives from commanders, directly target Palestinians whether or not they pose a real or immediate threat.
Testimonies by Israeli soldiers in Gaza display a disregard for Palestinian lives and a military culture where Palestinians are dehumanized, equated with “terrorists”, trivializing the killing of civilians.
The report noted that between the 10 October ceasefire in 2025 and 30 September 2026, Israeli attacks killed at least 1,431 Palestinian people in Gaza, including 300 children and 130 women.
In its latest update, Gaza’s health ministry said that 74,561 Palestinian people have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza since October 2023, when Isreal launched its assault on the territory following the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.
The report also accused Israeli forces of having committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank. It lists extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence. Israel has dismissed the findings of the report and has denied committing genocide in Gaza.
Netanyahu casts his ballot and urges his supporters to vote, saying 'this is an emergency hour'
Benjamin Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political survival, has just cast his ballot in Jerusalem.
In a post on X this morning, the Israeli prime minister wrote “right-wing voters, this is an emergency hour” as he urged them to get out and vote to counter any left electoral gains.
“Higher-than-usual turnout rates in the left’s strongholds. Right or Palestine, for real,” Netanyahu wrote.
Police believe the arrest of three people in southern Israel who are suspected of being involved in voting bribe attempts was a single incident and not part of a larger campaign, according to Dean Livne, acting director-general of the Elections Committee.
Early voting figures show highest turnout in decades
Citing figures released by the Central Elections Committee, the Israeli newspaper Ynet is reporting that voter turnout in the election reached 16.68% by 10am local time (8am GMT), the highest level recorded at that hour since 1981.
Over 1.2m Israelis had cast their ballots by 10am, according to the data, a rise of 0.78 percentage points compared with the same stage of the previous election in 2022.
In Sanhedria cemetery in north Jerusalem, ultra-orthodox voters came to the tombs of revered rabbis before they cast their ballots. There was no question of which way they were going to vote: for the parties representing Ashkenazi and Sephardic ultra-orthodox. But some at the Sanhedria cemetery, the young especially, made clear they only would do so reluctantly.
Yair Shuker, aged 19, said only one issue was important to him. “The election is about whether we will live by the Torah, or there will be no Torah. There will be a Jewish state or there will be no Jewish state,” he said.
And for him - as with almost all Israel’s ultra-orthodox (the Haredim) - the critical measure of the state’s level of observance is whether the Haredim would continue have exemption from military service.
“There are some who study the Torah, and some who stand and defend the land,” Shuker said.
The exemption for ultra-orthodox religious students dates back to the founding the state, but has long been a sort of tension among Israeli Jews, all the more so since the 7 October attack in 2023 and the start of the Gaza war. Israel’s supreme court ruled in 2024 that the blanket exemption for haredi men had no basis in law.
In return for their support in keeping him in power, Benjamin Netanyahu promised the ultra-orthodox parties (the Sephardic party Shas and the Ashkenazi United Torah Judaism) new legislation that would perpetuate the exemption, but has failed to deliver on that promise due to splits in his coalition. As a result both parties left the government, though Shas remained part of the coalition.
Whatever their feelings about Netanyahu, both would vote against a secular-led government led by the current opposition parties, which have pledged to end the exemption once and for all, and enforce military service if necessary.
Shuker said he did not trust either coalition, but would vote because he had been told to. “The rabbi has asked us to vote for Shas, so I will vote,” he said. A 23-year-old Ashkenazi ultra-orthodox, who identified himself as Yaacov K, expressed the same sense of disillusion mixed with duty. He said:
I’ll tell you the truth. To me and most of the people around me, we don’t believe in anyone.
If you’re asking me, I’ll never go and vote. But I have a rabbi and the rabbi told me listen, you have to go and vote. And if he says you have to go and vote, then that’s what I do. I don’t even start thinking if it’s worth it for me or not worth it for me.
The open distrust and contempt for Netanyahu, coupled with obedience and party discipline, could be one reason that the prime minister’s bloc has over-performed by a seat or two in past elections, compared to his poll numbers. That could be crucial if the pattern is repeated.
Azriel Zadok, a rabbi who had come for morning prayers at the Sanhedria cemetery, argued that the mass ultra-orthodox vote was essential to preserve Israel’s Jewish identity from “the left”.
“We have no problem with the secular. We pray for them, and we pray for the soldiers,” Zadok said. “Our problem is with the leftists we are trying to decide for us how we should live.” “They want us to go to the beach on Saturday and they want us to marry outside our faith. We want to remain Jews,” the rabbi added.
The centre left is only a small part of the opposition bloc, and it does not propose to change the ultra-orthodox lifestyle. But the bloc is united on the insistence that the Haredim should do their part in the defence of the nation. It is the most divisive issue among Israeli Jews voting today.
According to Israel’s Hareetz newspaper, United Arab List (Ra’am), an Islamist party headed by Mansour Abbas, has filed a complaint to the Central Elections Committee, alleging that a systematic campaign has been launched to disrupt voting for the party.
In a statement, the party said police arrested several of its leading activists in southern Israel’s Negev region before dawn with no clear justification, according to Hareetz.
The party also said there is a widespread shortage of its Arabic-language ballot slips in several areas, including the cities of Nazareth and Shfaram in northern Israel. We have not yet been able to independently verify these claims.
About 15 million people live in areas under Israeli control. Just over 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel live within the country’s pre-1967 borders, known as the “green line”, and have full voting rights.
In the occupied West Bank, more than 500,000 Israeli settlers can vote. They live among 3.1 million Palestinians who are subject to military rule and do not have the right to vote.
In occupied East Jerusalem more than 230,000 Israelis with voting rights live among 350,000 Palestinians who cannot vote.
Two million Palestinians in Gaza, who live under Israeli military occupation, according to the international court of justice, also have no vote.
How does the system work and when might we get results/a new government?
Emma Graham-Harrison
The Knesset, the Israeli parliament, has 120 seats, with lawmakers voted in through a system of proportional representation. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.
When the results are in, the president invites the party with the largest number of seats to try to agree a governing coalition. Exit polls are released at 10pm Israeli time (8pm GMT), and the first indication of actual voting counts usually emerges in the early hours of the morning.
Getting full results could take much longer, with the outcome potentially hanging on the electoral fortunes of two small parties, which need to win 3.25% of the overall vote to take up seats in the Knesset. Polling puts both around this threshold. If they cross it, they each get four seats, which would have a significant impact on coalition building options.
The far-right Amcha Yisrael is led by the former general Ofer Winter, who has pledged to back Netanyahu for prime minister if he gets into the Knesset. The Reservists is a rightwing Zionist party focused on ensuring universal conscription whose leaders sit between the two blocs.
They have ruled out joining any government supported by either the ultra-Orthodox – key Netanyahu allies – or Palestinian parties whose backing Gadi Eisenkot is likely to need. If it goes down to the wire, counting could take more than a day.
Palestinians with Israeli citizenship constitute about a fifth of the population but are consistently under-represented in the parliament.
Benjamin Netanyahu and most of his chief rivals have said they won’t form a coalition with parties (broadly) representing Palestinian citizens of Israel - even if that means political gridlock.
But after the votes are counted these parties could hold a critical balance of power, as my colleagues Emma Graham-Harrisonand Quique Kierszenbaum highlight in this story. Here is an extract from their report:
Palestinian citizens of Israel are forecast to secure between 12 and 15 seats, divided between the Islamist Ra’am and the Joint List alliance of three smaller parties, Hadash, Balad and Ta’al.
The mathematics of power are clear, even though most of the Jewish Israeli opposition has ruled out a coalition with Arab politicians, and Netanyahu and his allies have been doing everything they can to make such an alliance politically toxic.
There is recent precedent for breaking promises not to work with Palestinians, however. The Ra’am leader, Mansour Abbas, in 2021 took his party into a historic coalition government with Naftali Bennett, now part of the opposition bloc, and Netanyahu himself had previously started coalition negotiations with Abbas.
One prospective voter, Mohammed, works at a hi-tech company, managing both Jewish and Arab employees, which he sees as a template for a different future for Israel.
Although disappointed that most Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out a coalition with Palestinian parties, he understands the political logic, and he expects their position to shift once results are in.
“At the end of the day, everything is mathematics, right? One plus one is two. They cannot do anything without [those seats]. So they must do [some kind of deal] and they will do it.”
Who are Netanayhu's main opponents in the general election?
A consistent majority of Israeli polls show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition bloc with the ultra-Orthodox and the far right will fall below the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government.
But even though there is a clear anti-Netanyahu majority, polls indicate that the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc will also fall short of the required seats, meaning weeks or even months of political wrangling may be in store as parties make deals and trade concessions.
So who are Netanyahu’s leading rivals in the race?
As we have mentioned in a previous post, the man leading the field to potentially replace Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot, is a former head of the Israeli military who formulated the notorious Dahiya doctrine of using “disproportionate force” to cause damage and destruction.
Naftali Bennett is a former prime minister and former chair of the settler council, who supports annexing much of the West Bank.
Avigdor Lieberman wants to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and replace it with an Israeli-Jordanian confederation (though apparently he did not consult the Jordanians about this plan).
The Democrats, the only remaining political home for Israel’s Zionist left, are led by Yair Golan, a former general and deputy head of Israel’s military.

AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:01:13 UTC
14:01:13 KST

AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says
OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.
OpenAI has announced that its AI models have made several scientific discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics.
The AI giant said on Monday that the three new discoveries concerned the fields of harmonic analysis, complexity theory and quantum field theory.
Among the discoveries, AI models proved the local smoothing conjecture, one of the central propositions of harmonic analysis, in every spatial dimension for the first time, according to OpenAI.
Researchers in harmonic analysis, a branch of mathematics that studies how complex signals and functions can be broken down into elementary waves, had previously only proved the theory in three dimensions.
‘Historic development’
Alex Iosevich, a professor of mathematics at the University of Rochester who specialises in harmonic analysis, said OpenAI appeared to have “cracked” the conjecture in a “historic development”.
“The conjecture was formulated by my PhD adviser, Chris Sogge, so it is near and dear to my heart, and the news was a shock at first,” Iosevich told Al Jazeera.
“Now I am filled with joy and optimism, because the scientific enterprise as a whole is going to make giant leaps as a result of the AI revolution, and we have the chance to be a part of this historic development.”
Iosevich said he expected the field of theoretical mathematics to “change drastically” due to AI.
“I feel a twinge of sadness as a result,” Iosevich said.
“Many theoretical mathematicians I know feel the same way, but I firmly believe that these feelings will soon give way to the realisation that there is so much we can now accomplish.”
“Problems in pure mathematics did not arise in a vacuum,” he added. “Many of them came out of concrete physical considerations, and these connections can now be explored rapidly and decisively.”
According to OpenAI’s announcement, its models also disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which relates to the time it takes to solve complex computational problems, and provided “mathematically rigorous” proof of quantum chromodynamics, which studies the interaction of quarks and gluons.
Ryan Williams, an expert in computational complexity theory at MIT, said a confirmed refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis would be a major development.
“The ETH has been widely believed true since the late 1990s and a great deal of theoretical computer science was built on it being true,” Williams told Al Jazeera.
“We are working to verify and examine their proof and determine if it holds up,” Williams said.
“Their proof proposes a mysterious new method to more efficiently solve a variety of fundamental problems that have a wide range of potential applications.”
Williams said that while the development would not have real-world applications in the short-term, it could potentially lead to many “future real-world benefits for society”.
“It is hard to predict what will be possible next, because it’s a shocking development,” he said.
The ChatGPT creator said it had reached out to scientists outside the company to turn its “raw research data into scientific understanding”.
The San Francisco-based company said it decided on several different methods for releasing the findings based on consultations with three expert groups chosen to act as “shepherds”.
While the groups collaborating on the mathematics and computer science problems opted to make the AI-produced data public immediately, the physics group decided to defer the release in order to write up their own interpretation of the findings, OpenAI said.
“All of these approaches involve tradeoffs,” OpenAI said.
“On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community,” the $852bn start-up said.
“On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.”
OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.
Last month, Claude creator Anthropic announced the discovery of a new enzyme said to resemble CRISPR, the groundbreaking gene editing mechanism used in treating conditions such as cancer and sickle cell disease.
Anthropic’s announcement drew mixed reactions among scientists.
While some researchers hailed the finding as an exciting development, others suggested that the AI company had exaggerated its significance.
