14:00:04 KST

For a very long time, I dreamed of being cured. I was born in 1981. I learned to walk early enough, but I stumbled and fell more easily than other children. My parents began to worry that something was wrong, that my muscles were weaker than they should be. Eventually, at the age of three, I was diagnosed with a form of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). In the 1980s, the precise mechanics were not yet understood, but the condition was known to be hereditary, probably linked to a recessive gene. It was also known to be progressive. As I aged, my muscles would not keep pace. At eight, I began to use a wheelchair for longer distances. By the time I was 18, I rarely walked outdoors any more.
It is hard to be young and to know that you are growing weaker rather than stronger. I had all the same aspirations that my nondisabled friends did, but I lived in fear of the future in a way they did not. I spent a lot of time thinking about what my life would have been like if I didn’t have SMA. The images in my head were of something like a double: myself, only rid of this one deficit, imprecisely defined, but encoded somewhere in my body.
In the 1990s, the human genome began to be mapped. Medical genetics grew ever more precise. I was vaguely aware of this, of the fact that genetic conditions such as mine were being better understood with every year. With that understanding came the possibility, however faint, that there might be some form of treatment for me beyond the interminable hours of painful, barely-worth-it physical therapy I took after school.
At some point, it did strike me that before medical genetics could even begin to pursue a treatment, an SMA gene would be identifiable in embryos. My other self might be me, cured. Or he might be someone living in my stead, while I’d never been born at all.
As science progressed, this other self came to seem more concrete, more knowable than ever. It was an immensely attractive image. In almost every other respect, I was happy to be me. I didn’t bother to ask who I might have been if my eyes were blue, like my sister’s, instead of brown. I didn’t ask whether I’d have been happier with a talent for music instead of languages. Only this one error in my genome would need to have been corrected, and I would have been me, only better.
Eventually, this perfect shadow-self faded away, for many reasons. But last year it came back to haunt me, as I read about a series of adverts placed by a company called Nucleus Genomics. Throughout the New York City subway system, Nucleus promised prospective parents that they could now have their “best baby”. By way of posters claiming that “height is 80% genetic” and “intelligence is 50%”, potential customers were led to a website detailing an expensive, comprehensive IVF procedure. Up to 20 embryos would be screened for every genetic disorder under the sun, but also for eye and hair colour, and for traits ranging from strength and longevity to insomnia and male-pattern baldness.
It was a sales pitch perfectly tailored to the present moment. We already seek to optimise ourselves in every way, through healthy, precisely monitored living. Through the measurement and quantification of exercise routines, nutrition and even sleep patterns, we can assess whether we are living our lives in the best possible way, so why not have the best baby as well? Although we may not be immortality-seeking billionaires, we are all constantly living under the relentless imperative to strive for human perfection, in our own generation and the next. And although it has taken on a new, consumerist form, centred on the individual self, that imperative has a familiar name: eugenics.
Genomics companies tend to avoid the label eugenics, and for good reason. Although the word derives from the Greek for “good birth”, in the wake of the second world war, eugenics was broadly disavowed as a racist, pseudo-scientific movement. Its stated aim was to improve the human species, but its most tangible results were the involuntary sterilisation and forcible institutionalisation of “inferior” people in many countries and, in Nazi Germany, the mass murder of people deemed a threat to the master race.
In the preceding decades, however, eugenics was popular among scientists, politicians and the general public. Although many of its champions were elitist, sexist and racist reactionaries, there were eugenic progressives, eugenic socialists and eugenically minded feminists. While some eugenicists advocated the forced sterilisation of people deemed unfit to reproduce, some advocated women’s right to birth control as a means of social improvement. After all, the belief that many traits in human beings were strongly hereditary was not incompatible with the belief that humans also needed good sanitary conditions, public health and welfare systems, and access to education if they were to realise their full potential.
It is impossible to understand the appeal of eugenics without realising that it held both utopian and dystopian elements. This is particularly important, because the return of eugenics also involves both. And eugenics really has returned, including under its old name. What may be called the neo-eugenic revival sometimes takes an explicitly racist, white-supremacist form. It talks about birthrates, IQ levels and the impending “civilisational collapse” of the west. It focuses on what it sees as distinct, unequal racial groups. It harkens back to classical eugenic dystopias, such as the influential American writer Madison Grant’s The Passing of the Great Race, published in 1916, an inspiration for Tom Buchanan’s racist rants in The Great Gatsby.
This form of neo-eugenics is easy to dismiss for people who think of themselves as enlightened. However, another form of neo-eugenics is arguably much more pervasive. It is careful about words and labels, and it eschews the state management of populations for a focus on individual freedom of choice. In one sense, this form of eugenics never really went away.
Towards the end of the last century, some philosophers and bioethicists began to defend what they called “liberal eugenics”. Nicholas Agar and Julian Savulescu are among the figures who have argued that this form of eugenics, driven by parental freedom of choice, is something entirely different from the repressive eugenics of the past, which sought to mobilise the state to marginalise or even exterminate entire groups.
The origins of this reorientation are much earlier. According to the historian Nathaniel Comfort, eugenics was already beginning to shift its attention from the population to the individual during the middle of the 20th century, in tandem with the rise of medical genetics. This was partly because repressive eugenic policies were controversial, and partly because medical genetics was a burgeoning science, very different from the pseudo-scientific assumptions of the past. In the US, eugenic records offices kept a hodgepodge of observations based on prejudices about race, class and gender. Medical genetics clinics were building knowledge and tools with actual, and growing, predictive power. Today, prenatal screening procedures have been part of standard medical practice for decades, mostly directed at the identification of disabilities and illnesses. Down syndrome is becoming very rare in countries that facilitate screening. Denmark, for instance, now sees the termination of over 95% of pregnancies where Down has been identified.
Of course we want the best for our children. In a neoliberal society, one obsessed with maxxing every aspect of life, the “best” might easily come to mean competitive advantage. A company such as Nucleus knows this. Playing on the term “generational wealth”, its website suggests that customers can purchase “generational health”, providing a kind of embodied insurance policy against deteriorating public health and social services. In the 20th century, eugenics was a project for the nation state; in the 21st century, it has reinvented itself as the logical extension of capitalist individualism.
There are still problems with the science. Nucleus’s claims about height and intelligence being genetic to a particular degree refer to population-level estimates of how much of the variation in a group is due to genetics (and are contested, at that). They do not mean “you can reliably decide how smart and tall your child will be”, even if that was a likely takeaway for some people. But in a way, applying population-level logic to individuals makes perfect sense. States need to manage their populations for instrumental purposes – to keep the economy growing, to avoid public health emergencies and to have enough soldiers available to fight wars.
For a long time, this management was carried out in paternalistic or authoritarian ways. But, as the philosopher Michel Foucault argued, a signal feature of the modern state is that it operates through governmentality – by providing the incentives for citizens to manage themselves in ways that align with state interests. If we, as individuals, freely decide to treat ourselves and our families as miniature populations to be optimised for health and productivity, that saves the state quite a lot of effort. But what does this mean for our sense of ourselves?
As the biologist and historian Adam Rutherford has pointed out, eugenics was always about control. The word itself was coined in 1883 by Francis Galton, a cousin of Charles Darwin who saw evolution as a process to be managed and directed. With the discovery of natural selection, it seemed obvious to Galton that “what nature does blindly, slowly, and ruthlessly, man may do providently, quickly, and kindly”, as he put it in his seminal 1904 essay, Eugenics: Its Definition, Scope, and Aims.
An enduring image from the early decades of the movement is the “eugenics tree” commissioned for the Second International Congress of Eugenics, held in New York City in 1921. Growing from roots labelled with disciplines across the natural sciences, social sciences and humanities, the tree is surrounded by the words “eugenics is the self direction of human evolution”. In that image, the accumulation of knowledge as well as biological processes are provided with a teleology. But what are their goals? What is all the control, management and optimisation really for?
To Galton, and to the generations of committed eugenicists who succeeded him, eugenics was politically and morally necessary in order to prevent societal disaster due to degeneration. Following earlier thinkers such as Thomas Malthus, they worried that too many poor and undesirable people were reproducing. In a short time, the superior peoples, whether defined as the upper class or as “Anglo-Saxons”, “Nordic types” or “Aryans”, would be outbred and outcompeted by their natural inferiors.
Eugenics’ proposal of wholesale management of the population was thus made in service of a particular ideal of humanity, where the universal “best” was defined in a strikingly narrow way. Through the notion of “hereditary genius”, Galton presented the privileges of wealth and class as innate qualities; while he explained undesirable traits such as “vagrancy” and “criminality” as the causes, rather than the consequences, of poverty, deprivation and marginalisation. Galton’s eugenic utopia was an idea that reflected the prejudices of a particular place and time.
The same is true of liberal eugenics in our own time. We may question whether the genomics companies’ promises of “best babies” are credible. But it may be more important to ask what their notion of the “best” is. What do they see as valuable and worthless in a human life?
Liberal eugenics accentuates the positive. In an attempt to distance itself from the forced sterilisations of the past, it prefers to focus, as Nucleus does, on human improvement and enhancement. But as Rutherford notes, in biology you cannot select for something without selecting against something else. Positive eugenics and negative eugenics are two sides of the same coin; without an idea of what is undesired, there can be no notion of the desirable.
For the Victorian eugenicists, the “best” was an amalgam of racial fantasies about “Nordic” or “Aryan” types conflated with the privileges of the upper classes, defined against the undesirable character of brown and black people, and the underclass. For the new eugenics in its liberal form, positive qualities coalesce around productivity and competitive advantage. The ideal human is strikingly close to the ideal worker, someone who is smart, efficient and unlikely to ever take a sick day.
Against this ideal stand the unwanted lives of people with disabilities and chronic illnesses. Intellectual disability was among eugenics’ biggest bugbears, but a range of other conditions recur as targets to be eradicated. In a way, this is unsurprising. Disability really does mean disadvantage. That is something I know in my bones – and my muscles. Disability, as the scholar Tom Shakespeare has written, is a predicament. It means limitation and restriction; it can mean pain and suffering. There are simple reasons why I longed so deeply for a cure. The reasons why and how that longing began to fade are more complex.
As it turned out, medical genetics really did produce an effective treatment for spinal muscular atrophy. About a decade ago, a drug called nusinersen was being developed. Some studies suggest that if it is administered early enough, it can wholly counteract the symptoms of the condition, while arresting its progression in adults. But medical genetics also proved that I didn’t have SMA after all. The original diagnosis was made on the basis of muscle biopsies and clinical guesswork. When a test for the genetic markers for SMA became available, mine came back negative. Instead, I was shown to have an even rarer condition – rarer, and less likely to attract research funding. I am tempted to quote Franz Kafka, who once remarked that there is infinite hope in the universe, only not for us.
But, in truth, that isn’t quite apt. Losing both the original diagnosis and the possibility of a treatment felt like a wave of sorrow, tinged with relief. Strange as it may seem, it also gave me a greater sense of freedom, that my life was really my own.
Don’t get me wrong. If there was an actual cure for my condition, I would take it. But there won’t be one, at least not for me. Too much time has passed; too much of my life is behind me. It is my life as it unfolded, and I try my best not to compare it to lives I didn’t live.
It is easier to think this way in your forties than in your teens. In the company of my nondisabled friends, I see plenty of injuries, illnesses and vaguely defined aches. We all have the markings of life. It’s not exactly that my disability ceases to matter as I grow older. In one way, it’s quite the opposite, as I feel the physical impact of the world on my muscles and joints. But I do feel a sense of convergence with my kith and my kin about the tenuousness and frailty of it all, about the need to take care of each other, as we hurtle towards what is coming.
Call it a kind of realism. Those of us who have kids know another side of it. If you plan to have a particular kind of child, you are setting yourself up for failure. Every parent I know has had to abandon their notions of what they thought their children would be for the reality of their particular children. I don’t think any one of them subscribed to the idea of an ideal baby. I hope they didn’t. Such an ideal is a terrible thing for parents as well as children to live up to.
This is the most corrosive effect of liberal neo-eugenics: in positing that an individual ideal of embodiment is something that can be specified, quantified and realised, it creates a framework for torturing both our children and ourselves. Why are we not this perfect thing? Why are we not fitter, happier, more productive? I’m not particularly sentimental about the value of disability in any particular case, but I think it is crucial to acknowledge disability as part of human variation. In treating ever more traits and qualities as things to be measured, ranked and diagnosed, we are doing the opposite – turning variation itself into something like disability.
For me, hope comes from working to change the world so that it accommodates imperfection. One of the reasons I dislike liberal eugenics is that its individualist ethos runs counter to political measures that have mattered immensely in my lifetime. I believe we should direct our efforts toward making better societies rather than making better people.
During the postwar era, in parallel with the eugenic shift from the population level to the individual level, disability began to become a socio-political issue rather than a medical one. What the sociologist Mike Oliver once called the “personal tragedy theory” of disability was challenged by a social model that explained how people with a range of different impairments and illnesses were made disabled by societal structures.
Essentially, what constitutes “disability” varies with place and time. Although dyslexia can be hugely disadvantageous in the modern world, in a nonliterate society it amounts only to neurological difference. The kind of mobility impairment that I have – that is, being unable to walk for more than a few steps, or get up from the floor – is restricting under any circumstances. But it is orders of magnitude more disabling in a society without wheelchairs, or wheelchair accessibility. In between these extremes, there are conditions, illnesses and impairments that amount to disability in some contexts but not in others.
The goal is not to abolish cures, but to abolish the idea that only cures, or the prenatal optimisation of an embryo, can make for a life worth living. For the disability movement, the aim has always been to make a better world for everyone: a world where people with all kinds of bodies can thrive and flourish. That includes both people who were born disabled and people who had disability thrust upon them. It is a project that accounts for human variation, and the variability of life.
That is why it stands opposed to the neo-eugenic notion that there is a “best baby”; the best, in the singular, is not something the human species should be striving towards at all. It also bears remembering that the majority of disabilities do not stem from wholly genetic causes, but from an interaction of human genetic variation with the wear and tear of the world. There are good reasons to research cures, treatments and interventions whenever possible; there are equally good reasons to temper our expectations for how the human species may be perfected.
Rosemarie Garland-Thomson, a scholar of disability and bioethics, has put forward the “case for conserving disability”. It is a provocative case, for the obvious reason that disability, and chronic illness, are qualities which entail vulnerability and dependence on others. But, then again, so does the human condition. We are born helpless, and we age into helplessness. Even if we come into the world equipped for perfect health, we are always at risk of illness and injury. Neo-eugenics offers a vision of total independence, of a disconnect from society. Measured against such an ideal, all of us fall short. However strong and self-reliant we may think ourselves to be, we are a social species, with few prospects of surviving, let alone thriving, on our own.
The aim of control, and so of predictability, is intrinsic to eugenics’ notion of the ideal society. But who wants to live in a fully controlled, fully predictable world? A world where an external entity tells you how to live your life down to the last detail, what to eat, when and where to move, what to watch, all in the name of becoming your best possible self? Oh, right.
Against this vision of total algorithmic control, we must appeal to the unpredictability of the human condition. Shortly after the second world war, Hannah Arendt wrote her magnum opus The Origins of Totalitarianism, in which she traced the construction of “superfluous people” – whole swathes of the population made disenfranchised and killable by states that saw them as useless at best and dangerous at worst. Eugenics was central to this idea of superfluousness: of people who were incidental to the future of the species, or the nation, or the race.
Arendt described totalitarianism as, among other things, a vision for the absolute closure of the future, against all alternatives. In a subsequent book, titled The Human Condition, she laid out the alternative principle, by which human societies could grow and develop. That principle was plurality – the encounter with difference. Only this encounter provided the possibility for what Arendt saw as humanity’s highest calling – namely action: something with unforeseeable consequences and unpredictable results.
With her notion of plurality, Arendt was not referring to disability as such. But the concept can be extended to human embodiment. As humans, we are very much alike, but we are not the same. We may share the same bodily needs that must be met if we are to flourish, but our varying capabilities, talents and preferences mean that flourishing may look very different from one case to the next. Against the narrow-minded eugenic idea of “the best baby”, we can perhaps set another concept of Arendt’s: what she called natality. With each birth, with each new person, something wholly unique comes into being. And the world is made anew.

A leaderless revolution has swept Serbia. The world should be watching | Aleksandar Matkovic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:00:04 UTC
14:00:04 KST

More than a decade ago, the WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange told an interviewer in Belgrade that Serbia was “a country where the future happens first”. The phrase circulated widely on Serbian social media in the weeks before Sunday’s election, but in a way that could not have seemed possible 10 years ago. Who would then have imagined that Serbia today could be at the forefront of global democratic change?
The images from Belgrade on Sunday night – people dancing and crying in the streets, while in Novi Sad, the city that sparked the student movement, a flag bearing the image of the convicted war criminal Vojislav Šešelj, which had hung from a building since the 1990s, was torn down – reinforced the feeling that the future had truly arrived.
Watching my home country from abroad, I found it hard not to share in the excitement and emotion. I became involved with the student movement behind this electoral earthquake and was an election candidate for it, for about six months before moving abroad. My involvement began while lecturing in Belgrade at the university’s blockaded faculties in 2024 and 2025. During these extraordinary blockades, something happened that was not widely discussed in the western media: the emergence of a collective sharing of intelligence and a process of shaping opinion that would become key to Sunday’s outcome.
For almost two years, students debated almost every aspect of Serbia’s economy and society – from lithium mining and resource exploitation to the economic power of local oligarchs, as well as issues such as healthcare and education. Sometimes discussions lasted six hours. All of this happened before the students developed any joint programme or formed an organisation capable of outmatching the traditional liberal parties. In a sense, knowledge came first, and organisation followed.
Sunday’s election victory for what became the Student List, therefore, emerged from a novel political culture: a leaderless movement based on collective self-governance and political education, unseen in the Serbian political arena since the collapse of Yugoslavia.
Given Serbia’s recent history, how was this remarkable democratic experiment even possible? One answer lies in the movement’s ability to rally a wide range of people who, despite different political convictions, wanted to counter the perceived corruption of Aleksandar Vučić, the authoritarian president. With the economy dependent on foreign direct investment after the destruction of Yugoslavia, the political leadership formed close ties with foreign-owned corporations. Vučić’s name was often intertwined with the activities of multinationals such as Rio Tinto, the Anglo-Australian mining giant that sought to extract the country’s lithium.
In this context I received death threats following the publication of a critical scientific paper on the contested lithium issue; many of my colleagues faced similar intimidation. But the mistreatment of Serbian citizens who challenged large-scale investment projects also began to shape public consciousness in Serbia. Vučić’s party was accused of standing by and even participating, while opposition parties offered only lacklustre responses.
From the students’ standpoint, party leaders were seen as easy to corrupt when confronted with the financial power of international projects. And so, to change the system, you had to start by changing the political structures that enabled it.
In this sense, this was not just another election; it was a monumental struggle between the old, which was dying, and the new, which was struggling to be born – to paraphrase Antonio Gramsci. In Serbia, the new movement has arisen out of the old: it began with faculty occupations, blockades and plenary assemblies, before evolving today into the largest political force in the country.
By winning the parliamentary election, the Student List has broken the monopoly of political parties. It has become more popular than both the rightwing government and virtually all the opposition parties across the spectrum, most of which did not even win enough votes to meet the electoral threshold. Thus, the “old”, in Serbia’s case, at least, is confirmed as dead.
And what the Serbian people chose was not another party but a list of 250 candidates, 134 of whom hold PhDs, 44% of whom are women, and 135–140 of whom are now projected to enter parliament. Behind them stood an organisation unlike anything seen in traditional, leader-based political parties. In this way, “a bunch of students”, as the Economist described them, has created something that should be studied as it goes beyond the traditional ways of doing politics.
Will a leaderless movement be able to govern? This is where things get tricky. In the context of what the historian Adam Tooze calls the world’s “polycrisis”, a collective intelligence based on self-organisation may be a tempting answer. After all, the student protests in France, Italy and Belgium, along with protests in Spain and Albania, have emerged in response to interlocking crises of housing, education and environmental destruction. For these crises elsewhere in Europe, so evidently mismanaged by governments, the lessons of the Serbian experiment may become crucial.
On the other hand, one should not idealise the situation. The list comprises ideologically opposed blocs, from rightwing adherents to leftwingers and liberals. Most of those elected have never before held political office, and the parliamentary system will require them to nominate a prime minister and, in future presidential elections, a presidential candidate. Will the Student List bring the same energy to the national assembly without jeopardising the very method that made it so strong? Moreover, for Vučić, losing the election does not necessarily mean losing the system. On the contrary, his concession of defeat may also have been a strategic move, allowing him to keep the party apparatus intact for a comeback.
Whatever happens, one question has been put on the table: to what extent are self-organisation and decentralised decision-making a basis for government? For the time being, people are celebrating on the streets of Belgrade, Novi Sad and many other cities and towns across Serbia. But the real fight has only just begun. The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics.
- Aleksandar Matković is a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Environmental Science and Technology in Barcelona and a fellow at the Transnational Institute in Amsterdam. He works on environmental history, political economy and the history of Yugoslavia

Four takeaways from Anthropic’s potentially record-breaking stock market filing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:00:04 UTC
14:00:04 KST

- 1. Explosive and expensive growth Here’s what you need to know: Anthropic is making a lot of money. It’s also losing a lot of it. The five-year-old firm has been valued between $1.5 and $2tn by some investors but did not list a target valuation in its S-1. Founded in 2021, the company has seen explosive growth every year of its existence. Anthropic brought in $16.3bn in revenue and lost $80bn in just the first half of 2026, though much of that was due to a $72.4bn one-off charge. In 2025, the company brought in $4.585bn and lost roughly $33.9bn, per the filing. Securing computing power accounts for the vast majority of Anthropic’s costs. The company spent nearly $9bn on AI infrastructure in the first half of this year, up from $2.3bn in the same period last year. Anthropic, unlike OpenAI, has made it clear that its customers are largely other businesses. “Frontier AI is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest,” the company executives wrote in the filing. The company said its top five customers account for 25% of its business – which makes it risky business.
- 2. ‘A country of geniuses in a datacenter’ Anthropic says there is considerable potential for AI to reach levels of intelligence that would be akin to what its executives called “‘a country of geniuses in a datacenter’ – millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionize every area of human endeavor: software, physics, math, biology, medicine, finance, economics, commerce, robotics, military and intelligence capabilities”. Noticeably, the company mentioned military capabilities despite being embroiled in a standoff with the Trump administration over its refusal to limit restrictions on the way the Department of Defense could use Claude. The company highlighted four specific categories of opportunity at the start of the filing: Acceleration of progress in biology and medicine; economic growth; spreading said growth globally; and streamlining government services (such as social services and medical programming). The company said it was already working with several pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies and improved the process for clinical trials, which is “cutting the time it takes to write clinical trial reports from months to minutes”. The company’s executives claim they have also made biological discoveries with Claude, including a “molecular machine” that has the “potential to be developed into a novel biotechnology tool”. One purported use case: gene editing.
- 3. AI ‘safeguards are incomplete’ The company discusses risks in two contexts: the dangers that AI itself poses to society and human beings, and the ways Anthropic’s business could go awry. Risks that AI poses were broken down into four main categories: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. While Anthropic put a great deal of emphasis on the guardrails it has implemented to block attempts to misuse its models, it also includes one big caveat later in the filing: those safeguards may not work. Anthropic’s most capable models are capable of providing “meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote in the filing. The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended”. Already, Anthropic has detected what it believes is the first documented case of a large-scale cyber-attack with little human intervention. The company believes a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated a Claude code tool “into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”, per the prospectus. The company said it recognized AI may be used by authoritarian governments to “deepen repression” and develop “high-tech surveillance states”. Anthropic presented less of a defense or potential safeguard against those uses and instead said it was committed to working with “free societies to provide a counterweight to authoritarian abuse and to promote freedom and democracy”. The firm seems to suggest that its work with what it describes with scant details as “free societies” will cancel out in some way the AI-enabled repression of authoritarian regimes. The company had a falling out with the Trump administration after the firm said it would not change its restrictions to allow its models to be used to build domestic surveillance or autonomous lethal weapons.
- 4. 92 pages of financial risk Anthropic goes into detail in laying out 92 pages of risks to its business. Investors are making sense of a type of company that is fairly new to the public market in a highly competitive space with everything to lose. The company acknowledges that much of its success is tied to its top executives and whether they stay at the firm, being able to edge out its main competitors Google and OpenAI, navigating the tumultuous regulatory landscape around AI and datacenters and surviving any public relations fallout over its AI models being used to do things they are not supposed to do, like create bioweapons. The company’s focus on enterprise customers means that if any of its top buyers leave, the company could take a huge hit. Anthropic’s structure as a public benefit corporation – which is a designation for a for-profit company that balances financial interests with achieving a stated social good – may make it harder to achieve its short – or medium-term financial goals, the company said. The firm is obliged to report on its progress in meeting its public benefit goals in the same way it has to report its financials. There’s also all the risk related to any AI-enabled catastrophic event – the sort of doomsday scenario Anthropic employees have been warning about. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has called for a pause on AI development to ensure firms are developing it responsibly to avoid any such catastrophe. In addition to the public harm and potential fallout over a scenario where Claude went rogue, Anthropic said they worry they will be subject to a great deal of liability, especially considering insurance options for AI are still evolving. “We may be unable to obtain coverage for certain AI-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to potentially significant uninsured losses,” the filing reads. The bedrock of Anthropic’s AI infrastructure is concentrated in the US, making it extremely vulnerable to regulatory changes, power grid constraints, natural disasters and opposition to AI or datacenters. The filing specifically calls out datacenter moratoriums that have been passed or are being considered as among the big issues they are concerned about. “We are expanding our data center capacity internationally as part of our efforts to diversify our infrastructure footprint and reduce concentration risks,” the filing reads. The company, which says a big part of its value proposition is its talent, also said it worries about US immigration policies affecting its ability to recruit and retain highly qualified employees. The Trump administration has targeted H-1B visas, a tool tech firms have come to rely on to attract and hire from the global pool of tech and engineering talent.

The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

When Leighann McCready phoned her 19-year-old daughter, Jaysley Beck, on 15 December 2021, she got no reply, but brushed away her worries. “Jays always, always answered her phone, but it was early, eight in the morning,” she says. Beck, an army soldier in the Royal Artillery, had been at a party the night before at her Wiltshire barracks. She was probably asleep.
It was a busy time, the Christmas countdown. Soon, Beck was expected to be back home in Cumbria, where her parents – McCready and Anthony Beck – own a village pub. McCready had already bought matching Christmas pyjamas for Beck and her older sister Emilli to wear on the day.
Beck had been preparing for the holidays, too. She had been Christmas shopping two days earlier, calling and consulting throughout the day with her mum, who was transferring the cash to cover it all. She’d bought presents for herself and her sister: a Gucci bag, a belt and a purse. For her dad, she’d bought tickets for a James Blunt concert for the two of them to attend together in February. At the end of the spree, Beck had messaged her mum: “We’re two so lucky girls aren’t we, Mum? Thank you, thank you, thank you. I love you with all my heart!”
Despite all this, as the hours passed that Tuesday in December, with still no word from Beck, McCready began to feel a deep foreboding. She knew that, in the preceding weeks, her daughter had been struggling through a strange and intense period of escalating harassment from her line manager. With this in mind, Emilli offered to call one of Beck’s friends at the barracks, who assured them that Beck was probably fast asleep. “He said he was five minutes away and he’d go and wake her,” says McCready. “That five minutes just seemed like forever. I continued ringing Jays’ phone – until somebody else answered it. The voice said: ‘Hello, can I ask who I’m speaking to?’ And I just knew. They didn’t even have to tell me.”
Gunner Beck had taken her life, alone in her bedroom. Her suicide threw a spotlight on the British army and the treatment, safety and protection of female recruits. For the last five years, ever since Beck’s death, McCready has fought for answers and accountability. She has found some, but believes there is still far more to uncover. At every step – the service inquiry, the inquest and a subsequent police investigation – McCready has been in the public eye, talking to the press, advocating for her daughter. Now, she features in a Stacey Dooley documentary, Death in the Barracks, which follows the family’s continued search for justice. She still can’t quite believe that any of it is real.
“Grief is not what you see on TV, where you instantly fall to the floor and break down in tears,” says McCready, who has worked for 30 years in the care sector, much of it as an end-of-life nurse. “The moment I found out, I automatically went from being a mum, a partner, a daughter, to quite literally feeling as if I was putting my uniform on. It was about protecting a family and guiding them. No matter how many interviews I do or how many times I see Jays’ photo in the news, it doesn’t register. That isn’t my daughter – and this isn’t my life. I call it my ‘invisible uniform’ and I have never taken it off.”
Beck had joined the army at 16. “As a child, I used to call her my baby muck-magnet,” says McCready. “She was a cheeky little chops – pulling out her pigtails, collecting snails. She loved helping her dad with DIY. You always knew when Jays was around.” Aged 15, she’d returned from a school careers day intent on joining the army. McCready wasn’t keen. “I hadn’t expected that in a million years,” she says. “I thought it was a phase, but she was determined. She put her heart and soul into it. I remember her running round the village wearing backpacks weighted with bricks to build her strength up. She was only tiny – probably a size six in clothes.”
After Beck’s initial military training, her family attended her passing in parade at Army Foundation College Harrogate. “It was magical,” says McCready. “I was a proud mum.”
Beck settled happily into army life – but in her final six months, that changed. In July 2021, at a training exercise, Beck was sexually assaulted by Michael Webber (then 39, married, and a battery sergeant major). She escaped, then spent the night hiding in her car. When Beck reported the incident to senior officers, she was advised not to be “a female troublemaker”, and was urged to think of Webber’s career, and his family. Eventually, after she reported it a second time, Webber was asked to write Beck a letter of apology. He was promoted shortly afterwards. This meant that, three months later, when her line manager, bombardier Ryan Mason, 32, began showing an obsessive interest in Beck, she had no faith in any complaints process, and nowhere to turn.
McCready had known all this as it happened. “Jays told me everything,” she says. Her daughter had even shared Mason’s messages on a family WhatsApp – he sent more than 4,600 in two months. The family had tried to advise and support her, but they were hundreds of miles away, and military protocol was a strange, sealed world. “When she was assaulted by Michael Webber, she’d said: ‘Get off me, sir.’” says McCready. “I remember my first reaction was: ‘How, Jays, did you call him “sir”?’ Some of it was over my head.”
In the days after Beck’s death, as their home filled with military personnel, McCready became determined to bring all she knew to light. “Jays was not going to be another statistic. She was not another ‘sudden passing’,” she says.
“I was not a ‘grieving mum’. You have to be stronger than that,” she continues. “I had to keep going for Jays and also for Emilli. What would she do if I broke? She’d crumble, she wouldn’t be far behind me.” Christmas was days away, so McCready asked Emilli how they should spend it. Should they even get a tree? “Emilli said: ‘Lets do the tree, and let’s still go to Auntie’s as planned for Christmas Day.’ So that’s what we did,” says McCready. “It didn’t feel right, but nothing would have felt right. I printed up a big picture of Jaysley and asked if I could put it in the tree so she’d be watching.” McCready didn’t touch any alcohol – in fact, she hasn’t had a drop since losing her daughter. “I don’t want alcohol to affect my emotions,” she says. She doesn’t watch TV either. “I don’t think it’s good for my mindset. I remember trying to settle down one night – I think it was [with] Gogglebox – and the first thing that was shown was a mortuary. I couldn’t turn it off quick enough.”
Her “invisible uniform”, her years in end-of-life care, guided all her decisions in those first weeks. “I knew I needed to be kind to my mind, to bubble-wrap it and protect it,” she says. “I chose not to see Jays after her passing and I don’t regret it. I know from my work that it’s just a shell left behind, and do I want to see my daughter’s shell? Instead, I can close my eyes and she’s that happy little girl – she’s smiling, she’s singing, she’s running round the block with her backpack on. I didn’t deal with the coroner – I didn’t want to know details.”
What she did want, instantly and urgently, was to visit Beck’s room in Larkhill garrison. She had to push for access. “I was told I was not allowed, so we had a meeting. I explained how much I needed this moment. I wanted to lie on my daughter’s bed. I wanted to know the last bit of music she played – Jays loved music, we always shared songs and playlists. What was the last bit of laundry she put in her laundry basket? How do her clothes smell?”
The family were finally allowed entry on 28 December, although they were initially informed that they had to be accompanied. “I said: ‘Absolutely not.’” McCready had another motive, too. “I needed to gather as much information to find out what happened,” she says. “I wanted the letter of apology from Michael Webber – I knew exactly where she’d filed it. I wanted her smart watch and her laptop. I got all of them. I did want her phone, too – but Wiltshire police had already taken that.” Months later, when the police had done nothing with the phone, McCready returned to Wiltshire to collect it, having argued successfully that she had paid for it – so it was in fact hers, not Beck’s.
“Not only had I put my invisible uniform on, in my mind, I was also becoming a detective,” McCready says. “I sat down with a roll of wallpaper and I did a timeline.” She also found a lawyer through the Centre for Military Justice. “We’ve been on this journey together and we’ve had to push for every single inquiry and investigation since.”
There have been some answers. After the inquest, the coroner’s summing-up report found Mason’s “intolerable harassment” and “the daily barrage of messages, calls and face-to-face encounters” to have been a significant factor in Beck’s suicide. As her line manager, Beck found Mason possessive and manipulative, setting the rota so that they were always together. He said that he loved her, composed messages that ran to essays, called her at night and engaged in lengthy conversations, sometimes until 4am (when she had to be up at 6am).
On 7 December 2021 – a week before Beck’s death – Mason and Beck had been staying in a hotel for a recruitment event when Beck left suddenly in the night, after calling a friend while in tears, who drove over and took her back to barracks. At the inquest, giving evidence, Mason said that he did not know the reason for Beck’s sudden departure that night. (He left the army the day after the recruitment event.)
The summing-up also found that the earlier mishandling of Beck’s sexual assault complaint against Webber had left her “with a feeling of injustice but, more importantly, [a loss of] faith in her ability to complain effectively”. After the inquest, Webber was charged with sexual assault and, last October, pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to six months.
Other factors were identified as “significant” by the coroner, foremost Beck’s “turmoil” around her intimate relationships. In November 2021, she had separated from her long-term boyfriend – although the two remained friends. She’d then embarked on an affair with a married sergeant. She was a 19-year-old girl, says McCready, making some mistakes and finding her way – and none of this explains why her daughter, who had never reported any mental health problems, should so suddenly end her life.
“Truth be told, there are still so many unanswered questions,” says McCready, “but I’m trying not to let them into my head. It won’t change anything for Jays. Instead, I’m trying to focus on changing things for the next people.” She welcomes MoD plans to tackle “unacceptable behaviours” in the military, including a Violence Against Women and Girls taskforce and a tri-service team, covering the army, navy and RAF, which will take serious complaints out of the single chain of command.
“It’s going in the right direction,” she says, “but it’s not enough. The reporting system has to be independent, separate from the army. I’m still contacted daily by soldiers, veterans and their families who have their own stories of rape, assault, bullying, harassment – and it’s not just females.” She hopes the Dooley documentary will encourage more to come forward, and she’s in the process of establishing a formal organisation, Jaysley’s Voice, to advocate on their behalf.
Meanwhile, Christmas – that most difficult anniversary – is coming. This year, McCready and Anthony are flying out to Thailand to meet Emilli and her partner, who now live in Australia. “We’ve promised each other that we’ll always be together at Christmas,” says McCready. “Emilli went travelling 10 months after we lost Jaysley, so we’ve met her in Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, Bali. She keeps us busy, living the best life possible, which is exactly what Jays would have wanted for her. She’d have wanted that for all of us.”
Sometimes, McCready wonders if she has left any time and space for grief. She has rarely cried, she says, and opted against counselling. Could it all come crashing down? “I do ask: ‘Is this it?’” she says. “What am I waiting to feel like? Am I in denial?” Usually, though, she prefers to believe that Jaysley is close by, holding her together, protecting her from the worst of it, still on guard. “Maybe she’s saying: ‘This is how it will be for you, Mum, I’m not going to let you be hurt,’” says McCready. “For me, she’s still here.”
Stacey Dooley: Death in the Barracks screens Tuesday 27 October at 9pm on BBC Three; 10.40pm on BBC One; and iPlayer

Israel votes: polls open as 7.3 million Israelis choose their next government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:59:00 UTC
13:59:00 KST

Polling stations opened across Israel at 7 a.m. Tuesday as the country began voting in its 26th Knesset election, with more than 7.3 million eligible voters choosing the lawmakers who will shape the country's next government. The election brings 36 competing party lists into a contest for the 120 seats in parliament, with most polling stations remaining open until 10 p.m.
For voters, the process is straightforward: arrive at an assigned polling station, select a party ballot and cast a vote. Behind the scenes, however, the election is one of the country's largest logistical operations, involving nearly 300,000 people and thousands of polling stations spread across cities, towns and rural communities.
Schools, community centers and other public buildings have been transformed into voting locations, with 12,335 polling stations prepared nationwide. The Central Elections Committee has printed an estimated 450 million ballot slips, using approximately 250 tons of paper, to ensure that voters can choose among the competing lists.
"The Central Elections Committee has nearly 100,000 election-day workers at polling stations and regional committees. The parties employ another 200,000 people. That's almost 300,000 altogether," acting committee director-general Dean Livne told ynet. He said preparations intensified in July, when the Knesset entered its election recess, setting off a race to have everything ready for voting day.
The election is also taking place under the shadow of the war, with special arrangements in place for Israelis who remain displaced from their homes. Residents from communities including Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz and Holit have access to designated polling stations, while soldiers can cast their ballots at military bases. Voting arrangements have also been established for hospitalized patients, nursing home residents and people with mobility limitations.
Authorities have introduced free travel on Israel Railways and eligible intercity bus routes longer than 15 kilometers to help voters reach polling stations. The arrangement began Monday evening and will continue throughout election day.
Election officials say extensive safeguards are in place to protect the integrity of the vote. Ballots are counted manually, with representatives from different political parties present during the process. Police officers will also be deployed at polling stations across the country.
The first results are expected during the night, after most polling stations close at 10 p.m., but the political picture may remain uncertain well beyond then. Between 600,000 and 650,000 Israelis are expected to vote using special double envelopes, which are counted separately and could influence the final distribution of seats.
Election officials hope to complete the count by Thursday afternoon, although the official deadline for publishing the results is November 4. Until then, the country will be watching not only which party emerges strongest, but which political alliances can assemble the parliamentary majority needed to form Israel's next government.

Alibaba wins injunction against Pentagon contract restrictions tied to China blacklist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:58:00 UTC
13:58:00 KST

Alibaba wins injunction against Pentagon contract restrictions tied to China blacklist
- A US federal judge ordered the US government not to block Pentagon contracts because Alibaba shares lobbyists with contractors, giving the company a legal win.
- Alibaba was added to a Pentagon list of firms said to aid China’s military, but it says its business is for retail, logistics and enterprise technology.
- The injunction does not remove Alibaba from the list, and the company is still challenging the designation in court.
AI generated
NEW YORK – A US federal judge on Oct 26 granted Alibaba Group Holding’s request for a preliminary injunction, ordering the US government not to deny Pentagon contracts to companies because they, their parent companies or subsidiaries do business with firms that engage in lobbying activities for the e-commerce giant.
Alibaba sued the US government in June after the Pentagon added it to a list of companies allegedly aiding China’s military, alongside internet search provider Baidu, electric vehicle (EV) maker BYD and other major Chinese manufacturing and technology firms.
The ruling on Oct 26 means Alibaba will be able to retain US lobbyists who also represent Pentagon contractors, removing a potential obstacle to the company’s efforts to challenge its designation as a Chinese military company.
Alibaba fired dozens of its Washington lobbyists after the Pentagon action in June, said a source with direct knowledge of the matter who was not authorised to speak to the media.
The designation does not impose formal sanctions, but restricts Pentagon contracts with listed companies and, from 2027, purchases of their products or services through third parties.
Other listed Chinese tech firms were also concerned about the designation’s impact on international lobbying activities as well as the indirect procurement ban, which would completely remove Chinese products from US defence contractors’ supply chains, the source added.
Alibaba has denied any military ties, saying its products and services are built for retail, logistics and enterprise technology, rather than defence or intelligence.
“The determinations have no basis in fact or law,” Alibaba said in its lawsuit in June, seeking its removal from the list.
The injunction on Oct 26 does not remove Alibaba from the Pentagon list, which the company is continuing to challenge in court.
It did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the injunction.
Companies take legal action
Alibaba is one of several Chinese firms taking legal action to challenge their placement on the Pentagon list.
In September, two subsidiaries of the world’s largest EV-maker BYD sued the US Department of Defense over a federal law banning any Pentagon contractors from hiring lobbyists that also work with blacklisted firms, arguing that it breached BYD’s First Amendment rights.
In August, DJI, the world’s largest drone-maker, appealed its inclusion on the blacklist with the court finding merit in its argument that unclassified records did not support the conclusion that the company contributed to the Chinese defence industrial base.
The appeals court ordered the lower court to reconsider its decision to reject DJI’s bid to be removed from the Pentagon list and the case is ongoing.
Also in August, biotech firm WuXi AppTec won a preliminary injunction from a US federal court, which blocked its inclusion on the list. WuXi said the Pentagon designation was politically motivated. REUTERS

Melania Trump’s chief adviser: Russia pledges to respect Oleshky residents’ evacuation choices
Marc Beckman, senior advisor to U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, made this statement in an interview with Ukrinform.
When asked whether the residents of Oleshky would be able to freely choose their evacuation destination without pressure from the Russian occupation authorities, he noted: “Russia has assured the Ukrainians, as well as the Americans, that it will respect the wishes of the people who live in Oleshky,” he said.
According to Beckman, Ukraine and Russia “worked together to put a series of safeguards.”
“Once they are informed of where individuals and their families would like to go—whether to Ukraine, Russia, or to remain in their homes in Oleshky—those safeguards will hopefully provide enough protection to ensure that everyone’s wishes are respected,” he explained.
The First Lady’s chief advisor emphasized that the leadership of Ukraine and Russia, at both the governmental and military levels, has planned the humanitarian operation down to the day and hour.
He did not rule out extending the ceasefire if both sides conclude that it is necessary to deliver humanitarian aid and prepare for evacuation.
According to Beckman, the start date for the ceasefire was determined after technical and logistical issues were worked out jointly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership.
“The date of October 29 was chosen because both the Ukrainian government and military, as well as the Russian government and military, believe it is the earliest and best date to ensure the safety of all residents of Oleshky, bring in humanitarian aid—including medical personnel, medicine, clean water, food, and more—and begin preparing for the evacuation,” he explained.
Beckman did not disclose details of the guarantees provided by Russia or the mechanisms for responding to possible violations of the ceasefire. According to him, Ukrainian and Russian officials have asked that this information not be made public for the time being.
He also reported that Ukraine and Russia have agreed on the composition of civilian teams that will work with the residents of Oleshky, assess their needs, and assist with the evacuation.
The Ukrainian group will be led by Dmytro Lubinets, the Verkhovna Rada’s Commissioner for Human Rights, who will work on the ground alongside other Ukrainian representatives. The Russian side has also designated its representative and other civilian participants in the operation.
Beckman highly praised Lubinets’ work, calling him a person who is extremely devoted to Ukraine and the Ukrainian people and who makes every effort to overcome obstacles.
As previously reported, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump proposed a ceasefire to deliver humanitarian aid to the residents of Oleshky and prepare for the evacuation of civilians.

Netanyahu besieged by failure; An election of life and death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:55:55 UTC
13:55:55 KST

A prime minister who for years has justified his policy with the promise of providing Israel's security, defeating enemies, and achieving "absolute victory" must now answer a fundamental question: if his strategies have been so successful, why has the Iran file remained one of the most important axes of threat and security propaganda for Israel?
Netanyahu has been placed in a situation where his political defeat could mean the end of a long period of power-seeking and security claims. Although the election result is not yet clear, political evidence and domestic criticisms show that he faces one of the most difficult tests of his political career. The security failure of October 7, 2023 and its consequences have severely called into question the credibility of Israel's security establishment.
From the Promise of Absolute Security to a Crisis of Trust
For years, Netanyahu tried to present himself as a politician who, better than any rival, is capable of confronting security threats. However, the operation of October 7, 2023 showed how vulnerable this claim of comprehensive security was. The surprise of Israel's intelligence and military agencies, the entry of Hamas forces into the areas and settlements around Gaza, and the killing and capture of a large number of Israeli settlers dealt a historic blow to this regime's security image.
Afterward, the Netanyahu cabinet launched extensive operations in Gaza, and the scope of Israel's confrontation with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran also expanded. Netanyahu tried to present the military achievements of these operations as a sign of the restoration of Israel's deterrence power; but his fundamental problem persists: the power of military destruction is not the same as the realization of strategic objectives.
When the conflict becomes prolonged, human and economic costs increase, and the government still speaks of the necessity of continuing operations to reach final victory, this question becomes more serious: has the chosen strategy been able to create lasting security, or has it merely formed a new cycle of conflict?
Iran; A File Netanyahu Cannot Close with Slogans
Iran has been one of the main axes of Netanyahu's security strategy. He has repeatedly placed confronting Iran's nuclear program, missile capability, and regional influence at the top of his policies and has tried to present this file as evidence of the necessity of continuing his leadership.
However, the result of a military campaign cannot be measured merely by the aggressor side's declaration of victory. The real criterion is the extent to which the declared objectives have been realized, a lasting change in the balance of power, and the ability to prevent the return of the crisis. If, after extensive operations, the possibility of renewed confrontation with Iran is still raised, this situation shows that the issue has not been settled from a strategic perspective.
Channel 12 recent report about the alleged dispute between Netanyahu and Eyal Zamir, the Chief of the General Staff of the military, over the possibility of a new military operation related to Iran has highlighted this very contradiction. According to this report, the proposed action could have led to a broader confrontation with Tehran. Israeli officials have denied or questioned the details of this dispute, but the publication of such a report on the eve of elections reveals the sensitivity of the Iran file.
Yair Lapid, the opposition leader, also criticized the prime minister's performance, saying Israel's security should not be turned into a tool for election propaganda. Referring to Netanyahu's promises about Iran, he stressed that the prime minister has repeatedly spoken of "absolute victory" but has not reached the expected results.
This criticism from within the Israeli regime's political structure is considered a blow to Netanyahu's victory narrative; because it shows that even his domestic rivals do not consider the repetition of Iran threats as equivalent to strategic success.
The Axis of Resistance; The Strategic Costs of a Multi-Front Confrontation
The Iran file is not Netanyahu's only testing ground. Gaza, Lebanon, and other regional arenas have also become parts of his cabinet's security record. On these fronts, Israel has been able to deal heavy military blows to some groups of the Axis of Resistance; but inflicting a military blow alone does not mean eliminating the capacity for resistance or achieving a regional order in accordance with Tel Aviv's wishes.
In Gaza, extensive military operations could not easily realize all of Israel's declared objectives. In Lebanon, too, the weakening of Hezbollah's capability cannot be considered equivalent to the complete elimination of this actor without examining the political and security situation after the conflict. At the regional level as well, the confrontation with Iran has shown that military pressure does not necessarily lead to the opposing side's political surrender.
Therefore, the main issue for Netanyahu is not merely the number of operations carried out or the extent of damage inflicted on the opposing side; the issue is whether these operations have been able to turn the declared strategic objectives into a lasting result or not.
Netanyahu faces a fundamental contradiction: the more he speaks of final victory, the more the continuation of threats and the necessity of new operations highlight the question about the realization of that very victory.
The Election; The Final Test of Netanyahu's Record
Israel's electoral competition is being held under conditions in which none of the main camps, according to published polls, has a definitive and obstacle-free path to forming a cabinet. Achieving a majority of 61 seats out of the Knesset's total of 120 seats will depend on coalition-building and post-election negotiations. Therefore, even the electoral performance of the parties alone does not determine the fate of the future cabinet.
However, Netanyahu's issue is not just the number of seats for the Likud party. He must answer for the security failure of October 7, the costs of prolonged conflicts, the condition of reserve forces, internal disputes, and the gap between promises of victory and actual results. His opponents are trying to turn the election into an opportunity to end his period of leadership; his supporters continue to rely on his political experience and security policies.
Under such circumstances, the election for Netanyahu has a meaning close to political life and death: preserving power can give him the opportunity to continue his narrative of regional developments, but losing power will confront his position and political credibility with a serious challenge.
Ultimately, Netanyahu's record cannot be assessed with election slogans or claims of absolute victory. In realizing the promise of lasting security and converting military operations into a decisive strategic victory, he has faced serious failures. Iran remains at the center of Israel's security calculations, and the fronts associated with the Axis of Resistance, despite heavy military blows, have become unresolved files in Tel Aviv's regional strategy.
This is precisely Netanyahu's main weakness on the eve of the election: he can once again speak of victory, but he cannot eliminate the gap between his promises and strategic results merely by repeating this word. The October 27 election is, more than anything, a test for measuring this very gap and the extent of Zionist society's trust in his leadership.
MNA

Flavio Bolsonaro backs off Brazil election challenge as his party concedes defeat
- Flavio Bolsonaro dropped plans to challenge Lula’s victory, and the Liberal Party formally conceded defeat while criticising higher public spending before the vote.
- Bolsonaro then shifted to a new bid to disqualify Lula’s ticket, calling the result unfair and saying “the system won”, but the claim looks unlikely to succeed.
- He will organise opposition in Congress, while Flavio Bolsonaro was ordered by police to hand over passports and stay in Brazil amid a Supreme Court-linked investigation.
AI generated
Flavio Bolsonaro abandoned plans to challenge the result of Brazil’s presidential election, while his Liberal Party went a step further and formally conceded defeat to re-elected President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
In a statement signed on Oct 26 by its president, Valdemar Costa Neto, the party recognised the election result while criticising the increase in public spending in the run-up to the vote and its potential impact on the race.
The statement marks a sharp retreat from Bolsonaro’s initial response to the Oct 25 vote, when he said he would seek to have the election annulled.
Bolsonaro’s decision to drop that challenge was initially confirmed by a member of his campaign.
A second person said the campaign had already known the challenge was unlikely to succeed, but had kept it alive as a way to rally supporters.
Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly.
Bolsonaro had said he would seek to have the election annulled after the Supreme Court ordered voting hours extended by two hours. Both his campaign and Lula’s had requested the extension.
According to the electoral authorities, just over 34,000 votes were cast after regular voting hours, a negligible number compared with Lula’s roughly 4.4 million vote margin of victory.
In a social media video posted in the late afternoon on Oct 26, Bolsonaro said he would seek to have Lula’s ticket disqualified, another long-shot strategy with little chance of success.
He said the case would centre on what he described as false information and the use of public funds for measures announced in the final weeks of the campaign, which he called “vote buying”.
“I wasn’t the one who lost. The system won,” Bolsonaro said.
Lula’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bolsonaro’s allegations.
Bolsonaro also said he would organise the opposition to Lula’s government, pointing to the strength of his Liberal Party in both houses of Congress.
“I will bring together the elected lawmakers and senators to organise our strategy and turn the Lower House and the Senate into our fortress against the barbarity that is already taking shape with four more years of Lula,” he said.
In the same video, Bolsonaro said he had visited his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, on the morning of Oct 26.
The elder Bolsonaro is under house arrest in Brasilia for attempting a coup after his own 2022 election loss.
Flavio Bolsonaro said that after the meeting, he was served an order by the federal police requiring him to surrender both his regular and diplomatic passports and informing him that he was barred from leaving Brazil.
He said the order was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same judge who sentenced his father to 27 years in prison.
Bolsonaro said the measure followed comments by his brother Eduardo, who said on a podcast that Flavio Bolsonaro should leave Brazil if he lost the election.
In the same ruling, Moraes barred Bolsonaro from contacting lawyer Willer Tomaz, according to a person familiar with the matter. The two are under investigation on suspicion of involvement in a money-laundering scheme. Both have denied wrongdoing.
The order was not public, and the Supreme Court did not immediately respond to a request for comment. BLOOMBERG

Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:53:11 UTC
13:53:11 KST

Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bonn
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Bonn have discovered that spiders experience distinct stages of sleep, including a REM-like state that shares surprising similarities with human sleep. During this stage, the spiders move their eyes and twitch their muscles, behaviors also associated with REM (rapid eye movement) sleep in humans and other vertebrates.
The findings provide the first comprehensive experimental confirmation that spiders experience genuine, regulated sleep rather than simply remaining inactive. They also raise intriguing questions about how sleep evolved and whether animals with very different nervous systems might share some of its fundamental features.
Researchers at the University of Bonn's Institute of Organismic Biology made the discovery while studying the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a small but remarkably sophisticated predator.
A Tiny Spider With Remarkable Hunting Skills
The Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata is only about the size of a one-euro coin when fully grown, but its hunting abilities make it particularly interesting to scientists.
Unlike many spiders that primarily capture insects, members of the genus Portia specialize in hunting other spiders. They use a variety of sophisticated strategies to catch their prey, including imitating the vibrations made by struggling insects trapped in spiderwebs.
These deceptive signals can lure web-building spiders toward what appears to be an easy meal, only for them to encounter the hunting Portia instead.
Such complex behaviors suggest that these spiders have unusual learning abilities, making them valuable subjects for investigating the relationship between sleep, nervous system function, and cognition.
Scientists Discover Two Distinct Stages of Spider Sleep
Although sleep has been extensively studied in humans and other vertebrates, scientists still know relatively little about how it works in animals with very different nervous systems.
To investigate whether spiders experience genuine sleep and whether that sleep includes different stages, the researchers closely monitored Portia fimbriata over several days and nights.
They discovered that the spiders exhibit two clearly distinguishable sleep stages. One of these resembles REM sleep, the phase in humans associated with rapid eye movements, muscle activity, and vivid dreaming.
During this REM-like stage, the spiders displayed characteristic eye movements and muscle twitches. These observations suggest that some features of sleep previously studied mainly in vertebrates may also occur in spiders.
The researchers emphasize that identifying REM-like movements does not establish whether spiders dream. However, the discovery provides important evidence that sleep in these animals is more complex than previously understood.
How Researchers Confirmed That Spiders Really Sleep
To study the spiders' sleeping behavior, the team placed individual Portia fimbriata spiders in plastic dishes measuring 12 centimeters in diameter. They monitored the animals under different lighting conditions to examine their daily activity and rest cycles.
Infrared cameras allowed the researchers to observe the spiders throughout the night without relying on visible light. Detailed recordings captured their sleeping positions, periods of quiet rest, and episodes of REM-like movement.
The team also conducted experiments to determine whether the spiders were genuinely asleep rather than simply sitting motionless.
Using sound stimuli, the researchers measured how quickly the spiders responded to disturbances. These tests helped distinguish sleep from ordinary inactivity.
Another important part of the investigation involved sleep deprivation. The researchers examined whether the spiders displayed "sleep rebound," meaning they compensated for interrupted sleep by increasing their subsequent sleep.
Together, the behavioral observations and experimental tests provided strong evidence that Portia fimbriata experiences regulated sleep with distinct stages.
Studying Spider Sleep Presented Unusual Challenges
Determining whether a spider is truly asleep is considerably more complicated than observing a sleeping human.
Because spiders sense their surroundings differently from people, the researchers first had to identify a sound stimulus that would produce a consistent response during their experiments.
They also needed to avoid assuming that the observed eye movements and muscle twitches necessarily represented the same processes seen during human REM sleep.
One major limitation was that the researchers could not measure the spiders' brain activity. Instead, they relied entirely on carefully documented behavior to identify different sleep states.
This required extensive high-resolution video recordings collected over many days and nights, producing enormous amounts of data for analysis.
Despite these obstacles, the combination of behavioral monitoring, response testing, and sleep disruption experiments allowed the researchers to build a detailed picture of how these spiders sleep.
What Spider Sleep Could Reveal About Evolution
The discovery has implications that extend well beyond spiders.
Most scientific knowledge about sleep comes from studying vertebrates, particularly mammals and birds. Finding comparable sleep features in animals with radically different nervous systems could help researchers understand when and why different types of sleep evolved.
The results also open new opportunities in behavioral science, neuroscience, and chronobiology, the study of biological rhythms.
By investigating sleep in a wider variety of animals, scientists hope to identify features that are shared across species and uncover the fundamental biological functions that sleep may have served early in evolutionary history.
The researchers argue that future investigations should move beyond traditionally studied animals and include species with unusual adaptations or much simpler nervous systems.
Such comparisons could reveal whether certain sleep mechanisms are widespread throughout the animal kingdom or developed independently in different evolutionary lineages.
Even after decades of intensive research, many basic questions about sleep remain unanswered, including important mysteries surrounding human sleep.
Could Spiders Dream? Scientists Have More Questions
The University of Bonn team is now expanding its research to investigate how sleep, particularly REM-like sleep, varies across different spider species.
Scientists are also comparing spiders sleeping in natural environments with those observed in laboratories to determine how surroundings influence their behavior.
Another major goal is to investigate the relationship between sleep and cognitive abilities. Researchers want to understand what happens inside the brains of spiders and insects during sleep, and whether different sleep stages contribute to learning and other mental processes.
Environmental changes are also becoming an important focus. The team plans to examine how climate change and human activities, especially artificial light at night (ALAN), may interfere with the sleep patterns of spiders and other arthropods.
For now, the findings establish that even a tiny jumping spider can experience a surprisingly complex form of sleep. Whether spiders actually dream remains unknown, but their nighttime behavior is offering scientists new clues about one of biology's most enduring mysteries.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Bonn. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Nadja Geiger, Maxim Q. Capelle, Phillip Rosentreter, Marie E. Herberstein, Armin Bahl, Massimo De Agrò, Barrett A. Klein, Daniela C. Rößler. Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (45) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2618030123
