Taiwan university develops drone swarm technology for maritime patrols
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:51:04 UTC
13:51:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ocean Affairs Council said Monday it is funding National Cheng Kung University’s development of AI drone swarm technology to expand maritime patrol coverage.
The council said in a press release that the project combines AI, fixed-wing drones capable of vertical takeoff and landing, and coordinated flight technology. It aims to enable multiple drone types to work together on maritime patrol missions.
NCKU aeronautics and astronautics Associate Professor Chueh Chih-che (闕志哲) is leading the research team. His team is developing the system to automate coordinated missions involving multiple drone types.
Chueh’s team uses 3D models and flight simulations featuring the JUMP-20, V-Bat, and Flexrotor. Researchers analyze aerodynamic parameters and flight controls to support autonomous navigation, route planning, and coordination between drones.
The team uses multi-agent reinforcement learning to refine drone task allocation, route planning, and coordination. It has also incorporated a minimum vertical separation of about 30 meters and obstacle avoidance into the control system.
The council said the team has completed simultaneous flight simulations for two groups totaling 20 drones. The next stages will include prototype integration and flight tests at sea to assess performance under different conditions.

Taiwan’s working-age population projected to shrink by 4.51 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:50:48 UTC
13:50:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is projected to see more than two people reach age 65 for every person entering the working-age population over the next 20 years, raising concerns about labor shortages and the financial sustainability of social insurance programs.
The National Development Council’s latest population forecast projects that the population aged 15 to 64 will shrink by 4.51 million between 2026 and 2046, equivalent to an average daily decline of 618 people, per Liberty Times. The projected loss exceeds the 4.06 million decline forecast for 2024 to 2044 in the council’s previous report, reflecting a downward revision to fertility assumptions.
The working-age population is also expected to grow older, with people aged 45 to 64 projected to account for more than half of the total, up from 46.3% in 2026. That age group currently numbers approximately 7.29 million.
Meanwhile, the number of people turning 15 and entering the working-age population over the next 20 years is projected to total just 3.1 million, Liberty Times reported. The figures concern age groups rather than actual retirements or entry into employment.
An official cited by Liberty Times warned that the widening gap could undermine the financial foundations of Taiwan’s social insurance and pension programs, including labor insurance, public-sector pensions, and National Health Insurance. These systems rely on contributions from the working population to help fund benefits, leaving them increasingly vulnerable as the number of contributors shrinks relative to beneficiaries.
Policy responses include raising the effective retirement age, redesigning jobs to accommodate older workers, increasing women’s labor force participation, and attracting international talent, according to Liberty Times. Without such measures, Taiwan’s social insurance systems and public finances could face mounting pressure as the working-age population shrinks.

Lake Balkhash receives 40 billion of cubic meters of water as Kazakhstan steps up conservation efforts
Nearly 40 billion cubic meters of water have flowed into Lake Balkhash over the past three years, helping stabilize the lake’s water level, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, around 15.9 billion cubic meters of water were directed into the lake in 2024, followed by around 13.9 billion cubic meters in 2025. Since the beginning of 2026, more than 9.7 billion cubic meters of water have flowed into the lake.
Water is released into Lake Balkhash from the Kapshagay Reservoir, which is fed by the transboundary Ili River. The reservoir reached 98% of its capacity this year, compared with 100% in each of the previous two years.
“The inflow of water from the Ili River remains at its long-term average level. This helps maintain Lake Balkhash’s water level at the optimal elevation of 341 meters according to the Baltic height system,” said Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Nurzhan Nurzhigitov.
He added that work is underway with French experts to develop a master plan for the conservation of Lake Balkhash through 2040. Field studies have been completed, and the results are currently being analyzed.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kazakhstan attracted more than 192 billion tenge in water sector investments.

Israel heads to the polls as shift to the right dominates critical election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:44:14 UTC
13:44:14 KST

Israel heads to the polls as shift to the right dominates critical election
Netanyahu seeks to extend rule at helm of far right alliance facing off against predominantly right-wing bloc.
Israel is heading to the polls on Tuesday in a closely contested election that is being described as one of the most important in its history.
The vote is the first since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, as well as a wider conflict that has seen Israel carry out attacks on Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Syria and Qatar.
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to extend his tenure after leading the country’s most right-wing governing coalition which brought together far-right ultranationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
Wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza and faced with a long-running corruption trial, he is fighting for his political survival against a self-styled Zionist opposition bloc that has fundamentally embraced a right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges. Questions over accountability for alleged security failures, disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab-led parties dominated the campaign.
This has further dampened already low expectations that the vote would offer any meaningful improvement to the lives of Palestinians, as deadly attacks continue almost daily in Gaza despite a yearlong “ceasefire”, while settler pogroms and Israeli army raids have intensified in the occupied West Bank.
“The entire Israeli political system operates within the racist framework of Jewish supremacy,” Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani, a noted Israeli sociologist, told Al Jazeera.
“None of the leaders who present themselves as an alternative to Netanyahu can genuinely be described as left-wing. The horrifying reality we are witnessing is not simply the product of Netanyahu or the far right. It is rooted in Zionist political thought itself, which is structured around the principle of Jewish supremacy. There is no way around this fundamental fact,” he said.
Democracy?
Israel’s shift to the right did not begin with the establishment of Netanyahu’s most recent government in 2022, or what polls show to have been the rightward lurch that took place across Israel following the Hamas-led attack of 2023. Rather, the collapse of the peace process with the Palestinians and repeated security crises over the past few decades have combined to systematically erode the political centre and left, giving rise to landmark legislative milestones such as the 2018 Nation-State Law, which formally enshrined Jewish supremacy and the continued and violent expansion of illegal Israeli settlements into occupied Palestinian territory with little or no government restraint.
However, if the drift to the right was there beforehand, most analysts agree that its speed has accelerated to unprecedented heights under the latest Netanyahu government, which faced accusations of seeking to reshape the country in its own image.
They point to attempts to strip the Supreme Court of its power to review government actions and the flouting of its rulings on conscripting the ultra-Orthodox minority whose political support helped sustain the governing coalition, as well as the presence of figures such as far-right provocateur and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and religious Zionist Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s finance minister.
Together, in return for their seat at the table, both ministers offered crucial support to the controversial judicial overhaul that Netanyahu – himself on trial for bribery, fraud and breach of trust, charges he denies – launched in the early months of 2023 and which continues to this day. Similarly, both ministers have provided encouragement and cover for the surge in violence across the West Bank, while deflecting attempts to hold the coalition accountable for the alleged security failures that preceded the Hamas-led attack.
“If Netanyahu loses the election and, say, [Gadi] Eisenkot becomes the new prime minister, the main initial change will be the atmosphere, the vibe, as Netanyahu stirs deep emotions domestically,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
“Those who admire him, and there are many in Israel, regard him as God. Those who hate him, and there are many in Israel, hate him deeply,” said Bregman. “He’s a very divisive figure. A new prime minister is likely to calm things down.”
With the vote closely watched across the region and beyond, analysts also say the stakes go beyond the names on the ballot and cut through to the very nature of the character and future of Israel.
“The decision facing Israel of whether to retain a Netanyahu-led government or not is ultimately the decision on whether to live in a functioning democracy or a democracy in name only,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.
“It’s the choice between maintaining the occupation of the West Bank or annexing it entirely and the population’s ‘voluntary migration’ from there, as figures within the government have actually suggested.”
A respect for process and the rule of law would likely return to government in the event of an opposition win, added Bregman, a sharp contrast with what he described as Netanyahu’s approach to government. However, to expect too great a change in the overall direction of policy would be to miss the point.
“Don’t be mistaken,” he cautioned. “Israel, particularly after 7 October, turned sharply to the right, and any new government will reflect and mirror this reality.”
Peace?
What will not be on the ballot, analysts and observers say, is any opportunity to challenge a foreign and security policy that has underpinned the killing of more than 74,000 people in Gaza, the increased violence across the West Bank and the launching of multiple wars, including one on Iran that has seen key energy routes choked and has left global markets reeling.
None of the mainstream candidates for office in October have talked about including Arab-led parties in any potential coalition. In Israel’s popular media, references to the leaders of Ra’am or the Joint List are typically used by rival candidates to denounce each other for considering a future coalition with Palestinian politicians, now or in the past.
Shenhav-Shahrabani, the sociologist, said the ultra-Orthodox parties would still be welcome in government after the vote by either coalition, while the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel – one-fifth of the total population – would be excluded by a system built upon prejudice.
“The distinction is not between democratic and anti-democratic forces, but between Jews and Palestinians. As long as there is no genuine binational political vision, racism and the systematic restriction of Palestinian rights will remain fundamental features of Israeli society,” he said.
If that framework shapes who is allowed into government, it also shapes what the campaign is about. Netanyahu’s challengers largely framed their disagreements with him as questions of competence, timing and accountability for the alleged failures that preceded October 7, rather than challenges to the way Palestinians are treated.
For critics, that omission is not an oversight but a reflection of where the Israeli mainstream now sits: among the issues at stake in the election, none amounted to a referendum on the genocide in Gaza. “How can it be a referendum on genocide, or anything to do with the treatment of Palestinians in Gaza?” asked Daniel Levy, a former Israeli government adviser.
“You would have to have one side arguing it was a good thing and the other arguing it was a bad thing, let alone acknowledging that it was a genocide. So, no, obviously none of that is on the ballot,” he said.
“The treatment of Palestinians by the Israeli state and military is a consensus among Zionist parties,” added Levy, with differences among them primarily resting on “whether it’s the state’s job to oppress Palestinians, or if the settler militias also have a role – a significant role – to play”.

Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign disavowed a pro-Palestinian group’s new ad that critics say invokes antisemitic tropes about US support for Israel.
The ad comes from Rebellion PAC, which is fronted by left-wing political commentator Cenk Uygur. It depicts a couple in a supermarket saying they cannot afford groceries because they have to set money aside “for killing Palestinians.” It concludes by stating that the Michigan Democrat’s GOP opponent “is for they/them,” referring to Israelis.
In a statement to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, an El-Sayed campaign representative said the ad “is not affiliated in any way” with his campaign and that it did not speak for him.
“Abdul is focused on pushing back against Trump’s agenda that is raising prices for Michiganders,” campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner said in the statement. “No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign.”
The campaign did not address how El-Sayed viewed the messaging behind the ad, and did not respond to a follow-up from JTA about the ad’s content.
Rebellion’s ad repurposes an ad originally released in 2024 for Uygur’s presidential campaign — but with a new ending that backs El-Sayed and knocks his Republican opponent, former US Rep. Mike Rogers.
“Why does Mike Rogers care so much about what Israelis want and so little about what you want?” the new ad asks. A voiceover then riffs on Republican ads from 2024 that attacked Democrats over LGBTQ issues.
“Mike Rogers is for they/them,” the voiceover states over photos of Israeli politicians Benjamin Netanyahu, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. “Abdul El-Sayed is for you.”
A spokesperson for Rebellion PAC told JTA that the group is spending $1,000 on the ad, and that it will run online. Uygur, on X/Twitter, stated on Friday that the ad would run “in Michigan.” Tensions among Jewish voters in the state are high: Many have expressed discomfort with El-Sayed’s strong criticism of Israel. The candidate has condemned antisemitism and looked to make inroads with Jewish voters.
Critics are misusing antisemitism, spokesperson claims
“If you think this ad is antisemitic, you’ve lost your mind, and you don’t know it,” the Rebellion PAC spokesperson, Kara Eastman, told JTA. “It’s saying we’re giving too much money to a foreign nation — and they’re misusing it. There’s nothing more normal than that. But when someone criticizes the government of Israel, and you hear ‘they hate all Jews,’ get clinical help.”
Shortly after Eastman’s response to JTA, Uygur himself added on X, “If you think this ad is antisemitic, you’re in a cult and don’t know it. You think Israel is owed all the money it wants from the US and if Americans don’t hand it over — without complaint — they’re antisemites. That’s insane, but you don’t realize it because you’ve lost your mind.”
Michigan US Rep. Haley Stevens, a favorite of the pro-Israel community who endorsed El-Sayed after losing to him in the primary, called the ad “fearmongering” and “wrong.” She added that its makers were “blaming the high costs of our goods on the only Jewish homeland in the world.” Melissa Byrne, a progressive activist and former staffer for Jewish progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders, wrote that Uygur “clearly wants Abdul El-Sayed to lose by doing this ad.”
A spokesperson for Michigan Jews for Democracy, an ad hoc group of Jews in the state who have pledged to vote for El-Sayed, called the ad “crap” in an interview with JTA.
“If they honestly think this is going to help, then they honestly have no idea what is going on in this state or this race,” Stacie Chaiken, the group’s representative, told JTA. “They’re just playing into the hands of people who are really trying to hurt him.”

i24NEWS will be publishing its own exit poll tonight at 10:00 pm to reveal which political parties will come out on top, following a complete counting of the votes
It is election day in Israel, and across the nation, millions of people are heading to the polls in what has been one of the most contentious and divisive elections in recent history. According to Israel’s Central Elections Committee, there are over 7.3 million eligible voters, 12,018 polling stations, about 100,000 workers, and 450 million ballots printed, all on a whopping NIS 690 million ($223.3m) budget. However, about 11% of eligible voters, or 810,000 people, are living abroad and only an estimated 67,000 are flying into Israel to vote. Twenty regional election committees are operating nationwide, and 660 intercity public transport lines, including all Israel Railways lines, will run free on election day.
Tuesday’s election will be the first one since November 2022, before October 7, with approximately 333,000 more people eligible to vote. Will Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Likud Party be able to fend off their opponents and retain a majority coalition? Or will opposition leaders be able to garner enough votes to secure their own leading coalition? Make sure to tune in to i24NEWS for all your election coverage. Learn about the latest from the polls, what leading politicians are saying, and the final results, from 11:30 am to until the final ballot is counted. i24NEWS will be publishing its own exit poll at 10:00 pm.
Israeli elections: new guidelines to ease queues
Faced with long lines at polling stations, the Central Electoral Commission authorized secretaries to identify the next voter while the previous person votes behind the curtain. The instruction aims to expedite the voting process.
Gadi Eisenkot pays his respects at his son's grave before voting
Yashar! party leader Gadi Eisenkot and his wife Chana visited the grave of their son, Gal Meir, at the Herzliya military cemetery on Tuesday before going to vote in the 26th Knesset elections.
Reserve Staff Sergeant Gal Meir was killed in December 2023 during fighting in the northern Gaza Strip.
Central Elections Committee chair hosts Herzog at control center; Sohlberg says disagreement is “fundamental from the outset”
Central Elections Committee Chair Justice Noam Sohlberg hosted President Isaac Herzog at the committee’s Control Center in the Knesset on Election Day.
The two toured the committee’s departments, and Herzog observed the teams’ work and how the election process is being conducted across the country.
The center serves throughout the day as a hub for reports from the field, giving a national overview and helping coordinate responses to needs and incidents at polling stations.
“Election Day is no ordinary day; it is a day of celebration,” Sohlberg said. “We do not hide our disagreements, nor can they be swept under the rug. Polarization exists, and everyone is entitled to hold their own views. The disagreement is not an afterthought; it is fundamental from the outset.”
He added: “In a week’s time, we will meet with the President once again and present the election results, the will of the voters. This is our strength as a nation.”
Central Elections Committee: No reports of Likud tracking voters via app, claim online is incorrect
The Central Elections Committee said a claim circulating online that Likud representatives are tracking voters at polling stations and reporting on them through an app is incorrect.
“As of now, the Committee has received no reports of any such activity,” it said.
The committee did receive a specific report of photography at a polling station in Moshav Yarhiv, where a polling committee member who was taking photos stopped after the guidelines were explained to her and she realized her mistake.
The committee reiterated that party representatives at polling stations are strictly prohibited from conveying information to their parties about an individual’s arrival at a polling station or the fact that they voted, including through apps, and said the guidelines are binding on all parties and their representatives.
Shas Party Chairman Rabbi Aryeh Deri has just cast his vote at a polling station in the Har Nof neighborhood of Jerusalem

Over 95% of polling stations open as voting begins in Knesset elections; isolated delays possible
Reports from the field indicate that over 95% of polling stations have opened, with further updates expected in the coming minutes.
The absence of a report at this stage does not necessarily mean that a polling station has not yet opened.
Isolated delays in opening may occur, which is not unusual for the early morning.

The IDF said on Tuesday it apprehended an Egyptian civilian overnight after he crossed a border fence from Egyptian territory into Israel near Nitzana.
In the initial interrogation, he admitted to security officials: "I came to wage jihad, to kill Jews and to liberate the occupied lands." The suspect was transferred to Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) for interrogation.
The arrest comes amid warnings from Israel's top officials, like Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, who have warned about the heightened risk of terror attacks the country faces during its election process.
Extra Election Facts
Approximately 15.1% of eligible voters living in Israel are young people aged 18-24, 27.6% are aged 25-39, and 31% are aged 40-59. The share of eligible voters aged 60 and over is approximately 26.3%.
Meanwhile, just over 5 million (77%) of eligible voters living in Israel are Jews. About 1,159,000 (18%) of eligible voters are Arabs (Muslims, Arab Christians, and Druze). Another 346,000 (5%) are others, defined as non-Arab Christians and residents without religious classification.

Brazil’s Liberal Party accepts runoff results despite Flavio Bolsonaro’s call for annulment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Laura Gamba Fadul
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL) formally recognized the results of Sunday’s presidential runoff which confirmed President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s reelection over its candidate, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who continues to dispute the vote count.
In a statement posted Monday on social media, PL President Valdemar Costa Neto said that while the party accepts the official tallies certified by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), it will demand answers regarding pre-election social spending implemented by the ruling Workers' Party (PT).
“We acknowledge the presidential election results, as announced by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), but we believe that the concerns raised need to be properly addressed within a balanced and democratic political debate,” Costa Neto wrote. “We will continue to monitor the facts and seek answers with responsibility, transparency, and respect for our institutions.”
The PL statement came shortly after TSE President Justice Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Federal Court (STF) by former President Jair Bolsonaro, confirmed the final election results. Nunes Marques expressed "absolute confidence in the entire electoral process," effectively shutting down speculation regarding electronic ballot integrity.
Lula secured a historic fourth non-consecutive term with 51.76% of valid votes (over 60 million ballots), defeating Flavio Bolsonaro, who garnered 48.24%. The result sealed a dramatic comeback from the Oct. 4 first round, in which Bolsonaro led by nearly two percentage points.
Despite his party's official acknowledgment, Flavio Bolsonaro doubled down on his refusal to concede, insisting Monday that he will push forward with legal petitions to annul the election.
“It is impossible to recognize the elections under these conditions. I am going to request that these elections be annulled,” Bolsonaro said in a statement, alleging "unprecedented abuses of political and economic power.”
In a video message addressed to his supporters Monday, the senator announced plans to leverage conservative gains in the National Congress.
He vowed to mobilize the right-wing bloc to transform the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate into a "fortress against the barbarism" he claims will define Lula's upcoming term.
Costa Neto highlighted the PL-led coalition's substantial congressional footprint, which includes 121 federal deputies, 29 senators and six state governorships.
While the PL leadership indicated that it will pursue grievance mechanisms regarding government spending through formal institutional channels, it stopped short of endorsing Bolsonaro’s demand for a complete annulment of the vote.

Electronics, high-tech manufacturing drive double-digit growth in China's industrial profits
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:20:28 CST
13:20:28 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Robust growth in the electronics industry and high-tech manufacturing helped drive a double-digit increase in the profits of China's major industrial firms during the first nine months of 2026, official data showed Tuesday.
Profits of major industrial firms rose 15.5 percent year on year to 6.03 trillion yuan (about 897.7 billion U.S. dollars) during the January-September period, maintaining double-digit growth since the beginning of the year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
In September alone, industrial profits increased 14.4 percent year on year.
The electronics industry emerged as a key growth driver, with profits doubling from a year earlier and contributing 9.6 percentage points to the overall increase in industrial profits.
Meanwhile, profits in high-tech manufacturing surged 52 percent year on year, outpacing the overall industrial average by 36.5 percentage points, as demand in areas such as AI computing power and data center infrastructure continued to expand.
In the first three quarters, high-tech manufacturing accounted for 25.5 percent of the total profits generated by China's major industrial firms, up 6.2 percentage points from a year earlier.
As high-end manufacturing continues to advance and new quality productive forces take shape at a faster pace, China's industrial sector is steadily shifting toward a more advanced and innovation-driven structure, NBS statistician Yu Weining noted.
Earlier data showed China's industrial sector continued to gain momentum in the first three quarters of 2026, with the value-added industrial output increasing by 5.3 percent year on year. ■

China calls for ending conflicts to better protect children
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:19:56 CST
13:19:56 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy said Monday that the most direct and effective way of protecting children is to end conflict and violence, calling for greater efforts to promote peace.
China urges all parties to conflicts to abide by the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, cease hostilities, strictly fulfill their obligations under international law, and refrain from attacking civilians and civilian facilities, such as children and schools, said Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations.
"All parties should follow the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security, properly address differences through dialogue and consultation, and promote political settlement of hotspot issues," he told the Security Council.
There is also a need to step up humanitarian support and improve access to conflict-affected areas to ensure that children receive the necessary assistance and psychological support in a timely manner, he said.
Fu stressed the need to improve protection mechanisms and strengthen accountability.
Noting that children in the occupied Palestinian territory, Haiti, and elsewhere are on the front lines of conflict and violence and have long suffered grave violations and threats, Fu said China supports the Security Council in resorting to necessary tools to ensure strict accountability for wanton abuses of children.
China supports Vanessa Frazier, the UN secretary-general's special representative for children and armed conflict, in fulfilling her mandate and duties, and calls for stronger UN monitoring and reporting, he said.
Development is the fundamental solution to the root causes of conflict, said Fu. "We need to support the governments of the countries concerned in guaranteeing basic needs such as food, education, health care, and employment, and in improving the environment for children's growth and development, so that children can break free from the shadow of war and the cycle of violence."
China welcomes Jainaba Jagne's appointment as the first Special Envoy for Children Affected by Armed Conflict of the African Union (AU), and supports the United Nations in working closely with the AU to help conflict-affected countries strengthen their capacity to protect children, he said.
China will continue to assist developing countries to the best of its ability, including those in Africa. China stands ready to work with the international community to silence the guns and strengthen support and assistance, so that children around the world can grow up healthy and strong in an environment of peace and stability, and create a better future, said Fu. ■

Instagram ramps up video strategy in escalating TikTok, YouTube rivalry

Instagram ramps up video strategy in escalating TikTok, YouTube rivalry
- Instagram is expanding video with Features, Series and a revamped Live tool to compete with TikTok and YouTube, and to build a bigger social entertainment platform.
- Reels has driven record engagement, but longer videos need new formats because clips over three minutes are not pushed to new viewers.
- Instagram is also testing TV viewing and plans wider rollout, but leaders say the TV push is still early and will take years.
AI generated
Meta’s Instagram is pushing deeper into video with new products to help it compete more aggressively with TikTok and Google’s YouTube, and lay the foundation for its big swing in television.
The new products include Features, which are horizontal videos of as long as 90 minutes, and Series, designed for episodic, short-form microdramas. The company is also rebooting Instagram Live, which has been around for a decade, to make the streaming feature more ubiquitous and discoverable across the app, even to non-followers, in the Reels tab.
“Our goal is really to be the best place for social entertainment,” said Tessa Lyons, Instagram’s vice-president of product overseeing the video expansion under Instagram chief Adam Mosseri. “To do that well, we need to broaden the way that we enable people to tell stories through video and enable audiences to discover them.” A huge part of that is TV, she added, where people are spending more time streaming videos – especially creator-led content.
The shift comes as Instagram is seeing all-time highs in engagement driven mainly by video, Meta chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg said when the company reported third-quarter earnings on Oct 21. At the same time, the platform, which first rose to prominence as a photo-sharing app, faces intensifying competition with TikTok and YouTube and has been somewhat slower in developing a more entertainment-focused strategy.
TikTok has already helped popularise microdramas, short-form soap operas for smartphones that took off in China and are gaining traction across the West, while YouTube recently introduced Shorts series to help creators organise their work into episodes and seasons. YouTube has been investing for close to a decade in its “living room” strategy, aimed at getting YouTube videos onto every screen in the home, making the video giant all but synonymous with modern-day TV.
Lyons acknowledged “we are in a very competitive market”, but said Instagram has a unique advantage because it was built more on social connections and the premise of sharing with friends, a key value-add for creators eager to grow and nurture relationships with their fanbases.
“Creators don’t just want to put content out in the world,” she said. “They want to feel like they’re building a community around that content that’s deeply engaged with them.”
The success of Instagram Reels has also set up the platform to excel in other video formats, Lyons added, noting that people reshare those short, vertical video clips in direct messages 4.5 billion times a day.
But Reels has a key limitation: Those over three minutes long are not recommended to new audiences, so comedians, podcasters, video bloggers and others have had to drive viewers off Instagram to keep them watching and engaging with content. Features is aimed at solving that problem by keeping users on-platform and enabling creators to experiment more freely with the length of their videos on both mobile and TV. Beginning Oct 26, a beta version was available to tens of thousands of creators in the US.
Series, the medium tailored to booming short-form dramas, is in testing with a smaller subset of creators in the US, Mexico and India. Instagram’s surfacing of live streams in recommendations and Reels is also in testing, set to launch in Indonesia and Brazil by the end of 2026. Within the app, all of these formats will eventually be shown alongside Reels.
Instagram has been pursuing TV as a big swing in the US since 2025, when it unveiled its first dedicated TV app allowing users to watch Reels on a larger screen. Since beginning as a test on Amazon’s Fire TV platform in December, those efforts have expanded to Samsung and Google TV. Instagram for TV launched on Oct 26 on Apple TV in the US, eventually moving beyond Reels alone to include the newly announced video formats, and soon, viewers will also be able to use their phones as remotes. Still, Lyons cautioned, “the TV bet is really early” and will be a multi-year journey.
“We are not at a stage right now where we’re trying to grow the TV bet – we’re really trying to figure out what’s working for audiences on TV – but we do think that that’s going to be a key part of the next few years of Instagram”, including outside the US in the near future, she said.
“If behaviour (and) the consumption of these platforms are moving to TV,” Mosseri said in 2025 in an interview with Bloomberg, “then we need to move to TV too.” BLOOMBERG

Indonesia Announces New Measures to Improve Stock Market Transparency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:14:00 UTC
13:14:00 KST

Indonesia yesterday introduced a host of additional measures to address stock market manipulation, in order to stave off a potential downgrade of the country’s investment status by the global index provider MSCI.
On October 16, MSCI announced that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status” due to its lack of action to increase the transparency of its stock market. The announcement led to an immediate plunge in the Indonesian stock market, which shed 15 percent of its value over two days of trading.
Amid a defiant response from President Prabowo Subianto, who last week accused MSCI of trying to “intimidate” Indonesia, Indonesian officials have promised action to address the index provider’s concerns. Last week, the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) said that it would exclude stocks with high shareholding concentrations from its main Jakarta index starting on November 2.
At a press conference yesterday, IDX chief Jeffrey Hendrik said it plans to expand the membership of a committee that will come up with a list of stocks with high shareholder concentration to include independent parties, Reuters reported. These could include a number of Indonesian academics as well as F. Taylor Chapman, an American businessman currently serving on the board of the new Indonesian state investment fund Danantara, who will act as a representative of foreign investors.
Hendrik said that the IDX also plans to launch investigations when it detects possible coordinated trading aimed at manipulating share prices. It will also freeze suspicious investor accounts.
“We encourage the IDX to strengthen the mechanism and methodology of trading supervision, including its capacity to identify patterns of irregular transactions, detect coordinated trading and strengthen the mechanism to respond to such events,” said Hasan Fawzi, the financial regulator’s capital market supervisor, according to Reuters.
The Indonesian announcements reflect the seriousness of MSCI’s threat to recategorize Indonesia as a “standalone” market. Given its status as the primary benchmark for institutional investors, such a downgrade could potentially trigger billions of dollars in capital outflows.
MSCI initially threatened to downgrade Indonesia in January, but only to “frontier market” status, which is a rung above the “standalone market” category. At the time, it expressed concerns with a host of issues, including coordinated share purchases, the high concentration of ownership in certain companies, and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.
Whether these measures are enough to stave off a downgrade when MSCI makes its determination next June remains to be seen. After MSCI’s January announcement, Indonesia announced a long list of reforms to address MSCI’s concerns, including a doubling of the minimum free float for listed companies to 15 percent. Top executives of the exchange and regulatory body also stepped down.
However, in its October 16 announcement, MSCI said that despite these promised reforms, “significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement.” For this reason, it said, “a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.”
As Larry Luckey wrote in these pages last week, Jakarta’s proposed reforms are all sensible, “but announcing new regulations and actually enforcing them are two different things.”

Israelis vote in tense election seen as a referendum on Netanyahu
Israelis are voting Tuesday in the first general elections since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu facing a fight for political survival. The vote follows three years of regional wars, with Netanyahu running neck and neck with centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot.

Israelis are voting in a pivotal election Tuesday as their country is embroiled in unresolved wars, still reeling from Hamas' 2023 attack and deeply divided over the character of the state and the right person to lead it.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces off against an array of parties seeking to oust the longtime leader from power. Opinion polls have suggested a tight race with his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Read moreIsraeli candidate Eisenkot pledges to unite country as Netanyahu deems him 'soft' on Iran
In Israel's fragmented parliamentary politics, no single party has ever won an outright parliamentary majority, so political leaders must forge coalitions.

But in a close race in which nonaligned Arab parties are pushing for heavy turnout, there is a chance that neither Netanyahu's religious and ultranationalist coalition nor the group of parties looking to remove him has enough support to win a parliamentary majority. That could set off weeks of negotiations before a leader is declared.
Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if they agree to support one candidate over the other.
Read moreJewish ‘supercop’ runs on Arab ticket in Israeli polls – and sparks a storm
Already, some emotions were high as polls opened. In Kiryat Shmona, a Netanyahu stronghold near the border with Lebanon, one man kicked and tore down a poster of Eisenkot.
Hanging over the election are lingering tensions with Iran. Netanyahu ramped up threats against the country ahead of the vote. He appeared in a video this week standing beside a missile-defense battery and warned Tehran it would face “a devastating blow” if it attacked Israel.
Referendum on Netanyahu's lengthy leadership
The election is Israel's first national vote since the October 7, 2023, attack that sparked the war in Gaza and related conflicts across the region. In Tel Aviv, families of some of those killed on October 7 or former hostages held a moment of silence before polls opened. “Remember all those whose voices are no more,” said Yona Adam, whose daughter Mapal Adam was killed.
The vote serves not only as a referendum on Netanyahu's lengthy leadership but also on what kind of country Israel should be – heavily influenced by religious and nationalist forces, or more firmly anchored in liberal and secular values.
Read more‘I don't recognise the country I grew up in anymore’: Some Israelis tempted by exile
At stake is the fate of a country whose policies and leadership are being sharply criticised by its traditional allies. Since the 2023 attack, Israel has found itself increasingly isolated over its conduct in Gaza and in the occupied West Bank, where violence by Jewish settlers has intensified. Public support among Americans has plummeted and stalwart partners in Europe and elsewhere have slapped sanctions on Israel in recent months.
For Israelis, the election presents a chance at charting the country's course after Netanyahu's latest, and especially turbulent, four-year term.
Netanyahu's supporters see him as a steady hand and a consummate statesman who they believe has triumphantly guided Israel through multiple wars. They think he is protecting Israel’s Jewish identity while keeping in check what they see as an interventionist judiciary.
His Israeli detractors see him as a polarizing leader who, beset by an ongoing corruption trial, dragged on the war in Gaza and its hostage crisis for political reasons. They say he is undermining Israel's independent judiciary and weakening its democratic underpinnings. And they accuse him of abetting a system that has allowed ultra-Orthodox religious Jews to avoid enlistment in Israel's compulsory military.
Read more'The Bibi Files': Documentary reveals the police interrogations behind Netanyahu’s graft trial
Eisenkot is viewed by supporters as a capable leader with sterling security credentials who, along with his likely governing partners, could act as a bulwark against creeping illiberalism. As someone personally touched by the conflict – his son and two nephews were killed in Gaza – his backers believe that he feels deeply the pain that still courses through Israel three years after the attacks.
Parties that would likely throw their support behind Eisenkot have vowed to improve Israel's international standing and work to conscript ultra-Orthodox men while bolstering the independence of the judiciary.
'Not afraid to take action'
Zipporah Bennett, an 85-year-old retiree, said she was voting for Netanyahu "because he has had the experience of navigating the country through a lot of difficult seasons".
"He has the full support of the American government," she said, "and I believe he's a man who's not afraid to take action."
Netanyahu returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket.
The opposition has scorned the premier for his backing of ultra-Orthodox parties fighting to keep exemptions for religious Jewish students from drafting into the military, which faces personnel shortages.
But one of the biggest criticisms levelled at Netanyahu is his failure to take responsibility for the October 7 attack, the deadliest day in the country's history.
Eisenkot, 66, has pledged to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the attack, something Netanyahu's government has resisted.
Seeking to unseat the premier is an informal bloc of parties led by Eisenkot's Yashar and spanning from the right to the centre-left.
Eisenkot has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state and expressed support for Israeli settlements, but has promised to crack down on violent settlers.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu have publicly said they would partner with the predominantly Arab lists, which represent some 21 percent of Israel's population and who could become kingmakers if the results are as close as expected.
Final results could take days to trickle in and it is highly unlikely that any single party will come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member parliament.
Cobbling together any coalition could take weeks or months, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.

Election Day 2026 is a day for democracy and a chance for unity - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:09:34 UTC
13:09:34 KST

Israelis heading to the polls on Tuesday will be making choices shaped by three extraordinary years. The October 7 massacre, the wars that ensued, and the strain on families, soldiers, and communities have changed the questions voters are asking of their leaders.
Political disagreements have become deeply personal, and the next government will inherit decisions with consequences far beyond one Knesset term.
Even so, Election Day deserves a measure of joy.
Across Israel, citizens will walk into polling stations, choose a ballot, and exercise their democratic right. Some will vote with conviction, others with reservations.
First-time voters will join parents and grandparents who have cast ballots through decades of upheaval. The results will divide winners from losers, but the act of voting belongs to everyone.
The agenda waiting for the next government ranges from accountability for October 7 to Israel’s security and place in the world.
One of the next government’s first tests will be how to investigate the failures that allowed Hamas’s October 7 attack.
Demands for a state commission of inquiry have become a central election issue, particularly for bereaved families who want answers and accountability. The argument over the form of that investigation will not disappear when the votes are counted.
The dispute over haredi military service is equally consequential. After years of fighting and repeated reserve call-ups, the burden of service weighs heavily on many households. Parties remain divided over exemptions, enforcement, and the kind of draft legislation the next coalition should pursue. What leaders agree to in coalition talks will affect both the IDF and Israeli society.
Decisions await on the future of Gaza and the peace plan
Beyond Israel’s borders, decisions await on the future of Gaza and the peace plan intended to shape its recovery and security. Israelis must consider what arrangements could prevent Hamas from again threatening their communities, who should govern Gaza, and what role international partners should play.
The Palestinian question also remains unresolved. Debates over a possible Palestinian statehood, settlement expansion, and violence in the West Bank carry direct implications for Israel’s security and relations with its allies.
International pressure, including the threat or use of sanctions, adds another dimension to choices that cannot be postponed indefinitely.
This also explains why the ability to vote should inspire pride. After so much loss and uncertainty, Israelis still have the power to influence who will make those decisions. A citizen can fiercely disagree with a neighbor over Gaza, conscription, or the government’s record and still respect that neighbor’s equal place at the ballot box.
The Jerusalem Post also calls for a modest widening of the political camps and the formation of a broad Zionist government. Israel’s challenges demand leaders willing to work across familiar dividing lines.
Cooperation will require difficult compromises, but the next coalition should strive to represent a wider range of Israelis and offer the country a measure of stability.
That appeal should remain in voters’ minds beyond Election Day.
Once the ballots have been counted and the parties know how many seats they have won, the democratic marathon enters its next stage. Seat totals will establish the balance of power in the Knesset, but coalition negotiations will determine the priorities, partnerships, and commitments of the government that emerges.
The public should remain part of that conversation. Israelis can continue asking their elected representatives what they intend to do about an October 7 inquiry, military service, Gaza, and relations with the Palestinians and the wider world. They can make clear that a broad Zionist coalition, if it is achievable, should be pursued with seriousness and goodwill.
Israelis should allow themselves to enjoy the day
Results may come quickly; building a government will take longer. Its quality will be judged by the agreements reached and the decisions that follow, long after election-night speeches have faded.
For now, Israelis should allow themselves to enjoy the day. Bring children to the polling station. Talk with friends and relatives, including those voting differently. Appreciate the chance to participate in a national decision even when the outcome is uncertain.
Cast a ballot with hope, then keep paying attention as the next government takes shape.

Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:02:26 UTC
13:02:26 KST

Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience - KNAW
- Summary:
- Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.
- Share:
Some people have the brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease but never develop dementia. While others experience worsening memory and thinking problems, these individuals remain mentally sharp despite signs of the disease in their brains. Scientists have long struggled to explain why.
Now, researchers at the Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience have uncovered a promising clue. Their findings suggest that a rare group of brain cells, known as immature neurons, may behave differently in people who resist Alzheimer's symptoms. Rather than simply replacing damaged cells, these neurons could help protect the brain from the harmful effects of the disease.
This remarkable ability is known as cognitive resilience. It describes how some people maintain their memory and thinking abilities even when their brains show signs of damage or disease.
"Around 30 percent of older adults who develop Alzheimer's disease never experience its symptoms," says Evgenia Salta, senior author of the research. "We really don't know why. That's a big mystery, and a very important one."
Understanding this mystery could transform how scientists approach Alzheimer's, shifting attention from what causes brain cells to deteriorate toward what allows certain brains to remain healthy and functional.
Can the Aging Brain Repair Itself?
One possible explanation for cognitive resilience is that some brains have a greater ability to repair or protect themselves as Alzheimer's progresses.
"Perhaps they can add new brain cells to a network that is degenerating," Salta says.
This possibility involves a biological process called adult neurogenesis, which refers to the production of new nerve cells (neurons) in an adult brain. Neurons are specialized cells that transmit information throughout the nervous system, allowing us to think, learn, remember, and respond to our surroundings.
Scientists have established that adult neurogenesis occurs in several animal species. Whether it continues to happen in the adult human brain, however, has been a subject of scientific debate for decades.
If the human brain can produce new neurons later in life, those cells might help maintain important connections as aging and disease damage existing networks. However, finding immature neurons does not necessarily prove that they were recently formed.
To investigate this possibility, Salta and her colleagues examined donated human brain tissue obtained through the Netherlands Brain Bank, a research resource that collects and preserves brain samples.
The researchers compared three groups: people without detectable brain pathology, patients who developed Alzheimer's dementia, and individuals whose brains showed Alzheimer's pathology but who remained cognitively resilient.
The team concentrated on a small region within the brain's memory center, an area believed to be among the few locations where new neurons might develop.
Finding the relevant cells was far from straightforward.
"These cells are extremely rare, so we had to develop new ways to find them," Salta says. "We really zoomed in on the exact spot where we expected them to be."
The researchers also developed new approaches to analyzing their data, allowing them to identify the cells more precisely without relying heavily on assumptions drawn from animal studies.
Scientists Find Immature Neurons in Brains Over 80
The search revealed something remarkable. Immature neurons were present across all three groups, including in the brains of older adults.
These cells resemble neurons that have not yet fully matured, suggesting that the aging brain may retain cellular features associated with development and adaptability.
"Even at an average age of over 80, we still found these immature neurons in all groups," Salta says.
But the most intriguing discovery came when researchers compared the brains of people who had developed dementia with those who had remained mentally sharp despite Alzheimer's pathology.
Initially, the scientists expected resilient individuals to have substantially more immature neurons. If these cells help replace damaged neurons, having greater numbers might explain why some brains withstand the disease.
Instead, the difference in cell numbers was much smaller than anticipated.
That unexpected result pointed toward another explanation. The important distinction might not be how many immature neurons a brain contains, but how those cells respond when the brain comes under attack.
A Hidden Defense Against Alzheimer's Damage
When the team examined the activity of immature neurons more closely, they identified striking differences between the groups.
In cognitively resilient individuals, the cells showed signs of activating biological processes associated with survival and protection against damage.
"In resilient individuals, these cells seem to activate programs that help them survive and cope with damage," Salta says. "We also see lower signals related to inflammation and cell death."
Inflammation is part of the body's normal defense system, but when it becomes persistent in the brain, it can contribute to damage and interfere with communication between neurons. Cell death, meanwhile, gradually disrupts the networks responsible for memory and thinking.
The findings suggest that immature neurons in resilient brains may be better equipped to withstand these harmful conditions.
More surprisingly, their role might extend beyond protecting themselves.
"It might not be (only) about replacing lost neurons," Salta explains. "It could be that these cells support the surrounding tissue and help the brain stay functional and 'youthful'. They may act as a sort of fertilizer in a garden that has started falling apart."
In other words, rather than serving only as replacements for dying neurons, immature cells could potentially help maintain the environment surrounding existing brain cells.
Such support might allow neural networks to continue functioning even as Alzheimer's related damage accumulates.
Why Scientists Are Cautious About the Discovery
Although the results offer an intriguing explanation for cognitive resilience, Salta emphasizes that the researchers have not established exactly what these immature neurons do.
Their conclusions about the cells' possible protective roles are based on patterns observed in brain tissue, not direct experiments demonstrating those functions.
"We assume the cells' function based on the data, but we cannot confirm it in this type of study," she explains.
That distinction is particularly important because research on adult neurogenesis has attracted considerable public attention, sometimes leading to claims that go beyond what scientists have demonstrated.
The presence of immature neurons does not establish that new neurons are continuously being produced in older humans, nor does it prove that these cells are responsible for preventing dementia.
Other biological mechanisms almost certainly contribute to cognitive resilience as well.
"This is one piece of a very large puzzle," Salta concludes. "There will never be just one factor that explains resilience."
Could Alzheimer's Research Shift Toward Protecting the Brain?
The findings raise a broader question about aging: Why do some people's brains remain relatively stable while others experience progressive cognitive decline?
"Somewhere along this trajectory, there's a kind of decision point," Salta explains. "Some people remain stable, others develop dementia. We want to understand what drives that difference."
To explore this further, the researchers plan to investigate how immature neurons communicate and interact with neighboring brain cells. Understanding those relationships may reveal whether the cells actively contribute to resilience and how their protective responses might work.
The research also reflects a growing change in how scientists think about Alzheimer's disease.
Traditionally, much of the field has focused on understanding the processes that damage the brain, including the accumulation of abnormal proteins and the loss of neurons. Increasingly, researchers are also asking why some brains remain functional despite those changes.
By identifying the mechanisms behind this natural resistance, scientists hope to uncover new ways to preserve memory and cognitive abilities as people age.
"Cognitive resilience is extremely exciting," Salta says. "If we understand what protects these brains, it could eventually lead to new therapeutic strategies."
Although practical treatments remain a distant possibility, the discovery suggests that even in old age, the human brain may possess protective abilities that scientists are only beginning to understand.

He insisted that territorial questions could be addressed only by national leaders, while technical delegations could negotiate other aspects of a settlement.
Zelensky said US negotiators had presented several proposals following talks in Oslo on Oct. 20, which American envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently took to Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
He emphasized that the document was not a completed peace plan submitted to Putin for approval.
“Russia does not decide,” Zelensky said, explaining that the proposals were intended for discussion among the parties involved in ending the war.
He added that Russian demands could not determine Ukraine’s security arrangements.
“The limitation of our army and Ukraine’s neutrality are not up for discussion,” he said.
Ukraine wants to retain 800,000 troops
Zelensky said the size of Ukraine’s postwar armed forces would remain an internal decision, dependent on financing and the security arrangements eventually agreed upon.
“If I have enough money, I want to maintain an army of 800,000,” he said.
He stressed that he would not negotiate the size of Ukraine’s military with Russia or, for that matter, with the US.
The president said NATO membership could change Ukraine’s military requirements, but the decision would depend on the alliance’s readiness to help finance and equip Ukrainian forces.
Without NATO membership, Ukraine would require other credible guarantees alongside a large, well-funded army equipped with modern weapons and technology.
He said Washington’s proposals also covered economic questions, reconstruction and territorial matters, although he declined to reveal all details because of understandings with American negotiators.
US says Putin agreed to November trilateral talks
Zelensky said the Oslo negotiations had also helped reopen a diplomatic channel with Moscow.
According to the Ukrainian president, US officials traveled to St. Petersburg after the meeting and subsequently informed Kyiv that Putin had agreed in principle to trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US in November.
Abu Dhabi was among the locations discussed, although Zelensky said the talks could also take place elsewhere in the Middle East or Europe.
Kyiv wants European representatives involved and hopes technical negotiations can lead to a meeting between national leaders.
Zelensky said such a meeting could address territorial disputes, while other discussions could explore an energy ceasefire, a maritime ceasefire to protect Ukrainian exports and imports, and further prisoner exchanges.
He welcomed the return of 270 Ukrainian prisoners but said a comprehensive all-for-all exchange would require negotiations at the leaders’ level.
The president said Russia was also seeking security guarantees in discussions with Washington. He acknowledged that he did not know the full details of Putin’s conversations with American envoys, including whether economic issues influenced Moscow’s position.
Oslo talks restore intelligence and satellite capabilities
Zelensky described the Oct. 20 Oslo meeting as productive, saying it helped resolve two of Ukraine’s three immediate disputes with Washington.
He identified the problems as limited US intelligence sharing on Russian ballistic missile launches, restrictions affecting Starlink and Starshield satellite capabilities, and shortages of air defense systems.
According to Zelensky, intelligence sharing on ballistic threats had been fully restored, while satellite capabilities returned to the speeds required by Ukrainian forces.
He said that during overnight checks with defense officials, the satellite service had resumed operations at speeds corresponding to 420 kilometers (261 miles) per hour, following earlier restrictions.
Ukraine’s military welcomed the restoration, he said.
The president thanked American officials and Ukraine’s negotiating team for resolving both issues, adding that public attention may also have helped.
However, the shortage of air defense weapons remained unresolved.
Zelensky said the Oslo meeting had produced tangible results but warned that the situation could change, particularly amid US domestic political developments.
Witkoff and Kushner did not visit Bucha
Zelensky also disclosed that he had invited US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to visit Bucha during their earlier trip to Kyiv, but they did not go.
The president said he had taken them to St. Sophia Cathedral to show them Ukraine’s historical heritage and the reality of life in a country resisting Russia’s invasion.
He wanted the American delegation to experience Ukraine firsthand rather than rely on narratives emerging from its contacts with Moscow.
Zelensky said he had also hoped to show the envoys Bucha, the Kyiv suburb where Russian atrocities occurred in 2022.
“We offered,” Zelensky said when asked whether the Americans had been invited.
He said he wanted them to see both the consequences of Russian occupation and how communities were rebuilding.
“They did not find the time, but they found time for many other things,” he said.
The president acknowledged that the reasons for not visiting Bucha could have varied.
Nevertheless, he said showing the envoys Kyiv’s historic sites and the resilience of its residents had helped create an emotional connection with Ukraine.
He noted that St. Sophia Cathedral predates Moscow itself, underscoring Ukraine’s long history and independent identity.

Dammed Between Energy and Water Scarcity: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the Nile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Every large dam divides as much as it connects, and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is no exception. A monumental feat of architecture and engineering, the mega-dam has brought everyone together, for better or worse, to interrogate who gets to declare sovereignty over the riches of the river, be it water or momentum, and to challenge colonial-era Nile treaties.
Inaugurated in September 2025, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, or GERD, is a grand concrete structure on the Blue Nile in western Ethiopia within the Benishangul-Gumuz region, just 30 kilometers upstream along the river and east of the border with Sudan. It is built as a major source of hydroelectric power, being consistently ranked in the top 3-30 globally, and symbolizes Ethiopia's national sovereignty, rise to exponential economic development, and technological self-determination. So, why has it become the center of a protracted dispute over regional water security and international law between Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt?
The Architecture of the Dam
Related Article
Ecologies of Repair: Reconciling Our Relationship with Water
To understand the debate, the architecture must first be outlined. The GERD, a gravity mega-dam built under the management of civil engineering company Webuild (née Salini Impregilo) for the Ethiopian Electric Power, is comprised of a roller-compacted concrete (RCC) main dam, a concrete-faced rockfill saddle dam, and a system of spillways and hydroelectric power stations at the base. Designed for a 6,000 MW capacity, documented as 5,150 MW in recent literature, and meant to double the country's electricity generation, the dam is 1.8 kilometers long and rises to a 175-meter height. The main dam, located only 14 kilometers from Sudan, holds back a reservoir that can contain 74 billion cubic meters of water — named Lake Nigat — that is 3.5 times the surface area of Addis Ababa.
Moreover, the 5-kilometer-long, 50-meter-high saddle dam crescents a lower area of the surrounding reservoir basin for passive water retention, where the average annual outflow of the entire reservoir amounts to approximately 50 billion cubic meters of water. The two hydroelectric power stations, flanking the river bank on both sides and consisting of 13 Francis turbines, produce an average of 15,700 GWh/year.
The system of spillways provides safety for the dam by discharging floodwater without causing damage as well as maintaining the reservoir level below the designated threshold. They include a main service-gated spillway, a free-flow crest spillway, and an emergency side-channel ungated spillway capable of handling severe flooding.
Webuild's internal laboratories tested and manufactured the materials for long-term structural stability and mechanical performance. This was achieved through an advanced, internally and internationally researched RCC mix designed with a low cement, low water content, and extended setting times. In addition, an integrated network of galleries in the main dam accommodates high-sensitivity precision instruments including vertical pendula, to monitor hydrostatic pressure, structural shifts, joint integrity, and turbine performance in real-time. This continuous operational data is channeled directly into a centralized database at the right bank control center, allowing engineers to conduct proactive maintenance and ensure maximum structural reliability.
The structural resistance of its reservoir allows the GERD to alter seasonal water patterns, manage floods, and generate hydropower. However, considering its location on an international and transboundary river system, filling the reservoir raises questions regarding water requirements and storage timelines. The project's multi-stage filling cycles have proceeded unilaterally, without transparency between the upstream country and its downstream neighbors, fueling geopolitical tensions. Operating the GERD depends on hydrological regulation, as lack of coordination in operations and transparent data-sharing could disrupt existing downstream infrastructure — a prime example being Sudan's Roseires Dam, due to its proximity to the GERD.
Egypt argues that Ethiopia's unilateral operations can cut down water flow, which is a national threat to its people and economy. It also supports its claims by addressing Ethiopia's "unilateral exploitation" of its transboundary waters in the Omo, Jubba and Shebelle basins, and the harm it causes its neighbors, Somalia and Kenya.
Resolving this issue peacefully would foster vital regional cooperation on the White Nile too, where uncoordinated dam releases from Uganda have triggered downstream flooding in South Sudan, increasing people's displacement and disease outbreaks.
But how did we get here, anyway?
Historical Hegemony
During the initial survey for the GERD, carried out in the 1960s, Ethiopia lacked the internal stability to progress with it. It was kept discreet until sufficient work was done because it was known that its development would carry a heavy geopolitical weight, especially on downstream countries in the basin.
This weight is amplified, considering the Nile Basin countries are 11, some of which are upstream, downstream, or both in relation to other countries. The solely upstream nations include Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, while the sole downstream nation is Egypt. Sudan and South Sudan are both upstream and downstream, with South Sudan being upstream relative to Sudan and Egypt, and downstream relative to Uganda, since the White Nile is sourced by rivers flowing into Lake Victoria. The Blue Nile, supplying 85% of the Nile River, originates at Lake Tana in the Ethiopian Highlands, where it flows into Sudan and finally converges with the White Nile at Khartoum to form the main Nile River flowing through Egypt into the Mediterranean Sea.
Historically, Nile Basin hydropolitics have been shaped by Egypt's hydrohegemony, a legal history formed from a century of colonial-era 'treaties' — the Nile Treaties — towards a multilateral agreement that still conflicts with water rights. The 1902 Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement originally secured Egypt's control of the Nile by restricting Ethiopia from modifying the Blue Nile without British consent. This was further amplified by the 1929 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty — an exchange of notes more than a treaty, which essentially allowed Egypt to veto upstream projects or embark on unilateral development — and the subsequent 1959 Nile Water Agreement, which granted exclusive annual allocations of 55.5 billion cubic meters to Egypt and 18.5 billion cubic meters to Sudan. Reality, however, is more nuanced: while these inequitable, colonial-era treaties should be abolished or reassessed, Egypt remains a water-scarce nation, where the Nile supplies more than 90% of its freshwater needs, and approximately 95% of its population lives along its course.
Also, unlike other riparian nations in the basin — excluding Eritrea, an observer in the Nile Basin Initiative, due to its minimal hydrological footprint, and Sudan, facing severe infrastructure collapse — Egypt relies on the Nile as an existential lifeline. Since the GERD sits on the Blue Nile, which supplies the vast majority of the Nile's total flow, it signifies a major shift in regional power that ends the 'monopoly' of the river and creates a threat to downstream countries' agriculture and water security, especially during multi-year droughts. To challenge asymmetric control, the Nile Basin Initiative (NBI) was launched in 1999, with the Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) following soon after in 2010, one year before the Renaissance Dam's groundbreaking in 2011.
Preoccupied with the internal politics of the Arab Spring, Egypt was unable to effectively oppose or block the project. Its isolation deepened when Sudan softened its earlier objections into a moderate neutrality. Sudan's position has since shifted repeatedly, from rejection to neutrality or support and back again, driven largely by internal fragmentation and domestic politics. The debate over the dam's benefits and drawbacks has also shaped these shifts. On the one hand, the dam promises more stable irrigation, lower dredging costs, and better flood management. On the other, it carries serious long-term risks: floodplains depleted as sediment builds up in the reservoir basin, disrupted local ecosystems, and a lack of cooperation between the three countries.
The pressure culminated in the 2015 Declaration of Principles on GERD, which remains the primary trilateral framework between Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt. In it, the three countries acknowledged the dam and committed to the principles of international water law. They have still not reached a binding agreement on how the reservoir is filled or on how to manage droughts.
Divisions persist on a wider scale too. When the Nile Basin Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) came into force in October 2024, Egypt and Sudan refused to sign it. Both want to protect their access to a vital resource and the veto rights they claim under colonial-era treaties.
The Architecture of Geopolitics
Concrete structures can control physical water flows, but they rarely can resolve political friction. Ethiopia positions GERD as a shared resource built for its people and neighbors, vowing to export surplus to promote its own economy as well as support the continent, but hydrological uncertainty remains the biggest issue in the absence of a clear, definitive binding agreement meant to operate the dam. An exemplar model for sustainable and equitable transboundary water governance can be found in the Senegal River Basin Development Authority (OMVS) — Organisation pour la mise en valeur du fleuve Sénégal — that utilizes a framework of collaborative benefit-sharing and joint infrastructure ownership.
Ultimately, unlocking the GERD's true potential as a driver of East African economic integration hinges on overcoming impasses to secure its downstream neighbors and provide a new example of equitable water governance, environmental safety and sustained trilateral cooperation. Otherwise, how can shared river basins foster a nation's right to build its economic future against the security of its neighbors?

Taiwan rebuffs China’s commemorations for post-World War Two ‘restoration’ of island
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:59:31 CET
12:59:31 KST

TAIPEI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Taiwan’s defence minister on Tuesday said China was waging “cognitive warfare” after Beijing marked the anniversary of Japan’s handover of the island to Chinese rule with satellite images of Taipei and a military propaganda poster.
Japan took over Taiwan from China’s Qing Dynasty in 1895 and ruled it until 1945, when it transferred the island to the Republic of China government. Both Beijing and Taipei commemorate the event, now in its 81st year.
On Sunday’s anniversary of the handover, China released high-resolution satellite pictures of Taipei, including the train station and the National Palace Museum. The museum holds a vast collection of treasures brought to Taiwan in 1949, when the Republic of China government fled there after losing a civil war to the communists.
The Chinese military’s Eastern Theatre Command also published a poster with a map of Taiwan superimposed on images of fighter jets and warships, with the title “Remember the history of the restoration”.
Speaking to reporters at parliament in Taipei, Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said China was using the anniversary to carry out “cognitive warfare”.
“We must stress that the People’s Republic of China was established in 1949. The War of Resistance has absolutely nothing to do with the People’s Republic of China — this is a clear, objective fact,” he added, referring to World War Two and the Japanese invasion of China which began in 1931.
Taiwan’s military marked a different anniversary, the start of an unsuccessful late-October 1949 invasion attempt by the People’s Liberation Army of Kinmen, islands which sit next to the Chinese coast and remain under Taiwan control to this day.
Koo said that was a date much more worthy of remembering.
“This reminds us once again that China’s determination to annex the Republic of China and Taiwan by force has never changed. We should be even more vigilant,” he added.
Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control. The democratically elected government in Taipei rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims.
Neither government formally recognises the other, and their shared World War Two history is a frequent source of tension.
(Reporting by Ben Blanchard; Editing by Saad Sayeed)
