TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Wei Chuan Dragons defeated the CTBC Brothers 6-0 in Game 6 of the Taiwan Series at the Taipei Dome on Monday, securing their sixth Chinese Professional Baseball League championship with a 4-2 series victory.
Starting pitcher Cristopher Mercedes delivered a dominant performance, throwing eight scoreless innings, striking out six, walking two, and surrendering just two hits. Relievers Lin Tzu-yu (林子昱) and Lin Kai-wei (林凱威) combined to finish the shutout in the ninth inning, per CNA.
The Dragons won the first three games of the best-of-seven series before the Brothers rallied to win the next two, forcing a sixth game. The Dragons broke open a 1-0 game with five runs in the bottom of the eighth, including a two-run home run by catcher Jiang Shao-hong (蔣少宏).
The victory marked the Dragons’ sixth Taiwan Series title overall and their second since returning to top-flight competition in 2021. The team previously won championships in 1990, 1997, 1998, and 1999 before disbanding, then claimed its fifth title in 2023.
Manager Yeh Chun-chang (葉君璋) secured his third championship as a manager and his second with the Dragons since their return. His championship record also includes titles won during his playing career.
Yeh became emotional while speaking to reporters after the game, saying the team’s success stemmed from everyone’s efforts to improve the club.
“This team has achieved good results because everyone worked together. Everyone and every aspect of the team tried to make this team better,” he said. “Thinking about all of this, it’s impossible not to be emotional.”
Mercedes was named Taiwan Series Most Valuable Player after winning Games 2 and 6. Across his two starts, he pitched 14 innings and allowed one earned run, finishing with a 0.64 earned run average.
The Dominican pitcher did not allow a hit until the sixth inning of Game 6. After previously pitching for Japan’s Yomiuri Giants and Taiwan’s Uni-Lions, he achieved his championship goal with the Dragons.
“This game was the best I have ever pitched in my career,” Mercedes said. “I am so excited. I have never won a championship like this before.”
Dragons center fielder Kuo Tien-hsin (郭天信) said the experience of winning the 2023 championship had changed how he approached this year’s title run. He hoped to help younger teammates manage their nerves and learn from the experience, per CNA.
“Last time (2023), I just blindly fought hard and eventually won the championship. This time is different,” Kuo said.
“There are quite a few players younger than me on the team, and I hope they can learn something and be less nervous on the field. I am also someone who thinks a lot, and I hope to help them as much as possible.”
This year’s Taiwan Series, dubbed the “Dragon-Elephant showdown,” was the first championship series between the Dragons and Brothers. All six games were held at the Taipei Dome, with the schedule disrupted by a typhoon.
The six games drew a combined attendance of 230,615, setting a record for a single Taiwan Series. Games 1, 4, and 5 each drew 40,000 spectators, per UDN.

New report tracks how Russia helps China build better drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:54:05 UTC
12:54:05 KST

Russia's defense cooperation with China extends far beyond imports of dual-use goods, with evidence pointing to sharing drone design technology, providing testing services, and joint research, according to a new report from U.S. think tank C4ADS.
The report adds to earlier findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China's military collaboration with Russia throughout the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit that investigates security threats, released a report in October that maps lesser-known layers of cooperation between the two countries' defense industries, drawing on Russian trade records, corporate filings, leaked documents, and academic papers.
The investigation found that Russian designs for rocket-launched drones likely helped shape weapons China unveiled in 2025 and that Russian wind tunnels kept testing aircraft models for China's top arms maker after the invasion of Ukraine.
The report also documents how researchers from the two countries are jointly developing algorithms that could underpin combat drone swarms. Moreover, it shows that some suppliers to Russia's defense industry are moving production to China.
Beyond China’s well-documented supplies of components, raw materials and machine tools to the Russian defense industry, and Russia's recently revealed sales of airborne combat vehicles and munitions to China, the two industries increasingly work together further upstream, sharing designs, testing services and research.
read also
Joint drone development
A notable example involves the Science and Production Association SPLAV, Russia's leading maker of multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS). SPLAV is subject to multiple international sanctions and export controls.
Trade records show SPLAV sent Chinese arms giant Norinco technical documents for a "reconnaissance rocket" in 2014–2015, and apparently again in April 2022, less than two months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The rocket is most likely SPLAV's 9M534, which releases a reconnaissance drone in mid-flight.
In March 2025, China unveiled the Feilong 60A, a loitering drone launched from Norinco's SR-5 rocket system and reportedly capable of operating in swarms. Three months later, Norinco tested Sky Eye, a drone fired from a cannon. Both drones are similar to the Russian 9M534.
C4ADS believes the Russian technical documents helped speed up Norinco's work on both systems, though it notes that this conclusion rests mainly on how closely the Chinese and Russian systems resemble each other.
Russia's aerospace testing base is also working for Norinco, which now faces U.S. sanctions and Japanese and Taiwanese export controls.
The Russian state-owned Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI), which is under multiple Western sanctions, tested Chinese scale aircraft models in its wind tunnels and returned them to Norinco with the test data at least nine times between 2022 and 2024. The work comes as Norinco has been expanding into military drones over the past decade.
read also
The cooperation also extends to universities and research institutes. Drones have become a growing focus of joint research by Chinese and Russian scientists, according to C4ADS.
Researchers from the two countries co-authored 86 academic papers on drones and other unmanned systems between 2022 and 2026, an average of about 17 a year. In the dozen years from 2009 to 2021, they produced only 36 such papers, or about three a year.
Evgeny Neretin, a department head at the Moscow Aviation Institute, has co-authored multiple papers with researchers tied to Chinese defense laboratories — labs that also funded the work. The papers deal with algorithms for autonomous drone combat and, more recently, for keeping several drones in formation while they track targets, a likely building block for drone swarms.
In June 2025, the Chinese government approved the creation of a joint educational institute between the Moscow Aviation Institute (sanctioned by the U.S. and EU), and China's military-linked Northwestern Polytechnical University (subject to U.S. and Japanese export controls).
read also
Russian weapons, made in China
The C4ADS report also indicates that some Russian makers of machine tools and chips are moving production to China.
Stankomashstroy, a sanctioned Russian machine-tool maker, plans to move production of advanced five-axis machine tools to an industrial park in China's Shaanxi province.
In 2025, the company sold equipment to the Votkinsk Plant, which builds ballistic missiles, and to Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol, a producer of air defense systems and long-range attack drones.
Illustrating Moscow's reliance on Beijing for chips, Russia's sanctioned state-owned chipmaker Element set up at least four subsidiaries in China in 2025 and began assembling chipsets there. In 2026, Element also bought power electronics intellectual property from the Chinese defense contractor Shijiazhuang Tonhe Electronics.
According to C4ADS, these moves would likely help Element produce military-grade microelectronics despite Western sanctions and export controls. They also fit a recent Kremlin initiative to build up Russia's chip industry.
A deepening alliance
The C4ADS report adds fresh details to previous findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China and Russia's military partnership.
While China officially claims neutrality in Russia's war against Ukraine, Beijing remains Moscow's key trading partner, economic supporter, oil buyer, and provider of dual-use equipment.
According to leaked Rostec documents, China bought Russian airborne combat vehicles, ammunition, and parachute systems after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dozens of Chinese officers and arms industry staff visited Russia during the war to negotiate the deals.
Separate Kyiv Independent investigations found that Chinese suppliers have helped keep Russia's missile and drone production pipelines running.
Machine tools shipped mostly from China fueled the expansion of the Votkinsk Plant, which makes ballistic missiles — including intercontinental ones.
Chinese and Hong Kong companies also supplied parts to the maker of Russia's Lancet attack drones and remain the main channel for Western chips used in Russian weapons.

Did you wake up to an email from Meta recently about your new Meta Account?
Or maybe you received a pop-up message on your Facebook or Instagram account?
Well you're not alone.
In April, Meta announced it would be unifying access to its accounts across the company's apps with some Australians already seeing the changes.
Here's a rundown of what's changed and how it affects you.
What's changing and why?
Meta is changing its current Accounts Centre with an updated system called Meta Account.
The idea of the new system is to bring account management for the company's various apps and devices under one system.
These include:
- Messenger
- Threads
- Meta AI
- AI glasses
- Meta Quest headsets
Meta says WhatsApp will not be added to a Meta Account by default. It will only be in your Meta Account if you choose to add it or you've previously added it to your Accounts Centre.
The switch should not change your profiles or how you use these apps.
Meta says it's designed to make "signing in and managing your settings easier".
Here are a few updates you can expect, according to Meta:
- One password
- Easy set up for new apps and devices
- Boosted security with passkeys
- 24/7 protection
- Personalised security recommendations
Can you opt out?
No.
The change is automatic and being rolled out gradually.
You should receive a notification on your social media platform and email when your account is updated.
But Meta says you can still control and choose which profiles are in your Meta Account at any time.
For example, you can have a Meta Account for your Facebook and another Meta Account for your Instagram profile.
Settings that are specific to each app will also remain independent.
"For example, who can see your Facebook posts is a Facebook setting," Meta's website says.
"Similarly, whether someone can tag you in a photo on Instagram is an Instagram setting."
So how can I keep my apps separate?
Here's a step-by-step guide to create separate Meta Accounts for each of your apps:
- Click your profile picture in the top right of Facebook
- Select Settings & privacy, then click Settings
- Click Meta Account, then click Manage account
- Click Manage on your app of choice
- Click Move out of this Meta Account
When it comes to your passwords, Meta should use the same login info you use currently. It's up to you if you want to create a single password or passkey to use across all apps and devices.
Is it safe to put all your apps under the same Meta Account?
Macquarie University cyber security lecturer Jennifer Williams says while the new account system is likely no more or less secure than the old one, a breach of the new system would have a greater impact.
"An attacker would be able to gain access to all of your private messages on Instagram, Facebook, and, for those who have connected it to their Meta account, WhatsApp," Dr Williams says.
"They could use information from those messages to blackmail the user, impersonate them and send messages to their friends and family, or make posts on their behalf."
But Dr Williams says in the end, security comes down to the user's practices.
"If they do not use strong, unique passwords or two-factor authentication, then there is a greater risk of a breach of their account."
Ryan Ko, director of the Cyber Research Centre at the University of Queensland, says the more significant question is privacy.
"A unified identity makes it easier for Meta to track and profile its users, which then enables them to sell on to their clients," Professor Ko says.
"When Meta Account users' profiles connect activity across services, it creates a richer and more comprehensive profile of the user.
"The security risk is concentrated access; the privacy risk is concentrated knowledge of the user."

Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire for aid mission

Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire for aid mission
October 27, 2026
Russia and Ukraine began a localized ceasefire early Tuesday to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.
Both sides confirmed that the truce took effect at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT), following an agreement brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had stopped shelling in the Kherson sector to prepare for the humanitarian operation.
Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets also confirmed that Kyiv was observing the agreement.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.
However, it could not be independently verified whether fighting had decreased.
What is the humanitarian situation in Oleshky?
Around 2,000 people, including up to 50 children, remain trapped in Oleshky, according to Ukrainian and US estimates. The town had about 24,000 residents before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The United Nations says residents face severe shortages of food and medicine. Mines and drone attacks have made it difficult for them to leave.
Former residents told news agency AFP earlier this year that people remaining in the town were starving, sometimes hunting pigeons or surviving on food grown in their gardens.
"They've forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there's not even flour left," said Olga, who was in contact with two families still in Oleshky.
Oleshky lies across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson.
Russian troops captured the town during the first days of the invasion in 2022. It suffered further destruction in June 2023 when the collapse of the Kakhovka dam caused widespread flooding.
What role did Melania Trump play in the ceasefire?
The White House said last week that Melania Trump had helped secure the agreement after holding talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine.
Her office said the first lady had also met United Nations officials who briefed her on conditions in Oleshky.
Announcing the agreement on Friday, Trump said civilian officials from both countries would visit residents to assess their needs.
Doctors, food, drinking water and medicine are expected to reach the town before evacuation corridors are opened.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.
Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing residents from leaving, an allegation Moscow denies.
Neither side has provided details about who will monitor the ceasefire. Reports have also differed over its duration, with one account saying it could last through Saturday.
What happened in Kyiv after the ceasefire began?
Russian missile attacks continued elsewhere in Ukraine as the localized ceasefire began.
Explosions shook Kyiv shortly after 3 a.m. local time Tuesday, according to witnesses, while air raid alerts sounded across several regions.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the attacks had damaged the Southern Bridge and associated subway infrastructure. City authorities said traffic on the bridge had been suspended.
On Monday, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 10 others, including students at a dormitory. Further attacks caused casualties in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after the attacks.
Could the Oleshky ceasefire help revive Ukraine peace talks?
The limited truce in Oleshky comes ahead of another round of US-mediated peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, expected in November.
Negotiations have been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.
Previous attempts to establish ceasefires have repeatedly failed amid deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine.
More than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed, while millions have been forced to flee their homes.

Malaysia’s 2027 Budget: Fiscal Consolidation Continues Apace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:51:00 UTC
12:51:00 KST

The Malaysian economy is coasting these days. Growth for 2026 will be around 5 percent, with similar levels projected for 2027. Investment in manufacturing and digital services is flowing in, and the current account and trade balance are running large surpluses thanks to booming exports. The deficit is shrinking, even as fuel subsidies rise to cushion consumers from spiking energy prices. Inflation is stable, and fiscal reforms have succeeded in widening and diversifying the tax base, reducing exposure to volatile petroleum rents. For Malaysian fiscal planners, 2027 is coming up roses.
This kind of stable, sustained economic growth is music to the ears of fiscal forecasters because it means tax revenue will continue to grow in proportion to GDP. Not only that, but it will grow in a largely predictable manner. This is obviously important when making a budget because decisions about future spending and borrowing depend on how well you forecast revenue and growth. If growth misses the forecast, revenue comes in below target and the deficit widens. This has been a recurring theme in the Philippines in recent years.
It seems unlikely Malaysia will have a similar issue. Steady, predictable growth means more accurate revenue forecasts, making it easier to control spending and trim the deficit, something Malaysian fiscal planners are particularly fond of. Government expenditures mostly focus on maintaining and upgrading systems and services, and it is unusual to see big budget-busting social or infrastructure programs. As soon as the economy stabilized after the pandemic, Malaysia pivoted toward fiscal consolidation and sought to get the deficit under control through a combination of spending cuts and tax hikes.
This has continued apace in recent budgets, and it is working. The deficit in 2026 is projected at 3.6 percent of GDP, a steep decline from the high of 6.4 percent in 2021. Fiscal consolidation continues in 2027, with the deficit shrinking to 3.3 percent of GDP. That would be the lowest level since 2017. This is expected to happen even as approved government spending for 2027 rises to 458 billion ringgit ($112 billion), a 3.7 percent increase year over year.
Such is the power of tax reform. Historically, Malaysia has been highly dependent on dividends and taxes derived from extracting, refining, and selling petroleum products such as natural gas and oil. In 2019, dividends from state-owned oil and gas firm Petronas and excise and other taxes on petroleum-related activities accounted for 32 percent of government revenue. By 2026, it had fallen to 15 percent, and is expected to remain around that level in the 2027 budget. More than 80 percent of government revenue now reliably comes from non-petroleum sources, mainly taxes.
This is good news because while rents from natural resources like oil and gas can be an important contributor to government operations, they are unpredictable. Prices go up and down, and as the world pivots toward cleaner energy, any government that relies excessively on exploiting fossil fuels to shore up its revenue could be left holding the bag in a couple of decades when renewables are more dominant. By then, it will be too late.
Tax reforms, particularly a recent hike in the sales and service tax, have shifted revenue toward a more sustainable and diversified tax base. Revenue from this tax is set to increase from 10.5 percent of the total in 2019 to 19.2 percent in 2027. The sales and service tax is expected to contribute 73 billion ringgit in 2027, around $18 billion. Few people are happy to pay higher taxes, but during disruptive and uncertain transitional periods, such as the one we are currently living through, expanding the tax base and shoring up the country’s fiscal health is boring but sound medicine.
Evidence of this can be found in the one major line item where Malaysia continues to spend big: subsidies. Malaysia spent around $18 billion on subsidies in 2026, and is targeting roughly the same amount for 2027. A lot of this will go toward cushioning consumers from spiking energy prices. Fiscal planners would prefer to see subsidies go in the opposite direction. Indeed, they started cutting subsidies soon after the post-pandemic economy began stabilizing.
But with an unexpected shock to global energy prices that most rational people would not have seen coming, tax reforms and prudent fiscal management give Malaysia sufficient policy space to increase spending and shell out $18 billion in subsidies in successive years while still narrowing the deficit. That is the kind of fiscal math finance ministers in some neighboring countries can only dream about.

Scientists video REM-like sleep in Australian jumping spider species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:49:29 UTC
12:49:29 KST

Scientists video REM-like sleep in Australian jumping spider species
In short:
A new study has found a species of jumping spider, Portia fimbriata, experiences at least two sleep stages, including a REM-like stage.
An Australian expert says the study is the "most complete behavioural case for sleep in any arachnid".
What's next?
The team is now looking at how spiders sleep in the wild, including across Australia.
While not everyone gets to enjoy some peaceful shut eye, it seems that more creatures than we thought enjoy a good kip.
Subtle eye flickers and leg curls captured on video confirm a small Australian jumping spider experiences the same kinds of movements we do during sleep, according to a new study.
Study co-author Daniela Rößler, a behavioural ecologist from the University of Bonn, said the sleep patterns of Portia fimbriata were structured in at least two parts.
"Spiders have distinct sleep stages, and that the architecture of their sleep mirrors key features of vertebrate sleep far more closely than anyone expected," she said.
The research, which the team hopes can help scientists understand how sleep has evolved through the animal kingdom, was published today in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
How to wake a spider
Portia fimbriata, which is found across Northern Australia, is a "dream species" for studying sleep, study co-author Nadja Geiger said.
"She is diurnal, highly visual and famously clever,"
Ms Geiger said.
"She also has a very clear night-time resting posture, sleeping upside down in a little web … this makes sleep easier to identify and study."
The team recorded the arachnids throughout the night, then carefully analysed the footage to identify the stages.
The spiders groomed themselves while they snoozed and drooped down slowly over the course of the night in a phase the researchers called quiescent.
This was followed by a REM-like sleep stage, complete with leg curls, eye movements and arm twitching as the spiders dosed.
Loading...
Once the researchers had observed these two different phases, they could see what happened when they tried to wake the spider up.
"A hallmark sign of sleep is … [responding] slower or not at all to external stimuli," Ms Geiger said.
They woke the spiders up with a loud noise while they were still for more than 15 minutes in the quiescent stage, as well as when they showed signs of REM-like sleep and when they were visibly awake.
Similar to humans who have been woken from a nap, it took the spiders longer to respond when they were in this quiescent and REM-like state.
"This effect was particularly strong during the REM-like phase," Ms Geiger said.
"Responses were significantly delayed, and some spiders did not respond at all."
Spider sleep a (not so) controversial idea
Thomas White, an entomologist at the University of Sydney who studies invertebrate behaviour, said some people might think associating similar behaviours to animals that were so distantly removed from us was controversial.
"With spiders, you're talking about animals that have diverged 500 million years ago from all other vertebrates," Dr White said.
But he noted that scientists were becoming less hesitant as evidence mounted that similar behaviours occurred.
"We readily see our dog lying down and its eyes are twitching and it's kicking its little paws. Essentially what [the researchers] are showing here is that something similar," he said.
"Yes, [spiders] diverged a very long time ago, but if we're willing to extend that inference to our dogs, our cats, or even animals that are quite unlike us like reptiles, then what's stopping us from extending that inference … in animals that are very unlike us?"
Dr White said that the study built on research from the same team a few years ago that found some possible REM-like sleep in jumping spiders.
"But this goes a step further in mapping out different behavioural facets of sleep-like behaviour," he said.
"This paper is far and away the most complete behavioural case for sleep in any arachnid."
What can spider sleep tell us?
According to Dr Rößler, understanding how spiders sleep may help researchers explain why sleep exists at all.
"If animals with such different brains and sensory worlds show structured sleep with REM‑like phases, it suggests that the basic architecture of sleep may be far older and more widespread than we thought," she said.
"Comparing sleep across such different animals can help us understand how sleep evolved, which features are ancient, and what functions different sleep stages may serve."
The researchers are now looking at studying sleep in spiders in the wild, including fieldwork in northern Queensland and Western Australia.
"This allows us to ask how natural conditions and anthropogenic changes, such as artificial light and habitat disturbance, influence sleep outside the laboratory," Dr Rößler said.
"We'd love for this kind of research to help spread a little more curiosity and appreciation for these charismatic animals."

China's industrial profits grew at a faster pace in September, though a deepening divergence across the economy continued to weigh on business earnings.
Profits at industrial firms rose 14.4 percent from a year earlier last month, quickening from a 4.2 increase in August, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Tuesday.
Profits were up 15.5 percent in the first nine months, compared with a 15.7 percent increase in the January-August period.
While export-oriented firms brace for greater uncertainty, as expanding trade surpluses heighten the risk of external pressures, firms tied to domestic demand continue to grapple with subdued consumption, casting a shadow over the sustainability of profit growth.
The sectoral divide remained pronounced.
Profits in the computer, communication, and other electronic equipment manufacturing category soared 103.8 percent in the first nine months, whereas the furniture manufacturing sector posted a 51.3 percent decline, making it one of the weakest performers and highlighting the uneven nature of China's economy.
A stronger-than-expected 4.5 percent expansion in the third quarter put China within reach of its annual growth target of 4.5 to five percent, but disparities across different parts of the economy suggest the recovery remains unbalanced, with persistent weakness in some sectors continuing to erode corporate profitability.
That pressure has become increasingly visible at the company level.
Net profit at the world's largest electric vehicle battery maker, CATL, slowed sharply in the past quarter, as intense competition in the EV battery market squeezed margins at a time when China's auto sales were in a downturn.
Industrial profit figures cover firms with yearly revenue of at least 20 million yuan from main operations. (Reuters)

G Flip and Chrishell Stause have broken up and like many in the queer community, I’m in mourning  | Rebecca Shaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:44:59 UTC
12:44:59 KST

In this current bummer of a world, we often wake up to bad news. This morning, it was devastating. I picked up my phone and saw multiple texts asking me how I felt about the fact that … Chrishell Stause and G Flip have broken up.
If those names seem like some sort of gibberish to you, I won’t expect you to understand the seismic shift. While I was sleeping soundly in Australia in the knowledge that love exists, Strause, from the LA “real estate” show Selling Sunset, posted a vulnerable and deeply sad video where she revealed that she and Australian drummer G Flip have parted ways after being married for several years.
Her clear, genuine sadness, her talk of feeling like a failure – it moved me. I posted about it on Instagram and in came the flood of responses: Nooooo. Love is dead. Love isn’t real. Whose fault is this. I’m devastated. I’m in mourning. And so on and so forth. Many queer people in particular have been sliced in the heart by this news. Every group chat I’m in is talking about it (not all instigated by me).
I’ve started seeing comments under posts about the breakup such as “Who?” or worse, “Who cares?” and I have to tell you that I care. We care. To me, and people like me, this relationship was a beautiful queer success story.
Chrishell comes from a poor background, and her previous marriage ended in a brutal public dumping by actor Justin Hartley. She joined Selling Sunset as a real estate agent and soon became the main character as she compellingly rebuilt her life. During the process she met and fell in love with a non-binary drummer from Australia.
Watching someone from such a hyper heterosexual world like Los Angeles real estate, from a hyper heterosexual show like Selling Sunset, begin to dip her toe into the queer world was amazing. Watching her experiencing a truly fulfilling romantic relationship and falling for someone who loved her back and encouraged her to be her true self was a balm. Bringing that queer dynamic to the world of reality TV was also deeply enjoyable.
I think everyone tuned into this public relationship was happy to see Chrishell glowing. She and G Flip travelled together, their love always seeming to become stronger and more joyous. Chrishell seemed to love Australia, and in fact became part of Australia, endearing herself by travelling to all sorts of places G Flip’s music took her, such as Wollongong. When she ordered a flat white in a Selling Sunset scene at a cafe, I felt national pride. When the show introduced wide American audiences to their relationship, and to Chrishell’s hyper femme love for the non-binary G Flip, the couple received homophobic hate. But their love endured.
Until now.
Of course, we don’t know what happened. We know that Chrishell seems heartbroken, posting a video because she felt she owed it to the fans of their relationship, the ones who have been so supportive. We know that she seems confused, saying it won’t be hard for her to be respectful of G Flip “because I am in love with this person”, and adding she doesn’t “have all the information and the reasons” for the breakup.
We know that G Flip posted, saying that their head and heart feel very heavy. Ultimately, as much as I would love a full investigative report, a timeline, perhaps a podcast series, we are strangers to these two people and their relationship. Their love seemed genuine and real, and as we all know, that sometimes isn’t enough. Chrishell also said she is “definitely never doing this again”. I hope she doesn’t mean true love, I hope she means that after her public marriage breakup with Justin Hartley and her very visible relationship with G Flip, she won’t be bringing an audience along with her next time.
It must be pretty exhausting to have your romantic life turned into a spectator sport, even if the spectators are mostly well-meaning strangers, such as lesbians who love your love.
So for now, I and many others will be in a short period of mourning. It’s yet another loss of a nice thing. I will be lighting a candle and accepting condolences. And then, I will be trying to get on with my life, just as Chrishell and G Flip will. Love may not be dead, but it certainly had a difficult morning.
- Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in Sydney

Security is handled across several departments: the Australian Federal Police is responsible for assessments and security details, the Department of Home Affairs looks after home security, and the Department of Finance handles offices and transport.
All three coordinate to share information, Finance secretary Matt Yannopoulos confirmed in a late-night Senate estimates sitting on Monday.
But the updated protection would not be enough to shield women in the public eye from abuse, Gallagher warned, urging social media companies to take action when threats are posted on their platforms.
Debate on proposed social media reforms set to return
Her comments come before the government's Digital Duty of Care bill returns for debate in the lower house.
Under the proposal, social media platforms would be forced to protect users under 18 from content that promotes crime, eating disorders, pornography or misogynistic content, as well as posts that cause distress.
Representatives from the media regulator and the eSafety commissioner will likely field questions about the proposed legislation during Senate estimates on Tuesday.
MPs from across the political divide paused proceedings on Monday for a full day of tributes to Haines.
'I felt like I couldn't breathe'
As the sun set over the capital, Labor backbencher Ali France described learning of the attack.
"I felt like I couldn't breathe, my chest hurt, and like the speed of light, my brain went straight to her fight for life," France recounted in parliament.
"The flashes of fear that she may have had, the confusion of not knowing what was hurt or who was hurt, the urgency and the heroism of bystanders, her staff, and first responders.
"I went there because I know it."
France was seriously injured saving her youngest son Zac from an out-of-control vehicle in a shopping centre car park in 2011 and had a leg amputated.

JORGE DIEGO ETIENNE (JDE) EXHIBITS 15 YEARS OF PHYSICAL PROTOTYPES
Presented at the Museo Franz Mayer in Mexico City, Mockups Before Fuckups surveys nearly 15 years of design practice by Monterrey-based consultancy JDE, founded by industrial designer Jorge Diego Etienne. On view from October 16th, 2026, through February 14th, 2027, the exhibition focuses on the iterative processes preceding market production, exhibiting preliminary sketches, scale models, working prototypes, material experiments, 3D printed studies, and unreleased design concepts.
EXPANDED ARCHIVE BRINGS UNRELEASED DESIGNS AND COLLABORATIONS
The exhibition layout is structured around the studio’s five methodological stages and fifteen core design principles, framing physical prototyping and error mitigation as fundamental risk-reduction tools. Spanning varied typologies, including tableware, furniture collections, public spaces, and urban infrastructure, the displayed works feature Etienne’s early aluminum pen holder Choose Your Bullets, custom tableware developed for Michelin-starred restaurant Pangea, and research pieces from the Galeana collectible design series, alongside corporate collaborations with TANE, Libbey, Coca-Cola, Tupperware, and Cemex. Curated with the assistance of Roble Vargas, this expanded edition follows an earlier presentation at Centro Cultural Plaza Fátima in Monterrey and is accompanied by a monographic publication edited by designaholic (books).

EU gas prices hit four-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:31:28 UTC
12:31:28 KST

EU gas prices hit four-year high
European natural gas prices have surged to their highest level in four years amid the Iran war and the EU’s continued push to phase out Russian energy, according to data from online aggregator Trading Economics.
On Monday, wholesale prices briefly surpassed €97 ($108) per megawatt-hour, reaching levels not seen since December 2022. The increase came as gas storage facilities in the EU were just 74.62% full as of October 25, well below seasonal averages.
Liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for around a fifth of global LNG trade before the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran earlier this year, remained around 80% below pre-conflict levels.
Some EU countries have already begun drawing on stored gas as temperatures drop. Trading Economics forecasts that European gas prices will reach €98.20 per megawatt-hour by the end of the fourth quarter of 2026.
In the UK, the month-ahead gas contract rose by 4% to its highest level since December 2022, according to The Guardian. Brent crude, which climbed to $117 per barrel last week, has since eased slightly but remains at around $115.
British households could face a 27% increase in energy bills in January, pushing the average annual dual-fuel bill to nearly £2,200 ($2,940), according to a forecast by energy supplier EDF. An earlier forecast by Cornwall Insight projected a 16% increase to £2,000.
In August, The Guardian reported mounting concerns in the EU over low gas storage levels and soaring prices ahead of winter. In September, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen warned that the bloc faces its worst energy crisis since 2022.
In mid-October, German media reported that Berlin plans to make households and businesses pay for a national emergency gas reserve costing more than €3 billion over ten years. The government-controlled stockpile would be reserved for emergencies, including sabotage and infrastructure failures, rather than being used to lower gas prices.
The opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) party called for energy ties with Russia to be restored, following US President Donald Trump’s example. On October 13, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said Germany should seek its own diesel deal with Russia, praising Trump’s agreement with the country as a pragmatic approach.
Following the EU’s sweeping sanctions on Russia in 2022, the bloc experienced one of its worst energy crises in decades. Gas prices soared above €300 per megawatt-hour, driving up costs for industries and households and contributing to surging inflation.
The EU has continued its efforts to phase out Russian energy. While Russia accounted for around 45% of EU gas imports in 2021, the share fell to around 12% by 2025.
Moscow has described the EU’s efforts to sever energy ties with Russia as “suicidal.” Last week, Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev argued that the bloc would eventually have to restore ties because “cooperation with Russia economically will be inevitable.”
Dmitriev blamed the EU’s problems, including high energy costs, on its leaders, saying they refuse to acknowledge and correct their mistakes.

DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:30:04 UTC
12:30:04 KST

Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged for the third time with federal crimes, according to a court filing unsealed Monday in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., at Comey's request.
Comey is accused in the new case with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it.
He is also charged with conspiring with others to violate the law against sharing such information.
The charging document, known as an information, says Comey, "through one or more co-conspirators," directed an unnamed individual "to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication."
Comey is seeking to dismiss the new case, according to a court filing by his lawyers, which says the information relates to the "alleged disclosure of classified information" to The New York Times on Oct. 5, 2016.
Comey's lawyers told a judge in that filing that the alleged disclosure "was investigated by two separate U.S. Attorneys over the past ten years. Both declined to prosecute."
Comey has been repeatedly targeted by the Department of Justice under the administration of President Donald Trump, who fired him as FBI director in 2017. Both men have been fierce critics of one another since then.
"For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement, according to The Associated Press.
The DOJ filed the information against Comey on Oct. 5 and asked a judge to seal it, citing the risk that an ongoing criminal investigation would be compromised by the charges becoming public. Judge Trevor McFadden granted that request that day.
Attorneys for Comey, whom the DOJ agreed should be notified of the information, filed a motion to dismiss the case on Oct. 9, arguing that the 10-year statute of limitations to file a grand jury indictment relating to events of Oct. 5, 2016, had expired.
Comey's lawyers accused the DOJ of filing "a faulty information under seal" in an effort to put the statute of limitations on hold.
The attorneys on Monday asked McFadden to unseal the information, and the judge agreed to do so.
Comey separately is currently seeking the dismissal of an indictment obtained by the DOJ in North Carolina federal court on charges of threatening Trump's life by posting a photo of seashells on a beach on social media. He previously successfully won dismissal of another indictment accusing him of falsely testifying to Congress.
The new criminal complaint came to light hours after a federal judge in New York ruled that the Department of Justice had unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, last year as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
"Well, they're back — again," James Comey said in a video message on Substack addressing the new case.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said. "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
"And I'm still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers that will stand up in court and fight the latest and whatever comes after this," Comey said. "The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It's really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America."
In the pending indictment in North Carolina, Comey in late April was charged with threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
Prosecutors claim that the number "86" — which is often used in restaurants to indicate a menu item is no longer available — was code for suggesting someone kill Trump, who is the 47th U.S. president.
Comey has denied any wrongdoing in that case and is seeking to have the indictment tossed out by a judge.
Comey was first indicted in September 2025 by a federal grand jury in Virginia on charges of making a false statement and obstruction, in connection with testimony he gave before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 30, 2020.
Comey, in that testimony, denied authorizing another person at the FBI to serve as an anonymous source in news reports regarding an investigation of Hillary Clinton and her emails when she was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2016.
That first indictment was dismissed by a judge on Nov. 24, 2025, after the judge ruled that Lindsey Halligan, a then-interim U.S. attorney who obtained the indictments, had been invalidly appointed.
On the same day the judge tossed Comey's case for that reason, the same judge dismissed an unrelated indictment obtained by Halligan against New York Attorney General Letitia James, who had been accused of bank fraud and making false statements to a financial institution in connection with a home mortgage she obtained in 2020.
James, like Comey, has been a staunch critic of Trump, and a target of the president's ire.

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has abandoned plans to seek the annulment of Sunday's presidential runoff, but will pursue separate legal action against incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's campaign over power abuse, Brazilian media reported Monday.
Lula won Sunday's runoff with 51.79 percent of valid votes, defeating Bolsonaro, who received 48.21 percent, according to results released by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.
Bolsonaro, the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party, refused to concede defeat in remarks in Brasilia late Sunday, saying he would seek to have the election annulled.
Earlier Sunday, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ordered polling stations nationwide to extend voting by two hours in response to disruptions caused by public transport stoppages and heavy rain.
The extension applied only to polling stations that were still open when the decision was made by the Superior Electoral Court. Stations that had already closed were not reopened.
Bolsonaro argued that the measure disadvantaged voters in areas where polling stations were not reopened and said his legal team would challenge the election results.
However, his allies and lawyers persuaded him to drop the plan, arguing that a challenge to the validity of the election had little legal basis and was unlikely to succeed in the country's electoral and supreme courts, Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported.
Instead, Bolsonaro plans to file an Electoral Judicial Investigation Action, seeking to have Lula's ticket disqualified over alleged abuses of political and economic power during the campaign, CNN Brazil reported, citing members of Bolsonaro's campaign.
"What he did was an unprecedented abuse of political and economic power, creating a complete imbalance in the electoral contest," Bolsonaro said in a video posted on social media.
Valdemar Costa Neto, president of the Liberal Party, said Monday that the party had recognized the election result.
Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes has ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports to the Federal Police and barred him from leaving the country.
The ruling is part of an investigation involving Bolsonaro and lawyer Willer Tomaz, according to Brazil's public news agency Agencia Brasil.
Moraes also prohibited Bolsonaro from contacting Tomaz, Brazilian media reported. Both men are under investigation by the Federal Police on suspicion of money laundering and illegal foreign exchange transactions. ■

S. Korea's real GDP grows 1.0 pct on quarter in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:26:01 CST
12:26:01 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's economy delivered a better-than-expected performance in the third quarter, driven by a semiconductor export boom, strong facility investments and significant growth in government spending, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP), adjusted for inflation, expanded 1.0 percent in the July-September quarter compared to the previous quarter, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
It was more than three times higher than the 0.3 percent growth forecast estimated in August by the central bank, which projected an annual growth outlook of 3.3 percent for 2026.
The quarterly growth rate rebounded sharply from negative 0.1 percent in the fourth quarter last year to 1.8 percent in the first quarter this year, before maintaining positive momentum with an increase of 0.6 percent in the second quarter and 1.0 percent in the third quarter.
Outbound shipments of the export-driven economy mounted 2.3 percent quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter thanks to strong demand for semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment.
Soaring demand for locally-made semiconductors was led by expanding global investments in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Imports gained 2.4 percent due to higher inflows of crude oil and semiconductor manufacturing machinery.
Facility investments jumped 4.1 percent on the back of robust demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, while construction investments added 0.7 percent in the third quarter after falling 0.1 percent in the previous quarter.
Investments in intellectual property products grew 2.3 percent due to increased spending on software and research and development (R&D).
Private consumption, another growth engine of the Asian economy, showed a slight setback with a decrease of 0.2 percent amid lower expenditure on both goods and services.
Fiscal spending climbed 1.9 percent, affected by higher government spending on health insurance benefits.
Amid the better-than-expected economic increase and the still high inflationary pressure, the BOK delivered a back-to-back rate hike in July and August, raising its benchmark interest rate to 3.00 percent.
By industry, the seasonally adjusted production among manufacturers swelled 2.0 percent in the third quarter on a quarterly basis, spearheaded by computers, electronic and optical devices.
Output in the service industry rose 0.2 percent, and production in the construction sector advanced 2.0 percent on an expansion in civil engineering projects.
Those in the agriculture, forestry and fishing, and the electricity, gas and water supply sectors increased 5.9 percent and 3.7 percent, respectively.
Real gross domestic income (GDI), which measures the actual purchasing power of income generated from domestic production activities, expanded 3.4 percent in the third quarter compared to the previous quarter.
From a year earlier, the real GDI surged 18.8 percent in the July-September quarter, representing the fastest growth in nearly 49 years since the fourth quarter of 1977.
It was powered by soaring global prices of locally-made semiconductors that improved the country's terms of trade. ■

‘A national emergency’: Bay Area Israelis fly home to vote in pivotal election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:13:03 UTC
12:13:03 KST

This article was produced by J.–The Jewish News of Northern California in partnership with the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Ayelet Frank was one of the first people to check in on Sunday, Oct. 25, for a nonstop flight from San Francisco to Tel Aviv. A resident of Redwood City, California, since she left Israel in 1984, she is flying back for one reason: to vote in the Oct. 27 election.
It’s the first time in her more than 40 years abroad that she is going back to cast a ballot.
Election about Israel's very existence, Frank says
“This election is unique. It’s very different than any other,” she told J. “It’s about Israel’s very existence. This election is between the destruction of the country, or building it up in a positive way.”
A native of Kibbutz Ein Harod in the Jezreel Valley, she is spending only two days in Israel before returning to California. It’s a long way to travel just to vote, but, she said, “It’s that important.”
Frank was one of 271 passengers on El Al flight 48, which landed in Israel less than 24 hours before the polls open. It was the first nonstop flight from San Francisco to Israel since the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack. Many on board were part of what one organizing group estimates is a wave of 67,000 Israelis abroad flying home for an election widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In a tight race, the Israel Democracy Institute said that many voters could swing nearly two Knesset seats.
Those travelers are spending thousands of dollars for the chance to cast their ballots in what many are calling the most consequential election in Israel’s history.
The mood in the boarding area at the San Francisco International Airport was buoyant. Lots of people seemed to know one another and were running up to hug friends and chat excitedly. There were families with children and plenty of babies in strollers and carriers. There were a smattering of black kippahs as well as one Hasidic family. There were also Israeli residents returning home from vacation in the Bay Area. But judging from the conversations as well as from people interviewed by J., most passengers were Israeli expats flying back to vote.
Capitola resident Udi Pardo left Israel in 1983, a year before Frank. Most of his family still lives in Israel and he visits twice a year. But for him, this was his first time flying home for an election.
“I never tried to go and vote before because I don’t live there,” he said. “But now it’s a national emergency. I can’t not go.”
“Israel is on the verge of an abyss,” he continued, saying that he has not yet decided between Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar and Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad — both center-right parties opposed to Netanyahu’s government. “We need to bring back sanity to Israel and to Israeli politics and reestablish liberal democracy because it’s about to disappear.”
First election since October 7 Massacre
The Oct. 27 election is the first since the Hamas attack and the war that followed. The stakes are so high, pundits say, that Israelis living abroad are flying home to vote in what appear to be unprecedented numbers. Israel does not allow absentee voting, except for diplomats and other state employees posted abroad, so expats who want to cast a ballot must do so in person.
The 67,000 estimate comes from Fly & Vote, a project of the U.S.-based America Israel Democracy Coalition to help expats navigate the logistics of participating in the election. The group cautioned that the figure is based on a voluntary August survey and its own registration data, not a count of arrivals. No comparable data exists for previous elections.
Israel’s Likud-led government has tried to impede Fly & Vote’s efforts with legal action, which was blocked in October by Israel’s Supreme Court. The government reportedly also considered closing or slowing down traffic at Ben Gurion International Airport in the days before the election. Analysts say this is because Netanyahu and his allies believe that many, if not most, of those responding to Fly & Vote’s initiative will vote against the current government.
Indeed, that seemed to be true of most of the expats on this El Al flight from San Francisco. Every person interviewed spoke about the “need for change” in Israel’s government, and those who declared their support for candidates mentioned either Eisenkot or leaders of other anti-Netanyahu parties. The Silicon Valley-based Israeli expat group UnXeptable, which emerged to protest Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul and has become a major anti-Netanyahu voice globally, had a large presence on the flight, with about a dozen key members sporting light blue T-shirts emblazoned with the date of the election and the Hebrew words for “Flight for Change.”
They were handing out shirts to any other passengers who would take them, some of whom put them on right away. Local TV stations showed up for an UnXeptable press conference held at the check-in counter.
Roni Bar-Niv of Sunnyvale is one of several people interviewed who is spending just a few days in Israel, in her case enough time to vote, turn around and fly back to the Hebrew-language school she runs near her Silicon Valley home.
In the 26 years since she left Givatayim, a suburb of Tel Aviv, Bar-Niv said, she visits Israel four or five times a year but she, too, has never flown back to vote until now.
“I thought I didn’t need to vote because I don’t live there,” she said. But everything changed, she added, after Oct. 7. “If we pay taxes — we have an apartment there — and if we send money for the war effort, and if we have children there — my daughter made aliyah five years ago — we need to go and vote,” she said. “The direction our country is going is very bad, for Israelis living there and for us also.”
Berkeley resident Rivka Amado left Jerusalem 22 years ago. A retired ethics professor and Ladino singer, she said it’s the duty of Israeli expats to show up.
“This election is critical, and it’s important for every Israeli to vote, whether you live here or there,” she said.
The surge in emigration since Oct. 7 has also swelled the pool of Israelis abroad. Some 82,800 Israelis left the country in 2024, according to Israel’s Central Bureau of Statistics, up from 55,000 in 2023. More than 69,000 left in 2025, the Times of Israel reported, the second straight year that emigration outpaced immigration.
Gilad Kariv, an opposition lawmaker from the Democrats party who chairs the Knesset’s Diaspora Affairs Committee, has warned of a “tsunami of emigration,” according to the Jerusalem Post. He has called it a “strategic threat to the future of Israel” tied to the government’s conduct.
J Street regional director Shimrit Braun Kamin (left) hugs Galit Lipsitz Goldental near the El Al counter at San Francisco International Airport, Oct. 25, 2026. (Aaron Levy-Wolins/J. Staff/Report for America)
Experts point to the war in Gaza and opposition to Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul as driving forces, suggesting that many recent emigrants are critical of the government.
Thirty-seven parties are on the Oct. 27 ballot, but only about a dozen are expected to clear the 3.25% electoral threshold needed to win Knesset seats. With Netanyahu’s Likud party polling neck-and-neck with his main opponent, Eisenkot’s Yashar party — the final pre-election polls show Yashar winning 22 to 23 seats to Likud’s 19 to 21 — every seat matters.
Neither party is projected to win a clear majority, meaning either one will have to negotiate intensely to form a governing coalition.
That’s why these expats have ponied up the dough, packed their bags and jumped on planes.
Eyal, a tech designer in his 40s who has been living in Mountain View since 2004, declined to give his last name because of his former job in the Israeli military. This, too, is his first trip home to vote.
In general, he said that he agrees with Israelis who believe expats should not have a voice in elections that no longer affect them personally.
“But in this particular election, I think a lot of Israelis want us to come and vote,” he said. “I know my parents do.”
Shlomi from Sunnyvale, who left Israel more than 15 years ago and also declined to give his last name, is worried that if there is not a new government, Israel’s brain drain will accelerate.
“We are in the final moments,” he said, likening Israel’s political situation to a soccer game. “If the government doesn’t change, I think a lot of good people who contribute to the future of the country will leave Israel.”
Shlomi is also worried that Israel will lose its partnership with the United States.
“It’s not about right or left,” he said, declining to say how he’ll vote. “It’s about dignity, about taking responsibility, about leaders that actually make decisions for the people rather than their personal benefit.”
Iddo Tal, a Jerusalem native, has lived in Palo Alto for 15 years, where he is a tech entrepreneur and teaches fundraising to startup founders around the world. He has launched “five start-ups and two kids,” he said, joking that “the kids have been a huge success.”
Unlike most of those interviewed, he has traveled back to vote before. He made the trip to visit his parents but timed it around an election.
“They always say every election is historic, and they’re always right,” he said.
Tal believes expats should vote, saying it keeps Israelis at home and abroad closely connected. “There’s something very exciting about making the Israeli diaspora part of Israel [proper], by coming back to fight, to raise money, to vote,” Tal said.
Hadar Aviram teaches law at UC Law San Francisco while studying to become a rabbi through Hebrew Union College. Born in Israel, she grew up “all over the world” and landed in San Francisco in 2001 for grad school. She wore one of the blue UnXeptable shirts and has joined some of the group’s protests.
“Let’s start with taking accountability for the Oct. 7 massacre and the ensuing war,” she said. “And long before that, we were all hostages to this hateful, bigoted, corrupt government.… I’m flying to release us from him, and him from us.”
She bristles at people who don’t understand why Israelis like her feel so strongly about this election.
“If some of those ignorant folks ask what Zionism is, I invite them to look around at all the people here who have packed their bags and emptied their savings accounts because they want to save their country,” she said, waving at the crowded boarding area. “When you love something very, very, very much, you are willing to go to great lengths to save it.”

Israelis ready to cast their vote in an election that could end Netanyahu's rule
Unknown

2026-10-27

Key Events
Updates
These Palestinians woke up on Israel's Election Day still unsure whether to vote or boycott
On Tuesday, as Israelis head to the polls, some Palestinian citizens of Israel still have a decision to make: whether or not to vote at all. Even after months of campaigning and growing fears of another Netanyahu government, some are still trying to reconcile their political principles with the possible consequences of staying home.
For four Palestinians who spoke to Haaretz, the dilemma has persisted right up to Election Day. Some have spent years boycotting Israeli elections but are now considering casting a ballot. Others, who have voted in the past, are questioning whether participation serves any purpose.
A, a 31-year-old civil engineer from Haifa, says the closer it gets, the less certain he feels. He is "50-50" on whether he will vote, torn between a long-standing boycott of Israeli elections and the fear that abstaining could leave his people more exposed to the policies of a far-right government.
Police release one of three men arrested on suspicion of election bribery involving United Arab List party
The Be'er Sheva Magistrate's Court released one of three suspects, Bedouin residents of southern Israel, who were arrested overnight into Tuesday after police allegedly found them in possession of envelopes containing cash and ballots for the United Arab List.
The prosecution appealed the release to the Be'er Sheva District Court, which is expected to hear the appeal tomorrow.
The court granted a police request to extend the detention of the two other activists arrested in the case until Sunday to allow for further investigation.
How are Israel's new immigrants planning to vote in this election?
Over 100,000 immigrants have arrived in Israel since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's last election victory in 2022, according to Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics. Today, many of them are voting for the first time.
Aglaya Shmidt, who emigrated from Russia after friends who shared her left-wing perspective started to get arrested, thinks her outsider perspective gives her an important voice in this election.
"I do have friends who were born here, went to the army, and I feel like it's a bit harder to see perspective," she says. "I feel like people who went through the army, or through the education [system], it's a bit harder for them to see that there might be some problematic things that the army could do, for example."
Yashar party leader Eisenkot visited his son's grave before casting his vote
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot visited his son's grave earlier on Tuesday, before casting his vote.
Eisenkot's son, Gal Meir Eisenkot, was killed in December 2023 during a hostage rescue operation in Gaza. He was 25 at the time.
Election monitors report Haredi Public party ballot slips removed or hidden in ultra-Orthodox communities
Civil Election Guard, an organization deploying more than 20,000 observers at polling stations nationwide, reported a series of disruptions and the removal or concealment of ballot slips for the Haredi Public party in ultra-Orthodox communities.
The Haredi Public seeks to offer an alternative to the established ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas. The party is not expected to cross the electoral threshold, according to recent polls.
According to the organization, 23 incidents were recorded at 20 different polling stations in Modi'in Ilit, Bnei Brak and Jerusalem between 7:56 A.M. and 2:07 P.M. Entire stacks of the party's ballot slips were taken from voting booths or hidden beneath those of other parties, sometimes repeatedly at the same locations.
In Modi'in Ilit, observers reported that an entire stack of ballots disappeared within seconds. In Bnei Brak, a voting booth was found to have no ballot slips for the party while voters were casting their ballots. The organization said seven incidents occurred within just 13 minutes, between 1:54 P.M. and 2:07 P.M., and that these incidents were reported to the relevant authorities.
Inspired by an ancient Jewish sage, Israeli stages weeklong protest outside president's house in Jerusalem
A man has been camping outside President Isaac Herzog's house in Jerusalem for the last week, vowing not to move until "the government of October 7 moves out of office." Surrounding himself with a two-metre-wide circle of stones, he stepped out for the first time on Tuesday morning to cast his vote, dressed in biblical-style clothing.
Nir "Honi" Yanovsky, a 44-year-old Jerusalem resident, took inspiration from "Honi the Circle-Drawer," a Jewish sage who lived in the first century B.C.E. According to the Mishnah – Judaism's earliest rabbinic text compiled around 200 C.E. – Honi, during a severe drought, drew a circle on the ground and declared that he would not leave it until God sent rain. And so it happened.
"When Honi the Circle-Drawer drew a circle in the ground, he did so because he felt there was no other choice, that the nation was facing a state of emergency. Two thousand years have passed, and Israel is once again in a state of emergency," Yanovsky said.
According to Yanovsky, he spoke with hundreds of people throughout the week, some of whom even travelled from distant parts of Israel to show their support.
U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee: 'Arabs vote same as Israelis'
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee marked Israel's Election Day with a post on X, writing: "All voting is in person, ID required. No mail-in or absentee ballots. Arabs vote same as Israelis."
Today is election day in Israel, which is a national holiday. All voting is in person, ID required. No mail-in or absentee ballots. Arabs vote same as Israelis. Contentious process, but it's a democracy-not many of those in this region!
RECAP: Millions of Israelis vote in record-high election turnout by 2 P.M.
Here's what you need to know as Israelis cast their ballots
■ Voter turnout as of 2 P.M. has reached 44.9 percent, the highest at this hour since 1973, when the data was first measured, the Central Elections Committee said.
■ Launching a scare campaign, PM Netanyahu sent voters a recorded message, accusing the left and Arab parties of trying to "steal the election."
■ Senior Israeli military officials accuse PM Netanyahu's Office of orchestrating a campaign to discredit IDF Chief of Staff Zamir, saying reports of a clash between the two over a potential strike on Iran before the election were part of a political effort to portray the military's top brass as obstructing military action against Tehran.
■ Adalah, the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, told Haaretz it had received reports of systematic delays at polling stations in Arab communities across Israel.
■ A man carrying a knife was arrested after approaching Democrats party leader Yair Golan in Tel Aviv while allegedly carrying a knife, the party said.
■ A man was filmed assaulting Together party activist, tearing down party banners in Northern Israel's Tiberias.
■ The civilian election watchdog said it had received numerous reports of attempts by polling-station committee members or party representatives to tally voters in violation of Central Elections Committee regulations.
■ The Yashar party said it had contacted the Central Elections Committee following reports from several polling stations that its ballot slips had been removed, damaged or marked in ways that could lead to votes being disqualified.
■ Mansour Abbas' United Arab List filed a complaint with the Central Elections Committee, saying a campaign was being carried out to disrupt voting for the party, including the arrest of several party activists and ballot slips being removed or defaced in several Arab localities.
■ Naftali Bennett's Together party filed another complaint with the Central Elections Committee after it received reports of the use of the Elector app to monitor voters at polling stations in a community in northern Israel.
■ Three residents of Bedouin communities in the Negev were arrested on suspicion of election bribery after being found with envelopes containing cash and ballots for the United Arab List.

Russia-Ukraine ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump takes effect in Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:10:19 UTC
12:10:19 KST

A localised humanitarian ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has taken effect in Oleshky city, following a diplomatic initiative brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow emergency aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
The ceasefire started at 01:00 GMT on Tuesday. The White House confirmed that the first lady served as the "exclusive intermediary" in securing the operational pause.
The arrangement addresses critical shortages of food, potable water, and medical supplies in the frontline settlement, situated on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.
The remaining population faces mined roadways, recurring military bombardments, and severe electricity shortages.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," Melania Trump said.
"It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."
Military implementation
Russian Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced that Moscow would observe a "regime of silence" from 4 am Moscow time on October 27.
"To ensure the safety of the population and the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be conducted, and the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy to the settlement of Oleshky, Kherson Region, will be facilitated," Gerasimov said.
Ukraine's General Staff confirmed it would observe the ceasefire from 3 am Kiev time to facilitate aid deliveries and guarantee safe passage for departing civilians.
Under the framework, civilian representatives from Ukraine and Russia will assess local requirements.
Residents choosing to leave will receive transport to destinations in either country, with an American media organisation accompanying field teams to record proceedings.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov noted the mission could last several days.
Oleshky, seized by Russian forces in 2022, had a pre-war population of roughly 24,000.
Today, only 1,700 to 2,000 residents remain, predominantly elderly individuals unable to flee earlier.
The town suffered catastrophic damage in June 2023 when the destruction of the Nova Kakhovka Dam triggered massive flooding across the Dnipro basin, an act for which Kiev and Moscow continue to trade blame.

Nicknamed “Asian Elvis,” Tang entered the final ranked second in qualifying, scoring 14.566 points with a difficulty score of 6.000 and an execution score of 8.566, per Nownews. For the final, his coaching team raised his routine’s difficulty score to 6.600, helping propel him to the top of the podium.
Tang delivered a fluid routine featuring his signature aerial twists and earned an execution score of 8.366. His total of 14.966 points secured the gold medal.
The championships ran from Oct. 17-25 in Rotterdam, Nownews reported. Tang’s victory marked a historic milestone for Taiwan, which had previously won two silver medals and one bronze at the world championships.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) congratulated Tang on his achievement, praising his performance on the world stage and his contribution to Taiwan’s sporting success. He also encouraged the rest of the national team to continue striving for top honors.
Since the Asian Games in Nagoya last month, Tang has worked with coach Huang Bo-rui (黃柏瑞) and a sports psychologist to refine his mental approach, treating finals more like practice sessions, per UDN. He said he aimed to compete in a relaxed state, without adding too much ceremony or pressure, allowing him to perform with greater composure.
Tang, who turned 30 last month, has overcome multiple serious injuries during his career, including three surgeries on his right elbow and a ruptured left Achilles tendon during a domestic trial three years ago. He won bronze in the men’s horizontal bar at the 2024 Paris Olympics and helped Taiwan claim bronze in the men’s team event at the Asian Games last month.
Those medals and his world championships gold have boosted his confidence ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
His wife, Tseng Jo-yu (曾若語), traveled to Rotterdam to support him at the world championships, as she did when he won his Olympic medal in Paris, UDN reported. Tang described her as an “invisible coach” whose support motivates him to continue improving.

By Trevor Hunnicutt
CORINTH, Mississippi, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump campaigned on Monday in deeply Republican Mississippi, predicting victory for a Republican Senate candidate based on what he deemed to be a booming US economy, while also repeating his claim that oil prices would soon plummet.
Trump, a Republican, has been on a campaign blitz through normally safe Republican states ahead of the November 3 vote, with party strategists telling Reuters they are on edge about races from Alaska to South Carolina, in part because of voter discontent over how Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war have fueled inflation.
Sounding hoarse from his recent series of campaign rallies, Trump remarked, “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.”
Trump is expected to visit Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, Florida and Iowa in the final days of the campaign, with voter concerns over affordability likely to weigh on Republicans, pollsters say.
Trump acknowledged the war in Iran has pushed up oil prices, but said it was a small price to pay to stop Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
“I thought the price of oil was going to go much, much higher,” Trump said.
“It’s worked out fine and it’ll be over soon,” Trump said about the war.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are on the ballot, with public opinion polls suggesting the Democrats will regain control of the House and have a chance to retake the Senate.
A Republican victory would preserve Republican control of Congress, which Trump has enjoyed since returning to the White House after the 2024 election, while a Democratic victory could impede the president and trigger congressional investigations into his administration.
In Mississippi, an unexpectedly competitive US Senate race has given Democrats a rare opening ahead of next week’s congressional elections.
Democrats last won a Senate seat in Mississippi in 1982. Trump carried the state by nearly 23 percentage points in 2024, and he won the northeastern Mississippi county he was set to visit on Monday by 68 percentage points.
But several election analysts no longer regard US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith’s reelection as a sure bet. The Trump-endorsed Republican faces Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney from the Columbus area, and independent Ty Pinkins, a military veteran and attorney who previously ran statewide as a Democrat.
“Cindy’s doing great but I’ve just got to make sure,” Trump said. “I can’t take a chance.”
After listing a series of economic achievements, many of them exaggerations or unverifiable claims, Trump said, “I can’t help Cindy Hyde-Smith any better than that.”
Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign in support of Colom last week, and Democrats have dispatched big-name figures from former Vice President Kamala Harris to former presidential primary candidate Pete Buttigieg to campaign alongside the Democratic candidate.
Colom came to Corinth on Monday, posting pictures of himself meeting with voters outside the venue where some 5,500 Trump supporters gathered inside.
“Walking the line outside the Trump rally in Corinth, I was reminded that more unites us than divides us here in Mississippi,” Colom said on X. “When I’m elected to the U.S. Senate, I’ll represent every Mississippian — whether you voted for me or not.”
Democrats are contesting all three Republican-held House seats in Mississippi, but none is viewed as a likely pickup opportunity. A fourth seat, represented by US Representative Bennie Thompson in a heavily Black district, is considered safe for the Democrats.
