You bought it, but do you control it? The hidden power behind smart devices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:01:59 UTC
12:01:59 KST

You bought it, but do you control it? The hidden power behind smart devices
When a stolen smartphone can be remotely disabled and a connected car can be tracked or prevented from starting, the question of who controls a device after it is purchased becomes more complicated. Recent reports of stolen iPhones being blocked in France have brought this issue into focus. How far does a manufacturer’s control over a connected device extend, and where does the owner’s right to control their property begin? Qazinform News Agency examines how remote security technologies are reshaping the concept of digital ownership.
How technology can stop stolen devices
On Oct. 17, shops in Paris, Marseille, Lille, Bordeaux, Lyon and other French cities were targeted during looting alongside demonstrations. Electronics, including smartphones and tablets, were among the goods stolen.
A video shared on social media showed a message on a stolen iPhone instructing the holder to return it to an Apple Store in Lille. The message said the device had been locked and was being tracked, warning that local authorities would be notified.
According to French media outlet BFM Tech, manufacturers can remotely disable stolen smartphones and tablets, while mobile operators can blacklist their International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) numbers to prevent them from connecting to cellular networks. A blacklisted phone may, however, remain usable over Wi-Fi.
Yernar Yeleuov, a cybersecurity engineer at the School of Cybersecurity at Astana IT University (AITU), said anti-theft protection works through several mechanisms, including account-based locks, remote commands and network blocking.
Apple’s Activation Lock and Android’s Factory Reset Protection can prevent someone from setting up a stolen phone after a factory reset without the previous owner’s credentials. Services such as Find My and Find My Device allow owners to lock a screen, display a message or erase data remotely.
But these systems are not foolproof. A remote command may not reach a phone that remains disconnected from the network. IMEI blocking also depends on the networks and databases involved, while stolen devices may be dismantled for parts or targeted through phishing attacks designed to steal account credentials.
“These mechanisms are a strong deterrent that reduces the value of a stolen device, but not a guarantee that it will be returned,” Yeleuov said.
From smartphones to connected cars
The same principle is increasingly relevant to vehicles. In April 2026, Stellantis announced an expanded connected-services offering that includes Stolen Vehicle Tracking Assistance through its Connect PLUS package. In July, Ford Canada expanded the availability of vehicle theft-prevention features to selected models, including theft alerts, recovery assistance and a remote Start Inhibit function that can prevent a vehicle from starting remotely under specified conditions.
However, the technology that helps recover stolen property can also create new cybersecurity risks.
“If a vulnerability is found not in a single car but in the manufacturer’s servers or API, the entire fleet is at risk at once,” Yeleuov said.
Connected vehicles also collect location data that can reveal where people live, work and travel. If these systems are compromised, the consequences may extend beyond vehicle theft to unauthorized access and privacy violations.
Yeleuov said critical vehicle systems, including brakes and steering, should be isolated from infotainment systems and external communication channels. Remote commands must be securely authenticated, and an immobilization function should never stop a moving vehicle.
Who controls a device after purchase?
A smartphone or connected car is more than a physical product. It also depends on software, online accounts and services that may remain under a manufacturer’s control.
“The honest answer is that buyers today almost never get full control,” Yeleuov said. “Legally, you own the hardware, but the software that makes this hardware useful is usually licensed rather than sold.”
This distinction matters when companies change software, discontinue services or restrict features. A device may remain physically intact but lose some of its functionality if it depends on a manufacturer’s servers or subscription.
The end of software support can create a further risk: devices that no longer receive security updates may retain vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.
Yeleuov distinguishes between protective measures, such as security updates and anti-theft tools, and commercial restrictions that can limit repairs or access to features. Both can affect how much control consumers retain after purchasing a product.
Balancing security and ownership
Remote blocking and tracking can make stolen devices harder to use, but consumers also need protection against mistaken restrictions, unauthorized tracking and sudden service shutdowns.
Yeleuov said safeguards should include transparent policies, secure authentication, notifications when remote actions are taken and accessible procedures for appealing incorrect blocks. Consumers should also know before buying a connected product which functions can be controlled remotely and how long software support is expected to last.
“The keys to a device should be in the owner’s hands, not the manufacturer’s,” he said.
Kazakhstan’s IMEI registration system provides a mechanism for managing mobile devices on local networks, but the broader issue extends beyond stolen phones. As more products become connected, ownership increasingly depends on the software and services that determine how they can be used.
The challenge is to ensure that technology protects consumers without making them unnecessarily dependent on the companies that manufacture their devices. Buying a product gives consumers its physical hardware, but meaningful ownership also requires transparency, security and clear limits on remote control.
The issue is part of a broader debate over digital security in Kazakhstan. In September, Qazinform reported that more than 100 experts gathered in Astana for KazHackStan 2026 to discuss emerging cyber threats and the future of cyber resilience.

South Korea’s GDP grows 1% in Q3 on strong exports and investment
The growth in July-September accelerated from 0.6 percent in the previous quarter and surpassed the central bank’s August forecast of 0.3 percent. On a year-on-year basis, the economy expanded 3.4 percent.
South Korea’s export performance was driven by booming global demand for semiconductors amid the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Exports reached a record $120.9 billion in September, up 83.5 percent from a year earlier, with semiconductor shipments exceeding $60 billion.
Facility investment rose 4.1 percent from the previous quarter, while construction investment increased 0.7 percent. Government spending also advanced 1.9 percent. The BOK said South Korea’s economy grew a cumulative 3.6 percent during the first three quarters of 2026.
“If the economy maintains the on-quarter growth pace in the fourth quarter, GDP will likely grow 3.6 percent for the full year,” said Lee Dong-won of the BOK’s statistics department.
The central bank may revise its August full-year growth forecast of 3.3 percent upward, with updated projections scheduled for release next month.

Azerbaijan secures $40 million ADB loan to boost women-led businesses and farming
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) and Bank Respublika Open Joint Stock Company have signed a $40 million loan agreement to expand access to financing for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) and agricultural borrowers in regions outside Azerbaijan’s capital, Baku, Qazinform News Agency cites the press service of ADB.
Under the agreement, at least 20% of the loan proceeds will be allocated to women-owned MSMEs, while at least 50% will support borrowers engaged in agricultural production, processing, and trade. The funding is expected to facilitate the adoption of modern drip irrigation systems and encourage the cultivation of crops and fruits suited to varying weather conditions.
The initiative aims to promote business growth, create jobs, increase incomes, strengthen resilience to natural hazards, and contribute to the diversification of Azerbaijan’s economy.
“This financing aligns well with ADB’s country partnership strategy for Azerbaijan, 2025–2029, by promoting private sector-led growth, strengthening food security, improving resilience, and expanding access to finance for women-led businesses in areas outside the capital,” said Sunniya Durrani-Jamal, ADB country director for Azerbaijan.
She added that the project builds on the bank’s existing cooperation with Bank Respublika and expressed ADB’s commitment to deepening the partnership to achieve these objectives.
Established in 1992, Bank Respublika is Azerbaijan’s fifth-largest bank by assets, holding a 4.4% market share. It serves retail, MSME, and corporate clients through a network of 40 branches, 24 of which are located outside Baku.

'Veto should be held by all permanent members': India at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:01:03 UTC
12:01:03 KST

Parvathaneni Harish called for comprehensive Security Council reforms, arguing that all permanent members of an expanded Council must have equal rights and responsibilities
NEW DELHI: India has called for comprehensive reforms of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), saying all permanent members of a reformed Council must have the same rights and responsibilities, including the power of veto.Delivering India's statement at the United Nations, India's permanent representative Parvathaneni Harish said the veto should be exercised with restraint and must not become a tool for narrow political interests, particularly on matters concerning international peace and security.
India also opposed proposals to create a separate category of permanent members without the veto or with fewer powers, arguing that such an arrangement would deepen existing inequalities within the Council."India's position on the veto is principled and well known. It is aligned with the Common African Position. We reiterate that as long as the veto exists, it must be held by all permanent members of a reformed Council. Fairness and justice demand that all permanent members enjoy the same rights and responsibilities," news agency ANI quoted Harish as saying."A new category of permanent members, with or without the veto, would only further complicate a discussion that is already difficult, and would further entrench the very inequity we are seeking to correct.
Periodic elections and the concept of permanency are fundamentally contradictory," Harish added.Harish said the veto had been used 331 times on around 200 resolutions during the UN's history. He noted that most vetoes, or threats to use them, had come from three of the five permanent members -- China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States."The record of the Veto is stark. Over the life of this Organisation, the veto has been exercised 331 times on around 200 resolutions. We also note that two out of the five permanent members have not exercised a veto for over three and a half decades, and most of the vetos or threats of vetos have emanated from only three of the P5," he said.He also questioned the effectiveness of accountability measures introduced in 2022, under which the UN General Assembly holds a debate whenever a permanent member exercises its veto. The continued use of the veto since the mechanism was adopted showed that it had not brought the expected change, he said.
He also highlighted what he described as an “effective or de facto veto” in the Council's working methods. Under the practice of consensus, a single member can block presidential statements, press statements and decisions of sanctions committees, sometimes without providing an explanation, he said."The veto is not only what is cast in the open. There is also the 'effective or de facto veto' that every Council member, elected and non-elected, holds over presidential statements, press statements and the decisions of sanctions committees, where the unwritten rule of consensus allows a single member to hold or block a proposal, most often without explanation," Harish said.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

BAROMÈTRE DU REJET : Le Pen, toujours moins rejetée
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

BAROMÈTRE DU REJET : Le Pen, toujours moins rejetée
La nouvelle édition de l'enquête mensuelle de Cluster 17 pour POLITICO montre que Marine Le Pen est encore moins rejetée par les Français qu'au mois de septembre. Reste un mince motif d'espoir pour le bloc central.
Par SARAH PAILLOU et PAULINE DE SAINT REMY à Paris
Les mobilisations et violences d’octobre ont renforcé le rejet de Jean-Luc Mélenchon et amoindri celui de Marine Le Pen.| Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images
Les candidats du bloc central, Edouard Philippe et Gabriel Attal, sont bien placés pour le savoir : s’ils peinent à progresser dans les sondages d’intentions de vote — voire, s’ils reculent — c’est qu’après deux quinquennats d’Emmanuel Macron, l’heure est au dégagisme.
Comme le montre la dernière enquête de l’institut Cluster 17 pour POLITICO, parue lundi 26 octobre, ce sont les incarnations d’une rupture radicale avec le macronisme qui, à ce stade de la campagne, ont le vent dans le dos : Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Mais les représentants du camp central ne souffrent pas que d’un simple désir d’alternance : s’ils décrochent, c’est qu’ils suscitent désormais chez les Français un rejet aussi fort, voire plus puissant, que le Rassemblement national ou La France insoumise. Impossible donc, pour les partis ayant déjà exercé le pouvoir, de continuer à parier sur des électeurs prêts à tout pour barrer la route de l’Elysée aux “extrêmes”.
Advertisement
Pour l’emporter en 2027, un prétendant à la présidence doit donc formuler un nouveau vœu : plutôt que de rêver d’être majoritaire dans le pays, se contenter d’espérer être le moins exécré des compétiteurs. Ce que mesure notre baromètre mensuel du rejet, réalisé par Cluster 17 pour POLITICO, dont la deuxième livraison montre que les grandes tendances observées en septembre s’accentuent et témoigne d’un moment de la campagne “plutôt favorable aux droites” (traditionnelle et extrême), analyse Jean-Yves Dormagen, le président de l’institut.
Logique : notre enquête a été menée du 19 au 22 octobre, juste après les casses et pillages du 17 octobre.
Cluster 17 a, de nouveau, demandé à 3 000 personnes quelle était la probabilité, sur une échelle de 0 à 10, qu’elles votent “un jour” pour chacun des candidats à la présidentielle testés — 0 correspondant à une impossibilité totale de glisser ce bulletin dans l’urne, 10 indiquant que les sondés jugent “tout à fait possible” de le faire.
Seul motif de satisfaction pour Edouard Philippe et Gabriel Attal : la priorité des Français est davantage de faire barrage au camp RN ou au camp Insoumis plutôt qu’au bloc central. | Daniel Perron/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Tous les candidats testés demeurent rejetés par une majorité de Français. Les plus répulsifs restent les mêmes, mais ils voient augmenter le taux de Français excluant totalement de voter pour eux. L’Ecologiste Marine Tondelier arrive ainsi toujours en tête du classement du rejet, à 71% (+3 par rapport au mois dernier) — à égalité cette fois avec Eric Zemmour, non testé dans notre précédente enquête.
Mélenchon de plus en plus repoussoir
Même logique pour Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Toujours en deuxième position des personnalités les plus rejetées, l’Insoumis l’est encore plus qu’en septembre. Les interrogés sont désormais 69% à juger inimaginable de choisir un bulletin au nom de l’Insoumis (ils étaient 66%).
Les violences du week-end des 17 et 18 octobre ont “radicalisé sur la droite un certain nombre de personnes”, juge Dormagen. Et ainsi conforté l’image négative de “JLM”, augmentant la perception de LFI comme “un mouvement radical, qui incarne une rupture brutale”.
Advertisement
Le moment profite, en miroir, aux figures supposées incarner l’ordre, la fermeté, l’autorité, au premier rang desquelles Marine Le Pen. La candidate RN est désormais celle qui réunit le moins de sondés estimant strictement impossible de voter un jour pour elle : ils ne sont plus “que” 52% (- 4).
A ses côtés au même score : le social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann. L’eurodéputé Place publique se maintient quasiment à son niveau du mois dernier.
Misant sur une promesse du retour de l’ordre lui aussi, l’ancien ministre de l’Intérieur Bruno Retailleau est lui aussi moins repoussé qu’en septembre. Les sondés sont 54% (-4) à refuser catégoriquement de voter pour lui. Il rejoint ainsi le mouchoir de poche des personnalités les moins rejetées, avec Marine Le Pen et Raphaël Glcuksmann.
Edouard Philippe est à peine plus rejeté que ces personnalités. Avec 56% de Français excluant à jamais de voter pour lui, il se voit doublé de peu par le sénateur vendéen.
Le bulletin Gabriel Attal est, en revanche, de moins en moins envisagé par les interrogés comme une possibilité. Les sondés sont 59% à trouver inimaginable de voter pour le candidat Renaissance — une augmentation de trois points, comparé à notre sondage précédent. Supposition de Jean-Yves Dormagen, qui ne parie pas sur une hostilité des sondés à son égard : outre le rejet qu’il suscite, “la candidature d’Attal se heurte depuis le début à un enjeu de légitimité. Y compris dans son espace électoral potentiel, les gens ont du mal à comprendre pourquoi il est candidat.”
Le député des Hauts-de-Seine est ainsi quasiment aussi inenvisageable pour les Français que… François Hollande, nouvellement testé. L’ancien président, qui rêve d’un retour en grâce dans le cœur des Français, a visiblement du pain sur la planche : 61% des sondés jugent impossible de voter pour lui.
Advertisement
Un espoir pour le camp central ?
Reste, malgré tout, une (petite) raison d’espérer pour les anciens Premiers ministres d’Emmanuel Macron. Cluster 17 a cette fois demandé aux sondés quelle était leur priorité (à l’exclusion des deux autres) : empêcher la victoire du RN et de ses alliés, de LFI et de ses alliés, ou des partis ayant soutenu le président ?
Réponse : les Français ne sont que 14% à dire que leur objectif principal est une défaite du camp “macroniste”. Alors que faire barrage au camp Insoumis est prioritaire pour 43% d’entre eux, et celui du RN pour 30%.
De quoi laisser penser, donc, que si tous les camps restent majoritairement rejetés — fût-ce d’une courte tête —, tout espoir pour un représentant du bloc central de faire “barrage” à l’extrême droite n’est pas complètement vain. Encore faudra-t-il accéder au second tour.
(*) Etude Cluster 17 pour POLITICO réalisée auprès d’un échantillon de 3 000 personnes, représentatif de la population française grâce à la méthode des quotas, interrogées par questionnaire autoadministré en ligne, du 19 au 22 octobre 2026. Les données ont fait l’objet d’un redressement sociodémographique, à partir des données de l’Insee, ainsi que d’un redressement politique fondé sur la reconstitution des votes au premier tour de l’élection présidentielle de 2022 et aux élections européennes de 2024. La marge d’erreur se situe entre 0,8 et 1,8 point.

====================================================================================================

Tobacco lobby steps up Brussels push as EU rewrites rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

European lawmakers have held four times as many meetings with tobacco and nicotine lobbyists in the past two years compared with the entire previous parliamentary term, according to data analyzed by POLITICO.
Since this Parliament took office in the summer of 2024, more than 400 meetings have been declared, compared with about 100 in the 2019-2024 term, according to data collected by the Smoke Free Partnership, a coalition of NGOs, from the Transparency Register. European lawmakers are required to publicly disclose their meetings on the register.
Meanwhile, most meetings this term were with right-leaning MEPs. Some 75% were with lawmakers from the center-right European People’s Party, the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists and the far-right Patriots for Europe groups.
Advertisement
Meetings with tobacco and nicotine groups have ramped up this term as the EU seeks to overhaul several key pieces of tobacco and nicotine legislation. The EU has also proposed measures this session to curb heart disease and cancer, plans that also affect the sector.
Some MEPs have called out the tobacco industry’s access to lawmakers as they negotiate measures to prevent addiction and disease caused by the sector’s products, such as in a cardiovascular disease strategy report and cancer plan.
“I find it scandalous and shocking that there are more meetings with the tobacco industry than the NGOs and the associations that advocate for stop smoking,” Tilly Metz, a lawmaker with the Greens/European Free Alliance, said.
“When you are working on health files, it is completely incompatible to regularly meet with the tobacco industry,” she said. Metz referenced the World Health Organization’s tobacco control treaty, which says policymakers should meet with tobacco lobbyists only when strictly necessary to discuss the sector's regulation.
The tobacco industry and MEPs who regularly meet with industry say they have done nothing wrong.
British American Tobacco’s head of fiscal affairs, Simon Trussler, said that like any other business in Europe, it had legitimate experiences and arguments to put forward “because we see what's going on on the ground.”
Advertisement
Marlboro manufacturer Philip Morris International, whose meetings accounted for the most of any tobacco company, pointed out its contribution to the European economy and that the firm is “undergoing a deep transformation towards a smoke-free future.”
“We are proud to contribute to the democratic dialogue and to engage with any MEP, from any political group, who is open to discuss on the basis of science and facts and our determination to be part of the solution," said the company, which also sells nicotine pouches, vapes and heated tobacco products.
Global treaty debate
One concern raised by Metz and other MEPs is whether World Health Organization tobacco control rules are being followed correctly.
The WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control stipulates that public health policies need to be protected against industry’s commercial interests. It doesn’t ban lobbying, but guidelines to implement the treaty say that policymakers should limit interactions with the sector to what is strictly necessary for the purposes of regulating it, and ensure transparency of those meetings.
Industry maintains it operates within the rules and presents its perspective transparently. The sector also points to a 2022 European Court of Justicejudgment stating that the treaty doesn’t prohibit industry participation in implementing tobacco control; it is “intended solely to prevent the tobacco control policies of the parties to the convention from being influenced by that industry’s interests.”
In addition, the sector argues that the WHO framework doesn’t cover tobacco-free nicotine products. These products are especially in the firing line for stricter regulations as Europe seeks to overhaul tobacco products and advertising rules, as well as EU minimum taxes.
Advertisement
BAT’s Trussler said the company complied with all regulations and was transparent in how it did so. The WHO’s framework on tobacco control has been “misquoted and misunderstood,” Trussler claimed.
The company also argued that the FCTC's scope is limited to products made from tobacco leaf.
That’s not the position of the World Health Organization. Kristina Mauer-Stender, WHO Europe’s regional adviser on tobacco control, pointed out the scope of the treaty “extends beyond reducing tobacco consumption.”
Article 5.2(b) requires parties to adopt and implement effective legislative and other measures “for preventing and reducing tobacco consumption, nicotine addiction and exposure to tobacco smoke,” she said. “Therefore, preventing nicotine addiction is an explicit objective of the Convention's implementation, rather than merely an indirect consideration.”
The Conference of the Parties’ decisions have also progressively addressed novel and emerging tobacco and nicotine products, she added.
Clusters
The data comes following criticism that the European People’s Party watered down language on tobacco in a non-binding cardiovascular disease report this summer.
Advertisement
EPP lawmakers suggested changing the wording around nicotine having the “same” regulation as tobacco to instead having “appropriate rules.” This was supported by two MEPs who had held the third most meetings with industry — Jessica Polfjärd and Elena Nevado del Campo.
The final report adopted by the European Parliament reflected the proposal.
Socialists and Democrats MEP Romana Jerković, who led the report in the health committee, said at the time she wished it could have been more ambitious on tobacco.
Lobbying has also intensified as the European Commission prepares to release several updated regulations on tobacco and nicotine products.
The Smoke Free Partnership says spikes in meetings cluster around key policy initiatives, such as the taxdirective. “While meetings alone cannot prove direct influence on decisions, they highlight the industry’s opportunities to shape the legislative debate,” Director Erin Roman said.
However, transparency around industry meetings was not sufficient, Roman said, adding that meetings should only be “strictly necessary for effective regulation.”
Advertisement
To another Socialists and Democrats MEP, the lobbying has gone too far.
“Amendments weakening new tobacco products rules in a plan to fight Europe’s biggest killer didn’t come from nowhere: the groups meeting the industry most are the ones watering down the rules,” Spain’s Nicolás González Casares said.
Political trends
MEPs who have met with industry the most this parliamentary term mostly hail from the right.
Patriots MEP Auke Zijlstra held the most meetings with 14, followed by ECR’s Pietro Fiocchi with nine. The EPP’s Michalis Hadjipantela, Elena Nevado del Campo and Jessica Polfjärd all declared eight.
Zijlstra said he always spoke with any industry when a legislative proposal was on the table that would impact them.
“I do not think that I had too many meetings regarding tobacco and nicotine legislation. Taking an interest in the field is an absolute part of the job, and I don’t understand MEPs who have an opinion without,” he added.
Advertisement
He also denied the industry was overrepresented in meetings with lawmakers, saying, “There are a lot of consumers out there.” He encouraged NGOs to ask for more meetings to explain their point of view.
The Smoke Free Partnership said it had faced “significant pressure” on its resources due to the withdrawal of EU operating grants last year. “We have continued engaging with policymakers and coordinating independent public health expertise, but reduced funding means difficult choices about what activities can be prioritized,” it said, adding there was an imbalance between industry’s resources.
A spokesperson for Hadjipantela said he engages with a broad range of stakeholders as he’s a member of six committees. He “remains fully independent in his assessments and decisions,” the spokesperson said, adding: “Meeting with a stakeholder does not imply endorsement of their views or interests.”
Meanwhile, Nevado Del Campo said her meetings with tobacco representatives were because of the large number of tobacco producers in her region, and she had a duty to listen to the sector as it was a large employer. She also met with groups on the other side of the debate. “My commitment is with a healthy Europe and, at the same time, to those farmers who get up every day to work the fields of Extremadura and boost our regional economy.”
Fiocchi and Polfjärd did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication.
Topics and countries
A large number of meetings covered the tobacco taxation directive, which is currently making its way through the Council of the EU. The directive will put minimum taxes on nicotine and tobacco products and expand the definition of what is covered.
Advertisement
Other topics discussed and declared included tobacco products and advertising directives, as well as “harm reduction.”The Commission is currently drafting revisions of the products and advertising rules.
Lawmakers declared at least 178 meetings with Philip Morris International representatives — far more than any other tobacco manufacturer. Second was British American Tobacco with 60.
Further data shared with POLITICO by Transparency International EU shows that PMI ranked fourth behind Meta, Google and Apple as companies that had met the most MEPs and their assistants. A POLITICO investigation last year revealed PMI also successfully lobbied the European Commission.
The Transparency Register data also shows which countries are more willing to listen to tobacco lobbyists.
MEPs from Italy, the bloc’s leading tobacco leaf producer, met with the industry far more than other nationalities — more than one in five declared meetings of tobacco industry representatives in the Parliament involved an Italian lawmaker.
This was in part driven by Italian company Manifatture Sigaro Toscano meeting exclusively with Italian MEPs. Just under half of BAT’s meetings were with Italian MEPs. The country was also well represented in meetings with PMI, although German lawmakers declared having met the company slightly more.
Advertisement
The dataset, which relies on lawmakers' declarations of their meetings, likely offers a conservative snapshot of tobacco lobbying in Parliament. POLITICO removed declarations with insufficient information, but also added meetings declared more recently.
Large tobacco companies are broadly working to migrate consumers onto nicotine products under what they describe as a “harm reduction” approach. They argue nicotine and smoke-free products are better alternatives to smoking tobacco and so need to be enticing enough for people to use over cigarettes.
Proponents dispute this, saying people don’t need to be exposed to addictive products. They also point to the high use of nicotine pouches and products among young people, who otherwise weren’t smoking.
At least 28 meetings in the dataset referenced public health measures, rather than tobacco regulation or taxation, although this is likely non-exhaustive, as a large number of self-declared descriptions remain vague. Two meetings explicitly mentioned cardiovascular diseases.
Greens MEP Metz was part of a group of lawmakers who pushed to restrict tobacco lobbyists’ access to EU lawmakers and accused the Parliament of failing to live up to its obligations under the WHO tobacco control treaty. But this push failed earlier this year.
Metz said she will “continue to fight” for Parliament to fully respect the framework controlling tobacco.

Truce begins in wartorn Ukraine city after it was announced by Melania Trump
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:58:48 GMT
11:58:48 KST

Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive
- Published
A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents have been trapped without food, water and electricity.
Ukrainian officials and Russia's defence ministry say the limited ceasefire is being respected. The truce, which the White House said was secured by US First Lady Melania Trump, is meant to allow aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation on Friday.
Oleshky, along the front line in the Kherson region, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and on the other by Russian forces.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.
There are concerns that the truce will not hold, with one resident saying: "I don't believe in Russia's humanity."
Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, remain in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, Kyiv believes, with only 1,700 still living in the city itself.
Before the war it was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escape is highly dangerous because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water for three years.
Pope Leo XIV appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
The current truce is supposed to allow supplies in and enable roads to be cleared of mines to allow people safe passage out in an evacuation planned to take place on Friday.
One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a land mine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations.
"I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.
Many told the BBC last month there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
It is hard to make contact with people in Oleshky as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians, making it difficult to verify reports the ceasefire is being implemented.
Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, initially including how and where to register for it. Some people want to know if they can bring their pets. Others are questioning what future they will have if they opt to leave their homes.
"It is critically important that this mission to rescue our people proceeds successfully and safely," Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Zelensky's office, said on Tuesday.
Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".
While people are optimistic about leaving, there are also fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could see them be taken away and tortured.
Someone who has been speaking to family in Oleshky said they fear shooting could restart during evacuations and Ukraine will somehow be blamed for not upholding the truce.
Last month, the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
In response to the situation, the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (03:00 in Ukraine; 01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.
The truce is due to be in place until 23:59 local time on 1 November, according to Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament.
Ukrainian officials say parliament's commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has travelled to the areas to co-ordinate the operation.
"This is part of a humanitarian mission being carried out with the mediation and co-ordination of US First Lady Melania Trump, in co-operation with Yana Lantratova, Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights," Lubinets wrote on social media.
Ukraine's military general staff said that silence was being observed over the operation for humanitarian purposes, and urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there". However, he said some would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.
The White House said last week that "non-military, civilian leaders from both countries would work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require".
While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".
While a truce is under way in Oleshky, elsewhere strikes continue.
On Monday evening, attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv hit a university and a bridge, killing one person and injuring 14 others.
In Russia, one person was killed and six others were injured after a Ukrainian drone strike on Bryansk.
Additional reporting by Paul Kirby, Hafsa Khalil and Sareen Habeshian

Local ceasefire in besieged Oleshky begins, Ukrainian, Russian officials say

A localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine went into effect in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky on Oct. 27, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets and Ukraine's Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, Kyrylo Budanov, announced in statements.
"A ceasefire came into effect today at 3 a.m. Kyiv time (4 a.m. Moscow time) in designated areas related to the humanitarian mission," Lubinets said.
The temporary halt in fighting is meant to allow an aid mission into the city in southern Ukraine later this week. Fighting is supposed to remain frozen until at least Saturday, according to the Associated Press.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," Lubinets said. He added that the agreements were reached in negotiations with Yana Lantratova, head of the Russian negotiating team.
Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, confirmed a "bilateral ceasefire" has begun in the embattled Ukrainian city of Oleshky, in a later statement on social media on Oct. 27.
The ceasefire will last until Nov. 1, David Arakhamia, the parliamentary leader of the president's Servant of the People party, said in a later post on social media.
The Russian Defense Ministry also announced that Russian forces had stopped fighting the area in preparation for the humanitarian mission.
The ceasefire, credited to the mediation of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, covers Oleshky and surrounding areas in Kherson Oblast. It is meant to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of humanitarian aid.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson, it has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering.
Residents face severe shortages of food, water and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
The move comes as the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city has drawn international attention in recent weeks, including from Pope Leo XIV.
Within minutes of the Oleshky ceasefire beginning, Russian forces launched a wave of ballistic missiles at other parts of Ukraine, including Kyiv.

Prediction markets open new front for US election misinformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:55:00 UTC
11:55:00 KST

Prediction markets open new front for US election misinformation
WASHINGTON – The US midterms are playing out against a controversial new scoreboard as the nation votes in its first major elections since prediction markets went mainstream.
With hundreds of millions of dollars on the line, experts are warning that the proliferation of live odds into news coverage and on social media could sow confusion – and provide fodder for misinformation.
Concerns range from motivated actors taking extreme measures to sway markets, to voters overtrusting the odds and baselessly blaming fraud where election results differ.
US President Donald Trump has already made unsubstantiated allegations of fraud central to his political movement ahead of the Nov 3 vote.
Polymarket and Kalshi are allowing users to buy and sell contracts on thousands of outcomes related to the midterms, despite surveys showing most Americans oppose betting on elections.
The companies have also partnered with prominent news organisations.
“They’re more and more becoming part of how Americans understand elections,” said Davina Hurt, government ethics director at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics.
“Elections are not games,” she told AFP. “My concern is that we’ve reached a point where financial market expectations carry more weight in the public’s mind than the votes themselves.”
‘Not a promise’
Prediction market trading has surged amid legal battles over whether they should be regulated as federal commodities or under state gambling laws.
Kalshi said its markets offer unique data distinct from polling, that probabilities do not guarantee outcomes, and that efforts to manipulate the odds are cancelled out by other buyers.
“Kalshi should be seen as a complement to traditional polling,” head of communications Elisabeth Diana told AFP.
“On prediction markets, you trade what you think will happen. On polls, you say what you want to have happen.”
Yet, experts expressed fears over markets being misconstrued, especially as Polymarket and Kalshi issue race “projections” on social media.
A high probability “is not a promise”, Hurt said. “When the prediction fails, that’s not evidence that elections fail. But people are going to read that in.”
Los Angeles
When Republican Spencer Pratt lost the Los Angeles mayoral primary in June, right-wing influencers pointed to prediction market odds which showed him favoured to advance to the general election as evidence of fraud.
Some X posts spreading misinformation carried “paid partnership” tags, prompting backlash and action from Polymarket and Kalshi.
“The June primary reinforced how quickly expectations about election outcomes can become confused with actual election results,” said Michael Sanchez, spokesman for the Los Angeles County’s registrar’s office.
In a recent memo shared exclusively with AFP, Kalshi told its paid partners they “shall not call into question the integrity or accuracy of any official vote tally result, legal ruling, or other official or formal determination in connection with the election”.
Partnerships will be terminated with those who post without evidence “that an election result has been corrupted, rigged, compromised, or otherwise improperly administered”, it said.
Polymarket did not respond to requests for comment.
Bracing for confusion
For the first time, researchers who monitor election misinformation at University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public are tracking how prediction markets are misrepresented online.
“There’s more reason to create these rumors because there’s that sort of financial element tied to it,” senior research scientist Rachel Moran told AFP.
“It’s becoming a significant part of our work.”
Jared DeMarinis, elections chief of Maryland, has asked the state to investigate whether election betting via prediction markets is legal under local law.
He told AFP he is prohibiting poll workers from placing election-related bets.
He still worries lopsided odds could depress turnout and inspire false claims that wear down his team, already facing pressure from Trump’s administration.
“Election administrations are all under attack,” he said. “Now you’ve just put more gasoline on this by having money involved.”
“You just don’t want to have the legitimacy of the outcome in question.” AFP

US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:50:31 UTC
11:50:31 KST

One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

Putin to take part in Eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:38:24 UTC
11:38:24 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will take part in the Eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit in Moscow.
The event is scheduled to begin at 12:45 p.m. Moscow time (9:45 a.m. GMT) at the International Trade Center. According to the Kremlin, the Russian leader will welcome the guests before a group photo. The plenary session, chaired by Putin, is set to begin at 1:00 p.m.
The Russian president will deliver the opening address, highlighting the importance of natural gas as a source of energy that supports economic growth. He will also discuss problems facing the gas industry and outline priorities for solving them.
Putin will then give the floor to GECF Secretary General Philip Mshelbila and the heads of delegations from member states. Representatives of several observer countries, including Mozambique, Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia and Senegal, are also expected to address the forum.
The Russian president is also expected to hold five bilateral meetings during the day, including with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Qatari Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Mozambican President Daniel Chapo, Equatorial Guinean President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo and Libyan Presidential Council Chairman Mohammad al-Menfi.
Gas Exporting Countries Forum
The Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) is an intergovernmental organization that aims to strengthen cooperation and dialogue among gas-producing and exporting countries and promote stability and safety in the global gas market. The forum’s first ministerial meeting took place in Tehran in 2001.
The GECF member states are Russia, Iran, Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru and Senegal participate as observer countries.
GECF member states account for about 70% of the world’s proven gas reserves, 38% of global gas production, 42% of global gas exports and 47% of liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.

Bessent dines at Cheesecake Factory, slams Obama over Trump joke

Let them eat cheesecake?
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday became the latest right-wing critic to accuse former President Barack Obama of elitism for mockingly comparing President Donald Trump's ostentatious White House renovations to the Cheesecake Factory.
But Bessent, a former hedge fund manager whose net worth has been estimated at around $600 million, put his money where his mouth is — dining at the chain restaurant and praising its food before giving the Democratic ex-president a slice of his mind.
"This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader's tomb," Bessent told a Fox Business reporter who asked about Obama's remark as he left the restaurant near the White House. Bessent was apparently referring to the Obama Presidential Center, a monolithic structure that opened in June.
"I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try," Bessent said. Obama vacationed on Martha's Vineyard as president, and he and his wife Michelle now own an estate on the exclusive island.
Bessent said he ordered "what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger."
That's a "Charbroiled Cheeseburger Served on a Toasted Brioche Roll with Grilled Onions, Sriracha Mayo and Au Jus for Dipping," one of the "Glamburgers" on Cheesecake Factory's famously sprawling menu. The burger, which comes with french fries or a green salad, currently costs $22.95 at the restaurant's downtown Washington location.
"I recommend the Cheeseburger Spring Rolls," Bessent added in a follow-up post on X directed at Obama.
Bessent's biting comment followed those of other Trump allies who claim Obama sneered at working-class Americans when he tore into Trump over his extensive White House construction and decoration projects.
"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV!" Obama said of Trump during a speech at an Ohio rally for gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown on Saturday.
"There's gold everywhere. What's up with the gold?" Obama went on. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."
The crowd erupted in cheers and laughter at the remarks from Obama, who has previously poked fun at Trump's gold-heavy remodel of the White House.
Since retaking office, Trump has devoted significant amounts of time to discussing his renovations, including in the Oval Office, which now features heaps of gold leaf among many additional decorations. He has also built a White House helipad, the still-under-construction White House ballroom and an array of other projects.
Trump on Monday afternoon defended his White House redesign at length while claiming Obama had failed to address needed repairs.
"We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly," Trump said as he headed to Mississippi for a campaign rally. "Guys like Obama don't see it. You don't see dirt. He doesn't see filth. He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building."
"It has to be clean," Trump continued. "The columns can't be broken. The bricks can't be falling off from under the plaster. And for you to say it's a cheesecake factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president." 
Detractors insisted Obama's use of the Cheesecake Factory as an example of cheap, gaudy decor amounted to no less than class warfare.
"Classic Obama snobbery," Republican commentator Matt Whitlock wrote on X. "Cheesecake Factory is a great option for people who can't afford a private chef at their Martha's Vineyard estate."
GOP pundit Scott Jennings called Obama "undefeated at condescending to regular folks," while claiming the former president "has never been in a Cheesecake Factory."
That backlash quickly sparked its own backlash.
"This is actually a condescending view of working-class people," wrote Derek Guy, a popular menswear influencer, on X.
"I grew up in a working-class immigrant family and we ate at Red Lobster and The Cheesecake Factory for 'fancy nights out.' But even we understood that the White House should not look like the inside of a Red Lobster," Guy wrote. "Working-class people are not culturally illiterate just because their experiences are shaped by their limited means."
The food fight is taking place just days before the Nov. 3 midterm election, where most polls and analyst projections indicate Democrats are poised to make significant gains in Congress.
The election cycle has been defined by Americans' widespread unhappiness with high costs, which has dragged Trump's approval ratings to new lows and imperiled Republicans' majorities in the House and Senate.
The Cheesecake Factory is set to report its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.

'Our last chance to save the country': We meet Israelis flying home to vote at Ben Gurion Airport

Just ahead of Israel's 26th Knesset election, more Israelis living abroad arrived at Ben Gurion Airport to take part in the democratic process. "I left behind a 6-year-old child and my partner. I even parted with 1,000 euros just to come here and vote," Joelle Peleg, a resident of Brussels, Belgium, said upon her arrival Monday,
According to data from Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics, approximately 810,000 eligible Israeli voters live abroad, and tens of thousands have traveled to Israel to influence the country's political future. Fly&Vote, an initiative aimed at helping Israelis overseas exercise their voting rights, estimates that 67,000 have returned to cast their ballots, equivalent to roughly one and a half Knesset seats.
Peleg, who has lived in Brussels for 12 years, said after landing, "I came to vote because things are terrible under the current government. A lot of people on my flight felt the same way I do, and I hope we'll be the force that brings victory."
Lior Fores, who arrived after a long flight from New York, said she had marked the date of Israel's election in her calendar months ago. "I came specifically to vote. This is a critical moment," she said.
Mor Ben Ami also flew in from New York for a brief visit to her homeland. Her 48-hour itinerary includes visiting her parents, casting her ballot and flying back home.
"It feels like our last chance to save the country," Ben Ami said. "We made enormous efforts to get here. There has been a lot of discussion about these elections in the American Jewish community. The goal is to make things better for us abroad as well, because we're the ones who have to explain what's happening here."
Tamar Sofer-Geri and her partner, Noam, arrived after a long flight from San Francisco. "This is the first time we've come back to vote in the 30 years we've lived there," Sofer-Geri said.
Noam added, "We've been involved in what's happening all along. We were here for the protests against the judicial overhaul."
Eilon Caspi, who has lived in Connecticut for more than 20 years, said, "This time, I felt there was so much at stake. The country is at a critical crossroads, and it's important to get it back on the right track. I knew I had to come. I'm appalled by what's happening in Israel."
But some Israelis were heading in the opposite direction, choosing to forgo voting and take advantage of the opportunity to travel abroad.
Lilach and Assaf Ben Rahamim from Haifa, who had already postponed their honeymoon because of the war with Iran, decided they were not going to miss out on the golden beaches of Southeast Asia this time.
"We would have liked to vote, but that's just how it worked out," Assaf said. "We're disappointed we won't be here. We hope that when we return, there will be a government and we won't find ourselves caught in another round of elections."
Lilach added, "We'd like to see the right-wing bloc become a little stronger, but above all, we want a national unity government."
Aviv, an Israeli living in London, said at the departures hall, "I really wanted to stay and vote, but changing my flight would have cost 1,000 shekels. I'm really disappointed. Part of me didn't even want to make this flight."
Shalom, who was also flying to London, said: "What helped me decide to fly was that I wasn't even sure whom to vote for. I'm not worried. From the looks of things, there'll be another election, and then we'll come back to vote."

Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:32:38 UTC
11:32:38 KST

Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Mayo Clinic
- Summary:
- Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health. The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging.
- Share:
Seven studies from Mayo Clinic are revealing new details about senescent cells, often called "zombie" cells because they stop dividing but remain active in the body. These aging cells release inflammatory substances that can contribute to diseases associated with growing older.
The research, published in Nature journals, was conducted by scientists at Mayo Clinic's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging. Rather than simply confirming that senescent cells play a role in aging, the studies investigate how to recognize different types of these cells, why they produce harmful inflammation and how their effects might be reduced.
The findings also contribute to a nationwide effort to create detailed maps of senescent cells throughout the human body. Known as the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) Consortium, the project brings together researchers across the United States and receives funding from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund. Its goal is to document where senescent cells occur in different tissues and how they change throughout a person's lifetime.
"This body of work is moving the aging field forward to precisely identify, understand and target the specific senescent cells that contribute to age-related dysfunction, which is the necessary groundwork to develop new therapies that support healthy aging," says Marissa Schafer, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic scientist whose laboratory directed several of the investigations.
Scientists Discover That Zombie Cells Are Not All Alike
Identifying senescent cells reliably has long been a major obstacle for scientists studying aging. The new research shows that these cells are much more varied than previously understood. Their characteristics differ depending on where they are located in the body and which biological processes caused them to become senescent.
To help address this challenge, researchers developed a tool called the SenMayo gene set. It uses patterns of gene activity to identify senescent cells more consistently across tissues and experimental systems.
Scientists tested the approach using bone biopsies from older adults. They also found that the gene signature became less prominent after senescent cells were removed in preclinical experiments. Since its development, SenMayo has become a widely used resource for researchers investigating aging and related diseases.
Mayo Clinic endocrinologist Sundeep Khosla, M.D., served as senior author of the study, "A new gene set identifies senescent cells and predicts senescence-associated pathways across tissues." Other Mayo Clinic researchers who contributed to the paper include Nathan LeBrasseur, Ph.D., Diana Jurk, Ph.D., João Passos, Ph.D., and LaTonya Hickson, M.D..
A Hidden Connection Between Mitochondria and Chronic Inflammation
Other studies explored one of the most damaging features of zombie cells: their tendency to generate ongoing inflammation.
The researchers discovered additional biological processes that explain why senescent cells continue producing inflammatory signals. Several of these processes involve malfunctioning mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing much of a cell's energy.
In one pathway, DNA and RNA originating from mitochondria activate immune responses that contribute to inflammation. Another involves changes in mitochondrial metabolism that influence inflammatory gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms affect how genes are switched on or off without changing the underlying DNA sequence.
The discoveries suggest that researchers may eventually be able to interfere with the processes responsible for chronic inflammation while leaving the senescent cells themselves intact. This would offer another approach to treatment beyond attempting to destroy every harmful aging cell.
Dr. Passos served as senior author of three papers examining these mechanisms and the diversity of senescent cells:
- "Distinct senotypes in p16- and p21-positive cells across human and mouse aging tissues"
- "Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP"
- "Mitochondrial RNA cytosolic leakage drives the SASP"
Experimental Treatments Show Promise Against Aging Cells
The Mayo Clinic team also investigated possible ways to reduce the number of senescent cells or limit the damage they cause.
The approaches included senolytic medications, which are designed to eliminate senescent cells, a natural compound present in tomatoes, and genetic techniques intended to target particular populations of aging cells.
When tested in older mice, these interventions produced encouraging results. Depending on the approach, researchers observed reductions in inflammatory measures and improvements in several aging-related outcomes, including physical frailty, inflammation in the brain and performance on cognitive tasks.
Another investigation uncovered a possible way to measure aspects of biological aging through blood testing. Researchers identified IL-23R as a potential biomarker that might eventually help scientists evaluate aging-related changes and determine whether future treatments are working.
These results remain preliminary in terms of medical applications. More research will be necessary to establish whether the approaches are safe and effective in people. Nevertheless, the experiments provide valuable clues for developing treatments that more precisely address the cellular processes involved in age-related diseases.
Dr. Schafer was the lead author of two studies examining biomarkers and possible interventions:
- "IL-23R is a senescence-linked circulating and tissue biomarker of aging"
- "Spatial mapping and senolytic targeting of senescent and disease-associated microglia in aged mouse brain white matter"
A New Direction for Healthy Aging Research
Together, the seven studies represent an important shift in how researchers approach cellular aging. Scientists are moving beyond the broad observation that senescent cells contribute to age-related decline and toward identifying which populations cause the greatest problems, what makes them harmful and how those specific effects could be controlled.
The findings also challenge the idea that eliminating senescent cells must always be the primary treatment strategy. By understanding the molecular pathways that trigger persistent inflammation, researchers may be able to develop therapies that block damaging signals without removing the cells responsible for producing them.
Mayo Clinic researcher Darren Baker, Ph.D., served as senior author of the paper "Senotypes define the diverse landscape of senescent cells," which examines the varied characteristics of these aging cell populations.
The work also supports Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative. This program aims to equip physicians with better ways to identify and intervene in harmful biological changes before they develop into disease or advance into conditions that are difficult to treat.
By revealing how zombie cells differ, why they promote inflammation and which processes might be targeted, the research offers a more detailed roadmap for future treatments designed to support healthier aging.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Mayo Clinic. Original written by Alison Satake. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Dementia accounts for over 10 pct of deaths in Australia for 1st time
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:32:27 CST
11:32:27 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, accounted for more than 10 percent of all deaths in Australia in 2025 for the first time, remaining the country's leading cause of death, according to official data released on Tuesday.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said 19,019 people died from dementia in 2025, accounting for 10.1 percent of all registered deaths, up from 18,291 in 2024.
Ischaemic heart diseases remained the second leading cause of death, claiming 16,228 lives, or 8.6 percent of the total, with the mortality rate falling to its lowest level since official records began in 1968.
Cerebrovascular diseases, lung cancer and chronic lower respiratory diseases rounded out the five leading causes of death, which together accounted for 33.3 percent of all registered deaths.
A total of 188,421 deaths were registered across Australia in 2025, an increase of 1,153 from the previous year. However, the age-standardized mortality rate fell from 507.8 to 495.5 deaths per 100,000 people, indicating a return towards pre-pandemic mortality trends, the ABS said.
Over the past decade, deaths caused by dementia increased by 37.3 percent, while deaths from ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases declined by 16.2 percent and 12.1 percent, respectively.
The report also showed that accidental falls rose to the seventh leading cause of death in 2025, with 5,519 fatalities, an increase of 59.5 percent compared with 2016.
Meanwhile, influenza and pneumonia accounted for 4,382 deaths, ranking 11th among the leading causes of death and representing 2.3 percent of all fatalities.
The male age-standardized death rate dropped to a record low of 581.3 deaths per 100,000 people in 2025, according to the ABS. ■

S. Korea's consumer sentiment weakens in October
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:32:26 CST
11:32:26 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's consumer sentiment weakened in October owing to domestic stock market corrections and persistent geopolitical risks in the Middle East, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The composite consumer sentiment index (CCSI), which gauges the sentiment of consumers over the economic situation, fell 1.2 points over the month to 105.4 in October, turning downward from an increase of 2.1 points in the previous month, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The reading stayed above the benchmark 100, which indicated that optimists outnumbered pessimists, but stubborn geopolitical tensions and volatile local stock market chipped away at consumer confidence.
The results were based on a survey of over 2,000 households nationwide conducted between Oct. 13 and Oct. 20.
The sub-index for prospective household income edged down 1 point to 101, pressured by equity market corrections and climbing market interest rates.
The index for prospective domestic economic conditions declined 2 points to 88 due to stock market volatility and heightened uncertainties over the Middle East conflicts that overshadowed the positive impact from robust exports.
The BOK delivered back-to-back rate hikes in July and August, raising its benchmark interest rate to 3.00 percent.
Inflation expectations, which measure the outlook among consumers over headline inflation for the next 12 months, stood unchanged at 2.7 percent in October compared to the previous month.
Upward pressures from higher global oil prices were neutralized by downward factors, such as the BOK's rate hikes and the government's maximum petroleum price ceiling policy. ■

Australian cyber incident responses up 21 pct year-on-year: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:31:48 CST
11:31:48 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Australian authorities responded to almost 300 more cybersecurity incidents in 2025-26 than the preceding year, a report has revealed.
The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) on Tuesday released its annual cyber threat report for 2025-26, warning that Australia continues to be targeted by adversaries that seek to compromise government agencies, businesses and individuals to steal money and information.
It said that the Australian Cyber Security Center (ACSC), a subsidiary of the ASD, responded to 1,524 incidents in 2025-26, up 21.6 percent from 1,253 in 2024-25.
Of the 2025-26 incidents responded to by the ACSC, a subsidiary of the ASD that leads national cyber security operations, the report said that 576 targeted federal government agencies and services or critical infrastructure compared to 461 in 2024-25.
Another 383 incidents in 2025-26 targeted state governments, academia or research and development, large organizations or supply chains compared to 352 in the previous year.
The number of incidents targeting national security or systems of national significance declined from 50 to 23.
None of the 1,524 incidents resulted in a denial of essential systems, but 40 were classified as extensive incidents, including one that targeted the federal government or critical infrastructure.
"AI has been the defining force in the cyber threat landscape over the past year, allowing malicious actors to find vulnerabilities faster and exploit them at unprecedented scale, speed and sophistication," Defense Minister Richard Marles wrote in the report.
He said that Australia's successful adoption of AI would depend on balancing its benefits with a clear understanding of its risks.
The ASD report said that the ACSC notified entities of potential malicious activity more than 4,400 times in 2025-26, an increase of almost 80 percent year-on-year.
It said that the ACSC received 82,000 cybercrime reports from Australians, which was consistent with 2024-25. ■

PYONGYANG, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- A ceremony commemorating the 76th anniversary of the Chinese People's Volunteers (CPV) entering the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) to fight in the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea was held at the China-DPRK Friendship Tower here on Sunday.
On the DPRK side, present at the ceremony were Kim Hyong Sik, vice chairman of the Standing Committee of the Supreme People's Assembly, and other senior officials from relevant departments of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea (WPK), the government and the military.
On the Chinese side, attendees included Qi Han, charge d'affaires ad interim of the Chinese embassy in the DPRK, and other embassy diplomats, Hong Zongming, vice minister of the Ministry of Veterans Affairs, and a visiting delegation he headed, as well as representatives of China's representative office in the DPRK for commending the CPV martyrs, and Chinese-funded institutions and media organizations, overseas Chinese and Chinese students in the DPRK.
The commemoration began at around 10 a.m. local time, with the military band of the Korean People's Army playing the national anthems of China and the DPRK in succession. All participants stood solemnly in an orderly formation and observed a moment of silence to pay tribute to the CPV martyrs who sacrificed their lives in the war.
Kim said the traditional DPRK-China friendship was forged in blood as the two sides stood together through life-and-death struggles during the war.
"Under the strategic guidance of the top leaders of the two parties and two countries, bilateral relations have continued to be elevated to a new and higher level," he said.
The Party, government and people of the DPRK will never forget the immortal exploits of the CPV martyrs, and will continue to make every effort to properly maintain and manage memorial facilities dedicated to the CPV martyrs in the DPRK, said Kim.
Qi said that the traditional China-DPRK friendship was forged and meticulously nurtured by the older generation of leaders of the two parties and two countries, and cemented in blood by the military personnel and people of both countries during the war.
In recent years, under the personal planning and strategic guidance of Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, and Kim Jong Un, general secretary of the WPK, the traditional friendship between the two countries has demonstrated great vitality, Qi said.
"China stands ready to work with the DPRK to implement the important consensus reached by the top leaders of the two parties and two countries, inherit and carry forward the great spirit demonstrated in the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea, and keep pushing the bilateral relations forward," she added.
Hong expressed gratitude to the DPRK's Party and government for their sustained and extensive efforts to maintain and manage the memorial facilities dedicated to the CPV martyrs in the DPRK.
"The top leaders of the two parties and two countries have attached great importance to the commendation work in honor of the CPV martyrs," Hong said.
He added that relevant departments and agencies of China and the DPRK will resolutely implement the important consensus reached by the top leaders of the two parties and two countries, and keep making unremitting efforts in the commendation work through close cooperation and concerted coordination.
Following the memorial ceremony at the tower, China's representative office in the DPRK for commending the CPV martyrs hosted a reception on Sunday evening to mark the anniversary, during which Qi, Hong and Kang Chol Ho, vice minister of the DPRK's Ministry of Urban Management, delivered their speeches.
On the same day, commemorative activities were also held at the CPV martyrs' cemeteries in Hoechang, Anju, Kaesong and other places in the DPRK, where local officials and residents paid tribute to the fallen by laying wreaths. ■

Russia halts strikes on Ukraine’s Kherson as Oleshky ceasefire takes effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:29:00 UTC
11:29:00 KST

Russia halts strikes on Ukraine’s Kherson as Oleshky ceasefire takes effect
The localised ceasefire, secured by US First Lady Melania Trump, will allow evacuations and aid deliveries to Oleshky.
Russia has suspended strikes on the Ukrainian province of Kherson as a localised ceasefire takes effect ahead of a humanitarian mission led by the United States’ First Lady Melania Trump.
The pause in fighting started at 01:00 GMT on Tuesday, according to the Russian Ministry of Defence, to allow for an aid mission into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Kherson later this week.
The mission will enable aid deliveries and allow evacuations from the front-line town, which is suffering acute shortages of food, medicine and other basic supplies.
The agreement was announced on October 23 and brokered by the US first lady, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo XIV, as Washington seeks to revive peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv after more than four and a half years of fighting.
Up to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky. They have been unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the United Nations.
Matthias Schmale, the UN’s resident and humanitarian coordinator in Ukraine, told Al Jazeera that civilians were trapped in the town “without a guaranteed safe exit route”.
The assessment was based on interviews UN human rights monitors conducted with residents who had managed to get out “at great risk”, he said, as well as on information from credible civil society organisations.
“We hope that the announced ceasefire focused on Oleshky will bring the much-needed relief to their situation and allow both humanitarian aid to reach them as well as enable those who want to leave to do so safely,” he said.
The town, which had a pre-war population of 24,000 people, lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in the partially occupied Kherson region, opposite Kherson city, which is held by Ukrainian forces. Russian troops seized Oleshky during the first days of their February 2022 invasion and have controlled it ever since.
Oleshky has suffered extensive war damage and was hit hard by flooding after the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka Dam in 2023.
The localised ceasefire is due to last through Saturday, or longer, amid deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine that has thwarted previous attempts at ceasefires.
Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.

Russia expanding recruitment of African mercenaries amid heavy losses in Ukraine war – Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

02:27:00 UTC
