Russia expanding recruitment of African mercenaries amid heavy losses in Ukraine war – Bloomberg
As reported by Ukrinform, Bloomberg reported this, citing a presentation obtained from people familiar with the work of Ukrainian intelligence.
Russia is now turning its attention to countries with low levels of democracy, limited press freedom and weak judicial systems.
The countries where Russia has stepped up recruitment include Zimbabwe, Burundi and Sierra Leone.
According to the presentation, between January 1 and September 30, Russia recruited 699 men from Burundi, compared with 30 for the whole of 2025, and 530 Zimbabwean nationals, up from 65 previously.
Other countries where a significant increase in recruitment has been observed include the Democratic Republic of Congo, Sierra Leone, Sudan and Cameroon.
Moscow took this step after Kenya and South Africa introduced measures to prevent men from leaving the country to take part in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The Russian recruitment program is aimed at “offsetting massive losses and a shortage of people to mobilize.”
Russia has never publicly acknowledged recruiting foreigners to take part in combat operations against Ukraine.
The Kremlin has claimed that Russia has sufficient manpower to continue the war. Last month, Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin dismissed suggestions that he was preparing to announce another wave of mobilization in the country.
However, concern is growing in a number of African countries over Russia’s efforts to recruit their citizens. Given the relative poverty in Africa, people can be more easily lured to Russia, often with false promises of civilian employment, for example in catering or transportation.
Recruits are also offered substantial one-time payments upon signing a contract, high salaries and the opportunity to obtain Russian citizenship.
As reported by Ukrinform, in the spring of this year, the Center for Countering Disinformation under Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council said the Kremlin had changed its approach to recruiting foreigners into the Russian army for the war against Ukraine, with recruitment now being carried out on a systematic basis.

This could be the biggest investment bet in the history of global capitalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:22:26 UTC
11:22:26 KST

analysis
Anthropic eyes biggest ever IPO as AI funding starts drying up
Anthropic is the next cab off the rank for mega-tech initial public offerings (IPO), and is slated to surpass SpaceX as the biggest capital markets fundraising in history.
An IPO involves a company asking big financial institutions and "mum and dad" investors for cash via the stock exchange.
Elon Musk's SpaceX played this game in June, raising $US85.7 billion ($121 billion), with a listing price of $US135.
It hit the boards of the Nasdaq and subsequently shot up to $US161, with unprecedented investor interest pushing the company to a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.
Prominent US analyst Dan Ives, in an interview from New York, said history was about to repeat itself with the listing of Anthropic.
"If you think about SpaceX obviously being the biggest IPO that we've seen this year, and this is, it's groundbreaking," the partner at Yorkville Ives said.
"It's a watershed event, not just for tech, but the AI revolution in terms of the role Anthropic plays."
Anthropic is a self-described AI safety and research company. Many Australians would be familiar with its Claude AI assistant product.
Locally, there's some healthy scepticism.
"Anthropic is trying to pull off a historic IPO right as the AI funding well is completely running dry," fund manager Roger Montgomery said.
On a wing and a prayer
When consumers spend on credit, it's often due to a lack of cash flow.
Companies are no different. They ask share investors (equity) and lenders (debt) for cash to operate.
The big difference is that firms will look to finance investments for future growth.
Investors, naturally, want to know they will not just get their money back but also have their investment grow over time.
This usually means the company needs to be generating a profit.
SpaceX was risky in that it was operating at a significant loss when it asked share investors for cash.
But it didn't matter. Elon Musk sold investors a dream, and the tech giant's Starlink operation acted as a much-needed cash cow for investors.
Anthropic is in a similar position, but its CEO Dario Amodei wants even more money.
The company is looking to raise about $US100 billion.
Analysts valued Anthropic earlier this year at $US2 trillion, but a recent financial results update showed the company revalued downwards to $US1.5 trillion.
There's no problem generating revenue — the company's third quarter revenue rose to $US16 billion.
"Anthropic's growth puts it in rarefied air," Betashares's head of investment strategy, Cameron Gleeson, said.
"Its annualised revenue run rate reportedly topped $US65 billion at the end of July, around seven times its level at the end of 2025, and many expect it to approach $US100 billion by year-end.
"It has overtaken OpenAI in business adoption, where much of the potential to monetise AI lies, and achieved this with a workforce of around 5,300."
Spending bonanza
Anthropic's costs are damaging its bottom line.
Like many big tech companies, Anthropic is building its business rapidly to meet expected demand.
It means building cloud computing infrastructure, AI training chips, and data centre capacity.
In the second quarter alone, it spent $US5.6 billion on computing power to run its Claude models.
Adding salt to a wound, the cost of debt, which big tech companies are increasingly chasing, is becoming more expensive as inflation affects the global economy and interest rates rise.
The fundamental problem is that if, for example, the demand for SpaceX and Anthropic's products does not justify the spending being undertaken by these companies, the entire artificial intelligence trade is at risk of collapsing.
Loading...
"[It's] basically playing chicken with a market where Elon Musk is warning that debt is impossible to get, over 200 over-leveraged neoclouds are going belly up, and [the failed] Firmus IPO," Roger Montgomery said.
In other words, the fund manager believes investors who want the huge artificial intelligence trade to keep going will invest in Anthropic or risk a Wall Street crash.
"I think they're trying to get ahead of the bubble possibly bursting,"
he said.
And while Ives is confident the IPO will be a success, he says the company has not yet produced the sort of numbers that would justify its current valuation.
"For investors, they're going to basically need to look past this year," he said.
"I think Anthropic, being that they're the centrepiece of the AI revolution, you're going to see probably a strong appetite for this offering."
Loading
Australia at the table
As with the SpaceX IPO, Australians will be able to apply for shares in Anthropic.
Macquarie Capital will act as sub-underwriter and Australian coordinator for the listing.
Ives says it's up to investors to weigh up the risks.
"We're all going into it. Whether it's here in the US, Australia, wherever we are … we're all going into this fourth industrial revolution together,"
he said.
"And there's a lot of opportunity and growth, but there's also risk."
You could argue this is modern capitalism's biggest ever test.
Massive AI tech companies have a spending addiction. They need the cash to invest to hyper-scale, to try and produce the amount of product or service necessary to meet forecast demand.
Now, having largely exhausted debt markets, they're looking to raise equity.
Simply put, if something disrupts this trade, there is no government on the planet, nor central bank, that could clean up the damage caused without major disruption to the global economy.

Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d'Or award in London

Bayern Munich and England striker Harry Kane won the 2026 Men's Ballon d'Or on Monday, becoming the first English player to claim football's most prestigious individual award since Michael Owen in 2001.
The awards were presented at the 70th Ballon d'Or ceremony at the London Palladium, marking the first time the prestigious event was held in the British capital.
Kane, 33, claimed the award for the first time after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025-26 campaign, including 61 goals in 51 matches for the German side, which won a domestic double.
The England captain also scored six goals at the 2026 World Cup, helping his country finish third.
Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second in the Men's Ballon d'Or voting, while Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal took third place.
Kane became the fifth English player to win the award, joining Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen, who last claimed the prize in 2001.
He succeeded Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembele, who won the award in 2025.
Meanwhile, Putellas, 32, claimed her third Women's Ballon d'Or after winning in 2021 and 2022, matching former Barcelona teammate Aitana Bonmati's record.
The Spanish midfielder captained Barcelona to a quadruple in the 2025-26 season, winning Liga F, Copa de la Reina, the Spanish Super Cup, and the Women's Champions League.
She was also named the Champions League Player of the Season and helped Spain win the Women's Nations League.
Putellas joined London City Lionesses in July after her trophy-laden spell with Barcelona.
Other award winners
Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal won Men's Young Talent of the Year for the third consecutive year, while Barcelona forward Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second successive year.
Spain's World Cup-winning coach Luis de la Fuente was named Men's Coach of the Year, while Barcelona's Pere Romeu received the women's coaching award.
Athletic Bilbao's Unai Simon won Men's Goalkeeper of the Year, with Barcelona's Cata Coll claiming the women's honour.
Bayern Munich's Kane also received the Men's Striker of the Year award following his prolific campaign, while Mexican forward Charlyn Corral became the first Mexican to win the Women's Striker of the Year award.
Barcelona were named Women's Club of the Year, while Paris Saint-Germain claimed the men's club award.
Arsenal and England winger Bukayo Saka received the Socrates Award for his humanitarian work, including funding 120 medical operations for children in Kano, Nigeria through a partnership with charity BigShoe in 2022.

What's next?
ABC Sport will have a live blog of Melbourne Cup Day on Tuesday, November 3.
Melbourne Cup-winning jockey Craig Williams hopes racing's version of a blind date will quickly evolve into a successful partnership as he eyes further glory in the race that stops a nation.
Williams, who won the 2019 Cup with Vow And Declare, jumped at the chance to link up with James J Braddock for Irish master trainer Joseph O'Brien this year.
But the veteran hoop hasn't yet ridden the four-year-old son of Zarak and won't sit on him until moments before the gates fly open at Flemington.
"Joseph said he's got it under control and it looks like I'll see him in the mounting yard on the first Tuesday in November," Williams said.
"That's not unusual for us these days. You fly into different parts of the world and ride horses for the first time. It's part and parcel of the job.
"It's pretty exciting that he's definitely a well-credentialed horse for this year's Melbourne Cup."
Named after the 1930s heavyweight boxer who inspired the film Cinderella Man, James J Braddock is one of a handful of runners O'Brien will have in the Cup field as he seeks to add to previous wins with Rekindling (2017) and Twilight Payment (2020).
Trustyourinstinct, is second-favourite behind Ciaron Maher's Point Of Law.
While buoyed by James J Braddock's European form, Williams said co-owner Ozzie Kheir "bullied" him into committing to the ride last month.
"Everyone's got a list and he was right up the top of our short-list," Williams said.
"When I had a conversation with Ozzie I only had the next eight hours to make a decision, otherwise they will move and have to lock someone in.
"I spoke to my manager … we decided to take the plunge and let's hope on the first Tuesday (of November) at 3.15pm that it's the right plunge to do.
"He's got over here, he's got the right form reference, and (now) it's how he turns up on race day and how he acquits himself and how good he is."
James J Braddock has been gelded since finishing third in the Group 1 Epsom Derby, when he got worked up in the preliminaries, and sixth in the Irish Derby.
He will carry 53.5kg in the Cup and co-owner Kevin Blake said the raider has been "absolutely bouncing" since arriving at Werribee's international horse centre from Ireland last week.

A tariff truce between the European Union and United States is potentially at risk due to a multibillion-dollar loan approved by the bloc's investment bank for Airbus this summer, President Donald Trump's top trade official said Monday.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer expressed concern that his office had received "no details about this loan" and pressed for the situation to be "resolved as soon as possible".
"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," Greer said in a statement.
"This situation injects substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector," he continued.
In June, the European Investment Bank (EIB) said it would provide Airbus with a record three billion euros ($3.4 billion) in financing to boost its research and development.
Read moreFCAS project failure: 'France, Germany characterised by totally different strategic cultures'
"This new financing – unprecedented in the EIB's history – aims to provide Airbus with not only the capacity but also the flexibility needed to invest in long-term research, development and innovation across both commercial aviation and the security and defence sectors," EIB vice president Ambroise Fayolle told AFP at the time.
The United States and European Union had been squabbling over alleged unfair trade practices since 2004, with both sides claiming the other provided support to private companies, such as aircraft manufacturers Boeing and Airbus, in violation of international trade agreements.
The 17-year-long feud saw the United States and EU impose tariffs on billions of dollars worth of each other's products.
But in 2021, a five-year deal was agreed between both sides under former president Joe Biden's administration.
Both sides have not reimposed the tariffs since.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

‘Russian breakfast’ could soon be on the menu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

02:17:04 UTC
11:17:04 KST

‘Russian breakfast’ could soon be on the menu
A ‘Russian breakfast’ featuring traditional national dishes could soon appear on menus at hotels, cafes, and restaurants across the country, under a proposal by Moscow’s Industry and Trade Ministry.
In a document published on Monday, the ministry noted that hotels and restaurants typically offer international options, such as full English, continental, and French breakfasts, while largely overlooking local culinary traditions.
As a result, domestic tourists are often deprived of familiar morning meals, while foreign visitors have no opportunity to experience the country’s cuisine, the ministry said.
“This situation has a negative impact on tourism: Research shows that interest in local cuisine is one of the key factors people consider when choosing a country or region to visit,” it said.
“As a cultural and gastronomic phenomenon, the Russian breakfast does not merely exist – it is genuinely authentic and possesses clearly recognizable characteristics.”
The proposed menu could feature blini (thin pancakes), syrniki (pan-fried cottage cheese cakes), porridge, meat and fish dishes, and caviar. Suggested drinks include herbal teas, berry-based fruit beverages, and kvass, a fizzy fermented drink traditionally made from rye bread.
Participation would be voluntary, with establishments encouraged to expand their existing offerings rather than replacing international favorites.
The ministry also suggested creating a special ‘Russian breakfast’ emblem to help hotels, cafes, and restaurants identify and promote traditional dishes.
The initiative aims to showcase the country’s culinary heritage, attract tourists, and support domestic food producers.

TAICHUNG (Taiwan News) — Chef Justine Li (黎俞君), founder and executive chef of Fleur de Sel in Taichung, has been named a knight in the Order of Agricultural Merit by the French government.
Frederic Laplanche, director of the French Office in Taipei, presented the medal during a ceremony at his residence.
Established in 1883, the honor recognizes distinguished contributions to agriculture, gastronomy, and food culture.
Li is the first Taiwanese chef and restaurant owner to receive the award.
Founded in 2004, Fleur de Sel has served French fine dining in Taiwan for more than two decades.
Early in her career, Li traveled to France to study at culinary academies and language schools and train alongside Michelin-starred chefs.
She continues to lead her team on annual trips to France to exchange techniques and explore regional cuisines.
Laplanche praised Li for spending two decades introducing French culinary culture to Taiwan by blending classical technique with local ingredients, while inspiring young Taiwanese chefs to train abroad.
Delivering her acceptance speech entirely in French, Li expressed gratitude for the recognition, noting that French cuisine had taught her so much and continues to inspire her today.
Over time, she incorporated her Taiwanese roots, home flavors, and Taiwan’s seasonal ingredients, finding her own style and voice at the intersection of two cultures.
Known as the “Godmother of Western Cuisine in Taiwan,” Li has kitchen staff who have worked with her for more than 15 years.
To maintain the physical stamina required for daily prep work and menu development, Li has followed a weight-training routine for more than a decade.
To mark the honor, Fleur de Sel launched its autumn tasting menu, highlighting seasonal produce, wild game, and mushrooms.
The new menu features sweet autumn crab balanced with yuzu and fennel, as well as tuna and Wagyu tartare combining land and sea ingredients with precise knife work, accented with caviar and perilla flowers.
A slow-caramelized French onion soup built on a beef consomme base recreates a recipe from Li’s student days in France.
For the main course, roasted pigeon is infused with subtle longan wood smoke, served with burdock root and autumn persimmon.
The meal concludes with a dessert pairing seasonal lotus seeds with sweet osmanthus honey, a reimagining of the classic Mont Blanc inspired by memories of Li’s grandmother.
Fleur de Sel launches autumn menu. (Taiwan News, Lyla Liu video)

Prospects for Kazakhstan’s partnership with Belgium and EU discussed in Brussels
Roman Vassilenko, Ambassador of Kazakhstan to Belgium and Luxembourg and Head of the Mission of the Republic of Kazakhstan to the European Union, addressed a briefing at the Press Club Brussels Europe dedicated to the outcomes of the State Visit of King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium to Kazakhstan, as well as prospects for cooperation with Belgium and the European Union, Qazinform News Agency cites the Kazakh MFA press srervice.
The discussion on October 24 brought together G. Dubois, Deputy Director of the Central Asia and Caucasus Department at the Belgian Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Marilyn Josephson, Foreign Policy Adviser to the President of the European Council; and representatives of the diplomatic corps, the media and the expert community.
In his remarks, Ambassador Vassilenko highlighted the historic significance of the first-ever State Visit by a Belgian monarch to Kazakhstan, which took place on 12–14 October, underscoring its important role in strengthening political dialogue and expanding trade and economic ties between the two countries.
The Ambassador provided a detailed overview of the visit’s tangible outcomes, including the adoption of a Joint Statement by the two Heads of State and the signing of a Roadmap for Cooperation for 2027–2029 by the two countries’ foreign ministries. A total of 40 documents were announced during the visit, including 16 commercial agreements and 22 agreements between universities and research institutions.
Particular attention was paid to implementing the agreements reached in transport and logistics, critical minerals, agriculture, healthcare, education and advanced technologies. In this context, the Ambassador highlighted opportunities to develop cooperation between the Port of Antwerp-Bruges and Kazakhstan’s ports of Aktau and Kuryk, as well as joint projects in critical raw materials processing, scientific research and artificial intelligence.
Ambassador Vassilenko noted that bilateral trade had more than tripled over the past decade, reaching approximately EUR 765 million in 2025. More than 100 Belgian companies are currently operating in Kazakhstan.
Turning to cooperation with the European Union, the Ambassador emphasised Kazakhstan’s role as the EU’s key trade and economic partner in Central Asia. In 2025, trade between Kazakhstan and the European Union exceeded USD 45 billion. Priority areas for further cooperation include the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, energy security, critical raw materials and digital technologies.
In this regard, the diplomat also highlighted the significance of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Brussels in June this year and the first Central Asia–EU Summit, held in Samarkand in April 2025.
Ahead of Republic Day and the 35th anniversary of Kazakhstan’s Independence, Ambassador Vassilenko also outlined the country’s socio-economic achievements, ongoing political reforms and priorities for digital transformation.
For his part, Gommaar Dubois, representing the Belgian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, highly commended the outcomes of the State Visit, noting its extensive political, economic and academic programme. According to him, the participation of a substantial Belgian delegation comprising 115 members, together with events held in Astana and Almaty, helped establish direct contacts between the business and scientific communities of the two countries.
The Belgian diplomat also drew attention to the entry into force, on 1 November this year, of the agreement between the Benelux countries and Kazakhstan on visa-free travel for holders of service passports. He noted that the agreement would facilitate more frequent official contacts, including with the institutions of the European Union.
Marilyn Josephson, Foreign Policy Adviser to the President of the European Council, emphasised that diversifying economic ties and strengthening connectivity remain key priorities for the further development of the EU’s partnership with Kazakhstan. She highlighted opportunities for cooperation in digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, energy security, renewable energy, green hydrogen and critical raw materials.
The EU representative paid particular attention to the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, which has been designated a flagship project under the EU’s Global Gateway initiative. According to her, unlocking the corridor’s full potential requires investment in railway and port infrastructure and logistics hubs, alongside the simplification of border-crossing and trade procedures.
Marilyn Josephson noted that, following the intensification of high-level political dialogue in 2025–2026, the priority should now be to translate political commitments into tangible results, including increased trade and investment and stronger scientific, educational and business ties.
During the discussion, participants exchanged views on the next steps towards implementing the agreements reached, attracting investment, enhancing transport connectivity and expanding cooperation between businesses, universities and research institutions in Kazakhstan and Belgium.
Earlier, Ambassador Roman Vassilenko met with Kazakh students studying at universities across Belgium and Luxembourg.

Russia, Ukraine begin localised ceasefire to allow for humanitarian operation in Oleshky
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:11:10 CET
11:11:10 KST

By Dan Peleschuk and Anna Voitenko
KYIV, Oct 27 (Reuters) -
A ceasefire began on Tuesday around the Ukrainian town of Oleshky after more than four years of Russian occupation which have left trapped and starving residents desperate for food, water and medicine.
The local ceasefire, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump with the involvement of Pope Leo, is intended to allow aid into Oleshky and enable those who want to leave to do so. Some residents say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild weed added.
Russia and Ukraine both said they were abiding by the local ceasefire around the frontline city, which went into force at 3 a.m. Ukrainian time (0100 GMT) as part of stuttering US efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine and is due to last until November 1.
The ceasefire does not apply elsewhere, and Russian forces again pounded the Ukrainian capital Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, killing at least one person, local officials said.
Kyiv residents said they hoped the Oleshky ceasefire would finally bring some relief to locals, but optimism was tinged with concerns that Russia would not abide by the terms of the agreement.
“I want to hope that things will indeed work out this way, that the agreement will actually be implemented, and that the Russian side will keep its word,” Olha Haiduk, 59, told Reuters.
The head of President Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s ruling faction in parliament, David Arakhamia, called it the “biggest de-escalation since 2022.”
RUSSIAN OCCUPATION
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, opposite Kherson city, which is held by Ukrainian forces. Russian troops seized Oleshky during the first days of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and have controlled it ever since.
Oleshky has suffered extensive war damage and was hit hard by flooding after the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023.
The United States has said only a few thousand people remain in the town from a prewar population of 24,000. Residents and officials have reported severe shortages of food, medicine and other basic supplies, and Oleshky has been largely cut off from running water, electricity, gas and central heating.
Residents have offered harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads just to access food and water, one of which they call the “road of death”.
Ukrainian and Russian officials have said humanitarian corridors will be established to allow aid deliveries and the movement of residents. This is expected to involve demining of roads and could take several days.
One resident who managed to flee Oleshky told Reuters many of those remaining in Oleshky are sick or elderly, and that it would be difficult for them to relocate.
Ukraine and Russia blame each other for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky. Drones present the greatest threat to civilian life, and the town is within easy reach of unmanned aerial vehicles belonging to both armies.
White House envoys have talked to both sides in recent days as part of the US efforts to mediate an end to Europe’s deadliest conflict since the World War Two.
Zelenskiy said last week that three-way talks would continue in Abu Dhabi in early November. Russia’s pace of battlefield gains has slowed this year, but it has said Kyiv must cede the remaining 20% of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine that it still controls before Russian forces stop fighting.
Nataliia Bondar, a 52-year-old accountant in Kyiv, said she was pessimistic about Washington’s ability to negotiate with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Unfortunately, it seems to me that they are somewhat in their own world and do not understand the true nature of this man,” she said. “That you should not negotiate with him.”
NEW STRIKES ON KYIV
Russia’s overnight strikes damaged a university campus and Kyiv’s important Southern Bridge, in what Zelenskiy described as “a serious escalation” against Ukrainian logistics.
A Ukrainian military source said the bridge had been hit with four Iskander ballistic missiles.
Zelenskiy said energy facilities, logistics and infrastructure in 10 other regions also came under attack overnight.
Moscow’s defence ministry said it had struck transport infrastructure in Kyiv, a logistics hub in the Kharkiv region, as well as industrial facilities and cargo vessels in attacks aimed at military targets.
In Russia, a drone attack killed one person in the western city of Bryansk near the border with Ukraine, authorities said. One person was killed and 30 injured in a strike on a bus in a Moscow-held part of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, officials said.
Reuters could not immediately independently verify the reports. Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
(Additional reporting by Jekaterīna Golubkova in Tokyo and Tom Balmforth in London; Editing by Timothy Heritage)

By Kanishka Singh
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Dozens of countries including the US and major European powers said Sudan was experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security and urged parties to the conflict in the country “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance.”
The countries jointly said that in the face of a potential famine, they were calling on the international community to scale up funding and urging financial institutions to adapt their ongoing programs to the food security situation.
“Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action,” the joint statement released by the US State Department said.
“The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people.”
Sudan’s army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when the two fell out over issues including how to integrate their forces in a planned transition to civilian rule.
In June, the United Nations-backed global hunger monitor, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, said 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger. Farmers have struggled to harvest their crops since the civil war flared in 2023 and have also recently been battling a drought.
The joint statement urged parties in the conflict to authorize humanitarian operations through all crossline and cross-border routes, including air access into Darfur.
It also called on them to “sustain presence and protection of humanitarian personnel” throughout Sudan and refrain from strikes on civilian infrastructure.
The statement was signed by the US, Australia, the UK, France, Germany and the European Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, among others.
The State Department said last month that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary nor either of their respective leaders “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan.”
The war has displaced more than 14 million people and unleashed waves of ethnically driven killings.
A UN probe said in July RSF forces carried out mass killings, rapes and forced starvation in a city they besieged and captured last year, as part of an intentional policy amounting to genocide.
Washington has also accused the RSF of committing genocide and the army of carrying out war crimes. Both have previously denied abuses.

US appeals court denies Trump admin request to block California from counting mail ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:08:15 UTC
11:08:15 KST

A US appeals court has ruled against President Donald Trump's administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens.
The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday marked the latest setback in Trump's efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the November 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
The majority decision said the Justice Department failed to give a lower-court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, so it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in. The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Tuesday in the case.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government "asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state's traditional domain, upending the state's policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike."
The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent a state from counting votes, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people on its list had actually submitted a mail ballot.
Justice Department officials said on October 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting.
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state.
'Reckless political stunt'
Trump has long argued that California's immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on October 15 in federal court in Los Angeles.
The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration's list from the rest of the ballots and not count them until it verified that the people who cast them were citizens.
The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
California says the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data."
"At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt," lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing. "At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election."
The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots. It has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters' sensitive personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one.
"Today's ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump's disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country's democracy," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat.

“I’m really good in real estate and fixing things. I fix things very good, very beautifully, and I always build beautiful and inexpensive,” Trump told a rally in Corinth, Mississippi.
“I can do it naturally. It’s a natural thing. It actually relaxes me,” he said.
Obama said over the weekend that Trump’s renovations made the White House look like “Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory.”
“He said, ‘This isn’t a Cheesecake Factory.’ Can you believe it? Which is a very successful company. He doesn’t like successful companies,” Trump said.
Trump said the White House was in “horrible condition” when he took over, adding: “The plaster was falling off the exterior.”
He said ornamentation around several windows had “fallen off or half fallen off,” adding: “We made a mold of the good one, and we put it on the other one, and we got it all beautiful.”
Referring to the ballroom being built in the East Wing, Trump said: “I would have done it the first time, but I was under siege by the radical lunatics. ... So I didn’t have time.”
Trump also said the White House is “a symbol of America” and must be maintained properly.

The Ultrawealthy Produce More Carbon Pollution Than Nearly Half of Humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:02:53 UTC
11:02:53 KST

The ultrawealthy are responsible for more carbon pollution than more than half of humanity, according to a new report published Monday by Oxfam, a global organization fighting against inequality.
“We are seeing the ways that the ultra rich in the U.S. and around the world contribute disproportionately to creating the climate crisis,” says Rachel Carle, senior advisor on climate justice at Oxfam America. “They are also insulated from the impacts of the climate crisis, and are profiting off of the disasters that they have created.”
Billionaires and the ultra-rich are burning more carbon than than most of the world. The world’s richest 1%—just 8 million people who make, on average, $442,000 a year—produce far more emissions than the poorest 3.5 billion, states the report. Someone in the richest 0.1% emits 48 times more CO2 than the average person in the U.S. over the course of a year.
Oxfam used climate attribution models and a consumption-based emissions dataset developed by the Stockholm Environment Institute to calculate emissions by income group. Keeping emissions in check is a key part of addressing the climate crisis. This month, the United Nations warned that, in order to keep warming below 2°C, urgent action must be taken to drastically reduce global emissions by 18% by 2030.
Research has long shown that wealthier countries drive a disproportionate share of global emissions. But emissions disparities exist within countries as well. The U.S., for example, is the second largest carbon emitter behind China—but not everyone is responsible for the same share of emissions. The report finds that, in just under four months (118.3 days), someone in the richest 0.1% living in the U.S., those making an average of $1.98 million a year, emits more CO2 than what someone in the poorest half of the country (those making an average of $25,600 a year), has emitted over the last 30 years.
One of the biggest sources of emissions? Private jets—which, in 2025, were responsible for 16 million metric tons of CO2, the emissions equivalent of the annual energy use of over 2 million homes. The U.S. has the highest concentration of private jet use—with the majority of all private jets (68%) taking off from the U.S. Combined, all of the world’s private jets emit more in 2 seconds than someone in the world’s poorest 50%, those annually making an average of $1,500, would emit in a year. According to the report, last year private jets spent more than 6.5 million hours in the air.
“We see that the ultrarich consume differently than everyday people,” says Carle, who adds that the ultrarich are also far more likely to invest in polluting companies. A list of 217 companies that “profit from either creating climate disasters, preparing for them, or recovering from them,” analyzed in the report shows they made $1.8 billion on average in 2025, and paid out more than $1 billion to shareholders.
This has a direct impact on the climate, the report finds. The researchers constructed emissions pathway models to attribute the emissions of different income groups, and found that the richest 1% are responsible for 20% of global warming since 1990—20 times more than their share of the world’s population. Someone from the richest 1% contributed 34 times more than the average person to extreme heat events, the report states, and one year's worth of emissions from the richest 1% will cause an estimated 1.9 million excess heat deaths.
Yet, the ultrawealthy are less likely to face the impacts of their emissions. Those with lower incomes are significantly more likely to suffer from the impacts of climate disasters and extreme weather events—and often lack the funds to recover from disasters. Wealthy individuals, on the other hand, are more likely to live in safer locations or have the funds to ride out a disaster—purchasing private resources, like firefighters and generators, or paying a premium for emergency shelter.
The authors suggest taxing the emissions of the super-rich. This could be done through taxes on high-emitting luxury items and activities, like private jet use, to disincentivize their use, suggests the report, or via windfall taxes on profits from fossil fuel companies. The report envisions that these taxes could be used to help level the playing field when it comes to climate adaptation, like increasing climate financing in the Global South, or investing in adaptation measures around the world.
“We hope that people take away that there are a lot of opportunities to address inequality in ways that protect the planet and protect communities,” says Carle. “Polluters need to pay for the harm that they’ve caused.”

Russia, Ukraine begin Oleshky ceasefire but keep up strikes elsewhere
KYIV – Russia and Ukraine have begun a regional ceasefire to allow the start of a humanitarian effort in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, both sides said on Oct 27, but they continue strikes elsewhere, including the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv.
The ceasefire should enable deliveries of aid as well as evacuations from the frontline town in southern Ukraine that is grappling with acute shortages of food and medicine.
“As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments,” Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said in a Facebook post confirming Russia’s timing of its halt.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Telegram that it stopped shelling in the direction of the Ukrainian city of Kherson from 4am Moscow time (9am Singapore time) to prepare for the effort in Oleshky, just across the Dnipro River from Kherson.
Lubinets added that the deal was reached in coordination with US First Lady Melania Trump in cooperation with Russia’s commissioner for human rights, Yana Lantratova.
New strikes on Kyiv force traffic halt
New strikes on Oct 27 hit the Southern Bridge and subway infrastructure in Kyiv, forcing a suspension of traffic, city officials said, while a Reuters witness heard explosions.
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro in Ukraine’s southern region of Kherson, opposite the city of Kherson, which is held by Ukrainian forces.
Russian troops seized Oleshky during the first days of their February 2022 invasion and have controlled it ever since.
White House envoys have talked to both sides in recent days to try and find a solution as the US looks to mediate a peace deal to end the war, Europe’s deadliest conflict since the World War II.
On Oct 23, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said peace negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to meet at a technical level in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi to continue the talks.
Fresh attacks
A Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one and injured 15, including students in a dormitory, since the evening of Oct 26. The attacks also killed and injured people in the cities of Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
On the Telegram messaging app, the Russian defence ministry said it has hit transport infrastructure in Kyiv, a logistics hub in the Kharkiv region as well as industrial facilities and cargo vessels elsewhere it cited as being put to military use.
A drone attack killed a man and wounded six people in the western Russian city of Bryansk, close to the border with Ukraine.
Another person was killed and 30 injured as a drone hit a bus in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s south-eastern region of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said.
Reuters could not immediately independently verify the reports. Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians. REUTERS

Department sinks PM's claim $6m golf club grant was to fix sewage issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:53:00 UTC
10:53:00 KST

PM admits Marrickville Golf Club grant is not to fix sewage issues, after department sinks his claim
In short:
Department officials rejected the prime minister's claim that a $6 million grant promised to Marrickville Golf Club was meant for fixing sewerage issues.
The prime minister admitted his initial claim to the House of Representatives that the grant was for sewerage fixes was wrong.
What's next?
The national audit office is considering deeper scrutiny of the $500 million grants program under which the Marrickville Golf Club received funding.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been forced to admit that a $6 million grant he promised to Marrickville Golf Club is not for fixing sewerage issues, as he previously asserted to the House of Representatives.
Following the ABC's report revealing Mr Albanese held an undisclosed honorary membership to the club, the prime minister chastised the national broadcaster and told MPs the grant funding was to stop raw sewage flooding into the nearby Cooks River.
"When it floods in Marrickville, raw sewage flows into the Cooks River. That is what the funding is for," he told the House of Representatives last month.
But the Infrastructure Department sank that claim under questioning at Senate estimates on Monday, confirming the project did not include any sewerage works.
The vast majority of the $6 million grant will go towards a major redevelopment of the Royal Marrickville clubhouse, including a new bar, new furnishings and outdoor dining, a "dog-walking station", and office and meeting spaces, as well as a redesigned pro shop.
But $1 million will go towards stormwater harvesting upgrades that will help to water the greens, and $500,000 will be spent on "botanic plantings" and landscaping, according to Inner West Council meeting minutes.
Mr Albanese admitted to the chamber he was wrong to say the grant was to fix sewage issues.
"That was not correct. The state government had moved in and are funding the project," Mr Albanese said.
"The NSW government is funding the sewerage-related aspects of the club, which has been an issue for a very long time.
"The funding was going to be for sewerage; the NSW government has stepped in, which is appropriate because NSW run water and sewerage."
Earlier, Manager of Opposition Business Dan Tehan attempted to compel Mr Albanese to provide an explanation on whether he had misled the house by repeatedly stating the grant was for sewage fixes.
"This is an opportunity for the prime minister to clear the air. This is an opportunity for the prime minister to be frank with the house," Mr Tehan said.
"Just admit you got it wrong and tell the truth."
PM's claim rejected
Mr Albanese's admission came after Infrastructure Department officials on Monday rejected his claim that the grant's purpose was for sewerage fixes.
"It does not include sewerage works," a department official confirmed under questioning.
Mr Albanese has a decades-long association with the club and held an undisclosed honorary membership there, but has defended the grant as necessary for the community and says he did not give the final approval for it.
Last month, when pressed on the grant, Mr Albanese repeatedly said the purpose was to fix septic issues causing raw sewage to spill into the Cooks River.
"It has existed for a long time, almost 100 years, and they have a septic tank. Because it is on the flood plain, when it floods in Marrickville raw sewage flows into the Cooks River — that is what the funding is for," Mr Albanese told the House of Representatives.
The prime minister also chastised the ABC for its reporting on the grant and Mr Albanese's undisclosed honorary membership of a club with which he has a decades-long association.
"What it's for — because the ABC were told information they chose not to publish appropriately — what it's for, is at the moment because it's on a flood area by the Cooks River, when it rains and there's flooding, raw sewage goes into the Cooks River. That's what it's for, for fixing that," Mr Albanese claimed regarding the grant.
"And the ABC should do better."
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie, who has pursued the issue at an inquiry and at estimates, said the prime minister should apologise.
"This prime minister is a man who clearly can never admit when he has got it wrong. He was given three opportunities in Question Time in the house to apologise for misleading parliament on his commentary last month," Senator McKenzie said.
"The prime minister does need to apologise for misleading parliament, because our democracy is based on trust."
Documents released under freedom of information laws show the brief prepared by the department to Transport Minister Catherine King, and shared with the prime minister's office, contained no mention of septic issues or sewerage works as part of the $6 million grant.
That brief said the clubhouse refurbishment would include furniture, lighting, bar area and alfresco dining upgrades, public toilets, a dog walking station and dedicated space for local environment groups.
The brief was shared with Mr Albanese's office just days before the ABC put questions to the office about the grant and his honorary membership.

In brief

- State-backed hackers have used AI to target systems at greater scale and speed.
Artificial intelligence poses an "unprecedented" threat as foreign governments turn it loose to hack computer networks and critical infrastructure, Australia's cyber security agency warns.
The Australian Signals Directorate said rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models could be of huge benefit if harnessed for good, even using some AI tools to compile its own annual "cyber threat" report.
But recent months had also shown how AI was helping criminals and state-sponsored hackers launch attacks at "greater scale than ever before", the directorate said in the report, released on Tuesday.
"AI has been the defining force in the cyber threat landscape over the past year, allowing malicious actors to find vulnerabilities faster and exploit them at unprecedented scale, speed and sophistication," the report read.
"In recent weeks, new threats have emerged from the unintended actions of AI agents and model testing."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Global concerns about the power of advanced AI tools are mounting after a string of hacking incidents involving models from leading developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
The report documented a stark increase in cybersecurity incidents.
The Australian Signals Directorate issued more than 4,400 warnings about potentially malicious activity over the past year — an 80 per cent increase compared to the prior 12 months.
"State-sponsored cyber actors continued to target Australian organisations primarily to gain access to sensitive or non-public information," it said.
"This activity extends beyond government networks, and includes critical infrastructure entities, private businesses and individuals."
The report said hackers linked to China, Russia and North Korea had targeted Australia or its allies in recent times.
Defence Minister Richard Marles said the nation could not ignore the AI revolution.
"AI is here, and it's real. People need to engage," he told reporters.
"There's no turning the clock back in relation to that. Malicious actors are using AI to find vulnerabilities in systems."
Marles urged Australians to update their computers and "harden their systems".
Governments and firms have in recent days been rushing to fix critical flaws in a programming language that runs a large share of the world's websites.
The vulnerability was found using a powerful model from OpenAI.

US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
October 27, 2026
The US Justice Department has launched a third attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of illegally disclosing national defense information in 2016.
Court documents unsealed on Monday reveal allegations that Comey directed a subordinate to share classified information with a journalist.
The case marks another escalation in President Donald Trump's long-running conflict with the former FBI chief, who has denied wrongdoing.
What are the latest allegations against James Comey?
The case centers on an October 2016 New York Times article about a secret US surveillance order involving internet company Yahoo.
The order reportedly required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. It had been issued by a secret intelligence court.
Prosecutors allege that Comey instructed a staff member to contact a New York Times journalist to correct inaccurate information published by news agency Reuters the previous day.
According to the Justice Department, this resulted in the illegal transfer of classified national defense information to an unauthorized person.
However, the allegations have already been investigated twice.
Federal authorities began examining the disclosure in 2017. Prosecutor John Durham recommended against bringing criminal charges in December 2018, according to Comey's lawyers.
A second investigation, launched in 2019 under the code name "Tropical Vortex," was also closed without charges in February 2020.
How are Comey's lawyers fighting the new charges?
The Justice Department filed a legal document known as a "criminal information" in early October, shortly before the 10-year deadline for prosecuting the alleged offense.
Unlike an indictment, a criminal information does not require approval from a grand jury or judge.
Prosecutors say the filing allows them to extend the statute of limitations, which determines how long authorities have to bring criminal charges.
Comey's lawyers dispute that interpretation. They argue that federal law explicitly requires an indictment within 10 years and that the government's filing does not meet that requirement.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case. A ruling is still pending.
Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, also pointed to the two earlier investigations.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
Responding to the latest allegations in a video posted on Substack, Comey condemned the prosecution.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," he said.
"I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
What other criminal cases does James Comey face?
The latest case is the third criminal proceeding brought against Comey since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
In September 2025, prosecutors charged him with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding.
A federal judge dismissed the case after finding that the Trump-appointed prosecutor who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.
In April 2026, Comey was indicted again, this time over an Instagram photograph showing seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
The Justice Department interpreted the numbers as a threat against Trump, arguing that "86" referred to killing someone and "47" identified Trump as the 47th US president.
Comey denied threatening Trump's life and has sought to have that case dismissed.
Why has Trump targeted former FBI director Comey?
Comey was appointed FBI director in 2013 by Democratic President Barack Obama.
His relationship with Trump deteriorated shortly after the president took office in 2017.
Comey resisted Trump's request to pledge personal loyalty during a private dinner.
Trump fired him in May 2017 while the FBI was investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and possible connections to Trump's campaign.
The investigation was subsequently taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller. It established that Russia had interfered in the election but found insufficient evidence to prove criminal coordination between Moscow and Trump's campaign.
The two men have remained bitter political opponents. Trump has repeatedly accused Comey of treason, while Comey compared the president to a mafia boss in his 2018 memoir.

Investigations conducted this year have uncovered other attempts targeting facilities in Romania, including international military sites and facilities used to train Ukraine's Armed Forces.
The service warned that these actions are intended to intimidate, undermine defence capabilities and weaken countries' contributions to European and regional security.
Romanian intelligence also highlighted that recruitment for sabotage operations typically takes place through social media. Recruits are initially offered money for individual tasks, such as monitoring or photographing specific sites. The assignments then become increasingly serious and may escalate to acts of destruction, arson or even murder. If recruits refuse, their handlers may resort to pressure and blackmail.
These networks exploit financial vulnerability, addiction or criminal records. To conceal their identities and movements, members often use transport, accommodation and payment methods registered in other people's names. They also communicate using SIM cards from third countries and encrypted messaging apps.
"The Intelligence Service, together with the Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism, General Directorate for Defence Intelligence and the Ministry of Internal Affairs, is continuing to investigate sabotage operations detected within the country," the statement said.

1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:35:08 UTC
10:35:08 KST

1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
- Summary:
- New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
- Share:
An archaeological site in the Jordan Valley is rewriting the timeline of early human migration. New research shows that 'Ubeidiya is at least 1.9 million years old, placing humans in the region hundreds of thousands of years earlier than previously believed. The revised dating makes 'Ubeidiya, alongside Dmanisi in Georgia, one of the oldest known sites of early human activity outside Africa. The findings suggest that ancient human populations, using different types of stone tools, had already spread into the Levant during a crucial early period of human expansion beyond Africa.
The research was led by Prof. Ari Matmon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Prof. Omry Barzilai of the University of Haifa, and Prof. Miriam Belmaker of the University of Tulsa. By combining three advanced dating methods, the team established a more reliable timeline for 'Ubeidiya, a site that has played an important role in research on human evolution.
Their findings indicate that the site is at least 1.9 million years old, making it one of the earliest known locations where ancient humans lived outside their African homeland.
Ancient Stone Tools Reveal Early Human Activity
The 'Ubeidiya Formation has attracted scientific attention for decades because of its early evidence of the Acheulean stone tool tradition. This technology is known for large tools shaped on both sides, including hand axes. The site also contains a rich collection of animal fossils, representing species originally associated with Africa and Asia, including several that are now extinct.
Despite its importance, researchers have struggled to establish exactly when early humans occupied the area. Previous estimates generally placed 'Ubeidiya between 1.2 million and 1.6 million years old, but those dates relied on comparisons with other archaeological and geological evidence rather than direct measurements.
To resolve the uncertainty, the researchers collected new samples from the site and analyzed them using three complementary dating techniques. Each provided an independent source of evidence about the age of the ancient deposits.
The first technique, called cosmogenic isotope burial dating, uses rare isotopes that form when cosmic rays interact with rocks exposed at Earth's surface. After the rocks become buried, these isotopes decay at known rates. Measuring what remains allows scientists to estimate how long the rocks have been underground.
The researchers also investigated evidence of Earth's ancient magnetic field recorded in sediments deposited at the bottom of a lake. As these sediments accumulated, they preserved the orientation of the magnetic field at the time. Comparing these records with known magnetic reversals showed that the deposits formed during the Matuyama Chron, a period that began more than two million years ago.
A third technique involved fossilized shells from Melanopsis, a genus of freshwater snails found within the sediment. Using uranium-lead dating, the team was able to establish a minimum age for the geological layers containing the ancient stone tools.
Together, the three approaches pointed to a much older age than earlier estimates.
A 1.9-Million-Year-Old Discovery Changes the Human Migration Timeline
The combined evidence indicates that 'Ubeidiya dates back at least 1.9 million years, significantly changing the timeline of early human settlement beyond Africa.
This places the Jordan Valley site at approximately the same age as Dmanisi in Georgia, another major location for understanding early human migration. The similarity in age suggests that ancient human populations were expanding into different regions around the same time.
The findings also raise intriguing questions about how these early migrations unfolded. Evidence from the two sites suggests that different groups of ancient humans may have carried distinct stone tool technologies out of Africa during overlapping periods.
These included the Oldowan tradition, associated with relatively simple stone tools, and the more sophisticated Acheulean tradition, known for carefully shaped tools such as hand axes. Rather than spreading in a single technological sequence, these different approaches to toolmaking may have traveled beyond Africa at roughly the same time as separate groups of early humans entered new environments.
Solving a Three-Million-Year-Old Dating Puzzle
The researchers also had to explain an unexpected complication in their results. Initial measurements of cosmogenic isotopes suggested that some rocks were approximately three million years old, considerably older than indicated by the site's magnetic, fossil, geological, and archaeological evidence.
Further investigation revealed why the measurements appeared to conflict.
The sediments had undergone a complicated history of repeated deposition, burial, exposure, and movement within the Dead Sea rift and the surrounding landscape. Some of the material had been buried long before it was eventually transported and deposited again near the ancient lake at 'Ubeidiya.
This recycling meant that the geological history recorded by certain rocks extended much farther into the past than the formation of the archaeological layers themselves.
As the researchers explained:
"The exposure-burial history that emerges from the model implies recycling of sediments previously deposited and buried in the rift valley... and then redeposited along the 'Ubeidiya paleo lake shoreline."
By accounting for this complex sediment history, the team reconciled the conflicting measurements and strengthened the evidence for the site's revised age.
The results establish 'Ubeidiya as one of the oldest known centers of early human activity outside Africa. They also suggest that the movement of our ancient relatives into new territories was already underway 1.9 million years ago, potentially involving multiple populations with different toolmaking traditions.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- A. Matmon, A. Kuzmenko, R. Shaar, P. Nuriel, A. Hidy, M. Guillong, R. Blevis, N. Wieler, S. Vainer, Y. Asscher, M. Belmaker, O. Barzilai. Complex exposure-burial history and Pleistocene sediment recycling in the dead sea rift with implications for the age of the Acheulean site of ‘Ubeidiya. Quaternary Science Reviews, 2026; 378: 109871 DOI: 10.1016/j.quascirev.2026.109871

Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in Oleshky brokered by US first lady takes effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:33:54 UTC
10:33:54 KST

Kanyshai Butun
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky brokered by US first lady Melania Trump took effect at 0100GMT on Tuesday to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
An official press release was issued Friday by the White House confirming that the first lady had served as the "Exclusive Intermediary" to secure the localized agreement.
The development came amid worsening shortages of food, medicine and clean water in Oleshky, a frontline town located on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine's southern Kherson region. Residents must also contend with limited access to electricity, mined roads and recurring military attacks, according to the White House.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster,” Melania Trump said. “It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”
Russian Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov said Moscow would implement a “regime of silence” in the Kherson direction from 4 am Moscow time on Oct. 27 to facilitate humanitarian operations.
“To ensure the safety of the population and the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be conducted, and the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy to the settlement of Oleshky, Kherson Region, will be facilitated,” the Russian Defense Ministry quoted him as saying.
Ukraine’s General Staff said it would implement a localized ceasefire from 3 am Kyiv time the same day to deliver humanitarian aid to Oleshky’s residents and ensure the safe, unhindered evacuation of civilians.
Under the arrangement, civilian representatives from Russia and Ukraine will assess residents’ needs. Those wishing to leave will receive coordinated transportation to destinations in either country, while a US media organization will accompany the teams to document the process, according to the White House.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the duration of the operation remained uncertain but noted that it could last several days.
The truce comes as Moscow and Kyiv trade blame for the worsening humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, a city that Russian forces captured in 2022.
Oleshky had a prewar population of around 24,000, but estimates suggest that only 1,700-2,000 people remain, many of them older residents unable to leave.
The collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in southern Ukraine in June 2023 triggered massive flooding in nearby communities, including Oleshky, that destroyed homes and forced thousands of people to flee, with Ukraine and Russia each accusing the other of deliberately destroying the dam.

Bolsonaro’s party accepts Brazil election after Trump calls vote ‘rigged’
Trump pushes unsubstantiated claims about Brazil’s presidential vote but says he ‘didn’t take sides’ in the race.
The political party of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has acknowledged the result of Brazil’s presidential run-off, despite the right-wing candidate pledging to annul the outcome.
On Monday, Valdemar Costa Neto, the leader of the right-wing Liberal Party, issued a statement saying his political group had accepted the outcome of the vote.
Still, he echoed Bolsonaro’s concerns about the circumstances surrounding the election.
“We recognise the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
On Sunday, Bolsonaro was defeated by left-wing incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by a margin of more than 4.4 million votes.
Bolsonaro has yet to formally concede. In a post-election speech, he called the election results “unacceptable”, citing a last-minute extension to voting hours.
“We will take legal action,” he told supporters. “I will request that these elections be annulled.”
In a video posted on social media on Monday, Bolsonaro also announced that federal police asked him to hand over his passports amid speculation that he could leave the country following his loss.
He said that he would comply with the order and had no plans to leave.
He said the decision came from a Supreme Court justice, and was based on a comment by his US-based brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who told a US podcast two days before the election that “if my brother does not win, I am in favor that he would leave the country.”
Eduardo cited investigations against his brother.
Brazilian police are probing Flavio Bolsonaro over alleged corruption linked to the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.
“I never had any intention of leaving the country. I will surrender my passports and defend myself against this travesty,” Flavio Bolsonaro said.
The right-wing candidate also took up the mantle as “leadership of the opposition” in a separate statement.
Extended voting
An extension to Sunday’s vote had been sought by the campaigns of both candidates — but for different reasons.
Bolsonaro’s camp had pointed to inclement weather that impeded some voters from reaching polling stations. Parts of southern Brazil, considered a right-wing stronghold, had experienced heavy rains on Sunday.
Lula’s campaign, meanwhile, pushed for longer voting hours after it accused some cities of limiting public transportation on election day.
The left-wing leader’s allies framed those reductions in service as an attempt at election interference, aimed at preventing Lula’s working-class base from voting.
Media reports indicated that Pablo Souza, a transportation official in the city of Salvador, was arrested on Sunday over the matter.
In response to the petitions, Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin agreed to extend voting by two hours.
Whereas polls across the country had been slated to close at 5pm Brasilia time (20:00 GMT), Zanin’s order allowed those that had not already closed to remain open until 7pm (22:00 GMT).
Following his loss, Bolsonaro cried foul, saying that the justice’s decision had disadvantaged his voters.
He pointed to Zanin’s relationship with Lula as support: Lula had appointed Zanin to the high court in 2023, and Zanin had formerly served as the left-wing politician’s personal lawyer.
“With a simple stroke of a pen, at the request of a former partner, [Zanin] changed the rules of the game mid-match,” Bolsonaro said in his address on Sunday night.
But experts signalled they were sceptical of Bolsonaro’s claims of malfeasance.
An analysis by Pedro Burgos, a professor at the Brazilian educational institute Insper, found that the extension resulted in 35,000 additional votes across the country, less than 0.03 percent of the total.
That amount was far short of Lula’s 4.4 million vote advantage. The incumbent won more than 64.25 million votes, compared with Bolsonaro’s 59.83 million.
Still, some right-wing allies rallied to Bolsonaro’s support. US President Donald Trump, who has clashed with Lula in the past, told reporters that the vote seemed “rigged”.
“Elections have to be indisputable and it looked very bad to me,” Trump said on Monday. “It looked like another rigged election, frankly.”
Still, Trump stopped short of suggesting that he would get involved on behalf of Bolsonaro, saying instead he “did not take sides” in the election.
Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept his loss has raised concerns about whether he will abide by the democratic process or follow in the footsteps of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who served as Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2023.
After his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election, the ex-president refused to acknowledge the outcome.
Instead, he and his allies sought to overturn the results, including through a legal challenge, and prosecutors accused him of plotting a coup to prevent the legal transfer of power.
Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence on coup-related charges.
Separately, he was also barred from serving in public office for eight years, after a court found he had misused his public office to spread misinformation about the election.
Flavio Bolsonaro, along with his siblings, has sought to have his father released. The family has denounced the elder Bolsonaro’s trial as a case of political persecution.
Still, it is unclear whether Flavio Bolsonaro will continue with his legal challenge over Sunday’s election.
The Brazilian news outlet Folha de S Paulo reported on Monday that legal advisers and political allies have convinced Bolsonaro to abandon his quest to have his loss annulled, citing the large margin of Lula’s victory and its validation by the Supreme Court and election authorities.

The joint statement urged parties in the conflict to authorise humanitarian operations through all cross-line and cross-border routes, including air access into Darfur.

- The race is close and important for Senate control, but Trump’s low approval in Michigan may also hurt Republicans, despite strong crowd support.

PORT HURON, United States – US President Donald Trump turned to Islamophobic stereotypes to motivate Michigan Republicans on Oct 25, claiming at a rally that Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee, if elected, would bring a wave of jihadis to the country.
“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump told more than 4,000 supporters gathered in Port Huron, a working class, waterfront city in a deep-red congressional district about 95km north-east of Detroit.
Trump called El-Sayed, 41, whose family emigrated from Egypt, a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” – a baseless claim.
He then contrasted El-Sayed, a Muslim who was born in the US, with his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, who is white and also born in the US.
“I call him apple pie,” Trump said of Rogers, who is 63. “He’s like, perfect, this guy. He’s like central casting. He’s what your state is all about.”
Trump’s comments, coming in a key midterm battleground nine days before the elections, underscored the dark themes and personal vilification he and his allies have embraced as part of their closing pitch.
And, while he has often used crude and racist language, Trump’s message in Michigan seemed aimed at overtly stoking a fear of Muslims to get voters to the polls.
But a broader question about Trump’s rally here – which followed several in North and South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, among other stops – is whether his presence helps or hurts Republican turnout in a year when polls show deep dissatisfaction with the president.
His audience in Port Huron seemed enthusiastic, and thousands strained to take Trump’s picture as he took to the stage. But he held the rally in a conservative district of a state that pollsters believe is swinging back to Democrats.
Trump’s deep unpopularity has complicated Republicans’ path to victory.
While Trump carried Michigan by 2 points in 2024, just 34% of likely voters now approve of him, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid-September.
Polls indicate that El-Sayed has a narrow edge over Rogers in a race that will be pivotal to determining control of the Senate.
Trump’s attacks on El-Sayed on Oct 25, questioning his loyalty to the United States, began before he got on Air Force One outside of Washington and accelerated after he landed in Michigan.
Speaking in a town on the Canadian border, Trump did not dwell on his battle with Prime Minister Mark Carney, one of the few world leaders who has directly confronted him on tariffs and other issues, and he did not repeat his frequent call for Canada to give up its independence and become the 51st state.
Instead, he focused on El-Sayed, his religion and his relatives. Trump also disparaged Jewish voters who were considering voting for El-Sayed.
“Any Jewish person who supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” Trump said, adding that he “cannot understand how anybody who’s Jewish can even think about voting for this guy”.
Hundreds of Jewish voters in Michigan publicly announced they were backing El-Sayed, while others have said they are voting for Rogers or threatened to withhold their support.
Trump made the statement after claiming that El-Sayed’s half sister, Eman Abdelhadi, celebrated the Oct 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis by Hamas fighters.
She posted a video on the first anniversary of the attack that said that “no matter how great the brutality, the oppression, the intensity of what we’re going through, the horizon of justice is just around the corner”, but did not mention the massacre directly and did not celebrate the violence.
El-Sayed’s campaign told Fox News that he disagreed with her “on a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use”.
El-Sayed has repeatedly disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement, and has said comments about his name and faith are attempts to distract from voters’ economic woes. His aides have said claims of ties to overseas terrorist groups are racist and Islamophobic.

It was addressed to Mohammed Morsi, then the new Egyptian president, from a party that represents the political wing of the Muslim Brotherhood.

In fact, Trump was forced to drop that demand and instead signed a new treaty with Denmark, which handles Greenland’s foreign affairs, that envisions opening two new US bases on the island and bars similar arrangements with foreign powers, notably China. But it does not change Denmark’s sovereignty, as Trump initially insisted.
He also drew cheers when he insisted Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, and vaguely said the war with Iran would be resolved soon.

Like other Republicans, Rogers has largely avoided talking about Trump in ads and on the campaign trail.
Speaking at the rally in Port Huron, Rogers again accused El-Sayed of having family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. “I’ve never called him a terrorist,” Rogers said of El-Sayed.

After holding forth on the potential demise of the nation in Michigan on Oct 25, Trump spent five full minutes admiring the body and physicality of Senator Jon Husted, the Republican running for re-election in Ohio, and rapper Nicki Minaj, who traveled with Trump to the rally.
