During her absence, President Nicolas Maduro was captured in an extraordinary US military operation, after which his deputy Delcy Rodriguez assumed power as interim leader with Washington's backing.
With Machado observing transition talks from Panama, the US State Department pushed for a reconstituted Supreme Court by the end of this year alongside sweeping reforms to the National Electoral Council—steps deemed vital for credible elections.
Rubio underscored that Washington maintains substantial influence over the process and will hold authorities to strict milestones.
"What if they just try to wait us out for two years? That's not going to happen," Rubio said, warning that anyone attempting to derail the agreed roadmap is doing "great harm to Venezuela."
Rodriguez on Monday dismissed Machado's return as a "show."

Bayern Munich and England striker Harry Kane won the 2026 Men's Ballon d'Or on Monday, becoming the first English player to claim football's most prestigious individual award since Michael Owen in 2001, while Spain's Alexia Putellas secured her third Women's Ballon d'Or.
The awards were presented at the 70th Ballon d'Or ceremony at the London Palladium, marking the first time the prestigious event was held in the British capital.
Kane, 33, claimed the award for the first time after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025-26 campaign, including 61 goals in 51 matches for the German side, which won a domestic double.
The England captain also scored six goals at the 2026 World Cup, helping his country finish third.
Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second in the Men's Ballon d'Or voting, while Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal took third place.
Kane became the fifth English player to win the award, joining Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen, who last claimed the prize in 2001.
He succeeded Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembele, who won the award in 2025.
Meanwhile, Putellas, 32, claimed her third Women's Ballon d'Or following her previous victories in 2021 and 2022, equaling former Barcelona teammate Aitana Bonmati's record.
The Spanish midfielder captained Barcelona to a quadruple during the 2025-26 season, winning Liga F, Copa de la Reina, the Spanish Super Cup and Women's Champions League.
She was also named the Champions League Player of the Season and helped Spain win the Women's Nations League.
Putellas joined London City Lionesses in July after her trophy-laden spell with Barcelona.
- Other award winners
Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal won Men's Young Talent of the Year for the third consecutive year, while Barcelona forward Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second successive year.
Spain's World Cup-winning coach Luis de la Fuente was named Men's Coach of the Year, while Barcelona's Pere Romeu received the women's coaching award.
Athletic Bilbao's Unai Simon won Men's Goalkeeper of the Year, with Barcelona's Cata Coll claiming the women's honor.
Bayern Munich's Kane also received the Men's Striker of the Year award following his prolific campaign, while Mexican forward Charlyn Corral became the first Mexican to win the Women's Striker of the Year award.
Barcelona were named Women's Club of the Year, while Paris Saint-Germain claimed the men's club award.
Arsenal and England winger Bukayo Saka received the Socrates Award for his humanitarian work, including funding 120 medical operations for children in Kano, Nigeria through a partnership with charity BigShoe in 2022.

Trump administration loses push to block California votes from alleged non-citizens

Trump administration loses push to block California votes from alleged non-citizens
- A US appeals court blocked Trump’s bid to stop California counting mail ballots from over 20,000 registered voters the government says may be non-citizens.
- The 9th Circuit said federal action would upset state election powers and risk “disorder and confusion” before the Nov 3 midterms.
- California called the case a “reckless political stunt” that could “disenfranchise thousands”, while evidence says non-citizen voting is very rare.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – A US appeals court on Oct 26 ruled against President Donald Trump’s administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely non-citizens.
The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump’s efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the Nov 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in.
The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Oct 27 in the case.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government “asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged non-citizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election.
The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent votes from being counted by a state, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people allegedly registered to vote in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.
Justice Department officials said on Oct 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting.
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives – 52 – than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump’s fellow Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its so-called “sanctuary state” policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has long asserted that California’s immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including non-citizen voting, is exceedingly rare.
A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which non-citizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration’s list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.
The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
California says the state’s safeguards against non-citizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data”.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing.
“At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration’s methods for scrutinising state voter lists to identify non-citizens risk wrongly flagging naturalised US citizens for removal from the rolls.
The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed non-citizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots.
It has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters’ sensitive personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one.
“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy,” said California Attorney-General Rob Bonta, a Democrat. REUTERS

27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The US Justice Department has filed criminal charges against former FBI Director James Comey for the third time, accusing him of leaking national defense information in October 2016, according to court records unsealed Monday.
 
The two-count criminal information, filed under seal on Oct. 5 in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges that Comey “knowingly and willfully communicated, delivered, transmitted and caused that information to be communicated, delivered and transmitted to a person not entitled to receive it.”
 
Prosecutors allege that on Oct. 5, 2016, Comey, “through one and more co-conspirators directed Individual #1 to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication.”
 
The information ended up in a New York Times article, according to The Wall Street Journal.
 
The filing was signed by Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter.
 
The department said the filing, made exactly 10 years after the alleged disclosure, was meant to preserve the case before the statute of limitations expired while it seeks a grand jury indictment.
 
Comey has moved to dismiss the case in sealed proceedings, arguing that an indictment is required within 10 years and the filing does not suffice.
 
“An indictment fundamentally differs from an information,” his lawyers said in a court filing.
 
In a video posted on social media, Comey said: “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.”
 
“Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary,” he said.
 
Asked about the charges as he arrived at Joint Base Andrews after a rally in Mississippi, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know too much about it. I just heard about it.”
 
“I think he’s a dirty cop, James Comey, but I know nothing about it,” he said.

Trump says Brazil election looked ‘rigged’, defeated Bolsonaro’s party recognizes Lula win
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:37:31 CET
08:37:31 KST

By Oliver Griffin and Eduardo Simões
SAO PAULO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential vote ”looked like another rigged election,” although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in Sunday’s presidential election, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula’s victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party’s head Valdemar Costa Neto.
“We recognize the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party’s statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. “It looked very bad to me.”
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
“I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” Trump said. “The extension given was very strange.”
Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil’s electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump’s remarks were “totally wrong” and “unfounded.”
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil’s former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
MARKETS ROILED BY LULA WIN
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil’s real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
“The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure,” said Pantheon Macroeconomics’ chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula’s victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.
(Reporting by Oliver Griffin, Luciana Magalhaes, Gabriel Araujo, Eduardo Simoes, Lisandra Paraguassu and Andre Romani in Sao Paulo, Ricardo Brito in Brasilia, and Trevor Hunnicutt and Costas Pitas in Washington; editing by Brad Haynes, Gabriel Stargardter, Andrea Ricci, Rosalba O’Brien and Lincoln Feast.)

Harry Kane completed his long quest for football's highest individual honor on Monday, with the Bayern Munich and England striker winning the Ballon d'Or after a record-breaking season that cemented his status as one of the game's greatest goalscorers.

"Wow, wow, wow!" Kane said after taking the stage. "I am almost speechless. Being here in London makes it extra special. It feels like a good omen for me tonight. Thank you to everyone who voted for me. I can imagine it was tough this year.

Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or Féminin for the third time.
Kane's move to Bayern in 2023 brought the team trophies that had long eluded him. In 2025-26, he coupled that success with goalscoring numbers that made him the leading Ballon d'Or candidate.
The England captain produced the most prolific campaign of his life, scoring 61 goals in 51 games for Bayern across all competitions as the German giants completed a domestic league and cup double.
By the end of the season, Kane had established himself as Europe's leading goalscorer, turning every competition into a showcase of his finishing ability.
His influence stretched far beyond club football. As England embarked on another attempt to end decades of hurt at the World Cup, Kane once again emerged as the team's driving force.
He scored six goals during the tournament and led England to the semi-finals, combining his clinical finishing with the leadership and composure that have defined his international career.
In many ways, the award represents the culmination of a remarkable journey. Few players have experienced a career arc quite like Kane's.
Once struggling to establish himself at Tottenham Hotspur as a youngster, being sent out on numerous loans, he developed into one of the most complete center forwards of his generation, capable of scoring every type of goal while also functioning as a playmaker.
The Ballon d'Or has often rewarded players whose success was built on flair and spectacle, but Kane's triumph is a tribute to consistency, intelligence and productivity on an exceptional scale.
Week after week, he delivered. Match after match, he decided contests. There were no prolonged slumps and few quiet nights.
His numbers were almost impossible to ignore.
Kane finished the campaign with 73 goals for club and country, a total rarely seen in the modern era. More importantly, those goals arrived in moments of genuine significance, helping Bayern collect trophies and driving England deep into the biggest tournament in the sport.
Fierce competition
The competition for this year's award was fierce. Kylian Mbappe broke World Cup scoring records. Lamine Yamal helped Spain to World Cup glory. Yet voters ultimately chose Kane, whose excellence lasted the entire season.
At 33, Kane has finally claimed the game's highest individual honor, adding a Ballon d'Or to a legacy that already places him among football's greatest strikers as England's all-time leading marksman and their record World Cup scorer.
Putellas was presented with the women's award after winning the treble with Barcelona in the 2025-26 campaign, in addition to the Spanish Super Cup. She moved to Women's Super League side London City Lionesses in July after 14 years at Barca.

China steps up snow leopard protection as population reaches 5,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

08:36:34 KST

China steps up snow leopard protection as population reaches 5,000
China has continued to strengthen its network of protected areas in key habitats, establishing two national parks and 78 other protected areas in key regions, TV BRICS reported.
Since systematic conservation efforts began in 2013, China’s snow leopard population has doubled, rising from approximately 2,500 to around 5,000, whilst its range has expanded to approximately 2.08 million square kilometres.
According to China Daily, a TV BRICS partner, citing data from the National Forestry and Grassland Administration, China is currently home to more than 60 per cent of the global snow leopard range and is the country with the largest snow leopard distribution area and population in the world.
The snow leopard, often hailed as the "King of the Mountains", is a Class I specially protected animal in China; its presence is regarded as a key indicator of the integrity, stability and health of mountain ecosystems. Two national parks and 78 other key protected areas have been established in critical habitats, with over 800,000 square kilometres of habitat under strict protection – meaning nearly 40 per cent of the species’ potential habitat is now under regulatory control.
Significant progress has been made in restoring populations in areas where snow leopards had previously disappeared. In the Helan Mountains region, China launched the country’s first snow leopard reintroduction.

The package included €1 billion of investment in university campuses; a move to increase student grants with inflation; and the opening up of a further 15,000 higher education places for students.
“It’s clear we have to ease the pressure being felt in the education system,” French Education Minister Edouard Geffray told a press conference.
There was no overall figure for how much funding the package would require.
High borrowing needs are already complicating efforts to agree on a budget for 2027.
The protests, initially triggered by student discontent, have shown little sign of ending after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears that the state had lost control of the streets.
Earlier, Macron acknowledged it was likely there would be more unrest this weekend ahead of a bigger nationwide day of protests set for Nov 5.
On a tour to survey the damage in Marseille and to thank emergency services after protests on Oct 24, he said he would keep security measures in place and work to move protests outside city centres.
Candidate Le Pen, already the front runner in the 2027 presidential election, has benefited from the unrest and perceptions that the authorities are struggling to keep the peace.
An opinion poll published on Oct 25 put her at 32% to 33.5%, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, at 17%.
Surveys suggest that she would easily defeat Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May 2027.
Far-right gangs confront far-left activists
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez earlier said that 1,435 people were arrested nationwide during demonstrations on Oct 24 and that police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities.
“We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses,” he said.
“In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement.”
A sell-off in French government bonds paused on Oct 26 after rating agency Moody’s on Oct 23 refrained from downgrading the country’s sovereign debt.
But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage.
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of Oct 17, adding this had led to sharp falls in sales.
“We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce,” he told Radio Classique. REUTERS

Europe's five main NATO members said Monday they were prepared to assume "greater responsibility" within the alliance while continuing to view the United States as an "indispensable ally".
Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Britain (the E5 group) said after talks in Paris that "Europe must assume greater responsibility for its own security" and shoulder a greater burden within the alliance.
"We are determined to work in close coordination with the United States and all Allies in order to implement this concrete ambition," they said in a statement.
"The United States is and will remain an indispensable Ally, and continued United States engagement in European security is essential to a strong and credible NATO."

June 2025 decision to hold SIR taken unanimously, EC tells SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
23:18:52 UTC
08:18:52 KST

EC tells SC that the June 24, 2025 decision to conduct nationwide SIR was unanimous, denying opposition claims that CEC Gyanesh Kumar acted unilaterally.
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission Monday filed an affidavit in SC that the chief election commissioner and the two election commissioners had unanimously taken the decision on June 24, 2025 to conduct nationwide SIR of electoral rolls and that there was no difference of opinion.The affidavit by deputy EC Bhanu Prakash Yeturu came with an unusual declaration that it was being filed with the approval of the CEC and the two ECs. “At the very outset, I state that the present affidavit has been approved for filing before the SC by a unanimous decision of the three members of the Election Commission, that is the 2 election commissioners and the chief election commissioner,” the affidavit said.
The assertion contradicts the charge that CEC Gyanesh Kumar, at Modi government’s instance, unilaterally decided to conduct SIR of electoral rolls — the mainstay of the opposition’s “vote chori” campaign.The affidavit was filed in response to petitions, including one filed by Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders, following a news report that the two ECs — S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi — had approached the cabinet secretary because of their differences with the CEC over SIR-related issues.“Allegations based on the communication between ECs and the cabinet secretary are misconceived,” the EC said, adding that the letters by Sandhu and Joshi pertained to administrative matters.
No substance in claim that Form 6 was amended by SIR orders: EC
An office order came to be issued on July 28 by an IAS officer of the rank of additional secretary who had been posted on deputation to the commission pertaining to internal work allocation. On July 29, the two election commissioners wrote separate letters to the cabinet secretary in relation to this order and the conduct of the officer. In view of the joint direction of July 30 by the two ECs, the order of July 28 was never implemented,” the commission said. Responding to the petitions by Rahul and other INDIA bloc netas, the EC said all the petitions were based on a news article alleging that the commission had not been functioning in accordance with the procedure mandated in law, and allegations were also made questioning the integrity of the commission.It also issued a strong denial of the allegation, another key plank of the opposition’s offensive, that Form 6, as provided under Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, was amended by the commission by the SIR orders of June 24 and Oct 27 last year and May 14 this year. “There is no substance in the contention that Form 6 has been amended by the commission vide the SIR orders.” EC said Form 6 could be amended only by the Centre and what was changed was the introduction of a declaration to “enable the person seeking registration as a voter to dispense with the need for filing documents during the claims and objections period”.The ‘declaration’ was a document provided by the SIR orders and was not a part of Form 6, which was the statutory form for inclusion in the electoral rolls, it said, adding there was no significant change in the earlier and present declaration. The declaration that the affidavit was approved by the two ECs is significant because of the charge that the CEC’s “unilateral” calls on SIR-related issues were violative of the law, which required the poll body to take decisions unanimously or, when not possible, by majority. The opposition has demanded removal and prosecution of Gyanesh Kumar for violating the law.Denying the charge, the affidavit said that while the CEC, the ECs and even other officers may have expressed different views during deliberations, the decisions were taken in accordance with law. “The views by ECs/CEC of the commission during the decision-making process on the subjects before them are considered for arriving at the decision. It is upon consideration of all the views placed before the commission that the decision is taken and the orders are issued in accordance with the process,” the EC said.Explaining the process of decision-making in which views of all divisions concerned with the subject are considered in detail, the EC said, “In any such decision-making process, any suggestion, observation or query by the CEC or ECs either to the ECs or CEC or to any officer of the commission does not constitute a decision of the commission under Section 18 of the CEC and ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.”It said the statute prefers a decision by unanimity but also provides for decision-making by majority in the three-member EC. The commission said the CEC and ECs had taken a unanimous decision on June 29 that “in case any person to whom notice has been issued during the ongoing SIR, for being unmapped and/or logical discrepancies, BLOs will visit the homes of such persons for collection of documents and thereafter upload them in the ECINet, for decision by the ERO”.
“Such person shall not be called for hearing to the ERO/AERO officer. Only in exceptional circumstances, as defined by the ERO/AERO, will the hearing be held, preferably online. Any adult member of the family can be authorised by the elector to attend the hearing on their behalf,” EC said. Referring to the allegation relating to deletion of 97 voters in Goa, the commission said it had directed that no eligible voter should be left out of the rolls and pursuant to this, the BLOs conducted a house-to-house visit and found that 88 of the 97 had already filled Form 6 for inclusion of their names. Of the remaining nine, six were out of the country and three were Portuguese passport holders.

US, Canada reportedly working on deal to ease tariffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
23:15:06 UTC
08:15:06 KST

The US and Canada are working on a deal to ease tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, two US and four Canadian sources told Reuters, as the two governments try to repair relations that soured after trade talks broke down in August.
The talks focus on tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including up to a 50 percent tariff on Canadian steel and a 25 percent tariff on autos, with negotiators discussing potential relief from those duties.
Tariffs on Canadian imports have become a political liability for the Trump administration, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade war with Canada.
One Canadian source briefed on the negotiations said a deal on steel and auto tariffs was possible before the November 3 elections, while US sources said the Trump administration wanted Canada to make further concessions.
The Section 232 tariffs are administered by the Commerce Department, putting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick rather than the US Trade Representative's office at the centre of the negotiations, sources on both sides of the border said.
Lutnick and Canada's Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-US trade, have been in regular contact recently, one of the sources said.
"Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our US counterparts on a range of priorities," a spokesperson for LeBlanc, said in a statement. "We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests."
The US Trade Representative's Office and Canada have also been in contact in recent days regarding the overall architecture of any deal and all other trade issues, a USTR official said.
Ottawa sees progress
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said there had been "a slight intensification" in talks with the US, adding that Ottawa had not changed its stance.
"To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the US is coming closer to our position," he told reporters, but did not give details.
He said Ottawa had set firm limits that led it to reject the terms put forward in August.
"We had very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August," Carney said.
He added that Canada remains willing to reach an agreement on the right terms.
"Canada's ready to sign an agreement that is in the interests of Canadians, all Canadians," he said.
A Canadian industry source said a deal could come quickly, but not necessarily a broad one. "If it happens, it'll happen fast. But my sense is it'll be a narrowed deal, if it even happens," the source said, according to Reuters news agency.
US and Canadian trade talks collapsed in August over issues such as whether to cut duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are critical for Canadian factories.

Canadian youths ask court to impose binding climate protections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

Canadian youths ask court to impose binding climate protections
- 15 young Canadians are suing the federal government, saying climate change is a “grave threat” and that courts must protect their constitutional rights to life and security.
- The case, first filed in 2019 and now at trial after a 2023 appeal ruling, is the first in Canada to test whether climate protections are a constitutional issue.
- Plaintiffs say they have already suffered harm, including wildfire evacuations, while the government argues climate change needs a global solution and Ottawa cannot meet the duty they seek.
AI generated
VANCOUVER — A landmark trial pitting young Canadians against the federal government over its alleged climate policy failures opened on Oct 26, with lawyers for the youths describing climate change as a “grave threat” that cannot be left to politicians alone.
The lawsuit, brought by 15 plaintiffs aged 17-25, is part of a growing global movement among environmental activists seeking to use courts to force government accountability on climate change.
The plaintiffs’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, delivered opening arguments in a Vancouver court on Oct 26, challenging the notion that the government response to human-caused global warming can be “left to where the political winds are blowing at any given moment.”
“This case is about the most fundamental rights of children in Canada,” she argued, saying courts, which are not subject to political pressures, must step in to compel the government to implement actions that address climate change.
Overall, the plaintiffs plan to prove that successive governments have violated their constitutional rights to life and security by failing to protect them from the threats posed by climate change.
Canadian targets currently call for a 40-45% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 2005 levels, but Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has already indicated those benchmarks may be missed.
A global problem
The lawsuit, first filed in 2019, was initially dismissed. In 2023, a federal appeals court ruled the youths were entitled to a trial.
The case is unprecedented in Canada, where federal courts have never tested whether climate protections are a constitutional issue.
A government lawyer, BJ Wray, argued the plaintiffs are seeking to impose “an obligation on the government that the government has no way of satisfying”.
“Climate change is a global problem that can only be remedied with a global solution,” Wray argued, saying the plaintiffs might still experience harms from climate change even if Ottawa were legally bound to specific greenhouse gas emission targets.
The first plaintiff to testify was 20-year-old Kira Young, from Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories, which, like the rest of northern Canada, is warming at a faster rate than southern Canada.
Young recounted an August 2023 wildfire that forced her family to evacuate, driving through smoke and flames as the blaze approached the family home.
“I was terrified,” she said, adding that she feels compelled to fight for a future where fewer people need to pack up their lives “in less than 36 hours” to escape a fast-moving wildfire.
The plaintiffs plan to show the court that they have already suffered extensively from climate change and that the damages at issue are not speculative future risks.
Emerging body of law
Globally, environmental campaigners have brought hundreds of cases seeking government action on climate change.
Maria Antonia Tigre, director of Global Climate Change Litigation at Columbia University’s Sabin Center, noted that climate judgments are “travelling across jurisdictions”.
The Canadian case “could really contribute to that developing body of law”, she said.
Canada is enduring more frequent and destructive wildfires, increased flooding and more frequent episodes of extreme.
Carney remains popular nationally but has faced criticism from people concerned about the environment.
The prime minister says US President Donald Trump’s trade war has forced Canada to re-orient its economy away from dependence on the United States.
Part of his economic strategy includes boosting oil production in the western province of Alberta, including through a proposed new pipeline to the Pacific coast.
That project, along with other moves like scrapping the carbon tax on individual households, prompted the resignation of former cabinet member Steven Guilbeault, the architect of the robust climate protections pursued by Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau. AFP

Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
23:14:39 GMT
08:14:39 KST

Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or
- Published
Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year.
Putellas, 32, captained Barcelona to Champions League glory as part of a quadruple in 2025-26, before joining Women's Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July.
She joins Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati on three Ballon d'Or Feminin crowns - her former Barcelona colleague won the award in 2023, 2024 and 2025 after Putellas did so in 2021 and 2022.
The past six Ballons d'Or have been won by the Spanish pair, with Norway's Ada Hegerberg (2018) and Megan Rapinoe of the United States (2019) the only non-Spaniards to claim the prize.
Putellas' latest victory caps a remarkable return to the pinnacle of world football after suffering a career-threatening anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in 2022.
"All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl," Putellas said.
"Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself."
She collected the most votes from an international panel of journalists across Fifa's top-50 ranked countries, with Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor coming second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third.
Meanwhile, England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or, becoming the first English player to do so since Michael Owen in 2001.
The numbers don't lie
While Barcelona are always overwhelming favourites to win the three competitions on offer in Spain, Putellas' performances last season showed that she is still among the world's elite.
Nicknamed 'La Reina' - meaning the queen - Putellas scored 21 goals and provided 13 assists in all competitions, ranking her third and second respectively among players across Europe's top five leagues.
Seven of those goals came in the Women's Champions League as Barcelona claimed a fourth continental title in six seasons.
Only Pernille Harder (eight), Alessia Russo (nine) and Ewa Pajor (11) scored more, all of whom are strikers by trade.
But Putellas' contributions to Barcelona's attacking play went far beyond scoring goals herself.
In Liga F - which Barcelona won for a seventh consecutive season - she finished joint-sixth for assists (seven) and fourth for open-play chances created (40).
Across Europe's top five leagues, only Claudia Pina (199), Vicky Lopez (183) and Georgia Stanway (168) recorded more sequence involvements ending in an open-play shot than Putellas (151).
In all competitions, she created more chances (89, 19 of which were big chances) and completed more passes ending in the final third (965) than any other player in Liga F, the Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de Espana.
Only Bayern Munich's Klara Buhl created as many chances as Putellas in the Champions League last season (36), the most by a player in a single edition of the competition since Caroline Graham Hansen in 2021-22 (38).
From watching Iniesta to winning it all
Putellas was born and grew up in the Catalan municipality of Mollet del Valles, about 12 miles north-east of Barcelona.
She began playing football in the street, and soon became a Barcelona fan and a regular attendee at Camp Nou.
With matches always on the TV at home, former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta and Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho quickly became her idols.
After attending a summer football camp run by Xavi and playing for local side CE Sabadell, Putellas spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy.
Spells at Espanyol and Levante followed the disbandment of her girls team, before she eventually returned to Barca in 2012.
Cue the start of a 14-year career with her childhood club during which she won 38 trophies, including 10 league titles and four European cups.
But after winning the Ballon d'Or for the first time in 2021, one of the toughest moments of Putellas' career came when she suffered an ACL injury on the eve of Euro 2022, ruling her out of the tournament.
Though she retained the Ballon d'Or later that year, it took a while for her to return to her best level. Playing only a bit-part role in Spain's triumphant 2023 World Cup campaign would have stung.
After scoring in the 2024 Champions League final and improving further the following season, in 2025-26 she shouldered much of Barcelona's creative burden as Aitana Bonmati missed five months through injury and ended the season a quadruple winner.
If that was not enough, the midfielder scored twice in a 4-0 thrashing of England in June that secured Spain's place at the 2027 World Cup at the Lionesses' expense.
With her contract at Barcelona expiring and keen for a fresh challenge, Putellas made the decision to leave her childhood club. She, and her fans, were distraught.
She had several offers from England, Mexico and the United States, but joined the ambitious project of US billionaire Michelle Kang at London City Lionesses in July.
"I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player," Putellas told BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast in August.
With three goals and one assist in seven WSL games for her new club, it is clear Putellas is still deserving of her nickname.

Konotop remains without electricity for fourth day, with "no forecasts for power restoration"
The city of Konotop in Sumy Oblast has been without electricity for a fourth consecutive day following Russian strikes on the night of 23-24 October, with no forecast for when power will be restored.
Source: Konotop Mayor Artem Semenikhin, speaking to Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne and posting on Telegram; Sumyoblenergo, the regional power distribution company
Details: Semenikhin said that as of the night of 26-27 October the city is still without electricity. Most of Konotop has also lost its gas supply.
Quote from Semenikhin: "The city has no electricity and most of it has no gas. Educational institutions have been damaged and even our hospital is now running on generators. Water is also being supplied on a schedule: from 06:00 to 09:00 and from 18:00 to 21:00."
Details: Semenikhin added that the situation regarding the electricity supply remains uncertain.
"Unfortunately, there are no forecasts for when power will be restored. No forecasts at all," he wrote.
Meanwhile, Sumyoblenergo said emergency repair crews are working around the clock to deal with the damage caused by strikes on energy facilities. However, the timeframe for the work depends on the security situation and whether crews can access the damaged sites.
Background:
- On 24 October after 03:00, Russian forces launched a large-scale drone attack on the Konotop hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories . They hit energy facilities, a school and houses, causing a blackout.
- On the afternoon of 24 October, a Russian drone struck a civilian agricultural business in the Konotop district. A 31-year-old farm worker was killed and four other people were injured.

England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
23:06:00 UTC
08:06:00 KST

Harry Kane: Bayern Munich striker wins Ballon d'Or
October 27, 2026
England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or for the first time on Monday, becoming the first English player to receive the prestigious football award since 2001.
The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker was honored at a ceremony at the London Palladium after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for club and country last season.
The Ballon d'Or, awarded by French magazine France Football, is one of football's most prestigious individual honors, recognizing the world's best players.
The last English player to win the award was former Liverpool striker Michael Owen, who claimed the prize 25 years ago.
Why did Harry Kane win the 2026 Ballon d'Or?
Kane's remarkable goalscoring record helped Bayern Munich secure a German league and cup double last season.
The former Tottenham Hotspur forward also led England to the World Cup semifinals, the country's best finish since winning the tournament in 1966.
Kane has finished as the Bundesliga's leading scorer for three consecutive seasons. He was also Europe's top club goalscorer during the 2025-26 campaign.
At Monday's ceremony, Kane thanked his Bayern Munich teammates for their support.
"Without you guys (his Bayern Munich team-mates) and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much," he said.
Kane also paid tribute to his former club Tottenham Hotspur, which he joined at the age of 11, as well as his England teammates and family.
"To my wife Kate, my best friend. We've been through ups and downs. You are my biggest support and I felt like you wanted this more than me," he said.
Reflecting on his career, Kane encouraged young footballers to pursue their ambitions despite setbacks.
"I hope my journey, it wasn't straightforward, I didn't go straight to the top, I had to experience a lot of loan moves and fight my way to get to where I am now. I hope that can give you inspiration."
Kane faced strong competition from Barcelona's Spanish teenager Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid's French forward Kylian Mbappe.
He joins Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen among the English players to have won the award.
Who else won at the 2026 Ballon d'Or awards?
Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas claimed the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her career, having previously won the award in 2021 and 2022.
The 32-year-old was recognized after a successful season with Barcelona, winning the treble and scoring 21 goals across all competitions.
Putellas also played a key role in Barcelona's Champions League triumph, contributing seven goals and seven assists during the campaign.
She joined English club London City Lionesses in July after spending 14 years at Barcelona.
Her victory ended a run of three consecutive Ballon d'Or wins by fellow Spaniard Aitana Bonmatí.
Barcelona's Lamine Yamal won the Kopa Trophy for the best young male player for the third consecutive year, while his teammate Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second year running.
Barcelona coach Pere Romeu was named women's coach of the year, while Spain manager Luis de la Fuente won the men's coaching award.
Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon received the men's Yashin Trophy, with Cata Coll winning the women's equivalent.
Barcelona was named women's club of the year, while Paris Saint-Germain took the men's award.

Netanyahu camp presses for unity government with Eisenkot - report
Netanyahu has reportedly told officials that a coalition with Eisenkot could allow him to govern without far-right partners, an idea Trump is receptive to, according to The Washington Post
Prime Minister Netanyahu’s allies are promoting a potential unity government with his rival Gadi Eisenkot after Israel’s election, with President Donald Trump receptive to the idea, according to a Washington Post report.
The newspaper, citing three people familiar with the discussions, reported that Netanyahu has privately told American and European officials that a partnership with Eisenkot could allow him to form a more moderate coalition without far-right allies, including Jewish Power leader Itamar Ben Gvir.
Netanyahu has also presented himself to US officials as the strongest Israeli partner for a renewed US-Israeli campaign against Iran, the Post reported.
The prospect of a unity government has reportedly been discussed by Trump’s representatives with Israelis even as recent polls showed Eisenkot ahead of Netanyahu. A Likud official told the newspaper that Trump wanted a stable government to be formed quickly after the vote, "what Trump wants is a stable and reliable Israeli government that can be formed as soon as possible after the election.”
If Eisenkot rejects a partnership and coalition talks reach an impasse, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker prime minister and seek another election, the Post reported.
The Trump administration, however, is reportedly divided over the proposal. Some US officials believe Netanyahu could govern more moderately without Ben Gvir’s influence, while others distrust the prime minister 'because of his history of breaking with political allies.'

Evening sessions urged as fraud, money-laundering cases pack Hong Kong courts
District Court waits exceed target by 3.5 times amid 68 per cent caseload spike, prompting calls for evening hearings and more judicial hires
The long wait for criminal cases to be heard in Hong Kong’s courts could persist because of a surge in fraud and money laundering litigation, the judiciary has warned, as the Law Society suggested extending sitting hours into the evening.
In a paper submitted to the Legislative Council’s panel on administration of justice and legal services, the judiciary said that the total caseload in 2025 reached about 537,000, around 4 per cent higher than the annual average over the previous five years.
As of July this year, criminal cases had waited an average of 358 days to be heard in the High Court, while those in the District Court waited 354 days on average – the longest among all courts.

Romania's Intelligence Service said on Monday it had identified a sabotage network coordinated by Russia, which it believed was responsible for a fire in September at an industrial site in central Romania near a state-owned weapons company.
The European Union and NATO states share a land border of more than 600 km (370 miles) with Ukraine, and centrist president Nicusor Dan has said it is the target of a hybrid war waged by Russia to destabilize nations that support Kyiv.
The attacks range from drone incursions into Romanian airspace to cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns, acts of sabotage and attacks on cargo vessels near Romanian waters, Dan has said.
Russia's embassy in Bucharest could not immediately be reached for comment outside business hours, but Moscow has repeatedly denied such accusations.
Romanian organized crime prosecutors said they were seeking the extradition of two Belarusian suspects apprehended in Germany and one Ukrainian detained in Poland who were all suspected of involvement in the arson case.
The Intelligence Service said all three were part of the network coordinated by Russia, whose coordinators had assigned it targets including "state and private weapons production facilities, as well as other objectives of military and industrial interest."
NATO members Romania, Bulgaria, Poland targets of recent Russian attacks
A year ago, Poland and Romania detained eight people suspected of involvement in a Russian plan to send exploding parcels to Ukraine.
Dan accused Russia of escalating its attacks on NATO's eastern flank this month after a series of drone strikes on cargo vessels in the Black Sea.
At least eight cargo ships have been hit off the coast of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks. Some 34 sailors are reported dead or missing.

SC to UP police: Educate officers on investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:57:52 UTC
07:57:52 KST

Supreme Court slams UP police for "slipshod investigation", orders Rs 6 lakh compensation for man held six years without evidence.
NEW DELHI: In a severe indictment of Uttar Pradesh police for carrying out a “slipshod investigation” that resulted in a man being in custody for six years when there was no evidence against him, Supreme Court Monday said the state cannot shirk its responsibility to protect citizens and directed it to pay a compensation of Rs 6 lakh to him.“This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person’s life and liberty,” SC noted at the outset of its verdict.On Sept 30, in a separate matter, the top court had slammed UP police for not naming the accused in a road accident case.
Appalled at the way UP cops carried out probe: SC
It would be better if investigations in all criminal cases were handed over to CBI if the state police works with an agenda and does cover-up jobs, court had said, noting the accused had not been named despite the complainant catching him on the spot and handing him over to police.In the present case, a bench of J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said there was no evidence to implicate the person in a kidnapping and murder case. It noted he was never named in the FIR and police made him an accused on the basis that he was seen in CCTV footage. SC said it was “appalled at the manner in which investigation was carried out”. “It is unfortunate that despite no evidence against the petitioner, he was imprisoned for six years as an undertrial.
Based on a slipshod investigation, a haphazard prosecution was carried out, which resulted, fortunately, in the acquittal of the accused. We cannot but deprecate the manner in which the probe was carried out and prosecution conducted,” SC said. “State police would do well to educate their officers in the process of investigation.”
Making the state accountable for police’s misdeed, the court said six years have been erased from the man’s life on the strength of a concocted story built on mere surmises and conjectures, and the state has to pay compensation.“The state cannot shirk from its responsibility to protect its citizens, especially when a person arraigned in a criminal case is presumed innocent until proven guilty. The investigation and prosecuting agencies exist not merely to, and by whatever means, bring in a conviction. They should recognise themselves to be essential stakeholders in the justice delivery system, ensuring justice, not only to the victim, the de facto complainant and the injured but also to the accused,” the SC bench said.

Russia increases diesel production after Trump deal – Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:50:47 UTC
07:50:47 KST

Russia increases diesel production after Trump deal – Reuters
Russia has significantly increased production of diesel in the wake of an agreement reached between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, Reuters has reported, citing industry sources.
Daily output rose from 160,000 tons in early October to 180,000 tons after the Russian government introduced new export quotas in mid-month, the agency said. Moscow has eased its restrictions on diesel exports, allowing Russian companies to ship up to 500,000 tons of fuel to international markets in October while ensuring domestic demand remains fully covered.
Exports of diesel, marine fuel, and gas oil had been banned until October 31, as the government sought to stabilize the domestic market, which was suffering from increased seasonal demand linked to the harvest season.
According to sources cited by Reuters, domestic demand in Russia is now expected to fall to around 140,000 tons per day as the harvest campaign is largely over. This would free up as much as 40,000 tons of diesel per day or more than 1 million tons per month for export, according to the news agency’s estimates. Between 0.2 and 0.3 million tons are likely to be purchased by Russia’s neighbors, the sources said.
Trump and Putin agreed on diesel supplies during a phone call on October 9. Following the conversation, the US president announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, another million tons shortly thereafter, and potentially further shipments depending on refining capacity. Washington subsequently issued a temporary sanctions waiver permitting Russian diesel imports, reversing restrictions introduced under former US President Joe Biden in 2022.
Last week, Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak said Moscow had already dispatched three tankers carrying diesel to the US under the agreement. He also announced that Russia would “ensure additional supplies of diesel fuel to world markets and the United States” to help ease the global diesel shortage. Deliveries would continue on a regular basis, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said at the time.
The diesel deal provoked tensions between Washington and Kiev. Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to stop attacking Russian refineries, accusing Kiev of exacerbating the worldwide diesel shortage and hurting American consumers and farmers hit by high fuel prices.
Zelensky hit back, calling Trump’s claims “totally false” and accusing him of “deflecting the focus away from Iran.” He was referring to the US-Israeli military operation against Iran, which led to severe shipment disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz – one of the key seaborne oil transportation routes.
Russia has historically been the world’s second-largest diesel exporter, behind only the US, accounting for around 10% of global exports. Disruptions to Russian supplies can drive up prices even in countries that do not directly import diesel.

From Wall Street to Silicon Valley, Anthropic IPO poised to have massive 'trickle-down effect'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:50:07 UTC
07:50:07 KST

The tech industry needs this to go well. So does Wall Street.
Anthropic's IPO filing on Monday puts the Claude creator in position to pursue what could be the largest initial stock offering in history. Investors are already measuring the 5-year-old company's potential market cap in the trillions, putting it in a category with the world's most valuable companies.
It's a critical moment for the whole tech sector, as the artificial intelligence boom has been largely driven by two companies: Anthropic and OpenAI. The latter has confidentially filed to go public, but has said a debut likely won't take place until 2027.
Meanwhile, the stock market is showing signs of jitters on the AI trade. Neoclouds and data center companies have been getting pummeled, prompting Australia's Firmus to withdraw its IPO plans and for SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm unit to do the same.
Now, all eyes turn to Anthropic, which is betting that investors will look past over $80 billion in losses in the first half of the year, and see the 14-fold increase in revenue as a reflection of seemingly insatiable demand for the company's leading models and services.
"If it underperforms expectations, it'll be a little bit of a house of cards," said Jai Das, co-founder of Sapphire Ventures whose career in tech investing dates to the 1990s.
Anthropic's business is deeply entwined with tech megacaps. Close to half its revenue comes from Claude being sold through cloud divisions at Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet, which all hold investments in the company. In the IPO, some $77 billion in notes can be issued to Amazon, Broadcom and Google, while Microsoft and Nvidia agreed to invest $15 billion as the company builds up its computing capacity. Chips from Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Amazon and Google are powering Anthropic's development.
Cloud providers are ratcheting up capital expenditures to meet demand, and memory manufacturers are fighting shortages to prioritize AI chips. And there's the debt factor. Alphabet, with its investment-grade credit rating, committed to backstopping Anthropic for a data center in Texas. Broadcom, which helps Google develop chips for AI labs, is creating financing pools to help Anthropic and OpenAI deploy high-performance models, CEO Hock Tan told analysts earlier this year.
For public market investors, more than one-third of the value of the S&P 500 comes from tech's trillion-dollar companies, which are all, to varying degrees, going deep in AI. Beyond that, there are software giants like Adobe and Salesforce that have integrated with Anthropic's Claude assistant.
Market reset?
And in the private markets, check sizes have ballooned but IPOs are few and far between. Bessemer Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures both told CNBC that Anthropic is their biggest investment ever.
"If they don't perform well, they will become the bellwether for AI," said Brad Bernstein, a managing partner at growth equity firm FTV Capital. "Their valuation will reflect that performance variation, and then it'll just be a trickle-down effect to all the stuff going on with the excess capital that's getting poured into the venture AI world. Everything is going to have to sort of be reset."
Anthropic will be the third company to go public with a valuation above $1 trillion, after Saudi Aramco and Elon Musk's SpaceX, which debuted in June. OpenAI could be the fourth.
Revenue at Anthropic has been multiplying at a staggering pace as businesses adopt the company's coding and productivity tools. Second-quarter revenue soared to $11.56 billion from $787 million a year earlier.
The company held almost $132 billion in cash, equivalents and short-term investments at the end of June. And after five quarters of operating losses, Anthropic reported $974 million in operating income for the second quarter.
"It is, I think, better than feared," said Rohit Kulkarni, partner and chief AI officer at Burnham Park Capital Markets, referring to the financials. "There could have been more negative tidbits."
One source of concern in some corners of the investing universe is the emergence of so-called open-weight models, which are cheaper for businesses to access and allow for customization and flexibility in terms of where users access the models.
In the prospectus, the only two competitors Anthropic named were OpenAI and Google, though the company said it faces competition from a "broader set of model providers," including open-weight or open-source models.
Anthropic says it's all very early, with Fortune 500 companies committing less than 0.1% of their total expenses to its models and services in the latest quarter. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs, says that's part of the investment thesis.
"I think there's going to be room for frontier models like Anthropic and OpenAI and SpaceX, and I think there will be room for open-weight models," Monaghan said. "It's way too soon to say that one is going to disintermediate the other."
With hyperscaler spending on AI infrastructure set to reach into the trillions of dollars, Sapphire's Das said there's understandable concern about a market glut. But he compares it to the telecommunications and dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when companies flooded the market with fiber-optic equipment. Eventually, the infrastructure got used, although plenty of companies went belly up in the interim.
"Long term, I don't think there is a lack of demand," Das said.
Downside risks
A lackluster debut could push out OpenAI's offering even further and cause investors to rethink its lofty valuation. At the same time, rising interest rates mean it's getting costlier for companies to raise debt.
David Trainer, CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, wrote in a report last month that the AI boom has been built on the view that cheap credit and access to the capital markets will be "readily available."
"If AI liquidity dries up, and there are clear signs it is, we see large, 20%, downside risk in the S&P 500, with most of that concentrated in the valuation of AI-related stocks," Trainer wrote.
Industry experts take a different approach, focusing on the power and rapid proliferation of the technology. Claude Opus 5.5 Max performs better than any other model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an industry benchmark.
Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy said the technology is only becoming more essential.
"Anthropic and OpenAI have by now demonstrated their ability to stay at the frontier of AI and keep pushing innovation," Ramaswamy said. "They're incredible companies that are doing a big service to humanity by expanding the frontier of what is possible, and we are very much rooting for them to be public and very successful companies."
Still, Snowflake is experimenting with low-cost open-weight models from China's Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and Zhipu.
"We spend a lot on internal AI because we want to get as much efficiency as we can," Ramaswamy said.
