‘We Have Friends, No Enemies’: Timor-Leste’s First Year in ASEAN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:45:00 UTC
07:45:00 KST

On October 26, Timor-Leste marks the first anniversary of its admission to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), a milestone that followed 14 years of efforts and a much longer history of struggle for independence. Its accession as the bloc’s 11th member was celebrated as the completion of Southeast Asia’s regional family. Yet behind the diplomatic celebrations lies a more complicated reality. Timor-Leste is entering an organization whose political traditions and practices do not always sit comfortably with the principles that have shaped its own foreign policy.
While Timor-Leste’s resistance against Indonesian occupation is well known, considerably less attention has been paid to its foreign policy and relations with major powers. Dili has occasionally taken positions that have unsettled its neighbors. Myanmar’s military authorities expelled Timorese diplomats twice, first in 2023 following Dili’s engagement with the opposition National Unity Government (NUG), and again in February 2026, following the filing of a criminal complaint in Timor-Leste against senior Myanmar military officials over alleged atrocities. The second expulsion came barely four months after ASEAN accession, exposing the tensions between Dili’s commitment to international justice and the bloc’s longstanding principle of non-interference.
These tensions extend beyond Myanmar. Timor-Leste’s relationship with Indonesia remains shadowed by unresolved questions of justice, accountability, and reparations, while its relationships with China, the United States, and Australia require careful navigation amid intensifying geopolitical competition. At home, ASEAN membership brings demanding economic and institutional obligations, growing concerns over transnational crime and the responsibility of chairing ASEAN in 2029. For a small state whose independence depended heavily on international solidarity, membership offers greater diplomatic influence, but also new pressures to compromise. How Dili manages these competing pressures will reveal much about the kind of regional actor it intends to become.
In this inaugural interview for Conversations on Southeast Asia, a new Diplomat interview series hosted by Khoo Ying Hooi, Timor-Leste’s Vice Minister for ASEAN Affairs, Milena Maria da Costa Rangel, speaks about the country’s first year in ASEAN and the political and practical choices confronting Dili.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Timor-Leste joined ASEAN on October 26, 2025, with substantial legal and institutional commitments under its accession roadmap and access to development assistance through the Initiative for ASEAN Integration (IAI). One year on, how far has Dili progressed in fulfilling these commitments, and how much of the promised assistance has actually materialized? Beyond the diplomatic achievement of accession, what tangible benefits can ordinary Timorese, particularly businesses and young people, expect?
We remain grateful for the welcome and solidarity extended to Timor-Leste by ASEAN member states. But becoming a member is only the beginning of a much longer process.
Our first year of membership has focused on translating the achievement of accession into coordinated implementation across government. On the legal instruments, Timor-Leste had acceded to most of the 66 instruments under Priority 1 of the accession roadmap [the Roadmap for Timor-Leste’s Full Membership in ASEAN] before joining ASEAN. Two instruments relating to the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement and the ASEAN Comprehensive Investment Agreement remain under discussion, particularly regarding the common legal framework and domestic procedures required by member states.
We are also working with the ASEAN Secretariat to review the economic agreements under the remaining priorities. Some agreements have expired, have not entered into force, or have been replaced. As a result, the number under Priority 2 has been reduced from 48 to 35, and under Priority 3 from 106 to 62. The review has also identified 45 additional agreements that Timor-Leste will need to address. Domestic preparations for accession to the remaining economic agreements are under way.
In terms of assistance, Timor-Leste has benefited from the IAI since May 2024, even before becoming a full member. We are now covered by IAI Work Plan V for 2026–2030, which offers technical assistance and capacity-building in trade, agriculture, education, skills development, and institutional strengthening.
We have established a national task force with focal points in relevant ministries to identify priorities and develop proposals. So far, we have developed six initial project concepts, three of which have been finalized and submitted to the ASEAN Secretariat. They cover areas including sustainable tourism, youth capacity-building, digital skills for primary school teachers, and more resilient coffee production. The challenge now is to turn these proposals into funded projects that produce practical results.
For businesses and young people, ASEAN membership opens access to a much larger market and new opportunities in trade, investment, education, and skills development. But these benefits will not come automatically. Our businesses still face challenges in production capacity, competitiveness, and meeting regional standards. We also need to improve young people’s skills and qualifications so they can make use of these opportunities.
We recognize that many of the obligations require action now, while some of the economic benefits will take longer to emerge. That is why we are taking a phased approach, based on national priorities, institutional capacity, and the timelines agreed with ASEAN.
On October 21, the Council of Ministers approved the National Roadmap for the Implementation of ASEAN Economic Commitments for 2026–2030, accompanied by 19 sectoral strategic action plans and 19 sectoral work plans. These set out the reforms and responsibilities across government. Our focus is not simply to meet legal requirements, but to use membership to support economic diversification, stronger institutions, private sector development, and better opportunities for our people.
Turning to relations with Indonesia, the two countries often present their relationship as a model of post-conflict reconciliation. Yet the 2008 Commission of Truth and Friendship (CTF) acknowledged the serious violations committed during the 1999 violence, while justice and reparations remain unresolved for many victims. Has political reconciliation moved ahead at the expense of justice? Now that both countries sit together in ASEAN, is this chapter effectively closed?
Timor-Leste and Indonesia share a difficult and bitter history. Over the years, however, we have made significant progress in building a peaceful and constructive relationship based on mutual respect, dialogue, and cooperation. This reconciliation is something both countries can be proud of.
At the same time, reconciliation does not mean forgetting the past. We recognize the suffering of victims and their families, and we understand that justice, accountability, and reparations remain important. The CTF helped acknowledge what happened in 1999. At the national level, the Commission for Reception, Truth, and Reconciliation documented past human rights violations in its Chega! report and made important recommendations.
We need to continue preserving historical memory, supporting victims, and advancing a national reparations policy. Membership of ASEAN does not close this chapter. It provides an additional setting for cooperation between two sovereign neighbors, while the needs and dignity of victims remain important in their own rights.
Indonesia is one of our closest neighbors and an important partner in trade, investment, education, security, and regional cooperation. For us, reconciliation means acknowledging the past, addressing its consequences, and building a better relationship for the future. But there is still work to be done on the recommendations of the Chega! report. In that sense, reconciliation remains an ongoing process.
One of ASEAN’s most contentious issues is Myanmar. Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s military-backed leader, has visited five ASEAN member states, most recently Malaysia. These developments raise concerns about the gradual normalization of Myanmar’s military-backed leadership, despite the lack of meaningful progress on ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus. How does Timor-Leste view these developments? What is Dili’s position on engagement with the NUG, and how should Myanmar’s representation in ASEAN relate to progress on the Five-Point Consensus?
Timor-Leste’s position on Myanmar is guided by our commitment to peace, democracy, and international law. These principles remain central to our foreign policy as we engage with other ASEAN member states.
We recognize that the situation in Myanmar is complex, and we are deeply concerned about the continued violence, humanitarian suffering, and its impact on civilians. We believe inclusive dialogue is essential.
Engagement with all relevant stakeholders, including different political groups, should contribute to ending the violence, facilitating political dialogue, and achieving meaningful reconciliation and lasting peace.
Regarding the NUG and other stakeholders, our position is that an inclusive process is indispensable to a peaceful and sustainable solution. We should not focus on only one group while excluding others. At the same time, we respect Myanmar’s sovereignty and recognize its importance in addressing the crisis.
ASEAN membership does not require Timor-Leste to abandon its principles. It provides another platform through which we can advance them collectively. We continue to support the full and effective implementation of ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus as the principal framework for addressing the crisis, and we support ASEAN’s established position concerning Myanmar’s representation at high-level meetings. Engagement should help reduce violence, improve humanitarian access, and create conditions for an inclusive, Myanmar-owned political process.
We take note of the engagement by some ASEAN member states with the Myanmar authorities and will continue to follow developments closely. One thing is certain: Myanmar remains an integral part of the ASEAN family.
Timor-Leste has long emphasized democracy and human rights in its foreign policy, reflecting its own struggle for independence. ASEAN, however, places considerable weight on non-interference. How does Dili reconcile these competing commitments?
We do not see respect for sovereignty and the promotion of human rights as mutually exclusive. Timor-Leste’s approach is to uphold these commitments together. Respect for non-interference is essential to relations among sovereign states, while dialogue, humanitarian cooperation, and collectively agreed ASEAN action can also address matters of shared concern.
Our own history reinforces the importance of dignity, self-determination, and peaceful solutions. Within ASEAN, we seek to contribute constructively through consultation and cooperation, with respect for the Charter and international law.
The objective is not to choose one principle and disregard another, but to ensure that ASEAN’s principles work together in support of peace and the well-being of its peoples.
A series of police operations this year uncovered online scam operations in Timor-Leste, raising concerns about the spread of transnational criminal networks into the country. Why has Timor-Leste become vulnerable, and how will the government’s National Integrated Plan to combat online scams, organized cybercrime, and human trafficking for 2026–2031 translate into practical cooperation with ASEAN partners?
Online scams, cybercrime, and human trafficking are linked to organized criminal networks operating across borders. This is a regional problem, but also a global one. Timor-Leste is not immune to these risks. We are still building our institutions and strengthening our legal and law enforcement systems. These activities threaten our national security, economy, international reputation, and investment environment, so we take them seriously.
Our authorities have already investigated and disrupted suspected scam operations despite limited resources. The government has also taken steps to revoke online gambling and betting licenses and restrict related activities. As you rightly mentioned, the National Integrated Plan for 2026–2031 is aimed at strengthening the response to online scams, organized cybercrime, and human trafficking. But adopting a plan is only the beginning. The real challenge lies in implementation and enforcement.
ASEAN membership gives us more opportunities to work with our neighbors, including through ASEANAPOL [Association of Southeast Asian Nations Chiefs of Police] and other regional mechanisms. Cooperation must involve information-sharing, joint investigations, tracing financial flows, and preventing criminal networks from simply relocating across borders.
Public awareness is equally important, especially among young people and vulnerable communities who may be targeted through fraudulent recruitment or promises of easy employment. We recognize that gaps remain in our regulatory and enforcement capacity. Addressing them will take stronger domestic coordination and sustained cooperation with regional and international partners. No country can deal with these networks alone.
Timor-Leste elevated its relationship with China to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2023 while maintaining close ties with the United States and Australia. As U.S.-China rivalry intensifies, how does Dili seek to preserve its foreign policy independence amid competing major-power interests? Does ASEAN offer smaller states meaningful protection from external pressures, or is the organization itself increasingly constrained by these rivalries?
Our foreign policy is guided by our national interests and by the principles enshrined in our Constitution. We believe in maintaining friendly relations with all countries. Our philosophy is that we have friends, no enemies. Our foreign policy starts at home. Our international engagement is rooted in our national values, our commitment to peace, and our respect for international law.
We value our relationships with China, the United States, Australia, and other partners because each contributes in different ways to national development. The Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with China offers opportunities in infrastructure, agriculture, and economic development. At the same time, we have strong partnerships with Australia, the United States, and other countries in education, security, and institutional development. We see these partnerships as complementary rather than competing.
On defense and security cooperation, our priority is to strengthen national capacity, protect sovereignty, and contribute to regional peace and stability. The same principle applies to infrastructure and foreign investment. Cooperation has to serve our national development priorities.
We recognize that major-power competition creates challenges, especially for small states. But our approach is not about choosing sides. It is about making independent decisions based on our national interests and long-term development needs.
This is where ASEAN membership is important. ASEAN provides countries of different sizes with a platform to engage in regional discussions, deepen cooperation, and uphold shared principles such as sovereignty and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Its members have different perspectives and interests, and reaching common positions can be difficult. Nevertheless, dialogue and the search for consensus remain important. We believe ASEAN unity and centrality are essential to regional peace and stability.
During Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s visit to Dili in January 2026, the two countries signed the New Partnership for a New Era, with Canberra pledging additional assistance for Timor-Leste’s ASEAN integration. Yet the development of Greater Sunrise remains unresolved. Has ASEAN membership strengthened Dili’s diplomatic leverage with Australia, and how can Timor-Leste ensure that its regional priorities remain independent of Canberra’s strategic interests?
Australia is our immediate neighbor and has been an important development partner since the restoration of our independence. Its support for national development, human capital, and institutional capacity-building has been significant. We particularly value its assistance with our integration into ASEAN.
The New Partnership for a New Era reflects our shared commitment to economic development, education, security, and regional integration. But I want to emphasize that Timor-Leste’s foreign policy and regional priorities are guided by our own national interests and development needs. Strengthening our relationship with Australia and deepening our engagement within ASEAN are not competing objectives.
Greater Sunrise is important to our economic future and to the bilateral relationship. The 2018 Maritime Boundary Treaty was a major achievement. It demonstrated that disputes can be resolved peacefully through dialogue and international law. We continue to work with Australia and the Greater Sunrise joint venture to move the project forward. Significant progress has been made, but further negotiations are needed. Our priority is to ensure that the project creates jobs, supports economic development, and delivers long-term benefits to our people.
Australia also has a long history of engagement with ASEAN. For Timor-Leste, membership creates additional opportunities to work directly with our regional neighbors, build partnerships, and pursue our own development priorities.
Timor-Leste is scheduled to assume the ASEAN chairmanship in 2029, only four years after its accession. Yet the government’s own preliminary assessment identified significant gaps in infrastructure, accommodation, trained personnel, and logistical capacity. With less than three years remaining, what measurable progress has been made, how much funding has actually been secured, and what concrete benchmarks will determine whether Dili is ready to take on the chairmanship?
We recognize that assuming the ASEAN chairmanship in 2029 will be a significant responsibility for Timor-Leste. We also see it as an opportunity to strengthen national institutions, develop human and technical capacity, and contribute more actively to ASEAN community-building.
Chairing ASEAN involves much more than hosting high-level meetings. It requires adequate infrastructure, accommodation, transport, security, trained personnel, funding, and coordination across government. Our preliminary assessment has identified gaps, and we are taking them seriously.
We started preparations early. In February 2026, the government established the ASEAN Chairship National Organizing Committee, or ACNOC, chaired by Prime Minister Xanana Gusmão, with an executive committee led by Foreign Minister Bendito dos Santos Freitas. Its work covers five priority areas: human resources and institutional capacity; infrastructure and facilities; security and public order; communication and diplomacy; and finance and coordination.
Work is underway to expand and modernize Dili’s international airport, and preparations are progressing for an international convention center and other meeting facilities. We are strengthening officials’ skills in protocol, diplomacy, meeting management, security, communications, and logistics. We are also receiving assistance and training from other ASEAN member states.
On the financing side, we are assessing budgetary requirements, identifying funding sources, and coordinating with development partners. Funding for preparations in 2027 and 2028, and for some infrastructure work before 2029, is part of that process. We are aware that plans and coordination structures are not enough. We need clear timelines, adequate funding, implementation, and regular monitoring.
If those gaps cannot be resolved in time, would Dili consider postponing its turn?
Our focus remains on preparing to assume the ASEAN Chairmanship in 2029. We are approaching that responsibility seriously, through coordinated planning, measurable milestones, and cooperation with ASEAN partners. We want this responsibility to leave a lasting legacy for better infrastructure, stronger institutions, more skilled personnel, and a greater capacity to contribute to regional cooperation.
There are options that could be considered; we would discuss such arrangements with other member states if necessary. Any matter affecting ASEAN’s collective arrangements would be considered through the appropriate ASEAN processes. For now, our priority is to address the identified gaps and ensure that our preparations deliver lasting benefits for Timor-Leste.

France is sharply ramping up production of HAMMER air bombs, which the Ukrainian Armed Forces use to destroy Russian targets
Ukraine

France is sharply ramping up production of HAMMER air bombs, which the Ukrainian Armed Forces use to destroy Russian targets
Kyiv • UNN
Safran plans to produce up to 2,000 HAMMERs annually starting in 2027, strengthening potential deliveries to Ukraine. Kyiv has received licenses for local production.
The French company Safran plans to increase production of AASM HAMMER guided aerial bombs to 2,000 units per year as early as 2027. These munitions are actively used by the Ukrainian Air Force to strike Russian forces. Defense Express reports this, citing La Tribune, writes UNN.
Details
In recent years, the company has significantly expanded its production capacity. While Safran manufactured only 200 aerial bombs in 2022, it produced more than 1,000 in 2025. In 2026, it plans to produce approximately 1,400 units.
As early as next year, production could increase to 2,000 aerial bombs. The company has also halved the production cycle and continues to invest in expanding its facilities.
Why the increase in production is important for Ukraine
AASM HAMMER bombs have a solid-fuel booster that allows them to be launched from a lower altitude than conventional glide bombs. This reduces the risks to Ukrainian pilots during combat missions.
The increase in production creates opportunities to scale up supplies to Ukraine, although the specific volumes of future deliveries have not yet been announced.
At the same time, Ukraine has already obtained the necessary licenses to localize AASM HAMMER production.
In addition, Safran is developing a long-range HAMMER XLR version weighing 1,000 kg. Thanks to its turbojet engine, its maximum range is expected to increase from 70 to 140 km.

'Complete fabrication': Netanyahu, Katz deny plans to fire IDF chief Zamir ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:41:53 UTC

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Office and Defense Minister Israel Katz denied reported plans to dismiss IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir on Monday, amid reports of tensions between the political and military leadership over Iran, a day before the Knesset elections.
Katz condemned the reports, claiming they were part of an attempt to harm the Likud Party ahead of Tuesday's elections.
"The reports published this evening about an intention to dismiss Chief of Staff Zamir are a complete fabrication and an outright lie," the defense minister said.
According to Katz, the reports were part of a series of security-related claims circulated over the past 24 hours that he alleged were intended to damage Likud's election chances.
Katz stressed that he had personally recommended Zamir's appointment as IDF chief of staff and that their cooperation would continue.
"We are working together for the security of the State of Israel, with unprecedented historic achievements, and that is how I intend to continue acting in the future," he said.
Netanyahu's Office also rejected the reports concerning relations between the prime minister and the IDF chief of staff, issuing a brief response: "Complete fake news from beginning to end."
Netanyahu personally denied the reports in a post on X/Twitter on Monday, writing: "More fake news from the panic-mongering Channels 12 and 13 on the eve of the elections: I do not intend to dismiss the chief of staff, and we will continue working together for Israel's security. I do intend to eliminate the Iranian nuclear threat once and for all. I will do so together with my friend President Trump, and we will also sign peace agreements with additional countries."
Eisenkot: Zamir will remain in office, Netanyahu will leave after elections
Former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar Party, declared on Monday that Zamir would leave his position only when the law stipulates, while Netanyahu would leave office after the elections and the formation of the next government.
"Tomorrow, the people of Israel will elect a prime minister whose considerations will always be for the good of Israel, who will never act out of political interests at the expense of Israel's security and IDF soldiers," Eisenkot said.
Reports of Netanyahu-Zamir confrontation over Iran
The denials follow reports over the past 24 hours of unusual tensions between Netanyahu and Zamir concerning the possibility of an Israeli strike on Iran.
Channel 12 News reported on Sunday evening that Netanyahu and Zamir had clashed over the Iranian issue, while defense officials sought to emphasize that military decisions were made solely on professional grounds.
The IDF Spokesperson's Unit addressed the reports on Monday, stating that the military was on high alert across all fronts.
The statement stressed that the IDF's operational activities and guiding considerations were based solely on security, professional, and national interests, and that any portrayal suggesting otherwise was misleading.
Earlier, Katz also denied claims of disagreements between the political leadership and the military over Iran.
According to Katz, coordination between the prime minister, the defense minister, and the IDF was complete, and there had been no intention to initiate an Israeli attack on Iran before the elections.
However, he made clear that Israel would respond forcefully if attacked by Iran.
The statements came one day before polling stations were set to open, with relations between the political leadership and the military's top brass at the center of public debate.

Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of midterm election - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:41:32 UTC
07:41:32 KST

US President Donald Trump's public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from last week's record low, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.
Trump's fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party's majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.
The five-day nationwide poll also showed that registered voters broadly favored Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would pick for Congress in what is known as a "generic ballot" question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today.
That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on October 19. The latest poll additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term as president.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
Steep Senate climb for democrats
Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate.
It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favored Democrats over Republicans by 9 points, 53% to 44%.
The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent gasoline prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction.
Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach to the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue.
The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 percentage points for registered voters.

Grok Says Its AI-Generated Version of ‘The Odyssey’ Is ‘Not Historically Accurate’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:40:37 UTC
07:40:37 KST

You don’t hear the defenders of so-called Western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.
Maybe that’s because their rabid denunciations of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of Homer’s epic were buried in an avalanche of money. The July blockbuster has grossed nearly $1.8 billion worldwide, silencing the right-wingers who predicted a massive flop due to diverse casting and deviations from the source material.
Perhaps the loudest of these preemptive critics was Elon Musk. The world’s richest man spared no vitriol for what he considered a desecration of the ancient Greek narrative; four days after its release, he vowed to produce a superior version. “Before this year ends,” Musk wrote on X, “Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”
A little more than three months later—long after the discourse moved on—the public finally has a first glimpse of what we might call the Grodyssey, an Odyssey rendered through prompts fed into xAI’s video and image generation model. Rather than a “full-length movie,” it’s a seven-minute “episode” of an apparently ongoing series, depicting how Odysseus, king of Ithaca, resists a call to war against Troy but is ultimately compelled by an oath of loyalty to sail there with his army.
“Odyssey with Grok Imagine,” Musk announced Friday on X when sharing the clip, produced by AI entertainment company Wonder Studios X. The subdued post received just 18,000 likes, notably less engagement than other recent posts in which Musk cast doubt on the results of Brazil’s elections, complained about pronouns, and disparaged “legacy news.”
Grok’s introductory episode bears many hallmarks of AI slop. The movements of faces don’t match the dialog, which is further undercut by stilted and unnatural delivery. Besides Odysseus, none of the principal characters are introduced by name, and the pacing issues are laughable: The Ithacans arrive on the shores of Troy immediately after leaving their homeland, for example. Even the blue checks on X were harsh in their assessment. “Someone actually watched this and still decided to post it?” wrote one user. “Fire that person.”
But Musk’s stated goal wasn’t to deliver a better-looking or more narratively cohesive version of The Odyssey. He and his culture war comrades dubiously claimed that they were against Nolan’s casting of Black and trans actors, the Americanized English spoken by the characters they played, and various designs of ships and armor in the film because they were “historically inaccurate.” Hence Musk’s guarantee of a “historically accurate” corrective.
So, did Grok Imagine succeed on that front? Asking Grok for a self-evaluation yields an interesting answer. “No,” the chatbot says when queried about whether this Odyssey snippet is historically accurate. “Grok Imagine’s Episode 1 (and the broader promised series) is an adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey, not a historically accurate reconstruction of real events.”
The AI model further notes that the characters have no basis in the historical record, and that the poem is dominated by “myth” and “invention” rather than confirmed events. “Homeric society mixes possible Bronze Age elements (palace-centered kingdoms, certain warrior practices) with later Iron Age features,” it also states. “Many details are anachronistic or literary.”
In laying out the reasons that the episode “does not meet a strict historical standard,” Grok points out that the characters speak modern English with British accents, “not Homeric Greek or any reconstructed Bronze Age language.” Visually, it says, the production reflects “modern cinematic tropes and AI training data,” not “primary archaeological evidence.” (The bot cites the appearance of cavalry in a battle scene as an error when compared with standard reconstructions of the period.) Grok concludes that “the Odyssey itself is not a historical document, and the production makes no serious attempt at archaeological or linguistic fidelity beyond a general ‘ancient Greek epic’ aesthetic.”
Of course, the creative license that comes with adapting a millennia-old legend swarming with gods, witches, magic, and monsters was understood by just about everyone but Musk and a handful of cranks insisting that Nolan had contradicted some fundamentally true account of heroic adventure. Even Grok can tell you that its master’s fit of pique led him to promise the impossible—as he so often does.

Carers allowed to earn over the weekly limit without losing out as ‘cliff-edge’ abolished in the budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:30:53 UTC
07:30:53 KST

The controversial rule that led to unpaid carers being punished with penalties amounting to thousands of pounds is to be abolished, the Guardian can reveal.
The chancellor, John Healey, is to announce a new digital taper system for carer’s allowance in Wednesday’s budget, effectively ending what is regarded as one of the UK benefit system’s most feared and unfair administrative practices.
The scandal was highlighted in a Guardian investigation that revealed how hundreds of thousands of carers have, through no fault of their own, run up life-changing debts in recent years after overstepping weekly earnings thresholds by just a few pence.
Those hefty debts were then ruthlessly chased down by welfare officials who pursued carers using legislation designed to recover funds from drug dealers and organised crime bosses. Some unpaid carers were convicted of fraud as a result.
The cliff-edge rule dictates that if a carer earns even a penny more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – they forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, currently £86.45. A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40.
Although the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) was aware when carers breached earnings limits, it refused to warn them, insisting the onus was on carers to report any changes.
Thousands of carers spent long periods unaware of the breach, in some cases for years, resulting in overpayment debts typically of £2-£5,000 but in some cases as much as £20,000.
Under new rules set to be announced in the budget, the introduction of a tapered system instead of a cliff-edge means only £1 of carer’s allowance will be removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit, meaning carers are no longer left financially worse off for working additional hours or receiving a pay rise.
The announcement is one of five more “everyday fixes” announced by Healey ahead of his budget on Wednesday. His room for manoeuvre is severely constrained by the tight fiscal backdrop, a result of global events including the conflict in Iran.
Treasury insiders have warned that the budget will be low-key, with difficult tax and spend decisions put off until the spending review next year. But there is anxiety among some Labour MPs over the scale of the announcements, after Andy Burnham came to power promising major change.
Among the other measures to come is making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent – with the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles locked in, and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles to 35p per mile. The Treasury said the move would benefit about 3 million people – employees and self-employed – who use their own vehicle for work.
The chancellor’s intervention on the draconian cliff-edge rule comes after an award-winning Guardian investigation which revealed how the DWP had for years known of the profound distress it caused carers – including warnings from a DWP whistleblower – but did nothing about it.
The Guardian’s reporting triggered a government-commissioned independent review of carer’s allowance overpayments by disability rights expert Liz Sayce, published last year. It found unpaid carers suffered depression and hardship on a huge scale after falling foul of a series of systemic injustices, including the cliff edge.
In one case highlighted by the review, a carer was penalised when the national minimum wage had increased at a faster rate than the earnings limit. This put her 15p a week above the limit, even though her hours had not changed. Months later, she was told she had incurred a £2,000 penalty for above-limit earnings totalling just £5.
The review found the outdated design of carer’s allowance, coupled with longstanding DWP failures in its administration, meant about 180,000 carers ran up overpayment debts amounting to £300m between 2019 and 2025.
Campaigners welcomed the decision, calling it a “long-overdue reform” although there was disappointment the technical demands of building a new digital system to run the taper means it will not be introduced before the end of the decade.
Carers UK said the cliff-edge plays havoc with carers’ attempts to work part-time around their minimum 35 hours a week of caring duties, with many giving up paid work or refusing promotions, overtime or bonuses because of the risks.
John Healey, the chancellor, told the Guardian the carer’s allowance system had worked against carers. “That means doing an extra shift or getting a small pay rise can actually leave someone worse off. That cannot be right.
“So at this budget on Wednesday, we’re ending that cliff-edge. Carer’s allowance will instead taper as earnings increase, giving carers the freedom to work a little more and earn a little more without suddenly losing all their support.”
As well as unpaid carers, Healey’s budget will benefit an extra 150,000 new parents – including self-employed fathers and partners who have previously missed out – with parental support worth up to £194 a week.
Ministers are also removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on paraffin.
There will also be hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, to make it more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue.
Healey will also reportedly raise the minimum wage by about 4% to about £13.20 an hour. However, in a sign of government concern over rates of youth unemployment, the chancellor is said to be about to raise youth rates by roughly the same amount, rather than the inflation-busting levels seen in previous budgets.
Labour came to office in 2024 promising to raise the youth rate, which applies to workers under 21, to the same level as the full rate. But ministers have become concerned in recent months that raising the minimum wage for younger workers could be dissuading companies from taking on young employees.
“We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn’t mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren’t fair,” Burnham said.
“If you’re a nurse driving to work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket.”
Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said: “We have listened to [carers’] concerns about the cliff-edge built into the system which leaves them financially worse off for taking on a few more hours, or getting a modest pay rise, and intend to bring that to an end.”
Kirsty McHugh, chief executive of Carers Trust, said: “It is great news that the government is acting to remove the carer’s allowance cliff-edge. This is an important and long-overdue reform.
“We would urge the government to use this change as a springboard for a wider and deeper reform of carer’s allowance – a benefit that remains stuck in the 1970s and must be made fit for the future.”
Emily Holzhausen, Carers UK director of policy, said: “We have countless stories from carers who have shared their deep fears of going just a few pence over the earnings limit and losing all of their benefit.
“It’s absolutely right that the chancellor is thinking of practical changes that will make their lives easier. A taper on the earnings limit should give families much more choice about working and still caring.”

US Justice Department charges former FBI Director James Comey for third time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:30:28 UTC
07:30:28 KST

Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged by federal prosecutors with transmission of national defence information and conspiracy to transmit national defence information, marking the third criminal case brought against him by President Donald Trump's administration, according to court documents made public.
The case, which played out under seal from October 5, accuses Comey of sharing sensitive national security details during his tenure as FBI chief.
The charges stem from an article published by The New York Times on October 5, 2016, concerning Yahoo's role in adapting spam filters to assist US intelligence surveillance.
Special Assistant US Attorney Dustin Farahnak wrote in a filing unsealed on Monday that Comey directed staff to contact reporter Charlie Savage to correct reporting that had appeared in Reuters, and "thereby illegally transferred classified information."
Dismissal motion
Comey's defence attorneys filed a motion to dismiss the charges, arguing that the counts are based exclusively on a disclosure that occurred exactly ten years before the government filed its criminal information.
The defence contends the case is time-barred by the statute of limitations, arguing that prosecutors were required to secure a grand jury indictment within ten years rather than filing charges via a criminal information.
Comey has not been indicted in the matter.
In a video statement released after the filings were made public, Comey dismissed the allegations: "Well, they're back again. It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
Comey has remained a prominent target of the Trump administration since opening the FBI investigation into 2016 Russian election interference, leading to his dismissal as director in May 2017.
This action is the third prosecution launched against him.
A previous case was dismissed by a judge, while another indictment in April charged him with making a threat against President Trump through an online image.

Breadcrumb
Jordan strikes groups in Syria after church attack
The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.
It said air force jets had "destroyed several terrorist positions" and killed and wounded "numerous members" of groups linked to the perpetrators of the church attack.
Syria's state news agency SANA, citing a local health official, said the strikes across Daraa province in the country's south had killed eight civilians, including women and children.
Syria's government said that Jordan did not coordinate with it before launching deadly strikes on the country's south.
A Syrian government statement carried by state news agency SANA said "no prior coordination with the Syrian side was carried out concerning the military operation" by Jordan.
It said that authorities were investigating the strikes and discussing them with Amman while stressing the need for joint security coordination in border areas.
SANA quoted Syria's foreign ministry as saying that it had informed Jordan of "our complete reservation regarding the conduct of operations inside Syrian territory without prior coordination".
"Communication and coordination" was underway with Jordan "to address the repercussions of this incident in a manner that preserves security and the sovereignty of Syrian territory", it said.
Syria also closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions due to developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement.
On Friday, gunmen killed nine people during a funeral service at the Greek Orthodox St George's Church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate, southern Jordan.
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three percent of the population.
Major General Abdullah al-Maaytah, Jordan's director of public security, on Monday named the three detained suspects as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.
The trio, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage, were cornered at an abandoned house where they had barricaded themselves inside and opened fire on security forces.
"All three terrorists have been injured. They have been taken to hospital and are still receiving treatment," Maaytah told a press conference.
'We will show them'
One of the suspects was in critical condition, Jordan's state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka reported. It added that there were no casualties among the security forces.
"This country must remain an oasis of security and stability, and we affirm that Jordan will remain impervious to anyone who dares to challenge it," Maaytah said.
Under Jordanian law, murder is punishable by death by hanging.
A number of weapons and a large quantity of ammunition were seized from the three suspects, the Public Security Directorate said.
Jordan's King Abdullah II said in a post on X that security forces "chased them to the very end".
"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he wrote.
Earlier, the king visited wounded victims of the church attack in a hospital, dressed in military fatigues and carrying a pistol on his hip.
"We will show them," he vowed.
Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al-Mamlaka on Monday that the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".
"There is no indication of any external contacts or collaboration with foreign parties," he said.
Government communications minister Mohammad al-Momani said, "we stand ready and will strike with an iron fist, without mercy or leniency, against anyone who attempts to undermine Jordan's security".
Attacks on houses of worship in Jordan are rare. In 2016, an attack in Karak targeted a security centre and police patrols, leaving 10 people dead.
On Friday, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning for the victims of the church attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.
Eight of the nine victims were laid to rest on Sunday next to the church in a funeral that drew a huge crowd amid a large security presence, AFP images showed.
The ninth person, Mohammed al-Qasous, was buried in south Amman on Monday.

====================================================================================================

Daylight Saving Time Ends This Week. Here’s How to Best Prepare Yourself for the Time Change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:25:08 UTC
07:25:08 KST

The clocks in most of the U.S. will fall back an hour this weekend as Daylight Saving Time once again comes to an end.
Early Sunday morning, most of the country will switch back to observing Standard Time, resulting in earlier sunrises and earlier sunsets. The looming clock change comes as some lawmakers, with the backing of President Donald Trump, have been trying to push a bill through Congress that would make Daylight Saving Time permanent and end the biannual time change. But the bill has been met with pushback from other lawmakers and sleep experts.
Here’s everything you need to know about the clock change this fall, and the state of the bill that’s trying to put a stop to the cycle of changing the clocks twice a year.
When do the clocks fall back in 2026?
Daylight Saving Time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m. local time. At that time, the clocks will fall back an hour, to 1 a.m. local time.
How can I prepare for the clock change?
Dr. Alex Dimitriu, a psychiatrist and sleep medicine physician, likens the practice of changing the clocks twice a year to “an hour of jet lag,” adding that it can be an adjustment for many people. But the transition to Standard Time also means that people will gain an extra hour of sleep.
“Typically, moving to Standard Time is actually in sync with our circadian rhythm,” says Dr. Andrea Matsumura, a sleep medicine physician and spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. “Most people have a fairly easy transition into Standard Time; it’s the Daylight Saving Time that you have to do a lot more work to adjust [to] losing an hour of sleep.”
In the days leading up to the start of Daylight Saving Time—which will happen next March—Matsumura typically advises that people start going to bed a little earlier to help make the time change “a little less painful.” But there’s less preparation needed in the days leading up to Standard Time; in fact, Matsumura recommends that people simply stick to their regular sleep schedule ahead of Nov. 1.
Matsumura does suggest that people continue to take steps that normally help improve sleep, such as getting some daylight when they wake up in the morning and not drinking caffeine too late in the afternoon. Similarly, Dimitriu recommends that people do some physical movement in the morning, such as going for a walk, and avoid eating food too late in the evening.
What’s the status of the bill that would make Daylight Saving Time permanent?
Most states in the U.S. change their clocks twice a year: once in March as Daylight Saving Time begins, and again in November for Standard Time. Under the current federal law, states are permitted to opt out of Daylight Saving Time and remain in Standard Time year-round. Hawaii and most of Arizona have chosen that option, and so observe Standard Time throughout the year. Federal law does not, though, allow states to remain in Daylight Saving Time year-round.
A bill known as the Sunshine Protection Act, if passed by Congress and signed into law by the President, would change that. The measure would result in the country observing Daylight Saving Time year-round, though individual states could choose to forgo that path and instead stay in Standard Time permanently.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House with bipartisan support in July. But the measure is facing an uncertain fate in the Senate. Earlier this month, Senate Majority Leader John Thune told POLITICO that “there’s no clear path forward or consensus” on the bill yet.
Some lawmakers in the upper chamber, such as Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, have criticized the proposal. Critics have argued that permanent Daylight Saving Time would mean much later sunrises in some parts of the country, resulting in people going to school and work in the dark.
Sleep experts, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, have also objected to the bill because they say that Standard Time aligns better with people’s circadian rhythms.
Still, Trump has slammed critics of the Sunshine Protection Act and continued to push for the bill. At the beginning of October, he accused Cotton of “holding up” the bill, and urged his followers on Truth Social to “call Tom on his cellphone” to express support for the Sunshine Protection Act.

Protests in Europe: Fact-checking viral videos amid claims of 'chaos'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:18:34 UTC
07:18:34 KST

Protests in Europe: Fact-checking viral videos amid claims of 'chaos'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
As young people protest poor school conditions and the rising cost of living across Europe, misleading videos are spreading online. Footage from Poland in 2017, military preparations in Portugal and a protest in Argentina have all been falsely presented as recent demonstrations in Europe, painting a misleading picture of unrest. Vedika Bahl fact-checks three viral videos to uncover what they really show and how old footage is recycled to spread misinformation and attract clicks.
As young people take to the streets across Europe to protest poor school conditions and the rising cost of living, misleading videos circulating online regarding the demonstrations.
Footage from Poland, Portugal and Argentina has been falsely presented as evidence of recent unrest in Europe, with some posts suggesting the continent is descending into chaos. Others may be seeking to attract clicks and engagement.
One viral video, viewed more than a million times on X, appears to show enormous crowds gathered in Poland. Social media users claimed it depicted millions of people taking part in recent protests. But the footage is nearly nine years old. It shows Poland’s annual Independence Day march and was already circulating online in 2017.
The video has repeatedly resurfaced with misleading captions over the years. It was also previously shared as footage of unrest in France and was debunked earlier this year by FRANCE 24’s fact-checking service, The Observers.
Another video has been used to spread false claims about protests in Portugal. Posts on social media claimed the country had deployed its army to suppress demonstrations, warning that Portugal was on the “brink of social explosion”.
The footage shows military vehicles driving through the streets of Porto, accompanied by dramatic music. While the video was indeed filmed in the Portuguese city - with the famous Chapel of Santa Catarina is visible in the background - it does not show troops being deployed against protesters.
Instead, the footage shows preparations for Army Day, held from October 20 to 25. According to the city’s official website, thousands of soldiers arrived in Porto for a multi-day programme of events showcasing the military.
There have been no credible reports of the army being deployed to quell the recent protests. Demonstrations, including those calling for more affordable housing, have been handled by police. On Sunday, police dismantled housing protest camps in Porto and Lisbon, with more than 30 people arrested.
The same military footage has also recently circulated on TikTok with a different false claim: that it shows French police being deployed against protesters in France, despite Portuguese architecture being visible in the video.
A third video was shared by an account known for spreading false information, allegedly showing Italian protesters tearing down a US flag as onlookers cheered during a demonstration against rising fuel prices.
However, a reverse image search revealed that the footage dates back to August and was filmed in Buenos Aires, Argentina.The video shows the American flag being removed from the facade of a hotel near Argentina’s National Congress during a protest linked to a law introduced by President Javier Milei concerning private property.
The footage has no connection to protests in Italy.

Justice department charges ex-FBI director James Comey for third time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:17:09 UTC
07:17:09 KST

The justice department charged former FBI director James Comey on Monday with two counts of leaking information related to national defense, the third time the Trump administration has filed criminal charges against one of Donald Trump’s most despised foes.
The charges, filed in federal court in Washington DC, provide few details about what Comey is alleged to have leaked. The government alleges that the former FBI director leaked the information in 2016 and conspired with an unnamed person to give the information to a national news outlet.
Patrick Fitzgerald, Comey’s attorney, said the charges were related to a 5 October 2016 New York Times article that had already been investigated by prosecutors. The case was filed through a criminal maneuver known as an “information” – meaning it was not approved by a grand jury. While prosecutors will eventually have to have the charges approved by a grand jury, filing the charges through an information appears to have been an effort to quickly get the criminal charges in against Comey before the 10-year statute of limitations expires.
“Ten years after the article was published, the government filed an ‘information’ against Mr Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes he did not commit,” Fitzgerald said in a statement.
In a court filing unsealed on Monday, Comey’s lawyers argued the indictment should be dismissed because the statute of limitations had expired and it had been twice investigated and determined no charges should be filed. They also argued that the law required an indictment, not an information, within the 10-year statute of limitations.
Trump fired Comey in 2017 as he worked on an investigation into whether Trump allies colluded with Russia during the 2016 presidential election. The former FBI director has since become an outspoken critic of the president.
Last year, the justice department charged Comey with lying to Congress, but the charges were thrown out after a judge found the prosecutor handling the case, a White House ally installed to bring the case, was unlawfully appointed.
Earlier this year, the justice department filed charges against Comey in federal court in North Carolina for posting a picture of a formation of seashells spelling out “8647” – which for some people is a shorthand way of saying get rid of Trump. Legal experts have said that case is thin.
“Well, they’re back again. It would almost be funny if wasn’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice. One that we cannot become numb to,” Comey said in a video posted online.

Turkey-Libya maritime boundaries deal 'remains null and void,' Greek foreign minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:10:23 UTC
07:10:23 KST

The joint statement responded to the recent decision by Libya's House of Representatives to ratify the 2019 memorandum.
Greece's foreign minister said on Monday that a 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime boundaries deal remained "null and void" as he delivered a joint statement on behalf of Greece, Egypt, Cyprus, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union.
"The memorandum in question remains null and void and without legal effect, runs counter to international law and cannot serve as a lawful basis for the delimitation of maritime zones, nor can it produce legal consequences for third states," Giorgos Gerapetritis said.
The statement responded to the recent decision by Libya's House of Representatives to ratify the 2019 Turkish-Libyan memorandum on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean, which, it said, "raises serious concerns for regional security and stability."
The statement also highlighted a broader challenge to the international legal order, namely "the need to ensure that arbitrary bilateral agreements do not undermine the established rules of international law or prejudice the rights of third states."
Gerapetritis underlined that international law and, in particular, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), as well as customary international law, provide the legal framework for the delimitation of maritime zones.
These rules, he said, are "of fundamental importance for safeguarding predictability, legal certainty and peaceful relations among states."
He also warned that accepting bilateral agreements that disregard the applicable rules and principles of international law "would create a dangerous precedent, undermining the international legal order and the principles on which the peaceful settlement of disputes is based."
According to the statement, the memorandum violates these fundamental principles as it "ignores the geographical reality and the rights of all the coastal states involved over maritime zones, including the rights of islands in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea."
"The subsequent decision of Libya's House of Representatives does not alter this legal reality," it added.
The signatories reaffirmed their commitment "to the reunification of Libya's institutions and to the prospect of a united and prosperous Libya," while stressing that a stable Libya, engaging actively in regional cooperation, was essential for peace and security in the Mediterranean.
They also said that the country's political transition and its relations with its neighbours "must be governed by respect for international law and good-neighbourly relations."

Ukrainian Troops Evacuate Two Wounded Soldiers by Air With StarGate CASEVAC Drone in One Week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:07:08 UTC
07:07:08 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Troops Evacuate Two Wounded Soldiers by Air With StarGate CASEVAC Drone in One Week
Ukrainian troops evacuated two seriously wounded soldiers from the battlefield using the StarGate unmanned aerial CASEVAC platform after ground vehicles could not reach their positions, according to footage and information published online by the 475th Separate Assault Regiment CODE 9.2.
The two soldiers, 25-year-old Yevhen, call sign “Izium,” and 24-year-old Artem, call sign “Kolobok,” suffered severe limb injuries while positioned in a gray zone about five kilometers from the Russian border.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Difficult terrain, water obstacles, and the threat of Russian FPV drones made evacuation by ground transport impossible, leaving an airborne extraction as the only available option.
Over the course of one week, CODE 9.2 planned and completed two separate evacuation missions with support from SkyFall, the Ukrainian defense technology company that developed and manufactures StarGate.
The operations required coordination between several units, additional personnel and equipment, and fire support. Ukrainian forces used heavy Vampire strike drones to suppress Russian positions during the evacuations.
During one mission, StarGate flew nearly 30 kilometers to reach the wounded soldier and another 30 kilometers back with him onboard.
Russian forces were actively using electronic warfare in the area in an attempt to suppress GPS navigation completely. Despite the interference, StarGate continued flying using its onboard AI-based navigation system and was able to complete the mission.
The regiment now plans to turn the experience into a permanent capability.
“Going forward, we plan to make changes to the organizational structure of our regiment and create a separate air ambulance section within the medical company,” CODE 9.2 commander Oleksandr Nastenko, call sign “Flint,” stated.
“It will specialize directly in evacuating wounded personnel from the battlefield by air transport,” he added.
StarGate is Ukraine’s first specialized unmanned aerial platform developed specifically for battlefield CASEVAC missions. SkyFall designed the system for situations in which conventional vehicles cannot reach wounded troops or where sending ground transport would be too dangerous.
The drone can carry up to 150 kilograms and reach speeds of up to 105 kilometers per hour. Its evacuation module is based on certified medical stretchers, while onboard AI, navigation, and redundant communications systems allow it to continue operating when GPS is jammed or communications are lost.
Days earlier, Ukrainian forces evacuated a soldier who had survived 491 days in an isolated frontline position and lost both feet after being wounded by Russian drones. Conventional ground evacuation was impossible because of mines and intense drone activity, prompting several Ukrainian units to adapt a heavy hexacopter to carry him out.

Russia’s Black Sea Fleet Hasn’t Left Port in Five Months, Firing Kalibrs From Novorossiysk
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet has avoided open waters for five consecutive months, launching Kalibr cruise missiles directly from its base in Novorossiysk, Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk reported on October 26, according to NV.
Speaking on Ukraine’s national television, Pletenchuk explained that Russian commanders likely fear losing their warships at sea. As a result, they have opted to conduct missile launches from their own naval base, despite the potential dangers of such operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“It’s better to launch missiles from their own harbor, even though if something detonates there, everyone nearby will be in serious trouble. So yes, they decided to stay home,” Pletenchuk explained.
However, the restrictions on Russian naval movements have not eliminated the threat of Kalibr missile strikes against Ukraine. Pletenchuk noted that Russian submarines face greater operational limitations because they do not launch missiles from inside the harbor and have also stopped venturing into open waters.
Kalibr is a family of Russian sea-launched cruise missiles deployed aboard surface warships and submarines. Its 3M-14 land-attack variant has an estimated range of 1,500 to 2,500 kilometers and carries a warhead weighing approximately 450 kilograms, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The missile’s long range allows Russian warships to strike targets across Ukraine while remaining in port. This enables Moscow to maintain a naval missile threat without exposing its surface vessels to the same risks of operating in open waters.
Meanwhile, Russian military aviation continues to operate over the Black Sea around the clock, conducting patrols and strikes both day and night. Russian drones also remain active in the area.
Pletenchuk emphasized that Russian aircraft and helicopters maintain a distance of at least 100 kilometers from Ukraine’s coastline.
He recalled that Ukrainian forces had previously used naval drones to shoot down Russian aircraft and helicopters, demonstrating the expanding capabilities of Ukraine’s unmanned maritime systems.
Earlier, on September 9, several branches of Ukraine’s security and defense forces struck the naval base in Novorossiysk, hitting military harbor facilities, warships, and Kalibr missile carriers, along with a terminal involved in oil shipments.
At the port’s fuel oil terminal, a commercial logistics hub with an annual throughput capacity of 4 million metric tons, at least one petroleum storage tank was set ablaze.

Lula has maintained his innocence, accusing his political opponents of using the judicial system against him.
Trump previously urged the Brazilian authorities to drop the case against Jair Bolsonaro, calling his prosecution a “witch hunt.” His administration has also faced allegations of attempting to influence Brazil’s 2026 presidential election in favor of Bolsonaro’s son.
Brazilian police opened a preliminary inquiry into suspected US interference but closed it due to insufficient evidence. Reuters separately reported that two senior State Department officials had pushed for sanctions aimed at weakening Lula and boosting the Bolsonaro family’s political fortunes. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud will send workers to document Israeli Arab voters on Election Day, and may use the footage as false evidence for a conspiracy theory that the election was rigged, Haaretz has learned.
Likud over the past few weeks has set up unofficial teams to "observe" voters in Arab communities, sometimes citing voter fraud. These teams are designated to stand outside polling stations in Arab communities, document voters and report back to headquarters in real time.
Concurrently, Likud officials are preparing to launch a postelection campaign centering on voter fraud in the case that Likud suffers major losses.
Likud members have discussed and planned scenarios of major election losses, a source close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said. Some are pushing for a "stolen election" campaign that echoes U.S. President Donald Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election.
There is no information to suggest that the prime minister attended these meetings. At this stage, senior party officials are seemingly planning the campaign as a possibility for after Election Day.
Other sources close to Netanyahu say that several party officials are pressuring the prime minister to implement the plan, and that Netanyahu is considering the matter.
This is not the first time Likud planned to use a "rigged election" conspiracy theory to curry favor among voters and sow distrust in the electoral process. Likud's Yoav Kisch claimed there had been voter fraud on election night in 2022 when he spoke to Channel 14.
"I appeal from here to the chairman of the Central Elections Committee: We have dozens of cases of fraud, of harm to voting at polling stations in the Arab community," he said then. But Likud won the most seats in the election, and the claims were short-lived.
"2022 was a trial run for the current election," a senior Likud official involved in Election Day operations says, referring to claims of fraud and other matters.
The Likud system to document Arab Israeli voters at polling stations could be used to disseminate the voter fraud conspiracy theory.
The system is one of the party's largest investments this election campaign, standing at an estimated cost of millions of shekels. All team members were recruited and will be paid.
The system, which first took shape in the previous election, is unofficial and will not use the Likud representatives who work inside polling stations. Therefore, it is not subject to the Central Elections Committee's strict regulations.
"Suppose a woman comes to vote wearing a burqa," a Likud source said, "and then a few minutes later another woman arrives wearing a burqa – perhaps it's the same one? We will try to check and verify this." The teams, however, have no legal authority to verify voters' identities.
According to Likud sources, it is not unlikely that the videos from Election Day will be distributed as false evidence that the election was rigged. Since the videos will not feature the inside of polling stations, it will be difficult to legally oppose their distribution.
In addition to the dedicated teams, other Likud observers across the country will report any unusual incidents to the party, as is customary for every party in every election campaign. However, these reports are also meant to be forwarded to an established "fraud war room."

Former FBI director James Comey hit with third set of charges under Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:03:26 UTC
07:03:26 KST

Former FBI director James Comey hit with third set of charges under Trump
Comey, who was fired during Trump’s first term, has been accused of unlawfully divulging national security information.
James Comey, the former director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), is facing a third set of criminal charges under the administration of United States President Donald Trump.
On Monday, sealed documents came to light showing that the Trump administration has accused Comey of two counts related to the unlawful dissemination of “information related to national defence”.
Comey, a high-profile Trump critic, has not been indicted in the case. He has denied any wrongdoing.
But it is the third time the Trump administration has sought to level criminal charges against the former FBI director since the president returned to office in January 2025.
In an October court filing, prosecutors accuse Comey of ordering his FBI colleagues to leak information to the news media.
“The defendant [Comey] through one or more co-conspirators directed Individual #1 to disclose national defence information to a reporter for a national news publication,” the court filing reads.
In a video published on the online platform Substack, Comey once again denounced the Trump administration’s attempts to prosecute him as a campaign of political retribution.
“Well, now they’re back again. It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to,” Comey said.
“Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent, and I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”
Comey also noted that Trump is only midway through his second term, and he hinted that he expects more criminal charges to come his way.
“The next couple years are going to be hard for all of us,” Comey added. “It’s really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America.”
The latest charges pertain to a New York Times article from October 5, 2016, which describes how the email platform Yahoo was ordered to scan traffic on its site for a specific computer signature allegedly tied to a “terrorist” organisation.
Prosecutors have accused Comey of directing sensitive information to be disclosed to the reporter on that story, Charlie Savage.
In a statement released to news media, Comey’s defence lawyer Pat Fitzgerald framed the charges as feeble, claiming that the government had already investigated the matter twice before.
“Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone,” the statement said.
Fitzgerald pointed out that government prosecutors had not sought an indictment, which involves presenting charges to a grand jury that must then choose whether to approve the criminal charges.
Instead, they are seeking to charge Comey through a process called a “criminal information”, which allows prosecutors to bypass a grand jury.
“Ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an ‘Information’ against Mr Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury,” Fitzgerald said. “It purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit.”
Federal Judge Trevor McFadden, from the US District Court in Washington, DC, is overseeing the case. He is a Trump appointee.
Trump has long sought the prosecution of Comey, whom he fired from the role of FBI director in 2017, during his first term as president.
Comey had been FBI head since 2013. But his dismissal came as the FBI investigated the possibility of collusion between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, a probe that Trump has repeatedly denounced as a “hoax”.
Following Trump’s second inauguration in 2025, his administration has sought the prosecution of several of the president’s critics, including Comey.
In September 2025, Trump appeared to request that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi look into Comey and other perceived political adversaries.
“Nothing is being done. What about Comey, Adam ‘Shifty’ Schiff, Leticia???” Trump wrote to Bondi in a social media post, referencing the former FBI director, a Democratic senator and New York Attorney General Letitia James. “They’re all guilty as hell, but nothing is going to be done.”
Trump concluded his post by telling Bondi not to “delay any longer” before pursuing the three critics.
“JUSTICE MUST BE SERVED, NOW,” he wrote.
Five days later, on September 25 of that year, Comey was indicted on charges of lying to Congress and obstructing a legislative proceeding.
The case was ultimately dismissed on the basis that the prosecutor in charge, Lindsey Halligan, was unlawfully appointed.
A second indictment came on April 28. In that case, the Trump administration accused Comey of threatening the president by posting a photo on social media of seashells, arranged to form the message “86 47”.
Forty-seven is a reference to Trump, the 47th president, and “86” is a rhyming word for “nix”, common in the service industry as code for throwing out a dish or customer.
The Trump administration, however, has argued that “86” implies violence. That case is ongoing.
Earlier on Monday, before the third set of charges was revealed, a federal judge in a separate case ruled that Comey’s daughter, former assistant US attorney Maurene Comey, had been unlawfully fired last year under Trump’s second term.
The younger Comey has maintained her termination was retaliation against her father. The court determined she was entitled to “retroactive reinstatement” and backpay.
James Comey has denied all accusations of criminal wrongdoing, and his legal team has sought to have the latest set of charges dismissed.
