Why Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Is Missing So Many Key Figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:27:15 UTC
06:27:15 KST

Anthropic filed its hotly anticipated IPO prospectus on Monday, spelling out parts of the company’s business, strategy, and risk profile ahead of its public debut. Though the filing, known as an S-1, is several hundred pages long, it has some notable omissions—namely, certain financial figures.
“Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $_____ for the three months ended September 30, 2026,” reads the first of dozens of such examples.
It’s relatively common for companies to redact certain information in their S-1 filings, and Securities and Exchange Commission rules allow for a certain degree of leniency around the practice, particularly when it comes to information considered “confidential.”
Still, it’s helpful to know what, exactly, these companies decide to leave out. In Anthropic’s case, the missing details largely revolve around financials for its most recent quarter, which concluded at the end of September, and lease agreements tied to its compute investments. While experts expect many details to be disclosed before Anthropic goes public, their current absence may hint at the uncertainties of investing in artificial intelligence, as companies work to secure sufficient compute.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.
Michael Dambra, an accounting and law professor at the University at Buffalo School of Management, tells WIRED that there are “practical reasons” for Anthropic’s third-quarter numbers to be absent: September 30 was only a few weeks ago, and “closing the books for a company of this size takes time.”
Companies can also be liable for misstatements in their registration statements, “so there is a strong incentive not to publish numbers before they have been fully vetted,” Dambra says. SEC rules require that “Anthropic would need to update the filing with third-quarter financials” if the company goes public any later than about mid-November, he says.
As for data center lease agreements, Erica Neuman, an accounting professor at Youngstown State University, says it’s “not unusual” for companies to redact confidential details from “contract exhibits,” which could include lease terms.
However, Neuman adds that it’s worth scrutinizing whether Anthropic’s redactions would prevent, or make it more difficult, for investors to analyze Anthropic’s financial obligations and whether they may impact the company’s cash flow.
Many of Anthropic’s financial obligations relate to compute, which is the “most significant operating cost in our business,” according to the S-1. It’s also a business risk for the company, and it’s laid out both in terms of undersupply and overinvestment. (Parts of the AI industry have been warning that chip constraints could slow the progress of AI.)
Anthropic’s prospectus puts more emphasis on the risks of overinvestment, stating that the company needs to make forward investments in compute resources that will seem “irresponsibly large” at first glance.
Chips, Anthropic explains, are approached as a “single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners,” including Amazon, Google, Nvidia, and AMD. The company notes that it has entered into contracts “with an aggregate committed spend of more than $____, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.” Some of these contracts are set to be completed before December 2030, while others may extend through 2045.
Though the prospectus touches on Anthropic’s compute uncertainties due to factors like limited land and power resources, Patrick Moorhead, CEO and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, believes investors are owed more detail.
“It’s about characterizing the odds and impact individually across each of the areas. Anthropic owes investors more information, such as a probability of these individual issues, characterizing the percentage chance and the degree of the impact,” he tells WIRED. “Not ‘could materially impact.’”
Anthropic does provide some eye-catching estimates in footnotes. Since December 31, 2025, it has started or amended “compute and infrastructure” leases with “future minimum payment obligations” worth approximately $417 billion in aggregate. Since June 30, it has added an additional $245 billion to its future payment obligations, all related to infrastructure agreements. It also expanded “certain existing commercial agreements” that it caveats “have not yet been finalized,” for an additional $125 billion to $150 billion.
Include “short term” agreements with “minimum non-cancelable payments,” Anthropic says, and that’s another $21 billion. In total, it will owe, at minimum, an estimated $808 billion if it follows through on all of this.
Ben Bajarin, chief executive and a principal analyst at Creative Strategies who tracks the chip industry, says that this is likely just the first draft of Anthropic’s prospectus, and he expects a lot of gaps to be filled in an updated version.
Despite how common S-1 redactions are, Dambra describes them as “controversial.” While companies may argue that they’re “protecting proprietary information,” Dambra says that skeptics accuse them of using redactions “opportunistically” in order to “avoid disclosing politically or socially sensitive information.”
However, Dambra argues that redacting information may come at a cost. He notes that companies with redactions in their S-1s were also more likely to “underprice” their shares at the initial public offering.
When companies redact information in their S-1, Dambra says, they typically understand that they’ve created an “information gap” between them and outside investors. Understanding that investors will treat this gap with “suspicion,” companies may feel inclined to “entice” them to participate in the IPO by setting a lower starting price.
It’s unclear what Anthropic’s opening price may end up being or how investors may be interpreting the redactions in the company’s S-1. But according to Bajarin, the whole AI industry is one form of “blank” or another when it comes to crunching the numbers based on access to chips and infrastructure right now. So, yes, it’s all a risk.
“All of this,” he says, “just shows how absurdly early we are in enterprise adoption of an AI market that will be more than $3 trillion yearly and likely growing.”

Algeria plans to deploy its troops to Niger to protect oil and gas facilities and combat terrorist groups. This could become the country's first foreign military operation since 1973. Meduza reports, UNN writes.
Details
The decision to deploy troops is being made amid expanding military cooperation between Algeria and Niger. One of the operation's main tasks will be to protect energy infrastructure owned by Algerian companies.

First foreign military operation in more than half a century

The current operation will mark a significant shift in Algeria's military policy, as the country has not involved its regular army in combat operations abroad for decades.
At the same time, the exact timing of the troop deployment, the size of the contingent, and the duration of its stay in Niger have not yet been specified.

PM Modi outlines key milestones in 139th 'Mann Ki Baat' (file photo)
NEW DELHI: High fever and laboured breathing threatened the life of Oho-Tahane, a child from Jarawa tribe of Andaman and Nicobar Islands. With specialist care out of reach, health workers turned to e-Sanjeevani for remote consultation. The doctor diagnosed pneumonia, and timely expert intervention helped the child’s condition improve rapidly.Oho-Tahane, a member of one of India’s most vulnerable tribal groups, is among over 50 crore cases, many in far flung areas, facilitated by the national telemedicine service since its launch in Nov 2019.The service’s achievement was highlighted by PM Narendra Modi in his ‘Mann Ki Baat’ address Sunday, as he also cited how e-Sanjeevani enabled a doctor to guide a medical team in treating Kunhi Koya (60) in Kalpeni, Lakshadweep, and helped ensure medical assistance for pregnant Kunjang Dolma in Himalayan region of Zanskar.Developed by C-DAC Mohali under the health ministry, e-Sanjeevani facilitates 2.5-3 lakh daily consultations, offers services in 15 languages and is available across all 36 states and UTs. Women account for 57.1% of the platform’s utilisation, while people aged 46 and above account for 40.1% of consultations. Those aged 60 and above account for 16.2%. The platform has recorded a peak of 6,30,315 consultations in a single day.
Modi credited the platform’s reach to dedication of doctors, public trust and the effective use of technology. He highlighted 1.9 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, saying they were bringing healthcare closer to rural communities and evolving into wellness centres for village panchayats. Regular health check-ups were becoming more common in rural areas, he said, with e-Sanjeevani playing an important role.
The PM also highlighted advances in brain research, referring to Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT-Madras, which he inaugurated this month. The centre has developed a brain imaging technology platform to create high resolution digital 3D images of human brain. Its mission is to map and study 100 human brains in detail using Param Shakti supercomputer..Modi said the initiative could deepen understanding of the brain, particularly as conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and dementia lack a definitive cure. Data from the 100 brains will be available as an open-source resource for researchers, the PM added.

Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Germany planning to buy ‘drone missiles’ from Ukraine – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:21:08 UTC
06:21:08 KST

Germany planning to buy ‘drone missiles’ from Ukraine – media
Germany is preparing to buy a batch of low-cost cruise missiles from Ukraine to expand its long-range strike capabilities, according to several media outlets.
The deal could be finalized in the coming weeks, the Financial Times reported, citing officials familiar with the matter. It would initially involve a small batch of missiles for testing by the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, early next year. If the tests prove successful, Berlin could reportedly place a follow-up order for several hundred missiles.
Dubbed ‘Bars’ – meaning snow leopard in both Russian and Ukrainian – the cruise missiles, sometimes referred to as “drone missiles” in Ukraine, are jet-powered weapons with a range of up to 1,000 km and a payload of up to 105 kg.
Germany and Ukraine signed a deal to jointly produce Bars missiles in July 2026. Under that agreement, Berlin would finance production, with all the missiles produced being delivered to Ukraine.
The potential purchase comes amid a surge in German arms procurement as Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government seeks to turn the Bundeswehr into Europe’s strongest conventional army, citing the threat of a potential conflict with Russia. Moscow has repeatedly dismissed such claims as “nonsense,” insisting that it has no intention of attacking any NATO member.
Armament drive
Bloomberg reported earlier this week that Berlin was planning to acquire “thousands of precision deep-strike weapons” from several European and American companies. One proposed contract with US firm Covenant for the delivery of thousands of ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles could be worth more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion), according to the report.
Berlin emerged as Kiev’s single biggest military donor after Washington drastically scaled back its aid under US President Donald Trump. Merz has prioritized military spending, including assistance to Kiev, despite acknowledging that Germany’s economy is in a “structural crisis.” His government amended the constitutional debt brake to fund the buildup and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion for defense and €11.5 billion in military aid for Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Germany’s central bank has warned that the country is on course to record its largest budget deficit since reunification by 2028.
Cashing in on war?
Ukraine, in turn, appears to be actively seeking to cash in on weapons exports, including sales to its Western backers. In February, David Aloian, deputy secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council, told Reuters that the country expected to generate billions of dollars in revenue from it this year alone.
Kiev halted all weapons exports following the escalation of the conflict in 2022, but Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky reversed that decision when he announced plans to open nearly a dozen weapons export centers across Europe in early 2026.
The plans have not stopped Kiev from seeking further financial and military assistance from Western nations. Last month, Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeny Khmara suggested that Western donors supply Kiev with highly sought-after US-made Patriot interceptors from their own stockpiles, which would then be replenished with 1,000 missiles it plans to purchase with EU funds at some point in the future. In October, Zelensky himself lashed out at the country’s backers over their reluctance to cover a major budget shortfall.
Trump accused Ukraine in mid-October of selling American-supplied missiles on the black market. He also claimed that Kiev had failed to account for billions of dollars in American military and financial aid.
Ukrainian arms manufacturers have been implicated in some of the nation’s numerous corruption scandals. Fire Point – a defense contractor personally promoted by Zelensky during his visits to Western nations – was reportedly effectively owned by the Ukrainian leader’s longtime former business partner, Timur Mindich, known as ‘Zelensky’s wallet’ in Kiev. The businessman fled Ukraine last year after a major corruption investigation named him as one of its primary suspects.

JetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but the New York carrier said strong travel demand is helping to offset higher fuel prices as it seeks to calm investors after shares fell to a new low Monday.
JetBlue stock was up nearly 19% in early trading Tuesday.
JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million.
"Resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue well ahead of our initial expectations, allowing us to recapture more of the increase in fuel costs than we initially expected," CEO Joanna Geraghty said in an earnings release. "That momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, and Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver exceptional results even as we significantly grow capacity."
JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.
JetBlue executives are set to hold an earnings call on Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET, where they will face questions from analysts about the company's long-term health amid sustained losses. A group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.
The airline said its revenue per available seat mile, a key metric measuring how much operating revenue a carrier generates for every seat flown one mile, would be up as much as 22% in the fourth quarter, bringing the annual increase to an expected 13.5% to 14.5%
The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.
JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday.
"Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."
Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Loss per share: 60 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 55 cents expected
- Revenue: $2.81 billion vs. $2.82 billion expected
JetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.
Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares, which are up more than 20% this year.
JetBlue has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals.
It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines.

With the November 3 elections just eight days away, polls show Democrats pulling ahead as Republicans fight to retain control of both chambers of Congress.

Israeli forces continue to kill and injure civilians, including children, who approach or cross the Yellow Line in Gaza, the commission said in its latest report.

The Trump administration told Venezuela's interim authorities "weeks and weeks ago" that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado needs to be allowed to return to the country ahead of potential elections next year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday.
Rubio told reporters in a call that the government of acting President Delcy Rodríguez replied to the U.S. by saying that Machado was free to enter the country. Machado returned to Venezuela over the weekend.
"Weeks and weeks ago, we spoke to the interim authorities and just said, 'Look, our expectation is that she’s a Venezuelan, she belongs in her country. That’s the country she’s from. She should be allowed to return. She should be allowed to return unperturbed,’” Rubio said.
He noted that the U.S. had not discouraged Machado from returning to Venezuela except immediately after devastating earthquakes in June. He said that was because the U.S. believed the priority should be in getting humanitarian and emergency relief into the country.
Rubio spoke after Venezuelan authorities and opposition figures agreed last week on a blueprint to reform the country’s electoral process in order for free and fair elections to take place at some point in 2027.
He said the Trump administration, which captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January military operation and brought him to the U.S. to face drug-trafficking charges, would be watching events closely and urging all sides to comply with the new process.
"Obviously, we need to use our leverage with the government for the interim authorities to ensure that the process is moving forward in a responsible way," Rubio said. "Our goal here is to have an election."
Machado had been in hiding in Venezuela for most of 2025 before making a clandestine escape that December to Norway, where she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. She later gave her medal to President Donald Trump.
She returned to Venezuela on Sunday, her first appearance since the U.S. deposed Maduro and replaced him with Rodriguez, who had been his vice president and has now exceeded the time she was authorized to serve, with no election yet scheduled.
Rubio said the U.S. goal is to help put in a place a sustainable election architecture that will give all parties confidence in the vote.
To get there, Rubio said Venezuela must stabilize its economy and rebuild its institutions, including its courts and electoral council, and provide an open space for political expression that will hinge on press freedom and access to all media outlets, including online platforms.

Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of midterm election, Reuters Ipsos poll finds
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:15:21 CET
06:15:21 KST

By Jason Lange
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump’s public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from last week’s record low, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.
Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party’s majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.
The five-day nationwide poll also showed that registered voters broadly favored Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would pick for Congress in what is known as a “generic ballot” question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today.
That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on October 19. The latest poll additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his second term as president.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
STEEP SENATE CLIMB FOR DEMOCRATS
Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate.
It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favored Democrats over Republicans by 9 points, 53% to 44%.
The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent gasoline prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction.
Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach on the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue.
The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 points for registered voters.
(Reporting by Jason Lange in Washington; editing by Scott Malone, Will Dunham and Sanjeev Miglani)

Pentagon’s FORTRESS Plan Prepares US Bases to Operate 90 Days Without Outside Support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:11:09 UTC
06:11:09 KST

- Category
- World
Pentagon’s FORTRESS Plan Prepares US Bases to Operate 90 Days Without Outside Support
The Pentagon is preparing major US military bases to operate independently for at least 90 days during a major conflict that could disrupt power grids, supply chains, communications, and other critical infrastructure, Fox News reported on October 25.
The requirement is part of a broader initiative called FORTRESS , which is intended to keep US forces functioning even if the civilian systems they normally rely on are damaged or unavailable.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We don’t want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can’t. It’s an intolerable risk,” Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told Fox News.
According to documents reviewed by Fox News, major military installations in the continental US would be expected to sustain essential operations independently for at least 90 days, including electricity, water, fuel, and communications.
FORTRESS envisions portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage, and microgrids that could allow military bases to disconnect from civilian power networks during prolonged outages.
“Power is combat now. Without electricity, you lose communications, water, logistics, assembly lines and just basic military command structures,” Parnell stated.
Fox News reported that the Pentagon is also preparing for major disruptions to global supply chains during a large-scale war. The initiative calls for strategic reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts, and medical supplies.
For the most important defense dependencies, FORTRESS would require at least two qualified supply or production pathways, reducing the risk that the loss of one factory, supplier, or industrial capability could interrupt military operations.
The outlet also noted that the Pentagon is preparing civilian factories to shift toward defense production during a crisis through the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network.
The plan calls for manufacturers to be identified in advance, with technical requirements, cybersecurity protections, contracting arrangements, and conversion procedures established before a conflict begins.
Fox News reported that FORTRESS also includes recurring industrial stress tests and mobilization exercises intended to determine whether US manufacturers could maintain production during prolonged disruption.
The initiative also includes measures to strengthen military communications, navigation, and satellite capabilities against interference.
The outlet reported that the Pentagon is preparing for operations in which GPS signals are jammed or space-based systems are disrupted, reducing dependence on vulnerable civilian and commercial infrastructure.
“The next conflict will likely be fought on multiple fronts,” Parnell told Fox News. “When that happens, global supply chains will break.”
He described FORTRESS as an insurance policy intended to ensure US forces can continue operating during a prolonged, multi-front war even if critical infrastructure and supply networks fail.
The FORTRESS plan builds on earlier Pentagon efforts to expand the US defense industrial base beyond conventional military contractors. In April, UNITED24 Media reported that US officials were exploring whether companies including General Motors and Ford could shift civilian factories toward weapons, ammunition, and military equipment production during periods of heightened demand.

Poland and Britain Deepen Ties With Strategic 3-Year Defense Agreement
Poland and the United Kingdom are set to sign a 3-year defense cooperation plan.
The agreement will be formally signed by Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and British Defense Minister Wes Streeting, according to the Polish Ministry of Defense on October 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Streeting will travel to Poland for high-level talks with Kosiniak-Kamysz, followed by the official signing ceremony and joint statements from both officials.
This upcoming agreement builds on a prior defense partnership pact inked by the two nations in May 2026.
That agreement focused on tech integration, joint military exercises, enhanced cyber security measures, and the development of next-generation medium-range missiles and air defense ammunition.
The alliance also aligns with broader efforts to strengthen ties between London and the European Union.
On May 27, 2026, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer signed a historic Security and Defense Partnership Treaty in London, officially designating Russia as the primary threat to European stability.
The agreement was designed to elevate bilateral military cooperation to its highest level and enable rapid, direct defense responses in the event of a regional crisis without awaiting unanimous consensus from NATO’s 32 members.
Tusk underscored that while Poland remained fully committed to the transatlantic alliance, building swift, bilateral mechanisms with key allies like the UK and France was essential to counter regional aggression effectively—particularly as Washington prepared to gradually reduce its military footprint on the continent.

People with migrant backgrounds make up 5.4% of S. Korean population in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:04:55 UTC
06:04:55 KST

People with migrant backgrounds make up 5.4% of S. Korean population in 2025
The share of people with migrant backgrounds living in South Korea rose in 2025 to 5.4 percent, up from the previous year, data showed Monday, with those in their 20s leading the gains, Yonhap reported.
The total migrant population came to 2.81 million in 2025, up from 2.71 million a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics. South Korea's total population stood at 51.82 million.
The data ministry defines people with a migrant background as immigrants or those with at least one parent from overseas.
The category includes foreign nationals, naturalized South Koreans and second-generation immigrants.
Foreign nationals accounted for 75.1 percent of the population with a migrant background, followed by second-generation immigrants at 14.1 percent.
Another 9.1 percent acquired South Korean citizenship through naturalization or recognition of parentage, a legal process in which a parent recognizes a child born out of wedlock as their own.
By gender, males accounted for 52.5 percent, and females made up 47.5 percent. There were 110.7 males for every 100 females.
The working-age population, comprising people aged 15 to 64, stood at 2.3 million in 2025.
By age group, people in their 30s accounted for the largest share at 23.7 percent, or 667,000, followed by those in their 20s at 21.6 percent, or 607,000. People in their 40s numbered 439,000, or 15.6 percent of the total.
The number of people in their 20s rose by 36,000 over the period, the largest increase among all age groups.
The report also showed 56 percent of people with a migrant background lived in the greater Seoul metropolitan area, with 17.1 percent residing in Seoul.
South Chungcheong Province had the highest proportion of residents with a migrant background at 8.3 percent, followed by North Chungcheong Province and Gyeonggi Province, both at 6.5 percent. The figure for Seoul stood at 5.1 percent.
The southeastern city of Daegu had the lowest proportion at 2.9 percent.
The number of people aged 24 and younger with a migrant background rose 6.6 percent from a year earlier to 790,000.
By their parents' nationality, those with Vietnamese parents accounted for 28.1 percent, followed by those with Chinese parents at 15.7 percent. Those with ethnic Korean parents of Chinese nationality accounted for a separate 11.4 percent.
Other major countries represented by their parents' nationalities included Uzbekistan, the Philippines, Cambodia, Mongolia, and Nepal.
As written earlier, South Korea is set to expand international flights in the winter season.

Part of London's iconic Oxford Street pedestrianised ‘forever’

Part of London’s iconic Oxford Street pedestrianised ‘forever’
LONDON – A stretch of London’s iconic Oxford Street was made traffic-free “forever” from Oct 26, as pedestrians took over the country’s most famous shopping street, absent of the capital’s red double-decker buses and black cabs.
Shoppers walking along the street told AFP this was a “good idea”, but drivers of London’s famous black taxi cabs rejected the move as “crazy”.
“This is a momentous day for Oxford Street, but also for London,” Mayor Sadiq Khan told reporters on the thoroughfare, one of the busiest shopping zones in Europe.
“I want to be supporting our shops in Oxford Street and have a kilometre worth of this street – almost half of this street – traffic-free forever,” Khan said, adding the pedestrianisation would increase the number of shoppers.
Those walking in the area on a rainy Monday said they backed the move.
“Overall, I think it’s a very good idea. It should have been done before,” said John Oxford, an 83-year-old professor of virology.
“It gives people more of a chance to actually explore the shops, explore the iconic Oxford Street,” said Madaki Kanya, a 19-year-old visiting from Manchester in north-west England.
“It’s a lot more comfortable walking around, not dodging the cars and the traffic,” agreed Paul Facer, 62, from Weymouth in the south-west, who was visiting with his wife.
‘Decades of decline’
The street brings in some £3.1 billion (S$5.3 billion) spending annually, but has faced challenges, including shops shuttering during the Covid-19 pandemic and a loss of footfall due to a shift to online shopping.
“Over the last couple of decades it’s been in decline, I’d say managed decline,” Khan told BBC Radio 4 about the street lined with luxury retailers, clothing chains, and department stores.
“I’m not willing to stand by as shops leave this street, as jobs leave this street,” he said.
But the scheme has proved controversial among residents worried about traffic jams in neighbouring areas as well as among disability rights activists.
Black cab driver Jason Harvey, 51, told AFP that “to pedestrianise any part of Oxford Street is crazy”, citing needs of people with disabilities and young children.
Another taxi driver, Brendan Cooper, said people with disabilities will “have to walk 150 yards around the back of the stores to get a taxi”, calling this “just ridiculous”.
Khan insisted there were cab ranks and bus stops near the street so people can still access the area with ease.
“For centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way,” he added, saying the move would “revitalise” the road and make the capital “greener”.
Around half the street has been pedestrianised, with plans to close off the rest to vehicles depending on the success of the first phase.
“Today marks an exciting new chapter for Oxford Street as work begins to transform one of the world’s most iconic high streets,” said Meave Wall, chief retail and digital officer at the Selfridges department store, which opened on the West End road more than a century ago. AFP

Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of US midterms, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds

- Reuters/Ipsos found Democrats ahead by 47% to 36% in the generic ballot, or 50% to 41% with undecided voters included.
- Inflation and living costs are shaping the race. Voters see Democrats as stronger on the economy, and Democrats seem more eager to vote.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump’s public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from his record low a week earlier, ahead of the Nov 3 US midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Oct 26.
Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party’s majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.
The five-day poll, which was conducted nationwide, also showed that registered voters broadly favoured Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would vote for in what is known as a “generic ballot” question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today.
That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Oct 19.
The poll that closed on Oct 26 additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his second term as president.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress.
While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
Steep Senate climb for Democrats
Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate.
It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favoured Democrats over Republicans by 9 percentage points, 53% to 44%.
The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent petrol prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction.
Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach on the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue.
The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 points for registered voters. REUTERS

Serbia's Gen Z protesters topple Vucic's political establishment in landmark election victory. What's next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:58:42 UTC
05:58:42 KST

Vucic swept aside in Serbian elections. Can Belgrade break free from Russia’s orbit?
The Student List's election victory ends more than a decade of Aleksandar Vucic's rule, hinting at a new chapter in Serbia's relations with the EU, Russia, and China.
Supporters of the Student List opposition movement walk on a portrait of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic following his concession of defeat on Oct. 25, 2026 in Belgrade, Serbia. (Pierre Crom/Getty Images)
Belgrade erupted in celebration on Sunday night as Serbia's Gen Z-led protest movement transformed nearly two years of anti-corruption demonstrations into an electoral victory over the political establishment of former President Aleksandar Vucic, who had held power for 14 years.
Among the crowds was Dijana Hrka, whose 27-year-old son Stefan was one of 16 people killed when a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad on Nov. 1, 2024.
Hrka, who had been demanding accountability for the tragedy and had previously gone on hunger strike, broke down in tears after Vucic conceded defeat.
"I have been waiting for this moment for almost two years," she told N1 television, struggling to speak through her emotions. "This is the victory of all of us, the victory of our children."
read also
Change at the ballot
Protests in Serbia erupted following the Novi Sad disaster but soon evolved into a nationwide challenge to the government, mobilizing students, academics, workers, and citizens who had never before engaged in political activism.
By Sunday night, the movement had achieved what years of fragmented opposition efforts had failed to accomplish — a decisive electoral victory over Vucic's political camp. The Student List
The Student List — an electoral alliance formed by Serbia's anti-corruption protesters, bringing together 250 academics, professionals, and public figures — won almost 53% of the vote.
The coalition led by Aleksandar Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party secured less than 39%, according to preliminary results published on Oct. 26.
"The feeling is almost surreal," Dr. Mario Reljanovic, who ran on the Student List ballot, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The overwhelming support received by the Student List is a sign that we have managed to give the people of Serbia hope that a different society is possible, (a society) based on justice, the rule of law, solidarity, and the removal of party influence from the public sector," Dr. Reljanovic added.
The turnout, at almost 69%, was the highest since the fall of the Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. The students are projected to secure around 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, giving them a majority to form a government without needing coalition partners.
"The election result marks the end of a government that displayed authoritarian tendencies," Serbian political scientist Aleksandar Ivkovic told the Kyiv Independent.
"It ended much the same way as the regimes of Viktor Orban in Hungary (2026), Milo Djukanovic in Montenegro (2023), and Nikola Gruevski in North Macedonia (2022), which were similarly authoritarian, and were deeply entrenched in corruption and organized crime."
The result marks a potential turning point not only for Serbia's domestic politics but also for its relations with the European Union, Ukraine, Russia, and China.
The Student List has pledged to pursue EU-oriented reforms and keep Serbia on a European path, a commitment that could reshape the country's relations with Brussels and redefine its place in Europe.
Political outsiders take center stage
The Student List's electoral success was built on an unusually broad mobilization. Long marches from towns across Serbia culminated in a mass rally in Belgrade shortly before the vote. Queues formed outside polling stations on election day, while Serbian citizens abroad also turned out in large numbers.
Formally known as the "Students Are Winning" activist group, the opposition electoral list was formed over the past few months to turn the student protest movement into an electoral alternative without becoming a conventional political party.
"The Student List is a phenomenon that will be studied for decades to come," said Ivkovic. "It is a movement, not a political party designed to last."
The students avoided presenting a single dominant leader and instead emphasized civic participation, professional expertise, and accountability. The campaign was deliberately collective. Rather than putting forward a familiar party leader, the student movement assembled a list of 250 candidates from different professional backgrounds, including academics, doctors, lawyers, farmers, athletes, and cultural figures.
The first on the list is Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist and professor at the University of Novi Sad's Faculty of Medicine.
Srdanovic, who could become the new prime minister, became widely recognized in 2025 after publicly supporting student protests and university blockades, including demonstrations over the past two years. The candidates earned voters' trust primarily through their professional achievements rather than previous political experience. Around 170 people on the list hold doctoral degrees.
"While many come from academia, the list also includes farmers, lawyers, journalists, teachers, and cultural workers, reflecting the movement's emphasis on expertise and diversity of backgrounds," says Dr. Reljanovic, who holds a PhD in Law.
He expects that the same principle is expected to guide ministerial appointments.
"Given that ministerial portfolios have until now been treated and distributed as political party spoils, this represents a different approach to forming a government, one in which professionals with relevant expertise will predominate."
The Student List's program centers on restoring the rule of law, freeing the judiciary and media from political influence, investigating corruption, reviewing public contracts, and improving education and healthcare. It has also promised to direct money recovered from illegal enrichment towards economic development and public services.
"The purpose of the Student List will be fulfilled once it achieves the student movement's key demands — freeing institutions from political influence, holding those responsible for the Novi Sad canopy collapse and similar scandals to account, and improving media freedom and electoral conditions," Ivkovic added.
Ivkovic believes that once the goals set by the Student List are met, Serbia's political landscape is likely to reorganize.
"Many established parties may not survive in their current form, but Serbia will quickly return to a system where old and new parties will compete in a conventional, multiparty system."
read also
What's next for Serbia?
The immediate task for the Student List is to form a government and begin implementing its 11-point program of institutional transition, which will require decisions on the judiciary, public administration, media regulation, and the security sector.
The movement will also have to decide how to approach Serbia's relationship with the European Union. Its victory has been welcomed by European leaders, who have signaled that the EU is prepared to support democratic reforms and Serbia's European future.
"I do not expect radical foreign-policy shifts, but I expect a significant change in relations between Serbia and the European Union," Marko Todorovic, senior researcher at Belgrade-based think tank Center for European Policy (CEP), told Kyiv Independent.
"Above all, I expect an end to anti-European rhetoric and the creation of space for more objective information for citizens about the EU and the benefits of European integration," he added.
Serbia, an EU candidate country since 2012, has faced mounting criticism from Brussels over stalled reforms and remains one of the few European countries that has refused to join Western sanctions against Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"I do not expect sudden breaks in relations with either Russia or China, but I expect both countries to lose their current symbolic significance in Serbia's foreign policy," Todorovic added.
Over the last 14 years, Serbia remained an EU candidate country while preserving close relations with Russia, particularly in energy, and deepening economic ties with China. Belgrade condemned violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity at the United Nations but refused to join Western sanctions against Moscow.
Serbia also remains one of Europe's few remaining buyers of Russian natural gas, underscoring a dependence that leaves Moscow supplying about 80% of its total gas imports. Therefore, the question of sanctions against Russia is likely to remain one of the most sensitive tests for the new government.
As he conceded, Vucic suggested that a change of government could lead to sanctions being introduced against Moscow by March or April. However, Todorovic cautions against treating that possibility as an imminent policy shift.
"For now, there are no indications that sanctions against Russia will be introduced within such a short period. On the contrary, the student movement stated during the campaign that it opposed their introduction," he added.
A more democratic Serbia could offer Ukraine a more predictable partner.
"Serbia will certainly remain consistent in supporting Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, with the expectation that humanitarian aid and other forms of bilateral cooperation with Ukraine will continue," Todorovic added.
End of a decade of centralized power
Vucic's defeat marks the end of an era in which Serbia's president sought to maintain close ties with both Brussels and Moscow while consolidating political power at home.
His Serbian Progressive Party came to power in 2012, and Vucic served as prime minister from 2014 to 2017 before becoming president.
During that period, the government promoted infrastructure projects, attracted foreign investment, and presided over economic growth. At the same time, critics accused it of weakening democratic institutions, exerting pressure on independent media, and allowing political influence to permeate state institutions.
Several controversies came to define the period, while the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy became the most consequential crisis of Vucic's rule. Protesters argued that the tragedy exposed systemic failures in public oversight and government responsibility. The authorities rejected many of their political accusations, while investigations and legal proceedings continued.
The Student List has promised to investigate corruption, strengthen independent institutions, and redirect public resources towards citizens. Delivering on those promises will require not only political will but also the ability to govern a diverse coalition and overcome resistance within the existing state apparatus.
"There is enormous excitement at the prospect of having the opportunity to implement a concrete and detailed program to rebuild institutions, the economy, culture, and science, all of which have been undermined," Dr. Reljanovic said.
"We must use the mandate we receive to lay the foundations for a different way of running the country, so that politics is no longer synonymous with crime and corruption, and so that a cult of personality and a subservient relationship between citizens and those in power can never exist again."

Victor Osimhen scored twice in the first half on Monday as Galatasaray defeated cross-town archrivals Fenerbahce 2-1 in round nine of the Turkish Super Lig.
The Nigerian striker struck in the 29th and 44th minutes at RAMS Park in Istanbul, while Irfan Can Kahveci pulled one back for the visitors with an acrobatic effort in the second half.
Galatasaray made a promising start, with Baris Alper Yilmaz forcing Fenerbahce goalkeeper Ederson into a save from a tight angle in the 15th minute.
Fenerbahce came close to taking the lead in the 26th minute when Davinson Sanchez's attempted clearance from N'Golo Kante's cross struck the post.

Ederson prevented the Nigerian from doubling his tally in the 38th minute, diving to push his low effort from a tight angle out for a corner.
However, Osimhen struck again in the 44th minute, heading home after redirecting Sanchez's powerful first-time effort following a long throw-in by Ismail Jakobs.
Galatasaray dominated the opening half, registering 11 shots, including six on target, while Fenerbahce failed to produce a single attempt before the break.
The hosts continued to threaten after halftime, with Jakobs hitting the crossbar with a header in the 55th minute following Roland Sallai's cross.
Fenerbahce, however, pulled one back in the 62nd minute when Irfan Can Kahveci controlled Oguz Aydin's pass and scored with an acrobatic bicycle kick despite goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir getting a hand to the ball.
The visitors pushed for an equalizer in the closing stages, but Milan Skriniar's header was cleared near the goal line in the 90th minute.
Galatasaray substitute Leroy Sane then forced Ederson into another save in stoppage time as the hosts held on to secure all three points.
The victory lifted Galatasaray back to the top of the Turkish Super Lig standings with 22 points after nine matches, while Fenerbahce dropped to fifth place with 16 points.

EU mobilizes $5.4B in military support for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:57:14 UTC
05:57:14 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The Council of the European Union on Monday adopted eight decisions mobilizing about €4.9 billion ($5.4 billion) in support for Ukraine under the European Peace Facility (EPF).
The decisions provide €4.7 billion ($5.2 billion) to partially reimburse member states for military aid already delivered to Ukraine and an additional €230 million for the EU Military Assistance Mission in Support of Ukraine, known as EUMAM Ukraine, the council said in a statement.
The package marks a major step toward implementing an agreement among member states to mobilize €6.6 billion under the facility. That agreement also includes €1 billion in new military aid and further support for the training mission in 2027.
According to the council, the latest decisions bring overall support for Ukraine under the EPF to €10.8 billion, including €9.9 billion for military aid reimbursements and €950 million for military training.
Amid Ukraine’s ongoing war with Russia, which began in February 2022, the decisions reaffirm the bloc’s “continued firm and unwavering support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders,” the statement said.
The EU has also channeled €3.5 billion in extraordinary revenues generated by immobilized Russian assets through the facility to meet Ukraine’s ammunition, air defense, and drone needs.
Of that funding, more than €1.5 billion worth of military equipment was procured directly from Ukraine’s defense industry.
Established in March 2021, the EPF finances actions under the EU’s common foreign and security policy to prevent conflicts, preserve peace and strengthen international security, including military and defense assistance to partner countries.

UN sounds the alarm over Israel's West Bank military operation
October 26, 2026
The Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron was met with sharp criticism from the head of the UN as well as the UN's human rights commissioner in comments made on Monday.
The criticism comes after an Israeli military operation was launched in the occupied West Bank in response to a shootout on Friday that left two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen dead. Three more Israeli soldiers were also injured.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the military to demolish buildings in the West Bank city of Hebron and to close off the West Bank. It came just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday.
What did the UN say about Israeli operation in the West Bank?
The United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that "settlements are expanding, evictions are unrelenting with Palestinians driven from their lands," in a post on X.
"We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment, with the spectre of ethnic cleaning looming ever larger," he wrote.
The UN Human Rights High Commissioner Volker Türk also issued a statement condemning Israeli actions, saying the "aggressive operation" has resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely."
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing," he said.
A UN report, also released on Monday, that accuses Israel of committing war crimes in the West Bank, was rejected by the Israeli Foreign Ministry as "propaganda."
The ministry said that the findings were "not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."
What is the Israeli operation in the West Bank?
Israeli troops entered the Deir Baha neighborhood, where the assailants lived, and ordered residents to pack up and leave.
The Hebron municipality said that more than 3,000 people, including 200 babies, were ordered to leave.
The Israeli military said at the weekend that its troops were carrying out precise, targeted and thorough searches to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure and locate weapons, alongside questioning suspects" in Hebron.
The military said the operation was expected to continue "for several days" and would focus on Deir Baha.
The largescale response to the firefight in the West Bank comes in the run-up to elections in Israel on Tuesday that could bring an end to Netanyahu's premiership.
Netanyahu has frequently painted himself as the only person who can keep Israel safe but his opponents have accused him of lacking a plan.

Anthropic has taken the wraps off its US initial public offering (IPO) filing, bringing the Claude maker a step closer to a landmark debut that is set to test investor appetite for the rapidly growing AI industry.
The San Francisco-based developer behind AI chatbot Claude has now set the stage for one of the largest market debuts in history.
The company expects to target a market valuation between $1.5 trillion and $1.75 trillion, according to its regulatory filing.
The nearly 240,000-word prospectus showed that the firm recently told backers its third-quarter revenue surged nearly 50% from the previous quarter to $16.8 billion, reaching adjusted profitability.
The listing would be one of the largest debuts ever attempted, potentially reshaping benchmark indexes, investor flows, and the broader narrative driving US equities.
"A successful IPO from Anthropic could crack open or slam shut the IPO market, even well into 2027," said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, a provider of IPO-focused research and ETFs.
Multi-class corporate governance
Anthropic reported a net loss of $81 billion in the first half of the year, driven primarily by more than $72 billion in charges related to changes in the valuation of convertible notes.
The remainder of the losses was largely tied to nearly $9 billion spent on computing power and cloud infrastructure, while the firm outlined plans to commit close to $800 billion toward computing capacity over the next decade.
Investment bank Goldman Sachs secured the lead advisory role for the public offering alongside Morgan Stanley.
The filing also detailed a multi-class corporate governance structure with five distinct share tiers.
Under the proposed framework, Anthropic's seven founders will retain 50.1% of total voting power through Class F shares, while its Long-Term Benefit Trust will hold Class T shares that let it appoint the majority of the board of directors.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former researchers and executives from OpenAI, including Chief Executive Dario Amodei.
The listing is scheduled for after the US midterm elections in November but before the Thanksgiving holiday.

US court rules daughter of Trump critic James Comey was illegally fired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:55:37 UTC
05:55:37 KST

US court rules daughter of Trump critic James Comey was illegally fired
Maurene Comey had argued that she was fired because her father, former FBI chief James Comey, was a target of Trump’s ire.
A United States judge has ruled that former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey was illegally fired by the administration of President Donald Trump.
US District Judge Jesse Furman said on Monday that the Trump administration had overstepped the boundaries of executive authority when it fired so-called “inferior officers” without cause.
He rejected the administration’s position that the president had the power to undertake such firings, regardless of the protections implemented by Congress.
“To accept defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation’s constitutional system,” Furman wrote.
He also dismissed the idea that federal prosecutors like Comey are an extension of the president’s “conclusive and preclusive” powers.
“Defendants invented a new and expansive theory of executive power,” Furman wrote of the Trump administration. “They have also utilised that theory to remove other Executive Branch employees who have long held protections from removal.”
The ruling is a setback for the Trump administration, which has sought to fire federal employees seen as out of step with the president’s priorities.
Critics have also accused Trump of seeking retribution against perceived enemies. Comey is the daughter of former government official James Comey, who led the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) from 2013 to 2017.
He was fired during Trump’s first term and has since become one of the Republican leader’s most visible critics.
Maurene Comey’s legal team had argued that her position was terminated because of Trump’s antipathy towards her father.
In Monday’s decision, Furman granted her request for back pay from the date of her firing on July 16, 2025, through December. He also said she is entitled to “retroactive reinstatement” for that time period.
Maurene Comey had served as an assistant US attorney for the Department of Justice since 2015, based in Manhattan.
She had brought cases against such high-profile figures as convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his associate Ghislaine Maxwell and music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs.
In her lawsuit, Comey alleged that her firing had violated federal laws prohibiting the termination of civil servants for political reasons.
She also pointed to the separation of powers under the US Constitution, which allows Congress to pass regulations governing federal employees, so long as they do not interfere with the president’s authority.
The Department of Justice, under Trump, has countered that the president has wide latitude to fire federal employees without cause.
In response to Monday’s ruling, the administration has said it “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course”.
Since returning to office for a second term, Trump has sought to reduce the size of the federal government and remove prosecutors and investigators involved in cases he disagrees with.
He has also pushed the Justice Department to prosecute several of his critics, including James Comey.
In a social media post on September 20, 2025, Trump called on then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to pursue charges against James Comey and several others.
“There is a GREAT CASE, and many lawyers, and legal pundits, say so,” Trump wrote.
“We can’t delay any longer, it’s killing our reputation and credibility. They impeached me twice, and indicted me (5 times!), OVER NOTHING. JUSTICE MUST BE SERVED, NOW!!!”
James Comey was fired when the FBI was investigating potential links between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. That investigation was a frequent subject of Trump’s anger.
Shortly after the September 2025 post, the Department of Justice charged Comey with lying to Congress. A judge dismissed the case in November after finding the prosecutor who brought the charges, Lindsey Halligan, had been unlawfully appointed.
In April, James Comey was charged again in a separate case accusing him of threatening Trump by sharing an image of seashells on social media.
The seashells were arranged to form the numbers “86 47”. The term “86” is used in the restaurant industry in the US to refer to throwing someone out of a bar, but the Trump administration argued that it is a threat associated with organised crime.
The “47”, it added, was a reference to Trump, the 47th president.
The ex-FBI chief has denounced the case as an example of political persecution under Trump.

The Defense Minister called on Germany, Britain, France, Poland and Italy to transfer 10% of their stocks of interceptor missiles. Ukraine is also asking for man-portable air-defense systems and funding for the joint production of drones.
Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara addressed representatives of the defense ministries of the E5 countries: Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Poland, and Italy. The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine reported this, UNN writes.
The first critical priority is air defense. Ukraine already has contracts for the future delivery of interceptor missiles and is offering partners an exchange: to transfer some missiles from their existing stocks now in exchange for deliveries that are to reach Ukraine later

Man-portable air-defense systems are equally critically needed to counter jet-powered drones. Ukraine is counting on financing for new procurements and on the transfer of systems from partners' existing stocks.
The second priority is unmanned systems. Ukrainian manufacturers can double drone production in 2027. Timely funding is needed for this.
We propose not simply increasing procurement, but scaling up the joint production of Ukrainian drones in other countries. This will make it possible to increase production and provide Ukraine with the drones it needs. In addition, it will strengthen the defense capabilities of our partners
The minister stressed that Ukraine seeks a just and lasting peace. Achieving peace requires strength, a readiness to defend oneself, and decisions made in a timely manner. The task is to ensure that Ukraine has the necessary weapons when they are needed.

30 Kilometers With a Wounded Soldier: CODE 9.2 Conducted Two Air Evacuations Using the StarGate Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:49:26 UTC
05:49:26 KST

Over the course of a week, the CODE 9.2 regiment carried out two air evacuations of the wounded from the battlefield using the StarGate drone — these are the second and third known instances of such an evacuation in the world.
The regiment told Militarnyi that ground transport could not reach the positions where the wounded were located.
They evacuated 25-year-old Yevhen, call sign Izium, and 24-year-old Artem, call sign Kolobok.
Both soldiers had suffered severe injuries to their limbs and were stationed in the gray zone, approximately five kilometers from the state border with Russia.
Air evacuation remained the only available way to transport them to medical personnel.
The SkyFall team — the developer and manufacturer of StarGate drones — also joined in preparing for the operation.
Once the operation began, heavy Vampire strike drones were used to engage enemy positions.
During one of the missions, the StarGate drone traveled nearly 30 km one way to the soldier’s position and the same distance back, this time with the wounded soldier on board.
In the area of operations, the enemy actively employed electronic warfare measures in an attempt to completely jam the GPS signal.
Despite this, thanks to its onboard AI-based navigation system and the pilots’ skill, the drone was able to continue flying without satellite navigation and successfully complete the evacuation mission.
“Going forward, we plan to make changes to our regiment’s organizational structure and establish a separate medical aviation unit within the medical company. It will specialize specifically in evacuating the wounded from the battlefield by air,” emphasized Regiment Commander Oleksandr Nastenko, call sign Flint.
Previously, soldiers from the 92nd Separate Mechanized Brigade and the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade for the first time evacuated a wounded soldier using a hexacopter.
StarGate is Ukraine’s first specialized unmanned aerial platform for evacuating the wounded from the battlefield (CASEVAC), developed by the technology and defense company SkyFall.
It was created at the request of the military for situations where ground transport cannot reach the wounded or where its use is too dangerous.
The drone can carry up to 150 kg of payload and reach speeds of up to 105 km/h.
The evacuation module is based on certified medical stretchers.
Onboard artificial intelligence, navigation, and redundant communication systems allow the mission to continue even if the GPS signal is jammed or communication is lost.

Why Africa needs Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:48:42 UTC
05:48:42 KST

Why Africa needs Russia
There were times, in the mid-to-late 20th century, when the Soviet Union was deeply engaged with Africa. It not only welcomed decolonization but actively promoted it and it supported national liberation movements from Algeria to Angola and from Guinea-Bissau to Zimbabwe. It assisted newly independent nations economically, helping them build factories, hospitals, and schools. A number of African countries became Moscow’s political allies and received arms and advisers to strengthen their security.
Having long since recovered from the collapse of the USSR, today’s Russia is again turning its attention to the African continent. Both Africa and Russia, however, are very different from what they were sixty or seventy years ago. Russia’s interest in Africa is largely an expression of its comeback as a world power. It also reflects Moscow’s recognition of African countries’ rapid economic and demographic growth, and their potential as an important component of the 21st-century multipolar world order, which encompasses not just states but civilizations.
Russia, however, is not looking to impose an ideology on its partners because it has no ideology to export in the first place. Nor does it go to Africa primarily in search of natural resources, which it possesses in abundance within its own borders. Russia doesn’t need military bases in Africa as part of its grand strategy, which remains firmly focused on its own neighborhood in Eurasia. Rather, it sees Africa as part of what it calls the Global Majority, the part of the world where it has partners with whom to cooperate, as opposed to the West, which has shut itself off from Russia.
What Russia has to offer could be of considerable interest to Africans, given Russia is among the world’s major producers of energy and food. Over the decades, it’s built a reputation as a reliable supplier of both, and neither global energy nor food security can be assured without Russia. Disruptions in these markets are the result of Western sanctions and other attempts to undermine Russia’s strength. One of Moscow’s major projects is the North-South Transport Corridor, which would link Russia, the world’s fourth-largest economy in purchasing power parity (PPP) terms, with India, the third-largest, via Iran. Once fully operational, this corridor would also provide Russia with a gateway to East Africa.
Russia has already established itself as a security provider for African countries facing serious challenges. Under the banner of the Africa Corps, Russian military advisers and specialists are working in several West African countries belonging to the Alliance of Sahel States (Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso), as well as in the Central African Republic. They have managed to thwart a number of large-scale coup attempts and military offensives masterminded and supported from abroad. Such security assistance is essential to upholding the sovereignty of nations that have requested it.
Russia, of course, is much more than a military power. Among other things, it is a leader in digitalization. Moscow is one of the world’s most advanced capitals in this field. Russia is ready to share its expertise in establishing and improving electronic government services. Since Soviet times, Russian scientists have conducted pioneering research into deadly viruses and vaccines to combat them. A vaccine against Ebola was developed in 2019 by the Russian research institute Vector, located in Siberia, while the Sputnik V vaccine, developed against COVID-19, proved highly effective in fighting the pandemic.
In 1960, Peoples’ Friendship University was founded in Moscow for international students. The following year, it was named after Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the independent Congo (formerly Belgian Congo). At present, some 35,000 young Africans study at Russian universities, mostly majoring in medicine, energy, and engineering – fields in which Russian universities have historically been particularly strong.
To date, three African countries – South Africa, Egypt, and Ethiopia – are full members of the 10-member BRICS grouping. This format offers a novel, non-hierarchical and genuinely consensus-based approach to addressing economic, financial, environmental, educational, and other global issues. The BRICS way of doing business supports sovereignty and rejects diktat. Russia, which helped initiate the formation of BRICS just over two decades ago, works to ensure that the group remains true to its founding principles.
Russia has never been a colonial power in Africa and has never attempted to plunder its resources. It regards Africans as partners and African civilization as an equal in the emerging world order. This week’s Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow will bring the two even closer.

The issue was that foreign charitable contributions were deliberately presented as investments and commercial payments to circumvent Indian regulations governing foreign funding of news organisations. “The service agreement was a device for regular foreign funding rather than a genuine commercial arrangement,” a senior official said.“An email dated Aug 21, 2017, from the portal’s former HR head Amit Chakraborty explicitly discussed changing NewsClick’s company documents to obtain foreign investment without permission from the ministry of information and broadcasting. The email stated: The purpose of the same is that we want foreign investment without the permission of the ministry of information,” according to the agency.Sources said ED had relied on statement of the portal’s Prashanth Radhakrishnan that JEF owned peoplesdispatch.org only from April 2021 and NewsClick owned it previously. It was NewsClick’s team that determined content quality and terms, supporting its contention that JEF’s payments were not ordinary arm’s length purchases.
Sources said NewsClick is also being investigated for Tricontinental and other international funding connections, keeping in mind a Jan 2018 email discussing how Tricontinental could begin operations in India through a private limited company receiving US investment, rather than immediately seeking approval to receive foreign grants as a non-profit.“This has acquired wider relevance following recent Fox News reports concerning tech entrepreneur Neville Roy Singham, Tricontinental and their alleged links to international protest movements, including demonstrations in Paris,” an official said.

Cuba to present UN resolution demanding end to US embargo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:41:00 UTC
05:41:00 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Cuba will present a resolution to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday and Wednesday demanding an end to the decades-long US economic embargo, Cuban radio station Radio Angulo reported Monday.
"They are trying to change historical positions at gunpoint," Cuban UN Ambassador Ernesto Soberon said, accusing Washington of pressuring countries ahead of the vote, Radio Angulo reported.
The annual vote will mark the 34th time Havana has brought the resolution before the UN General Assembly since 1992.
The diplomat said the US State Department, its UN mission and American embassies around the world had launched efforts to weaken traditional support for the Cuban resolution.
Soberon said the vote comes amid increased US pressure on Cuba, including energy restrictions and sanctions targeting third countries.
He also cited prolonged power outages and difficulties accessing medicines, food and drinking water as consequences of the embargo.
The resolution, titled "Necessity of Ending the Economic, Commercial and Financial Blockade Imposed by the United States of America against Cuba," calls for the removal of US restrictions on the island.
The resolution is nonbinding, meaning the UN General Assembly cannot compel Washington to lift the embargo, which remains under US jurisdiction.
The United States has maintained the embargo against Cuba for more than six decades. It was formally established in February 1962 under then-President John F. Kennedy.
The resolution received 165 votes in favor, seven against and 12 abstentions at last year's UN General Assembly session, according to official figures.
The latest vote comes as Cuba faces a severe economic crisis marked by fuel shortages, power outages and difficulties accessing essential goods.

The administrations of the ports of Houston, Beaumont, and Corpus Christi in Texas, as well as the ports of New York and New Jersey, also received the letter.
The letter urges the banks and port authorities not to facilitate the "purchase, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing, or distribution" of Russian diesel fuel in the United States.
First tanker carrying Russian diesel has set off for the US - Reuters23.10.26, 11:43 • 5668 views
In addition, the recipients are asked not to facilitate any operations involving the supply of Russian diesel to other markets under the recent easing of sanctions. Citing expectations of increased congressional oversight, the lawmakers are demanding the preservation of a broad range of documents and communications related to "proposed or actually completed" transactions. These include contracts, transportation and shipping documents, vessel records, correspondence with suppliers, intermediaries, and US government officials.
The lawmakers want confirmation by Wednesday that the documents have been preserved, as well as information about any potential or actual transactions involving Russian diesel fuel.
