What Vucic’s defeat means for Serbia’s foreign policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:38:40 UTC
05:38:40 KST

What Vucic’s defeat means for Serbia’s foreign policy
Those expecting Belgrade to tilt towards the West may need patience while the new government deals with domestic issues.
Serbia has reached a watershed moment following 14 years of authoritarian rule by Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
Sunday’s election delivered a historic victory for the opposition Student List, ending the political dominance that Vucic and the SNS had exercised/enforced for 14 years.
As Belgrade prepares for a turbulent transition and the upcoming presidential elections in December, international observers and regional neighbours have been asking whether Vucic’s departure will prompt a shift in Serbia’s foreign policy.
However, while international analysts often anticipate a quick foreign policy pivot toward the West whenever an authoritarian regime falls, experts warn that internal consolidation will take immediate priority and any transformation will be gradual.
Domestic cleanup before regional reset
SNS’s defeat has brought a mixture of cautious optimism and uncertainty across the Western Balkans. Serbia’s relations with Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Kosovo have often been frayed by Vucic’s nationalistic rhetoric.
Aleksandar Popov, director of the Centre for Regionalism in Novi Sad in Serbia, told Al Jazeera that a rapid reset in regional relations was unlikely.
“These questions will not be on the agenda immediately,” he said, referring to relations with Serbia’s neighbours.
The new authorities will first have to tackle domestic problems, he said, including dealing with a system that has “captured all democratic institutions”, as well as problems in the judiciary, prosecution service, police and media sector.
“Tidying up at home” will take priority before “solving problems with the neighbours”, Popov said, despite noting that the outgoing regime had done everything possible to undermine regional relations.
While relations with Croatia are “not frozen” neither are they “the way they should … be between neighbours”, being marked by frequent sharp words.
Amid recent mass protests in Serbia, Vucic accused Zagreb of organising a “colour revolution”.
In addition, “relations with Montenegro are disrupted and issues with Bosnia and Herzegovina remain unresolved,” he said.
Stabilising the region
Croatia is the thorniest case, Popov suggested, noting that relations deteriorated as the SNS clashed with Croatia’s ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), which stems from a similar nationalist-populist stable.
“Zagreb would fire a poisoned arrow at Serbia and that gave Belgrade an argument to retaliate,” he said, describing a system that “functioned on the production of internal and external enemies”.
Meanwhile, behind the public hostility, lay a quiet convergence on Bosnia and Herzegovina, he argued, with Belgrade backing Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik and Zagreb favouring a third entity.
He expressed hope that a new government in Serbia led by experts and civic leaders, would work towards stabilising the region and revive Serbia’s hopes of joining the European Union.
“The previous government sabotaged EU integration and the EU will not accept a country without good neighbourly relations. The new government’s task will be to repair those damaged ties,” Popov said.
Russia and Ukraine
Beyond the immediate neighbourhood, global powers are closely watching Belgrade.
Under Vucic, Serbia maintained a delicate balancing act, refusing to impose sanctions on Russia despite heavy pressure from the EU, while simultaneously allowing ammunition to flow indirectly to Ukraine.
Of all elements of Serbian public policy, foreign policy will transform the least under the forthcoming governmental changes, Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy at King’s College London, predicted to Al Jazeera.
“Many international and domestic structures that shape Serbian foreign policy will remain in place,” he said, adding that Moscow never fully trusted Vucic, but viewed him instead as “the devil they knew”.
Russian influence will take a blow, with the end of uncritical glorification of Moscow in Vucic-controlled tabloids and media and intelligence cooperation to be downgraded, he said, but the new government is unlikely to adopt a hawkish stance overnight.
Serbian interests can continue to be served by ties with Russia, he asserted. “The country still needs preferential gas prices, the Kosovo dispute remains unresolved and parts of the public remain disillusioned with the West.”
“The new Serbian government will not see value in joining EU sanctions or adopting a hawkish stance toward Moscow,” Vuksanovic continued.
“Regarding Ukraine, Serbia will maintain its policy of not recognising the annexation of Crimea and Donbas. However, there is a question mark over ammunition deliveries, as the opposition viewed Vucic’s weapons sales to Kyiv as a cynical ploy to buy Western tolerance for his domestic rule.”
Ties with Israel
Another critical dimension of Serbia’s external relations is its close relationship with Israel. Under Vucic, Serbia established a strong partnership with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, marked by arms trade and technology exchanges.
Bosko Jaksic, a foreign policy analyst, told Al Jazeera that while ties will not be severed, recent controversial agreements will face scrutiny.
“The new government has no reason to abandon cooperation with Israel, but it will certainly re-examine newly concluded contracts – primarily those concerning Serbian ammunition exports to Israel and Israeli surveillance equipment exports to Serbia,” Jaksic said.
The analyst also noted that Netanyahu’s government has lost another “authoritarian, nationalist ally” in Europe after Viktor Orban’s removal in Hungary earlier this year. However, Serbia’s future stance will also depend on political developments in Jerusalem.
“How Israel positions itself toward the new authorities in Belgrade depends largely on the outcome of Israel’s own elections,” Jaksic added.
Multiple chairs
Looking at the broader geopolitical alignment, he emphasised that Serbia’s foreign policy will inevitably undergo a review.
He suggested that “the policy of ‘sitting on multiple chairs,’ which brought Serbia more harm than good, will certainly be re-evaluated”, and that it is realistic to expect Belgrade to strengthen ties with the EU.
But as Serbia enters a new political era, the international community should expect a period of intense internal reform rather than sudden geopolitical realignments, all of the analysts agree.

Iraq and Jordan signed nine cooperation documents Monday covering education, the environment, culture, and economic affairs, according to the Iraqi prime minister’s office.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and his Jordanian counterpart Jafar Hassan presided over the signing ceremony in the Jordanian capital Amman, the office said in a statement.
The documents included memorandums of understanding on competition and preventing monopolies, plus environmental protection, consumer protection, and documents and archives.

Hassan reaffirmed Jordan’s commitment to continued cooperation and coordination with Iraq to advance integration across various sectors, according to the Iraqi statement.

====================================================================================================

Why Indian women work where they 'can', not always where they 'want'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:35:03 UTC
05:35:03 KST

India’s first district-level jobs data shows women work most where they have the least choice, and least where the jobs on offer don’t fit their lives. TOI went to six districts at the extremes
Two job markets. Share of people aged 15+ working or looking for work, lowest and highest district, and the typical district (median)
Pick any district in India. At least 59 of every 100 men there are working or looking for work. In the typical district, it is 79.
For women, it depends on the address: 82 in 100 in Gujarat's tribal belt, fewer than 10 in North East Delhi.
In 396 of the 584 districts, fewer than half of women are in the job market.
For men, there is no such district.
Nowhere do women match men. The closest is Mandi in Himachal Pradesh: 69.6% of women against 74.2% of men.
We sent reporters to six districts at the two ends of three measures: how many women are in the job market, how many young women are neither working nor studying, and whether young women are doing better than women overall.
The six districts
Three questions, two ends of each
Profiled districts come from the top and bottom of each ranking; rankings exclude Delhi. Teal marks the higher-performing end, orange the lower. Tap a district to jump to its story.
Map shows India's official boundaries (DataMeet India, CC BY 4.0). Not to scale. Gujarat and Mizoram are survey district groups and are marked at their centre.
Part 1
Women in the job market
Share of women aged 15+ who are working or looking for work
82.1%Gujarat's tribal beltHighest in India
vs
10.0%Yamunanagar, HaryanaLowest outside Delhi
In the six tribal districts of eastern Gujarat, 82 of every 100 women aged 15 and above are working or looking for work. No district in India scores higher.
In Haryana's Yamunanagar, it is 10. Only North East Delhi, at 9.8, is lower.
The gap is widest in the villages: 86.5% of rural women in the Gujarat belt are in the job market, against 7.2% in rural Yamunanagar.
In the Gujarat belt's towns, the figure falls to 37.1%.
Now count only women who were working or seeking work in the week before the survey. The Gujarat figure drops from 82.1% to 57.7%.
A lot of this work comes and goes with the farming season.
Wearing her pink uniform, Anita Tadvi takes her e-rickshaw to the Statue of Unity in Ektanagar every morning. As tourists begin arriving at the world’s tallest statue in Narmada district, the 25-year-old’s day gathers pace. She drives them around the premises as driver and guide, one of many in this tribal Gujarat belt east of Narmada who are reaping the benefits of tourist inflows since Sardar Patel’s iconic statue was inaugurated in 2018.
In India’s first district-level periodic labour force survey (PLFS) released in Sept, the Dahod-Narmada-Dang-Tapi-Chhota Udepur-Mahisagar belt recorded the country’s highest female labour force participation rate of 82.1%. The rural rate was even higher, at 86.5%, suggesting village economies are driving the standout number.
Across these districts, women are working because households need two earners, men migrate for work, farms and livestock require family labour, and govt schemes, NGOs and self-help groups have opened up small livelihood routes.
“Statue of Unity has brought many opportunities for women in our district. When I learnt about the requirement for e-rickshaw drivers three years ago, I discussed it with my husband and in-laws. They immediately agreed,” Tadvi said.
She took driving lessons, obtained a licence and joined a group of around 90 women who drive e-rickshaws at the monument.
Self-help groups that teach making everyday products such as soaps, bamboo items, bags and festive decorations have brought more informal jobs. Tourism has poured into this basket.
“Women in the tribal belt are productive and earn more than men. They not only work outside the house but also shoulder responsibilities at home, leaving them with hardly any free time,” said Vadodara-based entrepreneur Swati Bedekar.
Dinesh Patel, a farmer from Mahisagar district, said many women work as farm hands and can be hired from the labour market. “I need farm labourers regularly in my corn fields. I prefer to hire women as they are productive and dedicated. In our district, women easily find farm jobs,” Patel said.
But high participation does not automatically mean secure work.
Madhu Gayakwad, who is from Dang and heads the sociology department at VNS, said employment opportunities for women had increased but remained uneven and there is scope to do more to improve livelihoods. As PLFS shows, tribal Gujarat’s women are working. The next benchmark is to make this income sustainable enough to change their lives.
Close behind the men. Here, 89.8% of men and 82.1% of women are in the job market, a gap of 7.7 points. Only seven districts in India have a gap under 10 points.
2Yamunanagar, Haryana
Factories at every turn. Yet 9 in 10 women stay out
Jaskaran Singh
Alka Mehta lives in a district crowded with factories, but none of them holds much appeal for her. Yamunanagar’s plywood units, paper mills, sugar mills and manufacturing plants generate jobs across the district. But Mehta, a homemaker, sees much of that work as too physically demanding for women like her.
“Women cannot work there because the factories require hard and skilled work,” she said.
That disconnect between the jobs Yamunanagar offers and the work many local women are prepared to take up may help explain one of the starkest findings of the PLFS. Only 10% of women aged 15 and above in the district are working or looking for work — the lowest female labour force participation rate (LFPR) outside Delhi.
The problem isn’t a straightforward absence of work.
My husband earns well, so I do not need to work. I work at home and spend my time taking care of my children
Geeta Arora, homemaker, Yamunanagar
That divide is visible in the district’s brick kilns. Women account for around half the workforce there, said Attar Singh, an advocate who works on labour-related issues. But most of them are migrants from Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Assam.
The women who do enter paid work are usually concentrated elsewhere — in schools and colleges, govt departments, shops, businesses and other service-sector jobs.
Education is not the obvious missing link. Women made up about two-thirds of students in Yamunanagar’s general arts and science colleges in 2023-24.
And educated women instead looked towards govt jobs, education and private-sector employment, including IT, software and businesses, said Suman Bahmani, mayor of Yamunanagar-Jagadhri Municipal Corporation.
That preference narrows the field considerably in a district whose industrial economy is built heavily around manual and factory work.
Sangeeta Singhal, a local, said women were far more likely to work in “businesses, shops, schools, colleges and other service-sector activities” than take up labour-intensive jobs because of their physically demanding nature.
For many families, there is another reason women stay out of the labour market — they can afford to. Geeta Arora, a homemaker, explained her choice. “My husband earns well, so I do not need to work. I work at home and spend my time taking care of my children,” she said.
The jobs are there. But for many of Yamunanagar’s women, they are not jobs they see themselves doing.
Delhi does worse. Six of India's 10 lowest districts on this measure are in Delhi, and none of Delhi's districts reaches 19%. In rural Yamunanagar, the figure is 7.2%.
Part 2
Neither working nor studying
Share of young women (15–29) not in a job, education or training
2.8%*Chamba, Himachal PradeshAmong the lowest in India
vs
73.9%Kendrapara, OdishaHighest in India
In Odisha's Kendrapara, 74 of every 100 women aged 15–29 are not in a job, not in education and not in training. That is the highest share in India.
Among young men in the same district, the figure is 21.6%.
In Himachal's Chamba, the survey puts it at 2.8%: among the lowest anywhere, though the estimate rests on a small sample.
Chamba's young women are busy. 70.7% of its women are in the job market, much of it on family farms. In Kendrapara, 28.6%.
3Chamba, Himachal Pradesh
Busy, yes. But mostly on the family farm
Rohit Mullick
In Sadal panchayat in Chamba, nearly every girl now goes to school or college, says up-pradhan Pritam Singh. The problem begins after the degree.
“With no industries and government vacancies extremely rare, educated women are left with no viable choice other than returning to the fields to assist their families with manual agricultural work,” he said.
That gap between being counted as working and having a secure job helps explain one of the more striking results of the PLFS. Chamba has one of the country’s lowest female youth NEET rates — only 2.8% of women aged 15-29 are neither in employment, education nor training — alongside a high female labour force participation rate of 70.7%.
On the ground, much of that participation is tied to agriculture, often on family farms, in a district where formal employment is scarce.
“The predominance of agriculture in the local economy means that women’s participation, including work on family farms and allied activities, is equal to men’s,” said Kulbhushan Upmanyu, president of Himalaya Niti Abhiyan, a social action collective.
People work in the fields only because family members help for free
Kulbhushan Upmanyu, Himalaya Niti Abhiyan
But he cautioned against treating that participation as evidence of good employment. Mountain farming, he explained, often generates too little income to function as a viable livelihood. “People work in the fields only because family members help for free,” Upmanyu said. In some areas, he added, fields are being left uncultivated because farming no longer pays.
For younger women, education is the other half of the PLFS story.
Schools have become more accessible across the district, while ITIs, colleges and skill programmes have expanded. That keeps many girls and young women within education for longer and helps push down the NEET rate.
The difficulty comes in converting education into jobs. While formal job opportunities are limited in Chamba, tourism is concentrated in pockets such as Dalhousie, Bharmour and Pangi and remains seasonal.
But the more consequential transition is still ahead — turning education and labour-force participation into jobs that actually pay.
4Kendrapara, Odisha
3 in 4 young women here are neither in college nor a job
Diana Sahu
Gayatri Lenka should have been in college. Instead, she lends a helping hand to her mother at home at Kalapada village all day, washing, sweeping and fetching water in the morning, working in the kitchen in the evening. Her college books lie untouched.
Gayatri dropped out. “I wanted to study further but finances were a problem. This year, govt made education free for all, but I can’t go back to college. My mother now depends on me for household chores,” she said.
PLFS paints a dismal picture of the Odisha district when it comes to its young women, with 73.9% of those aged 15 to 29 not in employment, education or training.
Like Gayatri, poverty forces girls into unpaid household work. Some wait for marriage. And some may migrate for work, which does not show up in the local employment picture.
Nearly 30km away, in Pattamundai, 22-year-old Monalisa Lenka has been at home for more than a year after completing her graduation. She did not find any local skilling programme that could improve her employment prospects. “The only options here are tailoring or making mats,” she said.
Kendrapara does not have large industrial employers.
“Skill-training opportunities are available, but they are not equally accessible to girls across the district,” said Chittaranjan Das, principal of Kendrapara Autonomous College.
Labour rights activists pointed out there is temporary migration from coastal pockets of the district to other states, and so women who might be earning otherwise don’t reflect as doing so in the local data.
Not just the young. Among all women aged 15–59 in Kendrapara, 63.4% are neither working nor studying. In the typical district, the figure is 40.9%.
Part 3
A generation apart
Share neither working nor studying: young women (15–29) compared with all women of working age (15–59)
15.2%Young women, Mizoram outside Aizawlvs 47.2% of all women: 32 points lower
vs
63.7%Young women, Tenkasivs 38.7% of all women: 25 points higher, the widest such gap in India
In Mizoram outside Aizawl, 15.2% of young women are neither working nor studying. Across all women of working age, it is 47.2%.
The young are far more likely to be in classrooms or jobs.
In Tamil Nadu's Tenkasi, it runs the other way. 63.7% of young women are outside work and education, against 38.7% of all women. No district has a wider gap of this kind.
Each dot is a district. Above the line, young women are worse off than women overall. That is the case in 251 of 558 districts with reliable estimates.
In 66 districts, young women's rate is at least 10 points higher. 28 of them are in five southern states: Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Keralam.
5Mizoram, outside Aizawl
Study, work, then marriage. Maybe
HC Vanlalruata
In an earlier generation, girls in Mizoram often began working in agricultural fields as young as 13 and married early. Today, more young women are staying in education longer, pursuing training and finding jobs before marriage.
The PLFS shows a striking divide between age groups. Across Mizoram’s districts outside Aizawl, only 15.2% of women aged 15-29 are neither working, studying nor training, compared with 47.2% of women aged 15-59 — a 32-percentage-point gap, among the widest in the country.
Older women worked too — in cultivation, markets, homes and family businesses. What appears to be changing is the path some younger women are taking into adulthood, with greater emphasis on education and financial independence before marriage.
Kimkimi, an assistant professor at a college around 100km from Aizawl, offers a glimpse of how women’s timelines have changed. Now in her mid-40s and unmarried, she spends weekdays teaching and returns to her parents’ home on weekends, where much of her time goes into academic work and writing her dissertation. “You could say I’m married to my job,” she said.
Work opportunities have widened alongside education. Women are deeply embedded in Mizoram’s markets and small businesses. Educated young women are increasingly entering banks, financial institutions and private companies. And govt jobs remain highly sought after.
As women spend longer in education and enter marriage with incomes of their own, the older assumption that men will earn while women depend on them starts fading.
The shift is far from complete. Agriculture remains central in many parts of Mizoram, the state’s hilly terrain limits expansion, and the private job market remains small. But the PLFS figures show how differently younger women are engaged in work, education or training today.
6Tenkasi, Tamil Nadu
Mothers roll beedis. Their educated daughters wait for work
Ram Sundaram
For decades, beedi-rolling was a steady provider of jobs in Tenkasi. Today, it’s the likely architect of a puzzling picture PLFS has thrown up — 63.7% of women aged 15 to 29 in the district are not in employment, education or training. The figure falls to 38.7% when women aged 15 to 59 are counted, a 25-point gap.
Older women remain connected to work through agriculture, beedi-rolling, VB-G RAM G and home-based production. Their daughters are more likely to have pursued education and gone to college. But these educated young girls are less likely to find jobs that match their education in the district.
A district labour department officer said the software firm, Zoho, offers some opportunities, but openings in the private sector remain limited. Some data-entry firms pay about Rs 5,000 for shifts lasting 10 to 12 hours. This eventually forces young women to take low-paid jobs in garment stores, jewellery shops and photocopy centres. Home-based beedi-rolling is, meanwhile, offering half the jobs it was a decade ago.
But moving into salaried work is not simple. Travelling farther for better jobs is difficult. M Thangam, an All India Democratic Women’s Association functionary, said caste identities remain deeply rooted, with such divisions visible from school age. Some parents hesitate to let daughters work far from home, fearing relationships and marriages outside their caste, she said. This is where Tenkasi’s education story and its employment reality collide.
Some young women bridge this gap by taking small local jobs and returning home to help mothers with beedi work. This informalisation of the beedi industry could be another reason why young girls who may be working from home don’t show up in the job data. For younger women, however, neither farm work nor beedi-rolling has replaced the shortage of suitable salaried jobs. That is the gap PLFS points to.
Looking, not finding. Of Tenkasi's women who are in the job market, 10.6% are unemployed, four times the typical district's 2.7%.
For context
How women compare with men
In 160 districts, a larger share of men are in the job market than women in India’s best district
The lowest share of men in the job market anywhere is 59.2%, in Uttarakhand's hill districts. Women's share is below that in 508 of 584 districts. Only three districts — Gujarat's tribal belt, Hamirpur* (Himachal Pradesh) and Nabarangapur (Odisha) — have a women's figure as high as men's in the typical district (79.2%). And the highest figure for women anywhere, 82.1% in Gujarat's tribal belt, is lower than men's figure in 160 districts.
Share of men (15+) in the job market: number of districts at each level
In 270 districts, a larger share of young women are neither working nor studying than young men in India’s worst district
In the typical district, 40.1% of young women are neither working nor studying, about 5 times the rate for young men (7.6%). The highest figure for young men anywhere is 41.3%, in Odisha's Anugul. Young women's rate is higher than that in 270 districts, and higher than young men's own rate in 572 of the 581 districts with figures for both.
Share of young women (15–29) neither working nor studying: number of districts at each level. Higher is worse.
What the terms mean
Women in the job market
Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR): share of people aged 15+ who are working or seeking/available for work, by usual status (principal and subsidiary activity, 365-day reference period). "In the week before the survey" is the current weekly status (CWS) measure.
Neither working nor studying
NEET rate: share not in employment, education or training. Unpaid helpers in family farms and enterprises count as employed.
A generation apart
NEET rate for ages 15–29 compared with ages 15–59. The 15–59 group includes the 15–29 group, so the true gap between younger and older women is wider than the figures shown.
District
The survey's basic stratum. Some strata combine several districts, for example Dahod, Narmada, Dang, Tapi, Chhota Udepur and Mahisagar in Gujarat. 584 strata in 30 states and UTs. "Typical district" is the median.
Rankings
Profiled districts come from the top and bottom of each ranking; rankings exclude Delhi. Delhi's figures are mentioned in the text for comparison.
* Small-sample estimate
Relative standard error of 40% or more; treat with caution. Rankings marked "reliable estimates" leave these out. # marks strata with fewer than 250 households surveyed.
Source: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Periodic Labour Force Survey 2025, district-level key estimates (rural + urban). Photographs: TOI.

Canada-US trade stalemate set to outlast US midterms: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:34:48 UTC
05:34:48 KST

Merve Aydogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Canada and the US are not expected to reach a trade deal before next week’s American midterm elections, Canadian public broadcaster CBC News said on Monday.
Citing three unnamed sources, the report said Canadian government officials told industry groups in recent weeks that no agreement is anticipated before the Nov. 3 elections, adding that there is no substantial engagement between the two sides despite ongoing contact between officials.
The sources said the White House is fully focused on the campaign, with President Donald Trump spending much of his time at rallies as polls suggest his Republican Party could lose the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate.
Canada-US Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc later confirmed the position in CBC interview.
"We have continued to remain engaged with the United States. But we’re not going to rush into some particular circumstance and … agree to something that we don’t think is in Canada’s sovereign interest or economic interest," he said.
Brian Clow, a former deputy chief of staff to former-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, said optimism in some circles had rested on the trade war’s unpopularity with some American voters. "But that window appears to be entirely closed," he said.
In a post on his Truth Social platform in August, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts, and steel to 50% as of Jan. 1, 2027. LeBlanc said Washington has not taken any official step yet but described the threat as "obviously of concern."
Meanwhile, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer denied that Canada is being singled out, saying tariffs are "not focused on any one country," according to the CBC.

Israeli tourists accused of shoplifting in Indonesia forced to pay heavy fine to leave island
Unknown

05:34:47 KST

A group of about 20 Israeli women traveling in Indonesia was accused of shoplifting on the island of Gili Meno, prompting local authorities to search their belongings and threaten them with arrest after security camera footage allegedly showed one member of the group stealing merchandise.
The women, who were on an organized two-week trip, ultimately paid $3,000 to local shopkeepers to resolve the dispute and avoid further escalation, according to members of the group.
The incident occurred Friday as the tourists, accompanied by a local guide, visited shops on Gili Meno, one of three small islands off the coast of Lombok, northeast of Bali.
Several hours later, a German national who owns one of the stores accused the Israeli visitors of stealing rings, perfume and swimsuits. Other shopkeepers subsequently made similar allegations.
According to the women, the shopkeepers did not initially identify a specific suspect, instead accusing the entire "Israeli group" of theft.
The allegations quickly spread on social media, where shopkeepers posted security camera images of the tourists in a local Facebook group, publicly identifying them as suspected thieves.
"Thieves. If anyone sees this guest, please detain her," one post read. "The group is from Israel and the guide is a woman with a Balinese accent. They bought and took several items from our boutique. Please provide information."
'They treated us as a group, not as individuals'
The confrontation escalated when local law enforcement personnel and shopkeepers arrived at the hotel where the Israeli tourists were staying and began searching their bags.
The women demanded that authorities search only the belongings of the person allegedly shown stealing in the security footage, rather than treating the entire group as suspects.
Local officials refused, arguing that they could not rule out the possibility that the suspected thief had acted with others or passed stolen merchandise to fellow travelers.
"It was extremely unpleasant, and the worst part was that they treated us as a group rather than as individuals," one tourist said.
Another described the experience as humiliating.
"People stood on the sidelines filming us like a bunch of monkeys," she said. "It was humiliating beyond description."
According to the women, the searches uncovered only empty lipstick boxes.
Before the searches were completed, one shopkeeper offered to settle the matter in exchange for a payment ranging from $2,000 to $6,000.
The parties eventually agreed on $3,000, an amount the shopkeepers said would cover the losses from the alleged thefts.
"We had no choice. We were forced to pay," one woman said. "We understood that we had to get out of there and avoid getting the local guide into trouble."
Suspected tourist denies stealing
The woman accused of theft refused to contribute to the payment, insisting she had stolen nothing and was being subjected to what she described as a "lynching."
Other members of the group said the security camera footage clearly showed the alleged theft.
They warned the woman that her actions could trigger a diplomatic incident, but said she continued denying the allegations and refused to accept responsibility.
In a response to ynet, the accused tourist rejected the claims.
"It's all nonsense. I didn't take anything. It's just a conspiracy," she said. "The shop owner wanted to make money, and the proof is that they turned our bags upside down and found nothing."
Israeli Embassy intervenes as tourists fear arrest
As the confrontation unfolded, a representative of the Israeli Embassy in Singapore, which handles Israeli diplomatic matters involving Indonesia, maintained contact with the group and advised the women on how to proceed.
The embassy representative also recommended that the woman suspected of theft remain inside the hotel.
The tourists said they feared that all of them could be arrested, regardless of whether they had been involved in the alleged shoplifting.
"It was a traumatic incident," members of the group said. "All we wanted was to get off that island and take the ferry to Bali."
The confrontation began Friday, and the women left Gili Meno by ferry for Bali on Saturday evening. They returned to Israel the following day.
The tourists said they were relieved that the incident occurred near the end of their two-week trip.
Despite the confrontation, they emphasized that they had not experienced hostility because of their Israeli nationality during the rest of their visit.
Gili Meno is the smallest and quietest of Indonesia's three Gili Islands, known for its secluded beaches and popularity among couples seeking a peaceful tropical getaway.
The island lies off Lombok's northwestern coast, northeast of Bali, and attracts visitors looking for a quieter alternative to the region's busier tourist destinations.

====================================================================================================

Big donors, bigger stakes: Money shapes US midterm races
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:32:24 UTC
05:32:24 KST

In the US, winning an election is a multibillion-dollar undertaking.
Few countries spend on elections at the scale of the US, where the 2024 federal cycle cost nearly $16 billion. Even in a midterm year, when the presidency is not on the ballot, candidates, parties, billionaires, corporations and interest groups are pouring record sums into contests that will determine control of Congress.
By the end of June, congressional candidates had spent more than $2 billion, 16% above the same point in the 2022 midterms.
Candidates' committees raise money to hire staff, organize voters and buy advertising. Individuals can contribute up to $3,500 per election to a federal candidate, while qualifying multicandidate political action committees, or PACs, can give $5,000.
Corporations and unions cannot contribute treasury funds directly to federal candidates. Outside spending, however, operates under different rules. Super PACs cannot donate directly to candidates or coordinate their spending with campaigns, but they can accept unlimited sums from individuals, corporations and unions to support or oppose candidates.
The framework largely dates to 2010, when the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision lifted restrictions on independent corporate and union spending, followed by an appeals court ruling that cleared the way for unlimited contributions to groups spending independently.
Political parties can contribute directly to candidates and spend on their behalf, while some nonprofits can finance political activity without disclosing all their donors, contributing to what campaign-finance advocates call "dark money."
The result is that candidates may control only a portion of the money spent to influence their races.
Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 24 show $3.1 billion in independent spending on House and Senate races, including $2.3 billion in the general election.
Political advertising across federal, state and local contests had surpassed $10 billion by mid-October. AdImpact projects a record $11.6 billion, exceeding both the $8.9 billion spent during the 2022 midterms and $11.2 billion in the 2024 presidential cycle.
Senate Leadership Fund had reported about $292 million in independent expenditures by late October, followed by Democratic-aligned WinSenate at $221 million and Republican-aligned No Going Back PAC at $220 million.
The money is concentrated among donors, too. The Washington Post found the 50 largest donor sources had supplied $2.77 billion by Oct. 23. Elon Musk led individual donors with $446 million, followed by Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein with $150 million and Jeff and Janine Yass with $110 million.
Texas illustrates how outside spending can upend the picture suggested by candidates' own fundraising. Democrat James Talarico had raised $146.3 million, against Republican Ken Paxton's $22.3 million. Yet outside groups had spent $298.5 million supporting Paxton or attacking Talarico in the general election, compared with $79.9 million benefiting Talarico's side.
"Billionaires are spending millions attacking me," Talarico said in a campaign ad. "I don't take corporate PAC money. I'm running to ban dark money so billionaires can't buy our elections."
Daniel Lobo-Lewis, executive director of the Washington-based Political Integrity Project, said candidates increasingly see funding sources as an issue voters can judge.
"Politically, I can use it against my opponent, but in order to do that, I have to be clean," he told Anadolu.
His group grades candidates using public campaign-finance data and asks them to pledge to reject corporate PAC money, back a congressional stock-trading ban, restrict lawmakers becoming lobbyists and support campaign-finance reform. More than 100 candidates had signed, he said, including about 70 who advanced to the general election.
Public concern crosses party lines. An April Pew Research Center survey found 74% of Americans regarded money in politics as a "very big problem," including 70% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents and 79% of Democrats and Democratic leaners.
Few groups illustrate the reach and controversy of outside money better than the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
AIPAC's traditional PAC had raised $57.8 million through Oct. 14 and bundled about $44 million in individual donations for candidates by Oct. 24. Those bundled funds belong to individual donors, not AIPAC itself.
Its affiliated super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), had raised $112.8 million and reported $54 million in independent spending through Oct. 24.
AIPAC says it seeks to elect pro-Israel candidates from both parties and defeat those it considers hostile to the US-Israel relationship.
Its largest 2026 intervention came in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, where UDP spent $20.7 million opposing Abdul El-Sayed and $10.6 million supporting Rep. Haley Stevens.
El-Sayed, a critic of unconditional US military aid to Israel, linked the spending to his advocacy for campaign-finance reform.
"When you launch a campaign and you're trying to get money out of politics, that invites record amounts of spending against you," he told Detroit public radio station WDET afterward.
Cory Archibald, co-founder of TrackAIPAC, launched in 2024 to challenge the pro-Israel lobby's influence, said wealthy interests across industries exercise disproportionate power.
"If somebody's got $100 million that they're waving around saying, 'Do what I say, or I'm going to spend this against you,' that's a problem," she told Anadolu, citing cryptocurrency and pharmaceutical interests alongside AIPAC.
But she argued that AIPAC differs from domestic industry lobbies because it seeks to shape US foreign policy in another country's interests.
"AIPAC's goal and the Israel lobby's goal is to influence American foreign policy to benefit a foreign government, even when that happens at the expense of American interests," she said.
Archibald said AIPAC faces growing resistance from a younger generation of politicians more willing to criticize Israel, a shift that began before the war in Gaza. She said the group responded by sharply increasing its direct election spending in 2022.
More than 40 candidates aligned with TrackAIPAC had won primaries this year, she said, including over 20 in districts where she expected them to enter Congress. Their arrival, she argued, could change congressional debates on US military aid to Israel.
Other industries are also spending heavily to influence Washington.
Cryptocurrency-linked groups tracked by FEC-based PaidForPolitics had raised $324.6 million and spent about $162 million supporting or opposing candidates by late October. Defend American Jobs alone accounted for more than $101 million in independent spending.
Artificial intelligence regulation has sparked another spending battle. Groups seeking lighter oversight had raised $125 million and spent about $36 million on elections, while groups advocating stronger regulation had spent roughly $25.6 million.
Yet even unprecedented spending does not guarantee victory.
"Money, you can't win without money, but money won't make you win," Lobo-Lewis said.

Ukraine’s Satellite Disruption Exposes a Central Risk of Modern Warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:28:45 UTC
05:28:45 KST

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk claimed over the weekend that the Ukrainian military had “violated” the terms of service for Starlink, the company’s commercial satellite internet network, which has become central to the country’s defense against Russia. Musk said SpaceX had restricted Starlink to prevent that alleged misuse. Ukrainian officials disputed his claim. His allegation came after over a week of uncertainty about why the services had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials reported on Oct. 14 that restrictions affecting SpaceX’s satellite communications were disrupting drone operations, blocking a key line of defense amid daily Russian air attacks. Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink for frontline communications, drone capabilities, and reconnaissance; the throttled connection ultimately led to the cancellation of several missions, officials said.
The restrictions also affected Starshield, a military-grade satellite communications service that uses Starlink technology but is supplied through U.S. government contracts.
Over a week after the disruption began, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Oct. 24 that both services had been fully restored. It reported that connections remained stable even when terminals were moving at speeds above 400 km/h.
At the time, the cause for the interruption had not yet been clarified, but Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara emphasized the importance of a strong and stable connection, calling it “vital for our front line, for our military personnel, for the operation of drones, and for logistics and communications.”
Musk maintains that the United States government controls changes to Starshield, leaving questions about who authorized its restrictions—and why.
U.S. President Donald Trump declined to identify those involved in the decision, while a Reuters report from Oct. 15 cited multiple officials who said the order came from inside the White House. The sources did not identify who authorized or implemented the restrictions, but a senior U.S. official denied that it was Trump, the report said.
Experts say that the disruptions expose a growing vulnerability in modern warfare: military reliance on a single private technology supplier.
The company that controls the technology can ultimately wield significant influence over military operations, leaving governments dependent on decisions made by executives and billionaire owners outside traditional diplomatic channels, experts warn.
Why U.S. control of Starshield matters for Ukraine
Ukraine’s access to satellite communications depends on decisions made in Washington as well as at SpaceX. That leaves Kyiv navigating both a private supplier’s restrictions and a fraught relationship with the Trump Administration.
In recent weeks, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising global fuel prices and called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop those attacks—despite the fact that experts have primarily attributed the price surge to the U.S. war with Iran.
Trump said on Oct. 15 that Zelensky was “more difficult to deal with” than Russian President Vladimir Putin and on Oct. 19 suggested that it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”
Alex Crowther, an adjunct professor at Florida International University’s Jack D. Gordon Institute for Public Policy, says the Starshield dispute goes beyond Trump’s souring relationship with Zelensky to a more basic question: Who has the authority to restrict Ukraine’s access?
“Usually when [a foreign entity] signs a contract with an American company, it says who has the capability to turn this stuff on and off, and the circumstances under which they can turn it on and off,” Crowther says, questioning who has that authority over the services Ukraine relies upon. “Is it Starlink, which is private, or is it Starshield, which is an American government contract? Is it Musk? Is it Hegseth? Is it Trump?”
“Nobody knows the rules right now,” he says.
Lance Hunter, a professor of political science at Augusta University, tells TIME that this dispute exposes the potential issues of having three different actors—the Trump Administration, SpaceX, and Ukraine—with potentially incompatible priorities.
How dependence on SpaceX limits Ukraine’s military autonomy
Hunter says that what is unfolding in Ukraine underscores warfare’s growing dependence on digital technology. Beyond traditional “tanks, bombs, planes,” he says that includes factors like artificial intelligence, drones, and navigation jamming.
Reliance on ongoing technology services creates a different relationship from a traditional arms purchase, Hunter says.
He points to traditional arms deals in which a private company sells a government a set amount of missiles or interceptors.
“Let's say you purchase a piece of weaponry or vehicle or any type of object that helps you in the conflict: You own it at that point. You have control over it,” Hunter tells TIME.
The relationship between Ukraine and SpaceX, however, is different; purchasing the technology does not guarantee operational sovereignty.
“Ukraine has a lot of transmitters which interface with Starshield and Starlink, and they're very much dependent on SpaceX as far as allowing them to use those when they need to,” Hunter continues. “There's not just a one-time dependence buying the technology; it's continual now.”
That gives the company more “influence and leverage” over conflicts than it has before, he adds.
It shifts the way that countries like Ukraine need to think about who they are willing to work with and how they weigh the potential costs.
Why Ukraine cannot easily replace Starlink and Starshield
In a perfect world, Hunter says, Ukraine would diversify its technology suppliers to decrease reliance on Starlink.
The country has already been expanding its domestic weapons production, including interceptor drones. But it remains dependent on foreign suppliers for critical air-defense weapons like the U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles.
That dependence has left it vulnerable to shortages and delays. On Oct. 26, Zelensky said Ukraine had been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve supplies of missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air-defense systems.
But replicating satellite communications networks presents a different challenge. Starlink technology is not something a government can easily reproduce domestically, Hunter says, and few providers worldwide offer comparable capabilities.
“Starlink has a monopoly on that technology to a degree, as far as the speed, the availability, the flexibility,” he says. “It's not like they can just flip a switch and diversify that technology. It takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of resources. It takes a lot of effort, and also in Europe we don't see that same level of technology with some of the European countries and also with some of the private companies.”
In the end, he says that Ukraine is stuck between “a rock and a hard place” as the country tries to negotiate its relationships with the Trump Administration and, separately, with Musk.
“You're reliant on the politics of those bodies all matching up,” he says of Ukraine. “All of a sudden, you kind of lose that autonomy.”
“If they really push back against the U.S. government or SpaceX, they have the potential of receiving less of the technology and being cut off to a greater extent,” he adds. “But if they don't really push at all and advocate for their interest as well, then they could be in a weaker position as far as having leverage exerted over them.”
Why Ukraine disputes Musk’s Starlink claims
In a social media post on Oct. 24, Musk said that SpaceX had restricted Starlink access deliberately because Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite network for offensive drone strikes.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in one post. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be.”
Musk explained that Starlink continues to be “critical to the defense of Ukraine,” but that it could not be used for offensive military operations.
Ukrainian officials promptly disputed Musk’s claims.
Defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote in a Telegram post that operational and speed restrictions are in place that make it “physically impossible” for the military to use Starlink for medium- or deep-range offensive strikes.
“It is very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine,” he wrote. “Starlink does not function over the territory of Russia.”

I haven't tested the kit (yet), but either way, these vacuums are at a great price for Dyson Week, especially with these accessories added on.

Conflict-related sexual violence more than doubles as women's share of civilian deaths rises: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:27:00 UTC
05:27:00 KST

Diyar Guldogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Women and girls are facing increasingly deadly consequences of armed conflict, with their share of civilian deaths doubling since 2021 and verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence rising sharply, UN Women officials warned Monday.
Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda, UN Women's deputy executive director for normative support, UN system coordination and programme results, told reporters that women and girls were bearing a growing share of the human cost of wars that she described as "preventable."
More than 37,000 civilians were killed in armed conflicts in 2025, with women and girls accounting for one in four deaths, twice their share in 2021, Gumbonzvanda said.
She added that at least 25 women and girls were killed every day, while more than 750 million lived within 50 kilometers (31 miles) of an armed conflict.
"The conflicts that have disappeared from our screens, but not from the lives of women and girls enduring them. And for women and girls who survive, the burden is relentless," she said.
Gumbonzvanda also warned of a sharp increase in conflict-related sexual violence, saying the UN verified 9,788 cases in 2025, more than double the number recorded in 2024 and nearly four times the figure reported in 2022.
"Women are paying the price of war," she said.
Gumbonzvanda urged governments and the international community to end armed conflicts, protect civilians, uphold international law and hold perpetrators of abuses accountable.
She also called for women to be included as decision-makers in all peace negotiations and for greater funding for women-led organizations working to save lives and build peace.
 
Sarah Hendriks, director of the Policy, Programme and Intergovernmental Division at UN Women, warned that the growing number of conflicts worldwide was worsening conditions for women and girls.
More than 185 conflicts were recorded globally in 2025, including 65 state-based conflicts, Hendriks said.
"Wars are multiplying; the ways that wars are fought are changing, and it is women and girls who are paying the price," she added.

Rubio says Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure must be replaced before a vote
Italy

2026-10-26

05:26:01 KST

By Simon Lewis and Matt Spetalnick
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure was designed to rig elections and so must be quickly replaced before a valid election can be held.
Rubio spoke to reporters by phone a day after opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to Venezuela for the first time since the US captured the country’s then-President Nicolas Maduro in January and took him to New York for trial.
The US believes that talks currently underway between the interim government in Caracas and opposition politicians are expected to see a new supreme judicial tribunal in place by the end of this year and a new electoral council shortly thereafter, a senior US State Department official said earlier.
“I think we’re making real progress in that regard,” said Rubio, who has acted as US President Donald Trump’s point person on Venezuela. “But if anybody tries to derail that process, they’re doing a great harm to Venezuela.”
Maduro’s government had set up the country’s electoral infrastructure to rig elections so must be quickly changed, Rubio added.
But Rubio stopped short of giving a target date for elections. Machado has said elections should be held by mid-2027, though Trump has previously said he did not believe Venezuela was ready for a nationwide vote.
Machado’s return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining her ties with Trump’s administration.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Machado, who was prevented from challenging Maduro for the presidency in 2024, had been out of the country for 10 months and spent the previous year in hiding following the disputed election.
Washington has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but has praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez and supports a negotiation process between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups that do not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement.
Rubio said the only time he had “discouraged” Machado from going back to Venezuela was in the immediate aftermath of devastating earthquakes in the summer, because the country was grappling with a humanitarian crisis.
But Rubio said that weeks ago the US told Venezuela’s interim authorities that Machado “belongs in her country” and “should be allowed to return unperturbed,” and the government had agreed.
Asked about Machado’s criticism of an oil deal that Trump had struck with the interim rulers, Rubio insisted that the agreement was a good one for both countries but that she had a right to express her opinion on the matter.
Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez, a former deputy to Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country.
But some critics have accused Trump of a neo-colonialist approach to Venezuela aimed at exploiting its natural resources.
A faction of the opposition and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Machado’s political movement.

Britain told to plan for war without Trump’s America
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:25:26 GMT
05:25:26 KST

Defence spending should go to five per cent of gross domestic product immediately, the country should be prepared for a wider European war and planning should assume Britain may have to fight without the United States, according to a security academic at the University of Leicester.
Dr Simon Bennett, director of the Civil Safety and Security Unit in the university’s School of Business and author of a 2025 book on security lessons from the war in Ukraine, set out the argument in comments issued through the university press office.
Bennett said: “Given these facts, we must prepare ourselves to fight alone. Like Keir Starmer, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is in denial about Trump. The American president is a lost cause. Better to focus finite energies and budgets first, on supporting Ukraine, and secondly, on preparing this country for a wider European war. Defence spending must be increased to 5% of Gross Domestic Product immediately and, as suggested by former Secretary of State for Defence Lord Hutton of Furness in the 17 October edition of The i Paper, the British public must be told the truth about Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign.”
On the range of threats he believes the country is exposed to, Bennett said: “The United Kingdom faces a spectrum of threats. The country has suffered two Kremlin-initiated chemical warfare attacks, in London in 2006 (Polonium) and in Salisbury in 2018 (Novichok). The Council on Strategic Risks recently highlighted the UK’s vulnerability to biological weapons. Prime Minister Burnham, it is time to focus on what really matters – giving Ukraine the weapons it needs and securing a vulnerable United Kingdom. Do not prostrate yourself before Trump, as your predecessor did. As Volodymyr Zelensky and Mark Carney have shown, the only way to deal with Trump is to stand up to him.”
Bennett is asking for far more than the government has signed up to. Ministers have committed to NATO’s target of three and a half per cent of gross domestic product on core defence by 2035, with a further one and a half per cent on defence-related resilience and infrastructure making up the alliance’s headline five per cent figure. Bennett is calling for core defence spending itself to reach five per cent now, a distinction ministers have had to set out repeatedly.
Lord Hutton of Furness, whose intervention Bennett cites, was Secretary of State for Defence from 2008 to 2009. His argument that the public must be told the truth about Russian hybrid warfare runs close to what ministers have themselves begun saying. Wes Streeting told the Defence Committee this month that hybrid activity of this kind amounts to state backed terrorism, and Louise Sandher-Jones confirmed in a written answer last week that “we know Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe.”
Ministers have also confirmed that government messaging on defence and security will build ahead of Exercise ALBISTON SHADOW and NATO’s crisis management exercise in spring 2027, and the Cabinet Office launched its Be Ready campaign this month asking households to prepare to look after themselves for three days.
The two chemical incidents Bennett refers to are the poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko with polonium-210 in London in 2006, which a public inquiry found was probably approved by the Russian president, and the Novichok attack on Sergei and Yulia Skripal in Salisbury in 2018, which killed Dawn Sturgess and which Britain attributed to the GRU. The Council on Strategic Risks is a Washington-based institute publishing on biological, climate and nuclear security.
Bennett’s case rests on his reading of the American president, whom he describes as a Russophile and, in his words and expressly as his opinion, a traitor to the West’s liberal-democratic values. He said he predicted in March 2025 that Trump would ally the United States with Russia through accords and treaties, and took criticism for saying so at the time.

UN urges Iraq, Kuwait to intensify search for 315 people missing since 1990 invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:25:11 UTC
05:25:11 KST

Diyar Guldogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The UN on Monday urged Iraq and Kuwait to accelerate efforts to determine the fate of 315 people still missing following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, as investigators continue searching burial sites believed to contain their remains.
"More than thirty-five years after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, this humanitarian file remains unresolved," Senior UN Representative Mari Yamashita told a Security Council meeting.
Yamashita said the fate of only 290 of the original 605 missing Kuwaiti and third-country nationals had been clarified over the past three decades.
Of the 315 people still missing, 308 are Kuwaiti nationals, she said, adding that the last confirmed identification took place in August 2023.
She said extensive efforts have been undertaken to locate the missing, including excavations at suspected burial sites across Iraq, particularly in the south of the country.
Yamashita said Iraqi authorities have excavated approximately 14,000 trenches at the Khamisiyah site and conducted numerous field missions to other locations of interest.
Khamisiyah remains a priority because investigators believe it may contain the remains of 150 to 180 missing Kuwaiti nationals, potentially accounting for roughly half of the unresolved cases.
In September, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and Iraqi authorities conducted a joint field mission to the site.
Yamashita expressed hope that the findings would lead to further excavation work as soon as possible.
 
Kuwaiti archives, property remain missing
The UN representative also highlighted the unresolved issue of Kuwaiti property taken during Iraq's invasion, including the country's national archives.
Although some materials have been returned, progress has been "limited," she said.
Items were transferred to the Kuwait National Library in 2019 and the country's Ministry of Information in 2022, while additional books and microfilm recordings were returned in 2025.
Yamashita called for a "clear pathway" to identify and locate the remaining property, suggesting that a proposed Joint Iraq-Kuwait Committee could provide a framework for regular dialogue and cooperation.
She also welcomed a recent meeting between Kuwait's crown prince and Iraq's prime minister on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, where the two countries announced a working group to address outstanding bilateral issues.
"Such engagements remain important in sustaining the constructive environment needed to advance the humanitarian objectives of this mandate, to strengthen mutual confidence, and to support continued cooperation in the future," she said.

Hours earlier, senior government security officials said their security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout on Monday over the church violence that killed nine people.
"God willing, they only represent themselves," said Jordan's Director of Public Security, Major-General Obeidallah al-Maaytah.

"The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications of any links between them and other cells," al-Faraya added.
At least 34 injured after gunmen attack funeral service

There has been no claim of responsibility for the church attack.

'Legitimazes Jihad': Foreign Affairs Ministry slams UN report accusing Israel of genocide

The Foreign Affairs Ministry on Monday called the report from a United Nations commission accusing Israel of genocide a "propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel’s right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."
The UN commission released a report Monday accusing Israel of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank and Gaza.
The report also mentioned wrongdoings by the Palestinian Authority, claiming that it had pushed for arbitrary arrests, detention, torture and the targeting of journalists, activists and human rights defenders.
In contrast, Hamas is named exactly twice, and neither mention accused Hamas of committing a crime or other wrongdoing.
The UN reported an increase in the number of Palestinian deaths in the West Bank, with almost 500 Palestinians killed annually in the West Bank since 2022, which were the highest numbers recorded since the UN started collecting data on the topic in 2005.
The report also claimed that Israel is continuing to commit “genocidal acts” with the “intent to destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part” in spite of a ceasefire agreement that went into effect in October 2025.
The report focused on Palestinian casualties in the West Bank due to Israeli military action and settler violence, as well as analysis of elected MKs and senior military officials.
“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, an Indian jurist who currently serves as the chair of the Commission of Inquiry.
Report cites increase in West Bank airstrike deaths
The Commission reported a sharp increase in Palestinian deaths caused by airstrikes in the West Bank since October 7, 2023. Six Palestinians were killed by airstrikes between 2008 and October 6, 2023, compared with 254 between October 7, 2023, and September 30, 2026, according to the commission’s findings.
It said airstrikes had become more frequent following the launch of Operation Iron Wall in January 2025, particularly in refugee camps and areas around Jenin, Tulkarm, Tubas and Nablus.
The Commission described the operation as a shift toward widespread destruction of Palestinian housing and infrastructure and the clearing of refugee camps. It cited the IDF's stated aim to “dismantle and restor[e] the operational freedom of action for IDF forces”, while reconstruction of the infrastructure is considered to be “endangering the citizens of the State of Israel and the military forces”.
Commission's analysis of statements by Israeli officials
The commission also cited statements by Israeli officials including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and IDF Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth in assessing Israeli military conduct and the intentions behind operations in the West Bank.
Smotrich referred to “two million Nazis” in the West Bank in November 2023, citing a poll on Palestinian support for the October 7 Hamas massacre. In November 2024, he said “The only way to remove the danger of a Palestinian terror state from the agenda is to apply Israeli sovereignty to Jewish settlement in the entire Judea and Samaria,” he said.
In January 2025, he wrote that Fondouk, Nablus and Jenin should “look like Jabalia,”.
The Commission also highlighted a reported May 2026 statement by Bluth that Israeli soldiers were “killing like we haven’t since 1967.”
Report alleges sexual violence against detainees
The Commission said it had verified four additional cases of sexual violence against Palestinian detainees since its March 2025 report on gender-based violence. Two victims were from the West Bank. The cases included alleged gang rape, genital violence, groping, threats of sexual violence, forced nudity, and searches conducted without an apparent security justification.
One case involved a male detainee at Megiddo Prison in 2025. He was allegedly blindfolded, forced to remove his lower garments, and repeatedly raped with objects during interrogation.
The Commission alleged that guards mocked and photographed him, threatened to mutilate his genitals and threatened sexual violence against his family and colleagues. The detainee reportedly suffered serious injuries, including rectal bleeding, without receiving medical treatment.
The Commission claimed that the cases it investigated involving torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence were not isolated incidents. It alleged that these acts formed part of a broader attack against the civilian population and concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed crimes against humanity involving torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence.
Israel has rejected previous allegations by the Commission of Inquiry that its forces systematically used sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinian detainees, describing the claims as unfounded and disputing the Commission's verification methods. In a March 2025 response, the Foreign Ministry said the IDF had rules prohibiting such misconduct and mechanisms for investigating allegations.
Commission also reports abuses by Palestinian Authority
The report also accused the Palestinian Authority of suppressing political dissent through arbitrary arrests, detention, torture and the targeting of journalists, activists and human rights defenders.
It cited reports of excessive force during West Bank protests in October 2023, when at least two men, a boy and a girl, were killed in Ramallah, Tubas and Jenin. The PA accepted responsibility for the death of the boy, who was run over by a security forces vehicle during clashes with protesters.
The Commission also investigated the December 2024 killing of a Palestinian journalism student in Jenin refugee camp who had documented alleged abuses by Palestinian security forces. Witnesses said a security force member had threatened to shoot her the previous day. She was killed by a single shot to the neck near her home.
The report said information conflicted on whether clashes were underway at the time. Palestinian security forces had a significant presence in the area, and their spokesman blamed the killing on “outlaws,” saying the case was under investigation. The Commission said key witnesses had not been asked to testify.
It also reported cases of arbitrary detention, including instances in which the PA allegedly ignored court orders for detainees' release.
The Commission concluded that the PA had violated the right to life and the right to security of person and had failed to conduct prompt, effective and impartial investigations into killings or provide effective remedies to victims and their families.

Israel’s moment of truth: Knesset election pivotal to future US-Israel relationship - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:18:24 UTC
05:18:24 KST

The upcoming election in Israel will likely prove pivotal in determining whether the ongoing erosion in support for Israel in the United States devolves further into a full rupture that makes both Americans and Israelis less secure.
As Americans, we are not interested in picking winners and losers. Israelis should decide such things, but our friends there should understand the consequences of their decisions.
Our colleague Mark Dubowitz has recently warned of possible American financial warfare against Israel. Some of this risk is linked to a growing campaign of antisemitism and anti-Zionism that has exploded since the October 7 terror attacks plunged the Middle East into conflict. But some of this is also linked to senseless violence in the West Bank and other concerns.
If the next government in Israel, regardless of who leads it, fails to punish and end lawlessness and cruelty by anarchists in the West Bank, there could be painful consequences.
We firmly support Israel’s right to exist and defend itself and believe that America is safer, and US interests in the Middle East are more secure, when a strong Israel works closely with Washington. We are proud that America and Israel have fought together to defend common interests and to counter common enemies.
Enemies of US engaged in unprecedented cooperation, understand value of partnerships
America’s enemies – namely the Axis of Aggressors, consisting of China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea – are engaged in unprecedented cooperation. Our foes understand the value of partnerships.
America needs partners, too, especially capable and motivated partners like Israel. We need Israel’s muscles in the Middle East so we can focus more on deterring and defeating aggression by Beijing, Moscow, or Pyongyang. Americans also benefit from Israel’s defense-technology expertise and defense-acquisition agility, which can help ensure American warfighters wield the best weapons.
But we are witnessing a sad paradox with Israel. On one hand, Israel has demonstrated that it is the most powerful military in the Middle East, worthy of closer cooperation with the United States. Israel has battled back and gained the upper hand in a regional war that it neither started nor wanted. And yet, in the United States, Israel is more unpopular than it has been in years. This is clear in recent polls from Pew, Gallup, and the Ronald Reagan Institute.
This is a strategic liability for Israel. A steep decline in approval could lead the next Congress and US administration to adopt policies that undermine our bilateral relationship, including defense cooperation. That would materially damage the security of both the US and Israel.
Some in Israel may respond by shrugging and saying, “Fine, Israel will just become independent and self-sufficient in its defense production and arm itself.”
But that is not possible. Israel is heavily reliant on major American-made platforms and will remain so for decades.
True defense production independence doesn’t just require assembly lines in Israel. It also requires suppliers and raw materials in Israel. Many of the inputs for Israeli-produced weapons are imported, meaning a hostile administration could try to block them.
Israel’s enemies are actively working to drive a wedge between Washington and Jerusalem. The goal is to slowly but surely deprive Israel of the means to defend itself. Unfortunately, those enemies are capitalizing on some Israeli unforced errors.
It is certainly true that some of the withering criticism of Israel will continue regardless of the country’s policies. It is also true that enemies are increasingly well-organized and funded, and they are conducting information warfare against the United States and Israel.
But explaining the negative shift in opinion in America solely through those dynamics is simply unrealistic. Such efforts ignore the agency of the Israeli government and encourage a dangerous apathy in terms of undertaking necessary reforms. The rule of law and the distinction between combatant and noncombatant are a primary difference between defenders of Western civilization and the terrorists who murdered innocents on September 11, 2001, and October 7, 2023.
US-Israel security cooperation needed more than ever
As threats to Americans grow, we need US-Israel security cooperation more than ever. And Israel needs continued American diplomatic and defense cooperation. But this could prove difficult if some Israeli policies continue.
Battles against the terrorist regime in Iran and its proxies will continue, as will the fight against disinformation and blind hate that unfairly targets Israel. But that does not absolve Israel from making some crucial decisions about its own conduct. The fate of the US-Israel alliance could hang in the balance.
Bradley Bowman is senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD). Jonathan Schanzer is executive director at FDD.
