Report: Netanyahu lawyer's firm received $1.25 million from key trial witness James Packer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:40:59 UTC
03:40:59 KST

Australian billionaire James Packer paid at least $1.25 million – 1.78 million Australian dollars or 3.85 million shekels – to the law firm of Amit Hadad, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's attorney, the Australian newspaper The Age reported Monday.
Packer is also a witness in Netanyahu's corruption trial, in which Hadad represents the prime minister.
The investigation, published on the eve of Israel's election, uncovered a trail of monthly bank transfers of $50,000 over the past two years, from a bank account controlled by Packer's company to the account of the law firm representing Netanyahu.
On the same day the investigation was published, Hadad filed a motion on behalf of Netanyahu's defense team requesting that Packer and two of his employees be allowed to testify from abroad, with their testimony broadcast by video link to the judges in Israel.
According to the investigation, the first monthly payment was made on September 23, 2024, from a Citibank account belonging to Packer's legal firm to an account held by Hadad, Roth, Shenhar at Mizrahi Tefahot Bank. A source familiar with the details reportedly said the payments urgently needed to be investigated to determine whether Netanyahu had received an undisclosed benefit from Packer.
Packer insisted that the bank transfers to Netanyahu's lawyers were payments for work carried out on his behalf, including "deal finding" in Israel, where he has business interests, and that they were unrelated to Netanyahu's trial.
The Australian newspaper also reported that a Netanyahu spokesperson asked for comment replied: "I couldn't give a monkey's about your questions. We are very busy. We have an election on right now."
Packer did not deny making the monthly payments but declined to comment. Hadad also declined to comment.
Packer's representatives responded that the law firm represents him in his "personal and business affairs." "Any claim that I paid even a single cent toward the legal defense of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is false. Anyone who claims otherwise risks being sued."
Packer was expected to testify as a key prosecution witness in Netanyahu's corruption trial in Case 1000, in which he and businessman Arnon Milchan are alleged to have provided Netanyahu and his wife with gifts and other benefits worth hundreds of thousands of shekels.
Packer gave a statement to police during the investigation, but in February 2024, prosecutors announced that they would not call him to testify at the trial. During the phase of the trial devoted to prosecution witnesses, prosecutors were unable to contact Packer to arrange for him to travel to Israel.
Meanwhile, attorney Amit Hadad filed a motion on Netanyahu's behalf Monday requesting that Packer and two of his employees, Ben Tilley and Guy Jolland, be questioned abroad. The defense requested that their testimony be broadcast by video link to the judges in Jerusalem, as was the testimony given by Arnon Milchan from England during the trial.
During the cross-examination of Hadas Klein, Packer's former personal assistant in Israel, the defense submitted letters from Tilley and Jolland challenging her testimony that most of the champagne and cigars purchased for Packer went to Netanyahu and his wife.
In the motion, Hadad stated that he represents Packer in Israel on matters unrelated to Netanyahu's trial.
In the letters, the two described their visits to Israel between 2013 and 2016, when they were members of Packer's staff. Tilley testified that he smoked a cigar every evening during each of the 83 days he spent in Israel, as did Ian Morris, another Packer employee.
Jolland described the hospitality at Packer's properties, including a suite at the Royal Beach Hotel in Tel Aviv and a villa he purchased in Caesarea. He claimed that the properties were always stocked with food and wine for entertaining guests, including a supply of rosé champagne, and that Packer himself regularly drank rosé champagne.
Hadad is seeking to call Packer, Tilley and Jolland as defense witnesses to challenge the testimony of Klein and driver Yonatan Hasson regarding the quantities of cigars and champagne transferred from Packer to the Netanyahu family.
Hadad explained that the defense has no way to compel the witnesses, who live abroad, to testify in Israel because they refuse to travel there. However, they have indicated that they would comply with any lawful court order issued by the courts in their countries of residence.
He attached a letter written by Jolland on Packer's behalf, stating that Packer refuses to come to Israel because of the treatment he received from law enforcement authorities.
Netanyahu had a close personal relationship with Packer, which also involved attempts to advance business and media interests. Packer, who came to Israel in 2013 through businessman Arnon Milchan, grew close to Netanyahu and admired him.
One of the clearest signs of their relationship was Packer's purchase of a villa next to the Netanyahu family home in Caesarea, after Netanyahu encouraged him to buy it. The Netanyahu family treated the property almost as their own home. Family members had dinner there and sometimes took boxes of cigars and cases of champagne from the house. Netanyahu also regularly swam in his neighbor's pool.
Packer also developed a friendship with Netanyahu's son Yair, who frequently stayed at Packer's properties, including the Royal Beach Hotel, a penthouse at Robert De Niro's hotel in New York, a villa in the ski resort town of Aspen, Colorado, and a yacht moored in Ibiza.
Testifying at his trial last year, Netanyahu confirmed that Milchan had introduced him to Packer at a dinner. "My impression of him was positive, and I think it was mutual," Netanyahu said. "We developed an emotional connection. I'm good at reading people, as I always have been, and I could see that he was genuinely someone who, I would say, had no ulterior motives. What he wanted was closeness."
Netanyahu also claimed that Packer had told him he was the most impressive person he had ever met.

Ukrainian Intelligence Reveals How Russia Targets Africa to Recruit Soldiers for Ukraine War
Russia has significantly expanded military recruitment across Africa, targeting poorer countries to replenish its forces amid heavy battlefield losses in Ukraine, Bloomberg reported on October 26.
The outlet cited a presentation by people familiar with Ukraine’s intelligence service detailing Moscow’s growing reliance on African recruits. The campaign aims to “offset massive losses and a shortage of people to mobilize,” the document stated.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the intelligence assessment, Russia has increasingly targeted countries with weak democratic institutions, limited press freedom, and inadequate judicial protections.
The recruitment campaign has expanded particularly rapidly in Burundi, Zimbabwe, and Sierra Leone, following efforts by Kenya and South Africa to prevent their citizens from joining Russian forces.
Between January 1 and September 30, 2026, Russia recruited 699 men from Burundi, compared with just 30 throughout 2025. In Zimbabwe, recruitment increased from 65 men in 2025 to 530 during the first nine months of 2026.
Significant increases were also recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan, Cameroon, and Sierra Leone.
Russia has also begun recruiting military personnel in Madagascar for the first time since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Following a military coup in 2025, Madagascar strengthened cooperation with Moscow, receiving Russian military equipment and food supplies.
Russian personnel have also provided military training to Malagasy forces.
Recruiters reportedly exploit economic hardship by promising high-paying civilian employment in Russia, including positions in catering and transportation.
Some prospective recruits are misled about the nature of their employment and subsequently deployed to the battlefield in Ukraine. Other incentives include substantial signing bonuses, high salaries, and the possibility of obtaining Russian citizenship.
The intelligence materials also described an online recruitment advertisement circulated in Zimbabwe, promoting a “program for specialists from Zimbabwe.” Applicants were directed to an online eligibility assessment, without explicit warnings that military contracts could lead to frontline deployment.
The surge in African recruitment is part of a far broader foreign-recruitment drive that has grown sharply since 2022, when only 94 such contracts were recorded. For 2026, Moscow set a target of 18,500 foreign recruits, and by mid-October, 16,168 had already signed contracts.
Russia has also used legal and administrative restrictions to pressure migrants living in the country without citizenship. This approach presents military service as one of the few routes to legal residency and a Russian passport, while circumventing opposition from countries across Asia, Africa, and Latin America that officially reject the recruitment of their citizens into foreign armed forces.

Delivery of grain storage sleeves to agricultural enterprises begins – URCS
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:40:42 EET
03:40:42 KST

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the United Nations World Food Programme, the international non-profit organization Mercy Corps, and the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) have begun distributing grain silos to agricultural enterprises in Sumy region for crop storage.
"The first 57 grain storage sleeves have been delivered to three agricultural enterprises in the Sumy region. They will provide temporary storage for almost 10,000 tonnes of grain," the URCS said on Facebook on Monday.
In total, the program calls for the distribution of 1,516 grain bags to 257 agricultural producers in Sumy and Donetsk regions. The aid will reach 48 communities in nine districts. The program is being implemented with the support of the U.S. government in close cooperation with the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine, as well as the governments of Canada, the European Union, and the Howard G. Buffett Foundation.

The Guardian view on Lula’s comeback: a victory for Brazil and the world, as well as a Trump rebuff | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:40:14 UTC
03:40:14 KST

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win in Brazil’s presidential election is a triumph for him, his country and the world. The 80-year-old incumbent snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, blocked the rise of the far right and saved the planetary air-conditioning system of the Amazon from irreparable destruction. Known universally as Lula, he made history by becoming the first candidate to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round. In triumphing against Flávio Bolsonaro, the leftist stopped what could have been the most dangerous consolidation of authoritarian rule in Brazil since military rule ended. A Bolsonaro presidency could have used a rightwing Congress to extend presidential terms and pack the supreme court, entrenching power for generations.
Lula seemed to have been energised by his first-round defeat by Mr Bolsonaro. The three-time president initially pitted his extraordinary life and record against a 45-year-old senator married to controversy. But voters wanted answers to economic insecurity, rising prices and poor public services. Lula reversed course in the second round, offering immediate relief from everyday costs and indebtedness – including to the rising number of self-employed voters whom his rightwing opponent had been courting. Popular mobilisation transformed the runoff into a race to stop a Bolsonaro restoration with student protests, mass demonstrations and a 10 million-strong “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel. It seemed to work. Nearly 5 million more people voted in the second round of the Brazilian election than the first.
Mr Bolsonaro’s desperate refusal to concede follows his father’s playbook. In 2022 then-president Jair Bolsonaro did the same, claiming fraud. The elder Bolsonaro’s attempted coup saw him jailed for 27 years. This time Lula’s margin of victory – 4.4m votes – over the younger Bolsonaro was twice that achieved over the father. His win has also been recognised by rightwing regional leaders, conservative newspapers and even a prominent evangelical ally of the Bolsonaros. It may be significant that defeat denied Mr Bolsonaro a presidential shield from allegations of corruption and money laundering. Whether he remains in Brazil after his term as senator expires in February remains to be seen.
After the Bolsonaro clan, the next biggest loser from the results of the Brazilian election is Donald Trump. Lula’s win broke a run of seven rightwing presidential wins across Latin America, a regional advance for which Mr Trump had claimed credit. While rightwing leaders in Chile, Paraguay and Peru congratulated Lula on his victory, the White House remained silent. The US president has only himself to blame: he tried to use tariffs to pressure Brazil over the elder Bolsonaro’s prosecution and its courts’ enforcement actions against American tech companies. Mr Trump’s meddling handed Lula a winning argument for Brazil’s sovereignty.
Brazil remains divided, with a rightwing Congress ready to obstruct Lula – particularly on the environment. But few are better placed to negotiate than the former trade unionist who founded the Workers’ party. Lula’s victory provides an elected counterweight and that matters for labour rights, public services, Indigenous communities and global climate policy. The win shows the wider democratic left that a broad coalition can defeat the right. Can governing produce the secure livelihoods, strong state provision and meaningful opportunities that make that coalition durable? The next four years in Brazil may provide an answer.

‘Students Have Won’: Overwhelming Turnout Shatters Serbia’s Entrenched Regime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:39:00 UTC
03:39:00 KST

When a handful of university students first spilled onto the streets two years ago to protest the deadly collapse of a railway station canopy, Serbia’s state-run media dismissed them as unruly kids merely looking for an excuse to cut class.
They were grieving the 16 people crushed to death and demanding accountability for what they condemned as lethal state corruption and crony contracting, bearing banners that read: “Corruption kills” and “Your hands are bloody.”
But those scattered demonstrations soon swelled into a generational revolt. Over two relentless years, the students slept in occupied lecture halls, barnstormed rural strongholds where state television branded them foreign mercenaries, and punctured a pervasive climate of fear with biting wit and viral banners.
On Sunday, the kids actually did it.
In a stunning ballot-box upset that shattered Aleksandar Vučić’s 14-year grip on power, Serbia’s student-led movement defeated the Balkan country’s formidable ruling machine, clinching a triumph so historic that even its young architects were left reeling in disbelief.
“Fantastic. I can’t believe it,” Ilija Ratković, 30, told OCCRP. “A regime that ruled for 14 years, was corrupt, and killed people in Serbia is out.” He admitted he never expected Vučić to yield quietly: “I expected him to fight to the end.”
The movement’s slogan, “Students are winning” (Studenti pobeđuju), mobilized Serbians at home and abroad to vote for the “Students’ List”—a slate of candidates chosen by activists to replace Vučić’s state apparatus. Though convinced the regime would try to manipulate the count, organizers aimed to counter fraud through overwhelming turnout, operating on a simple premise: elections can be stolen, but not in a landslide.
“The higher the turnout, the less chance he has to steal it,” one voter who identified himself as David told OCCRP ahead of the poll.
Then came Sunday. Even after Serbia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs adjusted overseas polling hours to align with Belgrade’s time zone, thousands of diaspora Serbs lined up outside embassies and consulates in Australia and the United States in the dead of night. Some traveled thousands of kilometers from Brisbane to Sydney. In New York, voters showed up at 2:00 AM singing defiant songs, with several wearing pajamas, bathrobes, and sleep masks to mock a rule they viewed as blatant voter suppression.
Inside Serbia, queues at polling stations stretched around city blocks. Voters brought sandwiches and flasks of tea and coffee, waiting patiently for hours to cast their ballots.
A video circulating on social media on Monday perhaps best captured that determination: just one minute before polls were set to close, a man was filmed carrying a woman wearing house slippers toward a polling station entrance. “She delivered a baby two days ago!” he shouted to the people at the door, as another bystander rushed over to help carry her inside. She was the final voter admitted to the station.
“Change requires participation. Citizens who do not participate in the democratic process – not in the public square through protest and engaged debate, nor through the ballot box – will achieve nothing,” political analyst Jasmin Mujanovic wrote in a commentary.
With turnout approaching 70 percent—nearing a historic record—Vučić did the unthinkable roughly an hour and a half after polls closed at 8:00 PM. Preempting the official election commission tally, he conceded defeat from party headquarters, announcing that based on his party’s samples, the youth-led Students’ List had won decisively, projecting roughly 2.2 million votes for the “List” compared to 1.72 million for his party.
His admission unleashed an immediate explosion of jubilation across the country. Car horns blared, red flares illuminated squares, and crowds of weeping, laughing students spilled into the autumn night, dancing well past dawn.

The Guardian view on Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to power | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:38:53 UTC
03:38:53 KST

This weekend it will be two years since the collapse of a shoddily constructed train station canopy in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. The tragedy, killing 16 people, was swiftly attributed to state corruption and failures of regulation, sparking student-led protests across the country.
Some of those demonstrators dared to imagine that they could become the catalyst for a democratic revolution.
On Sunday, that is more or less what happened. After sustaining their protests and turning them into a political movement, the students resoundingly defeated Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government in a snap legislative poll called by the president himself. Their victory constitutes one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history.
For well over a decade Mr Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) have exerted a domineering grip over civil society and the media, ruling through a combination of cronyism, patronage and bullying authoritarianism. As a report by international observers confirmed on Monday, the government made full, unscrupulous use of such tactics to ensure there was no level playing field for the vote. That it was nevertheless routed by a leaderless movement of 20- and 30-somethings will have been noted across a continent in which youth protest is challenging political priorities.
As in Hungary, where a focus on corruption helped the opposition to unseat Viktor Orbán after 16 years in office, the students’ campaign for basic democratic renewal struck a deeper chord than perhaps even they thought possible. Posing the choice for voters as “Serbia or mafia?”, they put forward a Student List of civic candidates dominated by academics, but also featuring farmers and well-known athletes. A turnout of almost 70% – the highest in a Serbian election since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992 – delivered them a comfortable majority.
What comes next will necessarily be an experiment in doing things differently. By standing apart from established structures of politics, the student insurgents embodied a freshness of approach and won the trust of the public – including in rural areas presumed to be bastions of Vučić support. In the immediate future, the new government is likely to function as a kind of constituent assembly, dedicated primarily to cleaning up civil society and rolling back the abuses that saw Serbia plunge towards the bottom of European corruption rankings.
Politically, the priority will be to consolidate this domestic agenda by winning the forthcoming presidential election. which is due by late December. But in the longer term there will be less straightforward debates to be had. Mr Vučić’s defeat is good news for the western Balkans as a whole, where he has been a consistently disruptive presence. But on foreign policy issues such as joining the European Union and relations with Russia, opinion across the student movement is divided.
As a new government seeks to re-establish the rule of law and a properly functioning and accountable state, Brussels must do all it can to assist that process while outlining a plausible and attractive path to EU membership. Mr Vučić’s Serbia, like Mr Orbán’s Hungary, became a soft autocracy where power was so entrenched that it was hard to imagine how it could be dislodged. But now there are new and better possibilities. In extraordinary fashion, the students’ inspiring journey from principled protest to power has shown just what the art of politics can deliver.

Russia accuses Ukraine of intensifying attacks on Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:38:05 UTC
03:38:05 KST

Kanyshai Butun
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Russia on Monday accused Ukraine of intensifying attacks on the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant and the nearby city of Enerhodar.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova criticized international organizations, particularly the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), for what she described as a restrained response to Kyiv’s “provocative actions.”
“We are compelled to note that international bodies, first and foremost the IAEA, have responded with great restraint to Kyiv’s provocative actions,” she said, accusing them of failing to explicitly identify Ukraine as responsible.
Zakharova claimed that Ukrainian forces had targeted civilian facilities earlier in the week, including an art school and a fire and rescue station operated by Russia’s Emergencies Ministry.
“Unable to strike the ZNPP directly, the Kyiv regime continues its futile attempts to destabilize the plant’s operations by intimidating its personnel,” she said, alleging that Kyiv sought to increase casualties and create a radiation-contaminated zone in the Zaporizhzhia region.
She also criticized Western support for Ukraine, saying it was creating radiological risks in Europe and endangering its own citizens.
Zakharova said Moscow was informing the international community about Ukrainian attacks and taking measures to protect the plant, its personnel and Enerhodar residents.
The situation around the ZNPP, Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and one of the world’s 10 largest, remains tense amid persistent concerns about a potential nuclear disaster, as Moscow and Kyiv frequently accuse each other of carrying out attacks around the facility in southeastern Ukraine.
IAEA personnel have been stationed at the plant since Sept. 1, 2022. Russia has controlled the facility since March 2022.

Ukraine adopts EU-linked law giving veterans priority in government hiring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:37:29 UTC
03:37:29 KST

Ukraine’s parliament on Oct. 26 passed a law reinstating open competitions for civil service and local government positions, advancing long-delayed reforms tied to EU funding.
The law fulfills Ukraine's commitments under the Ukraine Facility, an EU financial assistance program launched in 2024, and unlocks 137 million euros ($153 million) in budget funding, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
Open and transparent job hirings will be reinstated gradually, he added. The law also gives veterans priority for civil service jobs.
President's Office Head Kyrylo Budanov, a former spy chief, said Ukraine should create conditions for veterans "to realize their potential in state institutions, local government, the economy, and the country's leadership."
"Ukrainian veterans have unique experience in leadership, responsibility, management, and decision-making under the most challenging conditions," Budanov said.
"Veterans must be among those shaping Ukraine's future."
According to Ukrainian officials, there are around 2 million veterans in Ukraine. The Veterans Affairs Ministry said that after the war ends, veterans and their close family members could make up one-sixth of the country's population, or up to six million people.
Over the past year, several prominent figures with military backgrounds have taken up senior positions in Ukraine's government. Around 66% of Ukrainians have a positive attitude toward veterans participating in politics, while 19% are neutral and 7% view it negatively or somewhat negatively, according to a 2025 poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).

AFRL Targets New Hypersonic Engine Tech Prototypes Within 4 Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:37:28 UTC
03:37:28 KST

The Air Force Research Laboratory wants industry to advance concepts for affordable hypersonic munition engines to prototype demonstrations within three to four years.
AFRL released a request for information early this month, seeking white papers on technical requirements by Nov. 16. The notice is one of the first updates in months on its push for affordable rocket engines for hypersonic munitions.
The Hermes Rocket Lab effort began in 2020 under AFRL’s Rocket Propulsion Division with a Broad Agency Announcement seeking novel concepts and research and development proposals to accelerate rocket engine technology.
The latest white paper notice focuses on a specific kind of tech called rotating detonation rocket engine combined-cycle, or RDRE-CC.
RDRE-CC systems use continuous detonation waves rather than deflagration, the combustion process used in conventional engines. The approach produces higher pressures and improves efficiency and thrust-to-weight ratio. The technology could increase range, speed, and payload while reducing rocket engine production costs.
According to the lab’s notice, RDRE tech is at the proof of concept stage—in government parlance, at technology readiness level 3 of 9. AFRL wants industry to demonstrate a prototype in an “operationally relevant environment” within three to four years—the step associated with technology readiness level 6.
Specifically, AFRL wants the prototype demonstration to be a “ground-launched, sounding-rocket-boosted flight demonstration to validate the system’s operational viability for future High-Speed Affordable Mass Munitions.”
The Rocket Propulsion Division at Edwards Air Force Base, Calif., began HAMM market research in August and explored rocket-based combined-cycle technologies. That work led to the current RDRE-CC white paper notice.
HAMM covers both high-supersonic and hypersonic speeds, with its most ambitious efforts targeting the hypersonic range.
An AFRL spokesperson declined to answer specific questions on the latest notice from Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“AFRL continues to monitor opportunities and information obtained through Request for Information (RFIs) and may release further details at the appropriate time,” spokesperson Aleah Castrejon wrote in an email.
Industry Efforts
The Air Force is already developing hypersonic munitions like the Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon and the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile. Both those use scramjet and boost-glide systems that are more expensive to produce.
Other approaches include pulse detonation engines, oblique detonation wave engines, and advanced supersonic combustion engines. But critics have noted challenges with each: Pulse detonation engines are more complex and costly to build; oblique detonation engines are harder to start and face challenges at lower speeds; and advanced supersonic combustion engines often need external boosters. Ramjets may also offer lower thrust-to-weight ratios than RDRE-CC technology could achieve.
Companies are already developing RDRE-CC in various modes.
GE Aerospace uses Turbine-Based Combined Cycle, combining a standard turbofan with a rotating detonation dual-mode ramjet.
In 2023, GE laboratory tests validated continuous rotating detonation in supersonic airflow, a potential foundation for transitioning to Mach 5+ speeds.
The company teamed up with Lockheed Martin this year to demo a liquid-fueled rotating detonation ramjet for high-speed and hypersonic standoff missile use.
RTX, which includes Raytheon and Pratt & Whitney, uses an air-breathing, high-pressure combustion engine with rotating detonation combustors.
The company began continuous-detonation research in 2011 and was later selected by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency for its Gambit effort, which sought to develop a rotating detonation engine.
Venus Aerospace uses a compact RDRE and rocket-based combined-cycle system dubbed the Venus Detonation Ramjet, which combines RDRE with a Ramjet to attempt to reach Mach 6 speeds without separate propulsion systems.
In 2023, the company achieved long-duration, hot-fire tests of storable, liquid-propellant RDREs and ran drone-scale model flight tests for subsonic and low-supersonic stability.
In 2024-2025, Venus demonstrated the VDR2 on test stands with DARPA.
Aerojet Rocketdyne, part of L3Harris, works with pressure-gain combustion and RDRE tech to build both air-breathing and rocket applications. The company has conducted more than 500 static test firings in a variety of RDR and RDE configurations using multiple propellant combinations. They previously worked with AFRL and the Department of Energy on pressure-gain combustion modeling and other testing.
IN Space, LLC focuses on injector designs, ignition systems, 3D manufacturing tech, and hot-fire testing to build high-thrust RDRE.
In 2021, they worked with AFRL to test a 22kN-thrust RDRE using liquid oxygen and gaseous methane at Purdue University, Ind. Over the following two years, they worked with NASA to test 3D-printed RDRE combustors.

26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
US House Judiciary Committee Democrats on Monday released a new staff report alleging that President Donald Trump was implicated in accounts of sexual assault involving 11 women connected to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and calling for an independent investigation into Epstein’s associates and the Justice Department’s handling of relevant records.
The report, released by Rep. Jamie Raskin, the committee’s ranking Democrat, said five women directly accused Trump of rape or sexual assault in Epstein’s company or presence.
It also describes accounts from other women who alleged that the late Epstein or his longtime associate Ghislaine Maxwell – also convicted of sexual crimes – attempted to introduce or direct them to Trump.
Drawing on survivor accounts, interviews conducted by committee staff, FBI records and documents released under the 2025 Epstein Files Transparency Act, the report examines alleged connections among Trump, Epstein, and Paolo Zampolli, who until recently served as a senior Trump administration official and diplomat.
The report argues that the available evidence warrants investigating whether Trump and Zampolli were involved in Epstein’s trafficking and abuse network during the 1990s. That potential involvement remains an allegation, not an established legal finding.
"Donald Trump says he knew Jeffrey Epstein ‘just like everybody in Palm Beach knew him.’ Not exactly,” Raskin said in a statement accompanying the report, referring to Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida.
“Evidence involving 11 women tells a completely different and far more damning story about their relationship and the abuse of young women and girls that took place in their network," he added.
Raskin accused the Justice Department of withholding evidence and limiting inquiries into Epstein’s possible accomplices.
Raskin called for an independent special counsel to investigate the allegations and ensure that state and foreign prosecutors have access to relevant evidence.
"The women who survived Epstein deserve to be heard, Congress must have the complete files required by law, and an independent special counsel must investigate Epstein’s co-conspirators and DOJ’s (Justice Department) cover-up and ensure that state and foreign prosecutors have the evidence they need to pursue justice,” he said.
Epstein was found dead in his New York jail cell on Aug. 10, 2019, while awaiting trial on charges of sexually abusing and trafficking underage girls.
Released case files named prominent figures, including Donald Trump, Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, and the former Prince Andrew, though being named does not establish wrongdoing.

US Democrats prepare for investigation into Trump-Putin diesel deal
Democrats in the US Congress are demanding that major banks and ports preserve documents relating to transactions involving Russian diesel, as they prepare for a possible investigation into Donald Trump's arrangements with Moscow.
Source: Axios
Details: A letter dated 24 October was sent to six major banks, including JPMorgan, Bank of America and Goldman Sachs, as well as the port authorities of Texas and New York.
The lawmakers are asking them to preserve contracts, shipping documents, vessel records and correspondence with suppliers, intermediaries and US officials. They expect confirmation by Wednesday 28 October.
An investigation will become a priority for Democrats if they regain control of one or both chambers of Congress after the 3 November elections.
The initiative is being led by Senator Jeanne Shaheen. Republican Senator Thom Tillis also signed the letter.
The lawmakers are questioning the legality of the imports and warning that they could help finance Russia's war against Ukraine. The US Treasury Department considers the arrangements legal, while the White House has accused Democrats of focusing on investigations into Trump.
Background:
- In October, Trump suspended the enforcement of some sanctions and tariffs against Russia that conflicted with his plans to bring Russian diesel to global markets.
- On 26 October, Reuters reported that Russian refineries had begun increasing diesel production after receiving export quotas.

18:36:00 UTC
03:36:00 KST

The 2026 midterm elections in the United States represent a consequential juncture in the evolution of the U.S.-led international order and, by extension, Australia’s strategic environment. Their significance lies not merely in the redistribution of legislative power in Washington, but in what the electoral outcome may reveal about the durability of President Donald Trump’s political mandate, the institutional constraints on executive authority, and the future trajectory of U.S. engagement with its allies.
For Australia, the implications are particularly profound. Its post-war strategic posture has rested on the assumption that U.S. military predominance, institutional continuity, and alliance commitments will provide an enduring foundation for national security. However, as the last two years reveal, the contemporary United States presents a more complex proposition. It remains inextricably linked to Australian security, while its domestic political polarization, transactional approach to alliances, and increasingly protectionist economic orientation have introduced significant uncertainty into the strategic calculus of middle powers.
The consequences of the midterms must therefore be assessed through three interrelated dimensions: the domestic institutional constraints they may impose on the Trump administration, the implications for the credibility of U.S. strategic commitments in the Indo-Pacific, and the extent to which changes in U.S. trade and industrial policy may affect Australia’s economic sovereignty.
The Congressional Balance of Power and U.S. Policy Continuity
The U.S. midterm elections determine the composition of the House of Representatives and a portion of the Senate, thereby influencing the legislative environment within which a president exercises executive authority. Their effects, however, extend beyond the immediate capacity to enact legislation. They can alter congressional oversight, appropriations, appointments, policy implementation, and the political incentives governing presidential conduct. A strengthened Republican congressional majority would potentially consolidate Trump’s capacity to pursue an agenda centered on economic nationalism, immigration enforcement, industrial protection, and a more explicitly transactional conception of international relations.
For Australia, the implications would be ambiguous. Greater legislative alignment could facilitate the implementation of U.S. defense and industrial initiatives, but at the same time could equally reinforce policies that subordinate alliance management to narrowly defined domestic economic interests.
In particular, a congressional majority sympathetic to protectionism could legitimize further restrictions on international trade, including measures affecting allied economies. Canberra’s diplomatic relationship with Washington would not necessarily insulate it from such pressures. Indeed, the fundamental tension between strategic partnership and economic nationalism may become more pronounced precisely because Australia is both a close security ally and an independent trading nation.
On the other hand, a Democratic victory in either chamber would produce a different, although not necessarily more predictable, policy environment. Legislative resistance and intensified oversight could constrain the administration’s capacity to enact its domestic program. Nevertheless, congressional opposition would not automatically reverse executive trade measures, eliminate presidential discretion in foreign affairs, or restore the policy assumptions associated with earlier administrations. Here, a divided government may generate policy instability rather than moderation, particularly where disputes over appropriations, executive authority, and national security priorities impede coherent long-term planning.
For Canberra, the critical variable is therefore not simply which party controls Congress, but whether the electoral outcome increases or diminishes the predictability of U.S. statecraft. In this regard, Australia should not merely equate Republican control with strategic reliability or Democratic control with international engagement. Both parties operate within a political environment increasingly shaped by strategic competition with China, an overstretched U.S. foreign policy, concerns about domestic industrial capacity, and demands for a more equitable distribution of alliance costs. These structural pressures will only persist beyond the 2026 electoral cycle.
AUKUS and the Problem of Strategic Continuity
As has been well documented, the AUKUS partnership represents perhaps the clearest expression of Australia’s dependence on sustained American strategic commitment. Its submarine pathway and its Pillar II advanced technology initiatives are designed to strengthen deterrence, improve interoperability, and reinforce the capacity of the United States and its partners to respond to an increasingly contested Indo-Pacific.
At the same time, however, AUKUS also exposes an inherent asymmetry in Australia’s strategic position. The program requires decades of investment, complex industrial coordination, technological integration, and political continuity, whereas the U.S. political system operates through short electoral cycles and increasingly polarized partisan competition. The durability and cogency of the partnership therefore depends not simply on presidential support, but on sustained congressional appropriations, industrial capacity, and institutional commitment across successive administrations.
A change in congressional control could have vast material consequences even if formal support for AUKUS remains intact. Congressional scrutiny of submarine production schedules, shipyard capacity, workforce availability, technology transfers, and the allocation of U.S. defense resources could affect the program’s implementation. Such scrutiny would not necessarily constitute opposition to Australia; it might instead reflect legitimate concerns about whether the United States possesses the industrial capacity, not to mention political will, to fulfill its commitments while meeting its own naval requirements.
The broader implication is that Australia must distinguish between the durability of the alliance as a strategic concept and the reliability of particular programs as instruments of policy. Canberra should pursue bipartisan institutional engagement, demonstrating that AUKUS strengthens U.S. security, supports defense sector employment, and contributes to regional stability.
Equally important is the development of domestic defense-industrial capacity and capabilities that reduce Australia’s vulnerability to delays in U.S. production. The objective should not be strategic self-sufficiency, which is neither feasible nor necessarily desirable, but greater strategic resilience.
Trade Protectionism and Australia’s Economic Vulnerability
The economic reverberations of the midterms may also prove as consequential as their strategic implications. The defining tension in the Australia-U.S. relationship is the coexistence of deep security integration with an increasingly contested economic relationship. Whereas the alliance is premised on mutual strategic advantage, U.S. trade policy under Trump 2.0 has increasingly reflected the proposition that international economic relationships should be evaluated through their contribution to domestic production, employment, and national bargaining power.
For Australia, this creates a structural vulnerability. The United States is concurrently a security guarantor, a major source of investment and technology, and an economy whose trade policies can impose costs on close partners. Australian exporters may therefore find themselves exposed to policy decisions driven less by bilateral diplomatic considerations than by U.S. domestic political imperatives.
A Republican electoral victory could strengthen the political legitimacy of protectionist measures, although it would not necessarily produce a uniform escalation of tariffs. Conversely, Democratic gains could increase scrutiny of the administration’s economic policies without fundamentally displacing the bipartisan turn toward industrial protection and strategic supply chain security. The U.S. emphasis on domestic manufacturing, technological sovereignty, and reducing dependence on Chinese supply chains is not exclusively a Trump phenomenon; it reflects a broader reassessment of the relationship between economic interdependence and national security.
Australia must consequently resist the assumption that favorable diplomatic relations will reliably translate into preferential economic treatment. In this regard, critical minerals, energy, advanced materials, and defense-related technologies offer opportunities for cooperation, provided that agreements deliver commercially sustainable outcomes rather than merely political symbolism. Equally, diversification should not be understood as a retreat from the U.S. relationship. It is a means of reducing the economic costs associated with policy volatility and strengthening Australia’s bargaining position within the alliance.
China and the Strategic Balance in the Indo-Pacific
The regional outcomes of the midterms extend beyond the bilateral alliance. Australia’s strategic domain is defined by the interface between U.S. power, Chinese ambitions, and the calculations of regional states seeking to preserve autonomy amid intensifying great power competition.
A politically strengthened Trump administration might adopt a more assertive posture toward China, particularly in areas involving military deterrence, technological competition, and economic security. Such an approach could align with Australia’s concern about coercion and the deterioration of the regional balance of power.
Nonetheless, greater rhetorical or economic confrontation should not automatically be interpreted as a strengthening of regional security. As has already been evident across the last two years, a more transactional U.S. foreign policy has engendered uncertainty about the circumstances in which Washington is willing to support its partners, the conditions attached to that support, and the relative priority assigned to different theaters.
Alternatively, a Democratic-controlled Congress might seek greater oversight of the administration’s foreign policy, potentially reinforcing institutional scrutiny, and encouraging more deliberate consultation with allies. Still, partisan conflict could also undermine the coherence of U.S. external engagement, particularly if disputes over appropriations or executive authority hinder policy implementation.
For Australia, the central issue is credibility rather than electoral ideology. Deterrence depends not only on military capabilities but also on an adversary’s assessment of political resolve, alliance cohesion, and the likelihood that commitments will be honored under pressure. Canberra must therefore evaluate concrete indicators, including defense appropriations, force posture, operational coordination, diplomatic consultation, and the implementation of agreed commitments, rather than treating U.S. domestic politics as a reliable proxy for strategic behavior.
At the same time, Canberra must recognize that its interests are not identical to Washington’s. Its prosperity and security depend on maintaining a stable regional order, functioning economic relationships, and effective diplomatic channels. An escalation in China-U.S. confrontation could impose substantial costs on Australia even where the underlying U.S. objective is strategically defensible. The appropriate response is neither unconditional alignment nor strategic equidistance, but calibrated alliance management that combines credible defense cooperation with independent assessment of Australian interests and sustained regional diplomacy.
Strategic Autonomy and Australia’s Policy Response
The midterms raise a more fundamental question concerning Australian strategic autonomy. For decades, Australian governments have sought to reconcile dependence on U.S. military power with the economic importance of Asia, particularly China. This balancing act has become more difficult as strategic competition increasingly encompasses trade, technology, infrastructure, energy, and supply chain security.
A politically weakened Trump administration might become more unpredictable as it seeks to demonstrate presidential authority or mobilize domestic support. Alternatively, a congressional opposition could constrain certain initiatives and encourage greater scrutiny of executive decisions. Neither outcome necessarily implies a more conciliatory U.S. approach toward China. The danger for Australia is that domestic political conflict in the United States could produce abrupt policy changes, leaving regional partners to absorb the resulting uncertainty.
Here, Canberra should therefore invest in regional institutions, practical economic cooperation, and sustained diplomatic engagement with Southeast Asia and the Pacific. These relationships cannot substitute for the U.S. alliance, but they can strengthen Australia’s influence and reduce the extent to which its regional position depends on decisions made in Washington.
Strategic autonomy should not be confused with equidistance between the United States and China, nor does it require Australia to abandon its longstanding security commitments. Rather, it denotes the capacity to make independent judgments, maintain credible national capabilities, and preserve diplomatic options when allied preferences and Australian interests do not perfectly coincide. The objective is to transform dependence into managed interdependence: retaining the advantages of U.S. security cooperation while ensuring that Australia possesses sufficient economic, diplomatic, and military capacity to navigate periods of uncertainty.
Conclusion: “Sing Me Songs of No Denying”
The ramifications of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections for Australia will depend on the interaction between congressional control, presidential authority, and the deeper structural changes reshaping U.S. domestic and international policy. A Republican victory could consolidate Trump’s political agenda, while Democratic gains could constrain his legislative ambitions and intensify congressional oversight. Neither outcome, however, should be interpreted as a definitive resolution of the uncertainties and concerns confronting the Australia-U.S. relationship.
The more resultant development is the possibility that U.S. policy volatility has become a persistent feature of the strategic environment rather than a temporary consequence of one administration. For Australia, this will necessitate a recalibration of assumptions about alliance management, economic interdependence, and national security.
The appropriate response is neither to distance Australia from the United States nor to assume that historical ties guarantee future consistency. It is to pursue a mature alliance strategy grounded in institutional engagement, reciprocal contributions, and independent national capacity. Ultimately, Australia’s security will depend not simply on who controls Congress, but on its capacity to operate effectively in an international system where U.S. power still remains prevalent, but overstretched and increasingly difficult to predict. The midterms should therefore be understood as a test of Australia’s preparedness and capacity to adapt to a more volatile era of U.S. leadership.

Hind Rajab Foundation files UK criminal complaint against Israeli soldier over Gaza war crimes

The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has filed a criminal complaint with UK authorities against Israeli soldier Lidor Dafna over alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide committed in the Gaza Strip, Anadolu reports.
The foundation said in a statement Sunday that Dafna, a reservist serving as a D9 armored bulldozer operator in the 603rd Combat Engineering Battalion of the 7th Armored Brigade, participated in military operations in Gaza and Lebanon from November 2023 onward.
The foundation said it has reason to believe he is currently in the UK.
The complaint focuses on the destruction of Great Ocean Mills, an industrial flour-producing facility in the Morag Corridor between Khan Younis and Rafah, on May 25, 2025.
According to the foundation, footage posted by Dafna on social media shows a bulldozer demolishing the facility’s wheat silos.
The foundation said Israeli forces subsequently occupied the building, converted it into a military base and reportedly used it to shoot Palestinians seeking food aid at a nearby Gaza Humanitarian Foundation site.
The foundation said the destruction occurred when Israel had sealed Gaza to food, fuel and medicine, with flour reportedly selling for as much as $70 per kilogram and half a million people facing starvation.
The foundation also said that the 603rd Battalion carried out more than 60 controlled demolitions of buildings, including mosques and residential blocks, and contributed to widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure and agricultural land during the establishment of the Morag Corridor.
READ: Rights group urges US to arrest Israeli commander linked to Hind Rajab’s killing
The foundation said its investigation indicates that Dafna may be criminally responsible for extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity, intentionally targeting civilian objects, using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare, extermination as a crime against humanity and genocide.
The foundation called on British authorities to open an investigation, arrest and question Dafna, citing Article 146 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which requires states to search for individuals alleged to have committed grave breaches of the convention.
Dyab Abou Jahjah, the foundation’s director general, said: “Lidor Dafna filmed himself destroying one of the last remaining food production facilities serving a starving population, then posted the footage on social media as a trophy.”
“The United Kingdom now faces a simple test: will it arrest and prosecute a man, who remains an active soldier of an army carrying out such crimes, or once again permit a perpetrator of genocide to walk freely on its soil and return to Gaza to continue committing his crimes?” he added.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Israel votes Tuesday in closely contested election as Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:34:36 UTC
03:34:36 KST

Israelis head to the polls Tuesday in a closely contested parliamentary election that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's long rule or leave the country facing another political deadlock, with neither major bloc projected to secure a governing majority.
The vote will be Israel's first general election since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the subsequent Israeli offensive on the Gaza Strip, as well as military confrontations with Lebanon and Iran.
It will also be the first Israeli general election held on schedule since 1988, following decades in which successive governments collapsed before completing their four-year terms.
Around 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, including approximately 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Voting will take place at 12,018 polling stations, with approximately 18,000 ballot boxes deployed nationwide.
Most polling stations will open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 10 pm (2000GMT). Election day is a public holiday.
Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing for seats in the 120-member Knesset, where a governing coalition requires the support of at least 61 lawmakers.
Under Israel's proportional representation system, voters choose parties rather than individual candidates. Parties must secure at least 3.25% of valid votes to enter parliament.
No party has ever won an outright Knesset majority, making coalition negotiations decisive in determining who becomes prime minister.
Final surveys published by Israel's three main television broadcasters put former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party narrowly ahead of Netanyahu's Likud.
Yashar is projected to win 22 to 23 seats, compared with 19 to 21 for Likud.
The B'Yachad, or Together, alliance led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid is projected to finish third with 14 or 15 seats.
Other opposition parties include the Democrats, led by former general Yair Golan, and former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beytenu.
The three surveys project Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc winning 50 seats, while the opposition bloc is forecast to secure between 52 and 56.
Palestinian-led parties are projected to win a combined 14 to 16 seats.
The figures suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government.
Winning the largest number of seats does not automatically determine who becomes prime minister.
President Isaac Herzog will consult the elected parties before assigning the task of forming a government to the lawmaker considered most likely to command a parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu, 77, is seeking another term after serving as prime minister for more than 18 years across three separate periods.
His campaign has focused heavily on national security, portraying his experience and military policies as essential to confronting regional threats.
However, he faces criticism over his government's failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attacks, its handling of subsequent conflicts and its opposition to establishing an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures.
Netanyahu is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies, and faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
His potential coalition partners include far-right parties led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, alongside the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have advocated expanding illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, rejected Palestinian statehood and encouraged Palestinians to leave Gaza.
The ultra-Orthodox parties have meanwhile faced mounting criticism over demands to preserve military-service exemptions for religious students as the Israeli military struggles with personnel shortages after years of conflict.
Eisenkot, 66, served as chief of the Israeli military from 2015 to 2019 and joined Netanyahu's emergency government following the Oct. 7 attacks.
He later left the government after criticizing Netanyahu's management of the Gaza offensive and the absence of a clear political strategy.
His son was killed while serving with the Israeli military in Gaza in December 2023.
Eisenkot has campaigned on government accountability, political stability and restoring public confidence in state institutions.
He supports establishing an official inquiry into the Oct. 7 security failures and ending broad military-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men.
Despite positioning himself as an alternative to Netanyahu, Eisenkot maintains similar positions on several major security issues.
He opposes establishing a fully sovereign Palestinian state under current conditions and says Hamas' military capabilities and rule in Gaza must be dismantled.
The election therefore presents voters with competing approaches to leadership, governance, judicial independence and relations with far-right parties, even as the two leading candidates share positions on key security issues.
The Joint List and Ra'am, the principal parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, could play a decisive role if neither major bloc secures 61 seats.
Polls project the Joint List winning around nine seats and Ra'am securing between five and seven.
An Eisenkot-led government could require support from one or both Palestinian-led parties, either through formal coalition participation or outside parliamentary backing.
Such an arrangement would face political obstacles.
Lieberman has rejected joining a government dependent on Palestinian-led parties, while other opposition figures have been reluctant to commit to such an agreement.
Netanyahu has repeatedly invoked the possibility of Palestinian-led parties influencing the next government to mobilize right-wing voters.
Several possible outcomes could emerge from Tuesday's vote.
Netanyahu could form another government if his bloc secures enough additional seats or attracts lawmakers from outside his existing alliance.
An Eisenkot-led coalition would likely depend on an agreement involving Palestinian-led parties, defections from other camps or difficult compromises among ideologically divided opposition leaders.
A unity government involving Likud and major opposition parties is another possible arrangement, although Eisenkot and several allies have ruled out serving under Netanyahu.
If neither side assembles a majority, Netanyahu could remain caretaker prime minister during prolonged coalition negotiations, potentially leading to another election.
The performance of smaller parties polling near the 3.25% electoral threshold could prove decisive. Parties that fail to meet the threshold win no seats, potentially weakening their political allies and shifting the balance of power between the competing blocs.
Exit polls are expected immediately after voting ends at 10 pm local time Tuesday.
Initial official results will begin emerging overnight, although counting ballots from military personnel, hospitals, prisons and other special voting arrangements could take several days.
Official results are scheduled to be published by Nov. 4, after which coalition negotiations could continue for weeks.

Netherlands readies its army for large-scale conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:33:38 UTC
03:33:38 KST

- The Netherlands will buy more CV90 infantry fighting vehicles, bridge-laying tanks and a replacement for its Kodiak breaching vehicle, the defense ministry said.
- Germany’s FFG will supply ACSV tracked support vehicles and Wisent 2 recovery vehicles, but quantities and costs were not disclosed.
The Netherlands will buy more CV90 infantry fighting vehicles, additional bridge-laying tanks, a replacement for its unreliable Kodiak combat engineer vehicle, and new tracked support and heavy recovery vehicles from Germany’s FFG, Dutch State Secretary for Defense Derk Boswijk told parliament in a letter on Oct. 26, the Dutch Ministry of Defense said.
The ministry did not disclose how many vehicles it will buy, what the package will cost, or when deliveries will begin, but said the equipment will mainly go to the Royal Netherlands Army’s heavy and medium infantry brigades as the army prepares for a possible large-scale conflict.
The new CV90s will equip an armored infantry battalion that has yet to be formed and will be based at the Nassau-Dietz Barracks in Budel, in the south of the country. The Netherlands is buying them through a joint program led by Sweden, home of CV90 maker BAE Systems Hägglunds, together with Estonia, Finland, Lithuania and Norway, which the ministry said will speed up deliveries. The Dutch army already operates 122 CV90s, which are going through a mid-life upgrade valued at about $500 million.
The ministry said the army’s current breaching vehicle, the Leopard 2-based Kodiak, is outdated and not protected well enough against current and future threats, and that breakdowns and failures have limited how often it can be used. Its replacement will need to clear heavy defensive lines, minefields, walls and other obstacles so tanks and infantry can push through, a task that proved costly for both sides in Ukraine, where dense minefields stalled armored assaults. The ministry did not name the replacement.
The Netherlands is also buying more bridge-laying tanks, which carry folding bridges to span rivers and other gaps, and will probably join an existing German contract to get them.
From FFG Flensburger Fahrzeugbau Gesellschaft, the Dutch army will receive the Armoured Combat Support Vehicle, or ACSV, a tracked support vehicle already used by the Norwegian army, in several versions including an ambulance, command post, minelayer and driver training vehicle. FFG will also supply the Wisent 2, a heavy armored recovery vehicle built on the Leopard 2 chassis that can tow and lift damaged or stranded tanks and armored vehicles. The army currently has 25 older Bergepanzer 3 recovery vehicles, a fleet the ministry has said is too small for the planned expansion of its armored forces, which includes newly ordered Leopard 2A8 tanks, Defence24 reported in March.
Dutch companies will take a large share of the work. Van Halteren Technologies will assemble the ACSV and the Wisent 2 recovery vehicles in the Netherlands and maintain them, while KONI Nederland and Neways Electronics will supply parts and Avient Protective Materials will provide high-strength fibers for the ACSV’s ballistic protection.

Halis Sunnetci
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Trabzonspor overturned a two-goal deficit to secure a dramatic 4-3 away victory over Rizespor in the Turkish Super Lig on Monday, extending their winning streak to six matches across all competitions.
The visitors trailed 2-0 at halftime in the Black Sea derby but scored three goals in nine minutes after the break before Franculino struck a late winner to complete his brace.
Rizespor took the lead in the 12th minute when Mithat Pala delivered a low cross from the right flank, allowing Gennaro Borrelli to control the ball and finish from close range for his first goal for the club.
The Italian striker doubled the hosts' advantage in the 32nd minute, converting a low pass from Adedire Awokoya Mebude following a swift counterattack.
However, Trabzonspor emerged strongly after halftime, pulling one back in the 49th minute through Melih Kabasakal, who tapped into an empty net after Ernest Muci's pass.
Just two minutes later, Aral Simsir equalized with a delicate first-time lob over goalkeeper Yahia Fofana after being played through by Muci.
Trabzonspor completed their comeback in the 58th minute when Fofana parried Muci's effort into the path of Franculino, who converted the rebound from close range.
Rizespor responded in the 69th minute as Qazim Laci unleashed a powerful strike from nearly 30 yards, with the ball hitting the post before finding the top corner to make it 3-3.
But Franculino had the final say in the 84th minute, collecting a long pass from Muci before driving into the penalty area and firing a powerful shot into the top corner.
Muci played a key role in Trabzonspor's comeback, setting up three goals, including Franculino's late winner.
The victory extended Trabzonspor's winning streak under head coach Thomas Reis to six competitive matches and lifted the Black Sea side to second place with 19 points after nine league matches.
Rizespor remained 13th in the standings with 10 points.
 
Besiktas beat Basaksehir 2-0
In another ninth-round fixture, Besiktas secured a 2-0 home victory over Istanbul Basaksehir thanks to second-half goals from Oh Hyeon-gyu and Junior Olaitan.
The hosts came close to breaking the deadlock in the 17th minute when Dusan Vlahovic's header struck the crossbar following Wilfred Ndidi's cross.
After a goalless first half, substitute Oh put Besiktas ahead in the 76th minute, capitalizing on Hamza Gureler's failed clearance before rounding goalkeeper Muhammed Sengezer and slotting into an empty net.
Olaitan sealed the victory in the 89th minute, collecting a loose clearance from Emin Bayram following Leandro Trossard's low cross and firing a powerful shot into the top corner.
The result lifted Besiktas to fourth place with 18 points, while Basaksehir remained 12th with 11 points.

A woman living in Nigeria who was infected with the Ebola virus and her spouse, a Swiss diplomat, have been admitted to hospitals in Switzerland after they were flown in from Nigeria on Monday, Swiss authorities said.
The man was admitted to the University Hospital Zurich, while his wife was taken for treatment at the Geneva University Hospital, the Canton of Geneva said.
"This situation does not pose any risk to public health in Switzerland," the Swiss government said in a statement.
The patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is Nigeria's first Ebola case in more than a decade.
The outbreak, which started in Democratic Republic of Congo, has now been reported in four countries in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
WHO, Switzerland, Africa's top health agency says patient contracted Ebola in Uganda, Uganda denies
The patient arrived in Nigeria after spending two weeks in Uganda, raising concerns over potential transmission in a country that was declared Ebola free in August.
Ugandan officials claimed that the patient had recently been in the DRC, where the outbreak is still spreading, but the World Health Organization and Africa's top health agency said on Thursday that they had not received confirmed information that the woman had traveled there.
The Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs had on Thursday told Reuters that the woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling in Uganda.
Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases and that if it did, it would make that information public.

Israel’s 'hasbara' overhaul raises questions over who is in charge - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:32:44 UTC
03:32:44 KST

On Sunday, July 12, a debate took place in the Knesset on a subject that the parliament rarely discusses: the work of the National Public Diplomacy Directorate; in other words, Israel’s hasbara.
The Knesset’s own account of the debate conceded that it was occurring “after years of instability.” That was the least of the fundamental, indeed institutional, problems revealed.
Eden Bar Tal, director-general of the Foreign Ministry, openly admitted to the committee that, until the end of 2024, public diplomacy had scarcely featured in the ministry’s mission. Its concerns had historically been “almost solely diplomatic.”
Only from the end of 2025, in accordance with a permanent government resolution, did communications and public diplomacy acquire priority. “Public diplomacy,” Bar Tal declared, “is now the main role of the Foreign Ministry.”
The change in government policy was backed by a dramatic budget increase. “In previous years, public diplomacy activity amounted to NIS 25 million-NIS 27 million per year for the Foreign Ministry throughout the world,” Bar Tal revealed. “In effect, it was zero resources. Today, the budget that was set amounts to about NIS 1.2 billion.”
This extraordinary turnaround is almost certainly due to the appointment in April, shortly after completing her five-year term as Israel’s ambassador to the UK, of Tzipi Hotovely as head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate. In the few months she has held office, she has been heavily involved in rebuilding the organization she inherited, as well as actively mounting two vitally important promotional campaigns.
She told the Knesset committee that on taking up her post she had discovered substantial organizational problems. “I want to say directly and candidly that I discovered great difficulties,” she said, “but we are rebuilding the directorate.”
However, merely reconstructing the directorate that Hotovely now heads, essential as that is, may not create the well-functioning and effective national hasbara operation the nation urgently requires. It is the overall organizational set-up that seems problematic.
For example, two distinct bodies within the Israeli administration are rendered in English as “Public Diplomacy Directorate.” The National Public Diplomacy Directorate, headed by Hotovely, sits in the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). Its name in Hebrew includes hasbara.
The Foreign Ministry’s Public Diplomacy Department is a separate unit within that ministry. The word “National” is attached only to Hotovely’s unit.
Her organization is charged with setting and coordinating public diplomacy policy right across government, including the Foreign Ministry, the IDF, the intelligence agencies, the police, and the Government Press Office.
The Foreign Ministry, on the other hand, which operates its own Public Diplomacy Department, conducts Israel’s diplomacy abroad, supports Israeli embassies, manages media relations and digital outreach, promotes cultural and scientific cooperation, and relations with Jewish communities.
Moreover, as Bar Tal informed the Knesset committee, it is the Foreign Ministry that administers the principal public diplomacy budget.
Since the two bodies operate in the same broad policy field, questions must arise about the boundaries between their respective responsibilities.
How is this arrangement, which looks like a recipe for operational confusion and inter-departmental rivalry, meant to operate?
The current relationship is best described as coordination rather than command. Hotovely’s National Directorate is a senior-level coordinating body operating from within the PMO, while the Foreign Ministry is both a participant in that coordination and an implementing ministry with its own overseas public diplomacy apparatus.
In practice, the National Directorate convenes a national public diplomacy forum bringing together representatives from across government. The Foreign Ministry’s Public Diplomacy Department then translates policy into work carried out through embassies and consulates, such as press engagement, digital diplomacy, branding, briefings, cultural and scientific diplomacy, and responses to hostile narratives such as Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) campaigns.
The arrangement is not necessarily dysfunctional, since national coordination and diplomatic implementation can be complementary functions. But the arrangement strikes an outside observer as fragmented and lacking a clear management structure.
Is this division of labor supported by sufficiently clear lines of authority? If not, there is the risk of duplication, competing priorities and uncertainty over accountability.
In “rebuilding” her directorate, Hotovely will certainly have in mind the potential problems posed by the current set-up.
Meanwhile, she has not allowed the grass to grow under her feet. In September, she mounted a major publicity campaign in New York ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the UN General Assembly.
Around 500 billboards and dozens of trucks with digital screens were deployed, alongside online promotion. The messaging focused on Iran’s security threat, the US-Israel partnership, and the argument that Israel and the US were defending the free world.
In October, Hotovely was heavily engaged in promoting a film that countered the anti-Israel messages in the film NAZA, which claimed that the collateral death toll in the Israel-Hamas war was deliberate and institutionalized Israeli military policy. The film won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.
Hotovely presented certificates of appreciation to the creators of NAZA – The Real Story, a film featuring Israeli military personnel’s testimony, and intended to rebut accusations concerning the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza.
The film was available free online, and on October 14 the Algemeiner reported “it has already been viewed more than 43 million times, according to the site.”
Eylon Levy, a former spokesperson in the National Public Diplomacy Directorate, spoke to the Knesset committee in July.
'Waging a delegitimization campaign against us'
“Regrettably, in the past few years, our enemies have been playing on an empty field,” he said. “The most prestigious organizations around the world are waging a delegitimization campaign against us, aimed at persuading normative people that we deserve to be destroyed, but we aren’t returning fire.”
Hotovely is supremely well-qualified for the job she has taken on. Her career has combined domestic Israeli politics, diplomacy, and public advocacy abroad, and the Israeli cabinet unanimously approved her appointment. If anyone can construct the effective hasbara operation that Israel so desperately needs, it is Hotovely.
Whatever the political hue of the government that emerges as a result of this week’s election, the nation would be well served if she remains in post.
The writer, a former senior civil servant, is the Middle East correspondent for Eurasia Review. Follow him at: www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com
