Young men open up about looksmaxxing, toxic influencers and being a good man
It seems like the manosphere is lurking behind every corner.
From alarming headlines to documentary deep dives, what was once a fringe ideology has come full thrust into the mainstream.
And with young men shown toxic content within 23 minutes of creating a social media account, it's becoming an inescapable part of growing up in the internet age.
We asked young men what they're seeing online and how it's shaping their concept of masculinity.
Jak, 18, Melbourne
For me, it started with workout videos. It was generic stuff, like encouraging men to go to the gym, showing them proper form, that kind of thing.
Typically, you'd see a video of a guy, shirtless, ripped, big muscles, with electronic music playing in the background, saying, "You need to go to the gym. You need to lock in. You need to be strong and become the man you should be."
At first I thought, "Hell yeah." The message seemed to be that you need discipline and strength.
But I realised that the main idea is often that you're not good enough in various ways, and in order to be better you have to do X, Y and Z.
Over time, my algorithm became filled with people pushing peptides and steroids. Any influencer I watched long enough eventually started selling a course, supplements, or some kind of product.
A lot of it was saying that if you get big muscles you'll get women, and if women don't want you after you've built your body, then they're stupid.
I never tried to seek out the misogynistic side of these videos; it just came to me.
I was just thinking, "How did I go from gym videos to this?"
A lot of this content paints the idea that the world is out to get men, and I think some of that has bled into the real world.
Things that wouldn't have seemed normal before now feel normalised.
A couple of years ago, making fun of women wasn't really OK. Now you can be watching videos with friends, and if a woman starts speaking, someone says, "Shut up," and everyone laughs.
Recently, I worked on a Year 12 project about the manosphere. I learned a lot about how it can affect your mental wellbeing without you even realising.
Since doing that project, I've hopped off most social media.
At first, my friends thought I'd died. Then everyone thought I was crazy. A lot of people wanted to know what I actually do with my time.
But since leaving social media, I've just spent more time doing things I actually enjoy. I feel more confident and more present.
I wish people understood that no young man goes online intending to become misogynistic. A lot of it happens subconsciously and over a long period of time.
The core ideas are usually self-improvement — the ideas themselves are positive.
It's the way those ideas get twisted that becomes harmful.
Noah, 18, Canberra
I spend a lot of time on Instagram. I'm somewhat of an influencer — I post a lot of short films and stuff, and I teach people how to make them. I've gained a bit of a following, about 40,000 followers across platforms.
On social media, I'm drawn to a lot of political stuff. I'm very involved with current affairs and politics. I love watching big debates on YouTube.
I don't support manosphere content, but I pay attention to it because I think it's an important topic.
Regardless of whether you like it or not, it's going to be in your feed. It's not something you can ignore.
I first started doing content through the gym, so I understand how insecurity builds and how body dysmorphia presents. I feel like a lot of what the manosphere does is create insecurity, then try to sell a fix.
In my content, I make a conscious effort to show all sides of myself because I know everyone puts on a facade online. I'm guilty of it sometimes — I tend to show the good things rather than the bad — but I do post a lot of stuff that's more raw than other people.
In my friend group, we're very against the manosphere — we know that it's not an accurate reflection — but it has affected us. I know I had more drive to make money once I saw these influencers posting online saying, "You'll never get a girlfriend if you don't have money."
Status is another pressure I feel, especially with social media. Everything's about followers. If I post a video that doesn't do well or doesn't get a certain number of followers or likes, I feel this sense of impending doom.
There's also the big looksmaxxing craze — I see a lot of that on Instagram.
I know people who buy courses from influencers online and do things to alter their face or take peptides to try to fix their skin or lose weight. I've got friends who aren't very tall and they'll fold up socks and put them in their shoes to raise their height because they feel so insecure.
It feels like looks, money and status are the three pillars of being a man. In the world of social media, you can post and pretend you have all these traits, but none of it's real.
I think it's easy to be a decent person but hard to be a man.
The definition is changing a lot; what a man was 50 years ago compared to now is very different.
My idea of how to be a man changes a lot.
I want to get stronger, I want to look better, I want to make more money. There's pressure to do those things.
Then a lot of the time I think it doesn't matter.
I feel like you just need to ignore what a man is supposed to be and just try to be the best version of yourself.
Flynn, 24, Melbourne
Honestly, it felt like the flick of a switch. I'd never heard of Andrew Tate before but once I saw one video, I couldn't stop seeing them.
I was 20 at the time. All my friends were in the exact same demographic. We were talking about Tate, talking about different videos.
I think there was an element where we all recognised he was a bit extreme, but young men are often trying to make the darkest joke or say the most outrageous thing.
I'd always been passionate about filmmaking. I loved cameras and being on film when I was a kid, and I was pretty obsessed with becoming famous.
By Year 7, I was already editing videos; in Year 10, I tried vlogging. From there, it became skits, hot takes, opinion pieces and comedy.
The idea of being a content creator seemed exciting.
At first, my content was pretty harmless. I just enjoyed making funny videos and they generally got positive reactions.
Then I started consuming manosphere content. To me, it felt like being part of a cool club, like you understood something everyone else didn't.
It was all about "escaping the Matrix" and becoming an alpha male and a boss. It gave you a sense of belonging.
At the same time I was feeling frustrated. Not because I hated myself, but because I wasn't famous yet, I wasn't rich yet, I wasn't achieving all the things I felt I should be.
Around that time, my TikTok account started getting serious traction.
I posted some controversial videos that went viral. In one, I asked if it was OK to be a straight white male in Australia and went on a bit of a rant about women. It was probably one of the worst videos posted to TikTok that year.
The backlash was horrible – and rightfully so. It blew up internationally and got massive traction.
The irony is that it gave me exactly what I wanted, which was attention, fame, infamy, whatever you want to call it.
That made things worse because I doubled down. Every video of people responding to me reinforced my prejudice at the time and made me more bigoted and angry.
The sad thing is that I was always a pretty kind and compassionate kid. I grew up in a progressive household. Mum and Dad were very politically engaged, and my family had always taught me to treat people with respect.
It was the combination of anger, frustration, constant exposure to manosphere content and being mentally unwell.
Around that time, I had started cycling through periods of mania and depression. Eventually that developed into a psychosis and I was hospitalised for three weeks. I received a bipolar diagnosis.
It was this forced reset. I had nothing to do except get my medication sorted and get help.
I had a really great team around me: psychiatrists, psychologists, mental health professionals, supportive parents and an incredible friendship group.
Through time, maturity and a lot of conversations, I just got better. I eventually found my way back to who I originally was.
I'm 24 now and I don't get served any of that manosphere content anymore. Even if I did, I can engage with it objectively. It's not really a danger to me now.
But I don't know what it's like being 12 or 16 and seeing that stuff every day.
What I'd want young guys to know is that these influencers you're idolising and looking up to really aren't that cool.
If you want to get fit, healthy, disciplined and financially responsible, there are much better role models and communities for that; you don't need the manosphere to learn those things.
And honestly, being kind might sound lame, but it's actually one of the most important things you can be.
If you want to be anything, be kind.
Bodie, 27, Adelaide
I met a lot of my friends through online gaming.
I've always seen some of them as the "edgy" type, but after COVID things started to change.
People wanted something to blame for their problems, then Andrew Tate appeared.
The message became, "It's not your fault, it's women's fault."
People who felt disenfranchised suddenly had a major figure saying what they had been thinking all along.
Over time, my friends' attitudes gradually changed. They started making transphobic jokes, misogynistic jokes — the sort of "women should stay in the house" attitude.
Gamers will always get angry. I get angry too and swear sometimes. But I have absolutely no tolerance for that kind of manosphere culture because I think it genuinely harms people.
It was upsetting because these were people I'd spent years with. I've got autism and I was diagnosed with ADHD as a child, so I know what it's like to be targeted.
I'm not really a confrontational person, but I just thought, "I'm not dealing with these a**holes anymore". I left the server, and that was enough for them to block me and label me the bad guy.
What's sad is that some of the people I once called friends have turned into genuinely unpleasant people.
When I think about my former friends, I don't necessarily think they followed Andrew Tate directly, but they definitely followed that broader manosphere culture.
I think algorithms are a massive part of it. You watch one innocent video and suddenly you're sent down a pipeline.
The problem is that the manosphere deals in half-truths. These influencers give some genuinely useful advice, and then they use that credibility to push an ideology. That's how they hook people.
They see desperate young men as money bags; it's basically a get-rich-quick scheme. They give people a narrative, someone to blame, and that makes cruelty feel justified.
I look at my little brother. He's 14 now. He's a good kid, but I'm worried because kids are exposed to this stuff.
I'm always wondering what the best approach is, the best way pull him up on certain comments. I trust my dad to steer him in the right direction if he notices something concerning.
When you're young you think you have to be perfect. You think you can never be wrong.
But going through all this has made me more confident in who I am. I can see those patterns; I can recognise the grift immediately.
Now, the people I'm around are mostly people I work with. I spend my time with decent people, and they usually think similarly to me.
I'm not the most socially competent person, so I try to make up for that by making people smile.
I want to be someone that people feel safe around.
I want to be the kind of man people can look up to.

Top cyber spy braces for more AI-powered hacking attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Disruptions 'inevitable' as AI-powered cyber threats grow, Australian Signals Directorate says
In short:
The Australian Signals Directorate says more disruptions to essential services are likely as AI increases the risk of cyber attacks.
AI is turbocharging the number and potency of cyber threats Australia faces from criminal networks and state-aligned operators, the agency says.
The ASD has also revealed previously secret details of its offensive operations, including the targeting of criminals hoarding and selling personal data on the dark web.
Australia's top cyber spy is warning the country to prepare for more frequent disruptions to everyday services amid a surge of AI-powered cyber attacks.
Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) director-general Abigail Bradshaw said artificial intelligence frontier models had "redefined" the threat facing Australia.
"What is inevitable is that with each capability increase, we are likely to see more disruption," she said.
"Disruption can look like what we've seen over the last few weeks, with websites that require patching having to be taken down in order to be secured.
"Disruption could look like data breaches. Disruption could look like service disruption.
"Virtually any service that you rely on in your life today is enabled in some respect by a digital network."
The warning comes just days after a number of government websites, including the ASD's, were brought partially offline after vulnerabilities were found.
Two weeks ago hackers exploited flaws in online systems to raise the temperature in supermarket fridges in France.
Today the ASD is publishing its annual cyber threat report, which details a 20 per cent jump in cybersecurity incidents the agency was required to respond to last financial year.
But Ms Bradshaw said the defining event of the past year was the release of frontier models such as Anthropic's Mythos.
Models such as Mythos were touted as being too dangerous to release publicly due to their capability to find vulnerabilities in cyber defence systems.
A swarm of AI agents was responsible for breaching Australian health data security, in what was described as the first autonomous hack of a government website.
Ms Bradshaw said that incident led to a reworking of the relationship between agencies such as the ASD and the massive American companies at the forefront of the technology.
She said the ASD had worked "very quickly" to set up protocols to act as an "early warning system" with AI companies, including OpenAI.
"These protocols have been shared with all of the labs, and all of the Five Eyes [intelligence agencies]," she said.
"We now have an equal expectation about the sorts of things that agencies like ASD need to be engaged on ahead of model testing."
Dismantling dark web operators
Responding to cyber incidents makes up a large portion of the ASD's work, but the agency is also keen to talk up the success of its offensive operations.
It revealed details of a recent effort to take down criminal groups selling and operating a piece of malware known as Amadey.
Hidden inside free software, Amadey steals the personal data or login details of its victims and transmits it back to criminal groups, where it is then sold on the dark web.
The ASD said in one case, it was found hidden in a free, illegitimate version of Photoshop editing software.
It also found evidence of the software being sold on the dark web for about $US500 ($712).
ASD operators were able to access the back end of Amadey's operation and found the criminal network had access to 180,000 computers across the globe, including in Australia.
"The next steps that we took were to disconnect that Amadey controller from all those victims," ASD acting deputy director-general of intelligence Tauri Gregory said.
"And so, effectively, that cyber criminal can no longer access those 180,000 computers and no longer steal data from all those people.
"If ASD had not acted here, you'd have 180,000 businesses or individuals whose data was being stolen and be either sold on the dark web or monetised in other ways, or used to inform follow-on crimes such as fraud and identity theft."
In another case, the ASD was tipped off to the sale of 5 terabytes of data stolen from a business that was unaware it had been hacked.
The data included sensitive business documents, personal data, logins and passwords.
Mr Gregory said the agency was able to break in and destroy the data before it could be sold.
"To give some context, we think there are about 4.8 million files which were stolen from Australians, which we destroyed in that operation, as well as hundreds of thousands of files from other victims around the world," he said.
Mr Gregory said AI was increasing the scope and scale of attacks, but it was also an enormous asset to those trying to defend against them.
"We are using AI to generate software capabilities much more quickly, and so we use it to support our software engineering and development of new tools and capabilities directly," he said.
An accelerating threat
The agency has previously joined international partners in warning of Chinese-aligned actors building hidden networks of hijacked devices that can be used for espionage or offensive operations.
It has also warned that some state actors want to maintain access to essential services and infrastructure that could be disrupted if conflict were to break out.
Ms Bradshaw said strategic tensions in the region would increase that threat.
"The natural progression of this is, as the world becomes uncertain, of course nation states will try to reduce that uncertainty by obtaining more information," she said.
"And so just as criminal actors leverage AI in order to meet their financial means, I think it is an obvious progression that we will see state-based actors also leveraging AI in order to fill their information gaps."
Ms Bradshaw said there was a huge amount of work to do in both corporate and government systems to better prepare for and defend against cyber threats, particularly in replacing vulnerable "legacy" systems.
She said it also meant learning how to best use AI as a defensive tool.
"There is much more that we need to do and, in the current context, that is now a matter of urgency," Ms Bradshaw said.

Almost half of all comments on MPs' social media flagged as abusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Labor MPs turn to AI to combat online abuse as thousands of threats flagged
In short:
Social media companies are facing calls to take greater responsibility for online safety after new data exposed the extent of abuse aimed at politicians.
Almost 5,000 threats and violent comments were directed at a sample of 22 Labor MPs and senators trialling a new AI moderation tool in the past three months.
What's next?
MPs are demanding tech giants do more to tackle online abuse and threats.
Almost 5,000 threats and violent comments have been flagged on the social media accounts of 22 Labor politicians in just three months as MPs have turned to technology to combat online abuse.
New data from an AI tool being trialled by some senators and MPs has exposed the scale of hostility elected representatives face, with about half of the more than 460,000 comments analysed between July and October classified as abusive.
About 190,000 of the screened comments were personal attacks, with gender-based abuse, racism and transphobia the categories most commonly identified by an AI-powered plug-in, called Areto.
There were 2,497 threats and 2,487 comments using violent language, with examples including "someone shoot this dopey b***h" and "you need to be hung for treason".
In one post, an MP was called a "brain dead b***h", while in another comment a person said they "prefer assassinations".
Labor MPs using Areto told the ABC the tool protected both staff and community members, with abusive content clearly differentiated from genuine political criticism.
The safety of politicians has become a focus in the wake of the attack on Indi MP Helen Haines, for which the motive remains unknown.
Senior public servants have also warned that social media clips of various parliamentary committee hearings were fuelling abuse towards bureaucrats.
Abuse has 'chilling effect' on community
A few female Labor members began experimenting with Areto, which uses AI to identify and hide abusive and threatening comments, earlier this year before a trial was then extended to others in the caucus.
Analysis of the results for 22 parliamentarians using the tool in the past three months found high-profile accounts typically received more attacks, with one MP recording 57,522 abusive comments.
Facebook carried about 94 per cent of all comments, of which 51 per cent were abusive, compared with 42 per cent of the small number of comments on Instagram and 21 per cent of the comments on TikTok.
Finance and Women's Minister Katy Gallagher, who has started using Areto, said the volume of abuse online was "extraordinary".
"It is having a chilling effect on genuine community engagement," she said.
"For women, the abuse is usually sexualised, a lot about physical harm that will be done to you or your children."
Senator Gallagher said the automated AI tool was not filtering critical comments about the government or policy, but was giving her staff and others "respite" from abusive content.
"It's not a perfect solution, and I don't think anyone expects it to be, but the platforms themselves are not dealing with this," she said.
Minister told 'you're next' after Haines attack
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said the behaviour of the social media platforms was "pitiful", accusing them of prioritising profits over safety.
"These platforms are profiting off people treating each other with disrespect, anger, aggression and abuse. Then they play dumb at the devastating social effects that are happening across the country," she said.
Ms O'Neil said the fact that Areto existed was a "tragedy", but it was essential in helping to manage the mental health of her team.
"Female MPs shouldn't have to have a program that screens for death and rape threats, but that's where we are,"
she said.
Ms O'Neil said the majority of public interactions she had as an MP were respectful, but she sensed the "online environment is seeping into the way people behave in real life".
"No-one should feel sorry for us; that's not what this is about," she said.
"Politicians just happen to be in the public conversation right now, but it doesn't matter if you're an AFL footballer or a nurse working in a hospital, or a retail worker … Anyone who interfaces with the public is feeling this declining respect."
Ms O'Neil said the abuse directed at politicians went beyond the "democratic process" of "people being upset with government and wanting to convey that".
"I don't see a straight line between that and, 'You're next s**t,' being written on my social media wall two days after Helen Haines [was attacked]."
MP's children the target of racist abuse
Bonner MP Kara Cook has been trialling Areto for the past six months. She said as someone who did most of her own social media, she had noticed a vast improvement.
"For me, having a safe space for people locally to be able to genuinely express their views has been positive because I want to hear those," she said.
Areto has hidden 15,244 comments, mostly on Ms Cook's Facebook page, which were identified as "abusive", with racism, gender microaggression and transphobia the most common categories of attack.
Ms Cook, who has three First Nations children, said posts about her family often attracted "overwhelmingly racist comments".
"I've never hidden who I am as a person from my community … and I don't want that to change, but I also want to protect my family from that abuse," she said.
The first-term MP, who was a domestic violence lawyer and has previously served as a local councillor, said the day after she was elected to federal parliament, her home address and pictures of her house were published online.
"From that moment it was very clear to me that I'd entered a very different environment to any other workplace I'd ever been in," she said.
Ms Cook also said tech companies had an "obligation" to stop threatening and racist abuse appearing on their platforms.
She said the attack on Ms Haines needed to be a "pivotal moment" when Australia changed its approach to the safety of everyone, particularly women.
Public service hits out at 'ridicule' and 'vile abuse' of officials
At a Senate estimates hearing on Monday, top public servant Steven Kennedy said officials were also subject to increasing abuse online, and that parliamentarians were partly to blame for sharing "misleading" clips.
Those concerns were first aired in September when a senior defence official told a committee she did not want her answers clipped up for social media.
That request was rejected, with opposition and crossbench parliamentarians outraged by the idea.
But Mr Kennedy, who heads the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, said while he did not propose censoring footage, the "health and safety" of officials was a concern.
"Conduct that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets witnesses is inconsistent with the behaviour code for parliamentarians," he said.
"Evidence has been edited [for social media] in ways that invite ridicule, hostility or abuse directed at individual public servants … Unfortunately, some public servants have been the subjects of vile abuse."
Mr Kennedy urged parliamentarians to moderate comments on their social media posts and to delete abuse directed at officials.

Israel’s democracy faces its greatest test as Netanyahu clings to power - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

As Israel’s elections draw closer, the Israeli government has once again reaffirmed its illiberal orientation and embarked on a troubling escalation, with a series of controversial decisions affecting civil liberties and the rule of law.
Two journalists, one German and the other Italian, who had come to cover the election, were denied entry visas to Israel, for no apparent reason. And no explanation was provided for the suspension of the aliyah process for two young left-wing Jews, which was forcefully condemned by Labor Party lawmaker Gilad Kariv.
This arbitrary decision, which runs deeply counter to the very idea of Zionism, follows the expulsion of two Jewish women from Israel for their own activism in support of Palestinians, along with a 10-year ban on entering the country.
In another display of demagoguery reflecting his authoritarian drift, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to identify the soldiers who testified anonymously in the film NAZA and bring them to justice, after reiterating his call to strip the film’s directors of their citizenship.
This threat against the film’s witnesses retrospectively vindicates their decision to remain anonymous, a practice criticized by those who have attacked the film. The documentary is certainly not beyond reproach, particularly because of its analogy with the Holocaust. Yet its critics have failed to take sufficient account of the authoritarian drift of Israel’s current government.
As with the two young Jews whose aliyah process has been suspended and the journalists denied entry visas, the real objective of these maneuvers is not necessarily to target the individuals concerned. Rather, it is to create a climate of fear and intimidation that encourages others to think twice before speaking out or taking action.
This well-established method in authoritarian regimes applies, for example, to future young left-wing Jewish activists who might one day consider immigrating to Israel and who could be deterred from doing so by the prospect of being targeted.
These reprehensible intimidation tactics also serve populist and electoral demagoguery. Netanyahu is capitalizing on Israelis’ sense of isolation and of living in a besieged fortress – a feeling he has helped foster – and turning it into electoral fuel by dismissing all critical voices as “hostile.”
When the government itself is not making threats, far-right thugs, often affiliated with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, regularly disrupt public meetings and leaflet distributions organized by Yair Golan’s party, the Democrats.
They use hooligan-style tactics all too familiar to Palestinians in the West Bank, who are attacked by violent settlers, a journalist from The Washington Post, or European diplomats, while the authorities look on with culpable indulgence.
All these incidents reflect tensions within Israeli society, but also the nervousness of a prime minister clinging to power.
Opposition fears election interference
Attacks by the Right on expatriate voting, the Likud’s efforts to ban Arab parties, threats to bomb Iran before the elections that could lead to their cancellation, and the party’s allegations of possible foreign interference, intended to cast doubt on the election’s legitimacy, help explain the fears expressed by opposition figures.
They are also wary of Netanyahu’s political exploitation of security concerns.
Netanyahu is so attached to power that it is difficult to believe he would accept the ballot box’s verdict if it went against him, much like his “friend,” US President Donald Trump, who has just endorsed him.
These warning signs could help pave the way for such a scenario. This volatile situation, combined with the prime minister’s cynicism, explains Golan’s recent remarks in which he warned of a scenario resembling January 6, 2021, when Trump’s supporters stormed the Capitol.
In 1999, shortly before suffering a resounding defeat, Netanyahu repeatedly said of his opponents, “They are afraid,” in an attempt to dispel his own fears.
Today, as then, Netanyahu is afraid. Of judges. Of critics. Of voters. Of defeat. That fear makes him unpredictable and dangerous, ready to do anything to remain in office.
Israeli democracy is rightly a source of national pride. A small country under threat, Israel has never abandoned the practice of holding elections despite geopolitical tensions and a wartime atmosphere, and no election in its history has ever been contested. It will face its greatest test on October 27 and in the days that follow.
The writer, who was born and raised in France, is the correspondent of French Jewish radio, Radio J, and of the French paper librejournal.fr in the US, where he has been living for 16 years. He also holds US and Israeli citizenship. The opinions expressed are his own.

Hind Rajab Foundation files UK criminal complaint against Israeli soldier over Gaza war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:58:57 UTC
02:58:57 KST

Aysu Bicer
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has filed a criminal complaint with UK authorities against Israeli soldier Lidor Dafna over alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide committed in the Gaza Strip.
The foundation said in a statement Sunday that Dafna, a reservist serving as a D9 armored bulldozer operator in the 603rd Combat Engineering Battalion of the 7th Armored Brigade, participated in military operations in Gaza and Lebanon from November 2023 onward.
The foundation said it has reason to believe he is currently in the UK.
The complaint focuses on the destruction of Great Ocean Mills, an industrial flour-producing facility in the Morag Corridor between Khan Younis and Rafah, on May 25, 2025.
According to the foundation, footage posted by Dafna on social media shows a bulldozer demolishing the facility's wheat silos.
The foundation said Israeli forces subsequently occupied the building, converted it into a military base and reportedly used it to shoot Palestinians seeking food aid at a nearby Gaza Humanitarian Foundation site.
The foundation said the destruction occurred when Israel had sealed Gaza to food, fuel and medicine, with flour reportedly selling for as much as $70 per kilogram and half a million people facing starvation.
The foundation also said that the 603rd Battalion carried out more than 60 controlled demolitions of buildings, including mosques and residential blocks, and contributed to widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure and agricultural land during the establishment of the Morag Corridor.
The foundation said its investigation indicates that Dafna may be criminally responsible for extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity, intentionally targeting civilian objects, using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare, extermination as a crime against humanity and genocide.
The foundation called on British authorities to open an investigation, arrest and question Dafna, citing Article 146 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which requires states to search for individuals alleged to have committed grave breaches of the convention.
Dyab Abou Jahjah, the foundation's director general, said: “Lidor Dafna filmed himself destroying one of the last remaining food production facilities serving a starving population, then posted the footage on social media as a trophy.”
“The United Kingdom now faces a simple test: will it arrest and prosecute a man, who remains an active soldier of an army carrying out such crimes, or once again permit a perpetrator of genocide to walk freely on its soil and return to Gaza to continue committing his crimes?” he added.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its mandate on Oct. 31, ending a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN missions supporting peacebuilding, governance and state-building in the country, a UN official said Monday.
In a statement, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, said the mission would cease operations in accordance with Security Council resolutions and a request from Somalia’s federal government.
“This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,” Dujarric said.

Guterres reaffirmed that the UN would continue supporting Somalia through its resident agencies and programmes, working with Somali authorities, the African Union and other international partners to promote peace, stability, human rights and sustainable development, Dujarric said.
“Recognizing the significant political, security, humanitarian and development challenges that remain, the Secretary-General calls for sustained international support to consolidate progress, advance inclusive political dialogue and reconciliation, strengthen institutions, and promote and protect human rights,” he added.
Dujarric stressed that Guterres reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to the people of Somalia and to supporting Somali-led efforts to build a peaceful, stable and prosperous future.

Russia Plans to Export Grain Through Ochamchire Naval Base in Abkhazia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:57:20 UTC
02:57:20 KST

Amid Ukrainian strikes on ships, Russia plans to use the Ochamchire base in occupied Abkhazia to export grain.
Sources at Bloomberg reported that logistics operator Modern Way made this proposal to Russia.
Several Russian traders and brokers are considering this proposal, which involves shipping grain to Turkey in containers.
The port of Ochamchire has limited throughput capacity, and transporting grain in containers is an expensive and atypical solution.
Grain is typically transported by bulk carriers — ships designed to carry bulk cargo. A standard 20-foot container holds about 23 metric tons of grain, and loading it requires additional costs and time.
Russia accounts for about one-fifth of global wheat trade, and its Black Sea ports used to handle about 90% of exports.
According to Bloomberg, Ukrainian attacks have virtually halted grain shipments from Russia’s main export hubs.
Russian traders are increasingly using containers that travel thousands of kilometers across Russian territory to reach various ports — from St. Petersburg to Vladivostok on the Pacific Ocean. However, these alternative routes have not yet been able to meet the necessary transportation volumes.
The terminal is ready to begin shipping grain to the Turkish city of Gebze.
To this end, a product quality control service is expected to be operational by the end of next month. A Modern Way employee reported this to Bloomberg.
According to information on the company’s website, Modern Way transports containers by sea and rail and has offices in Russia and China. In addition, the company provides air freight and warehousing services.
Construction of the container port at the Ochamchire naval base was completed last year with financial support from Russia.
Earlier, in October 2023, Militarnyi reported that Russia plans to establish a naval base on the Black Sea coast of the occupied territory of Georgia.
Abkhazia has been under Russian control since the early 1990s, following an armed conflict between Georgia and Abkhaz forces supported by Russia in 1992–1993.
Since then, the region has been controlled de facto by authorities backed by Moscow.
Russia recognized Abkhazia’s so-called independence following a direct military invasion of Georgia in 2008.

Israel enters election silence period ahead of Tuesday's parliamentary vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:56:49 UTC
02:56:49 KST

Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Israel entered an election silence period Monday ahead of Tuesday's parliamentary elections, with restrictions on campaign activities taking effect at 7 pm local time (1700GMT), an Anadolu correspondent reported.
Under Article 129 of the Knesset Elections Law, campaigning at gatherings and marches, through loudspeakers, and on radio and television is prohibited from 7 pm on the eve of the election and throughout polling day, according to the Knesset's official website.
Most polling stations will open at 7 am (0500GMT) Tuesday and close at 10 pm (2000GMT). In communities with no more than 350 eligible voters, voting will take place from 8 am (0600GMT) to 8 pm (1800GMT).
Vote counting will begin after polling stations close at 10 pm, when Israeli media outlets are also expected to release exit poll results, according to Israel's Channel 12.
Under Article 11 of the Basic Law: The Knesset, the Central Elections Committee has eight days after election day to publish the official results in the official gazette, setting a deadline of Nov. 4.
 
More than 7.3 million eligible voters
A total of 37 parties and electoral alliances are contesting seats in the 120-member Knesset, with 13 projected to secure parliamentary representation.
The main contenders include Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and Yashar, which is contesting its first election under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Opinion polls suggest Yashar could emerge as the largest party, challenging years of Likud dominance.
According to the Central Elections Committee, 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote in elections for the 26th Knesset.
Voting will take place at 12,018 polling stations, with approximately 18,000 ballot boxes deployed nationwide and around 100,000 personnel working on election day.
Of the polling stations, 6,209 will be accessible to people with disabilities.
Twenty regional election committees will oversee preparations and voting operations in their respective jurisdictions.
To facilitate access to polling stations, 660 intercity public transport routes and all Israel Railways services will operate free of charge on election day, according to the committee.
 
Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
Forming a government requires the confidence of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset.
The previous Knesset dissolved on July 17, paving the way for the Oct. 27 election.
Netanyahu has led the current government since December 2022, heading a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel's history.
He is standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies.
The International Criminal Court has also issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu over war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.

Paralelo Transversal organises Chilean house under cantilever roof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:56:31 UTC
02:56:31 KST

Paralelo Transversal organises Chilean house under cantilever roof
Chilean studio Paralelo Transversal has designed a rectangular house with a large hip roof and a terrace that cantilevers over a ravine in Puerto Varas, Chile.
Completed in 2025 on a 1.2-acre site near Lago Llanquihue, the 155-square-metre house, known as Casa Ensenada, was oriented around its roof.
“In southern Chile, rain is not an exception but part of everyday life, so we wanted the roof to become more than a protective element,” architect Sebastián Silva of Paralelo Transversal told Dezeen.
“It creates a place beneath the rain, extending daily life beyond the enclosed rooms while bringing the different parts of the project together under one continuous gesture.”
The roof serves as the organising element for the program, circulation, relationship to the landscape and the home’s structure.
“Its section thickens toward the center while remaining remarkably thin at its perimeter,” Silva said.
“This allows it to be perceived as a light, continuous sheet while providing the structural depth required for long-span trusses capable of resisting both Chile’s seismic conditions and the strong winds of Patagonia.”
The house sits on a sloped site with a stream. Residents and visitors approach along the stream before the access ramp turns towards the house, where they enter at the junction of public and private zones.
The narrower side of the plan contains a large, open kitchen, dining and living room that bleeds onto the cantilevered terrace.
Oriented toward the northeast to capture winter sunlight, the house opens its living spaces to the landscape – the valley of Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park on one side and Calbuco Volcano on the other – through floor-to-ceiling windows with thin black frames.
The other side of the house widens to hold three suites. On either side of the house, the perimeter wall pushes under the roof canopy to form a covered bench and a planted garden.
The warm, contemporary material palette continues across the exterior and interior with exposed concrete slabs, large spans of glazing, tongue-and-groove timber and standing-seam metal roofing.
The concealed joints allowed the roof to be precise while reducing the visual impact of construction tolerances. The team collaborated closely with engineers and local builders to achieve its long spans and thin edge.
“Looking back, we believe the project fulfilled its original ambition of integrating architecture and landscape without compromising comfort, construction logic or budget,” Silva said.
“More importantly, it reinforced our belief that a project becomes stronger when one clear architectural idea is capable of organizing structure, climate, materiality and space simultaneously.”
Previously, Paralelo Transversal created a sail-like skylight that brought sun, shadows and air into a home on the outskirts of Santiago.
Other homes recently completed in Chile include a mass timber forest hideaway by Iragüen Viñuela Arquitectos and a seaside home with stacked terraces by Croxatto and Opazo Architects.

====================================================================================================

How Venezuela’s earthquake amputees adapt to life without limbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:55:59 UTC
02:55:59 KST

Ricardo Contreras’s new leg rests on a wooden countertop.
More than four months after twin earthquakes struck Venezuela, the 24-year-old is still recovering from his injuries.
When he was trapped beneath the rubble on the night of June 24, he waited hours to be rescued. His left leg had been pinned beneath a fallen door frame, limiting its blood circulation. It had to be amputated.
“One of the biggest achievements is that we survived,” Ricardo said, glancing towards his 16-year-old brother, Andres Contreras. “At first, when I found out Andres was well, I didn’t care about my leg too much. I would have chosen a thousand times over for Andres to be OK.”
But now Ricardo is adapting to his new reality.
He and his brother are still undergoing physiotherapy for their injuries. On a scorching afternoon, he sits in a small workshop in the hills of northwestern Caracas, waiting to do rehabilitation exercises to prepare for his new prosthetic leg.
“Now it’s about regaining a little of the independence I had before the earthquake, because that’s what limits me most," Ricardo said.
But recovery is only part of the challenge he is facing. His parents died in the collapse.
Resources and aid have also grown scarcer, particularly as global attention faded and international donations dried up.
As of September, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said it had secured only $29.5m of the $65.7m needed to continue its earthquake support in Venezuela, a shortfall of 55 percent.
Separately, that same month, the International Red Cross said its Venezuela response effort was only 39.8 percent funded.
Not only are survivors like Contreras left to grapple with loss of limbs and family members, but they now face the prospect of lifelong health costs — with dwindling support.
From rescue to recovery
More than 6,500 people have been confirmed dead as a result of the earthquakes, according to government authorities.
At least 226,696 people have received hospital treatment for injuries. The government says it has compiled a census of amputees, but no details have been made public.
At Ortoprotecnica, a Caracas workshop that makes prosthetic limbs, director Bianca Damaso is helping survivors like Ricardo through the next stages of recovery.
For those who have lost limbs, it typically takes two to three months of physiotherapy, rehabilitation and preparation to be ready for a prosthesis — sometimes longer depending on how their wounds heal and any pre-existing health conditions.
“It’s a very individual process where you have to support each person from where they are, because some are very anxious to have the prosthesis already, but their skin hasn’t even healed yet,” Damaso explained.
She said there are more than 100 types of knees to choose from, as well as more than 200 skin shades.
But the process does not end with the first fitting. Children may need five or six replacement prostheses as they grow, while adults might require ongoing adjustments and repairs.
Then there are the psychological hurdles. Many earthquake survivors wonder about practical realities like whether they will walk again, whether they will need a wheelchair or whether they will be able to urinate independently.
Many, in Damaso's experience, also question whether they will find a partner who will love them.
"Right now, the challenges for them are going to be more than just physical. They’re mental battles," Damaso said.
There is one rule she is adamant about in her workshop: “We tell them that the only thing that’s forbidden here is saying, ‘I can’t.’”
Karina Bechara, who lost both her legs in the earthquakes, is hoping to stand on her new feet by December 1. For now, she relies on a wheelchair.
“That motivates me every morning to get up and say, 'One day less to go.' It's painful, yes, but we're getting closer to the goal,” Bechara told Al Jazeera.
Before the earthquake, Bechara ran her own business and had an active life, training regularly with high-intensity CrossFit workouts. Her children saw her as an independent mother who did not depend on anyone.
“Now I am the opposite, a mum who needs their help, a dependent mum,” Bechara said.
After the earthquakes struck, Bechara was stuck in the rubble for 23 hours, immobilised by a piece of heavy furniture that crushed her legs.
She describes her recovery as an “emotional rollercoaster”. She said she allows herself to cry on the harder days but tries to keep looking ahead.
“Because if I don’t see the future for myself, no one else will.”
More than just limbs
But readjusting to routines can be difficult for those who have sustained life-altering injuries — not to mention other losses.
So far, Ricardo is optimistic about his daily activities. He has resumed work at his family's truck parts business, as well as his university studies. A new semester of classes has started, and he uses crutches to get around.
“I was really quite nervous. I was even worried about where the classes will be because we have three floors and also the distances are long,” Ricardo said.
But his concerns quickly melted away. The professors even moved his lessons to ground-floor classrooms to make the courses more accessible.
“It was actually great going back," Ricardo explained. "My classmates have always been there, helping me.”
The most difficult adjustment, however, has been grappling with the loss of loved ones.
“If my leg hurts, I take a pill, but with that, there’s nothing I can do. There’s no cure, there’s no remedy, there’s nothing,” Ricardo told Al Jazeera.
His mum and dad both died from suffocation during the earthquakes while the family was waiting to be rescued. Their building was one of dozens in the state of La Guaira to collapse.
“I fell in the bathroom hugging my mother, and Andres fell near my father. She was telling me she was fine, but I saw that her head was covered with concrete, with a wall on top, and dust,” Ricardo said.
Before the earthquakes, he remembers his mother cooking, singing and spoiling the family dog, who also died in the destruction. He credits his father with teaching him and Andres the value of work and the importance of being strong.
The brothers often look through photographs of their parents on their phones. One shows their family home, overlooking the sea. Another has them by the pool.
“As time goes on, the crying is the same, but the reason is different. Instead of crying so much from sadness, it's more like remembering the good times,” Ricardo said.
Following his parents' death, Ricardo has taken on additional responsibilities beyond school and work.
He is now Andres's legal guardian, and he is hoping the pair can soon find a home of their own through a government housing programme for earthquake victims.
His university has also offered him a full scholarship to finish his studies, to help relieve the financial burden.
Money, however, is still expected to be tight. The average salary for a private-sector worker in Venezuela is not much more than $200 a month.
“Of course, I'm worried about my financial situation,” Ricardo said, explaining the family business has slowed since the earthquakes.
“Sometimes it's hard to cover all the expenses, given everything that's happened, but we find a way. I think that's what Venezuelans do: We’re always finding a way to make things work.”
The cost of recovery
The Juan Pablo Dos Santos Foundation, a Venezuelan nonprofit, is among the groups helping earthquake amputees. Its founder and namesake, Dos Santos, lost his legs in a car accident in 2019.
He remembers realising the scale of June's tragedy when, at the first hospital he visited, he encountered a ward with 12 children. All of them had either lost limbs or were facing amputation.
“It's very difficult for everyone in general but especially for children, who suddenly lost so much. They lost family members, their homes, their schools, their abilities, and on top of that, they're missing a part of their body,” he told Al Jazeera.
One of his priorities was to show them what their lives could look like after amputation, telling them of his own achievements as an athlete and model.
But alongside the physical and psychological challenges, he knew they would face another obstacle: the cost of prosthetics.
“A prosthesis for a below-knee amputation, which is a transtibial prosthesis, can cost between $3,000 and $5,000," Dos Santos said. "And a prosthesis for an above-knee amputation can cost between $7,000 and $12,000."
The price tag for artificial limbs with electronic components — that react to the body's muscles — can stretch even higher, into the tens of thousands of dollars.
Even before the earthquake, the foundation had a waiting list of hundreds of people who needed a prosthetic limb but could not afford one.
After the seismic disaster, some 200 people were added to its database, Dos Santos said.
He explained that the foundation focuses on functional prostheses rather than the most expensive technology, partly because patients also need to be able to afford adjustments, repairs and replacements.
For many families, the cost is simply beyond reach.
The foundation is now planning to set up a specialist orthotics and prosthetics centre in Venezuela, which it says is essential to provide ongoing support for amputees.
Navigating the healthcare system
Medical professionals also see continued care as fundamental to recovery.
“For patients who suffered serious injuries or amputations, being saved and discharged from hospital is only the beginning. The recovery can be long, and that’s where we encounter many limitations,” Ana Rosario, the president of the Caracas Nurses Association, told Al Jazeera.
She said the earthquake compounded problems in Venezuela’s health system, which was weakened by years of economic crisis.
There are often too few nurses for the number of patients. Hospitals sometimes relied on supplies donated by citizens and organisations to help meet their needs.
“Although healthcare is technically free, patients may still have to pay for medicines, medical supplies, tests, transport and rehabilitation,” Rosario said. “And these are costs that can continue for months.”
For families who cannot afford them, the consequences can be serious.
“We see it every day: Families ask for help through social media, look for donations, go into debt, or simply have to wait,” she said. “When a test, medication or procedure is delayed, recovery can also be delayed, and new complications can arise.”
For survivors like Ricardo, private donations through organisations such as the Juan Pablo Dos Santos Foundation are helping pay for prosthetic limbs and rehabilitation.
“A few days ago, I saw my leg being made, and that got me really excited,” Ricardo said.
Though Ricardo is his guardian, Andres explained they help care for one another as they each recover from their injuries.
“Just getting out of the wheelchair was already a big step," Andres said of his brother. "He’s getting better every day. Honestly, it makes me so happy that he’ll be able to walk again."
The brothers attend physiotherapy sessions together, with Andres encouraging his older brother as he learns to walk again.
“My brother makes me feel like a world champion,” Ricardo said, laughing as his younger brother breaks into a smile.

Algeria’s president orders troop deployment to neighbouring Niger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:55:47 UTC
02:55:47 KST

Algeria’s president orders troop deployment to neighbouring Niger
Niger requested troops to secure shared energy interests in what would be Algeria’s first deployment abroad since 1973.
Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has ordered troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy and economic interests shared by both countries.
The decision, announced by Algeria’s presidency on Monday, came after both chambers of parliament approved the deployment in an emergency session on Sunday.
The presidency said authorities in Niger had requested military assistance.
If carried out, it would be Algeria’s first overseas military deployment since 1973, when it sent soldiers to support Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war.
The move marks a departure from Algeria’s longstanding reluctance to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
A 2020 constitutional reform allows the president to authorise overseas deployments with the approval of at least two-thirds of legislators in each parliamentary chamber.
Algeria sent fighter jets and support aircraft to Niger in August after what Algerian officials described as an attempt to destabilise its military government.
The presidency said the deployment decision was made under provisions of Algeria’s constitution allowing the military to operate abroad with parliamentary approval.
It has not been announced how many soldiers will be sent or when.
Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after Sunday’s parliamentary vote that the soldiers would protect economic infrastructure, particularly Algerian oil facilities in Niger.
He said Algeria was “not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger”, describing the mission as a response to changing security conditions in the Sahel region.
Algeria’s state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has been working with Niger on the proposed Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline. It would carry natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria for export to European markets.
Niger and neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso have faced years of attacks by armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).
All three countries are governed by military leaders who seized power in coups and subsequently formed the Alliance of Sahel States, a regional political and security bloc.
The deployment follows an improvement in relations between Algeria and Niger, which has been led by General Abdourahamane Tiani since a 2023 military coup that Algeria initially condemned.
Tensions deepened in April last year after Algerian forces shot down a Malian drone near the border, prompting the three alliance members to recall their ambassadors from Algiers.

Quebec’s new separatist government wants a bigger role in EU ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:55:04 UTC
02:55:04 KST

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon makes a speech after winning the election to become the next premier of Quebec, in Montreal, Canada on Oct. 5, 2026. | Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Quebec’s new separatist government is treating this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal as the start of a wider diplomatic push to get the province in the room whenever Ottawa and Brussels strike deals that concern its powers.
The separatist Parti Québécois returned to power this month at the head of a minority government in the province, promising to assert greater control over Quebec’s affairs and eventually hold another referendum on independence.
“Quebec has to be at the table, and Canada understands that very well,” Hélène Drainville, the province’s delegate general to the Benelux and the EU institutions, said in an interview in Brussels.
Advertisement
Prime Minister Mark Carney hosts Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa on Thursday and Friday for a summit the two sides have billed as a step change in relations, driven by Donald Trump’s tariffs and a shared need for new partners. Von der Leyen has even proposed to make Canada an “associate member” of the EU — an offer that goes too far even for some of the bloc’s member countries.
Early drafts of a joint summit declaration include a digital trade deal, a pact to let the European Investment Bank finance Canadian critical minerals projects, and a consignment of Canadian water bombers for Europe’s emergency services.
While Canada is responsible for negotiating the text, much of it lands in areas where its 10 provinces have extensive powers, such as over natural resources, education and health. Quebec is the second-largest province by population after Ontario and has a territory more than twice the size of France — with which three-quarters of its people share French as their mother tongue.
“Canada negotiates the umbrella agreement, and where we come in is when what’s negotiated touches our areas of jurisdiction,” said Drainville, who has been in post for a year. Natural resources are a provincial matter, she added, noting that Quebec has deposits of 22 of the 34 minerals on the EU’s critical list.
The province is already talking to the European Investment Bank and DG GROW, the European Commission’s industry department, about the bank’s entry into Canada, she noted.
Asked whether Quebec’s interests line up with those of Ottawa, Drainville said federal and provincial officials have already set up joint working groups to implement the summit’s outcomes. “Right now, all the signals are green,” she said.
Advertisement
New arrival
The cooperation comes at an unusual moment. Quebec’s new premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, won power on Oct. 5 while promising a third referendum on sovereignty, though not as long as Trump is in the White House. His cabinet includes the new position of minister for “accession to independence.”
However, support for independence in the province is the lowest it has been for three decades, around 29% in a poll from earlier this year — hardly a popular mandate for the project.
The Parti Québécois has nevertheless pledged to double Quebec’s 34 offices abroad. A party blueprint published last year would raise the number of countries with a Quebec office from 19 to 38 and, if the referendum delivers a “yes” to sovereignty, would turn those delegations into embassies and consulates.
“Quebec is going to start to exist and shine everywhere in the world,” St-Pierre Plamondon said last year, describing the representative network as a prerequisite for independence.
Drainville said the new government, which has been in office for three weeks, has not yet set its line on Europe.
“Our political leaders haven’t taken a position yet, which is normal,” she said. “But if they decide to double [the network], it’s because they believe in this partnership.” As for the associate-member label, she declined to engage: “We’re not really into semantics. That’s Canada.”
Advertisement
What Quebec does want from the EU, she said, is “win-win partnerships,” noting that the province and Ottawa complement each other and are stronger together when it comes to relations with Europe.
It hasn’t always been so amicable.
Quebec’s diplomatic ambitions date back to the 1960s, when the provincial government asserted the right to pursue international relations in areas under its constitutional jurisdiction.
Its international aspirations became politically contentious when French President Charles de Gaulle publicly embraced Quebec’s independence movement in 1967 — ending a speech in Montreal by proclaiming: Vive le Québec libre! (“Long live free Quebec!”)
The Brussels office opened in 1972, and the province now counts 10 posts in Europe, which Drainville called the most of any Canadian province.
Quebec never consented to the constitutional changes Canada enacted in 1982, and its 1995 independence referendum failed by the narrowest of margins (49.4% to 50.6%). A decade ago, Quebec lobbied Europe for a seat at the table in negotiations on the CETA EU-Canada trade deal.

Oil spill off UAE widens, satellite images show, prompting more beach closures
Satellite images show that an oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated 24 October show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is nearing the shores of northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along the coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Friday that it was working to contain oil leaking from an offshore tanker, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill came from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
Images from the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker.
Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday that it temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution.
"The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed," Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Centre, told Reuters.
In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Saturday that they would close all beaches in the emirate until further notice.
The UAE's marine life "is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters," including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, says on its website.

Cabinet publishes resolution on updating system for granting deferments from conscription
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:53:48 EET
02:53:48 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has published a resolution on updating the organization of deferments from conscription for those liable for military service during the period of mobilization and under martial law.
Specifically, in accordance with Resolution No. 1328 dated October 23, central executive authorities, other state bodies, public administration entities with jurisdiction covering the entire territory of Ukraine, as well as regional and Kyiv city state administrations (or military administrations, where established), are required within ten days of the resolution’s entry into force to ensure the review and harmonization of the criteria used to designate enterprises, institutions, and organizations as "critically important" for the functioning of the economy.
Following this review, an analysis must be conducted to determine whether enterprises still meet these criteria. If a criterion—on the basis of which an enterprise was originally designated as "critically important"—is removed, the decision designating that enterprise as "critically important" must be revoked.
The Government has established that decisions designating enterprises as "critically important"—in effect as of the date this resolution enters into force—shall remain valid for the duration for which they were originally issued, unless they have since been revoked.
It is noted that decisions by the Minister of Defense to increase the quotas for the deferment from military service ("reservation") of liable individual, adopted prior to the entry into force of Resolution No. 1608, shall remain in effect for the entire duration of the enterprise’s designation as "critically important," but no later than December 8, 2026. Decisions by the Ministry of Defense to increase such quotas, adopted after December 8, 2025, shall remain in effect for the duration of the enterprise’s "critically important" status, but not beyond the specific timeframe stipulated in the relevant Ministry decision.
Furthermore, the Cabinet of Ministers has established a Coordination Center for the organization of the deferment from military service for liable individuals during periods of mobilization and wartime.
Enterprises may be designated as "critically important" to the functioning of the economy and the provision of essential services to the population during special periods if they operate within the following sectors: the defense-industrial complex; the fuel and energy complex; housing and utility services; the extractive industry; the manufacturing (processing) industry; the agro-industrial sector (including the assurance of food security); retail trade; construction; transport and logistics; information technology; banking; healthcare; and communications. This also applies to entities engaged in emergency rescue and other urgent operations (emergency rescue services), as well as those operating in sectors approved by the Coordination Center, following a substantiated request from a central executive body or another state authority responsible for developing and/or implementing state policy in the relevant field. It has been established that the number of individuals liable for military service who are eligible for deferment (exemption from mobilization) may exceed 50%, subject to the recommendations and proposals of the Coordination Center.
Substantiated proposals to increase the number of deferments are to be submitted to the Coordination Center by the relevant government authority. Grounds for the Coordination Center to refuse to consider such proposals include, among other things, the documented, systematic violation of legal requirements regarding the organization and maintenance of military registration by the head of a critical institution, specifically, the occurrence of two or more such documented violations within the preceding 12 months, and/or the imposition of administrative liability upon the head for committing such violations.
Furthermore, it is established that for individuals liable for military service who hold positions within the representative offices of donor institutions or with entities implementing international technical assistance projects, the number of those eligible for deferment shall not exceed 50% of the total number of such employees directly engaged in the tasks of a single project, and in any case, shall not exceed 7 individuals.
Pursuant to a decision by the State Secretary of the Cabinet of Ministers, made in light of the Coordination Center’s recommendations, the number of individuals eligible for deferment may exceed 7, provided it does not exceed 50% of the total number of employees liable for military service.
For critical institutions, defined by the Ministry of Defense as critical within the defense-industrial complex, the fuel and energy sector (including their contractors), or as domestic manufacturers of transformer equipment for the energy sector, the number of employees liable for military service, who are eligible for deferment, may reach up to 95%. This applies to entities engaged in the construction, repair, restoration, manufacturing, and/or supply of equipment, the provision of services, or the execution of other engineering and technical activities aimed at ensuring the uninterrupted operation of the unified [energy/power] system.

Ukraine Hits Russian Drone Workshop and Control Post, Targeting Frontline Attack Capability
Ukrainian forces struck Russian military communications facilities, command posts, drone infrastructure, and supply depots across three regions on October 25 and overnight into October 26.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced the strikes on its official Facebook page on October 26, identifying targets in the Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, and Luhansk regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"This disrupts the enemy’s communications and command and control of its troops," the General Staff wrote, describing the strike on a Russian military communications hub near temporarily occupied Melitopol.
According to the military, Ukrainian forces targeted:
- a Russian military communications hub near Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- Russian command posts near Myrnohrad in the Donetsk region and Chervonohirka in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- a Russian UAV control post near Vyshneve and a drone workshop near Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- Russian military equipment and supply depots near Komisarivka and Katerynivka in the Luhansk region.
The General Staff explained that the strikes on command posts were intended to disrupt Russian battlefield coordination, while targeting drone infrastructure could reduce Moscow's ability to attack Ukrainian military positions and frontline communities.
The attacks on supply depots were also intended to undermine Russian logistics by destroying materiel needed to sustain military operations. The General Staff did not disclose the weapons used, the number of Russian casualties, or detailed damage assessments for the targeted facilities.
"Operations against the enemy’s key military targets will continue until Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine ends completely," the General Staff stated.
Days earlier, Ukrainian forces carried out a similar wave of strikes across the same three regions on October 19 and overnight into October 20.
Targets included a command post near Fedorivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, a military repair unit near Kalmiuske in the Donetsk region, and logistics depots near Kripenskyi, Rivnopil, and Lahidne.
Russian troop concentrations were also hit near Horlivka, Selydove, Svatove, and several settlements in the Zaporizhzhia region.

Russian Spy Network Exposed in Alleged Scheme to Stage Fake Pro-Nuclear Rally in Budapest
Russian intelligence-linked operatives allegedly attempted to stage a paid demonstration outside Hungary’s parliament in Budapest to promote a nuclear power project backed by Russia’s state-owned Rosatom, according to a new investigation based on leaked intelligence documents.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The alleged operation was uncovered by InformNapalm and Ukrainian Militant, which published their findings on October 26 after examining correspondence, internal documents, and digital records obtained by the hacker group 256 Cyber Assault Division.
Investigators identified Russian Colonel Timur Sirtlanov and Lieutenant Colonel Irina Parman, both linked to military unit 33949, previously identified in open-source investigations as a structure associated with Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
A leaked email dated September 16 reportedly showed Sirtlanov asking Parman to conduct psychological profiling ahead of a postponed operation in Budapest. The correspondence referred to an “active measure,” a term used by Russian intelligence services for covert influence operations targeting foreign governments and public opinion.
The planned demonstration was intended to generate public support for Paks II, a nuclear power plant expansion project involving Russia’s Rosatom.
Organizers reportedly recruited Russian-speaking residents through Facebook advertisements and coordinated preparations in a private Telegram group called “Friendship of Peoples,” which had 106 members.
Participants were instructed to prepare banners and promotional materials supporting the nuclear project. Organizers also offered additional financial compensation, although investigators found no evidence that payments were actually made.
InformNapalm further traced promotional materials to Parman after discovering that a PDF file contained the author name “Irina Larina,” matching a surname she had previously used online.
The rally was initially scheduled for September 20 outside Hungary’s parliament before being postponed to September 26. However, organizers canceled the demonstration approximately 30 minutes before it was due to begin.
The alleged Russian influence operation emerged amid worsening relations between Moscow and Budapest. On September 8, Hungary expelled ten Russian diplomats over activities incompatible with their diplomatic status.
Meanwhile, the Paks II project has faced increasing scrutiny. Hungarian authorities launched an investigation into financial transactions associated with the project in August, following a European Union court ruling in 2025 overturning the European Commission’s approval of state aid for its construction.
Earlier, in May 2026, Hungary expelled a Russian diplomat identified as an undercover officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. According to VSquare, the diplomat had allegedly spent years cultivating contacts within Hungarian institutions and gathering intelligence on government officials and the Paks II nuclear power project.

You’ll Never Guess What Ukraine Uses to Keep Drones Flying at −20°C
Ukraine’s defense industry builds drones capable of reaching deep inside Russia and cruise missiles carrying massive warheads—but when temperatures plunge to −20°C (−4°F), one surprisingly effective engineering solution is considerably less sophisticated: salo .
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point on October 26 revealed that extreme cold can cause frost to form on drone cameras and cables while batteries discharge significantly faster, threatening the reliability of unmanned systems operating through the winter.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One workaround is a simple layer of salo used to help shield vulnerable components from freezing conditions.
It is an unusually low-tech solution from a company responsible for some of Ukraine’s most advanced long-range weapons.
Fire Point manufactures the FP-1 deep-strike UAV and FP-2 strike drone, as well as the FP-5 Flamingo ground-launched cruise missile. The company is also developing the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles, with the latter designed for strikes at ranges of up to 850 kilometers.
Its FP-1 and FP-2 drones are already used extensively for strikes deep inside Russia, while the Flamingo has become another component of Ukraine’s expanding domestic long-range arsenal.
Yet battlefield engineering is not always about finding the most technologically sophisticated answer.
At around −20°C, preventing a camera, cable, or other exposed component from freezing can matter just as much as advanced guidance software or propulsion.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine and Norway were accelerating development of the Fire Point FP-5.x FREYJA anti-ballistic missile defense program, with initial components already showing progress and the first tests targeted for the end of 2026.
