What Israel's election could mean for the West Bank's future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:51:28 UTC
02:51:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Beyond the ballot: The West Bank's future after Israel's election
Ramallah - Driving in the occupied West Bank, motorists are confronted with a barrage of campaign billboards for the Israeli elections.
The messages are geared towards Israeli settlers in the territory, not the Palestinians barred from voting.
Many of the posters express support for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power party, as he draws his core voter base from settlers.
But there are also numerous posters for Prime Minister Netanyahu’s Likud party, including an ominous ad along the road to Jerusalem featuring Zohran Mamdani and Ayatollah Khomeini, warning against the power of Palestinian allies.
Against this radicalised backdrop, Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday in an election that many hope will spell the end of Netanyahu’s 19-year non-consecutive rule as prime minister.
The election comes in the wake of growing domestic resentment against Netanyahu over reports of his advanced knowledge of the 7 October attacks.
Netanyahu’s Likud is seemingly facing an uphill battle against a bloc of four Jewish opposition parties that have joined forces to defeat him: the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beitenu party, and the Together alliance.
After the bloc’s establishment, the parties announced their goal was to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.
The elections are projected to be a near deadlock with no bloc winning an absolute majority. That outcome would trigger a period of negotiations and coalition building, where different parties must agree to come together to form a government.
But as settler violence reaches record levels in the West Bank, many Palestinians are left wondering: will any electoral outcome change the facts on the ground?
West Bank violence surges ahead of election
Approximately 750,000 Israelis live in settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem today, illegal under international law.
The settlers comprise a disproportionately powerful bloc in Israeli politics, despite accounting for around 7-8% of the total Israeli population.
Under Netanyahu’s current administration, which has brought settlers from the far-right fringes into a governing coalition, the settlers’ political influence has coincided with a rapid acceleration of settlement expansion.
But it’s unlikely that another government would slow the pace of settlement building.
“In order to ameliorate pressure from the settler lobby, the left often are tempted to expand settlements even more than the right,” Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, a political commentator and former Israeli diplomat, tells The New Arab.
“It [the opposition winning] might even lead to an increase in settlement construction in order to pay them off for concessions.”
As settlements expand, so does the pressure on Palestinians living nearby. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded an average of six settler attacks per day this year thus far.
Those numbers were released before the autumnal olive harvest commenced, when violence dramatically escalates as settlers launch coordinated attacks against Palestinian farmers in their olive groves.
And after two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on an Israeli checkpoint on 23 October, Ben-Gvir suggested that Palestinians should be barred from driving on the roads in the West Bank - or the land of Judea and Samaria, as he refers to it.
The Israeli army subsequently launched a collective punishment operation and began home demolitions across the neighbourhood where the shooters hailed from, displacing 400 families thus far.
Netanyahu has promised the biggest military occupation in the West Bank since 1967, though many experts say he may be bluffing to bolster support for Likud ahead of the elections.
The election will now take place against a backdrop of expanding settlements, escalating settler violence, and increasingly severe restrictions on Palestinian movement, fuelling fears that tensions across the West Bank are near boiling point.
“There are a lot of people in the Israeli security forces who want Palestinians to have a better quality of life, just so that the West Bank doesn't explode into another Intifada,” says Ben-Ephraim.
Projected electoral outcomes
Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot of Yashar!, is seen as the leading centrist alternative for Prime Minister.
Eisenkot has promised to rein in settler violence while firmly opposing a two-state solution. Once the Israeli army Chief of Staff, Eisenkot was the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine in 2006, which advocates "disproportionate force” against Israel’s perceived enemies.
“None of the Israeli governments that would come is going to give a Palestinian state to the Palestinians, but change may come, depending on how you define change,” Muhanned Qafesha, a Palestinian journalist from Hebron, tells The New Arab.
An Eisenkot government could mean greater restrictions on settler violence and a slight change in settlement policy, without fundamentally interfering with the settler project.
Alternatively, if Netanyahu secures another term or temporarily heads a caretaker government if a stalemate arises, the settlers in his administration may feel their time is limited and accelerate their existing plans for the annexation of the West Bank.
As it stands, neither major political bloc is projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
While the opposition bloc has sworn not to form a coalition with either of the Palestinian parties on the ballot - the left-leaning Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) - that pledge may not hold, as they could be a potential lifeline to forming a government.
“The two Arab parties can maybe win like 15 seats or something, and this will make a huge difference because if they can make a coalition with the opposition, they can kick out Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir,” Qafesha tells The New Arab.
“I do believe that the opposition in Israel is saying they won’t form a coalition with the Arabs because they want to get as many votes from the Jewish community as possible. But if they need the Arab parties to form a coalition to kick out Netanyahu, they might do it,” he adds.
But any coalition will also depend on parties that oppose Palestinian statehood, and thus a fundamental shift in Israel’s approach to the occupation is virtually impossible.
Even if Eisenkot eventually forms a government, his fragile coalition across the ideological spectrum would struggle to agree on significant changes towards settlement policy in the West Bank.
Will the opposition improve life in the West Bank?
The 3.4 million Palestinians living in the West Bank under military occupation cannot vote in Israeli elections, but Palestinian citizens of Israel can.
Arab voters have long boycotted Israeli elections, but there has been a recent push for their participation - with a record turnout for the group anticipated.
The vast majority of Palestinians in the West Bank want Palestinian citizens of Israel to vote in the elections to improve their daily lives, explains Qafesha, who himself cannot vote.
He believes an administration without settlers at the helm may alleviate some of the daily struggles in the West Bank.
“We live in hell. We just want to breathe,” Qafesha says.
But if Netanyahu finally goes down, some Palestinians believe Western governments may attempt to rehabilitate Israel’s image under a new administration - and lift the recent round of European sanctions against settlements that were years in the making.
“The upcoming election is between fascists and ultra-fascists. If Netanyahu loses the chance to lead the next government, his loss can be used to alleviate the pressure that is just starting to build from the international community,” Mazin Qumsiyeh, Director of Palestine’s Natural History Museum in Bethlehem, tells The New Arab.
Yet Qafesha remains adamant that the reality on the ground is more important than the views of the international community, which could promote a new government as an example of Israel’s return to democracy.
“Over the past three years, Israel has killed more than 100,000 Palestinians in Gaza. What has the world done for us? Has anything changed in our life? I don't want the view of the world to change at the expense of the blood of Palestinian children, whether it's in Gaza, West Bank, or Jerusalem,” says Qafesha.
An opposition government less reliant on far-right parties could potentially curb some of the policies driving unchecked violence and forced displacement, ameliorating a few of the numerous obstacles to a dignified life under occupation. But any improvement would likely be limited in scope.
“If the opposition wins, the intensity of the ethnic cleansing will probably somewhat lessen, but it's only temporary,” concludes Ben-Ephraim.
“I think that the Israeli public opinion has turned so far in favour of genocide and ethnic cleansing that it will just be a respite at best.”
Kate McMahon is a freelance journalist and foreign correspondent focused on the Middle East and South Asia. She reports on environmental change, human rights, and geopolitical conflicts

Polish city of Przemyśl suspends cooperation with Lviv over Year of UPA decision
Councillors in the Polish city of Przemyśl agreed on Monday 26 October to suspend cooperation with Lviv following a recent decision by the Lviv Oblast Council to designate 2027 as the Year of the UPA The UPA, or Ukrainian Insurgent Army, was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. and Roman Shukhevych, one of its commanders-in-chief.
Source: Przemyśl Mayor Wojciech Bakun on Facebook, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Twenty-one councillors voted in favour of the resolution to suspend the partnership with Lviv. No one voted against or abstained.
According to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), Przemyśl councillors said the decision adopted by the Lviv Oblast Council on 20 October "insulted" the memory of Polish victims of crimes committed by the UPA and ran counter to efforts to build relations based on historical truth and mutual respect.
The resolution requires Przemyśl Mayor Wojciech Bakun to take legal steps to terminate the 1995 cooperation agreement.
However, it also provides for cooperation between the cities to resume if the Lviv Oblast Council definitively repeals or formally withdraws the resolution and Lviv's city authorities clearly distance themselves from initiatives that "glorify structures responsible for crimes against civilians".
The mayor must inform Lviv's city authorities of this position and report to Przemyśl councillors on the measures taken and the date on which the agreement will cease to be in force.
"After a lengthy discussion on the matter, all councillors unanimously decided that we would suspend all joint activities until Lviv's authorities clearly state their position on the promotion of ideologies directed against Poland and the Polish people. I would like to thank the councillors for taking this position and demonstrating that we will not remain indifferent to provocative and anti-Polish actions," Bakun wrote.
Background:
- On 20 October, the Lviv Oblast Council voted to declare 2027 the "year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army and Oleh Olzhych". The decision immediately drew criticism from Polish officials.
- Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk later said that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had made it clear that he would not support further steps by the Lviv Oblast Council to declare 2027 the year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych.
- The city council of Wrocław, Poland, unanimously condemned the decision by the Lviv Oblast Council to declare 2027 the year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army.
- Meanwhile, Kraków's new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, has proposed suspending the city's partnership with Lviv in response to the Lviv Oblast Council's decision to declare 2027 the year of the UPA.

Algeria's Kaylia Nemour wins double gold at gymnastics worlds
Algerian gymnast Kaylia Nemour won gold on the balance beam on Sunday at the 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships, a day after claiming another gold medal on the uneven bars.
The two gold medals came after a difficult start for the 19-year-old, whose poor vault performance on Friday dashed her hopes of an all-around medal in Rotterdam.
"I'm extremely happy, but I'm completely in shock. In shock at this gold medal on beam," Nemour was quoted by International Gymnast as saying. "My goal was to do a nice routine, and that's what I did, so I was already proud of myself. And with the score, I was hoping it would be enough for a medal. And now, having the gold medal is unimaginable. I think I'll need a lot of time to digest it. Maybe a month, knowing me."
Nemour was first to compete in the uneven bars final, scoring 14.566 before seven other gymnasts took their turns. China's Zhang Qingyang finished second with the same score, with Nemour taking gold on the execution-score tiebreak.
"I knew there was the Chinese gymnast, last year's world champion, who is extremely strong, with a big start value and exceptional cleanliness," she said. "And then we had the same score, so I think it was the execution score that made the difference, and it's exceptional."
Nemour's success at the championships was celebrated by Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on social media on Sunday.
"Warmest congratulations, Kaylia... Like all Algerians, I am happy and proud of you for this double gold at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in the Netherlands," Tebboune wrote.
"You always deserve our full appreciation for making the nation’s flag proud. Long live Algeria."

"Ukrainian athletes will not go there" — Bidnyi on Ukraine's participation in the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships in Moscow
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine will appeal the IWF's decision to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow. If the competition is held in Russia, Ukrainian athletes will not participate.
Ukraine will appeal the decision by the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow and will boycott the competition if it takes place in Russia. Ukrainian Minister of Youth and Sports Matvii Bidnyi said this in a comment to UNN.
Details
"Ukraine will use all legal, political and diplomatic instruments to ensure that the decision by the International Weightlifting Federation to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow is reviewed. Our principled position is to be present on the international stage, win, raise the Ukrainian flag and not vacate the arena for Russian propaganda. However, in the case of the 2030 World Championships, if this competition does indeed take place on Russian territory, Ukrainian athletes will not go there," Bidnyi said.
He stressed that Ukrainian participation in a tournament on the territory of the aggressor state, from where orders to kill civilians and destroy our cities are issued every day, is absolutely impossible for security reasons and morally unacceptable.
"We are currently initiating official appeals to the IWF and the IOC, as well as consolidating the support of international partners and the sports ministers of EU countries and the Council of Europe, in order to prevent the World Championships from being held in Moscow and secure a new, transparent selection process for the host country," the minister added.
We remind you
The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) granted Russia the right to host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships for adults. The competition will be held in Moscow. This is the first case since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in which an international federation governing an Olympic sport has entrusted Russia with hosting a World Championship of this level.
Ukraine is preparing an appeal to the IWF and the IOC demanding a review of the decision to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow. Matvii Bidnyi called on partners to prevent the competition from taking place in Russia.

Tax service advises gas producers to report export volumes of gas injected into storage for royalty administration
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:47:56 EET
02:47:56 KST

The State Tax Service (STS) recommends that gas-producing companies notify it in writing of the volumes of domestically produced gas exported after being injected into underground gas storage facilities (UGS).
According to a statement on the agency's Telegram channel, the information should be submitted together with monthly acts documenting the movement of natural gas in storage facilities. This will allow tax authorities to administer subsoil-use royalty payments without making additional requests to taxpayers.
The STS recalled that certain provisions of Ukraine's Tax Code exempt companies from paying royalties on extracted gas injected into UGS facilities until it is sold. The obligation to pay royalties resumes in the reporting period in which the gas is sold, with the amount due calculated based on the actual volume sold.
The procedure for exporting domestically produced gas was approved by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 1251 of October 7, 2026.

Israel's Hebron raid displaces nearly 4,000 Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:47:51 UTC
02:47:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's Hebron raid displaces nearly 4,000 Palestinians as homes turned into military outposts
Israeli forces have forced nearly 4,000 Palestinians from their homes in Hebron since Friday, leaving hundreds of families displaced as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly rejected military advice to end the operation in the southern occupied West Bank.
The number of displaced Palestinians reached around 3,971 on Monday, according to figures reported by Palestinian news agency WAFA. This includes approximately 200 children under the age of two, at least 258 elderly people and 137 pregnant women.
Riyad Khamis, spokesperson for Hebron’s Follow-up, Support and Relief Committee, said 619 families had been affected, including 266 unable to find safe accommodation.
More than 80 Palestinians have been arrested, while hundreds of others have been detained and interrogated, according to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club. Israeli troops have also raided and ransacked hundreds of homes, leaving residents unsure when they will be allowed to return.
Hebron's Governor Khaled Dudin reported that Israeli authorities established 128 gates and 120 checkpoints across the southern governorate, saying that it fragments the area and severly restricts movement as well as access to healthcare and basic services.
The Israeli operation followed a shooting attack on Friday in which two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near Hebron. Israeli forces killed both gunmen.
Netanyahu subsequently ordered the evacuation of residents from the neighbourhood where the attackers lived ahead of house-to-house searches. The ensuing assault has extended to Palestinian homes, businesses and industrial facilities.
In a statement issued on Monday, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) warned that these actions "raise grave concerns about ethnic cleansing and collective punishment".
"Palestinians in Hebron are being driven from their homes and cut off from healthcare and basic supplies," Aseel Baidoun, MAP's Deputy Director of Advocacy and Communications, said. "This is collective punishment. People are being punished simply for being Palestinians."
A home turned into a military outpost
For Ramadan Faisal al-Hashlamoun, a 47-year-old Palestinian displaced with his family, the uncertainty centres on a house he says Israeli soldiers have turned into a military outpost.
Speaking to The New Arab, Hashlamoun said troops entered his home and took it over because it overlooks the main road. He has been unable to return since.
His household numbers 10, including children, the youngest of whom is aged 12. The family has been split apart since residents were ordered to leave the entire area, he said.
"You can only feel at ease in your own home," he told The New Arab.
Hashlamoun said neighbours had heard the sound of objects being smashed inside his house, leaving him deeply worried about the condition of his belongings, including money, gold and other personal possessions. Unable to enter, he has no way of checking what has happened to them.
He also said Israeli forces had marked four X signs on the exterior walls of the house – a mark that has since been circulating in images across social media on multiple houses whose inhabitants had been forcibly displaced.
Israeli occupation forces mark several Palestinian homes with "X" signs in the Ein Deir Bahha neighborhood of Hebron, south of the occupied West Bank, after forcibly displacing their owners. https://t.co/3lNmvZ4yO7
— Quds News Network (@QudsNen) October 24, 2026
At the time of the interview, his family had received no aid or essential supplies, although Hebron Municipality had contacted them. He told The New Arab that his immediate concerns were the separation of his family and the uncertain fate of their home.
Local relief officials said on Monday that a first batch of aid and basic supplies was being distributed to displaced and affected families. Hundreds of other residents remained trapped inside homes in neighbouring areas, according to WAFA.
Israeli forces have sealed off the neighbourhoods of Deir Baha and al-Jilda, where much of the displacement has taken place, while imposing closures at entrances to Hebron and surrounding towns and refugee camps. The restrictions have disrupted movement and access to homes, businesses and services.
A staff member at a MAP local partner in Hebron described the sudden incursion, saying it was "unexpected to see this kind of mass forced displacement" where residents including persons with disabilities, pregnant women, and children "left their homes carrying whatever they could. A lot of those who were displaced are elderly people with chronic illnesses, meaning there is a need for medicines as well."
Netanyahu reportedly rejected an end to the operation
The sudden displacement of thousands of residents comes as Israeli media reported that Netanyahu had rejected Israeli Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir's recommendation to end the operation, despite being told its objectives had been 'achieved' and there was no justification for continuing to prevent residents from returning home.
Israel’s public broadcaster Kan reported on Monday that Zamir had recommended ending the operation, telling Netanyahu during a situational assessment on Sunday that its objectives had been met.
According to Kan’s reporting, Zamir said there was no operational justification for continuing the raid and no legal justification for keeping displaced Palestinians from their homes.
Netanyahu nevertheless insisted that the operation continue despite the military having wanted to announce as early as Saturday night that the operation was winding down.
The reported disagreement emerged a day before Israel’s general election, as displaced Palestinian families remained unable to return.
“Across the West Bank, we are living in high uncertainty, especially with Israeli elections this week; there is no safe place due to the situation deteriorating day by day," MAP's staff member said.
"We are wondering if this will last days, weeks, or months. People are worried about forced displacement and it's becoming a real fear, especially when looking at what happened in Jenin and Tulkarem in the past couple of years. We are losing trust in the international community."

ZURICH, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis will travel to North Korea this week for political talks and for the formal reopening of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang, his government said on Monday.
• Cassis, whose visit begins on Thursday, will meet North Korean authorities during the formal office opening on October 30
• Talks will include the resumption of bilateral consultations between the countries’ foreign ministries, security on the Korean peninsula and geopolitical issues
• Cassis will afterwards travel to Seoul for talks with South Korean officials
• The Pyongyang office reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing, which retains responsibility for diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea
• The office, operational since October 19, restores Switzerland’s permanent diplomatic representation in North Korea
• While Switzerland has actively re-engaged with Pyongyang in recent years, the EU has essentially frozen out direct dialogue with North Korea

Analysis-Now home, Venezuela opposition leader Machado walks tightrope with supporters, Trump
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:47:11 CET
02:47:11 KST

By Mayela Armas and Julia Symmes Cobb
CARACAS/BOGOTA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who returned on Sunday after nearly a year away, will walk a tightrope as she seeks the elections her supporters want without running afoul of a US-backed negotiation process between the interim government and other opposition groups.
Machado’s return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Washington has said she has every right to be in Venezuela, but has praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez and supports a negotiation process between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups that do not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement.
The talks, which have continued this month, would remake the electoral council and top court ahead of eventual elections. Both bodies are staffed by ruling party loyalists and backed ousted President Nicolas Maduro in a disputed 2024 presidential election, despite tallies published by Machado’s movement that showed her candidate had won. The US military captured Maduro in January.
Machado supporters, tens of thousands of whom swarmed her caravan between Barquisimeto and Caracas on Sunday, waving flags, chanting her name and festooning her with rosaries, are eager for elections and call her the next president. She has said a presidential vote should happen in 2027.
Machado’s team did not respond to a request for comment.
Asked whether Machado would participate in the negotiations, Rodriguez said she hopes the dialogue will lead those who called for sanctions against the country — a common ruling party critique leveled at Machado — to feel remorse. Rodriguez added that the talks offer a chance for all voices to be heard.
“I hope both the dialogue and the program for democratic coexistence and peace can provide a space where all voices can be heard, where voices seeking the good of the country can be heard,” the acting president said during a visit to a military hospital in Caracas, where she urged politicians to concentrate on serious issues and not put on a “show.”
Though Machado cultivated Trump as an ally for years, he said last month it was too soon to consider democratic elections. On Sunday, Trump said he had been unaware of her return plans, though a person briefed on her movements disputed that.
RISK OF SHORT CIRCUIT WITH WASHINGTON
Machado’s eagerness for a vote could “short-circuit” the relationship with the US and its three-phase stabilization, recovery and transition plan for Venezuela, said Ricardo Rios, head of Poder y Estrategia, a political risk consultancy.
“The idea (at the negotiations) is to hold a regional election before a presidential election. She will probably push for electoral guarantees and for a presidential election to be held as soon as possible,” Rios said.
But much remains to be defined before voters cast ballots.
“What guarantees does the ruling sector have to leave power (if it is defeated)?” Rios asked. “That still needs to be defined in order to make this viable, because otherwise, no matter how popular she is, it complicates matters.”
US AND EU URGE DIALOGUE
Machado’s safe return was a direct outcome of the negotiations, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a longtime champion of Machado, said on Sunday, adding he expects all political actors to support the talks.
Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure was designed to rig elections and so must be quickly replaced before a valid election can be held, he told reporters on Monday. He did not provide an estimated date for elections.
“I think we’re making real progress in that regard,” Rubio said. “But if anybody tries to derail that process, they’re doing a great harm to Venezuela.”
The EU echoed that sentiment, saying on Monday authorities and all political actors should advance “an inclusive, Venezuelan-led dialogue towards free and fair elections.”
The negotiations will lead to a top court being in place by the end of this year and a new electoral council shortly thereafter, a senior US State Department official said earlier.
“The reception (Machado) got yesterday will only reinforce the tendency to demand instant results,” said Phil Gunson, senior analyst for the Andes region at the International Crisis Group think tank. “Not only might that provoke a reaction from government hardliners, but it could — if successful — produce a political rupture instead of a peaceful transition, with inadequate post-electoral guarantees and a potentially ungovernable country.”
The opposition included in the talks, led by Dinorah Figuera, a lawmaker elected in 2015 to the last Venezuelan legislative body recognized by the US, said Machado’s return was a significant step in the US plan.
“Her role is also tied to how she interprets the signals from the United States, which has called for reconstruction and reconciliation. She has to be an ally in the negotiations,” said Oswaldo Ramirez, managing director of ORC Consultores.
“Rubio sent a clear message,” he added. “I don’t see her trying to torpedo the negotiations. She can’t stray outside the lines.”
(Reporting by Mayela Armas in Caracas and Julia Symmes Cobb in Bogota; additional reporting by Deisy Buitrago in Caracas and Simon Lewis in WashingtonEditing by Rod Nickel and Nick Zieminski)

E5 Defence Ministers' Statement: 26 October 2026
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:44:22 GMT
02:44:22 KST

E5 Defence Ministers' Statement: 26 October 2026
E5 Defence Ministers' Statement.
Our countries share the assessment that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability. Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine, on the one hand, and its continued violations of Allied airspace, acts of sabotage and growing use of multi-domain hybrid attacks, on the other, do not undermine our unity, solidarity and cohesion. On the contrary, they strengthen our determination to pursue the efforts already undertaken to safeguard the integrity and security of Allied territory, through a 360-degree approach that takes into account threats from all strategic directions.
We, the Defence Ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom (the Group of Five/E5), share a deep conviction: Europe must assume greater responsibility for its own security. We are determined to work in close coordination with the United States and all Allies in order to implement this concrete ambition. The United States is and will remain an indispensable Ally, and continued United States engagement in European security is essential to a strong and credible NATO.
This greater responsibility must begin with the empowerment of European Allies within NATO.
With the aim of building a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO, we are already taking concrete measures to implement the commitments taken in The Hague, emphasized in Ankara, and to meet agreed capability targets.
We will assume greater political and military leadership within the Alliance, modernising forces and capabilities, including through closer defence-industrial cooperation based on common and standardised requirements,. We reaffirm our commitment to further strengthening NATO’s collective defence in order to rapidly adapt to current and future challenges, including with a more proactive deterrence and defence posture.
We will bolster our contributions to enhance readiness, resilience and our ability to respond to evolving threats across all domains, by promoting the development of the necessary capabilities, in line with NATO-agreed priorities and targets, including through an appropriate, tailored and effective mix of complementary capabilities to meet the full range of operational requirements.
NATO remains the cornerstone of our collective security. The Group of Five/E5 will support greater European ability to act through different frameworks and initiatives, including the European Union, complementing the sovereign responsibilities of States and intergovernmental cooperation.
We emphasise the importance of a nation-led, coordinated approach, aligned with NATO. We commend the European Union’s efforts to support nations in meeting NATO’s defence capability requirements and in strengthening European defence readiness. The EU’s regulatory and financial capacity is a valuable tool in support of our nations’ efforts and ambition. EU defence initiatives should complement NATO, avoid duplication and remain open, under certain conditions, to meaningful cooperation with non-EU NATO Allies.
We will maintain our unwavering commitment to supporting Ukraine in its fight back against Russian aggression. Ukraine’s ability to defend itself now and in the future is critically important to Euro-Atlantic collective security.
We stress the need to keep supporting Ukraine by all available means — politically, militarily and financially.
We reaffirm our determination to continue tackling the activities of Russia’s shadow fleet, in accordance with international law and in coordination with relevant partners.
We stand united with Ukraine in its determination to secure a lasting peace, underpinned by robust security guarantees. The Coalition of the Willing will contribute to robust and credible security guarantees once a cease-fire or a peace agreement is in place.

Likud files police complaint against Eisenkot campaign manager over Polymarket post
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:40:00 UTC
02:40:00 KST

Likud filed a police complaint on Monday against Ronen Manelis, campaign manager for Gadi Eisenkot, accusing him of breaking Israel’s election campaigning law by sharing a post on X that gave Eisenkot strong odds of becoming prime minister after the upcoming election. Attorney Ilan Bombach filed the complaint on Likud’s behalf.
At the center of the complaint is a Polymarket post that Manelis reshared on his X account on Sunday. The post said that former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party, is expected to become Israel’s next prime minister after Tuesday’s election, replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It gave Eisenkot a 52% chance of winning the post, compared with 28% for Netanyahu, and included a photo of Eisenkot in IDF uniform.
The complaint included a screenshot of Manelis’s repost, showing the original Polymarket post, the figures and a chart comparing Eisenkot’s and Netanyahu’s chances.
Likud claims Manelis shared post without clarifying context
Likud argues that the figures do not come from a public opinion poll conducted using accepted statistical methods, but from a platform that forecasts the outcomes of future events. Even so, the complaint claims, Manelis shared them without making clear that they were not a statistical survey and could not be used to draw conclusions about voting patterns or public opinion.
The figures reflect the probability of a political outcome, not a candidate’s level of support among voters. Eisenkot’s 52% chance of becoming prime minister does not mean that 52% of the public plans to vote for him.
In his letter to the police, Bombach stressed that, in Likud’s view, this is not merely a technical violation, but an attempt to influence voters through illegal means.
Post was shared 'to influence the voting public," complaint claims
The complaint claims the offense was committed “in order to influence the voting public, under aggravating circumstances and through prohibited means.” Likud views it as especially serious that the post was shared by Manelis, who runs the campaign of one of the candidates. “There is a significant and pressing public interest in investigating and bringing the offender to justice,” the complaint said, calling on police to investigate the post and pursue charges to the full extent of the law.
However, the claim that Polymarket’s figures count as an election poll under the law is Likud’s own legal interpretation, not a ruling by any authority. The question is a substantive one, since the platform presents the probability of future outcomes rather than the results of an opinion poll. Whether the law’s rules on publishing election polls apply to this kind of data may prove central to how the complaint is handled.

Pope Leo meets with AJC delegation, reaffirms condemnation of antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:55 UTC
02:39:55 KST

American Jewish Committee (AJC) leaders met with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Thursday, marking the first lay leadership delegation to visit the pontiff since the beginning of his papacy.
During their visit to Rome, the AJC delegation also held discussions with senior Vatican officials, including Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin and Vatican Secretary for Relations with States Archbishop Paul Gallagher. They also met with diplomatic figures and representatives from the Italian Jewish community.
The ties between AJC and the Catholic Church stretch back more than a century to at least 1915, with the Holy See and the advocacy group maintaining a decades-long partnership that included a pivotal role in the formulation of Nostra Aetate, the landmark 1965 Vatican declaration that transformed Catholic-Jewish relations by rejecting antisemitism, affirming Judaism's eternal covenant with God, and building new bridges of understanding.
Vatican continues to uphold cooperation with Jewish community
Although recent disagreements and divergent viewpoints regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict have occasionally created friction, AJC noted that the Vatican continues to uphold the core principles of the historic document. This enduring commitment was highlighted in a letter sent to Rabbi Noam Marans in May 2025, where Pope Leo pledged “to continue and strengthen the church’s dialogue and cooperation with the Jewish people in the spirit of the Second Vatican Council’s declaration Nostra Aetate.”
The delegation was led by AJC Chief Executive Ted Deutch, President Bobby Lapin, and Director of Inter-religious Affairs Rabbi Noam Marans, alongside AJC Chair of Inter-religious Affairs Dr. Joyce Silberstang, AJC Associate Director of Inter-religious Affairs Rabbi Allyson Zacharoff, AJC Representative in Italy and Liaison to the Holy See Lisa Palmieri-Billig, and dozens of other AJC leaders.
During the audience, the delegation presented the Pope with a piece of commissioned artwork titled Honoring a Sacred Relationship. Created by Rabbi Matthew Berkowitz, Izzy Pludwinski, and Yair Medina in Jerusalem, the piece displays key passages from Nostra Aetate, written in both the original Latin and an official Hebrew translation. Encircling these texts is a decorative border inspired by an 1822 illuminated Jewish marriage contract from Ferrara, Italy, with the ketubah design purposefully chosen to symbolize the enduring covenant and lasting bond between the Church and the Jewish people.
During the papal audience, Pope Leo addressed the delegation about the longstanding relationship between the Church and the organization, stating, “It is a pleasure to welcome you to the Vatican on this day when the Church remembers in a special way my beloved predecessor, Saint John Paul II, whose efforts contributed so greatly to fostering the friendship between Jews and Catholics.”
Pope's commitment to combat antisemitism
The Pope also recalled remarks made to the committee’s board of governors in 1995, noting that his predecessor observed that “dialogue between Christians and Jews must find eloquent expression in the life of both of our communities.”
“These words remain relevant today, as reflected in your organization’s longstanding commitment to dialogue and to cooperation with the Catholic Church,” Pope Leo said. “I, therefore, welcome this opportunity to express gratitude to all who continue to build relationships, grounded in sincerity and mutual respect, between our respective communities.”
Reaffirming the stance of the Church, the pontiff added, “In this regard, on the occasion of the 60th anniversary of the Declaration Nostra Aetate from the Second Vatican Council, I affirmed that ‘the Church does not tolerate antisemitism and fights against it, on the basis of the Gospel itself.’”
Deutch highlighted the importance of the meeting during a time when inter-religious dialogue faces ongoing challenges.
“When Pope Leo XIV reached out to AJC on the very first day of his papacy, he reaffirmed the enduring importance of the relationship between the Catholic Church and the Jewish people,” Deutch said. “At a time when dialogue across faiths is more important than ever, this gift celebrates a relationship sustained by decades of trust, dialogue, and shared values, rooted in the historic breakthrough of Nostra Aetate. We thank His Holiness for his partnership, generosity, and unwavering support for Jews across the world.”
Lapin stated, “It is a great honor to represent AJC as we met Pope Leo.”
He added, “We are proud of AJC’s long history of leadership in Catholic-Jewish relations, and are grateful for Pope Leo’s commitment to this relationship and leadership in combating antisemitism.”
Marans noted, “It is particularly poignant that we are able to reaffirm our joint commitment to Catholic-Jewish relations in person not only with Vatican officials, but with Pope Leo himself, who on the occasion of his inauguration, reached out directly to AJC and the Jewish community.
The rabbi added: “AJC is deeply moved that this group of Jewish leaders was welcomed to a papal audience while His Holiness continues to recover, and is among the first to meet him as he resumed his schedule of public meetings – a clear demonstration of the value he places on maintaining and fostering the enduring relationship between the Church and the Jewish people.”

Award-winning producer receives £400,000 payout from BBC over workplace antisemitism claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:52 UTC
02:39:52 KST

An Oscar- and Emmy-winning producer has received a payout of more than £400,000 from the BBC after claiming she was victimized and forced out of the corporation following the October 7 attacks.
Lucie Kon left the broadcaster in April, just 19 days after winning an Oscar for her work, following a dispute over antisemitism in the workplace. Having built a stellar career on major programs including Panorama, Today, BBC Breakfast, and Storyville, her commissioned and produced films have earned an Emmy, an Oscar, a BAFTA, and many other prestigious industry honors.
Speaking to The Telegraph on Sunday, Kon alleged that her professional treatment shifted rapidly after the October 7 attacks in Israel. As footage and news of the atrocities emerged, she had messaged a colleague on WhatsApp asking if they had seen what was happening in Israel and remarking that Hamas were evil. In response, the colleague told her that “Zionists” were evil.
“I was like, ‘What?’ And she went, ‘Evil Hamas, evil Zionists,’ a bit like it was a joke, like they were the same and they’re not the same, and that was a particularly tasteless thing to say at that particular moment in history,” Kon said.
Later, when Kon sought to raise concerns about the treatment of Jewish staff and insisted that staff should at least be able to describe Hamas as committing acts of terror, another colleague told her that if she wanted to refer to Hamas as terrorists, she was required to call Israel a terrorist state as well.
Kon helps set up WhatsApp group for Jewish BBC employees
Pushed by the worsening workplace environment, Kon helped set up an internal WhatsApp group for Jewish employees at the corporation and wrote to then-Director General Tim Davie to raise concerns.
Shortly afterward, as more footage of the atrocities emerged, Kon proposed producing a film about the events of October 7 to a colleague who had previously made inappropriate remarks. When she mentioned the idea, the colleague dismissed it, saying they had already made enough films about Israel, but Kon’s manager later called her over to discuss the project.
“She said, ‘Lucie, we probably will do the Nova film,’” Kon recounted. “And she said to me, ‘But if we do it, we need to contextualize why Hamas did what they did.’”
When Kon questioned this requirement, explaining that the project was intended as a straightforward account of what happened that day rather than a deep dive into the historical and political context of the region, her manager’s manager informed her that she could no longer oversee the film. When Kon asked why, the manager told her it was “because you’re Jewish” and stated she was partial.
Kon noted that the manager then stated the person who was going to look after the film instead was the very same colleague who had previously told her that if Hamas were terrorists, the Israelis were terrorists too. An arrangement was later reached where Kon could oversee the film, but only under the strict supervision of someone else to ensure she remained impartial.
Kon subsequently raised a formal grievance. News of the grievance quickly reached the colleague who had made the remarks about Zionists, and that colleague wanted nothing more to do with Kon. This meant the two could no longer attend meetings together, and Kon was instructed not to come into work.
Six months later, she received the outcome. “It wasn’t upheld,” Kon said. “I was told that a lot of the things that I’d said people didn’t remember saying. And I was told that I’d been told - that I hadn’t been told I couldn’t work on the Nova film because I was a Jew - that they were worried about my mental health.”
When she appealed the decision, that appeal was also unsuccessful. At the time of her appeal, the BBC moved her colleague away from the Strand to work elsewhere, while Kon was told she could no longer travel, commission, or speak on behalf of the BBC because it would be unfair to her colleague.
Kon continued working from home while her appeal was considered, but by December, the stress took a toll, and her health began to deteriorate. After submitting a doctor’s note for stress-related sick leave, she was called into a meeting where she was told her job was being put at risk of redundancy. Having returned from sick leave, she applied for a newly created position but was rejected and made redundant in April.
BBC refuses to apologize, call Kon victim of antisemitism
According to The Telegraph, she brought unfair dismissal proceedings against the BBC, which agreed to pay her substantial compensation, partly funded by the license fee, without admitting liability. The corporation refused to apologize or admit she was a victim of antisemitism.
The Telegraph noted that she is the first person known to have been given a settlement by the BBC after alleging antisemitic behavior among colleagues. Speaking about the broader climate for staff after her departure, Kon reportedly told The Telegraph that other Jewish colleagues are still being bullied and abused, adding, “I know that nothing has changed because I’ve spoken to quite a few people since I left. Friends who are still struggling, still suffering, who feel embarrassed to say that they’re Zionist or that they’re a Jew.”
“I went from being a journalist and commissioner at the BBC who was Jewish to being a Jewish journalist at the BBC,” Kon said. “It was like I had Jew stamped on my forehead. I think I became a problem. I think I made too much of a noise about being a Jew inside the BBC.”
Kon added, “A colleague of mine said to me a while ago that if you say you’re a Zionist at the BBC, you might as well say that you were the person who had their foot on the neck of George Floyd. You’re a murderer. You’re an evil colonialist. You are a racist, and I’m not any of those things, and neither are the other people I know who are Zionist.”
“I stood up for who I was,” Kon said. “I stood up for what I believed to be right. The BBC says, ‘Bring your authentic self to work.’ And I did, and I lost my job as a result.”
A BBC spokesperson said in a statement, “We are grateful that Ms. Kon acknowledges that the BBC is not institutionally antisemitic. The BBC processes did not uphold any of Ms. Kon’s allegations of antisemitism. However, the outcome acknowledged shortcomings and the personal impact on Ms. Kon. We would like to acknowledge that Ms. Kon was a valued member of staff with many years of dedicated service to the BBC.”

President Isaac Herzog diverted from his efforts to promote a national unity government to receive the credentials of five new ambassadors to Israel on Monday.
Under the country’s current government, Maj.-Gen. Emmanuel Bayingana of Rwanda, Christophe Parisot of France, Arad Benko of Austria, Stella Ronner Grubacic of the Netherlands, and Evelyn Korantemaa Ofosu-Amable of Ghana were the last ambassadors to present their credentials.
They will serve out their terms under Israel’s next government.
Israel and Rwanda established relations in the early 1960s, but severed them in 1973. Decades later, in 1998, Israel and Rwanda renewed their relations, which have remained cordial. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Rwanda in 2016, and Rwanda President Paul Kagame visited Israel in July 2017 in return.
Since taking office in the immediate aftermath of the Rwandan genocide, Kagame has spent the past 26 years rebuilding his country and forming strong international partnerships. Israel and Rwanda cooperate on many levels, including innovation, technology, agriculture, and security. Rwanda and Israel signed several bilateral agreements earlier this year when Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe visited Israel.
Bayingana said that he would work to further expand the relationship between the two countries.
Neither Herzog nor Parisot tried to pretend that relations between France and Israel were rosy. However, Parisot noted that, despite their diplomatic challenges, the people-to-people relations and cultural ties between France and Israel remained strong.
Herzog and Parisot also discussed the chaos and unrest that have overtaken France in recent weeks. Herzog recalled how different Champs-Élysées had felt when he accompanied his late father, then-president Chaim Herzog, on a state visit to France in 1988.
Herzog recalls time of 'amazing' French-Israeli relations
Herzog also recalled a time when relations between France and Israel were so positive they were “amazing.”
Parisot later wrote in the guest book that he would devote all of his energy to improving relations between the two countries.
Benko previously said returning to Israel felt like coming home. Indeed, it was. He was born in Haifa; he left the country as a child, and returned some 20 years ago as a spokesman for the Austrian embassy. He said that when he left Israel, he had a hard time in school because the only language he spoke was Hebrew. Aside from the usual diplomatic subjects and antisemitism, Benko and Herzog also discussed the Jews of Austria.
Michal Herzog, the president's wife, seldom sits in on the presentation of diplomatic credentials. This time, however, she attended the meetings with both the French and Austrian ambassadors and joined the ensuing conversations.
While welcoming Rubacic, Herzog spoke of the “special relationship” between Israel and the Netherlands. But he also expressed concern over the discourse emanating from Holland and some of the government’s own negative comments. He warned that Israel and Holland’s relations were currently under strain. Rubacic replied that she was happy to be in Israel and stressed the importance of highlighting the good relations between the two countries, which are based on shared values.
The significance Israel attaches to its ties with the Netherlands was evident in the brief, closed-door tete-a-tete Herzog had with the ambassador after the formalities concluded.
Most African countries with which Israel has diplomatic ties are proud of their culture and heritage. Ghana is no exception. Ofosu-Amable and her entourage arrived at the President’s Residence in national dress. Herzog was struck by the swell of colors and commented on it. He also noted that Israel’s relations with Ghana span seven decades, dating back to when former premier Golda Meir made her historic visit to Africa.
Israel trained Ghanaian soldiers early in relationship
In the early years of their relationship, Israel helped to train soldiers in Ghana’s army. Ghana stands out for the confidence it places in its women. Many of the country’s diplomats and high-ranking officials are women, and the ambassador is among them.
Where Israel and Ghana differ is their stance on a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Ghana’s President John Mahama told Ofosu-Amable that she must remember that her mission is to uphold Ghana’s longstanding commitment to the two-state solution.

====================================================================================================

Form a government, you can hate each other on your own time - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:47 UTC
02:39:47 KST

Before casting his vote in Israel’s first national election, Rabbi Moshe Yekutiel Alpert told off the polling committee.
Its chairman was two minutes late.
On January 25, 1949, Alpert got up at 5:35 a.m., put on his Shabbat clothes, and headed for a Jerusalem polling station. His home in the Beit Yisrael neighborhood had been damaged by shelling; he was staying elsewhere while it was being repaired. He carried his Israeli identity card, he wrote, with the same joy of carrying a Torah scroll during Simchat Torah celebrations.
He arrived at 5:50. The chairman appeared at 6:02. Alpert reminded him that proceedings were supposed to begin at six. The man apologized.
As the oldest person present, Alpert was invited to vote first at that station. He received “voter number one,” said Shehecheyanu, the blessing of gratitude for reaching a special occasion, and cast his ballot.
His father and grandfather had never had the same opportunity.
I shared the story this week. The Jewish state was eight months old, and Alpert already expected it to run on time.
It’s a familiar mix of reverence and impatience. Israelis can be fiercely attached to their country and furious with it, often in the same conversation. People expect a great deal from a place their families have paid a great deal for. From abroad, the anger can be easier to hear than the attachment.
Today, Jewish and Arab Israelis will again choose the people who govern them. I hope we allow ourselves a little of Alpert’s pleasure before we begin arguing about the exit polls. The ability to vote a government out is worth appreciating, including when a government we favor loses.
Israel needs several years where its citizens can make plans again
What I want from this election is a few years in which Israelis can make plans again.
Three years after October 7, consider what that would mean for a reservist trying to keep a business alive. Someone has to cover the work while he is away. His spouse has to rearrange work and childcare. Eventually, decisions about next month become decisions about whether the business has a future.
Families rebuilding their homes need to know that funding and official attention will last until the work is finished. They should be able to plan around a budget that survives the next coalition dispute.
I believe only a broad Zionist government can give this country the political stability it needs for that work. Likud, former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, and other Zionist parties should negotiate an agreement to govern together for several years.
That will require leaders to sit with people they have spent the campaign attacking and explain the arrangement to voters who believed those attacks.
Some will have to accept a job smaller than the one they wanted. They should tell us which demands they are prepared to set aside. I would find that interview considerably more useful than another account of why everything is someone else’s fault.
There is a reason these concessions are so hard. In Israel, a political allegiance often comes with a family history. It may include a grandparent’s experience of immigration, a parent’s sense of being looked down on, or a lasting belief that people like us were denied a fair hearing. Calling an entire camp ignorant or dangerous reaches well beyond the politician at its head.
An election settles who has the votes to govern. People still have to live together afterward. A citizen should be able to lose an election and feel at home in their country. Leaders who want a broad coalition will have to show they understand one another’s voters.
Start the negotiations by asking what 70 or 80 percent of Israelis could support. I would begin with security preparedness, restoring damaged communities, and arrangements that let reservists serve without ruining their livelihoods. Agree on what can be done, how much it will cost, and who is responsible. Give ministers enough time in office to be judged on whether they delivered.
A coalition agreement might even contain a deadline unrelated to the next leadership rotation.
Independent October 7 commission must be part of coalition agreement
An independent, credible examination of October 7 must be part of that agreement. Families deserve to know how the state failed them. Officials and commanders need to answer for their decisions. A coalition assembled to restore public trust will have to accept findings that may be uncomfortable for its own members.
Before accepting another promise, I want to know whom that candidate appointed, what improved while they were in office, and what they did when something went wrong. The politician I like deserves the same questions. Newcomers can be judged on their experience and the seriousness of their plans.
Theodor Herzl, the founder of modern political Zionism, described Zionism in 1904 as “a never-ending ideal.” Even after the Jewish people obtained a homeland, he wrote, the pursuit of “ethical and spiritual fulfillment” would continue.
In our time, that responsibility includes a government office being responsible for treating a bereaved family, the education available to a child far from the center of the country, and the willingness of a prime minister to accept scrutiny.
The late chief rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook approached the problem from another direction. He wrote about the religious, national, and universal human concerns within Jewish society, arguing that each had value and could restrain the others’ excesses. He also understood how hostility between camps could consume them.
A religious minister and a secular mayor can have different ideas about the purpose of Jewish sovereignty and still agree on how to get a school built. They can resume the philosophical argument after the classrooms open.
The Jewish Agency’s Board of Governors has been meeting in Israel this week. The gathering brings Israeli leaders and Jews from abroad into the same room on the eve of the election.
Having spent years covering Jewish life abroad, I wish more Israelis were interested in what those communities are trying to achieve.
A minister visiting a Jewish school should ask how it keeps tuition affordable and what its pupils know about Israel. There is a great deal to learn from people who have to persuade families to choose a Jewish education.
We Israelis often ask Diaspora Jews to understand the pressures we live under. We should also be equally willing to learn about the pressures they face. The government answers to Israel’s citizens; its decisions can still affect a Jewish family thousands of miles away.
The next prime minister should put regular consultations with Jewish communities abroad in the diary and give the relevant ministers responsibility for following up. The Jewish Agency and other communal bodies can bring in voices from beyond the familiar leadership circles. Publish the commitments, then report what happened to them.
I would put affordable opportunities to study and spend time in Israel high on that list. Help young immigrants find their feet here. Give young Israelis more chances to encounter Jewish life abroad. A friendship formed over a semester has time to develop beyond the positions people take in an argument about the news.
A Jewish child abroad should be able to cultivate a relationship with Israel that lasts through several changes of government. She ought to have friends here, places she wants to revisit, and enough knowledge to form her own opinions.
I want my own children to make their lives here, and I want them to be able to plan beyond the next emergency. They will have plenty to complain about. I would like them to grow up expecting a government to finish the work it starts.

The regime change we need for Thames Water | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:41 UTC
02:39:41 KST

Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained (Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question.
Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed.
Nationalisation changes who owns the shares. It does not change the rules. A publicly owned Thames under the present regime would inherit the same debt and the same incentive to defer repair; within a decade “public control” would mean ill-regulation by another name.
The Cunliffe review’s single water regulator closes one gap. It leaves the larger one: water is still regulated apart from the air, land and soil it moves through, though sewage in a river is a land, soil and water problem at once.
The prime minister’s 10-year plan needs a single environmental regulator, with a duty of candour, for air, water, land and soil, with three plain service duties: the service is delivered to standard, the money raised is spent on the service, and the charge is fair to the household that pays it. That, not ownership alone, is what a well-regulated industry looks like.
 
Terry Barker
 
Honorary professor of environmental sciences, University of East Anglia
Your report that Andy Burnham has instructed his team to explore radical solutions to the Thames Water crisis is welcome. But one solution already exists: the special administration regime (SAR), which could bring the company under temporary public control to stabilise and restructure it in the public interest.
The forthcoming clean water bill may revisit legislation enabling greater public ownership, but reform must not delay action under existing powers. The Water Industry Act 1991 provides for special administration where statutory conditions are met. Thames Water’s financial instability, service failures and environmental record provide compelling grounds.
We at River Action urge the government and Ofwat to petition the high court to place Thames Water into an SAR. A creditor deal will not address the causes of its decline. An SAR offers restructuring that prioritises customers, communities and the environment over creditors.
The government should also commission an independent feasibility study of alternative ownership, governance and financing models, including public, mutual and not-for-profit options.
No new legislation is needed: the powers and grounds to intervene in Thames Water already exist. Water is an essential public service. Its future must be secured in the public interest.
 
James Wallace
 
CEO, River Action
If Thames Water is effectively bankrupt, I can’t see why shareholders should get compensation. Broke is broke. Rather than old-style nationalisation, I would turn it into a social enterprise and put it under the control of its engineers.
There would be no shares, no dividends, and all profits would be reinvested in infrastructure, such as pipes and new reservoirs.
 
Philip Clayton
 
London

Bigger does not always mean better in hospital care | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:24 UTC
02:39:24 KST

The closure of maternity units is always a temptation when the NHS runs into staffing problems, largely of its own making (Up to 20 maternity units in England may have to shut, NHS leader warns, 19 October).
In my area the quality of care has already been called into question at the largest local unit, and directing mothers to chance their luck there seems to be an undeserved reward. Likewise a nearby large trust has had the quality of its neonatal care called into question. Closing small units is unlikely to provide the quality gain that is sought.
The problem for the NHS is that there is a freedom of ability to employ consultant staff. If you have the money, get on and advertise. This means that the supposedly better, larger units will be able to hoover up all the people they want. The smaller units don’t get a chance.
The reason people want to work at big centres is because for the same pay they don’t have to work so hard, or have the same level of responsibility. Government policy has created specialist units in large centres with the belief, promulgated by the medical profession, that bigger means better.
When I was appointed as a consultant in 1988, before trusts were invented, the regional health authority made the appointments and made sure that senior medical staffing was fairly spread. You could not have 20 specialists in one district general hospital (DGH) and none in the next.
Centralising services on fewer sites is a disaster for local populations. If a DGH loses its obstetrics department, paediatrics would be immediately under threat. It would mean more children would have to travel. Accident and emergency departments would lose specialist support from paediatricians and gynaecologists. Fine if you have a broken arm, not so fine if you have meningitis etc.
So, when reviewing the future of obstetrics and midwifery, how about considering the people who live in the area and not just the needs of professors?
How about planning to relatively overstaff small units to make sure that they can provide for the needs of the population they serve, and ensuring that the newly qualified are directed towards these posts? After all, the NHS is paid for by everyone, so everyone should get a decent quality of care, without having to travel 50 miles in the dead of night.
 
Dr Paul Godwin
 
Keighley, West Yorkshire

France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:10 UTC

I’m writing in response to your editorial (The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment, 19 October). While the focus is on Emmanuel Macron, let us not forget the hierarchical structure of French administration, from mayors to MPs to senators to prefects and heads of region. All are part of the government, but few stood up to bring leaky school roofs and missing teachers to national consciousness. I deplore the senseless destruction of shops and state buildings. But I also deplore the fact that students had to protest to be heard. In the many administrative tiers of this highly hierarchical country, no one acted and inertia prevailed.
Centrally, the government is financially challenged but refuses to acknowledge that having a huge deficit, an ageing population and a low retirement age are perhaps connected. Thus, this sclerotic system presses on until the next crisis.
Neither side of the populist fringe offers a viable path forward. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise actively avoid confronting the retirement timebomb, preferring politically expedient promises over fiscal reality.
If a system treats retirement as a sacred cow even when the meaning of work is being redefined at lightning speed by AI, if it’s acceptable to have productivity grind to a halt in August because the wisdom of asking employees to all take four to five weeks off in the same month while we live in a 24/7 world is never questioned, and if that same system lets young people study by rote in leaky classrooms while offering its over-60s free social dinners, let us not be surprised if the pressure valve is showing signs of fatigue. My concern is how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion.
 
Muriel E Cockcroft
  
France

The arc of Trump: How the president lost the coalition that put him in the White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:36:55 UTC
02:36:55 KST

President Donald Trump forged an extraordinary coalition to win office in 2024, stitching together his base with unusual support from some traditional Democratic groups like Hispanics and young people. It was enough to sweep the battleground states and catapult him into office for a second term.
The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey shows that coalition is now seriously weakened.
Since the beginning of his second term, the president's net approval rating among Latino voters has dropped from -22 to -38, and declined from -28 to -53 among 18- to 34-year olds. Black respondents have moved from -55 to -67.
Among all registered voters, his approval has fallen from -7 at the start of his term to -19 in the most recent survey.
The decline in the president's approval carries over into the Republican base. Approval from self-described Trump voters has fallen from a net +85 in 2025 to a net of +65. Net approval has even turned negative in the South, from +2 in 2025 to -20 in the latest survey.
The results of the latest poll show why Republicans are facing an uphill battle in the midterm elections next week. Trump is not on the ballot — but his presence will be felt.
Read the full survey results here.
To be sure, Republicans in the survey still give the president an 82% approval rating, and those who say they identify with the MAGA movement are at 90%. But interest in the election is 10 points lower among Republicans than it is for Democrats, and in tight races, the party that better turns out its voters will have an advantage.
The survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide found 44% of respondents say their biggest worry if Republicans control Congress is allowing President Trump to operate beyond his constitutional power. By contrast, 28% say their biggest worry for Democratic control is passing policies of Democratic Socialists. For either party's control, registered voters worry that Congress won't do enough to bring down prices.
The survey was conducted Oct. 14-18, and was co-led by Democratic pollster Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Public Opinion Strategies. It carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.
As a second-term president who had skipped four years between terms, Trump's arc of approval has followed an unusual path. The president left office above water on the economy, with 48% approving and 41% disapproving — high numbers for a president whose last year was overwhelmed by the Covid pandemic.
But there was no second-term honeymoon. Trump was immediately underwater in his economic approval rating in the April 2025 CNBC survey. That could have reflected immediate public discontent with the tariff regime and resulting market turmoil. The president's economic approval rating remained negative through most of his first year.
The bottom dropped out, however, with the launch of the Iran war. By April 2026, the president's net economic approval rating was plying depths last seen under President Joe Biden amid the aftermath of the pandemic, when the country was facing high inflation and elevated unemployment.
In the first quarter of this year, Trump's net economic approval dropped 10 points to -21. It has plunged to -31 in the latest survey. Economic disapproval rose to 65%, the highest for any president CNBC has measured back to President Barack Obama, and one point higher than Biden's worst showing. The survey shows increasing disapproval of Trump's handling of inflation. Over the same time, shooting of Americans by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers began to dominate headlines, eroding support for one of the president's major policy initiatives.
The survey this quarter appeared to pick up growing frustration with a host of issues, from immigration to the economy, among those demographic groups that had supported the president in unusual numbers in 2024, with sharp declines in economic and overall approval among Latinos, young people and those in the $50,000 to $75,000 income group.
Most ominously for the president, views on the economic outlook fell 22 points for Republicans. Though still net positive, it was the lowest level of economic optimism for Republicans since Biden.
These downbeat views on the economy do not automatically translate to votes for Democrats. The survey showed a 7-point preference for Democratic control of Congress, a 3-point gain from the July survey. While Republican economic pessimism grew, so did their preference for a Republican-controlled Congress, from 85% in July to 87% in October.
Blue-collar workers show how the president has maintained his base amid growing concern about the economy. Their net economic approval of the president has plunged 22 points to -15 from the beginning of Trump's term to now. But their overall presidential approval remains +6, just a four-point drop. They still prefer a Republican-controlled Congress by 21 points, though that is down from 33 points in July.
The days and weeks leading up to the election have seen the president barnstorming through red states, a sign of concern with the base's enthusiasm. But it also creates the possibility that he could fire up his base and bring them out to stanch potential Democratic gains.
The survey shows that the extra votes from the coalition that put Trump in the White House in 2024 would be a reach for Republican congressional candidates in 2026.
