OAC and university developing maritime AI drone system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:42 UTC
01:48:42 KST

The Ocean Affairs Council (OAC) yesterday said it is funding a National Cheng Kung University (NCKU) team to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered system to coordinate different types of drones to enable wide-area maritime surveillance and sustained monitoring.
Developing a multilayered coast guard surveillance network and enhancing maritime domain awareness are core strategies to address maritime law enforcement needs and various forms of “gray zone” harassment from China, the council said.
Regional conflicts in the past few years have shown that drone technology has evolved from single-aircraft operations to coordinated missions involving multiple types of drones and fleets operating in swarms, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Ocean Affairs Council
The AI-powered drone swarm system being developed by the research team achieved a breakthrough by coordinating different drone fleets, providing wide coverage and continuous monitoring over territorial waters, the council said.
“This system would bolster Taiwan’s maritime defense, rescue capabilities and whole-of-society defense resilience,” it said. “It has laid a solid technical foundation to build a smart and multilayered coast guard patrol system and demonstrated Taiwan’s research and development capacity in marine technology and smart aerospace sectors.”
The team, led by the university’s aeronautics and astronautics associate professor Chueh Chih-che (闕志哲), built an intelligent multiple drone operating system by integrating AI, vertical takeoff and landing fixed-wing drones, flight dynamics, and swarm coordination and control technology.
The team explored the strengths and control models of three types of drones used in the project — Jump 20, V-Bat and Flexroter — through 3D shape modeling, aerodynamic parameter analysis and “six degrees of freedom” flight simulation, the council said.
The team further used AI multi-agent reinforcement learning technology to enable multiple drones to autonomously assign missions, plan flight paths and coordinate with one another, flying in formation like a flock of geese.
To improve formation flexibility and flight safety, the research team incorporated “leader-follower formation control” and “intelligent dynamic obstacle avoidance,” enabling the drone swarm to adjust its flight path according to mission requirements and autonomously respond in real time to sudden environmental changes or obstacles, the council said.
The team has completed simultaneous flight simulations of two drone fleets, comprising a total of 20 drones, it said.
To avoid drone swarm collisions, the team has incorporated into its control algorithm the 3D separation distance and a minimum vertical separation of 30.5m, the council said.
The team would further test the reliability and feasibility of drone fleets under different marine environments by conducting hardware-in-the-loop and prototype integration tests, as well as real-world flight tests over open water, it said.

2026 Elections: China trying to isolate Puma Shen: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:38 UTC
01:48:38 KST

China is attempting to isolate Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) by pressuring people and businesses associated with him, a source familiar with national security cases said after a celebrity’s statement denying support for Taiwanese independence.
Television host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) faced a backlash from Chinese authorities and Internet users after on Oct. 4 attending an event marking the opening of Shen’s campaign headquarters. Tsai on Sunday night in a post on Chinese social media apologized, saying that he had never supported Taiwanese independence.
Beijing cannot easily use the Chinese market to pressure Shen directly, so it is targeting Taiwanese entertainers and companies that attend his events or appear alongside him, the source said yesterday.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
By threatening their commercial interests, Beijing hopes to deter others from participating in Shen’s campaign and limit his ability to secure resources and support, they said.
Tsai had attended Shen’s event to familiarize himself with Shen ahead of a potential interview with the candidate, Tsai’s manager said.
However, business partners in China continued to distance themselves from Tsai.
The pressure could lead businesses and people to avoid even routine professional interactions with political figures, as the risk lies not only in what a person says but also in which events they attend and who they appear alongside, the source said.
If potential supporters become reluctant to meet a candidate, accept invitations or publicly collaborate with them because of their business interests in China, the candidate loses not only potential campaign surrogates, but also opportunities to explain their positions and attract new supporters, they said.
Beijing has said that it would target people and businesses associated with political figures, they said, citing the Chinese government’s investigation and penalties against Taiwan’s Far Eastern Group in 2021.
At the time, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office said businesses would not be allowed to make money in China while funding people it described as advocates of Taiwanese independence. It also identified affiliated companies and financial backers as targets for punishment.
Shen yesterday said the timing of Tsai’s post denying support for Taiwanese independence appeared to have been determined by outside forces, adding that it showed signs of Chinese interference in Taiwanese people’s ability to make their own decisions.
He was referring to the statement issued a day before his opponent — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), who is seeking re-election — was slated to launch his campaign headquarters.
Tsai, who previously said he would attend the event, showed up yesterday.
Shen said that Tsai was the top trending topic on Chinese social media yesterday, adding that topics in the top three positions on the platform’s trending list were generally determined by Chinese authorities.
Regardless of whether Tsai had been directed to issue the statement, the incident showed signs of Chinese intervention, Shen said.
The interference was not necessarily in the election itself, but in Taiwanese people’s ability to make their own decisions, he added.
Chiang yesterday said he respected Tsai’s post and political position, adding that he would not accept threats against people because of their political views.
In local media, Tsai’s post was widely compared to a 2016 incident in which Taiwanese K-pop star Chou Tzu-yu (周子瑜), more commonly known as Tzuyu, issued a video apologizing for holding a Republic of China (Taiwan) flag on television.
Chiang was asked about the comparison and whether the controversy could affect his election campaign.
Chiang said he welcomed Tsai’s attendance at the opening of his campaign headquarters, adding that regardless of whether Tsai or any other citizen supports him, he respects their opinions and is committed to serving them as mayor.
Chiang also criticized the tendency to attack, boycott or ostracize people because of their differing political views.
“I absolutely will not permit or accept such anti-democratic intimidation,” he said.

Taiwanese gymnast wins gold at world championships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:37 UTC
01:48:37 KST

Taiwanese gymnast Tang Chia-hung (唐嘉鴻) on Sunday won gold in the men’s horizontal bar final at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.
Tang scored 14.966 in the final. He had advanced to the final in second place with a score of 14.566 points in qualifying, with a difficulty score of 6.000 and an execution score of 8.566.
In the final, he raised his difficulty score to 6.600, the highest among the eight finalists. Although he did not fully steady himself on landing, his score was still enough to claim the gold medal.
Photo: Iris van den Broek, EPA
Taiwan had previously won two silver medals and one bronze at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships. Chang Feng-chih (張峰治) took silver in the men’s vault in 1993, while Lee Chih-kai (李智凱) won silver in the men’s pommel horse in 2019 and bronze in the same event in 2018.
With his gold medal, Tang became the first Taiwanese gymnast to win a title at the world championships.
Tang said he had found a way to reset his mindset after finishing fifth and missing out on a medal in the horizontal bar final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Japan.
Photo: Patrick Post, AP
He said he had reviewed his performance with coach Huang Bo-rui (黃柏瑞) and a sports psychologist after the Asian Games.
He decided to treat the world championships final as a practice session and compete without pressure, which helped him stay calm and in control without overthinking.
This approach seemed to work quite well, he said with a laugh, adding that he now felt more confident about qualifying for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics at next year’s world championships.
Tang said he was unsure how he had performed after his unsteady landing and kept wondering how he had made such a mistake.
He said he was most grateful to everyone who had supported him, including his coaches, teammates and athletic trainers.
“We won this gold medal together, helping take Taiwan’s gymnastics another step further on the world stage,” he said.
Tang said he struggled with his preparations during the first week of training under the pressure of back-to-back major competitions. His wife, Tseng Jo-yu (曾若語), arrived in Rotterdam a day before the event and gave him a much-needed boost.
“I was physically and mentally exhausted during the training camp and didn’t feel I was in my best form, but after my wife arrived, simply having a meal and chatting with her made me feel recharged,” he said.
Tang, who has been married for two years, said his wife is his “invisible coach.”
She understood how he was feeling, kept him grounded when he got overly excited and encouraged him when he was feeling down, he said.
Huang said he had been sleeping poorly in the days leading up to the world championships because of the high level of competition, but Tang continued to train as usual after qualifying, without making any special adjustments.
Tang’s routine had the highest difficulty score in the field, so he would be hard to beat as long as he completed it, Huang said, adding that he had urged Tang to stay calm and avoid putting too much pressure on himself.
This year’s Artistic Gymnastics World Championships were held from Oct. 17 to Sunday.

The Ministry of Health and Welfare in November last year launched a pilot program with 13 UCCs in the six special municipalities to provide emergency treatment for mild illness and injuries on weekends and on holidays to relieve pressure on crowded emergency rooms.
With schools and work suspended nearly nationwide due to Typhoon Champi on Friday, the long holiday weekend became a four-day weekend for many people.
Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times
About 75 percent of clinics were open yesterday and some hospitals also resumed outpatient services, which helped relieve overcrowding at emergency departments, Shih said.
In addition, a new UCC would open at Tainan’s Da-an Women and Children Hospital on Sunday, he said.

Before the Double Ten National Day three-day weekend, the ministry had announced that during long weekends through the end of this year, a 50-percent surcharge would be added to consultation fees, nursing fees and pharmacist service fees at primary care clinics and hospitals’ outpatient and emergency departments, Shih said.
Eighty percent of the surcharge must be distributed to on-duty staff, he said.
To alleviate overcrowding at National Taiwan University Hospital’s emergency department, the Taipei Department of Health is planning to set up a UCC near the hospital at the Huashan Market, Shih said.
Preparations for the center are under way, and the department hopes to open it before the Lunar New Year holiday next year, he said.
Between July and Oct. 18, the most common reasons for visiting the nation’s 13 UCCs were for fever and respiratory infections (46 percent), followed by minor wounds (13 percent) and gastrointestinal discomfort (9 percent), National Health Insurance Administration data showed.

“Ocean Wave” — a pun on 洋 (“ocean”) in Shen’s name and a nod to the “Han wave” (韓流) that led to Han Kuo-yu’s (韓國瑜) surprise 2018 Kaohsiung mayoral victory — refers to the campaign movement built around Shen’s Taipei mayoral bid.
The Ocean Wave has revived people’s expectations for a concrete policy vision for the city and responded to their hope for a new, policy-oriented election culture, the source said.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
People want to see candidates refraining from attacking their rivals and adopting new practices, such as whispering slogans at night to avoid disturbing residents, they said.
The core value of the Ocean Wave is creating a healthy election culture and demonstrating respect for citizens, they said.
Shen’s candidacy for Taipei mayor has triggered momentum for civic self-determination, they said, adding that rather than being an extension of last year’s mass recall movement, his campaign should be defined as a comprehensive expansion of a new citizen movement.
Shen has invited citizens to share their opinions and get involved in discussions to shape the city’s future blueprint, including the street-side soapbox sessions that invited people to voice their concerns, the Heart Policy Island interactive Web site launched last week and the “Municipal Debug Hackathon” that solicited ideas from the public, the source said.
Those efforts put the new movement into practice and have won growing support from moderate voters, they said.
While the mass recall movement fell short of its goal, it was still a display of civic will, they said.

The amendments have exacerbated intergenerational division and increased the burden on young people, while once again drawing public attention to the opposition party’s indiscriminate budget cuts, the source said.

輕鬆華語GO: EASY CHINESE GO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:35 UTC
01:48:35 KST

對話 Dialogue
華華：最近天氣終於涼快一點了，我想找一天去騎腳踏車。
Huáhua: Zuìjìn tiānqì zhōngyú liángkuai yìdiǎn le, wǒ xiǎng zhǎo yì tiān qù qí jiǎotàchē.
Photo: Unsplash / 照片：Unsplash
清清：我也想去！秋天最適合騎車了，不會像夏天那麼熱。
Qīngqīng: Wǒ yě xiǎng qù! Qiūtiān zuì shìhé qí chē le, bú huì xiàng xiàtiān nàme rè.
華華：你平常都去哪裡騎？
Huáhua: Nǐ píngcháng dōu qù nǎlǐ qí?
清清：我很喜歡去河濱自行車道，一邊騎車一邊看風景，很舒服。
Qīngqīng: Wǒ hěn xǐhuān qù hébīn zìxíngchēdào, yìbiān qí chē yìbiān kàn fēngjǐng, hěn shūfu.
華華：聽起來不錯，不過我很久沒騎了，可能騎一下就累了。
Huáhua: Tīng qǐlái búcuò, búguò wǒ hěn jiǔ méi qí le, kěnéng qí yíxià jiù lèi le.
清清：沒關係，我們可以慢慢騎，累了就停下來休息。
Qīngqīng: Méiguānxi, wǒmen kěyǐ mànmàn qí, lèi le jiù tíng xiàlái xiūxi.
華華：那我們這週六早上六點出發吧！騎完車再去附近吃早餐。
Huáhua: Nà wǒmen zhè zhōuliù zǎoshang liù diǎn chūfā ba! Qí wán chē zài qù fùjìn chī zǎocān.
清清：蛤？六點也太早了吧！我可能爬不起來，我們晚一點出發吧！
Qīngqīng: Há? Liù diǎn yě tài zǎo le ba! Wǒ kěnéng pá bù qǐlái, wǒmen wǎn yìdiǎn chūfā ba!
翻譯 Translation
Huahua: The weather has finally gotten a little cooler lately. I’d like to go cycling soon.
Qingqing: Me too. Autumn is the perfect time for cycling. It’s not as hot as summer.
Huahua: Where do you usually go cycling?
Qingqing: I really like cycling along riverside bike paths. It’s relaxing to ride while enjoying the scenery.
Huahua: That sounds nice, but I haven’t ridden a bike in a long time. I might get tired pretty quickly.
Qingqing: That’s OK. We can take it slow and stop for a break when we get tired.
Huahua: Then let’s head out at six this Saturday morning. After our ride, we can get breakfast somewhere nearby.
Qingqing: What? Six is way too early. I might not be able to get out of bed. Let’s leave a little later.
生詞 Vocabulary
1. 終於 (zhōngyú) finally; at last
2. 涼快 (liángkuai) cool; pleasantly cool
3. 河濱 (hébīn) riverside; riverbank
4. 自行車道 (zìxíngchēdào) bike path; bicycle path
5. 週六 (zhōuliù) Saturday
6. 蛤 (há) Huh?; What?
7. 爬不起來 (pá bu qǐlái) can’t get out of bed;
can’t get up
8. 出發 (chūfā) set out/off; depart; leave

Who is the Hebrew-speaking ‘fox applying for the henhouse guard job?’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:47:39 UTC
01:47:39 KST

Who is the Hebrew-speaking ‘fox applying for the henhouse guard job?’
Lana Nusseibeh’s close alignment with Israel shadows her bid to lead the UN
TEHRAN — Having spent years whitewashing Abu Dhabi’s submission to Israeli interests, Lana Nusseibeh is now being promoted by her handlers to run the United Nations.
Nominated on Oct. 21, the 48-year-old minister of state is the newest and most contested entrant in the race to succeed António Guterres, and the objections started within hours.
Nusseibeh was born in 1978 into a family in al-Quds (Jerusalem). Her grandfather Anwar sat in Jordanian governments, her father Zaki advises the UAE’s rulers, and her uncle Sari is a philosophy professor.
She read history at Cambridge, then took a master’s in “Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies” in London, where her teacher Colin Shindler later called her “instrumental” in the 2020 normalization deal. She is fluent in Hebrew.
In 2013, she became the UAE’s first female ambassador to the UN and stayed eleven years, twice presiding over the Security Council.
‘The fox applying for the henhouse guard job’
Weeks before the Abraham Accords were signed, she told the Emirati outlet The National that the “empty chair policy” toward Israel “had produced no peace.” She went on to host Israel’s then-UN envoy, Gilad Erdan, at the Emirati mission.
In March, she rushed to condemn Iran’s defensive counterstrikes against U.S. bases across the region, while ignoring the underlying U.S.-Israeli campaign of aggression that precipitated them. She uttered not a word regarding the loss of Iranian civilian lives, including the devastating American attack on an elementary school in Minab that killed 155 civilians, over 120 of them children.
Her defenders point to her September 2025 warning against Israel annexing the West Bank as proof of her independence. But a closer look shows she was actually protecting the anti-Palestine Abraham Accords, which formal annexation would have destroyed.
The UAE has kept and even upgraded its ties with Israel through every month of the ongoing genocidal war on Gaza, whose toll now exceeds 74,000.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reacted to her nomination in an X post. He called the bid a runway-clearing exercise for the “Greater Israel” project and a way to whitewash genocide, then added that “the fox is updating the LinkedIn profile to apply for the henhouse guard job.”
He attached excerpts of an interview in which she defends normalization with the genocidal Israeli regime.
The field and the arithmetic
Behind the sudden push lies Security Council arithmetic. In the Oct. 16 straw poll, front-runner Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica, who leads UNCTAD, secured nine “encourage” votes but faced “discourage” votes from two permanent members.
With IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi and Guyana’s diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett capturing only two votes apiece, the Security Council vote ground to a halt, opening the door for Abu Dhabi’s push.
Into that deadlock stepped a candidate whom some observers now call the front-runner. Nusseibeh has quickly drawn support from a broad pro-Western coalition.
Key Washington voices, including Brett McGurk, as well as Israeli outlets such as Ynet and The Times of Israel, along with members of Tel Aviv’s foreign policy establishment, have welcomed her bid. Perversely and tragically, she is also backed by the Arab-led Persian Gulf Cooperation Council and the Palestinian Authority’s UN delegation.
Proxy networks and the independence question
Sudan poses a steep hurdle for Nusseibeh’s candidacy, casting a direct spotlight on Abu Dhabi’s aggressive regional posture.
A UN fact-finding mission reported in September reasonable grounds to believe UAE-linked entities armed and trained the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), fueling a devastating civil war and enabling genocidal massacres.
This policy forms part of a broader imperial strategy: across North Africa and the Horn, Abu Dhabi has cultivated proxy networks and armed non-state actors, from Khalifa Haftar’s forces in Libya to the Southern Transitional Council in Yemen and separatist movements in Somalia, fragmenting sovereign states to secure ports, gold-smuggling routes, and strategic influence.
In Sudan, this patronage network translated into direct logistical support for the RSF, causing deep friction across the Global South and making the UAE complicit in severe war crimes.
Justin Lynch, managing director of the Conflict Insights Group, told the AP that Nusseibeh operated as Abu Dhabi’s primary point person on Sudan, routinely offering assurances that the UAE was not aiding the RSF even while Washington and other Western capitals privately knew otherwise.
Lynch noted that the Secretary-General’s core duty is protecting civilians from atrocities such as the El Fasher siege, warning that “handing the job over to the diplomat who ran cover for it would be an insult to the survivors.”
Similarly, Nathaniel Raymond, executive director of Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab, cited an insurmountable “dual loyalty” and conflict of interest.
Pointing out that the RSF’s assault on El Fasher was made possible by UAE-supplied drones, mortars, and logistics, Raymond argued that the UN should not mark the anniversary of the El Fasher massacre by appointing an official from the very state credibly accused of enabling the carnage.

Turkish steel output grows despite trade barriers, trade minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:47:37 UTC
01:47:37 KST

Kazim Kaan Ulu and Emir Yildirim
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Türkiye's steel industry holds a leading position in Europe, but EU and US protectionist measures are hindering the global green transition, Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat said on Monday.
Bolat addressed 400 industry representatives from 80 countries at the Steel Networking Summit 2026 in Istanbul.
He said the Turkish steel industry drives the national economy and supports the auto, transport, energy, machinery and defense sectors, having produced 38.1 million tons of crude steel last year to rank seventh worldwide and first in Europe.
"Türkiye boasts $17.1 billion in steel exports and a network of over 200 countries within a global steel trade market projected to reach $615 billion by 2025," he said.
"That 42.3% of our steel exports are destined to the EU is a testament to our sector's international competitiveness," he added.
Bolat noted that Türkiye's steel production capacity relies on environmentally friendly, scrap-based electric arc furnace technology, adding that the country imported 18.8 million tons of steel scrap to produce 27.5 million tons of crude steel.
The minister criticized US and EU decisions on the steel sector, saying the measures affect exporting countries as well as investors and end consumers.
"These unilateral restrictions were implemented without the necessary consultation or negotiations, and they are inconsistent with international trade rules," he said.
"These barriers limit the efficient circulation of scrap-based, low-carbon steel, undermining the goals of green transition in the steel and industrial sectors," Bolat added.
"The annual trade volume between Türkiye and the EU is $233 billion, and over the past five years, this figure exceeded $1 trillion, representing a balanced and mutually beneficial bilateral trade volume," he said, noting that the bloc's protectionist measures are causing concern.
Despite deep economic integration, the EU's 50% reduction in steel quotas effective July 1 and the implementation of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism burden exporters, according to the minister.
"In January-September, Türkiye's steel product exports covered by the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism to the EU fell 1.7%, while exports to non-EU countries rose 10% — our steel exports to the EU saw a 6.7% decline," Bolat said.
He said the Trade Ministry provides advisory support to counter the negative impact of trade barriers through Green Deal Compliance Projects so Turkish firms can meet new emissions standards without facing excessive costs.
"Under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's leadership, the economy saw an annual real growth rate of 5.35% over the past 24 years, and the economy posted positive growth over the last 16 years except for 2009," he said.
"Since the second quarter of the COVID-19 pandemic, the growth rate rose over the past 24 quarters, or six years; the average growth over the past six years has been above 5%," Bolat added.
Bolat said Türkiye's gross domestic product surged from $238 billion to $1.7 trillion over the 24-year period and is projected to hit $1.8 trillion by year-end, with per capita income expected to surpass $20,000, up from $18,000 last year.
"Our total exports, including both goods and services, account for 25% of the national income, and coupled with imports, Türkiye's total foreign trade amounts to $860 billion, making up more than 50% of national income," he said.
He added that Türkiye has become a key player in global trade through its exports, imports and international investments.

“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” the New York Times quoted Trump as telling more than 4,000 supporters gathered in Port Huron.
Through such inflammatory rhetoric, Trump is seeking to mislead the American public while crossing all bounds of decency and morality.
He called Dr. El-Sayed, whose family immigrated from Egypt, a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member,” a baseless claim. He then contrasted Dr. El-Sayed, a Muslim who was born in the United States, with his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, who is white and also born in the United States.
“I call him apple pie,” Trump said of Rogers, who is 63. “He’s like, perfect, this guy. He’s like central casting. He’s what your state is all about.”
Trump’s comments, coming in a key midterm battleground nine days before the elections, underscored the dark themes and personal vilification he and his allies have embraced as part of their closing pitch. And while he has often used crude and racist language, Trump’s message in Michigan seemed aimed at overtly stoking a fear of Muslims to get voters to the polls.
But a broader question about Trump’s rally here — which followed several in North and South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, among other stops — is whether his presence helps or hurts Republican turnout in a year when polls show deep dissatisfaction with the president. His audience in Port Huron seemed enthusiastic, and thousands strained to take Trump’s picture as he took to the stage. But he held the rally in a conservative district of a state that pollsters believe is swinging back to Democrats.
Trump’s deep unpopularity has complicated Republicans’ path to victory. While Trump carried Michigan by two points in 2024, just 34 percent of likely voters now approve of him, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid-September.
Polls indicate that Dr. El-Sayed, 41, has a narrow edge over Mr. Rogers in a race that will be pivotal to determining control of the Senate.
Trump’s attacks on Dr. El-Sayed on Sunday, questioning his loyalty to the United States, began before he got on Air Force One outside of Washington and accelerated after he landed in Michigan.
Trump also disparaged Jewish voters who were considering voting for Dr. El-Sayed.
“Any Jewish person that supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” Trump said, adding that he “cannot understand how anybody who’s Jewish can even think about voting for this guy.”
Hundreds of Jewish voters in Michigan publicly announced they were backing Dr. El-Sayed, while others have said they are voting for Rogers or threatened to withhold their support.
Dr. El-Sayed has repeatedly disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement, and has said comments about his name and faith are attempts to distract from voters’ economic woes. His aides have said claims of ties to overseas terrorist groups are racist and Islamophobic.
Trump deepened his critique as the day went on, saying that someone with Dr. El-Sayed’s background “would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane. They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate.” He also said that Dr. El-Sayed should not be given access to classified information.
At his own rally on Sunday in Grand Rapids, Dr. El-Sayed said the Republican strategy was “to point at me and my name and my faith. But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas.”
Trump and some other hardline Republicans fail to realize that such incendiary remarks against their political opponents, particularly those of Muslim background, could backfire and alienate a large segment of the American public.

Serbia’s Student List preparing for talks on forming government despite no clear leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:46:27 UTC
01:46:27 KST

Serbia’s triumphant but untested Student List movement is preparing to start talks on forming a government capable of reversing 14 years of increasingly authoritarian nationalist rule, after a seismic weekend election win.
Supporters of the movement, which has no experience of government, took to the streets in the west Balkan country on Monday after the strongman former president, Aleksandar Vučić, was defeated in a historic landslide.
Vučić conceded defeat late on Sunday, bringing his domination of Serbian politics to an abrupt end and capping two years of anti-government protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
With 100% of ballot samples counted, projected results from the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy in Belgrade showed the Student List on 53% of the vote, giving it 141 MPs in the 250-seat parliament, while Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) won 39%, giving it 103. The remaining seats went to national minority party lists.
As yet, there are few clues as to how the winning movement, built around collective decision-making, will actually govern. Its candidates included academics, actors and farmers as well as students, but it is deliberately leaderless with no hierarchy, so it is unclear who it will appoint as the prime minister and cabinet.
Prominent Student List figures include: Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist who headed the candidate list; Dejan Šoškić, a former central bank governor; and Radomir Saičić, a chemistry professor at Belgrade University who spoke on behalf of the List after its victory.
Much like Péter Magyar’s Tisza party, which ended Viktor Orbán’s 16 years of illiberal government in Hungary this spring, the List faces public institutions staffed with civil servants loyal to the outgoing regime, complicating the task of institutional overhaul.
“Everyone in the student movement, and every candidate on the list, has a complete and very clear understanding of the weight of the responsibility before us,” said Ana Mirković, a university educationist, psychologist and Student List candidate.
“We do not see the election result as gaining power and privileges, but as taking on a historic debt to our own people and to our own children.”
Mirković told the Guardian the movement’s first priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.
Vučić’s 14-year rule has been described as a “textbook regime” of autocracy, with his party extending control over the media, judiciary and other state institutions and elections marred by registration irregularities, media bias and voter bribes.
The students’ platform centres on a pledge to fight corruption and restore the rule of law, including creating an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors, not the interior ministry, and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime.
It also aims to ban appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies and to promote financial accountability and public scrutiny – by new independent bodies – of all major state infrastructure contracts to curb the misuse of public funds.
Mirković said the new government would dismantle a “system of intimidation” that encouraged “fear and polarisation”, by “urgently opening up” the media, putting an end to pressure on public-sector workers and “stopping institutional violence”.
She added that the aim was to “rebuild society from the ground up: full disclosure of all contracts and financial flows; depoliticising and strengthening the judiciary; renewing the education and healthcare systems”, and that state capture should “never again” be possible.
The Student List deliberately kept divisive foreign policy issues, including relations with the EU and Russia, in the background. The Kremlin said on Monday it hoped the new leaders “understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests”.
Dušan Vučićević, an analyst, said that, from the outset, the movement “insisted as much as possible that Serbia must first and foremost address domestic political issues – the literal dismantling of every institution, from the national to the local level”.
The students’ win marks a profound political shift in Serbia and could potentially offer inspiration to other student movements that have cropped up across Europe in recent weeks demanding better education standards and prospects.
However, Vučićević said it was distinct from other protests. “This experiment in grassroots democracy ultimately secured more than 50% of the vote,” he told Agence France-Presse, but it was “unclear whether a similar model could work in other countries”.
Nikola Burazer, programme director at the Belgrade-based Centre for Contemporary Politics, said on Monday that the movement’s decision-making process also needed to “be sped up”, as its process for choosing candidates “actually took a long time – months”.
He added: “After people are done celebrating and thinking about what happened yesterday, we will focus a bit more on what’s coming up, and how the government will look. Twenty-four hours ago that all seemed like a fantasy.”
On Sunday, Vučić, who maintained close ties with Russia throughout his tenure, blamed his party’s defeat on “the direct support of various European countries and the US deep state, the one that is also against President Trump”.
International leaders, meanwhile, joined a chorus of welcome to the students on Monday. “This is clearly a new chapter in the history of the country and its people,” said the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
“We wish Serbia success, real development, and warm relations with the European community. We in Ukraine thank Serbia for respecting our people, our state, and our independence. And we always celebrate our shared achievements.”
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Berlin would “actively support Serbia’s European path” after the victory, saying the students “with their demand for the rule of law, fighting corruption and fundamental freedoms, have reached the people”.
Serbia’s constitution requires the new parliament to convene within 30 days of the official election result, and sets a 90-day deadline after that for formation of the new government.
The country must also hold new presidential elections before 27 December, since Vučić stepped down to run for prime minister.

Lula defeats pro-Israel Bolsonaro, dealing Trump a major Latin American blow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:45:07 UTC
01:45:07 KST

Lula defeats pro-Israel Bolsonaro, dealing Trump a major Latin American blow
TEHRAN — Brazilians re-elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday, October 25, giving the 80-year-old leftist a fourth term and the Trump administration its most consequential defeat in the Western Hemisphere. Lula took 51.8 percent to Senator Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.2, a lead of more than 4 million votes, three weeks after trailing by 2.2 million. No one had ever won Brazil’s presidency after finishing second in the first round.
The result ends a run of seven straight right-wing presidential wins in Latin America over 18 months. Brazil was supposed to be the prize that completed the set.
Washington’s failed push
Trump never formally endorsed Bolsonaro, but his administration played its hand anyway. It imposed double-digit tariffs and sanctions on Brazilian officials to stop the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro, now serving 27 years for a coup plot that included plans to assassinate Lula.
In May, it designated Brazil’s two largest criminal factions as terrorist organizations, which Lula warned could become a pretext for intervention. Reuters reported that the State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
Flávio made the alliance his pitch, promising to join the U.S.-led “Shield of the Americas” security coalition “with great enthusiasm and great honor.”
Lula answered with sovereignty, turning the tariffs into the rallying cry “Brazil belongs to Brazilians.” On election night, he said the country “does not accept being anyone’s backyard.”
The stakes extend to minerals. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest known rare earth reserves and about 90 percent of global niobium, used in jet and rocket engines.
After USA Rare Earth, partly owned by the U.S. government, closed a $2.8 billion takeover of the miner Serra Verde, Lula’s government moved to tighten oversight of critical minerals. “With Lula, the U.S. is on shakier ground,” Monica de Bolle of the Peterson Institute told AP.
Israel had a stake too. Bolsonaro campaigned as openly pro-Israel, promising to move Brazil’s embassy to al-Quds (Jerusalem) in 2027 and to restore full ties with Tel Aviv.
Lula has long backed Palestinian statehood, and he has criticized both Washington and Tel Aviv over the genocidal war on Gaza. Brazil joined South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice and recalled its ambassador from Israel in 2024.
Benjamin Netanyahu made no secret of his preference. He appeared by video at Flávio’s campaign launch in July, and after the first round he phoned the senator and invited him to visit Israel.
The next day he posted on X, congratulating Bolsonaro, wishing him a great victory and writing, “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.” The vote came two days before Israelis head to the polls for the first time since October 7, 2023.
How Lula turned the race around
Lula’s first-round campaign was listless, and polls favored Bolsonaro. Then it changed.
The president, who said last year he owned no cell phone, began filming selfie videos aimed at younger voters, and ally André Janones launched a WhatsApp channel, “Lula’s Army,” that grew from 50,000 followers to nearly 11 million on a platform long dominated by the Bolsonaro movement. Turnout climbed to more than 128 million, the highest in 20 years.
The government added cash: a 15 percent increase in its flagship social program, a ban on online betting, debt relief, small-business tax amnesties and free weekend public transit.
Economists put the cost near $8.8 billion next year, and opponents call it vote buying. Lula gained more than 10 million votes between rounds, including 1.3 million in the Bolsonaro-leaning south.
Flávio’s self-inflicted defeat
Bolsonaro ran to free his father, pardon the rioters who stormed government buildings in Brasília and impeach the powerful Supreme Court justices who jailed them.
Lula kept the 2022 coup plot in view and attacked Flávio over alleged links to Rio’s militias, which the senator denies. Bolsonaro’s allies were reportedly discussing cabinet posts before the count.
Then came Friday’s debate, where Flávio mocked Lula as “nine-fingers,” a jab at the digit lost in a factory accident at 17.
Lula looked into the camera. “I was a minor and working at night, because either I worked or I did not eat,” he said. Polls before the exchange gave Bolsonaro a 2-point lead. Lula won by about 3.5.
Thomas Traumann, a political analyst and spokesman for former leftist President Dilma Rousseff, called the result “a defeat of Bolsonarismo, more than a victory for Lula.”
Flávio refuses to concede, calling the two-hour voting extension ordered by Justice Cristiano Zanin a “dirty trick” and demanding annulment.
Yet his own campaign sought an extension citing rain and flooding; the electoral court chief says it changed nothing, and no Brazilian presidential election has been annulled since democracy returned.
Congratulations from Tehran, silence from Washington
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian sent Lula a congratulatory message, hoping friendly ties between Tehran and Brasília would grow in the new term and that cooperation would serve both peoples and strengthen multilateralism, development and international peace.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei also congratulated the Brazilian people and their president, calling the majority’s choice of their country’s political direction deeply meaningful.
Brazilians, he said, showed they do not yield to insinuations and decide what serves their own country.
Russia, France, the European Commission, Mexico, Canada, India, and also congratulated Lula. Trump’s White House stayed silent on Monday, as did Argentina’s Javier Milei.
Nevertheless, Lula starts January 5 from a weak position. Conservatives dominate Congress, debt is high, and Brazilian assets sold off sharply on Monday. Still, he enters office with a mandate Washington tried to prevent and cannot easily ignore.

Hezbollah readies for new regional war with funds from Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:45:02 UTC
01:45:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Hezbollah readies for new regional war with funds from Iran, sources say
Lebanese armed group Hezbollah has spent three months preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.
The group, founded by Iran's Revolutionary Guards in 1982, has been dealt severe blows in two wars with Israel since 2024, with thousands of fighters and many of its leaders killed, and much of its arsenal destroyed.
Invading Israeli forces now occupy its heartland of villages in southern Lebanon, and political pressure has built up in Beirut for its disarmament.
It nevertheless remains committed to fighting Israel and has used a lull in hostilities since June to rearm, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into Israeli positions, two Lebanese security sources told Reuters.
One of the sources, and another close to Hezbollah, said the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities. That is in addition to around $200 million that the group received from Tehran to aid displaced families in its Shia heartlands, which Reuters reported earlier this month.
The group has been restoring command-and-control structures that broke down in key battles, according to one of those sources and three other security officials familiar with the group's operations.
In response to questions from Reuters, Hezbollah's media office said Israel's occupation of Lebanese land made any resistance to it a legitimate right. It rejected the suggestion that its command-and-control systems had broken down.
Israel's military declined to comment. Iran's permanent mission to the United Nations in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters questions.
A US State Department spokesman said Washington would keep strangling Hezbollah's finances through sanctions and other measures. A US Treasury spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to move money.
Hezbollah on alert
Hezbollah's effort comes amid continued tensions in the wider Middle Eastern conflict ignited by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February.
Hezbollah opened fire in support of Iran on 2 March, triggering an Israeli offensive that killed more than 4,000 people and uprooted a quarter of Lebanon's population, mostly members of Hezbollah's Shia Muslim constituency.
Hostilities largely abated over the summer as an interim Iran-US deal included a Lebanon ceasefire and Washington-mediated talks between Lebanon and Israel. Full-scale hostilities have not resumed in Lebanon despite the collapse of the US-Iranian deal, though Israel continues deadly strikes in the south.
Hezbollah is on alert for a possible US-Iran escalation, potentially reigniting the Lebanon front.
Sources told Reuters the group has not yet fully prepared its stockpiles or fighting force.
Hezbollah is still restocking, acknowledging this month that explosives seized by Lebanese authorities belonged to it and were intended for use against Israel. A Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters they were specifically for its explosive drones.
Israel's remote warfare proved a challenge, sources say
The group will also need to repair its command-and-control capabilities after losses on key fronts, including the flashpoint town of Bint Jbeil and the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, according to one Lebanese source and three security officials.
They said Hezbollah's tactic of operating in small units and rationing the use of anti-tank rockets left some units isolated on those fronts, struggling to confront Israel's remotely operated systems, including weaponised drones and armed remote-controlled vehicles.
The Israeli military told Reuters it uses remotely-operated systems to monitor southern Lebanon and reduce troops' threat exposure.
Hezbollah has not explicitly said whether it would take part in the eruption of fresh hostilities, but its media office said it was wary of giving Israeli leaders any justification to escalate in Lebanon, particularly as the group was concerned about its constituents being displaced once more.

Pope says happy to return to South America as trip confirmed
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:45:01 CET
01:45:01 KST

Pope Leo XIV said Monday he was happy
to be able to return to the continent where he lived after his
November 6-17 trip to South America was confirmed including
Peru, where he worked as a missionary for many years before
becoming papal representative there and whose citizenship he
holds along with his US one.
                                    
"I am happy to be able to return to the continent where I
experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a communiqué
from the Holy See Press Office, which confirmed that the Pope's
trip to South America will proceed as scheduled.
                                    
"May this journey be an occasion to open our hearts to one
another, to strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters,
and to renew our commitment to proclaim the Gospel with joy!
"The Pope," the statement reads, "is following medical
recommendations with scrupulous care and attention, while
remaining deeply determined to continue serving the Church.
                                    
"The Holy Father looks forward to this journey with great joy
and enthusiasm; it will offer an opportunity to strengthen the
bonds of communion with local Churches, encourage the faithful
in their mission, bring a message of faith, hope, and peace to
the peoples of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, encounter their
faith, and share the hope and peace that Christ brings to our
world."
Leo's apostolic journey to South America his sixth international
trip.
                                    
He will be in Uruguay November 6-8, visiting Montevideo,
Paysandú and Florida, then travel to Argentina, where he will go
to Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján November 8-11, and
subsequently stay in Peru until November 17.
                                    
The American pontiff spent large chunks of his life in Peru
after first going there as a missionary in the 1980s and served
as the bishop of Chiclayo between 2015 and 2023.
                                    
He also acquired Peruvian citizenship.
                                    
Chiclayo and the capital Lima are among the Peruvian cities he
will travel to.
                                    
Leo's predecessor Pope Francis never returned to his homeland of
Argentina during his 12-year pontificate.

Ukraine Has Been Waiting Nearly a Month for Hegseth’s Signature on Missiles for the Patriot and NASAMS Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:44:53 UTC
01:44:53 KST

Ukraine has been waiting nearly a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on delivering missiles for the Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated this.
He said Ukraine is working on several fronts: with the United States, European countries, and other partners with stockpiles of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles for the Patriot systems.
“In particular, we have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth’s signature on the missiles for the Patriot and NASAMS systems. I have instructed my team to discuss this once again with the American side. Discussions are also ongoing with other countries,” Zelensky said.
It was previously reported that contracts to supply missiles for the Patriot system are on Hegseth’s desk, but he has not yet signed them.
A high-ranking Ukrainian official described the batch of missiles—which, according to him, is awaiting Hegseth’s approval—as “significant.”
“It’s hard to call this a monthly delivery, since there’s no established standard for how many missiles are needed each month. However, it is a significant volume,” the official said.
Over the past 90 days, the U.S. has transferred only 24 anti-aircraft missiles for Patriot systems to Ukraine.
At the same time, Washington is delaying approval of missile deliveries that Ukraine has already paid for.
“In the early days of the war in the Middle East, countries used about 2,000 missiles in the first 48 hours. In the first 48 hours—2,000 missiles they received from partners. I, on the other hand, have received 24 missiles from our strategic partner over the past 90 days,” Zelensky stated earlier.
The NASAMS anti-aircraft missile system also uses American missiles, including the AIM-120 AMRAAM, the extended-range AMRAAM-ER, and the short-range AIM-9X Sidewinder Block II.
In Ukraine, the primary publicly confirmed missile for NASAMS is the AIM-120 AMRAAM, designed to intercept aircraft, cruise missiles, and other aerial targets.

Lithuania eyes June 2027 EU vote to end seasonal clock changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:44:20 UTC
01:44:20 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Lithuania expects an EU vote on ending seasonal clock changes in late June 2027, during its presidency of the Council of the European Union, public broadcaster LRT reported Monday.
Deputy Transport Minister Lukas Paskevicius said the issue would first be discussed at an informal meeting of EU transport ministers in February.
“In February 2027, we will discuss this issue at an informal meeting of EU transport ministers, and toward the end of Lithuania's presidency, in late June, a vote will be held. We will see what the decision will be,” he said.
Lithuania will hold the council’s rotating presidency during the first half of 2027. Ending twice-yearly clock changes has been included in its proposed presidency agenda, pending final approval by parliament.
Paskevicius said Lithuania had discussed the initiative with ministers from France, Spain, Germany and the Nordic countries, as well as members of the European Parliament.
The EU is awaiting a European Commission study, expected in February 2027, assessing the potential effects of ending seasonal time changes on the economy, agriculture, public health and other sectors.
Member states remain divided over whether to adopt summer or winter time permanently, according to the deputy minister.
Southern European countries tend to favor summer time for its brighter evenings, while Nordic countries have concerns over darker winter mornings, he said.
“Our goal is to abandon seasonal time changes altogether, regardless of whether summer or winter time is chosen. Surveys show that most Lithuanian residents prefer remaining on summer time,” Paskevicius said.
The commission proposed ending seasonal clock changes in 2018, and the European Parliament backed the proposal in 2019. Progress subsequently stalled amid disagreement among member states.

Key Israeli health committee faces tough choices as funding increase stays flat for fourth year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

01:43:54 KST

Israel's health basket committee began deliberations Monday on which drugs and medical technologies to add to the state-subsidized health care system in 2027, with an additional 650 million shekels ($211 million) allocated for new treatments – the same amount added to the basket's budget annually since 2023, despite advances in medical technology and an aging population driving increased health care needs.
When asked by Haaretz about the budget increase, Health Ministry Director General Moshe Bar Siman Tov said, "The healthcare system's needs don't start or end" with the committee's work, citing the system's "many diverse needs," including increasing the number of doctors and building infrastructure. At a press conference marking the committee's convening, Health Minister Haim Katz said, "I know that however much we give, it's never enough."
This year, the committee will consider innovative cancer drugs, expanding routine childhood vaccinations to include Bexsero, a vaccine against meningococcal disease, and widening access to contraceptives and mammography screenings. It will also examine expanding eligibility for diabetes medications, including drugs taken orally rather than by injection.
The committee's makeup for 2027 was approved only on Sunday, later than the usual schedule, under which it is appointed by the end of September and begins deliberations after the Jewish High Holy Days. Delays in appointing the committee over the past three years pushed the introduction of new treatments into the health basket to February and March.
Because of the delay in appointing the committee, its deliberations may extend into the beginning of next year, delaying the addition of new drugs to the health basket and potentially forcing patients who need them to incur significant out-of-pocket expenses.

Russia’s trade with African countries exceeded $27B in 2025: Kremlin aide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:42:30 UTC
01:42:30 KST

Kanyshai Butun
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Russia's trade with African countries exceeded $27 billion in 2025, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Monday, highlighting agriculture as a key area of cooperation, state media reported.
Russia exported 1.5 million tons of mineral fertilizers to Africa in 2025, with shipments exceeding 2.2 million tons in 2026, Ushakov said, according to the state-run news agency Tass.
Russia also supplied more than 18 million tons of grain to African countries in 2025 and exported another 13 million tons in the first nine months of 2026, he said.
Moscow is also expanding its diplomatic presence across the continent. Since 2022, Russia has opened three embassies, in South Sudan, Gambia, and the Union of the Comoros, while five other diplomatic missions have resumed operations in Burkina Faso, Equatorial Guinea, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Togo, Ushakov said.
He added that Russia cooperates with African countries through international organizations, particularly the UN, on issues including counterterrorism, drug trafficking, and cybercrime.
His remarks came ahead of the Russia-Africa summit, scheduled for Oct. 28-29 in Moscow, with 48 African countries confirming participation, including 22 represented by their heads of state.
 
Gas Exporting Countries Forum
Ushakov also highlighted the role of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), saying global natural gas demand is projected to rise 28% by 2055, from 4.2 trillion cubic meters to 5.4 trillion cubic meters.
He said the global gas industry needs a platform for professional, depoliticized dialogue amid heightened tensions in the Middle East, attacks on Russia's Nord Stream pipelines and Western restrictions on gas purchases, equipment, and technology.
Russia considers reliable and stable gas supplies essential to meeting growing global demand, Ushakov said, describing Moscow as a responsible participant in the global gas market and a reliable supplier.
He added that Russia holds the world's largest natural gas reserves and ranks second globally in terms of production.
The GECF summit is scheduled for Tuesday in Russia, with participants expected to adopt the Moscow Declaration at the conclusion of the event, Ushakov said.

Maccabi Tel Aviv searches for answers as struggles on the court continue

Maccabi Tel Aviv is in crisis mode after falling to Real Madrid in Euroleague play and then suffering a stunning overtime loss to Maccabi Rishon Lezion in Israeli league action.
Oded Katash’s yellow-and-blue is struggling to find its footing following Iffe Lundberg’s injury, with other players yet to step up in his absence.
Maccabi Rishon Lezion stunned Maccabi Tel Aviv 93-90 in overtime over the weekend, handing the yellow-and-blue its first Israeli League loss of the season and extending the club's struggles following the defeat to Real Madrid. In a thrilling contest, Maccabi Tel Aviv erased a 20-point deficit to force overtime, but the hosts held on to secure an impressive upset.
Chaunce Jenkins scored 18 points, Justin Tillman added 17, and Qua Grant and VJ King each contributed 16 in the win. Roman Sorkin led Maccabi Tel Aviv with 23 points, while Jaylen Hoard added 13 and Keaton Wallace scored 12 in the loss.
Maccabi head coach Katash summed up the defeat.
Katash: Team knew game 'wasn’t going to be easy'
“We talked before the game, and I said we knew it wasn’t going to be easy. They did what they needed to do and were very aggressive. Everyone knows the schedule we have, and they ran the floor and dictated a fast pace. We shot 2-for-18 from 3-point range in the first half. You have days like that, and you can lose games because of them.”
Kaplan was pleased with his team’s response.
“That’s the power of Maccabi Rishon and its fans. We just need to play hard. Basketball is secondary, and when you come in with the right energy and believe in yourselves, you can play good basketball and win. Credit to the fans for the atmosphere and to the players for their fighting spirit. We took a very painful hit on Monday, and I’m glad we’ve at least started to respond. We still have a lot to make up for.”
In Euroleague action, Maccabi Tel Aviv fell 113-99 to Real Madrid, which set a team record with 21 three-pointers as six players scored in double figures. The defeat left the yellow-and-blue with a 2-5 record ahead of a challenging double week.
Katash’s team came out firing, scoring at will as Clark led the way to give Maccabi a 52-51 halftime lead. However, Real Madrid turned up the offensive pressure after the break, with Timothe Luwawu-Cabarrot, Andres Feliz and Facundo Campazzo leading the charge to secure the victory.
Clark scored 20 points, Colson added 19, and Yam Madar contributed 14 in the defeat. Campazzo led Real Madrid with 21 points, Feliz scored 18, and Luwawu-Cabarrot and Alberto Abalde each added 15.
Katash reflected on the defeat, pointing to his team’s inability to maintain its first-half momentum.
“We had a good first half, but in the second half we just ran out of steam and were tired, especially our guards. Playing against a team like Real is tough, and you have to pick your poison. But when their guards hit their shots and had good possessions, it was just very difficult for us. However, we can take some good things from this game.”
Hoard acknowledged that Maccabi needed to improve its ball movement and find ways to come up with wins without Lundberg.
“We stopped moving the ball, and anytime that happens, it puts us in a hole. It’s not the first time. I’m not sure what we can do to correct it. We have to do it the same way as we did against Valencia. We can’t use Iffe’s absence as an excuse, and we have to find ways to get wins. We have to stay together on the defensive side and share the ball on offense.”
Brissett: 'Not great to lose,' team has to 'be better'
Brissett also stressed the need to learn from the loss.
“Two completely different halves, and we have to learn from this. It’s not great to lose, and we have to be better when a team goes on a run. We let this slip away, and we’re not happy with the result. We have to get better.”
In other Israeli League action, Hapoel Holon eased past Hapoel Beersheba 91-75 after jumping out to a commanding 30-12 lead in the opening quarter and cruising to victory.
Claudell Harris led Holon with 22 points, Brandon Jones added 20, and Adama Sanogo scored 18. Tyreek Smith led Beersheba with 25 points, while Brian Cameron contributed 15 and MJ Walker added 14 in the loss.
“We played solid defense and also had a solid performance on offense,” Holon coach Predrag Krunic said. “It was really important to win this game as we have to integrate some new guys into the team, and we showed character to take this victory.”
Beersheba coach Doug Spradley was disappointed with his team’s lack of intensity.
“We had a lack of intensity at times. Our concentration on both sides of the ball wasn’t good enough. We had guys who didn’t show up for some reason. We showed no intensity and no heart. Holon was the more aggressive team. We have to learn from this and move forward.”

Pope says happy to be able to return to continent where he lived
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:42:09 CET
01:42:09 KST

Pope Leo XIV said Monday he was happy
to be able to return to the continent where he lived after his
November 6-17 trip to South America was confirmed including
Peru, where he worked as a missionary for many years before
becoming papal representative there and whose citizenship he
holds along with his US one.
                                    
"I am happy to be able to return to the continent where I
experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a communiqué
from the Holy See Press Office, which confirmed that the Pope's
trip to South America will proceed as scheduled.
                                    
"May this journey be an occasion to open our hearts to one
another, to strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters,
and to renew our commitment to proclaim the Gospel with joy!
"The Pope," the statement reads, "is following medical
recommendations with scrupulous care and attention, while
remaining deeply determined to continue serving the Church.
                                    
"The Holy Father looks forward to this journey with great joy
and enthusiasm; it will offer an opportunity to strengthen the
bonds of communion with local Churches, encourage the faithful
in their mission, bring a message of faith, hope, and peace to
the peoples of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, encounter their
faith, and share the hope and peace that Christ brings to our
world."
Leo's apostolic journey to South America his sixth international
trip.
                                    
He will be in Uruguay November 6-8, visiting Montevideo,
Paysandú and Florida, then travel to Argentina, where he will go
to Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján November 8-11, and
subsequently stay in Peru until November 17.
                                    
The American pontiff spent large chunks of his life in Peru
after first going there as a missionary in the 1980s and served
as the bishop of Chiclayo between 2015 and 2023.
                                    
He also acquired Peruvian citizenship.
                                    
Chiclayo and the capital Lima are among the Peruvian cities he
will travel to.
                                    
Leo's predecessor Pope Francis never returned to his homeland of
Argentina during his 12-year pontificate.

In a social media post on Instagram, the Berlin-Mitte branch of the Junge Union wrote that the “so-called student protests” scheduled for Oct. 31 “must be prevented.” It added: “Paris has shown what haters of the free, democratic world can wreak. We demand that the Bundeswehr be involved preventively to defend our free order. To prevent terror like in Paris.”

The CDU youth group’s proposal sparked a debate on social media, with critics saying the demand is unconstitutional, as Germany’s Basic Law generally limits the armed forces to defense duties. Domestic deployments are permitted only for military support of police against armed insurgents when state and federal police are overwhelmed and the free democratic order is threatened.
The planned student protests are being organized by groups including “Gen Z steht auf” (Gen Z stands up) and “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z takes charge). They focus on better school funding, affordable living, climate protection, opposition to possible conscription and concerns about surveillance.
“We clearly distance ourselves from any kind of violence,” Akram Selo, co-initiator of “Gen Z steht auf,” told local media.

Protesters kill longtime nurse treating Ebola patients in Congo
KINSHASA, Oct 26 - Youths killed a longtime nurse treating Ebola patients in eastern Congo and other health workers were sheltering under police guard, health officials said on Monday, in the latest in a series of attacks that have been fuelled by misinformation.
The nurse worked at the general hospital in the town of Bafwasende in Tshopo province, where he sought to help residents understand and protect themselves from Ebola. He was attacked and killed on Friday.
"We are shocked at how the population turned against this nurse. It is impossible to believe that he was mistaken for a stranger," a local health official told Reuters.
A colleague survived the attack and was recovering in hospital, the official said. Other health workers were sheltering at the general hospital under police guard, too afraid to go home, while the army also briefly deployed to the area, he said.
"None of the nurses have slept at their homes because they fear for their security," the official added.
Tshopo is among eight provinces in Congo that are battling a fast-spreading outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus. Congo's public health institute on Friday reported 9,964 total confirmed cases with around a 48.6% fatality rate since the outbreak was declared in May
Attacks on health workers have targeted hospitals, vehicles and staff involved in the Ebola response, underscoring the challenge of building trust among the population.
The local health official said that youths in the area had previously attacked another colleague, setting his house on fire, without providing a date for that incident.
Reuters has previously reported how the rapid spread of health misinformation posed a threat to health workers in eastern Congo even before Ebola began to spread, with multiple health workers killed in Tshopo after they were accused of spreading an imaginary disease that caused male genitals to atrophy.
"The killing of a nurse yesterday in Bafwasende is a loss to the Ebola response and an even greater loss to patients," Julien Harneis, the senior United Nations Ebola coordinator, said in a post on X on Sunday. REUTERS

Details
According to the investigation, at around 10:00 p.m. on October 25, 2026, in the village of Soshychne, Kamin-Kashyrskyi district, a police officer from one of the units of the Main Directorate of the National Police in Kyiv, driving an Audi, hit two pedestrians who were walking along the roadside.
After the collision, the driver did not stop to help the injured people and fled the scene of the accident.
A 43-year-old man and a 39-year-old woman sustained moderate bodily injuries. Both are in hospital.
The law enforcement officer was detained shortly after the accident. According to the results of the examination, the alcohol content in his blood was 2.07 per mille
Under the procedural guidance of prosecutors from the Volyn Regional Prosecutor’s Office, he was notified of suspicion under Part 1 of Article 286-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (violation of road safety rules while intoxicated) and Part 1 of Article 135 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (abandoning a person in danger).
The vehicle bearing signs of damage was seized. Prosecutors filed a motion with the court seeking its seizure.
The issue of choosing a preventive measure for the suspect is being decided.

Serbia's student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:35:44 UTC
01:35:44 KST

Serbia's student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
BELGRADE, Oct 26 - By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday's election, Serbia's student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing - something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience of.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.
But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?
The answers will determine the political stability of Serbia, the largest economy in the Western Balkans, and its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.
The students' victory "is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging," Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday.
WINNERS, BUT CAN THEY STICK TOGETHER?
The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024 and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.
Despite not having a figurehead, the students won widespread support, before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.
The movement and some of the top candidates on its list have given some idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centred on institutional overhauls.
It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia's former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia's accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.
Prominent figures include the head of the students' candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory. But there is no certainty that any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.
"(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia's culture; we will just have to see if it lasts," said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.
"We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system."
REFORMING PUBLIC INSTITUTIONS
Under Serbia's constitution, the students' candidates have 90 days to form a government once parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.
Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid growing public and private debt levels, while any attempt to end corruption will require an overhaul of the police and intelligence services and judicial reform.
State institutions require "detoxification" after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.
Prelevic warned that Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS
In Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.
"We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector," Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia’s RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia's foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.
Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia's four-year-long invasion.
European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country in its fight against corruption.
"I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing - someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms," said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement.
