Lula’s Victory in Brazil Is a Defeat for Trumpism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:35:00 UTC
01:35:00 KST

On Oct. 25, Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won an unprecedented fourth term, defeating the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro with 51.79 % of the vote, a margin of nearly 4.4 million votes. For the 80-year-old Lula, who had trailed his opponent by 2.2 million votes in the first round of elections just three weeks earlier, the victory was a remarkable comeback.
Brazil is the largest country and economy in Latin America, and the contest had become a test of whether the region’s rightward shift could be stopped. Lula’s victory interrupted that drift and dealt a setback to President Donald Trump’s ambition to build a hemisphere of governments aligned with his politics. Yet interpreting the result as a triumph for the left would be a mistake.
Consider the first round of the elections in Brazil: more than 33 million Brazilians did not vote in the first round, an abstention rate of 21.08 %, the highest for a presidential election first round since 1998. Millions more cast blank or invalid ballots. Voting is optional for Brazilians aged 16 and 17 and for those 70 or older, but the scale of abstention points to a broader problem of political alienation. The high rejection rates for both candidates suggest that, for many voters, the election was not about electing a president but to ensure his opponent is not elected.
Flávio, whose father and former president Jair Bolsonaro is serving 27 years in prison for crimes against democracy, won the first round, with 2 million more votes than Lula, and his Liberal Party’s formidable showing in Congress in early October shocked the liberal world. He ran as his father’s proxy. He promised to pardon his father and his accomplices and to carry forward his political legacy.
The new expectations of Lula’s children
It seemed puzzling that Lula needed such a dramatic comeback to win re-election when unemployment in Brazil stood at 5.3 %, near a historic low. The International Monetary Fund projected that Brazil would become the world’s eighth-largest economy in 2027. Poverty in the country had fallen substantially during Lula’s third term, while real wages rose and food insecurity declined. Violent deaths had fallen to their lowest level in over a decade. Deforestation of the Amazon had fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1988. Incumbents have been re-elected in Brazil with far less to show for their time in office.
The children of Lula’s social policies came of age in a rapidly changing world, and in a country where formal employment, labor unions, and traditional social protections have struggled to serve an increasingly informal workforce. Some turned toward market-oriented politics. Others found a sense of belonging in conservatism, part of a broader rightward turn among young men around the world.
Brazil’s left governed for much of their formative years. Lula’s successor, Dilma Rousseff, was impeached in 2016 amid a bitter political crisis and corruption scandals that implicated political figures across party lines. For many Brazilians, the political establishment became synonymous with impunity and self-preservation. They saw Lula’s Workers’ Party as the establishment. And while Lula’s earlier corruption convictions had been annulled, the allegations continued to shadow him.
Meanwhile, lethal violence had become a defining feature of everyday life. Brazil had urbanized rapidly without addressing deep inequality or reforming a public-security system inherited from the military dictatorship. Overcrowded prisons became recruiting grounds for criminal factions.
In Rio de Janeiro, militias made up largely of serving and former police officers and other security personnel initially claimed to protect residents from drug traffickers. They evolved into criminal enterprises that extorted communities, struck deals with drug factions, and infiltrated local governments. Yet responsibility for confronting them remained fragmented. State governments control most policing, leaving the federal government with limited direct authority over local law enforcement.
Flávio understood how to exploit voters’ distrust and frustration. His promises of tougher security resonated with Brazilians desperate for protection. His campaign drew comparisons to the hardline model of President Nayib Bukele of El Salvador. Yet Bolsonaro Jr. also faced questions about his own associations with criminal figures in Rio, undermining his claim to offer a solution to the country’s security crisis. During the campaign, new revelations about his ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the disgraced banker and owner of Banco Master at the center of a vast financial scandal, added to those doubts, even as he denies wrongdoing.
Flávio's brother, Eduardo, had lobbied the Trump Administration to punish Brazil over the prosecution of their father. Washington imposed tariffs on Brazilian exports, explicitly linking the measures to the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro. The tariffs threatened Brazilian businesses and proved deeply unpopular, leaving Flávio defending a political alliance whose costs would be borne by Brazil.
How Lula fought back
Lula’s campaign had expected these vulnerabilities to suffice. When Flávio entered the presidential race in Dec. 2025, early polls placed Lula comfortably ahead. His first-round defeat jolted the progressive camp out of its complacency. Lula’s campaign returned to the streets of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro and intensified its presence on social media, seeking to mobilize the voters who had stayed home in the first round. Lula’s people reorganized their digital outreach to speak more directly to younger Brazilians and informal workers.
Lula, who had initially seemed detached from younger voters’ digital habits, embraced viral content and selfies. His coalition expanded beyond the traditional left, drawing in moderates and voters who feared another Bolsonaro presidency. His campaign also challenged what it described as algorithmic bias on platforms such as Instagram, securing an electoral court ruling requiring equal treatment of candidates’ content.
The most potent opening for the Lula campaign came from Washington. Trump praised Flávio’s first-round performance as a “very, very big victory,” helping Lula recast the runoff as a contest over national sovereignty. The tariffs had already alienated Brazilian exporters and moderate voters.
In televised debates and rallies, Lula accused the Bolsonaro family of serving American interests and warned that Flávio would surrender control of Brazil’s natural resources to foreign interests. He also attacked his rival’s support for sweeping cuts inspired by President Javier Milei of Argentina. For voters outside the left, defending national sovereignty offered a reason to support Lula despite their reservations about his government.
On São Paulo’s Paulista Avenue, Brazil’s main stage for political protests, a protester wore a Trump mask and carried a Flávio puppet. The image captured the choice Lula wanted the voters to see. This was no longer simply a referendum on his record. It was also a choice about whether Brazil would let an American president shape its politics.
Lula’s campaign turned a contest he had been losing into a choice between an imperfect incumbent and a candidate whose victory threatened democratic institutions and national autonomy. Abstention fell from 21.08 % in the first round to 19.22 % in the runoff. On election day, severe weather and heavy rainfall in southern Brazil kept some voters from reaching the polling booths. Transportation disruptions also hampered voting in cities including Salvador and São Paulo. A last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting hours by two hours, allowing more voters in working-class strongholds to cast their ballots.
Lula’s victory is both a reprieve and a warning. It shows that a broad democratic coalition, mobilizing in the streets and online, can defeat a far-right candidate even amid a regional shift to the right and pressure from Washington. But the victory has not resolved Brazil’s divisions. Lula must govern a country where about half of those who cast valid ballots chose his opponent. He has won four years. He has not won back the country.
Flávio has challenged the result and demanded that the runoff be annulled. His party holds a powerful position in Congress, where conservative and center-right forces can obstruct Lula’s agenda. The election has given Brazilian democracy breathing room, but the battle for Brazil’s democracy has only begun. What Lula does with his mandate will determine whether he can make it count.

Lebanon watches Israel vote amid fears of renewed war
Lebanon is closely watching Tuesday's Israeli parliamentary election and the US midterms on 3 November amid fears of renewed war in the region, as Lebanese officials intensify contacts with Hezbollah to prevent the country from being drawn into another conflict.
The concerns centre on the possibility of new US-Israeli attacks on Iran following the elections, with Lebanon particularly vulnerable as diplomatic negotiations remain stalled and Israeli military operations continue in the south.
The New Arab has learned that intensive domestic and international contacts are under way to keep Lebanon out of any wider confrontation.
Consultations are taking place between advisers to Lebanon's three top leaders - the president, prime minister, and Speaker of Parliament, while Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri has been urging Hezbollah not to get involved if war erupts between Iran and the United States and Israel.
Hezbollah has expressed concern for Lebanon's stability, but its position remains dependent on developments on the ground and Israeli actions inside Lebanon, according to information obtained by The New Arab.
The group has also discussed the possibility of military support with Iranian officials, although there is considerable hesitation about taking such a step given the potentially devastating consequences of another war, particularly for Hezbollah's support base.
The consultations follow media reports that Hezbollah had assured Berri it would not intervene militarily in support of Iran, despite having previously joined the war on 2 March.
A Hezbollah parliamentary source told The New Arab that the group prioritised Lebanon's stability and accused Washington and Israel of threatening the country.
"Instead of focusing on us, the Lebanese state should act to stop Israeli attacks and stop submitting to American dictates that will bring no good to our country," the source said.
Asked whether Hezbollah had promised Berri not to intervene, the source declined to confirm the reports.
"We are confident in Iran's capabilities, and as we always say, the final word belongs to the battlefield," the source said.
Hezbollah denies taking orders from Iran
Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah separately rejected claims on Monday that the group's military decisions were dictated by Tehran.
"The resistance's decision is a Lebanese decision taken by its leadership, and no one abroad or at home dictates it," he said in a statement distributed by Hezbollah's media office.
Fadlallah insisted that Iran had never asked Hezbollah to intervene militarily on its behalf against US-Israeli attacks.
"On the contrary, when we meet Iranian officials, they ask what we want and what is in our interest and Lebanon's interest so they can support us," he said.
He also rejected calls for Hezbollah's disarmament while Israeli forces continue to occupy Lebanese territory, arguing that the issue should be addressed through national dialogue after Israeli withdrawal, the return of displaced residents and the release of prisoners.
Lebanese officials are concerned that Israel could intensify military operations after Tuesday's Knesset election, potentially provoking a Hezbollah response and reigniting the war.
Israel has continued its attacks despite the framework agreement signed on 26 June, while insisting on maintaining its designated security zone in southern Lebanon.
The continued military operations and Israel's refusal to compromise have obstructed negotiations, including military-level talks held in Tampa, Florida, last week.
On Saturday, Israel's public broadcaster reported that the military had raised its alert level ahead of the election, deploying tens of thousands of soldiers across several fronts, including Lebanon, Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Military officials said there was no specific intelligence warning of an imminent attack, but confirmed preparations for an exercise simulating a surprise assault.
Israeli artillery targeted Khiam, Zawtar al-Sharqiya, Mansouri, Wadi al-Hujeir and Wadi al-Slouqi in southern Lebanon on Monday, highlighting fears that renewed fighting could erupt regardless of the election outcome.

Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant seeks to cut costs while pouring money into artificial intelligence.
Staff on select teams in the United States, Canada, India and Britain at vice president level and below will be eligible, a Microsoft spokesperson said on Monday, while some groups of employees, including some working on data centres, sales and marketing, are excluded.
"This offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below," Microsoft said in a blog post on Monday.
The company said it was a time-limited, voluntary programme and built on insights gained from a previous voluntary retirement programme.
The voluntary exit offer will impact key divisions, including AI experiences, Copilot, finance, human resources, Xbox and Windows + Devices, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters news agency.
It will exclude units such as marketing, commercial business and security, the source added.

'The Iranian people will neither compromise nor surrender'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:31:55 UTC
01:31:55 KST

'The Iranian people will neither compromise nor surrender'
Lawmaker and former FM tells Tehran Times that Iran’s resistance has exposed limits of US military power, sanctions and political influence
TEHRAN — Military attacks and economic pressure will not force Iran into submission, says former foreign minister Manouchehr Mottaki, who argues that Washington has failed to translate its superior resources into its desired outcomes.
In an interview with the Tehran Times, Mottaki, now a lawmaker and member of Parliament’s Economic Committee, discusses the country’s wartime governance, its response to renewed sanctions and its diplomatic efforts at recent Inter-Parliamentary Union assemblies. He acknowledges the economic hardships facing Iranians but maintains that public grievances should not be mistaken for a willingness to yield to foreign pressure.
Mottaki also assesses the potential consequences of the upcoming U.S. congressional elections and how the Trump administration’s failed war against Iran could shape the president’s political future.
The following is the text of the interview:
Could you please elaborate on the activities of the Parliament since the beginning of the 40-day war? Did the security threats from the United States and Israel against the lives of the representatives lead to any temporary suspensions of parliamentary functions?
War inherently carries specific consequences. The aggressors in these two wars imposed upon us have shown no regard for international law or human rights, as evidenced by their targeting of innocent civilians—children, women, and athletes—alongside their conflict with our military forces. They have created an ugly reality in this American-Zionist war. It is only natural that when they are committed to sowing fear and terror—striking schools, seminaries, and civilian areas like Lamerd and Koushk, or attacking weddings and funerals—they would also attempt to assassinate officials of the Islamic Republic whenever possible, as their terrorist acts have clearly demonstrated.
Consequently, yes, measures were taken within Iran to mitigate the fallout from the enemy’s actions. For example, government cabinet meetings, parliamentary sessions, and other official state gatherings were not held in their traditional, established locations. We, as representatives, continued to carry out our committee work and oversight duties, but we suspended open parliamentary sessions due to these specific threats. Cabinet meetings were still held, but not at the presidential office.
However, while these security measures were necessary, they did not disrupt the administration of the country. As you have observed throughout the past year and a half of the war, despite the inevitable pressures—particularly regarding food and basic supplies, which are usually the first sectors to suffer—there has never been a shortage of goods in the market or a lack of food for our people. This success demonstrates that the government, drawing on the experience of the eight-year [Iran-Iraq] war, had a firm grasp on wartime management and successfully adapted to the circumstances. Thus, while we faced significant difficulties, these challenges were unable to disrupt the cycle of governance, notwithstanding the damage inflicted upon our people and our nation.
In recent months, you have participated in international forums several times as the head of the Iranian parliamentary delegation. What was the reaction of foreign representatives during these trips? Has their perspective on Iran changed?
The two recent assemblies where I and several other representatives attended were held in March in Istanbul, and in early October in Arusha, Tanzania, for the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) conference, which typically convenes twice a year. Part of our work in these assemblies involves dividing ourselves among the working committees—numbering three, four, or five, such as the Committee on International Peace and Security, the Committee on Women, the Committee on Youth, the Committee on Environment, and the Committee on United Nations Affairs—where we present our positions on various thematic issues.
Another key component is the General Assembly, where countries can propose emergency items. In Istanbul, three emergency items were proposed, while in Arusha, four were brought forward. Naturally, the Assembly must vote on which topic becomes the official emergency item for debate, resolution, and final decision.
One point of particular significance to us was the maneuver carried out by Bahrain at both the Istanbul and Tanzania conferences. Bahrain was essentially a party to the war, having allowed U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf for 40 years—dedicating 135,000 square meters of its small territory to the Americans to do as they pleased, alongside hosting the U.S. Fifth Fleet. However, the war resulted in the disruption and closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which had been open prior to the aggression of these very countries. We have consistently sought to remove these obstacles and restore conditions so that the Strait can be safely utilized for international shipping, tankers, and vessels, in accordance with established regulations and Iran's rightful regional role.
In both Istanbul and Arusha, the Bahraini delegation submitted a draft emergency item aiming to condemn Iran for supposedly attacking them, while completely ignoring the fact that we were merely defending ourselves against aggression. When an enemy attacks you, you must strike back— ‘al-‘aynu bil-‘ayn, wal-sinnu bil-sinn’ [an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth]; just as they transgress against you, you must confront them. Instead of apologizing or explaining their predicament, Bahrain adopted an air of entitlement, claiming that Iran had attacked them. In Istanbul, their move to condemn Iran ended in total failure.
In Tanzania, they no longer dared to directly target Iran with a condemnation. Instead, their text called for the support of "freedom of navigation". Of course, Iran is not opposed to freedom of navigation, but tabling a one-sided text that ignores the root causes of maritime insecurity is entirely inappropriate, especially coming from them. We dealt Bahrain a heavy defeat in Istanbul, where their proposal was rejected.
In Tanzania, four texts were submitted: one from Bahrain, one from Iran, one from Ukraine, and one concerning the humanitarian crisis and thousands of deaths from flooding in Nepal. We maintained our resolution, while others pressured Nepal and Ukraine to withdraw their proposals so that Western, Arab, and Zionist delegations could unite behind Bahrain's text. Ukraine gave in to their enticements and withdrew, but Nepal refused to withdraw, and neither did we. We forced a vote. Despite intense lobbying by Western nations, their followers, and a significant bloc of Arab states, Nepal’s proposal—appealing to humanitarian and emotional considerations—secured the highest number of votes, delivering another defeat to Bahrain.
Another major part of these assemblies involves the floor speeches, where delegations frequently criticize other countries—such as Ukraine against Russia, European nations against Russia, or various countries targeting China. Britain, Germany, and Bahrain all made statements against us in their speeches. According to assembly rules, any country directly referenced has the right of reply to address those remarks.
Two of those replies regarding Britain and Germany were delivered by me, while Bahrain was addressed by Dr. Hosseini, a member of our IPU delegation and the Chairman of the Parliament's Economic Commission, since I was engaged in a meeting at the time. The video of my response to Bahrain that went viral actually originated from the Istanbul session six or seven months ago, where I also answered Australia and Ukraine.
In this recent session, however, three countries spoke against us: Britain, Germany, and Bahrain. Bahrain was answered by Dr. Hosseini, while I responded to Britain and Germany. The British representative—a female MP—made relatively mild remarks against Iran. Germany, however, brazenly violated the rules. Typically, a right of reply is only granted if your country was specifically mentioned in the preceding speech. I had not mentioned Germany in my address, yet this female German delegate requested the right of reply. At the very end of the day, as the final speaker on the roster, she took the floor and spewed nonsense against Iran—talking points straight out of the playbook of Israel Radio.
The morning session concluded, and the afternoon session began. Although the official male representative of Germany was scheduled to speak that afternoon and delivered his remarks without mentioning us, I took the floor. I stated that I had no objection or protest regarding the remarks made that afternoon by this gentleman—this German gentleman—and that I actually agreed with and thanked him for mentioning the Persian Gulf. However, I turned my attention to the rude German woman who had improperly claimed a right of reply that morning, and whom the inexperienced chairperson had mistakenly allowed to speak, even though she had no such right since Germany was never mentioned.
I stated that her remarks were the voice of Israel Radio, which clearly revealed her true identity—acting within this assembly essentially as an agent of the Mossad, which is entirely beneath the dignity of this gathering. I told her and any other potential spies in this assembly: tell the Israeli regime that the Iranian nation will break Netanyahu’s and Trump’s teeth, and the nation of Iran will take revenge for the blood of its martyred Imam [Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei]. I even held up a picture of the martyred Imam. That was our response to the German woman.
Regarding the British representative, she made a brief, passing remark while speaking on the assembly's theme of good governance and empowerment. In my response, I expressed astonishment that a British representative had the audacity to lecture us on good governance. If Britain wants to examine its record of governance, it should reflect on its long history of global colonization, the torture it inflicted, its mistreatment of women, and the slaves it shipped to the West.
Fifty years ago, I was a student in India. If you visit India and ask the local people about the 120 years of British colonial rule, you will learn firsthand how they treated the Indian people and the brutal tortures they employed—whether in India, Kenya, or elsewhere. Britain is in no position to lecture a country like Iran. I advised her—she is a member of the British Foreign and Security Policy Committee—to spend an evening walking the streets of London to see how young Londoners view Britain's shameful complicity in illegal U.S. wars. When Bush and Trump launched unauthorized attacks against Iraq without UN approval, Britain was the sole country to join that unlawful aggression. We successfully presented a clear indictment of British crimes during our response.
Now, regarding your question about the feedback from other delegations and countries: because we arrived straight from the battlefield, our speeches were naturally combative. We spoke swiftly, clearly, and decisively in defense of our martyrs, our nation, our ideals, our country's demands, and to demand justice for the blood of our people. Many delegations, even European ones, approached me afterward to say, 'We agree with everything you are saying, but we lack the courage to say it ourselves.'
I spoke with one European delegation head for perhaps half a minute—or rather, half an hour. Many delegations from Asia, Africa, Latin America, and Venezuela itself—when the Venezuelan delegation took the podium, they declared that their president had been kidnapped and that American thieves had transgressed against their country, abducting their president and his wife—completely transformed the atmosphere of the meeting.
When I stated in my speech that America is afflicted by the most foolish president in its history, you could see smiles on the faces of nearly all the delegations, as if everyone fully agreed with the portrayal of Trump we presented, but lacked the courage to voice it publicly.
Thus, it was a very successful assembly. This time, we defeated Bahrain, the Europeans, and the faction of Arab states that had rallied to support Bahrain. I very much doubt that Bahrain will ever dare to propose another emergency resolution against Iran in future IPU assemblies.
We know that the United States currently places heavy emphasis on economic warfare against Iran, hoping to force the country into submission by inducing a form of economic collapse. Given that you are a member of Parliament's Economic Committee and receive reports regarding the country's economic and livelihood conditions, do you think such a scenario is probable?
A nation that others might superficially dismiss as a mid-tier, third-world country has found itself locked in a multi-front war—military, economic, and political—against the world's foremost self-proclaimed superpower and the most bloodthirsty regional regime in history, whose very existence has been intertwined with slaughter, terror, and massacres. This war was unjustly imposed upon us: a 12-day war followed by a 40-day war across three different arenas.
On the military front, their initial assumption was that they could very quickly destroy and eliminate our navy in the Persian Gulf. Relying on their air superiority, regional bases, and the confident assumption that they could effortlessly neutralize our air defenses, they believed they would swiftly dismantle our defense capabilities and subsequently obliterate our missile bases. During the 12-day war, our launcher crews did indeed attempt to fire their missiles, but many of them were targeted and martyred by Israeli and American aircraft the moment they launched.
Between the ceasefire of the 12-day war and the outbreak of the 40-day war, however, we implemented critical adjustments within our defense sector and among our launcher crews. Consequently, in the 40-day war, they realized things were no longer as they had expected. In the 12-day war, after eight days had passed, the Americans realized that Israel was not winning. Within a couple of days, fearing that Israel would suffer a defeat reminiscent of the 33-day war, they pushed for a ceasefire, which was established after 12 days.
Then, in the roughly seven-month interval between the 12-day and 40-day wars—spanning from July to March—they orchestrated a coup d'état, which in its own right was a full-scale war. To put it in perspective: if during the 1953 coup we had just one Shaban-e Bi-Mokh [notoriously CIA-backed thug], here they deployed a hundred Shaban-e Bi-Mokhs—individuals who had trained for years, engaged in espionage, and maintained direct connections with American and Israeli intelligence services. They brought them into the field, and although they caused considerable bloodshed—martyring well over three thousand of our people, the coup ultimately collapsed.
Following that failure, they entered the 40-day war. To keep things brief: both they and the international community ultimately acknowledged that America was the military loser of the 40-day war. Why do we assert that they were defeated in both the 12-day and 40-day wars? Because any aggressor launching an attack does so with a specific objective; they do not end a conflict until that objective is achieved. Requesting a ceasefire midway through a war is an admission that they failed to reach their goals, which means they accepted defeat and sued for peace.
On the military front, it became evident to them that they were incapable of confronting Iran. Having failed in a comprehensive war, they shifted to a limited conflict. This time, they resorted to tactics in responding to our naval and missile capabilities that were difficult for them to even fathom. They had assumed that if they encountered trouble in the Persian Gulf, they could simply retreat to Jordan; but this time, they found Jordan turned upside down—their AWACS aircraft were hit, their F-35 fighter jets were struck, and so forth. Whispers began circulating that they needed to relocate all their assets directly to the occupied territories. This institutionalizes America’s military defeat, both in the comprehensive war and in the limited engagements against Iran.
Trump waged this economic war once before during his previous presidential term. As you may recall, in his very first year, Trump entered the arena with full force, proclaiming: "I will destroy Iran, I will paralyze Iran, I will impose lethal sanctions," proudly flashing his signature on television every new sanction document, driving Iran's oil exports to zero, and shouting various slogans. Yet, not only did he fail to force Iran into submission or break its resolve, but the fallout from his actions and foreign policy resulted in him losing his re-election bid. Everyone expected Trump to secure a second term [in 2020], but he failed—right up until his recent revival of economic sanctions and pressure campaigns.
Although they are attempting to showcase new tactics, the 47-year-old Islamic Republic is standing—and has continually stood—firm against these sanctions. Our role model is the Prophet of Islam, who stood firm and resisted during the economic blockade imposed upon him by the patricians of Quraysh in an enclosed valley—and of course, how economic prosperity eventually blossomed through resistance at battles of Badr and Khandaq.
In these very days when they imagine their pressures have multiplied and are bearing fruit, international economic institutions are actually speaking of the revitalization of Iran’s economy and the effectiveness of our stabilization measures. That the country's economic conditions face difficulties under these pressures is entirely natural—just as we face severe hardships during military onslaughts, where some of our infrastructure was targeted, our leader was martyred, thousands of our people were killed, and various hospitals, Red Crescent facilities, and other centers were struck. Russian oil refineries ramp up diesel production after deal with the US - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
In October, Russian oil refineries increased diesel production to 180,000 tonnes per day after export quotas were approved. The quotas were granted as part of a deal with the US.
Russian oil refineries increased diesel fuel production in October after the government granted export quotas as part of a supply deal the Kremlin concluded with the United States, two industry sources close to the situation told the publication. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Traders said that from October 1, the Russian government allowed exemptions to the existing ban on diesel fuel exports, allocating quotas that enable Russia to supply fuel under a deal with Trump.
Since Russia's ban on diesel fuel exports came into force in August, Russian oil companies have been forced to cut production to meet domestic demand, while also limiting supplies to Central Asian countries in accordance with intergovernmental agreements.
Industry sources said that diesel fuel production in Russia in the first half of October fell to approximately 160,000 tonnes per day from 175,000 tonnes per day in September. After the new export quotas were approved in the middle of the month, production began to rise to 180,000 tonnes per day.

Strikes are impacting people's access to healthcare in Yemen
Share
Crisis Update26 October 2026
Over the past few days, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) teams in Aden and Mocha have been exposed to a series of incidents that further restrict humanitarian access and the provision of medical care to people in Yemen.
This morning, on Monday 26 October, three strikes hit the coastal area of Mocha. One of them fell only 150 metres away from Mocha General hospital, where our teams are working in the maternity and paediatric wards. While all staff and patients are safe, the strike caused damages to the building that may weaken the structure in the longer-term — a building already weakened by years of regular blasts.
The strike also created panic among patients, medical staff, and civilians, further limiting their safe access to healthcare. Such incidents are preventing patients from coming to the hospital, fearing for their lives. With every strike around the hospital, there is a decrease in the number of patients coming to seek care.
A few days earlier, while an MSF plane was about to take off from Aden’s airport on a routine flight intended to carry humanitarian workers, a missile hit the vicinity of the airport. The plane was forced to stay on the ground, and the staff were asked not to board but to seek shelter inside the airport instead. Aden's airport is the main entry point for humanitarian workers, supplies, and medical equipment to the southern parts of Yemen, and accessing it safely is crucial.
These incidents, among others, are exposing MSF and other humanitarian organisations in Yemen to more threats, directly impacting the capacity to urgently operate and reach people, at a time where their needs are highest and the provision of humanitarian care is essential.
We reiterate to all parties to the conflict that humanitarian and medical workers, as well as medical facilities and patients, and access to care, must be protected.

The mega proposals were approved by the ministry's highest decision-making body, the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) chaired by defence minister 
Rajnath Singh
. Out of the total acceptance of necessity (in-principle approval) given, around 82% of the procurements will be made from Indian Industry.
For the 
Indian Army
, the approval was accorded for the procurement of high mobility vehicles (HMVs), self-propelled tracked gun system, gun shot response systems (GSRS) and light multi-role helicopters (LMRH), a defence ministry’s release said on Monday.

While HMVs will enhance operational capabilities, logistical support and mobility in challenging terrains, the self-propelled tracked gun system will provide matching mobility and firepower to mechanised formations. GSRS will serve as a force-multiplier, providing real-time situational awareness to the forces.
LMRH will be used by both the Indian Army and Indian Air Force for reconnaissance and surveillance, combat, search and rescue of troops, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief. 
The IAF, along with the Army, plans to procure 200 helicopters, out of which 80 helicopters are allocated specifically for the IAF and 120 for the Indian Army. rima dain frames exterior living zones with custom architectural outdoor rugs
marbella-based studio rima dain outlines how custom proportions, UV-stabilized synthetic flatweaves, and water-permeable backings transform outdoor rugs into structural zoning elements for residential and hospitality terraces.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
RIMA DAIN TREATS OUTDOOR TEXTILES AS ARCHITECTURAL ZONING TOOLS
Marbella-based studio Rima Dain develops technically engineered, flatwoven outdoor rugs designed to structure seating zones across Mediterranean residential and hospitality terraces. In exterior architecture and landscape design, outdoor rugs function as foundational spatial dividers, defining boundaries for lounge zones and anchoring furniture across stone, tile, and timber decks. When left unresolved, terraces often present proportion issues where seating groupings appear isolated on expansive paving. Rima Dain approaches exterior rug design through architectural proportion, geometric zoning, and technical textile performance, treating the ground plane as an integral component of the exterior furniture plan.
Caletta Rug in Bronze / Sand
PROPORTION AND GEOMETRIC SIZING CALIBRATE FURNITURE FOOTPRINTS
For Rima Dain studio, specifying an outdoor rug requires careful consideration of scale and layout geometry. In lounge zones, standard spatial planning dictates that front furniture legs rest on the textile, with full-perimeter coverage preferred for larger layouts to unite disparate pieces. In outdoor dining settings, extending the perimeter by 60 to 75 centimeters beyond the tabletop ensures that pulled-out dining chairs remain entirely on the woven surface. For linear or irregular architectural terraces, custom dimensions allow rugs to align with structural columns and boundary walls, establishing clear functional zones across open footprints.
Dune Rug in Olive / Sand
Synthetic FLATWEAVES WITHSTAND DEMANDING EXTERIOR settings
Material engineering and drainage determine an outdoor rug’s longevity across harsh climates and high-traffic hospitality environments. Synthetic flatweaves manufactured from UV-stabilized polypropylene or recycled PET yarns resist moisture absorption, staining, and fading while collecting less debris than high-pile alternatives. Permeable backings and non-slip outdoor underlays are essential on stone paving and timber decking to promote water evaporation, prevent surface mold, and eliminate slipping hazards in poolside and resort settings.

Exclusive: EU to give Frontex new powers to deport migrants from outside Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:25:26 UTC
01:25:26 KST

Under new rules, the EU border agency will be allowed to transfer migrants between third countries, expanding its operations beyond Europe and facilitating deportations from return hubs.
The EU’s border agency Frontex is set to gain new powers to return irregular migrants from one non-EU country to another, further extending European migration policy beyond the bloc’s borders, according to several EU officials who spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity.
The reforms, which the European Commission will unveil on Tuesday, will give Frontex greater operational powers outside EU territory, in a move likely to provoke a backlash from civil society organisations.
Frontex officials can currently assist national authorities in returning irregular migrants from EU countries to their countries of origin, as well as patrol the bloc’s external borders and coastlines.
Under the new rules, the Warsaw-based agency will also be able to support authorities in third countries, such as North African governments, in returning Central African citizens to their countries of origin before they even attempt to reach European shores.
“The more people you return before [they reach Europe], the less you have to return after,” an EU official told Euronews.
Frontex officials will also be allowed to take part in deportations from return hubs, which a recently approved law allows EU countries to establish in third countries. Five EU governments are currently negotiating the creation of the first hub, which is expected to become operational in 2027.
Migrants whose asylum applications or right to remain in the EU have been rejected and who are hosted in these hubs are ultimately expected to be returned to their countries of origin. Frontex’s involvement could prove instrumental in carrying out the final transfers.
“It's no longer only an agency supporting EU countries at their borders. [...] It's a deportation agency, increasingly operating far away from the actual border of the EU,” Josephine Solanki, a researcher from the Amsterdam-based think tank Transnational Institute, said in a press briefing ahead of the reform.
Several NGOs and civil society organisations are demanding that any expansion of Frontex's mandate be accompanied by stronger oversight and accountability mechanisms to safeguard migrants' fundamental rights. They argue that the agency has already been implicated in rights violations during its operations within Europe.
Any cooperation with a third country will, however, require a specific agreement with the country concerned, similar to the “status agreement” Frontex already has in place with several non-EU countries, including Albania, Serbia and North Macedonia.
These agreements allow Frontex officials to be deployed to carry out specific tasks, including joint operations and rapid border interventions on the territory of partner countries.
The EU is currently negotiating an agreement with Senegal. Meanwhile, a Frontex liaison officer for Senegal, whose expanded mandate also covers Mauritania and Gambia, was appointed in 2023 under informal “working arrangements.”
The reform will also introduce a rapid-response force to be deployed in the event of sudden, large-scale arrivals of irregular migrants, as well as an online surveillance unit tasked with monitoring social media to prevent large-scale movements.
The aim is to avoid situations such as the mass entry into Ceuta last July, when around 90,000 migrants forced their way across the border between Morocco and the Spanish exclave.
European Commission Vice-President for Security Henna Virkkunen and Home Affairs Commissioner Magnus Brunner are expected to present the reform after the Commission’s weekly College meeting on Tuesday.
Frontex is also set to receive €12 billion under the EU’s next seven-year budget, doubling its previous allocation.

Ukraine strikes Russian plant producing missile, bomb batteries in Yelets, General Staff says
A fire broke out on the territory of the Energia plant following an overnight attack on the battery plant in the city of Yelets in western Russia overnight on Oct. 26, Ukraine's General Staff said later that day.
The plant is the sole Russian manufacturer of batteries for glide bomb guidance and correction modules, the General Staff said without specifying the extent of the damage.
It added that the plant, located about 250 kilometers (about 155 miles) from Ukraine, also produces batteries for Iskander-M ballistic missile systems and sea-based cruise missiles.
"The strike complicates the Russian Federation's military's production of power sources for missiles, guided bombs, and other weapons," the General Staff said in its Telegram post.
Earlier on Oct. 25, Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channel Exilenova Plus reported that smoke rose over the whole territory of the Energia plant after several missiles appeared to have hit it in the afternoon. The General Staff has not specified what weapons were used to strike the Energia plant in Russia.
In its statement, the General Staff said that Ukraine had also "destroyed" the main microchip production workshop of Proton-Electrotex Enterprise in Orel, western Russia, on Oct. 23. It added that the attack would likely complicate the Russian production of components used to produce cruise and ballistic missiles, which are often deployed to target Ukrainian cities.
The Russian Defense Ministry has not reacted to the General Staff's statement. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claim.
The attack comes as Ukraine intensifies its long-range attacks inside Russia and across Russian-occupied territories, often targeting defense industrial plants, airfields, and oil refineries.
Earlier on Oct. 26, independent Russian media outlet Astra reported that a chemical plant producing dual-use goods in the southwestern Russian city of Voronezh was likely hit in a Ukrainian drone attack.

Analysis: No Elon Musk, Russian soldiers in Ukraine are not 'kids' who have 'no choice but to fight and die'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:40 UTC
01:24:40 KST

Analysis: No, Elon Musk, Russian soldiers in Ukraine are not 'kids' who have 'no choice but to fight and die'
"We should (have) some sympathy for the poor Russian conscripts too. Those kids have no choice but to fight and die in drone strikes."
For anyone watching and understanding Ukraine's years-long struggle for survival, the words of SpaceX founder and world's richest man Elon Musk ring with deep moral bankruptcy.
But more importantly, Musk's post on Oct. 25 — made in the middle of a hurricane scandal around the near-trillionaire's throttling of Starlink internet terminals used by the Ukrainian military — badly misrepresents the reality of how Russia staffs its wartime military.
The misconception that Russian soldiers are forced to fight against their will in Ukraine is one that has consistently reached the most powerful men in the United States.
Earlier this year, U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly lamented the deaths of soldiers on both sides, seemingly equating their suffering and the circumstances under which they found themselves in the trenches.
"Every day people are dying. Young handsome soldiers are being killed. Young men, like my sons. On both sides. All over the battlefield," he said in February.
"Young, young, beautiful people. They’re like your kids, two million of them — and for no reason."
But this sentiment ignores one important fact — Russian soldiers are not young men forced to fight in Ukraine against their will.
Most Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine chose to do so voluntarily, and did so not for values, but for cold, hard cash.
“Many think that the Russians are forced to fight. In fact, the Kremlin is afraid of mobilizing its people,” Kateryna Stepanenko, Russia research fellow at the Institute for the Study of War, told the Kyiv Independent.
Instead, Russian President Vladimir Putin relies on paying vast sums of money in order to entice people to sign up voluntarily, which they continue to do in droves — up to 40,000 a month according to NATO estimates from August.
"The moral equivalence of these two armies is impossible," Pavel Luzin, an independent Russian military analyst, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russia’s side is completely immoral, and the vast majority of its soldiers went to war voluntarily — driven by financial and psychological interests, not by coercion.
“One side is an occupying force trying to subjugate another country and its people. The other is fighting for its freedom. These are fundamentally different causes."
How does the average Russian soldier die on the front?
Russia effectively operates with two armies — a conscript army and a contract army.
The conscript army is the standing force used to defend Russia itself. The Kremlin conducts conscription twice a year, in spring and fall, requiring eligible men to serve for one year. By law, conscripts cannot be sent abroad to fight.
Instead, the Kremlin has relied on its contract army, which consists of paid volunteers and soldiers who sign short-term contracts with the Defense Ministry.
The way Moscow wages its war dictates that the Russian army fighting in Ukraine requires a constant inflow of warm bodies.
Since the Battle of Bakhmut in 2022-23, Russia's offensive tactics have relied mainly on a near-endless stream of dismounted infantry assaults.
As the war has transformed over time, so have these attacks, with assault squads shrinking first from 6-10 infantrymen around 2023, to the small infiltration teams of two soldiers — sometimes just one at a time — sent to seep through Ukrainian lines.
What has stayed consistent is the fact that these men for years are treated by their command as single-use soldiers.
Interviews with Russian POWs consistently tell a story of the assault soldier's mission being nothing more than to advance to a given point on the map, often past enemy lines, and wait for more orders.
While some may pierce through and survive to be reinforced and later sent out again, many are killed or wounded before reaching their assigned objectives, eliminated by a Ukrainian drone, shell, or mine.
But amazingly, despite this grim everyday reality of Moscow's war machine, Russia is able to continue without resorting to forced mobilization, as tens of thousands of Russians continue to sign up voluntarily every month.
"Money remains central to how the Kremlin sustains its forces."
Motivation and coercion
Money remains the main motivator for Russian soldiers signing up to fight in Ukraine.
Recruits are offered sign-up bonuses and monthly salaries several times higher than the national average. Federal-level sign-up bonuses from the Defense Ministry are complemented by bonuses paid out by Russian regions, operating under strict recruitment quotas imposed by Moscow.
For many from poorer regions, joining the army means solving years of financial hardship in a single decision.
"They’re incentivized not only by finances but also by numerous social benefits. These include free education, housing subsidies, discounts on cars, and other privileges that make service more attractive," Stepanenko said.
Some also enlist to resolve personal or legal problems.
"There’s recruitment among prisoners and people facing financial or legal issues, like those with unpaid loans or minor criminal charges. For them, signing a contract can mean avoiding debt or punishment," Stepanenko said.
This supply of recruits is complemented by men from Russia's prison system, as well as foreigners, an important exception to the largely financially driven domestic recruitment system.
Migrants from Central Asia and other countries are another target group. Many are pressured to enlist through the threat of deportation or the loss of Russian citizenship.
Russia has also recruited smaller groups of foreign nationals from countries such as Cuba, Syria, Nepal, and sub-Saharan Africa, through local intermediaries or misleading job offers that later turned into military contracts.
"There’s a lot of coercion. Recruitment sometimes involves abuse, manipulation, or pressure in workplaces to meet quotas. But there’s also a large number of people who willingly sign contracts to fight in Ukraine because of the financial rewards. Money remains central to how the Kremlin sustains its forces," Stepanenko said.
Putin's social contract
Well into the fifth year of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia continues to sustain a large army without declaring general mobilization or facing mass protests.
"Putin has two overriding priorities — to subjugate Ukraine and to stay in power. When he announced partial mobilization in the fall of 2022, his popularity dropped the most," Max Bergmann, director of the Europe, Russia, and Eurasia program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), told The Kyiv Independent.
"Another mobilization risks provoking backlash not only against the war, but against his rule itself."
To avoid that, the Kremlin promotes the idea that participation in the war is voluntary. It presents those who fight as contract soldiers, rewarded with high pay and other benefits.
"There’s a kind of social contract between Putin and Russian society. Putin will not mobilize the broader Russian society and will pay those who serve, as long as people do not oppose the war," Stepanenko said.
“So far, it has worked — there have been no large-scale protests across Russia."
Mobilization around the corner?
Even though recruitment numbers remain steady, Russia's military has performed poorly on the battlefield over 2026 compared to years past — taking far less territory despite high losses, failing to capture the Donbas region, and even losing ground to Ukrainian counteroffensives.
According to Kyiv, the Kremlin is planning a so-called "peripheral mobilization" of 300,000 people before the end of 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027.
The term "peripheral" refers to Kremlin's alleged intention of drafting large numbers of people without announcing it publicly, and focusing efforts on more remote, disadvantaged regions — the same areas that have provided most of the volunteer recruits.
The new forced draft was expected to come after United Russia's planned victory in Russian State Duma elections in September, but five weeks later, it hasn't, with only a few reports of ramped up coercive recruitment.
If large-scale mobilization is eventually announced again in Russia, the experience of 2022 would suggest a likely exodus of military-aged men and other forms of day-to-day avoidance.
But even then nowhere in that picture is any expression among ordinary Russians — especially those invading a neighbor with weapon in hand — that their country's war against Ukraine is inherently wrong.

Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:37 UTC
01:24:37 KST

A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing last year of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was unlawful.
Judge Jesse Furman, in his ruling, also granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay as an assistant U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York from her termination on July 16, 2025, through Dec. 20, 2025, when the judge inferred she accepted another job.
The DOJ said it would appeal Furman's ruling in which the judge rejected the department's arguments that the attorney general had authority to dismiss Comey without cause. The case is in in U.S. District Court in Manhattan.
Comey's lawyers, in a statement, said, "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
"As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system,'" the lawyers said. "This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."
Before her termination, Comey was involved in a series of high-profile federal prosecutions, including ones against the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean "Diddy" Combs.
Her lawsuit against the DOJ argued that her termination violated federal law and the Constitution and stemmed from President Donald Trump's longstanding animus toward her father, whom Trump had fired as FBI director in 2017.
James Comey is currently under federal indictment that accuses him of threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells forming the number "86 47." His attorneys are seeking to have that case tossed out.
James Comey, who denies any wrongdoing, previously had another federal indictment against him filed by the DOJ under Trump dismissed.
Maurene Comey's suit said the DOJ did not give "any explanation whatsoever for terminating Ms. Comey," and, "In truth, there is no legitimate explanation."
"Rather, Defendants fired Ms. Comey solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B. Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both," the suit said.
Furman, in his ruling for Comey, referenced that claim, but his decision was based on other grounds.
The judge rejected the DOJ's arguments that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi could remove a federal prosecutor "at will" and without cause and that current Attorney General Todd Blanche could ratify that act after the fact as he did in May as acting attorney general.
Furman also rejected the DOJ's argument that even if the Civil Service Reform Act requires removal of a prosecutor for cause, an attorney general's firing of her constituted an implicit determination that she was removed "for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service."
"The Court need not dwell long on Defendants' second statutory argument justifying Comey's removal," Furman said, referring to that claim.
"That is because the argument borders on frivolous."
The judge noted that Comey was fired despite having had excellent performance reviews.
"Comey's supervisors and peers consistently lauded her work, describing her as a 'brilliant lawyer and a gifted supervisor,' 'the lawyer the office turns to when legal excellence is a must,' and 'an outstanding AUSA in every respect' with 'judgment, work product, and courtroom advocacy [that are] among the finest in the country,'" Furman wrote.
The DOJ admitted that Comey's termination "was not 'for cause' and was not based on her
performance," Furman noted.
In addition, the judge said, the DOJ's argument that Comey's termination was lawful ignored parts of the Civil Service Reform Act, which "required that Comey be given advance written notice (subject to certain exceptions not relevant here); 'a reasonable time' to respond orally and in writing; representation; and 'a written decision and the specific reasons therefor at the earliest practicable date.'"
"Defendants concede, as they must, that Comey was not afforded these procedural protections," the judge said.
Furman also said the DOJ all but admitted that its argument that the attorney general had power to fire Comey under Article II of the U.S. Constitution — which establishes the executive branch of government — sought "to overturn nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."
"This Court, however, is bound to follow the Supreme Court's precedents unless and until the Supreme Court overturns them," Furman wrote.
The DOJ, in a statement, said, "The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."
That appeal would happen after Furman issues a final judgment in the case.
The judge reserved judgment on Comey's claim that her firing violated her First Amendment rights. Furman gave her until Nov. 9 to file arguments on why that claim should not be dismissed as moot given his order in her favor on other grounds.
The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to a post by the DOJ's Rapid Response account on X, which said, "The Department disagrees with this decision, which obstructs President Trump's constitutional authority to fire individuals who wield executive power on his behalf. We intend to appeal the decision in due course.
Comey, in a note to colleagues at the U.S. Attorney's Office after she was fired, wrote, "If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decisions of those who remain."
"Fear is the tool of a tyrant, wielded to suppress independent thought. Instead of fear, let this moment fuel the fire that already burns in the heart of this place," she wrote. "A fire of righteous indignation at abuses of power. Of commitment to seek justice for victims."

‘Everything destroyed’: Hebron businesses count cost of Israeli assault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:24 UTC
01:24:24 KST

‘Everything destroyed’: Hebron businesses count cost of Israeli assault
Israeli demolitions and road closures have devastated businesses in Hebron, leaving owners facing millions in losses.
Hebron, occupied West Bank – Sufyan al-Qawasmi stood near the rubble of his factories in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron, lamenting the business he watched vanish beneath the debris.
Israeli bulldozers demolished the factories on Friday without any prior warning or notice, following a shooting attack carried out by two Palestinians that morning near Hebron’s western entrance. The attack killed two Israeli soldiers, as well as the two Palestinian gunmen, and prompted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to announce a large-scale military operation across Hebron and order preparations for a wider closure of the illegally occupied West Bank.
Demolitions are regularly used by Israel to punish Palestinians, typically the family members of attackers, but in al-Qawasmi’s case, for the misfortune of being close to the site of an attack. Human rights groups decry the practice, which is regarded as collective punishment.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich justified the demolitions as “establishing deterrence and exacting a price”.
The Israeli bulldozers destroyed a business that al-Qawasmi’s family had built up for his whole life, and provided a livelihood for more than 70 people. The first factory, which produced ceramics, is the same age as he is – it was established 50 years ago. Fifteen years later, the family opened a marble factory.
Their business flourished, becoming one of the most significant industrial operations in the West Bank, with goods exported to Israel.
In the space of a few hours on Friday, the ceramic factory and marble factory were gone, as well as several neighbouring buildings, including a three-storey house and various commercial facilities. Simultaneously, the city faced an Israeli military incursion that included the closure of all entrances, raids, arrests, and the forced evacuation of more than 3,000 Palestinians from their homes, severely disrupting the lives of residents and the city’s commercial activity.
The message was clear: the whole city would be punished for the actions of the attackers.
A devastating loss
Al-Qawasmi says he was given no chance to retrieve goods from the family businesses’ warehouses and factories before the demolitions began, leaving the stock buried under the rubble, where it remains.
“We managed to retrieve some marble slabs and store them in facilities belonging to friends nearby, but most of the stock was destroyed,” he told Al Jazeera.
Al-Qawasmi says that 1,300 square metres of their business’ property was destroyed, including the family’s offices. He estimates the losses at no less than 60 million shekels ($19m).
Those losses are devastating for al-Qawasmi’s family, but also for the wider economy in Hebron and the Palestinian economy as a whole.
According to the Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Hebron serves as a primary pillar of the Palestinian economy, contributing approximately 42 percent of the Palestinian gross domestic product (GDP). It is home to more than 23,000 economic establishments, including more than 5,000 industrial and artisanal facilities that employ approximately 40,000 workers.
Hebron’s economy is notably diverse, encompassing sectors such as stone and marble, plastics, metals, food production, leather and footwear, and glass, alongside robust commercial and agricultural activity.
Adnan al-Natsha, vice president of the Hebron Chamber of Commerce, told Al Jazeera that there are no precise figures yet regarding the total losses resulting from the Israeli military operation so far. He noted that work is currently under way to compile statistics on the damage inflicted on businesses and homes, losses estimated to be in the millions of dollars.
Al-Natsha explained that the extensive Israeli measures, including closing off areas of the city, displacing residents from their homes, demolishing buildings and shutting down commercial shops, have exacerbated the already difficult economic situation in Hebron – which already has an illegal Israeli settlement in its commercial centre that severely disrupts Palestinian movement and trade there.
“Business owners have been unable to operate their facilities because workers couldn’t reach their workplaces, and employees have been unable to get to their jobs. The impact of these measures is not limited to Hebron; it extends to the Palestinian economy as a whole,” he stated, adding that work was ongoing to assess the losses and damages of the ongoing Israeli operation so far.
Paralysed commerce
The Israeli military continues to lock down Hebron, including the installation of checkpoints, earthen berms, and concrete blocks across the city, as it conducts raids. As a consequence, economic activity has been severely disrupted.
Ibrahim Ahmaro, who owns a vegetable shop in the al-Jalada neighbourhood, one of the areas targeted by the Israeli operation, told Al Jazeera that he had been arranging his stock on Friday, preparing for Saturday, which is typically the busiest day for commerce due to the arrival of buses carrying Palestinian citizens of Israel shopping for cheaper produce.
Military vehicles suddenly stormed the area, and soldiers forced Ahmaro to leave his shop immediately. He says that he wasn’t given an opportunity to turn on the refrigeration units, which would have kept his goods from spoiling, nor allowed to retrieve his vehicle, which remained parked in front of the shop.
“My brother, the staff and I all left, thinking it would only be for a few hours. Instead, we were met with a total lockdown of the area, and we were unable to reach our shops, meaning everything inside was lost after being left unattended for days,” he added.
On Sunday morning, Ahmaro was able to return to check on his stock, despite the heavy military presence in the area. As soon as he entered, he said soldiers attacked him inside the shop and forced him out. He pleaded with them to let him remove at least a few crates; they granted him a few minutes to do so.
“I placed the crates 400 metres away from the shops so that local residents, facing the lockdown, could take whatever they needed. My losses on these goods alone exceed 50,000 shekels [$16,200],” he said with a sigh.
Economic expert Ali Oweiwi said that the Israeli military’s restrictions and lockdowns imposed on Hebron have created significant challenges for commercial and industrial establishments, which rely on road access to transport production supplies and distribute their products.
He explained that the impact of the closure is not limited to retail shops but extends to companies, factories, suppliers, and the transport and logistics sector, not to mention the workers who are forced to take alternative routes to reach their workplaces, all of which ultimately affect consumers.
Oweiwi said that if the Israeli operation concludes within a day or two, the economy might recover relatively quickly. However, if it persists for more than 10 days, it could lead to significant problems, including the accumulation of goods, disruptions to transport and a decline in productivity due to the difficulty of moving both workers and merchandise.
Israel – which will vote for a new parliament in pivotal elections on Tuesday – has not announced an end date for the lockdown in Hebron.
“The destruction of facilities specialising in vehicle dismantling, spare parts, and tile shops has resulted in losses estimated at 70 to 80 million shekels ($22.7m to $26m), in addition to the seizure of dozens or perhaps hundreds of vehicles belonging to the owners of these establishments,” Oweiwi said.

Italy flotilla torture case against IDF officials even broader than ICC war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:23:43 UTC
01:23:43 KST

Italy’s criminal probe of flotilla activists’ torture claims against Israel impacts far more IDF officials than even the pending file before the International Criminal Court (ICC), multiple Israeli officials with knowledge of the case have confirmed to The Jerusalem Post.
Since 2007, flotilla activists have periodically sought to block Israel’s blockade to prevent weapons smuggling to Hamas in Gaza.
Although the activists claim they are seeking to bring Gazans humanitarian aid, Gazans have been receiving over 600 trucks of aid per day since the October 2025 ceasefire – almost triple what they were receiving pre-war.
Gazans’ overall situation is still far worse because the Strip is years away from being rebuilt, but there is no actual food shortage.
ICC seeks to arrest Netanyahu, Gallant, may target other Israeli officials
Currently, the ICC is confirmed to be seeking to arrest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant, with reports that it is also seeking to arrest minister Betzalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, and possibly also Defense Minister Israel Katz, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, and former IDF chief Herzi Halevi.
That is still a short list, and most of the officials are government officials because Israel has not probed its government officials.
In contrast, the Italian criminal probe relating to Israel’s treatment of arrested activists from the September-October 2025 and April-May 2026 flotillas not only includes many of the same ministers, but it also implicates a long list of IDF and prison service officials, of around a dozen.
In fact, the IDF officials being targeted are even more noteworthy than the prison service officials, given that there is some cloud of impropriety hanging over the prison service since it has been managed in recent years by Ben-Gvir.
Ben-Gvir himself was condemned by the entire Israeli government for various actions he undertook and statements he made relating to the flotilla activists.
But the IDF officials include completely apolitical and generally highly regarded officials, such as: former navy chief David Saar Salame, current Navy Chief Eyal Harel, each of their top advisers Tal Politis and Guy Levy, Ashdod Naval Base Chief Eitan Paz, and the Shayetet 13 Naval Commander.
While none of the activists’ claims against Israeli officials have been proven, there have been Israeli officials concerned that police and prison guard officials, who are under Ben-Gvir’s command, may have roughed up some of the activists.
Put differently, even if some of the most sensational charges might be untrue or exaggerated, some officials recognize that some of the lesser claims against officials under Ben-Gvir may be true.
Yet, there are no Israeli officials who believe that the navy’s conduct was anything other than highly professional, leaving many mystified as to what prosecutors from Italy – a country which has been one of Israel’s stronger allies even after October 7- could really be trying to get after going after IDF and naval officials.
The Post understands from officials with knowledge of the case that the prosecution is being run by a local Italian prosecutor, who is not coordinating with the Italian federal government.
Italian prosecutor rogue prosecutor, Israeli officials tell 'Post'
In other words, Israeli officials speaking to the Post portrayed the prosecutor as a rogue prosecutor who is using an Italian law for universal jurisdiction that the government would not have intended or expected to use against an ally like Israel, as much as it may have been passed to go after a traveling warlord from a more broken non-democratic country.
Further, the case has been a major domestic politics issue within Italy, such that some officials may see it as advantageous internally to make noise about such a case, without necessarily moving it forward to the end, something which could take many years in any event.
Around the time of the flotillas, Italy suspended certain defense cooperation arrangements with Israel, and the sides have sparred publicly over the treatment of some activists who were recently detained in the West Bank while assisting Palestinians with the olive harvest.
However, Israeli officials still view this criminal proceeding as being in conflict with overall Italian government policy, which has not sought to inflame relations.
Rather, multiple sources with knowledge of the case said that the long list of IDF officials who are considered highly professional simply indicated how politicized and disjointed the specific prosecutor likely was.
Moreover, they indicated that once a criminal probe is opened, it is always easier to add other suspects into the probe, even if they have less of a true connection to the heart of the issue.
The Israeli minister, IDF officials, police, and prison officials were all put under official investigation in Italy on October 16.
The move expanded an investigation that was previously focused on Ben-Gvir.
The case concerns alleged torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of boats headed towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026, the Rome prosecutors’ office said in a statement.
Probe opened after activists launched complaints
Investigators opened the probe after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions in September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.
Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission had reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism.
Notably, being insulted and being accused of terrorism might be problematic or fully justified, but would usually not be criminally probed.
Activists involved in the second mission alleged even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark, the use of rubber bullets, and tasers, a statement said.
Once again, some of these actions would clearly be criminal, but using a non-lethal taser to subdue a person resisting arrest is standard even in the West.
Investigators had identified various individuals forming the military and police chains of command involved in the operations, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors said they had sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information needed to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility. They did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
Questioned about their response, multiple Israeli authorities declined to address the issue, signaling that Israel may view the request as invalid if it is not endorsed by the Italian federal government or may choose to deal with it through diplomatic channels as opposed to strictly technical channels.
An interesting question would be whether Israel might comply more if the requests were more limited to Ben-Gvir and some of his officials, who took videos of themselves at minimum verbally harassing detainees.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
Being placed under investigation in Italy does not imply guilt and does not automatically lead to a trial. However, if the probe determines that charges are warranted, prosecutors could lodge a formal request for trial.
Reuters contributed to this report.
