Israel elections: Netanyahu, Trump, and the battle for Israeli democracy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:04:14 UTC
01:04:14 KST

One day before Election Day, most people in Israel are on edge since, more than ever, the future of the state appears to be at stake, and a clear-cut decision by the voters does not appear to be at hand.
At present, there are two alternatives. The first is that Israel will continue to deteriorate into becoming an authoritarian state, under yet another all-right religious government, in which its center-left and Arab populations will be subject to progressively growing oppressive measures and physical attacks by unruly right-wing bullies.
As in the current government, the new government’s leader will again be Benjamin Netanyahu, who was and still is bent on a continuous bleeding war, irrespective of its cost or consequences.
It will be a coalition of parties who seek the unilateral application of Israeli sovereignty in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, and turning Israel into a more religious state than it is today.
The second alternative is that Israel will continue to exist as a more or less liberal state, which tries to remain both Jewish (in terms of its serving as the national home of all sections of the Jewish people) and democratic (in terms of being tolerant to all its citizens, whether Jewish or Arab, religious, secular, or everything in between), and attentive to the rules of international law to the maximal extent, without endangering Israel’s survival.
At this stage, in the existing circumstances, I do not believe that a well-functioning national unity government – which is what Israel most urgently requires – is an option, as long as Netanyahu is still the leader of the Likud.
Unfortunately, also the prospects of a stable government in which one of the sides has a clear majority are close to nil, especially if predictions that the Arab population will turn out to vote in large numbers and thus increase the number of Arab MKs to as many as 16 will materialize.
When US President Donald J. Trump announced his “complete and total endorsement” for Netanyahu on October 18, nine days before polling day in Israel, his accompanying words undoubtedly warmed the hearts of all those in Israel who support another Netanyahu-led government, while disgusting and angering its opponents, both Jewish and Arab, who happen to constitute a majority of the Israeli electorate.
This majority disagrees with Trump’s statement that “Netanyahu has been a great warrior prime minister, and an even greater partner for peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Most of this majority sees Netanyahu as the man who bears most of the responsibility for the greatest catastrophe to have befallen the Jewish people since the Holocaust – the massacre of October 7, 2023 – but who, over three years after its occurrence, still refuses to accept any responsibility for it, or to appoint a national commission of inquiry to examine the events that preceded it.
It also believes that despite some brilliant military operations in the last three years, Netanyahu has, time and again, promised a total victory over Iran and its proxies but has failed to bring about even a single victory, while managing to isolate the State of Israel in the international arena and turn himself into a person wanted for trial by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Trump’s endorsement statement also rejected all the other potential candidates to head Israel’s next government, even though the Israeli elections are not about electing a prime minister but about electing parties to the Knesset, which may become part of a coalition government.
At the moment, it doesn’t look like Netanyahu, even with Trump’s endorsement, will manage to muster sufficient parties, with sufficient Knesset seats, to form such a government.
Trump ended his endorsement by stating to the Israeli voters that “Bibi Netanyahu will never let you down!” Time and again, Netanyahu has let a majority of Israel’s citizens down – not least of all over the return of all the Israeli hostages – both alive and dead.
In fact, it is Trump himself who was responsible for bringing them all back home – not Netanyahu, who kept sabotaging efforts to reach an agreement with Hamas over the release of the hostages, when more of them could have been brought back alive. There were allegedly strategic considerations for this enervating action of his.
Apparently, we must also thank Trump for dissuading Netanyahu from attacking Iran two weeks ago and thus sabotaging tomorrow’s elections. Nevertheless, Trump remains guilty of unwarranted intervention in the Israeli elections.
Incidentally, though it is generally assumed that international law categorically rejects intervention by states in the elections of other states, in fact, so far, no treaty-based solutions to the problem of foreign election interference have been formulated.
What does exist is an International Court of Justice ruling from 1986 that the principle of nonintervention is a pillar of customary international law.
In addition, traditional international law prohibits actions that are coercive by nature – i.e., intervention that compels a target state to act against its will.
Finally, there are several UN General Assembly resolutions that explicitly condemn direct or indirect interference, foreign financing of political groups, or attempts to sway domestic electoral processes.
Strictly speaking, what Trump has done is not illegal under international law but is certainly enervating and objectionable to those who believe that Netanyahu’s continued premiership is dangerous to Israel’s continued existence as a liberal democratic state. Some even believe that it endangers Israel’s existence altogether.
Final words
A few words should be mentioned about the ugly and libelous campaign by the Likud and its non-haredi partners against Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is one of the current promising candidates for the premiership of the opposition parties, and has been unjustifiably belittled and mocked.
The worst manifestation of this was the disgusting referral to him, by Channel 14 moderator and close associate of Netanyahu, Yinon Magal, as “an oriental-Moroccan monkey, who is backed by the Ashkenazi elites that manage him.”
It doesn’t matter whether Magal used the word “monkey” in the physical sense, or – as he later explained – as the word used in the Israeli underworld to mean a front man, puppet, or straw man. In both senses, the meaning of the word “monkey” is disgusting, demeaning, and meant to belittle and insult.
Hopefully, tomorrow will go by peacefully – both in verbal and physical terms.
And just one final word to Netanyahu personally. The way to deal with threats of international economic sanctions against Israel, which you mentioned several days ago, is not by moving over to crypto or turning Israel into a super-Sparta, but by changing your policies that have led to the threats of sanctions against our state.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

Starshield Speed Caps Fully Lifted in Ukraine, General Staff Data Shows
Starshield speed restrictions affecting Ukrainian military operations have been fully lifted, according to data from Ukraine’s General Staff on October 26.
Testing has confirmed stable satellite communication connections at speeds of up to 470 kilometers per hour.
The first incident was recorded at 1:43 a.m. on October 14, when Starshield connections began dropping on fast-moving Ukrainian systems. Before that point, no speed restrictions had been detected.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Starshield is the military-focused version of SpaceX’s satellite communications service used by Ukrainian forces to maintain connectivity for drones, aircraft, logistics, and other fast-moving battlefield systems. UNITED24 Media reported that the service is also used by interceptor drones hunting Russian jet-powered Shahed-type UAVs, making stable high-speed connections important for air defense.
Initial monitoring found that the connection limit was effectively triggered at around 60 kilometers per hour. Ukrainian units reported losing connectivity at different speeds, but later analysis identified a two- to three-minute delay between exceeding the limit and the eventual loss of connection.
SpaceX technical support maintained that the restriction should have applied only at 161 kilometers per hour.
By 8:13 p.m. on October 14, Ukrainian monitoring confirmed that the limit had shifted to approximately 161 kilometers per hour.
The restrictions disrupted Starshield, SpaceX’s military-focused satellite communications service used by Ukrainian forces for drone operations, logistics, and other missions requiring stable connectivity while moving.
On October 24 at 1:10 a.m., monitoring recorded a decline in the number of connection errors. By 6:10 a.m., Ukrainian specialists concluded that the restrictions were no longer active.
Tests were subsequently conducted at speeds of up to 470 kilometers per hour without the previous connection limits reappearing.
The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Elon Musk personally ordered the Starshield slowdown, despite later writing that speed and usage limits were controlled by the US military and ultimately the president.

"Strasbourg Calling" The secrets of the Italy-Albania migration deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:01:56 UTC
01:01:56 KST

Author
Irina Nedeva
Article
2026 Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize
"Strasbourg Calling" The secrets of the Italy-Albania migration deal
Giacomo Zandonini and Maite Vermeulen reveal the costs of detaining migrants and the obstacles to public scrutiny of the centres in Albania
Monday 26 October 2026 16:51
Monday, 26 October 2026, 16:51
Giacomo Zandonini and Maite Vermeulen
PHOTO European Parliament Multimedia Centre
Font size
The 2026 Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize for Journalism was awarded to an investigation by the Dutch platform De Correspondent into the agreement between Italy and Albania, which provides for the detention of migrants and the processing of their asylum applications on Albanian territory.
The investigation was conducted by Italian journalist Giacomo Zandonini and Dutch journalist Maite Vermeulen. Over 18 months, they tracked how the agreement operates, as several EU member states consider it a possible model for future European migration policy.
The journalists uncovered serious obstacles to public scrutiny of the system. They were denied access to the centres operated by Italy in Albania, while key information, including the number of people detained, is not made publicly available.
To investigate how the centres operate and how public funds are spent, the authors submitted more than 30 freedom of information requests in six European countries, as well as to the European Commission, the Council of the EU and the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, Frontex. They also interviewed detained migrants, lawyers, government officials, members of parliament and local residents in Albania.
The investigation also examines possible violations of human rights and the rule of law. According to the authors, the costs of the centres are covered through emergency procedures that bypass the usual public procurement rules, while staff are required to sign confidentiality agreements.
The award was presented at a ceremony in the European Parliament in Strasbourg by a representative of the independent jury, which includes journalists from all 27 EU member states. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola and Vice-President Pina Picierno, who is responsible for the prize, attended the event.
“Nine years after the brutal murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia, our determination to see justice done remains unwavering,” Roberta Metsola said. She stressed that the courage and commitment to the truth demonstrated by the Maltese journalist continue to inspire others, and that the European Parliament will continue to support journalists and defend press freedom.
A total of 344 entries were submitted for the 2026 competition. The jury selected ten finalists, from whom the winner was chosen. The prize also carries a monetary award of €20,000.
Finalists for the 2026 European Parliament Prize for Journalism await the announcement of the winner
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
About the Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize
The prize is awarded annually with the support of the European Parliament in memory of Maltese investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, who was killed by a car bomb on 16 October 2017. She was known for her investigations into corruption, money laundering, organised crime and links between political power and business.
The award recognises journalistic investigations that uphold the European Union’s fundamental values: human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights.
Previous recipients have included an investigation into the financial networks behind Russia’s “shadow fleet” in 2025, the disappearance of unaccompanied migrant children in Europe in 2024, and the migrant shipwreck off Pylos in 2023.
Nine years after Caruana Galizia’s murder, five people have been imprisoned for their involvement in the crime. The question of the legal accountability of the person who commissioned the murder remains unresolved.
Who Was Daphne Caruana Galizia?
Daphne Caruana Galizia was a Maltese journalist, blogger and anti-corruption activist who produced in-depth investigations into corruption, money laundering, organised crime, the sale of citizenship and links between the Maltese government and the so-called Panama Papers.
After facing harassment and threats, she was killed in a car bomb explosion on 16 October 2017. Public outrage over the authorities’ handling of the murder investigation led to the resignation of Prime Minister Joseph Muscat.
Members of the European Parliament criticised shortcomings in the investigation and, in December 2019, called on the European Commission to take active measures. They have continued to revisit the case, including through a resolution adopted in 2023 that condemned the limited progress in bringing those responsible to justice.
To date, five people have been imprisoned for carrying out the murder. However, the person who masterminded the killing has yet to be convicted.

The Anthropic IPO Is Also a Doomsday Primer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:01:55 UTC
01:01:55 KST

Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.
While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.
“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)
Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.
The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.
Or, as the Anthropic filing puts it: “Risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models.”
The prospectus repeatedly makes the point that RSI could lead to AI models that develop faster than the company’s safeguards, and that the company may not even realize it has lost that race until it’s too late. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
It also gets specific about what might happen after that. “As AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the prospectus says, “there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” This is Skynet territory.
Speaking of robots, Anthropic flags concerns about those as well. “When our models direct physical equipment,” the filing says, “errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible.”
You might think, given the apparently existential stakes, that serious consideration would be given to whether RSI should be pursued at all, much less embraced. In an industry as competitive as frontier AI, though, it’s become fait accompli. Here’s how Anthropic describes that same process elsewhere in the prospectus, this time in a section about the startup’s “core advantages:”
“We refer to this recursive dynamic as ‘closing the loop,’” the prospectus says, “and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.”
Failure to “close the loop,” Anthropic later says, could result in “falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities.” In other words, the same systems that are causing all that existential concerns are the ones Anthropic sees as critical to its success.
Every AI company is dealing with this same tension. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral for loudly resigning, he put curbing RSI at the top of his wish list for the industry. Employees at Google DeepMind and elsewhere have had similar revelations. There are multiple bills in Congress, including one cosponsored by Bernie Sanders, that propose a ban on RSI. At the same time, these are for-profit companies, and there are trillions of dollars at stake.
It’s a tricky dynamic to navigate. Recursive self-improvement could become a runaway train that destroys humanity. But until then, just look at how fast it can go.

Saddam Haftar is eyeing the throne in Libya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:01:19 UTC
01:01:19 KST

Saddam Haftar is eyeing the throne in Libya
As the US looks to broker a unity deal, Saddam is trying to position himself as the main contender for the presidency.
Eastern Libya spent nearly seven years denouncing the maritime memorandum Turkiye struck with its rivals based in Tripoli. Last week, it needed a single sitting of the legislature to embrace it.
On October 20, the House of Representatives (HoR) in Benghazi ratified the deal. The European Union condemned the vote, as did Greece, Israel and Egypt.
Yet the ratification was less a Turkish triumph than the final act of a sequence choreographed by Saddam Haftar, the son of Khalifa Haftar, the military commander who controls eastern Libya. The ultimate goal is the Libyan presidency.
The United States is currently trying to broker a power-sharing arrangement between Tripoli and Benghazi. Championed by Massad Boulos, US President Donald Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, the deal could install Saddam as Libya’s president.
For that to happen, however, he needs the backing of Ankara, whose sway over western Libya gives it a decisive voice in any such settlement. The ratification of the maritime deal, therefore, is meant to secure Turkiye’s blessing.
The opening move in Saddam’s pursuit of the presidency was a palace coup: a fortnight before the vote, the HoR unseated its speaker, Aguila Saleh, who had spent 12 years in this position. It thus removed both Cairo’s principal ally in the east and the most stubborn obstacle to the memorandum’s ratification.
Yet Saleh’s ouster was never only about Egypt, and the same stone felled a second bird. As speaker and nominal supreme commander, he embodied the de jure authority from which Khalifa’s own command flows, and with a weighty tribal constituency among the Obeidat tribe, he was one of the few men capable of complicating, or even arbitrating, any transfer of power. Removing him cleared Saddam’s path to a handover already quietly under way, which the elder Haftar’s advanced age could hasten at any moment.
Saleh’s successor, Al-Salhin Abdulnabi, a fellow Obeidi, who chaired the HoR’s Libyan-Turkish friendship committee, is able to defuse the risk of tribal backlash while signalling where the chamber now takes its cues.
Whether the gambit pays off will be decided in Washington. Saddam is counting on the Trump administration’s appetite for a Libyan deal, sharpened by Turkish and Emirati lobbying and by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s rapport with Trump.
He hopes it can prevail over the objections of Athens and Nicosia and the displeasure of Israel, which is uneasy about Ankara’s reach. This is directly pitting Trump’s transactional instinct against a longstanding US partnership with the Greek-Cypriot-Israeli axis.
The broadside against Israel may even pay a domestic dividend, allowing Saddam to pose as standing up to Israel while dispelling perceptions of a covert channel to it.
Europe, meanwhile, has sidelined itself into near-irrelevance: when Benghazi expelled the EU’s migration commissioner and three member-state ministers on arrival in July 2025, European capitals responded with something closer to grovelling than resolve.
Less than a year later, Athens was hosting Saddam, who duly sidestepped any commitment on an alternative maritime memorandum.
That deference flows from the EU’s navel-gazing fixation on migration that has reduced its Libya policy to counting the boats leaving Libya’s eastern coast for Crete. A Union that implores Saddam to police the very waters now in dispute is in no position to make him pay for redrawing them.
Abu Dhabi, for its part, has every reason to look the other way because it wants Saddam to succeed. None of Khalifa’s sons has been more faithful to the Emiratis, and seeing their most loyal client installed at the apex of the Libyan state would cap a decade of investment in the Haftar project. Whatever their past flirtation with Greece and Cyprus, a maritime line drawn in Ankara’s favour is a modest price for that outcome, though the closeness of that embrace may yet constrain him.
Egypt remains the real question mark: Cairo’s statement objected chiefly to the memorandum’s encroachment on Egypt’s exclusive economic zone and was framed almost entirely in legal terms, a sign perhaps that it is keeping its political options open.
Its relationship with Ankara has been transformed, with the two now aligned on Sudan and the Red Sea. A shared wariness of Israel’s expansionist ambitions has only drawn them closer.
Offering commercial deals could go some way towards softening Egyptian opposition. But Cairo could also lean on its rapport with Ankara to champion an alternative Haftar heir. It would not have to look far for a candidate: Saddam’s brother Khaled, the Libyan Arab Armed Forces’ chief of staff, is considerably closer to Cairo and publicly criticised the US initiative in April.
Should that happen, Saddam would have little left to bargain with, having cashed in his most valuable chip with the Turks, and the strongest card he still holds is one Abu Dhabi would never let him play.
Cutting off support for Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces would win favour in Ankara and Cairo alike, both backers of the Sudanese army, but that would jeopardise the one relationship he cannot afford to lose.
Squeezed between a patron in Abu Dhabi he dare not cross and a partner in Ankara that has already pocketed its reward, Saddam is betting that he can keep both on side long enough for Washington to see the deal through. That he is prepared to run such risks may say as much about desperation as acumen, for the alternative to an institutionalised succession is one contested, perhaps violently, by his siblings or by the constituencies left out of the new order.
History, in Libya, has a mordant sense of humour. The maritime memorandum was the price Tripoli paid for the Turkish intervention that helped halt Khalifa Haftar’s offensive at the gates of the capital and sent his forces and mercenaries into headlong retreat in 2020. Where the father tried and failed to storm Tripoli, the son now hopes to be ushered in on a red carpet woven from the very document that sealed his father’s defeat.
Should he succeed, the instrument of the Haftars’ most humiliating setback will have become the cornerstone of their dynasty. Should Washington baulk, it may instead become the epitaph of the son’s ambitions.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Frequent cannabis use linked to higher odds of nighttime breathing problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:00:47 UTC
01:00:47 KST

Adults who use cannabis are more likely to report loud snoring and pauses in breathing during the night, according to new research published in Sleep Health: Journal of the National Sleep Foundation. The findings indicate that more frequent cannabis consumption corresponds with higher odds of experiencing these nocturnal breathing issues, even after accounting for factors like body weight and tobacco smoking. This relationship raises important questions for the growing number of people who turn to cannabis as a sleep aid.
Sleep-disordered breathing is an umbrella term for medical conditions characterized by abnormal respiratory patterns or insufficient ventilation during rest. The most common form is obstructive sleep apnea, a disorder in which the muscles in the back of the throat relax too much, causing the upper airway to narrow or collapse entirely. People with this condition require extra physical effort to breathe, often resulting in loud snoring, gasping, or brief, repeated stops in breathing known as apneas. Standard treatments like continuous positive airway pressure machines, oral appliances, and surgery can be effective, yet many patients find the devices uncomfortable or difficult to tolerate over the long term.
At the same time, cannabis has become increasingly accessible across the United States, and difficulty sleeping is one of the most common reasons people cite for using it. While users frequently report that the plant helps them rest, controlled clinical trials examining cannabinoids and sleep have produced mixed outcomes.
For example, a 2023 clinical trial covered by PsyPost found that consuming medicinal cannabis oil improved sleep duration and increased midnight melatonin levels in adults with insomnia, whereas a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that a cannabis compound called cannabinol reduced nighttime awakenings when taken alone but showed no benefit when combined with cannabidiol, another cannabis compound. Observational tracking also points to potential drawbacks, such as a 2026 longitudinal study of military service members that linked current cannabis use to worse overall sleep quality and longer times needed to fall asleep.
When it comes to breathing disorders specifically, tetrahydrocannabinol, the primary psychoactive compound in cannabis, has shown some potential to stabilize breathing in animal experiments and small human trials using oral pills. However, the broader clinical evidence remains inconsistent, leading the American Academy of Sleep Medicine to formally advise against using cannabis to treat obstructive sleep apnea. Most everyday consumers inhale cannabis rather than taking standardized pills, exposing their airways to smoke and heat that could inflame the tissues of the throat.
The new research, led by Tyler J. Gallagher, a resident physician in the Caruso Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery at the Keck School of Medicine of the University of Southern California, and co-first author Matthew E. Lin of the David Geffen School of Medicine at the University of California, Los Angeles, sought to evaluate how everyday consumption relates to signs of breathing issues at night.
“While some studies have explored cannabinoids as potential treatments for obstructive sleep apnea, there has been relatively little population-level research examining whether real-world cannabis use is associated with common signs of sleep-disordered breathing, such as loud snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep,” Gallagher told PsyPost. “We sought to better understand this relationship using a nationally representative sample of US adults.”
To investigate this connection, the authors analyzed information from the 2017 to 2018 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, a state-based telephone survey coordinated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Although nearly 900,000 adults completed the main survey during those two years, only Minnesota and Tennessee included optional survey modules asking about both cannabis habits and sleep breathing symptoms. From the respondents in those two states who had complete data, the researchers selected a stratified random sample of 14,485 adults designed to match the demographic profile of the broader United States population.
Participants were asked how many days they had used marijuana or cannabis during the past 30 days, as well as their primary method of consumption and whether they used it for medical or recreational purposes. The researchers grouped the respondents into three categories: non-users (zero days in the past month), non-regular users (1 to 15 days), and regular users (16 to 30 days). Signs of sleep-disordered breathing were assessed using two yes-or-no questions asking if anyone had ever observed the respondent stop breathing during sleep, and if the respondent had ever been told that they snore loudly.
Of the participants, 13,461 reported no current cannabis use, 438 were classified as non-regular users, and 364 were regular users, meaning about 5.5 percent of the sample currently used cannabis. Smoking was by far the most common consumption method, reported by about 87 percent of both non-regular and regular consumers, followed by vaporizing and eating. Among non-regular users, 61.6 percent used cannabis strictly for recreational reasons, whereas 37.6 percent of regular users reported using it strictly for medical reasons and another 24.7 percent used it for both medical and recreational purposes.
Overall, signs of sleep-disordered breathing were common across the entire cohort, with 44.7 percent reporting either loud snoring or witnessed apneas. In the unadjusted raw numbers, 44.3 percent of non-users reported at least one of the two breathing signs, compared to 48.4 percent of non-regular users and 55.2 percent of regular users. Specifically, witnessed breathing pauses were reported by 15.3 percent of non-users, 17.1 percent of non-regular users, and 19.8 percent of regular users. Loud snoring was reported by 41.3 percent of non-users, 44.5 percent of non-regular users, and 50.0 percent of regular users.
To account for other differences between users and non-users, the researchers ran statistical models that applied national survey weights (statistical adjustments that make a sample better mirror the U.S. adult population) and controlled for a wide range of potentially confounding factors. These adjustments accounted for age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, income, health insurance status, diabetes, body mass index, alcohol consumption, traditional cigarette smoking, and electronic cigarette use. Even after factoring out the influence of tobacco smoking and body weight, cannabis use remained independently associated with higher odds of sleep-disordered breathing symptoms.
Compared to non-users, non-regular cannabis users had 41 percent higher odds of reporting witnessed apneas, 26 percent higher odds of reporting loud snoring, and 33 percent higher odds of experiencing either symptom. The association was more pronounced among regular consumers. Those who used cannabis 16 to 30 days per month had 73 percent higher odds of witnessed apneas, 68 percent higher odds of loud snoring, and 82 percent higher odds of reporting either sign compared to non-users. These figures describe odds rather than probabilities, so the absolute differences are smaller than the percentages might suggest; in the raw numbers, about 55 percent of regular users reported at least one sign, compared with about 44 percent of non-users.
“While the impact of infrequent use is relatively small, the odds of irregular breathing during sleep almost double with more frequent cannabis use, making this a strong association worthy of consideration before frequent cannabis utilization,” Gallagher explained.
The researchers also analyzed cannabis consumption as a continuous spectrum from zero to 30 days. In the weighted models, each additional day of cannabis use per month was associated with an approximate 2 percent increase in the odds of reporting witnessed apneas, loud snoring, or either sign, an estimate the authors note is clinically small and serves as a general summary across use levels rather than a strict per-day effect. When the authors repeated the analysis without the national survey weights, regular cannabis use remained linked to both breathing signs, though the estimates were smaller (for example, 36 percent higher odds of either sign rather than 82 percent). In that analysis, non-regular use was no longer linked to loud snoring or to either sign, and its link with witnessed breathing pauses sat right at the threshold of statistical significance.
“The strength of the association and its greater magnitude among more frequent users were notable, particularly given that some studies have investigated cannabinoids as potential treatments for sleep apnea,” Gallagher said. “These findings may reflect differences between isolated cannabinoids studied in clinical settings and real-world cannabis use, including differences in composition and method of consumption.”
The authors proposed two primary biological mechanisms that might explain why cannabis consumers report more signs of airway obstruction at night. Because roughly 87 percent of the consumers in the sample smoked their cannabis, physical irritation from smoke is one possible contributor. Unlike tobacco, cannabis smoke is typically inhaled through deeper breaths without a filter, and it burns at a higher temperature, which can cause thermal injury and inflammation in the throat tissues that narrow the upper airway.
A second potential mechanism involves the way cannabis interacts with the autonomic nervous system, which regulates involuntary body functions. While small doses of cannabis tend to stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, the body’s “fight or flight” system, higher doses activate the parasympathetic nervous system, which promotes physical relaxation. Frequent users may develop tolerance and consume larger quantities, and the resulting parasympathetic activity may cause the muscles that hold the upper airway open to relax excessively during sleep, making the throat more likely to collapse.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the survey captured information at a single point in time, the study cannot establish whether cannabis use causes sleep-disordered breathing or if the relationship works in the opposite direction. People who suffer from undiagnosed sleep apnea often experience fragmented, unrefreshing sleep, and it is possible that some of these individuals turn to cannabis in an attempt to self-medicate their exhaustion or insomnia. The researchers also could not account for factors such as sleeping pill or sedative use, heavy drinking, or psychiatric conditions, any of which might influence both cannabis use and nighttime breathing.
The reliance on self-reported telephone survey data also introduces constraints. Asking participants if they have been told they snore or stop breathing is less reliable than conducting an overnight medical sleep study, and people who sleep alone may be unaware of their nighttime breathing habits. Additionally, the survey only tracked how many days a person used cannabis over the past month, without measuring the exact dosage, potency, or ratio of specific compounds like tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol.
The data came from just two states, Minnesota and Tennessee, because they were the only ones to include both sets of questions, and roughly 98 percent of the original survey respondents were excluded for that reason or because of missing information. Survey weights help align the sample with national demographics, but the authors note that applying them to such a small subset is debated among statisticians. In addition, the breathing questions asked whether these symptoms had ever been observed, while the cannabis question covered only the past month, so some symptoms may have predated participants’ current cannabis habits.
Gallagher emphasized that reporting these symptoms is not the same as receiving a formal medical diagnosis. “While obstructive sleep apnea – a clinically defined and hazardous intermittent airway obstruction during sleep – is a type of sleep-disordered breathing, this study cannot make conclusions about the association between cannabis use and sleep apnea or other associated long-term risks,” he noted.
Future research will need to incorporate objective sleep testing, such as polysomnography, an overnight sleep study that monitors breathing, oxygen levels, and brain activity, to verify whether cannabis habits correspond with clinically diagnosed sleep apnea. Scientists also need to compare different delivery methods, such as edibles versus inhalation, to separate the chemical effects of cannabinoids on throat muscles from possible damage from inhaling hot smoke.
“Further research is required to examine the long-term effects of cannabis use on sleep and to determine the effects of cannabis dosage, different cannabis compositions, and different methods of consumption on sleep-disordered breathing,” Gallagher said. “Additionally, the long-term consequences of these impacts must be studied.”
Until those relationships are clarified, the authors suggest that physicians should counsel patients about the potential respiratory risks of using cannabis, particularly for individuals who already show signs of sleep-disordered breathing. “People experiencing persistent snoring, pauses in breathing, or other symptoms of sleep apnea should seek medical evaluation rather than trying to utilize cannabis to manage their sleep,” Gallagher advised.
“This study highlights the importance of evaluating the broader health effects of substances that people increasingly use for self-management,” Gallagher added. “Cannabis may have benefits for certain symptoms or conditions, but those potential benefits should be considered alongside possible risks. Sleep-disordered breathing is particularly important because it can go unrecognized for years while causing significantly worse quality-of-life. We hope these findings encourage further research and help clinicians have more informed conversations with patients who use cannabis for sleep-related concerns.”
The study, “Cannabis use and associated sleep-disordered breathing among US adults,” was authored by Tyler J. Gallagher, Matthew E. Lin, Ian Kim, Ziva D. Cooper, Sebastian M. Jara, and Eric J. Kezirian.

EU set to miss 2030 marine protection targets, auditors warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:00:37 UTC
01:00:37 KST

Despite designating 14% of its waters as protected areas, the EU has placed less than 1% under strict protection, leaving marine ecosystems vulnerable to damaging fishing practices and putting its 2030 biodiversity targets at risk.
The EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 targets for protecting marine biodiversity, with many designated marine protected areas offering little meaningful protection against damaging activities such as commercial fishing, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) warned on Monday.
Around 14% of EU waters are currently designated as marine protected areas, but less than 1% are under strict protection, exposing a gulf between the bloc’s environmental ambitions and the reality at sea.
The EU aims to protect 30% of its marine waters by 2030, including 10% under strict protection. But auditors warn that simply expanding the network of protected areas will not be enough without tougher restrictions on activities that damage marine ecosystems.
“The EU has made some progress in designating marine protected areas, but our audit shows that the true challenge is turning designation into actual protection," said Iliana Ivanova, the ECA member in charge of the audit.
Imposing tougher restrictions could, however, prove politically contentious, particularly if fishing communities and other affected industries bear the costs without adequate consultation or support.
While countries such as France and Sweden have made progress through community involvement and new bans on bottom trawling, Ireland has been hampered by major data gaps and legal delays.
Protected on paper but not in practice
A chronic shortage of staff, inadequate funding and lengthy administrative procedures also hamper enforcement. Authorities may identify harmful or illegal activities but lack the resources or legal powers to stop them.
"Turning political ambition into tangible results for marine ecosystems will require faster action, applicable protective measures and a more coherent network across the EU’s seas,” Ivanova added.
Protected status does not necessarily mean that damaging activities are restricted. Fishing restrictions, for example, apply to only a small proportion of designated areas, despite the threat posed by commercial fishing and other activities that damage the seabed.
As a consequence, designating protected areas is politically easier than imposing the restrictions needed to make them effective.
Those restrictions could affect fishing fleets operating across national borders, creating tensions between biodiversity objectives and the economic interests of coastal communities.
The EU auditors are calling for the European Commission and EU countries to move beyond national approaches towards more harmonised and enforceable conservation rules.
“To ensure that marine protected areas function effectively, we need the European Commission and member states to join forces, as well as engagement with local stakeholders,” Ivanova said.
Funding gaps and local opposition hamper protection
Fragmented financing is also a barrier to effective protection, the ECA report warns.
Conservation efforts rely on national budgets and different EU funding instruments, leaving protected areas facing problems with staffing, resources and long-term planning.
Even if stricter rules are imposed, securing support from the communities affected by them can also be a challenge, according to the EU auditors.
"The process for adopting conservation measures affecting fishing fleets of several member states can be complex and lengthy because it may require negotiations between member states that have fishing interests, as well as with various stakeholders. It can take many years, and few conservation measures have been adopted since 2013," reads the ECA report.
Monica Verbeek, executive director at the NGO Seas At Risk, said Europe does not lack policies, solutions or scientific knowledge.
"Where measures are implemented consistently and at a sufficient scale, nature responds. But recovery at scale is still not happening. We cannot afford another decade of ambitious targets followed by insufficient implementation," Verbeek said.

Israel’s top court rejects bid to ban firearms at polling stations ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:56:52 UTC
00:56:52 KST

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Rania Abushamala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Israel’s Supreme Court has rejected a petition seeking to prohibit polling station officials and party representatives from carrying firearms inside voting facilities during Tuesday’s parliamentary elections, according to the Arab rights group Adalah.
In a statement Monday, Adalah said the court dismissed the petition, which it filed with the Joint List, on Sunday evening.
The petition followed announcements by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party that they planned to deploy around 2,000 observers to polling stations in Arab towns and cities with mixed Jewish and Arab populations.
Adalah said the plans raised concerns that armed observers could “intimidate Arab voters, which could also spark violent confrontations.”
The petitioners cited previous incidents in which voters had reportedly been intimidated by people brandishing firearms, warning that the presence of armed civilians could lead to the unlawful use of lethal force.
They argued that the risks were heightened when weapons were carried by untrained civilians sent to polling stations in Arab communities amid what they described as “a racist incitement campaign that portrays Arab citizens as a threat.”
 
Court defers to police judgement
According to Adalah, the state argued that there were no grounds for judicial intervention in the police’s professional assessment, which found no concrete threat or operational need to impose a firearms ban.
The state also said there were no indications of plans to disrupt voting or threaten voters.
The court accepted the state’s position and declined to intervene in decisions made by the police and the Central Elections Committee chair not to impose a ban, Adalah said.
According to the group, the court emphasized that police have broad discretion in matters of security and public order, with judicial intervention limited to exceptional circumstances. It also found that police had considered the petitioners’ concerns in their election preparations.
There was no immediate comment from the court on Adalah’s account.
 
Intimidation of voters
Responding to the ruling, Adalah said the state and the Central Elections Committee had ignored the petition’s central argument: that organized groups of armed right-wing activists inside polling stations could intimidate Arab voters.
The group said the committee chair’s decision to allow party representatives to carry firearms relied on a police security assessment conducted before Likud and Religious Zionism announced their election-day plans.
“The Court’s decision allows those taking part in Netanyahu and Smotrich’s provocation to show up at polling stations in Arab communities like armed militias,” Adalah said.
Israel holds parliamentary elections Tuesday amid a closely contested race between Netanyahu’s bloc and its opponents. Arab voter turnout could play a significant role in determining the balance of power in the 120-seat Knesset and the prospects for forming the next government.
Polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Jewish opposition parties will secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority, potentially leading to a unity government, another election or an alliance with Arab parties.
Both blocs have so far ruled out forming a governing coalition with Arab parties.

Alaska Senate: Peltola seeks quick dismissal of DOJ election lawsuit before midterm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:55:37 UTC
00:55:37 KST

A federal judge Monday night fast-tracked the Department of Justice's lawsuit seeking to block prompt certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses the race because of potential voter confusion from another candidate who shares his name.
Judge Sharon Gleason's order sets the stage for her to potentially rule on a request by the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola to dismiss the suit before Election Day, Nov. 3.
The winner of the race could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate starting in January.
Gleason granted a motion by Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to expedite consideration of the case in U.S. District Court in Alaska.
The judge ordered the DOJ to respond by 5 p.m. Alaska Time on Tuesday to motions to intervene in the case by Peltola's campaign, the DSCC, the League of Women Voters and the advocacy group Common Cause. Gleason said she intends to rule on the motions to intervene by late Wednesday afternoon.
If she grants the motions to intervene, Gleason said the DOJ should be prepared to respond to the motion to dismiss the case by Peltola's campaign and the DSCC by 5 p.m. Thursday.
Shortly after Gleason issued her order, Alaska election officials filed a motion asking the judge to dismiss the lawsuit "immediately, with prejudice, because the complaint has no legal basis." The filing was the first by state officials in the case.
The motion, which seeks a decision by Nov. 2 — the day before the election — says Alaska's Division of Elections "has taken significant steps to distinguish" between the two Sullivans on the ballot, "so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which."
The motion said that "the United States lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate."
"This lawsuit and this requested relief cast a cloud over Alaska's election that is contrary to the public interest and that the Court should not allow to linger," lawyers for the officials said in a court filing.
A lawyer for Peltola's campaign and the DSCC in a court filing Sunday said they are "seriously concerned" President Donald Trump, a Republican, and Attorney General Todd Blanche will use the lawsuit to "lay the groundwork for unlawful efforts to challenge a potential Peltola victory" if the complaint remains pending as of Nov. 3.
The Department of Justice filed the suit Thursday. Trump later that day said he ordered it.
The DOJ's suit asks a judge to bar Alaska from certifying the Senate race results if incumbent Sen. Sullivan loses by a margin that could be attributable to voters mistakenly casting their ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan.
The DOJ, in that case, would want an investigation to determine whether enough voters were confused by the men's names to swing the vote to another candidate, presumably the former Rep. Peltola.
The DOJ claims that Daniel J. Sullivan's "sole purpose" of running "is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan."
Daniel J. Sullivan, in an email to the Alaska Beacon on Monday, said, "This experience has been beyond anything I could have ever imagined."
"To say that it has now become overwhelming and intimidating is an understatement. It is unending stress, at times paralyzing and I am looking forward to it being over," Sullivan said, according to the news outlet.
"I ran because I was unhappy with the status quo and wanted to be a voice for common sense, Alaska values and change," Sullivan said. "With the litigation and threats, I was never really able to get up and running like I wanted, but I did the best I could under the circumstances."
"As for the DOJ lawsuit against the state, it seems a gross misuse of the Justice Department for a situation that has already been litigated and resolved by the Alaska Supreme Court," he said, referencing a court action that put his name on the primary ballot after election officials initially rejected it.
"I think the Division of Elections did a notable job of differentiating two candidates on the ballot with similar names and the primary showed there was little if any confusion," he said. "Alaskan voters are smart and I have faith in their ability to make an informed decision on their ballots."
In their motion to expedite the case, Peltola's campaign and the DSCC said, "DOJ filed this lawsuit in the midst of the ongoing general election, less than two weeks before election day, raising issues governed exclusively by state law that were definitively resolved by the Alaska Supreme Court months ago."
"DOJ seeks an unprecedented order precluding certification of the U.S. Senate election if the candidate the President favors loses narrowly," the filing said.
"As the proposed Motion to Dismiss reflects, DOJ's claims are utterly without legal basis," the filing said.
"The Court should not allow this lawsuit to hang like the Sword of Damocles over the ongoing election, lending false legitimacy to the President's and the Attorney General's ongoing efforts to spread false narratives about Alaska's elections as voting continues and as results begin to be tabulated next week."
The DOJ declined to comment Monday on the motions, but pointed to an X post by Blanche on Sunday.
"The Department of Justice does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska's election," Blanche had said. "This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska's governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead."
"The lawsuit was written by Justice Department attorneys and the Department did not coordinate with any campaign or candidate, but rather relied solely on federal law," Blanche said.
The department has not said how any investigation before certification of the election could determine whether a voter was confused about which Sullivan they were voting for. The ballot for the election notes that Sen. Sullivan — whose name is listed as Dan S. Sullivan — is an incumbent and a Republican. There are no words next to the name of the other Sullivan, whose name is spelled out Daniel J. Sullivan.
Peltola on Friday night told MS NOW's Nicolle Wallace that the DOJ's suit "is exactly the kind of corruption that Alaskans are sick and tired of."
"This is clearly a very desperate attempt to cling to power, using his allies in Washington, D.C., to rig the system even further," Peltola said.
Peltola's campaign on Sunday said that on Saturday night she and her family "sustained minor injuries" that required medical attention after a vehicle transporting them en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives Annual Banquet was struck by another driver.
As a result, Peltola posted events in Fairbanks and Bethel on Sunday and Monday. The campaign said that those events would be rescheduled.

Sudanese recount horrors in el-Fasher at the hands of UAE-backed RSF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:54:24 UTC
00:54:24 KST

Sudanese recount horrors in el-Fasher at the hands of UAE-backed RSF
Three weeks ago, Hala, a Sudanese woman, left the refugee camp in Tawila and returned to the city of el-Fasher.
She took a bag and got into a small vehicle operated by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group that took over the North Darfur capital a year ago, raping, killing and looting thousands of civilians like Hala.
When she arrived in el-Fasher, which is about 60km east of Tawila, she noticed that everything had changed. Houses had been looted or destroyed. The streets looked different.
RSF fighters immediately approached her as she got out of the vehicle. “They asked me where I was going,” Hala told the campaign group Avaaz, in an interview shared with Middle East Eye.
“I told them I was going to our family home because I needed to collect some documents, including my birth certificate and ID. They asked me how many days I was planning to stay and where exactly our house was located. They wanted to check whether I was lying to them or not.”
Hala, who used a different name for security reasons, had to describe the location of the house. She told the fighters she would need more than a day because it was a mess and she had to locate many documents. The house has no electricity, making the task harder.
“They agreed and issued me an entry permit for el-Fasher. It was a piece of paper with my name, their signature, and the date,” Hala said.
“Dealing with them is very difficult; they can easily enter your house and threaten to rape you if you refuse to go with them. They might rape you if you refuse, beat you, and if you argue with them, you could end up in prison,” she said.
“For women, travelling to el-Fasher is extremely dangerous. Most of the people who go there are fathers and elderly people because young people's lives are at risk in el-Fasher. Even elderly people often face problems with RSF fighters,” Hala told MEE.
The day after she returned to the city, she was threatened. “Some RSF fighters saw me in the street and started speaking to me using abusive and insulting language. But there were other civilians in the street, so they did not physically assault me and eventually allowed me to return home,” Hala said.
“The strangest thing is that they might assault you and then tell you that el-Fasher belongs to you, that this is your home, and that you are welcome to return at any time. But there is no security in el-Fasher at all. Women face sexual violence, and anyone who refuses the RSF's demands can be tortured or beaten.
"I returned to Tawila, and I will never go back to el-Fasher again, even if the situation improves and life changes.”
Killing on an industrial scale
On 26 October 2025, after over 500 days of siege, the RSF launched its final offensive on el-Fasher.
What followed was the largest single massacre to have taken place during Sudan’s war, which began in April 2023 between the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and has led to the largest humanitarian crisis in the world.
Researchers at Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab said the speed and industrial scale of the killing could only be compared to the whole of the Rwandan genocide.
RSF fighters, backed by the United Arab Emirates, which continues to deny its involvement, filmed themselves massacring civilians. Survivors described RSF fighters raping young women and girls, executing civilians, moving survivors to makeshift clinics to take blood from them, and exhorting ordinary people and their families.
RSF in el-Fasher
“In one of the streets they brought dozens of families outside the houses,” Mohamed Hassan, from el-Fasher, told MEE over the phone.
“They separated the men from the women and children. They lashed and insulted the women verbally and they fired on the men randomly. If they decided that you are a SAF or Joint Forces soldier, they will kill you immediately,” he said, referring to the allied militia fighting alongside the army.
Hanin, a Sudanese mother who escaped to Tawila, where she remains, described how she got out. “I left el-Fasher with only my daughter in my hands. I thought that once I reached Tawila, my daughter and I would finally be safe. I am still waiting for that feeling of safety to come,” she told MEE.
“I survived horrible things. There are things that happened to me that I struggle to speak about. I am a mother, and I tried to protect my daughter. I cannot explain what it does to you to see your child suffer violence and know that you could not stop it. We survived, but survival does not mean we are no longer hurting.”
Anna, an aid worker, said: “There are currently RSF prisons in el-Fasher.
“They are using old buildings as detention facilities, and the conditions of detainees are much worse than ours because they are not given food or medical care when they become sick.”
Where did everyone go?
Six weeks before the RSF took the city, roughly 107,000 had fled the capital of North Darfur. About 260,000 people were still inside the city when the assault began. Doctors Without Borders asked the question that still hangs over Sudan: where did everyone else go?
The true death toll may never be known. Monitoring groups counted at least 6,000 dead in the first 72 hours using satellite imagery, but the RSF has kept el-Fasher sealed behind a communications blackout, and human rights investigators have not been allowed in.
A year on, bodies keep surfacing and the count is still rising. In the North Kordofan town of Bara this week, 200 mass graves were found where volunteers have recovered more than 600 bodies, most of them civilians whom witnesses say the RSF killed in the same October offensive that took el-Fasher.
In the year since, the verdicts have come in one after another. In February, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan determined that the RSF committed acts of genocide in el-Fasher and that genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference from its conduct.
The US government and a string of human rights groups, including the Raoul Wallenberg Centre for Human Rights and Amnesty International, have determined that the RSF has committed genocide in Darfur.
In July, Amnesty called the atrocities perpetrated in el-Fasher “a stain on the conscience of humanity”.
Walled in
The massacre was the last stage of a genocidal process.
The RSF besieged el-Fasher from May 2024 to October 2025, creating berms around the city to act as physical barriers trapping civilians. It shelled the city almost daily and cut off food and medicine. The World Food Programme reported that trade routes into el-Fasher were blocked and captive residents were surviving on animal fodder and food waste.
A doctor who spent almost two years living and working inside a hospital in el-Fasher spoke to MEE about the siege.
“Over time, the hospital became our entire world. We slept there, ate whatever food we could find and spent most of our days and nights caring for patients. For months, many of us barely saw our families,” he said.
“As the siege tightened, keeping the hospital functioning became increasingly difficult. Medical supplies stopped reaching the city, essential medicines ran out, and our equipment gradually broke down. We lost reliable access to electricity and clean water. Even finding enough food for ourselves became a daily struggle.”
Generators could only be run for two hours at night. Life-threatening emergency operations were carried out using mobile phone flashlights. Antibiotics ran out. Surgical gauze was unavailable.
“We had to improvise constantly, knowing that every compromise carried risks for our patients,” the doctor said. “Pregnant women arrived after travelling through dangerous roads, often in critical condition. We treated premature babies who depended on equipment we struggled to keep running,” he told MEE.
“Children suffering from malnutrition and civilians wounded by shelling, as well as people with chronic diseases, were also losing access to the regular treatment they needed.
“What made everything worse was that we were experiencing the same conditions as our patients. Some colleagues became severely malnourished. Others continued working while sick or injured. We were exhausted, but there were still people waiting for treatment,” the doctor said.
“One of the most painful experiences for a doctor is watching a patient deteriorate when you know exactly what treatment they need but have no way of providing it. That happened far too often in el-Fasher.”
The cover-up
The RSF punished anyone who tried to break the blockade. Young people and traders who brought food past the berm told Human Rights Watch about deadly RSF attacks on those runs.
Survivors spoke about the execution of people caught with supplies. During that period, a young woman, Qisma Ali Omar, was hung by her arms from a tree with her feet bound and videotaped for the world to see.
When the city fell on 26 October last year, the RSF went first to the places where civilians had taken refuge. Close to 500 people were killed at the Saudi Maternity Hospital, where patients and medical staff were sheltering alongside displaced families, mostly women and children.
UN investigators later documented mass killings at el-Fasher University and the Saudi Hospital, on the roads out of the city and at the berms built to trap its people.
Amnesty verified videos of an RSF commander executing civilian captives. Other footage showed dozens of dead civilians in a trench that ran along the berm. The RSF spent months building the walls that became the edge of a mass grave.
Then came the cover-up.
Between 26 October and 28 November 2025, Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab identified 150 clusters of objects consistent with human remains. Twenty showed signs of burning. Fifty-seven disappeared completely within four weeks. At the Saudi Hospital, satellites captured a pit of what appeared to be bodies burned again and again through November.
A pile of suspected bodies beside the berm was later cleared away. The RSF tried to erase the evidence. Its leader, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, better known as Hemedti, announced an investigation into what he called violations committed by his soldiers during the capture of el-Fasher.
Life under occupation
El-Fasher today is a city of ruins and captives.
When a UN team finally entered in December, under close supervision, it called the city a crime scene and found few people left. One in six of those screened had severe acute malnutrition.
Those who escaped did not escape the RSF. Survivors say the group still detains men fleeing el-Fasher and demands ransoms of up to $3,000. One monitoring group documented the detention of nearly 68,000 civilians. Tawila, once a small town, now hosts around 800,000 displaced people, most of them from el-Fasher.
Khadijah is one of them. Her journey traces the RSF's path across Darfur. “I'm an elderly woman from el-Geneina,” she told MEE, referring to the city in West Darfur, where the dead were also left lying in the streets as the RSF took over in the summer of 2023.
“I fled to el-Fasher seeking safety. But conflict followed, forcing me to displacement again. Now, I live under a tree on a farm, exposed to the elements. There is little food here, and I have no shelter. The cold is unbearable. I'm struggling to survive.”
Mudathir Mohammed Diqourni, of an el-Fasher resistance committee, warned that RSF militias are destroying farms across South and Central Darfur.
“They are also deliberately targeting farmers, shooting and killing them as they head to their farms or attempt to protect their crops and agricultural properties,” he said.
Hunger is pushing villagers toward Tawila in search of relief. Diqourni calls this demographic engineering, an effort to drive the last residents of rural Darfur into camps or across the border “through a policy of systematic impoverishment and starvation”.
Its most haunting image is of farmers “racing against the Janjaweed's camels in the fields” to save scraps of fodder for their own animals.
Arms networks
From el-Fasher, the RSF carried the war back east into Kordofan, and south to the Ethiopian border.
The paramilitary does not arm itself. The UN’s fact-finding mission has found reasonable grounds to believe that private companies and recruiters operating from the UAE have routed supplies through Chad and southeastern Libya, as well as Bosaso in Somalia.
MEE has reported extensively on this supply network and on the use of army bases in Ethiopia to assist the RSF.
These routes were used, Mona Rishmawi, a member of the UN’s mission, said, to provide “weapons, drone-related equipment, logistical assistance and personnel… to commit the atrocities in el-Fasher.”
The US remains the UAE’s top source of weapons.
In May 2025, the Trump administration pushed $1.4bn in Chinook helicopters and F-16 parts to Abu Dhabi despite a congressional hold. In March this year, it approved more than $8bn in new weapons, drones and missiles, with billions more in sales that never had to go before Congress.
British weaponry has been found on battlefields in Sudan and the UK government has been accused of failing to stop the el-Fasher massacre because it feared the UAE.
In Bara, the volunteers are still digging. Khadijah still sleeps under a tree on a farm. The UN has named the network that armed their killers, and Washington has named the genocide.
“In Tawila every day, I see people around me getting weaker,” Hanin told MEE.
“People who were laughing and talking just days ago become too weak to stand. Sometimes, I wake up and learn that someone has died because they had nothing to eat.”
Hala said: “El-Fasher has completely changed. We have now reached a point where, if you want to visit your own home, you need permission from the RSF. That alone shows the situation we have reached. We just hope the war ends and things get better.”

Report: Hezbollah rebuilds drone arsenal with Iranian cash, braces for renewed war with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:53:49 UTC
00:53:49 KST

Lebanese security officials familiar with Hezbollah's activities say the terrorist group has spent the past three months preparing for a possible resumption of fighting with Israel, following a substantial infusion of Iranian funding. Despite suffering heavy losses in successive wars with Israel, Hezbollah remains committed to fighting and has used the lull in hostilities since June to rearm, focusing on acquiring explosives and producing attack drones capable of striking Israeli positions.
One Lebanese security source and another person close to Hezbollah told Reuters that the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to strengthen its military capabilities. The funding comes in addition to approximately $200 million transferred from Tehran to assist displaced families in Hezbollah's Shiite strongholds, as Reuters reported earlier this month.
According to the sources, Hezbollah is also working to restore command-and-control structures disrupted during major battles with Israel. The group's media office rejected claims that its command systems had collapsed, arguing that Israel's occupation of Lebanese territory made resistance a legitimate right.
The IDF declined to comment, while Iran's permanent mission to the United Nations in Geneva did not respond to Reuters' questions. A U.S. State Department spokesperson said Washington would continue restricting Hezbollah's finances through sanctions and other measures, while a Treasury Department spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to transfer it.
Hezbollah on alert for renewed fighting
Hezbollah remains on alert for a possible escalation between the United States and Iran that could reignite fighting in Lebanon. However, Lebanese security sources said the group has yet to fully replenish its weapons stockpiles or restore its fighting force.
The organization acknowledged this month that explosives seized by Lebanese authorities belonged to Hezbollah and were intended for use against Israel. A Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters the materials were specifically intended for explosive-laden drones.
Hezbollah also faces the challenge of rebuilding its command capabilities following losses on key fronts, including the southern Lebanese town of Bint Jbeil and the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge. Lebanese security officials said the group's tactics, which relied on small combat units and rationed anti-tank rockets, left some fighters isolated and struggling against Israel's remotely operated weapons, including armed drones and remote-controlled military vehicles.
The IDF told Reuters it uses remotely operated systems to monitor southern Lebanon and reduce the exposure of its troops to threats. Hezbollah has not explicitly stated whether it would join a renewed conflict involving Iran, but its media office said the group was careful not to provide Israel with justification for further escalation, particularly because of concerns that its supporters could once again be displaced from their homes.
