‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:51:18 UTC
00:51:18 KST

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return to Brazil after winning a historic fourth term in power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro.
“This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.
A few hours earlier, Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from a first-round defeat in early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff.
“Today is a historic day,” Lula declared, before telling a sea of elated supporters: “Democracy always, dictatorship never again. Democracy always, fascism never again.”
Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.
But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo and cities all across Brazil. He won with 64.2m votes to Bolsonaro’s 59.8m, a 51.79% to 48.21% victory. It was at least 10m more votes than Lula secured in the first round.
While Bolsonaro initially refused to concede, his party acknowledged the election results on Monday, nearly a full day after Lula’s win.
“We recognize the presidential election results,” the Liberal party head, Valdemar Costa Neto, said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.“
Lula’s health minister, Alexandre Padilha, told the Guardian shortly after the result was confirmed: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defence of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme-right candidate entailed.
“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha said at the hotel where the president’s team was following the count in São Paulo.
Bolsonaro rejected the result, following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.
The US administration had been rooting for a Bolsonaro victory that would have seen the pro-Donald Trump so-called “orange wave” continue its sweep across the region into Latin America’s largest democracy. Trump took almost 24 hours to comment and, on Monday, appeared to endorse Bolsonaro’s claim when asked about Brazil’s election.
“It looked terrible to me. I thought it was a terrible look. I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election, frankly,” the US president said.
When asked if he intended to do anything in response, Trump said: “Well, I’m not running Brazil. I’m running the USA. And I just thought that the election was – I like Lula. I get along with him very well. I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated. The extension given was very strange.”
Other leaders and governments from across the political spectrum were quicker to recognise Lula’s victory. Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum, tweeted: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, wrote: “The global progressive resurgence has just begun.”
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called Lula’s victory “a historic win for the global progressive movement” and said his government looked forward to continuing to collaborate on “shared values of democracy, social justice and climate action”.
Rightwing South American leaders also recognised Lula’s victory, with Chile’s president, José Antonio Kast, calling Lula to offer congratulations and Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, saluting “the Brazilian people for this democratic day”.
Even Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella – who had publicly backed Bolsonaro and appeared in a recent live broadcast with him on social media – acknowledged Lula’s win, tweeting: “When the people decide at the ballot box, their will is respected because it is sacred. That’s what democracy is all about!”
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.”
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said: “China respects the choice of the Brazilian people.”
Besides Trump, one of the few powerful international voices of dissent was Elon Musk, who claimed the “math doesn’t add up” for Lula’s comeback, ignoring the fact that it did because of the historically low level of abstention in the second round.
In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the US had been accused of seeking to influence the result through a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure. Erika Hilton, a transgender lawmaker who recently became the most voted-for woman in Brazil’s congress, said those efforts had failed. “We have defeated the interference of the US government, which thought it could turn our country into its back yard. Brazil and the Brazilians are too gigantic to be anybody’s back yard,” she said.
Lula’s victory will also have profound consequences for the environment and the Amazon rainforest in what is the world’s most biodiverse nation. On the eve of the vote, the former environment minister Marina Silva had warned that Bolsonaro, if elected, would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rainforest destruction started by his father, whose 2019-22 administration coincided with a surge in deforestation.
On Sunday night, Silva was in a buoyant mood, telling the Guardian: “My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people.”
She said: “The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations.”
For Flávio Bolsonaro, the future looks bleak. As the scale of Lula’s victory became clear on Sunday night, the mood at the Brasília mansion where Bolsonaro was watching the count soured, with what had initially resembled a lively birthday party turning into something closer to a wake. Like football supporters heading for the exits midway through the second half because their team was being thrashed, crestfallen guests began heading home.
One of them approached the dozens of journalists waiting for Bolsonaro’s speech to shout that it was the “north-east’s fault”, insulting the region where Lula has historically won most of his votes.
One photograph circulated by Lula supporters showed a dejected Bolsonaro in tears, although it had been taken on the eve of the vote. Another image showed a red-faced Bolsonaro flanked by visibly mortified allies as they came to terms with their defeat. São Paulo’s pro-Bolsonaro governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, sat next to him covering his face with his hand.
On Paulista Avenue, where huge crowds had gathered to hear Lula speak, one reveller wore a costume of Flávio Bolsonaro behind bars. Some suspect the senator is likely to flee the country to the US once his term runs out in February and he loses parliamentary immunity. Bolsonaro is facing a series of federal police investigations over suspected misdeeds including money laundering, although he maintains he is innocent.
Lula supporters delighted in the idea that the far-right politician may soon join his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his coup attempt, in jail.
“Oh, how awful! Poor little thing!” João Maluf, a 27-year-old psychologist, shouted sarcastically as he held up his mobile phone to the crowd to show them a photograph of a visibly distraught Bolsonaro. “We want rid of these fucking Bolsonaros,” Maluf said.

Digital Communications and Video Frequency Selection: TAF Industries Unveils Upgraded Kolibri 13” FR1 Repeater Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:50:34 UTC
00:50:34 KST

Ukrainian company TAF Industries has released an upgraded version of the Kolibri 13″ FR1 relay carrier.
Viktor Tymoshenko, the company’s Brand Manager, told Militarnyi more about the modifications during the Future Forces Forum in the Czech Republic.
The main change is switching to digital communication between the operator and the carrier. Control commands and video transmission from the carrier now use a single digital channel. This improves the safety of the carrier’s crew, as the digital video feed cannot be intercepted to determine the pilots’ location.
The upgrades also include changes to the signal relay system for strike drones. The module transmits control commands to FPV drones during combat missions.
The repeater is available in several configurations with different video communication frequency bands for long and short ranges. These include the 6000–7200 MHz and 7000–8000 MHz bands for long ranges.
The link between the relay and the strike drone is analog. However, the developers are already working on a fully digital version.
“To receive video from the strike drone, a horn antenna is installed in the nose of the carrier. Its advantage is that it effectively filters out external radio noise, allowing it to receive a clean video signal,” Viktor Tymoshenko shared.
The carrier has a modular design, with the repeater installed as a separate unit.
The military selects the required frequency configuration when placing an order. The upgraded platform has already been codified, making it eligible for purchase using e-Points.
However, demand for the upgraded Kolibri 13″ FR1 is currently high, with orders booked two months in advance.
“This is the result of continuous iterations in collaboration with the military. They tell us what they need, we develop a product that we believe will meet those needs, test it together, and make adjustments,” the company representative concluded.
In July, The Fourth Law and TAF Industries codified the Kolibri 10″ Advance FPV drone with Level 1 autonomy.

EXPLAINER - Serbia's students won the election, but who will govern?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:50:14 UTC
00:50:14 KST

A student-led movement that emerged after a deadly railway station collapse has won Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, challenging the political camp led by President Aleksandar Vucic, which has been in power for more than a decade.
Vucic conceded defeat following Sunday’s snap election, putting the Student List, a slate of candidates selected by student assemblies, on course to form the next government.
The movement has brought together academics, doctors, artists, farmers and activists under a campaign promising to tackle corruption and restore public trust in state institutions.
But while students organized the campaign and selected its candidates, none stood for parliament themselves.
And despite its electoral victory, the movement has yet to announce who will lead the next government.
The protests erupted after a concrete canopy collapsed at Novi Sad railway station on Nov. 1, 2024, ultimately killing 16 people.
The disaster, at a recently renovated station, sparked accusations of corruption, poor oversight, and failures in public procurement.
Tensions escalated after students and lecturers holding a vigil in Belgrade were attacked weeks later.
Four days later, students at the Faculty of Dramatic Arts began a blockade, demanding accountability for the attacks. Other universities soon joined.
The students organized through plenums, assemblies where participants debated and voted on decisions, rather than appointing a single leader.
Their initial demands included the release of documents relating to the station's reconstruction, prosecution of those who attacked protesters, dismissal of charges against detained students and increased university funding.
The movement soon spread beyond campuses, drawing support from teachers, farmers, professionals and other citizens.
Months of demonstrations contributed to the resignation of Prime Minister Milos Vucevic in January 2025, although the protests continued after Djuro Macut formed a new government in April.
One of the largest demonstrations took place in Belgrade on March 15, 2025, drawing an estimated 275,000 to 325,000 people, according to the independent Archive of Public Gatherings, and between 88,000 and 107,000, according to official estimates.
The movement also had support beyond those attending rallies. A CRTA survey published in January 2025 found that 61% of respondents supported the protests and blockades, including some people closer to governing parties.
By May 2025, students were demanding early parliamentary elections.
Rather than establish a conventional political party, the movement formed a citizens' group and selected candidates through more than a year of assemblies, discussions and collective work.
Its electoral slate, known as "Student List - Students Win," featured 250 candidates from different professions and regions.
Students themselves were excluded from the list, as were former members of governing coalition parties and former officials of parliamentary opposition parties. The candidates include doctors, university staff, artists, entrepreneurs and activists from different parts of Serbia.
The campaign relied heavily on volunteers traveling across Serbia, meeting voters and presenting the election as an opportunity to challenge entrenched political power.
With almost 99% of votes counted, the Student List had secured 52.7% of the vote, compared with 39.2% for the alliance led by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party, according to preliminary election commission figures. That would give the Student List 139 seats in the 250-member parliament.
The Student List has not publicly named a candidate for prime minister.
However, two prominent figures have attracted the most attention: cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, who heads the parliamentary list, and former central bank governor Dejan Soskic.
Srdanovic is a professor at the University of Novi Sad's Faculty of Medicine and has worked at the Institute for Cardiovascular Diseases of Vojvodina since 1997.
A prominent supporter of the protests, he has advocated improvements to Serbia's healthcare system, particularly primary and secondary care.
During the campaign, he emphasized direct engagement with voters. Following the election, he also called for better relations with neighboring countries and the international community.
Soskic, an economics professor at the University of Belgrade, served as governor of the National Bank of Serbia from 2010 to 2012.
He resigned after proposed legislative changes that he argued threatened the central bank's independence.
His economic background has made him a prominent figure in discussions about the direction of a future government.
Vucic claimed during the campaign that Soskic was the students' preferred candidate for prime minister, but the movement has not confirmed that.
Radomir Saicic, another candidate, has said lawmakers would decide on a prime minister in consultation with the student movement.
The Student List brings together figures from academia, sports, culture and grassroots activism.
Dejan Bodiroga, a former basketball star and current Euroleague Basketball president, is among its most recognizable names.
A three-time EuroLeague champion who played for clubs including Real Madrid, Barcelona and Panathinaikos, Bodiroga is 24th on the list.
Saicic, ranked 91st, is a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade and a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts.
An outspoken supporter of the protests, he has also criticized the authorities' handling of Kosovo.
Sociologist Jovo Bakic, 76th on the list, is known for his criticism of Vucic's administration.
A professor at the University of Belgrade, Bakic has researched nationalism, political sociology and Europe's far right.
After Vucic conceded, Bakic told N1 that he had expected a decisive student victory but had not expected Vucic to acknowledge defeat. He called for action against organized crime.
Farmer Zlatko Kokanovic, 17th on the list, is a leading opponent of Rio Tinto's proposed Jadar lithium and boron mining project.
He has pledged to seek a permanent ban on lithium and boron exploration and extraction, bringing environmental concerns into the movement's political agenda.
Playwright Zeljko Hubac, third on the list, and actor Tihomir Stanic, eighth, are also prominent figures from the cultural sphere.
Hubac helped establish the citizens' group through which the movement contested the election, while Stanic publicly supported its campaign.
Other candidates include Mirjana Nikolic, rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade, civil engineering academic Sanja Fric, geological engineer Zoran Djajic and lawyer Sarah El Sarag.
Their varied backgrounds reflect the movement's attempt to build a political alternative far beyond Serbia's established parties.
The Student List's 11-point program focuses on fighting corruption, strengthening institutions and improving living standards.
Its proposals include protecting courts and prosecutors from political interference, investigating officials' assets and confiscating illegally acquired property.
It also promises greater transparency in public procurement, audits of infrastructure projects and reforms to public broadcasters and media regulators.
Appointments to state-owned enterprises would be based on professional qualifications rather than political connections, the plan adds.
The program also includes free school textbooks, affordable housing, greater support for farmers and domestic businesses, and improved access to medicines and healthcare in rural areas.
On employment, it proposes reducing the maximum duration of fixed-term contracts from 24 to 12 months.
Many of these pledges address grievances that fueled the protests, particularly corruption, weak institutions and declining trust in public services.
Winning the election does not automatically give the Student List control of the government.
Under Serbia's Constitution, the president nominates a prime minister after consulting representatives of the parties and lists elected to parliament.
The nominee then presents a proposed Cabinet and government program to the 250-member National Assembly. At least 126 lawmakers must vote in favor for the government to take office.
Election-night projections suggested the Student List had secured enough seats to reach that threshold on its own, although the final allocation depends on certified results.
The new parliament must convene within 30 days of the official declaration of results. If lawmakers fail to elect a government within 90 days of the assembly's formation, parliament is dissolved.
The process is complicated by Vucic's resignation as president on Sept. 27 to pursue the premiership.
Parliamentary Speaker Ana Brnabic, a close Vucic ally, is serving as acting president pending a separate presidential election due before the end of the year.
The Student List’s parliamentary victory now puts the movement in a strong position to challenge Vucic’s camp for the presidency as well.

US to host G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta this weekend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Diyar Guldogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
By Diyar Guldogan
WASHINGTON (AA) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Atlanta, Georgia, on Friday to host a two-day G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, where diplomats from the world’s leading economies will discuss shared economic and security challenges, the State Department said Monday.
The meeting is part of Trump’s administration’s effort to refocus the G20 on economic growth, economic security, and policies intended to deliver results for Americans, the department said in a statement.
Rubio will convene the top diplomats to advance practical cooperation on issues affecting the global economy, it said.
"As a global hub of diplomacy, connectivity, and commerce, Atlanta offers the perfect backdrop for these discussions," it said of the Southern US city.
The US plans to use the meeting to address geopolitical crises that contribute to economic instability, including threats to freedom of navigation, energy and food security, and global supply chains, said the statement.
The talks are also expected to help establish priorities ahead of December’s G20 leaders’ summit, where heads of government meeting in Miami, Florida will address broader economic issues.

Cabinet under pressure from both sides as budget talks resume
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:47:19 UTC
00:47:19 KST

Cabinet under pressure from both sides as budget talks resume
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet is resuming talks with seven opposition parties this week as it tries to secure the votes it needs to steer its budget for next year through parliament.
Prime minister Rob Jetten and finance minister Eelco Heinen still hope they can win support from both sides for a broad deal, despite warnings from party leaders that their demands are irreconcilable.
The largest opposition party, the left-wing Pro, is calling for the coalition parties to scrap plans to raise income tax to fill the gap created after it abandoned its welfare cuts, under pressure from Pro and the trade unions.
Pro and the pro-European party Volt say the money should be raised instead through higher taxes on savings and investments, but Heinen’s party, the liberal-conservative VVD, want to replace the wealth tax system with a capital gains tax.
The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA needs the support of at least two opposition parties to secure its legislation through parliament.
Pro and Volt have enough seats in the two houses of parliament to guarantee a majority, but the VVD fear that making too many concessions on the left will damage their already precarious standing in the opinion polls.
Asylum and nitrogen
Many VVD voters were dismayed by Heinen’s proposed reforms to the “box 3” wealth tax, which would have led to people with modest investment portfolios paying more, prompting the finance minister to go back to the drawing board.
Opposition parties on the right, such as JA21, are pressing the cabinet to tighten the rules on asylum further as the price for their support.
JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans wants the status of all 70,000 Syrian refugees in the Netherlands to be reviewed and asylum claims to be processed outside the EU. The party also wants to water down the so-called “spreading law” so that the government in The Hague cannot force municipalities to take in minimum numbers of asylum seekers.
Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen is also expected to take part in the talks, suggesting the cabinet is prepared to compromise on its plans to cut nitrogen pollution, even though Pro has warned the reforms “must not be weakened”.
Another pivotal issue is likely to be the proposed surrogacy law, which the orthodox Protestant party SGP wants the cabinet to withdraw.
The bill was put in the spotlight last week when Jetten and his partner Nicolás Keenan announced they were having a baby next year with the help of a surrogate mother.
At the moment there is no law regulating surrogacy in the Netherlands. Couples who make their own arrangements must have the child adopted before they are legally recognised as parents.
The SGP have said they will not support the cabinet unless it withdraws a bill that would recognise the rights of parents who have children born through surrogacy immediately.
The party also wants the government to intervene to stop hospitals offering to perform abortions after 22 weeks without a compelling medical reason.

Israel committing crimes against humanity in occupied West Bank: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:44:59 UTC
00:44:59 KST

UN panel accuses Israel of ‘extermination’ in West Bank, genocide in Gaza
Report finds extermination, torture and rape in the West Bank and says genocide in Gaza is continuing despite a ceasefire.
A United Nations commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, torture and rape, while also continuing “to commit genocide in Gaza” despite a ceasefire brokered by the United States.
The report, published on Monday by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, examined killings and physical and mental harm inflicted by state actors from October 7, 2023, through September of this year.
It was released the day before Israel’s general election.
The commission found that the situation in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, had “deteriorated gravely” since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
It said Israeli military operations, reinforced by sustained violence by settlers, amounted to a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians, and that Israeli authorities “intended to collectively punish” residents of the occupied West Bank for the Hamas-led attack on Israel.
“The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core,” the report said.
Extermination
The commission also found a sharp rise in deaths from air strikes in the territory.
Six Palestinians were killed in air attacks in the occupied West Bank from 2008 to October 6, 2023, it said, compared with 254 from October 7, 2023, to September 30, 2026.
“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unlivable,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, the commission’s chair.
“Meanwhile, Israel’s expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross” the so-called Yellow Line that demarcates Israeli-controlled areas in the enclave, he said.
Israel’s mission in Geneva called the report part of the commission’s “misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal”.
“The international community must reject these distortions, repudiate the commission’s findings and demand its immediate dissolution,” the mission said in a statement.
Continued genocide
The commission, which does not speak for the UN as a whole, first concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza during the war that followed the October 7 attacks. Israel has flatly rejected the UN commission’s finding.
In its new report, the commission said Israeli forces had continued to commit “genocidal acts” against Palestinians in Gaza despite the ceasefire brokered by the US last October, with attacks intended to “destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part”.
At least five Palestinians, including a seven-year-old girl, were killed in Israeli air attacks across Gaza on Monday, according to medical officials there. The Gaza Health Ministry says at least 74,500 people have been killed in the genocidal war, which has displaced nearly all of the territory’s population.
The report also examined abuses by Palestinian security forces. It found that the Palestinian Authority had targeted people who voiced dissent, and that the killing and wounding of journalists and human rights defenders had steadily narrowed space for civil society.
The three-member commission was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021.
Navi Pillay, a former South African High Court judge who led it until last November, won the Nobel Peace Prize this month.
West Bank lockdown
The report was released as Israeli forces carried out a crackdown in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron after a shooting near the city last week. Israel imposed a lockdown on Hebron on Friday, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans to extend it across the entire West Bank.
Later on Monday, Volker Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights, condemned the Hebron operation. He said threats to empty and erase neighbourhoods raised “serious concerns of ethnic cleansing”.
According to Turk, the lockdown had already forcibly displaced more than 2,000 Palestinians, led to the demolition of homes and prevented residents from moving freely.
“The sweeping steps taken raise grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force – which must end,” he said.
“The Israeli lockdown is confining many to their homes and their immediate neighbourhoods. Declarations by senior Israeli government officials indicate that the measures implemented are punitive in nature and designed to instil fear. This is unacceptable,” Turk added.
Some Israeli ministers have previously called for the occupied West Bank and Gaza to be ethnically cleansed.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told Ynet News last month that Israel should “go to war” in the occupied territory and repeat what it “did in Gaza”. He added that Israeli forces had “cleared out” Palestinian refugee camps in the occupied West Bank.
Turk insisted that people displaced under the clampdown must be allowed to return home and that “Israel must ensure compensation and reparation for unlawful evictions and demolitions”.
“Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law,” he said.

Quebec beats Switzerland in improv world finals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:44:16 UTC
00:44:16 KST

Quebec beats Switzerland in improv world finals
On Saturday in Geneva, Quebec won the World Improvisation Theatre Championship, beating Switzerland in the final at the Bâtiment des Forces Motrices (BFM). The competition, which brought together five French-speaking teams, attracted more than 4,600 spectators over ten days for 11 matches.
Thirty amateur players from Switzerland, Quebec, France, Belgium and Algeria took part in this year’s tournament, the organisers said. The qualifying matches were held at the Salle Centrale de la Madeleine, in the centre of Geneva, ahead of the final at the BFM.
Switzerland had hoped to secure a third title in this competition, which was established in 1991. In the end, however, they were defeated in the final by Quebec, which has thus cemented its place amongst the tournament’s most successful nations.
Belgium still on top
Described by its organisers as the world’s oldest theatrical improvisation tournament, the championship rotates between several French-speaking countries and returns to Geneva every four years. Belgium, France, Quebec and Switzerland take turns to host it.
More
Monumental sadness: Geneva theatre takes on DRC-Glencore injustice
Belgium remains top of the all-time winners’ list with 12 victories, but Quebec is now closing in with 11 titles. Switzerland, this year’s runner-up, has two titles to its name, won in 2006 and 2016.
The concept of the improvisation match originated in Quebec in 1977, borrowing some of its rules from ice hockey. Two teams compete by inventing stories on the spot based on themes that are revealed at the last moment.
However, this highly structured format is no longer the only one to grace the stage. The art form has diversified significantly, with full-length formats, improvised musicals and improv wrestling. There is just one constant: no script is written in advance.

Taiwan-Vatican Ties: The Dynamic Interplay Under Pope Leo XIV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:44:00 UTC
00:44:00 KST

Pope Leo XIV succeeded Pope Francis in May 2025, becoming the 267th Pontiff of the global Catholic Church. According to academic and media analyses, Pope Leo XIV’s diplomatic strategy continues Pope Francis’ approach of “engagement” and “openness,” placing a particular emphasis on “peace” and the “de-escalation of potential armed conflicts.”
For Taiwan, the most closely watched diplomatic development during Pope Francis’ tenure was the 2018 provisional agreement on appointing bishops, signed between the Holy See and the People’s Republic of China (PRC). This agreement led the Chinese government to formally recognize the Pope as the Catholic Church’s supreme religious leader, facilitating the joint appointment of multiple bishops by Beijing and the Vatican under its framework. Since taking office, Pope Leo XIV has not altered the Sino-Vatican agreement; instead, he has accelerated the bishop-appointment process, ushering in a “rejuvenated” roster of Chinese bishops.
The Holy See remains the Republic of China (Taiwan)’s sole diplomatic ally in Europe. Since 2000, public discourse has frequently debated whether the Holy See might sever formal diplomatic ties with Taipei in favor of establishing relations with Beijing. Pope Leo XIV’s continuation of his predecessor’s approach to China implies a further deepening of Sino-Vatican relations. However, from Taiwan’s perspective, society should not underestimate its own standing. In fact, since Pope Leo XIV assumed the papacy, the Pontiff has received numerous Taiwanese organizations and individuals.
Furthermore, Pope Leo XIV has not shied away from being photographed alongside the Taiwan national flag. These gestures show that the Chicago-born Pope is friendly toward Taiwan, understands Taiwan’s significance to the global community, and recognizes the distinct differences between Taiwan and the PRC.
When discussing Taiwan-Vatican relations, the analytical lens must not be restricted solely to the continuation of the Sino-Vatican agreement or ongoing negotiations. Instead, one must examine whether the practical, multifaceted ties between Taiwan and the Holy See have correspondingly deepened. From Taipei’s perspective, the answer is a resounding yes.
From September 23 to 26, 2026, Chen Chien-Jen, former vice president of Taiwan and current president of Academia Sinica, attended the Pontifical Academy of Sciences (PAS) meeting and its biennial plenary session at the Vatican. Chen presided over the seventh session, titled “Medicine, Neuroscience, and Human Well-being.” Following the meeting, Chen and the PAS issued a joint statement titled “The Future of Science in a Changing World,” serving as an action plan for the international scientific community. Through the Holy See’s global platform, Taiwan once again showcased its scientific prowess to the world.
Shortly after, from October 7 to 15, Bishop John Lee Keh-mien, president of the Chinese Regional Bishops’ Conference in Taiwan, along with Professor Chou Te-yu and Consultor Yeh Chia-yen – members of the Holy See’s Dicastery for the Laity, Family and Life – attended a major conference at the Vatican. Hosted by Pope Leo XIV, the event marked the 10th anniversary of Pope Francis’ apostolic exhortation, Amoris Laetitia. The grand-scale conference welcomed 187 invited guests, including 111 presidents of episcopal conferences from around the globe. Taiwan was not only present, but Taiwanese scholars attended in their official capacities as members of the Vatican’s Dicastery, underscoring Taiwan’s deep engagement with the Holy See.
Furthermore, on October 19, Pope Leo XIV appointed new members to the Holy See’s International Theological Commission. Sister Hu Shu-qin, an associate professor at the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine, was appointed as a new member of the Commission for the 2026-2031 term. Sister Hu is the first ethnic Chinese theologian to be appointed to the Commission since Archbishop Savio Hon Tai-Fai, S.D.B., who served from 2004 to 2014. Her long-standing dedication to theological education and academic research in Taiwan has deepened Taiwan’s participation in global Catholic theology, further demonstrating the Vatican’s high regard for theological development in Taiwan.
Immediately following, from October 22 to 24, the Vatican’s Dicastery for Evangelization hosted the “The Church of the Sheaves” international conference in Rome. Under the theme “A Church for All: Synodal in Method, Missionary in Spirit, Credible in Love,” the event gathered over a hundred scholars worldwide. Grounded in the spirit and method of synodality, the conference emphasized mutual listening and sharing, signaling a shift in the Catholic Church’s approach to evangelization from the traditional model of missionaries transmitting and teaching, to local churches sharing and receiving each other’s gifts to enrich one another.
Professor Tan Liang-chen, an assistant professor and well-known public Catholic theologian at the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine, was selected to attend the Rome conference. He brought Taiwan’s voice – and the voice of the Taiwanese Catholic Church – to the West and the Vatican, sharing it with the universal Church.
The relationship between Taiwan and the Holy See is concretely built upon these small yet monumental steps. Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been advancing an “Integrated Diplomacy” strategy, using “Values,” “Alliances,” and “Trade” to expand Taiwan’s friendships – a deeper diplomatic approach increasingly evident in Europe. The good that Taiwan can bring to the world extends beyond high-tech industries like semiconductors and AI; it also includes the vibrant space for religious faith nurtured within Taiwan’s free society.
The stable, deepening relationship between Taiwan and the Holy See is the fruitful result of joint efforts by Taiwanese civil society, the local Catholic Church, and the government. These rich fruits stem from the relentless educational and research dedication of the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine and Fu Jen Catholic University. More importantly, they rely on tireless diplomats on the front lines in Rome and on Ketagalan Boulevard in Taipei. Even when the road ahead is fraught with challenges, they keep working diligently, paving bridges for the present and the future, which is why Taiwan-Vatican ties remain so steadfast.
In the face of shifting Sino-Vatican dynamics, Taiwan has no reason to worry; in the eyes of the Holy See, Taiwan remains an undeniably “precious” presence.

Egyptian parliament authorises military aid for Saudi Arabia

Egyptian parliament authorises military aid for Saudi Arabia
Legislators approve military support amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, but Cairo has ruled out strikes on Yemen.
Egypt’s parliament has authorised President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to provide military support to Saudi Arabia as attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis intensify.
The House of Representatives, chaired by Speaker Hisham Badawi, approved the mandate in a vote on Monday.
A parliamentary statement shared with the Reuters news agency said el-Sisi had been authorised to “undertake necessary” measures to support Saudi Arabia in defending itself, should Riyadh request assistance.
The move raises the possibility of Egypt becoming more directly involved in a conflict which has consumed the Gulf and the Red Sea in recent weeks. It follows Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s international airport and facilities belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, Aramco, disrupting flights and oil exports.
The Houthi armed group that controls Yemen’s capital Sanaa is fighting the Saudi-led coalition, which backs the internationally recognised government.
Fighting has intensified in recent weeks, deepening the humanitarian crisis that has already devastated Yemen.
‘Purely defensive’
Hussein Haridy, an Egyptian former assistant foreign minister, said Cairo’s involvement in the conflict would be limited to defensive action.
“The decision adopted by the Egyptian parliament today, of course, fully authorises the president, in his capacity as the commander in chief of the armed forces, to take any measures that the situation would warrant in order to provide Saudi Arabia with whatever it would need to defend its territory and its infrastructure against any outside attacks,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The mission, from an Egyptian point of view, is purely defensive in the sense it’s not directed at any party in the region, whether a state or a group. So now it’s a precautionary measure.”
El-Sisi had also said on Wednesday that any Egyptian military action would be limited to protecting Saudi territory and borders, rather than launching attacks on Yemen.
Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Cairo continued to favour a diplomatic settlement after visiting Riyadh on Wednesday.
The vote followed closed-door parliamentary discussions and an earlier postponement of the military aid authorisation for Saudi Arabia, which is one of Egypt’s most important economic partners.
Egypt’s constitution requires approval from two-thirds of legislators before troops can be sent abroad on combat missions.
Egypt also has a direct stake in Red Sea security. Houthi attacks near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the key route to and from the Suez Canal, have disrupted shipping and reduced canal revenue.
Egypt joined a previous Saudi-led campaign in Yemen in 2015, largely helping secure shipping routes with naval forces.
Cairo has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
El-Sisi also met United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in Cairo on Monday to discuss regional tensions and peace efforts.
According to Egypt’s presidency, Guterres praised Cairo’s efforts to prevent escalation in the Gulf and said diplomacy could help address disputes over Iran’s nuclear programme and shipping.
In a post on X on Monday, Guterres urged “maximum restraint”, warning that further fighting could spiral out of control.

Saudi Arabia to store oil in Singapore to bolster Asia supply security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:40:02 UTC
00:40:02 KST

SINGAPORE (Reuters) -- Saudi Arabia plans to store crude oil at Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027 to strengthen supply security in the region, energy ministers from both countries said on Monday.
The move comes after the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran severely disrupted energy supplies to Asia shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, prompting countries to draw down inventories and raising concerns about stockpile levels globally. Asia imported two-thirds of its oil supplies from the Middle East before the war.
"Saudi Arabia and Singapore are announcing our joint intent to establish an arrangement for Saudi crude oil to be stored at the Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027," Tan See Leng, minister for energy, trade and industry, told the Singapore International Energy Week conference.
"This arrangement enhances the resilience of the Saudi crude oil supply chain in Southeast Asia, as well as contributes to Singapore's energy security and resilience in the event of supply disruptions."
Tan said Saudi Aramco will sign a memorandum of understanding with the Energy Market Authority and JTC Corp. on Monday and aimed to conclude negotiations in a few months' time.
"Bringing supply closer to key Asian markets would strengthen the flexibility of our supply network and support Singapore's security of supply and preparedness," Saudi Arabian Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al-Saud said in a video recording at the conference.
Located at a depth of 150 meters below the ground, the rock caverns at Jurong Island can store up to 1.47 million cubic meters, or roughly 9 million barrels of liquid hydrocarbons such as crude oil and condensate.
Saudi Aramco currently stores crude in Japan and South Korea, where local governments have priority to buy the supplies in the tanks in the event of an unexpected shortage.
The crude storage capacity in Okinawa was expanded to 8.2 million barrels in September 2017 in an agreement with Japan Oil, Gas and Metals National Corp. (JOGMEC), Aramco Japan said on its website.
In 2023, Aramco inked a deal with Korea National Oil Corp. to store 5.3 million barrels of oil in South Korea's reserve facilities in the port of Ulsan for five years.
Elsewhere, Japan is in talks with Asian countries to boost crude reserves across the region, part of the Partnership in Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia) initiative proposed earlier this year by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi backed by $10 billion in financial support.
While China, Japan and South Korea have built large oil stockpiles, most other Asian countries have less of a buffer in the event of supply shocks.

Iran's Greco-Roman team win 2026 World Championship
TEHRAN – Iran have secured the Greco-Roman team title at the 2026 World Wrestling Championships in Astana, Kazakhstan, following an outstanding performance by their wrestlers on the international stage.
The Iranian squad clinched the championship ahead of the conclusion of the Greco-Roman competitions, underlining the country's dominance in one of its most successful sporting disciplines.
Iran made an impressive start to the tournament, collecting one gold, two silver and one bronze medal in the first four weight categories before securing additional places in the finals.
Gholamreza Farokhi delivered Iran's first gold medal in the 82kg division, defeating Turkey's Yuksel Saricicek 5-1 in the final.
At 55kg, Payam Ahmadi claimed silver after losing 3-1 to Azerbaijan's Eldaniz Azizli in the gold-medal contest.
Ali Ahmadi Vafa also earned silver in the 60kg category, narrowly missing out on gold after being pinned by Japan's Koto Gomi despite holding a 7-1 lead.
Iran's fourth medal came through Ali Oskou in the 77kg division. He secured bronze with a 4-3 victory over Uzbekistan's Nekibov.
The Iranian team's impressive campaign continued as Saeid Esmaeili and Alireza Mohmadi advanced to the finals in the 67kg and 87kg categories, respectively.
Esmaeili defeated Azerbaijan's Hasrat Jafarov in the semifinals, while Mohmadi booked his place in the final with a commanding 10-1 victory over Armenia's Gevorg Tadevosyan.
Danial Sohrabi at 72kg and Fardin Hedayati at 130kg also won two gold medals, while Olympic and world champion Mohammadhadi Saravi seized a bronze medal at 97kg.

Documents
Details
As seen in the Security Defence Review, the Army are at heightened readiness due to a new era of threat. This has placed greater demands on the Defence Training Estate across the UK, which is being used for training more regularly and at shorter notice.
As such, the firing time notifications published on Gov.UK have been standardised to show the daily timings for when live-firing is permitted on the UK DTE. This is a change from the previous method of showing when training bookings had been made in advance.
This to ensure safety of all users, as it is not possible to change Gov.UK notifications at short notice. Broadly, the only guaranteed safe times for access are before or after the firing times provided on this page, however there may be exceptional circumstances where extensions have been requested.
If you wish to use the DTE for recreation, please always refer to onsite safety warning signals to understand if the site is safe to access before doing so.
Your safety
Danger - When warning signals are displayed, regardless of the timings, do not cross the range boundary.
Warning signals are red flags by day and red lamps by night; range boundaries are marked by red and white poles.
Red flags and red lamps indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries.
Do not enter the danger area when in use, this could result in loss of life.
Do not touch any military debris, it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) via 0191 239 4261 or the police.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas

Europe’s voters keep throwing leaders out. Who has the answers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:38:22 UTC
00:38:22 KST

Europe’s voters keep throwing leaders out. Who has the answers?
This past election day did deliver one bombshell: Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections. Hardly anyone seems to have seriously expected that. Calling the election was a gamble, of course, but he still had reason to believe he could pull it off.
The reasons will take time to untangle. Vucic himself spoke of a “revolution” backed by Europe. Others, with some justification, see an “Orban scenario”: accumulated fatigue with one man’s prolonged rule, during which his personal traits and interests came to exert too much influence over national policy.
Clearly, more than one factor was at work. Just as clearly, Serbia is entering a new era. Vucic’s increasingly elaborate and convoluted balancing act will likely give way to an attempt to steer the country sharply toward the European Union. Hungary’s experience is telling in this respect. And Russia should expect little good to come of it.
Serbian society, however, is different from Hungary’s. There really is considerable sympathy for Russia. Whether that sentiment can rally a new opposition, this time against a firmly pro-EU course, should become clear soon enough. The EU will try to make the most of the defeat of yet another set of “pro-Russian forces.” Whether that will bring Serbia any closer to EU membership is another question entirely.
Whatever the outcome, if there is a common thread running through elections across Europe, it is probably this: people in different countries are disillusioned with the status quo and the establishment, whatever its political stripe – even when those establishments stand at opposite ends of the spectrum.

Ilayda Cakirtekin
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Italian President Sergio Mattarella on Monday called for rapid action against "improper and uncontrolled" use of artificial intelligence and warned against manipulation of information with fake news, according to local media.
"We must act swiftly and effectively to prevent the improper and uncontrolled use” of artificial intelligence, Mattarella said at the opening ceremony of the Festival of Regions, ANSA news agency reported.
He stressed the need for establishing and implementing an appropriate regulation.
"Already today, it is evident how the manipulation of information, including through the spread of false news using the capabilities offered by the internet, can influence public opinion and shape its views and choices," Mattarella also said.
He warned against the risk of losing control over technological processes with the development of models through machine learning.
"The need is to put the brakes on an increasingly intense competition among a limited number of players, with outcomes that science is currently unable to predict," Mattarella noted.
"If we limited ourselves to being spectators of the expansion of computing power in every direction, the fundamental values of the centrality of human life and, at the same time, our democracy could be undermined," he further warned.

Israel election: How it works and what it means for Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:35:53 UTC
00:35:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel election 2026 explained as Netanyahu faces key vote
Israeli voters head to the polls on Tuesday in a closely fought election that will determine Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political future and the direction of Israel's policies towards Palestinians.
The vote pits a coalition of opposition parties led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot against the far-right bloc led by Netanyahu, whose opponents accuse him of undermining Israel's democratic institutions.
It is the first Israeli election since the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 and Israel's subsequent genocidal war on Gaza, which has been followed by wider regional conflicts involving Lebanon, Iran and Yemen.
While much of the campaign has focused on Netanyahu's leadership, the war and domestic divisions, the outcome will also affect millions of Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank who have no vote in the election.
Palestinian citizens of Israel, meanwhile, could play a decisive role in determining the balance of power in the Knesset, even as the main Jewish-led political blocs remain reluctant to cooperate with them.
How will the vote work?
Polling stations will open at 7am on Tuesday and close at 10pm.
Major Israeli news organisations will publish exit polls shortly after voting ends, with counting beginning the same evening.
More than three dozen parties are contesting the election, with around 7.4 million people eligible to vote at polling stations across Israel.
Israel uses proportional representation, meaning voters choose a party rather than an individual candidate. The 120 seats in the Knesset are allocated according to each party's share of the national vote.
Candidates enter parliament according to their positions on their party's electoral list.
Parties must win at least 3.25% of the vote to enter the Knesset, equivalent to four seats.
No single party has ever secured an outright majority, meaning Israeli governments have always depended on coalitions.
When will the results be announced?
The official results must be declared by 4 November, although the likely distribution of seats should become clear as early as Wednesday morning.
Attention will then turn to coalition negotiations, with parties seeking to assemble a parliamentary majority of at least 61 seats.
After the official results are announced, President Isaac Herzog will consult parliamentary factions before selecting a Knesset member to attempt to form a government.
These negotiations could take weeks, particularly if neither of the main blocs wins enough seats to govern.
What are the polls saying?
The final opinion polls suggest that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition coalition led by Eisenkot is on course to secure a majority.
Surveys published over the weekend put the opposition on 54 to 56 seats, compared with around 50 for Netanyahu's Likud-led alliance.
Eisenkot's Yashar party was projected to become the largest party with 22 to 23 seats, ahead of Likud on 19 to 21.
The polls also pointed to gains for the far right, with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party projected to win eight seats.
But the remaining seats could prove crucial.
Parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel were projected to win between 14 and 16 seats, potentially leaving them with considerable influence over whether a government can be formed.
Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Palestinian-led parties, leaving questions over how the opposition could secure the parliamentary support it needs.
Could Palestinian voters decide the election?
Palestinian citizens of Israel account for a substantial share of the electorate, but their political representation has long been constrained by divisions between parties, low turnout and the reluctance of major Jewish-led parties to include them in governing coalitions.
This election could nevertheless give their parties considerable influence over whether Netanyahu remains in power.
The two main Arab-majority electoral lists are Ra'am, also known as the United Arab List, and the Joint List, bringing together Hadash, Balad and Ta'al.
Their performance will depend partly on turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes could influence both the number of seats won by Arab-led parties and the overall balance of the Knesset.
In an interview with The New Arab, Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh highlighted the importance of Palestinian voters in an election where neither main bloc appears assured of a majority.
The campaign has also been marked by attempts to exclude Palestinian-led parties and candidates.
Israel's Central Elections Committee voted in September to bar the Joint List and Ra'am from contesting the election, but the Supreme Court overturned the decision.
The court nevertheless upheld the disqualification of Abu Shehadeh over an article in which he described the 7 October attacks as an important historical event.
The episode has renewed questions about the political rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the limits placed on their participation in Israeli politics.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly portrayed the possibility of opposition cooperation with Arab-led parties as a campaign warning, seeking to pressure his rivals into ruling out such an arrangement.
What about Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank?
Millions of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip cannot vote in the election that will help determine the policies governing their lives.
The next Israeli government will have a major influence over military operations, movement restrictions, settlement expansion and the future of Gaza.
In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians face an expanding network of military checkpoints, road closures and settler attacks.
Israel has also announced the closure of land crossings into the West Bank for election day, adding to restrictions that have intensified since October 2023.
In Gaza, the central questions include whether Israel will ease its blockade, withdraw troops from occupied areas, allow displaced Palestinians to return home and permit reconstruction after three years of devastating war.
However, Netanyahu's principal challengers have offered little indication that a change in government would bring a fundamental shift in Israeli policy towards Palestinian statehood or the occupation.
Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state, while other prominent opposition figures have supported Israel's military campaigns and taken hardline positions towards Gaza.
Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, whose party is part of the opposition coalition, has criticised Netanyahu for being too soft on Gaza and called for the Palestinian Authority to be dismantled.
Meanwhile, far-right ministers Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have advocated annexing Palestinian territory and ethnically cleansing the Palestinians.
The election could therefore change Israel's leadership without necessarily bringing major changes to the policies Palestinians face.
What are the main election issues?
Netanyahu's opponents have sought to make the vote a referendum on his leadership, focusing on the security failures surrounding the 7 October attack, his long-running corruption trial and Israel's growing international isolation.
According to the Israel Democracy Institute, the October 2023 attack is expected to play an important role in the voting decisions of more than two-thirds of the electorate.
Other major issues include military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews and Netanyahu's attempts to overhaul the judiciary in 2023, which sparked widespread protests.
The election also comes after years of Israeli military operations in Gaza and regional conflicts involving Hezbollah, Iran and the Houthis.
Yet there is considerable overlap between the main Jewish-led parties on questions relating to Palestinian rights, the occupation and Israel's military operations.
While opposition politicians have criticised Netanyahu's handling of the wars and the diplomatic damage caused by his government, few have advocated a fundamental reversal of settlement expansion or a renewed peace process leading to Palestinian statehood.
The most explicit calls for annexation and Palestinian displacement have come from the far right, particularly Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
What happens if coalition talks fail?
If neither bloc can assemble 61 seats, Israel could face prolonged negotiations over a possible minority government or another election.
A minority government would need support or abstentions from parties outside the governing coalition to survive key parliamentary votes.
That could make Palestinian-led parties particularly important, even if they are excluded from formal coalition agreements.
If negotiations fail altogether, another election could be called in 2027, with Netanyahu potentially remaining as caretaker prime minister until a new government takes office.
The result could therefore leave Israel facing continued political deadlock, with Palestinian parties holding potentially important seats but little guarantee of a role in government.
For Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, the immediate consequences will depend less on which party wins the most seats than on the policies the next government adopts towards the occupation, military operations, settlements and displacement.

Nearly 30,000 excess cancer cases linked to inequalities across EU countries: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:35:27 UTC
00:35:27 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The incidence of nearly 30,000 additional cases of lung and cervical cancer was estimated across EU countries in 2024 due to disparities in cancer incidence rates, with some countries seeing rates more than seven times higher than others, according to a study presented Monday.
The findings were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress in Madrid by Italian epidemiologist Diego Serraino, the ANSA news agency reported.
Based on European Cancer Information System estimates, the study identified 29,412 excess cases in countries where incidence exceeded the EU average.
For lung cancer among men, incidence ranged from 38 cases per 100,000 people in Sweden to 130 in Hungary, with 11,105 excess cases seen across 12 countries.
Among women, Denmark saw 83 lung cancer cases per 100,000 compared with 20 in Lithuania, contributing to 13,441 excess cases across 11 countries.
Cervical cancer showed even greater disparities, with Romania seeing 36 cases per 100,000 women compared with just five on the island nation of Malta.
Of the 4,866 excess cervical cancer cases identified across 10 countries, Romania accounted for 2,475.
Researchers emphasized stronger anti-smoking measures to reduce lung cancer risks, alongside human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, and regular screening to prevent cervical cancer and detect precancerous lesions early.

Helsing Developed the Contra Autonomous AI-Controlled Air Defense System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:34:34 UTC
00:34:34 KST

Helsing has developed the Contra autonomous AI-controlled air defense system, which independently controls interceptors.
Militarnyi reported this based on the company’s presentation, which took place at its new office in Berlin.
Contra enables the simultaneous detection and engagement of hundreds or thousands of air targets—including drones and missiles. To do this, the system integrates sensor and weapons data into a unified air picture and autonomously decides on target interception while maintaining human oversight.
The system was designed from the outset to integrate third-party equipment. Specifically, this includes other interceptors, laser systems for countering UAVs, anti-drone cannons, and net-based interception systems.
“Contra is capable of defending against massive attacks, missiles, and the latest generation of attack drones. It is a single system for various tasks, independent of the type of equipment,” the company states.
As part of the Contra project, Helsing has developed two high-speed interceptors: the AD-1 Inferno, powered by a jet engine, and the AD-2 Ambush, powered by a solid-fuel rocket engine.
“They are designed to outperform even the fastest threats posed by jet-powered drones and cruise missiles in terms of speed and effectiveness,” the company says.
Helsing has already signed a contract to supply Contra, while the AD-1 and AD-2 interceptors are currently undergoing testing.
Contra is powered by Altra—Helsing’s military artificial intelligence, command, and control platform.
Altra integrates data from radar, electro-optical, infrared, and acoustic sensors from various manufacturers via open, published interfaces. The platform also enables interoperability with the SitaWare system and national combat management systems.
Contra is designed to operate even under conditions of electronic warfare, loss of communication channels, and failure of individual system components.
The AD-1 is a jet-powered interceptor designed to fill gaps in defense capabilities. It is intended for situations where threats outmatch electric interceptors in flight performance and traditional missile systems are too expensive for widespread use.
The Inferno launches immediately upon target detection and receives guidance commands during the cruise phase from the Contra system’s ground-based radar stations.
The interceptor can remain airborne for extended periods in standby mode, operate as part of a swarm, and re-engage targets in flight.
The AD-1 is designed for mass production in Europe under European control. According to the developers’ concept, it is intended to provide a more favorable cost-to-effect ratio for the defending side in terms of weapons and interception capabilities. The AD-1 integrates into the Contra system at the basic architecture level.
The AD-2 is an interceptor equipped with a solid-fuel rocket engine, designed to rapidly intercept targets in the upper threat range.
It can destroy high-speed, single-use strike drones flying at high altitudes, as well as subsonic cruise missiles beyond the AD-1’s range.
The Ambush is designed for mass production. This enables defense forces to maintain intensive interception of large numbers of targets without relying on a single production line.
The AD-2 integrates with Contra at the system’s basic architecture level and receives guidance commands during the cruise phase from Contra’s ground-based radar stations.
Most affordable homing heads use electro-optical (EO) or infrared (IR) cameras.
Electro-optical cameras are unable to reliably track targets in the dark, and both types of cameras may perform poorly in cloudy or foggy weather.
According to the developers, the AD-1 and AD-2 radar homing heads overcome these limitations. They are also built with standard, commercially available components.
AI optimizes the interceptor’s flight path to maximize the probability of a successful hit.

Kyiv • UNN

Details

This disrupts the enemy’s communications and troop control

Mecca pact countries in Iran in bid to stop war restarting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:33:13 UTC
00:33:13 KST

- Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in Tehran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from resuming.
- Parliament authorised Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia to defend itself - a move that could push Cairo more directly into the conflict between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
- The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.
- A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Monday.
Israel prepares to vote as Netanyahu faces a tight fight
Campaigning and ballot preparations mark the lead-up to Israel’s election Tuesday, widely seen as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins, after Trump said they should "finish the job".
"US President Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president. And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again," Netanyahu said in a televised appearance late on Sunday night.
"He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me."
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Monday that a vessel was on fire off the coast of Iraq, without specifying the cause of the incident or the status of the crew.
"UKMTO has received multiple third-party reports of a vessel on fire, 63 nautical miles southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq," it said.
"Crew status, damage assessment, and environmental impact are unknown at time of report," the agency added.
Al-Faw is a port town that sits on the Gulf, neighbouring Kuwait and Iran.
Syria closes main border crossing with Jordan after strikes
Syria closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions due to developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement.
The closure came after Jordan's air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria, saying suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there.
The Nassib border crossing is Jordan's only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.
Syria says Jordan did not coordinate before strikes
Syria's government said Monday that Jordan did not coordinate with it before launching deadly strikes on the country's south in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week.
A Syrian government statement carried by state news agency SANA said "no prior coordination with the Syrian side was carried out concerning the military operation" by Jordan, adding that authorities were investigating the strikes and discussing them with Amman while stressing the need for joint security coordination in border areas.
Syria says death toll in Jordan strikes rises to 8
Syria said the death toll in Monday's strikes in its south had risen to eight, as Jordan said it had targeted "terrorist organisations" after a deadly jihadist attack on a church.
Health officials said "hospitals in Daraa province have received eight victims, including an elderly man and three children", in addition to four wounded, raising an earlier toll of five dead.
Jordan strikes militant groups in Syria after church attack
The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.
It said air force jets had "destroyed several terrorist positions" and killed and wounded "numerous members" of groups linked to the perpetrators of the church attack.
Syria's state news agency SANA, citing a local health official, said the strikes across Daraa province in the country's south had killed five civilians, including women and children.
Iran security chief says 'very good discussions' held
Iran's security chief said on Monday he held "very good discussions" with the three member nations of the Mecca defence pact, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, after their first meeting in Tehran.
"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television after the meeting with top officials from the three countries. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen."
The meeting, proposed by Pakistan, brought together senior officials from the three countries and Iran for talks in the Iranian capital.
Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said earlier Monday that the meeting aimed to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis".
UN probe accuses Israel of 'extermination' in West Bank
Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the West Bank, while continuing to commit "genocide" against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, United Nations-mandated investigators said Monday.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said Israeli forces had also committed other crimes against humanity and war crimes in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.
The commission, which does not speak for the UN itself, first determined in a September 2025 report that Israel had committed "genocide" in the war on Gaza.
In a new report, which comes the day before Israel's general election, the investigation found that in the West Bank, through military operations reinforced by sustained settler violence, Israel has waged a "widespread and systematic attack" against civilians.
"The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core," it said.
Iran says agreed with Mecca pact countries on security
Iran said Monday it had agreed with three countries party to the Mecca pact, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, that regional security should be ensured by countries in the region itself and not by foreign actors.
"The outcomes we agreed on were that security in the region where we live should be endogenous, meaning it should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention in this region," Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said after the meeting.
Israel dismisses UN-backed probe's report on genocide
Israel on Monday dismissed as "propaganda" a new report issued by UN-mandated investigators accusing it of committing the crime against humanity of extermination in the West Bank and genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
The Israeli foreign ministry said on X that the investigators' finding "is not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens".
At least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in the Gaza Strip since the so-called ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025.
UN raises 'ethnic cleansing' concerns over Israeli operation
Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron, launched after a deadly attack by Palestinian gunmen, raises serious concerns of "ethnic cleansing", the United Nations warned Monday.
Israel's "aggressive operation" has already resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely", UN rights chief Volker Türk said in a statement.
"The sweeping steps taken raise grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force, which must end."
He said the lockdown was confining many to their homes and immediate neighbourhoods.
Gaza truce has not stopped Israel from committing genocide
A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Monday. They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the West Bank.
In response, Israel's mission in Geneva called for the commission's dissolution and said on X the report marked an example of the body's “misinformation campaign to demonise the state of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal."
Israel has long criticised the commission's output and denied accusations of genocide in Gaza and sexual assault by its forces.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for a just settlement of the Palestinian issue and comprehensive reform of the UN Security Council during talks with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Guterres welcomed Egypt's efforts to consolidate the Gaza ceasefire agreement, praising Cairo's role in facilitating the delivery of humanitarian aid and ensuring it reaches those in need.
"Lasting peace in the region could not be achieved without a just settlement of the Palestinian issue," Guterres said, stressing that it would remain the central issue in the Middle East until a final resolution is reached.
The UN chief also expressed deep concern over developments in the occupied West Bank and urged the international community to fulfil its responsibilities by taking action to halt violations against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.

India-US trade deal stalled over tariffs and politics – media

India-US trade deal stalled over tariffs and politics – media
India’s interim trade deal with the US remains stalled as New Delhi reportedly refuses to accept a proposed 18% tariff rate and weighs politically sensitive agricultural concessions ahead of next month’s US midterm elections.
India wants to retain the current additional 10% levy on covered exports and could reassess negotiations after the November 3 elections, the Hindu BusinessLine reported on Sunday, citing sources familiar with the talks.
Under a framework agreed in February, Washington proposed reducing tariffs on several categories of Indian goods to 18%, from penalties of up to 50% imposed last year. In return, India agreed to lower duties on US industrial goods and selected agricultural products.
However, the negotiating landscape changed after the US Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump’s sweeping emergency tariffs later that month. Washington subsequently imposed a separate additional 10% duty on covered Indian imports under Section 301 of US trade law.
Around 55% of India’s exports to the US are subject to the additional levy, while products including generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones remain exempt, according to India’s Commerce Ministry.
New Delhi is seeking assurances that future US tariffs will not leave its exporters at a disadvantage to competitors in Vietnam, Bangladesh, and Indonesia, the BusinessLine reported. India also wants protection against further duties after an agreement is signed.
Agricultural market access remains another obstacle to finalizing the deal. Washington is seeking concessions on American farm products, including those from Republican-leaning states, while India has sought to protect sensitive sectors such as dairy, poultry, rice, and wheat.
Granting such concessions while accepting higher tariffs would be difficult to defend domestically, sources told BusinessLine. New Delhi is therefore reportedly inclined to wait until after the US elections before deciding how to proceed.
The deadlock comes despite US Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying last week that 99% of the agreement was complete and that a deal could be finalized within weeks.
Trump also described the negotiations as “pretty close,” even as Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar cautioned that the remaining stages could prove difficult.
Trump waived key Russia-related sanctions and tariffs earlier this month, easing a major obstacle to the negotiations. However, a separate US investigation into alleged industrial overcapacity remains unresolved, leaving uncertainty over possible future duties on Indian goods.
