How long will Turkey keep its troops in Syria and Iraq?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:13:27 UTC
00:13:27 KST

Breadcrumb
How long will Turkey keep its troops in Syria and Iraq?
Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler has clarified that Turkey will retain its military presence in Iraq and Syria until certain conditions are met.
The original justifications for Turkey’s cross-border deployments have dwindled in recent years. Now, analysts believe Ankara is offering new justifications for its open-ended military presence in these neighbouring states.
“We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria,” Guler said in a recent interview.
“When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered.”
Open-ended conditions
Turkey sent troops into Syria in 2016. Its cross-border operations primarily focused on targeting the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
The SDF were a coalition formed by the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK)’s main Syria affiliate, which became an invaluable ad hoc US ally against Islamic State (IS).
Early this year, following a Turkish-backed offensive by the new Syrian government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa, the SDF agreed to integrate its fighters into the new Syrian military.
Complete SDF integration could remove Turkey’s decade-long justification for retaining troops in much of northern Syria.
“Ankara conditions its decision to withdraw from Syria not only on border security and the elimination of the terrorist threat in Syria, but also on the al-Sharaa government’s ability to establish state authority throughout the country,” Suleyman Ozeren, a lecturer at the American University and senior fellow at the Orion Policy Institute, told The New Arab.
“This condition could signal Ankara’s desire to maintain a Turkish military presence and use it as leverage against, for example, Israel if tensions in southern Syria escalate into military confrontation between Syria and Israel.”
Consequently, Turkey’s military presence in Syria may continue even if there is a successful Kurdish peace process in Turkey.
“There may be mainly two minimal conditions: the total and actual disarmament of the PKK-linked groups in both Iraq and Syria, and the absence of Israeli military pressure on Syria,” Ozeren said.
In Iraq, Turkey has made repeated forays into northern Iraq’s Nineveh province and Iraqi Kurdistan as part of the conflict with the PKK. Turkey has had bases in these areas since the 1990s.
In the second half of the 2010s, it advanced deeper into the mountains of Iraqi Kurdistan, establishing and maintaining a vast network of outposts and forward-operating bases in strategic areas to relentlessly pressure the Kurdish fighters.
Now, with a major peace effort underway aimed at having the PKK lay down its arms for amnesties and a conclusive end to the conflict possibly on the horizon, Turkey’s justifications for these bases could become defunct.
Muaz Al-Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the conflict-tracking organisation Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), specified that Guler’s remarks aren’t a withdrawal signal.
Rather, he was merely articulating the “latest version of an open-ended condition” which Ankara adjusts as events change.
“In 2024, Turkey tied any exit from Syria to a new constitution, elections and full border security. Earlier this year it said the Damascus-SDF deal was still not enough,” Abdullah told The New Arab.
“Withdrawal is possible, because the presence is costly for Turkey economically and politically, but it will be slow and conditional.”
He also outlined how the minimum conditions for withdrawal differ by country.
“In Iraq, the PKK must be disarmed and out of Sinjar and Qandil,” Abdullah said.
“Since the (Turkey-Pakistan-Saudi Arabia) Mecca alliance, Ankara’s concerns now also include the weapons of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and the threat they pose to Turkey’s ally Saudi Arabia, including PMF drone attacks on the Kingdom,” he added.
“In Syria, the minimum is a completed SDF integration, PKK cadres out of the northeast, and a Syrian army able to hold the border on its own.”
Reality on the ground
ACLED data has documented a rapid decrease in Turkish strikes in Iraqi Kurdistan in the past two years since the latest PKK peace talks began. In 2024, Turkey executed 4,861 strikes in the region. That fell rapidly to 634 in 2025, then to zero so far in 2026.
“The security case for staying is weakening, but the political conditions are not yet met,” Abdullah said.
In September, Turkey agreed to gradually withdraw from the Bashiqa base in Nineveh in tandem with Iraq’s removal of PKK-affiliated fighters from Nineveh’s Sinjar, the homeland of the Yazidi minority subjected to the 2014 IS genocide.
Abdullah described Turkey’s willingness to hand over Bashiqa as a “low-cost concession” rather than the start of any strategic withdrawal. Turkey only established its presence there a decade ago to train local forces battling IS. It is also the furthest base from Turkey’s border.
Nevertheless, it’s important since it is linked to a network of forward bases along the border that support Turkey’s broader counter-PKK mission.
“The handover is also a trade, not a gesture,” Abdullah said. “In return, Baghdad committed to establishing full state authority in Sinjar and removing PKK-linked groups."
The agreement also specifies a “gradual handover” tied to security steps taken on the Iraqi side. As a result, the withdrawal timeline is wide open to delay.
“The real test is on the ground,” Abdullah said. “An Iraqi commander expects Bashiqa to be vacated by the end of this year. If it is, that is a genuine signal. A phased withdrawal begins only when the forward bases start closing, not Bashiqa.”
Therefore, statements and agreements don’t reflect reality on the ground. What would be considered a clear signal that the Turkish withdrawal has begun, the ACLED expert added, is an “actual withdrawal on the ground rather than another statement of agreement between the two sides.”
Syria's status quo
Turkey’s support for Syrian government forces in their January offensive against the SDF proved vital. Ankara is still supporting Syrian government forces in their efforts to establish complete authority in hitherto SDF-controlled areas.
The situation remains unsettled, with ACLED’s Abdullah pointing to reports of armed groups, including the PKK-affiliated Revolutionary Youth Movement, opposed to the Damascus-SDF agreement still operating in those areas. Still, Turkey-Syria collaboration isn’t limited to the SDF.
“Basically, while the Turkish concerns are mainly related to the SDF/PKK activities in Syria, it is also related to the IS activities in Syria,” Abdullah said.
“So yes, the nature of the Syrian-Turkish relationship has changed mostly from cross-border operations and military support on the ground to more of intelligence and training collaboration.”
In his interview last week, Guler noted that Turkey has established “close coordination in the field of security” with Syria’s post-Assad authorities and seeks to “strengthen the capacity” of the new armed forces “to ensure the security of our borders.”
“While the al-Sharaa government has been pushing to take full control of the northern border and end Turkish military control there, Ankara has been pushing for at least a measured understanding with Damascus that would allow Turkish military presence to continue,” Ozeren said.
The Orion Policy Institute’s senior fellow contends that if the present Kurdish resolution process ultimately results in the PKK’s total disarmament and the return under amnesty of ex-PKK fighters to Turkey, then Ankara’s pretext for its military presence in Iraq will become unviable.
“However, two developments could alter the security landscape across the region: an expansion of the Saudi-led conflict with Iran-backed Houthis into a regional conflict, and an escalation of the US and Israel war against Iran into ground operations,” Ozeren told The New Arab.
“Such developments would force non-state actors, including PMFs in Iraq and PKK-linked groups in Iran and even Iraq, to reconsider current arrangements.”
That possibility could especially become a reality if Turkey decides to “pursue military involvement” through its commitments under the Mecca Defence Pact.
"If, and this is a big if, Damascus establishes full governance across the country, Turkey’s security- and defence-oriented influence may diminish, as the al-Sharaa government has tried to diversify its defence and military engagements with other actors,” he said.
In September, President al-Sharaa said that his country is “now entering the stage of giving legal status to the Turkish bases in northwestern Syria,” subject to the approval of the Syrian People’s Assembly.
He clarified that Syria does not have a long-term need for such foreign bases but also wants to “maintain diplomatic relations and mutual respect with neighbouring and friendly countries.”
ACLED’s Abdullah assesses that Sharaa’s statement implies that Syria doesn’t want any long-term Turkish presence on its soil to avoid turning the country into an arena of regional conflict.
That is especially urgent considering the growing tension between Turkey and Israel, which could transform Syria into a flashpoint between these two regional heavyweights.
Israel’s repeated targeting of Syrian airbases that Turkey evaluated for potential use demonstrated how quickly Turkey’s presence could potentially draw Syria into a regional confrontation.
“At the same time, Damascus cannot yet do without Turkish support,” Abdullah said. “As-Suweida remains unresolved, and IS and other groups may expand their activity.”
“Legal status for the bases is Damascus’s way of regulating Turkey’s presence now, so it can reduce that presence later."
In early August, Syria reached a memorandum of understanding on the future conditions of Russia’s access to the coastal naval and air bases of Tartus and Hmeimim under which the bases will become joint training centres after a three-month transitional process.
While Abdullah anticipates that’s the direction Damascus is pushing regarding the Turkish presence, he stressed that any comparison with Russia has significant limits.
“Russia’s presence is two bases far from Syria’s borders, and their value to Moscow is regional reach," he said. “Turkey’s presence sits on a 900-km land border and is tied to a security concern Ankara considers existential. That makes it much harder to reduce to a residual training mission.”
“Expect a smaller footprint over several years, but not a Turkey that fully leaves northern Syria.”
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.

Jordan arrests three following deadly terror attack on church

Jordan's strikes on Syria over church terror attack kill several civilians
Jordanian authorities on Monday arrested three suspects over last week's terror attack that killed nine people in a church funeral procession in the village of Hammoud. Jordan's military later launched strikes on "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria in retaliation for the attack by alleged Islamic extremists, killing at least eight civilians including women and children, a health official said.
The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.
It said air force jets had "destroyed several terrorist positions" and killed and wounded "numerous members" of groups linked to the perpetrators of the church attack.
Syrian authorities reported civilian casualties from the raids, with health officials in Daraa province saying six people, including three children and a woman, were killed.
Syria's civil defence agency reported seven deaths in total, six people in Daraa and one in neighbouring Sweida province.
On Friday, gunmen killed nine people during a funeral service at the Greek Orthodox St George's Church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate, southern Jordan.
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three percent of the population.
Major General Abdullah al-Maaytah, Jordan's director of public security, on Monday named the three detained suspects as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.
The trio, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage, were cornered at an abandoned house where they had barricaded themselves inside and opened fire on security forces.
"All three terrorists have been injured. They have been taken to hospital and are still receiving treatment," Maaytah told a press conference.
Read moreJordan's strikes on Syria over church terror attack kill several civilians
'We will show them'
One of the suspects was in critical condition, Jordan's state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka reported. There were no casualties among the security forces, it added.
"This country must remain an oasis of security and stability, and we affirm that Jordan will remain impervious to anyone who dares to challenge it," Maaytah said.
Under Jordanian law, murder is punishable by death by hanging.
A number of weapons and a large quantity of ammunition were seized from the three suspects, the Public Security Directorate said.
Jordan's King Abdullah II said in a post on X that security forces "chased them to the very end".
"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he wrote.
Earlier, the king visited wounded victims of the church attack in hospital, dressed in military fatigues and carrying a pistol on his hip.
"We will show them," he vowed.
Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al-Mamlaka on Monday that the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".
"There is no indication of any external contacts or collaboration with foreign parties," he said.
Government communications minister Mohammad al-Momani said "we stand ready and will strike with an iron fist, without mercy or leniency, against anyone who attempts to undermine Jordan's security".
Attacks on houses of worship in Jordan are rare. In 2016 an attack in Karak targeted a security centre and police patrols, leaving 10 people dead.
On Friday, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning for the victims of the church attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.
Eight of the nine victims were laid to rest on Sunday next to the church in a funeral that drew a huge crowd amid a large security presence, AFP images showed.
The ninth person, Mohammed al-Qasous, was buried in south Amman on Monday.

The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children that are born to a woman through her reproductive years under current age-specific fertility rates.

Israel is not abandoned: Record-breaking numbers reveal a global movement of support - opinion

For months, the headlines have told us that the younger generation is turning against Israel. We have watched images of campus protests, heard the chants of hostility, and been told repeatedly that the next generation has abandoned the Jewish people.
But on October 7, something extraordinary happened. Something the headlines could not ignore. Something that shattered the narrative.
On the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, Friends of Zion sponsored a record-breaking 24-hour global broadcast that reached more than 250 million people across 167 countries.
At a time when Israel faces relentless attacks on its legitimacy, and the Jewish people continue to endure a rising tide of antisemitism, millions of people around the world chose to watch, listen, pray, and stand with Israel.
The broadcast reached more than 3.8 million people in Syria, 1.2 million in Egypt, and 1.1 million in Algeria. In Brazil, the broadcast reached more than 8.5 million people, following a public appeal by Senator Flávio Bolsonaro encouraging Brazilians to watch.
Let that sink in. Millions of people in nations where public support for Israel can be politically complicated were exposed to a message of solidarity, remembrance, and hope.
This was not a small gathering preaching to the choir. It was a global declaration that the Jewish people is not alone.
The numbers tell a different story
Perhaps one of the most significant findings was the age of the audience. Some 59.8% of the social media audience was between the ages of 25 and 34.
We have been told that young adults have turned their backs on Israel and that support for the Jewish state is destined to disappear. Yet this global initiative reached tens of millions of people through social media, with a substantial share of its audience among younger adults.
We must be careful not to confuse the loudest voices with the majority, or viral outrage with the convictions of an entire generation. A protest does not speak for every student. A hashtag does not represent every young adult. And the most hostile voices on social media do not have the final word on the future of Israel.
The October 7 broadcast demonstrated that a significant global audience remains willing to engage with a message of support for Israel and remembrance of the victims of terrorism.
The battle for the next generation is not over. In fact, it may be one of the most important battles we face.
A generation worth fighting for
The numbers from this broadcast should challenge every pastor, parent, educator, and Christian leader.
We must meet the next generation where they are, communicate with clarity, tell the truth with courage, and equip them to recognize antisemitism even when it is disguised as fashionable political rhetoric.
We cannot surrender the universities. We cannot abandon social media. We cannot allow the next generation to learn the history of Israel exclusively from those who deny the Jewish people’s history, distort the facts, or excuse terrorism.
We must offer something stronger than slogans: truth supported by history, conviction grounded in faith, and a vision of human dignity that refuses to dehumanize the Jewish people.
The Friends of Zion initiative demonstrated what can happen when technology, media, faith, and a clear moral purpose converge. A message that began with a commitment to remember and stand with Israel crossed borders, reached millions, and entered conversations around the world.
That is a foundation on which we must build.
The future is not written by the headlines
I have spent decades working to mobilize Christians to stand with Israel. I have learned that history is not changed by those who wait for public opinion to become comfortable. History is changed by those who stand for what is right when doing so is difficult.
The record-breaking reach of this October 7 broadcast should encourage us, but it should also challenge us. We cannot assume that millions of views automatically translate into millions of committed advocates. We must turn awareness into education, education into conviction, and conviction into action.
We must continue building bridges between Christians and Jews, training young ambassadors, confronting antisemitism, and ensuring that the next generation understands both the historical and biblical significance of Israel.
The enemies of Israel want us to believe that the world has turned away, that the younger generation is beyond reach, and that standing with the Jewish people is a losing cause.
On October 7, millions across the world encountered a different message. Across 176 countries, a global broadcast brought remembrance, solidarity, and support for Israel to an audience that stretched across cultures, borders, and generations.
The headlines may tell one story. The evidence tells another story.
We must never surrender the next generation. We must never abandon Israel. And we must never allow the forces of hatred to have the final word.
The future belongs to those willing to fight for truth and defend the innocent.
The world is watching. The next generation is listening. And our response today will help determine what they believe tomorrow.

The agreements represent a major milestone in Cyprus's efforts to strengthen its position on the energy map of the Eastern Mediterranean, while also contributing to the diversification of Europe's natural gas supply sources.
The President of the Republic of Cyprus, Nikos Christodoulides, received an Eni delegation at the Presidential Palace, headed by the group's Chief Operating Officer of Global Natural Resources, Guido Brusco. This was followed by the contract-signing ceremony covering the design, equipment procurement, construction and installation of the infrastructure required for the development of the field.
The president of Cyprus, Nikos Christodoulides, issued a written statement on the agreement, in which he says among other things that "The signing of contracts worth up to $1.8 billion dollars for the development of the 'Kronos' field, and by extension the first commercial exploitation of Cypriot natural gas, constitutes a strong vote of confidence in our country's energy prospects, with particular geopolitical and economic significance."
In his speech, Brusco described the development as a historic milestone for Cyprus, as it is the country's first hydrocarbon field development project.
More than 3 trillion Cubic feet of gas
According to Brusco, the Kronos field holds estimated reserves of more than 3 trillion cubic feet (TCF) of natural gas, with production forecast to rise to as much as 500 million cubic feet per day once operations have stabilised.
The gas will be transported to Egypt, where it will be processed using existing infrastructure, including facilities linked to the Zohr field off the coast of Egypt.
It will then be fed into the Damietta liquefied natural gas plant, from where it will be exported to international markets, chiefly in Europe.
Using Egypt's existing infrastructure is a central pillar of the plan, as it enables the development of the field through regional energy partnerships and facilitates the commercial exploitation of the gas.
"Historic milestone for Cyprus"
The Eni executive underlined that the company has been active in Cyprus since 2013, investing for more than a decade in expertise, human resources and technological infrastructure.
He said the move of the Kronos project into the implementation phase is the result of this long-term effort and cooperation between the Republic of Cyprus, Egypt, Eni and TotalEnergies.
"It is our first development project in Cyprus and confirms our commitment to being a long-term partner in the country's energy future," he noted.
At the same time, he described the project as the starting point for a new chapter in Cyprus's energy industry, with the potential to strengthen the country's role on the regional energy map.
Brusco also referred to Egypt's contribution, stressing that cooperation between the two countries has shaped a viable route for the commercial exploitation of Kronos gas.
In closing, he emphasised that the start of implementation marks the launch of a complex energy project that demands high-level expertise, close coordination between all stakeholders and strict compliance with safety standards.
Kronos field: Production targeted to start in 2028
Eni and TotalEnergies decided in July to accelerate the project's roll-out, setting a target of starting production in the first half of 2028.
A key advantage is the ability to use existing infrastructure that is expected to reduce development costs and shorten the time needed to build the necessary facilities.
Cooperation between Cyprus, Greece, Egypt and Italy at the heart of energy strategy
Beyond the economic and commercial dimension of the project, the development of the Kronos field highlights the strategic importance of strengthening energy cooperation in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Cooperation between Cyprus, Greece, Egypt and Italy can become a key pillar of a broader energy corridor linking Eastern Mediterranean fields with the European market. Cyprus has the potential to produce new volumes of natural gas, Egypt has the processing and liquefaction facilities, Greece offers a strategic location and interconnections for channelling energy flows towards south-eastern and central Europe, while Italy provides an important entry point to one of the European Union's largest energy markets.
The harnessing of these capabilities creates scope for infrastructure investment, deepening trade ties and the development of new energy transport routes. At the same time, it can strengthen the negotiating position of European countries and mitigate risks arising from dependence on a limited number of suppliers and supply routes.
Europe's energy security and diversification of supplies
For Nicosia, the significance of the agreements goes beyond their immediate economic value. According to daily newspaper Phileleftheros, revenues from gas sales are not expected to begin flowing straight away.
Eni's commitment is a vote of confidence in Cyprus's prospects and reinforces the case for tapping Europe's own energy resources in order to reduce its reliance on external suppliers.
These developments take on particular importance at a time of heightened tensions in the Middle East and concern about the impact of the confrontation between the US and Iran around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important energy shipping lanes.
The risk of disruption to energy flows across the wider region underscores Europe's need to secure alternative supply sources and strengthen strategic partnerships with countries that possess energy resources and the infrastructure needed to export them.
In this context, the development of new fields in the Eastern Mediterranean can help diversify Europe's energy mix, limiting the risks associated with excessive dependence on specific countries or transport routes.
However, the actual contribution of Cypriot gas to Europe's energy security will depend on when production starts, the available export capacity, the commercial agreements in place and the conditions prevailing in global markets.
The exploitation of Kronos does not automatically mean replacing supplies from the US or Russia, but it can add another option to Europe's energy portfolio.
The companies implementing the project
As part of advancing the project, contracts are to be signed with specialised companies that will undertake specific tasks for the development of the field and the necessary infrastructure.
In particular:
- Baker Hughes: Design, supply and construction of subsea production systems.
- Dalmine: Works related to natural gas export pipelines and MEG transfer.
- TechnipFMC: Execution of works for flexible production lines.
- McDermott: Transport, offshore installation, tie-in and commissioning of subsea pipelines and equipment.
- Oceaneering: Construction of the main subsea control cables.
- CMHI: Construction and installation of a floating control unit.
- Petrojet: Construction of a new onshore natural gas pipeline in Egypt between Zohr and Damietta.
- Saipem: Provision of offshore drilling services using the Saipem 10000 drillship.
New energy projects in the Eastern Mediterranean
The Kronos field is part of a broader surge of activity in hydrocarbon exploration and development in the Eastern Mediterranean.
US energy giant Chevron is continuing talks on the development of the Aphrodite field, with its partners Israel's NewMed Energy and the UK's Shell.
At the same time, according to media reports, Shell has reached an agreement to sell its stake in the field to Hungarian energy group MOL, with the transaction expected to be completed in early 2027.
The progress of these projects will play a decisive role in Cyprus's ability to turn natural gas discoveries into commercially exploitable resources and to strengthen its participation in regional energy value chains.
The stakes, therefore, go beyond the development of another gas field. They concern the Eastern Mediterranean's ability to evolve into a reliable energy corridor for Europe, through investment, regional partnerships and infrastructure that connect production with European markets.
In this endeavour, closer cooperation between Cyprus, Greece and Egypt is particularly important, as it can combine the region's production potential with Europe's need for a safer, more diversified and competitive energy supply.

Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win
Published October 25, 2026last updated October 27, 2026
What you need to know
- Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro
- It was a tight runoff, with Lula winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, official results showed
- In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race
- Bolsonaro refused to concede, but his party recognizes Lula's victory
- Trading was suspended on the stock market for half an hour on Monday morning as shares and Brazil's real currency tumbled
- Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win
- Germany's Merz said he looks forward to 'deepening strategic ties' with Brazil
- US President Trump said the vote 'looked terrible,' but added, 'I like Lula'
This blog is now closed.
Keep reading for developments from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25, with continued coverage into Monday, October 26.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Thank you for reading
Thank you or obrigado for following our live news blog coverage of the Brazilian presidential election runoff.
We're sure to have more coverage of Brazilian politics, Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro in the coming days and weeks.

Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula's election victory
Brazil's Liberal Party has acknowledged President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's election victory, breaking with its own candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede defeat.
"We recognize the presidential election results," party leader Valdemar Costa Neto said in a statement on Monday. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified."
The statement marks a clear break with Bolsonaro's position. The senator has vowed to seek the annulment of Sunday's runoff result, claiming that a two-hour extension of voting favored Lula.
The extension was ordered due to transport problems in several cities that made it difficult for voters to reach polling stations. Bolsonaro's own campaign had also requested more voting time in some regions because of heavy rainfall.
According to electoral officials, the extension did not change the outcome of the election.
Bolsonaro has yet to publicly respond to his party's statement.
Flavio Bolsonaro says he is banned from leaving Brazil after election defeat
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro says he has been ordered to surrender his passports and is banned from leaving the country.
The right-wing senator said federal police approached him after he visited his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.
"I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," Bolsonaro said in a video posted on social media.
He called the move "a clear attempt to intimidate me" and claimed the order came from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Neither the court nor federal police immediately confirmed the reported ruling.
Bolsonaro said the decision was based on comments by his brother Eduardo, who had suggested he should leave Brazil if he lost the election. He denied having any plans to flee the country and said he would comply with the order.
Trump says Brazil vote 'looked terrible to me' but adds, 'I like Lula'
Ask, and you shall receive — sometimes anyway! Now a senior US government representative has commented on Brazil's vote.
Leaving Washington for a midterm election campaign rally, President Donald Trump told reporters that it "looked terrible" to him.
"I didn't take sides but it looked like another rigged election frankly... it looked so corrupt, so terrible," he said.
Asked by a reporter if he wanted to "do something about the election," Trump seemed to suggest he did not, albeit repeating his criticism of the mechanics of the vote.
"Well, I'm not running Brazil. I'm running the USA. I just thought that the election was, uh — I like Lula, I get along with him very well — I just think it had a very bad look, the election. The way it was tabulated, you know? The extension given was very strange."
US yet to comment on Brazil election
As of 3:20 p.m. in Washington D.C. (1920 GMT), the upper echelons of US government were yet to respond to the election in Brazil on Sunday.
The only October 26 State Department press releases concerned Austria's national day and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's planned trip to Georgia later in the week for a G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting.
Rubio had not opined on his social media channels and US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account — which only tends to pick up on stories with a tape delay unless they involve Trump directly — had remained inactive since Sunday night.
Lula and his Workers' Party often had strained relations with US governments, especially Republican ones, but this has been particularly pronounced in Trump's case.
Recap — Why is Bolsonaro crying foul after the voting extension?
Just joining us and wondering how Brazil's runoff vote had a considerably clearer margin of victory than predicted and yet still ended in controversy and the losing candidate refusing to concede defeat?
Challenger Flavio Bolsonaro's objections were focused around the evening extension of voting past the planned closing time of 5 p.m. across the country.
The decisions by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice on Sunday followed a complaint over allegations of pro-Bolsonaro mayors being behind public transport irregularities that may have hampered people's plans to vote.
On election night, Bolsonaro then told journalists it was "impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded."
For now it's unclear whether, as the dust settles, Bolsonaro will continue to resist the outcome and try to encourage protests in the way his now-jailed father Jair Bolsonaro did four years ago.
But two factors in particular seem to speak against the prospects of a potential Bolsonaro challenge.
Firstly, his fairly sizeable margin of defeat — losing by slightly more than 4 million votes rather than just a few thousand — makes it much more unlikely that a two-hour extension at polling stations could have even the theoretical potential of swaying the result.
And beyond that, his camp appealed for and successfully secured permission to keep polling stations open in some of Bolsonaro's southern strongholds, after torrential rains interfered with would-be voters' travel plans.
African leaders congratulate Lula, seek to 'advance shared interests'
Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was one of several African leaders to congratulate Lula on Monday, saying that his renewed mandate offered an opportunity to strengthen bilateral ties.
"As two leading nations of the Global South, we can promote economic integration and advance our shared interests in a rapidly changing global order," Tinubu said online, saying he looked forward to expanding cooperation in a raft of areas.
Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu also extended her "sincere congratulations" to Lula.
"Tanzania values its longstanding friendship with Brazil, and looks forward to continue building on this foundation to further strengthen bilateral relations and deepen cooperation, for the mutual benefit of our two nations," Suluhu said.
Seychelles President Patrick Herminie called the runoff election result "a powerful affirmation of the trust the Brazilian people have placed in President Lula's leadership," in comments published by his office online.
He said Lula's win was "a testament to his lifelong commitment to the dignity and well-being of ordinary men and women," saying the Seychelles shared Lula's values like "social justice, equality of opportunity, the protection of workers and the most vulnerable, and a model of development that places people at its center."
Herminie expressed a desire to deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in tackling climate change, protecting the oceans and advancing the interests of the Global South.
Putin congratulates Lula, praising his 'personal contribution' to bilateral ties
Russian President Vladimir Putin offered congratulations to Lula in a telegram published by the Kremlin on Monday.
"It is difficult to overstate your personal contribution to strengthening the strategic partnership between Brazil and Russia," the telegram stated.
Putin, a leader of a fellow BRICS alliance member, is one of few world leaders to have worked with Lula across all of his presidential terms, starting in 2003.
Putin also congratulated Lula on his upcoming 81st birthday, which falls on Tuesday.
The Russian president's spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow earlier in the day that the Kremlin welcomed Lula's re-election.
WATCH: Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a historic fourth term after defeating far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro in a runoff election.
It's a historic political comeback for Lula who trailed in the first round.
DW reports from Rio de Janeiro.
Sao Paulo stock exchange halts trading over sharp drop after Lula win
Trading on the Sao Paulo stock exchange, the largest in Latin America, was suspended for 30 minutes on Monday after plummeting nearly 17% in the wake of the re-election of left-wing Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who defeated conservative Flavio Bolsonaro.
The sharp drop in the benchmark Ibovespa index triggered a 30-minute "circuit breaker" mechanism provided for "periods of sharp market decline," according to a stock exchange statement.
Meanwhile, the US dollar surged 12% against Brazil's currency, one of the real's biggest daily moves on record.
Prices of raw sugar, one of Brazil's most important exports, slid nearly 5% on the collapsing exchange rate.
Prediction markets had indicated a Bolsonaro win but the right-wing senator's refusal to concede defeat and his pledge to challenge the election result have added to investor uncertainty.
"Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result, or at least allows the constitution to run its course," Chris Turner, a strategist at ING in London, told the Reuters news agency as attention turned to Lula's choice of finance minister — a clue as to his fiscal approach.
"The key signal for markets will be the next Lula administration's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the appointment of a new finance minister in coming weeks," RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Graham Stock told Reuters.
Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.
"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.
Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.
Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win
Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index Bovespa falling nearly 15% in early Monday trading
On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.
Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.
Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.
Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.
"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He said Russia hoped for more of the same.
Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.
However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.
Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.
It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.

Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.
China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."
Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."

"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."

"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.

From the Mecca defence pact to Tehran talks: Is the Middle East’s security landscape shifting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:07:28 UTC
00:07:28 KST

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are pursuing talks with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of the Mecca Defence Alliance.
Senior military and security officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are holding talks with Iranian officials in Tehran as diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States continue.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are members of the Mecca Defence Alliance, a security alliance established amid regional instability and concerns over threats linked to Iran and its allies.
The three countries have now turned to direct talks with Tehran about regional security, even as the alliance faces growing pressure from attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are attending the talks in Tehran on Monday, according to Saudi and Iranian officials.
They are reportedly meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has described the meeting as a potential step towards establishing cooperative regional security mechanisms.
Speaking at his weekly news conference in Tehran, Baghaei reiterated Iran’s longstanding call for what it describes as "endogenous security," a framework that would rely primarily on the capabilities and interests of regional countries.
The Mecca pact: collective defence against regional threats
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August 2026. Under the pact, an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all three, requiring the others to provide assistance.
The agreement brings together Saudi Arabia’s financial resources and influence in global energy markets, Pakistan’s nuclear capabilities and Turkey’s advanced defence industry and NATO membership.
Although the agreement was signed amid growing concerns over Iran and its allied groups, Turkish officials have insisted that it is not directed against Tehran or any other specific country.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in an Aug. 8 interview with Anadolu that the agreement did not identify any country as a common threat. He explained that countries would not be considered targets unless they attacked a signatory.
The agreement has received approval in Pakistan, while Turkey has submitted it to parliament but has yet to complete the ratification process.
Houthi attacks put collective defence to the test
Escalating missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi Arabia have presented the Mecca alliance with its first major test.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct. 5, the three countries agreed to move towards implementing their collective defence commitments, including measures to ensure the rapid deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments were outlined in a joint statement published by Turkey’s Foreign Ministry.
Ankara, however, has drawn a line between supporting Saudi Arabia’s defences and joining offensive military operations against the Houthis inside Yemen.
At an Oct. 8 news conference in Ankara, Fidan said the agreement was defensive and ruled out sending Turkish troops to another country to carry out attacks.
Turkey has instead been assessing possible contributions in areas such as air defence, electronic warfare and technical assistance.
The three nations are therefore pursuing direct engagement with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of an alliance designed to deter attacks on its members.
Why engage with Tehran?
Pakistan has played a mediating role between Tehran and Washington in recent months. Saudi Arabia is seeking to contain the threat posed by Houthi attacks on its territory and infrastructure, while Turkey has sought to prevent further regional escalation.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said in an Oct. 26 post on X that the Tehran visit was part of continued efforts by the Mecca pact countries to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.
He said the talks were also intended to support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan.
The Saudi statement suggests that talks with Iran are being pursued alongside the alliance’s defence commitments, rather than necessarily representing a fundamental change in the pact’s purpose.
Military deterrence or regional security?
Tehran’s emphasis on locally driven security arrangements appears, at least in principle, to share some common ground with the Mecca pact’s stated objective of strengthening security cooperation among regional states.
Significant differences remain, however.
Saudi Arabia maintains extensive security ties with the United States, Turkey is a NATO member, and Pakistan continues to pursue defence partnerships with several major powers.
Meanwhile, no agreement on a new joint regional security mechanism has been announced.
Nevertheless, the Tehran meeting highlights a notable development: Three countries that have established a mutual defence alliance in response to mounting regional security threats are now also pursuing direct dialogue with Iran.
The key question is whether this dual approach can have a lasting impact on regional tensions.

UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:07:23 UTC
00:07:23 KST

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

SIR row: EC rejects oppositions charges, files 15-point counter-affidavit in SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:05:52 UTC
00:05:52 KST

The affidavit was approved unanimously by the CEC and both Election Commissioners
NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Monday filed a counter-affidavit in the Supreme Court defending its functioning and the conduct of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The poll body rejected allegations of irregularities and questioned the basis of a petition challenging its decision-making process.According to Bar and Bench, the poll body said the petition was built entirely on a single news report. The affidavit, approved unanimously by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, addresses concerns over the Commission's internal decision-making, alleged changes to voter enrolment forms, deletion of names and the functioning of its electoral databases.
The response came after a plea filed by Rakesh Kumar Singh in the apex court. The petition sought the suspension of the CEC and challenged his alleged unilateral decision-making powers. It also sought to declare the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and all related actions invalid.
In its counter-affidavit, the EC made the following submissions, as reported by Bar and Bench:
Affidavit approved unanimously by all three members: the CEC and both Election Commissioners
All three SIR orders (June 2025, October 2025, May 2026) were unanimous decisions of the Commission
Notes, queries or suggestions by the CEC or ECs while a file moves are not decisions of the Commission
Files go to one EC, then the other EC, then the CEC. In urgent cases, approval is taken electronically and recorded on file later
Any officer issuing orders beyond delegated powers will face action
July 28 work allocation order was issued by an Additional Secretary on deputation. Both ECs wrote to the Cabinet Secretary the next day. The order was never implemented after the ECs' joint direction of July 30
Form 6 has not been amended. Only the Centre can amend it. The SIR declaration is a separate document
Admits the online display could be read as an amendment. From October 21, the online application will be split into Form 6 and the declaration, as in the physical form
Unmapped voters need not attend hearings. BLOs will collect documents from their homes. Hearings only in exceptional cases, preferably online
ECINet: no name is added or deleted except by order of the ERO. A committee with experts from IIT and IISc has been set up to check compliance
Goa: of 97 "left out" voters, 88 had already been enrolled, 6 were abroad and 3 held Portuguese passports
West Bengal appeals against inclusion of voters were filed by officers of the CEO, West Bengal, under Supreme Court orders. "These matters were not brought to the Commission"
Plea to restrain the CEC is not maintainable. CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge
Commission never released or authorised the release of any internal note or file to the media

Trade, space cooperation to top agenda at Turkic states summit in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:05:25 UTC
00:05:25 KST

Ankara is preparing to host the 13th Organization of Turkic States (OTS) Summit on Thursday and Friday to assess progress and cooperation in trade, investment, energy, digital infrastructure and space.
Organised under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought, and Deed,” the event will be hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Cooperation among member states spans a wide range of areas, including transport, digital technologies, agriculture and space.
Türkiye will assume the OTS' rotating presidency from Azerbaijan, and participating leaders are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration at the summit, along with other agreements to deepen institutional cooperation.
Digital cooperation will be the central focus, as Türkiye has recently become the third country after Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan to ratify a digital economy partnership agreement to facilitate e-commerce and cross-border data activities.
Technical collaboration between OTS member states continues to expand to encompass new areas, including a project to establish a joint digital agriculture data platform and a framework agreement signed at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) to coordinate a joint CubeSat project.
Ahead of the event, the Turkish Union of Chambers and Commodity Exchanges (TOBB) will host the Turkic World Business and Investment Forum on Wednesday to focus on the Middle Corridor, border logistics and customs.
Turkmenistan's President Serdar Berdimuhamedow will meet with the Turkish business community on Friday.
Türkiye's diplomatic ties with other OTS member states are deepening amid growing economic relations.
Türkiye's annual trade volume with full member states, namely Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, totalled $17 billion last year, comprising $9.6 billion in exports and $7.3 billion in imports.
Türkiye achieved and maintained net exporter status with the member states, as exports rose from $6.2 billion against $4.2 billion in imports in 2021 to $6.9 billion against $6.2 billion in 2022, $8.8 billion against $6.4 billion in 2023 and $10 billion against $6.5 billion in 2024.
Kazakhstan was the largest Turkish export destination in 2025, with $3.2 billion, followed by Azerbaijan with $3 billion, Uzbekistan with $2.1 billion and Kyrgyzstan with $1.3 billion.
From January to August 2026, Türkiye's exports to full OTS member states reached $6.1 billion against $5.4 billion in imports, led by $2 billion in exports to Kazakhstan, $1.9 billion to Azerbaijan, $1.3 billion to Uzbekistan and $832.8 million to Kyrgyzstan.
The OTS continues to expand with observers such as Turkmenistan, Hungary, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) and the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO).

How Zelensky's team sent Brussels scrambling over a meeting that never was
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:04:30 UTC
00:04:30 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky's planned Oct. 26 trip to Brussels descended into a diplomatic guessing game, with conflicting signals from his own team leaving EU and NATO officials scrambling to establish whether he was coming — and who was supposed to meet him.
At the center of the confusion was a proposed four-way meeting between Ukraine, the U.S., the EU, and NATO on efforts to end Russia’s war. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were expected to join the talks and brief European officials on their recent meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
But the meeting was never officially confirmed. An official from Zelensky's office leaked word to the press that the president would come anyway, setting off a scramble among European officials to prepare for a visit that remained uncertain.
The result was a rare public breakdown in coordination: Ukrainian officials gave reporters one account, European officials prepared to travel to Brussels, and Kyiv ultimately pointed to a change in U.S. plans to explain the confusion.
As a result, European officials began the day scrambling to answer the most basic question: Was the meeting even happening?
A trip announced, then thrown into doubt
The first indication that something might be in the works came from Zelensky himself.
In an interview with Ukrainian state television on Oct. 25, the Ukrainian president said a meeting was expected in Brussels "this week."
"We had a briefing from the Americans, and now they no longer want just a briefing — they want to have a broad discussion about security, guarantees, the EU, and participation," he said. "And they want a meeting this week in Brussels."
Yet the plans appeared to change almost as quickly as they emerged. A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent late on Oct. 25 that Zelensky had planned to visit Brussels but that the trip had since been called off.
By the morning of Oct. 26, the story appeared to have changed again.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing unnamed sources in Zelensky's team, reported that the Ukrainian leader was going to Brussels.
Ukrainian and European journalists began reporting the visit, while EU and NATO officials appeared to be hearing about it at roughly the same time as everyone else.
Even after it became clear there would be no meeting in Brussels, European media reported it was canceled, even though it had never been confirmed in the first place.
The European Commission offered little clarity, saying it continued to participate in talks and efforts with allies and partners to achieve a just and lasting peace for Ukraine, but had "no further information to share." Behind the scenes, European officials were trying to work out whether the reports were real.
One senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent they had no idea Zelensky was coming.
"Now we are in fact trying to assess if they are surprise visiting," the official said. "We are leaving for Canada and do not currently expect to have such a meeting."
"We are traveling to Canada and not expecting visitors."
The timing made the confusion particularly awkward.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa were preparing to travel to Montreal for the Canada-EU Summit — hardly the ideal moment to improvise a high-level meeting with the Ukrainian president.
Washington's plans may have changed
Part of the confusion appears to have stemmed from uncertainty over the U.S. delegation. Witkoff and Kushner had been expected to join the meeting, but Kyiv learned that Trump had decided to keep them in Washington around the time of Israel's Oct. 27 elections.
"Donald wants those two to be in Washington with him," a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
Without the two envoys, the meeting seemed pointless.
When Ukrainian reporters pressed Zelensky's office for confirmation that the Ukrainian president would travel to Brussels, presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said Kyiv could not confirm the meeting "due to a change in plans on the part of the U.S."
That explanation helped clarify why the plans might have shifted, but it did little to explain why European officials had been left trying to determine whether the Ukrainian president was arriving in the first place and who was responsible for the false leak.
A communications breakdown
The conflicting accounts sparked a heated exchange among senior members of Zelensky's communications team over why reporters had received different information about the trip, the Kyiv Independent can reveal.
One Ukrainian official suggested the confusion may have stemmed from a simple problem: not everyone on the team is "on the same page."
A senior EU official offered a more diplomatic — if pointed — assessment of the recurring coordination challenges.
"We love (Ukrainians), but (they are) sometimes a bit chaotic."
The episode came as Kyiv and its partners were trying to coordinate the next stages of talks to end Russia's war. On Oct. 23, Zelensky said Ukrainian, Russian, and U.S. negotiating teams would meet in Abu Dhabi in November to begin peace talks.
An EU official told the Kyiv Independent that European partners still expected another round of discussions on the continent before those multilateral talks.
"We do expect a session of talks in Europe in the coming weeks before the expected Abu Dhabi multilateral talks," the official said.
Whether that meeting will take place remains uncertain.
"That may or may not happen given the temperaments of all involved."

Ukraine will demand the cancellation of the permit for the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships in Moscow
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:04:30 EET

Ukraine will demand the cancellation of the permit for the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships in Moscow
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is preparing an appeal to the IWF and the IOC demanding a review of the decision to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow. Matvii Bidnyi called on partners to prevent the competition from taking place in Russia.
Ukraine is preparing an appeal to the International Weightlifting Federation and the International Olympic Committee regarding the decision to grant Russia the right to host the 2030 World Championships. Youth and Sports Minister Matvii Bidnyi stated this on social media on October 26, UNN reports.
Details
"We are preparing official appeals to the International Weightlifting Federation and the International Olympic Committee regarding the shameful decision to grant Russia the right to host the 2030 World Championships. We call for this decision to be reviewed and for a new, transparent selection process to be held to determine the country that will host the championships," Bidnyi wrote.
He noted that he would raise this issue with international partners, in particular at upcoming official events with the sports ministers of the countries of the Council of Europe and the EU.
"We seek to consolidate the international position—we call on the international sports community to publicly oppose holding the championships in Russia. As long as Russia continues its war against Ukraine, holding international competitions on its territory is unacceptable. This decision is especially cynical now, when, on the eve of winter, Russia is intensifying its strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, killing people and threatening Europe. Against this backdrop, the international federation is inviting the global sports community to gather in Moscow, from where orders for these crimes are issued. In effect, it is asking them to turn a blind eye. For the Kremlin, such a championship would become an instrument of propaganda and Putin’s political rehabilitation. This is a dangerous signal that a country can continue waging war while simultaneously returning to international sport. It encourages impunity and shows contempt for the principles that global sport should protect," the minister added.
Bidnyi emphasized that Ukraine "will use all available mechanisms and will continue working with international partners to call for this championship not to be held in Russia."
As a reminder
The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) granted Russia the right to host the 2030 Senior World Championships. The competition will be held in Moscow. This is the first case since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in which an international federation of an Olympic sport has entrusted Russia with hosting a World Championships event of this level.

SBU: Head of Russian occupation administration in Kherson region, Saldo, notified of suspicion regarding illegal transfer of Ukrainian children
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:04:26 EET
00:04:26 KST

The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) has documented further crimes committed by Vladimir Saldo, the head of the Russian occupation administration on the left bank of Kherson region. According to the SBU, he and two accomplices were involved in the illegal transfer of Ukrainian children following the seizure of the regional center.
"The investigation established that on October 7, 2022, the individuals in question organized the illegal removal of students from Kherson Vocational Shipbuilding Lyceum to so-called 'sanatoriums' in temporarily occupied Crimea," the SBU stated on its Telegram channel on Monday.
It was determined that the students were first transported by bus to a river port, and from there, taken by boat to the left bank, where further transport awaited to carry them to the peninsula.
"To facilitate this illegal removal, Saldo enlisted the help of Viktor Loginov, former Russian military serviceman who, at the time of the crime, held the position of 'deputy director of the lyceum,'" the agency specified.
According to investigators, in order to conceal the illegal transfer of the children, Loginov personally entered fictitious information into the educational institution's official records.
"A second accomplice, Nikolai Dolzhenko, a teacher at the lyceum, which had been seized by that time, accompanied the students along the entire route to Crimea," the message notes.
The message emphasizes that, through these actions, the individuals involved violated Article 49 of the Geneva Convention (IV) relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War, which prohibits the forcible transfer of protected persons from occupied territory.
Based on the evidence gathered, investigators from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) have notified Saldo and two of his accomplices in absentia that they are suspected of committing crimes under Part 2 of Article 28 and Part 1 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (war crimes committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy).
"As the perpetrators are currently hiding in a temporarily occupied part of Ukrainian territory, comprehensive measures are underway to bring them to justice," the SBU noted.
The Ukrainian security service also pointed out that, in a separate criminal proceeding based on evidence provided by the SBU, Saldo has already been sentenced in absentia to 15 years in prison.
The investigation was conducted by investigators from the Main Investigative Directorate under the procedural guidance of the the Prosecutor General’s Office.

WASHINGTON, October 26. /TASS/. US Congress representatives are threatening businesses, demanding that they refuse to participate in agreements to supply Russian diesel fuel to the US market, Axios reported.

The politicians urged American businesses to refrain from "purchasing, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing, or distribution" of Russian diesel in the US or the financing of its acquisition. At the same time, the lawmakers required the business community to "preserve a wide range of potential records and communications related to ‘proposed or actual’ transactions" of this kind, including correspondence with "suppliers, intermediaries and US government officials." Finally, the authors of the letter also ordered them to identify all other companies and contractors involved in such transactions. Businesses are required to report on their completed work by October 28.
The letter was sent to J.P. Morgan, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley. The document was also sent to the ports of Houston, Beaumont, and Corpus Christi in Texas, as well as to ports in New York and New Jersey.

Most Ukrainians see anti-corruption progress despite scandals, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:04:05 UTC
00:04:05 KST

Around 55% of Ukrainians believe genuine efforts are being made to fight corruption and that progress is being achieved, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) published on Oct. 26.
The findings come amid persistent public concern over corruption, which remains one of Ukraine's most pressing issues even as the country nears the fifth year of Russia's full-scale invasion. A string of high-profile scandals has implicated top officials and allies of President Volodymyr Zelensky over the past year.
KIIS asked respondents how they viewed the media reports on corruption scandals. While 55% said the reports pointed to genuine efforts to tackle corruption and positive developments, 41% said Ukraine was "hopelessly corrupt," seeing no signs of progress.
The remaining 4% were undecided.
The share of respondents who saw progress fell slightly from 57% in December 2025, while the share who viewed Ukraine as "hopelessly corrupt" rose from 35%.
The recent survey was conducted among a representative sample of 1,031 adults across all regions of Ukraine except for areas under Russian occupation, between Oct. 8 and 26.
A separate KIIS poll published earlier this fall found that 72% of Ukrainians believe the level of corruption has increased since Russia launched its all-out war. Only 6% said it has decreased.
Corruption was also the most frequently cited concern, named by 50% of respondents, followed by Russia's mass missile and drone attacks at 40%.
The same poll found that 72% of Ukrainians believe Zelensky bears personal political responsibility for corruption among his associates.

Latvia plans minimum wage increase – proposed amount falls short of initial calculations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:01:58 UTC
00:01:58 KST

After the National Tripartite Cooperation Council failed to reach an agreement on raising Latvia's minimum wage to 835 euros, the Ministry of Welfare has proposed increasing it by 40 euros to 820 euros per month next year, according to draft regulations prepared by the ministry.
The current minimum monthly wage in Latvia is 780 euros. Both the Ministry of Welfare and trade unions had supported raising it to 835 euros.
The draft regulations have been submitted for consultation until 9 November and will still require government approval. The changes are intended to take effect in 2027.
The Ministry of Welfare states that, based on the reference value established in Latvian legislation, the minimum monthly wage should be set at 835 euros next year.
However, no agreement on this amount was reached during meetings of the National Tripartite Cooperation Council on 30 July and 8 October this year.
The reference value used to calculate the minimum wage is 46% of the average gross monthly salary over the latest available 12-month period, as calculated by the Central Statistical Bureau (CSB).
The calculation is based on the average gross monthly salary of 1,815 euros recorded in 2025.
This produces a reference value of 834.90 euros, rounded to 835 euros.
Consequently, the minimum wage proposed by the Ministry of Welfare in the draft regulations is 15 euros lower than the amount calculated using the statutory reference value.
According to CSB data cited in the draft's explanatory memorandum, an average of 131,815 employees, or 17.1% of all employees, earned the minimum wage or less last year.
This represented a decrease of 2.3 percentage points compared with 2021, when 19.4% of employees received wages at or below the minimum level.
The Ministry of Welfare explains that increasing the minimum wage will raise labour costs for employers whose employees currently earn less than the proposed 820 euros per month for normal working hours.
However, the ministry does not expect the changes to increase employers' administrative burden, as information about employee income and taxes must already be submitted to the State Revenue Service every month.
According to the ministry's assessment, a higher minimum wage will improve the purchasing power of low-income workers and have a positive effect on domestic demand.
It could also encourage investment in technology and productivity improvements, while helping to reduce the shadow economy in sectors with a higher proportion of minimum-wage workers.
At the same time, the ministry acknowledges that industries employing a large proportion of workers earning the minimum wage or salaries close to it could face increased pressure from rising production costs.
In the short term, the increase could also negatively affect small and medium-sized enterprises in regions with lower economic activity and income levels, particularly where a significant proportion of employees earn the minimum wage or close to it.
The fiscal impact of increasing the minimum wage to 820 euros has already been incorporated into macroeconomic forecasts, tax revenue projections and state budget expenditure estimates, as well as Latvia's Fiscal Structural Plan for 2025–2028.
As a result, the proposed amendments will not change the tax revenue or state budget expenditure figures already forecast.
The Ministry of Welfare cannot accurately calculate the potential additional costs for municipal budgets because it does not have data on employees of local government institutions whose monthly wages for normal working hours are below 820 euros.
As previously reported, the Ministry of Welfare stated in its July report on the minimum wage that, based on the reference value established in legislation, Latvia's minimum monthly wage should be set at 835 euros in 2027.
However, on 19 September 2024, when reviewing an information report on state budget revenue and tax policy, the government outlined a medium-term minimum wage schedule.
Under that plan, the minimum monthly wage would be set at 780 euros in 2026, 820 euros in 2027 and 860 euros in 2028.

Ukraine’s SOF Receive New Heckler & Koch G95 Rifles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:01:19 UTC
00:01:19 KST

Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SOF) have received German G95 assault rifles, which are also being introduced into service with the Bundeswehr.
A SOF soldier shared with Militarnyi his impressions of using the new weapon.
According to him, the G95 has a smooth trigger pull, manageable recoil, and is low-maintenance in the field.
“Smooth trigger pull, recoil, low-maintenance. Overall, a good-quality weapon. Better than the M4A1,” the serviceman said.
The G95 belongs to Heckler & Koch’s HK416 family and uses 5.56×45 mm ammunition. The Bundeswehr selected rifles from this family as part of its transition from the standard-issue G36 to a new small-arms platform.
It is currently unknown how many G95s Ukraine’s SOF have received or as part of which transfer they were delivered.
The delivery of G95 rifles to SOF is also notable because the platform is based on the HK416, a rifle family widely used by special operations units in various countries.
The G95 is the Bundeswehr’s new standard-issue 5.56×45 mm assault rifle, developed by Heckler & Koch based on the HK416 platform. It is intended to gradually replace the G36 in German troops. The first production rifles of the new standard began reaching Bundeswehr combat units in December 2025.
The Bundeswehr is set to receive two main versions: the G95A1, with a 419 mm barrel, and the more compact G95KA1, with a 355 mm barrel. The shorter version is intended to become the standard rifle for most service members. Without additional equipment, they weigh approximately 3.4 kg and 3.3 kg, respectively.
The rifle uses a short-stroke gas piston system with a rotating bolt. It has a rate of fire of about 850 rounds per minute and a stated effective range of up to 450 meters. The controls are ambidextrous, designed for use with either hand.
Separate from the G95A1 and G95KA1, the G95K is a shorter version of the HK416 that German special operations forces have used since 2019.
Militarnyi previously reported on Ukrainian troops’ experience with the German G36 and G3 rifles. Service members spoke positively about the compact G36K and G36C variants, while noting that the 7.62 mm G3 is significantly heavier than Kalashnikov rifles.
