Elering launches tender for €30M crisis management center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:01:00 UTC
00:01:00 KST

Elering launches tender for €30M crisis management center
Estonian electricity and gas system operator Elering has launched a tender to build a crisis management center, expected to cost €28.7 million excluding VAT.
The center will be built adjacent to Elering's head office on Kadaka tee in Tallinn, and must meet state defense security requirements. It is expected to be completed within two years.
Hannes Kont, head of Elering's crisis preparedness unit, said that due to the changed security situation, Elering has launched a highly extensive crisis preparedness program, within the framework of which investments are being made in infrastructure security. The establishment of a new crisis management center forms one part of this.
"We must ensure that system dispatchers can monitor and control the situation via secure data channels at any given moment. Looking at what is happening in Ukraine and at the threat assessments issued by the state, the necessary level of security has become considerably more precise and higher. We must do this in a much more secure environment than before," Kont said.
"What those technological solutions are, how we at any moment have a literally microsecond-level overview of the state of both the electricity and gas infrastructure — those details we will certainly not disclose," Kont went on, citing security concerns.
Kont said Elering wants to conclude the construction contract by the beginning of next year at the latest. Tender participants must submit a preliminary bid with a deadline of 20 months. "Naturally we are in a hurry, but we will see what the market offers. Our ambition is to sign the contract by the start of 2027, which means the crisis management center could be completed by the end of 2028 or the start of 2029."
Elering is a state-owned transmission operator which runs Estonia's electricity and gas transmission systems. Security concerns have driven investment in critical infrastructure. The center is part of a wider crisis preparedness program.

00:00:49 KST

As world leaders race to congratulate Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, after he pulled off a dramatic comeback to claim a re-election victory over his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, US President Donald Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei — both of whom had endorsed Bolsonaro — have yet to publicly acknowledge the outcome.
Lula's win was acknowledged by left and right-wing leaders alike, despite his challenger Bolsonaro refusing to accept the loss. Lula received 51.8 percent of the vote in Sunday's run-off in the South American country's election compared to 48.2 percent for Bolsonaro.
In Argentina, neither Milei, the Foreign Ministry under Pablo Quirno, nor other senior officials had issued an official statement or congratulatory message by midday on Monday.
Milei had openly backed Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, and repeatedly attacked President Lula da Silva during the campaign, calling him a "communist", "thief", "leftist thief", and other insults.
He congratulated Bolsonaro after the first round and had expressed hope they would work together.
Milei has not commented after Lula win, prompting a Brazilian official of Itamaraty (foreign ministry) to joke: "What happened? Digital blackout?
Trump's ties with Bolsonaros
In the US, neither the White House, the State Department, nor the president has offered an official congratulatory message so far.
Multiple outlets in Latin America, citing the Spanish news agency EFE, reported that Trump claimed Brazil had applied the "Joe Biden playbook", noting that Bolsonaro led in the first round and was the clear favourite for the run-off, but that "the communists do not give up power once they get it".
Trump has consistently backed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, describing legal investigations against him as a "witch-hunt" akin to his own.
After Jair was barred from running and imprisoned, his son Flavio ran in the presidential election against Lula. In June 2026, Trump hosted Flavio at the White House, posting on Truth Social to describe him as a "smart young man who loves his Country, Brazil, very much!"
Following his first-round performance against Lula, Trump publicly hailed the result on social media as a "great victory" and "very, very big victory."
US administration also imposed tariffs linked to the elder Bolsonaro's cases on Brazil, revoking some visas, while Lula had been criticising US influence and emphasising Brazilian sovereignty.
In his recent UN address and victory speech, Lula reaffirmed that Brazil is "no one's backyard."
American progressive figures, such as Senator Bernie Sanders, praised the outcome, while several other Democratic and state officials also expressed support.
"Congratulations to Lula on his extraordinary reelection victory in the Brazilian presidential election. Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers & democracy — and will continue to do so in the next four years," Sanders posted on X.
Stage set for political and legal confrontation
While Trump has yet to react, his son Donald Trump Jr criticised the extension of voting hours, an aspect of the outcome Bolsonaro is now contesting.
"If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they're just choosing to be silent because it's all for the cause," Trump’s son argued.
Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered Sunday's polls to remain open for two additional hours, at the request of both candidates.
Lula made the request because of issues with public transportation in metropolis Sao Paulo and northeastern city Salvador, two of his strongholds. Bolsonaro requested it after heavy rains in the south, which he won by a strong margin in the first round.
Bolsonaro, however, has claimed that Zanin, a former Lula lawyer, had changed “the rules of the game in the middle of the game."
"I do not recognise this," he told supporters after the election loss. "There is no way I can accept this outrage that was committed against Brazil. I will take legal action and I will not give up on Brazil."
Lula's victory meant Brazil did not follow Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru—all supported by US President Trump — in swinging to the right.
It also left Latin America's two most populous nations, Brazil and Mexico, under left-of-centre leadership, complicating Trump's efforts to expand US influence across the region.
Bolsonaro's remarks set the stage for a political and legal confrontation between the two rival factions in Brazil, while attention is also now on the US president.

====================================================================================================

‘Hybrid weapon of war’: Why climate disinformation could be a growing public health threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:00:46 UTC
00:00:46 KST

“Climate disinformation is not only a problem of false rumours and mistruths; it is also a problem of power, incentives and accountability.”
WHO member states are being urged to recognise climate disinformation as a public health threat as vested interests attempt to “sow doubt and confusion”.
Health and civil society organisations have called on 194 countries to make information integrity a core part of climate and health policy, preparedness and response.
It follows the EU-backed landmark declaration to crack down on fake news and conspiracy theories that was launched at the COP30 summit in Belém last year.
A new report, ‘Protecting Health in the Age of Climate Disinformation’, is said to be the first instance of the health community addressing how climate disinformation harms human health around the world – from undermining emergency warnings and public-health guidance to delaying policies on air pollution, clean energy and fossil fuels.
The report, produced by the WHO Civil Society Working Group on Climate and Health, argues that a “healthier information environment” is not a communications luxury but a “condition for climate justice, public health and the right to a healthy future”.
What is climate disinformation?
Climate disinformation refers to the intentional spread of false or misleading information about climate change and climate action.
This includes the complete denial of global warming as well as conspiracy theories.
It differs from climate misinformation, which is defined as false or out-of-context information that someone is presenting as fact.
While misinformation does not carry the same level of intent as disinformation, it can result in equally dangerous consequences.
How climate disinformation is impacting public health
The report highlights several case studies where climate disinformation has interacted with existing inequalities and power structures.
For example, after the 2023 Maui wildfires, false claims circulated online that residents who applied for disaster assistance could have their land or property seized by the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
Fact-checkers established this was false, but the rumour had potential to deter survivors from seeking aid at precisely the moment they needed housing support, financial assistance, medical care and recovery services.
“In a disaster setting, misinformation is not just confusing,” the report reads. “It can directly obstruct access to life-saving and stabilising support.”
In Europe, clean air policies such as low-emission zones – designed to reduce people’s exposure to harmful traffic-related pollution – are often targeted by misleading narratives.
The debate around London’s Ultra Low Emissions Zone (ULEZ), which imposes a charge for vehicles that do not meet emissions standards, has included concerns about affordability and implementation, particularly for low-income households, workers, small businesses, and people who depend on older vehicles.
But the report states that these concerns have also been “amplified and distorted” by misinformation, politicised attacks on air quality evidence, fake social media claims, and in some cases even violent backlash against ULEZ infrastructure.
“The backlash against ULEZ shows how disinformation can turn a public health intervention into a culture-war issue,” the report states.
“Instead of focusing debate on how to reduce pollution while protecting those least able to bear transition costs, misinformation can shift attention toward fear, mistrust, and false claims. This risks weakening public support for policies that protect lungs, hearts, pregnancies, children, and communities most exposed to polluted air.”
Other case studies in the report highlight the interests and power structures that “enable disinformation to flourish”, including fossil fuel greenwashing and conflicts of interest.
Dr Jeni Miller, Executive Director of the Global Climate and Health Alliance, and co-chair of the WHO Civil Society Working Group on Climate and Health, says governments must integrate tools for mis- and disinformation response into how they prepare and communicate heat, wildfire, flood, storm, drought and infectious disease scenarios.
“Climate disinformation is not only a problem of false rumours and mistruths; it is also a problem of power, incentives and accountability,” Miller adds.
“WHO, its member states, health institutions and the health community must go beyond simply providing better information and messaging – they must establish robust conflict-of-interest safeguards against fossil fuel greenwashing, and against those who wield climate disinformation as a hybrid weapon of war.”
Dr Laura Jung, Chair of the Working Group on Environment, World Medical Association, argues that the public health impacts of climate disinformation can be “immediate”.
“Misleading information can for example discourage people from evacuating during wildfires or floods, undermine confidence in heat and air-pollution warnings, interfere with access to disaster assistance, and create confusion about health risks during emergencies,” she explains.
How to spot climate disinformation
As part of the efforts to address the issue of fake news, the European Commission’s Directorate-General for climate action recently launched a campaign called #ClimateFactsMatter.
It aims to “empower people” to see through climate disinformation and reveals the main techniques used to mislead the public.
The campaign urges members of the public to always check the source of an article they’re reading, fact-check ‘expert’ comments, look out for loaded, emotional language, and fact-check stories claiming to have a ‘quick solution’ to climate change.

Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:00:28 UTC
00:00:28 KST

Politicians from both left and right have criticized independent Danish MP Jacob Harris for planning to meet Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, on 10 November.
Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen, Denmark’s former defense minister, expressed strong opposition to the meeting in a post on X.
“I actually thought it was a bad joke when I read it,” he wrote, adding that “we must fight Putin. Not drink coffee with his ambassador”.
“It is completely, completely the wrong way to go, and it actually makes me furious. While Russian missiles rain down on Ukrainian cities, while innocent civilians are being killed, and while Russia is waging hybrid warfare against Denmark and our allies, a Danish member of parliament apparently believes that the time has come to sit down at the table with Putin’s representative,” Lund Poulsen wrote.
Mohammad Rona, political spokesperson for the Moderates, and Mette Abildgaard, parliamentary group leader for the Conservatives, also criticized Harris.
“Why is Harris turning his back on Denmark? Harris’ loyalty apparently lies somewhere else. Sad that a Danish parliamentarian can sink so low,” Rona wrote on X.
Abildgaard wrote: “He becomes a useful idiot in the Russians’ propaganda machine. If he wants to be a great diplomat so badly, then apply for a job in the Foreign Service instead.”
Sigurd Agersnap, political spokesperson for the Socialist People’s Party (SF), described the planned meeting as “deeply naive”.
Harris risks giving the Russian ambassador exactly what he needs: “An image that Danish politicians are softening toward Russia while the attacks on Ukraine continue,” Agersnap said in a written comment to Ritzau.
“Of course we must have diplomacy. But a lasting peace requires that we stand firm on the Ukrainians’ right to freedom and self-determination. Harris does not help that by showing up for this meeting,” he added.
Trine Pertou Mach, the Red-Green Alliance’s foreign affairs spokesperson, told DR that the meeting was “decidedly stupid”.
Harris announced the planned meeting with Barbin in a Facebook post on Thursday. He also said he expected criticism from fellow politicians.
He has defended the decision, arguing that meeting a foreign ambassador is not an act of disloyalty.
“Speaking with a foreign ambassador is not treason. Seeking diplomatic solutions is not treason. And working to ensure that Denmark is not dragged into a war is certainly not treason either,” Harris wrote on Facebook.
Harris is an independent member of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. He was elected in March as a member of Borgernes Parti, or the Citizens’ Party, but was expelled a few days later.
He has since established a “working partnership” in parliament with fellow independent Cecilie Liv Hansen, who supports his decision to meet the Russian ambassador.
“I think it is reasonable to meet with ambassadors, regardless of where they come from. Jacob Harris has also tried to reach out to several, including the Ukrainian one,” Hansen told DR.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four and a half years ago. Denmark and several other countries have supported Ukraine since then, including through financial assistance and weapons deliveries.

Economic pain collides with regulatory changes for small businesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Economic pain collides with regulatory changes for small businesses
In short:
Small business operators are navigating tough economic conditions, changes to payday super, a ban on debit and credit surcharges, an increase in wages and changes to trusts.
According to CreditorWatch, one in 10 invoices were more than 60 days overdue in September.
What's next?
The Reserve Bank meets next week, with an interest rate hike increasingly expected.
Small businesses are unlikely to receive a reprieve from tough conditions, with another potential interest rate hike looming and fuel costs continuing to climb.
The unfavourable economic climate has collided with a string of policy changes facing operators, who say a growing regulatory burden has only increased their costs.
The changes include the introduction of payday super, a ban on debit and credit surcharges, an increase to minimum and award wages, and changes to how trusts will be taxed.
Industry associations have voiced concerns about the cumulative impact on small firms, creating additional red tape at a time businesses were already navigating higher costs.
"It's just killing us, killing our industry," builder Steve Bright told The Business.
He went into construction for the love of the trade, but running his own firm, a typical day at work now looks very different.
"Instead of getting out and building a house, we're spending more than half our time in an office doing paperwork," he said.
He is one of about 2.7 million small business owners navigating the current conditions.
Mr Bright has hired extra staff to help implement the policy changes in his business.
"We've got full-time people that do it now ... it's just another cost that we've got to wear."
Simon Croft from the Housing Industry Association said reforms have often been viewed in a "policy silo".
"It's that layering effect of simultaneous changes that then also … trickle down to their business operations."
Sunshine Coast designer and planner Debbie Johnson is rethinking her plans to pass her business onto her son after a tough year.
"I really don't know that as a mother, I would like to see [my son] coming in and taking this business over. It's not like you work 38 hours a week and you get your holiday pay and your sick pay," she said.
"It's very difficult when you want to deliver services for your clients and, I suppose, the regulations that you're working within keep changing because it's disruptive to your focus of what your core business is."
Cashflow crunch worsening
The data demonstrates the cashflow crunch facing businesses at the same time as they adapt to regulatory change. An increasing number have fallen behind on payments.
Credit reporting agency CreditorWatch found "serious arrears" hit an 8.5-year high in September.
Its latest Business Risk Index showed more than 50 per cent of invoices were not paid on time.
One in 10 invoices were more than 60 days overdue, which CreditorWatch chief executive Patrick Coghlan said was the highest level of "serious arrears" since April 2018.
"Even though we're at almost record insolvency levels, the indicators that we're seeing show that that's likely to increase,"
he said.
"It's rarely one decision that gets made or one event that takes place that knocks a business over.
"It's generally [the] cumulative effect of all of these changes that really just continues to put pressure on small businesses."
Inflation and interest rate squeeze
In a week, the Reserve Bank's interest rate-setting board will decide whether to increase borrowing costs for a fifth time this year.
Like households, many businesses have been squeezed by high inflation and rising rates.
"The biggest single factor that is squeezing small business and the economy in general is higher fuel costs and therefore higher transport costs," said Westpac's chief economist, Luci Ellis.
The costs have often been passed on to consumers, as with last month's ban on debit and credit surcharges, which had hospitality venues increase their pricing.
"There have been a few instances of firms, particularly cafes, where it seems prices have increased even more [than the surcharge price]," Dr Ellis said.
"These are often places that have been dealing with other cost pressures, and this has just given them permission to adjust their prices."
Economic concerns overshadow regulatory changes
A survey by small business accounting platform MYOB found 38 per cent of small businesses have seen a drop in revenue from a year ago.
Loading...
Sixty-five per cent reported being concerned about cashflow for the coming year, and 69 per cent were worried about attracting new customers.
MYOB's chief executive, Paul Robson, said the payday super and surcharge policy changes have required small businesses to adapt.
"These two shifts have taken place within a relatively short period," he said.
"However, for the most part, our research suggests that concerns around regulatory changes are still behind cost factors including fuel, energy and interest rates."
Charlie Sheppeard, from competing accounting platform Xero, said slow sales growth in certain sectors made it harder to adapt to changes such as the surcharge ban.
"That leaves little room to absorb additional costs,"
he said.
"It is particularly challenging for sectors like retail and hospitality, where customer card transactions are common, and margins are already thin."
In a statement to the ABC, Small Business Minister Anne Aly said the government knows businesses have been managing rising costs and adjusting to changes, and took the challenges seriously.
"That's why the Albanese Labor government is delivering billions in business tax relief," Dr Aly said, citing the $20,000 instant asset write-off being made permanent, and backing payment reforms, which the RBA has said will lower business costs by $910 million a year.

Will Donald Trump or AI blow up financial markets first?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

analysis
Will Donald Trump or AI blow up financial markets first?
It's an unpalatable choice.
But investors now must consider which poison will cause the least harm.
With civil unrest running rampant across the developed world and global investors desperately seeking exits from the great artificial intelligence boom, a double dose of debt worries has suddenly infected the world of finance.
One is a problem that has been decades in the making, as governments have spent their way out of various crises with nary a care about the cost.
The other has arisen in a frighteningly short time, driven by a manic investment boom that used trillions of dollars of borrowed cash to fund a technology with debatable benefits for society.
Over the past eight weeks, competing demands from those two piles of debt have coalesced into a dramatic repricing of borrowing costs.
Financial markets are perennially worried about the next crisis.
But they now find themselves debating whether a sovereign debt crisis would be worse than an undoing of a technology boom that has driven stock markets since before the pandemic.
The one thing over which there is no dispute is that, if there is a meltdown, interest rates will provide the trigger.
The US Federal Reserve meets tonight and tomorrow, and while there is little chance of an official US rate hike this time around, markets are convinced that December will likely see an increase.
Either way, it's academic.
The US government has seen the cost of its long-term borrowings soar in recent months as bond markets, concerned about the mounting cost of its war in Iran coupled with US President Donald Trump's massive tax cuts, have pushed debt costs higher.
America's debt is now equivalent to 126 per cent of its economic output, the highest it has been in the post-war era, with no plan to reverse the trend.
The annual interest cost on that $US40 trillion ($56 trillion) debt has topped $US1trillion, creating a snowballing budget deficit.
The great AI unravelling
They've been falling like bowling pins in recent weeks.
It began with the Firmus float flop, an audacious $44 billion grab for cash that may have gotten across the line just a few months earlier.
Last week, NextDC — a long-established Australian data centre builder with a strong track record — saw its share price plunge 42 per cent after Melbourne residents successfully delayed a monster computer shed in the suburbs.
A similar incident occurred in Sydney recently, when Goodman Group canned a data centre in the northern suburbs.
It's a story resonating across the developed world.
CoreWeave, a US neocloud like Firmus that rents out its chips and computing power to AI firms, has seen its stock drop 36 per cent in the past month on concern over its mounting debts.
The Nasdaq exchange, dominated by global technology firms, has just endured its worst fortnight since April as developed nations have collectively turned their backs on AI infrastructure.
The AI giant behind Claude, Anthropic, will be hoping the mood is different by the time it floats on Wall Street, which could be just weeks away.
But a recent Gallup poll in the US found 71 per cent of Americans opposed data centres. Of those questioned, only 53 per cent opposed nuclear power plants.
Continuing those delays will dramatically slow the expected rollout of AI technology to businesses and firms.
That, in turn, could undermine revenue for AI firms and destabilise those that have taken on huge debts to fund their investment.
Those concerns have escalated dramatically in the past two months.
ASIC takes a deep dive
It's not all bad news.
Unlike the global financial crisis, where debt problems emerged out of left field, monetary authorities and market regulators are warning and preparing for the worst this time around.
In Australia, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) is taking a helicopter view of national financial markets to ensure they are operating for the interests of all.
From the deeply troubled Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) to private credit markets, fixed income, commodities and foreign exchange, it is holding round table talks to improve their operation and eliminate friction points.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant says the watchdog has two key themes running across all markets: resilience and transparency.
"Resilience gives you strength, transparency gives you trust," she says.
And the corporate watchdog is aware of the growing risk facing Australian investors and institutions.
"Global markets are becoming more integrated and are open more hours than ever.
"Capital flows are going offshore as much as onshore because of the dominance of tech stocks.
"There's high and strategic risk … and giant pools of savings in Australia."
During the 2008 financial crisis, a complete absence of transparency from ratings agencies, auditors and little-known corners of debt markets trading instruments that were mostly unregulated created panic across the financial system.
No-one knew who owed what or which bank held a toxic pile of worthless IOUs. As trust evaporated, the system ground to a halt.
Loading...
ASIC's overview won't stop a market crash. But it will limit the potential for regulators to be blindsided.
"We're seeing movements in spreads and volatility that we haven't seen for a long time," Constant notes.
The view from the helicopter may improve market efficiencies, she adds, the benefits of which will flow through to Australian investors, including those exposed through their superannuation funds.
"We don't want to be a regulator that fears the risk of the challenges ahead.
"It's about adapting to it with that trust and with that strength, that resilience and transparency give."
The AI payday
The prospect of a simultaneous sovereign-debt crisis and a stock-market collapse of hugely indebted companies terrifies many investors.
But some argue that an implosion in one area may ease problems in the other, as interest rates would fall sharply.
Either way, it would still hurt.
Loading
In the early days, big tech companies funded their AI dreams through their enormous cash flows.
But as capital expenditures escalated and the boom expanded beyond the technology itself and into hardware like chips and then architecture like data centres, everyone turned to debt markets.
Even the giants, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, have raised more than $US200 billion between them this year alone.
Nvidia, the world's biggest company, has raised more than $US80 billion this year and routinely finances data centre firms like Australia's Firmus to roll out new data centres using its chips, making it a financier and supplier.
Then there are the "innovative" financing arrangements such as "Special Purpose Vehicles" financed by industry suppliers and investors, along with what is known as "chip financing" as well as debt guarantees and lease arrangements that cloud the boundaries between financing definitions.
And these figures barely scratch the surface. Private credit firms, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and a host of financiers have gleefully handed over cash.
For years, technology and artificial intelligence have had investors enthralled and have driven stock markets to record levels.
Australia's superannuation funds have dived in with their ears pinned back, delivering double-digit returns to members.
But now comes the reckoning.
What if the rollout stalls because no-one wants a big humming data factory in their backyard?
What if China produces an ultra-cheap version of AI that undercuts Silicon Valley?
Or perhaps something more fundamental, like the pencilled-in sales revenue falls short and simply isn't enough to make the interest payments on the debt?
No wonder Wall Street is getting cold feet.

'Travesty of justice': SC flays UP Police for 'slipshod probe' in murder case, orders reparation for undertrial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:58:39 UTC
23:58:39 KST

The verdict came on a plea challenging an Allahabad high court order in January that had denied the man bail. The Supreme Court had directed the trial court on March 23 to conclude the proceedings within three months. The trial was subsequently completed, and the accused was acquitted.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the Uttar Pradesh government to pay Rs 6 lakh in reparation to a man who spent six years in jail as an undertrial in a murder case before being acquitted. The apex court said that the years lost to a faulty investigation were a travesty of justice.Slamming the state police for a “slipshod investigation” and the prosecution for its haphazard handling of the case, a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran called the man a “victim of the system”. It said six years of his life had been erased based on a “concocted story” built on mere surmises and conjectures.The man had been in custody since November 14, 2019, in a murder case registered in Agra.The Supreme Court noted that the trial court acquitted him after finding that none of the four circumstances cited by the prosecution, including electronic evidence, had been proved.“This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person's life and liberty,” the bench said.The court directed the state to pay the compensation within one month, acknowledging that the amount was small compared with the years he had spent behind bars.
“We, hence, direct the state to pay an amount of Rs 6 lakh; though paltry in comparison to the years spent in custody, within a period of one month to the petitioner herein,” it said.The verdict came on a plea challenging an Allahabad High Court order in January that had denied the man bail. The Supreme Court had directed the trial court on March 23 to conclude the proceedings within three months. The trial was subsequently completed, and the accused was acquitted.The bench said the case highlighted the failure of investigating and prosecuting agencies to safeguard an individual's liberty despite the presumption of innocence.“The state cannot shirk from its responsibility to protect its citizens, especially when a person arraigned in a criminal case is presumed innocent until proven guilty,” it said.The court stressed that the role of investigating and prosecuting agencies was not simply to secure convictions, but to ensure justice for all parties, including the accused.“They should recognise themselves to be essential stakeholders in the justice delivery system, ensuring justice, not only to the victim, the de facto complainant and the injured, but also to the accused,” the bench said.The judges also expressed concern over the wider implications of such cases, saying they had encountered similar failures but that this one stood out for its severity.
“We come across such travesty of justice in many matters, but in some, so blatant and shocking, as in this case, which requires reparation to the accused, who in turn is a victim of the system,” it said.The bench directed that a copy of its verdict be sent to the Uttar Pradesh director general of police and the state's home secretary. It also urged the police to train officers in proper investigative procedures, criticising the manner in which the case had been handled.The court said the acquittal was fortunate, given the consequences of the flawed investigation and prosecution for the man's life and liberty.

Russell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was “normalised and dismissed” by those around him, his former personal assistant has told a court.
Helen Berger alleged she had seen Brand treat women badly and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend walking in on him having sex with someone in his dressing room.
She also told the court she had overheard the comedian receiving oral sex in a toilet cubicle and once found a celebrity leaving his bedroom in the morning.
Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Wearing a grey suit and white shirt, Brand sat still in the dock as statements from prosecution witnesses were read to Southwark crown court on Monday.
Berger worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when he was at the height of his fame. She said the job was one of the hardest she had had because Brand had “non-stop energy”, and she left because she was “sick of him” and burnt out.
“Though I’d worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level. I think everyone else normalising and dismissing Russell’s behaviour made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is,” Berger said in a May 2024 witness statement to police.
Describing his behaviour, she added: “He was always in his underwear, he loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on. I remember Sadie Frost came over to interview him. He did the whole interview in his underwear and no shirt and an open robe.”
At the time, Brand had filming commitments for Channel 4’s Big Brother as well as MTV and the BBC, a radio show, a national comedy tour, a weekly Guardian column, and was writing a book.
“In addition to his busy work, he had an insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night. He was very open about what his needs were,” Berger said in the statement, which was read out by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC.
“He never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed,” Berger alleged. “There were times when I was at his house and he would be on a deadline … and he would get antsy and joke with me: ‘May I go and have sex now?’”
She recalled Brand turning to the website Myspace to find random women to sleep with and how women, including an unnamed celebrity, would often be at his flat in Camden, north London, for sexual liaisons. “He was like a peacock, women always approached him,” she said.
When Brand was recording an MTV show, Berger alleged, he told her to ask women for their phone numbers, which she said made her feel uncomfortable.
She alleged that on other occasions she had to keep Brand’s mother and girlfriend away from his dressing room because he was having sex, and she overheard him receiving oral sex in a women’s toilet. Berger described overhearing Brand talking and recognising his trademark cowboy boots in the cubicle next door.
Berger recalled that when Brand was headlining the Edinburgh festival, he ended his show by asking that anyone with “a vagina and heartbeat” meet him at a pub afterwards. Many women showed up, Berger said, and she later found him having sex in the shower at the apartment he was renting.
“I never witnessed Russell doing anything against the law,” she said, before adding: “I did see Russell treat women poorly.”
She recalled how he was once “hitting on” a woman who revealed she had a boyfriend, before Brand “turned in a way” that startled his then PA. “He literally just switched off his charm and moved on to the next woman,” Berger said.
The court also heard a witness statement from the manager of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Brand when she worked at Channel 4 in 2009. The manager said she recalled the alleged victim telling her that Brand’s associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy had “told her she had to give Mr Brand a massage” or he would not continue with the day’s recording.
The manager recalled being told that Bayles and Roy “were both there the whole time and watched and laughed while Mr Brand sexually assaulted her right in front of them”.
The sister of a woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted and then orally raped by Brand at a Soho bar in 2004 told the court she was “upset and almost in shock” the next morning.
In 2023, the woman called her sister in tears and told the “full story” of what had happened, the court heard.
“It sounded like she was struggling to catch her breath,” the witness recalled. “She said his [Brand’s] eyes had gone completely black and he was possessed or had been a completely different person.”

Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:58:00 UTC
23:58:00 KST

Why Ukraine may be aiding Mali rebels against Russia
October 26, 2026
Ukraine is fighting Russia — and the conflict may extend into Africa's Sahel region.
According to an investigation published by US media outlet CNN in September, around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting Tuareg rebels in northern Mali. Their common enemy: the military government in Bamako and its Russian allies.
But how reliable is the information? And what price could Kyiv pay for engaging in Africa?
Marta Oliynyk-D'omochko, coordinator of the African Studies Program at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, sees a strategic motive. "Ukraine's main interest is to weaken Russia's influence around the world," she told DW. If Russia's military influence were rolled back, she added, the economic opportunities arising from it would also diminish.
Russian historian Irina Filatova, professor emeritus at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, also considers Ukrainian support for the Tuareg movement plausible. However, she said she has no independent evidence to confirm such involvement.
Kyiv's alleged partners are controversial. The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) cooperates with the Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated with al-Qaeda.
Ukraine's suspected role in Mali dates back to 2024
In July 2024, DW reported on possible involvement by the Ukrainian military intelligence service (HUR) in an ambush on Russian Wagner fighters near Tinzaouaten in northern Mali.
At the time, HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov said the Tuareg rebels had received information they needed to carry out the attack. Ukraine denied direct involvement.
Paramilitaries from Russia's Wagner Group and Malian troops suffered heavy losses in the July 2024 attack.
CNN's investigation has reignited the question of whether the Russia-Ukraine war is also being fought on African soil.
Signals from Kyiv, but no confirmation
The suspicions were renewed by a post on X by Kyrylo Budanov. The former head of Ukraine's military intelligence, now chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on September 7 that Ukrainian intelligence protects the country's interests worldwide — "from Russia to Africa … in the burning desert sands and in the snows of icy Antarctica...".
Budanov did not explicitly mention Mali and his post does not confirm any specific operation. CNN reported that the Ukrainians provided drone training, operational planning and remote support for drone missions. DW has not independently verified those claims.
DW reached out to the HUR for comment. Among other things, DW wanted to know whether personnel had been deployed to Mali, whether the political leadership had approved such a mission, and what measures were in place to ensure that the JNIM — which cooperates with the FLA — does not indirectly benefit from Ukrainian support.
DW did not receive a specific response. An HUR spokesperson said the agency might provide information at a later date. The extent of any potential Ukrainian involvement therefore remains unclear.
Why Mali matters to Kyiv
Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali increasingly turned away from Western partners and toward Russia. The Wagner Group was subsequently replaced by the Africa Corps in 2025 as Moscow reorganized its military presence.
Russia has sought to consolidate its influence in the Sahel region and present itself as a reliable security partner.
Ulf Laessing, former head of the Sahel program of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Mali and now head of its Syria and Iraq program, said Russia is continuing to expand its activities in Africa.
"I have received information that the Africa Corps still uses Syria and Libya as transit points for flights from Russia, including for refueling and loading, to support its operations on the continent," Laessing told DW.
From Ukraine's perspective, it could be attractive to exert pressure on Russian forces in Africa.
Filatova sees a strategic logic to this: "The Ukrainians regard Russian troops anywhere in the world as legitimate targets." Setbacks in Mali could tie up Russian resources and undermine Moscow's reputation as a security partner, she argued.
However, Oliynyk-D'omochko stressed that the relationship with the Tuareg is not a comprehensive alliance. The FLA is not seeking to replace the government in Bamako. Instead, it is focused on northern Mali and is pursuing self-determination or extensive autonomy.
Oliynyk-D'omochko describes the relationship as a tactical arrangement: "It is more of a situational alliance against a common enemy than a comprehensive partnership."
Are Mali's Tuareg rebels cooperating with jihadists?
The FLA is fighting for an independent state in the north of Mali, a region predominantly inhabited by Tuaregs. JNIM, by contrast, aims to impose strict Islamic rule. Both groups oppose the military government and its Russian allies, but their objectives differ.
Any potential Ukrainian support for the FLA would not, in itself, prove that Kyiv is directly supporting JNIM. However, jihadists could benefit indirectly if they conduct joint operations with FLA or gain access to knowledge and equipment.
Cooperation between Tuareg and Islamist groups dates back more than a decade.
After the ousting and killing of Libya's longtime dictator Muammar al-Gaddafi during the Arab Spring in October 2011, heavily armed Tuareg fighters returned to Mali and took up the struggle for an independent state.
In the process, separatist ambitions became intertwined with Islamist movements. Iyad Ag Ghaly, the current leader of JNIM, was himself involved in the Tuareg rebellion before turning to jihadism.
According to Oliynyk-D'omochko, the cooperation is primarily tactical in nature. The two sides have collaborated during past uprisings but later fell out. It remains unclear how long the current alliance will last.
For Kyiv, this also poses a political risk. In many African countries, the Tuaregs are viewed as separatists. Cooperation with them could therefore create the impression that Ukraine is interfering in another country's internal affairs.
Mali and its neighbours accuse Ukraine of aiding rebels
Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso accuse Ukraine of supporting armed groups and threatening their territorial integrity. The three Sahel nations, all ruled by military governments, have severed diplomatic relations with Kyiv and deepened their cooperation with Russia.
In September, Mali's Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine at the United Nations of "providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," reported Agence France-Presse. Diop did not provide evidence for his claim.
The three nations' governments have may have an interest in legitimizing their partnership with Moscow and portraying Kyiv as a destabilizing actor.
Oliynyk-D'omochko has found no definitive proof of the allegations, yet warned of the potential consequences for Ukraine's Africa policy. Kyiv advocates equal partnerships with African countries. Any alleged cooperation with separatists could undermine that message and affect how potential partners view Ukraine.
What price could Ukraine pay?
Engagement in Mali could offer Ukraine a relatively low-cost way to weaken Russian interests beyond Europe. A small team of specialists could train local fighters and improve their capabilities in the use of drones.
But a potential partnership with the FLA carries political risks. Because the Tuareg separatists cooperate with the JNIM, Kyiv could face accusations of indirectly supporting jihadist fighters. That could undermine Ukraine's efforts to strengthen its relations with African countries.

Russia-Ukraine war reaches orbit: What a close satellite encounter means for space operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:57:28 UTC
23:57:28 KST

In mid-October, a Russian military satellite in low-Earth orbit came dangerously close to a commercial US spacecraft reportedly serving Ukrainian military needs.
The approach was so extreme that the two spacecraft may have been “just a few meters” away from each other at one point.
Satellite trackers called the non-consensual manoeuvre a “worrisome cat-and-mouse game” in space between Russia and Ukraine, the two countries at war since February 2022.
Experts say the incident is an indication that space is increasingly turning into the final frontier for drawn-out geopolitical wars that countries can’t settle using conventional tools.
Russia’s Kosmos-2612 moved dangerously close to ICEYE-X36 equipped with a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) – a technology that can see through clouds during both day and night to create two-dimensional images of objects on Earth.
The satellite is owned by ICEYE US, an American subsidiary of Finland-based ICEYE. Analysts say ICEYE-X36 is likely used by Ukraine for satellite imagery. Kiev has formal access to data collected by the Finnish company’s constellation of SAR satellites.
ICEYE has been supplying satellite data and images to the Ukrainian armed forces since 2022.
Ukraine relies heavily on satellite networks such as Starlink, Starshield, and ICEYE to monitor Russian troop movements and run drones that both intercept missiles and strike targets.
Any disruption in the satellite network by Moscow would substantially degrade Kiev’s ability to launch precision weapons and execute interceptions.
Ukraine’s dependence on its so-called eyes-in-the-sky was on full display last week when Elon Musk’s SpaceX imposed speed restrictions on Starlink and its military-grade Starshield service.
US President Donald Trump had to intervene on Ukraine’s behalf as Musk restored internet speeds to previous levels.
Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in the department of space engineering at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, tells TRT World that the encounter was unusual in its closeness.
“We have never seen two satellites coming so close without cooperation between the operators of both satellites,” says Langbroek, who first reported the close encounter.
Earlier uncooperative approaches in space had taken place at distances of tens of kilometres, rather than a few hundred metres, he says.
Langbroek links the episode to a broader pattern that includes Russian satellites approaching other countries’ satellites apparently for eavesdropping, reported hacks of satellite feeds, on-orbit exercises involving close approaches, and tests of anti-satellite weapons.
“Space is quickly developing into a potential battlefield,” he says.
No wonder the language around space operations has also become militaristic of late: the US Space Force now treats space as a “battle domain” and has acknowledged possessing “space weapons”, he says.
Modern military operations now depend heavily on space-based communications, live data streams, including from drones, and satellite intelligence.
In the same vein, civilian life has also grown equally dependent on space-based communications, Langbroek says.
The result is heightened vulnerability for everyone, he adds.
“This is not just a military threat. It is a threat to us all,” he says.
Langbroek notes that the traditional divide between military and civilian satellites has blurred of late.
Commercial systems, such as those operated by ICEYE and Starlink, now support military tasks, he says.
Russia already considers any commercial satellite used by Ukraine as a legitimate target.
Consequently, satellite systems that multiple countries and ordinary users rely upon can become targets, potentially harming states that are not parties to the conflict, he says.
Militarisation of Earth’s orbits
Mark J Sundahl, director of the Global Space Law Centre at Cleveland State University, tells TRT World the stalking of satellites in space is on the rise.
The phenomenon is fanning global concerns about the growing militarisation of Earth’s orbits, he says.
“All kinetic warfare that could result in the creation of massive debris clouds that will stay in orbit for hundreds of years must be prohibited,” he says.
Sundahl says such action is already inconsistent with Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, which requires states to exercise “due regard to the corresponding interests” of other countries.
Generating debris clouds that threaten civilian satellites would constitute a “clear violation” of that obligation, even though he notes that not everyone shares this interpretation of the law.
“The common orbital infrastructure that we all share for purposes of telecommunication, navigation, and other daily needs cannot be put into danger due to terrestrial conflicts,” Sundahl says.
Ilyas Golcuklu, head of the private international law department at Altinbas University in Istanbul, tells TRT World that the non-consensual close approach between a military and a commercial object in space is no longer a hypothetical exercise.
“Space has already become a new frontier for geopolitical conflict,” he says.
With the growing volume of objects in orbit, distinguishing commercial from military assets will become harder, he notes.
“The escalation of national rivalries into space is a justified concern for all humankind,” he says.
Lack of established norms
Clear and widely accepted norms for uncoordinated proximity operations in space remain mostly non-existent.
Langbroek attributes this mainly to the opposition by major space powers, which have resisted rules that might constrain their own extraterrestrial activities.
In wartime, rules of conduct are often the first to be broken, he says.
“Any form of uncooperative proximity should not be performed, because of the risks involved. Yet, it happens,” he says.
Golcuklu notes that space approaches conducted for peaceful purposes – such as refuelling, repairing a component, or removing space debris – rely on technologies that are essentially identical to those needed to spy on or disable a rival satellite.
Distinguishing legitimate activity from hostile intent – and closing the regulatory vacuum – has become increasingly challenging, he says.
“Minimum safe distances” or “keep-out zones” must be devised as quickly as possible by the UN before the risks become too big to handle, he adds.
For example, experts consider the risk of a minor miscalculation resulting in collisions and creating space debris as serious.
Langbroek notes that a kinetic attack – whether by collision or by a projectile – would generate large amounts of on-orbit debris that endangers satellites belonging to countries uninvolved in any conflict.
Even non-kinetic methods, such as disabling electronics with an electromagnetic pulse, would leave the targeted satellite itself as debris, adding to collision hazards, he says.
During close approaches, the risk of an unintended collision is real: if the operator of the approached satellite becomes nervous and attempts an evasive manoeuvre, the geometry can become hazardous, he says.
Even controlled approaches in space can go wrong.
“It really is a risky thing to bring your satellite so close to another satellite, especially without coordination with the owner of that satellite,” Langbroek says.

“If such a solution could be found, there would be no need to look for people on the streets,” he said.

Full worker deferments would come with conditions
The proposal builds on changes outlined by the government on Friday, Oct. 23.

'No fuel to keep babies warm': shortages push hospitals in Yemen's Taiz to brink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:55:34 UTC
23:55:34 KST

'No fuel to keep babies warm': shortages push hospitals in Yemen's Taiz to brink
GENEVA, Oct 26 - Fuel shortages in Yemen's besieged city of Taiz have forced one hospital to cut the number of incubators it can operate from 40 to 10, putting newborn babies at risk as weeks of fighting choke off vital supplies and deepen a humanitarian crisis affecting hundreds of thousands of people.
"There's no oxygen, there's no fuel to run the incubators, to keep the babies warm," said Nada Ahmed, a nurse in the neonatal unit of the Yemeni-Swedish Hospital for Maternity and Childhood.
Nawal Najeeb, a supervisor in the neonatal unit, warned the facility could be forced to halt operations if fuel supplies do not arrive.
"It will be a catastrophe for the babies, a catastrophe of deaths and disabilities."
Taiz has been largely isolated since October 3, with fighting preventing humanitarian supplies from entering and civilians from leaving, following an escalation in clashes between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
FUEL PRICES SURGE
Key supply routes, including the Taiz-Aden corridor, have been blocked by Houthi forces, worsening shortages of water, food and fuel. The city hosts nearly half of the 250,000 people displaced by the latest fighting, according to the United Nations.
In Taiz city, 42 health facilities are reporting acute shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said.
Fuel prices have surged to 2,000 Yemeni rials per litre, driver Abdullah al-Radfani told Reuters.
Oxfam Yemen's policy, advocacy and media manager, Fatma Jaffar Shotah, described one dialysis patient who has to spend two nights at a healthcare centre rather than travelling home between sessions because regular journeys have become unaffordable, the cost rising from half a dollar to around $10.
"Fuel shortage inside the city is having catastrophic impacts on people's lives," she said.
The strain is being felt beyond Taiz. Aid group Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said fuel shortages were causing power outages at hospitals and primary healthcare centres in the southern governorates of Aden and Lahj, affecting operating theatres and intensive care units.
HUNGER AND MALNUTRITION
UN agencies and aid groups also warned of worsening hunger and malnutrition. The World Food Programme says that more than 800,000 people have been cut off from food assistance in Taiz and surrounding areas.
UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said 52,000 of the 168,000 children screened in Taiz so far this year are acutely malnourished, including more than 11,500 suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
Although UNICEF has put in place nearly 8,000 cartons of life-saving therapeutic food, enough to sustain treatment services for around three months, Pires warned that worsening insecurity and movement restrictions could hamper future deliveries and prevent families from reaching treatment centres.
MSF said growing displacement was aggravating child malnutrition in southern Yemen, an area which has already faced a long-standing hunger crisis, as families flee fighting in the north and along the west coast.
Between September 15 and October 22, MSF screened 299 children under 5 at its mobile clinics in Aden and Lahj. Forty-four children, or 14.7%, were suffering from moderate acute malnutrition, while 28 children, or 9.4%, were severely malnourished and in need of hospital care.
"In each location we go, on a daily basis, we see at least one or two children who are in severe acute malnutrition," said MSF's mobile health activity manager, Sara Ghanem. REUTERS

Israel Police race to stop election disinformation as voting nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:51:40 UTC
23:51:40 KST

Israeli police are intensifying efforts to combat domestic disinformation campaigns ahead of Tuesday's national election, targeting fake social media accounts, artificial intelligence-generated videos and coordinated influence operations aimed at manipulating voters.
The operation, led by a specialized police intelligence unit known as Matzpen, will reach its peak on Election Day and continue until polling stations close at 10 p.m.
While the Shin Bet domestic security agency has spent recent months tracking foreign influence operations intended to affect the election's outcome, police investigators are focusing on individuals and groups operating inside Israel.
Matzpen, which operates within the Israel Police Intelligence Division and the national cybercrime unit of the Investigations and Intelligence Department, has been monitoring online activity for six months in an effort to identify and disrupt attempts to undermine the integrity of the vote.
Police announced Sunday that the unit had secured the removal of two networks engaged in what authorities described as improper activity on X and Facebook.
Separately, the Yashar! party, led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot, filed a complaint after unidentified individuals allegedly forged a public message purporting to come from the party.
Fake profiles, AI videos and coordinated manipulation
According to police, domestic actors are employing an increasingly sophisticated range of tactics to influence voters, including creating fictitious social media profiles, impersonating real individuals and circulating posts that either promote or attack political candidates.
Other methods include spreading fabricated news about political parties, impersonating candidates and publishing statements in their names, and distributing AI-generated videos designed to mislead viewers.
Authorities have also identified coordinated efforts to flood social media posts with favorable or defamatory comments, creating the appearance of public support or opposition.
The techniques can make it difficult for voters to distinguish genuine political debate from organized manipulation.
Police warn that social media users should approach election-related content with caution, particularly when its source or authenticity cannot be verified.
Despite the extensive monitoring operation, investigators acknowledge that they can identify and disrupt only a small proportion of the individuals and networks engaged in such activity.
Police officials say the practice is unlikely to diminish significantly unless those responsible recognize that they could face substantial fines or prison sentences.
Police prioritize disruption over identifying operators
Police say impersonation, fraudulent accounts and automated networks designed to manipulate public opinion can constitute criminal offenses involving impersonation or forgery, depending on the circumstances.
However, investigators acknowledge that their immediate priority is stopping harmful online activity rather than identifying and prosecuting every person behind it.
"We are currently focused on monitoring the internet to identify and thwart activity across the various online platforms," police said.
That approach means authorities are concentrating on detecting coordinated campaigns and securing the removal of offending content before it reaches more voters.
Under normal circumstances, Matzpen primarily monitors social media for incitement against the State of Israel and incitement to terrorism.
With the election approaching, however, the unit has shifted significant resources toward protecting the integrity of the democratic process.
Six months of monitoring ahead of Election Day
A senior official in Matzpen, which operates within the police Intelligence Division, told ynet that investigators have been preparing for the election for approximately six months.
"We have been involved in safeguarding the integrity of Israel's elections for six months now," the official said.
"We are confronting domestic actors who are trying to undermine the integrity of the elections, and we are working around the clock to monitor the internet and identify influence operations aimed at promoting or discrediting a candidate or political party."
The official said the intensity of the operation has increased as Election Day approaches.
"Our work is becoming increasingly intensive as we get closer to Election Day," the official said. "Tomorrow will be our busiest day, and until the polls close, we will work to thwart online activity by bots seeking to smear a rival party or promote a candidate or political party."
Investigators are also targeting accounts that impersonate real people or fabricate political identities.
"We are also disrupting the activity of online impersonators and fictitious personas that publish posts, tweets or TikTok videos containing fake news or impersonating candidates running in the election," the official said.
Working with social media companies to remove content
When investigators identify suspected coordinated manipulation, they work through the cyber department of the State Attorney's Office to request the removal of offending content.
The requests are directed to operators of major social media platforms, including X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook.
"When we identify such activity, we contact the operators of Twitter, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook through the cyber department of the State Attorney's Office and ask them to remove activity that we have been able to establish is improper," the senior official said.
The process requires investigators to establish that the targeted activity violates applicable rules or laws before seeking its removal.
Police have not disclosed how many individuals are suspected of operating the networks or whether the two networks removed from X and Facebook were connected to particular political parties or candidates.
The operation comes amid broader concerns about efforts to manipulate Israel's election through both domestic and foreign influence campaigns.
For police, the immediate challenge is the speed at which misleading content can spread across social media, particularly in the final hours before voting ends.
Authorities say they will continue monitoring the platforms until the last polling stations close Tuesday night, seeking to prevent coordinated disinformation campaigns from influencing voters before ballots are cast.

Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a highly anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.
According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.
“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”
The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.
Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.
While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”
Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.
It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply chain risk.
“While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the US government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” the filing concluded.
In September, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI—which filed confidentially for IPO in the summer—announced that it no longer intended to go public this year, citing concerns over the risks posed to humanity by AI.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI, who had reportedly lost faith in the lab’s ability to develop advanced AI models safely. Anthropic markets itself as highly safety-conscious; its CEO, Dario Amodei, has repeatedly commented on the risk that AI could eliminate scores of jobs, and act against human interests.
The filings also outline Anthropic’s ambition to develop sophisticated AI models capable of accelerating scientific discovery, curing disease, and spurring economic growth.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” the company wrote.
The company did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Hezbollah readies for new regional war with funds from Iran, sources say
BEIRUT, Oct 26 - Lebanese armed group Hezbollah has spent three months preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.
The group, founded by Iran's Revolutionary Guards in 1982, has been dealt severe blows in two wars with Israel since 2024, with thousands of fighters and many of its leaders killed, and much of its arsenal destroyed.
Invading Israeli forces now occupy its heartland of villages in southern Lebanon, and political pressure has built up in Beirut for its disarmament.
It nevertheless remains committed to fighting Israel and has used a lull in hostilities since June to rearm, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into Israeli positions, two Lebanese security sources told Reuters.
One of the sources, and another close to Hezbollah, said the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities. That is in addition to around $200 million that the group received from Tehran to aid displaced families in its Shi'ite heartlands, which Reuters reported earlier this month.
The group has been restoring command-and-control structures that broke down in key battles, according to one of those sources and three other security officials familiar with the group's operations.
In response to questions from Reuters, Hezbollah's media office said Israel's occupation of Lebanese land made any resistance to it a legitimate right. It rejected the suggestion that its command-and-control systems had broken down.
Israel's military declined to comment. Iran's permanent mission to the United Nations in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters questions.
A US State Department spokesman said Washington would keep strangling Hezbollah's finances through sanctions and other measures. A US Treasury spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to move money.
HEZBOLLAH ON ALERT
Hezbollah's effort comes amid continued tensions in the wider Middle Eastern conflict ignited by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February.
Hezbollah opened fire in support of Iran on March 2, triggering an Israeli offensive that killed more than 4,000 people and uprooted a quarter of Lebanon's population, mostly members of Hezbollah's Shi'ite Muslim constituency.
Hostilities largely abated over the summer as an interim Iran-US deal included a Lebanon ceasefire and Washington mediated talks between Lebanon and Israel. Full-scale hostilities have not resumed in Lebanon despite the collapse of the US-Iranian deal, though Israel continues deadly strikes in the south.
Hezbollah is on alert for a possible US-Iran escalation, potentially reigniting the Lebanon front.
The sources told Reuters the group had not yet managed to fully prepare its stockpiles or fighting force.
Hezbollah is still restocking, acknowledging this month that explosives seized by Lebanese authorities belonged to it and were intended for use against Israel. A Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters they were specifically for its explosive drones.
ISRAEL'S REMOTE WARFARE PROVED A CHALLENGE, SOURCES SAY
The group will also need to repair command-and-control capabilities after losses on key fronts, including the flashpoint town of Bint Jbeil and the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, according to one of the Lebanese sources and three security officials.
They said Hezbollah's tactic of operating in small units and rationing the use of anti-tank rockets left some units isolated on those fronts, struggling to confront Israel's remotely operated systems including weaponized drones and armed remote-controlled vehicles.
The Israeli military told Reuters it uses remotely-operated systems to monitor southern Lebanon and reduce troops' threat exposure.
Hezbollah has not explicitly said whether it would take part in the eruption of fresh hostilities, but its media office said it was wary of giving Israeli leaders any justification to escalate in Lebanon, particularly as the group was concerned about its constituents being displaced once more. “Conversations with other countries are also ongoing,” he added.

Patriot missiles
Ukraine could have had enough Patriot air defense missiles to sustain its systems for several years if more interceptors had not been expended in the Middle East, Yuriy Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Ukrainian Air Force Command, said on the RBC-Ukraine podcast.
Ihnat revealed that Ukrainian forces have developed tactics for using the US-made systems more efficiently during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Unlike crews that keep Patriots at fixed positions, Ukrainian operators can set up ambushes, engage targets, and quickly relocate to avoid detection.
Ukrainian crews have also learned to conserve expensive interceptors, typically using one missile per target. By contrast, air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight missiles at a single target, including relatively cheap Shahed drones.
A senior Ukrainian Air Force officer previously told The Times that Gulf forces were using excessive numbers of interceptors and that Ukraine’s battlefield experience had not been fully incorporated despite Kyiv sharing operational data with allies.
Ukraine’s missile shortages remain acute. Earlier, Zelensky said Ukraine received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite needing around 350 per month to counter Russian ballistic attacks.
He has requested 300 interceptors from European partners for the winter, but efforts to secure missiles from existing European stockpiles have faced resistance, including from Greece.
