US singer Chris Brown spared jail for UK nightclub attack
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:23:15 CET
23:23:15 KST

By Sam Tobin
LONDON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US singer Chris Brown was spared an immediate prison sentence in Britain on Monday for attacking a music producer with a tequila bottle in a London nightclub in 2023, with his fans cheering as the musician walked free from court.
Brown, 37, was given an eight-month suspended sentence at London’s Southwark Crown Court over the attack on Abraham Diaw at the Tape nightclub in February 2023 that lasted around 20 seconds.
Diaw was hit twice in the head with a bottle, which was then swung twice more at him in what prosecutors described as “a vicious and unprovoked attack”.
The R&B star and his vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu, 40, pleaded guilty to a charge of affray in July, having denied more serious charges of attempting to inflict grievous bodily harm and assault causing actual bodily harm.
NO SPECIAL TREATMENT
Judge Tony Baumgartner said: “This was serious, public violence. In your case, Brown, it involved the repeated use … of a bottle, including twice striking Diaw to his head.”
The judge told Brown: “Your fame, commercial success and professional standing do not entitle you to special treatment – the law applies equally to everyone.”
But Baumgartner said he could suspend Brown’s sentence for 12 months, meaning he will not go to prison unless he commits another offence in that period. Akinlolu was also spared an immediate jail sentence.
“Violence will not be accepted on the streets of London,” Detective Chief Superintendent Christina Jessah from the Metropolitan Police said in a statement. “Regardless of an individual’s profile or status, we will pursue those responsible and work tirelessly to bring them before the courts.”
BROWN’S FANS CHEER SUSPENDED SENTENCE
Brown, winner of Grammy awards for best R&B album in 2011 and 2025, has previously admitted other violent offences in the US, having been charged with assaulting his then-partner, singer Rihanna, in 2009, with a photo of her bruised face making headlines around the world.
Prosecutor Heidi Stonecliffe said Brown pleaded guilty to the 2009 assault of Rihanna and was sentenced to five years’ probation. He also admitted a 2013 assault on a fan he was accused of punching when he asked for a photograph.
Brown remains hugely popular and has sold tens of millions of records worldwide, with dozens of fans queuing outside court from around 0700 GMT, about an hour before the building opened.
His lawyer Sallie Bennett-Jenkins said Brown was profoundly sorry for the incident and described him as “a dedicated, loving and loyal father to four children”.
“This was an ugly and unattractive incident, we would be the first to accept,” she added. “It was, however, an incident that was very short-lived.”
Brown thanked the judge before leaving the dock and nodding towards about two dozen of his supporters in the public gallery.
Other fans who gathered outside the building cheered as Brown left and went into a waiting car.
Brown was arrested in May 2025 having returned to Britain for the first time since the attack and was initially denied bail, throwing his worldwide “Breezy Bowl XX” tour into doubt.
But Brown was eventually released after promising to pay a £5 million ($6.7 million) security fee, allowing the tour to go ahead.
($1 = 0.7487 pounds)
(Reporting by Sam Tobin; Editing by William James and David Holmes)

Russia against forced evacuation, hope for deal compliance: Alyoshki situation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:23:02 UTC
23:23:02 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The Russian Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova responded to Kiev’s statements by saying that forced evacuation of families with children from Alyoshki in the Kherson Region is unacceptable.
Russia hopes that Ukraine will fulfill all agreements on the humanitarian mission in the city, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
TASS has compiled the key facts known at the moment.
Implementation of the ceasefire plan
- The United States has prepared a detailed plan for how the ceasefire regime in Alyoshki will function down to the minute, said Marc Beckman, senior adviser to the First Lady of the United States, in a comment to Vesti.
- On October 24, Lantratova said that both Russia and Ukraine are fulfilling their commitments under the agreements on the humanitarian mission in the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region.
Russia not amenable to forced evacuation
- Lantratova responded to Kiev’s statements by saying that the forcible removal of families with children from Alyoshki is unacceptable.
- She pointed out that if Ukraine wants people to make an informed decision, it should give them that opportunity by allowing them to live in peace and ordering its military to stop daily shelling of the town and mining of the roads.
- The ombudsman noted that people "are capable of making informed decisions on their own."
- "Everything must be done voluntarily, taking into account their interests specifically, and not those of the Kiev authorities, who have suddenly become concerned about the people living there," she said.
- Lantratova reminded that Alyoshki is Russian territory, where only Russian laws apply, and references to Ukrainian legislation carry no weight there.
Fake concern about residents
- Kiev is claiming in Ukrainian media that it is concerned about the residents of Alyoshki, Rodion Miroshnik, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s ambassador-at-large on issues related to the crimes of the Kiev regime, wrote on Telegram.
- However, he said that on October 24 between 7:15 a.m. (4:15 a.m. GMT) and 8:30 a.m. (5:30 a.m. GMT) 28 mines were launched at Alyoshki; at night, Ukrainian drones continued to remotely mine the access routes to the town.
- The civilian population of Alyoshki did not receive humanitarian aid from Ukraine; all reports to the contrary are false, Svetlana Popova, an evacuated resident of the town, told TASS.
Reaction to the ceasefire
- Lantratova thanked US First Lady Melania Trump and all members of the negotiation group for their cooperation in organizing a humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres welcomed the agreement, according to a statement by his official spokesman Stephane Dujarric.
- Guterres also expressed hope that this and other steps will help improve the dire humanitarian situation in Alyoshki and will make it possible to immediately provide vital assistance, as well as to carry out a safe and voluntary evacuation of the city’s residents in strict compliance with international humanitarian law.
- White House Communications Director Steven Cheung called the agreements an important step towards resolving the Ukrainian conflict.
- The humanitarian communication channel between Lantratova and Melania Trump’s team on Alyoshki will help convey the truth about the living conditions in the city, which remains under Ukrainian blockade, Miroshnik said.
- Konstantin Basyuk, deputy head of the Federation Council Committee on Defense and Security, expressed hope that the humanitarian corridor to the town would not be disrupted.
- Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow hopes that Ukraine will fulfill all agreements on the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- In his opinion, the agreements on the humanitarian operation could set a precedent for missions in other areas as well.
Agreement between Moscow and Kiev
- The White House said on October 23 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to cease fire in Alyoshki starting on October 29, 2026.
- It was noted that the countries agreed to cease all hostilities in Alyoshki to ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid and to prepare for the evacuation of the civilians through a special safe corridor.
- Reports also indicated that an independent media organization from the United States would monitor and document the actions of Russian and Ukrainian groups on the ground throughout the entire process.
- Later, Chief of the General Staff, Army General Valery Gerasimov, said that Russia would introduce a ceasefire in the Kherson direction starting at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27 to carry out the humanitarian operation.
- Ukraine’s General Staff said that it would observe the ceasefire starting from 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27 to carry out the humanitarian operation.
The situation in the city
- On September 21, Peskov described the humanitarian situation as critical.
- Kiev’s shelling and drone attacks made the delivery of any food or medicines to the town impossible.
- On September 1, a decisive attempt was made to break the blockade to deliver humanitarian aid, but Ukrainian militants fired on the convoy of vehicles and almost completely destroyed the cargo, said Miroshnik.
- Four vehicles loaded with ten tons of food were attacked at the entrance to the town.
- Residents of nearby settlements on the left bank of the Dnepr tried to deliver food to Alyoshki, but Ukraine prevented this, Svetlana Popova, an evacuated resident of the town, told TASS.
- Slightly more than 1,000 people remain in Alyoshki, Miroshnik said in a comment to Vesti.
- Previously, more than 20,000 people lived in the city, he said.
- Miroshnik noted that the situation deteriorated over the past four to five months.

'Rubens fans' protest against TotalEnergies’ museum sponsorship
Unknown

Environmental activists protested at the KMSKA, Antwerp’s Fine Arts Museum, on Sunday. The protesters are unhappy about sponsorship of the museum by French oil and gas producer TotalEnergies. They call themselves the ‘Rubens-fans’ and sang protest songs. They believe the museum is helping the company to polish up its image. The museum says it needs sponsorship and that it does, in fact, adhere to a code of ethics.
“Look at this painting that’s been restored by Total – KMSKA, this really isn’t on,” several environmental activists inside the museum shouted on Sunday. They criticise the KMSKA for accepting money from TotalEnergies in order to restore paintings.
“In this way, the museum is allowing itself to be used to boost the oil giant’s dubious reputation,” they say. Among other things, they point out that TotalEnergies has been found jointly liable for global warming.
‘Bribery and negligent environmental policy’
‘For decades, the French oil company has been guilty of bribery and negligent environmental policy and has been convicted in court for these offences. Furthermore, TotalEnergies intimidates critics by taking legal action against them.’
‘For example, in 2023, the company took Greenpeace to court after the environmental organisation had revealed that in reports TotalEnergies systematically underestimated its own emissions. In October 2025, however, Greenpeace was vindicated and a French court found the company guilty of greenwashing on account of deliberately misleading consumers about its emissions and climate targets.’
Funding needed
“We have indeed been working with TotalEnergies and many other parties since 2023 to restore a fantastic masterpiece by Rubens,” says Carmen Willems, director of the KMSKA. “At present, the KMSKA receives no government funding for restoration projects. Nevertheless, we are carrying out a number of them, all of which are entirely privately funded.”
“It is already very difficult just to keep a museum running, and these pieces are really in need of restoration. That is why we have launched a major campaign in which we have asked a number of companies to support us in this endeavour.”
According to Willems, TotalEnergies also meets the criteria for sponsorship. “It is a listed company and is required to report transparently and openly on the impact of its activities on people and the environment. In international rankings, it scores significantly higher than its competitors in its sector in terms of environmental policy and climate targets.”
This was not the first time that campaigners had criticised TotalEnergies’ sponsorship. The museum invited the campaigners, as it had done previously, to a meeting. “We will clearly explain our considerations regarding sponsorship policy. As a museum, we adhere to the code of ethics on sponsorship. But the campaigners never accepted our invitation.”

On Monday afternoon, two Palestinians were killed and another injured in an Israeli strike on a vehicle in Deir al-Balah.
Earlier on Monday, civil defence spokesperson Mahmoud Bassal reported that at least 13 people had been killed and 60 injured by Israeli fire and airstrikes across Gaza over the previous 24 hours.

Osama al-Kahlout, a resident of Deir al-Balah, said the Israeli army had advanced west of the demarcation line several times over the past week.
"These movements have forced residents to flee their homes and shelters, only to return when the forces pull back, leaving families in a constant state of uncertainty and fear," al-Kahlout toldThe New Arab.
Residents, he added, were growing "increasingly concerned that these advances could be part of a gradual effort to reposition troops and expand the Yellow Line westward, rather than temporary military operations."
The so-called 'Yellow Line', marked by large yellow concrete blocks, delineates areas under Israeli military control.
Although the initial arrangement under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan was intended to be temporary and followed by a gradual Israeli withdrawal, the Israeli military has instead expanded its area of control. Estimates now suggest Israel controls nearly two-thirds of the besieged Palestinian territory.

Military expansion ahead of elections
Ibrahim said the "repeated advances and withdrawals could indicate an attempt to gradually expand the area under Israeli control and establish new military positions."
"Maintaining Israeli military control over parts of Gaza and expanding the area under its control could serve the objectives of [Benjamin Netanyahu’s] far-right coalition, which opposes a full Israeli withdrawal and seeks to impose new realities on the ground," Ibrahim told The New Arab.
With Israel heading to the polls on Tuesday, Ibrahim argued that Netanyahu’s continued military operations in Gaza were closely tied to his political survival.
Netanyahu "seeks to project an image of strength and security to Israeli voters, particularly among right-wing constituencies that support maintaining military pressure on Hamas," he said.
The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Gaza, also faces fierce criticism from opponents over the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
Gaza has seen an escalation in Israeli attacks in the week preceding the general election. The total death toll since the start of Israel’s genocidal campaign has reached 74,555.
"Ultimately, the continuation of these operations risks deepening Palestinian suffering while leaving the political future of Gaza increasingly uncertain," Ibrahim said.

Lula’s comeback puts brakes on Latin America’s rightward surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:21:34 UTC
23:21:34 KST

Brazil’s re-elected leader now faces a hostile Congress at home and a Trump administration that had bet heavily on his rival.
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s narrow victory in Brazil’s presidential run-off on Sunday has ended a run of seven consecutive conservative wins in Latin American presidential elections over the past 18 months.
The leftist incumbent beat Flávio Bolsonaro by 51.8% to 48.2%. Bolsonaro has said he will challenge the result and seek its annulment, after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Voters across the region, frustrated by organised crime and economic hardship, have increasingly backed hard-line candidates, from Peru’s Keiko Fujimori to Chile’s José Antonio Kast. Washington has encouraged the trend with endorsements, bailouts and military aid.
“The US is certainly putting its finger on the scale to try to help the more hard-line right-wing elements in the region,” Kenneth Roberts, a professor of government at Cornell University, told the Associated Press.
Brazil, Latin America’s largest economy, would have been the biggest prize. Bolsonaro had pledged to join a US-led anti-cartel coalition and campaigned on his closeness to Trump.
Instead, Washington’s pressure may have helped Lula. The steep tariffs Trump imposed on Brazilian goods over the prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro for a coup plot triggered a nationalist backlash, which Lula channelled into the slogan “Brazil belongs to Brazilians”.
“To the extent that the regional superpower becomes a threat to Brazil’s democratic institutions, defending Brazilian national sovereignty also becomes a form of defending Brazilian democracy,” Roberts said.
'Brazil has leverage'
Lula has refused to join the US-led Shield of the Americas coalition. “We don’t accept being treated like children,” he said in May, after Washington designated Brazil’s two largest gangs as terrorist organisations.
Brazil also holds valuable cards: the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves and around 90% of global niobium output, both vital to defence industries.
"Brazil has leverage," said Monica de Bolle of the Peterson Institute for International Economics. “With Lula, the US is on shakier ground.”
Yet analysts warn against reading too much into one result. Conservatives strengthened their grip on Brazil’s Congress this month, leaving Lula struggling to pass reforms.
“Lula has his hands tied,” said Guilherme Casarões of Florida International University.
A setback for Trump
The defeat of a Trump-backed candidate comes just over a week before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
A CNN poll put Trump’s approval rating at a record low of 32%. An NBC News/Telemundo survey found 68% of Latino voters disapprove of his foreign policy, a significant shift among a group that helped return him to power in 2024.
Reaction split along party lines. Donald Trump Jr attacked the extension of voting hours, while Democratic congressman Ro Khanna urged the president to respect the result.
Both governments still have reasons to cooperate, with Washington seeking rare earths and Lula wanting tariff relief.
"Lula is pragmatic enough to work out some kind of modus operandi with the Trump administration," said Will Freeman of the Council on Foreign Relations, adding that the Bolsonaros’ allies in Washington were likely to lose influence after the family’s second straight defeat.

Elvis Presley music rights holders sue Anthropic over AI training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:21:20 UTC
23:21:20 KST

Efe Ozkan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The owners of rights to Elvis Presley’s music catalog have sued artificial intelligence company Anthropic, accusing it of using 274 songs recorded by the singer to train its Claude AI models without permission, The Guardian reported Sunday.
The lawsuit was filed Friday in the US District Court for the Northern District of California by a subsidiary of Authentic Brands Group, which acquired Presley’s intellectual property and trademark rights in 2013.
The plaintiffs include music publishers Raleigh Music Publishing and Abilene Music, as well as trusts linked to songwriter Luigi Creatore and the Aberbach family, whose publishing business controlled rights to songs recorded by Presley.
The lawsuit alleges that Anthropic copied the songs without a license or payment and retained the material in an internal repository for training future versions of Claude.
The catalog allegedly includes Can’t Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up, Don’t Be Cruel, A Little Less Conversation and Return to Sender.
The plaintiffs are seeking $150,000 for each of the 274 allegedly infringed songs, amounting to $41.1 million, with additional damages bringing their total claim to $48.6 million.
Lead attorney Richard Busch accused Anthropic of building its business on copyright infringement and said the plaintiffs were “deeply protective” of the songs.
Anthropic disputed the allegations.
“We disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully,” the company told NBC News.
The case is among a growing number of copyright disputes between AI developers and the music industry and could have broader implications for how copyrighted music is used to train AI models.

Finance ministry proposes abolishing child benefits amid sweeping reform suggestions
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:20:21 EET
23:20:21 KST

The Ministry of Finance has published a list of proposals aimed at strengthening Finland's public finances — with suggestions on how to reduce public expenditure, increase tax revenues and secure the foundations of the welfare state.
The ministry's report will be used to inform government formation talks after next April's parliamentary elections.
"Political decision-makers will be faced with numerous important decisions in the coming years as they seek to respond to evolving global challenges and build a better future," the ministry said in a press release.
The ministry noted in particular that Finland's general government expenditure as a share of GDP has been higher than state revenue every year since 2009, driving Finland into a "cycle of indebtedness".
"Public finances are in a weak state. We have not been bold enough over the past decades in making reforms and prioritising what we use our shared resources on," Director General of the ministry's budget department Mika Niemelä said, adding that resolving this situation "requires bold, determined action" from politicians.
Earlier this year, all but one of Finland's major political parties agreed to a public finance adjustment — otherwise known as a "debt brake" — of between 8 and 11 billion euros for the next parliamentary term, with only the opposition Left Alliance rejecting the deal.
The agreement sets limits on how much debt a sitting government can take on, regardless of which parties are in power.
While describing the scale of the necessary adjustments as "significant", the ministry added that securing the sustainability of public finances is possible.
Abolishing child benefits?
The finance ministry's Expenditure and Structural Survey, one of two surveys on which its report is based, is divided into different areas — such as healthcare and social welfare, social security benefits, education, as well as business and industry.
In total, the ministry makes about 400 proposals in relation to these areas of public finances.
Among the most significant proposed changes, the ministry suggests abolishing child benefits altogether, or ending various sibling and single-parent supplements. This would save the state about 1.2 billion euros, according to the ministry's calculations.
The ministry also wants to make cuts to social security payments such as basic social assistance, a last-resort form of benefit, and general housing allowance. Various reductions are also proposed to the state pension system, while certain conditions would be removed from earnings-related pensions.
Another significant proposal relates to the adjusting or dismantling of index-linked increases to spending. This means freezing the indices for a set period of time, lowering their level, or removing them altogether.
In practice, this would affect earnings-related pensions, social security benefits, as well as the services offered by municipalities and regional healthcare authorities. This would generate savings of around two billion euros over the coming decade, the ministry said.
Other measures
Among the ministry's other proposals are an overhaul of Finland's network of regional healthcare authorities, including a reduction in the number of wellbeing services counties (which currently stands at 21) as well as the ending of round-the-clock emergency care services in certain areas.
"These matters are of course among the politically most difficult, especially when it comes to reducing the number of regions and the network. This certainly won't be achieved during the next parliamentary term, and so it won't yet strengthen public finances," Niemelä noted.
In education, the ministry suggested making changes to staffing ratios, abolishing the practice of providing extra funding to schools in more disadvantaged areas, and rowing back on the extension of compulsory schooling in Finland to age 18.
In the area of state administration, the finance ministry proposed reducing the number of government ministries from the current level of 12 to nine.
In its press release, the ministry emphasised that its list of proposals is "not a recommendation of the Ministry of Finance or a proposal for what measures to implement", adding that the aim is to provide a wide range of options and estimates of how they would impact public finances.
Taxing questions
In addition to spending cuts and structural changes, the Finnish state also needs more tax revenue.
"We are not recommending one single package of tax increases, nor are we taking a position on how much taxation should be tightened. There is a long list of proposals here for politicians to choose from," Terhi Järvikare, Director General of the ministry's Tax Department, said.
These possibilities include raising income and corporate tax levels, as well as VAT rates.
"Raising VAT is less harmful than tightening taxation on labour and businesses. Reduced VAT rates are an inefficient way to support disadvantaged groups. There are more effective means available for that," Järvikare explained.
Changes to Finland's VAT rates could bring in hundreds of millions of euros, she added, noting further that any changes to taxation should have as little impact as possible on Finland's economic growth and employment levels.
"It would be good to find a few large packages rather than making many small measures. That would also make it easier to assess the effects," Järvikare said.

Aysu Bicer

Almost 1 kilometer of London's Oxford Street has become traffic-free, with Mayor Sadiq Khan describing the move as "a truly momentous occasion for the capital."
The traffic-free zone covers the stretch between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street, preventing buses, taxis, private hire vehicles, private motorized vehicles, cycles, scooters and pedicabs from entering the area. Vehicles will be diverted onto nearby roads.
Deliveries will be permitted between midnight and 7 am local time, while emergency services will retain access to the street, one of the world's busiest shopping areas.
Khan described the pedestrianization project as "a new vibrant destination" and said he was excited to see his vision for the famous shopping street finally come to life.
"Revitalising Oxford Street will boost jobs and economic growth in the capital, unlock the full potential of this key part of the West End and help build a better, greener and more prosperous London for everyone," he said.
"There has been talk of pedestrianising Oxford Street for decades. After so many false dawns, and now working with a Government who share the scale of my ambition, I'm proud that we're finally unlocking a new era for the street," he noted.
Khan hopes the move will create opportunities for a wider range of activities and public experiences, including sports, fashion and cultural events.

Sugar rush: blood bank acts to stem flow of free iced biscuits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

23:18:59 KST

Sugar rush: blood bank acts to stem flow of free iced biscuits
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch blood bank Sanquin has had to lock away the iced biscuits it hands out to donors after discovering it was haemorrhaging money through the heartwarming gesture.
A volunteer at the donation point in Delft told Omroep West the organisation had taken the drastic step because some visitors were abusing its generosity. “People were going out of here with their bags full,” they said.
Sanquin’s Instagram page promotes the pink-topped biscuits as a “well-earned tradition” to thank blood donors and restore their blood sugar levels.
But according to volunteers, the gesture is costing it around €1,000 a month in Delft alone, forcing it to put the biscuits behind the counter.
Instead there are now laminated menus in the café telling people they can ask for a biscuit after they have given blood.
Not all Sanquin donation points have withdrawn the biscuits. NOS found they were still on display in Utrecht and at a football club in Utrecht.
A spokesman for Sanquin’s head office said it was up to individual branches to decide, but confirmed that at some locations there were problems with “people taking more than we would reasonably expect.”
A volunteer in The Hague said: “We see people taking more than they should, but if they say they’re taking them home, should we be forbidding that?”

The government is relaunching the competition for the position of head of ARMA
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:17:47 EET
23:17:47 KST

The government is relaunching the competition for the position of head of ARMA
Kyiv • UNN
Applications to participate in the new competition will be accepted from October 26 to November 26, 2026. The previous selection process ended without a winner.
The Cabinet of Ministers announced a competition for the position of head of the National Agency for Finding, Tracing and Management of Assets Derived from Corruption and Other Crimes (ARMA). Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, UNN reports.
Details
"We are announcing an open and transparent competition for the position of head of the National Agency for Finding, Tracing and Management of Assets Derived from Corruption and Other Crimes. The Agency needs a leader trusted by both society and its partners. I invite everyone with management experience, an impeccable reputation and a desire to be useful to their country to participate," Koretskyi wrote.
Background
In June 2025, on Wednesday, 18 June, the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine voted in full for Draft Law No. 12374-d, which provides for reform of the Asset Recovery and Management Agency.
Under the adopted law, the head of ARMA may be:
-  a citizen of Ukraine who has a higher legal or economic education at a level no lower than specialist (master’s); 
-  at least five years of professional experience in the relevant specialty; 
-  at least three years of experience in managerial positions in state authorities, enterprises, institutions or organizations, regardless of their form of ownership; 
-  fluent in the state language and proficient in a foreign language that is one of the official languages of the Council of Europe; 
-  of proven integrity and competent; 
-  capable, based on their professional and moral qualities and educational and professional level, of performing the relevant official duties. 
On 25 September last year, the Cabinet of Ministers formed the Selection Commission that will choose the new head of the National Agency for Finding, Tracing and Management of Assets (ARMA).
Ukrainian and international experts joined the commission. They include:
-  Wolf-Tilmann Baumert - a German prosecutor and specialist in investigating economic crimes; 
-  Serhii But - chairman of the board of JSC "Prozorro.Sale"; 
-  Anzhelika Krusian - academic secretary of the Institute of State and Law of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine; 
-  Valentyna Lukianets-Shakhova - a researcher at the National Academy of Internal Affairs; 
-  Kateryna Ryzhenko - a representative of Transparency International Ukraine, who has monitored ARMA’s activities and promoted legislative changes for many years; 
-  Rita Simoes - a Portuguese prosecutor and expert at the Basel Institute on Governance in the areas of financial crime and asset recovery. 
On 9 December 2025, the announcement was made regarding the submission of documents for the position of head of ARMA; they had to be submitted by 19 January. At that time, 20 candidates applied for the position of head of ARMA.
However, on 19 January this year, the commission selecting the head of ARMA decided to extend the deadline for submitting documents by three weeks for everyone wishing to participate in the competition. The reason was the small number of candidates.
We have already received a number of document packages from candidates, and we would like to discuss the next steps. At least 13 candidates applied. Unfortunately, this is not the number that we, as a commission, would like to see in order to ensure, in our view, the most competitive and professional selection possible. Therefore, at this meeting I would propose discussing whether we, as a commission, are ready to extend the deadline for submitting documents in order to provide more opportunities for everyone interested
The first stage of the competition – testing on knowledge of legislation – took place on 11 March. Fourteen of the 15 applicants passed it. The second stage of the competition - general aptitude testing - took place on 24 March. Only one candidate - Viktor Dubovyk - passed it.
On 16 April, the Selection Commission interviewed Dubovyk at an official meeting.
As a result, Dubovyk received 4 votes from members of the Selection Commission; however, the commission stated that "the candidate cannot be included by the Selection Commission in the proposal to the Cabinet of Ministers for appointment to the position of Head of the National Agency."
The Commission referred to the law under which a decision is considered adopted if it is supported by at least four members of the selection commission, including at least two members of the selection commission appointed by the Cabinet of Ministers based on proposals from development partners.
Dubovyk received only one vote from an international member. It should be noted that Kateryna Ryzhenko and Rita Simoes opposed his candidacy.
They explained their position by citing doubts about the origin of some of Dubovyk’s assets and the candidate’s "superficial answers."
On June 10, the selection commission decided to conduct a repeat selection after all candidates had been eliminated in the previous one.
"I propose putting the following motion to a vote: to conduct a repeat competitive selection for the position of Head of ARMA,"
The relevant decision was supported by all members of the selection commission.
"The Commission understands that we must make every effort to ensure that the next, repeat competition proceeds with candidates from among whom we can propose one or several candidates for appointment,"
On October 19, the selection commission for the position of Head of ARMA held a meeting at which it approved updated procedural documents and officially announced the start of a new competition to select the Head of the Asset Recovery and Management Agency.
Documents may be submitted from October 26 to November 26, 2026 (inclusive).
The selection commission also allowed applicants to submit a certificate of proficiency in the state language throughout the selection process, but no later than three days before the interview.
We would like to remind you
Yaroslava Maksymenko has been appointed acting Head of the National Agency for Asset Recovery and Management.

NATO Brigade in Latvia launches 'most extensive' deployment exercises, Latvian army says
The NATO Multinational Brigade in Latvia has launched its most extensive force deployment exercises, the Latvian army said on Oct. 26, as the Baltic states bulk up their defensive capabilities amid growing threats from Russia.
The Resolute Reforger 2026 exercises, scheduled from Oct. 26 to Nov. 2, will involve about 3,000 soldiers and 1,000 units of equipment, moving on roads and railways, according to the Latvian army.
"The aim of the drill is to test the brigade's ability to move, supply, and guide units at long distances in cooperation with the National Armed Forces," the Latvian army said.

The training sites would feature soldiers and Canadian CH-146 Griffon military helicopters, according to the Latvian army.
The NATO Multinational Brigade in Latvia is a Canadian-led defensive formation that has taken center stage in protecting the alliance's eastern flank, heavily utilizing operational insights and lessons learned from the war in Ukraine.
Security concerns continue to grow in the Baltic region. NATO officials have warned about Russian drone incursions, airspace violations, sabotage, and other hybrid threats, while countries in the region have been strengthening air defenses. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, NATO has reinforced the eastern flank by deploying additional troops and preparing a rapid-response plan.
In an interview with the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 22, Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics said that NATO troops already stationed on the alliance's eastern flank would be ready immediately in the event of a Russian incursion.
"If someone plans something, we are not expecting two weeks' debate in Brussels," he said. "We are expecting a very, very swift response from NATO troops that are stationed in Eastern flank countries."

“Strasbourg Calling” Daphne Caruana Galizia’s son calls for a retrial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:17:12 UTC
23:17:12 KST

Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
The European Pariament Prize for Independent Journalism is named after Daphne Caruana Galizia
“Strasbourg Calling” Daphne Caruana Galizia’s son calls for a retrial
Impunity for attacks on journalists in Europe is a worrying sign
Interview with Interview with Matthew Caruana Galizia
Monday 26 October 2026 15:32
Monday, 26 October 2026, 15:32
Matthew Caruana Galizia
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
October brings back two names that Europe must not reduce to mere anniversaries: Anna Politkovskaya, the Russian journalist murdered in Moscow 20 years ago, in October, and Daphne Caruana Galizia, the Maltese investigative journalist killed in Malta nine years ago, also in October.
This year, the European Parliament’s commemoration of Daphne Caruana Galizia has been overshadowed by a new twist in the legal proceedings. On 2 September, a jury acquitted Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech of charges of complicity in her murder and criminal conspiracy. On 22 September, the Attorney General appealed the verdict, while an investigation into possible misconduct by jury members has further undermined confidence in the trial.
What remains of justice when people have been convicted of carrying out the murder itself, but responsibility for commissioning it continues to be contested in court? And what does this case tell us about the protection of journalists in Europe?
Matthew Caruana Galizia is the son of the Maltese investigative journalist and chairs the foundation established in her memory. Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed when a bomb planted in her car exploded.
“Our top priority at the moment is to fight for a retrial, because there were serious problems with the trial over the summer, particularly with the selection of the jury. So this is the most important issue for us right now. I see no reason why there should not be a retrial,” he told the BNR on the live "Strasbourg Calling" programme from the European Parliament in Strasbourg. He added:
Matthew Caruana Galizia and Irina Nedeva in Radio Studio 3 at the European Parliament on “Strasbourg Calling”, 21 October 2026
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova
“One of the most troubling aspects of our justice system is that jurors are not required to explain why they reached a particular verdict. This means they can base their decisions on corruption or prejudice without facing any consequences.”
According to him, Malta’s institutions remain crippled and unable to provide society with the democracy and freedom it needs.
“It is not enough for the Attorney General simply to bring charges. The justice system itself must deliver fair outcomes,” Matthew Caruana Galizia stressed, adding:
“And if we cannot obtain fair outcomes, then Parliament and the government should step in and amend the legislation so that fair outcomes become possible.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with Matthew Caruana Galizia was aired on the BNR's Horizon channel and can be heard HERE.

At the Port Huron rally, he said he is “polling at 99% in Israel,” which will hold national elections on Tuesday.
Trump did not cite evidence for the claim, and no publicly available surveys support it. While he has historically been popular among Israelis, a June poll by the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) found the Israeli public’s trust in him was declining. The poll said 12% of Israelis reported having a great deal of trust in Trump, down from 21% in May, while the share of Israelis who completely distrust him rose from 32% to 37%.
Trump joined his comments about Jews and Israel with anti-Muslim rhetoric about El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim in the Senate if he is elected.
El-Sayed 'on the side of the terrorists,' Trump says
Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” who was “on the side of the terrorists,” adding that he would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”
He threatened that “if Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”
Trump claimed that El-Sayed’s half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, celebrated the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. On the first anniversary of the attack, Abdelhadi posted a video that said, “no matter how great the brutality, the oppression, the intensity of what we’re going through, the horizon of justice is just around the corner,” according to The New York Times. She did not directly mention or celebrate the violence.
Trump also said that El-Sayed’s mother had “worked for an organization that gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda.” A Times investigation reported that El-Sayed’s mother worked as a nurse in Missouri for a Muslim aid group that was later designated by the US government as a supporter of terrorist groups. She was never accused of wrongdoing.
El-Sayed’s campaign has said that he “disagrees” with his sister on “a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use, including on foreign policy.” He was raised by his father and stepmother and has said that he had little relationship with his biological mother while growing up.
Former US president Barack Obama campaigned with El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday, praising his potential partnership with Democratic Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who has endorsed El-Sayed.
“Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa,” said Obama. “You got a Muslim man, you got a Jewish woman, fighting for you in the United States Senate. That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of.”

Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) organized a provocative rally in Budapest in support of Rosatom’s Paks II nuclear power plant construction project, aiming to influence Hungary’s political situation.
The international intelligence community InformNapalm reported this in cooperation with the Ukrainian Militant analytical group, based on an analysis of leaked CYBINT data.
The 256 Cyber Assault Division group uncovered the Russian intelligence operation after intercepting correspondence in which Russian Colonel Timur Sirtlanov instructed SVR Lieutenant Colonel Irina Parman to prepare an “active measure” in Budapest.
In Russian intelligence terminology, “active measures” refer to information campaigns, covert operations, and manipulations designed to influence public opinion and the policies of foreign states.
Both subjects of the investigation are linked to military unit 33949, which open sources and analytical reports identify as an official structure of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
Irina Parman specializes in profiling and the use of psychological methods in operational activities, as evidenced by the courses she took at the SVR Academy.

The attempt to stage a manipulative rally came amid worsening relations between Hungary and Russia following the expulsion of ten Russian diplomats over espionage activities.
The organizers canceled the planned rally at the last minute, so it never took place.

No winner in first round: Bulgaria sets presidential runoff for Nov. 1
The Iotova-Valchev ticket has secured 34.76% of the vote, while Gurov-Kandev has received 31.95%, with 99.95% of tally sheets processed by the district election commissions. The figures are as of 10 a.m. on Monday, according to data published on the Central Election Commission's (CEC) website.
Under the Constitution, a presidential candidate can be elected in the first round only if they receive more than half of the valid votes cast and more than half of all eligible voters take part in the election. If no candidate is elected, a new vote is held within seven days, with the two candidates who received the most votes taking part.
The results of the presidential and vice-presidential election show the following distribution:
Ilana Iotova/Kiril Valchev - 34.76%
Andrey Gurov/Georgi Kandev - 31.95%
Kostadin Kostadinov/Petar Volgin - 12.54%
Radostin Vasilev/Krasimir Manov - 4.61%
Ivelin Mihaylov/Yuliana Mateeva - 3.79%
Ivan Hristanov/Stoyanka Cherkezova - 2.39%
The “I do not support any candidate” option was chosen by 4.43% of voters.
A total of 6,637,238 voters were eligible to take part in Sunday's election, in which 27 presidential and vice-presidential tickets competed. Some 46,001 people were eligible to vote for the first time.
As previously reported, Bulgarian citizens were voting Sunday to elect the country's seventh president.

How will growing US-Ukraine tensions shape the course of the war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:16:07 UTC
23:16:07 KST

Growing tensions between Washington and Kiev are exposing differences that extend beyond the personal rivalry between US President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as the White House pursues closer ties with Moscow.
The latest signs of a US-Russia rapprochement emerged last week when US mediator Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg, with both sides issuing positive statements about renewing peace talks and ending the war in Ukraine.
Yet just hours after the statements, Russia and Ukraine exchanged a deadly barrage of attacks, underscoring the challenges facing efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict.
The growing US-Russia rapprochement, marked by Washington brokering a diesel deal with the Kremlin and lifting most US sanctions on Moscow, has frustrated Zelenskyy, who has recently publicly opposed Washington's softer approach toward Moscow.
Trump has also demanded that Zelenskyy stop targeting Russian refineries.
The disagreements mark a further deterioration in relations that have remained strained since a heated White House meeting in March, when Trump and Zelenskyy engaged in a public shouting match.
Although Zelenskyy subsequently sought common ground with Trump through European mediation, their latest exchanges suggest that the divisions between Washington and Kiev run deeper than disagreements over how to end the war, reflecting increasingly divergent geopolitical priorities and international alignments.
“I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” the US president said in a speech last week, underscoring his affinity for the Russian leader, who recently proposed a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump to address the war in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy has shown less hesitation in confronting the US administration, which has long provided Ukraine with weapons, funding and essential intelligence in its war against Russia.
“How can Trump be friends with him? I think that it’s a mistake. It’s his choice again and again,” Zelenskyy said in a recent Financial Times interview, referring to the political rapprochement between Russia and the US.
Rapprochement disrupts Ukrainian resistance
Growing differences between Washington and Kiev, coupled with Trump's rapprochement with Putin, could strengthen Moscow's position both on the battlefield and at the negotiating table, according to experts.
The deepening tensions between the US and Ukraine are “exerting a disruptive influence on the dynamics of the war in Ukraine, affecting both military operations on the ground and the parameters of a potential peace settlement,” Ozgur Korpe, an academic at National Defence University, tells TRT World.
“On the battlefield, uncertainty regarding US aid—compounded by political conditionality—is compelling Ukraine to adopt a more defensive, resource-conserving strategy, while simultaneously granting Russia greater latitude to maintain its offensive tempo and intensify pressure,” he says.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has faced disruptions to US intelligence sharing and Starlink satellite connections, which Kiev believes contributed to its vulnerability during recent deadly Russian missile attacks on the capital.
Shortages of missile interceptors, compounded by delays in US supplies, have further strained Ukraine's air defences.
According to Korpe, Ukraine's predicament reflects a well-documented phenomenon in international relations: when a weaker partner depends heavily on a stronger ally for security, declining support or growing uncertainty over assistance can undermine its willingness and ability to continue fighting.
Since the war began, Kiev has relied heavily on American political, economic, military and intelligence assistance.
Under the Trump administration, however, that support has declined, while the US president has increasingly portrayed Zelenskyy as an obstacle to a potential peace settlement.
Ukraine has sought to offset shortages of American weapons and disruptions to intelligence sharing with support from Europe.
But questions remain over whether countries such as France, the UK and Germany have the military capabilities to replace US assistance.
Domestic priorities
Trump and Zelenskyy have different pledges to their respective national audiences, making compromise increasingly difficult.
While Trump has long pledged to Americans to bring immediate peace to the Russia-Ukraine war, Zelenskyy aims to minimise any territorial concessions to Moscow to keep national support for his presidency strong.
The tensions between Washington and Kiev are “largely a product of US domestic political factors, with the Trump administration facing pressure due to rising energy costs amid prolonged wars in both the Middle East and the Russia/Ukraine conflict,” says Eugene Chausovsky, senior director of analytical development and training at the New Lines Institute.
With the US midterm elections approaching, Trump is seeking ways to ease economic pressures, particularly rising diesel prices and their wider impact on inflation.
“This frames the US agreement with Russia on allowing diesel shipments, as well as Trump’s frustration with Zelensky for Ukraine continuing to target Russian energy and refinery infrastructure at a politically sensitive time,” Chausovsky tells TRT World.
However, experts warn that the diesel deal is unlikely to immediately affect US fuel prices, as European countries continue to enforce their own sanctions on Russia.
Trump’s declaration of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia also failed, as both sides said they did not sign the agreement.
“Trump frames Ukraine not so much as a front line for the defence of liberal democratic norms, but rather as a costly foreign burden in the context of US domestic politics and a bargaining chip to be used at the negotiating table when striking a ‘grand deal’ with Russia,” Korpe says.
By contrast, Zelenskyy views Ukraine's struggle as existential and closely tied to the country's aspirations to join Western political and military institutions, according to Korpe.
Will Ukraine and the US break up?
Ukraine has long sought closer integration with Western political and military institutions, including NATO and the EU. But deteriorating relations with Washington have raised questions about whether Kiev can keep relying on American support.
Oleg Ignatov, a senior analyst on Russia at the International Crisis Group, says the Trump administration has recently changed its approach to negotiations aimed at ending the war.
“Previously, Washington tried to reach an understanding with Moscow first, then took its proposals to Ukraine and its allies, who rejected them.
“Now the United States is trying to secure support from Ukraine and its European allies first and find out what they are prepared to accept. It would then take those proposals to Putin,” Ignatov tells TRT World.
Last week, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, met Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo before Witkoff travelled to Saint Petersburg for further talks with Putin.
“This approach requires Zelenskyy to be clearer about the compromises Ukraine might accept. That is likely to cause friction between Kiev and Washington because their approaches still differ,” Ignatov tells TRT World.
If the US continues to push Zelenskyy to make further concessions to Russia, this approach could “lead to further friction or even conflict between Kiev and Washington,” Ignatov says.
Zelenskyy has insisted that any potential ceasefire must be backed by Western security guarantees without territorial concessions to Russia.
In a recent CNN interview, Zelenskyy maintained that Ukraine “will survive” and “will stay strong” despite tensions with Washington, while rejecting territorial concessions to Russia.
Although some analysts attribute the tensions partly to personal animosity between Trump and Zelenskyy, Korpe argues that the differences run deeper.
“The rift between the two leaders is not merely personal; rather, it is rooted in deeper disagreements regarding the objectives of the war and the vision for a final settlement.”
Korpe says institutions such as the US Congress and the Pentagon, alongside NATO, have helped prevent American support for Ukraine from collapsing entirely.
Nevertheless, “it is fair to say that the crisis of trust between the two leaders is moving distinctly toward a complete ‘break’,” he adds.
Chausovsky, however, offers a different assessment.
While Zelenskyy and the Trump administration remain at odds, he says, “these tensions should not be seen as a sign of a breakup” between Washington and Kiev.
Instead, Chausovsky describes the current friction as “rather a down period in the ebb and flow of their ties amid the protracted conflict with Russia.”
“Greater diplomatic activity can be expected as a result, though any sustainable ceasefire or peace agreement is unlikely to materialise in the short term,” he tells TRT World.

Syria arrests Assad's cousin and senior former regime officers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:16:04 UTC
23:16:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria arrests Assad's cousin and senior former regime officers
Syrian authorities have arrested several senior officers from Bashar al-Assad's former regime, including his cousin, as part of an ongoing crackdown on suspects accused of atrocities during the country's 14-year-long civil war.
Syrian Interior Ministry spokesperson Nour al-Din al-Baba announced the arrests on Monday, saying those detained included senior military and intelligence officials, former air force pilots and individuals suspected of involvement in massacres and attacks on civilians.
Among those arrested was Yahya al-Assad, a cousin of ousted president Bashar al-Assad who held the rank of colonel in Branch 105, a unit of the former regime's security apparatus.
Al-Baba said the detainees also included a major general who had commanded the 24th Division and the Air Defence Directorate, as well as senior officials from the Air Force Intelligence Directorate.
Another suspect was allegedly involved in the Tadamon massacre, one of the most notorious atrocities committed by Assad's forces during the Syrian uprising.
The arrests also included a fighter pilot accused of bombing Syrian cities, a brigadier general from the Political Security Directorate, the head of investigations at Air Force Intelligence and a judge who served in the former regime's Counterterrorism Court.
Other detainees included two brigadier generals from the Republican Guard, a senior officer at Tishreen Military Hospital, a military doctor, a helicopter pilot and another fighter pilot accused of taking part in attacks on civilian areas.
The arrests are part of efforts by Syria's new authorities to pursue former military and security officials suspected of committing abuses during the uprising against Assad, including aerial bombardments, arbitrary detention, torture and massacres.
Former regime pilots targeted
Syrian authorities have stepped up arrests of former air force personnel in recent weeks, targeting officers suspected of involvement in bombing campaigns against opposition-held areas.
In September, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of nine former regime pilots in Latakia province.
According to the ministry, preliminary investigations indicated that the pilots had participated in combat missions and airstrikes targeting several areas, including Eastern Ghouta, Aleppo and its countryside, Deir ez-Zor and rural Hama.
On 18 September, authorities detained five former air force officers and commanders in Tartous province, including pilots and officials who had held operational and field responsibilities.
Two days later, security forces arrested Brigadier General Zakaria Mohammed Sannoun, who served as head of operations in the 22nd Division between 2012 and 2020.
Authorities accused Sannoun of overseeing operations at the Hama, Tiyas (T4) and Shayrat military airbases during the conflict.
On 28 September, internal security forces arrested Colonel Khaldoun Hussein Mubarak in the Jableh countryside of Latakia province.
He was accused of participating in combat sorties against Syrian areas during the uprising.
The Interior Ministry has described the arrests as part of continuing investigations into former officers and military personnel suspected of war crimes and other violations, with judicial proceedings expected to follow.
Suspect in 2013 massacres arrested
The latest arrests come less than two weeks after Syrian authorities announced the detention of Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural and nicknamed the "Butcher of Baniyas".
Kayali was arrested on 15 October over his alleged role in the 2013 massacres in Baniyas and al-Bayda, in the Tartous countryside.
Syrian authorities accuse him of responsibility for the killings, which took place during the early years of the uprising against Assad.
The successive arrests mark a widening effort to track down former regime figures accused of involvement in atrocities committed during the conflict.
Authorities have said investigations will continue and that suspects will face further judicial proceedings over their alleged roles in abuses against Syrians.

This Tuesday, millions of Israelis will enter the voting booth with mixed emotions – feelings of trauma and pride.

Hezbollah is crushed.

Those with a proven track record in war and peace who have committed to Iranian regime change or a newly formed amalgamation of parties who agree on few things beyond their disdain for Netanyahu.

Imagine we are on the eve of a joint American Israeli attack against the remnants of the Iranian nuclear program, and the Pentagon is waiting to hear if Israel is on board, pending a decision from the Islamist Ra’am movement’s Shura Council of elders.
This isn’t a joke; it’s a dangerous possibility.

This comes alongside an unprecedented endorsement by US President Donald Trump, who clearly wants to keep the winning team together to finish the job.
Now is not the time to throw the dice on Israel’s security.
That’s why I solemnly believe that a vote for Netanyahu is a vote for victory.

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has extended the partial compensation scheme for the cost of Ukrainian-made industrial machinery and equipment for another two years, until September 30, 2028.
The relevant resolution extends the experimental project developed by the Ministry of Economy as part of the Made in Ukraine state policy, the ministry said.
The program provides compensation of 15% of the purchase price of Ukrainian-made industrial machinery and equipment, excluding value-added tax (VAT).
"The 15% compensation program for machinery and equipment has already demonstrated its effectiveness, so it is important to ensure its continued operation. It allows businesses to reduce the cost of modernizing production, while Ukrainian machinery manufacturers receive new orders, increase production and invest in their own development," Deputy Economy Minister Vitaliy Kindrativ was quoted as saying.
The program has operated since September 2024 and covers equipment manufactured in Ukraine with a localization level of at least 40%.
As of May 2026, buyers had purchased 476 units of Ukrainian machinery and equipment worth nearly UAH 1.2 billion under the program. Total partial compensation amounted to UAH 148.8 million, according to the ministry.
A total of 29 Ukrainian banks participate in the program.
The Federation of Employers of Ukraine previously named the continuation of existing support programs under the Made in Ukraine platform among the key industrial policy challenges requiring urgent attention from the new prime minister and government.

For Italian Language Week

26 October 2026, 15:14
ANSA English Desk

- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The Italian Embassy in Bratislava presents the sixth edition of the “Raccontare in Italiano” contest, open to students of Italian in schools and undergraduate programs in Slovakia.
The initiative, promoted as part of the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, is organized in collaboration with the Italian Cultural Institute in Bratislava and Eduitalia, an association of over one hundred schools, academies, and universities.
Participants must submit a short story of no more than 350 words, choosing from two themes: “Even if you don’t know it, you recognize it,” on the presence of Italian in unexpected contexts, and “Italian, the Language of Genius,” on the fields in which the Italian language excels, drawing on personal experiences or readings.

Israel heads to the polls: Netanyahu seeks to survive another election

Israel heads to the polls: Netanyahu seeks to survive another election
Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday in a closely contested parliamentary election that could end the nearly four-year rule of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition, following years of war, political scandals, mass protests, and deepening divisions within Israeli society.
The vote is widely viewed as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership, with the opposition blaming him for security failures surrounding the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and accusing his government of undermining democratic institutions.
The Hamas attack killed around 1,200 people and saw some 250 taken hostage. Israel responded with a military campaign in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to the local Health Ministry.
Despite their fierce political rivalry, the main Israeli election contenders differ less considerably over the country’s military policies and its approach to the Palestinians.
Netanyahu’s fight for political survival
Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who heads the centrist Yashar party, has emerged as Netanyahu’s strongest challenger.
Speaking at a mass rally in Tel Aviv on Sunday, Eisenkot urged traditional voters for Netanyahu’s Likud party to abandon the prime minister, claiming that Israel cannot survive another four years under his leadership.
“Anyone who thinks our Israel can survive another four years like these is living under a dangerous misconception,” Eisenkot said, according to the Times of Israel.
Netanyahu is also facing accusations of attempting to provoke a new war with Iran to postpone the election. Former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman has demanded a criminal investigation into the prime minister on suspicion of treason after Channel 12 reported a clash between Netanyahu and Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir over a proposed military operation.
“The man has gone off the rails,” Liberman said on Monday, accusing Netanyahu of putting his political survival ahead of national security. The prime minister denied the reported confrontation, and no criminal wrongdoing has been established.
Netanyahu also failed to persuade US President Donald Trump to launch strikes on Iran before the Israeli election, CNN reported, citing American and Israeli sources. The operation has reportedly been postponed, potentially until after the November 3 US midterm elections. Netanyahu’s office rejected the report.
The confrontation is not simply between the left and the right. Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid are also seeking to oust Netanyahu, but the opposition remains divided over domestic policy, coalition alliances, and who should lead the next government.
Four years of war and political turmoil
Netanyahu’s latest term has been marked by a series of crises, from mass protests over his judicial overhaul to the October 7 Hamas attack, which exposed major failures in Israel’s security apparatus and triggered years of warfare.
The attack remains a central election issue, with Netanyahu’s opponents accusing him of evading responsibility and blocking an independent state commission of inquiry. While the opposition demands a full investigation into the political and military failures, the prime minister has backed a government-appointed panel with more limited powers.
Israel’s subsequent military campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran have come at a heavy human, economic, and diplomatic cost. The Gaza offensive has devastated the Palestinian enclave, killing tens of thousands and displacing much of its population.
In September 2025, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Netanyahu is also subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. Israel rejects the genocide allegations and denies committing war crimes.
Another major dividing line concerns Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul, which triggered nationwide protests in 2023. His opponents have pledged to reverse measures they say undermine judicial independence. The prime minister is also standing trial on corruption charges, including bribery, fraud, and breach of trust, which he denies.
Another contentious issue is the exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from military service. Despite a 2024 Supreme Court ruling against blanket exemptions, Netanyahu’s coalition has continued to resist compulsory conscription for religious students, fueling resentment among Israelis repeatedly called up for military duty.
The economic toll has added to public anger. Rising defense spending, higher living costs, and a VAT increase to 18% in 2025 have put further pressure on households.
Yet the wars themselves have attracted relatively little debate among the main contenders, many of whom support Israel’s military campaigns. The deeper political battle is over Netanyahu’s leadership, accountability, and the direction of the Israeli state.
Election arithmetic: Can anyone secure a majority?
Recent surveys indicate a tight race, with Eisenkot’s Yashar holding a narrow advantage over Netanyahu’s Likud in several polls.
An October 21 Jerusalem Post analysis of four major surveys put Yashar at an average of 22.5 seats, compared with 19.75 for Likud. But neither Netanyahu’s allies nor the opposition appear assured of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-member Knesset.
Under Israel’s proportional representation system, parties must win at least 3.25% of the national vote to enter parliament. Votes for parties that fail to cross the threshold do not translate into seats, meaning even small shifts could tip the balance between rival camps.
The real battle may therefore begin after the ballots are counted. Smaller parties, particularly ultra-Orthodox factions, could determine who governs, with military conscription exemptions and religious education funding among their key demands.
According to a Jerusalem Post report published Monday, possible scenarios include opposition cooperation with ultra-Orthodox factions, reliance on Arab parties’ parliamentary support, or even another election if coalition talks fail.
Would a defeat for Netanyahu change Israel’s course?
A new prime minister would not necessarily mean a new direction for Israel’s military and foreign policies.
Despite their fierce opposition to Netanyahu, leading opposition figures broadly support maintaining Israel’s military superiority, confronting Iran, and retaining extensive security control over Palestinian territories. None of the principal contenders has made the establishment of a Palestinian state a central campaign commitment.
The election also comes amid renewed tensions in the occupied West Bank. Israeli authorities have imposed sweeping restrictions following a shooting near Hebron that killed two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen, including curbs on Palestinians entering Jewish settlements for work.
Meanwhile, thousands of Israelis have demonstrated against the government and violence toward Palestinians, even as younger voters increasingly identify with the political right.
Reporting from Tel Aviv, RT correspondent Charlotte Dubenskij described Israel as “a nation dramatically shifting towards the right,” with many young people citing the October 7 attack as a turning point in their political views.
The election could therefore remove Netanyahu from power without reversing the security policies that have defined his latest term.
What happens after October 27?
The vote could leave Netanyahu in power, hand the opposition a chance to form a government, or produce another parliamentary deadlock.
Under Israel’s parliamentary system, the president consults party leaders before choosing a lawmaker to form a government. Coalition talks can drag on for weeks, with smaller parties demanding concessions in exchange for their support. If no candidate can secure a majority, Israel could face another election.
The final result may therefore be decided not at the ballot box, but behind closed doors, as rival parties bargain over who will govern Israel next.
Yet even if Netanyahu loses power, the election may change Israel’s leadership without fundamentally altering its approach to the Palestinians or the regional conflicts that have defined his latest term.

Ukraine’s Defense Ministry discussed with a visiting European Union delegation how spending under the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan is monitored, including through competitive tenders, electronic procurement platforms and audits.
Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banyk said the ministry is updating defense procurement legislation to reflect wartime conditions and EU recommendations. It also plans to move purchases to competitive procedures and shift tenders to electronic platforms to reduce the human factor.

The Defense Procurement Agency is strengthening controls at all stages of procurement, conducting audits and carrying out risk-based checks on contractors, its acting director, Artem Romaniukov, said.
The agency is also cooperating with anti-corruption bodies to ensure international funds are used transparently.
The ministry said competition in defense procurement is growing, some tenders have been completed and deliveries to the military have begun. European defense companies have also taken part in competitive tenders announced by the agency in 2026.

Temu falls into line as EU backs its action plan after €200m fine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:11:03 UTC
23:11:03 KST

The Chinese-owned online retailer has promised stronger action to address several violations of the EU’s Digital Services Act, the European Commission said on Monday, following a €200 million fine in May.
The European Commission has said it has accepted Temu's action plan to address several violations of the bloc's Digital Services Act (DSA).
Temu has promised to carry out a risk analysis, to keep a close eye on measures to prevent the sale of illegal products on its platform and to step up its efforts if needed.
The Chinese retailer will also review how its recommender systems "may amplify the spread of illegal goods", the Commission said.
In May this year, Temu was fined €200 million by the EU for allowing the sale of illegal products like dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers on its platform.
The fine came after a formal investigation launched in October 2024 into whether Temu was meeting its obligations as a designated Very Large Online Platform under the EU's Digital Services Act.
Commission investigators said the platform failed to properly identify and address the risks posed by illegal and unsafe products sold to European consumers.
Today, Temu welcomed the approval of its action plan by European regulators. “We appreciate the Commission's constructive engagement with us throughout the process,“ the company said in a statement.
The plan "stands as a clear testament to Temu's commitment to investing in robust compliance infrastructure to ensure a safe, trustworthy shopping environment for all EU users”, it added.
The Chinese retail giant has 130 million users in the 27-nation EU, nearly a third of the bloc's population, making it one of the biggest online retailers in Europe.
Temu is one of several ecommerce platforms dealing with the EU’s new €3 fees on low-value packages since July, while those worth less €150 had entered the bloc duty free beforehand.
The new packaging rules have seen imports, especially from China, slump by 30% to 40% since coming into force.

Russian oil tycoons' bitter feud spills into Dubai courts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:10:51 UTC
23:10:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Russian oil tycoons' bitter feud spills into Dubai courts
A bitter feud between Russian oil traders has spilled into courts in Dubai and Brazil, with lawsuits worth hundreds of millions of dollars and allegations of stolen trade secrets and death threats.
The dispute involves Igor Soglayev, a former Deutsche Bank executive, and traders linked to the sanctioned Coral oil network, according to an investigation published by The Wall Street Journal on Sunday.
The fallout began when a tanker carrying Russian diesel worth tens of millions of dollars failed to deliver its cargo in Brazil.
The dispute has since led to claims exceeding $500 million, a $42 million arbitration award and a Dubai court order freezing assets worth up to $704 million.
Soglayev, who previously advised Igor Sechin, the head of Russian oil giant Rosneft, partnered with traders associated with Coral in early 2024.
He established Dubai-based DIA33 to trade Russian diesel and export it to Brazil, but the partnership collapsed following the failed shipment.
Coral-linked traders accused Soglayev of failing to pay for the fuel and secured a Dubai arbitration ruling ordering him to pay approximately $42 million.
Soglayev then filed lawsuits in Dubai and Brazil, accusing his former partners of undermining his business and misusing confidential commercial information.
He is seeking more than $500 million in damages and claims to have received death threats.
In June, a Dubai judge ordered the freezing of up to $704 million in assets belonging to the defendants and associated companies.
The order remains in place while appeals continue, although questions over the court's jurisdiction have complicated proceedings. No final ruling has settled the competing allegations.
The WSJ reported that the UAE court handling the main case has not made the proceedings public.
Accusations of stolen clients
The dispute has also reached Brazil, where DIA33 accused Coral of recruiting senior employees and using its customer base, offices and infrastructure to establish a rival business.
Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that a commercial court in Sao Paulo had identified indications of unfair competition.
Representatives of the defendants denied wrongdoing, arguing that the dispute stemmed from a business partnership that had never been fully formalised.
Coral has separately accused DIA33 of misappropriating a diesel shipment.
A sanctioned oil network
Coral Energy, renamed 2Rivers in 2024, has been a major player in Russian oil trading, with commercial roots in Azerbaijan and offices in Dubai and Singapore.
Western officials accuse traders associated with the network of helping Moscow maintain oil exports and finance its war in Ukraine despite sanctions.
Britain sanctioned the group in December 2024 and added five executives to its sanctions list in May 2025.
The European Union has also sanctioned associated entities, accusing them of facilitating Russian oil exports, disguising the origin of shipments and using vessels linked to Moscow's so-called shadow fleet.
The network has denied breaching sanctions and announced plans to wind down operations in August 2025, citing Western pressure.
Dubai has become an important hub for Russian oil trading since Moscow redirected exports away from Europe following its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

European Commission seeks to boost efficiency through artificial intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:10:23 UTC
23:10:23 KST

Melike Pala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday highlighted the potential of artificial intelligence to modernize the EU executive's administration, improve working methods, and make services less burdensome for businesses and citizens.
Speaking at a news conference in Brussels alongside European Commissioner for Budget, Anti-Fraud and Public Administration Piotr Serafin and Catherine Day, chair of the High-Level Group on the Future of the Commission's Civil Service, von der Leyen said technological advances offer new opportunities to improve administrative processes and make the EU more efficient.
"Artificial intelligence offers new ways to work, new ways to improve processes, and find less burdensome ways to make the European Union work for business and citizens," she said.
She stressed that the commission must equip its staff with the necessary skills and tools to make the best use of AI, while also investing in talent development, simplifying services and making better use of technology.
"We must give our colleagues the skills and tools to best use it, and we must develop talent, simplify services, and make better use of technologies," von der Leyen said.
Stressing the need for the commission to act "effectively and quickly," she said simplifying procedures, clarifying structures, and improving cooperation across departments would allow staff to focus their efforts on areas where they could make the greatest difference.
She identified making "every euro count" as the commission's second priority, emphasizing the need to ensure that public spending delivers added value and tangible results, particularly as Europeans continue to face cost-of-living pressures.
"Our ambition remains clear: to deliver the best possible public service for our European citizens," she said.
