The crews took shelter and escaped injury, but fire and rescue equipment was damaged. More than 50 rescuers were deployed, and authorities reported no casualties in the Odesa attacks.
At a second site in the region, four garages were damaged, a fire broke out and one car was destroyed.
In Zaporizhzhia, the overnight attack damaged private homes, a hotel, two buses and outbuildings. Three cars and dry vegetation caught fire, while rescuers searched the area for anyone trapped.
Acting regional military administration head Mykhailo Semikin initially reported two injured people, but later raised the toll to four injured: two women, aged 22 and 30, and two men, aged 40 and 61.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 140 Shahed-type attack drones and decoys overnight, including 70 jet-powered drones. It said air defences shot down or suppressed 112 drones, among them 56 jet-powered aircraft, as well as three Kh-59/69 guided missiles.
Emergency crews remained at the impact sites on Monday morning to extinguish fires, assess structural damage and restore services

Geneva to offer free home delivery of groceries to elderly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Geneva to offer free home delivery of groceries to elderly
Following a trial phase, the Swiss city of Geneva is making its free home grocery delivery service a permanent feature for people aged 65 and over. This service will now also be available to recipients of a care allowance.
These people can enjoy free delivery of their shopping once a week. Launched in the summer of 2025, the pilot scheme for free home delivery of groceries has been a resounding success, with an average of 260 deliveries made each month, the Department for Social Cohesion and Solidarity (DCSS) said on Monday.
The beneficiaries, currently numbering 300, have an average age of 79.
Building on this positive outcome, the DCSS has decided to make this initiative a permanent service, whilst expanding the group of beneficiaries. The aim remains the same: to promote independence, mobility and social connections, while making everyday shopping easier.
More
How the internet is reshaping global postal services
Deliveries are made by electric bicycle by the Genèveroule association. Purchases can be made at all food markets as well as in all Migros supermarkets located in the city. Deliveries are available from Monday to Saturday, limited to two bags weighing a maximum of 20 kilos.

France: Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:52:00 UTC
22:52:00 KST

Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests that rocked France
October 26, 2026
The French government is set to announce a series of "strong measures" to assuage protests which have rocked France in recent weeks, President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.
Speaking in the southern city of Marseille, Macron warned that fresh demonstrations planned for this coming Saturday were "risky" and said that protest routes would remain outside city centers in order to protect public order.
France braces for 'lively' Halloween
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told broadcaster BFM that he was expecting further disturbances on October 31.
"Halloween evening is traditionally always a bit lively," he said. "We expect it to be complicated again."
Prior to Macron's arrival in Marseille, the Elysee Palace said the president intended to "pay tribute to and thank the internal security forces that helped restore republican order" in France's second-largest city where protesters briefly stormed the city hall on October 17.
He acknowledged that French authorities had "not anticipated at all" the scale of demonstrations which descended into widespread violence in looting in several major cities, leading to suggestions the state had lost control of the streets.
Macron: 'Social media is damaging our democracies'
The French president also highlighted the role of social media in the protests, saying the online networks were "damaging our democracies" by "bringing young and not-so-young people to places where criminal acts, attacks and looting were taking place."
He described social media as "tools for mobilizing the worst impulses."
While Macron admitted that French security forces underestimated the extent to which "extreme left forces" would meet up "so early in the day" on October 17, Interior Minister Nunez highlighted the phenomenon of organized far-right mobs confronting left-wing activists in several cities.
"We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out to defend businesses," he told BFM.
"In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organized formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A presidential aide said Macron wanted to demonstrate that "the state is present, standing firm and fulfilling its mission to protect."
The president said that curfews enabled relative order to be maintained during last Saturday's protests (October 24), when authorities also deployed 70,000 police officers across the country, making 1,435 arrests.
"The state prevailed this weekend. The state was strong," government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told RTL radio.
France: Macron acknowledges 'legitimate' student demands
Nevertheless, President Macron also said he had instructed his government, led by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, to "respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement."
He said the government will soon announce several "concrete and huge" measures aimed at addressing student concerns over education and university admissions, following a nationwide consultation with high school and university student representatives.
"There are demands that must be heard and answered," confirmed government spokeswoman Bregeon.
"But to answer them, there is a prerequisite: a return to calm. We cannot have a functioning social dialogue in a climate of violence such as the one we experienced a week ago."
Edited by: Alex Berry

Elections in Israel: Can Netanyahu Hold on to Power?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:51:21 UTC
22:51:21 KST

Israelis will elect a new parliament next Tuesday. The main issues in the campaign are foreign and security policy, mistakes regarding the 2023 Hamas attack, military service for ultra-Orthodox Haredi Jews, and high inflation. The right-wing religious bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the more moderate forces led by former chief of staff of the Israel Defence Forces Gadi Eisenkot are neck-and-neck in the polls.
Opposition overtakes PM on the right
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Many of Netanyahu’s opponents share his worldview, political scientist Sergei Medvedev explains on Facebook (Russia) :
“The opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot has a slight lead in the polls. ... Nevertheless, the election is taking place on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s terms. The key leaders of the opposition bloc have adopted Netanyahu’s worldview on a number of key issues and have even shifted further to the right than he has. ... The majority of Israeli Jews now see the world as Netanyahu has long viewed it. This is Netanyahu’s great victory. But it is matched by his great defeat: much of the world now sees Israel as the residents of the Gaza Strip do.”
No healing without facing the past
To move forward, Israel must first come to terms with the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, La Libre Belgique (Belgium) argues:
“It is precisely in view of these painful wounds that Israeli voters will have to make their choice on Tuesday. Not in the hope of healing this or that wound by any means necessary, but in order to set their country on the path to genuine recovery. ... Three years on, Netanyahu is still refusing to allow a state commission to be set up to clarify political responsibility for the events of 7 October. ... Yet every Israeli has the right to know what led to that fateful day in October. No society can look calmly toward the future if it turns a blind eye to its past.”
Bulgarian Presidential Election Exposes Split Over Ukraine War
Display of direct access to Washington
According to military expert Alexandru Grumaz writing in Adevărul (Romania), Monday’s surprise visit by US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was aimed at helping Netanyahu score points with his voters:
“The fact that the US secretary of defence came to hold talks with him at a military base – eight days before the election – reinforces the image of a prime minister who has direct access to the decision-makers in Washington. For voters, the message is easy to understand: a change of government would also mean replacing the very person who maintains those relationships just when the country is in a dangerous phase. This is a powerful election argument, even if the partnership between two states should not depend on who is leading them.”
Even small changes are important
TVNet (Latvia) explains why a change of government does not necessarily mean a change of course:
“Overall, it’s clear that Netanyahu’s departure would not automatically mean that Israel is prepared to end the wars or support the Palestinians’ right to their own state. Many voters want a more responsible government but are still in favour of military operations. A victory for the opposition cannot therefore be interpreted as a clear demand for a change of course in relations with the Palestinians and other neighbours. Nevertheless, even small changes would be important for both sides.”
Last stop before the abyss
The Israelis must use their votes to stop Netanyahu, urges Le Temps (Switzerland):
“In recent years, Israel has undergone a fundamental transformation: it is a country governed by a prime minister who is under investigation by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity, and which finds itself in a state of open war with multiple neighbours in the region. ... Tens of thousands of Israelis have already fled the country. ... Netanyahu’s potential departure would certainly not be enough to change the country from the bottom up, however urgent that may be. But at the very least it could allow Israelis to halt their rapid descent into the abyss.”
Bellicose slogans poisoning the campaign
The situation may well deteriorate futher, El Periódico (Spain) de Catalunya fears:
“Israel’s founding Father David Ben-Gurion is said to have remarked: ‘The Land of Israel is our homeland, and we shall defend it with all our might.’ ... This bellicose mindset still prevails today – the idea that the first defeat will drive the Israelis into the sea, and it is poisoning the campaign slogans – against a backdrop of an exhausted Palestinian society, an uncontrolled energy crisis and uncertainty hanging over the entire region, from Egypt to Iran. ... This already toxic atmosphere could deteriorate further if the election result prolongs the formation of a government amid a sea of irreconcilable parties. Things are liable to get worse.”
Outcry of the ultra-Orthodox
According to the Kronen Zeitung (Austria), the compulsory conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews is making waves:
“With just under a week to go before the elections a campaign bombshell has exploded, stirring up emotions like hardly any other issue: the privileges enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox (known as Haredim), particularly when it comes to compulsory military service. Israel is at war and there is a shortage of soldiers. Now the army has made an example of them. It intercepted a flight bringing young Haredim returning home from New York at Tel Aviv airport. Two coaches were waiting outside: the one on the right to take them to collect their uniforms, the one on the left to take them to a military prison. An outcry from the Haredim ensued. For years their parties – as sought-after coalition partners – have been extorting precious privileges. ... The Haredim have become a test of faith in the truest sense of the word.”

Siher 'capable of developing revolutionary strategy'
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:50:56 CET
22:50:56 KST

Youssef Siher, a 30.year-old 
Italian researcher and freelance journalist with Moroccan roots
who has been accused of being the mastermind behind the shocking
rioting and looting that took place in Milan on the weekend of
October 17, is capable of developing a revolutionary strategy, 
prosecutors said Monday in their arguments in favour of his
being remanded in custody at a hearing Tuesday.
                                    
Siher, detained by order of the Milan Public Prosecutor's Office
for allegedly being the mastermind behind the social media
channel 'Movimento 17 ottobre' ('October 17th Movement'),
reportedly possessed a level of technical expertise that would
have enabled him to "develop a revolutionary strategy."
This is one of the points highlighted by prosecutors in their
request to validate the detention and impose pre-trial
incarceration—a request based on the assessment that there is a
risk not only of the individual fleeing, but also of him
reoffending.
                                    
In the request to validate the detention and impose a
precautionary jail measure—filed by prosecutor Francesca Crupi
of the counter-terrorism department, who is coordinating the
investigation alongside Chief Prosecutor Marcello Viola—it is
noted that Siher holds a "prominent profile within activist
circles."
He demonstrated "particular skill" by managing, in just a few
days, to build a social media group with nearly 9,000
followers—most of whom are inclined to engage in "criminal
conduct against public order."
Furthermore, regarding the risk of reoffending, he reportedly
possesses a "command of digital tools capable of developing a
revolutionary strategy," including the drafting of statements
designed to "gather thousands of people in public squares."
The instructions provided to users point to a "clear strategic
design," as the designated meeting points were chosen
specifically "to evade law enforcement oversight."
On Saturday, following intervention by investigators, the social
media channels were shut down; consequently, the previously
announced "instructions"—which included the names of specific
squares in Milan where participants were to gather—were never
disseminated.
                                    
No trace of these instructions has yet been found during the
digital forensic searches conducted on Siher's laptop.

Russia Says Ukraine Has Repeatedly Struck Oleshky With Artillery, Drones Ahead of Local Ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:50:09 UTC
22:50:09 KST

Russia's Defense Ministry on Monday accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine with artillery and drones ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week, something it said had prevented the delivery of food and medicine and stopped people from leaving.
Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed to a ceasefire in Oleshky that would go into effect on Oct. 27, allowing for the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.
Russia's Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that Ukraine had struck the town 18 times with artillery fire and carried out more than 120 drone attacks on it and the main roads around it in the week since Oct. 19.
Reuters could not independently verify that assertion, and there was no immediate response from Ukraine, which has in the past accused Russia of not letting aid in or people out of the town.
Also on Monday, the Kremlin said that the local humanitarian ceasefire agreed for Oleshky with the United States' help could set a precedent for similar ceasefires elsewhere in Ukraine.
The ceasefire comes as residents of the town, controlled by Russian forces since February 2022 and located close to the front line, have reported a deepening food crisis, with both sides accusing each other of blocking supplies.

UN inquiry says Gaza genocide continues despite ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:49:54 UTC
22:49:54 KST

A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the U.N. say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Oct. 26.
They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the West Bank.
In response, Israel’s mission in Geneva called for the commission’s dissolution and said on X the report marked an example of the body’s “misinformation campaign to demonize the state of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal.”
Israel has long criticized the commission’s output and denied accusations of genocide in Gaza and sexual assault by its forces.
The findings by the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which seeks to document in minute detail the allegations and evidence of crimes to bolster accountability for perpetrators, could be used by prosecutors at the International Criminal Court or in other jurisdictions to try to bring justice to victims and their relatives.
The report on Oct. 26 said Israel was “continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”
Much of the harm has come from Israel’s expansion deeper into Gaza during the ceasefire period, the report said.
Since October 2025, when the ceasefire was signed, Israeli forces have gone from controlling 53 percent of Gaza to at least 60 percent, the commission said.
In that time, Israeli fire across the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
The report also accused Israeli soldiers and prison guards of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians.
The commission said that it had recently documented six cases where Israeli guards were sexually violent toward male detainees from Gaza in the Sde Teiman military prison.
In one case, it says guards raped a Palestinian detainee with a stick, then forced him to put the stick in his mouth until he vomited. It also recalled another episode in which guards instructed a Palestinian man to urinate as they tied a plastic cord around his genitals.
The ceasefire scaled down a devastating war started by the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, when the militants killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. Israel responded with a campaign that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

Egypt authorises military support for Saudi Arabia as Houthi militia attacks escalate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:48:50 UTC
22:48:50 KST

Egypt’s parliament has authorised the country’s military to provide support for Saudi Arabia’s defence, lawmakers and local media reported, potentially bringing Cairo closer to a regional conflict intensified by attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militia.
President Abdel Fattah el Sisi asked parliament last week to approve military assistance if Riyadh requests help defending itself against the Houthis, whose operations threaten Saudi territory and the strategic Bab al Mandab Strait, a vital shipping passage linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and access to Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The parliamentary authorisation comes as attacks on Saudi Arabia have disrupted aviation and oil exports, raising concerns over regional security and international trade routes.
Cairo draws a line around its military role
Egypt has repeatedly condemned Iranian and Iran-backed attacks on Gulf countries but has not publicly joined direct combat in the current conflict.
Sisi has indicated that any Egyptian support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders, rather than launching attacks inside Yemen.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh last Wednesday to deliver a letter from Sisi to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Following the visit, Abdelatty said Cairo supported exploring “every opportunity” to resolve the Yemen conflict through diplomacy.
Egypt’s potential involvement would mark a significant development given its military capabilities and strategic position along the Red Sea.
The country has also been considering joining a mutual defence pact involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, signed in August.
Abdelatty said earlier this month that Egyptian membership remained “under serious consideration.”
A history of involvement in Yemen
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government in March 2015, primarily as a naval partner tasked with protecting Red Sea shipping lanes.
Cairo sent warships, pledged air support and deployed around 800 ground troops, although its direct combat role remained limited.
The country has a difficult history of military intervention in Yemen, having suffered heavy costs during its involvement in the 1960s. It has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
Saudi Arabia remains a key political and financial partner for Cairo, providing billions of dollars in assistance, central bank deposits and energy supplies during Sisi’s presidency.
Red Sea security raises regional stakes
The latest escalation has added another volatile front to the wider US-Israeli war on Iran. The Houthis, who control Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, have attacked targets including Riyadh’s international airport and Saudi oil giant Aramco, disrupting flights and oil exports.
The conflict also threatens maritime traffic through the Bab al Mandab Strait, a strategic chokepoint for shipping travelling between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Any sustained disruption could affect routes serving the Suez Canal, a major source of revenue for Egypt.
Saudi Arabia and Egypt have stepped up security discussions as the fighting intensifies. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo on September 15 to discuss security and navigation in the Red Sea.
The extent of any Egyptian military support will depend on Saudi Arabia’s requests and how Cairo balances its security commitments with efforts to prevent further regional escalation.

Vučić’s Defeat Is Not Yet a Victory for Serbia’s European Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:48:30 UTC
22:48:30 KST

Aleksandar Vučić has lost the election, and Ukraine now has good reason to take a close look at who has won. For Serbia’s citizens, worn down by 14 years of rule under the former president’s Serbian Progressive Party, the Student List’s victory offers grounds for hope that they will finally be able to hold those who govern them to account.
For Ukrainians defending their country against Russian aggression every day, it also matters what the winners intend to do with the relationship Belgrade has built with Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
With 98.8 percent of votes counted, the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy (CeSID), an independent Serbian election-monitoring organization, and Ipsos, the international polling company, project that the Student List will take around 140 of parliament’s 250 seats, enough to form a government on its own.
In a country where party membership has for years opened the doors of state institutions, that result matters enormously. The deaths of 16 people when the canopy of Novi Sad railway station collapsed turned a demand for accountability into a revolt against the way the country was governed. Citizens have every right to expect courts free from political pressure and close public scrutiny of how the state spends their money.
The scale of that change makes it all the more important to read carefully what the winners say about the world. The Student List brings together professors, doctors and other public figures chosen by students to represent them, yet there are no students among its candidates. Some very old political convictions sit alongside its youthful symbolism, particularly regarding Russia, Kosovo and Europe. That gives Moscow an opening to preserve its influence after the defeat of the man it has dealt with for so many years.
Serbia’s Student Movement Ousts Longtime Leader in Parliament Poll
In these pages in August, I strongly supported Vučić’s decision to receive Volodymyr Zelensky in Belgrade. I stand by that position after his electoral defeat. Ties with a country defending itself against aggression retain their value after the politicians who built them leave office. Were we to undo every sound decision a government had made simply because its author had lost an election, Serbia’s foreign policy interests would endure no longer than an election campaign.
Vučić and Zelensky established regular contact and a working relationship that allowed them to discuss practical cooperation despite the deep differences between Belgrade and Kyiv over Moscow. After Vučić’s visits to Odesa in 2025 and Kyiv in July this year, Zelensky was officially welcomed in Belgrade on August 8. Their talks covered energy, railways, trade and Ukraine’s reconstruction. Each endorsed the other country’s European aspirations, and Serbia reaffirmed its respect for Ukraine’s territorial integrity.
Those talks have been accompanied by concrete aid. By February 2024, Serbia had allocated €3 million for Ukrainian children and €1.5 million for internally displaced people, sent 14 trucks carrying humanitarian aid and donated ambulances. It also sent equipment to help restore the electricity grid. In August this year, the Ukrainian presidency confirmed a further €2 million for the energy sector. For a country whose power stations and grid are under systematic Russian attack, such support has an immediate practical value.
There is also a military dimension, which Belgrade has spent years describing in guarded diplomatic language. As far back as June 2024, the Financial Times reported an estimate that around €800 million worth of Serbian ammunition had reached Ukraine through intermediaries since the invasion began. These were commercial exports via third countries. This year, Christopher Hill, the former US ambassador to Belgrade, described American support for the purchase of that ammunition and said those involved in Belgrade knew who the end user was.
Vučić’s policy towards Russia provided ample grounds for serious criticism, from his refusal to impose sanctions to his attendance at Putin’s parade in Moscow. His visit to Odesa ended with his refusal to sign a joint declaration calling for increased pressure on Russia. Even so, Ukrainian diplomacy managed to secure tangible benefits from that contradictory relationship. Zelensky had a duty to seek help wherever he could obtain it, including in Belgrade.
Parts of the Serbian opposition judged his visit chiefly by how much it might benefit Vučić. Srđan Milivojević, leader of the Democratic Party, which backed the Student List, argued that Vučić was using Zelensky to signal his usefulness to Berlin, expecting it in return to accept whatever election result he declared. This reduced the visit of a president whose country was under attack to a weapon in a domestic political feud, leaving Ukraine’s interests almost entirely out of the picture.
Milivojević is fully entitled to doubt Vučić’s motives. But I also expect a politician who presents his party as pro-European to recognize Ukraine’s needs. Zelensky is answerable to people who need ammunition, medicines and electricity, and every meeting that can secure such support is justified by his country’s needs. To demand that he tailor his diplomatic contacts to the mood of the Serbian opposition would reveal how little we understand the responsibilities of a president whose country is at war.
A protest letter signed by a hundred intellectuals in response to the visit displayed even more open hostility. Its signatories declared Zelensky chiefly responsible for the war, denied that Russia was the aggressor and warned that his visit threatened Serbia’s relations with Russia. That position effectively grants Moscow the right to decide whom Belgrade may receive. Appeals to Serbian dignity end, on this reasoning, in acceptance of Russian tutelage over Serbian diplomacy.
By that logic, the Ukrainian president should be held responsible both for the war Putin started and for the discomfort his visit causes Putin’s admirers. Ukrainians are expected to understand Serbia’s historical traumas, Russia’s security demands and other people’s electoral needs, while their own right to survive is subjected to endless political qualifications. It is hard to imagine greater moral arrogance than demanding that a people under bombardment spare the feelings of those who justify bombing them.
The Student List’s representatives must now show what approach to Ukraine they intend to turn into state policy. Their campaign statement of September 30 explicitly pledged that Serbia would continue to reject sanctions against Russia. University professor Radomir Saičić, a member of the Serbian Academy and one of the Student List’s most prominent figures, advocated “productive relations with Russia” during the campaign, invoking historical ties and energy needs. For Kyiv, those positions matter more than photographs of celebrations on Belgrade’s streets.
Historical ties deserve respect, and energy dependence demands serious efforts to reduce it. When used as permanent excuses for giving in to Moscow, they become instruments through which Russia maintains its advantage. The new government needs to explain what Serbia gains by making its European future dependent on the Kremlin’s mood, and how far it is prepared to limit cooperation with Ukraine for the sake of that relationship.
Invoking Kosovo makes that choice particularly difficult to defend. Ukraine has not recognized its independence, maintaining a position Belgrade regards as essential to its national interests. Russia, meanwhile, occupies Ukrainian territory and seeks to redraw borders by military force. Politicians who demand that the world respect Serbia’s territorial integrity have an added obligation to uphold the same principle for Ukraine, including Crimea and the other occupied regions.
The question for the winners is how much of the sovereignty they demand for Serbia they are prepared to recognize for Ukraine. The right to choose a government and determine a country’s future is the very basis of their electoral victory. Ukrainians are defending precisely that right against a state that denies their country’s existence. It would be a bitter outcome if politicians brought to office by citizens who had freed themselves from fear showed more sympathy for Putin’s demands than for the people he is subjecting to violence.
There is also a very practical question: who in the new majority will decide the course of those relations? Will ministers have the political backing to continue cooperating with Kyiv when the nationalist wing of their alliance objects? Will decisions on exports, humanitarian aid and diplomatic contacts serve Serbia’s interests, or the need to keep the peace among people who, until yesterday, were united by their opposition to Vučić?
The Kremlin can exploit precisely these divisions. All it needs to do is raise the political cost of every decision that helps Ukraine, present it as a betrayal of friendship with Russia and provoke disputes within the new government. Delaying contracts, halting deliveries or withdrawing from joint projects could then be presented as temporary concessions made to preserve unity. Ukrainians and Serbian citizens alike would bear the consequences, while Moscow secured the outcome it wanted.
For the pro-European members of the winning alliance, this is where they must face the responsibilities they could avoid during the campaign. They will have to state what cooperation with Ukraine they support and which decisions they regard as unacceptable. Invoking the movement’s diversity will quickly lose its force once they are voting on budgets, appointing ministers and making commitments to other countries. Every concession to Russian interests will then carry their names and be backed by their votes.
I expect Moscow to use Serbia’s relations with Ukraine to test how much influence it can exert over the new government in Belgrade. Serbia now has an opportunity to make a democratic change of government the basis for greater independence in its foreign policy, and its new representatives have a strong enough mandate to take responsibility for that choice.
Ukrainians deserve to see that independence exercised in Serbia’s dealings with them as well. Their president must be welcome in Belgrade even when his visit displeases Moscow and offers no electoral advantage to his Serbian hosts. If, after a victory won on the promise of a freer Serbia, the Ukrainian president finds his scope for cooperation with the country curtailed, Vladimir Putin will have won a share of that victory. Responsibility for that outcome will lie with those who promised their citizens a free country, then allowed a foreign regime waging a war of aggression to set the limits of its foreign policy.

Türkiye plans $100 billion investment in power grids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:48:07 UTC
22:48:07 KST

Türkiye’s National Energy 2040 strategy envisages about $100 billion in investment in electricity transmission and distribution networks, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Oct. 26.
The strategy will be unveiled in Istanbul on Nov. 5, Bayraktar told an electricity distribution industry event in Ankara.
He said the spread of electric vehicles, greater use of electricity in industrial production, and growth in artificial intelligence and data centers would increase electricity demand and change consumption patterns. Expanding solar and wind capacity would also require networks to adapt.
“We cannot assess the energy transition solely in terms of investment in power plants,” Bayraktar said.
Transmission and distribution networks, storage capacity, digital technologies and system management capabilities needed to be developed together, he added.
Bayraktar also called for wider use of domestically developed software in electricity distribution systems and stronger protection against cyberattacks.
Electricity now accounts for 21 percent of Türkiye’s final energy consumption, up from 15 percent in 2002, he said. Its share has reached 30 percent in industry and 33 percent in buildings.
Greater electrification would help improve energy efficiency, expand the use of domestic and renewable resources, and reduce dependence on energy imports, Bayraktar said.
Strengthening electricity grids will be a priority on Türkiye’s agenda for COP31, the U.N. climate conference in Antalya on Nov. 9–20. Bayraktar said Ankara would seek greater international cooperation on modernizing distribution networks, integrating renewable energy and financing grid investment.

Vilnius hoped a change of government in Latvia would help unblock the Rail Baltica railway project that has been plagued by delays, Lithuanian Transport Minister Juras Taminskas said on Monday.
"The Estonians are executing the project, and like us, they are keeping to the deadlines. We face more challenges with the Latvians, but I believe that with the change of government, and if this prime minister remains prime minister in Latvia, which seems likely, the project should move past the deadlock there," Taminskas told reporters in Vilnius on Monday.
Following an agreement among the Baltic states to extend the deadline for completing the first phase of Rail Baltica to 2034, Taminskas reiterated that Lithuania remained committed to its plan to finish the project by 2030.
"There is not much flawed work on the Lithuanian side. There are certain alleged violations in construction committed by contractors. Legal remedies are being addressed by LTG Infra, and whatever was improperly built will have to be fixed or rebuilt," Taminskas said.
The minister said rising project costs were not unexpected, as delays had turned it into a decade-long undertaking.
Two weeks ago, the leaders of Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia and Poland urged the European Union to ensure adequate funding.
In Lithuania, 114 kilometres of the main line are under construction. Across the three Baltic states, nearly half of the railway line is either under construction or ready for construction. Poland recently approved the construction of an almost 95-kilometre section between Bialystok and Elk.
The first phase, which will connect the Baltic states to Europe with a single track, is estimated to cost 15.3 billion euros across the three countries. Installing a second track could raise the total project cost to 23.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica will connect Tallinn, Parnu, Riga, Panevėžys, Kaunas, Vilnius and Warsaw.
The railway line in Lithuania will stretch 392 kilometres.

The ASEAN-India Trade Agreement and Its Discontents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:57:00 UTC
21:57:00 KST

Even as India has embraced a renewed fervor for free trade agreements, one trade deal remains disfavored in Indian memory. The 2009 ASEAN-India Goods in Trade Agreement (AITIGA) is one of the oldest trade agreements signed by post-liberalization India as well as one of its most controversial. Atypically for an establishment that prefers to settle diplomatic disputes behind the scenes, Indian diplomats and trade officials are publicly trenchant in their criticism of AITIGA.
An oft-repeated narrative has emerged around the agreement: in the early 2000s, inexperienced Indian negotiators walked into an asymmetric deal, opening up their markets while getting little in return. Consequently, India’s trade deficit with ASEAN ballooned. Moreover, China exploited the AITIGA to route its goods into India through Southeast Asia.
This narrative stems from misremembering history. Rather than a powerful tool for ASEAN and China to penetrate the Indian market, the AITIGA is, in fact, a shallow and weak instrument. Moreover, it is shallow precisely because India preferred it that way. By repeatedly telling itself an alternative story, New Delhi has developed irrational fears over economic cooperation with Southeast Asia and injected unnecessary acrimony in the relationship. The myth of AITIGA as a bad deal is costing India diplomatically.
India started running a trade deficit with ASEAN in 1996, 13 years before the AITIGA was signed. The deficit stemmed from Southeast Asia’s shift from agrarian to manufacturing-led economies. The currency devaluations triggered by the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis further boosted the deficit. While the absolute figure of the trade deficit has ballooned over the last three decades, the India-ASEAN imports-to-exports ratio remains broadly similar to what it was in the 1990s.
After the 1997 crisis, ASEAN was looking to economically integrate itself with its East Asian neighbors. In the early 2000s, it began pursuing ASEAN+1 FTAs with its six immediate neighbors: China, India, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand. India had been excluded from the first wave of post-1997 regional integration – the ASEAN Plus Three, Asian Bond Markets Initiative, and Chiang Mai Initiative for currency swap. Eager not to miss out on another wave of regional integration, India agreed to negotiate the FTA.
Contrary to the myth, Indian officials were tough negotiators. After all, India had decades of experience negotiating economic deals in the GATT, WTO, and elsewhere. The negotiations were tortuous and took much longer than the other ASEAN+1 FTAs.
Moreover, there was a mismatch of approach. On the one hand, eager to gain access to the Indian market, ASEAN wanted to widen the FTA’s scope. On the other hand, India looked to protect its domestic industry by limiting the scope of the agreement. Indian businesses were lukewarm about seeking out greater market access in Southeast Asia.
India’s tough negotiating ensured that the AITIGA was the shallowest of the ASEAN+1 FTAs. Whereas all other agreements committed parties to tariff elimination coverage of more than 90 percent, the AITIGA’s promised coverage hovered around 79 percent. ASEAN mirrored India’s reluctance to open its markets. For instance, Indian critics of the AITIGA often point to the fact that Indonesia promised only 48.7 percent tariff elimination coverage to India. Notably, Indonesia offered above 91 percent coverage to all other ASEAN+1 partners, including Australia, with which it ran a trade deficit at the time.
AITIGA also ended up with the most stringent Rules of Origin among all the ASEAN+1 FTAs. It is the only agreement that demands dual compliance (35 percent local content and change in tariff subheading) for goods to qualify for preferential treatment. Its complex compliance rules and lower scope resulted in exporters avoiding using the AITIGA.
In AITIGA, India got what it wanted – an agreement that signaled India’s commitment to its Look East policy without exposing its domestic industry to excessive international competition. While economists may argue over whether Indian protectionism is good economic policy, the debate is irrelevant from a diplomatic standpoint. For whatever reasons, Indian economic managers prefer shielding the Indian market. The AITIGA was a natural outcome of such preference.
However, to then construct a narrative of the agreement as a bad deal in which India got duped is diplomatically damaging. To begin with, it erodes India’s credibility in the region as a reliable and competent partner. India began criticizing the AITIGA almost as soon as it was signed. The two sides agreed to open a review of the agreement in 2015 but still haven’t concluded it. Such long-drawn, dangling processes chip away at India’s image.
AITIGA’s beleaguered state becomes a particularly bad look when contrasted with other ASEAN+1 FTAs, especially the one with China. Beijing began negotiating its FTA with ASEAN around the same time as New Delhi. However, it not only concluded the negotiations fairly quickly, but China and ASEAN have since upgraded the agreement twice. Today, the ASEAN-China FTA is a powerful instrument that deals with a range of issues from digital trade to green technology.
The narrative of AITIGA as a loss for India has made New Delhi a less confident economic actor in Southeast Asia. The resultant hesitation has been evident in India’s exit from the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership as well as its reluctance to conclude bilateral FTAs with Southeast Asian countries such as Thailand and Indonesia. Today, even as India seeks out FTAs in the Middle East and Europe, it is too unsure of itself to look for a trade deal in Southeast Asia.
Tellingly, the acrimony over AITIGA has spilled over into other aspects of ASEAN-India economic cooperation, even the ones which are in India’s interests. For instance, the 2014 ASEAN-India Trade in Services Agreement needs urgent upgradation to account for all the advancements in the digital economy. Given that India enjoys a services surplus with Southeast Asia, New Delhi should be eagerly driving the process. However, so far the two sides have not even begun discussing the issue.
The self-created myths around AITIGA have cast a shadow on India’s Look/Act East policy. New Delhi needs to shed them to become a more confident, credible and engaged actor in the region.

Togo’s China Pivot: Building a Strategic Gateway to the Sahel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:18:00 UTC
21:18:00 KST

As Togo’s President of the Council of Ministers Faure Gnassingbé concluded his eight-day visit to China on October 16, much of the geopolitical attention surrounding the deepening relationship between Lomé and Beijing naturally centered on China’s expanding commercial and strategic influence in West Africa. Yet an equally important question deserves attention: What does Togo stand to gain from its growing partnership with China?
For Togo – a relatively small coastal country with significant maritime assets and ambitions to become a regional economic hub – China offers opportunities that extend beyond conventional bilateral cooperation. Togo is seeking to leverage its geographic position, particularly the strategic Port of Lomé, to strengthen domestic development while expanding its commercial influence across West Africa, including the landlocked countries of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).
During the visit, both countries elevated their bilateral relations to a “China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era,” alongside agreements spanning agriculture, industry, infrastructure, finance, and security.
From Togo’s perspective, three strategic opportunities stand out: building domestic productive capacity, consolidating its position as a maritime gateway to the Sahel, and expanding financial and strategic optionality.
Moving Beyond Raw Commodity Exports
One of the most important opportunities for Togo lies in leveraging Chinese investments, technology, and market access to accelerate domestic industrialization. The composition of Togo’s exports to China illustrates the challenge. According to U.N. Comtrade data reported by Togo, the country exported approximately $18.1 million in merchandise to China in 2025, compared with $14.8 million in 2024. Leading products included sesame seeds, unwrought aluminum alloys, cocoa beans, copper scraps, and manganese ores.
These figures reveal an export relationship still heavily concentrated in primary commodities, metals, and limited processing activities. They also illustrate the considerable scope for Togo to capture economic value domestically. During this visit, Gnassingbé toured a smart farming park in Shaanxi, and the Third Institute of Oceanography in the coastal city of Xiamen. He further expressed that Togo will learn from China’s comprehensive production ecosystems as it pursues a sustainable blue economy.
The significance of these engagements becomes clearer when considered alongside Togo’s existing industrial ambitions. At the Adétikopé Industrial Platform, a major industrial and logistics zone near Lomé, Chinese manufacturer Vivace Group inaugurated a building-materials factory in April 2025 following an investment of about $13.6 million. The facility has a reported annual production capacity of 10,000 tonnes and is intended to supply Togo and neighboring markets.
These developments suggest that Chinese engagement could complement Togo’s efforts to establish a broader industrial production ecosystem rather than remain predominantly a channel for merchandise imports. China’s zero-tariff access arrangements for eligible African exports and the newly signed phytosanitary protocol for Togolese soybeans could further expand export opportunities.
Position Lomé as the Gateway to the AES
The second opportunity concerns Togo’s maritime geography and its potential to becomes an increasingly important commercial intermediary between China and the landlocked economies of the Sahel. The Port of Lomé is central to Togo’s development strategy. Its maritime facilities and the connections to inland transport corridors give the country a structural advantage in serving neighboring economies without direct access to the Atlantic Ocean. For the AES countries of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, reliable access to coastal infrastructure remains essential for international commerce, industrial supplies, and economic development.
Togo’s ambition is to convert this geographic advantage into a durable regional logistic position. During his China visit, Gnassingbé emphasized maritime security, technological capacity, and the need to capture greater economic value from port activities. He spoke highly of China’s record in terms of global maritime governance. The China–Togo joint declaration similarly identified port cooperation, logistics infrastructure, and the development of Lomé as a West African commercial gateway as areas for further engagement.
The timing is particularly significant because Togo and the AES have been pursuing closer customs and trade coordination to harmonize their customs and trade frameworks. Experts from the four nations met in Ouagadougou between October 12 and 14, while Gnassingbé was in China. Their objectives revolved around defining the interconnection of custom IT systems, the adoption of community regulations, and boosting capacity for customs administrations. The strategic benefits of these developments cause a multiplier effect especially in coordination with China.
For Togo, the benefits could extend beyond port traffic to include warehousing, freight services, customs administration, logistics employment, industrial distribution, and greater regional diplomatic influence.
However, Togo must compete with alternative coastal corridors through Benin, Ghana, and Côte d’Ivoire. Its advantage will ultimately depend on transport costs, customs efficiency, infrastructure reliability, and the security of inland routes. This is where Togo’s relationship with China could become strategically consequential. Chinese capabilities in logistics infrastructure, industrial system, and transport technology could complement domestic and regional investments, helping Togo strengthen its competitiveness as a gateway economy.
Diversifying Togo’s Strategic and Economic Partnerships
The third opportunity concerns Togo’s ability to use its relations with China to diversify development financing, strengthen financial connectivity, and expand its room for strategic maneuver. Chinese financing has already played a role in Togo’s infrastructure development.
Research on China’s overseas lending estimated that Togo’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors reached approximately $740 million in 2021. This figure demonstrates the scale of earlier financing relationships, although it does not represent Togo’s current outstanding obligations. During Gnassingbé’s visit, the Togolese government also announced an agreement providing partial cancellation of debt owed to China.
Beyond conventional lending, the most significant new development concerns financial infrastructure. On October 10, the pan-African banking group Ecobank, headquartered in Lomé, signed a memorandum of understanding with China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) to strengthen renminbi-denominated payment connectivity between China and African markets. With operations across 34 African countries, Ecobank provides a potentially important institutional bridge between Chinese financial infrastructure and African commercial networks.
Gnassingbé reaffirmed Togo’s support for the One China principle, and both leaders spoke on the importance of connecting immediate security conditions to long-term development planning. The wider implications of these connections were expressed in the joint declaration on October 15 where Gnassingbé and Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivered five main points as the foundation of the China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era. First was to undertake joint contribution towards the promotion of an orderly and equal multipolar world. Second was to work together to implement the Global Development Initiative. Third was to implement the Global Security Initiative. Fourth was to collaborate toward implementing the World Civilization Initiative and finally, to establish the Global Governance Initiative.
By maintaining economic connectivity with the landlocked Sahel while deepening its engagement with China, Togo is positioning itself as an increasingly important intermediary in the region’s evolving economic architecture. However, the success of this strategy will ultimately depend on Togo’s ability to convert diplomatic agreements into financed projects, domestic technical capabilities, efficient institutions and productive economic activity.

Arakan Army Firms Up Relocation Plan For Villages on Bangladesh-Myanmar Border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:57:00 UTC
20:57:00 KST

The Arakan Army (AA) is preparing to relocate some villages from the restive Bangladesh-Myanmar border at a time when the outfit is also deeply engaged in fierce battles against the Myanmar military’s renewed attempts to reclaim territories in Rakhine State.
The plan being fine-tuned will move residents of select villages from the border to areas in different parts of Maungdaw district in Myanmar’s Rakhine State that are well connected by roads and rivers.
In an interview on March 2, Arakan Army (AA) chief Twan Mrat Naing told this correspondent about the relocation plan, which would focus on “remote villages” along the border, many of which are inhabited by the Buddhist Mro community.
Twan Mrat Naing explained that concern for “better security arrangements” for the residents was the primary reason for the decision to shift residents of a few villages to other zones. “Many villages are isolated and scattered. We will have to ensure that this isolation comes to an end. We will have to relocate them and move them to a place where we can provide security and keep an eye on them,” he said.
The AA chief did not spell out any deadline for completion or details of the project. But the concerns he expressed over the security of some villages has multilayered connotations for the current situation along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border and AA’s plan to take control of it.
The 271 km-long Myanmar-Bangladesh border includes a riverine border of 64 km, where the Naf River serves as the boundary between the two countries. In Myanmar, the border runs along the districts of Maungdaw in Rakhine State and Paletwa in Chin State, contiguous to Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh.
The two districts are both under AA’s control, but the focus of the relocation is on the border villages in Maungdaw, where the population of Rohingya Muslims is over 90 percent.
There is no clarity on how many villages there are along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border. Observers believe there were more Rohingya-inhabited villages before the ”clearance operations” of 2017, when many settlements were destroyed and ceased to exist. Currently, there are over a hundred villages, mostly inhabited by non-Rohingya communities such as Rakhine Buddhists, Mro, Khami, and Chakma.
ARSA’s Presence Along the Border
Underlying the AA’s decision to relocate border villages is its inability to establish absolute control along the border, unlike other parts of Rakhine State that it captured from the military two years ago.
Besides, the AA has to contend with the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), a Rohingya Muslim militant group, which is seeking to carve out a distinct region for the community in northern Rakhine State.
In 2016-17, ARSA carried out a series of attacks on police and military outposts in northern Rakhine State. The military retaliated with the “clearance operations,” resulting in the death of thousands of Rohingya and the displacement of over 700,000 people, now lodged at refugee camps in Bangladesh.
The situation changed in late 2023 when the Myanmar military joined hands with Rohingya rebel outfits, including ARSA and the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), to stall the AA’s campaign to capture Maungdaw. While the military could not prevent the AA from taking control of Maungdaw, the violence resulted in more Rohingya and rebel functionaries crossing over to Bangladesh.
ARSA has support in the Rohingya villages in north Maungdaw. It mounts operations intermittently against the AA and residents of non-Rohingya villages. Its functionaries also frequent the Mayu mountains, which cut across the townships of Buthidaung, Maungdaw, and Rathedaung.
ARSA has clashed with the AA often. It has also abducted and murdered non-Rohingya residents from villages located either near the border or the Mayu mountains. Its victims were mostly from the Rakhine Buddhist, Mro, Khami, Thet, and Chakma communities.
On November 12 last year, ARSA abducted and killed three people, including a 10-year-old girl from Kone Chaung village in Maungdaw. “They were in a group of six people. Three men managed to escape with injuries,” Soe May, a resident of the village, whose daughter was killed, told The Diplomat.
Possibility of Battles on Multiple Fronts
Currently, the AA is engaged in a fierce battle against the Myanmar military in Sittwe and the adjoining region. The Myanmar military unleashed a renewed offensive codenamed Operation 4926 to claw back territories it had lost to the AA in Rakhine State.
However, so far, the military has met with little success. Functionaries of the AA and its political wing, the United League of Arakan, who spoke to this correspondent, were of the view that the military might equip ARSA with weapons to launch more attacks against the AA in north Rakhine State. Reports have emerged of ARSA stepping up its campaign along the border even as the military offensive in Rakhine State deepens.
The AA is concerned about the vulnerability of non-Rohingya border villages to ARSA attacks. Residents of these villages often visit Bangladesh to purchase essential commodities and for medical treatment; this could cease if ARSA trains its guns on them.
A senior ULA functionary pointed out that the most vulnerable to ARSA attacks are about 20 villages located between border pillars 50 and 57, most of which are inhabited by the Mro and Rakhine Buddhist communities.
ARSA, along with the RSO, could target the AA and border villages from camps it has established on the Bangladesh side of the border. Traders from Maungdaw town who frequent the border, including some Rohingya, told The Diplomat that they have seen ARSA and RSO camps at Bandarban in Bangladesh’s Chittagong Hill Tracts.
“Some of these camps are not far from the outposts established by the Bangladesh Border Battalion. The border around Tombru in Bangladesh is the area where the ARSA is most active,” said Kyaw Aye Than, a trader based in the border village of Waylartaung, who occasionally lives in Maungdaw town.
The AA has diverted most of its resources to fight the military for control of Sittwe, the capital of Rakhine State. In addition, it has cadres stationed in the Bamar heartland such as Sagaing Region, Magwe, and Ayeyarwady, where it has teamed up with the local People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) in the movement against the military. The outfit would be overstretched if it were to divert more resources to confront ARSA along the border.
Two months ago, the AA launched its second compulsory recruitment drive under a special law called the National Emergency Defense Provision to increase its cadre strength.
The AA has reportedly learned of the “intimate ties” between ARSA and a section among the non-Rohingya villages, Twan Mrat Naing told me. A sustained collaboration between them could extend to information sharing, which would weaken the AA further in the border areas.
In addition to relocating villages, the AA plans to use technology to surveil the border areas. Drones, camera, and other equipment are being actively considered, the AA chief said.
Border Residents Have Started Relocating
Some non-Rohingya households from the border villages have started relocating to safe areas in Maungdaw, even as the AA is giving final shape to its relocation plans.
On February 10, I saw four huts being constructed near Kine Gree village, located about 20 km north of Maungdaw town. The residents, who belonged to the Mro community, hailed from Don Nyou village near pillar 52 on the border.
An elderly man named Kaing Htauk was among the group engaged in building the huts. He said that since last year 85 households had begun the process of relocating from Pyar Re and Kyauk Lone villages near border pillars 55 to 58. They are now building new homes on plots of land allocated by the ULA. He cited safety concerns as the reason for the move.
“ARSA camps and training facilities across the border in Bangladesh are not very far from our village,” Kaing Htauk said. “We were told by ARSA functionaries to join hands with them. They warned us of dire consequences if we did not.”
Two incidents prompted these residents to arrive at the momentous decision. In April last year, ARSA burnt an AA outpost. Five months later, six farmers, who crossed the border at pillar 52 to visit a market in Bangladesh, went missing. Alarmed villagers then began relocating from their villages.
“Residents of four villages comprising around a thousand people have already shifted to different areas in Maungdaw. More residents from other villages, mostly Mro, Rakhine Buddhists, and Khami, plan to do the same,” said Aung Hlaing, vice chairman of Mro Affairs Committee. He relocated three years ago from the border in a group of 30 people.
Most of the residents of the border villages were engaged in shifting cultivation or petty trade dependent on merchandise from Bangladesh. They face hardships in finding a livelihood in the new location, as it meant adapting to new occupations. While some of them have become daily wagers, others are cultivating food crops such as rice and vegetables and selling them in shops.
There is no fear of ARSA for these residents anymore, but they are now grappling with poverty, which they did not face in their former villages. Aerial attacks by the military are a constant threat they face, like other residents across Rakhine.

Laos Expected to Scuttle ASEAN’s South China Sea Code of Conduct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:34:00 UTC
15:34:00 KST

Throughout its year as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Philippines has aggressively sought to push the China-ASEAN Code of Conduct (CoC) for the South China Sea to the top of the regional agenda and end the long and drawn out diplomatic saga, which dates back more than two decades.
The CoC is part of a long (and thus far inconclusive) quest to find peaceful resolutions to the many maritime and territorial disputes that persistently plague the sea lines of communications across a waterway that accounts for almost a quarter of world trade. A CoC would enable ASEAN to negotiate with China as a united entity, and after all that is what ASEAN is supposed to be all about: a centrist political and trade bloc that can represent the interests of 11 Southeast Asian states on the world stage through a rules based order.
It’s a process that does not suit China, which has done its best to belittle and intimidate Manila and specifically Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, who has demanded respect for international law while juggling heated diplomatic tensions and the ASEAN chair. Publicly, Beijing maintains its policy of non-interference and at times even espouses the virtues of potentially resolving maritime issues with Southeast Asian states through ASEAN. But behind the public spotlight, China has persistently used its proxies to obstruct and scuttle the CoC.
Cambodia was particularly useful in this regard. At the 2012 ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, hosted by Phnom Penh, Prime Minister Hun Sen was signaling a significant shift in foreign policy toward China and the CoC was topping the agenda. The Philippines and Vietnam pushed to explicitly mention the ongoing Scarborough Shoal standoff and Chinese maritime encroachment in their Exclusive Economic Zones, but Hun Sen and his Foreign Minister Hor Namhong balked and declared that such disputes should be handled bilaterally.
For the first time in ASEAN history, no joint communique was issued at the end of the meeting. It was a major embarrassment for the Cambodians.
The CoC was effectively frozen, delays amid the COVID-19 pandemic followed, and whenever necessary Cambodia could be relied upon to do China’s bidding and scuttle the process.
That is what China wants; bilateral negotiations between individual states that enable it to reject international verdicts like the 2016 arbitral ruling on the South China Sea while protecting its expansive unilateral claims and military bases on artificial reefs.
China has also secured its state, military, and civilian investments along Cambodia’s limited coastline, but times have changed with the roaring days of the Belt and Road Initiative disappearing into the vacuum of history.
Given the colossal damage caused by online scam compounds, Beijing would prefer to exact penance out of Phnom Penh than scout for new investments, and the Cambodians, sources in ASEAN are saying, are not prepared to weather the diplomatic heat from blocking another effort to resolve the CoC.
Thus Beijing has considered and pressed its alternatives ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit, to be held in Manila on November 16–18 and chaired by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Myanmar could work, but it remains barred from ASEAN summits in retaliation for the ousting of Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government in early 2021 by a junta led by current regime president Min Aung Hlaing. That could change next year.
Timor-Leste, ASEAN sources say, is moving rapidly into China’s orbit, but as the newest member remains unwilling to upset Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, or Singapore on the CoC, nor to offend Cambodia after it shepherded Dili into the trade bloc.
That leaves landlocked Laos, an economic basket case in a region struggling for growth, and an absolute dependent on Chinese largesse. There are shades of the Khmer-Sino relationship from a decade ago now emerging between Vientiane and Beijing.
Late last month, China and Laos announced the opening of a Military Joint Support and Training base north of Vientiane, which has already earned comparisons with China’s development of the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia. Joint military exercises known as “Peace Train 2026” were held in September.
“Cambodia does not have the appetite for this,” said a Western source privy to CoC negotiations between ASEAN states over the last 12 months.
“It’s overwhelmed by the mess created by organized crime, the scam compounds and the conflict with Thailand. Phnom Penh is now moving closer to the United States and it just can’t deal with any more pressure. Myanmar, not yet; Timor-Leste, watch this space.
“Laos? Laos has been tapped by China and will have to defend its interests, and it’s the only country in ASEAN that Beijing can lean on, and it has been doing precisely that. Laos is going to shatter the Philippine dream of using the chair to pass the Code of Conduct. It’s as simple as that.”

China Pulls Out of Logistics Hub Project at Colombo Port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:17:00 UTC
14:17:00 KST

Last week, China Merchants Port Holdings (CMPH) pulled out of an agreement to build a $392 million South Asia Commercial and Logistics (SACL) hub at the Colombo port. The Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) agreed to pay $21.9 million to settle investments. This should not have come as a surprise given that the project was rife with delays from the start.
When the project was announced in April 2023, it was expected to be completed by the end of 2025. The SLPA and private sector firm Access Engineering were the other parties to the agreement and each holds a 15 percent stake in the project. The logistics hub was to be an eight-story, 5-million-square-foot facility with a storage capacity of 530,000 cubic meters (CBM). The SACL project was expected to provide direct employment to at least 1,800 people and create 10,500 other indirect jobs.
China has been a major financier and builder of Sri Lanka’s infrastructure. Chinese loans helped finance infrastructure projects, while Chinese companies made substantial investments in port operations. China Merchants developed the $500 million Colombo International Container Terminals facility, in which it holds an 85 percent stake, and secured a 99-year concession to operate Hambantota Port through a $1.12 billion agreement in 2017. Separately, China Harbor Engineering undertook the Colombo Port City development on reclaimed land adjoining the capital’s harbor. The proposed logistics hub would have expanded China Merchants’ existing maritime business into a larger warehousing and distribution operation, further linking Chinese investment to Sri Lanka’s ambitions to become a regional logistics center.
There were allegations against the SACL project from the beginning, including claims that the Ranil Wickremesinghe administration signed the agreement without following tender processes. The unions insisted that Sri Lanka would lose 2.8 billion Sri Lankan rupees annually (around $8.4 million) and that the agreement prevented the SLPA from granting other port logistics or warehousing operators royalty terms below those payable by this project, raising questions about the SLPA’s freedom to attract competing investment.
In March 2024, almost a year after the agreement was signed, it was revealed that the project had not yet commenced due to delays in approval for concessions. Almost another year later, the SLPA said the project was scheduled to commence in 2025 after the attorney general’s approval for the proposed concession agreement.
SLPA Chairman Admiral (Retd) Sirimevan Ranasinghe told the media that the delays in the project were due to difficulties in reaching an agreement on the concessions applicable to the project. When the agreement was signed, it was expected to enjoy concessions as a Strategic Development Project (SDP). However, this facility was withdrawn due to the objections of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which had long insisted that Sri Lanka suspend SDP concessions. Ranasinghe also said that the logistics center project would take around 42 to 45 months to be completed, which would have pushed the project’s completion to around 2029, four years after the original completion deadline of 2025.
In October this year, leader of the house Bimal Rathnayake told parliament that the deal was called off because the two sides could not see eye to eye on the agreement. He said the agreement allocated 10 acres between the East and West Container Terminals at the Colombo port. The agreement’s clauses were highly problematic, and despite several rounds of discussions, the two sides could not reach an agreement, Rathnayake said.
This falling out between CMPH and the SLPA raises a number of issues. The Colombo Port could have benefitted greatly from a logistics center. Had it been completed as scheduled in late 2025, it could have allowed Sri Lanka to earn more from cargo passing through.
The World Bank’s latest reports show both the strength of Colombo’s position and the danger of allowing it to weaken. The Connecting to Compete 2025 report said Sri Lanka is among the developing economies whose emergence as shipping hubs have given them unusually strong international connectivity. Yet the Container Port Performance Index 2025 placed Colombo 95th for vessel turnaround, behind Jawaharlal Nehru Port and Mundra, both in India, at 22nd and 30th places, respectively. Colombo’s performance scores also deteriorated sharply in 2024 and 2025.
The World Bank reports showed that while Sri Lanka has valuable shipping connections, it faces growing pressure to provide better service. The reports recommended that Colombo must earn more from the cargo those connections bring. Much of Colombo’s transshipment work involves transferring unopened containers between ships. A logistics center would have allowed operators to unpack selected shipments and prepare their contents for onward distribution.
There could also have been operational benefits. The Container Port Performance Index 2025 report said that inadequate storage and slow movement of cargo fill terminal yards, disrupt handling, and lengthen ships’ stays. A well-integrated logistics center could help by providing suitable space for cargo processing and storage, supported by efficient transfers and customs procedures.
In response to CMPH’s pullout, the SLPA has decided to call for tenders to develop a new logistics hub at Colombo port, under a public-private partnership (PPP) model. Colombo port is a busy place, and some believe that it will not be difficult to attract new investors to build the logistics center.
However, given international developments, geopolitical rivalries, and the expertise needed to develop a logistics center, finding a replacement investor will be difficult and time-consuming. The conflicts in West Asia have disrupted shipping routes, raised transport costs, and made future cargo flows harder to predict. Then, there are alternative ports for Colombo that are modernizing rapidly.
The falling out with CMPH, which already operates a major Colombo terminal and has obvious commercial interests in making the proposed center work, would be another obstacle in attracting a new investor. A replacement investor will want to know why that venture failed and whether the same difficulties could affect its own investment.
And if indeed the deal didn’t go through because the initial agreement of April 2023 did not follow due process and ignored IMF dictates about SDPs, prospective investors will wonder whether an agreement signed with the Sri Lankan government is a dependable basis for committing significant funds for long-term projects. Sri Lanka’s IMF program was approved on March 20, 2023, a month before the logistics hub agreements were signed on April 21. Negotiations with the IMF had begun much earlier, with a staff-level agreement reached on September 1, 2022. In December 2023, Sri Lanka committed to stop approving new SDP projects.
The Wickremesinghe administration was responsible for negotiating both the IMF program and the logistics investment. It can’t say that the IMF demands were unforeseen, as the government knew the fiscal commitments it had accepted from the IMF and the concessions the developer wanted.
CMPH is expected to recover approximately $20.83 million under the settlement, before winding-up costs. But it also spent time pursuing a project that never became operational. Returning most of the capital does not compensate for the forgone opportunities. So, a prospective investor may require a higher expected return, stronger compensation provisions, or more approvals completed before committing money.
A business that commits hundreds of millions of dollars to a long-term investment project like the SACL looks for stability and clarity. No investor would like to spend months agreeing on terms of a project, invest substantial time and resources, and then be compelled to leave because opportunity costs are great, especially at a time when the world is in flux. In recent years, successive Sri Lankan governments have shown international partners that they were unreliable. One of the National People’s Power (NPP) government’s main challenges is to change that perception. However, there has not been much to write home about in the past two years.
