Myanmar Using Fake Paperwork to Conceal Shipments of Iranian Jet Fuel, Reports Claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:27:00 UTC
07:27:00 KST

Myanmar’s military authorities have imported Iranian jet fuel using “sham paperwork” designed to circumvent the U.S. sanctions on both nations, according to reports published by Reuters and a local activist group yesterday.
The reports, which were based on shipping records, satellite imagery, and documents from Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator and Ministry of Commerce, show how both the origin and content of the shipments were falsified. These shipments of jet fuel, which were disguised as diesel, have allowed the Myanmar Air Force to sustain its brutal air campaign against those opposing its coup d’etat in February 2021.
It has been clear for some time that Myanmar’s military was receiving fuel shipments from Iran’s large tanker “shadow fleet” – both Reuters and the rights group Amnesty International have reported on the issue – but the exact mechanism by which the shipments were being concealed was previously unknown.
The Reuters report traced the journey of a particular vessel, the U.S.-sanctioned tanker Reef, which arrived in Myanmar waters in December of last year with some 113,000 barrels of fuel aboard. As the report detailed, the shipment was ordered by Myanmar-based energy broker Dynamic Wave, which signed a $15.8 million sales contract with Thailand’s Tawan-Oil Trading “to supposedly take delivery of a similar amount of South African diesel.”
But the vessel really contained jet fuel from Iran, which Reuters verified both via documentary evidence and satellite images and analysis provided by SynMax Intelligence, “which tracked the tanker’s journey from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas to Southeast Asia.”
Myanmar’s military junta, which in April pupated into a quasi-civilian government under coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, was involved in concealing the origin and nature of the shipment. Days before the Reef arrived, Reuters stated, Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator told the client of Dynamic Wave that it would issue import documentation that labeled the delivery as diesel “instead of jet fuel,” according to a copy of a November 30 letter seen by the news agency.
Reuters said that it received the document from the local activist group Justice for Myanmar (JFM), which also published a report yesterday providing more detailed evidence of how Myanmar and Iran had concealed the shipments. In its report, JFM stated that leaked import documentation “reveals a network of junta-linked businesses in Myanmar, Thailand, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), for fuel declared as originating in or transiting through Singapore and South Africa.”
Between December 2024 and November 2025, JFM said that it identified records from the Myanmar Commerce Ministry for six shipments of jet fuel that included more than 843,000 barrels of aviation fuel, valued at $109.5 million. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that shipments of jet fuel between Iran and Myanmar have continued into 2026, stating that a tanker reached Myanmar in September.
According to previous reports, Iranian “shadow tankers” have also used a number of other methods to conceal their shipments. They have “gone dark” and switched off their location signals when onloading or offloading aviation fuel. Fuel shipments have also been resold and transshipped multiple times in order to hide the source.
All of this demonstrates the lengths to which Myanmar’s military is prepared to go to ensure a continued supply of jet fuel, as well as the porous nature of U.S. sanctions against both Iran and Myanmar.
In March 2023, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions on two individuals and six entities linked to Myanmar’s jet-fuel industry, citing its deadly bombing campaign against civilian targets. In a statement at the time, Treasury said that the U.S. government “remains steadfast in its commitment to the people of Burma, and will continue to deny the military the materiel it uses to commit these atrocities.” Similar sanctions have also been imposed by the United Kingdom, European Union, Canada, and Australia.
These shipments from Iran have allowed the military to sustain its fierce air campaign against resistance groups and civilian populations that are believed to harbor them. As it has lost territory in various parts of the country, the Myanmar military has relied ever more heavily on its air force, one of its main advantages over the welter of rebel groups and civilian militias that oppose it.
According to the U.N. Human Rights Office, civilian deaths from airstrikes rose by more than 50 percent in 2025. The figure increased from 641 in 2024 to 982 last year. The latter figure included 232 children, which, as JFM noted, is more children than were killed by airstrikes in the previous four years combined.
The past several months have been marked by fierce bombing attacks in Rakhine State, where the military is battling to retake territory from the Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist group that has conquered most of the state since late 2023. Airstrikes on two camps for internally displaced people in AA-controlled Ponnagyun township earlier this month killed at least eight people. These came after a major aerial attack in neighboring Kyauktaw township on September 28, which killed 50 people and wounded at least 58, according to the AA and other local sources.
Given its importance to the military’s machine of repression, human rights activists have campaigned since the coup for foreign governments to cut off its supplies of jet fuel. However, the fact that fuel continues to flow between Iran and Myanmar, despite extensive sanctions, demonstrates how difficult it can be for the United States and its partners to establish firm control over complex and attenuated global fuel supply chains.
JFM yesterday concluded its report by urging like-minded governments to close the gaps that have permitted the Myanmar military access to jet fuel. It called on the Thai, Singaporean, and Emirati authorities “to urgently investigate the junta’s trade fraud and use of companies in their territory to source aviation fuel.” It also said that the U.S. and other Western powers should “sanction the junta’s whole aviation fuel supply chain network, including the companies and individuals identified in this investigation.”

The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has filed a criminal complaint with UK authorities against Israeli soldier Lidor Dafna over alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide committed in the Gaza Strip, Anadolu reports.
The foundation said in a statement Sunday that Dafna, a reservist serving as a D9 armored bulldozer operator in the 603rd Combat Engineering Battalion of the 7th Armored Brigade, participated in military operations in Gaza and Lebanon from November 2023 onward.
The foundation said it has reason to believe he is currently in the UK.
The complaint focuses on the destruction of Great Ocean Mills, an industrial flour-producing facility in the Morag Corridor between Khan Younis and Rafah, on May 25, 2025.
According to the foundation, footage posted by Dafna on social media shows a bulldozer demolishing the facility’s wheat silos.
The foundation said Israeli forces subsequently occupied the building, converted it into a military base and reportedly used it to shoot Palestinians seeking food aid at a nearby Gaza Humanitarian Foundation site.
The foundation said the destruction occurred when Israel had sealed Gaza to food, fuel and medicine, with flour reportedly selling for as much as $70 per kilogram and half a million people facing starvation.
The foundation also said that the 603rd Battalion carried out more than 60 controlled demolitions of buildings, including mosques and residential blocks, and contributed to widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure and agricultural land during the establishment of the Morag Corridor.
READ: Rights group urges US to arrest Israeli commander linked to Hind Rajab’s killing
The foundation said its investigation indicates that Dafna may be criminally responsible for extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity, intentionally targeting civilian objects, using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare, extermination as a crime against humanity and genocide.
The foundation called on British authorities to open an investigation, arrest and question Dafna, citing Article 146 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which requires states to search for individuals alleged to have committed grave breaches of the convention.
Dyab Abou Jahjah, the foundation’s director general, said: “Lidor Dafna filmed himself destroying one of the last remaining food production facilities serving a starving population, then posted the footage on social media as a trophy.”
“The United Kingdom now faces a simple test: will it arrest and prosecute a man, who remains an active soldier of an army carrying out such crimes, or once again permit a perpetrator of genocide to walk freely on its soil and return to Gaza to continue committing his crimes?” he added.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Israel votes Tuesday in closely contested election as Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:34:36 UTC
03:34:36 KST

Israelis head to the polls Tuesday in a closely contested parliamentary election that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's long rule or leave the country facing another political deadlock, with neither major bloc projected to secure a governing majority.
The vote will be Israel's first general election since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the subsequent Israeli offensive on the Gaza Strip, as well as military confrontations with Lebanon and Iran.
It will also be the first Israeli general election held on schedule since 1988, following decades in which successive governments collapsed before completing their four-year terms.
Around 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, including approximately 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Voting will take place at 12,018 polling stations, with approximately 18,000 ballot boxes deployed nationwide.
Most polling stations will open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 10 pm (2000GMT). Election day is a public holiday.
Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing for seats in the 120-member Knesset, where a governing coalition requires the support of at least 61 lawmakers.
Under Israel's proportional representation system, voters choose parties rather than individual candidates. Parties must secure at least 3.25% of valid votes to enter parliament.
No party has ever won an outright Knesset majority, making coalition negotiations decisive in determining who becomes prime minister.
Final surveys published by Israel's three main television broadcasters put former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party narrowly ahead of Netanyahu's Likud.
Yashar is projected to win 22 to 23 seats, compared with 19 to 21 for Likud.
The B'Yachad, or Together, alliance led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid is projected to finish third with 14 or 15 seats.
Other opposition parties include the Democrats, led by former general Yair Golan, and former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beytenu.
The three surveys project Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc winning 50 seats, while the opposition bloc is forecast to secure between 52 and 56.
Palestinian-led parties are projected to win a combined 14 to 16 seats.
The figures suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government.
Winning the largest number of seats does not automatically determine who becomes prime minister.
President Isaac Herzog will consult the elected parties before assigning the task of forming a government to the lawmaker considered most likely to command a parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu, 77, is seeking another term after serving as prime minister for more than 18 years across three separate periods.
His campaign has focused heavily on national security, portraying his experience and military policies as essential to confronting regional threats.
However, he faces criticism over his government's failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attacks, its handling of subsequent conflicts and its opposition to establishing an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures.
Netanyahu is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies, and faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
His potential coalition partners include far-right parties led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, alongside the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have advocated expanding illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, rejected Palestinian statehood and encouraged Palestinians to leave Gaza.
The ultra-Orthodox parties have meanwhile faced mounting criticism over demands to preserve military-service exemptions for religious students as the Israeli military struggles with personnel shortages after years of conflict.
Eisenkot, 66, served as chief of the Israeli military from 2015 to 2019 and joined Netanyahu's emergency government following the Oct. 7 attacks.
He later left the government after criticizing Netanyahu's management of the Gaza offensive and the absence of a clear political strategy.
His son was killed while serving with the Israeli military in Gaza in December 2023.
Eisenkot has campaigned on government accountability, political stability and restoring public confidence in state institutions.
He supports establishing an official inquiry into the Oct. 7 security failures and ending broad military-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men.
Despite positioning himself as an alternative to Netanyahu, Eisenkot maintains similar positions on several major security issues.
He opposes establishing a fully sovereign Palestinian state under current conditions and says Hamas' military capabilities and rule in Gaza must be dismantled.
The election therefore presents voters with competing approaches to leadership, governance, judicial independence and relations with far-right parties, even as the two leading candidates share positions on key security issues.
The Joint List and Ra'am, the principal parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, could play a decisive role if neither major bloc secures 61 seats.
Polls project the Joint List winning around nine seats and Ra'am securing between five and seven.
An Eisenkot-led government could require support from one or both Palestinian-led parties, either through formal coalition participation or outside parliamentary backing.
Such an arrangement would face political obstacles.
Lieberman has rejected joining a government dependent on Palestinian-led parties, while other opposition figures have been reluctant to commit to such an agreement.
Netanyahu has repeatedly invoked the possibility of Palestinian-led parties influencing the next government to mobilize right-wing voters.
Several possible outcomes could emerge from Tuesday's vote.
Netanyahu could form another government if his bloc secures enough additional seats or attracts lawmakers from outside his existing alliance.
An Eisenkot-led coalition would likely depend on an agreement involving Palestinian-led parties, defections from other camps or difficult compromises among ideologically divided opposition leaders.
A unity government involving Likud and major opposition parties is another possible arrangement, although Eisenkot and several allies have ruled out serving under Netanyahu.
If neither side assembles a majority, Netanyahu could remain caretaker prime minister during prolonged coalition negotiations, potentially leading to another election.
The performance of smaller parties polling near the 3.25% electoral threshold could prove decisive. Parties that fail to meet the threshold win no seats, potentially weakening their political allies and shifting the balance of power between the competing blocs.
Exit polls are expected immediately after voting ends at 10 pm local time Tuesday.
Initial official results will begin emerging overnight, although counting ballots from military personnel, hospitals, prisons and other special voting arrangements could take several days.
Official results are scheduled to be published by Nov. 4, after which coalition negotiations could continue for weeks.

Netherlands readies its army for large-scale conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:33:38 UTC
03:33:38 KST

- The Netherlands will buy more CV90 infantry fighting vehicles, bridge-laying tanks and a replacement for its Kodiak breaching vehicle, the defense ministry said.
- Germany’s FFG will supply ACSV tracked support vehicles and Wisent 2 recovery vehicles, but quantities and costs were not disclosed.
The Netherlands will buy more CV90 infantry fighting vehicles, additional bridge-laying tanks, a replacement for its unreliable Kodiak combat engineer vehicle, and new tracked support and heavy recovery vehicles from Germany’s FFG, Dutch State Secretary for Defense Derk Boswijk told parliament in a letter on Oct. 26, the Dutch Ministry of Defense said.
The ministry did not disclose how many vehicles it will buy, what the package will cost, or when deliveries will begin, but said the equipment will mainly go to the Royal Netherlands Army’s heavy and medium infantry brigades as the army prepares for a possible large-scale conflict.
The new CV90s will equip an armored infantry battalion that has yet to be formed and will be based at the Nassau-Dietz Barracks in Budel, in the south of the country. The Netherlands is buying them through a joint program led by Sweden, home of CV90 maker BAE Systems Hägglunds, together with Estonia, Finland, Lithuania and Norway, which the ministry said will speed up deliveries. The Dutch army already operates 122 CV90s, which are going through a mid-life upgrade valued at about $500 million.
The ministry said the army’s current breaching vehicle, the Leopard 2-based Kodiak, is outdated and not protected well enough against current and future threats, and that breakdowns and failures have limited how often it can be used. Its replacement will need to clear heavy defensive lines, minefields, walls and other obstacles so tanks and infantry can push through, a task that proved costly for both sides in Ukraine, where dense minefields stalled armored assaults. The ministry did not name the replacement.
The Netherlands is also buying more bridge-laying tanks, which carry folding bridges to span rivers and other gaps, and will probably join an existing German contract to get them.
From FFG Flensburger Fahrzeugbau Gesellschaft, the Dutch army will receive the Armoured Combat Support Vehicle, or ACSV, a tracked support vehicle already used by the Norwegian army, in several versions including an ambulance, command post, minelayer and driver training vehicle. FFG will also supply the Wisent 2, a heavy armored recovery vehicle built on the Leopard 2 chassis that can tow and lift damaged or stranded tanks and armored vehicles. The army currently has 25 older Bergepanzer 3 recovery vehicles, a fleet the ministry has said is too small for the planned expansion of its armored forces, which includes newly ordered Leopard 2A8 tanks, Defence24 reported in March.
Dutch companies will take a large share of the work. Van Halteren Technologies will assemble the ACSV and the Wisent 2 recovery vehicles in the Netherlands and maintain them, while KONI Nederland and Neways Electronics will supply parts and Avient Protective Materials will provide high-strength fibers for the ACSV’s ballistic protection.

Trabzonspor complete 2-goal comeback against Rizespor as Besiktas beat Basaksehir in Turkish Super Lig

Halis Sunnetci
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Trabzonspor overturned a two-goal deficit to secure a dramatic 4-3 away victory over Rizespor in the Turkish Super Lig on Monday, extending their winning streak to six matches across all competitions.
The visitors trailed 2-0 at halftime in the Black Sea derby but scored three goals in nine minutes after the break before Franculino struck a late winner to complete his brace.
Rizespor took the lead in the 12th minute when Mithat Pala delivered a low cross from the right flank, allowing Gennaro Borrelli to control the ball and finish from close range for his first goal for the club.
The Italian striker doubled the hosts' advantage in the 32nd minute, converting a low pass from Adedire Awokoya Mebude following a swift counterattack.
However, Trabzonspor emerged strongly after halftime, pulling one back in the 49th minute through Melih Kabasakal, who tapped into an empty net after Ernest Muci's pass.
Just two minutes later, Aral Simsir equalized with a delicate first-time lob over goalkeeper Yahia Fofana after being played through by Muci.
Trabzonspor completed their comeback in the 58th minute when Fofana parried Muci's effort into the path of Franculino, who converted the rebound from close range.
Rizespor responded in the 69th minute as Qazim Laci unleashed a powerful strike from nearly 30 yards, with the ball hitting the post before finding the top corner to make it 3-3.
But Franculino had the final say in the 84th minute, collecting a long pass from Muci before driving into the penalty area and firing a powerful shot into the top corner.
Muci played a key role in Trabzonspor's comeback, setting up three goals, including Franculino's late winner.
The victory extended Trabzonspor's winning streak under head coach Thomas Reis to six competitive matches and lifted the Black Sea side to second place with 19 points after nine league matches.
Rizespor remained 13th in the standings with 10 points.
 
Besiktas beat Basaksehir 2-0

The hosts came close to breaking the deadlock in the 17th minute when Dusan Vlahovic's header struck the crossbar following Wilfred Ndidi's cross.
After a goalless first half, substitute Oh put Besiktas ahead in the 76th minute, capitalizing on Hamza Gureler's failed clearance before rounding goalkeeper Muhammed Sengezer and slotting into an empty net.
Olaitan sealed the victory in the 89th minute, collecting a loose clearance from Emin Bayram following Leandro Trossard's low cross and firing a powerful shot into the top corner.
The result lifted Besiktas to fourth place with 18 points, while Basaksehir remained 12th with 11 points.

A woman living in Nigeria who was infected with the Ebola virus and her spouse, a Swiss diplomat, have been admitted to hospitals in Switzerland after they were flown in from Nigeria on Monday, Swiss authorities said.
The man was admitted to the University Hospital Zurich, while his wife was taken for treatment at the Geneva University Hospital, the Canton of Geneva said.
"This situation does not pose any risk to public health in Switzerland," the Swiss government said in a statement.

The outbreak, which started in Democratic Republic of Congo, has now been reported in four countries in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
WHO, Switzerland, Africa's top health agency says patient contracted Ebola in Uganda, Uganda denies
The patient arrived in Nigeria after spending two weeks in Uganda, raising concerns over potential transmission in a country that was declared Ebola free in August.
Ugandan officials claimed that the patient had recently been in the DRC, where the outbreak is still spreading, but the World Health Organization and Africa's top health agency said on Thursday that they had not received confirmed information that the woman had traveled there.
The Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs had on Thursday told Reuters that the woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling in Uganda.
Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases and that if it did, it would make that information public.

Israel’s 'hasbara' overhaul raises questions over who is in charge - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:32:44 UTC
03:32:44 KST

On Sunday, July 12, a debate took place in the Knesset on a subject that the parliament rarely discusses: the work of the National Public Diplomacy Directorate; in other words, Israel’s hasbara.
The Knesset’s own account of the debate conceded that it was occurring “after years of instability.” That was the least of the fundamental, indeed institutional, problems revealed.
Eden Bar Tal, director-general of the Foreign Ministry, openly admitted to the committee that, until the end of 2024, public diplomacy had scarcely featured in the ministry’s mission. Its concerns had historically been “almost solely diplomatic.”
Only from the end of 2025, in accordance with a permanent government resolution, did communications and public diplomacy acquire priority. “Public diplomacy,” Bar Tal declared, “is now the main role of the Foreign Ministry.”
The change in government policy was backed by a dramatic budget increase. “In previous years, public diplomacy activity amounted to NIS 25 million-NIS 27 million per year for the Foreign Ministry throughout the world,” Bar Tal revealed. “In effect, it was zero resources. Today, the budget that was set amounts to about NIS 1.2 billion.”
This extraordinary turnaround is almost certainly due to the appointment in April, shortly after completing her five-year term as Israel’s ambassador to the UK, of Tzipi Hotovely as head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate. In the few months she has held office, she has been heavily involved in rebuilding the organization she inherited, as well as actively mounting two vitally important promotional campaigns.
She told the Knesset committee that on taking up her post she had discovered substantial organizational problems. “I want to say directly and candidly that I discovered great difficulties,” she said, “but we are rebuilding the directorate.”
However, merely reconstructing the directorate that Hotovely now heads, essential as that is, may not create the well-functioning and effective national hasbara operation the nation urgently requires. It is the overall organizational set-up that seems problematic.
For example, two distinct bodies within the Israeli administration are rendered in English as “Public Diplomacy Directorate.” The National Public Diplomacy Directorate, headed by Hotovely, sits in the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). Its name in Hebrew includes hasbara.
The Foreign Ministry’s Public Diplomacy Department is a separate unit within that ministry. The word “National” is attached only to Hotovely’s unit.
Her organization is charged with setting and coordinating public diplomacy policy right across government, including the Foreign Ministry, the IDF, the intelligence agencies, the police, and the Government Press Office.
The Foreign Ministry, on the other hand, which operates its own Public Diplomacy Department, conducts Israel’s diplomacy abroad, supports Israeli embassies, manages media relations and digital outreach, promotes cultural and scientific cooperation, and relations with Jewish communities.
Moreover, as Bar Tal informed the Knesset committee, it is the Foreign Ministry that administers the principal public diplomacy budget.
Since the two bodies operate in the same broad policy field, questions must arise about the boundaries between their respective responsibilities.
How is this arrangement, which looks like a recipe for operational confusion and inter-departmental rivalry, meant to operate?
The current relationship is best described as coordination rather than command. Hotovely’s National Directorate is a senior-level coordinating body operating from within the PMO, while the Foreign Ministry is both a participant in that coordination and an implementing ministry with its own overseas public diplomacy apparatus.
In practice, the National Directorate convenes a national public diplomacy forum bringing together representatives from across government. The Foreign Ministry’s Public Diplomacy Department then translates policy into work carried out through embassies and consulates, such as press engagement, digital diplomacy, branding, briefings, cultural and scientific diplomacy, and responses to hostile narratives such as Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) campaigns.
The arrangement is not necessarily dysfunctional, since national coordination and diplomatic implementation can be complementary functions. But the arrangement strikes an outside observer as fragmented and lacking a clear management structure.
Is this division of labor supported by sufficiently clear lines of authority? If not, there is the risk of duplication, competing priorities and uncertainty over accountability.
In “rebuilding” her directorate, Hotovely will certainly have in mind the potential problems posed by the current set-up.
Meanwhile, she has not allowed the grass to grow under her feet. In September, she mounted a major publicity campaign in New York ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the UN General Assembly.
Around 500 billboards and dozens of trucks with digital screens were deployed, alongside online promotion. The messaging focused on Iran’s security threat, the US-Israel partnership, and the argument that Israel and the US were defending the free world.
In October, Hotovely was heavily engaged in promoting a film that countered the anti-Israel messages in the film NAZA, which claimed that the collateral death toll in the Israel-Hamas war was deliberate and institutionalized Israeli military policy. The film won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.
Hotovely presented certificates of appreciation to the creators of NAZA – The Real Story, a film featuring Israeli military personnel’s testimony, and intended to rebut accusations concerning the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza.
The film was available free online, and on October 14 the Algemeiner reported “it has already been viewed more than 43 million times, according to the site.”
Eylon Levy, a former spokesperson in the National Public Diplomacy Directorate, spoke to the Knesset committee in July.
'Waging a delegitimization campaign against us'
“Regrettably, in the past few years, our enemies have been playing on an empty field,” he said. “The most prestigious organizations around the world are waging a delegitimization campaign against us, aimed at persuading normative people that we deserve to be destroyed, but we aren’t returning fire.”
Hotovely is supremely well-qualified for the job she has taken on. Her career has combined domestic Israeli politics, diplomacy, and public advocacy abroad, and the Israeli cabinet unanimously approved her appointment. If anyone can construct the effective hasbara operation that Israel so desperately needs, it is Hotovely.
Whatever the political hue of the government that emerges as a result of this week’s election, the nation would be well served if she remains in post.
The writer, a former senior civil servant, is the Middle East correspondent for Eurasia Review. Follow him at: www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com

UK antisemitism watchdog GnasherJew exposes 40 antisemitic healthcare workers in NHS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:32:41 UTC
03:32:41 KST

An investigative resource published on the UK watchdog GnasherJew website has exposed approximately 40 medical professionals across the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) who have used their public social media platforms to disseminate antisemitic rhetoric, propagate conspiracy theories, and celebrate violence against civilians.
GnasherJew is a team of Jewish online investigators who identify, expose, and report on antisemitism, Holocaust denial, and extremism. The watchdog group's page of Antisemitic Healthcare Professionals states, “Over recent years, we have exposed doctors, healthcare providers, and other medical professionals for posting antisemitic content on social media, supporting terrorism, and discriminating against Jewish people.”
The dossiers listed on the page detail extensive online activity by practicing doctors, consultants, surgeons, and therapists.
Among the cases documented on the page is Dr. Mazin Fageir, a senior trauma and orthopedic surgeon at the Royal Free Hospital in London.
GnasherJew’s compiled dossier on him included screenshots of his X/Twitter posts showing that he shared a cartoon depicting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wearing an armband with a Star of David and pushing a coffin draped in a Palestinian flag into an Auschwitz concentration camp oven beneath the phrase "ARBEIT MACHT FREI," which translates from German to “work sets you free” and was the sign on the gate at the front of the camp.
Dr. Fageir praises Hamas rocket fire on Israeli homes
In another post from May 2021, during Israel’s war in Gaza known as Operation Guardian of the Walls, Dr. Fageir replied to a post reporting a rocket striking a civilian home in Givatayim, saying, “May you live under rocket fire forever, amen,” and adding that Israeli citizens would be “wiped out one day.”
The page also includes a dossier on Dr. Nizar Ali Mhani, an NHS consultant orthodontist and Cardiff University honorary clinical lecturer.
In the aftermath of the October 7 attacks, Dr. Mhani posted material comparing the actions of Hamas to the Jewish fighters of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, writing, “Would anyone have the audacity or idiocy to ever suggest that the brave Jews who resisted the Warsaw Ghetto genocide used civilians as human shields because they used bunkers and tunnels?”
Another case involves Dr. Asaad Nemer Shamallakh, an anesthetist practicing within the Swansea Bay University Health Board.
Following the outbreak of the war, Dr. Shamallakh published a Facebook post on October 8, 2023, mourning family members, including his uncle and multiple children and women, who he wrote were killed in a missile strike. Writing, “Yes, the Zionist succeeded in gouging out our eyes with them, but he ignited fire and a hell in our souls that will not calm down until we are victorious, take revenge and regain our freedom and our homeland,” he added that after initial grief, “infants, girls and women from the Shamallakh family were the victims of the pigs today... and then you ask why we hate them and fight them with our nails and teeth? Yes, tears fell profusely, and hearts were broken, but we soon returned to the battlefield.”
In another October 8, 2023 post, set against a red background, Dr. Shamallakh wrote: “I swear that the battles of Badr, Uhud and Khandaq, militarily speaking, are a drop in the ocean of the Palestinian battle now. You are the Companions of the Prophet.”
In another post that day, Dr. Shamallakh shared a graphic on Facebook that featured a rocket and star background with the caption, “Look.... watch... what does the Palestinian do .”
The dossiers on the page capture broader trends among the identified practitioners, ranging from the propagation of 9/11 conspiracy theories and Holocaust inversion to the open dismissal of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism.
GMC took 'little to no action' on reports, GnasherJew tells 'Post'
GnasherJew said in a statement to The Jerusalem Post that, “The GMC has taken little to no action on our reports, and its reported 19% regulatory action rate in antisemitism cases does nothing to reassure us. In our opinion, this failure to act tolerates and encourages antisemitism rather than confronting it.”
“In the cases of Dr. Nizar Ali Mhani, Dr. Mazin Fageir and Dr. Asaad Nemer Shamallakh, no action appears to have been taken despite the material documented in our investigations, which includes gross antisemitism, some at neo-Nazi levels, and some support for terrorism. Jewish patients deserve to feel safe in the British Healthcare system; instead, the GMC appears to be playing Russian Roulette with their safety,” GnasherJew told the Post.
A General Medical Council (GMC) spokesperson said, “We are very clear that antisemitism is completely unacceptable. Doctors and patients should have confidence that if a concern is raised with the GMC, it will be dealt with appropriately. We can and will investigate serious concerns that suggest patient safety or the public’s confidence in doctors may be at risk. Where complaints regarding antisemitism have been raised with us, approximately 19.5% of doctors have faced regulatory action. This includes two doctors who have been erased from the medical register, one who received a suspension, and two who were issued warnings.”
A spokesperson for the Royal Free London said, “Our priority is to ensure that everyone in our care, and everyone who works for us, feels safe, respected and valued, regardless of their background or beliefs. The Royal Free London should be a place where everyone is treated equally, with fairness, care, compassion and kindness. We expect that everybody who works here ensures that any content they publish online or elsewhere is consistent with the trust’s values and standards.”
These revelations come amid a widening scrutiny over allegations of antisemitism within Britain’s healthcare sector. Further light was cast on the issue by the Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA) in its recent documentary, Malignant: Antisemitism in the NHS, which compiled harrowing testimonies from Jewish patients and medical personnel detailing direct hostility within hospitals.
Among the incidents featured in the documentary is an account by Shelley Lipman, a registered nurse in Cambridge, who discovered a colleague performing a Nazi salute next to a patient’s bed after discussing her Jewish identity. The film also documented testimony from Shaul Freeman, a patient in Sheffield who alleged that a consultant surgeon made antisemitic remarks—including claiming that Jews shoot children “for fun”—while actively performing surgery to remove a tumor from his forehead.
Accompanying polling published alongside the documentary revealed that over four in ten British Jews who have used NHS services since October 7, 2023, took active steps to conceal their Jewish identity.
The Post contacted the General Dental Council (GDC), but Swansea Bay University Health Board did not respond to an email request for comment by publication time.
Inquiries regarding the allegations were submitted to the relevant NHS trust press offices and regulatory bodies, as well as the GDC for forwarding to the clinicians named; however, no response or comment was received by publication time.

Polish city halts ties with Lviv amid dispute over UPA commemorations

Councilors in the Polish city of Przemysl unanimously voted on Oct. 26 to suspend cooperation with Lviv, a city in western Ukraine, in protest against a proposal to honor the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its leader, Roman Shukhevych, in 2027, Polish broadcaster RMF24 reported.
The move adds to tensions between the two countries after Lviv's council adopted decrees on Oct. 20 declaring the next year as the Year of the UPA, the Year of Shukhevych, and the Year of Oleh Olzhych, a Ukrainian poet and political activist.
The dispute could spread to other Polish local authorities. The Lublin regional assembly also voted in support of severing ties with Lviv, according to RMF24.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has described Lviv's decision as "suicidal tactics," adding that he warned President Volodymyr Zelensky such gestures are not helping already patchy Ukraine-Poland relations.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry called Lviv's actions "counterproductive to our current efforts to further develop Ukrainian-Polish relations and resolve contentious issues amid Russia's full-scale aggression," in a statement to journalists on Oct. 21.
Sviatoslav Sheremeta, head of Lviv's regional council cultural committee, was declared by Warsaw as persona non grata and banned from entering the Schengen area until 2031.
In Poland, the UPA is associated with 1943-1945 Volyn massacres, a historical event during which tens of thousands of Poles were killed in what today is western Ukraine, but used to be under Nazi occupation.
"Roman Shukhevych was a criminal who collaborated with the Nazis and whose hands are stained with the blood of thousands of innocent victims—people killed simply because they were Polish," said Poland's charge d'affaires in Kyiv, Piotr Lukasiewicz.
Poland is an important ally in the realms of security and defense, especially at a crucial time when U.S. relations with Ukraine have become strenuous.
"Additional foreign policy challenges are the last thing Ukraine needs today," Sergiy Solodkyy, director of the New Europe Center think tank in Kyiv, told the Kyiv Independent.

Eurovision in crisis: Netherlands make U-turn and pull out of Eurovision 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:38:08 UTC
22:38:08 KST

The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to participate.
The Netherlands will not participate in 2027's Eurovision Song Contest after all.
NPO, the umbrella organization for public broadcasters in the country, has reversed its earlier decision to return to the contest, after Dutch public broadcaster AVROTROS had announced in August that it would not take part because of Israel's presence in the line-up.
The decision to return to the competition was met with widespread criticism and around 400 NPO employees signed a letter urging the organisation to reconsider its participation.
In a statement, NPO's director Jet de Ranitz said that NPO was unable to secure a broadcaster who would send a Dutch artist.
“In our coordinating role, we held discussions with the broadcasters to investigate whether there are any broadcasters willing to facilitate the participation of a Dutch artist. In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return,” De Ranitz said.
"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027." He added: "Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."
NPO will still broadcast the event.
Eurovision director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".
He said in a statement: "We recognise that opinions about the Contest are deeply and sincerely held at the moment, and that they differ widely, both within countries and between them. We do not dismiss any of those views. Public service media exist to serve their audiences, and it is right that our Members weigh these questions carefully, in dialogue with their own communities."
He added: "At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience. That spirit of unity is what the Contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."
"We are very happy that the 2027 Contest will still be broadcast in the Netherlands and look forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again whenever NPO, its members and audiences feel the time is right."
Ireland has already announced it will not take part in Eurovision 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.
The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.
Last year, five countries - Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia - boycotted Eurovision after organizers declined to exclude Israel over its military actions in Gaza and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
The Spanish broadcaster RTVE said at the time that it would not broadcast the contest or the semi-finals and criticised the decision-making process as “insufficient”. They said that the EBU’s decision to keep Israel as a competitor “increases RTVE’s distrust of the festival’s organisation and confirms the political pressure surrounding it.”
Irish broadcaster RTÉ stated: “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation remains unconscionable given the appalling loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there, which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk.” As for Slovenian broadcaster RTVSLO, they said last year that taking part “would conflict with its values of peace, equality and respect” and that it was pulling out of the competition "on behalf of the 20,000 children who died in Gaza".
The 2026 competition drew 131 million viewers, down 35 million from the year before.
Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year.

EU Commission proposes expanding powers of border police force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:36:04 UTC
22:36:04 KST

EU Commission proposes expanding powers of border police force
BRUSSELS, Oct 27 - The European Commission proposed a major expansion of the powers of the EU border agency Frontex on Tuesday, including giving it the capacity to act beyond EU territory, in the aftermath of the massive rush to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta last summer.
The proposal would significantly expand Frontex's mandate, providing additional resources and empowering the agency to support non-EU countries to return migrants to the countries of origin.
The proposed legislation is an attempt to make Frontex more reactive to large-scale arrivals at the EU's borders, such as in Ceuta on the North African coast, as European governments push for tougher migration policies despite concerns from rights advocates over accountability.
"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs and migration, told reporters.
"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can deploy within 24 hours and spot risks early, before an event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.
OVERSIGHT CONCERNS
But while the proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's role, it would also narrow the scope of its internal rights watchdog, with complaints referred to national authorities to handle.
The proposal comes as member states increasingly focus on returns, arguing that too many migrants ordered to leave the bloc ultimately remain.
Although irregular arrivals have decreased, the arrival of more than 72,000 people in Ceuta from Morocco in late July, most of whom later left, reignited debate over the EU's migration rules and was cited by several member states as evidence for stronger tools.
The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers, who would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.
The proposal would create a new EU Return Coordination Centre within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process, from voluntary return counselling to organising returns and reintegration support, the statement said.
The proposal would also create a new online monitoring centre to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.
The proposal was met with criticism from rights groups and lawmakers.
"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.
"We need a human rights-based approach to border management and Frontex plays a key role. But instead the Commission risks turning Frontex into a European version of ICE," she said. REUTERS

A Ukrainian company is beginning to assemble interceptor drones designed to launch from unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), with specialized launch boxes being developed for their deployment.
Taras Ostapchuk, founder of Ratel Robotics, announced the plans in an interview with Forbes, as cited by RBC-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The company has previously demonstrated the launch of strike FPV drones from its ground robots. It now plans to adapt the concept to counter aerial threats.
Ratel will initially focus on multi-rotor interceptor drones before moving on to fixed-wing, airplane-type models.
The company is also developing launch boxes for deployment from UGVs and integrated software to enable data exchange between ground and aerial platforms.
Under the concept, a UGV would carry interceptor drones to a designated position and launch them to engage enemy aerial targets.
Ostapchuk told Forbes that integrating different types of unmanned platforms was a key direction in robotics development. By combining their capabilities, the systems could enable operators to perform a wider range of tasks remotely.
Vsviti, which also cited the interview, reported that Ratel is currently focusing on multi-rotor interceptors that do not use jet engines. Fixed-wing drones are planned for a later stage.
The company is also working on unified software for ground, aerial and, eventually, maritime unmanned systems. The software is intended to improve data exchange and interoperability between different platforms.
Russian Commander Complains NATO Testing Drones on Ukraine’s Front Line
As part of this effort, the company is testing an autopilot system for ground robots that it plans to adapt for aerial drones.
According to Ostapchuk, Ratel has already invested approximately $200,000 in developing its aerial division. Developing fixed-wing drones could require several million dollars.
Ukrainian troops have completed their first logistics mission using a domestically developed amphibious UGV, traveling more than 40 kilometers (nearly 25 miles) across land and water to deliver supplies to frontline positions, Ukraine’s defense ministry said.
The vehicle can cross rivers, canals, and marshes without switching platforms, allowing it to continue operating where conventional ground robots might be unable to pass.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps has begun using unmanned ground vehicles for assaults on Russian positions. Its NC13 unit equipped kamikaze robots with Bullspike grenade launchers and deployed them against Russian troops, including positions inside shelters.
The corps has also tested dropping UGVs from Gryphon heavy bombers and used robotic platforms to strike Russian positions and logistics targets up to 15 kilometers (about 9 miles) from the front line.

BRUSSELS, Belgium — The EU is working on how to stop Russia from laundering its reputation through international sporting events, but as it talks, Moscow creates new facts on the ground.
"Sports and culture must not become vehicles for whitewashing Russian aggression," the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas told journalists on Oct. 13.
But since then, there have been at least two instances in which Russia has been able to advance its sports agenda.
Lithuania was stripped of its right to host an April 2027 international pentathlon tournament on Oct. 19 after it refused to grant visas to Russian and Belarusian athletes for the event.
And on Oct. 25, the International Weightlifting Federation announced that its 2030 championship would take place in Moscow, the first time such a high-level contest has been awarded to Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In both cases, the condemnations and expressions of disappointment have come thick and fast.
Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys called the pentathlon decision "shameful" and said the EU "must tighten restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes competing under national colors, expand visa bans and sanctions, and cut support for those enabling state-sponsored propaganda."
And Ukraine's Sports Minister Matvii Bidnyi told public broadcaster Suspilne that Kyiv would boycott the weightlifting tournament in Moscow.
The minister added that he considers the choice of host "an alarming and unacceptable signal," which "suggests that the influence of Russians in some international federations is extremely strong."
Likewise, European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova told the Kyiv Independent that the EU's executive arm "regrets" both of those decisions.
"In line with the autonomy of sport, international federations are responsible for decision-making on where to host international competitions. However, both federations and member states should act in line with EU sanctions and values," Hrncirova said.
Beyond criticism, the EU is also preparing measures in a bid to tackle the issue.
Kallas said on Oct. 13 that the EU's diplomatic arm, the European External Action Service, "together with the Commission, will put forward proposals on how to sustain Russia's isolation in global sports."
And Hrncirova said that "the Commission is facilitating and supporting coordinated action among member states and with like-minded international partners to resist the instrumentalization of sport by Russia and Belarus."
However, it remains unknown when the new measures will be announced. In the meantime, Russia's lobbying to return to sports continues unabated.
Russia's all-out war has taken a heavy toll on Ukraine, with hundreds of Ukrainian athletes and coaches killed and hundreds of sports facilities destroyed by Russian missile and drone attacks.

Tallinn mulling 1+1 and 2+1 lane options for Tulika tänav renovation
Preliminary designs have been released for the renovation of Tulika tänav and the section of Paldiski maantee that intersects with it in Tallinn's Kristiine district, and the street will be rebuilt with either 1+1 or 2+1 traffic lanes.
Ahead of the renovation of Tulika tänav, which connects the Kristiine traffic junction and the Sõle intersection, Tallinn is considering two options: rebuilding the street with either 1+1 or 2+1 traffic lanes.
Both solutions will include new sidewalks, cycle paths and street greenery. A traffic study has been carried out to find a suitable solution, and the final choice will be made after assessing spatial possibilities and the needs of different modes of transport.
Tallinn Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) said that he and Tallinn Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse (Center) prefer the 2+1 option.
"Our clear view is that this location cannot accommodate a 1+1 solution, and our firm preference is 1+2," he noted.
However, no decision has yet been made. "When making the final decision, we will naturally take residents' feedback into account," Järvan said.
The reconstruction will also include the renovation of water supply and sewerage facilities, the construction of a separate stormwater drainage system and improvements to street lighting.
Feedback on both options can be submitted until November 10.

Two Russian Starlink rival satellites set to fall from orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:28:40 UTC
22:28:40 KST

- Two Rassvet-3 satellites from Russia’s second 2026 batch are expected to reenter within a day or two after failing to raise their orbits.
- Most of the remaining satellites from both 2026 launches have reached a stable altitude of about 500 km, satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell said.
Two satellites from Russia’s Rassvet broadband constellation, the country’s answer to SpaceX’s Starlink, are expected to fall back into the atmosphere and burn up within the next day or two after failing to raise their orbits, Harvard-Smithsonian astrophysicist and satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell said, while most of the other Rassvet-3 satellites have now settled into their working altitude.
“Most of the rest are stable at 500 km,” said Jonathan McDowell, who published an updated chart of the constellation’s orbit raising showing the bulk of the satellites from both 2026 launches flattening out at about 510 km (317 miles), while two satellites from the second batch have sunk below 230 km (143 miles) and are dropping fast.
The two failing satellites come from the second group of 16 Rassvet-3 spacecraft that Bureau 1440 launched on a Soyuz-2.1b rocket from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on July 19, 2026, and by late August tracking data already showed a pair from that batch heading toward reentry without ever performing orbit-raising maneuvers, after they slipped below 300 km (186 miles).
Their loss would bring the number of Rassvet satellites lost since the program began flying operational spacecraft this year to three out of 32, after the constellation lost its first satellite in June, when Object 4 from the first batch, launched on March 23, 2026, reentered without having made a single maneuver.
McDowell’s chart also shows that a handful of other satellites from both batches are still below the target altitude, with one first-batch satellite holding at about 345 km (214 miles), another climbing past 470 km (292 miles), and one second-batch satellite at about 363 km (226 miles), although it does not indicate whether those spacecraft are still working.
Rassvet is being built by Bureau 1440, a private company that began as a research office inside Russian mobile operator MegaFon, and the system is meant to provide satellite internet across Russia, with partial commercial service planned for 2027, subscriber terminals said to weigh under 15 kg (33 pounds) and the company aiming for 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and up to 900 by 2035.
Neither Roscosmos nor Russia’s Ministry of Defense has announced the Rassvet launches, and in August the constellation was already providing at least two daily coverage windows over Ukraine lasting more than an hour each, raising concerns that Russian forces could eventually use it the way Ukraine’s military relies on Starlink.

PRESS RELEASE 160
Albares takes part in the annual Ibero-American Free Zones Conference, bringing together organisations from both sides of the Atlantic
The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, addressed the annual Ibero-American Free Zones Assembly, which opened in Cádiz on Monday, and called for a strategic awakening of a Europe that speaks with its own voice and works hand in hand with Latin America and the Caribbean, “because only through multilateralism can the world move towards progress”.
The Assembly, organised by the Association of Free Zones of the Americas (AZFA) and the Cádiz Free Zone Consortium, provides a forum for cooperation, knowledge exchange and the creation of opportunities among free zones, institutions, businesses, universities and specialists from Europe and Ibero-America.
Strategic awakening

Madrid Summit

The Minister described it as a Summit “that will strengthen the Ibero-American Community, an essential instrument for all of us, particularly in a geopolitical context as complex and uncertain as the present one. A community that offers us a space for dialogue, cooperation and trust, capable of providing stability and certainty in turbulent times, but also of delivering very tangible improvements in the lives of the millions of citizens who belong to it. A community that demonstrates, once again, that there is far more that unites us, and that many opportunities arise when we Ibero-Americans work together.”
The ocean that unites us
Under the theme “The Ocean That Unites Us”, this year’s event seeks to strengthen partnerships on both sides of the Atlantic and promote Cádiz as a connecting point between the two continents. It has brought together representatives of 53 organisations from 20 countries and territories (Spain, Colombia, Costa Rica, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Brazil, Panama, Honduras, Curaçao, Guatemala, Cuba, Paraguay, Afghanistan, Uruguay, Aruba, El Salvador, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Haiti and Peru).

Swedbank lays off 100 in Baltic states, warns AI could mean more cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:28:00 UTC
22:28:00 KST

Swedbank lays off 100 in Baltic states, warns AI could mean more cuts
Swedbank is laying off around 100 staff in Estonia and the other Baltic states, while the bank says Artificial Intelligence (AI) could lead to further layoffs in future.
Swedbank CEO Olavi Lepp said the company is laying off employees across the entire group, meaning both in the Baltic states and in its home nation, Sweden, with redundancies to total around 500.
"Naturally, in the process, we are also offering existing employees the opportunity to retrain for other roles, but this does not suit everyone and, unfortunately, layoffs are also needed," he said.
Lepp added that Swedbank employs more than 6,000 people in the Baltic states, of whom around 100 have been laid off. The layoffs are linked to a general restructuring of work and investments in development, he went on.
Lepp explained that when the bank experienced a period of very high profitability a few years ago, it decided to invest more in IT development and data modeling, adding some of the aims have been accomplished. "Today, when profitability is at normal levels, we do not need as many people," he said, adding that when development work is not being carried out on a large scale, it makes no sense to retain employees at the same level.
Lepp said in any case there will certainly be jobs in the future that require fewer people. "Then it depends on the company's own sales and strategy what it does next: whether it reduces the number of employees or tries to increase business volumes with its existing workforce."
He added that it is currently unclear whether companies developing AI will meet investors' expectations on profitability. "The big question is that when they become profitable, meaning they start charging the proper price for their services, how much will the software licenses and tokens that we pay AI companies for then cost?"
There are currently more than 90 applications across the Swedbank group in which AI is being tested. Lepp said that so far as Estonia goes, the primary objective is to do more business with the same number of people — increasing business capacity and market share, and in some contexts reducing costs.
In implementing AI, a company needs to carry out a standard cost comparison, and if using tokens is cheaper than employing people, layoffs or retraining will probably follow. "I would say that when it comes to tasks governed by fairly formal logic, the capabilities of artificial intelligence are certainly much greater than those of humans in a great many cases," Lepp went on.
The bigger question, he added, is whether there will be customers from whom profits can be earned. "There have to be people somewhere who consume these services, and they, too, have to earn their income from somewhere," Lepp noted.
Swedbank's net profit in Estonia for the first nine months of this year came to €193 million, €2 million more than in the same period in 2025.
