German Ambassador: Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:26:00 EET
22:26:00 KST

German Ambassador: Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way
Boris Ruge has been Germany’s new ambassador to Ukraine since August.
Ukraine is not new to him, though. Until recently Ruge was a senior NATO official, serving as Assistant Secretary General for Political Affairs and Security Policy – essentially the third-highest position in the Alliance’s civilian hierarchy. And, of course, he was closely involved with Ukraine and supported closer ties for Ukraine with the Alliance.
Now Ruge speaks on behalf of Berlin.
And when he tells European Pravda in this interview that Germany supports NATO membership for Ukraine, that represents a clear German position. But his statements on EU membership for Ukraine are even clearer and more detailed.
This and much more in the ambassador’s first interview in office.
"We are absolutely determined to stay here"
In your view, what does Ukraine mean to Germany?
Ukraine is a very important partner for Germany – in technical terms we could say a strategic partner, as we agreed in the spring of this year. We understand how important Ukraine is for European security, and we also understand its weight as a major economic player.
You’ve worked at NATO, so you’ll know that pretty much every member is described as "a highly valued ally". It’s the same for Ukraine, isn’t it?
No, it’s not the same for Ukraine. Ukraine is a big country, and it is, unfortunately, at the heart of the largest war in Europe since 1945, which has been going on for more than four years now – tragically so. The outcome of this war will determine Europe’s future security order.
As far as we are concerned, Europe’s future security order should include a Ukraine that is sovereign, independent and democratic – and able to move towards and join the European Union, certainly. And NATO as well: we said a few years ago that the future of Ukraine is in NATO.
All of these things matter. At the core is a fundamental point: Ukraine must be able to exercise its own choices and be part of what, in the old days, we would have called the free world. And I think that is very relevant today – if we look at what Russia represents today, it is definitely not the free world.
So, NATO membership, EU membership, and a democratic Ukraine. Those are encouraging messages at the start of our interview, and we’ll come back to each of them later. But first let me say that I’m particularly happy to see you here in Kyiv after last night’s missile attack [the interview took place on 22 October]. Do you know why I say that?
No.
Because we Ukrainians remember 2022, when one embassy after another was leaving Kyiv. Can we be certain that this won’t happen again?
Yes. I think you can be absolutely sure. You remember that Chancellor [Friedrich Merz] came to Kyiv on 4 October. And on 3 October, we were told [by Moscow] that all foreigners should leave Kyiv because it was dangerous and we risked losing our lives by staying here.
But the Chancellor was not deterred from coming here.
We are here. We know that the coming months will be difficult – over the past two months, we have already seen the security situation become more difficult. We need to handle that, and we need to look after the security of our people, but we are absolutely determined to stay here. It’s the same for all our European and NATO partners.
"EU membership won’t happen in 2027 or 2028. That's impossible. It's not doable"
You’ve already said that you see Ukraine as a member of the EU. But is that goal achievable within a reasonable timeframe? And what exactly is a "reasonable timeframe"?
That’s a good question. As we all know, to become a member of the European Union, a country has to adapt its legislation, regulations, institutions and so on. That’s not arbitrary, and it’s not something we’ve made up to make things complicated. It’s simply that the European Union is so highly integrated and demands so much of its members. Ukraine needs to go through those steps – and doing so will also make Ukraine a more European country in a broader sense.
I don’t think you will find a government in the European Union that is more forward-leaning on EU membership than Germany. I remember that you interviewed my predecessor, Heiko Thoms, about the letter that Chancellor Merz wrote back in May [on a special format for Ukraine’s integration into the EU].
Among other things, the letter called for full membership for Ukraine – I think it says so three times in a single letter – and, basically, for opening all negotiation clusters now.
And it says that, as Ukraine moves towards the European Union, Ukrainians – representatives of Ukraine – should be brought into the institutions: the Commission, the Parliament, the Council, the European Court of Justice. It’s a very forward-leaning, very positive vision of how we see Ukraine and of our wish for Ukraine to advance rapidly.
How long it will take is a very difficult question.
I think it's a good thing that
people here in Kyiv have moved away from the notion that it will happen in 2027 or 2028.
It will not happen then. It’s impossible. It’s not doable.
We’re now hearing hopes that Ukraine could join by 2030, and this is being discussed in Brussels as well, not just in Kyiv. Is that an achievable goal, even if it is an ambitious one?
2030 is ambitious. First of all, it depends on how Ukraine performs. And then, of course, the reality is that it’s also a very political process, because there are 27 members of the European Union and they all have a say. So it’s difficult to predict, but I think the geopolitical case for Ukraine joining the European Union is very strong.
What matters is that, together, we keep Ukraine on track, moving forward as fast as possible towards full membership – so that people in this country can feel that this is something they can work towards, and that they have a real opportunity to become a member of the European Union within a reasonable time.
Is it theoretically possible for Ukraine to join the EU while the war is still ongoing?
I don't know whether the European Union has taken a position on whether a continuation of the war would stand in the way of Ukraine becoming a full member. I don’t know that. I don’t believe that’s the case.
We should work with Ukraine, even under these very difficult circumstances, to move forward on the path to the European Union. And then we’ll take it from there.
"There's an understanding, but I remind people that this is the case"
The path to EU membership is first and foremost about reforms.
Last week, several laws were passed that are relevant to the European Union and to Ukraine’s membership – including the law on minorities, but many others as well. There’s a whole list of things – I think they’re very well known to the Office of the President, to the government, to the Rada [Ukrainian parliament] – that need to be done. And in some cases, draft laws or executive decisions are relevant to unlocking funding from the European Union for Ukraine, which is hugely important.
And we keep reminding people that, given the overall situation, we can only encourage Ukraine’s institutions to adopt this legislation as soon as possible, so that the funding the European Union has available for Ukraine can be released.
Do you think the Ukrainian government and our MPs understand that all the reforms must be implemented? That cherry-picking reforms is not an option?
I think there’s an understanding, but I can tell you that I do remind people that this is the case. To raise the very significant resources – the massive resources – needed to support Ukraine and help it defend itself, we also need to be able to tell people in the German parliament, the Bundestag, in the European Parliament and in the European Council that Ukraine is doing its part and delivering on the reform agenda.
Is Ukraine making tangible progress on the rule of law and the fight against corruption?
I mean, there are issues with corruption. There were very prominent cases. But at the same time, we can see that Ukraine has institutions, created after the Revolution of Dignity, that are able to investigate and prosecute people even in very high positions. That’s pretty significant. Maybe it’s not perfect, but nothing ever is.
There is real action on anti-corruption, and that’s extremely important because – again, in Germany – to make the case for supporting Ukraine, there has to be a credible anti-corruption architecture in place and credible action against people who misuse funds for their own purposes.
I remember interviewing German and other European ambassadors five or ten years ago, and even earlier. Time and again they would describe how corruption was hurting their investors. Is that still the case today?
I don’t think that is the main problem for German companies today. And that’s good.
"Russia has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way"
I’d like to ask you about the war, but first, let’s talk about what’s happening around these so-called peace negotiations. I think the best word to describe it is a mess. Would you describe it differently?
No, I don’t have another word for it. I think everyone, first and foremost the people in Ukraine, would like to see the war come to an end – after four and a half years of full-scale war and, before that, eight years of a bloody war at a lower level.
I can see that there is an American-led effort to bring the war to an end. But I would also say, as a German diplomat, that it is clear that Europe has to be part of the picture. The first point is that Ukraine and the people of Ukraine have to decide on what basis they are willing to end the war.
We are grateful to America for trying to bring the war to an end. But Europe – and Germany too – certainly has a big stake in how this war ends, and so we will be there and find a way of articulating our European interests and working with Ukraine to make sure that we end up with a result that is acceptable.
Is Europe playing a sufficiently meaningful role in the process right now?
What we can see is that, as you remember, the national security advisors of France, Britain and Germany have been to Kyiv twice most recently in September. We also had some national security advisors in Oslo just now. So there is a presence, recently in Miami as well.
At the same time, we’re hearing criticism from Poland, our closest EU neighbour. Polish officials don’t hide their frustration that they’re never invited to these discussions. What’s the reason for that?
I don’t know whether it’s true that they’re never invited. But Poland is clearly very important. It’s an important member state of the European Union and an important ally in NATO. It is a neighbour, and it is very much impacted by this war. So I think Poland’s desire to be closely involved is important, clearly. I think there are questions about what the formula will ultimately be.
In a sense, we could say that we have not yet entered into a proper negotiation process. And if we’re serious, we can also say that the Russian Federation has at no time in the past four and a half years negotiated in a serious way. They have always stuck to their basic demands, which essentially amount to Ukraine capitulating – so that is not a negotiation. So I would say we’re not yet in a real negotiation process, and we will see what format it takes.
So for now, as far as I understand, you don't see Russia being ready for serious steps.
Exactly. I mean, last night [21 October] is a demonstration that Russia talks in very vague terms about its willingness to engage, to meet and so on – and in the meantime it attacks Ukraine with its jet drones and ballistic missiles, killing civilians, attacking civilian targets and committing war crimes. So that’s not exactly the mindset of peace. I think we have to be very clear about that.
There was a change in the Ukrainian position beginning in 2025, when the president signalled that he would be willing to accept a ceasefire – a full ceasefire. Since then, we have been talking about the Black Sea deals, grain deals and energy ceasefires – all sorts of things. Russia has rejected every single one of them, and I think the record is perfectly clear.
"I wouldn't say NATO is stepping back. Part of the response is not visible"
Is there a risk that Russian attacks could extend beyond Ukraine?
Russia’s strategy consists of fighting on land. But the front line is relatively stable. Ukraine has done quite a good job of slowing Russia down and, obviously, of retaking territory recently as well.
There’s a war happening in the air, with cruise missiles and drones, where Russia is unfortunately having an impact on the energy infrastructure and attacking the economy – the steel industry, for example. And then there’s a third element: Russia’s hybrid campaign against NATO and EU states, which has been going on for years. Russia is not engaging in a military conflict with NATO, but it is pushing the limits of its hybrid campaign.
In my view, when an explosive-laden drone attacks Leipzig Airport, that’s no longer a hybrid attack. It’s more like a conventional attack, isn’t it?
In the case of Leipzig, Germany made an attribution. We did our homework: we didn’t go out the next morning and say it was Russia – our intelligence services did their homework, and then we attributed it to Russia. And then we took a number of measures: we closed the consulate in Bonn, we closed the Russian House in Berlin, and we did a number of other things to push back.
But you still consider it a hybrid attack?
You know, people argue about hybrid, and I accept that hybrid is perhaps a problematic term. You could say it’s grey-zone – a kind of grey-zone campaign that they’re waging.
But Russia is not engaged in a large-scale military campaign against NATO. And why is that? Because NATO’s deterrence against Russia has worked. So they have been trying to operate below the threshold of an actual military attack.
They've been testing us. And we have to find ways of pushing back.
I was in Berlin at the beginning of September for our ambassadors’ conference. Mark Rutte was there to speak, and he said – and I agree entirely – that if Russia engages in these hybrid operations, the response should be more support for Ukraine, not less, because Russia’s objective is to undermine our support for Ukraine.
And you could see it when Chancellor Merz came here on 4 October with a package of one billion [euros] in military support for Ukraine. So maybe people in Moscow should register that, despite Leipzig and everything else that has been going on against EU states, NATO states and Germany, our support for Ukraine has not gone down. It has gone up.
And yet I’m seeing attacks that ten years ago would have been considered conventional acts of military aggression – Russia is striking NATO member states with drones, targeting Turkish ships, and sinking ships in the territorial waters of Bulgaria or Romania. And nothing happens! There’s no response from the Alliance. So Russia keeps raising the stakes, and NATO is stepping back.
I wouldn’t say NATO is stepping back, but I can tell you that I’ve talked to many Ukrainian colleagues and I know that this is the perception here: that Russia is pushing and NATO has not come up with a strong response. I think part of the response is not visible. But I’ve been telling colleagues from NATO, my former colleagues, that this is the perception here and that they should think about it: The impression that NATO is not responding strongly enough to Russia’s campaign. I think that’s a point people should reflect on in Brussels.
"Germany wants Ukraine to be as close to NATO as possible"
I’m glad to hear that you see Ukraine as a future NATO member. But there’s one opponent to us joining, and that’s the United States. Do you think Ukraine will join the Alliance despite that opposition?
For Ukraine to join NATO, you need all 32 NATO allies to agree. And if you look at the procedure, there are actually several steps where 32 ambassadors need to raise their hand and say "Yes, we agree."
What we said in Washington – and that is the NATO position, as Mark Rutte has reminded people – was that the future of Ukraine is in NATO and that Ukraine is on a… I can’t come up with the adjective right now. Незворотній is the Ukrainian term.
Yeah, absolutely! Незворотній.
Irreversible! Sorry.
So you know the Ukrainian word better!:)
Exactly – so I do remember only the Ukrainian word.
It’s on an irreversible path to full Euro-Atlantic integration. When exactly that will happen is, again, a political issue. The difference today, at least from a German point of view, is that it’s very clear that Ukraine is not just the recipient of our assistance, but also a major element of Europe’s defence today.
We need Ukraine, with its armed forces and its expertise in modern warfare, to be part of our defence against a very aggressive and imperialist Russia whose ambitions go beyond Ukraine. That is our analysis.
What is your vision for Europe’s future security architecture, and what role would Ukraine play in it?
In my view, it revolves around NATO. I’m a former NATO person, so maybe that’s logical. But NATO is the organisation in charge of collective defence. I think the role that the United States plays in NATO is changing – we can see that – because of the change in US force posture globally. As you know, that has been going on for 20 years: Barack Obama talked about the pivot to Asia, and that was in the years after 2008. And now China has become even stronger, and the US is required to play its balancing role in the Indo-Pacific.
So Europeans will have to step up and play more of a role. But to my mind, Ukraine is already very, very close to NATO. We have the NATO-Ukraine Council, and we do a lot of things together. We have the Joint Analysis Training and Education Centre in Bydgoszcz, Poland, and we are learning from Ukraine today when it comes to unmanned systems.
We don’t know when Ukraine will be able to join NATO as a full member, but, from a German point of view, we want Ukraine to be as close to NATO as possible, because in reality you are already part of our collective defence.
What are the key elements of a peace settlement that is acceptable to Europe? And please don’t just say that it’s for Ukraine to decide. You have your own position too, don’t you?
Sure. Our position is that Ukraine should survive as a sovereign, independent, democratic nation that can make its own choices.
What about other conditions, particularly concerning Russia? Some people say that to secure a lasting peace, Europe would need to restore ties with Russia and resume supplies of Russian oil and gas through Ukraine. What’s your view on that?
I don’t believe that’s the case. If you look at the German-Russian relationship after 1991, you could say two things.
One is that Germany got it terribly wrong. We were wrong to assume that we could develop a partnership with Russia. Russia walked away from the partnership we tried to establish and turned into an aggressive, imperialist actor that is trying to overturn the entire political order of Europe. That’s one way of looking at it, and I think in many ways it’s accurate.
Another way of looking at it is that Germany and the rest of Europe tried very hard to build a constructive and positive relationship with Russia. You can see it in the NATO-Russia Council, and you can see it in the way we developed the energy partnership with Russia, and so on. So we tried, and it failed.
We made an honest effort to have a positive, forward-looking relationship with Russia, and Russia threw that out of the window and turned to the use of military force, aggression and this hybrid campaign, this manipulation of information and politics.
This attempt of ours was a failure. But what is important is that we sincerely made efforts to build forward-looking relations with Russia. So the people in Europe today, including in my country, Germany, who say we should go back to that and build a positive relationship with Russia have obviously forgotten that we spent 20 years doing exactly that, and it turned out to be a massive failure.
And it turned out to be the biggest failure on energy in particular. The idea at the time was that if Russia had a major market in Western Europe, it would have a stake in maintaining peace and building a positive relationship. But that is not what Mr Putin ultimately decided.
We are not going back to that. I don’t believe you will find a majority in Germany for that. Maybe people in Washington DC think we should re-establish that energy partnership between Western Europe and Russia, but I think in Western Europe you will find precious few people willing to make themselves dependent on Russia in any way today.
Interview by Sergiy Sydorenko

Giant metal 3D printer to build hypersonic systems in Indiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:24:52 UTC
22:24:52 KST

- Kratos has bought an AMCM M 8K large-format metal 3D printer with eight 1.2-kilowatt lasers for its hypersonic payload facility in Odon, Indiana.
- The system will support MACH-TB, the U.S. Department of War hypersonic test program for which Kratos is the prime contractor.
Kratos Defense & Security Solutions has bought one of the largest metal 3D printers on the market, an AMCM M 8K additive manufacturing system, for its new hypersonic payload facility in Odon, Indiana, where the company prepares the experimental test vehicles it flies for the Pentagon’s MACH-TB hypersonic test program.
Germany’s EOS, whose AMCM unit builds the machine, announced the sale on Oct. 27, 2026, saying the printer will be installed at the Kratos Indiana Payload Integration Facility near Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane Division, though neither company disclosed the price or when the system will begin producing parts.
The M 8K was developed for space and defense work and can print metal parts inside a build volume of 800 by 800 by 1,200 millimeters (31.5 by 31.5 by 47.2 inches) using eight high-power 1.2-kilowatt lasers, with built-in thermal management, gas flow control, filtration and in-process monitoring meant to keep large, complex components accurate and consistent from one build to the next.
“As we change the paradigm on low-cost, high-cadence hypersonic testing for programs like MACH-TB, this type of capability is critical to achieve the goal,” said Mike Johns, senior vice president of Kratos SRE.
Kratos is the prime contractor for MACH-TB 2.0, the U.S. Department of War’s effort to run frequent, affordable flight tests of hypersonic technologies, under a contract worth up to $1.45 billion awarded in January 2025, and printing large metal parts in-house is meant to help the company build test hardware faster and in greater numbers than traditional machining allows.
The printer will join a site that is still ramping up, after Kratos finished the $50 million, 68,000-square-foot (6,317-square-meter) Indiana Payload Integration Facility ahead of schedule in July 2026, with room to prepare up to six hypersonic payloads at once and plans for more than 100 high-tech jobs in its first phase.
“The M 8K was built for exactly these kinds of applications, large, complex parts where scale, precision, and process reliability all matter,” said Martin Bullemer, managing director of AMCM.

Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:23:32 UTC
22:23:32 KST

Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US elections
The US and Israel have teased strikes around their elections, particularly against Iran’s civilian infrastructure.
Israelis have gone to the polls to decide whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will remain in power. On November 3, midterm elections in the United States will take place and likely impact President Donald Trump’s final years in office.
Many Iranians are watching both elections closely, knowing that the way Israelis and Americans vote could have serious consequences for their future. Since Israel and the US launched an unprovoked war on Iran on February 28, Iranians have experienced bombings, a blockade and sanctions.
But despite a sharp decrease in US and Israeli attacks since a memorandum of understanding was reached between Washington and Tehran in June, the threat of war has re-emerged. Many political commentators believe that the US and Israel could restart the war after the elections, and Iranians are anticipating further strikes.
“I haven’t followed the Israeli election very closely. But I think there will be more fighting whether Netanyahu wins or Eisenkot or someone else,” 37-year-old Tehran resident Sajad told Al Jazeera, asking to remain anonymous due to security reasons.
He believes that the rhetoric of Israeli officials signals that their ambition in the war is still for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic, which has controlled Iran since a 1979 revolution.
This has gained some support from Iranians inside and outside the country, who are opposed to the government. But cyber intelligence operations by both Israel and Iran make it difficult to accurately gauge online reactions to the prospect of Netanyahu winning another election.
Iranian authorities have described pro-Israeli Iranians as “homeland sellers” and continue to severely punish any perceived cooperation with Israel based on national security charges.
They also fully blame the US and Israel for Iran’s nationwide protests in January, during which thousands of civilians are believed to have been killed. The United Nations says Iranian security forces committed crimes against humanity while cracking down on the protests.
Shayan, a 32-year-old Tehran resident, said he believes that any Iranians who might have hoped for the overthrow of the government at the start of the war are disillusioned after witnessing US and Israeli conduct since then, with thousands of civilians killed and the US blockade and sanctions hitting most people’s incomes.
“I think some people’s viewpoints adjusted after some of the comments from the US and Israel, and after they bombed infrastructure that we need to live, like oil and gas, power and steel,” he told Al Jazeera.
“I think most Iranians don’t have a choice in the matter, but want some stability and peace.”
President Trump has threatened to bring about the “death of a civilisation” in Iran and suggested the country’s map may look different after the war.
He has also repeatedly threatened to launch more major strikes against Iran’s power plants, bridges and other civilian infrastructure if hostilities resume. US media report that the country’s military is prepared to attack over the coming days if an order is given.
The other option Trump has threatened is prolonging a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place since July, which has stopped the country’s oil exports and significantly disrupted trade. Together with some of the most stringent sanctions imposed against any country, the US measures have made Iranians poorer and more isolated from the international community.
The Netanyahu government has also threatened to strike Iranian infrastructure again, including energy facilities. Defence Minister Israel Katz has repeatedly said in recent months that he wants to send Iran “back into the Stone Age”.
His election opponents and other prominent opposition figures, including Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid and Yair Golan, have all cheered the US-Israeli attacks on Iran both during the current war and during last year’s 12-day war.
They have also been united in wanting to remove Iran’s enriched uranium stockpiles from Iran and dismantle the country’s nuclear programme. Another goal is eliminating the Tehran-backed “axis of resistance” of armed forces who oppose Israel and the US across the region.
Israeli politicians, both the government and opposition, are generally united on the war aims of overthrowing the Iranian establishment, but differ on the method.
Eisenkot, for instance, has supported Netanyahu’s military strikes against Iran and praised Trump’s decision to launch attacks as courageous. But he also says that military operations cannot realistically overthrow the Islamic Republic, and that change must come from Iranians themselves.
Some Iranians have been mentally preparing themselves for conflict when the elections end.
Some Iranians said they have established groups with friends living in different parts of the country to warn each other of imminent strikes if they hear fighter jets flying overhead.
Some of the groups are in domestic messaging apps or over text message since Iranian authorities have said they will impose more internet and communication shutdowns if deemed necessary.
“In all seriousness, 90 million people have our eyes to the sky to see when there will be war. Damn this life we’ve lived,” a user named Ali wrote on X.

India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:15:32 UTC
22:15:32 KST

India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
Despite diplomatic thaw between New Delhi and Beijing, clashes along undemarcated border pose challenge to Modi’s strongman image.
New Delhi, India – India’s armed forces are locked in multiple ongoing face-offs with the Chinese army along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the chief of India’s paramilitary border force guarding the Himalayan frontier with China has said.
The remarks late last week by Shatrujeet Kapur, the director-general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) paramilitary force, come nearly four months after local civil society groups in the remote northeastern region told Al Jazeera that Chinese forces were increasingly encroaching on Indian territory and denying Indian troops access to patrolling points, angering locals.
Chinese President Xi Jinping was in New Delhi last month – his first trip to India in seven years – for the BRICS summit, where he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines, as the two capitals pursued a cautious thaw in bilateral ties. That thaw is partly driven by United States President Donald Trump’s trade war, which has pushed nuclear-armed rivals Beijing and New Delhi closer.
Yet the alleged Chinese incursions into India underscore how, despite warm handshakes in New Delhi, tensions along the 3,500-kilometre (2,200-mile) border between the neighbours threaten to undercut efforts to normalise ties.
They also pose a major political challenge to Modi, who has built an image as being strong on national security, but who has in recent years faced difficult questions about the relationship with China.
The face-offs with Chinese forces in Arunachal Pradesh – that “still continue”, according to Kapur – come six years after at least 20 Indian troops were killed in hand-to-hand combat with Chinese forces in mountainous Ladakh.
Though satellite imagery and multiple accounts, including from within the Indian security establishment, have since pointed to China effectively taking control of parts of previously disputed territory since that fight, the Modi government has refused to concede that it has given up any land.
And five days after Kapur’s comments on recent standoffs, the Indian government is yet to confirm the nature of the border tensions, instead offering more boilerplate criticisms of China.
Unresolved, lingering dispute
Kapur, the ITBP chief, was speaking at a felicitation ceremony for the paramilitary force’s personnel, where he revealed that commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the border with China.
Arunachal Pradesh’s remote Upper Subansiri region – where the ongoing face-offs are reported – had seen the first clash between independent India and China in August 1959, which killed at least two Indian soldiers.
Then-Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke of the remoteness of the region in his account of the clash, when he told Parliament that the border post under Chinese attack was roughly three weeks’ march from the nearest roadhead.
The decades-long India-China border dispute is rooted in a British-drawn border, called the McMahon Line. In 1914, British India and Tibet, not under Chinese control at the time, signed the Simla Convention, demarcating their border. Since gaining independence in 1947, India has treated the McMahon Line as its border with China. But China, which came under communist rule in 1949, rejects the line as the boundary with India, arguing that Tibet lacked the authority to conclude the agreement independently.
Beijing claims the entire state of Arunachal Pradesh and refers to it as “South Tibet” or “Zangnan”. China also controls Aksai Chin, a slice of the disputed Kashmir region that India and Pakistan claim in full.
In 1962, India and China agreed to treat the Line of Actual Control (LAC) – meant to acknowledge the actual areas they each control – as their de facto boundary while negotiating their broader border differences.
Those differences were never bridged in the following years, keeping the disputed frontier a persistent flashpoint in relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.
The dispute erupted again into a deadly confrontation in June 2020, when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in eastern Ladakh, with both sides accusing the other of crossing the LAC. At least 20 Indian soldiers were killed, and China later acknowledged four deaths among its troops.
Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, said that border tensions amid a thaw in bilateral relations now appear as “part of a pattern” – “likely a pressure tactic by Beijing,” he added.
And due to the undemarcated border, “stand-offs are bound to occur from time to time, some of which may go out of hand”, Donthi warned.
‘Chinese army on top of mountain’
But the 2020 clash also pushed Modi into a corner domestically, as the opposition parties pressured the government over its opaque handling of China. The Modi government also faced opposition complaints over restrictions on parliamentary scrutiny, questions about whether intelligence agencies had detected the Chinese troop build-up, and limited disclosure of operational details.
Contradictions between the government’s own stand and Modi’s claims also prompted accusations that he was trying to minimise – or even hide – the scale of the crisis along the border.
On June 17, 2020, soon after the Galwan clash, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar spoke to his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.
“The Chinese side sought to erect a structure in Galwan Valley on our side of the LAC,” the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said after the phone call. “While this became a source of dispute, the Chinese side took premeditated and planned action that was directly responsible for the resulting violence and casualties. It reflected an intent to change the facts on ground in violation of all our agreements to not change the status quo.”
Yet two days later, Modi said on Twitter, now X, that “neither has anyone been able to enter our territory, nor is anyone still on our territory” – an assertion that disputed the foreign ministry’s account. If no Chinese troops had crossed the LAC, why had Indian soldiers been forced to fight them, the opposition and other strategic analysts asked?
The government has never answered those questions, with Modi’s office only issuing a clarification that the prime minister meant that there were no Chinese troops still in Indian territory after the clash.
Six years since the Ladakh clash, the Chinese incursion has returned to challenge Modi’s strongman image at home – which has already taken a hit from youth-led protests in the country that forced out Modi’s education minister in July this year.
In his address, ITBP chief Kapur also recalled the 2020 clash, outlining a specialised training programme “to better equip personnel to deal with” a Ladakh-like situation.
Kapur, who is due to retire this week, also warned that China’s frontier military capabilities had advanced – and Indian forces may not be able to take a fight head-on by traditional methods.
The Crisis Group’s Donthi said that the Modi government “presents an image of a hard security state with zero tolerance for national security failures”. but “the power differential with China is quite sharp, so it tends to downplay any event that reflects poorly”.
The opposition Congress party’s top leader in Arunachal Pradesh state, Bosiram Siram, said that Chinese troops have intruded nearly 50km (31 miles) deep into Indian territory in remote Upper Subansiri.
A Siram-led party delegation visited border areas in August after initial reports of China’s incursions, and Siram added that “Chinese personnel are stationed up there”, referring to Indian territory.
“You can see the [Chinese] Army. They are on top of the mountains, while we are down below,” Siram added.
In response to the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that “the situation in India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns”. He did not comment on the ongoing face-offs.
No lasting solution in sight
BR Deepak, a professor of Chinese studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) in Delhi, said that the reports of Chinese incursion pose a challenge to Modi’s “credibility and accountability”.
Since 2012, India and China have relied on an official channel that deters border disputes from snowballing, without resolving the underlying question of where their Himalayan boundary lies.
The so-called Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC) has officials from both countries and operates alongside military channels.
Its latest round, the 36th WMCC, was held on August 6 – nearly a month after reports of Chinese incursion first emerged in Arunachal Pradesh. In September, a first-ever commander-level meeting was held in Arunachal Pradesh.
Deepak said that “the continuing face-offs show that these diplomatic efforts have not eliminated the friction.” He argued that “meetings at the military or local level can provide temporary relief and help prevent escalation, but they cannot, by themselves, deliver a lasting solution to a border dispute rooted in decades of historical, political and strategic differences”.
And in the absence of “clear political guidance and a coordinated response” in both capitals, Deepak said, any border-level arrangements will “remain fragile and reversible, as seen in [Ladakh] and now in Upper Subansiri in Arunachal Pradesh”.

NEW DELHI: Union petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri on Tuesday said that India was not under any pressure to stop buying Russian oil.During an interaction at the 29th Energy Technology and Innovation Meet, Puri said Indian refiners would purchase crude from suppliers offering the most competitive prices as the country prioritises energy security amid global market uncertainties."I have never felt any pressure," Puri said during the interaction at the 29th Energy Technology and Innovation Meet, which began here on Tuesday."India was not particularly buying Russian oil at present, but the decisions in this regard were guided by commercial considerations rather than pressure from any country," he added."At the point of negotiation, whoever is supplying a particular grade, we will buy from them. Prices come down sometimes," he further said.Puri also said India had diversified its energy investments and sourcing, adding that New Delhi's approach was guided by the need to ensure reliable supplies while managing costs for consumers and the broader economy."India had diversified its energy investments and sourcing," the minister said."India, as a major energy-consuming nation, could not compromise on its energy security amid geopolitical developments and volatility in international markets," he added.
Puri's remarks come days after US secretary of state Marco Rubio visited India against the backdrop of US’ Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act meant to penalise countries purchasing Russian oil and Trump’s subsequent suspension temporarily of related tariffs.
Rubio also said US was in discussions with Reliance Industries on creating capacity to refine Venezuelan crude, calling India a refining superpower and underlining that Washington understood India’s need to diversify its oil imports and saw Venezuela as a potential source of supply.Rubio said New Delhi had repeatedly expressed its desire to diversify its energy portfolio, describing it as a sensible strategy.“In the end, it’s not just about Russian oil; it’s about their desire to diversify,” he said, adding US was keen to be a source of energy supplies for India.

Zabuzhko: Ukraine had culture in 1995, but had lost it by 2005
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
15:13:29 EET
22:13:29 KST

Ukraine was under information and cultural occupation in the decade between the 1990s and 2000s, writer Oksana Zabuzhko said.
"In 1995, we had culture. In 2005, we no longer had it. We were a branch of the 'great Russian world,' which was engaged in the information occupation of Ukraine throughout the entire pre-war decade, starting around the turn of the 1990s and 2000s. This was the same preparation of Ukraine for co-optation into Russia, carried out on a massive scale and quite successfully in the information and cultural spheres. Accordingly, we were invisible to the outside world. The visibility of any nation is cultural visibility. As long as the political class does not understand this, this country will be condemned to struggle somewhere in the third ranks, among the countries of the Third World," Zabuzhko said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum, themed "People. Business. Economy. What Next?", in Kyiv, answering a question about whether Ukraine had achieved a cultural breakthrough.
She said that before the full-scale war, no one abroad was interested in engaging with the culture of "some invisible country whose future was still unknown."
"But once our glorious armed forces gave a thorough beating in the spring of 2022 to those who were considered the world's second army, my dream finally came true. In October 2022, Lesya Ukrainka's Cassandra premiered to great acclaim at London's Omnibus Theatre," the writer said.
In her view, the most relevant definition for Ukraine today was one given by political figure Vyacheslav Lypynsky: "The sum of values that, in the course of a community's life, have proved most conducive to that community's survival is called culture."
"Motivation wins, spirit wins, and so does what the Ukrainian soldier has and the Russian soldier lacks. That is a cultural difference. It is a sense of defending the values of one's community. Ask our soldiers what they are defending: their home, their land. At the level of one's home, one's land and one's family, at this level of rootedness, we have already defeated the Soviet regime and Russia in what they wanted to do to our ancestors during the Holodomor," Zabuzhko said.
Returning to the notion of a Ukrainian cultural "renaissance," she stressed that an artist would succeed with a domestic audience only if they articulated the collective unconscious. That was when queues would form for cultural products, as had happened with the play The Witch of Konotop at the Ivan Franko National Academic Drama Theatre.
"The state's role is to obtain information from experts about this very wild-growing garden: where to graft and where to water, which areas need watering, and where to put in money and later recoup it, whether through the state budget, patrons or fundraising. That is an entirely separate matter. What grows on its own does grow on its own, as we have seen over the past decade. They introduced quotas for Russian music on FM radio, and suddenly it turned out that a great deal of Ukrainian music had grown wild in the meantime, having spent the previous decade being considered unsuitable for the format," Zabuzhko said.
As reported, Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Culture Minister Tetiana Berezhna said that, given the vastly unequal resources available for culture in Ukraine and Russia, Ukraine needed to act asymmetrically. She also said there was currently demand among Ukrainian consumers for Ukrainian culture, demand among creators to produce it, and a need to introduce Ukrainian culture to international audiences.

Details

Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:12:24 GMT
22:12:24 KST

Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
- Published
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - a rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
The aim was looking at "future negotiations to help to end the war" in Ukraine, the offices of President Alexander Stubb and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said. Their initiative was not on behalf of "Europe as a whole".
After the call, Putin said "confrontational" EU and Nato policies were prolonging the war which began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken to the two Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin. Last week, Zelensky met them as well as US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
The Ukrainian leader said he was grateful for the "active support" of his Finnish and Norwegian counterparts.
Tuesday's 90-minute phone call was held from the Finnish capital Helsinki, and showed "big differences in views", Støre said.
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the call to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
The call was "frank and substantive", Stubb said, explaining that the war's outcome will "have a direct impact on our and the broader European security".
Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
He - like Stubb and Støre - had agreed to continue their direct phone communication, the statement added.
Støre said all their allies had been informed of the call ahead of time.
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "very sceptical" of Tuesday's dialogue, telling Danish broadcaster DR, it had not been "co-ordinated with any of the rest of us".
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates, was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US, Ukraine and its European allies have been souring since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia - allowing it to export oil to the US.
But last week, Stubb, Støre and Zelesnky met with Witkoff in the Norwegian capital, before the US special envoy travelled on to St Petersburg to meet Putin.
Following the talks, Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to resume three-way negotiations that Russia had stopped for months.
After speaking to the two Nordic leaders, Zelensky said part of their discussions with Putin had centred on November's trilateral talks to be held in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky said he had discussed with them "various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security".
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
As the US administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the European Union of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".

Japan moves to expose foreign government lobbying
A Japanese government panel began discussing a foreign agent registration system on Monday. The proposal marks a first step toward planned anti-espionage legislation, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Jiji Press.
The proposed system would cover individuals and organizations lobbying in Japan for foreign governments. Those acting under their instructions or contracts would need to register with Japanese authorities. Tokyo aims to make these activities more transparent.
The panel will draft recommendations ahead of the government’s planned national intelligence strategy. That strategy could be compiled as early as this fiscal year.
The government hopes to submit related legislation during parliament’s regular session next year.
Monday’s meeting took place at the prime minister’s office, the panel’s second gathering. A National Police Agency official called for penalties for malicious acts.
The official said attempts to influence political and administrative processes had increased in recent years. This made legislation an urgent priority.
The government also presented examples of similar systems in the United States, Britain and France.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Japan plans to review its fuel subsidies.

====================================================================================================

Greenhouse gas levels reach record high in 2025: WMO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:02:33 CST
22:02:33 KST

GENEVA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases in the atmosphere reached unprecedented highs in 2025, locking in more long-term temperature increases for the planet, according to a bulletin from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) released on Tuesday.
The global average surface concentration of CO2 in 2025 was 53 percent above the 1750 pre-industrial baseline, the WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin showed. Concentrations of methane and nitrous oxide -- the second and third most important long-lived greenhouse gases related to human activities -- also rose to a new record, with respective increases of 167 percent and 26 percent.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. CO2 has a very long lifetime and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries," Barrett said.
Growth rates of CO2 have tripled since the 1960s, accelerating from an annual average increase of 0.8 parts per million (ppm) per year to 2.4 ppm per year in the decade from 2011 to 2020. From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm, above the decadal average but slightly less than the exceptional surge of 2023/2024, according to the bulletin.
"The more modest growth rate from 2024 to 2025 reflects recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino," said WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova.
Nevertheless, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning, she said.
In 2026, the burning of fossil fuels and the development of a supercharged El Nino will impact land carbon sinks as it did in 2023/2024, said Tarasova, warning that "the risks of reduced CO2 uptake by the ocean are also increasing in our changing climate."
The Greenhouse Gas Bulletin, one of the WMO's flagship annual publications, provides authoritative scientific information for negotiators at the United Nations (UN) Climate conference. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Desert brine from former "sea of death" feeds fields across China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:02:28 CST
22:02:28 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Four hours south of Hami, after a long drive across the barren Gobi Desert of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, a sweep of blue-green water appears on the horizon.
It is not a lake. These are evaporation ponds, stretching across more than 160 square kilometers at a sprawling potash operation in Lop Nur, once known as the "sea of death" for its extreme aridity and forbidding terrain.
The desert is also home to Lop Nur Town. There are no families who have lived there for generations -- nearly everyone went there in the new century because of the potash resources beneath Lop Nur's salt crust.
POTASH BENEATH DESERT
Potassium is a key plant nutrient, helping crops develop stronger stalks and fuller grain. For years, China had relied heavily on overseas potash, with domestic self-sufficiency long below 30 percent.
Exploration in the 20th century uncovered a world-class sulfate-type potassium-rich brine deposit in northern Lop Nur. But finding the resource was one thing, and producing fertilizer from it on an industrial scale was another.
There was no established industrial process elsewhere to copy. The location also posed its own problems. Two decades ago, there were no roads, little fresh water and no settled population.
"When I first came to Lop Nur, the wind blew sand straight into the face. You could go through all four seasons without seeing any green," said Liu Qinyong, who has worked at SDIC Xinjiang Luobupo Potash Co. Ltd. for more than 20 years. "Everything had to be brought in from outside." SDIC is short for the State Development and Investment Corporation.
The first batch of Lop Nur-brand potassium sulfate was produced in 2003. The company later built a production complex with an annual capacity of 1.2 million tonnes, which reached designed capacity by the end of 2011.
The company has so far produced over 27 million tonnes of potassium sulfate, with its products accounting for nearly half of China's potassium sulfate market.
TURNING HARDSHIP INTO ADVANTAGE
Production in Lop Nur relies heavily on both evaporation and time.
Brine pumped from underground moves through a four-stage evaporation system, where different salts crystallize as the concentration increases. It takes nearly two years before potassium-bearing minerals are ready for processing. These minerals then undergo further processing, including purification, crystallization and drying, to produce potassium sulfate.
The extreme evaporation that makes Lop Nur so inhospitable does much of the concentrating naturally.
Water scarcity has also shaped the production system. Fresh water has to be piped in from Ruoqiang, about 240 kilometers away, while liquids left from processing are recycled within the system and brine is not discharged outside it.
Inside the plant, progress has often been measured in fractions of a percentage point.
Dong Guangfeng, head of the potassium sulfate plant, arrived in 2005, when there was only an industrial pilot facility. Over the following two decades, he and his colleagues worked to raise potassium content and develop a wider range of products.
The potassium oxide content of the company's potassium sulfate has risen from 51 percent to a stable 52.5 percent, while a high-end product reaches 53.8 percent. Its product range has also expanded to include granular and water-soluble fertilizers.
China's potash self-sufficiency has now risen to around 50 percent, Dong said, with Lop Nur contributing an important share of domestic supply.
The brine is also yielding another product. In 2023, the company put into operation a line that extracts lithium from residual brine after potash production. The facility can produce 5,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate a year, mainly for use in power batteries for new energy vehicles.
A TOWN TAKES ROOT
The industry has also drawn people.
Chen Liangzhi, from southwest China's Sichuan Province, was among the early arrivals. When he came to Lop Nur in 2000, there were no roads, electricity or running water.
He lived in a semi-underground shelter and ran a restaurant from a prefabricated metal room. At midday in summer, when surface temperatures could reach 50 to 60 degrees Celsius, the room became too hot for cooking. Chen would retreat underground and wait until late afternoon before lighting the stove again.
Today, his restaurant covers more than 100 square meters and serves business travelers.
Lop Nur Town was formally established in 2002. Its water, electricity and heating are largely supplied via facilities operated by the potash company, while garbage and sewage are handled through shared facilities. Medical workers from the People's Hospital of Bayingolin Mongolian Autonomous Prefecture are stationed at the local clinic.
"If you want people to stay, you first have to make them feel secure about living here," said Liu Xiangyu, deputy Party secretary of Lop Nur Town. Over 3,000 people now live in the settlement that grew around the potash industry.
Notably, far beyond Lop Nur, potassium from beneath its salt crust is reaching and nourishing farmlands across China. ■

====================================================================================================

The ASEAN-India Trade Agreement and Its Discontents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:57:00 UTC
21:57:00 KST

Even as India has embraced a renewed fervor for free trade agreements, one trade deal remains disfavored in Indian memory. The 2009 ASEAN-India Goods in Trade Agreement (AITIGA) is one of the oldest trade agreements signed by post-liberalization India as well as one of its most controversial. Atypically for an establishment that prefers to settle diplomatic disputes behind the scenes, Indian diplomats and trade officials are publicly trenchant in their criticism of AITIGA.
An oft-repeated narrative has emerged around the agreement: in the early 2000s, inexperienced Indian negotiators walked into an asymmetric deal, opening up their markets while getting little in return. Consequently, India’s trade deficit with ASEAN ballooned. Moreover, China exploited the AITIGA to route its goods into India through Southeast Asia.
This narrative stems from misremembering history. Rather than a powerful tool for ASEAN and China to penetrate the Indian market, the AITIGA is, in fact, a shallow and weak instrument. Moreover, it is shallow precisely because India preferred it that way. By repeatedly telling itself an alternative story, New Delhi has developed irrational fears over economic cooperation with Southeast Asia and injected unnecessary acrimony in the relationship. The myth of AITIGA as a bad deal is costing India diplomatically.
India started running a trade deficit with ASEAN in 1996, 13 years before the AITIGA was signed. The deficit stemmed from Southeast Asia’s shift from agrarian to manufacturing-led economies. The currency devaluations triggered by the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis further boosted the deficit. While the absolute figure of the trade deficit has ballooned over the last three decades, the India-ASEAN imports-to-exports ratio remains broadly similar to what it was in the 1990s.
After the 1997 crisis, ASEAN was looking to economically integrate itself with its East Asian neighbors. In the early 2000s, it began pursuing ASEAN+1 FTAs with its six immediate neighbors: China, India, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand. India had been excluded from the first wave of post-1997 regional integration – the ASEAN Plus Three, Asian Bond Markets Initiative, and Chiang Mai Initiative for currency swap. Eager not to miss out on another wave of regional integration, India agreed to negotiate the FTA.
Contrary to the myth, Indian officials were tough negotiators. After all, India had decades of experience negotiating economic deals in the GATT, WTO, and elsewhere. The negotiations were tortuous and took much longer than the other ASEAN+1 FTAs.
Moreover, there was a mismatch of approach. On the one hand, eager to gain access to the Indian market, ASEAN wanted to widen the FTA’s scope. On the other hand, India looked to protect its domestic industry by limiting the scope of the agreement. Indian businesses were lukewarm about seeking out greater market access in Southeast Asia.
India’s tough negotiating ensured that the AITIGA was the shallowest of the ASEAN+1 FTAs. Whereas all other agreements committed parties to tariff elimination coverage of more than 90 percent, the AITIGA’s promised coverage hovered around 79 percent. ASEAN mirrored India’s reluctance to open its markets. For instance, Indian critics of the AITIGA often point to the fact that Indonesia promised only 48.7 percent tariff elimination coverage to India. Notably, Indonesia offered above 91 percent coverage to all other ASEAN+1 partners, including Australia, with which it ran a trade deficit at the time.
AITIGA also ended up with the most stringent Rules of Origin among all the ASEAN+1 FTAs. It is the only agreement that demands dual compliance (35 percent local content and change in tariff subheading) for goods to qualify for preferential treatment. Its complex compliance rules and lower scope resulted in exporters avoiding using the AITIGA.
In AITIGA, India got what it wanted – an agreement that signaled India’s commitment to its Look East policy without exposing its domestic industry to excessive international competition. While economists may argue over whether Indian protectionism is good economic policy, the debate is irrelevant from a diplomatic standpoint. For whatever reasons, Indian economic managers prefer shielding the Indian market. The AITIGA was a natural outcome of such preference.
However, to then construct a narrative of the agreement as a bad deal in which India got duped is diplomatically damaging. To begin with, it erodes India’s credibility in the region as a reliable and competent partner. India began criticizing the AITIGA almost as soon as it was signed. The two sides agreed to open a review of the agreement in 2015 but still haven’t concluded it. Such long-drawn, dangling processes chip away at India’s image.
AITIGA’s beleaguered state becomes a particularly bad look when contrasted with other ASEAN+1 FTAs, especially the one with China. Beijing began negotiating its FTA with ASEAN around the same time as New Delhi. However, it not only concluded the negotiations fairly quickly, but China and ASEAN have since upgraded the agreement twice. Today, the ASEAN-China FTA is a powerful instrument that deals with a range of issues from digital trade to green technology.
The narrative of AITIGA as a loss for India has made New Delhi a less confident economic actor in Southeast Asia. The resultant hesitation has been evident in India’s exit from the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership as well as its reluctance to conclude bilateral FTAs with Southeast Asian countries such as Thailand and Indonesia. Today, even as India seeks out FTAs in the Middle East and Europe, it is too unsure of itself to look for a trade deal in Southeast Asia.
Tellingly, the acrimony over AITIGA has spilled over into other aspects of ASEAN-India economic cooperation, even the ones which are in India’s interests. For instance, the 2014 ASEAN-India Trade in Services Agreement needs urgent upgradation to account for all the advancements in the digital economy. Given that India enjoys a services surplus with Southeast Asia, New Delhi should be eagerly driving the process. However, so far the two sides have not even begun discussing the issue.
The self-created myths around AITIGA have cast a shadow on India’s Look/Act East policy. New Delhi needs to shed them to become a more confident, credible and engaged actor in the region.

Court orders Egyptian website closed in case seen as test for independent media
CAIRO, Oct 27 - A court ordered a leading independent Egyptian news site closed on Tuesday after its editor-in-chief was convicted of running the site without a licence and taken into custody pending bail, her lawyers and the outlet said.
Lina Attalah of the news site Mada Masr, which has won numerous international awards for its reporting, was fined 3 million Egyptian pounds ($53,400), her lawyers told Reuters.
The court gave her the maximum penalty, ordering the website to be shut down and its equipment confiscated, Mada Masr said in a statement.
After prosecutors referred Attalah to trial last Thursday, a group of 119 rights groups and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, called the case an "unprecedented attack on press freedom".
US Senator Chris Van Hollen said in a statement on the social media platform X on Friday that the charges were baseless and that "journalism is not a crime".
Egyptian authorities say the state is committed to upholding freedom of expression but that the media must operate within the law, respect national security and counter misinformation.
Founded in 2013, Mada Masr is the most internationally prominent independent outlet in a landscape mostly dominated by media owned by or closely affiliated with the state, and it regularly publishes on politically sensitive topics.
It has been blocked inside the country since 2017. Mada Masr says six cases have been brought against it and its journalists over the last six years, though rights groups say this is the first of its kind to be referred to trial.
The case against Attalah — named one of the world's 100 most influential people by Time magazine in 2020 — follows the arrest last month of the entire newsroom of the fact-checking outlet Matsaddash.
The CPJ said the arrests risked "deepening a climate of fear that threatens independent journalism".
Mada Masr says it has asked for a licence from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation repeatedly since 2018 but heard nothing back and only learned of a rejection when prosecutors raised the issue during an earlier case in 2022.
The outlet contested that decision in court, and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.
The council has not commented on the case but has said that it facilitates procedures for outlets which meet official requirements and is keen to promote freedom of expression. State authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In September, the US waived rights conditions, which include protecting media freedoms, on a portion of the roughly $1.3 billion of military aid it sends Egypt each year. REUTERS

The Netherlands is boycotting Eurovision again due to Israel's participation

The Dutch broadcaster NPO has withdrawn from Eurovision 2027 due to public sensitivity surrounding Israel's participation. The contest will be broadcast.
The Netherlands will not participate in the next Eurovision Song Contest, its broadcaster NPO said on Tuesday, citing the "sensitivity" surrounding Israel's participation. UNN reports this with reference to AFP.
Details
"We have known for some time that Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and leads to discussions and divisions... therefore, after consultations with the Broadcasters' Council, NPO has decided to withdraw from participation in 2027," NPO Director of Media Jurre Bosman said in a statement.
NPO Executive Chair Jet de Ranitz acknowledged that this would disappoint many Dutch Eurovision fans and stressed that the contest would still be broadcast on public broadcasters.
However, he said: "We must conclude that it is still too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027."
"Because of the sensitivity surrounding the issues currently being discussed, we have decided to take a step back for now," De Ranitz added.
The contest was recently hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel's participation, in protest against the country's deadly offensive in Gaza, which was triggered by Hamas militants' attacks in 2023.
Earlier this month, the Czech public broadcaster also withdrew from participation, but cited cost-cutting as the reason.
Ireland has already announced that it will not participate, while the head of Spain's public broadcaster spoke in support of a boycott.
This is only the second time that the Dutch broadcaster has withdrawn from the competition.

Denmark criticizes Finnish and Norwegian call with Putin on Ukraine
October 27, 2026
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized Finland's and Norway's leaders Tuesday after they held a joint phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.
The call came ahead of planned US-led peace talks, which European leaders are seeking to join.
Why did Denmark criticize the call?
Frederiksen said that Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store had gone "solo.”
"I'm very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn't been coordinated with any of the rest of us," she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordics leaders.
"I honestly don't know what those two countries think they can achieve with this."
"I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone," Frederiksen said.
Stubb and Store said they had consulted Ukraine before initiating the call.
They stressed that they represented their own countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe.
What did the leaders discuss with Putin?
Stubb described the conversation as "frank and substantive." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the call, the first between the three leaders.
"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.
Finland and Norway both border Russia and have supported Ukraine throughout the war.
Store said the leaders had emphasized de-escalation.
"The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations," he said.
How was Ukraine involved?
The call followed an October 20 meeting in Oslo involving Stubb, Store, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US envoy Steve Witkoff. US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner joined remotely.
Zelenskyy also spoke with the Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin.
"Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace," Stubb wrote on social media.
A US-mediated ceasefire in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky is set to last until November 1,
Ukraine's top negotiator Davyd Arakhamia said on Tuesday.
"This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," he said on Telegram, adding that every such step brings peace closer.

“I am proud to stand here on stage in solidarity with the Palestinian people,” Macklemore told the audience. “We will continue to fight for collective liberation until our last breath.”
Palestinian flags and keffiyehs were visible throughout the arena as the audience repeatedly chanted “Free Palestine.”
“Six weeks ago, two words is all that it took,” Macklemore said, referring to the declaration that led to his removal from Sheeran’s remaining concerts.
“Those two words are so threatening to some people that we’d rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean,” he said. “Somehow those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary.”
Macklemore was joined by Palestinian singer Lina Makoul, Palestinian American DJ Habibeats and the US political hip-hop group Dead Prez, alongside Irish performers Hozier, Kneecap and Beoga.
Actors Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon and the Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas also appeared in recorded video messages.

Beoga, who performed on Sheeran’s hit Galway Girl, also appeared after withdrawing from his tour in solidarity with Macklemore.
The rapper performed tracks including Thrift Shop, Same Love and Chant, as well as Hind’s Hall, his 2024 protest song supporting Palestinians and the student-led Gaza solidarity movement.
The Dublin concert was the first of three announced European performances, followed by shows in Paris on Thursday and London on Friday. All three dates sold out.
Proceeds will support organizations providing Palestinians with medical care, humanitarian assistance, education and community services.
Macklemore was removed from Sheeran’s tour after declaring “Free Palestine” and criticizing Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank during performances at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium in September.
Several other performers subsequently withdrew from Sheeran’s tour in solidarity. Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was made after promoters were told venues would not permit further concerts with the rapper on the bill.

Dutch chip firm Besi's shares jump as Applied Materials moves to double stake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:36:15 UTC
21:36:15 KST

Shares in Dutch chip equipment maker Besi jumped on Tuesday after US rival Applied Materials announced plans to lift its holding to roughly 20% from 9%, tightening ties built around technology used to make AI hardware.
Dutch company BE Semiconductor Industries (Besi), which makes machines used to assemble and package semiconductors, saw its stock climb more than 10% to over €160 per share by early afternoon on Tuesday.
The jump came after Applied Materials, one of the world's biggest makers of chipmaking equipment, announced late on Monday that it would increase its holding in Besi to about 20%, from the 9% it has owned since April 2025.
In a statement, Applied said it had signed an accelerated share purchase agreement to buy the additional stock, with delivery depending on a review under US antitrust law.
The California-based group called the stake a long-term investment and said it "currently has no intention to increase its investment in Besi beyond approximately 20%".
Nor will it ask for a place on the Dutch company's board, the firm added.
Prabu Raja, president of Applied's semiconductor products group, said in the same statement that the company was increasing its stake because hybrid bonding and next-generation ways of connecting chips are increasingly becoming critical to energy-efficient AI computing.
"We also look forward to furthering our strategic collaboration with Besi," Raja concluded.
Hybrid bonding and AI
The companies' collaboration on hybrid bonding dates back to 2020.
The technique joins chips directly to one another without tiny solder bumps, allowing them to be stacked more tightly, and is seen as key to the next generation of AI processors and memory.
On 1 October, in a joint statement, they widened the partnership to other packaging technologies, with Besi becoming an "innovation partner" at Applied's new research and development hub in Silicon Valley, known as the EPIC Center.
In that statement, Raja said advanced packaging had become a materials engineering challenge rather than a back-end assembly step.
Besi's CEO Richard Blickman called joining the centre "a natural next step".
Why not a takeover?
Applied's promise to stop at 20% also keeps it well clear of a key threshold. Under Dutch takeover rules, an investor that crosses 30% of a listed company’s voting rights must make an offer for the whole company.
A full deal would also face scrutiny in Beijing.
Both companies sell heavily into China, giving its competition regulator a say over any potential merger.
Roughly 30% of Applied's 2025 revenue came from China, while Besi runs a factory in the Chinese city of Leshan, in Sichuan province.
Applied has been in a similar situation before. In 2021, it abandoned a deal to buy Japanese chip equipment maker Kokusai Electric when Chinese approval failed to arrive in time.
Applied's move also comes after a steep slide in Besi’s share price.
The stock has lost about half its value since peaking at €317 in June, caught up in a wider sell-off in chip stocks.

Over 80% of domestic workers worldwide lack formal employment protections: ILO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:33:49 UTC
21:33:49 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
More than four in five domestic workers worldwide remain in informal employment, often without effective labor and social protection, despite progress in many countries, the International Labour Organization (ILO) said Tuesday.
In a new report marking 15 years since the adoption of its Domestic Workers Convention, the ILO estimated that 66.5 million domestic workers, or 83.1% of the global total, were informally employed in 2025, an increase of 5.1 million since 2019.
The global domestic workforce reached 80 million people, up from 75.6 million in 2019, with women accounting for 77.2% of workers.
Domestic workers earned an average of just 53.3% of the monthly wages of other employees, down from 56.4% in 2019. Informal domestic workers earned even less, at 48.7%.
The report also found that 35.2% of domestic workers worked at least 49 hours per week, including 14.6% who worked 60 hours or more.
Informality remained particularly widespread in Africa, affecting 93.3% of domestic workers, and was "nearly universal" in the Arab states. Even in Europe and Central Asia, which recorded the lowest regional rate, more than one-third worked informally.
"Progress in many countries shows that change is possible. But with more than 66 million domestic workers still in informal employment and their wages falling further behind those of other employees, much more needs to be done," said Patrick Belser, chief of the ILO's informal work branch.
The ILO urged governments to strengthen minimum wages, social security coverage, working-time protections, and enforcement of labor rights under Convention No. 189.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Far EasTone Telecommunications Co. announced Tuesday plans to develop direct-to-device (D2D) satellite services to extend mobile connectivity to areas beyond the reach of terrestrial networks.
The company signed a cooperation agreement with global D2D satellite communications provider Elveo Mobile to develop the technology. Far EasTone plans to gradually build up its satellite communications capabilities, spanning satellite broadband and D2D, according to CTEE.
Satellite broadband provides high-speed internet access in remote areas and specialized locations where reliable connections are essential. D2D technology, meanwhile, enables mobile phones to access network services through satellites when conventional mobile coverage is unavailable.
Far EasTone President Chee Ching (井琪) said next-generation communications would increasingly combine networks on the ground, in the air, and in space. She said the partnership is expected to strengthen network resilience.
Elveo CEO Ramu Potarazu said the company is building a satellite communications network backed by satellite assets and partnerships with more than 50 mobile network operators. He said the collaboration would help deliver reliable next-generation connectivity to Far EasTone subscribers and the Taiwan market.
Far EasTone said extreme weather and natural disasters can disrupt communications, making backup connectivity increasingly important. The company plans to combine terrestrial and satellite networks to maintain communications when conventional infrastructure is disrupted, with the aim of strengthening Taiwan’s overall communications resilience.
