TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's benchmark stock index fluctuated around the 46,000-point level Tuesday as selling in heavyweight stocks offset gains.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index, or TAIEX, fluctuated by 908.78 points during the session. It closed up 54.8 points, or 0.12%, at 46,096.23, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Turnover totaled NT$976.6 billion (US$30.1 billion). The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$150.91 trillion, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
Among the index’s most heavily weighted stocks, TSMC gained 0.63% to close at NT$2,400. MediaTek fell 1.25% to NT$3,960, according to Yahoo Stocks.
Foxconn added 1.02% to NT$247.5. Delta Electronics lost 3.21% to NT$1,510, and ASE ended down 0.46% at NT$651.
Bearing and linear guide sectors gained as demand for humanoid robot components continued to outpace available production capacity. The ongoing Japan International Machine Tool Fair, one of the world’s three major machine tool exhibitions, further fueled interest in related sectors, according to Sinotrade.
Hiwin Technologies hit its daily limit-up of NT$328 after reportedly securing a large order from a major US robotics manufacturer at the event. Expectations that automation and robotics orders would remain visible through 2027 supported Tbi Motion Technology and Chieftek Precision, which rose 7.14% and 6.67%, respectively.
Memory stocks attracted catch-up buying after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) said memory supply is unlikely to exceed demand by 2029, according to CNBC. Nanya Technology gained 6.52%, Winbond Electronics rose 5.5%, and Macronix International added 3.52%.
Specialty memory makers also advanced as demand for edge AI, smart wearable devices, and automotive electronics gradually recovered. ESMT gained 7.05%, Etron Technology rose 6%, and AP Memory added 2.39%.
Leading copper-clad laminate maker Taiwan Union Technology hit limit-down following reports that its anticipated orders for Amazon’s next-generation Trainium 4 AI chips could face competition from rival suppliers. Trainium 4 is expected to be an important potential source of orders for manufacturers in the sector next year.
Selling spread to other printed circuit board (PCB) upstream materials suppliers. Drill bit maker Topoint Technology fell 9.6% and copper foil producer Lcy Technology lost 8.45%.
PCB makers Co-Tech Development, Unimicron Technology, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, and Nan Ya PCB ended lower. PCBs serve as the base for assembling electronic components, with copper circuits connecting the components and carrying electrical signals and power, according to Stockfeel.
Glass fiber stocks faced profit-taking after substantial gains in previous sessions, despite continued tight supply of high-end, low-dielectric (Low-Dk) glass fiber yarn. Glotech Industrial fell 6.63%, Baotek Industrial Materials lost 6.16%, and Fulltech Fiber Glass retreated 5.76%.
Shin Zu Shing, a supplier of hinge components for foldable devices, fell 8.7% following reports of cracking sounds and abnormal bright lines on the inner display of Apple's first foldable iPhone. Peers Fositek and Jarllytec ended lower.
Analysts said trading volume remained insufficient to support a stronger advance, while the TAIEX continued to fluctuate near recent highs. They advised investors to monitor institutional trading activity and look for signs of stabilization in individual stocks' prices and trading volumes, according to CTEE.
They added that funds could rotate out of stocks that have already attracted substantial catch-up buying and into lower-valued shares showing improving price and volume trends. Stocks breaking through key resistance levels could also draw greater attention in the next round of sector rotation.

When will traffic on the Pivdennyi Bridge be restored: the situation at the impact site, a photo report
Kyiv • UNN
In Kyiv, the crater on the Pivdennyi Bridge is being cleared and the road surface is being repaired after the Russian strike. The timeline for restoring traffic will be determined after an expert assessment.
Work is ongoing in Kyiv on the Southern Bridge, which was damaged as a result of a Russian strike. Municipal workers are clearing the area and repairing the road surface. At the same time, the Kyiv City State Administration is awaiting expert conclusions, reports UNN.
What is happening on the bridge now
According to a UNN journalist who is at the scene, municipal services are patching the road surface. At the same time, traffic across the bridge is restricted for cars, so people are making their way to the other side on foot or on scooters that have come in handy.
At the beginning of the bridge, in particular on the right bank, a crater was formed by a Russian Iskander-M missile, which hit both metro tracks. Municipal services are currently working around it, welding, clearing the area, and dismantling the consequences of the Russian attack
At present, car traffic across the bridge is temporarily restricted. Instead, people are making their way to the other side on foot or on scooters.
When will repairs to the Southern Bridge be completed?
It is currently unknown how much time is needed for the bridge to resume operation. The press service of the Kyiv City Military Administration told UNN in a comment that they do not yet have the experts’ conclusions that would allow them to assess the duration of the work.
There are no details for now. The experts also cannot provide an estimate of the timeline. We are waiting for some details from them, but there are none at the moment
Thus, the exact timeline for the repairs and the restoration of traffic will become clear after the damage is assessed and specialists provide their conclusions.
Reminder
Because of the closure of the Southern Bridge in Kyiv, traffic is temporarily being redirected along detour routes. Oleksii Biloshytskyi, head of the Patrol Police Department of the National Police of Ukraine, explained in more detail which roads drivers of trucks and passenger cars can use

Anticyclone to bring dry weather and warm temperatures to Kazakhstan

Türkiye posts unemployment rate of 8.4% in September
The number of unemployed people aged 15 and over rose by 198,000 month-on-month to reach 2.97 million, the official figures showed.
Unemployment rates continued to differ significantly by gender, standing at 6.9% for men and 11.3% for women.
Among people aged 15-24, the jobless rate rose by 1.6 percentage points from August to 14.8%. The rate stood at 10.4% for young men and 23.3% for young women.
Meanwhile, the number of employed people in Türkiye declined by 49,000 to 32.45 million in September. The employment rate edged down by 0.1 percentage points to 48.3%, reaching 65.8% among men and 31.2% among women.
Despite the decline in employment, the country’s labor force expanded by 149,000 people to 35.41 million during the month.
The labor force participation rate increased by 0.1 percentage points to 52.7%. Participation stood at 70.7% for men and 35.2% for women, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.
Earlier, it was reported Türkiye's Central Bank lowered the policy rate to 36% after five consecutive holds.

UN commission finds Russia’s grid strikes are crimes against humanity, citing last winter at minus 21°C. Now they’re intensifying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:21:20 UTC
21:21:20 KST

Russian authorities committed war crimes and crimes against humanity through attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine said in a report to the UN General Assembly on 26 October.
International Criminal Court (ICC) warrants for former Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu and Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov, issued in June 2024, already covered alleged crimes linked to Russia’s 2022–2023 strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The UN commission’s new report reaches into last winter, 2025–2026, and the cumulative toll since 2022, documenting what the attacks did to civilians living through outages in freezing temperatures.
“As the cold season approaches, the attacks have intensified once again, raising serious concerns about the threats to civilians’ lives and health,” commission chair Erik Møse said.
Russian commanders knew heating facilities were vital
The commission said Russian commanders knew that heating facilities in large cities were indispensable to civilians, particularly during winter. Russian authorities also made official declarations about further attacks and referred to a plan to carry them out, it said. It found that Russian authorities intentionally directed attacks against civilian objects, constituting war crimes.
The commission also concluded that the attacks were carried out under a state policy aimed at depriving civilians of electricity and other essential energy-dependent services and causing suffering. It classified these acts as crimes against humanity in the form of “other inhumane acts.”
Minus 21°C, weeks without heat, and shelters out of reach for older people
Last winter, temperatures fell to minus 21°C as millions of Ukrainians endured prolonged disruptions to heating, electricity, water, and gas, the commission said.
The commission relied on the accounts of 255 people from Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr Oblasts, alongside officials, doctors, and nongovernmental organizations.
Older people and those with limited mobility were particularly affected. Fear of becoming trapped in elevators during blackouts prevented some residents from reaching shelters during air raid alerts. They remained in unheated homes, sometimes without access to life-support equipment.
A 53-year-old Kyiv resident told investigators he tried to stay awake at night because he feared he might not wake up if he fell asleep in the cold.
Meanwhile, school closures disrupted children’s education, and children fell ill in unheated homes, the report said.
Russia rejects the findings
Russia’s UN mission said Moscow did not recognize the commission’s mandate and dismissed its findings as “falsified data,” the Associated Press reported.
The commission also examined Ukrainian attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia and Russian-occupied Ukraine. It said it could not investigate their impact fully because Russia denied access and did not respond to its requests.
Foreign recruits trafficked to the front
The same report found “compelling evidence” that Russian authorities trafficked men from 29 countries into the Russian armed forces through deception and coercion.
Recruitment agents arranged visas and travel, presenting themselves as legitimate businesses. After arriving in Russia, the men were forced to sign military contracts in Russian and were sent to the front, where many were killed or went missing, the commission said.

Nobel Peace Prize committee welcomes Machado's return to Venezuela
COPENHAGEN, Oct 27 - The Norwegian Nobel Committee said on Tuesday it welcomed the return of opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to Venezuela, saying it hoped her presence would strengthen the democratic opposition and its peaceful campaign for democracy.
Machado, the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was greeted by tens of thousands of supporters on Sunday after 10 months abroad, following several failed return attempts that have strained her ties with US President Donald Trump's administration.
"The committee expresses its hope that her return will strengthen the democratic opposition and its peaceful struggle for democracy," the award body said.
Machado was barred from running against then-President Nicolas Maduro in the 2024 election and left the country after a crackdown on the opposition. The US military captured Maduro in early January and he was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez.
A few weeks later, Machado gave her Nobel Peace Prize medal to Trump in recognition of what she called his commitment to the freedom of the Venezuelan people.
Trump thanked Machado for the accolade but has repeatedly said that he himself deserved to receive the prestigious award, calling it disgraceful and embarrassing that the committee chose other candidates.
The awards committee said at the time the prize remains inseparably linked to the person or organisation that won it, though the medal can be given away.
"Much has changed in recent months, but the task remains urgent: Venezuela still requires a democratic transition founded on fundamental rights, political participation and free elections," the committee said on Tuesday. REUTERS

Romanian President Nicusor Dan on Tuesday condemned alleged Russian involvement in acts of sabotage on Romanian territory after an investigation into a fire at an industrial site in Brasov.

Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said in Chisinau that a defense industry sabotage network operating with Russian involvement had been dismantled, according to Romanian media.
“We will not be discouraged in our commitment to ensuring the security of Romanian citizens and Romania,” he said.
Romanian broadcaster Antena 3 CNN reported that three suspects, two Belarusian nationals and a Ukrainian, fled Romania after the fire and were apprehended in Germany and Poland. The broadcaster said they were preparing further acts of sabotage.

Christopher Moseley, champion of Estonian literature in English, dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:19:00 UTC
21:19:00 KST

Christopher Moseley, champion of Estonian literature in English, dies
Christopher Moseley, the Australian-born translator and language teacher who devoted his career to bringing Estonian, Latvian and Nordic literature to English-language readers, has died. He was 76.
Moseley was born in Australia and came to Britain in 1974 to study Scandinavian languages, but his interests soon moved somewhat eastwards to Finland and the Baltic states, even while the latter countries were still shackled under the Soviet occuption.
He studied Finno-Ugric languages in Finland and the UK, and his fieldwork on Livonian between 1987 and 1993 was his first direct work with a minority language. It led to his Master's thesis at the School of Slavonic and East European Studies (SSEES), part of the University College London (UCL), and later to his book Livonian (2002).
He also authored the Estonian language installment of British publisher Routledge's "Colloquial" range, and co-authored its Latvian course too.
For many years he taught Estonian language and Baltic literature at SSEES and UCL, along with evening courses in Estonian and Latvian. He also worked as a translator and journalist specializing in Baltic affairs at BBC Monitoring for nearly two decades, before becoming a freelance translator and editor.
Moseley's own translations from Estonian into English included A.H. Tammsaare's classic "Põrgupõhja uus Vanapagan", Andrus Kivirähk's "The Man Who Spoke Snakish", Indrek Hargla's "Apothecary Melchior" series, and Ilmar Taska's "Pobeda 1946". His final translation, Rein Raud's "The Sun Script", was published by Norvik Press just this year.
From 2008 Moseley was General Editor of UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger, which became a key reference for the world's threatened languages. He was also a dedicated member of the Foundation for Endangered Languages.
In 2018, he was one of the speakers at the opening of the University of Latvia's Livonian Institute.
The Estonian Literature Center remembered Chris as a warm and friendly person with unceasing passion for languages and literature.

Togo’s China Pivot: Building a Strategic Gateway to the Sahel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:18:00 UTC
21:18:00 KST

As Togo’s President of the Council of Ministers Faure Gnassingbé concluded his eight-day visit to China on October 16, much of the geopolitical attention surrounding the deepening relationship between Lomé and Beijing naturally centered on China’s expanding commercial and strategic influence in West Africa. Yet an equally important question deserves attention: What does Togo stand to gain from its growing partnership with China?
For Togo – a relatively small coastal country with significant maritime assets and ambitions to become a regional economic hub – China offers opportunities that extend beyond conventional bilateral cooperation. Togo is seeking to leverage its geographic position, particularly the strategic Port of Lomé, to strengthen domestic development while expanding its commercial influence across West Africa, including the landlocked countries of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).
During the visit, both countries elevated their bilateral relations to a “China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era,” alongside agreements spanning agriculture, industry, infrastructure, finance, and security.
From Togo’s perspective, three strategic opportunities stand out: building domestic productive capacity, consolidating its position as a maritime gateway to the Sahel, and expanding financial and strategic optionality.
Moving Beyond Raw Commodity Exports
One of the most important opportunities for Togo lies in leveraging Chinese investments, technology, and market access to accelerate domestic industrialization. The composition of Togo’s exports to China illustrates the challenge. According to U.N. Comtrade data reported by Togo, the country exported approximately $18.1 million in merchandise to China in 2025, compared with $14.8 million in 2024. Leading products included sesame seeds, unwrought aluminum alloys, cocoa beans, copper scraps, and manganese ores.
These figures reveal an export relationship still heavily concentrated in primary commodities, metals, and limited processing activities. They also illustrate the considerable scope for Togo to capture economic value domestically. During this visit, Gnassingbé toured a smart farming park in Shaanxi, and the Third Institute of Oceanography in the coastal city of Xiamen. He further expressed that Togo will learn from China’s comprehensive production ecosystems as it pursues a sustainable blue economy.
The significance of these engagements becomes clearer when considered alongside Togo’s existing industrial ambitions. At the Adétikopé Industrial Platform, a major industrial and logistics zone near Lomé, Chinese manufacturer Vivace Group inaugurated a building-materials factory in April 2025 following an investment of about $13.6 million. The facility has a reported annual production capacity of 10,000 tonnes and is intended to supply Togo and neighboring markets.
These developments suggest that Chinese engagement could complement Togo’s efforts to establish a broader industrial production ecosystem rather than remain predominantly a channel for merchandise imports. China’s zero-tariff access arrangements for eligible African exports and the newly signed phytosanitary protocol for Togolese soybeans could further expand export opportunities.
Position Lomé as the Gateway to the AES
The second opportunity concerns Togo’s maritime geography and its potential to becomes an increasingly important commercial intermediary between China and the landlocked economies of the Sahel. The Port of Lomé is central to Togo’s development strategy. Its maritime facilities and the connections to inland transport corridors give the country a structural advantage in serving neighboring economies without direct access to the Atlantic Ocean. For the AES countries of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, reliable access to coastal infrastructure remains essential for international commerce, industrial supplies, and economic development.
Togo’s ambition is to convert this geographic advantage into a durable regional logistic position. During his China visit, Gnassingbé emphasized maritime security, technological capacity, and the need to capture greater economic value from port activities. He spoke highly of China’s record in terms of global maritime governance. The China–Togo joint declaration similarly identified port cooperation, logistics infrastructure, and the development of Lomé as a West African commercial gateway as areas for further engagement.
The timing is particularly significant because Togo and the AES have been pursuing closer customs and trade coordination to harmonize their customs and trade frameworks. Experts from the four nations met in Ouagadougou between October 12 and 14, while Gnassingbé was in China. Their objectives revolved around defining the interconnection of custom IT systems, the adoption of community regulations, and boosting capacity for customs administrations. The strategic benefits of these developments cause a multiplier effect especially in coordination with China.
For Togo, the benefits could extend beyond port traffic to include warehousing, freight services, customs administration, logistics employment, industrial distribution, and greater regional diplomatic influence.
However, Togo must compete with alternative coastal corridors through Benin, Ghana, and Côte d’Ivoire. Its advantage will ultimately depend on transport costs, customs efficiency, infrastructure reliability, and the security of inland routes. This is where Togo’s relationship with China could become strategically consequential. Chinese capabilities in logistics infrastructure, industrial system, and transport technology could complement domestic and regional investments, helping Togo strengthen its competitiveness as a gateway economy.
Diversifying Togo’s Strategic and Economic Partnerships
The third opportunity concerns Togo’s ability to use its relations with China to diversify development financing, strengthen financial connectivity, and expand its room for strategic maneuver. Chinese financing has already played a role in Togo’s infrastructure development.
Research on China’s overseas lending estimated that Togo’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors reached approximately $740 million in 2021. This figure demonstrates the scale of earlier financing relationships, although it does not represent Togo’s current outstanding obligations. During Gnassingbé’s visit, the Togolese government also announced an agreement providing partial cancellation of debt owed to China.
Beyond conventional lending, the most significant new development concerns financial infrastructure. On October 10, the pan-African banking group Ecobank, headquartered in Lomé, signed a memorandum of understanding with China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) to strengthen renminbi-denominated payment connectivity between China and African markets. With operations across 34 African countries, Ecobank provides a potentially important institutional bridge between Chinese financial infrastructure and African commercial networks.
Gnassingbé reaffirmed Togo’s support for the One China principle, and both leaders spoke on the importance of connecting immediate security conditions to long-term development planning. The wider implications of these connections were expressed in the joint declaration on October 15 where Gnassingbé and Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivered five main points as the foundation of the China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era. First was to undertake joint contribution towards the promotion of an orderly and equal multipolar world. Second was to work together to implement the Global Development Initiative. Third was to implement the Global Security Initiative. Fourth was to collaborate toward implementing the World Civilization Initiative and finally, to establish the Global Governance Initiative.
By maintaining economic connectivity with the landlocked Sahel while deepening its engagement with China, Togo is positioning itself as an increasingly important intermediary in the region’s evolving economic architecture. However, the success of this strategy will ultimately depend on Togo’s ability to convert diplomatic agreements into financed projects, domestic technical capabilities, efficient institutions and productive economic activity.

Indonesia scouts for gasoline supplies from India
Indonesia is looking to secure gasoline supplies from India amid rising energy prices and friction with Singapore over toxic haze in the region from forest fires, according to reports.
Indonesian Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia is slated to visit India and China this week to secure more gasoline supplies, the Jakarta Globe reported. “I will travel to several countries, including India and China, to ensure supplies,” Lahadalia said in Jakarta.
Singapore, a major refining hub in the Southeast Asian region, accounted for half of Indonesia’s gasoline needs and supplied 28.36% of its oil and gas imports in the first half of 2026. However, Indonesia slashed its piped gas exports to the city state last week, days after Jakarta slammed neighboring countries that had complained about haze from intense forest fires on its territory.
The cuts have led to tensions between the two countries. Singapore depends on imported natural gas for about 95% of its electricity generation. The city state has not resorted to any retaliatory action, but its foreign minister is visiting Indonesia on Tuesday.
Jakarta is also facing severe fuel supply disruptions across its provinces, due to surging demand and distribution bottlenecks, apart from geopolitical uncertainties, Reuters reported.
Indonesia is not the first country to look toward India for its fuel needs amid the global oil crunch. Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio termed India a “refining superpower” as Washington sought to tap New Delhi’s oil refining capabilities to cool global fuel prices.
Indian refineries, especially the Jamnagar refinery complex owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani, are configured to process both Russian and Venezuelan heavy crude. The latter, especially, is considered key to lowering global fuel diesel prices, as it yields a higher volume of the fuel.

China Focus: Chinese research institutes, enterprises co-innovate from lab to factory
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
20:08:43 CST
21:08:43 KST

Huang Xiaohua, who is in charge of the Industrial Development Center at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, introduces the technology achievement supermarket in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 19, 2026. (Xinhua/Yu Fei)
SHENZHEN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- At a special supermarket in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province in south China, shelves are stocked not with fruits or vegetables, but cards featuring cutting-edge scientific achievements and top research talent.
The cards at the supermarket in the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology (SIAT) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences represent more than 1,000 frontier achievements arranged by track, covering medical equipment and scientific instruments, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics, advanced electronics and energy materials, and synthetic biology.
Every card carries a unique QR code, which helps entrepreneurs gain access to the technology's highlights, application scenarios, potential collaboration directions, together with the developer's contact information. If something catches their eye, they can connect directly, with no more wading through thick archives of research files.
In the past, researchers' achievements often lay dormant in academic papers and patent offices, while companies desperate for new technologies had nowhere to turn. Today, with the results stocked on supermarket shelves, complex academic papers are transformed into "visual products" that companies can grasp at a glance. Supply and demand finally meet face to face, and the commercialization of research achievements is put on the fast track.
The supermarket's entire inventory comes from the SIAT's 10 research divisions. Over the past five years, SIAT has produced an average of 6.6 patents per day, with new achievements hitting the shelves every month.
FROM LAB TO PRODUCTION
The supermarket is re-imagining the way scientific and technological achievements are commercialized: connecting frontier laboratory technologies precisely with industrial needs, so that more research results can travel from the lab bench to the production line more efficiently.
Huang Xiaohua, who is in charge of the Industrial Development Center at SIAT, said: "Through this matching platform, companies find technologies of interest, and technologies are directly exposed to real corporate needs."
Jiangsu Apon Medical Technology Co., Ltd., which has been deeply engaged in the brain-computer interface field for many years, is a "treasure seeker." The company urgently needed new technological breakthroughs in the neural regulation domain, particularly in non-invasive deep brain stimulation. The platform helped connect the company's technological request with relevant research from SIAT.
In 2025, the company precisely matched with SIAT's non-invasive brain regulation technology, and the two sides quickly reached a consensus, establishing a "brain-computer interface" innovation consortium in early 2026 to jointly tackle temporal interference stimulation technology, exploring diagnostics and treatments for epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and emotional brain disorders.
Since opening in February 2025, the supermarket has facilitated the commercialization of research achievements worth more than 200 million yuan (about 30 million U.S. dollars). In 2025, the SIAT's average achievement conversion rate exceeded 29 percent, and the success rate of technology matchmaking through the supermarket has risen by more than 10 percent, according to Huang.
The achievement supermarket has expanded beyond Shenzhen, taking root across China in cities including Zhuhai, Jiangmen, Ningde, Wenzhou and Wuhan.
INTEGRATED INNOVATION
The supermarket model is a vivid snapshot of the growing integrated innovation between Chinese research institutions and enterprises in recent years. Companies have moved beyond simply buying technologies to co-developing them with scientists, unleashing a stronger combined force for innovation.
Carbon dioxide emitted from industrial processes used to be taken as waste gas in many people's eyes. But as a result of the cooperation between SIAT and China Merchants Group, it has become a treasure.
The two sides have jointly developed a remarkable technological pathway: electrocatalytic processes powered by renewable electricity convert carbon dioxide into organic carbon feedstocks, which are then used in fermentation to sustainably produce flavors and fragrances, protein feed, bulk chemicals and other products, supporting food security and China's dual carbon goals of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060.
A joint laboratory for green conversion of carbon dioxide and biorefining has been established by the two sides, with cooperation funding approaching 100 million yuan. A 100-tonne-scale demonstration facility has already been commissioned, and a 1,000-tonne-scale platform has completed design verification.
The SIAT has also teamed up with China Nuclear Power Engineering Co., Ltd. to conduct research on and apply multimodal human-machine interaction systems for nuclear power plants, developing solutions oriented toward human-machine interaction needs in plant operations to reduce operator workload.
Cooperation with the Shenzhen Research Institute of the China National Coal Group Corporation focuses on another key technical frontier. The two parties are jointly developing high-performance proton exchange membranes based on ordered subnanochannels. The technology holds huge potential for long-duration energy storage, with promising prospects for further expansion into semiconductor, biomedical and environmental applications.
SIAT's research team has also partnered with China Resources Mixc Lifestyle to bring AI into property inspections, service dispatching, on-site handling, and operational evaluation. The system has been deployed in more than 1,000 property projects, improving overall operational efficiency by 35 percent.
China has recently released a set of guidelines on promoting the deep integration of scientific and technological innovation and industrial innovation.
Issued by the General Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council, the guidelines require efforts to deepen the implementation of the innovation-driven development strategy, with the goals of developing new quality productive forces and building a modern industrial system, and with a focus on establishing an enterprise-led, multi-stakeholder collaborative system for integrated industry-academia-research innovation, so as to form a new pattern in which sci-tech innovation and industrial innovation promote each other. ■

EU cybersecurity revision could cost the Netherlands up to 2.2 bln euros in first year

20:08:34 CST

THE HAGUE, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A proposed revision of the European Union's Cybersecurity Act, known as CSA2, could lead to losses ranging from 290 million euros (324.02 million U.S. dollars) to 2.2 billion euros (2.46 billion dollars) for Dutch businesses in the first year of implementation, according to a report by SEO Amsterdam Economics.
The report, titled The Price of Security and commissioned by the Netherlands China Business Council (NCBC), cautions that the impact could extend beyond businesses directly affected by the restrictions, spreading through supply chains and hitting firms in other sectors of the Dutch economy.
The legislation was proposed by the European Commission at the beginning of this year. The draft introduced "non-technical risks" in the name of cybersecurity and supply chain security. In particular, the draft would identify "countries posing cybersecurity concerns" and "high-risk suppliers," and exclude listed countries and suppliers from relevant EU supply chains across 18 sectors, including energy, transport, and information and communications technology.
However, the economic implications of restricting suppliers could be substantial, particularly for businesses that rely on existing information and communications technology infrastructure and have limited short-term alternatives, according to the report.
Companies may also need to modify existing systems, adjust production processes and reorganize supply chains to accommodate replacement products. These changes could generate additional costs beyond the losses estimated in the report.
"Security measures do not exist in an economic vacuum," NCBC Chairman Jochum Haakma said at a seminar on the report on Monday, adding that restrictions on suppliers, changes in procurement policies and the replacement of existing ICT infrastructure can affect entire supply chains, investment decisions and ultimately the competitiveness of the European economy.
In a letter to parliament on June 19, Dutch Minister of Justice and Security David van Weel said the government was concerned about the European Commission's proposed power to designate entire countries and suppliers as high-risk, citing potentially far-reaching economic, legal and geopolitical consequences, as well as insufficiently clear and detailed criteria and procedures.
The report notes that restrictions on supplier choice could also yield other adverse consequences, as diminished competitive pressure may result in higher prices, lower quality and reduced innovation.
"Strategic autonomy is an important European ambition, but autonomy should not lead to isolation," Haakma noted. ■

Record carbon dioxide levels will impact us for centuries, says UN weather agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Record carbon dioxide levels will impact us for centuries, says UN weather agency
Levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases in the atmosphere caused by burning fossil fuels reached record highs in 2025, locking in more long-term global warming, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said on Tuesday.
The agency’s latest Greenhouse Gas Bulletin indicates an average global concentration of CO2 at 426.8 parts per million (ppm) last year, or 153 per cent of the 1750 pre-industrial baseline.
“Every additional part per million matters because it traps additional heat. In effect, we are supercharging the ocean and the atmosphere. That means that heat waves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for,” WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett told journalists in Geneva.
Equally worrying, levels of methane and nitrous oxide – the second and third most important long-lived greenhouse gases caused by human activities – also hit a new peak in 2025.
“Another year, another new record. Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies,” Ms. Barrett stressed. 
“The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. CO2 has a very long lifetime and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries.”
When the Bulletin was first published in 2004, the annual average level of CO2 measured by WMO’s Global Atmosphere Watch network of monitoring stations was 377.5 ppm, compared with nearly 427 ppm today.
El Niño accelerator
Growth rates of CO2 have tripled since the 1960s, accelerating from an annual average increase of 0.8 ppm per year to 2.4 ppm per year in the decade from 2011 to 2020.
The “exceptional [3.5 ppm] surge” of 2023-2024 coincided with a strong El Niño “which reduced the efficiency of the biosphere through more drought, drier vegetation and more wildfires”, said WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova. 
She noted that although the 2.8 ppm annual increase from 2024-2025 represented a more modest increase, it was nonetheless “a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning. We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Niño which will impact land carbon sinks as it did in 2023-2024.”
CO2 growth rates triple
The agency’s Bulletin reports on the amount of gas that accumulates in the atmosphere and not new annual emissions. About half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere and the rest is absorbed by Earth’s land ecosystems and oceans.
The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Annual Greenhouse Gas Index shows that from 1990 to 2025, the warming effect on our climate caused by greenhouse gases increased by 56 per cent, with CO2 accounting for about 81 per cent of this increase, known as “radiative forcing”.
Energy transformation concerns
WMO noted that as countries transform their energy systems towards decarbonization, careful attention should be given to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulphur hexafluoride (SF6).
Widely used as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution, SF6 use has risen steadily in the past three decades in line with increased global electrification. “It has an atmospheric lifetime of over 1,000 years and has the highest 100-year global warming potential of approximately 24,300 times that of CO2. The increase of SF6 in 2025 was a record high,” the agency’s report notes.
Hydrogen concentration has increased by 5.3 per cent between 2010 and 2024. Hydrogen is being used as an energy storage medium for hard-to-decarbonize sectors such as steelmaking, shipping, and long-duration energy storage, as well as for renewable sources and as an energy source for transport. 
“Its leakage into the atmosphere from production facilities, pipelines, storage tanks, and fuel cells poses a growing concern,” WMO said, highlighting that although hydrogen is not a greenhouse gas, “it influences atmospheric chemistry” and has a strong indirect effect on warming, the agency explained.
“Both H2 leakage and SF6 persistence represent potential threats that could undermine the climate benefits of the energy transition,” WMO said. “Careful monitoring of the composition of Earth’s atmosphere is essential to detect, understand and prevent unintended consequences of these changes.”.
WMO releases the Bulletin to provide authoritative scientific data for negotiators attending the annual UN Climate conference. The aim of the Conference of the Parties meeting (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November is to turn climate commitments into concrete action.

‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:59:42 UTC
20:59:42 KST

When Bill Tuck first started installing air source heat pumps six years ago, other heating engineers were skeptical about whether the green technology would take off. “Now, the conversation is completely different,” he said.
“I’m getting approached by them saying: ‘Mrs Jones, my customer for 15 years, she’s enquiring about a heat pump. What can you tell me?’ The whole narrative has changed.”
But despite a surge in interest in cheap and sustainable ways to warm homes, the government is understood to be slashing the amount of money available to subsidise heat pumps as it looks for ways to cut spending in Wednesday’s budget.
Businesses that install the renewable systems are fearing the worst. “It’s going to damage us as a company,” said Tuck, the operations director at Sustain Homes in Watford. About 75% of his customers pay for their pump using the government subsidies. “It’s the foundation of the business. If that’s to go, it’s extremely damaging.
“Of course, we will do what it takes to keep everybody’s jobs going and the business afloat. But it’s a tough one – I don’t know how we will do that.”
The boiler upgrade scheme (BUS) was introduced in 2022 to help people decarbonise their homes and businesses. It provides upfront grants worth up to £9,000 to help property owners replace fossil fuel and direct electric heating systems with low-carbon alternatives such as heat pumps and biomass boilers.
Heat in buildings is responsible for approximately nearly a fifth of the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions, the latest government data shows. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has described the 2020s as a “critical decade for decarbonising heat”, but now appears to be putting the cost of decarbonising on to the consumer. The UK lags far behind other European countries with heat pump installation; Norway, the global leader, has 632 installed for every 1,000 households, while the UK has a paltry 3.5.
Jim Lacey, who has been installing renewables with his business JLN Plumbing & Heating for 20 years, said: “No one’s going to save the planet if it really hits their pocket.”
“We can go in [to homes] now and go: ‘It’s a few hundred pound more than having a normal boiler, but you save so much on your energy usage.’ That whole argument’s gone.”
Adam Killa, the founder of Ask Renewables in Burscough, Lancashire, saw what happens when subsidies are removed after the 2022 closure of the Renewable Heat Incentive, a scheme that paid households for generating clean heat.
“As soon as that stopped, we went from doing six, seven, eight [installs] a week down to zero. The customers say: ‘Well, I know they’re good, but 15 grand – I can buy a new boiler for three grand. What’s the point?’
While the government continues its drive to increase numbers of young people earning while learning, heat pump installers say cuts to the subsidy will put their apprentices – and the future of the industry – are at risk.
“Unless we start bringing the young generation through, we’re going to have a huge lack of installers, repair engineers, and more importantly, heat pumps as well,” said Tuck.
A nascent industry, installers fear manufacturers will go under too. According to the Heat Pump Association, about a third of heat pumps sold in the UK in 2024 were produced domestically.
“This isn’t just down to us fitting the heat pumps, it’s the people delivering them, it’s the people manufacturing them, it’s all the associated trades that go with it that make the little bits, the little bobs, everything,” said Lacey. “There’s so many knock-on effects”
James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the green thinktank Verdant, said removing money from green jobs and manufacturing would damage Andy Burnham’s mission to effectively reindustrialise Britain. “It’s at a point where his blank spot on climate is working hard against other things he wants to do,” he said.
Lacey said that, while he had not thought the grant would last for ever, he had expected business and consumers to be weaned off gradually as the technology became more widespread and production costs fell. “But to suddenly axe some off the BUS grant or get rid of it completely is just catastrophic for all the work that we’ve put in so far,” he said.
A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on budget speculation.
“We remain committed to bringing down bills for families now, while investing in the clean, homegrown energy and warmer homes that will protect households from volatile fossil fuel prices for good.”

India rejects ‘second-class’ permanent UN Security Council seats
Unknown

India rejects ‘second-class’ permanent UN Security Council seats
India has demanded equal veto rights for all permanent members of an expanded United Nations Security Council (UNSC), warning that creating a second tier of permanent seats would reinforce existing inequalities in the global body. 
New Delhi opposes proposals for long-term membership without veto powers, which would create “second-class” members while preserving the authority of the existing five, India’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Harish Parvathaneni, said during talks about reforming the UN in New York on Monday.
The Security Council currently has five permanent members – Russia, China, the US, the UK, and France – with veto powers, alongside ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. The council’s only expansion, in 1965, increased the number of elected seats from six to ten without changing its permanent membership.
In 1997, the then-UN General Assembly President Razali Ismail of Malaysia proposed expanding the Council, including adding five more permanent members but without veto powers.
“Fairness and justice demand that all permanent members enjoy the same rights and responsibilities,” Parvathaneni said, reiterating that veto powers must extend to new permanent members as long as the system exists.
📹 No Second-Class Permanent Seats: India Demands Veto Parity In Reformed UN Security Council Ambassador P. Harish emphasized that New Delhi’s position remains firmly aligned with the Common African Position, insisting that basic fairness and justice demand identical rights and obligations for all permanent members.
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 27, 2026
The Asia-Pacific region accounts for more than 60% of the world’s population, but has only one permanent seat; Africa and Latin America remain without permanent representation. The African Union formally presented its reform model, which calls for at least two permanent UNSC seats for Africa, carrying veto rights, earlier this year.
India and its G4 partners – Brazil, Germany, and Japan – have also called for negotiations on expanding both permanent and non-permanent membership.
The reform push has received backing from Russia. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow’s support for permanent seats for India and Brazil during the UN General Assembly in September, calling for greater representation of Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
Changes to the UN Charter would require ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five existing permanent members.

INTERVIEW – UN envoy likens spread of Islamophobia in Europe to 'metastasis'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:59:29 UTC
20:59:29 KST

- Moratinos urges stronger laws, education, monitoring to counter anti-Muslim hatred
- ‘You cannot close the door to the one who represents the whole of humanity,’ he says of Israel’s entry ban on UN chief
From threatening graffiti on mosques to attacks on worshippers, anti-Muslim hatred has left communities across Europe fearing for their safety. A deadly shooting near Paris on Friday has heightened those concerns.
The attack killed one person and injured five others, including a 12-year-old girl wearing a headscarf whose mother said she was shot eight times. Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh described it as “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic.”
Against that backdrop, the UN's envoy on Islamophobia warned that hostility toward Muslims was becoming embedded in Europe's political discourse and spreading through its institutions, likening its spread to a "metastasis."
“Europe, I think, is the most complicated case because Islamophobia has been introduced in the political discourse,” Miguel Angel Moratinos, the UN special envoy to combat Islamophobia, told Anadolu on the sidelines of the 9th Mediation Conference in Istanbul.
In England and Wales, police recorded 5,132 hate crimes targeting Muslims in the year ending March 2026, up 15% from the previous year, according to Home Office figures.
In Germany, monitoring organization CLAIM documented 4,096 anti-Muslim incidents in 2025, compared with 3,080 a year earlier. 
Its tally includes discrimination, threats and verbal abuse as well as physical violence, with two homicides and 214 cases of bodily injury.
“Normally in political elections you discuss economy, security, about the main concerns, but why we are discussing Islam? Why do we have to have this kind of concern about the Muslim communities?” he asked.
His concerns extend beyond Europe to the United States, Asia and parts of Africa.
In the US, President Donald Trump attacked Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a rally Sunday, calling him a "jihadist" who was "on the side of terrorists" and suggesting he should face special security screening before entering the Senate.
El-Sayed, who would become the country's first Muslim senator if elected, accused Trump of mocking his name and faith to distract voters from the effects of the president's policies.
Moratinos urged governments to challenge rhetoric that normalizes hostility toward Muslim communities and turn commitments against discrimination into action.
Having recently visited France, the UK, Germany and Spain to encourage stronger institutional responses, he called for legal protections, investment in education and better monitoring of Islamophobic incidents. 
 
Challenging prejudice
Outlining steps to combat Islamophobia, Moratinos said governments should strengthen legal frameworks and invest heavily in education to challenge prejudice and misinformation.
“Most probably the reason people are anti-Muslim is because they are ignorant,” he said.
“They don't know what is Islam, they don't know what a Muslim community is, they have not been informed, they have not been educated in respecting each other,” he added.
He also called for “monitoring mechanisms” to collect reliable data on Islamophobic incidents, helping authorities identify the sources of discrimination and decide how to respond.
The UN International Day to Combat Islamophobia represents progress, he said, but awareness must lead to practical measures.
“The UN can do what it can, member states can do what they can, civil society has to engage, religious leaders – everybody has to contribute to eliminate this plague,” he said.
 
Rethinking the post-9/11 approach
Moratinos also questioned the emphasis on security that has shaped international policy since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.
Drawing on his experience as the EU’s special representative for the Middle East peace process from 1996 to 2003, he said the attacks marked a shift away from political engagement and negotiations.
“From 9-11, we changed the approach and we chose security,” he said. “And security has led us to this catastrophic situation.”
Prioritizing military and security objectives over dialogue had deepened instability across the Middle East, he argued.
“Because when you try to get more security, you are more insecure,” he said. “Security for Israel, security for Lebanon, security for the Gulf, security for Iran, security, security, security, and security brings war, brings instability.”
Moratinos called for a return to negotiations that take account of the interests, concerns and aspirations of all parties, warning that military force cannot substitute for political engagement.
 
‘The force of law’
Turning to Palestine and other conflicts, Moratinos defended the importance of international law, arguing that crises make upholding shared principles more urgent.
“If we lose our soul, if we lose our values, the international community will be lost,” he warned. “The force of law will be much more sustainable than the law of force.”
He also called for changes to the way the UN operates, pointing to the power of its five permanent Security Council members – China, France, Russia, the UK and the US – to block action through their vetoes.
Moratinos called for updated rules to ensure the UN secretary-general can pursue diplomacy worldwide without governments denying his entry.
He described Israel’s decision to bar UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres from entering the country as “unacceptable.”
“He is the Secretary-General. He has to be welcomed in any capital, at any moment,” he said. “You cannot close the door to the one who represents the whole of humanity.”

Zelenskyy speaks with Finnish president, Norwegian premier following their call with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Burc Eruygur
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday held a phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store after the two Nordic leaders spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier in the day.
On US social media platform X, Zelenskyy said his call with Stubb and Store additionally took place as a continuation of their discussions in the Norwegian capital Oslo last Tuesday, which also involved representatives of the US, Europe, and NATO, and thanked the two for their briefing and active support for Kyiv’s diplomacy and peace efforts.
“Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said, noting they also discussed preparations for US-mediated trilateral peace talks planned for next month.
Saying that Finland and Norway, as countries bordering Russia, have a particular interest in “sound and reliable” security arrangements, Zelenskyy said they also discussed various formats for their engagement with partners in Europe that “could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security.”
“There must be peace, de-escalation is needed, and Russia must stop dragging out the war,” Zelenskyy added.
His statement came soon after Stubb and Store's phone call with Putin, which the Nordic leaders initiated to discuss the ongoing war, as well as diplomatic efforts to end it and promote peace and stability in Europe.
“The aim of the call was to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin. The call was related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi,” said a corresponding statement by the Finnish presidency.
Separately, a Kremlin statement said that the three leaders welcomed an agreement to resume trilateral peace talks in early November, noting that Putin had said that reaching a “just and lasting” settlement is only possible with “full and unconditional consideration” of Russia’s interests.
“At the same time, attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are leading to a prolongation of hostilities,” the statement said, adding that issues of ensuring security and stability in the Baltic Sea and Northern Europe were also discussed.
Moscow and Kyiv last held US-mediated peace negotiations earlier this year, with three rounds of talks this January and February, in Abu Dhabi and Geneva.

Israeli police foil stabbing attempt on opposition leader Yair Golan in Tel Aviv during election tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:51:41 UTC
20:51:41 KST

Lina Altawell
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Israeli police arrested a man carrying a large knife on Tuesday after approaching opposition politician Yair Golan during an election-day campaign appearance in Tel Aviv in a suspected stabbing attempt, Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported.
The incident occurred during a voter mobilization tour at Railway Park in Tel Aviv, the Democrats party, which Golan chairs, said in a statement.
The party said an unidentified man wearing a jacket approached Golan in a threatening manner before being intercepted by his security guards.
As the guards moved toward him, a large knife fell from his clothing, prompting the security team to restrain him and call police, according to the report.
Police subsequently arrested the suspect, the newspaper said.
The Democrats party said Golan’s security team prevented the man from acting and that no one was injured.
The suspect’s intentions have not been independently established, while police have yet to release details of the investigation.
Golan blamed political incitement for the incident.
“Incitement and violence will not deter us,” he said, while urging Israelis to vote in Tuesday’s elections.
The incident came as Israelis voted Tuesday in general elections for the 120-seat Knesset, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former army chief Gadi Eisenkot heading the main rival political camps.
Neither bloc is assured of securing the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority, raising the prospect of coalition negotiations after the vote.

EU Commission presents climate resilience framework amid rising costs of climate damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:50:47 UTC
20:50:47 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The European Commission on Tuesday presented a framework to strengthen the EU’s ability to anticipate, prepare for and manage climate risks, citing rising economic losses and the impact of extreme weather events.
The Commission said estimated economic losses from climate damage between 2022 and 2025 totaled approximately €200 billion ($232 billion), or around €50 billion ($58 billion) annually.
“Europe is warming at double the global rate,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, adding that climate resilience should be integrated into policies across the continent to support investment, innovation and long-term growth.
The framework proposes integrating climate resilience into major domestic and international policy areas and supporting local and regional authorities through pilot projects and advisory services.
The Commission said adapting Europe’s infrastructure and economy to future climate conditions is expected to require investment of around €70 billion ($81 billion) annually.
It added that investment in climate adaptation could generate returns exceeding 10 times initial amounts through avoided losses and damage.
The global market for climate adaptation solutions is projected to reach €3.5 trillion ($4.1 trillion) by 2050, the Commission said, presenting opportunities for European businesses developing resilience technologies.
Alongside the framework, the Commission proposed a Climate Resilience Law intended to establish a common reference trajectory for global warming and simplify national planning requirements through a single strategic plan for each member state.
The proposal cites scientific projections that global temperatures could rise to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels by 2030, 2C (3.6F) by 2050 and 3C (5.4F) by 2100.
The framework also envisages new digital tools to help public authorities, businesses and communities assess climate risks.
These include an interactive European Climate Viewer showing projected climate hazards and a platform to help users identify adaptation tools and solutions.
The Commission said it would begin implementing the framework immediately. It is also developing a European Heatwave Plan, a Climate Insurance Alliance and a European Water initiative, alongside measures to strengthen disaster preparedness.
The Commission plans to propose an EU strategic plan on climate resilience in 2028.

emma sicher grows biomaterials from wild berries and microorganisms

emma sicher grows biomaterials from wild berries and microorganisms
with bacteria and locally sourced plants, biodesigner emma sicher grows microbial cellulose into edible prototypes and packaging.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
emma sicher grows materials with microbes
Berlin-based biodesigner Emma Sicher is experimenting with materials grown by bacteria and yeast, turning microbial cellulose into everything from translucent packaging to edible food prototypes. Some of her samples resemble crinkled pieces of pink glass, while others form glossy, gelatinous spheres. Their unusual colors and textures emerge through fermentation, a process in which microorganisms help produce the material itself.
At the center of her practice is SCOBY, a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast commonly associated with kombucha. As the microorganisms grow in a nutrient-rich liquid, cellulose-producing bacteria form a gelatinous membrane at the surface. This can be harvested and processed into flexible sheets, or developed into different forms for food and material applications.
when microbial cellulose becomes food
Emma Sicher’s EATING SCOBY project explores the culinary possibilities of this cellulose-rich membrane. Developed during her MA in Eco-Social Design, the research involved food microbiologists and consultation with chefs. Among the prototypes are SCOBY chips that begin crunchy before becoming chewy and slightly gelatinous in the mouth. An experimental ice cream cone offers another application, with the possibility of an inner coating of melted chocolate.
A double-flavor popsicle takes the material in a different direction, with a consistency the designer compares to blended aloe vera. These familiar food formats make the unusual ingredient easier to imagine on a plate, while introducing new possibilities for its texture and presentation. The prototypes remain experimental, exploring how microbial cellulose might become part of future food systems.
packaging grown from food waste
Sicher first explored bacterial cellulose in her 2017 project From Peel to Peel, which proposed biodegradable food packaging grown from discarded fruit and vegetables. Apple peels and beetroot scraps became nutrients for microbial cultures, producing thin sheets that could be dried into wrappers and small containers. The packaging took on different colors depending on the ingredients, ranging from pale yellow to deep pink.
The dried material can resemble paper or leather, with its finish influenced by the surface on which it dries. Its tendency to absorb moisture presents limitations for conventional packaging, particularly for wet foods. Still, the project established an approach that continues throughout Sicher’s work: allowing biological processes to influence the properties of a material from the beginning.
growing materials from local ecosystems
More recently, Sicher has begun investigating how materials can be grown using microorganisms already present in the surrounding environment. In research published in 2026, she describes experiments with rowan berries foraged around Berlin and mirabelle plums collected in Brandenburg. Both successfully produced cellulose membranes through fermentation using naturally occurring microbial communities, without conventional kombucha starter cultures.
Other experiments combined elderberries with a fermentation starter made from wild mirabelle plums, producing an intensely colored membrane. Sicher’s research also draws on fermentation practices she studied with local practitioners in Thailand. Together, these investigations explore how the plants and microbial populations of a particular region might influence the materials cultivated there, introducing biological variations that would be difficult to achieve through standardized production.
designing alongside living organisms
Sicher also brings microbial experimentation into educational workshops, where participants learn to prepare plant infusions and cultivate their own SCOBY membranes. During a workshop at Elisava School of Design and Engineering in Barcelona, students worked with wet and dried cellulose, exploring how its texture and behavior change through processing. Her research with alternative plant infusions has similarly examined how botanical ingredients can influence the density and physical properties of the grown material.
Across these experiments, Sicher works with processes that depend on the behavior of other living organisms. She can select the plants and prepare the growing environment, but the microorganisms play their own part in forming the material. What emerges is shaped by those biological interactions, suggesting a way of making in which the surrounding ecology participates in the design process.

designer: Emma Sicher | @seeker_biodesign

NEW DELHI, October 27. /TASS/. Parliamentarians from the BRICS member countries have reaffirmed their unwavering support for a peaceful resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, as well as the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and the establishment of an independent, sovereign state, says a joint declaration issued following the 12th BRICS International Parliamentary Forum.
"We reaffirm our unwavering support for a peaceful resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict based on the ‘two states for two peoples’ concept, in which both states coexist peacefully and securely, in accordance with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions, and we also reaffirm the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination, freedom, and the establishment of an independent, sovereign state," the document states.

According to the document, the BRICS parliamentarians called for stepping up efforts, through dialogue and diplomacy, to achieve long-term mutual understanding that will contribute to establishing long-term peace, security, and stability in the region. They emphasized the need to work together to maintain the uninterrupted functioning of global trade, supply chains, and energy flows in accordance with international law the norms.
Russia’s parliamentary delegation led by State Duma Chairman Vyacheslav Volodin is in India, where it is participating in events at the 12th BRICS International Parliamentary Forum. This year, the forum is being held in the Indian capital, which currently holds the BRICS chairmanship. The main theme of the forum is "Fostering Parliaments for People-Centric Development."

With 11 more fatalities, deaths in Bangladesh from dengue rise to 400
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:49:10 UTC
20:49:10 KST

Sm Najmus Sakib
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Deaths from dengue infections rose to 400 in Bangladesh on Tuesday with the addition of 11 more fatalities registered in the past 24 hours.
The Health Services Directorate under the Health and Family Welfare Ministry also reported 2,071 new cases of hospitalizations in the same period, bringing the caseload since this January to 128,237.
Of the total hospitalized patients, 6,415 patients remained in hospitals across the country while the rest returned home after recovery.
Bangladesh this year has started reporting a growing number of deaths from an increased number of hospitals.
There were 269 deaths and 66,423 dengue cases recorded in the corresponding period of 2025, according to directorate data.
Bangladesh usually experiences its dengue season between June and September. The mosquito-borne disease has shown a sharp rise in infections and related deaths compared with the corresponding period last year.
Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes. There is no specific treatment for the viral infection.
The South Asian nation of 175 million saw its highest-ever annual number of dengue deaths in 2022, when 281 people died.
 
7 more children die from measles and suspected cases
Meanwhile, health authorities also reported seven more deaths of children involving confirmed measles and measles-like symptoms.
The total number of child deaths linked to measles infections rose to 1,240 since mid-March. Of these, 105 have been confirmed as definitely due to measles.
The directorate also registered 1,232 new suspected cases and 63 new confirmed infections nationwide. With this, the number of symptomatic measles cases reached 223,784, while confirmed cases stood at 23,541.
The Health Ministry has immunized around 20 million children in response to the outbreak, in addition to routine vaccinations and a catch-up campaign launched late last month.
Bangladesh historically had herd immunity against measles but has lost it in recent years due to declining vaccination coverage.

Twenty Vietnamese students participated last Saturday in Hanoi in a masterclass dedicated to Italian pasta, organized by the Italian Embassy in Vietnam to mark World Pasta Day 2026, with the support of Aliseo International Trade and Pegasus International College. The event featured Italian chef Nico Ceccomoro, who guided the participants through a journey exploring preparation techniques and regional culinary traditions. During the morning, the students explored the differences between fresh and dried pasta, learned about some of the main specialties from various Italian regions, and took part in hands-on exercises that culminated in the preparation of various dishes. Pasta is one of Italy’s most widely consumed agri-food products internationally: in 2025, Italy produced approximately 4.2 million metric tons of it, exporting over 60%. Ambassador Marco della Seta attended the event, presenting the students with certificates of participation and highlighting their contribution to promoting authentic Italian cuisine—recognized as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage—and to strengthening the presence of “Made in Italy” products in Vietnam.

Nearly 40,000 flee Ethiopia clashes into Kenya as rights commission urges urgent action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:48:36 UTC
20:48:36 KST

Andrew Wasike 
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Nearly 40,000 Ethiopians have sought refuge in Kenya after fleeing deadly clashes in their country, Kenya’s independent human rights commission said Tuesday, urging authorities to provide emergency assistance and protect civilians escaping the violence.
“The protection of life and human dignity cannot be postponed. KNCHR urges all responsible authorities and partners to act urgently, in coordination and with compassion, so that everyone seeking safety in Moyale is protected by the law and can access essential humanitarian assistance,” Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) Chairperson Claris Ogangah said in a statement.
The latest figure represents a sharp increase from the more than 14,000 displaced Ethiopians reported by the Kenya Red Cross over the weekend, as fighting between regional security forces and armed civilians from Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional states continues near the shared border.
The commission said it was concerned by reports that “approximately 40,000 people have sought refuge in Moyale after fleeing unrest in Ethiopia.”
More than 15,000 were reportedly staying in eight temporary shelters, including churches and schools, while over 20,000 others were being accommodated by relatives and friends.
The influx has placed considerable pressure on host communities, with shortages of food, clean water, shelter, sanitation and healthcare raising concerns about deteriorating humanitarian conditions.
KNCHR warned that overcrowding and inadequate sanitation could increase the risk of communicable disease outbreaks.
It also reported that two women had given birth at Manyatta Burji and another two at Bitiye, highlighting the urgent need for maternal healthcare, emergency treatment and postnatal services.
The commission called on the Kenyan and Ethiopian governments to coordinate efforts to address the violence and ensure the safe and humane movement of civilians across the border.
KNCHR emphasized that Kenya’s constitutional protections apply to everyone within its borders, regardless of nationality or immigration status.
It also reminded authorities of their obligations under international refugee law, including the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they face persecution or serious threats to their safety. 
Flag dispute triggers deadly fighting
The humanitarian crisis follows clashes involving security forces and armed civilians from Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional states, particularly among the Oromo Borana and Somali Garre communities.
Both groups inhabit areas around Moyale, where longstanding disputes over administrative boundaries and territorial control have repeatedly fueled tensions.
The latest violence was preceded by a dispute over the raising of the Somali Regional State flag and the opening of a new administrative office in an area of Moyale claimed by Oromia authorities.
Tensions intensified following the killing of a 13-year-old girl on Oct. 18, triggering protests, business closures and further confrontations between the communities.
Heavy fighting erupted on Oct. 22, with regional security forces and armed civilians exchanging gunfire as violence spread to several settlements in southern Ethiopia.
Representatives of the rival communities have accused each other of provoking the clashes, while residents have reported deaths, injuries and the destruction of homes and businesses.
The fighting has also disrupted transport and commercial activities along the Kenya-Ethiopia border, an important trade corridor connecting the two East African countries.
Kenyan lawmakers from Marsabit County earlier appealed to President William Ruto to engage Ethiopian authorities diplomatically and help restore calm.
KNCHR warned that humanitarian assistance must also take into account the needs of Kenyan communities hosting displaced families, saying coordinated intervention was essential to prevent conditions from deteriorating further.

Poland and UK support strong transatlantic alliance, Polish minister says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:38:03 CET

WARSAW, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Both Poland and the United Kingdom are in favour of strengthening the transatlantic alliance as there is no alternative to cooperation with the US, Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Tuesday.
“We share a similar view of the alliance with the United States. Both Poland and the United Kingdom support strengthening this alliance,” the Polish Defence Minister said during a joint press conference with British Defence Minister Wes Streeting.
He said both countries backed efforts to strengthen Europe’s defence capabilities and strategic autonomy, but not at the expense of ties with Washington.
“There is no alternative to transatlantic cooperation. Any other solution is simply worse, it is bad. But our capabilities, British capabilities, Polish capabilities, and European capabilities must be strengthened for production, for collective defense, for cooperation,” he said.
Poland and Britain signed a three-year defence cooperation plan on Tuesday covering joint military exercises and the development of defence capabilities.
Kosiniak-Kamysz also said Poland would seek to ensure that Britain could benefit from the European Union’s SAFE defence financing programme and assured that Poland will strive to “bring the United Kingdom closer to the European Union”.

Nova Poshta has set up its own air defence and is downing Russian drones
Nova Poshta (Nova Post), Ukraine's largest private delivery company, whose warehouses are constantly being damaged by Russian attacks, has set up a private air defence project and has already shot down Russian attack drones.
Source: Viachеslav Klymov, co-owner of the Nova Group of Companies, at the Kyiv International Economic Forum on 26 October, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine
Quote: "We are one of the few companies to have implemented this project. I don't want to disclose the figures, but we have shot down Shahed drones."
Details: Klymov stressed the importance of further developing private air defence projects, noting that businesses can take on functions that before Russia's full-scale invasion were considered the exclusive responsibility of the state.
He also believes businesses could establish their own firefighting services at their production facilities.
Klymov cited his company's experience, saying that employees put out a significant proportion of the fires caused by attacks themselves, without waiting for the State Emergency Service to arrive.
"Large businesses are now looking for fire engines in Europe so they can set up their own services. This is our property, so what's the problem? Can anyone stop me from putting out a fire myself on my own property?" Klymov said.
Background: In October, Nova Poshta opened Moldova's first parcel locker hub in Chișinău, with 624 parcel collection compartments in one location.

• This month anti-migrant protests in KwaZulu-Natal’s biggest city Durban and Johannesburg’s Soweto township turned violent, with vehicles torched and shops looted
• A foreign national was also allegedly beaten to death by a crowd in Durban last week
• The unrest followed disinformation about a July Constitutional Court ruling that asylum seekers cannot be denied access to South Africa’s asylum system solely for procedural reasons
