For Pope Leo, there was little choice but to go to Latin America
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:37:50 CET
20:37:50 KST

By Joshua McElwee
VATICAN CITY, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Since undergoing surgery on October 13 to treat lung cancer, Pope Leo has weighed a major decision: whether to press ahead with an intense, three-country tour of South America just 24 days after having part of one lung removed.
But in the end, according to a biographer and other experts, Leo had little choice but to continue with a visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru as the Vatican announced on Monday, to show he remains up to the job of leading the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics.
Leo, 71, was born in the US but spent decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. He is also devoted to that country, where he became a citizen and which he considers an adopted home.
“Cancelling would have meant … sending a certain message that this (surgery) has been a real rupture in this pontificate,” Massimo Faggioli, a papal historian, told Reuters.
“The message is now, ‘No, that health crisis is over. And I can do it,’” said Faggioli, a professor at Villanova University, near Philadelphia, where Leo earned one of his diplomas.
Elise Allen, author of a biography of the pope for Penguin Peru, said his decision “shows an incredible determination to continue with the mission that he believes has been entrusted to him by God.”
FOREIGN TRIPS NOW INTEGRAL PART OF PAPACY
Travelling abroad has become a major part of the modern papacy, with popes seeking to meet local Catholics, spread the faith, and conduct international diplomacy.
They often draw large crowds, and officials in Argentina have estimated that some seven million people will attend events with Leo over his three days in that country.
Making foreign trips has become an integral part of being pope, said Faggioli. “That has become the real test of the papacy, if you can do exhausting trips or not,” he said. “The papacy is … a global job and you have to be there in person.”
Leo’s November 6-17 South America tour is set to be one of the most intense taken by a pope in decades. He is scheduled to travel some 31,000 km (19,300 miles) over the 10-city tour and give 36 speeches.
The Vatican said on Monday that the pope was fit for the trip, citing Leo’s personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone.
Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, said the risks of complications for the pope related to the surgery now appear “quite low.”
He said that Leo being cleared to fly by his doctors should indicate that his operated lung has fully expanded and any surgical wounds are healing without signs of infection.
“My primary advice for patients in this situation is not to push themselves too far and to listen to their body when it asks for rest,” Liu told Reuters.
“I would expect his team would primarily be watching for any signs of exhaustion” during the trip, said the doctor.
CATHOLICS WILL WATCH TRIP CLOSELY
Leo is recovering from surgery two weeks ago in which doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung to treat lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The pope’s doctors said last week that further examinations of the tissue removed in the operation had confirmed the cancer was localized and he would not require any further ongoing cancer treatments.
The Vatican said on Monday the trip would go forward with no changes to the previously planned itinerary, which includes 12 flights and two helicopter trips.
The Vatican press office did not immediately respond to questions about whether there would be any additional emergency planning for the trip or additional medical personnel added to the tour.
“It is very intense and I think the risks are very real,” said Allen, the only journalist to interview Leo since his May 2025 election. “But obviously, Leo is confident in how he’s feeling and his medical team is confident in what they’re seeing.”
Faggioli said he expects Catholics across the world will be watching the trip closely, to see how Leo is faring.
“Everyone will look at every speech he gives, every hand he shakes,” said the academic. “This decision will keep some people, as we say in Italian, ‘sulle spine’ (on tenterhooks).”
(Reporting by Joshua McElwee, editing by Keith Weir)

By Tora Agarwala
GUWAHATI, India, Oct 27 (Reuters) - India has deployed hundreds of additional security personnel in its remote northeast, authorities said on Tuesday, after youth protesters clashed with police last week over a plan to build a mega-dam to counter a Chinese hydropower project upstream.
Protests in Arunachal Pradesh’s Siang Valley, which borders Tibet, turned violent last week, triggering clashes with police, who made at least 21 arrests.
Police fired tear gas shells, while youth protesters pelted stones and set fire to a police station and an office of the state-owned National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, authorities said.
“Forces are being increased in the places where it is required. We do not want any law and order problem,” SD Singh Jamwal, police chief of Arunachal Pradesh, told Reuters.
Sporadic protests have taken place in the Siang Valley in the last two years, the location of the proposed 11,200-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, which will be developed by state-run National Hydroelectric Power Corporation.
Villagers who oppose the project fear that the dam would submerge ancestral villages belonging to the Adi tribe.
“We will keep opposing this dam till they cancel it. If it is constructed, 27 of our ancestral villages will be completely submerged. At least 40 or 50 more will be affected,” Gegong Jijong of the Siang Indigenous Farmers’ Forum told Reuters.
The Siang river flows into Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet, where it is known as the Yarlung Zangbo. China announced plans in December 2024 to build the world’s largest hydropower dam upstream, triggering fears in New Delhi that its longtime strategic rival could weaponise its control of the river.
China claims Arunachal Pradesh, which it calls Zangnan, as part of southern Tibet. India says the state is an integral and inalienable part of its territory.
Arunachal Pradesh’s chief minister, a member of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, has called the Chinese project an existential threat and said the government would protect national interests while respecting the rights and aspirations of the people of Siang Valley.

Nearly all Saudi Arabia’s oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, both of which the Houthis have attacked in the past.
Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura’s terminal.
AIRSTRIKES
The Houthis said they had attacked two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the attacks.
On Tuesday afternoon, civil defence authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh.
The Houthis said they had repelled an advance by forces they described as Saudi-backed from the southern approaches to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces earlier this month pushed the Houthis out of coastal areas they had seized in September, loosening the group’s grip on a vital Red Sea oil route.
Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported Saudi strikes on the Yemeni city of Mocha. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
The fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce between the coalition and the Houthis, who control the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran to try to reduce regional tensions.
Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the three countries in a mutual defence pact, authorised Egypt’s military on Monday to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked.

Three Arab states back Greece in dispute over Turkey-Libya maritime accord
Italy

2026-10-27

20:37:43 KST

ATHENS, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Egypt, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates aligned with Greece to denounce a Turkey-Libya maritime accord as a threat to regional security and international legal order in a long-standing dispute over sea borders in the eastern Mediterranean Sea.
Libya’s eastern parliament last week approved a maritime boundaries deal with Turkey, originally agreed in 2019, drawing swift condemnation from Greece and Cyprus, which say it infringes on their own maritime claims.
In a joint statement delivered by Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis at the United Nations in New York on Monday, Greece and the three Arab countries said the maritime accord raised “serious concerns for regional security and stability” and could set a bad precedent by allowing “arbitrary bilateral arrangements” to undermine established rules of international law.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday that reactions from the European Union and others to the approval of the agreement had no legitimate basis, defending Ankara’s policy in the eastern Mediterranean.
The Arab support to Greece signals efforts to turn a bilateral dispute into a broader regional push for respect of maritime rules, increasing diplomatic pressure on Turkey and Libya over maritime zones and future energy projects in the Mediterranean Sea.
Since the 2019 Libya-Turkey deal, Greece has awarded a Chevron -led consortium a licence to look for gas off the island of Crete and has sought a separate agreement with Libya on demarcating their maritime zones.
Gerapetritis said on Monday that Athens stood ready to continue the effort and called on Libya to foster good relations with neighbours in line with maritime rules as part of a political transition.
Libya broke apart into rival eastern and western administrations more than a decade ago during a civil war after a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.
The Libya-Turkey accord was agreed by Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in the west, but the rival eastern administration under military commander Khalifa Haftar had withheld its approval for years.
Turkish support was crucial to repelling an assault by Haftar’s forces on Tripoli in 2019-2020.
But relations have steadily improved in recent years, with Turkish officials paying regular visits to Haftar’s de facto capital, Benghazi, and investing heavily in construction and other sectors.

Iraq revives shipping line after 50 years as Hormuz crisis bites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:37:29 UTC
20:37:29 KST

Breadcrumb
After 50 years, Iraq revives national shipping line as Hormuz crisis drives up costs
Iraq has resumed operations on its national commercial shipping line after more than five decades, as rising freight and insurance costs linked to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz place growing pressure on the country's import-dependent economy.
The relaunch marks an attempt by Baghdad to restore its presence in regional maritime trade, reduce reliance on foreign shipping companies and expand transport options for Iraqi businesses.
The General Company for Maritime Transport, which operates under Iraq's Ministry of Transport, announced on Monday that the vessel Basra had arrived at Umm Qasr port carrying containers from Jebel Ali port in the United Arab Emirates.
The voyage marked the first step towards reviving the Iraqi Line, the country's national commercial shipping service, which had been inactive for more than 50 years.
Ahmed Jassim, director-general of the company, said the resumption would provide traders and importers with additional shipping options while strengthening commercial links between Iraqi and Emirati ports.
He added that the initiative formed part of wider efforts to develop Iraq's national maritime carrier and expand its role in regional and international trade.
The transport ministry announced on 5 October that the shipping line was preparing to resume commercial operations, noting that its last voyages dated back to the mid-1960s.
The ministry also said Iraq's ports had a combined annual handling capacity exceeding 79 million tonnes and a container capacity of more than 3.6 million containers, with measures underway to ease congestion and improve roads and storage facilities.
However, Iraq's national fleet currently consists of just six vessels, raising questions about whether the revived service can compete with established international shipping operators.
Hormuz disruptions drive up shipping costs
The relaunch comes as instability in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime route connecting the Gulf to international markets, has increased freight and insurance costs and disrupted delivery schedules.
Jassim al-Moussawi, a member of Iraq's parliamentary Oil and Gas Committee, said developing the national fleet had become increasingly important as regional tensions drove up transport costs.
Speaking to The New Arab, Moussawi said Iraq needed a larger fleet of nationally owned vessels to reduce its dependence on foreign companies.
He estimated that transport costs had risen sharply because of regional disruptions, reaching almost half the value of exported oil, according to his calculations.
Expanding Iraq's maritime transport capacity could save the state treasury millions of dollars, he argued, by reducing freight and insurance expenses and improving the country's ability to respond to disruptions in international shipping.
Iraqi trader Halim Hamid also welcomed the reopening of the route between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr, describing it as an opportunity to provide importers with more shipping options.
"The resumption of the line between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr represents a positive step towards expanding shipping options for importers, particularly following the rise in freight and insurance costs and delays in the arrival of goods caused by the Hormuz disruptions," he told TNA.
Hamid said fluctuations in shipping costs and unreliable delivery schedules were affecting the price of imported goods in Iraqi markets.
He added that an effective national carrier could increase competition with foreign companies, provided it offered competitive rates, reliable sailing schedules and efficient customs clearance.
"The success of the line depends on providing integrated services covering booking, transport, unloading and delivery according to clear schedules," he said.
Traders, he stressed, make shipping decisions based on overall costs and reliability rather than the nationality of the carrier.
While expanding the service could gradually reduce import costs, Hamid cautioned that it would not necessarily lead to an immediate fall in consumer prices without sufficient shipping capacity and competitive logistics services.
Can Iraq's shipping revival deliver economic gains?
Economists say the return of the national shipping line could help Iraq develop an additional source of non-oil revenue by capturing a greater share of the country's substantial import and freight market.
Economic expert Karim al-Hilu said Iraq's heavy reliance on foreign shipping operators presented an opportunity for domestic companies to expand their role in maritime transport and logistics.
Citing Ministry of Planning figures, Hilu said Iraq imported approximately 23.46 million tonnes of goods through its ports in 2025, an increase of 10.5% from the previous year.
Despite the growth in cargo volumes, revenues at the General Company for Maritime Transport fell by 10.9% to 213 billion Iraqi dinars ($163 million), highlighting a gap between expanding trade activity and the earnings of the national carrier.
Iraq's merchandise imports totalled approximately $72.3 billion in 2025, including $49.3 billion transported through seaports, according to Hilu.
He said the figures demonstrated the potential for greater investment in shipping, warehousing, maintenance and other port-related services, which could create jobs and generate more economic value domestically.
However, Hilu warned that reviving the national line would require a carefully planned commercial strategy, particularly given the small size of Iraq's fleet and competition from international operators.
"Unplanned expansion could turn the project into a financial burden rather than a sustainable source of revenue," he said, calling for a clear operational and investment plan to ensure economic viability and strengthen the national carrier's regional competitiveness.

Iranian, Russian universities explore potential to boost co-op
TEHRAN - Iran’s Persian Gulf University and Russia’s Novosibirsk State University have discussed ways to strengthen scientific cooperation and expand joint research initiatives.
During an online meeting, the two universities outlined their respective capacities, explored potential areas of collaboration, and agreed to examine mobility programs involving industry participation in both countries.
Persian Gulf University initiatives are primarily focused on three strategic areas of excellence: energy, petroleum, gas, and petrochemistry; marine studies; and international business and commerce. By prioritizing these areas of scientific knowledge and academic activity, Persian Gulf University aims to strengthen its constructively important role in establishing and maintaining peaceful coexistence and sustainable development, as well as enhancing human prosperity and well-being in the Persian Gulf region.
The university’s internationalization project has begun in recent years, and there has been significant growth in the international indicators, including the number of international academic members, international students, and international events. The university’s mission is to become a third-generation international university with excellence in science, technology, and entrepreneurship to respond to the surrounding society’s needs and create value for society, develop competent citizens, and perform its social roles.
Persian Gulf University has an excellent reputation for teaching quality, academic research, and graduate employability. Admission is limited to students who pass the national entrance examination administered annually by the Iranian Ministry of Science, Research, and Technology.
Novosibirsk region is home to one of Russia’s most prominent universities—a symbol of the research-oriented university model in Siberia—situated in the heart of the science city, Akademgorodok.
Relying on high-quality education, fundamental research, and close collaboration with institutions of the Russian Academy of Sciences, the university holds a distinguished position within the country’s science and technology system.
The combination of a dynamic academic environment, an international scholarly community, and a focus on basic sciences and advanced technologies has established it as a key center for cultivating the next generation of scientists and innovators—both in Russia and globally.
Tehran, Moscow set to establish joint science and technology commission
Iran and Russia are preparing to establish a joint commission on science and technology, with a document on international scientific cooperation between the two countries set to be signed at a meeting of the commission.
In September, Ehsan Qaboul, head of the Ministry of Science, Research and Technology’s Center for International Scientific Cooperation, said Iran is firmly committed to expanding ties with Russia, outlining the next steps by Tehran and Moscow to strengthen bilateral cooperation, including the formation of the joint science and technology commission.
Qaboul added that the Minister of Science, Research and Technology is scheduled to travel to Moscow within the next three months to finalize the document on international scientific cooperation between Iran and Russia.
He also announced plans for 500 cooperation programs with Russian universities and scientific institutions.
The programs include holding 100 joint educational courses involving Russian professors, enabling 100 doctoral and master’s students to choose a second academic supervisor from among professors at
Russian universities, and organizing 100 technology events aimed at expanding bilateral cooperation from science and education into the technology sector.
Qaboul further said that 100 joint cultural events with Russian universities and academic and educational institutions, as well as 100 scholarships for Russian students, are also among the planned initiatives. The scholarships will give priority to students seeking to study Persian language and literature.
The official also stressed Iran’s support for Persian-language programs at Russian universities, saying Iranian professors are ready to teach Persian to Russian speakers either in person or online.
In June, Iranian Science, Research and Technology Minister, Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, and Russian Science and Higher Education Minister, Valery Falkov, reviewed strategies for developing scientific, educational, and academic cooperation between the two countries, with an emphasis on expanding professor and student exchanges, strengthening research cooperation, and facilitating academic interactions.
Simaei-Sarraf considered the development of Russian language chairs in Iranian universities and Persian language chairs in Russian universities as a sign of deepening scientific and cultural ties between the two countries.
Falkov, for his part, pointed out the beginning of a new university admission period in Russia and the welcoming of Iranian students to study at the country’s universities, emphasizing the importance of providing employment opportunities and utilizing the academic potential of graduates after their return to Iran.

The most haunted hotels in Europe you can book a stay in this Halloween
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:28:41 UTC
20:28:41 KST

From heartbroken lovers to airmen who have fallen to their untimely deaths, these hotels on the continent have guests with no respect for the 11am checkout time.
A spectre is haunting Europe. No, hang on. Spectres are haunting Europe, and apparently people are willingly sleeping in the same space as them.
While I personally would avoid any hotel that claims to be haunted, there are a number of properties across the continent that loudly and proudly shout about their paranormal guests, and with Halloween coming up, we thought it was time to spotlight them.
Here’s where to stay if you want a truly haunted Halloween experience.
Golden Fleece, York, UK
Billing itself as one of the most haunted cities in Europe, practically every street in York has a building with a ghost story attached to it.
The Golden Fleece, a pub on Pavement, claims to be the most haunted in the city, and for those who aren’t satisfied with just enjoying a pint among the spectres, you can also book a night in one of the rooms here.
According to York’s tourism board, paranormal guests you might encounter during your stay include Lady Alice Peckett, the wife of the pub’s owner from the early 18th century, and a British airman who fell out of a window here in 1944.
The Ancient Ram Inn, Gloucestershire, UK
Originally built in the late medieval period, The Ancient Ram Inn has had plenty of time to rack up supernatural figures that wander its halls while guests sleep.
Its owners say it’s the most haunted bed and breakfast in the UK, with some 20 ghosts, including a young girl named Rosie, reports Metro. One ghost hunter even claims to have encountered a female sex demon. Blimey.
The Shelbourne, Autograph Collection, Dublin, Ireland
When it comes to five-star hotels, you tend to have certain expectations: Top-notch service, fantastic bars and restaurants, and preferably a nice wellness area with a spa or swimming pool.
You probably don’t expect to run into the mischievous spirit of a seven-year-old girl named Mary Masters who died of cholera in 1791.
But that’s exactly what you’ll get at The Shelbourne, Autograph Collection in Dublin, according to the Irish Mirror, with sightings as frequent as two or three times a week.
Actress Lily Collins even claimed to have seen the ghost during a stay here while filming The Mortal Instruments: City of Bones.
Hotel Union Øye, Norway
While Mary Masters is supposedly limited to the sixth floor of The Shelbourne, the ghost said to be inhabiting Hotel Union Øye sticks to “The Blue Room”.
The tale goes that a servant girl named Linda started an illicit affair with one of Emperor Wilhelm’s officers, and The Blue Room was where the pair would meet.
It ended in tragedy. Unable to divorce his wife and be with the woman he loved, the officer killed himself. Linda, not wanting to live without him, killed herself by walking into the lake, never to be seen again.
Now, according to Norway’s tourism board, Linda’s ghost is said to be heard weeping in The Blue Room.
Toftaholm Herrgård, Sweden
Another broken-hearted ghost can be found at Toftaholm Herrgård in Sweden.
Servant Mats fell in love with the daughter of a count, who was promptly married off to the son of a nobleman. Upon discovering the news, Mats hung himself in one of the guest rooms of the mansion.
Describing him as a “gentle ghost”, the team behind Toftaholm Herrgård say guests claim to have seen him appearing behind women staying in the hotel, occasionally putting his hand on their shoulder.

Family Physician Program being implemented in 64 medical networks nationwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:27:26 UTC
20:27:26 KST

Family Physician Program being implemented in 64 medical networks nationwide
TEHRAN – The health ministry is implementing Family Physician Program in 64 medical networks across the country, providing services to some 3.5 million individuals in the initial phase, and diagnosing new cases of patients with diabetes, hypertension, and pre-diabetes.
Around 13.6 million people are currently covered by the program, including 7.7 million in urban areas and the remainder in rural areas, IRNA quoted Alireza Raeisi, an official with the health ministry, as saying.
Noting that the rural population has been fully assigned, the official said that the process of assigning individuals to Family Physician Program in the urban population is being completed, and urban coverage will expand with more physicians joining the program.
Around 2,528 physicians are operating in rural and urban pilot centers, and some 1,610 specialists will soon start providing essential services to the patients, he added.
Referring to the development of digital health infrastructures, Raeisi said integration of systems at different levels of service, the connection with insurance systems, the scheduling of appointments, the referral of patients, and the creation of management dashboards are parts of the adopted measures.
According to the official, some 408,000 referrals to higher health services, about two million prescriptions, and 753,000 medical tests have been recorded so far.
Up until now, 19,246 new cases of diabetes, 34,731individuals with high blood pressure, and 9,322 individuals with prediabetes have been diagnosed, amounting to 49 and 37 percent of expected target population with hypertension and diabetes, respectively.
The official went on to say that the subsequent phases of the program will include breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer screening tests, disease risk assessment, hearing screening tests, child care, identification of overweight and obesity, and childbearing counselling.
In July, the third phase of the Family Physician Program and referral system kicked off on July 28 in 19 cities, Alireza Raeisi, an official with the health ministry, said.
The program aims to make treatment referrals more concentrated and provide more convenient access to health services.
Successful implementation of the Family Physician Program is essential to the health system. There are no other options; the failure to implement the program would inflict the greatest damage on the health system, IRNA quoted Raeisi as saying.
“Over 100 countries worldwide have implemented the program, and an analysis of global experiences indicates that its full implementation is not feasible in the short term; rather, it requires developing a supportive culture, careful planning, patience, perseverance, and continuous follow-up. Nevertheless, based on existing experiences, we assess the program’s implementation process in the country as positive and promising,” Raeisi highlighted.
Referring to the implementation of the program in Fars and Mazandaran provinces, the official said that the unsuccessful experiences in these provinces resulted from improper implementation rather than a failure to fully implement it. Hence, the precise and principled implementation of the current program is of great importance.
The new phase of the program should be implemented in some cities, like Firouzabad, Jahrom, Larestan, Fasa, and Jouybar, in which previous phases of the program were implemented, to ensure its efficiency, he noted.
Drawing upon the experiences of the first and second phases, the implementation of the third phase should be pursued with enhanced speed, precision, and quality. Furthermore, the chancellors of the universities and the heads of the colleges should continuously oversee the selected networks, regularly monitor the implementation process, and collect necessary feedback. They will also need to consider the Social Determinants of Health (SDH), Raeisi further noted.
The rural family physician program started in 2005. Back then, it also targeted villages and cities inhabited by fewer than twenty thousand individuals to make treatment referrals more concentrated and provide more convenient access to health services, ISNA reported.
Periodic examinations and monitoring of people’s health status, easy and round-the-clock access to basic services and primary care, and frequent visits to doctors are the characteristics of a family physician.
Medical, dental, mental, midwifery, nutrition, laboratory, pharmaceutical, and medical imaging are among the services offered by the program.
Based on the Family Physician Program, a physician and a midwife offer services in rural areas; every 3,300 villagers have a physician, and there is a midwife per 5,200 people in villages.
The program will gradually target other parts of the country as well, ISNA quoted Health Minister Mohammad-Reza Zafarqandi as saying.
“It is a large-scale program based on social behavior change. Designing new patient pathways, reforming the referral pattern, and improving the healthcare network system requires careful coordination between the Health Ministry, governors, and other relevant institutions at the provincial level,” IRIB quoted Zafarqandi as saying.
So, it is essential to develop a national headquarters headed by the President to oversee the overall management of the program, he added.

The decision was made against the backdrop of repair work on the metro and bridge infrastructure. Starting October 28, the number of additional services will increase to 16 per day.
Details

The route will run in a semicircle through the Vydubychi, Berezniaky, Darnytsia, Rusanivka, Livoberezhna, Mykilska Slobidka, Voskresenka, Rainbow and Pochaina stations. Services will operate in both directions. The first additional evening train will depart from Vydubychi at 15:57, and from Pochaina at 15:59.

Passengers can purchase tickets for the additional services in the Ukrzaliznytsia mobile app.
Starting Wednesday, October 28, additional services will run during both the morning and evening rush hours. In total, the carrier has scheduled 16 additional services. The national railway carrier hopes that the combination of regular and additional trains will ensure that intervals on the semicircular route during rush hours are between 15 minutes.
The introduction of additional trains is intended to expand travel options between Kyiv’s right and left banks during periods of peak passenger traffic while repair work is being carried out on the capital’s transport infrastructure

Across China: Researchers propose new irrigation to balance water conservation, food security in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:17:46 CST
20:17:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A new study shows that China may better balance water conservation, food security and investment returns by adopting more efficient irrigation strategies, and expanding irrigated farmland only where conditions are optimal.
The study, published in the journal Nature Food, was led by researchers at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics (IAP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hohai University and Xiamen University, in collaboration with several other Chinese and international institutions.
As rising temperatures and droughts put more pressure on food production systems, irrigation is becoming more important for farmers adapting to climate change. But expanding irrigated farmland further burdens already limited water supplies. The researchers therefore look for ways to save water, protect cereal production and improve investment returns all at once.
The team examined 42,190 county-level agricultural statistical records, 3,576 household socioeconomic survey responses and 2,230 irrigation technology comparison trials. It also focused on China's three staple crops: maize, wheat and rice.
The study found that China's agricultural irrigation underwent a significant technological transition between 2010 and 2022. In 2010, earthen-channel water delivery and flood irrigation were still widespread. By 2022, these inefficient practices had declined substantially, while water-saving technologies had become more common. However, the pace of change varied widely across crops and regions.
Wang Jinxia, a professor at Hohai University in east China's Jiangsu Province, said upgrading irrigation and water-saving technologies has long been a key part of China's farmland water conservancy investment.
Wang explained that at the current rate of technology adoption, irrigation water use per area for the three staple crops is projected to fall by only 9.4 percent to 16 percent by 2030. This projected reduction would fall short of the 25.5 percent water-saving target set by the national agricultural sustainable development plan for 2015 to 2030. The plan sets a cap of 373 cubic kilometers on national agricultural irrigation water use by 2030.
The study showed that deploying the most efficient irrigation technologies across all existing irrigated areas could more than meet the water-saving target. However, even such widespread upgrades would not be enough to offset possible crop yield losses caused by future climate change, posing risks to food security.
The researchers therefore proposed a new approach: first improve water-use efficiency in existing irrigated areas, and then, within water resource constraints, use the water saved to convert some rainfed farmland into irrigated farmland. The strategy aims to reduce the adverse effects of future climate change.
The study also found different optimal strategies for the three crops. For maize, the preferred approach is to adopt more advanced irrigation technologies while moderately expanding irrigated areas. For wheat and rice, less expansion is needed, and medium-efficiency water-saving technologies in newly developed irrigated areas could be enough to ensure food security under future climate conditions, meet water-saving policy targets and maximize investment returns.
Zhang Tianyi, a senior scientist at IAP, said the real question policymakers need to answer is which crops need irrigation, where irrigated area should be expanded, by how much, what technologies should be adopted and whether the investments are economically viable.
He noted that previous studies had largely focused on projecting changes in irrigated areas without fully accounting for interactions among irrigation technologies or between existing and newly developed irrigated areas.
"By integrating multi-source data and developing a new analytical framework, the study aims to provide more actionable scientific evidence for these specific investment decisions," he said.
The researchers emphasized that irrigation is not the only solution. Agricultural production is also influenced by crop variety breeding, cultivation management, land management scale and other factors. Irrigation investment should therefore be coordinated with the development of stress-tolerant crop varieties, climate-resilient cultivation practices and the construction of high-standard farmland.
Chen Huang, a researcher from Xiamen University in east China's Fujian Province, said the study drew on three independent datasets collected through different survey and research approaches. Despite their different sources, the model was able to capture the decline in agricultural irrigation water use and the improvement in irrigation productivity in China over the past decade.
"Future research will further incorporate agricultural policy and economic factors such as farmland consolidation and changes in agricultural commodity prices to refine the assessment of irrigation investment," he said. ■

Researchers in Australia find potential new treatment for rare genetic disorder
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:17:43 CST
20:17:43 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have discovered a way to release a genetic "brake" that silences healthy genes in Prader-Willi syndrome, opening a potential new path to treating the rare genetic disorder.
Researchers at Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research (WEHI) found that removing a protein called SMCHD1 lifted the genetic "brake," allowing healthy but dormant genes to switch back on, according to a WEHI statement released Tuesday.
In Prader-Willi syndrome, the protein switches off certain genes essential for development and brain function, contributing to developmental delays, intellectual disability and an insatiable appetite that can lead to obesity. About 400,000 people worldwide live with the condition, the statement said.
The study, published in Science Advances, used CRISPR gene-editing, stem-cell and genomic technologies to examine the effects of removing SMCHD1 in patient-derived cells and animal models.
Current treatments mainly address symptoms rather than the underlying cause, often relying on multiple medications, surgeries and specialist care, providing limited relief, the researchers said, adding that potential new therapies targeting the cause of Prader-Willi syndrome are now advancing through a WEHI spinout company. ■

Feature: Lively celebrations mark end of Buddhist Lent, boat racing festival in Laos
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
19:17:43 CST
20:17:43 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 26, 2026 shows an illuminated boat along the riverbank in Vientiane, Laos. (Photo by Kaikeo Saiyasane/Xinhua)
VIENTIANE, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- In Laos, riverfronts come alive with glowing floating lights, bustling crowds and festive sounds as people gather to celebrate the end of Buddhist Lent and the boat racing festival, an occasion that brings together religious traditions, community spirit and vibrant festivities.
The end of Buddhist Lent, which falls on Oct. 26 this year, begins with religious observances as people rise early to visit temples, give alms and offer food to monks as a way of making merit.
In the evening, crowds gather along riverbanks to float decorative banana-leaf boats adorned with flowers, candles and incense sticks. The offerings are released onto the water as a gesture of respect for the river and, for some participants, a symbolic way of washing away bad luck.
For Channapha Khamdy, a 29-year-old resident of Lao capital Vientiane, the festival is an occasion not to be missed. "This is one of the most important festivals. Everyone should experience it at least once in their life," she told Xinhua.
This year, Channapha brought Thai and Chinese friends she had met while studying abroad to the Mekong Riverbank to experience the celebrations firsthand. "They flew to Vientiane just to attend the festival," she said.
Proud to share her country's traditions with her friends, Channapha highlighted the candlelight processions, lantern displays and illuminated fireboats along the riverbanks as must-see highlights of the celebration.
"Even though it is crowded, I still want to bring my friends out to experience the atmosphere for themselves. I believe these memories will stay with them even after they return home," she said.
In many parts of Laos, the end of Buddhist Lent is followed by traditional boat racing festivities. In Lao capital Vientiane, the boat racing festival, held on Tuesday, also provides an opportunity for local vendors to sell their products while visitors experience Lao culture through traditional goods, local food and festive activities.
Sommanivanh, a 42-year-old woman from southern Laos' Champasak province, came to the Mekong Riverfront with her family, drawn by the variety of products on display and the lively atmosphere surrounding the celebration.
"This is one of my favorite festivals of the year. I never miss the celebration," she said.
Sommanivanh also shared her impressions of this year's festivities, noting that she had seen more young people wearing traditional clothing, visiting temples and strolling around the festival. She described the trend as a positive way to showcase Lao culture and traditions to foreign visitors while helping preserve the country's cultural heritage.
The festival is not only an occasion for people to enjoy festivities around town, but also a time for families and friends to come together at home.
"Since my house is near the Mekong River, it is a tradition for me to welcome friends from near and far. We gather to eat, drink and celebrate together," Bee, a Vientiane resident, told Xinhua.
He added that during the festival, friends and visitors often come to his home carrying food and drinks to share, turning the occasion into a gathering filled with warmth and friendship.
"For us, it is a way to come together and strengthen our bonds, so that we do not grow distant from one another. That is one of the most beautiful things about the celebration," he said. ■

Israel elections 2026: 10 factors that could shape the vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:06:51 UTC
20:06:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel elections 2026: 10 factors that could shape the results
Israelis headed to the polls on Tuesday in what Israeli media report to be one of the country's most dramatic elections in recent years, with the political future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hanging in the balance.
The vote comes against the backdrop of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, growing political divisions and uncertainty over whether Netanyahu's right-wing coalition or the opposition, also rightwing politically, can secure enough seats to form the next government.
But the outcome will depend on more than which party wins the most votes. Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, the mobilisation of ultra-Orthodox voters and the performance of smaller parties could all influence the balance of power in the 120-seat Knesset.
The counting process could also take longer than usual, with an unprecedented number of special ballots expected to delay a clear picture of the results until Wednesday afternoon.
The following are 10 factors that could shape the election results:
1. How high will voter turnout be?
Voter turnout is one of the most closely watched indicators in Israeli elections, particularly because it can affect the prospects of smaller parties seeking parliamentary representation.
Turnout in the previous election stood at around 70%, while estimates suggest it could rise to 75% this time.
A higher turnout increases the number of votes a party needs to cross the electoral threshold, making it more difficult for smaller parties to secure seats.
This could have significant implications for both Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition, particularly if parties aligned with either camp fail to enter parliament.
2. Which cities will turn out in the largest numbers?
Beyond the national turnout figure, the geographical distribution of voters could provide important clues about the election outcome.
Traditionally, peripheral towns and settlements such as Ofakim, Yeruham, Kiryat Shmona and Sderot have been strongholds of Netanyahu's Likud party.
By contrast, more liberal cities, including Herzliya, Ramat Hasharon, Tel Aviv and Kfar Saba, have been more closely associated with the opposition's so-called "change camp".
That camp includes prominent political figures with military and security backgrounds, such as Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Yair Golan, alongside Yair Lapid and Avigdor Lieberman.
Turnout figures in these areas could reveal where political enthusiasm is strongest and where voter apathy may affect the results.
3. Why could special ballots delay the results?
Around 650,000 special ballots, known as "double envelopes", have been registered for this election, an unprecedented figure.
These ballots are used by eligible voters who cannot cast their votes at polling stations near their registered addresses.
They include soldiers, diplomats, Foreign Ministry employees, people with disabilities and settlers evacuated from their homes.
The special counting procedures mean that a clearer picture of the election results may not emerge until Wednesday afternoon.
The unusually large number of these ballots could also affect the final distribution of seats, potentially pushing some smaller parties above the electoral threshold.
4. Could Palestinian voters determine the balance of power?
Turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel is expected to be one of the most consequential factors in the election.
The Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List (Ra'am), led by Mansour Abbas, are running separately but have both launched extensive campaigns to encourage Palestinian citizens to vote.
Their performance could affect the prospects of both Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition.
If Arab parties secure more than 14 of the Knesset's 120 seats, analysts believe it would represent a significant achievement, while potentially making it harder for either political bloc to form a government.
However, concerns have emerged over the conduct of voting in Palestinian towns and cities. Several polling stations in Arab communities were delayed in opening on Tuesday morning.
According to sources speaking to The New Arab, some polling committee members claimed to have lost their way in Arab towns, while residents in certain areas alleged that the delays were deliberate.
Arab voters also complained about the absence of Arabic-language ballot papers at some polling stations, raising concerns about accessibility for citizens who are not proficient in Hebrew.
Another controversy concerns the presence of armed election observers.
On Monday, Israel's Supreme Court rejected a petition filed by the Haifa-based legal rights organisation Adalah and the Joint List seeking to prohibit observers from carrying weapons inside polling stations.
The petition followed announcements by Likud and Religious Zionism that they intended to deploy approximately 2,000 observers in Arab towns and mixed cities.
Petitioners warned that the presence of armed representatives from right-wing parties could intimidate Arab voters and provoke confrontations.
The Israeli authorities argued that there was no operational or security justification for banning weapons, saying armed observers would receive specific instructions limiting their use to self-defence.
The court declined to intervene in the decisions of the police and Central Elections Committee, saying the concerns raised had been considered in election security preparations.
Adalah criticised the ruling, arguing that it failed to address the potential intimidation of Arab voters by organised groups of armed right-wing activists.
5. Will young Israelis turn out in greater numbers?
Young voters could play a more prominent role in this election following a campaign heavily conducted on social media.
According to Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, political parties believe their online campaigns have encouraged greater engagement among younger Israelis, including those who previously showed little interest in electoral politics.
Celebrities and social media influencers have also joined the campaign, with several publicly revealing which parties they intend to support.
Their endorsements have generated debate among followers and helped bring political discussions to audiences that might otherwise have remained disengaged.
Party estimates suggest that younger voters could turn out in greater numbers than usual, potentially increasing their influence on the results.
6. How will ultra-Orthodox voters respond?
Israel's ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, community has traditionally voted in large numbers, often following the guidance of religious leaders.
However, analysts and prominent figures within the community say voting patterns are particularly difficult to predict this year.
One major source of dissatisfaction is the government's failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military conscription during the current parliamentary term.
The emergence of new Haredi parties challenging established political organisations has also created uncertainty.
Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, which represents sections of the ultra-Orthodox community, has undergone a leadership change, with Knesset member Yaakov Asher replacing veteran politician Moshe Gafni.
According to Yedioth Ahronoth, it remains unclear whether ultra-Orthodox voters will maintain their traditional party loyalties or use the election to register a protest vote.
Their decisions could have significant consequences for Netanyahu, whose governing coalitions have long relied on ultra-Orthodox parties.
7. Does winning the most seats guarantee power?
Not necessarily.
Although considerable attention is focused on which party will emerge as the largest in the Knesset, winning the most seats does not automatically give its leader the right to form a government.
Under Israel's political system, the president assigns the task of forming a government to the candidate considered most capable of assembling a governing coalition.
The president has considerable discretion in making that decision.
As a result, a party could finish first in the election but still find itself in opposition if another political leader can secure broader parliamentary support.
The ability to negotiate alliances and build a viable coalition may therefore prove more important than the number of seats won by any single party.
8. Why does the first mandate to form a government matter?
The candidate tasked with forming a government initially has 28 days to assemble a coalition.
That period can be extended by a further 14 days.
However, securing the first mandate is important for reasons beyond coalition negotiations.
According to the report, the candidate who receives the initial mandate also gains influence over the Knesset's Arrangements Committee, which plays a central role in parliamentary procedures before permanent committees are established.
Control over parliamentary arrangements can allow political factions to advance legislation and potentially replace the Knesset speaker.
This means the first candidate given the opportunity to form a government could influence parliamentary developments even if their coalition negotiations ultimately fail.
9. What role could the Elector app play?
Political parties are also relying on technology to mobilise supporters and monitor turnout throughout election day.
One tool attracting particular attention is Elector, a sophisticated voter-management application reportedly worth hundreds of thousands of shekels.
According to Israeli news website Ynet, the application contains information gathered about individuals who have declared support for particular parties or have been identified as potential supporters.
It allows campaign teams to monitor whether those voters have cast their ballots, providing parties with a clearer picture of their mobilisation efforts.
The system can help parties identify supporters who have not yet voted and focus their efforts on encouraging them to reach polling stations.
However, its use has raised questions about consent and the collection of personal information.
Central Elections Committee chairman Judge Noam Sohlberg expressed reservations about the application but ultimately permitted its use.
The effectiveness of parties' voter mobilisation operations could prove important in closely contested races.
10. Could the weather affect the result?
Even the weather could play a role in determining turnout.
Political parties are closely monitoring forecasts for rain in several Israeli cities on election day.
Rainfall could discourage undecided voters or those with little enthusiasm for participating from travelling to polling stations. This could be particularly significant for parties that depend on mobilising less committed supporters.

Amid Legal Uncertainty, US Lawmakers Warn Banks, Ports Over Russian Diesel Imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:06:48 UTC
20:06:48 KST

WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of US lawmakers have warned American banks, port authorities, and fuel-industry groups against facilitating imports of Russian diesel, raising the prospect of congressional investigations and legal action over President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian fuel.
In letters sent to the chief executives of major US banks and the heads of several port authorities, the lawmakers warned that importing Russian diesel could violate federal law and expose companies to civil and criminal liability.
They also said the imports would raise national-security concerns by providing Moscow with revenue to help finance its war against Ukraine.
The intervention comes after Trump recently announced an arrangement with Russian President Vladimir Putin under which Moscow would supply hundreds of thousands of metric tons of diesel to the United States, with additional shipments planned in the coming months. The US Treasury Department subsequently issued General License 135, granting a six-month exemption from certain sanctions restrictions.
The letters signal a potential new front in the political and legal battle over the administration’s Russia policy. Democrats could gain significant investigative powers if they regain control of one or both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections.
“Any importation of Russian diesel into the US raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations,” the lawmakers wrote.
The group includes Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren, as well as outgoing Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
They urged companies not to facilitate the purchase, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing, or distribution of Russian-origin diesel until the relevant legal requirements had been met.
The lawmakers also demanded that the companies preserve records of proposed or completed transactions, including contracts, shipping documents, payment records, port reservations and communications with suppliers and US government officials dating back to September 1.
Recipients were asked to confirm by October 28 that they had implemented the required preservation measures and to disclose whether they had knowledge of any proposed or actual Russian diesel imports.
The letters went to the chief executives of major US banks, including Goldman Sachs, as well as the port authorities of Houston, Corpus Christi and Beaumont in Texas and New York/New Jersey.
Public reporting and vessel-tracking data cited by the lawmakers indicate that ships carrying Russian diesel could arrive at Beaumont and New York/New Jersey as early as the end of October.
At the center of the dispute is whether the administration’s licensing action is consistent with restrictions established by Congress.
The lawmakers cited the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which generally prohibits imports of Russian-origin energy products unless the president certifies to Congress, following a period of consultation, that Russia has ceased military hostilities in Ukraine, poses no immediate military threat to NATO members, and recognizes Ukrainians’ right to choose their government.
They also argued that Section 216 of the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act requires congressional review before certain licensing actions that significantly alter US foreign policy toward Russia. The lawmakers said the administration had not fulfilled that requirement.
The administration maintains that its action is lawful and consistent with previous decisions by the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, which administers US sanctions.
The White House dismissed the lawmakers’ initiative as politically motivated.
“The Democrats are already telegraphing that, once again, they have no agenda to improve the lives of Americans and will instead continue their decade-long obsession with investigating President Trump,” spokesperson Taylor Rogers said.
The letters do not establish that any company has committed a crime. Instead, they warn that participating in the transactions could expose companies to legal challenges and investigations despite the administration’s assurances that the waiver is valid.
Representative Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, separately warned major fuel-industry associations that companies importing Russian diesel could face civil and criminal penalties, including up to 20 years in prison.
Raskin argued that Trump’s move could not override statutory prohibitions and warned that companies could be held accountable “whether in this administration -- or the next.”
Experts say the warnings could complicate the administration’s plans even if the waiver reduces the risk of sanctions violations under US executive-branch rules.
Michael Wain, a senior international trade policy adviser at the law firm Akin, told RFE/RL that the congressional pushback was noteworthy but that US imports represented only part of the picture.
“General License 135 covers a broad range of Russian diesel transactions and substantially reduces US sanctions risk for foreign firms that stay within its terms,” Wain said. However, he added, companies must still consider British, European Union and other jurisdictions’ sanctions rules.
A key question, he said, is whether foreign buyers previously reluctant to handle Russian fuel will now feel more comfortable doing so -- an outcome that may be part of the administration’s objective.
Glen Howard, president of the Saratoga Foundation and a longtime Russia strategist, said the letters could make major US banks reluctant to finance the transactions.
“It is very significant because it was sent to each of the major US banks and will likely cause them to freeze in place any efforts by the Trump administration to proceed with the sale,” Howard told RFE/RL.
He said the move suggested the administration had failed to adequately consider the deal’s legal obstacles and strategic implications. Howard speculated that the decision had been made by a small group of advisers without broader consultation across the administration.
The potential consequences extend beyond the immediate shipments. Banks and other intermediaries may be wary of congressional subpoenas, requests to testify or future legal challenges, even if they believe a transaction is permitted under the Treasury license.
Rachel Ziemba, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, said the warnings reinforced her view that most Russian diesel cargoes would be sold outside the United States.
“These warnings reinforce my view that most of any Russian diesel cargos will go to countries outside the US and that it is mostly diplomatic theater,” Ziemba told RFE/RL.
She said a meaningful increase in diesel supplies would likely require an energy cease-fire, which she said Russia was wary of agreeing to. Ziemba also said the administration believes its waivers are sufficient to overcome the legal obstacles identified by lawmakers, but that uncertainty could still deter American buyers and financial institutions.
“The concerns from the senators may give some US banks and buyers pause about purchasing the diesel, which is en route to the US as we speak,” Ziemba said.
Some cargoes could consequently be resold to other countries in the Americas, where demand for fuel remains strong.
Russia confirmed the arrangement after Trump announced it on October 9. Trump said Moscow would initially deliver more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons afterward. He said Russia could supply an additional 3 million tons, depending on the condition of its refineries.
Traders said the Russian government had begun granting exemptions to its diesel export ban on October 1 to allow shipments under the arrangement. Industry sources said Russian diesel production fell from about 175,000 tons a day in September to 160,000 tons a day in the first half of October, before recovering toward 180,000 tons a day after new export quotas were introduced.
The shipments could provide Russia with additional revenue, but legal uncertainty may deter some US buyers and redirect cargoes to other markets.

Tallinn's new cinemas are still working to build their audiences

Tallinn's new cinemas are still working to build their audiences
Two new movie theaters, which opened earlier this year in Tallinn, are working to differentiate themselves from the competition and build their audiences.
In the spring, Kai Cinema, previously part of Sõprus Cinema, began operating independently, while at the beginning of the summer, Cinamon, which had operated at T1 in Ülemiste, relocated to Kosmos.
Kai Cinema, which is part of the Kai Art Center, has now been operating independently for approximately six months. Program Manager Katariina Rebane said Kai Cinema does not compete directly with the capital's other arthouse movie theaters.
"If we think about what the market share of arthouse movie theaters is in general today, it is rather small. And Kai Cinema is also contributing to increasing the share of arthouse films and their audiences," Rebane said.
The cinema's program has become more extensive after the venue became independent, she added. There have been more special programs and screenings, benefiting both the art center and the local community.
However, Rebane admitted the movie theater is not currently profitable and she does not support raising ticket prices.
"We would rather people could still come to the movies at a lower price, get out of their homes and watch a film together with other people. Taking the economic situation into account, we certainly do not want to raise ticket prices at the moment. We hope the situation improves, and for now we are running the movie theater out of a sense of mission and enthusiasm. We want there to continue to be a movie theater here," she added.
In June, Kosmos Cinema reopened its doors in the city center. As a mainstream movie theater, Cinamon competes directly with Apollo.
"We try to do things differently from Apollo. Our difference lies not only in the location, but perhaps also in the emotional significance of the place. We show various cultural films, such as Japanese and Indian films, and organize various events for children and families," said Cinamon CEO Andac Bagioglu.
The theater manager said attendance figures depend largely on which films are currently being released.
"One of the drawbacks of the movie industry is that you have no control whatsoever over what you sell. When good films, such as 'Spider-Man' or 'The Odyssey,' or a good animated film reach the screen, everyone comes to the movies. But when it comes to average or lower-quality films that can also be watched on streaming services, people do not come to the movies," he acknowledged.

- On 23 October, Zelenskyy spoke with the US president's special envoys and said that a trilateral meeting at team level on ending Russia's war against Ukraine was planned for the first half of November.
- Yuri Ushakov, an aide to Putin, claims that Russia is ready to resume trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the Russia-Ukraine war after 4 November.

Danish PM sceptical about Finnish and Norwegian leaders' call with Putin
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has said she is sceptical about the phone call that Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held with Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Source: Mette Frederiksen in comments to DR, as reported by European Pravda

She stressed that she sees no signs that Russia wants peace with Europe.
Frederiksen said this is evident from both Russia's ongoing hybrid warfare and its daily brutal and aggressive attacks on Ukraine. She added that she believes Europe needs to maintain unity rather than act individually.

UK and Poland strengthen defences on Europe's Eastern flank
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:59:30 GMT
19:59:30 KST

UK and Poland strengthen defences on Europe's Eastern flank
Britain will be more secure as a result of a new defence agreement with Poland designed to deter Russian threats.
The Warsaw Defence Plan comes as Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and his counterpart Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz today meet in Warsaw. Under the agreement, the two nations will work together across sea, land, air, cyber and industry to strengthen security and deterrence across Europe’s Eastern Flank.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:
  Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies - from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century.
The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.
From collaborating on NATO exercises that deter our adversaries to working together to support Ukraine in its fight for freedom, we are committed to standing together for European security whilst boosting our economies with stronger defence industries.
The agreement sets out the first phase of defence cooperation under the new UK-Poland Security and Defence Partnership Treaty and demonstrates the UK stepping up on European security to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.
It will strengthen joint work on defence between the UK and Poland across a number of key areas, including:
- Collaboration on the manufacture and development of the next generation of air defence missiles.
- Co-development of drone and counter-drone technologies to deter threats to civilians and critical national infrastructure, as Russia steps up its campaign of drone incursions across the UK and Europe.
- Boosting cooperation on cyber security and resilience to help both countries defend defence and civilian sites from hostile threats.
- Sharing lessons and experience from developing frigate capabilities, the British Type 31 and Polish Miecznik, which are built from a common design.
- Increasing defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea.
The UK and Poland will also work together to further strengthen cooperation between their defence industries through closer defence procurement coordination, building on major deals such as Poland’s procurement of its Narew air defence system from MBDA UK.
UK and Polish defence industrial partners BAE Systems and Poland’s PGZ will expand large-calibre ammunition production capacity and capability. More widely, both nations’ defence industries will collaborate to promote defence education, training and workforce mobility to build shared expertise.
Continued UK and Polish participation in large-scale exercises such as Steadfast Defender, Polish Dragon and Joint Warrior will also ensure both nations remain ready to respond to the conflicts of the future, including counter-drone warfare, electronic warfare, and missile defence.
It comes as the UK and Poland plan for a major Coalition of the Wiling exercise in Poland next month, which will see thousands of personnel take part to ensure the Multinational Force Ukraine is ready to support the military training and post-war rebuilding that Ukraine will need.

Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation issues recommendations for development of social services in Kyiv region based on new study
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:59:21 EET
19:59:21 KST

Currently, the most in-demand services include social support, home-based care, transportation, and social adaptation. This is according to the findings of a study conducted by the Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation in cooperation with Kyiv Regional State Administration as part of the Seeing the Invisible project. The results were presented at a press conference held at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Tuesday.
"There is plenty of work for everyone: state, municipal, and non-governmental organizations alike. As part of the Seeing the Invisible project, we carried out a comprehensive study. It involved approximately 100 social sector professionals and over 600 residents of Kyiv region," said Vladyslav Zhyliaiev, an advocacy specialist at the Caritas-Kyiv Charitable Foundation.
According to him, the study’s results show that "the needs, as assessed by both residents and professionals, align very closely."
"I always say that if a person’s basic needs aren’t met, if they have nothing to eat, nothing to wear, or no way to pay for housing (which is especially true for internally displaced persons, or IDPs), then, unfortunately, we cannot even begin to discuss anything beyond that. That is why we keep urging the international community to focus on the needs of Kyiv region in particular, as it is in dire need of assistance," emphasized a representative from Caritas Kyiv.
"As the figures show, the region is constantly taking in internally displaced persons. It was one of the first to welcome them, and to this day, it continues to host the largest number. Consequently, while the needs are only set to grow, the available aid is shrinking; yet, we must continue to devote ever-greater attention to these internally displaced persons," he said.
Zhyliaev also noted that special attention should be paid to veterans and their families, families with children facing difficult life circumstances, children with disabilities, people with disabilities, and the elderly.
"What kind of services are needed most? These include social support, in-home care, material assistance, transportation services, social adaptation, supported living, and respite care. We can provide assistance to these families—who are in need—on several occasions, helping them overcome their difficult life circumstances and reach the level of stability they require," he emphasized.
According to the study, Zhyliaev pointed out, "the services that residents feel are most lacking include transportation, respite care, material assistance, social adaptation, and collaborative social work involving the non-governmental sector, municipal institutions, and the public sector."

Slovakia plans to develop cooperation with Russia in areas not covered by sanctions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
12:59:12 EET
19:59:12 KST

Slovakia plans to develop cooperation with Russia in areas not covered by sanctions
Kyiv • UNN
Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár said after his visit to Moscow that cooperation with Russia would be developed outside the scope of international sanctions. The opposition called the trip a disgrace.
Slovakia plans to develop cooperation with the russian federation in areas not covered by international sanctions. The country’s Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár said this after his visit to moscow on October 26. Slovak opposition politicians criticized the trip. DW reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Juraj Blanár headed the Slovak delegation at the 22nd meeting of the bilateral intergovernmental commission on economic and scientific-technical cooperation. The previous meeting took place in 2021. The russian delegation was headed by the Minister of Science and Higher Education of the russian federation, valery falkov. During his visit, Blanár also met with russia’s Foreign Minister sergey lavrov.
"The parties discussed Slovakia’s energy security, bilateral relations with an emphasis on economic cooperation, as well as the war in Ukraine. In particular, Juraj Blanár stated that it was necessary to maintain dialogue with russia in order to resolve 'situations arising in connection with the European Commission’s decisions to abandon russian energy resources' by the end of 2027. The Slovak Foreign Ministry’s website emphasizes that lavrov assured Blanár that russia 'is still ready to fulfill its contractual obligations.' Commenting on the war in Ukraine, the Slovak minister said that representatives of the two countries understood how 'important it is to take into account the root causes of this conflict and actively support dialogue with all parties' in order to end it," the publication writes.
According to Blanár, lavrov called his proposal to hold 'preliminary talks at a lower level' in Bratislava 'acceptable.'
At the same time, according to available information, Blanár’s visit drew criticism from opposition politicians. In particular, Gábor Grendel, a representative of the conservative Nova party, called the trip an 'international disgrace' and demanded that the minister explain 'what exactly his trip to moscow gave the citizens of Slovakia.'
Meanwhile, former Slovak Foreign Minister Ivan Korčok, who represents the liberal Freedom and Solidarity party, called Blanár the 'gravedigger of Slovakia’s foreign policy.' According to him, Blanár intended to ask Lavrov for permission to increase the number of employees at the country’s embassy in moscow. Other representatives of the Slovak opposition had previously made similar assumptions.
"However, Blanár’s visit at the head of a delegation was not the first trip by high-ranking Slovak officials to Russia in recent times. On May 8, the country’s Prime Minister Robert Fico flew to moscow. On the eve of Victory Day, he laid flowers at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, and the following day met with Russian President vladimir putin. At the same time, Fico did not attend the parade on Red Square," the publication notes.
Background
The Slovak delegation arrived in moscow for talks on energy and Russian gas. Bratislava fears arbitration claims of up to €16 billion.
