Polish far-right leader charged over confrontation with abortion doctor and inciting hatred against Jews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:59:04 UTC
19:59:04 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion.
The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections.
Do sześciu razy sztuka. Grzegorz Braun dostał zarzuty, w tym za uwięzienie ginekolożki Gizeli Jagielskiej
Wcześniej europoseł Grzegorz Braun pięć razy unikał przedstawienia zarzutów w Prokuraturze Okręgowej we Wrocławiu. Zainterweniował Prokurator Generalny Waldemar Żurek.…
— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026
As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges.
Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read.
In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges.
Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hannukah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”.
Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups.
Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison.
In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month.
The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher.
Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”.
For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term.
Finally, Braun has been charged with destruction of property for an incident during his presidential campaign in March this year when he vandalised an exhibition about the local LGBT+ community in the city of Opole, spray-painting “stop the propaganda of perversion” on it.
Police are investigating far-right presidential candidate and MEP Grzegorz Braun after he vandalised an LGBT+ exhibition.
The city where it took place immediately cancelled a meeting he was due to hold there and is seeking compensation for the damage https://t.co/EbDpMzmpFw
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 20, 2025
Braun has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him, as he has done with a string of other charges for various offences relating to his antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT rhetoric and actions.
In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”.
Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%.
If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition.

Tit-for-tat Sudan drone strikes kill 21, cause mass power outages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Retaliatory drone strikes between Sudan's warring factions killed at least 21 people in Darfur and caused widespread power outages in the east, witnesses and medics said Tuesday.
A drone strike on a market in Nyala, the de facto capital of Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Darfur, killed 21 people and wounded at least 40 others, a medical source and witnesses said.
One Nyala resident said a market in the city's north was struck by a drone on Monday around 8:00 p.m. (6 p.m. GMT).
Another said the market was frequented by young men, particularly Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters.
"Twenty-one people were killed in last night's bombing, and more than 40 others injured," a medic at Nyala Hospital said, though he was unable to identify how many were RSF fighters.
Sudan's military, at war with the RSF since April 2023, regularly strikes Nyala, where the RSF has declared an administration rivaling the army-backed internationally recognized government in Khartoum.
The RSF has in turn launched repeated strikes targeting Khartoum's airport, as well as dams and power stations across the country's east.
On Tuesday, "RSF militia drones targeted the Al-Markhiyat transformer station, disrupting the power supply across large parts of Khartoum and Al-Jazira states," a source in the national electricity company said on condition of anonymity.
The strike comes a day after a coordinated RSF drone attack on six power stations left millions without power in Al-Jazira, White Nile, Sennar and Gedaref states.
The war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks from across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October alone, drone strikes killed over 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a U.N. tally.
Since it began, the war has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate and has triggered the world's largest humanitarian crises.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people.
Close to 3 million people have returned to Khartoum state since it was recaptured by the army last year, but many have struggled to rebuild their lives in a scarred city.
Power and water supplies remain unreliable, much of the capital remains unsafe from unexploded bombs and many struggle to put food on the table in a collapsed economy.
On Monday, 30 countries including the United States, France and the United Kingdom warned that urgent action was needed to prevent famine expanding across the country.
Sudan is facing "an alarming deterioration" of food security, they said, citing the war, a currency in freefall, higher fuel prices due to the Middle East war and a drought induced by the El Nino climate phenomenon.
Sudan's Foreign Ministry Monday insisted the country's food security was "reassuring," in an attempt to "refute claims of famine."
It accused "some countries and organizations" of "politically exploiting the humanitarian situation."
The army has for years denied claims of documented famine and has been accused of blocking access to humanitarian aid.

Saab announces new Sea Giraffe AMB D radar

Saab announces new Sea Giraffe AMB D radar
Saab introduces Sea Giraffe Agile Multi Beam D (AMB D), the latest evolution of its Giraffe AMB radar family, providing naval forces with enhanced 3D surveillance and tracking of air and surface targets in increasingly complex maritime environments.
Sea Giraffe AMB D can detect, track and classify aircraft, drones, missiles and crewed or uncrewed surface vessels, with a range of up to 250 km for air targets and 50 km for surface targets. It provides early warning and accurate target information to support decision-making in distributed, multi-domain operations, where reliable sensors are the foundation of operational advantage.
Designed for demanding maritime environments, the radar combines advanced Electronic Counter-Countermeasures (ECCM) capabilities against jamming attempts, with a modular architecture that enables integration with other naval systems. Its software-defined architecture also enables continuous upgrades as operational requirements evolve.
“Sea Giraffe AMB D takes a proven naval radar capability to the next level, combining increased performance with a low footprint and an architecture built for continuous development. It is designed to meet the demands of today’s naval forces while giving customers the flexibility to evolve with future threats,” says Carl-Johan Bergholm, head of Saab’s business area Surveillance.
Building on more than 70 years of radar innovation and over two decades of ongoing operational success with Sea Giraffe AMB radars, the new Sea Giraffe AMB D leverages Active Electronically Scanned Array radar hardware with a new software architecture and modern processing capabilities to provide enhanced air surveillance performance.

Audi CEO Gernot Dollner defends appearance at Donald Trump rally in letter to workers
Unknown

Audi CEO Gernot Dollner defends appearance at Donald Trump rally in letter to workers
- Audi CEO Gernot Dollner defended joining Donald Trump’s Georgia rally, saying the US$4 billion plant announcement was “solely in the interest of the company”.
- The move angered German workers and union leaders, who called it “highly embarrassing” and “politically unacceptable”, and warned it could affect approval of the factory.
- The plant plan comes as parent Volkswagen cuts costs, reshapes its workforce, and faces weak demand, Chinese competition, and tariff pressure in the US.
AI generated
Audi chief executive officer Gernot Dollner said he acted in the interest of the carmaker when he took part in US President Donald Trump’s campaign rally that announced the company would build a US$4 billion (S$5.1 billion) plant in the country.
The two men shared the stage in Georgia over the weekend, days before the US midterm elections. The appearance triggered a wave of criticism in Germany as taking sides in the upcoming vote.
The Audi executive, who had travelled to the US for talks about the project, said the company was asked to announce the go-ahead for the facility together with Trump, Dollner said in a letter to workers seen by Bloomberg News. The decision to appear “was taken solely in the interest of the company”, it said.
“At the same time, we realise that the announcement was taken as signalling a political stance,” Dollner wrote. “We take this very seriously.”
The planned site in Georgia still needs to be greenlighted at Audi parent Volkswagen’s supervisory board level, where worker representatives hold half the seats. The furore about the Trump rally could complicate this step, and push the company into making concessions elsewhere.
VW as well as Audi are in the midst of tense talks on wages and tough savings measures with workers in Germany.
On Oct 26, Christiane Benner, the head of IG Metall union and VW’s deputy supervisory board chairwoman, called Dollner’s appearance “highly embarrassing” and pointed to labour’s leverage over whether the factory goes ahead. As part of the broad restructuring talks, VW is looking into alternative uses for its large Audi factory in Neckarsulm after earlier saying the plant could be shut.
“The way Gernot Dollner presented himself and Audi in the US is highly embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company and, above all, its employees,” she said.
VW’s works council chief Daniela Cavallo separately accused Dollner of providing “active campaign assistance”. She said Audi’s internal guidelines prohibit public-facing appearances with politicians standing for election during the final three months before a vote, and that he had signed those principles only months ago.
The plan to spend US$4 billion on a facility in the US lands in the middle of VW’s attempt to radically reshape its industrial footprint and shrink its domestic workforce in Europe.
VW CEO Oliver Blume is pushing to cut jobs and factory costs while investing more heavily in growth markets including the US. Europe’s largest carmaker is struggling with weak demand, fierce Chinese competition and the costly shift to electric and software-defined vehicles.
Audi is particularly exposed to the US trade shift because it still imports most of the vehicles it sells there, leaving the brand vulnerable to tariffs that have already raised costs across VW’s North American business. Dollner on Oct 25 said that the Audi brand is losing money in the US currently. BLOOMBERG

President Stubb, Prime Minister Støre hold phone call with President Putin
This was reported by the Office of the President of Finland, according to Ukrinform.
The office said the call was a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on 20 October and “held in consultation with Ukraine.”
“Stubb and Støre initiated the call to discuss Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe,” the press release said.
According to the office, “the call was related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi.”
It is emphasized that Stubb and Støre took part in the call as the leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole.
“Norway and Finland have always promoted peace and security in our region. The two countries have a shared interest in stability and predictability in the Baltic Sea region and the High North. This was highlighted in the call,” the press release said.
According to the statement, “Stubb and Støre emphasized that Finland and Norway will continue their longstanding support for Ukraine.”
They also emphasized that the war must end and negotiations resume
“The discussion was frank and substantive. We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions”, President Stubb said.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation”, Prime Minister Støre said.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this week in Brussels a security meeting involving representatives of the United States, Ukraine, the EU and NATO, at which initiatives to end the war will be discussed.

Taiwan receiving 6 MS-110 reconnaissance pods for F-16Vs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:36 UTC
19:50:36 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is scheduled to receive six US-made MS-110 Multispectral Airborne Reconnaissance System pods by the end of December, enhancing its F-16V fighter fleet's surveillance capabilities and speeding access to battlefield intelligence.
The defense ministry confirmed the updated delivery schedule in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan, per Liberty Times. The procurement program has a budget of NT$9.63 billion (US$302 million), with two pods already delivered and the remaining four expected by the end of the year.
The Air Force began installation testing and personnel conversion training in June. In August, F-16Vs operating from Hualien's Chiashan Air Force Base carried the first two pods on flights that completed the initial phase of flight-performance evaluations.
The MS-110 is expected to double the imaging capabilities of the Air Force's existing tactical reconnaissance pods, commonly known as the Phoenix Eye system, Liberty Times reported. Its seven spectral bands — blue, green, red, near-infrared, shortwave infrared, and two midwave infrared bands — enable multispectral imaging for target identification and surveillance.
Military sources said the system has an effective imaging range exceeding 148 kilometers and can capture high-resolution imagery at a rate of up to 26,000 square kilometers per hour. This would allow F-16Vs operating east of the Taiwan Strait median line to monitor Chinese coastal military deployments and troop movements without flying deep into contested airspace.
The system also lets the Air Force receive reconnaissance imagery in real time, rather than waiting for aircraft to land and retrieve recorded images, according to Liberty Times. Its digital data link transmits high-resolution imagery to ground stations while airborne.
If terrain or low-altitude flight disrupts the signal, the pod stores imagery internally and automatically transmits it when connectivity is restored. The Air Force has established four ground receiving stations that relay imagery through military data networks and fiber-optic connections to the Heng Shan Military Command Center and operational theater commands.

Underwater data centers may be coming to the U.S.—smack in the middle of endangered whale habitat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:19 UTC
19:50:19 KST

The battle over where to put data centers is heading below the waves: the Trump administration is considering proposals to build two massive underwater data centers off the country’s coast. The sites selected for the projects—one in Cook Inlet, Alaska, and one in the Gulf of Maine—are smack in the middle of two endangered whale populations’ habitats.
Whales are “skittish animals,” says Arial Brewer, a beluga researcher at the University of Washington and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “A massive-scale project like this could really stress them out in a lot of different ways.”
Data centers, with their thousands of servers, generate considerable heat that can damage equipment if not offset in some way. Land-based facilities use massive amounts of fresh water to cool down. By putting a data center underwater, the ocean can easily dispel that heat. “Cooling is a large part of what a data center costs to run, and seawater is a free sink,” says Vishal Misra, a computer scientist and professor at Columbia University.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Microsoft showed that the concept could work with a pilot project off California in 2015 and another off Scotland a few years later. Currently, there are only two operational underwater data centers in the world, one off the Chinese island of Hainan and another off the coast of Shanghai, and they’re a fraction of the size of the proposed centers at the two U.S. sites.
In the Maine project, a cluster of what official documents call “subsea-compute hives” or “data center pods” would rest on the seabed, powered by up to 50 tidal turbines across 27 acres. In Cook Inlet, the data center would be made up of 66 pods and more than 300 tidal turbines. Its footprint would span 1,650 acres—more than 1,000 football fields.
The locations were chosen by DeepGreen Holdings LLC—a U.S.-based developer—because of their potential for tidal power, which works by harnessing the movement of water.
But each spot is also home to beleaguered groups of whales. A distinct population of around 300 critically endangered beluga whales lives in Cook Inlet. And the Gulf of Maine hosts feeding grounds for the North Atlantic right whale, a species whose numbers have dropped below 400 individuals.
The primary concern over data centers underwater is the same as for those on land: they are exceedingly noisy. “Pumps, fans and especially turbine arrays make continuous low-frequency sound, and pile-driving during construction is louder still,” Misra says.
Shipping noise has doubled every decade since the 1960s, and there’s evidence to suggest that when the volume goes down, marine mammals are less stressed. One study found that when ship noise decreased immediately after 9/11, right whales in the Gulf of Maine had lower levels of stress hormones. As for the belugas in Cook Inlet, they are particularly sensitive to noise, Brewer says. Because of glacial runoff, the bay is very turbid. “It literally looks like chocolate milk,” she says, so the belugas there rely almost entirely on echolocation to feed, mate and move around.
The purpose for putting the data centers underwater—heat shedding—also threatens the whales. When a pattern of warming waters hit the Gulf of Maine in the early 2010s, right whales started to abandon their feeding grounds. “Ocean warming is a big, big deal to them,” says Philip Hamilton, a senior scientist at the New England Aquarium.
In Alaska, salmon are one of the main prey sources for belugas—and the fish need cold water to develop their eggs, keep their metabolism stable and prevent energy depletion during long migratory journeys. “All that hot energy, what’s that going to do to very delicate salmon populations that rely on cold water?” Brewer says.
Community backlash has been fervent: The city of Eastport, Maine, issued a moratorium halting all permits and applications for all industrial data centers. The local Passamaquoddy tribe has also publicly expressed that it has no interest in any sort of collaboration with DeepGreen. Several groups have filed motions to intervene with the proposal for Cook Inlet.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which oversees such energy projects, notes that these proposals are just that: proposals. “A preliminary permit does not authorize construction of any kind,” says Celeste Miller, a FERC representative.
Indeed, FERC found the original proposals for both projects “deficient,” citing a lack of details and insufficient identification of Indigenous tribes who have historic ties to the local areas. But the agency has accepted amended versions; the Maine project, which originally called for 170 turbines on 400 acres of seafloor, now has a smaller proposed footprint. The public comment period for Maine closed on October 19, but the one for Cook Inlet is open until November 2. After that, FERC will review the applications and comments and issue preliminary permit decisions.
“We have no intent to build at this stage,” Louis Wolfson, the luxury real estate developer behind DeepGreen, says. “If equipment cannot operate safely well within federal marine mammal thresholds, it will never be licensed or deployed.”
But over the past two years, the federal government has sought to strip back those very thresholds. For example, the Senate is considering a bill that would delay new protections for right whales against entanglements in fishing gear. And though belugas and right whales have historically been protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, proposed amendments to it would drastically draw back protections.
“It feels like every day they’re chopping at another protection,” Hamilton says.

Why we’ll never have another Black Death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:50:10 UTC
19:50:10 KST

Scientists disagree over how scared we should be by the mysterious death of a worker at a Russian plague lab. A young laboratory technician died earlier this month of an undisclosed illness after working on research at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East. Although officials have not released details about the cause of death, scientists agree that if it was caused by ordinary plague, the wider world has little to worry about. This bacterial illness is infamous for the explosive killing spree known as the Black Death, which wiped out between a third and half of the population of Europe between 1347 and 1353. Today, however, plague is curable and extremely unlikely to blow up into a new pandemic, experts say. That’s thanks to a combination of antibiotic development, scientific understanding and luck.
Experts who study plague are reluctant to say it’s been completely conquered. The World Health Organization (WHO) recently reported approximately 3,800 infections and 423 deaths from plague between 2019 and 2025. And scientists haven’t cracked all the mysteries behind the plague bacterium, known as Yersinia pestis—one of the biggest being how it hides for years in cryptic reservoirs only to spring out in unpredictable new waves of infection in humans or other animals.
The disease is endemic in rodents living in the Americas, Central Asia and Africa, says David Wagner, a plague expert who directs the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “It’s constantly cycling between rodents via fleas, and it just does that in perpetuity in a manner we poorly understand, despite 100 years of research.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Studies of ancient DNA show plague-infected prehistoric hunter-gatherers in Siberia 5,500 years ago. Plague is known for causing three major pandemics: in addition to the one that started with the Black Death, which peaked between 1347 and 1351 and was followed by outbreaks into the 18th century, there was the plague of Justinian from C.E. 541 to 549 and a third pandemic that started in the 1800s and spread to every inhabited continent by 1900. That last pandemic was accelerated by a boom in rail and steamship travel but was eventually quashed by advances in science.
In 1894 French-Swiss bacteriologist Alexandre Yersin isolated the plague bacterium and connected rat infestations to the disease. Rat eradication campaigns followed around the world, drastically slowing the spread of plague, Wagner says. Though it was really the fleas that spread the disease to people, rat control worked because fleas are very specific about hosts. Different animal species have their own flea species, so rats and plague-carrying fleas traveled together.
Quarantines also helped, Wagner adds, because doctors started to recognize that the bacteria could sometimes spread from person to person through respiratory droplets. In the 1940s, when antibiotics had become widely available, doctors started curing plague cases with the drugs. Several vaccines have been developed over the years and deployed in severe outbreaks, in which they offered partial protection. No vaccine has been deemed effective enough to gain approval from the WHO or the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but labs in Russia and the U.S. continue to work on them.
Today most plague cases occur in Madagascar. Because food can be scarce there and people fear theft, individuals will store rice in their dirt-floor homes, Wagner says, allowing close contact with the rats that infest the island.
Though fleas are picky about their hosts, plague-carrying fleas in the U.S. are commonly found on prairie dogs, thanks to the animals having some functional similarities to rats. The plague bacterium now infects all five known species of prairie dogs and is one of the factors that contributed to a population decline in these social, burrowing rodents of about 98 percent from their historical levels. Because prairie dogs are a food source for other animals, including the critically endangered black-footed ferret, plague has been wreaking ecological havoc.
Even now it’s not clear where Y. pestis hides out between detectable outbreaks, Wagner says, and it’s surprising that it can be transmitted both by respiratory droplets and through fleas. But important clues about how the sickness operates are emerging from the latest studies of bacterial DNA in ancient bones and teeth.
The plague bacterium appears to have emerged as a human pathogen more than 5,700 years ago, evolving from a soil bacterium called Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, says Hendrick Poinar, a biologist at McMaster University, who works with ancient DNA. For the next 3,000 years, it infected Late Stone Age hunter-gathers and Bronze Age herders. Scientists suspect it was transmitted from human to human via respiratory droplets or via contaminated food because it hadn’t yet acquired the genes needed to travel through fleas.
Despite the versatility of Y. pestis, we’re lucky it can’t spread between humans unless an infected person is very sick and the contact is very close. Because of this limitation, even the emergence of an antibiotic-resistant strain won’t necessarily spark a new pandemic, Wagner says, noting that such strains have already shown up in Madagascar.
Though most scientists aren’t too alarmed about the situation in Russia, some are speculating that the death was caused by some highly genetically modified version of the plague bacterium or a different germ entirely. There’s no evidence for this, though the lack of transparency from Russia is unnerving. Regardless of the cause, the death of the worker is tragic. But if it was caused by the plague we know, the rest of us need not worry.

HELSINKI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The leaders of Finland and Norway called Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine, breaking with a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin.
The phone call by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was a bid to influence the diplomatic process at a time when US President Donald Trump has shifted his position in favour of Russia and US ties with Ukraine have hit their lowest point in 18 months.
The Nordic leaders spoke by phone to Putin and afterwards to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, according to a Zelenskiy aide.
“The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” Stubb said in a joint statement with Stoere.
The Norwegian added: “The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation.”
Both leaders stressed their strong support for Ukraine, which they said would continue.
NO SIGN OF COMPROMISE FROM THE KREMLIN
The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not suggest that Putin had signalled any compromise from previously stated positions.
“It was emphasized that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account,” the Kremlin said.
“At the same time, attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities.”
Western European leaders have mostly shunned contact with Putin, while piling up sanctions on Moscow, since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022.
But that stance has left them sidelined as efforts to end the war have been led by Trump, who is seen in many EU capitals as unpredictable, erratic and prone to side with Putin at the expense of Ukraine.
That perception has been reinforced by deals this month in which Putin agreed to supply Russian diesel to the US and Trump eased sanctions on Russia while saying it was time for Ukrainians to replace Zelenskiy as their leader. Ukraine has also complained of disruption to intelligence-sharing by the US and to satellite internet services on which its military relies.
DANISH LEADER CRITICISES NORDIC PEERS FOR MAKING THE CALL
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticised the Finnish-Norwegian decision to talk to Putin, adding that she saw no signs that Russia wants peace.
“I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo,” Frederiksen told public broadcaster DR.
Stubb and Stoere participated in the call as leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole, they said, adding that the two Nordic nations will continue their longstanding support for Ukraine.
Russia has frequently accused European governments of stoking the war by arming Ukraine and refusing direct talks.
It has contrasted the stance of Western European leaders with that of Trump, who has engaged with Putin and tried — so far without success — to broker a peace agreement.
A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that French President Emmanuel Macron was the last EU leader to speak with Putin by phone. The call, which took place in July this year, was not made public and did not yield any results, according to the source.
The source said Putin told Stubb and Stoere that Russia would not compromise over its aim to capture the whole of Ukraine’s Donbas region. The Europeans responded by saying that a “just” peace is needed, this person said.

Ukraine improves jet-powered drone interception rates, but Starlink disruptions threaten progress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:49:20 UTC
19:49:20 KST

Ukraine made significant progress in countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some air defence units reporting interception rates around 80%. But recent restrictions on US satellite services exposed Kyiv's reliance on US technology as it races to develop cheaper, more effective interceptors.
Ukraine's improved interceptor drone technology has helped it counter Russia's jet-powered drones, but disruptions to US Starshield satellite services threaten those gains.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Ukraine's interception rate fell slightly from 77% to around 74% during disruptions to the military-grade satellite service between 14 and 24 October.
The figures nevertheless represent a marked improvement on early September, when Ukrainian officials reported intercepting around 60% of Russia's jet-powered drones.
Some Ukrainian air defence units have reported interception rates exceeding 80%, although these figures reflect individual units' performance rather than nationwide results.
The Starshield restrictions, which affected high-speed drone operations, were lifted on 24 October, according to Ukrainian officials. However, the disruption highlighted the country's dependence on US satellite communications to sustain its air defences.
ISW warned that maintaining and improving interception rates would require Ukraine to develop and deploy affordable, high-speed interceptor drones on a much larger scale.
Russia has increasingly turned to jet-powered versions of its Shahed-type attack drones, which travel considerably faster than conventional propeller-driven models, leaving Ukrainian air defence crews with significantly less time to detect and intercept them.
Ukraine relies on a combination of interceptor drones, fighter aircraft and ground-based systems to counter the threat.
Interceptor drones have proved particularly effective, according to ISW, but many depend on Starshield connectivity to operate at the speeds required to engage faster Russian targets.
Ukrainian forces also use F-16 fighter jets, either firing air-to-air missiles or engaging targets with onboard guns. Both approaches have drawbacks: missiles are expensive and scarce, while gun engagements demand considerable pilot skill and expose aircraft and crews to additional risks.
Using fighter jets against drones also increases maintenance requirements and diverts aircraft from other missions.
Ukraine has installed ground-based gun turrets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, although expanding these systems nationwide would require considerable time and resources.
The race for cheaper interceptors
The growing threat has accelerated efforts by Ukrainian manufacturers to develop faster, more affordable interception systems.
One such project is the F-Jet 80, a jet-powered interceptor being developed by Ukrainian company F-Drones, which plans to incorporate artificial intelligence into its guidance system.
The company aims to keep the unit cost at approximately $7,000, compared with an estimated $20,000 to $70,000 for other high-speed interceptor drones and around $1 million for an air-to-air missile launched from an F-16.
Although the F-Jet 80 remains under development, its manufacturer says it has already successfully intercepted several Russian drones.
For Ukraine, the challenge extends beyond developing effective technology to producing it in sufficient numbers to counter Russia's expanding use of jet-powered drones.
ISW argues that integrating affordable interceptor drones into Ukraine's existing air defence network offers the strongest prospect of sustaining high interception rates as the country approaches another winter of Russian aerial attacks.

Pope Leo to return to his adopted home on South America tour

By Marco Aquino
ZAÑA, Peru Oct 27 (Reuters) - As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America next week, many Peruvians remember him as the priest who helped feed hungry families, delivered aid after floods and walked alongside migrants in the country he would eventually call his own.
When the pandemic emptied the streets of northern Peru and one of the world’s longest quarantines left many struggling to eat, Bishop Robert Prevost, as Leo was known, helped launch a soup kitchen in 2020 in the small town of Zaña.
“He gave us an example of human charity, and we prepared the ‘aguadito con fe’,” recalled former cook Betty Burga Campos, referring to the traditional soup of rice, meat and vegetables that volunteers served.
Prevost left Peru for Rome three years later after Pope Francis tapped him to lead the Vatican office that recommends candidates for bishop appointments worldwide.
After rising from missionary and bishop in Peru’s far north to cardinal and ultimately pope, Leo, 71, is set to revisit the country where he became a citizen and built some of the relationships that defined his ministry, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer. The Vatican confirmed on Monday that his November 6 to 17 South America tour remained on schedule.
Across northern Peru, regional governments are refurbishing churches and residents are preparing celebrations for his visit, which also includes earlier stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
For many Peruvians, memories of the Chicago-born head of the Catholic Church are less about Vatican titles than muddy boots, long drives across the country’s rugged north and a hands-on approach to helping people.
“He had become Peruvian, even in the way he spoke. He no longer had much of that American accent,” said José Manuel Zamora Romero, a priest in Lambayeque who knew him for years.
The share of adults in Peru who identify as Catholic has fallen from 76% to 67% over the decade to 2024, according to Pew Research Center. The decline is often linked to social changes and distrust of institutions, following years of political instability that have caused Peru to cycle through nine presidents in a decade.
A BISHOP ON THE MOVE
Prevost arrived in Peru in 1985 at age 30. After years based in the United States and Rome with his Augustinian order, he returned in 2014 and became bishop of the Peruvian city of Chiclayo in 2015. In 2023, Pope Francis brought Prevost to the Vatican. Francis named him a cardinal later that year and he was elected pope in 2025.
Across northern Peru’s sun-baked farm belt, residents and priests recall a churchman constantly on the move.
For the future pontiff, “the distances were not limits, the distances were opportunities,” said David Farfán, a priest in Zaña, one of the towns on the pope’s upcoming itinerary.
Many remember Prevost riding horseback to isolated Andean communities. Others recall him driving hundreds of kilometers himself across Peru’s rugged north.
“His hobby was driving,” Zamora Romero said. “And I know he taught some priests to drive so they could get their licenses … and they all passed the test.”
That practical approach became evident during emergencies.
When severe flooding linked to the El Niño climate phenomenon inundated northern Peru in 2023, photos circulated on social media of Prevost wading through knee-deep water in rubber boots as he helped deliver aid.
When natural disasters occurred, “he was on the front lines to bring the help that the population needed,” said Rev. Jorge Villegas of Chiclayo, where the pope will spend two full days.
Residents pointed to moments like those as evidence of a bishop who preferred action over visibility.
“He wasn’t very focused on being with the press; he was more with the poor and in social conflicts,” said Verónica Castillo, a journalist in Chiclayo who witnessed his intervention during a 2015 labor conflict.
“He was a bishop who intervened, who took action, and people remember that,” she added, recalling how Prevost helped mediate the prolonged protest by workers against a sugar company, which turned violent.
‘PUT HIMSELF IN SHOES OF A MIGRANT’
Migration has reshaped much of Latin America over the past decade, as millions of Venezuelans fled economic collapse and political turmoil. Peru hosts the world’s second-largest Venezuelan diaspora community, with more than 1.5 million migrants. Many arrived without proper documentation and live with inadequate access to healthcare and basic services.
Prevost founded a Catholic organization in Chiclayo in 2018 to assist newcomers.
“He put himself in the shoes of a migrant first and foremost and knew what the situation was like,” said Augusto Martínez, who leads the organization.
The group has assisted thousands of Venezuelans.
As pope, Leo has called for migrants to be treated with dignity, condemned human trafficking and warned traffickers to repent or face divine judgment. He has criticized anti-immigration policies, including measures pursued by US President Donald Trump.
“He supported migrants on how to have a dignified life here in Peru,” said Lisbeth Coromoto Díaz, who received help through the Chiclayo organization and said he held Masses in honor of migrants.
Leo’s planned return to Peru has revived hopes among Catholics in Eten, near Chiclayo, that he could advance a long-running campaign to secure Vatican recognition of the town’s reported Eucharistic miracle. As bishop, he supported the cause, presenting historical records and thousands of testimonies of faith in Rome, linked to a 1649 apparition in which devotees say the image of the Christ Child appeared in a consecrated host.
Tourism officials are promoting routes tied to the places Leo lived and worked. Souvenir shops are stocking shelves with pope-inspired hats, key chains and pins.
In a shop window in the capital Lima’s Gamarra textile district, an image of Leo on a T-shirt depicts him smiling while enjoying a plate of Peruvian food.
“We’ve got the pope looking spirited; we’ve got the pope as a foodie, enjoying delicious ceviche and rotisserie chicken. We even have the play on words: ‘The Pope and the papa (potato) are Peruvian’,” said clothing maker Victoria Quiñones.
Quiñones predicted a 200% increase in her workload and was running low on fabric for the T-shirts.
Nearby, Maria Rodriguez, 70, was shopping for pope T-shirts.
“I’m buying several,” Rodriguez said.
“I’ll be wearing them all through November because I am Catholic: Roman and Peruvian,” she added.

MUMBAI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - An Indian court allowed Bollywood actor Imran Khan to remain in the country until at least November 2, local media said on Tuesday, pausing a government order that asked him to leave for breaching immigration laws by allegedly participating in a protest.
Khan, 43, is a US citizen and was asked to leave the country by October 28 after he was accused of joining protests in Mumbai against the country’s election chief this month.
Under Indian law, the participation of foreigners in political protests can be treated as a violation of immigration and visa rules.
Khan appealed against the order in the Bombay High Court, saying it was unconstitutional and arbitrary, local media reported.
There was no evidence to show that Khan participated in the protest and mobilised a crowd, his lawyer said in the appeal, legal website Live Law reported.
On Tuesday, the Bombay High Court postponed the hearing to November 2 due to technical reasons and said that the order Khan had challenged would remain on hold until then, legal website Bar and Bench posted on X.
There has been no official statement from Mumbai Police on Khan’s case. The city’s police chief did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
A nephew of actor Aamir Khan, Imran belongs to a prominent film family. He acted in several hit Bollywood films from 2008 to 2015, before suddenly retiring.
His partner, Lekha Washington, said in a post on her Instagram page on October 12 that she, Khan, his mother and a cousin walked toward the protest site to ask about a friend who had been detained by police and were immediately surrounded by media representatives.
“He (Imran) responded to the questions of the media, saying we have no demands, we are not part of an organisation,” Washington said in the post.
Both Khan and Washington posted pictures from inside what appeared to be a police van on the day of the protests, smiling into the camera.
The rally in Mumbai was one of several protests across the country demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over what opposition parties and activists say is a revision of voter lists that benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party.
(Reporting by Shilpa Jamkhandikar; Editing by YP Rajesh)

Upgraded Russian cruise missile crashes in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:38:35 UTC
19:38:35 KST

- Photos show Russia’s upgraded Geran-5 K5-K light cruise missile, serial number ANS-3031, lying in a field in Ukraine’s Odesa region.
- The new version has a redesigned airframe and modern navigation equipment, and the cause of its crash is not yet known.
Photos have emerged of Russia’s newest version of the Geran-5 light cruise missile, known as the Geran-5 K5-K and often described in the media as a jet-powered drone, lying in a field somewhere in Ukraine’s Odesa region after it came down during an attack, with the serial number ANS-3031 visible on the airframe.
It is not yet known why the Geran-5 K5-K crashed, whether it was hit by Ukrainian air defenses, brought down by electronic warfare or failed on its own, and Ukrainian officials have not commented publicly on the find.
The K5-K is an upgraded version of the Geran-5 cruise missile with a noticeably different design from the first versions of the weapon, and Ukrainian sources say the new variant has a modified fuselage, smaller swept-back wings, a tail without wingtips and an engine moved from an external pod into the fuselage, along with more modern navigation equipment.
Russian forces began using the new version in late September, and Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov has said it carries autonomous optical navigation that compares images of the ground below with stored data to correct its course without satellite signals, which makes it much harder to throw off course with jamming, while its designers are reportedly aiming for speeds of up to 900 km/h (559 mph).
Russia first used the original Geran-5 against Ukraine in early January 2026, when Ukraine’s military intelligence described it as a turbojet-powered weapon with a conventional cruise-missile layout, a warhead of about 90 kg (198 pounds) and an advertised range of roughly 1,000 km (621 miles), and said its design was substantially similar to Iran’s Karrar.
Ukrainian intelligence data give the baseline Geran-5 a length of about 6.5 meters (21 feet), a wingspan of 3.2 meters (10.5 feet), a takeoff weight of up to 850 kg (1,874 pounds) and a cruising speed of 450 to 600 km/h (280 to 373 mph), using a Chinese-made Telefly turbojet, a Kometa anti-jamming satellite navigation receiver and cellular modems.
Ukraine’s Defence Intelligence has said Russia produces about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 weapons a month at the Alabuga plant in Tatarstan, and that Moscow has been building additional production facilities there since May 2026.

Finnish, Norwegian Leaders Call Putin Ahead of Ukraine Peace Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:36:39 UTC
19:36:39 KST

Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday, during which the three leaders discussed ongoing efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
Moscow confirmed the call shortly after officials in Helsinki and Oslo released statements about the conversation, which marks the first time a leader from one of Ukraine’s European allies spoke to Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron’s phone call with the Kremlin chief in July 2025.
Stubb’s office said he and Støre initiated the call in order to “discuss Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe.”
It said the aim of the outreach, made in consultation with Ukraine, was “to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin,” adding that it was also “related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi.”
Both Finland and Norway said their leaders were speaking as representatives of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole.
“In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation,” Støre’s office said in its statement about the call with Putin.
The Kremlin said Putin “reiterated the root causes” of his decision to order the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In the phone call, he also “drew attention to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO member states, which he noted serve to prolong the hostilities.”
Stubb, Støre and Putin also discussed security and stability in the Baltic Sea and Northern European regions, the Kremlin’s readout said. The three leaders agreed to maintain direct contact moving forward, it added.
Tuesday’s phone call comes a week after Stubb and Støre met with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo. The purpose of the Oslo talks was to mend strained relations between Kyiv and Washington, as well as to seek a new path out of the war.
Witkoff later met with Putin in St. Petersburg to report on progress in efforts to end the conflict. The Kremlin said it is willing to resume U.S.-mediated peace negotiations in Abu Dhabi as soon as next month.

French teachers say government education measures to quell protests fall short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

19:36:11 KST

French teachers say government education measures to quell protests fall short
PARIS, Oct 27 - French teachers said on Tuesday that education reforms aimed at ending weeks of protests were insufficient and would not be enough to quell students' anger.
The French government on Monday announced a raft of proposals, including capping some class sizes at 28, billions of euros in loans for building renovation and a revamp of the university admissions system, to try to ease popular anger.
But Sophie Venetitay, the secretary general for teachers' union SNES-FSU, told reporters that the measures did not go far enough, saying the size of more classes should be capped and more people should be hired to improve learning conditions for students.
"Today, what the ministry has said is only the beginning of a response," she said. "It will not be enough to extinguish the anger."
High school students initially blockaded their schools to protest against inadequate staffing and resources, in a movement that has since broadened to encompass general trade unions and the so-called "Yellow Vests" to express anger about weakening public services and cost-of-living increases.
The French government, under pressure from bond markets to reduce its debt level, has little spare cash to respond to protesters' demands.
Budget Minister David Amiel said on TF1 the measures announced on Monday were expected to cost €5 billion ($5.6 billion) and would be offset with spending cuts elsewhere.
Student leaders also said the government's concessions were a good first step, but vowed to continue demonstrations, on Saturday and on November 5.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told RTL that there would be a heavy security presence on Saturday, which will come two weeks after large nationwide protests gave way to violence and looting that shocked the country and have spurred curfews and bans on large gatherings in France.
The turmoil has boosted the fortunes of French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is favoured to top the first round in the presidential election next spring. REUTERS

Limburg first region in Europe to host a CERN innovation hub in Hasselt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:27:09 UTC
19:27:09 KST

A CERN innovation hub is to be established at the Corda Campus, a large technology and business innovation campus in Hasselt (Limburg Province). CERN is the leading European centre for particle physics, based in Geneva (Switzerland). Over the past few decades, a great many new technologies have been developed there. The hub aims to make this knowledge more accessible to businesses in Limburg and the rest of Belgium.
CERN develops technologies that are among the best in the world. Although they are primarily intended for fundamental research, they also have applications outside particle physics, for example in medical imaging, advanced sensor technology and data processing.
The new innovation hub at the Corda Campus in Hasselt is designed to strengthen the link between CERN and the Belgian business community. The focus is on connecting CERN’s expertise with the needs of businesses and research institutions.
For example, both partners aim to launch new research and development projects and to stimulate the development of innovative products and applications.
First region in Europe
Limburg is the first region in Europe to have such an innovation hub. “This is an important recognition of our ambitions,” says Tom Vandeput, chair of the provincial development agency of Limburg province POM Limburg and provincial executive member for Innovation Policy.
The province is allocating an additional 3.6 million euros to the Big Science Hub over the coming years. The collaboration with CERN is a first concrete step within this broader initiative. Our aim is to give our innovative SMEs better access to international knowledge and technology and to strengthen their competitiveness.”
“This CERN innovation hub is the first of a limited number of hubs we are establishing this year to test the new collaboration model in practice,” adds Han Dols, Head of Innovation and Technology Transfer at CERN.
“Together with a partner that is strongly committed to regional innovation, we want to help businesses and researchers apply CERN’s knowledge to challenges in a wide range of fields. In this way, this hub can strengthen the Belgian innovation ecosystem, stimulate socio-economic growth and create tangible social added value.”
Through the Big Science Hub, POM Limburg aims eventually to become a permanent link between Belgian industry and major international research infrastructures.
This should enable Limburg province to secure a stronger position within the international Big Science landscape, opening up new opportunities for innovation, entrepreneurship and employment.

These measures are being implemented alongside operations led by the Paratroopers Brigade headquarters, under the command of Col. Roi Zweig, to combat nationalist crime in the Shiloh Valley, within the Binyamin Regional Brigade's area of responsibility.

A security official told Walla on Tuesday morning that IDF engineering forces were preparing to demolish illegal structures, terrorists' homes and monuments as part of efforts to combat incitement to terrorism and prevent potential copycat attacks.
The IDF also decided on Monday night to reinforce troops along the security barrier amid concerns that terrorists could infiltrate Israel.
Heller also emphasized the importance of strengthening coordination among security agencies on Election Day, including the Israel Police, the Israel Border Police in the West Bank and the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency).
The increased coordination is intended to ensure a rapid operational response to any incidents that may arise.

“Forest Carabinieri: ‘Biodiversity Keepers’,” an exhibition at UNESCO running through October 29
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:25:21 CET
19:25:21 KST

Thanks to the collaboration between the Carabinieri and Italy’s Permanent Delegation to UNESCO, an exhibition dedicated to the role of the Carabinieri as “biodiversity keepers” opened last night in Paris. Italy boasts the richest biodiversity in Europe. From Alpine forests to Mediterranean coastlines, its extraordinary landscapes are home to unique ecosystems, rare wildlife, and an unparalleled agricultural heritage. Through audiovisual experiences and interactive installations set within an “ideal forest,” visitors can discover the hidden wonders of Italian biodiversity while learning about the vital work of the Carabinieri Forestali in safeguarding forests, wildlife, and protected areas.
                                    
“The Carabinieri work daily to protect the territory: from combating illegal waste trafficking to defending agricultural and food excellence and natural reserves, our efforts safeguard the environment in all its forms. The exhibition we are inaugurating at UNESCO is a call to awareness and a concrete commitment to future generations to preserve the delicate balances of the planet,” stated Gen. C.A. Fabrizio Parrulli, commander of the CUFAA (Carabinieri Forestry, Environmental, and Agri-Food Units Command).
                                    
Indeed, peacebuilding and peacekeeping also depend on the protection of the environment and biodiversity. UNESCO has been active in this field since the 1970s through the “Man and the Biosphere” program, which aims to reconcile the needs of environmental protection with those of sustainable development. The program, for which Italy currently holds the rotating vice-presidency, manages a global network of nearly 800 Biosphere Reserves—21 of which are in Italy—that together cover 5% of the Earth’s surface. 
   “Here at UNESCO, the Carabinieri are known for their role in safeguarding cultural heritage. Today, it is also important to highlight their work—less well-known internationally but equally important—in defending biodiversity. This work benefits the community, and Italy wishes to present it as a best practice and a model that can be replicated on a global scale,” stated Ambassador Liborio Stellino, Italy’s Permanent Representative to UNESCO, addressing a large audience of diplomats and international officials.

Voter turnout in Israel’s general elections reached 31.5% by noon local time (1000GMT) on Tuesday, the highest level recorded at that hour since 1973, according to the Central Elections Committee.
 
A total of 2.39 million Israelis had cast their ballots by noon, an increase of more than 3 percentage points compared with the previous election, according to the committee.
 
Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich attributed the high turnout to exceptionally strong participation among Arab voters and in left-wing strongholds.
 
In a social media post, Smotrich said the increase in participation was driven by unusually high voting rates in Arab communities and areas traditionally supporting left-wing parties.
 
Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi also reported unusually high participation, expressing confidence in a strong electoral performance.
 
“Polling stations are packed like never before, and I am confident we will achieve a major victory,” Tibi said in a press statement.
 
The remarks come amid efforts by Arab political parties and opposition leaders to mobilize voters in a closely contested election that could determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power.
 
According to The Jerusalem Post, the communities of Ein Hod and Sde Nehemia recorded turnout rates of 25.7% and 25.4%, respectively, by 10 am.
 
Other communities, including Nes Harim and Odim, reported participation rates of 23.2% and 23%, respectively.
 
Earlier Tuesday, opposition leaders urged Israelis to vote in large numbers to end Netanyahu’s rule.
 
Opposition Yisrael Beiteinu party leader Avigdor Lieberman called for an end to the Netanyahu era, while Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the opposition Yashar party, urged voters to support political change.
 
More than 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election to choose members of the 120-seat Knesset.
 
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time (0500 GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 pm (2000 GMT).
 
The election is Israel’s first general vote since the start of its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
 
The vote comes amid deep political divisions over Netanyahu’s leadership, the Gaza genocide, Israel’s military confrontation with Iran and the country’s future political direction.
 
Netanyahu’s Likud-led coalition and opposition parties are competing to secure the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.
 
Recent opinion polls have suggested that neither bloc is assured of a majority, raising the possibility that Arab parties could play a significant role in determining the formation of the next government.

Jordan carried out air strikes in southern Syria late on Monday, killing at least five civilians, including women and children, according to Syrian state media. Meanwhile, Amman said the operation targeted Daesh sites following a deadly church attack in Jordan.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported strikes on several locations in Daraa province, saying seven people were killed. Two injured people in Muzayrib, in the western countryside, were taken to Tafas National Hospital, according to the provincial health director.
Among those killed was a 65-year-old man from Daraa city’s Tariq al Sadd neighbourhood who died from shrapnel wounds, the provincial health director said.
Jordan’s army said earlier that it had struck sites belonging to “terrorist organisations” in southern Syria linked to Friday’s attack on mourners at Hamoud Church in Jordan’s Karak province, which killed nine people.
The army said the strikes killed and wounded members of the groups and destroyed sites and vehicles, but did not identify the organisations or provide locations or casualty figures.
Jordan says strikes targeted Daesh
Jordanian government spokesman Mohammad al Momani said on Tuesday that the strikes killed more than 20 Daesh members and destroyed a major weapons depot.
He said the operation followed a period in which Jordan had “run out of patience” with terrorist group movements and threats to its national security.
“The operation was based on field intelligence aimed at neutralising confirmed threats and planned terrorist attacks against Jordan,” Momani said.
He expressed regret over civilian casualties, saying Jordan had avoided striking locations where intelligence indicated civilians were present.
Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects in the church attack on Monday after a shootout in Karak. All three were wounded, while no security personnel were injured, according to Jordan’s Public Security Directorate.
Damascus condemns strikes
Syria on Tuesday condemned the strikes by Jordan. A foreign ministry statement expressed "condemnation and rejection, in the strongest terms", calling the strike "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination".
It also said the attack was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty".
The Syrian government also said that the Jordanian strikes were conducted without prior coordination and that an investigation was under way.
Damascus said it was supporting those affected and had conveyed its objections to Jordan, stressing the need for joint security and field coordination on operations in border areas to safeguard Syria’s sovereignty and the security of both countries.
Jordan said it respected Syria and its people and that coordination between Amman and Damascus on counterterrorism and weapons and drug smuggling had been ongoing for years.
Momani said Jordan and Syria would establish a joint committee to follow up on the consequences of the operation and strengthen coordination against Daesh while protecting civilians.
He said Jordan supported Syria’s security, unity and internal stability and was committed to developing cooperation in confronting shared challenges.
“Jordan’s security and Syria’s security are one,” Momani said, adding that countering terrorism remained a shared objective.
The Syrian authorities said the strikes had killed seven people, while SANA reported five civilian deaths and two injuries in the attacks.

Eesti 200 MP: Casino tax cut needs time, over-regulation is the real issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:24:00 UTC
19:24:00 KST

Eesti 200 MP: Casino tax cut needs time, over-regulation is the real issue
A controversial online casino tax cut needs time to work out, Eesti 200 MP Tanel Tein said.
It is over-regulation and not the lower tax rate, which Tein's party sponsored, which is behind lower than hoped-for tax revenues, the MP went on.
The tax cut, passed last December, lowered the online casino rate from 6 percent to 4 percent, in increments over a two-year period. Receipts fell 9.7 percent in the first seven months of 2026, while the Cultural Endowment, one of the main recipients of the tax revenues, has forecast a €6–7 million shortfall for next year, directly as a result of the lower revenues.
Speaking to "Aktuaalne kaamera," Tein called comparing six months of receipts to a four-year strategy short-sighted, adding the Finance Ministry's forecasts do not represent money in the budget.
The gambling tax cut was your big mission in politics — do you concede failure?
Its aim was to bring extra funding to sport and culture; a private funding foundation and a sports facilities fund were set up at the Cultural Endowment for that purpose. The tax strategy is set up over four years, so assessing it after six months is very short-sighted.
Why do you say that? It can already be seen that the state budget has received half as much tax revenue.
No. If we compare the tax base we had in 2025, in 2026 it has grown noticeably. When we hiked the gambling tax from 5 to 6 percent, growth in the tax base fell sharply — and that is a very important signal that we need to grow the tax base, so there is something to tax.
The Ministry of Finance disagrees with you, while the Cultural Endowment's forecast is something else entirely compared with what you promised at the start of this year.
The Ministry of Finance's forecast is just that, a forecast; it is not money in the budget. And we have to ask why in earlier years growth in the tax base was nearly 40 percent, and during the tax rise it fell sharply to zero. That is a very important point, and it is the market participants themselves who must be asked. It is known that nearly two-thirds of tax revenue comes from foreign operators. To my knowledge, the Ministry of Finance has not spoken to them about what they will do if the tax rises or falls. But the bigger problem is over-regulation.
It is very convenient to blame other officials and institutions for over-regulating. You seem to think pawn brokers are over-regulated too. But the forecast has not matched reality.
A forecast is not money in the state budget. Take the simple example of the car tax: the forecast said €130 million would flow into the state budget, and in fact around €50 million did — so forecasts are very often wrong. We need to know the substance: why that taxpayer and that tax revenue comes to Estonia, what we need to do for it, what other countries are doing so that we are in the international market and competitive. I would very much listen to what the sector and the market participants themselves say on this point — and today they say we over-regulate.
Your own forecasts were €95 million in online casino tax revenue by 2029. Today it's clear that won't happen — what forecasts are you still waiting for?
Let's settle one thing: that was not a forecast, it was an assumption. It was a simulation of what would happen if we succeeded in bringing ten licenses a year to Estonia — and now we have to ask what we should do to bring those ten licenses a year.
What needs to be done? The Cultural Endowment says there is no money to fund projects.
At the Cultural Endowment we have to look at what other tax receipts have fallen. Alcohol and tobacco excise have fallen, [state lottery] Eesti Loto has fallen — all of them. And now the remote gambling tax is being made the political culprit, which in my view is not right. In previous years the remote gambling tax has continued to cover shortfalls in other areas, and that hasn't been talked about.
In your view, should the Riigikogu reverse the legislative amendment?
If our tax base falls, then that tax percentage could be 30. We won't get more tax from it; we need to get more companies here, and for that we need to know what we have to do. We must not over-regulate.
Background:
The tax cut was passed last December and lowers the rate from 6 percent to 4 percent by 2029. The Ministry of Finance forecast a €6–37 million shortfall across 2026–2029. Prime Minister Kristen Michal has said the government will revisit the cut if it brings no extra revenue.

Bluey getting run over by a car in a One Nation video will now be the subject of legal action by the ABC.
The Australian cartoon dog, now beloved around the world, appeared in a 2024 episode of the Please Explain series produced by the party.
In the episode, Bluey is hit by a car driven by former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the passenger seat.

"Probably the globally most loved character in a video that is both shocking and disrespectful to the children of Australia," he said.

Labor senator Varun Ghosh described Bluey's use as "heinous", particularly in light of the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines on 19 October, where she was hit by a car and lost both legs.

The broadcaster will write One Nation a cease and desist letter demanding the video be taken down, with Marks flagging that damages might be sought.

The episode remains on YouTube.

Ambassador Schiavo presents the Stella d’Italia to writer Amara Lakhous
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:17:21 CET
19:17:21 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Algeria, Alessandra Schiavo, presented the Italian-Algerian writer Amara Lakhous with the title of Knight of the Order of the Star of Italy, an honor conferred upon him by President of the Republic Sergio Mattarella back in 2021 but which could not be presented at the time due to the pandemic.
                                    
The ceremony, held at the Italian Residence, brought together members of the diplomatic corps, representatives of the Italian community and the “Scuola Roma” in Algiers, senior officials from the University of Algiers 2, the Faculty of Languages, and the Department of Italian Studies, the director of the Italian Cultural Institute in Algeria, Paola Cordone, and numerous Algerian publishers, journalists, and artists.
                                    
Ambassador Schiavo recalled the reasons for awarding the honor to this writer, who was born in Algiers and later moved to Rome during the “Black Decade.” Having acquired dual citizenship, Lakhous mastered Italian to such an extent that he has become one of the world’s rare examples of perfectly bilingual writers.
                                    
He is the author of a prolific body of work in Arabic and Italian—with some of his novels translated directly from the Italian text into numerous European and non-European languages —Lakhous has distinguished himself for his tireless commitment to promoting the Italian language and culture, which he now teaches in the United States at Yale, one of the most prestigious universities on the international stage.
                                    
“By making the encounter between languages one of the defining elements of his work,” said Ambassador Schiavo, “Lakhous has shed light on the themes of exile and identity, contributing to reflection on many contemporary urban contexts.”
Amara Lakhous’s visit to Algeria is part of the program promoted by the Italian Embassy and the Italian Cultural Institute in Algiers on the occasion of the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, dedicated this year to the theme “Brilliant Language: Conceive, Design, Create with Italian.” The program includes meetings with students and faculty from the Italian Studies departments of four Algerian universities (Annaba, Algiers, Blida, and Oran), as well as the author’s participation in the 29th edition of the Salon International du Livre d’Alger (SILA), scheduled for October 28 through November 7.
                                    
The book fair will mark the 20th anniversary of the Italian publication of “Clash of Civilizations Over an Elevator in Piazza Vittorio,” one of the author’s best-known novels and a significant work of contemporary literature on the transformations of multicultural societies.

Can Oleshky truce pave way for wider Russia-Ukraine peace?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

Kanyshai Butun
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
- Truce in Russia-controlled Ukrainain city of Oleshky aims to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations amid worsening humanitarian crisis
- Analysts say sustained ceasefire could build momentum for broader negotiations, but doubt it will hold amid failed truce attempts
A temporary ceasefire has taken effect in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, but analysts remain skeptical about whether it will hold.
The ceasefire, announced by US first lady Melania Trump, took effect Tuesday and could serve as a test of broader US-mediated efforts to end the war.
Eugene Chausovsky, senior director at the New Lines Institute, told Anadolu that a ceasefire sustained beyond a “few days” could signal that both sides were willing to consider similar arrangements across a wider geography of the conflict.
Failure to sustain it, however, would reinforce the "status quo" amid already high levels of mistrust, he said. 
Truce could test prospects for peace talks
The truce comes ahead of trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US scheduled for the first half of November, raising the prospect that a successful local arrangement could inject momentum into broader negotiations.
Chausovsky said a successful truce in Oleshky “could breathe new life” into the upcoming talks and have important implications for the overall conflict.
“It is possible that this localized ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a significant test for broader US-mediated ceasefire arrangements to be put into place between Ukraine and Russia,” he said.
Timothy Ash, an associate fellow in the Russia and Eurasia program at Chatham House, was more skeptical that a localized ceasefire would change the course of the war, saying Russian President Vladimir Putin still believed he held the upper hand.
"It’s possible that if the ceasefire holds it could generate some positive vibes around broader peace talks - but I doubt it," he told Anadolu.
Ash questioned whether the truce would alter Putin's approach to the war, arguing that Moscow's ambitions remained “maximalist," with Russia rejecting several ceasefire efforts and believing that US Donald Trump could reduce US support for Ukraine, weaken the Western alliance and ultimately make concessions to its demands. 
Humanitarian crisis
The truce comes as Moscow and Kyiv trade blame for the worsening humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, a city in Ukraine's southern Kherson region that Russian forces captured in 2022.
Oleshky had a prewar population of around 24,000, but estimates suggest only 1,700-2,000 people remain, many of them older residents unable to leave.
Thousands of people lost their homes to massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023, with both sides accusing each other of blowing it up.
Ukraine has accused Russia of trying to turn the city “into a death trap,” saying the only exit route and a nearby river are mined and monitored by attack drones.
“Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in homes, as Russians forbid residents from burying them. Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, preserves and even snails,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
He added that the local hospital had run out of medicine and residents feared they would not survive the winter.
Moscow has rejected Kyiv's accusations.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov described the situation in Oleshky as critical, saying Kyiv “is doing literally everything it can” to prevent food and medicine deliveries.
Trump described the situation as “dire,” saying that without intervention, bringing humanitarian aid into the city and evacuating the elderly would be “impossible.” 
Will truce hold?
Although Russia and Ukraine agreed to halt fighting in the area from Tuesday morning to facilitate the humanitarian operation, analysts remain sceptical that the ceasefire will hold, given the broader military and political objectives of both sides.  
“Failure of the Oleshky ceasefire would signify that diplomatic mediation efforts are still unable to overcome the competing objectives of Russia and Ukraine in their protracted conflict,” Chausovsky said.
“I think the war goes on and we see a winter of escalation by both sides,” Ash said.
