‘It’s magical’: London’s iconic Oxford Street goes vehicle-free
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:03:32 UTC
19:03:32 KST

‘It’s magical’: London’s iconic Oxford Street goes vehicle-free
The cars have gone, and so have the buses, but while retailers expect a boost, residents worry about change.
London, United Kingdom – “It’s magical,” says biology teacher Muneera Alfadhel from under her umbrella.
In fact, it is a characteristically rainy, grey day in London, but the weather is doing nothing to dampen her mood. She is among the first to walk down the middle of the iconic Oxford Street following its pedestrianisation.
For generations, shoppers have bustled along Oxford Street next to bikes, cars, black cabs and red double-decker buses. But on Monday, from Great Portland Street to Orchard Street, the road is now a pedestrian-only zone.
On Monday morning, by force of habit, most pedestrians are still sticking to the pavement. Mark Arbouine, a forensic scientist out for a stroll, is one of the few breaking ranks: “I saw there was no traffic today, so I thought, why not walk in the middle of the street and take advantage of it? I just think it’s great for the environment, great for shopping. It’s just so much easier to move around the street.”
This tiny strip of real estate is big business: about 1 percent of the UK’s annual gross domestic product (GDP) is generated along this 1km (0.6 miles) stretch of street. But despite its outsized importance, Oxford Street has in recent decades been hit by lower consumer spending, as well as falling rents and footfall, which is now just 57 percent of what it was in 2006, according to New West End Company, a retail trade body.
The Greater London Authority, also known as City Hall, believes pedestrianisation could, therefore, offer a lifeline.
City Hall analysis suggests the partial pedestrianisation of Oxford Street could generate more than $109m per year and support an additional 700 jobs. Following a weekend trial in October 2025, two-thirds of businesses in the area said they had higher or similar sales figures during the pedestrianisation.
This is the first step in a multi-phase regeneration project to add two public squares, 50 trees and hundreds of public seating.
Barbara Stoll, a leading campaigner on the benefits of greener, more walkable cities, was smiling as she observed the street. The air already feels cleaner, she noted.
“It’s amazing coming here this morning. Walking down the street, it was already so uplifting that the noise is considerably lower,” she said. “People are excited. I saw people coming up from the tube and looking around. Seeing that, it’s almost like children when it’s Christmas Day.
“So I think it’s absolutely wonderful, and so needed for London.”
Residents ‘haven’t really been listened to’
On Saturday, ahead of the change, not all shoppers were convinced. A French tourist said he would avoid Oxford Street altogether if buses and cabs were no longer allowed through.
“People with disabilities who cannot walk a lot – that would be really helpful if the buses move on and they don’t discontinue [them],” a shopper told Al Jazeera.
“It would be good. Sometimes you’re tired; sometimes it’s raining.”
The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street has been years in the making, and not without controversy.
London Mayor Sadiq Khan first tried it in 2017, following a manifesto pledge. But the plan fell apart in 2018, when Westminster Council – the local government authority responsible for Oxford Street at the time – withdrew its backing, saying residents did not support it.
Following a public consultation, Khan created the Oxford Street Development Corporation, taking responsibility for the street away from local officials and transferring it to the Greater London Authority and Transport for London.
With this second, successful attempt at pedestrianisation, doubts from local authorities have not gone away.
Residents are not being listened to, said Councillor Tim Barnes, the deputy leader and cabinet member for growth and planning for the City of Westminster.
“There has been a communication process with residents, but it’s been pretty much one way. Mostly, they are being told what’s going to happen to them and how it’s going to happen; what the format of the process is going to be in future. But realistically, those who know the street best haven’t really been listened to.”
He believes the economic benefits are overstated and do not consider the impact of displacing bus routes from a major road to the surrounding, smaller streets. That fear is shared by resident Nerma Cridge, who said London’s West End will become “completely unliveable, too crowded and too noisy at night”.
“We think all of this should be done in a much more productive relationship with communities,” she told Al Jazeera over the phone.
‘People just take back the space’
Concerns over the change will fade once residents see the real-world results in the coming months, Stoll believes.
“Examples from across Europe and the world, where such projects have already happened, prove that this only makes life better overall for local residents,” she said.
“Retail gets a boost. More people linger, more people come to the street, more people spend money in the shops, and even local shop vacancies reduce. The local air pollution significantly reduces, and as activity increases, people just take back the space.”
The Oxford Street Development Corporation will be testing and reviewing the results of the pedestrianisation in the coming months, and reviewing its findings early next year. Transitioning the rest of Oxford Street into a permanent, traffic-free public space is expected to go ahead by the end of next year.
Ahead of mayoral elections in 2028, the pedestrianisation could be one of the last major initiatives that Sadiq Khan signs off. A landmark project that will also become his legacy.

Limiting sugar in the first 1,000 days of life is associated with later dementia onset, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:00:34 UTC
19:00:34 KST

Limiting exposure to added sugar in the womb and during the first two years of life is associated with a lower risk of developing dementia decades later, according to a new study published in Neurology. By examining adults born around the end of post-World War II food rationing in the United Kingdom, researchers found that early-life sugar restriction corresponded with delayed dementia onset, healthier brain structure, and better scores on some cognitive tests in their 60s. The findings suggest that nutritional conditions during the earliest stages of human development may play a lasting role in how the brain ages.
Dementia is an umbrella term for progressive neurological conditions that impair memory, thinking, and the ability to perform everyday activities. The most common form is Alzheimer’s disease, which involves the gradual breakdown of brain cells and the buildup of abnormal proteins, followed by vascular dementia, which occurs when reduced blood flow damages brain tissue. Although lifestyle habits in middle and old age are well-known factors in cognitive decline, growing evidence points to the importance of the “first 1,000 days” of life, the developmental window spanning from conception to a child’s second birthday.
During this early period, the brain undergoes rapid growth, forming neural connections and building the structural foundation for lifelong thinking and memory. High sugar intake during pregnancy and infancy may disrupt this process by triggering inflammation or interfering with how cells respond to insulin. For instance, research covered by PsyPost in 2016 indicated that rats fed sugary drinks early in life developed changes in the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped brain region essential for memory, that resembled the biological effects of early-life stress. In humans, observational studies have similarly linked higher maternal sugar consumption during pregnancy and breastfeeding to altered brain tissue organization in newborns and slightly lower cognitive scores in young children.
Studying how infant diets affect human brain aging is difficult because tracking people from birth into their 70s rarely happens in controlled experiments. To overcome this challenge, scientists have turned to a historical policy shift in the United Kingdom: the end of wartime sugar rationing. Introduced in July 1942 during World War II, the rationing system strictly limited added sugar and sweets to levels comparable to modern dietary guidelines while keeping overall calories and basic nutrients sufficient, unlike historical famines that caused severe starvation. When the British government abruptly ended sugar rationing in September 1953, national sugar consumption jumped by more than 50 percent, even as total calorie intake rose by only about 5 percent and other food groups remained relatively stable.
Researchers have used this sudden dietary shift to examine how early sugar limits relate to adult health, starting with a 2024 study by another team that linked rationing exposure during the first 1,000 days to lower adult rates of type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. Extending this approach to respiratory health, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that rationing exposure during pregnancy and infancy was tied to better adult lung capacity and lower rates of asthma. In the realm of mental health, a 2026 cohort study of British adults found that experiencing sugar rationing across the first 1,000 days of life was associated with a reduced preference for sweet foods and a lower risk of adult depression and anxiety.
Building on this line of inquiry, the new study was led by Jiazhen Zheng, an assistant professor at the School of Life and Health Sciences at Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology in China, who also led the 2025 lung-health study. Zheng conducted the research at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) alongside co-corresponding author S. W. Ricky Lee of the same institution and their colleagues, examining whether early sugar restriction also relates to long-term dementia risk, brain structure, and cognitive ability in older age.
“While growing evidence suggests that early-life nutrition can shape long-term health, remarkably little is known about whether sugar exposure during this period is associated with dementia many decades later,” Zheng told PsyPost. “We were particularly interested in addressing this knowledge gap because most dementia prevention research focuses on risk factors in middle and older age. The end of sugar rationing in the United Kingdom in September 1953 provided a unique natural experiment to investigate this question.”
The researchers analyzed data from the UK Biobank, a large health study that recruited middle-aged and older British adults between 2006 and 2010. Starting with 74,213 participants born between 1951 and 1956, the team excluded 6,582 people born outside the United Kingdom, 2,424 from multiple births such as twins or triplets, 79 adoptees, 208 people already diagnosed with dementia at recruitment, and 108 who withdrew from the project. This left a final sample of 64,737 adults who were an average of 54.6 years old at enrollment, 56.4 percent of whom were women.
Using each person’s birth date relative to the September 1953 policy change, the authors sorted participants into groups reflecting how long they experienced sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days from conception. In total, 40,963 participants experienced rationing: 10,682 were exposed in the womb only, 15,025 were exposed in the womb plus up to one year after birth, and 15,256 were exposed in the womb plus one to two years after birth. The remaining 23,774 participants were born after July 1, 1954, meaning they were conceived after rationing ended and grew up in an environment of unrestricted sugar.
The team tracked hospital admissions and death registries through July 1, 2023, to identify new diagnoses of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, and vascular dementia. To account for other differences between the groups, the statistical models controlled for age, sex, race, birthplace, birth month, inflation-adjusted food prices, average national fat intake at birth, maternal smoking, breastfeeding, and parental dementia history. The researchers also adjusted for adult household income, neighborhood socioeconomic status, smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and chronic illnesses such as heart, kidney, and liver disease.
In addition to tracking dementia diagnoses, the authors examined a subset of more than 7,500 participants who underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scans at an average age of 61.8 years, alongside roughly 6,400 to 20,600 participants who completed computerized cognitive assessments. These brain scans measured total brain volume, gray matter (the outer layer of brain tissue rich in nerve cell bodies), white matter (the deeper nerve fibers that connect different brain regions), the hippocampus, and white matter hyperintensities, which are bright spots on a scan that indicate small blood vessel damage and tissue wear.
Building on the 2024 research linking rationing to metabolic and vascular health, the team also tested whether adult type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure explained the link between early sugar restriction and dementia, and they checked two conditions considered unlikely to be affected by early sugar intake, type 1 diabetes and melanoma (a form of skin cancer), as negative controls.
Over the follow-up period, 504 out of 23,774 unexposed participants (about 2.1 percent) were diagnosed with all-cause dementia, including 227 cases of Alzheimer’s disease (about 1.0 percent) and 178 cases of vascular dementia (about 0.75 percent). In raw numbers, the rationed groups had slightly higher dementia rates, largely because they were born earlier and were more than two years older on average than the unexposed group, with 251 dementia cases among the 10,682 people rationed only in the womb (about 2.3 percent), 388 cases among the 15,025 people rationed through age one (about 2.6 percent), and 456 cases among the 15,256 people rationed for one to two years (about 3.0 percent). Once the researchers adjusted for age and other background variables, the rationed groups showed a lower risk of developing dementia at any given age, though the association for those exposed only in the womb was smaller and not statistically significant.
Compared with adults who never experienced rationing, those exposed to sugar rationing in the womb plus their first year of life had a 21 percent lower hazard (the rate at which new cases appear at a given age) of developing all-cause dementia and a 23 percent lower hazard of developing Alzheimer’s disease. The association was slightly stronger for those exposed in the womb plus one to two years after birth, who showed a 23 percent lower hazard of all-cause dementia and a 28 percent lower hazard of Alzheimer’s disease.
For vascular dementia, the estimates pointed in a similar direction, though the results were not statistically significant. Looking at the timing of diagnoses, experiencing rationing from conception through ages one to two was associated with delaying the onset of all-cause dementia by 2.55 years, Alzheimer’s disease by 2.87 years, and vascular dementia by 2.49 years.
“The magnitude of the associations was particularly noteworthy,” Zheng said. “These are population-level estimates rather than predictions for any individual, but even modest shifts in dementia occurrence could have meaningful public health implications given the growing global burden of the disease.”
The results were less robust in one additional analysis. When the researchers accounted for the possibility that participants would die of other causes before developing dementia, rationing exposure was still linked to a roughly 15 percent lower likelihood of all-cause dementia, but the associations with Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia were no longer statistically significant.
The link between early sugar rationing and dementia was stronger in women than in men, which the authors noted might relate to biological differences in how female neural circuits respond to early nutritional environments. The results held steady regardless of whether participants carried genetic variants of the apolipoprotein E gene that heighten Alzheimer’s risk. Mediation analyses indicated that lower rates of adult type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure accounted for 18.0 percent and 11.6 percent of the association, respectively, or 25.5 percent when combined, while birth weight accounted for just 2.7 percent. As expected, rationing exposure showed no association with type 1 diabetes or melanoma, and the primary dementia patterns were supported by a validation analysis in an independent British aging study, with an American cohort serving as a comparison group.
The brain imaging and cognitive test results aligned with the clinical dementia findings. Compared with the unexposed group, participants who experienced early-life sugar rationing had larger total gray matter volumes, averaging 618.9 cubic centimeters versus 618.5 cubic centimeters (an adjusted increase of 3.27 cubic centimeters), and smaller volumes of white matter hyperintensities, averaging 3.72 cubic centimeters versus 3.84 cubic centimeters (an adjusted reduction of 0.64 cubic centimeters).
Rationed participants also performed better on tests of complex processing speed, verbal and numerical reasoning, nonverbal pattern reasoning, and a timed test of visual attention that involves connecting numbered circles in order. Differences in total brain volume, white matter volume, hippocampal size, working memory, verbal memory, and a harder version of the connect-the-dots test that requires switching between numbers and letters were not statistically significant. These differences were modest: the gray matter difference amounted to about half a percent of total gray matter volume, and the cognitive differences were similarly small.
“What struck us most was how strongly early-life nutritional exposure appeared to be associated with brain health more than half a century later,” Zheng explained. “Beyond dementia diagnoses, we also observed favorable differences in brain MRI measurements, including greater gray matter volume and fewer white matter hyperintensities, alongside better performance on certain cognitive tests. The convergence of these findings across clinical, structural, and cognitive outcomes was especially interesting and suggested that the associations might reflect broader processes of brain aging.”
These results are consistent with research covered by PsyPost in December 2025, which tracked broad diet quality across the lifespan starting at age four rather than isolating sugar restriction during the first 1,000 days of life, and similarly found that healthier early nutritional habits were associated with better cognitive performance and a lower risk of late-life dementia. They also align with another study covered by PsyPost in November 2025, which examined how chronic sugar consumption caused memory impairment and Alzheimer’s-related brain pathology in adult rats rather than how early-life sugar restriction affects long-term dementia risk in humans, yet similarly linked high sugar exposure to neurodegenerative decline.
“Our findings suggest that the nutritional environment during pregnancy and early childhood may have consequences for brain health that extend across an entire lifetime,” Zheng told PsyPost. “The key message is not that people should eliminate sugar entirely, but rather that limiting excessive added sugar during these sensitive developmental periods may be beneficial. Importantly, our findings demonstrate associations, not definitive causation.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because this was an observational study that relied on birth dates during a historical policy change, the researchers did not have direct measurements of how much sugar individual pregnant mothers or infants actually consumed. Although national surveys confirm that household sugar purchases surged right after September 1953, personal eating habits within both the rationed and unrationed groups likely varied from family to family. Because exposure was determined entirely by birth date, the rationed participants were also older, so the findings depend on statistical adjustments for age; the authors checked this by confirming that dementia risk did not drift among never-rationed participants born at different times after the policy ended.
“One important distinction is that our study does not prove that reducing sugar intake in infancy directly prevents dementia,” Zheng noted. “Other dietary, social, or environmental differences associated with the rationing period may also have influenced the results. Furthermore, our findings should not be interpreted as advocating extremely restrictive diets during pregnancy or infancy; adequate and balanced nutrition remains essential for healthy development.”
Another consideration is the age and makeup of the study population. Because participants were born in the early to mid-1950s, they were only in their late 60s and early 70s by the end of the tracking period in 2023, meaning the study primarily captured relatively early cases of dementia rather than diagnoses occurring in the 80s and 90s.
In addition, the UK Biobank consists of volunteers who survived into middle age and tend to be healthier, wealthier, and predominantly white (over 96 percent of this sample), which may limit how well the findings apply to more diverse or disadvantaged populations. The authors suggest that future randomized trials testing practical nutritional counseling to limit added sugars during pregnancy and infancy could help establish how early dietary habits shape brain development and long-term cognitive resilience.
“We hope to better understand the biological mechanisms linking early-life nutrition with brain aging and neurodegenerative diseases,” Zheng said. “In this study, type 2 diabetes and hypertension together statistically accounted for approximately one-quarter of the observed association, suggesting that metabolic and vascular health may play a role. Future research should examine additional biological pathways, clarify the most sensitive developmental windows, and determine whether these findings can be replicated in other populations with more detailed dietary information. Ultimately, we hope this work will help inform evidence-based nutritional recommendations across the life course.”
“I believe one of the broader implications of our work is that dementia prevention may need to be considered from a much earlier life-course perspective,” Zheng added. “We often think of dementia as a disease of old age, but some of the factors associated with vulnerability or resilience may originate decades before symptoms appear. Understanding these early influences could open new opportunities for preventive research and public health strategies.”
The study, “Association of Sugar Restriction in Utero Through Age 2 Years on Dementia Risk Later in Life,” was authored by Jiazhen Zheng, Gregory Y.H. Lip, Zhuoni Zhang, and S. W. Ricky Lee.

We advocate for disputes to be addressed through peaceful means and resolved through dialogue with all coastal states. We expect all stakeholders, particularly the European Union, to display the same constructive will,” he stressed.

Iraqi court sentences six French men to life in prison for Islamic State membership
Italy
Unknown Publisher

BAGHDAD, Oct 27 - An Iraqi court on Tuesday sentenced six French nationals to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years after convicting them of membership in Islamic State, a Reuters witness inside the courtroom said.
The men were among 47 French Islamic State suspects transferred from detention facilities in northeast Syria to Iraq last year under a broader relocation arrangement coordinated by US forces and Iraqi authorities.
The presiding judge said the sentences were imposed under Iraq’s counterterrorism law for joining Islamic State and spreading fear. He added that the court had opted for life imprisonment rather than the death penalty because the defendants were young.
A seventh French national, aged 23, was given a 15-year sentence, according to the Reuters witness.
Abbas al-Maliki, one of the lawyers for the defendants, said the group would appeal the sentence in the Court of Cassation.
Iraq opened the trial of the French nationals last month.
Islamic State seized large parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014 before being driven from its self-declared caliphate by a US-led coalition and local forces in 2019. Many of the group’s militants were detained, although remnants of the jihadist organization continue to operate.
The United States announced in January that it had begun transferring Islamic State detainees from Syria to Iraq amid concerns about the security of detention facilities in northeast Syria after Kurdish-led forces lost control of parts of the region.

Melbourne Celebrates the Legend of Pinocchio During the 26th Italian Language Week
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:57:15 CET
18:57:15 KST

The 26th edition of Italian Language Week Around the World concluded on Sunday, October 25; this year’s theme was “A Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian.” Sponsored by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation under the high patronage of the President of the Republic, the Melbourne event featured an evening dedicated to Carlo Collodi as one of its highlights. On October 21, marking the 200th anniversary of the author’s birth, the Consulate General of Italy and the Italian Cultural Institute, in collaboration with the Italian Studies departments at the Universities of Melbourne, Monash, and La Trobe, presented the event “Pinocchio: 200 Years of Collodi in Literature, Film, and Creativity” at the University of Melbourne, under the patronage of the Carlo Collodi National Foundation and the National Committee for the Celebrations of the Bicentennial of Carlo Collodi’s Birth. In her opening remarks, Consul General Chiara Mauri noted how Pinocchio has spanned generations, borders, and various artistic disciplines, representing one of the most beautiful creative expressions of our literature. Following a presentation by Roberto Vezzani, secretary-treasurer of the National Committee and librarian of the Foundation, a panel of specialists from the three universities explored Collodi’s work through the various lenses of literature, history, gastronomy, iconography, and cinema, as well as translation and education. Italian students also presented a performance inspired by the puppet’s adventures, while an exhibition of historical editions accompanied the evening. Finally, the event provided an opportunity for the official introduction of the new director of the Italian Institute in Melbourne, Stefano Scaramuzzino. In addition to this initiative, the Consulate General and the Italian Cultural Institute promoted a program of events in Melbourne organized in collaboration with their partners: a singing performance in Italian by the “Piccole Voci Geniali” choir and students from Victorian schools participating in the “Student Talent Show” as part of the Italian Melbourne Festa & Expo; the “Pinocchio in Schools” project organized by the local Com.It.Es at the city’s two bilingual schools; the Poetry Recitation Contest, organized by the Dante Alighieri Society of Melbourne; and the “Globo Talk Show,” segments recorded by students from the bilingual schools “Brunswick South” and “Footscray” at the Italian radio and television station “Il Globo.”

LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Two men were charged on Tuesday under Britain’s National Security Act following last month’s security incident at the RAF Fairford military base, with prosecutors accusing one of them of trying to assist Iranian intelligence operations in Britain.
RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five British men were arrested outside the base in southwest England in the early hours of September 27.
The circumstances of the incident, which remain largely unexplained, attracted huge international attention, coming at a time of heightened concern about the security implications for Western states of the war between the United States and Iran.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier this month that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Tehran’s ambassador to Britain has denied.
British national Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, was charged with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service between August 31 and September 28, with police saying the country is believed to be Iran.
Nouman Essghir, a 24-year-old dual British-Iranian national who was first arrested outside RAF Fairford on September 27, was charged with one offence of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on August 22.
The pair will appear at London’s Westminster Magistrates’ Court later on Tuesday.
Police said that six other people, four of whom are British nationals who were arrested outside RAF Fairford on September 27, remain on police bail.
The decision to bail suspects after an apparent major incident had drawn scrutiny, but on Tuesday police said that decision had helped secure charges against the two men.
“We know the decisions made during our investigations can sometimes appear illogical to those on the outside, but I want to make it very clear that there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them,” said Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK.
“In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I have announced today.”

Soccer-Chinese brands drop Mbappe over alleged Mao meme comments
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
10:56:51 CET

By Casey Hall, Helen Reid, Clare Jim and Aadi Nair
SHANGHAI/HONG KONG/LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - France soccer captain Kylian Mbappe apologised on Tuesday after Chinese brands cut ties with him over comments referring to the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong, underscoring how swiftly international celebrities can come unstuck in a crucial market.
Mbappe, 27, is heard in a video saying the funniest meme he had seen of himself was one where his face had been photoshopped on to that of “some guy — I think he’s a Chinese dictator”, an apparent reference to the composite image of him and Mao.
“During a recent interview, I reacted to an image of myself,” Mbappe said in a statement. “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.”
“I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” he added. “This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry.”
In China, satire or jokes about Mao, modern China’s founding leader who ruled the country from 1949 until his death in 1976, are considered disrespectful and remain a social taboo.
Mbappe’s faux pas highlights the risks for athletes and brands in China’s huge market. Mbappe, one of the world’s most prominent athletes, has ties with firms including sportswear brand On Holding, hotel chain Accor and Lego.
Other major firms and organisations that have previously incurred the wrath of Beijing, Chinese netizens and media include fashion brand Dolce & Gabbana, Swiss watchmaker Swatch and the National Basketball Association.
“Mbappe’s team knew, or should have known, what the true cost of Chinese brand endorsements was all about,” said Terrence Burns, sports sponsorship expert and CEO of the T. Burns Sports Group. “Athletes today are their own media outlets and their teams should train them as such.”
‘WHAT DID HE SAY?’
Chinese state media outlet China Daily said Mbappe’s remark had “triggered a backlash among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence”.
Many Chinese media outlets on Tuesday condemned Mbappe’s apparent remarks, but did not repeat them.
“What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it,” the state-backed Global Times said.
“The message from Chinese consumers is clear: Respect is not optional; one doesn’t get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance.”
The apology did not convince everyone straight away. “Not accepted. Not forgiven!!,” one user wrote on China’s social media platform Weibo. Another wrote: “He doesn’t realise he was wrong. He just knows to be afraid now.”
Brands including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech as well as Eastroc Beverage said they were ceasing all cooperation with Mbappe, who plays for Real Madrid, effective immediately.
The companies said they “firmly oppose and have zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.”
China’s state television has halted broadcasts of all matches and events involving LaLiga and Mbappe, and all advertisements involving Mbappe have been removed, state-backed media outlet the Paper reported on Tuesday.
Spain’s LaLiga President Javier Tebas issued an apology on X and said his organisation deeply regretted the alleged comments that have caused discomfort and offence in China.
“We are taking the measures within our reach and working directly with our partners and interlocutors in China to overcome this situation,” Tebas wrote. “A relationship built over so many years cannot be damaged by a single episode.”
Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said it would listen to what Mbappe had to say after his apology, and “even more importantly” watch what he does.
“We hope La Liga, Real Madrid, and Mbappe himself will genuinely learn a lesson from this, offer a sincere apology, and thoroughly correct their mistakes,” it said in a statement.
Real Madrid declined to comment.
Denmark’s Lego, which has a Mbappe building set on sale in China, said it could not comment. The Mbappe set still featured on Lego’s Chinese website on Tuesday.
On Holding and Accor did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
TRENDING ON WEIBO
As of 0700 GMT, four topics related to Mbappe were still among the top 10 trending searches on Weibo. Some netizens called for China to “blacklist” Mbappe and reduce his commercial value to zero. These comments received hundreds of likes.
Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappe’s face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for. Mbappe has been nicknamed “the dictator” in the European press.
“In attempting to laugh at himself and his reputation of being a dictator in the locker room, he apparently crossed a red line he didn’t know was there,” said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.
In an interview with L’Equipe last month, Mbappe said that although aspects of the meme trend were harmless fun, the viral ones depicting him as a dictator showed “a lack of political and human awareness”.
A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry said words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people “will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society”.

Open, check, store: What changes once a packaged food is opened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:56:42 UTC
18:56:42 KST

That satisfying pop of a jar lid, the snap of a foil seal, or the smooth peel of a fresh film, we’ve all experienced it. It’s that reassuring moment that says, 
“
This food is fresh, untouched, and safe.”
But here’s the catch: the moment you break that seal, the safety bubble vanishes. While modern food packaging uses clever barrier technology and vacuum sealing to keep food pristine on store shelves, it isn’t bulletproof once opened. Opening a package starts the countdown, shifting the responsibility of keeping food safe straight into your hands.
What the numbers tell us about food safety at home
Improper post-opening handling isn't just a minor oversight. It's a major driver of global food waste and foodborne illness:
- 60% of global food waste happens at home: According to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) Food Waste Index Report [1] , households account for over 60% of all food wasted worldwide, equivalent to over 600 million tonnes of food per year. Misinterpreting date labels and letting opened food spoil prematurely are two primary drivers.
- 1 in 10 people fall ill annually: Estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO) [2] highlight that roughly 1 in 10 people worldwide fall ill every year from consuming contaminated food. A common contributor in domestic kitchens is improper temperature control and cross-contamination after packages are unsealed.
- The ‘best before’ confusion: Data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) shows that 30% to 40% of the food supply is lost or wasted [3] . A significant portion stems from consumer confusion surrounding unopened "Best Before" dates versus actual post-opening shelf life.
What happens when you break the seal?
Inside an unopened package, food lives in a controlled environment. Once the package is opened, that protection is broken, and three key changes can begin to occur:
- Air enters (oxidation): Oxygen in the air reacts with fats, oil and certain vitamins. Overtime, this can cause food to become rancid, colours to fade and flavours lose their punch.
- Moisture changes: Dry foods, such as chips or cookies, can absorb moisture from the air and lose their crispness. Other foods may lose moisture and gradually become dry or stale.
- Microorganisms are introduced: Mold spores, yeasts, and bacteria naturally present in the environment can come into contact with the food. Given the right conditions, these microorganisms may grow and contribute to spoilage. 
The simple open-check-store checklist
Keeping food fresh after opening doesn't require complex science. It only requires just a few quick habits:
Quick hacks for common kitchen staples
- Sauces & dips: Some condiments, such as ketchup, can remain shelf-stable until opened, but mayonnaise, pesto, and cream-based dressings belong in the fridge the second they are opened. Always check the label for storage instructions.
- Canned goods: Have leftover tomatoes, beans or other canned foods? Never leave them in an open metal can in the fridge. Transfer them into a clean glass or food-grade plastic container before refrigerating. This helps preserve quality and prevents unwanted flavour changes.
- Dairy & milk: Store opened milk and dairy products on the inner shelf of the refrigerator where temperatures are more consistent. Avoid storing them on the door shelves which experience greater temperature fluctuation.
- Grains & spices: Store spices, flour, rice and cereals into sealed glass jars to keep pantry pests and humidity away.
Packaging helps keep food safe and fresh until it reaches your kitchen, but proper handling after opening is just as important. Paying attention to storage instructions, resealing products carefully and maintaining good kitchen hygiene, ensures every bite stays as fresh and safe as it should.

HSL raises ticket prices and introduces a fare cap for contactless payments
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:56:37 EET
18:56:37 KST

Helsinki Regional Transport (HSL) is introducing a price cap for contactless payments. The change is meant to make it easier for passengers to choose between a single ticket and a day ticket. The change takes effect on Monday, 2 November.
The cap is calculated starting from the first ticket purchase. The system then adds up the prices of all tickets bought with the same payment method.
However, HSL notes that a physical payment card and mobile payments linked to the same card are treated as different payment methods.
Once the combined total reaches the price of a day ticket, no further charges are made for additional journeys.
The fare cap depends on the zones you travel in during the 24 hours. A two-zone 24-hour ticket is €10.60.
In a press release, HSL said the cap means passengers no longer have to estimate how many trips they will make during the day.
The fare cap applies only to adult single tickets paid with contactless payment — it doesn't cover tickets bought through the HSL app or with an HSL card.
Fares rise
The HSL board meanwhile decided on Tuesday to raise ticket prices by an average of 1.8 percent at the beginning of 2027. In the most popular AB zone, the price of an adult single ticket will go up by 1.5 percent, from €3.30 to €3.35.
Children's single tickets and single tickets in the 50 percent discount group will stay the same in all zones.

Pärnu property prices unaffected by Rail Baltic delay

Pärnu property prices unaffected by Rail Baltic delay
Real estate agents have said the postponement of the Rail Baltic deadline until 2032 is still too recent to be reflected immediately in Pärnu's real estate market. Projects already underway are continuing as planned.
This is not the first time that the completion deadline has been pushed back, and entrepreneurs and residents hope they will be able to travel on the track from Tallinn to the summer capital Pärnu by 2032.
Ingmar Saksing, a real estate agent at LVM Kinnisvara, said investors have factored this into their plans.
"Today we can talk about growing interest in the area where a terminal will be built, as in Ülemiste in Tallinn. Following the same logic, it is clear that property prices in this area and interest in the area are higher than before," he said.
The Part spa hotel will be completed by next autumn, adding 450 hotel beds to Pärnu. Sari Sopanen, head of the major development project, said the railway delay has not changed the hotel's development plans, but the completion of Rail Baltic would certainly help increase the number of customers.
"If Pärnu were connected to two international airports, Tallinn and Riga, then of course that would be a very, very big advantage for our industry and for us as well," Sopanen said.
"We believe in Pärnu, our location is ideal, it is a very good spot on Pärnu beach," she added.
Property prices in the summer capital have been steadily rising by two to three percent annually over the past decade, including inflation. The delay in Rail Baltic's completion has not caused any major jumps in prices, in either direction.
"People consider other reasons much more when deciding to change their place of residence, plus the fact that the arrival of the railway in Pärnu does not mean that everyone will want to move to Pärnu. Perhaps they will just come during the day and travel back home in the evening," said Terje Võrk, a real estate agent at Arco Vara.
In recent years, new real estate developments have sprung up in several parts of the city. Saksing said this is welcome, because when supply emerges, demand will follow.
"In total, 400 apartments are under construction and on offer, and at the current pace it will take up to two years to sell them, assuming no more are added," Saksing said.

Privacy group files complaints against Scale AI over alleged worker surveillance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:56:00 UTC
18:56:00 KST

Privacy group files complaints against Scale AI over alleged worker surveillance
- Privacy group noyb filed five complaints against Scale AI in four EU countries over alleged illegal worker surveillance on Outlier, a platform used to create AI training data.
- The complaints say up to 19 trackers recorded keystrokes and mouse movements, and workers faced repeated ID and face checks that may break EU biometric rules.
- noyb wants fines and a review of task assignment. DiPLab also found bonuses and game-like rewards pushed workers to complete many tasks fast.
AI generated
European digital privacy advocacy group NOYB filed five complaints against Scale AI in France, Italy, the Netherlands and Austria on Oct 27, alleging it illegally monitored freelance workers who produce training data for artificial intelligence models.
The complaints target Outlier, a platform it operates on which more than 900,000 freelancers perform various tasks that are recorded to create AI training data for clients such as Meta, OpenAI and Google. Meta owns 49% of Scale AI.
NOYB is asking regulators to fine Scale AI and examine how the platform assigns tasks.
“You don’t work when you want,” said Thomas Le Bonniec, who spent two years studying the platform for Paris-based research collective DiPLab. “You work when the platform wants you to and there are tasks available.”
Scale AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The complaints seen by Reuters said up to 19 trackers follow workers while they work, including recording keystrokes and mouse movements every few seconds. An investigation by DiPLab found the resulting file could be rebuilt into a video that replays a work session from start to finish.
Workers must also submit identification documents and face video to identity verification firm Persona. The complaints said the checks were invasive, repeated without explanation, and broke European Union rules on biometric data.
Outlier also uses game-like mechanisms, and bonuses are a key part of its incentive system, DiPLab found.
Outlier offered bonuses of US$100 (S$128) to US$200 for completing 200 tasks in 24 hours, Le Bonniec said, citing interviews with workers during his investigation. Italy’s data protection authority fined delivery platform Glovo in 2021 over similar gamification, he added.
Four workers asked Outlier for copies of their data between December 2025 and May 2026. None received an answer, the complaints said. REUTERS

Swiss bankruptcies set to reach record levels in 2026

Unknown Publisher

Swiss bankruptcies set to reach record levels in 2026
Economic concerns, high energy costs and rising interest rates are taking their toll on businesses. This is leading to a rise in corporate insolvencies worldwide.
In Switzerland, bankruptcies are even likely to reach a record high, as a study by Allianz Trade shows. The new Swiss insolvency law is also contributing to this.
Allianz Trade’s experts expect the sixth consecutive rise in Swiss corporate insolvencies in 2026. With 15,000 cases, this would mark an all-time high. This would represent a doubling compared with 2022, and even a tripling compared with pre-pandemic levels. These findings are set out in the Insolvency Report published on Tuesday by the trade credit insurer.
However, this “unprecedented” wave of insolvencies can only be partly attributed to the macroeconomic and financial challenges facing companies. “The new insolvency law, which has been in force since 2025, is largely responsible for the high number,” said Jan Möllmann, head of Allianz Trade in Switzerland, according to the press release.
More
Bankrupt debtors to get second chance in Switzerland
Möllmann went on to say that the insolvency law automatically leads to an increase in the number of companies against which insolvency proceedings are initiated. “We currently expect the situation to stabilise at this new, high level in 2027 and 2028.”
According to the study, corporate insolvencies worldwide are likely to rise by 5% in 2026 and by a further 1% in 2027, having already risen by 6% in 2025. Due to the persistently uncertain geopolitical and macroeconomic environment, the expected peak in insolvencies is shifting by one year to 2028. After that, the number of corporate insolvencies is likely to fall slightly.

Jordan says it killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on Syria
Oct 27 - Jordan said on Tuesday its forces had killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on southern Syria the previous evening, following a deadly church attack in Jordan that authorities linked to militants operating across the border.
The strikes, which followed a rare attack in Jordan, have inflamed tensions between the two US allies.
Jordan has been a longtime partner to the US in its fight against extremism, while the Islamist-led government of Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who wants to restore the country's relations with the West after overthrowing longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, said it was seeking to curb extremism.
Syria said the strikes killed seven people, including three children and a woman. Jordan regrets the civilian casualties, Government Communication Minister Mohammed al-Momani said in a post on X.
Jordan said on Monday its air force had struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's church attack were linked to "terrorist groups" based there. Jordanian security officials said separately that security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law following a shootout linked to the church attack, which killed nine people.
Local resident Salah Mahwash, speaking to Reuters during the funeral of four people including three children in Al-Mismiyah in southern Syria, said:
“At around 10 p.m., there was an explosion and the sound of aircraft overhead. We went to the site, and it was a poor family whose father had gone missing during the events and was in Sednaya prison.
"Today, as you can see, these are people just trying to make a living, tending to their sheep and goats and doing manual labour. We condemn what happened in the Jordanian state, of course.”
Attacks such as the church shooting are rare in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East. No group has claimed responsibility for the shooting, although Jordan said the militants it targeted in Syria were members of Islamic State.
Monday's strikes have nevertheless sparked anger in Syria. While the Jordanian military said they were conducted in coordination with Damascus, Syria's government said they were carried out without prior coordination. It also said it would hold an investigation.
Statements in recent days by Jordanian authorities that there appeared to have been no prior planning of the church attack have added to the confusion, seemingly at odds with Jordan's justification for Monday's cross-border strikes.
Syria's Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as a violation of the country's sovereignty.
It said, however, that Damascus was coordinating with Amman and would establish a joint security committee to strengthen border security and prevent similar incidents.
Last year, Jordan and Syria agreed to form such a committee to secure their border, combat arms and drug smuggling and work to prevent any resurgence of Islamic State militancy. REUTERS

U.S., UK and Australia test Saronic drone boats together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:46:41 UTC
18:46:41 KST

- Saronic Technologies fielded three Corsair autonomous boats with U.S., British and Australian forces at Maritime Big Play Pacific in San Diego.
- The boats ran pier resupply partly under denied communications and a trilateral sense-decide-effect mission within a mixed uncrewed fleet.
Saronic Technologies’ Corsair drone boats, the same type the U.S. military used to strike an Iranian naval base in July, have operated alongside forces from the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia at Maritime Big Play Pacific, the AUKUS partners’ largest demonstration of uncrewed and autonomous technology, held in San Diego this October.
The Texas company said it fielded three Corsairs across the three nations and that the boats ran several mission scenarios, including resupplying a pier with parts of the mission carried out while communications were denied, and a trilateral “sense, decide, effect” mission in which the Corsairs operated as part of a mixed fleet of uncrewed surface vessels supported by uncrewed aircraft.
Saronic said the boats were controlled through its Echelon software, integrated into the Common Control System used to command uncrewed vessels, and it credited the U.K. Royal Navy with giving the company the opportunity to take part, though it did not say which navy operated each boat or how long the boats ran without human input.
Maritime Big Play Pacific brought more than 40 government and industry technologies from the three countries to San Diego under AUKUS Pillar 2, the part of the partnership focused on advanced military technology, with the program organized around anti-submarine warfare, integrated lethality, contested resupply, and subsea and seabed warfare, while the Royal Navy led the anti-submarine warfare strand with its own uncrewed surface vessels, underwater gliders, drones and subsea vehicles.
The Corsair is a 7.3-meter (24-foot) autonomous surface vessel that can carry up to 453 kg (1,000 pounds) of payload, has a range of about 1,852 km (1,000 nautical miles) and a top speed above 35 knots, and the U.S. Navy awarded Saronic a $392 million production contract for the boats in December 2025.
Task Force 59 began fielding Corsairs in the Middle East in late March 2026, mostly for surveillance and support, and on July 12, 2026, three Corsairs struck Iran’s Bandar Abbas Naval Base, targeting a submarine and ship maintenance facility, in what U.S. Central Command called the first time American forces had used sea drones in combat operations.

27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Jordan said Tuesday that its airstrikes in southern Syria killed more than 20 ISIS (Daesh) terrorists and destroyed a major weapons depot, while Damascus condemned the operation as a violation of its sovereignty and reported several casualties.
 
Jordanian government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said the strikes were conducted after Amman had “run out of patience” with the movements of terrorist groups and threats to its national security.
 
“The operation was based on field intelligence aimed at neutralizing confirmed threats and planned terrorist attacks against Jordan,” he said.

“Jordan’s security and Syria’s security are one,” he said, adding that combating terrorism remains a shared objective.
 
Momani also linked the security threats to a recent attack on a church in Jordan’s Karak governorate that killed nine people.
 
He reiterated Jordan’s support for Syria’s security, unity and stability, particularly in the country’s south.
 
Syria condemns strikes
 
Syria’s Foreign Ministry strongly condemned Jordanian airstrikes targeting several locations in the southern Daraa province a day earlier, saying they were carried out without prior coordination with Damascus.
 
In a Tuesday statement, the ministry said the attacks killed and injured several people, describing the operation as an “unacceptable violation” of Syrian airspace and national sovereignty.
 
Syrian authorities had earlier reported that seven people were killed in the strikes.
 
Damascus also condemned Friday’s attack targeting St. George Greek Orthodox Church in Jordan, offering condolences to the victims’ families and wishing the injured a speedy recovery.
 
However, the ministry stressed that the Jordanian military operation inside Syrian territory was unacceptable and violated the principles of good neighborliness and bilateral coordination.
 
It warned that certain parties were seeking to undermine relations between the two countries and fuel tensions, without elaborating.
 
The ministry said coordination was underway with Jordan to establish an urgent joint civilian and security committee to investigate the incidents, prevent their recurrence and strengthen security cooperation along their shared border.

Iraqi court sentences six French men to life in prison for Islamic State membership
BAGHDAD, Oct 27 - An Iraqi court on Tuesday sentenced six French nationals to life in prison and a seventh to 15 years after convicting them of membership in Islamic State, a Reuters witness inside the courtroom said.
The men were among 47 French Islamic State suspects transferred from detention facilities in northeast Syria to Iraq last year under a broader relocation arrangement coordinated by US forces and Iraqi authorities.
The presiding judge said the sentences were imposed under Iraq's counterterrorism law for joining Islamic State and spreading fear. He added that the court had opted for life imprisonment rather than the death penalty because the defendants were young.
A seventh French national, aged 23, was given a 15-year sentence, according to the Reuters witness.
Abbas al-Maliki, one of the lawyers for the defendants, said the group would appeal the sentence in the Court of Cassation.
Iraq opened the trial of the French nationals last month.
Islamic State seized large parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014 before being driven from its self-declared caliphate by a US-led coalition and local forces in 2019. Many of the group's militants were detained, although remnants of the jihadist organization continue to operate.
The United States announced in January that it had begun transferring Islamic State detainees from Syria to Iraq amid concerns about the security of detention facilities in northeast Syria after Kurdish-led forces lost control of parts of the region. REUTERS

Justice Department Files More Charges Against James Comey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

The Justice Department has brought charges against former FBI Director James Comey for the third time in 13 months, this time related to alleged leaks of national security information to the media.
According to court documents filed earlier this month and unsealed on Monday, federal prosecutors are accusing Comey of “willfully” mishandling information related to national defense in October 2016, resulting in the information appearing in media reports.
“Having reason to believe such information could be used to injure the United States and to the advantage of any foreign nation,” the court document said Comey “knowingly and willfully communicated, delivered, transmitted, and caused that information to be communicated, delivered, and transmitted to a person not entitled to receive it.”
The inquiry is the latest attempt to prosecute Comey, who is a prominent critic of President Donald Trump. Trump fired Comey in 2017 while Comey was leading the FBI investigation into potential ties between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. The first Trump Administration cited a memo related to Comey’s handling of the FBI investigation into Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton’s emails. Since then, Trump has publicly called for criminal investigations into Comey and celebrated the indictments he’s faced.
In a video posted on Monday, Comey said the latest investigation was an attempt to politically persecute him.
“They’re back, again,” Comey said. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.”
“I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people,” he added.
Comey’s attorneys argued in court filings that the alleged leaks had already been investigated twice during the first Trump Administration in 2017 and 2019, and neither had resulted in charges.
The Justice Department has pursued a number of investigations and indictments against prominent Democrats in recent weeks, appearing to break with the unofficial “unwritten 60-day rule” of avoiding filing new charges or taking public investigatory action that could influence an approaching election. Earlier this month, the Department secured a search warrant for the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D, Minn.), who called the effort “the latest escalation in [Trump’s] campaign of political intimidation.” The DOJ also secured an indictment against Virginia Senate Leader Louise Lucas, who led the Democrats’ counter-effort against Republican gerrymandering, on drug trafficking and money laundering charges. Lucas denied the allegations and said she would fight back against an attempt by “people in power … to silence those who stand up to them.”
What to know about the new Comey charges
According to court documents, prosecutors allege that around Oct. 4 and 5, 2016, Comey directed FBI staff to speak with the New York Times “about specific accuracy concerns” related to “misinformation which had appeared” in a Reuters report about Yahoo’s cooperation with U.S. surveillance.
In doing so, prosecutors contend, Comey “illegally transferred classified information.”
The Times article had described how Yahoo had adapted its existing email filtering system, used to detect spam, malware, and child sexual abuse material, to comply with a secret surveillance order to search messages for a computer “signature” associated with communications by a foreign, state-sponsored terrorist organization. The article said the Justice Department had obtained the order from a Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court judge in 2015 and that Yahoo was barred from disclosing it.
A spokesperson for the Times said the newspaper “does not comment on the sourcing behind our reporting, but we know from experience that prosecutions like this one are designed to discourage sources from providing journalists with the kind of valuable and illuminating information that the public needs to know.”
Comey’s lawyers argued in a motion to dismiss the case that the Trump Administration did not file an indictment within the 10-year statute of limitations. On Oct. 5, prosecutors filed the charges in a criminal information under seal in Federal District Court in Washington, which does not require approval from a grand jury or a judicial finding of probable cause, but have not obtained an indictment.
Previous charges against Comey
The Justice Department has brought multiple charges against Comey during Trump’s second term. It secured an indictment against him in September 2025 over allegations that he made false statements to Congress in 2020 related to alleged leaks to the media. The charges were thrown out by a federal judge in November, concluding that the prosecutor, Lindsey Halligan, had been unlawfully appointed.
Comey was also indicted in April over allegedly making a threat against Trump by posting on Instagram a photograph of seashells on a North Carolina beach arranged to spell “86 47.” Prosecutors argued that the arrangement was intended as a threat “to kill” Trump, who is the 47th President. Comey, who deleted the post after initial backlash, said he did not intend the photograph to be a threat against Trump, and that he understood the numbers to be a “political message.” The numbers “86” have commonly been used to mean “to throw out” or “to refuse service to,” according to Merriam-Webster, but have also been used in some instances to mean “to kill.”
That case is set to go to trial in North Carolina in February 2027.
Earlier on Monday, a federal judge in New York ruled that the Justice Department had unlawfully fired Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, in July 2025. The judge ordered her retroactive reinstatement with back pay, concluding that the Trump Administration had violated the Constitution and federal law by claiming the President had executive authority to fire civil servants.

Flavio Bolsonaro Barred From Travel Amid Money Laundering Investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Brazil’s Supreme Court has ordered police to confiscate the passports of Flávio Bolsonaro as part of a criminal investigation related to a money laundering scheme.
Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the ruling, which became public on Monday, a day after Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, lost the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro is being investigated for alleged links to a Brazilian lawyer, Willer Tomaz, who is accused of laundering more than $1 billion through a fraud scheme, the New York Times reported.
Bolsonaro, who has cast the investigation as political persecution, said in a social media video on Monday afternoon that the seizure of his travel documents was an attempt at intimidating him after he lost the election.
The action could inflame political tensions amid claims from Brazil’s right wing and abroad that the election was unfair. Bolsonaro initially said he would seek to annul the vote, although his Liberal Party later conceded defeat. In the video posted Monday, the right-wing senator said he would now seek to have Lula’s ticket disqualified, citing alleged disinformation and “vote buying.” He also said he would organize the opposition in Congress to Lula’s government.
“I wasn’t the one who lost,” he said. “The system won.”
Donald Trump, an ally of the Bolsonaros, said on Monday that the election appeared “rigged.” The U.S. President did not provide evidence for his claim.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” Trump said.
“I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” he added. “The extension given was very strange.”
Brazil’s Supreme Court had granted a two-hour extension to voting on Sunday, citing transport issues raised by Lula’s campaign. Bolsonaro’s campaign had separately requested a two-hour extension due to heavy rainfall in certain areas. Lula won the election by more than 4 million votes. Roughly 0.03% of the total votes—or less than 35,000 votes—were recorded in the extra two hours. Vice President Geraldo Alckmin told Rede Vanguarda that Trump’s claims were “completely wrong.”
Bolsonaro is also being investigated over alleged links to a disgraced banker connected to a corruption scheme. Bolsonaro allegedly raised millions of dollars from the banker to fund a biopic about his father.
Here’s what to know about the investigation.
What to know about the money laundering inquiry
The inquiry into Bolsonaro stems from a federal probe into unauthorized deductions from pension payments made by Brazil’s social security agency. The broader operation, launched in April 2025, investigated associations suspected of collecting unauthorized membership fees from pension benefits.
Evidence from the probe led investigators to examine suspected money laundering involving betting platforms and financial transactions linked to Tomaz, who denies wrongdoing.
Police reportedly discovered that Bolsonaro had “master user” access to bank accounts belonging to Alcazar Holdings, a company owned by Tomaz. In May 2025, a person working for Tomaz asked the bank to remove Bolsonaro’s access to the accounts, local media outlets BPMoney and Times Brasil reported earlier this month, citing police findings. Both Bolsonaro and Tomaz deny having a joint account or financial ties.
The order required Bolsonaro to surrender his passports and barred him from contacting Tomaz. Bolsonaro said he would comply with the order and that he had “never considered” leaving Brazil. He said that the ruling came after his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, had said on a podcast last week that he should leave the country if he lost the election.
Criticisms of Brazil’s justice system
Bolsonaro has repeatedly criticized Brazil’s judiciary and described the investigations into him as politically motivated. The country’s Supreme Court generally assigns cases through a lottery system, and the money laundering investigation was assigned to de Moraes on Oct. 16.
De Moraes was the lead justice in last year’s trial of Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to accept his election loss in 2022. A five-member panel of Supreme Court justices convicted Jair Bolsonaro, by a 4-1 vote, of attempting to overturn his election defeat and sentenced him to 27 years and three months in prison, which he is serving under house arrest due to poor health. Prosecutors alleged that the plot included plans to assassinate Lula. Jair Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.
In June, a Supreme Court panel unanimously convicted Eduardo Bolsonaro of coercion in judicial proceedings. Prosecutors alleged he had attempted to lobby the Trump Administration to use tariffs and sanctions, including on de Moraes, to pressure judicial authorities to drop its prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro. He was sentenced to four years and two months in prison, but remains in Texas, where has lived since 2025.
De Moraes has also faced scrutiny over reported ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the former owner of Banco Master, whose financing of a film about Jair Bolsonaro is the subject of a separate inquiry into Bolsonaro. The New York Times reported, citing a police dossier, that Vorcaro sent text messages to de Moraes asking for help to avoid arrest. In messages to other associates, Vorcaro reportedly mentioned paying millions to the law firm of de Moraes’s wife. De Moraes has denied wrongdoing and said he never acted to favor Vorcaro or Banco Master.
De Moraes also clashed with tech billionaire Elon Musk in 2024 over court orders to block accounts on Musk’s social media platform X. De Moraes temporarily suspended the platform in Brazil after it failed to comply with judicial requirements, which Musk had described as “the most draconian demands of any country on Earth.”

Is an Under-Sink Reverse Osmosis System Worth It? Benefits, Costs, and Drawbacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:35:00 UTC
18:35:00 KST

That funny taste in your tap water may be a harmless nuisance—or it may be cause for serious concern. Either way, you can do something about it by installing a reverse osmosis (RO) water filtration system in your home.
Stand-alone RO systems and pitchers sit on your countertop and generally require manual refilling from the tap. You’ll save space and avoid the hassle of constantly refilling the unit by installing an under-sink or under-counter model that connects directly to your plumbing lines. Either way, RO systems aren’t cheap. But for some homeowners, they may be an invaluable investment.
Featured in this Article
What Is Reverse Osmosis?
Osmosis is the movement of molecules—usually water—through a semipermeable membrane that blocks larger particles like salts and sugars from passing through. After osmosis, the concentration of particles on both sides of the membrane ends up in equilibrium. It’s how plants get water from the soil, and it’s how your kidneys filter junk out of your blood.
While osmosis is a spontaneous phenomenon that happens naturally, reverse osmosis requires pressure to force water through a membrane in the other direction, effectively removing all of those compounds from the water to render it pure. It’s how salt is removed from seawater to make it drinkable, and it’s one way tap water can be purified in your home.
RO differs considerably from traditional filtration systems, which rely on physical barriers, typically activated carbon, to manually capture particles that pass through. Eventually, these filters become saturated with sediments and other matter and have to be replaced. While carbon filters are fairly blunt, able to capture larger particles of at least 0.1 microns in size, RO systems have a much finer-grained membrane that captures contaminants on a microscopic level (typically down to 0.0001 microns).
Carbon filters can make your water taste and smell better, but with RO you are getting much, much cleaner water than what that inexpensive Brita filter can muster. (That said, RO can’t capture everything, and carbon filters are still useful for capturing certain volatile organic compounds through adsorption. Most RO systems also have an additional carbon filtration system included.)
Note that two types of RO systems are available: Tanked RO systems filter water slowly (albeit passively, without electricity) and sequester it in a (rather large) tank under your sink. Today, tankless RO systems are more popular, processing water on demand but requiring electricity to keep things flowing expeditiously. Tankless systems are considerably more expensive due to their inherent complexity.
What Are the Real Risks of Contaminants in Water Today?
“US tap water is safe for most people most of the time,” says John Voll, an industrial water treatment veteran and the founder of Tap & Air, a website that monitors water and air quality for hundreds of municipalities. “The problems are local, not universal.”
The first step to understanding your personal risk is to gauge whether your own water is up to snuff by simply looking up its most recent data report online. The Safe Drinking Water Act requires community water systems to publish an annual report on the quality of water they’re delivering, due by July 1 each year.
These are heady documents, so to keep things simple, Voll says to keep your eye on three key pollutant metrics: lead, nitrate or arsenic, and PFAS (so-called forever chemicals popular in nonstick cookware and other products). While the first two are serious issues, they’re fairly rare today. PFAS, however, are a particularly significant problem across the country. Voll says that 98 of the 200 largest US cities have at least one PFAS compound detected in their water supply. Reverse osmosis systems can handle them—as well as lead and other compounds. Carbon filters usually can’t.
“Most people don't need RO,” Voll says, “but some households clearly do, and the way to tell is to read your own water report first.”
What Are the Drawbacks of Using an RO System?
RO systems come with a host of downsides, but most are related in some fashion to cost.
- RO wastes water: The particulars of RO technology have historically meant it requires a large amount of unprocessed tap water to create a small amount of purified water, sometimes up to 4 gallons or more of tap to 1 gallon of clean water (called the pure-to-drain ratio). In recent years that number has dramatically shifted, with 4 gallons of tap water producing up to 3 gallons of clean water, or a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio.
- Filters are costly: RO systems can require up to six different filtration cartridges that must be replaced every year or two, depending on use. Much like printer ink, these costs can be easily overlooked when making your initial purchase. Plan to spend $50 to $200 annually on replacement cartridges, but check prices before you buy.
- RO can strip “good” minerals from your water: Calcium, magnesium, and potassium are all unable to pass through the RO membrane. RO systems also remove fluoride from your water, which many users may not desire and which dentists abhor. Some RO systems can remineralize water and/or raise the pH level of the processed water thanks to additional cartridges—but these, of course, mean further expense on replaceables.
- Plan for professional installation (and additional financial outlays): I try not to DIY too much when there’s even a remote potential for a water leak, so I get a plumber involved for installations like these. And since most RO systems require their own faucet, you’ll need to prepare to have a new hole drilled into your countertop for your tap if you don’t already have one available.
Do You Need an Under-Sink RO System?
Based on my analysis of my city’s water report, no I don’t really need an RO system, as there’s nothing hazardous to worry about. However, as the linked report notes, our water supplier uses chloramine as a disinfectant, and drinking that chloramine-treated water straight from the tap has a slight but noticeable, off-putting taste. This is exacerbated by the extreme hardness of the water; this part of Texas is basically built on top of nothing but limestone, and the resulting amount of calcium carbonate in the water can add a slightly bitter flavor, as well.
For me, RO is all about the way the water tastes. Any lingering contaminants that are removed along the way are just a bonus.
I tested the Waterdrop X12 for this story, hiring a plumber to remove a well-aged unit under the sink and replace it with this more capable one. The job was done in less than an hour.
Under-sink RO filters are separate from your existing plumbing, and most use three color-coded lengths of tubing to tie into it. One connects to your incoming water supply through an adapter valve, one clips into your wastewater drainpipe via an included fitting, and one connects to the faucet. I am confident I could have made these connections on my own—especially since I was replacing an existing system—but I’ve seen how even a small water leak can lead to devastating problems and was happy for the peace of mind that professional oversight supplied.
Once installed and powered up, the X12 launches a 35-minute priming process designed to flush the filters before first use. It seems like an awfully long time for the sink to run, and it is. If you have some way to capture and use all this extra water, plan ahead to collect it. After the session completed (it stops automatically), I was ready to start sipping from the tap.
The X12 is exceedingly simple to use. Tap the LED-equipped button on top of the faucet to start or stop the flow of water, or twist the same button to dial in the number of ounces you want to dispense (up to 999) before depressing it. This way, you can drop your 64-ounce Stanley Quencher in the sink and walk away without having to wait around or worry about an overflow, with a digital timer first offering a measurement of your water’s current TDS (total dissolved solids), then counting down the ounces as they’re dispensed. The good news is that you won’t have to wait long: The X12 blasts water out of its spigot faster than my kitchen sink does—a far cry from the sad dribble of H2O my old RO system provided.
The unit can also be switched into one of two alternate operating modes, including an energy-saving mode (which quiets the device) and “flow mode,” which is designed for high-use households. Both require pressing certain button combinations on the filtration unit. I have used the device in all three modes, and (contrary to other reviews I’ve seen) I’ve never found it to be noisy at all, even though it’s located just 20 feet from my bed.
As for the water, it tastes great. The remineralization feature and pH adjustment (to about 7.5, which I confirmed with a pH test strip) give the water a pleasant tang while avoiding any harshness or chemical flavors. Unfortunately it doesn’t come out particularly cold, which means having to add non-RO ice to the glass to chill it down. First-world problem, I know.
I was especially pleased to discover that the X12 has one of the best water efficiency rates in the business, with a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio (3 gallons of pure water production to 1 gallon lost). Replacement filters (three are needed in total) are sold à la carte for $30 to $160 each.
For an even more powerful version—ideal for larger households—consider the Waterdrop X16, which uses the same cartridges and offers the same features as the X12. WIRED editor Kat Merck, whose municipal water supply does contain PFAS, has had one installed for a year and a half without any maintenance or reliability issues.
