Battlefield in Kherson Region’s island area is now “transparent”,  military says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:34:37 UTC
18:34:37 KST

Battlefield in Kherson Region’s island area is now “transparent”, military says
Pavlo Drohal, spokesperson for Ukraine’s 30th Marine Corps, told Ukrinform about the situation.
“As for the island area in the Dnipro River delta, the enemy continues to make systematic attempts to advance onto the islands. They try to reach them in small boats, using small assault groups, and attempt to establish positions there so they can infiltrate closer to the right bank. Given the challenging geography and the large number of islands — this is not just the Dnipro River proper, but also its tributaries, forming an extensive island zone with a complex network of waterways — they continue these attempts systematically. The difference is that we can see them because technology makes the battlefield ‘transparent,’ and the airspace is under constant surveillance,” Drohal said.
According to him, Ukrainian defenders spot and destroy Russian troops, in most cases as soon as they begin moving. In autumn, the enemy is trying to use fog and rain as cover, but the outcome remains the same: these groups are destroyed.
“Regarding the attempt to land in Kherson’s Korabel neighborhood, yes, such an attempt was made last week. It was unsuccessful because the enemy was spotted, targeted with weapons, and destroyed,” the spokesperson said.
He added that rumors suggesting an enemy sabotage and reconnaissance group might nevertheless have landed and hidden in the neighborhood were unfounded.
“That is impossible. Those who attempted to land were destroyed. Our defenders are monitoring the area very closely and keeping track of everything happening there,” Drohal emphasized.
He also noted that Russian forces had conducted intensive assaults in the island area in spring and early summer, operating “nonstop.” At the time, there could be as many as 50 assaults a month. The number of attacks subsequently declined: there were no such attempts in July, but they resumed in August and continue to this day.
“In other words, the enemy is experiencing something of a seasonal surge. It is once again imagining that it can advance toward the islands, establish a foothold, and set up positions there. But doing so is extremely difficult in practical terms, and given our countermeasures and constant surveillance, it is virtually impossible,” the spokesperson stressed.
However, Drohal said these failed attempts had not deterred the Russian military command, which continued to send assault groups on missions that amounted to a death sentence, showing little regard for its personnel. Russian servicemen receive some training for combat in these conditions, he added, but the enemy’s assault groups “are not particularly well supplied.”
As for Kherson city, Drohal stressed that Ukrainian forces were doing everything possible to protect it. Although Russian forces launch a huge number of drones, Ukrainian defenders destroy or suppress 90–93% of them.
“We are equally successful in targeting enemy artillery along the Dnipro River axis. Since the beginning of summer, we have destroyed or damaged around 150 enemy artillery systems. Once a gun starts operating in our area, it is tracked almost immediately and survives for only two to three days. The Russian command shows little regard for its artillery either,” the spokesperson said.
The number of artillery attacks in autumn has fallen by a factor of 2.5 compared with spring. While there were around 2,000–2,500 attacks in spring, the current figure is approximately 1,000–1,200, Drohal said.
As reported, Russian artillery shelling along the Dnipro River axis has decreased significantly as Ukrainian Defense Forces successfully destroy Russian artillery systems.

Two men face UK national security charges following an incident near RAF Fairford, with police suspecting Iranian state involvement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

UK: 2 charged after incident near US-used airbase
October 27, 2026
British prosecutors said Tuesday that two men had been charged under the National Security Act in connection with a September incident near RAF Fairford, an airbase used by US forces to launch strikes on Iran.
US bombers were withdrawn from Fairford on security grounds shortly after the arrests immediately after the incident.
What have police said about the Fairford suspects?
The Crown Prosecution Service charged Mohmed A., 24, of London, with engaging in conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Counterterrorism police chief Laurence Taylor said investigators believed the country involved was Iran.
Nouman E., 24, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on August 22. Both men were due to appear in court later Tuesday.
Nouman E. was initially arrested near the Gloucestershire base on September 27 and rearrested on October 20.
A separate suspect, a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national also arrested on October 20, was released without charge over the suspected intelligence offense. He remains on bail following an October 1 arrest on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five other men also remain on police bail.
How did the Fairford investigation begin?
Armed police responded to reports of three suspicious vehicles near the base on September 27 and arrested five men. Scores of residents were evacuated as police and military bomb-disposal experts searched the area for explosives.
Police have said they consider Iranian state involvement "highly likely."
"We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state," said Laurence Taylor, head of UK counterterrorism policing.
He said police were working with MI5, Britain's domestic intelligence service, to counter the threat and urged the public to report concerns.
Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said it considers bases used to attack its territory legitimate targets.

====================================================================================================

A decade after liquor ban, Bihar faces a new drug question: What the numbers reveal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

NCB destroyed 1,170.15 kg of seized narcotics worth Rs 4.54 crore in Patna, Bihar, across four cases to prevent their recirculation in September (Credit: NCB's X)
Punjab is set to go to polls in 2027, and the BJP, seeking to form its first government in the state, has made the drug menace a major election issue. The party has been targeting the ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) over its handling of the problem. Union home minister Amit Shah has even promised to make Punjab "drug-free" by December 2029 if the BJP comes to power.But AAP has hit back. Its national convener Arvind Kejriwal questioned the BJP over the drug problem in states where it is in power, including Bihar, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Goa, asking why the same deadline had not been set for them.The political exchange has also put the focus on Bihar, where alcohol has been banned for a decade but recent drug seizures have raised fresh concerns. More than 4.13 lakh intoxicating injections were seized in Patna in the first eight months of 2026, while investigations have uncovered heroin consignments, codeine-based cough syrup and networks involved in preparing and distributing narcotics.But what do these seizures actually reveal? Is Bihar witnessing a rise in drug consumption, or is the state increasingly becoming a transit route for narcotics headed elsewhere? And has a decade of prohibition had any bearing on the availability and use of other intoxicants? Here's what the data reveals
Does Bihar have a new drug problem?
More than 4.13 lakh intoxicating injections seized in Patna in the first eight months of 2026.
A sharp rise in smack seizures. Growing quantities of codeine-based cough syrup being intercepted. Across Bihar, recent drug seizures and investigations point to a changing narcotics landscape, raising questions about what is entering the state, where it is going and who is using it.But do these seizures signal a growing drug problem within Bihar, or are they exposing the scale of a trafficking network that uses the state as a transit route? Police have traced consignments from the Northeast and Nepal-linked routes, while investigations in Patna have uncovered alleged local networks involved in preparing and distributing narcotics.The answers are not straightforward. Five years of seizure data show sharp fluctuations rather than a consistent rise across substances. Meanwhile, a debate over Bihar’s liquor prohibition has raised another question about whether the use of alternative intoxicants has changed since the ban came into force in 2016.What do the numbers reveal?Bihar’s drug seizure data over five years shows that ganja accounted for the largest quantities seized among the major narcotics listed, while seizures of heroin fluctuated sharply. Ganja seizures rose from 16,607 kg in 2020 to 33,603 kg in 2021, before falling to 23,023 kg in 2022 and 13,129 kg in 2023. They increased again to 18,356 kg in 2024.Heroin seizures fell from 363.77 kg in 2020 to 9.62 kg in 2021, before rising to 31.13 kg in 2022, 27.37 kg in 2023 and 53.35 kg in 2024. Hashish seizures also varied, peaking at 395.12 kg in 2021 before declining to 195 kg in 2024.A person whose circle consumes drugs said, on the condition of anonymity, that marijuana remained the most widely consumed substance in their social circle and that they had not noticed a significant shift in preferences towards other drugs.“In most circles, marijuana is most widely consumed, and I don't think synthetic drugs have made their way to Bihar,” the person said.The data records smaller seizures of other substances, including ATS, cocaine and LSD in certain years. While these figures show fluctuations in the quantities of narcotics seized, they do not establish a steady year-on-year rise in drug trafficking or consumption. Seizure figures reflect what enforcement agencies intercept and, on their own, cannot establish how many people use drugs or whether drug abuse is increasing in Bihar.
Where are the drugs coming from?
Police say a significant share of narcotics reaching Patna comes from the Northeast. The routes and methods of transportation vary according to the size of a consignment.Investigations have also pointed to supply chains passing through multiple states. In September, four people were arrested near JP Setu in Patna with 274 gm of heroin. Police traced the consignment to Assam, from where it allegedly travelled to Tamkuhi in Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh, before being sent towards Patna.Bihar’s location along the Nepal border adds another dimension to the problem. On October 25, Motihari Police, in a joint operation with the Bihar Special Task Force, seized smack valued at Rs 4 crore near Raxaul, close to the India-Nepal border.
Cops suggest that drugs in Bihar enters from multiple states
In a separate operation, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence’s Muzaffarpur unit and the Bihar STF busted a suspected network involved in smuggling Nepal-origin charas into India. Two people were arrested and 5.14 kg of charas, valued by officials at Rs 5.14 crore, was seized. Investigators said the consignment was intended for onward transportation to Indore in Madhya Pradesh.The cases point to Bihar’s role as a route for narcotics moving between regions. However, seizures along transport corridors do not establish how much of the intercepted supply is consumed within the state.
Is the trade limited to transportation?
Police investigations suggest that local networks are also involved in storage, preparation and distribution.In March, police found a rented room in Patna’s Ramakrishna Nagar area allegedly being used to prepare smack. A flat in Alamganj was allegedly used for distribution. Police recovered 1.68 kg of brown sugar and cash, along with cheques worth around Rs 70 lakh issued in the name of a police officer.The trade is not confined to substances traditionally associated with narcotics smuggling. Pharmaceutical products have also featured in investigations. In May, the DRI seized 7,500 bottles of codeine-based cough syrup from a pickup van outside Patna’s Rajendra Nagar Terminal. Investigators found that the consignee’s drug licence had been cancelled and that the firm did not exist at its stated address.Such cases raise questions about how pharmaceutical products enter illicit supply chains, how they are distributed and whether existing monitoring systems are able to detect diversion from legitimate channels.A Patna high court order has raised questions about how narcotics can travel long distances before being intercepted.In an order dated September 15, the court expressed concern over two minor boys who had travelled from Assam to Bihar in a car without a registration certificate. The vehicle was intercepted near Patna, and the directorate of revenue intelligence recovered more than 60 kg of cannabis from a concealed compartment.The court questioned how the vehicle had travelled uninterrupted from Assam to Bihar while carrying a commercial quantity of cannabis.Has prohibition changed pattern of substance use?Bihar banned the sale and consumption of alcohol in April 2016 under a policy introduced by the Nitish Kumar government. The prohibition was intended, among other objectives, to reduce domestic violence and encourage households to spend money on more productive needs.A research paper by the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), titled Macro Perspective of Bihar's Development Achievements, Unfinished Agenda, and the Way Forward, has questioned whether the ban achieved its intended outcomes.The paper said reported crimes against women had not declined following prohibition and that total reported crimes against women increased over the post-2016 period. It also pointed to concerns about the expansion of illicit liquor trade, enforcement challenges, corruption and the use of alternative intoxicants, including illicit drugs."In tandem, there was a significant rise in illegal liquor trade leading to higher alcohol consumption, increased crime and corruption, and an increase in the use of alternative additive substances, such as illicit drugs," the paper said.The authors argued that Bihar should reconsider prohibition and restore alcohol excise duty to historical levels. They estimated that doing so could increase the state’s own revenues by 14-15%.Some residents also believe prohibition may be one factor behind the availability of other intoxicants, although personal accounts cannot establish a direct link between the ban and drug consumption.“I would argue that it is a byproduct of the prohibition in the state, but that isn't the full picture,” another person who spoke on condition of anonymity said, referring to the perceived increase in drug availability.The person said their observations were based on the experiences of people in their social circle who use drugs, adding that young people and those in their 30s appeared to be among the users they had noticed.“In a state like Bihar, with a large chunk of youth population that haven't so far been backed with job opportunities, [this] has also contributed to the rise of drug consumption in the state,” the person said.They also flagged a lack of awareness about addiction and the support available to people who use drugs.“I feel like there is a lack of awareness against remedial methods, like what to do if someone you know has become addicted to drugs, what are you supposed to do then. I feel like there is a lack of rehabilitation system and awareness among the people needed to curb the drug menace,” the person said.
Is Bihar seeing a rise in consumption or a rise in detection?
The distinction matters because seizures measure what enforcement agencies intercept, not the total volume of drugs entering the market or being consumed.Bihar’s prohibition and narcotics enforcement policies also form part of a wider debate over how the state measures the effectiveness of its policing. A rise in seizures can reflect an increase in trafficking, improved detection or a combination of both.Bihar minister Madan Sahni has rejected the charge that rising seizures indicate a failure of prohibition. He said the increase was not confined to Bihar but was a phenomenon seen in other states as well."I must say that due to the alertness of the officials concerned, the quantity of the seizure of substances prohibited under the NDPS Act has increased in the state, but at the same time, people should know that the majority of the prohibited substances seized in Bihar are meant for supply to other states," he said.Sahni added that intercepting consignments within Bihar could create the impression that the drugs were intended for local consumption, even when they were being transported elsewhere. He also defended prohibition, saying it had been successful.The minister’s argument points to an important gap in the available figures. Without comparable data on drug use, treatment demand, drug-related health emergencies and the destinations of intercepted consignments, it is difficult to determine how much of the rise reflects local consumption.
RJD MP Manoj Kumar Jha, meanwhile, cited a media report and said the situation was out of control."An entire generation has been ruined. This is what happens when the government has no control. The situation here is completely out of control..." he said.
Does Bihar have a new drug problem?
Bihar’s recent seizure figures and investigations point to a changing narcotics landscape. Police have reported sharp increases in some categories, identified supply routes running through several states and uncovered alleged local networks involved in preparation and distribution. Seizures near the Nepal border have also highlighted the state’s role in cross-border trafficking.But the central question remains unresolved. Is Bihar facing a growing drug-consumption problem, a trafficking problem that extends beyond its borders, or both?

Trump's son spent two days hunting in Mongolia with a Russian oligarch
The eldest son of US President Donald Trump, Donald Trump Jr, went hunting in Mongolia at the end of August, where he may have spent several days in a camp with Kremlin-linked oligarch Umar Kremlev. The Financial Times established the circumstances of the trip on the basis of testimony from local guides and officials, flight data, social media posts and public documents.
Source: The Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The meeting took place at the end of August. The FT notes that Kremlev flew to the Mongolian capital of Ulaanbaatar by charter plane from Kazakhstan, after which he travelled to Donald Trump Jr's hunting camp in the western part of the country.
Travelling alongside Kremlev was Russian businessman Arthur Martirosov, a partner in the US-sanctioned venture fund Voskhod. According to the FT, Trump Jr and Kremlev spent two days together, after which the Russian returned to Ulaanbaatar.
One of the local participants in the trip said that Trump Jr and Kremlev were careful not to be photographed together during their stay at Trump Jr's camp.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr stated that the men developed a personal friendship through a shared passion for hunting, fishing and outdoor recreation. According to him, they were introduced by a mutual acquaintance from the hunting community, and there are no business relations between them.
Quote from spokesperson for Trump Jr: "Don has made clear that he has a personal friendship, not a business relationship, with Umar. Their friendship is largely based on their shared love for hunting, fishing and the outdoors. It shouldn't be a surprise to anyone that they went hunting together earlier this year."
Details: Meanwhile, counterintelligence experts warn that contacts between members of the US president's family and individuals with ties to the Russian authorities could pose national security risks.
"It really doesn't matter if people have the most above board intentions. The moment the Russian security and intelligence services figure out someone has a relationship with anyone of high value, they will try to weaponise that," said Holden Triplette, who served as director of counterintelligence on the US National Security Council during Trump's first term.
During his stay in Mongolia, Trump Jr also hunted a rare Altai argali – an endangered wild sheep – and met with Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh.
For reference: The 43-year-old Kremlev is president of the International Boxing Association, an organisation headquartered in Lausanne that oversees international competitions and sets rules and standards in the sport. Prior to this, starting in 2017, he headed the Russian Boxing Federation.
Background:
- In early October, Kremlev claimed that Trump's son returned the money that the Russian spent on post-wedding celebrations organised by him as a gift.
- Earlier, US Attorney General Todd Blanche made it clear that he would not conduct an investigation into Trump Jr's wedding, which was partially funded by Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev.
- Members of President Donald Trump's family have flatly denied knowing Kremlev, while Democrats on Capitol Hill have promised to launch an investigation.

Asia-Pacific Community: China-ASEAN youth dialogue focuses on tech-driven modern agriculture
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:58 CST
18:22:58 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A China-ASEAN Youth Dialogue convened here on Tuesday, focusing on how cutting-edge technology can drive modern agriculture.
The event brought together approximately 150 participants to share insights and experiences on using modern innovations, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), drones, and the Internet of Things (IoT), to modernize the agricultural sector across Cambodia and the broader ASEAN region.
Seak Leng, an undersecretary of state at Cambodia's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), emphasized that agriculture remains a priority sector for Cambodia, serving as a cornerstone for the national economy, food security, and rural livelihoods.
"In an era of rapid technological advancement, modernizing agriculture goes beyond just using machinery or modern equipment," he said during the event. "It also encompasses innovation, digital technology, data analytics, and research and development to boost productivity, quality, and value-added potential."
Leng highlighted young people as the primary catalysts for meaningful change within the sector.
"I am confident this event will spark creative ideas, facilitate knowledge exchange, and build strong partnerships among youth and key institutions from both countries," he said. "Ultimately, this will help transition Cambodia's agricultural sector into one that is more modern, efficient, climate-resilient, and highly competitive."
The dialogue was organized by China's Guangxi Radio and Television Station in collaboration with Cambodia's MAFF, Ministry of Information, National Television of Cambodia, and Royal University of Agriculture.
Nguon Samnang, vice president of the Cambodia Agricultural Science Academy, said the dialogue arrived at a pivotal moment, emphasizing that embracing innovations like AI, drones, and IoT is vital for modernizing the agricultural sector and ensuring sustainable growth.
"Many of the agricultural technologies and innovations developed in China can be adopted across the ASEAN region, including Cambodia, to boost farmers' livelihoods and support agricultural communities," he said.
He added that cooperation between China and ASEAN can be expanded through active exchanges among experts, youth, and young researchers, noting that the participation of both the younger generation and local farmers is essential for future agricultural development.
Leang Seiha, a fourth-year student at the Royal University of Agriculture in Phnom Penh, described the dialogue as a unique opportunity to exchange techniques, share ideas, and learn about China's modern agricultural practices.
"I would like to thank China for working closely with Cambodia to share its technical knowledge, as well as organizing training programs and seminars," she told Xinhua. "These platforms allow us, as students, to explore new technologies that can help modernize Cambodia's agriculture."
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said Chinese agricultural technologies-including spraying drones, IoT soil sensors, and high-yield crop seeds-are essential tools for modernizing farming across Cambodia and the wider ASEAN region.
"Adopting these scalable solutions helps local farmers boost yields, cut labor costs, build climate resilience, and meet global export standards," he told Xinhua.
He emphasized that China and ASEAN should prioritize expanding cooperation in key areas, including digital and smart agriculture platforms, agri-e-commerce supply chains, and green technologies like climate-resilient breeding.
Additionally, both China and ASEAN should establish dedicated youth agri-tech exchange hubs while increasing investments in vocational training and technical education for rural communities, Mengdavid added. ■

Over 3,000 Australians died by suicide in 2025: statistics bureau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
17:22:48 CST
18:22:48 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Over 3,000 Australians died by suicide in 2025, according to official data published on Tuesday, with males accounting for a significant majority.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said that 3,283 of the 188,421 deaths registered nationally in 2025 were classified as being due to suicide, making it the 15th most common cause of death.
The figure was a slight decrease from the 3,326 suicide deaths reported in 2024, but the ABS noted that the number is expected to rise as ongoing coronial investigations progress.
It said that 73.9 percent of all people who died by suicide in 2025 were males.
The median age at death for those who died by suicide was 45.0 years. For males, it was 45.5 years, and for females it was 43.8 years.
By comparison, no other cause of death that ranked in the top 20 nationally in 2025 had a median age at death lower than 65.5 years.
The ABS said that suicide was the leading cause of death for Australians aged 15-44 in 2025 and was the overall leading cause of premature mortality, with suicide victims accounting for 108,674 combined years of potential life lost. ■

Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
09:22:45 UTC
18:22:45 KST

Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
Exit polls are expected soon after voting closes late on Tuesday, but a final verdict might take days.
Israelis are voting in a closely watched election to decide on the direction of the country, three years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on southern Israel that set off the genocidal war on Gaza.
The first election since those attacks comes at a time when Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of its neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.
But the vote also comes amid growing domestic questions that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces over alleged failures that allowed the October 7 attack, his government’s handling of efforts to retrieve captives taken to Gaza, alleged corruption and disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service.
In final polls published Friday, Netanyahu’s coalition is expected to be neck and neck with – or trail slightly behind – the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
According to Israeli news outlet Haaretz, which has collated polls from Israeli news channels, as of Friday, an average of Channels 11, 12 and 13 predicts Netanyahu’s bloc will win 50 seats while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc will take 54 seats. The Israeli parliament, known as the Knesset, has 120 seats in all, so 61 is the mark that a grouping needs to reach a majority.
Here’s what you need to know about the election.
When do polls close in Israel?
On Tuesday, polls opened at 7am local time (05:00 GMT) and will end at 10pm (20:00 GMT).
About 7.3 million Israelis will be eligible to vote, including 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel. Israelis living abroad cannot vote because the country does not have a general absentee ballot, requiring voters to be physically present on election day.
Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception and cast their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.
When will Israel’s election results be announced?
News channels will broadcast exit poll results once the election ends, with the first indications likely within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or weeks to get a clear result.
Results will also be live on the Central Elections Committee website once polls close.
While a clear picture of the election results may come out quickly, if no party or coalition secures a majority, it could take much longer.
The final vote tally is expected by Friday, and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.
How does the electoral system work?
Under a proportional representation system, Israelis vote for a single party, not individual candidates.
The number of seats the party gains in the Knesset is linked to the proportion of the vote it receives. For example, if Netanyahu’s Likud party secures 50 percent of the national vote, it would take 50 percent of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats.
For a party to enter the Knesset, it must secure at least 3.25 percent of the national vote.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
How is Israel’s next prime minister chosen?
Once the final count is in, President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
The person nominated then has up to 42 days to form a government. As it stands, no single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks.
What happens if Netanyahu or his rivals cannot form a government?
If no government emerges, the current cabinet, Netanyahu’s government, will remain as a caretaker government.
But before that point, whoever gains the most votes will have different options to assemble support from smaller parties, including forming a minority government or working with another political leader to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.
If all negotiations fail, and no grouping is able to cobble together a workable government, new elections will have to be called.

UK prosecutors charge two after RAF Fairford incident
British Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir charged under the National Security Act.
British prosecutors say they have charged two men with offences under the National Security Act following an incident in September at RAF Fairford, an airbase in England used by the United States.
British Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir, both aged 24, were charged under the National Security Act, the Crown Prosecution Service said. They are due to appear in court later on Tuesday.
Abdulkarim is charged with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of the United Kingdom’s Counter Terrorism Policing, said police believed the country Abdulkarim was assisting was Iran.
Essghir was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
Both men live in Westminster, a district in London.
The airbase in Gloucestershire, southwestern England, had been used by US bombers to carry out attacks on Iran this year.
Essghir was arrested outside the base on September 27, when armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Dozens of residents were evacuated from their homes as police and experts searched for explosives.
Abdulkarim was arrested in the past week. Six other men remain on bail, all living in London and aged between 23 and 25, as investigations continue.
Shortly after the incident at the base, US B-1 bombers were withdrawn from the site.
“We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state and, as the Director General of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat,” Taylor said in a statement.
Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec, reporting from London, said police initially commented that they were considering all avenues and that they were not ruling out a state actor.
“But at the time, they didn’t go so far as to point towards Iran – although US President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were fairly quick to say they believed that there was credible evidence to suggest Iran was involved,” she said.
“It’s only in the past few days that police who have been in charge of this investigation have increasingly said they believe there is evidence that Iran is involved,” she added.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last week said the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Iran’s ambassador to the UK has denied.
Last year, the UK said there had been 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK.
In July, Britain used new powers to ban support for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and a linked group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which had claimed responsibility for seven attacks earlier this year at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities and Persian-language media.

Voters at polling stations reflected the divide. “He’s a man who’s not afraid to take action,” said 85-year-old Zipporah Bennett, explaining her support for Netanyahu. In Jerusalem, 65-year-old Alexandra said: “I want change in our country.”
Arab-majority parties, which represent around 21% of the population, could prove kingmakers if the result is as tight as expected, though neither leading candidate has publicly said he would partner with them.
The vote is being closely watched in Europe. The EU is Israel’s largest trading partner, but relations have come under strain over the war in Gaza. In April, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia renewed a push to suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement at a meeting of foreign ministers, but Germany and Italy blocked the move. alqudsWikipedia
Analysts caution that replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily mean a break with the policies driving European criticism, pointing out that Eisenkot has opposed Palestinian statehood. He has, however, promised to crack down on violent settlers. Al Jazeera
Polls close at 22:00 local time (21:00 CET). Final results could take days, and no party is expected to come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset, meaning coalition negotiations could last weeks or even months.

Actual Swiss wages increase by 0.5% in 2026

Actual Swiss wages increase by 0.5% in 2026
Actual and minimum wages in Switzerland are set to rise by an average of 0.5% and 0.8% respectively in 2026. This was announced on Monday by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), based on the provisions of the main collective labour agreements (CLAs).
The average increase of 0.5% in actual wages, agreed by the social partners in the main collective labour agreements, was broken down into 0.3% at individual level and 0.2% at collective level. According to inflation forecasts for 2026 (+0.6%), real wages in sectors covered by collective agreements are not expected to rise this year. The agreements on actual wages cover just under 700,000 people.
In detail, the increase in actual wages was 0.2% in the secondary sector and 0.8% in the tertiary sector. Among the economic sectors, the largest increases were recorded in transport and storage (+1.2%), Financial and insurance activities (+1%) and professional, scientific and technical activities (+0.8%). Manufacturing and construction saw more modest increases, of 0.3% and 0.2% respectively.
More
Median annual salary in Switzerland rose to CHF87,000 in 2025
As regards minimum wages, the average increase of 0.8% in 2026 follows rises of 1% in 2025 and 2% in 2024. More than 1.85 million people are covered by a collective labour agreement (CLA) that includes statutory provisions on minimum wages and for whom agreements have been concluded.
Minimum wage increases varied by sector: +0.3% in the secondary sector and +0.8% in the tertiary sector. Among the sectors, ‘unclassified activities’ (commercial employees and sales staff) stood out with +2.3%, followed by ‘financial and insurance activities’ (+1.8%) and ‘other service activities’ (+1.5%). The lowest increases were recorded in manufacturing (+0.1%) and accommodation and food service activities (+0.2%).

Putin to host 22 African leaders in Moscow
Russian President Vladimir Putin will host 22 African leaders at the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow this week for talks spanning economic cooperation, energy, and global affairs, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
Putin’s schedule includes 24 bilateral meetings across the Russia-Africa gathering and Tuesday’s eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit, Ushakov told reporters on Monday.
Five are scheduled for Tuesday, with the presidents of Mozambique, Equatorial Guinea, and Iran, as well as Qatar’s emir and Libya’s Presidential Council chairman. Another 11 are planned for Friday, including talks with representatives of Ghana, Mali, Mauritania, South Sudan, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, Togo, Eritrea, Somalia, and Comoros.
Ushakov said the discussions will emphasize “national sovereignty and fair access to food, resources, fertilizers, and modern technologies,” adding: “We have a busy... extremely packed week ahead.”
According to the Kremlin aide, delegations from 48 of Africa’s 54 countries have confirmed that they will take part in the October 28-29 gathering. Putin and Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the African Union chair, will co-chair the summit at the Grand Kremlin Palace.
He said the Russia-Africa summit will adopt a cooperation action plan for 2027-2029 and two declarations, one setting out joint positions and the other covering cooperation in AI. Another 33 intergovernmental, interagency, and commercial documents are set to be signed with African countries.
The accompanying Economic and Humanitarian Forum will cover agriculture, energy, mining, finance, and technology, with around 4,000 Russian and African entrepreneurs invited.
The gathering follows the 2019 Sochi summit, attended by 43 African heads of state or government, and the 2023 St. Petersburg summit, which drew delegations from 48 African countries, including 17 heads of state. Russia completed the delivery of 200,000 metric tons of free grain to six African countries in February 2024, fulfilling Putin’s pledge at the 2023 summit, according to the Agriculture Ministry.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said earlier this month that Western governments are attempting to pressure African states, including through financial blackmail, to deter them from attending the Moscow summit. Russia has positioned itself as a strategic ally to African countries, with governments across the continent seeking closer ties in education, energy, and security despite Western criticism.
Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop defended his country’s partnership during Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s February 2023 visit to Bamako, saying, “We are not going to continue to justify our choice of partners.”
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama, who is in Moscow for the Russia-Africa summit, reaffirmed his country’s nonaligned foreign policy in London last week, saying partnerships should deliver investment and fair returns rather than being determined by competition among outside powers.

Some semiconductor wafer manufacturers have already begun discussing their PC requirements for 2027 with Asus, he said. “The commercial market still has strong demand,” Liao said.
He added that many organizations had not fully allocated their budgets in 2025, while businesses and government agencies were now considering larger budgets for 2027. Unexpectedly rapid PC price increases had left some organizations unable to purchase all the equipment they needed, prompting them to plan more carefully for future procurement, per UDN.

Ukraine’s Ambassador to the United Kingdom and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), Valeriy Zaluzhny, believes that the war in Ukraine persists due to the weakness of the Western world and its security system—a system that requires a new military doctrine reflecting the realities of modern warfare.
"The West needs to step out of its comfort zone and into the reality of what war looks like in 2026; it must shed the illusion that outdated guarantees and doctrines can truly protect it and its children," Zaluzhny wrote in a Facebook post.
According to him, the Western security system remains rooted in a World War II-era doctrine, merely supplemented by expensive, high-precision weaponry whereas modern conditions demand a comprehensive overhaul of approaches to combat operations.
Zaluzhny emphasized that for the West to ensure its own security, it is not enough to simply procure new weapons or adjust tactics to account for the use of drones.
"The West needs a new doctrine to defend itself. For us in the military, a doctrine is a 'Bible of war'—it integrates all components of the armed forces—weaponry, tactics, structure, training, and funding—into a unified system," he noted.
Zaluzhny stated that such a doctrine would enable the assessment of the impact of new technologies, adaptation to change, and the planning of joint operations. "A relevant, up-to-date doctrine means security for your children and for your state. No other commitments will save you," he wrote.
He added that the West still possesses sophisticated and costly technologies that could help build a new security system; however, the key factor remains the willingness to step out of one’s comfort zone and take collective action. According to Zaluzhny, only by working together can the war for the future of our children be won.
Zaluzhny also mentioned that he addressed officers from various nations at the Joint Services Command and Staff College of the UK Defence Academy, where they are preparing for senior command roles, and noted the participation of Ukrainian military personnel with firsthand combat experience in the training program. Among them is a Hero of Ukraine, Lieutenant Colonel Serhiy Roschin, a squadron commander who has been defending the Ukrainian skies since 2022.

09:10:55 UTC
18:10:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Migrant worker groups protested outside the health ministry Tuesday, calling for stronger labor protections and better home care services amid concerns over pregnant caregivers, CNA reported.
Taiwan relies too heavily on families hiring migrant caregivers directly, worker groups said, leaving both workers and employers with too much responsibility. They urged the government to provide more affordable and flexible home care services.
The Taiwan Care Workers' Union said many migrant caregivers work long hours without clear limits. It urged the government to gradually replace direct household employment with a system in which professional care organizations hire caregivers and provide services to families.
Taiwan prohibits employers from firing migrant caregivers because they become pregnant. However, household caregivers are not covered by the Labor Standards Act, and their maternity leave is unpaid, per the labor ministry.
At a separate protest outside the labor ministry, employers and families raised concerns about finding replacement caregivers. They said families caring for people with severe disabilities could be left without enough support for months when their regular caregivers cannot work.
The Taiwan Association of Families with Disabilities and Migrant Caregiver Employers called for a government agency to oversee recruitment, insurance, training, and job placement to help families maintain care.
The labor ministry said that if a caregiver cannot perform the required work, both sides may agree to end the contract, allowing the employer to apply for a replacement under existing rules.
The health ministry said it would work with the labor ministry to improve care services and support for families. Since September 2025, households employing migrant caregivers have had greater access to government-supported services, including care provided outside the home.
The labor ministry said the government has allocated about NT$2 billion (US$63 million) for respite and short-term care services. Eligible households can receive a combined total of up to 52 days of support annually when regular caregivers are unavailable, per Liberty Times.

Prosecutors detained Wu at a Kaohsiung hospital on Monday after he failed to physically appear at a detention hearing that morning. Asked by the media about the incident, Wu said he had applied for two days of leave to prepare for heart surgery scheduled for Wednesday, per China Times.
Wu accused prosecutors of overstepping their authority, describing the incident as an erosion of human rights protections. After the presiding judge granted bail, Wu’s family posted the NT$7 million bond and took him back to the family residence, per ETtoday.
Wu’s defense team objected to his treatment, questioning whether prosecutors had obtained a medical assessment to determine if he was fit to leave the hospital, per SETN. The team emphasized that the court had approved his leave, adding that Wu had agreed to attend the evening hearing in person after prosecutors objected to his absence.
Wu’s lawyers questioned whether prosecutors’ insistence on detaining him at the hospital was intended to create what they described as the false impression that he was evading court proceedings.
The Taitung District Prosecutors Office responded by highlighting its efforts to verify whether Wu needed to remain hospitalized for further treatment, per Tai Sounds. It said the detention decision took both Wu’s health and the ongoing investigation into account.
Prosecutors also noted that the subsequent court proceedings would determine the legality of the detention.

Congo's Ebola cases surpass 10,000 as fears grow of wider African spread
Oct 27 - The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo has risen above 10,000, government data showed on Tuesday, a milestone that coincides with growing fears the epidemic could spread to more African countries.
The latest situation report from Congo's public health institute put the number of cases at 10,060, with those killed by the virus reaching 4,887.
The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, was announced in mid-May and has since become the largest and deadliest in Congo, surpassing a 2018-2020 epidemic.
It is now the second-largest and second-deadliest on record behind only the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first case and went on to announce nine cases in total, after a man who had travelled from Congo via Uganda died in Nairobi.
Last week, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case.
Health officials have been seeking to work out how and where the patient — the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who had not travelled to Congo — contracted the disease. The Swiss government said she was believed to have contracted it in Uganda.
The woman and her husband were flown to hospitals in Switzerland on Monday.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Ugandan officials say the country does not have any Ebola cases.
Uganda's health minister said on Sunday that Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Congo would be quarantined for 21 days. REUTERS

08:59:51 UTC
17:59:51 KST

The Turkish Trade Ministry has announced the signing of a declaration confirming Türkiye’s alignment with EU machinery safety legislation, fulfilling customs union requirements.
The regulatory harmonization “paves the way for the Turkish machinery sector to benefit from the free movement of goods across European markets.”
Ankara can now designate accredited notified bodies within Türkiye, enabling Turkish machinery exporters to conduct their conformity assessment and certification procedures at home instead of relying on foreign institutions.
The local assessments will be recognized under the same conditions as those performed by EU manufacturers.
The deal marks a major milestone in simplifying technical and administrative processes that Turkish exporters deal with when accessing the European single market.
The financial costs and administrative burdens associated with these regulatory procedures will be significantly reduced.
The alignment will reportedly benefit more than $10 billion worth of Turkish machinery exports to the EU per year.
Machinery sales make up 10 percent of Türkiye’s total export volume to the EU, according to the ministry.

GDELS and ARMMO team up on mobile anti-drone system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:58:47 UTC
17:58:47 KST

- ARMMO and Santa Bárbara Sistemas launched and flew the Bandit-X interceptor drone from an ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier during Spain’s ATLAS 26 exercise.
- ARMMO says Bandit-X exceeds 360 km/h, flies for 20 to 25 minutes and has an estimated range of 40 to 50 km.
Spanish drone maker ARMMO Defense Technologies and General Dynamics European Land Systems’ Spanish unit, Santa Bárbara Sistemas, launched and flew ARMMO’s Bandit-X interceptor drone from an ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier tracked armored vehicle during the ATLAS 26 counter-drone exercise in Huelva, Spain, turning the heavy vehicle into a mobile launcher for drones that hunt down other drones.
The two companies announced the demonstration on Oct. 27, 2026, along with a cooperation agreement to develop and integrate autonomous systems on armored vehicles and other ground platforms, and they said the launch was carried out in front of senior Spanish and NATO officers, including Spain’s Chief of the Defence Staff, Adm. Gen. Manuel Teodoro López Calderón, and Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation.
The launcher had already been spotted at the exercise, when Defence Blog reported that a tracked ASCOD carrier was seen with box-shaped launch containers marked with ARMMO’s logo on its open rear deck at the Médano del Loro training range, where ATLAS 26 ran from Oct. 19 to Oct. 23 under the direction of the Spanish Army’s Anti-Aircraft Artillery Command.
Bandit-X is a high-speed interceptor built to find and destroy hostile unmanned aircraft, and ARMMO says it flies at more than 360 km/h (224 mph), with plans to push that to 420 km/h (261 mph), stays in the air for 20 to 25 minutes and has an estimated operational range of 40 to 50 km (25 to 31 miles), depending on conditions and mission profile.
The company says the drone can navigate on its own when satellite navigation is jammed or denied, resists electronic interference and guides itself autonomously in the final phase of an intercept, and that it was validated during NATO experimental activities in Slovakia in 2026 and has been assigned a NATO Stock Number, which lets allied militaries identify and order it through their common logistics catalog.
The ASCOD Heavy Mission Carrier is a modular tracked platform from Santa Bárbara Sistemas that can be fitted for ground-based air defense, artillery, fire support, heavy recovery, logistics, electronic warfare, medical evacuation and counter-drone missions, and it uses the NEVA open digital architecture, built to NATO’s Generic Vehicle Architecture standard, so that systems from other companies can be added to the vehicle.
ARMMO, which operates an industrial site of more than 30,000 square meters (323,000 square feet) in Zafra, in Spain’s Badajoz province, also builds unmanned ground and surface vehicles and electronic warfare systems, and the agreement with Santa Bárbara Sistemas sets up a framework for putting its autonomous technologies on a range of ground vehicles.

Natural History Museum launches new tender for permanent exhibition project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:58:00 UTC
17:58:00 KST

Natural History Museum launches new tender for permanent exhibition project
The Natural History Museum has launched a new €3 million tender to find a contractor for one of the largest projects in Estonia's museum sector in the past decade.
The museum is seeking a contractor to design the new permanent exhibition and to implement it based on that design at the newly built wooden Nature House in Põhja-Tallinn. The two-part tender has a total value of €2,812,950.
Egle Hecht, acting director of the Estonian Museum of Natural History, said she hopes to see companies from both Estonia and abroad that have previously carried out similar museum projects among the bidders for the permanent exhibition tender.
"This is a very large international tender for Estonia's museum sector, the likes of which was last carried out more than 10 years ago when the Estonian National Museum was established," she said.
The previous tender failed.
"A total of three bids were submitted for the first tender for the core exhibition, but unfortunately none of them qualified. As these were predominantly some of the world's leading creative agencies specializing in exhibition construction, which often do not participate in public procurement tenders, it turned out that they misunderstood the tender conditions and made mistakes when submitting their bids. With the new tender, we hope to avoid similar situations," Hecht said.
The acting director said the museum's new core exhibition will tell the story of the coexistence of nature and humans through Estonia's natural environment. It is hoped it will be "more ambitious and exceptional than before in terms of its concept, size and execution."
"In every chapter, humans are one of the characters, equal among others. Alongside well-known and visible species, we emphasize the richness of microscopic life and its coexistence with other living organisms. We talk about different relationships in nature, also touching on, for example, how rich biodiversity influences culture and language, and vice versa. The new permanent exhibition offers something for all age groups, being accessible and taking different visitors into account," Hecht said.
The museum is also planning a separate children's exhibition, where they can learn about nature in a way that supports their natural curiosity.
Natural History Museum to fully open in 2028
The tender consists of two parts: the permanent exhibition and the exhibition for young children.
"We will open the children's exhibition together with the museum's first temporary exhibition in 2027, meaning there is less time to complete it, while the permanent exhibition will open in 2028. That is why the tender has been divided into two parts," Hecht said.
The acting director said the museum will open its doors with its first exhibition in 2027, as planned from the outset, although the exact date is not yet clear.
"Once the Taru Nature House is completed, the museum will only then begin moving into the building and constructing and setting up the exhibitions. The completion of the building will allow us to begin creating the exhibition," Hecht said.
The expected final deadline for the design and exhibition construction work under the procurement contract is April 6, 2028.
The deadline for submitting bids is in one month's time, on November 23. The work will be financed from external funds (the Cohesion Policy Funds Implementation Programme 2021–2027) and the Environmental Investment Center's environmental program.

Norwegian media companies take Meta to court over new commercial terms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:42:06 UTC
17:42:06 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
Major Norwegian media companies have taken Meta to court over its proposed new commercial terms, raising concerns about the potential use of news content to train artificial intelligence models, broadcaster NRK reported Tuesday.
Members of the Norwegian Media Association (MBL) argue that the new terms would grant Meta the right to scrape every article, photo and video published by editorially controlled media outlets.
Major media organizations, including NRK, TV 2, Schibsted, Amedia, Polaris, Aller, DN, Mentor Medier, NTB and Hordaland Folkeblad, have asked the Oslo District Court to suspend Meta’s new terms pending a judicial review of their legality.
“We believe that this should be legally assessed to see if this is actually in line with Norwegian law,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, chairwoman of the MBL.
NRK’s legal director Olav Nyhus also said they “in no way” want Meta to be able to use their content to further strengthen platforms such as Facebook and Instagram.
Nyhus added that it would not be easy to terminate agreements with Instagram and Facebook, as the platforms have become important channels for disseminating information.
“What Meta is doing is destroying the entire financial basis for journalism,” he said, adding: “We believe that Meta’s conduct and terms are a clear violation of competition law.”
Meta recently revised its commercial terms to remove language that raised concerns about the potential use of news websites to train artificial intelligence models.
The revised terms specify that automated website crawling is intended to develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products.
The provisions still allow Meta to use automated tools, including web scrapers, bots and crawlers, to access and collect content from websites associated with businesses using its platforms.
An earlier version of the proposed terms included language about using collected material to “train” Meta products, prompting concerns among publishers and legal experts over the potential use of copyrighted news content for AI development.
Meta subsequently removed the reference and clarified that the crawling provisions apply to advertising and business products.

EU readying for major Australian resources investment, ambassador says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:40:59 UTC
17:40:59 KST

EU readying for major Australian resources investment, ambassador says
SYDNEY, Oct 27 - The European Union expects a wave of investment into the Australian critical minerals sector as it pushes to diversify its supply chain away from China, the bloc's ambassador to Australia Lawrence Meredith said on Tuesday.
Australia and the European Union struck a free trade agreement in March after eight years of negotiations, removing tariffs on almost all goods and easing EU access to Australian critical minerals.
Once both parties sign and ratify that agreement, expected early next year, a 5.5% EU tariff on critical minerals will be removed.
"It is going to be a game changer," Meredith said.
In parallel, talks are "very close" for Australia to sign a memorandum of understanding with the European Investment Bank, which would act as the bloc's funding vehicle, Meredith added.
"The European Union will be massively investing in critical minerals. Since we wish to diversify away from China, then one of the most likely partners has to be Australia," he said.
EU policy proposals have laid out as much as €10 billion ($11.2 billion) for critical raw materials within the larger €409 billion competitiveness fund, as the EU debates its budget from 2028 to 2034.
Australia is one of several critical minerals "superpowers" in which the EU is looking to invest, including Brazil, South Africa and Canada. The EU also expects to invest along the supply chain, including in processing, Meredith said.
Australia said on Tuesday it would refresh its critical minerals strategy to place greater emphasis on refining and processing, as competition for investment intensifies and supply-chain concerns persist.
The bloc is looking initially at the minerals that Australia will prioritise for its strategic reserve: gallium, antimony and rare earths.
Australian companies going faster through the early project development would speed the investment process, he said.
"(The FTA) is a signal that Europe wants to do far more with Australia. We also have a security and defence partnership. A lot of that is dual technology, and it requires precisely these critical minerals," he said.
The European Union plans to mobilise €800 billion into defence under ReArm Europe by 2030.
Australia is also on track to join the EU's flagship funding program for research and innovation, Horizon Europe, next year.
Meredith said 2026 had been a "transformational" year for Australian-EU relations.
"You've seen a big surge in EU-Australia in 2026, and I'm very confident we will go to the next level in 2027." REUTERS

India ramps up oil imports from Middle East – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:40:20 UTC
17:40:20 KST

India ramps up oil imports from Middle East – media
India’s imports of Middle Eastern crude have surged to more than half of its total oil purchases, as steep Gulf discounts and soaring freight costs make Russian supplies less competitive for Indian refiners.
Middle Eastern crude accounted for 54% of India’s oil imports in September, up from 32% in August, while Russia’s share fell to 33.5% from 46.6%, according to ship-tracking data reported by Reuters. Russia nevertheless remained India’s largest individual oil supplier.
The shift is reflected in purchases by state-owned Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), which expects Russian crude volumes to decline significantly in November. Russian oil accounted for around 37% of BPCL’s crude sourcing during July-September.
India increased Russian oil purchases when the US-Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern supplies. However, Gulf shipments have since recovered to prewar levels, with producers offering steep discounts to attract buyers.
The conflict has driven up global tanker rates, making the longer voyages from Russian ports increasingly expensive. Average crude freight costs have risen nearly sevenfold over the past year, from around $3 per barrel to more than $20, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank cited war-risk premiums, higher fuel expenses, and costly ship-to-ship transfers.
Freight costs for Russian Urals crude shipped to Asia reached around $30 per barrel or more in early October. Transporting a tanker shipment from Russia’s Black Sea ports to India currently costs $27 million-$30 million, compared with approximately $19 million in September, Reuters reported.
Meanwhile, some Iraqi cargoes are being offered at discounts exceeding $25 per barrel against the Dubai benchmark before shipping, while selected Saudi shipments have been discounted by as much as $10, Bloomberg reported, citing traders. Russian crude, which previously sold at steep discounts, was being offered at around a $2 premium to the separate Dated Brent benchmark.
“Due to the increase in freight, we are not getting good offers from Russia,” BPCL finance director Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta told analysts on Monday.
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL), another state-owned oil company, is also adjusting its procurement strategy, increasingly buying crude on a delivered-price basis to manage shipping costs. HPCL Chairman Vikas Kaushal also confirmed that Gulf producers are offering discounts to offset the elevated freight rates.
Indian Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday that Middle Eastern supplies are increasing, and noted that Russian oil purchases depend on pricing and discounts compared with other grades.
Asked whether Washington had pressured India to reduce Russian oil imports, Puri said, “I never felt anything.”

U.S. Navy nuclear submarine arrives in Australia for maintenance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:40:18 UTC
17:40:18 KST

- USS Colorado (SSN 788) arrived at HMAS Stirling for a monthlong maintenance period involving more than 30 Australian civilian technicians from ASC.
- Colorado has been named the first U.S. Navy Virginia-class submarine assigned to Submarine Squadron 3 and will return in late 2027.
The U.S. Navy attack submarine USS Colorado (SSN 788) arrived at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia on Oct. 27 to begin a scheduled monthlong maintenance period. For the first time, Australian civilian technicians will carry out routine maintenance on a Virginia-class submarine in Western Australia, working alongside American shipyard specialists, with the U.K. Royal Navy also taking part in the work.
More than 30 trained and certified technicians from Australian shipbuilder ASC Pty Ltd. will work on the boat alongside specialists from Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility, the U.S. Navy yard in Hawaii where the Australian workers were trained.
The visit comes one day after Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and his Australian and British counterparts issued a joint statement on Oct. 26 naming Colorado as the first U.S. Navy Virginia-class submarine assigned to Submarine Squadron 3, the American squadron reactivated at HMAS Stirling in June. When Colorado returns in late 2027, it is set to help formally establish Submarine Rotational Force-West, the arrangement under which up to four U.S. submarines and one British submarine will operate on rotation from the base south of Perth.
“This maintenance period brings us closer to establishing SRF-West,” said U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Doug Adams, director of AUKUS, International & Systems. “Our Lead Maintenance Activity, Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility, is doing a great job ensuring the Australian personnel trained in Hawaii are ready and able to support our submarines.”
Colorado’s visit is the fourth submarine maintenance period in Western Australia since the AUKUS partnership was formed and the third in the past 12 months, and each one has handed Australia a larger share of the work. USS Hawaii (SSN 776) was serviced at Stirling in 2024 with help from the submarine tender USS Emory S. Land (AS 39), while USS Vermont (SSN 792) arrived in October 2025 for a larger and more complex maintenance package that was carried out without a tender. The British submarine HMS Anson followed with its own maintenance period in February 2026, and Colorado is the sixth nuclear-powered attack submarine to visit Stirling since the AUKUS partners announced Australia’s path to a nuclear-powered fleet.
The latest period will also be the first to use several new pieces of Australian-built infrastructure together, including a custom-made metal safety walkway around the submarine’s sail known as a “racetrack,” nuclear submarine upgrades to the base’s Diamantina Pier, a pure water plant, a high-pressure air compressor and a dehumidifier.
“During last year’s maintenance period, we successfully delivered pure water from an Australian-designed and built plant and validated the sail racetrack was fit for purpose. During the U.K.’s maintenance period in February, we validated the high-pressure air compressor and dehumidifier systems. Now, with the racetrack, we’re using it to conduct maintenance, utilizing the pier upgrades, and leveraging a workforce of about three dozen fully qualified and certified Australian civilian nuclear-powered submarine maintenance workers,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Jason Pittman, commander of Submarine Squadron 3.
Australian officials said the visits are building the country’s ability to keep allied submarines in port longer and return them to sea on time, which it will need before the rotational force begins operating.
“These maintenance periods have been critical to Australia being on track to start SRF-West in 2027,” said Royal Australian Navy Rear Adm. David Mann, head of the Australian Submarine Agency’s Virginia Division.
The British side will be directly involved in the work on the American boat, which officials presented as a way to bring all three navies closer to common maintenance practices.
“The more the three nations work together to maintain submarines – whether American or British – the faster we’ll be able to uplift our Australian partner’s knowledge and skills and increase commonality across our submarine forces,” said Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the U.K. Prime Minister’s Special Representative for AUKUS.
Under the first pillar of AUKUS, Australia plans to buy three in-service Virginia-class submarines from the United States before moving to the new SSN-AUKUS design, and the port visits are intended to prepare its workforce and facilities to maintain and operate a conventionally armed, nuclear-powered fleet of its own. Ahead of Colorado’s arrival, about 20 Australian civilian maintainers and 25 Royal Australian Navy divers, Fleet Support Unit officers and sailors had completed training at Pearl Harbor, and more than 230 others were still training in Hawaii, USNI News reported in June.
“The success of any maintenance period comes down to the people on the deckplates, and the Australian personnel stepping aboard our ship are true professionals,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Justin Reeves, commanding officer of USS Colorado.

U.S. Army launches Project Griffin to automate cyber defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:48:38 UTC
22:48:38 KST

- The U.S. Army selected Amazon Web Services and World Wide Technology on Oct. 23, 2026, for a $2.6 million Project Griffin cyber defense pilot.
- Project Griffin aims to build an autonomous, superintelligence-driven platform that helps U.S. Army cyber defenders detect, divert and deceive threat actors faster.
The U.S. Army has picked Amazon Web Services and World Wide Technology to help build an autonomous cyber defense system that can find and stop network threats with little human involvement, choosing the two companies on Oct. 23, 2026, for a Project Griffin pilot worth a combined $2.6 million.
The U.S. Army said it wants an autonomous, agentic platform driven by what it calls superintelligence, or SI, that can spot and neutralize cyber threats faster than human analysts, removing the weak points that come from manual data analysis and human action, though it did not say how the $2.6 million is split between the two companies or how long the pilot will run.
“Project Griffin is one of the first efforts under Project ARDS, which is advancing the Army’s adoption of SI-enabled cyber defense capabilities through rapid sprints in conjunction with industry partners. We will swiftly implement SI-enabled cyber tools to detect, divert and deceive threat actors, and rapidly adopt agentic SI to securely scale network defense and disruption,” said Brandon Pugh, principal cyber advisor to the secretary of the U.S. Army.
Project Griffin is one of three fast-tracked efforts under Project ARDS, short for Army Rapid Defensive of Cyber Systems, which Pugh’s office leads together with the assistant secretary of the U.S. Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, Army Cyber Command and the U.S. Army’s chief information officer to find, buy and hand over promising tools to the soldiers who defend its networks.
The pilot will be managed by Project Manager, Cyber Warfare, part of the Portfolio Management Executive for Intelligence and Spectrum Warfare, with Army Contracting Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, handling the contract.
“Through our flexible procurement methods, we were able to quickly seek out SI solutions that will advance the cyber warfighter,” said Col. David Bergmann, project manager for cyber warfare.

NEW DELHI: Union road transport minister Nitin Gadkari on Tuesday described the backlash against petrol blended with 20% ethanol (E20) as a “paid campaign”. His remarks came a day after the government notified changes to motor vehicle rules allowing flex-fuel vehicles to run on blends containing up to 100% ethanol.Speaking at an event organised by industry body CII, Gadkari said the opposition to E20 had intensified about three months ago but had since subsided.“Three months ago, huge noise (khub halla) was made against the E20 (20 per cent ethanol-blended petrol) fuel; now rage against E20 fuel is over...It was a paid campaign,” news agency PTI quoted Gadkari as saying.The government on Monday notified amendments to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, permitting flex-fuel vehicles capable of running on fuel containing up to E100, or nearly pure ethanol.Gadkari has repeatedly advocated greater use of ethanol as part of efforts to reduce the country's dependence on imported fossil fuels. He said expanding the use of alternative fuels could help the country save valuable foreign exchange by cutting fossil fuel imports.
The Centre’s nationwide rollout of petrol blended with 20% ethanol (E20) had triggered protests and political criticism earlier this year, with motorists raising concerns over reduced mileage and the compatibility of the fuel with older vehicles.
Opposition leaders questioned the government’s decision to make E20 the standard fuel at petrol pumps across India in April 2025.The row escalated after attorney general R Venkataramani referred to E20 as an “experiment” during a Supreme Court hearing, saying its results would be known next year. The remark went viral, prompting renewed criticism of the policy.The Centre subsequently clarified that the attorney general was referring to ethanol supply volumes, not describing the E20 policy itself as an experiment. Venkataramani also told Reuters that his comments had been misunderstood.The government and automobile industry cited studies indicating that E20 does not significantly damage metallic engine components, while acknowledging that fuel efficiency and compatibility can vary across vehicles.

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy on Monday called for efforts to properly solve the issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property from the Gulf War.
The issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property, a legacy of the Gulf War, has remained unresolved for 35 years and continues to tug at the heartstrings of the Kuwaiti people, said Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations.
"Properly addressing this historical legacy issue is of great significance for soothing the emotional wounds caused by the war, improving relations between Kuwait and Iraq, and promoting friendly cooperation among countries in the region," he said.
Achieving this goal requires not only the joint efforts of the parties concerned, but also the political support of the Security Council, said Sun.
In September 2025, the council unanimously adopted Resolution 2792, which decides to establish the position of senior representative of the UN secretary-general to advance the resolution of the issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property.
Since her appointment, Senior Representative Mari Yamashita has maintained close communication with both Kuwait and Iraq. Kuwait, Iraq, and the International Committee of the Red Cross have made great efforts in this regard, Sun noted.
"We hope that Kuwait and Iraq will further demonstrate sincerity, patience, and determination, build on the prior work, and, in keeping with the principle of mutual respect and friendly consultation, intensify their efforts and work in the same direction, so as to create favorable conditions for substantive progress on the issue," Sun told a Security Council briefing on the issue of missing Kuwaiti persons and property.
As a good friend and good partner of both Kuwait and Iraq, China will continue to play a constructive role in promoting a proper settlement of the issue, he said. ■

Defense Minister Martin Herem hires air defense expert Mati Tikerpuu as adviser
Reservist Colonel Mati Tikerpuu, an air defense specialist, starts work as an adviser to Defense Minister Martin Herem (Reform) next month.
Herem told ERR that Tikerpuu's two main tasks will relate to air alerts and public threats notification, as well as improving society's awareness of threats and how to reduce and mitigate them — whether by finding an alternative location, creating a shelter, or strengthening infrastructure by engineering means.
"Air alerts and public notification need to be at a better level; all providers of vital services, and society as a whole, need to be better informed about both the threats and the possibilities for reducing and mitigating them," Herem said.
Herem described Tikerpuu as a "very high level" air defense specialist, noting he has also served as a brigade commander. "He understands general military questions very well and will help move this issue forward quickly over the next six months," the minister, a former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF), added.
Tikerpuu, who will be a full-time hire, himself told ERR he has served in the defense forces for more than 30 years, over half of that working on air defense.
"I'm being hired to help the minister make informed decisions. But Herem himself also has a very clear ambition about where he wants to get to with these developments in the near future. We've had conversations about where to go and what to do. But as for various development ideas or proposals, I couldn't comment on them publicly right now," Tikerpuu said.
Tikerpuu is the former commander of the EDF's 2nd Infantry Brigade (South). He worked for nearly a year at the Center for Defense Investment (RKIK) as category manager for communications and radars, finishing in that role last December. Since then he has been working as development director for the drone sector with the volunteer Defense League (Kaitseliit).
He has served in the EDF since 1997. He starts in his new role in November.
A recent drone threat warning drill was assessed to have gone better than the previous two earlier this year, but improvements still need to be made, authorities say.
Herem has said improvements need to be made in air and also maritime defense more generally, and the option of purchasing light fighter jets for Estonia's Air Force (Õhuvägi), part of the EDF, is being weighed up. Their role would include countering drones.
