Anduril unveils family of air defence interceptors
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:17:33 GMT
17:17:33 KST

Anduril has revealed Steelfin, a family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles built on a common two-stage architecture so that one production line can turn out versions for everything from point defence to upper-tier ballistic missile defence, according to the company.
The company set out the problem it is addressing, saying adversaries have invested in large volumes of low-cost, mass-producible offensive weapons and that air defence batteries are too often forced to expend exquisite interceptors against lower-cost threats, straining stores of the most critical defensive weapons and putting defenders on the losing side of the cost exchange.
Steelfin pairs a first-stage booster, which can take different solid rocket motors to suit range, launch configuration or packing density, with a second-stage terminal interceptor sharing the same airframe, avionics, software, flight control system and interfaces across every variant. Open interfaces between the subsystems in that terminal stage let different seekers and mission systems be fitted without redesigning the missile.
Because the variants share an architecture and components, they move through the same production line using the same tooling, technicians and facilities, and Anduril said it is planning to produce on the order of several thousand Steelfin variants a year in the short term, with capacity designed to flex to demand. The same open interfaces allow commercial off-the-shelf components and competition between vendors, widening the supplier base.
The missiles are compatible with launch infrastructure already in service, including the M903A2 launcher used by Patriot, the Mk 41 vertical launching system fitted to warships, Typhon and emerging containerised launchers, and are designed to integrate with fielded fire control systems such as Aegis and IBCS. Anduril has completed ballistic testing with representative air vehicles and will begin flight testing next year.
The American company has built a European presence over the past two years, with Latvia selecting its Barracuda cruise missile family and a United Kingdom arm working on autonomy, counter-drone systems and command software. Its approach of designing weapons around mass production and common components is the same argument being made by Helsing, which launched its own pair of low-cost interceptors this week.

Fishing quotas for the Baltic Sea approved for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:16:59 UTC
17:16:59 KST

Fishing quotas for 2027 in the Baltic Sea and the Gulf of Riga have been approved this week at a meeting of the European Union (EU) Agriculture and Fisheries Council in Luxembourg. 
Following discussions among industry experts from the Baltic Sea Fisheries Forum (BALTFISH) in Luxembourg on the evening of 25 October, and subsequent negotiations at the Agriculture and Fisheries Council late on Monday evening, a compromise was reached on fishing opportunities in the Baltic Sea for next year.
The final decision largely reflects the common position agreed upon by the Baltic Sea countries.
Under the agreement, Latvia will be allocated a herring fishing quota of 4,581 tonnes in the Baltic Sea for 2027, representing a 71% increase compared with 2026. The European Commission (EC) had initially proposed an increase of 49%.
The cod bycatch quota will remain at 10 tonnes, unchanged from this year. Cod may only be caught as bycatch.
The European Commission had initially proposed reducing cod fishing allowances by 90% in subdivisions 22–24 and by 50% in subdivisions 25–32.
In the Gulf of Riga, the herring fishing quota has been approved at 20,550 tonnes, an increase of 11% compared with 2026.
Meanwhile, Latvia's sprat fishing quota will reach 40,340 tonnes, representing a 44% increase.
The salmon catch allowance in the Baltic Sea will remain unchanged at 3,366 fish.
The Ministry of Agriculture explained that the compromise revised the European Commission's initial proposals concerning cod bycatch limits and restrictions on recreational salmon fishing, including angling and fishing for personal consumption.
The permitted cod bycatch volumes and conditions will remain identical to those in force in 2026.
According to the ministry, these limits correspond to actual bycatch levels and therefore no longer threaten the continuation of fishing for other species along Latvia's Baltic Sea coast.
The Baltic Sea countries also rejected a proposed complete ban on recreational salmon fishing.
The ministry explained that there was no justification for prohibiting the catching of hatchery-raised salmon, which are identified by their clipped adipose fins.
Latvia's greatest concern was the European Commission's original proposal to reduce cod bycatch allowances by 50%, which the country considered unacceptable.
Negotiators successfully secured changes to that proposal.
The discussions also resulted in a 71% increase in fishing opportunities for herring in the central Baltic Sea, in line with scientifically permitted catch levels, compared with the European Commission's initial proposal for a 49% increase.
The Ministry of Agriculture noted that fishing opportunities in 2027 will also increase by 44% for sprat and 11% for herring in the Gulf of Riga.
Ģirts Krūmiņš, State Secretary at the Ministry of Agriculture, said the decisions are important for ensuring the responsible use of fish resources available in the Baltic Sea rather than leaving them to Russian fishing operations.
According to Krūmiņš, Russia has significantly exceeded its allocated fishing quotas for many years and has failed to respect the condition of fish stocks.
"I am very pleased that both sprat and herring quotas will increase substantially next year. We should make the most of these opportunities to generate the greatest possible economic benefit and added value," Krūmiņš said.
He emphasised that the increased quotas would strengthen Latvia's coastal communities and support local fishermen and fish processors, whose livelihoods depend directly on the resources provided by the sea.
Krūmiņš stressed that the most important achievement during the negotiations was preserving the existing cod bycatch quota, which the European Commission had sought to reduce.
"I believe our decisions must not threaten the survival of fishing in the Baltic Sea or the traditional coastal way of life, as adopting the European Commission's proposal would have done," Krūmiņš said.
He added that the agreement would help protect the livelihoods of Latvia's coastal fishermen and ensure they can continue their work.

Scandals and losses force revamp of Swiss supermarket chain Migros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:16:29 UTC
17:16:29 KST

Scandals and losses force revamp of Swiss supermarket chain Migros
Supermarket chain Migros, one of the largest employers in Switzerland, wants to call time on its tradition of decentralised operations by merging its regional cooperatives.
How did this come about and what happens next?
Migros group’s core business is barely profitable any more, and its supermarkets are struggling with low margins. This is evident from an analysis of the results of the ten regional cooperatives.
Last year, the Zurich regional co-operative made a loss of CHF180 million. Migros in Ticino, in southern Switzerland, is also in the red. Supermarkets in Ticino and Geneva face competition from low-cost chains based in neighbouring countries.
By dissolving the regional societies and merging them into a group cooperative, Migros aims to make savings and streamline operations.
More
Retail giant Migros confronts its complicated history with alcohol
The previous Migros structure gave each cooperative a great deal of power, giving rise to the term “regional prince”. Each regional cooperative has its own management with its own chair and keeps its own accounts with separate annual reports.
This decentralised organisation has led to several scandals. For a long time, for example, there was turmoil within the Neuchâtel-Fribourg cooperative.
+ How a new kind of Swiss store changed the way we shop
The Neuchâtel-Fribourg internal conflict escalated seven years ago when its then president was accused of fraud and embezzlement.
Migros group headquarters in Zurich attempted to remove the Neuchâtel-Fribourg leadership, which led to a vote of the 50,000 local cooperative members.
Irregularities occurred during the vote, involving forged ballot papers. The case highlighted the weaknesses of the decentralised organisation.
The regional cooperative in Zurich failed in a foreign venture that squandered several hundred million francs. In 2013, Migros Zurich took over the organic supermarket chain Tegut in Germany. But this resulted in financial losses and the German chain being put up for sale.
This example, too, highlighted the shortcomings of the decentralised organisation.
The Migros group merger will now centralise completely different cooperativee, both large and small. In terms of sales figures, the Zurich cooperative is the largest, with a turnover of around CHF4 billion.
The Eastern Switzerland cooperative, on the other hand, has the most employees, at 8,466. The smallest cooperative is in Ticino. However, all ten cooperatives support the merger.
It remains to be seen how many jobs will be cut following the merger. Since 2018, Migros has shed or outsourced almost 15,000 posts.
Migros has sold off a number of subsidiary companies, including Hotelplan, Globus, Melectronics, SportX, Micasa and Mibelle. The sale of Tegut in Germany will result in the loss of a further 7,000 jobs this year, with the employees transferring to the new owner.
The regional cooperative merger needs the blessing of Migros’s 2.3 million cooperative members who will vote on the proposal. A turnout of at least 25% and a two-thirds majority are required.

SEOUL, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A fire broke out on Tuesday in Guryong village, a shantytown in Seoul’s upmarket Gangnam district, affecting 77 households and 107 people, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
No injuries or casualties had been reported, a fire official told Reuters, and Yonhap said people had evacuated to an emergency shelter.
The fire agency has deployed 232 personnel and 70 vehicles to fight the fire, which began at about 3:50 p.m. local time (0650 GMT) in a temporary structure, Yonhap said. Six helicopters were sent to stop the fire spreading to a nearby mountain.
Guryong, often described as Seoul’s largest remaining shantytown, emerged in the 1970s and 1980s when families displaced by public works projects settled on the edge of Gangnam without permits. Its densely packed homes are built with flammable materials such as vinyl sheets and plywood.
A major fire in the village in January forced hundreds of residents to evacuate.

Prison sentences of up to one year for fraudsters who conned Prince Laurent and Princess Claire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:16:20 UTC
17:16:20 KST

Four defendants who defrauded Prince Laurent (pictured left), King Filip’s brother, and Princess Claire, his wife, of 17,000 euros have been sentenced to prison terms of up to one year. The couple, who live in leafy Tervuren (Flemish Brabant), clicked on a link in a fake text message in 2021.
Prison sentences of up to one year for fraudsters who conned Prince Laurent and Princess Claire
On 23 December 2021, Princess Claire received a message on her mobile phone purporting to be from Cardstop. Card Stop is the central 24/7 service in Belgium used to immediately block lost, stolen, swallowed, or compromised payment methods. The text stated that she needed to block her bank card. She had lost her card a few days earlier and didn’t suspect anything. She clicked on the link and entered her personal details on a fake website.
When Princess Claire became suspicious, she closed the website, but a few days later she realised she could no longer make any payments. Her bank confirmed that she had been the victim of phishing. A total of 17,776 euros was withdrawn from Prince Laurent and Princess Claire’s accounts. The account into which the prince receives his allowance was also affected.
Identity of fraudsters still a mystery
Almost five years later, the public prosecutor’s office has not managed to map out the fraudsters’ entire network. However, four so-called ‘money mules’ were tracked down. They had made their accounts available to the fraudsters to channel the money and were due to appear in court today.
One of the money mules will not face any punishment. The other three were given suspended prison sentences of between six and twelve months. Together, they must also repay 10,765.75 euros.
'Fake'
The investigators were also able to establish that the fraudulent message had been sent by a woman from Antwerp, but she pleaded not guilty.
Her lawyer, Walter Damen, argued that the woman’s telephone number had been spoofed. This is a technique used by fraudsters to display a false number with a message, in order to impersonate someone else. The woman was acquitted.

Earlier Monday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three drones over the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia, without identifying their origin or intended targets.
The coalition also announced strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen, saying it destroyed ballistic missile launchers, storage tunnels and a missile depot.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said the operations aimed to dismantle the group's ballistic missile network and disrupt its supply routes.
The renewed fighting between the two sides has shattered a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce that largely halted attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has also opened another front in regional conflicts involving the U.S., Israel and Iran.

The Oromiya regional government and a source linked to a rebel alliance fighting government forces in the northern Tigray region traded blame for the attacks.

Admit it: the English love affair with European food has grown stale – we need a native cuisine we can be proud of | Lewis Bassett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:05 UTC
17:00:05 KST

No discerning dinner party host in England would dream of serving their guests a traditional English ham. You might find jamón ibérico, of which Spain is so proud, but never stuffed chine, a shoulder cut of salted pork marbled with parsley, once a delicacy in Lincolnshire. It sometimes seems as if the English middle classes are so concerned with other countries’ proud artisanal products that they miss the potential of our own.
We’re more likely to find cookery writers and experts in nutrition advocate for Japanese foods than traditional English fare. The Chinese diet, too, has its passionate advocates in England. We barely need to mention the English middle classes’ long love affair with France and Italy and Spain.
Many well-to-do English eaters project ideals of rustic authenticity on to southern Europe, giving us the “modern European” cooking that has dominated the menus of many smart restaurants in England for decades. Yet perhaps this culinary culture is running out of road? Is it not a little dull to see aioli, burrata and fresh pasta almost everywhere? What happened to salad cream and whitebait and pickled herring and steamed puddings? Where did all the bath buns and sally lunns go? Are croissants really all we want from our bakeries? When did England’s middle classes fall out of love with English food?
My book The Full English explores these topics from the first-person perspective of a chef-cum-sociologist. I describe the history of England’s break with the tastes once shared by elites across medieval Europe, which provided us with our first recognisably national cuisine. For Georgian Britons, food, especially beef, spit-roasted and served with simple garnishes, was everything that France was not. France was said to be popish and tyrannical, and the courtly tradition of French food reflected that. France was viewed by British patriots as weak, because its population supposedly subsisted on weeds and frogs. Beef, by contrast, was hearty, honest and rooted in the self-reliance of the English country gentleman. Many middling and upper sorts in Georgian England, from William Hogarth to William Gladstone, joined clubs whose patriotic motto was “beef and liberty”.
But by the late 19th century, among a generation with no direct memory of the Napoleonic wars, elite food preferences changed again, no less because the elite itself had changed. Britain had already become a majority urban nation in 1851 (some 100 years ahead of southern Europe), and in English cities, merchants, financiers, capitalists and their associated professions – groups whose power came from money, rather than land or title – demanded French cooks and French restaurants as a modern move away from the country cooking of the older upper classes, one which reflected Britain’s new ease with France.
Later, in postwar Britain, an expanding middle class underwent a lifestyle revolution. Stiff hats, starched shirts and rigid table manners were out and the supposed informality of Mediterranean food was in, along with bare brick walls, furniture from Habitat, bric-a-brac and olives; all markers of what the cookery writer Elizabeth David deemed a new taste for “the luxury of authenticity”.
And why not? Fourteen years of rationing had undermined a native food culture already hindered by urbanisation and industry, both of which were enabled by our dependence on imported food. Then, on top of these features of Britain’s peculiar modernity, has been the long shadow cast by Georgian patriotism – which deemed French food as effeminate, and so committed us to a view that refinement in food is “posh”. No wonder the middle class in this country projected a greedy gaze upon an idealised, provincial France and Italy.
But might it be time to turn our hungry dreamings back to England? The other nations that make up the union have their own culinary traditions and often proud relationship to national identity. But in England, patriotism is often assumed to be a blight. Outside international football tournaments, one senses that flags are flown mostly out of fear and hatred, and almost never out of pride. A positive, prouder version of national identity could become a powerful way to rebuild connection in our increasingly fragmented society.
Nations are inventions, thus so too are national foods. Take the case of British bread. The modern artisanal sourdough loaf – so adored by today’s tote-bag yoga-ing classes – has its roots in France and California and was introduced to England in the mid-1990s. And yet its popularity has seen an explosion of native craft baking across the UK, producing a proud generation of artisans who have brought about a better, and at this point, recognisably British bread.
We need such inventions more than ever, since ours is a country with some of the most unhealthy and unsustainable eating habits in Europe. Roast beef or overfished seafoods cannot be the way to go. Old dishes and familiar ingredients can be adapted, and new traditions can be invented. Yet as the new British artisanal sourdough shows, middle-class trends can be unaffordable for many. Such exclusivity can breed resentment, in turn fuelling the popularity of foods and brands, such as Greggs, which reproduce our anti-posh, anti-artisanal culture and our habits of unhealthy, industrial eating.
For England to find a popular new culinary heritage, one centred on the dignity of craft production as much as health, will require state policy capable of lifting up our culinary standards across the board.
And here, pride can form a common ground for any politics leaning in that direction. As a chef, I know that when I have made a custard tart with a satisfying wobble or perfectly dressed a crop of garden beans with a pouting spike of vinegar, I feel a sense of self-respect. Investing in British culinary craft is a way to lend pride to our struggling nation; a decent native cookery culture will be one positive thing worth raising the flag for.
- Lewis Bassett is a chef and the host of The Full English Podcast, and the author of The Full English

"Things start in really simple gestures" says Es Devlin of her Design Museum retrospective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

British artist and designer Es Devlin explains how ambitious creative projects begin with simple ideas in this exclusive video interview with Dezeen, filmed at Es Devlin: Other Worlds, her first European retrospective at London’s Design Museum.
“This is literally my favourite project. A book which took me seven years to make and it contains everything I’ve ever made,” Devlin told Dezeen, referring to a companion book created to coincide with the exhibition.
The book, as well as the exhibition, brings together three decades of Devlin’s work across theatre, opera, concert stage design and large-scale public installations.
The exhibition explores how Devlin’s projects develop, from early drawings and models to monumental installations experienced by audiences around the world.
In the interview, she explains how she hopes the presentation will demystify the creative process and encourage visitors to pursue their own ideas.
“I really hope that when people leave this exhibition, they’ll see objects and traces of things which make them say, ‘Oh, I could do that’,” she said.
“It’s not a mystery. It doesn’t come by magic. It comes step by step, with attention, curiosity, work and collaboration.”
The exhibition begins with a replica of Devlin’s studio in Peckham, complete with her books, objects, models, drawings, tools and paints.
“I love visiting other artists and designers’ studios,” she said. “I think it’ll make people feel something about what these rooms feel like, where creativity is allowed to happen at all times.”
From the studio, visitors encounter Come Home Again, Devlin’s installation originally presented outside Tate Modern in 2022.
The original work featured illuminated cut-outs of endangered wildlife arranged within a cross-section of the dome of St Paul’s Cathedral.
Reconfigured beneath a mirrored ceiling for the Design Museum exhibition, it is followed by A 30-Year Desk, a series of concentric circular desks displaying archival objects, drawings and models from across her career.
The archive includes material relating to her designs for the 2018 theatre production The Lehman Trilogy, the Forest of Us installation in Miami and the closing ceremony of the London 2012 Olympic Games, alongside more than 30 models of projects that have previously been exhibited in Britain.
The exhibition culminates in An Infinite Library, an eight-metre-wide rotating sculpture containing more than 2,000 books that have shaped Devlin’s worldview.
The artwork was originally installed on the beachfront of the Faena Beach hotel in Miami Beach and has been reimagined for the Design Museum retrospective.
Arranged in bands of colour above a circular mirror, the books are illuminated by projections and accompanied by recordings of Devlin reading selected passages.
Devlin began her career designing sets for small-scale theatre productions in 1996 before moving into opera, dance and concert stage design. Over the past decade, she has increasingly focused on large-scale public artworks and installations.
For Es Devlin: Other Worlds, she brought together material spanning her career, including childhood experiments and paintings made shortly before the exhibition opened, to reveal the ideas and processes behind her finished projects.
“I began to develop an attitude on how to take things that are amassed in piles and are somewhat overwhelming, to spread them out along a timeline and make them digestible and legible to an audience,” she said.
“Actually, these things that seem huge and overwhelming and complicated, they start in really simple gestures.”
Es Devlin: Other Worlds runs at the Design Museum in London until 4 April 2027.

‘Unacceptable’: condemning writers over AI detector scores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

‘Unacceptable’: condemning writers over AI detector scores
When a detector flagged a bestselling novel as AI-generated, it sparked a controversy that had serious consequences for the author. Swiss experts and artists examine how much these tools can really prove and what their verdicts mean for creative work.
Haitian-Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien had a promising career ahead of him. His novel C’était ça ou mourir (It was either that or die), a critical and commercial success, was in the running for some of France’s most prestigious literary prizes, including the Goncourt. That was until an anonymous account on X accused him of writing almost the entire book using artificial intelligence (AI).
Orélien denied using AI to write the novel. But to his accusers, the evidence seemed unequivocal: Pangram, one of the most popular tools for detecting AI content, had classified more than 95% of the book as AI-generated.
From there, things took a turn for the worse for Orélien. His novel was removed from the Goncourt selection, also amid revelations by the press of plagiarism in earlier works, for which he apologised. His Canadian publisher cut ties with him after an external analysis uncovered further evidence of AI use. Orélien continued to deny having written the book with AI, while acknowledging that he had turned to it for historical research during the creative process.
From the beginning, the controversy divided the literary world between those who defended the author and questioned the reliability of AI detectors, and those who criticised him.
Beyond Orélien’s case, Swiss filmmaker, screenwriter and lecturer Manuel Flurin Hendry believes it’s unfair to damage a writer’s reputation based on a software-generated score. “The idea that you feed a text into Pangram and then socially execute a writer feels unacceptable,” Hendry told Swissinfo in an interview at the AI+X Summit in early October. Hendry defends artists’ freedom to choose their own tools.
Other Swiss writers and artists have openly experimented with AI. Author Charles Lewinsky incorporated entire passages generated by ChatGPT into his novel Täuschend echt. Photographer Matthieu Gafsou has used image-generation tools such as DALL·E in his artistic work.
These are just a few transparent examples of how AI has entered creative work in Switzerland. But deciding how to respond to undisclosed and potentially extensive use of AI is far more difficult. As is determining how much AI-generated material is acceptable in a work of art, and whether tools like Pangram can really be trusted as a definitive proof of fraud.
How reliable is Pangram?
For Hendrik Strobelt, a senior researcher at IBM in the United States, the question of Pangram’s reliability is complex. In 2019, Strobelt and his colleagues developed GLTR, one of the first experimental tools designed to help identify text potentially generated by language models.
At the time, OpenAI had just released GPT-2, the model on which GLTR was based. AI models tended to produce rather dull texts that were very similar in style, because this type of content was the most common, Strobelt explains.
Identifying whether a text might have been produced with the help of AI was therefore relatively straightforward: it was enough to look for the most likely words.
Then language models became more sophisticated. Strobelt believes that, with today’s advanced AI systems, it has become extremely difficult to establish clear rules to distinguish AI-generated text from human writing.
“Now these models are significantly larger. They can imitate styles if you prompt them accordingly,” the IBM researcher says.
Software such as Pangram uses a method known as “supervised classification”. It compares and classifies texts written before generative AI became widespread – which is presumed to be human-written – with “mirror” versions on the same topic, generated by different commercially available language models. During training the software learns to identify the differences between them.
The logic is that if a system can distinguish between texts that are very similar in subject matter, its predictions will become more accurate.
“You want to train on things that are very close to each other, to be sure that you get the hard tasks trained first,” Strobelt explains.
Pangram claimsExternal link an accuracy rate of 99.98% and a false-positive rate of 0.01%. Its high performance has also been supported by independent researchExternal link, including a studyExternal link published this year.
According to Paolo Italiani, an AI and machine-learning researcher at the Università della Svizzera italiana (USI), the longer a text is, the more reliable a detector’s assessment tends to be.
“It’s quite probable that at least a portion of [the text] is AI-generated,” he says.
The limits of AI detectors
Yet it remains difficult to understand exactly which features of a text these tools rely on to make their classifications, says Lonneke van der Plas, professor of natural language processing at USI.
Interpretability studies would be needed to gain more understanding, she explains. But because commercial tools such as Pangram are largely black boxes whose internal workings are not accessible to independent researchers, it is challenging to study how they reach their conclusions.
In theory, certain clues such as an overly linear argumentative structure could help determine whether a text was more likely written by AI or by a human, researchExternal link co-authored by Van der Plas highlights. But such features, she cautions, are not sufficient to establish a text’s origin with certainty.
Van der Plas also points out that detection tools tend to perform less reliably in languages other than English and in more specialised genres that may have been less well represented in their training data.
The problem becomes even more complicated when a text is the product of collaboration between humans and AI. Some tests showExternal link, detectors’ accuracy drops by around 20 percentage points in such cases. Pangram’s own technical reportExternal link also indicates that the software loses accuracy when faced with content that alternates between human-written and AI-generated sentences.
“This software has been mostly trained on either completely human-generated or machine-generated texts. As soon as they get something that it’s in between, they get into trouble,” van der Plas says.
A score is not sufficient proof
From a legal perspective, results produced by tools such as Pangram do not constitute proof that an author has committed fraud.
“A legal decision cannot simply rely on those technologies because they can be inaccurate” says Jacques de Werra, professor of intellectual property law at the University of Geneva.
If a case like Orélien’s were brought before a court, de Werra explains, other evidence alongside detector scores should be considered, including original manuscripts, successive drafts and even exchanges with AI systems. De Werra also points out that AI involvement in creative work does not automatically invalidate an author’s copyright claims.
“If a person can demonstrate that there is a sufficiently close creative link between the input, creative prompting, and the output, it could be possible to claim human creativity,” he says.
The key is whether the author’s creative contribution is sufficient. De Werra stresses, however, that there is no fixed numerical threshold that determines how much of a text must be written by a person for a work to be considered their own.
If a book moves you, does it matter if AI helped write it?
For Manuel Flurin Hendry, however, the issue goes beyond legal protection.
Hendry openly uses AI-based technologies, some of which he has developed himself, for various aspects of his work, from analysing screenplays to assisting his academic research.
Technology, he explains, opens new channels of inspiration, sometimes suggesting approaches he had not previously considered. It also frees up more time for the creative process.
“True human writing is thinking in action. It requires friction and to enter a state where one can just concentrate on their flow of thoughts,” he says.
And he poses a provocative question: why should it matter how much AI contributed to a work? “If it moves you. If you find it interesting. If it makes you think, what is the argument?” he asks.
What’s important, Hendry argues, is learning which tasks to delegate to AI and which are better done personally. Rather than rejecting technology, artists should be transparent about how they use it.
“If I pretend this is mine, but it’s totally AI generated, then it’s fake,” Hendry says.
What is at stake is not only an artist’s reputation, but above all the relationship of trust with their audience.

Qatar’s path to defence autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:55:01 UTC
16:55:01 KST

Qatar’s path to defence autonomy
Qatar and other Gulf states need to strengthen their defence capabilities and diversify security partnerships to reduce reliance on external protection.
Developments in the Gulf since the beginning of this year have raised fundamental questions about the security of the region in general and Qatar in particular. How can Qatar and other Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states become effective, independent military powers that do not rely on external security guarantees to ensure their safety?
The question for Qatar is how it can build, over the next five years, a national defence capability that would enable it to protect the state and its vital interests even in the absence of Gulf or regional support, or if the United States provides only limited assistance. The aim is to explore whether Qatar can achieve what might be described as defence autonomy, rather than isolation. In other words, Qatar should remain open to alliances and partnerships without making its security dependent on the decisions of another state.
Qatar is a small country in terms of geography and population, but it enjoys numerous advantages. It has highly valuable critical infrastructure, a sensitive geographical location and an economy that depends heavily on the uninterrupted flow of energy exports, trade and shipping to almost every part of the world. At the same time, it possesses substantial financial resources, extensive international relationships, a major military base hosting US forces, advanced air defence capabilities and a network of political relationships that give it influence beyond its physical size.
These advantages, however, do not amount to “strategic autonomy”. In a major crisis such as the one the region has been experiencing for several months, Qatar’s protection remains heavily dependent on the US. Nor does reliance on the collective capabilities of the GCC provide sufficient assurance that its member states would be able, or willing, to take risks in defence of another member.
Against this backdrop, Qatar’s policy objective over the next five years should be to design and build an independent national strategy based on the capacity to prevent threats, withstand attacks and maintain continuity. The goal should be to achieve defence autonomy, rather than to build an army capable of confronting a major regional power on its own.
Such a strategy would rest on six pillars:
- Air and missile defence
- Early warning capabilities and information sovereignty
- Protection of critical infrastructure
- Air and naval power
- Cybersecurity and electronic warfare
- Restructuring security and military policy around the principle of multiple security guarantees rather than dependence on a single guarantor
Defence autonomy
Qatar does not need to exhaust its resources building the capabilities required to fight an all-out war alone against a major regional power, regardless of which power that might be. Such an ambition would be unrealistic for a country with limited territory and population.
A more realistic objective is to achieve a degree of defence autonomy appropriate for a small state such as Qatar. This means being able to perform a number of essential tasks without waiting for assistance from others.
These include, but are not limited to:
- Detecting threats and identifying their nature before they reach Qatari territory
- Delaying or absorbing an initial strike
- Protecting the country’s leadership and strategic centres
- Maintaining energy and water supplies, electricity, communications, ports and airports
- Keeping political and economic activities functioning during a crisis
- Imposing sufficiently high costs on an aggressor to force it to reconsider its calculations
- Withstanding a prolonged crisis without making the state’s continued functioning conditional on the arrival of external forces
To carry out these tasks effectively, the strategy should focus on the following priorities:
First: Building an integrated Qatari air defence shield
This is the most important gap that needs to be addressed. Possessing advanced fighter aircraft and air defence systems is not enough to make Qatar militarily autonomous. What is needed is an integrated national air and missile defence system.
The objective by 2031 should not be to possess the best defence system, but one that continues to function even in the absence of US forces or any other external security guarantor.
Such a system should include:
- A multilayered Qatari radar network
- Integration of civilian and military radar systems
- A unified national command and control centre
- Integration of short, medium and long-range air defences
- Expanded counter-drone capabilities
- Stronger electronic warfare capabilities and equipment
- Low-cost interception systems for small targets
- Enhanced mobile protection for radar installations and command centres
- Large national stockpiles of ammunition and spare parts
Second: An air force designed for independence
Qatar currently possesses an advanced air fleet. But the independence of an air force cannot be measured by the number of aircraft it operates. The crucial question is whether the Qatari air force can sustain operations for several consecutive weeks if external supply lines are disrupted.
For the answer to be yes, Qatar must develop the capacity to continue air operations even without direct US or other foreign support, albeit at a reduced level.
This requires policymakers and those responsible for developing the national defence strategy to focus on the following priorities over the next five years:
- Increasing ammunition stockpiles, whether through domestic production or imports
- Expanding domestic defence manufacturing capabilities and strengthening maintenance capacity
- Training more Qatari personnel to carry out a range of functions, including maintenance
- Building up dispersed ammunition stockpiles rather than concentrating them in a single location
- Increasing stocks of drones and other unmanned aircraft
- Developing ground and aerial refuelling capabilities and strengthening logistical support
Third: The sea as a second line of defence
For Qatar, a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides, protecting its maritime domain is not merely a military concern. It is also an economic necessity of the highest importance.
Liquefied natural gas, oil exports and imports all depend on the security of the surrounding waters. Qatar should therefore develop a naval force suited to its needs, equipped with advanced technology and capabilities.
The objective is not to build a large fleet, but to make attacks on Qatar’s maritime infrastructure both difficult and costly.
This requires a focus on several important priorities:
- Continuously improving and expanding maritime surveillance capabilities to protect Qatar’s waters and offshore installations
- Strengthening and developing capabilities to counter maritime drones
- Enhancing the protection of ports and securing shipping routes
Fourth: A national resilience programme
The most serious vulnerability of a country with limited territory and population lies in its infrastructure. A successful attack on a small number of critical facilities could have severe and far-reaching consequences for the entire country.
Given the importance of this threat, the national defence strategy should include the establishment of what might be called a “national resilience and protection programme”.
Such a programme would aim to protect critical infrastructure, including gas and energy facilities, water desalination plants, power stations, telecommunications centres and towers, civilian and military airports, ports and fuel networks, hospitals, government institutions and data centres.
One aspect of this protection is ensuring that every sector has adequate backup capacity. If a major desalination plant were to stop operating for any reason, for example, an alternative source of supply should be available to prevent a water supply problem from escalating into a national crisis. The same principle should apply to every other sector.
Fifth: Qatar must know what is happening around it before the US does
Military independence begins with information. Qatar therefore needs to develop its own national capabilities in the following areas:
- Space-based reconnaissance
- Unmanned aerial vehicles
- Radar systems
- Electronic intelligence
- Artificial intelligence-driven data analysis
This does not mean that Qatar needs to launch large satellites for every mission. Instead, it should work towards building an integrated system combining commercial and military satellites, international partnerships and national capabilities for collecting and analysing data.
The underlying principle is that Qatar should not depend on an external party to inform it of a threat approaching its territory.
Qatar will undoubtedly continue to need intelligence from the US, France, the United Kingdom and other countries. Nevertheless, it must possess the independent capacity to produce its own national intelligence picture, assess the nature of threats and determine how to prepare for them at an early stage, before requesting assistance from allies or partners.
Sixth: Diversifying security guarantees
The events of this year have demonstrated to all GCC states the importance of diversifying their alliances and security guarantees rather than relying on a single external power, particularly the US.
That power could become involved in future international crises, decide for one reason or another to limit its direct involvement in regional crises, or even reduce its military presence.
This makes it necessary to adopt a forward-looking approach based on diversifying alliances and making the security of the Gulf a matter of global interest requiring international cooperation.
In this context, GCC states could benefit from partnerships with South Korea, Turkiye and certain European powers, as well as regional powers such as Pakistan and China in specific fields, without hastily abandoning cooperation with the US.
The objective is to reduce the risks associated with dependence on a single supplier or ally. Such diversification does not mean building an alliance against the US.
Achieving defence and political autonomy for Qatar by 2031 does not mean isolating the country from its partners or dispensing with existing alliances. Rather, it means developing national capabilities that can ensure the protection of the state and its vital interests under all circumstances.
This strategic objective requires the development of an integrated air defence system, stronger intelligence and cyber capabilities, and better protection of critical infrastructure. It also requires improving the effectiveness of Qatar’s air and naval forces to ensure resilience and allow state institutions to continue functioning during a crisis.
Defence autonomy also requires diversifying international partnerships and establishing multiple security guarantees to reduce dependence on any single external power.
The foundation of this strategy is a transition from dependence on external protection towards the ability to deter threats, withstand crises and make independent national decisions at the appropriate time, while remaining open to international cooperation and partnerships.

Israel elections: High Arab turnout seeks to punish Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:40:51 UTC
16:40:51 KST

Breadcrumb
As Israel's elections get underway, high Arab turnout seeks to punish Netanyahu's government
Palestinian towns and villages across Israel saw significant voter turnout on Tuesday morning as polls opened for the 26th Knesset elections. Voters began arriving at polling stations as early as 7am, with a heavy presence of Jewish observers, including representatives from far-right parties.
Despite reported delays in opening several polling stations due to administrative procedures, activists from both the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra'am) mobilised to urge Arab citizens to cast their ballots early in the day to avoid anticipated congestion during the afternoon and evening.
The elections come three years into Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, with widespread expectations of strong mobilisation by Palestinian citizens of Israel seeking to punish the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court, and his far-right coalition partners.
According to the Central Elections Committee, the total number of eligible voters stands at 7,331,981, an increase of 543,177 compared to the previous election. Arab citizens account for roughly 18% of the eligible electorate, numbering approximately 1.172 million voters.
Most opinion polls project an increase in Arab voter participation.
Data from the Midgam Research Institute indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in the previous elections.
Meanwhile, Yousef Makladeh, director of the Stat-Net research institute, which specialises in polling within the Arab community, projected that turnout could reach around 68% if current campaign momentum is sustained.
Polling analysts further suggest that if turnout exceeds 70% on election day, Arab parliamentary representation could climb to 16 seats.
Writer and researcher Marzouq Halabi told The New Arab that the anticipated mobilisation reflected a defensive response to the policies of Netanyahu's government, including the genocide in Gaza, forced displacement, home demolitions and growing anti-Palestinian incitement.
"This is purely defensive voting, more than anything else," he said, arguing that Palestinian citizens of Israel increasingly view the election as an opportunity to resist the far right rather than simply choose between competing political programmes," he said.
"They are not asking about party platforms; rather, they are asking how the fascist right can be repelled and its agendas obstructed," Halabi said.
He added that the vote was also about asserting Palestinian presence and identity in the face of attempts to marginalise and silence the community.
Maha Karkabi, a candidate representing the Joint List, similarly argued that higher Arab turnout could prevent some far-right parties from crossing the electoral threshold and potentially deny Netanyahu the parliamentary support needed to form another government.
"Most opinion polls indicate that a high Arab turnout will prevent extremist and racist right-wing parties from crossing the electoral threshold, and could, to a certain extent, prevent Netanyahu from forming a government with the far right," she told The New Arab.
Karkabi said the Joint List would nevertheless remain in opposition, ruling out participation in Israeli governments because of their policies towards Palestinians, including occupation, ethnic cleansing and home demolitions.
However, analysts cautioned that Netanyahu's defeat would not necessarily bring an immediate end to Israel's policies in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Muhanad Mustafa, a researcher at the Haifa-based Mada al-Carmel Center, told The New Arab that much would depend on the election results, but that even a victory for the opposition would be unlikely to produce an immediate change.
Instead, he suggested that an alternative government could gradually shift towards political arrangements centred on Israeli security interests, rather than the religious ideology that has shaped the current coalition's approach.
"An alternative government would not bear the burden of the 7 October failure, and its approach would be primarily security-driven rather than rooted in messianic religious ideology," Mustafa said.
He added that a more ideologically diverse coalition could be more inclined towards internal compromises when addressing Gaza and the West Bank, although this would not necessarily translate into a fundamental change in Israeli policy.
Discussing the broader political and psychological shifts within Israeli society since 7 October, Mustafa said that the war had intensified anti-Palestinian sentiment and normalised increasingly extreme attitudes towards Palestinians.
"The fundamental shift is the desire for revenge against the Palestinians and treating them as a dehumanised population that can be annihilated, with a sense of relief following such actions," he said.
Mustafa also argued that religious narratives portraying the war as part of a broader struggle for salvation had gained influence, while much of Israeli society continued to view the events of 7 October in isolation from decades of occupation, siege and settlement expansion.
He said this had reinforced a widespread denial of Palestinian humanity and obscured the broader political context of the conflict.
Beyond domestic political shifts, the vote has drawn intense international scrutiny amid concerns over a potential resumption of war on Iran and its geopolitical and economic consequences.
Meanwhile, many Israelis, including expatriates who travelled back specifically to vote, hope the election outcome could help restore Israel's international standing, which has suffered significant damage in global public opinion following the war on Gaza.
Honida Ghanim, director of the Palestinian Forum for Israeli Studies (MADAR), told The New Arab that Israel's international reputation had deteriorated sharply, particularly among Western publics, even as governments continued to provide political support.
"Israel's international standing has declined sharply, to the point that it is closer to a rogue state, at least at the level of public opinion, and the United States is the clearest illustration of this," she said.
Ghanim argued that the Trump administration had given Israel's far-right leadership considerable freedom to pursue its policies despite mounting international criticism and concerns over violations of international law.
She warned that one of the most dangerous election outcomes for Palestinians would be a political deadlock that left Netanyahu in power as caretaker prime minister for an extended period.
"The most dangerous possible outcome of the elections is therefore a stalemate, with Netanyahu's government remaining in office as a caretaker government for what could be two years under Trump," she said.
Ghanim warned that such a scenario could allow the Israeli right to intensify its policies of forced displacement and territorial control while enjoying continued backing from Washington.
Even a victory for former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, she argued, would be unlikely to reverse Israel's international isolation or produce a fundamental shift in its policies towards Palestinians.
She suggested that Western governments might seek to rehabilitate Israel's image by presenting a new leadership as a departure from Netanyahu's far-right coalition, but questioned whether such a distinction would be credible.
Ghanim pointed to changing attitudes towards Israel in the United States, the difficulty of forming a stable alternative coalition and the continued support among mainstream Israeli politicians for policies that violate international law.
She also cited UN Security Council Resolution 2334 of 2016 and the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion on Israel's occupation, arguing that settlement expansion had become so deeply embedded in the Israeli political system that a change of government alone could not resolve the underlying issues.
"Israel has moved beyond the stage of repair: the settlement, which the world has regarded as a violation of international law, most notably in UN Security Council Resolution 2334 of 2016 and the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion, is today Israel itself," Ghanim concluded.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Tofan emphasized that Moldova intends to adopt Ukrainian anti-drone tactics to secure its borders against growing aerial threats. Addressing Moldovan citizens from the Ukrainian capital, Tofan noted that Ukraine’s defense against aggression contributes directly to the security of Europe.

Germany: Car ramming injures several near Hannover
October 27, 2026
A BMW was driven deliberately into a group of people, leaving four to five of them with some serious but not life-threatening injuries in Neustadt am Rübenberge late on Monday night, police said on Tuesday morning.
A police patrol making routine traffic checks in town near Hannover in the state of Lower Saxony, intervened, shooting at the car to stop it.
"The officers witnessed the incident as it happened and opened fire on the vehicle after it had been driven into the group of people," the spokesperson said.
Organized crime suspected
Police announced that they had taken three people into custody at the BMW owner's address.
A police spokesperson added that initial findings indicated the ramming was an act of gang violence between organized crime families, that the individuals involved knew each other and that the perpetrators likely targeted the group of people and were not acting at random.
Several suspects had fled the scene of the ramming on foot, police had said.
"The sequence of events and the exact roles of those involved are still under investigation," the spokesperson said, adding that forensic analysis of the cars and ramming scene was ongoing.
A reporter for the German DPA news agency described several damaged cars, with flat tires, a smashed rear window and bullet holes.

this fictional beverage comes with a real warning about fake news
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:37:43 UTC
16:37:43 KST

this fictional beverage comes with a real warning about fake news
dysturb’s fake drink campaign arrives in paris and NYC to encourage media literacy and critical thinking in an age of misinformation.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
dysturb launches a beverage with 0% fake news
Paris-based nonprofit Dysturb has launched Source.s, a fictional beverage advertised across the streets of Paris and New York in October 2026. The campaign gives its imaginary drink a convincing product launch, with large-scale murals, posters, and promotional cans handed out to passersby.
At first glance, Source.s could easily pass for another new drink brand. Its aluminum can comes in pale blue with oversized navy lettering, while its advertising borrows the familiar promises of refreshment and well-being. While the brand is invented, the promotional cans themselves are real.
The packaging begins to give the idea away upon closer look. An ‘informational value’ label replaces conventional nutrition facts, listing 0% fake news and 100% critical thinking. Even the language of hydration gets a rewrite. The American campaign reads ‘hydrate your mind, filter your feed,‘ to turn a familiar wellness slogan into a reminder to question the information we consume. It’s a playful piece of packaging design, with an underlying concern about how readily we trust something that looks convincing.
between paris and new york
The campaign for Dysturb’s fake beverage Source.s takes two different forms depending on where it appears. In Paris, it borrows the visual language of a classic bistro drink. Its posters use oversized yellow typography against photographic backgrounds, while the cans themselves have the polished appearance of a commercial beverage. A monumental mural on the Quai de Valmy extends the campaign into the city, accompanied by smaller posters across several neighborhoods. The team also distributed cans along the canal and around nearby métro entrances.
In New York, the American version takes its cues from contemporary wellness branding. The same pale-blue can appears against bright skies and sunlit architecture, with a model holding it in the kind of lifestyle imagery associated with functional drinks. Large murals were erected near the Navy Yard in Brooklyn and in Manhattan.
Dysturb credits AI-generated imagery in the campaign, an interesting detail for a project concerned with the credibility of visual information. Both versions use recognizable advertising conventions to lend an invented product the appearance of legitimacy.
a health warning disguised as a drink campaign
The message becomes more direct in the posters’ smaller print, where Source.s borrows the language of consumer health warnings. One reads, ‘Excessive consumption of fake news is hazardous to democracy.’ Another compares questionable information to a contaminated source, extending the drink metaphor into the way misleading stories circulate online. QR codes appear alongside the advertising, giving passersby a way to follow the campaign beyond the posters.
For Dysturb, the fictional beverage offers a way to introduce a familiar problem through an unexpected format. The organization has spent more than a decade bringing photojournalism and public information into urban spaces, often through large photographic installations. With Source.s, it has adopted the techniques of commercial advertising itself. The campaign asks people to consider why professional graphics and familiar branding can make a message seem credible, even before its source has been examined.
free guides bring the campaign beyond the street
Source.s is part of Dysturb’s Anti Fake News Club, an educational initiative that also offers five free media-literacy guides in English, French, and Spanish. The downloadable materials address the mechanics of misinformation and the habits that shape how people encounter the news. Their practical exercises encourage readers to look beyond a headline, compare independent sources, and examine the origins of photographs.
One guide explains how cropping or a misleading caption can change the meaning of an image, while another examines the influence of algorithms on the information appearing in social feeds. The resources have been used in educational programs across schools and other institutions.
The organization is also developing JustCheck, a verification platform intended to help users evaluate questionable content. According to Dysturb, the proposed tool will accept everything from screenshots to videos and return a credibility assessment supported by evidence and sources.
For now, Source.s puts the same questions into a more immediate, physical setting. A fake drink appears on a café table or a neighborhood wall, complete with all the visual cues of a genuine product. Its real purpose becomes clear once someone stops to read the label.

According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 27 (starting at 18:00 on October 26), the enemy attacked with:
-  Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia's Bryansk region; 
-  280 Shahed-type attack UAVs (69 of them jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Millerovo, Kursk, Shatalovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske. 
Where Russia struck
"The main direction of the strike was Kyiv," the statement said.
How the air defense forces performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 257 enemy targets:
-  2 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles; 
-  255 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (56 of them jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs, and drones of other types; several attack UAVs are still in the air, and combat operations continue. 
Hits by the enemy's air-attack weapons were recorded at 25 locations, as well as the falling of downed targets (debris) at 16 locations.

KMT urges government to defend non-nuclear homeland policy

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The KMT called on the government and anti-nuclear advocacy groups to nominate representatives for debates on a referendum proposing the abolition of Taiwan’s non-nuclear homeland policy.
The Central Election Commission announced in September that it would hold five debates on Nov. 12, 14, 16, 18 and 20, per SETN. The referendum asks voters whether they support adopting nuclear energy to strengthen the economy and abolishing the non-nuclear homeland policy, per Global Views Monthly.
Presidential Office spokesperson Karen Kuo (郭雅慧) said Friday that Taiwan had already achieved its non-nuclear homeland policy. KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chair Chen I-hsin (陳以信) urged President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Monday to nominate representatives to defend the policy or apologize for what Chen considers to be the wrong policy for Taiwan.
Pro-nuclear advocate Huang Shih-hsiu (黃士修) reiterated Chen’s call, stressing that the KMT had already submitted its debate representatives, per ETtoday. He noted that the Control Yuan had previously criticized the Cabinet for failing to nominate representatives to defend government policies during the 2018 local elections.
Huang also urged the National No-Nukes Action Platform to nominate representatives, adding that the advocacy group had previously announced Oct. 15 as the date it would release its list of debate representatives.
In addition to calling for the release of the representatives’ names, Huang addressed criticism of the referendum.
Former CEC Chair Chen In-chin (陳英鈐) questioned the proposal’s effectiveness, saying the referendum does not specify whether it seeks to reopen existing nuclear power plants or establish small modular reactors, per Liberty Times. He added that the referendum would have no bearing on the results of nuclear safety inspections.
National Chengchi University Associate Professor of law Lin Chia-ho (林佳和) argued that the referendum, which calls for the abolition of Article 23 of the Basic Environment Law, should have been handled by the legislature, per Environmental Information Center. He said the move would allow lawmakers to shirk their responsibilities.
In response to Chen, Huang said the proposal envisioned using nuclear power to support carbon capture, desalination, or hydrogen production when installing new conventional reactors or small modular reactors.
Responding to Lin, Huang stressed that the referendum concerned abolishing the policy rather than specific legal provisions. He accused former President Tsai Ing-wen’s (蔡英文) administration of ignoring the results of a 2018 pro-nuclear referendum to pursue its non-nuclear homeland policy.
The 2018 referendum sought to repeal the legal requirement that all nuclear reactors in Taiwan cease operations by 2025, per Taiwan FactCheck Center. Although the referendum led to the removal of the relevant provision, then-Premier Lai Ching-te (賴清德) stressed that the government’s policy remained unchanged.
Academia Sinica research fellow Su Yen-tu (蘇彥圖) explained that arguments presented during the preceding debates were intended to inform voters rather than determine the referendum’s legal effect. He noted that the referendum itself focused on abolishing the legal requirement for all reactors to cease operations before 2025.
Former Taipei Bar Association Chair Huang Hsu-tien (黃旭田) suggested that the government could continue pursuing denuclearization if it opposed the use of nuclear energy.

Lai pledges better healthcare facilities, higher pay for Taiwan medical workers
Unknown

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will expand hospitals, improve medical workers' pay, and strengthen healthcare services under the government's Healthy Taiwan policy, President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Tuesday.
Speaking at a topping-out ceremony for a new emergency and critical care building at Taipei Hospital in New Taipei's Xinzhuang District, Lai said the project would improve care for local residents. He expressed hope that the building would open in 2028, CNA reported.
Lai said the government aims to increase average life expectancy by three years by 2032. It also wants to reduce the share of people's lives spent in poor health from 10% to 8%.
The president said Taiwanese are living longer, but the years spent in poor health have not declined. People spend about eight years of their lives with health problems or disabilities that may require medical care or daily assistance.
The government also aims to cut the age-standardized cancer mortality rate by one-third by 2030, Lai said. It has set a similar reduction target for the age-standardized mortality rate from chronic diseases, with prevention efforts focused on high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and high cholesterol, per CTEE.
Lai said achieving these goals would require more funding for hospital facilities, medical equipment, and healthcare services. He also called for higher pay and better working conditions for doctors, nurses, and other medical staff, measures outlined in the government's healthcare policy.
The government's Healthy Taiwan Cultivation Plan will invest NT$48.9 billion (US$1.5 billion) from 2025 to 2029. The program focuses on improving working conditions, training medical workers, introducing smart healthcare technology, and supporting sustainable medical services.
Lai also praised Taipei Hospital for its role during the COVID-19 pandemic, including its quarantine and screening work. He recalled approving the expansion project while serving as premier and thanked successive administrations for helping move it forward, per UDN.
The new building will have 16 floors above ground and four basement levels. The expansion was designed to increase hospital capacity and strengthen emergency and critical care services for residents of Xinzhuang and surrounding areas, per Economic Daily News.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Food and Drug Administration intercepted 24 metric tons of black peppercorns from Malaysia due to excessive pesticide levels, reports said Tuesday.
Authorities will check every shipment from the same importer arriving in Taiwan, per Liberty Times. The peppercorns were imported by Rich’s Spice International Inc.

During recent border checks, inspectors also found 0.8 milligrams of cadmium per kilogram in sea urchins from Vietnam, Liberty Times reported. The applicable limit was 0.3 mg/kg.
The sea urchin importer will also face increased inspections, the FDA said.

King Charles heads to Caribbean as calls for slavery reparations grow
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
08:25:21 CET
16:25:21 KST

By Michael Holden
LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - King Charles heads to the Caribbean this week on a tour which comes against the backdrop of increasingly vocal demands from the region that Britain pays reparations for its role in the slave trade.
Charles and his wife Queen Camilla will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana, before heading to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), the biennial get-together of the international organisation which he heads. The tour runs from October 27 to November 4.
At a previous meeting in 2022 of the leaders of the Commonwealth — a group of 56 nations which were mainly former British colonies — Charles expressed deep personal sorrow over slavery, and the issue is certain to be prominent once again.
Last month, CARICOM, the Caribbean Community, a group of 23 member and associate member states which includes the Bahamas, Barbados and Jamaica, said it would push for reparations to be on the CHOGM agenda.
“The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” CARICOM’s Secretary-General Carla Barnett said in a speech last month.
“It is about recognition, accountability and transformation, and about building a just and equitable future for the descendants of those who, as the chattel of colonial owners, endured untold suffering, loss of life and freedom.”
While Buckingham Palace has said the monarch would not shy away from Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade during his tour, he would not formally apologise for it as some have wanted, in keeping with British government policy which also excludes making any financial reparations.
“It is important to note here the work his majesty himself has done over many years both to acknowledge the wrongs of the past and to find creative ways to right inequalities that endure,” a palace spokesperson said.
Shirley Botchwey, the secretary-general of the Commonwealth, which encompasses some 2.7 billion people, said last week the time had come for discussions about reparations, be they financial or in some other form such as the return of artefacts.
As for an apology from the king, who remains the head of state of a number of Caribbean nations including both the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, she told Sky News: “It wouldn’t hurt to have that.”
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants, with Britain responsible for transporting an estimated 3.2 million people, making it the second most active European nation after Portugal.
(Reporting by Michael Holden; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria)

Good morning. It’s Tuesday, and this is what’s on today’s docket: Election fever spreads to Israel, Zelenskyy bemoans a lack of American Patriot missiles, and the European continent is only getting hotter, according to the EU climate chief. I’m Angela Skujins. Let’s dive in.
All eyes on Jerusalem: Roughly seven million eligible Israeli voters will head to polling stations today to cast their ballot in the country’s first legislative election since the 7 October attacks in 2023. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of the right-wing Likud party has dominated Israeli politics for the last two decades, and another victory would confirm unshakable confidence from his constituents, particularly after three years of war.
A defeat, however, could spell trouble. Netanyahu's main political rivals are led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose two sons were killed in combat. “What he is offering is an eternal war,” Eisenkot, the Yashar party leader, said in a radio interview. Although the pair share some policy positions — they both reject a two-state solution and favour a hard-line approach with Iran — Eisenkot is campaigning on a simple premise: he is not Netanyahu.
Yossi Mekelberg, senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, just said on Europe Today that a new government led by the opposition would bring about meaningful change. This would be manifested hopefully through a state commission into the 7 October attacks. “The more the (current) government rejects the idea, the more people are suspicious that they have something to hide,” he said. Watch.
Brussels watches: It remains to be seen whether the election will change how the EU engages with Israel. The capitals maintain an EU-Israel Association Agreement, which entered into force in 2000, that, among other measures, establishes a free trade area for industrial goods, agricultural trade preferences, and a framework for political, economic, and cultural cooperation.
According to Amnesty International, however, the EU and all its member states are under a “clear obligation” to prevent trade and investments that assist in the maintenance of Israel’s unlawful occupation of Palestinian territories, as set out in the International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion of July 2024.
Despite the agreement remaining in force, the EU executive has also tried — and failed — to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements. Meanwhile, relations between the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas and her Israeli counterpart Gideon Sa’ar remain fractious at best.
Hope is in the air: Diplomats wanted to remain tight-lipped when speaking to me about the election occurring just over 3,000 kilometres away, and what it means for relations between European capitals and Israel. However, one EU insider said there was “some hope” to find common ground with the new administration, whomever that may be.
Have I read that right? US President Donald Trump’s top officials allegedly want former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to be considered as the United Nations’ new secretary-general.
According to a Wall Street Journal report, Washington kingmakers have allegedly tapped the former prime minister for the top job, but nothing is certain yet. As my colleagues Sandor Zsiros and Ferenc Horvath report, the proposal could be a joint US-China-Russia bid, but securing the position is not as easy as it seems.
At least one UN member state has voiced its opposition, too. “I am certain that Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions,” Ukrainian Minister for Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha opined.
Speaking of Ukraine: Defence ministers from Europe’s biggest military powers — France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom — met in Paris Monday for a meeting centred on support for Ukraine and the spiralling war in Iran.
The strongest commentary to come out from the gathering was NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska, who stated that the ministers agreed “all allies” must “dig deep and do more — especially with air and missile defence” for Ukraine.
“We need to do it now, because every night the pressure from Russia is felt in almost every Ukrainian city,” she said.
Time goes by: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated on Monday he has waited “nearly a month” for US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to approve Patriot missiles, among other weapons, to counter Russia’s advances. “Conversations with other countries are also ongoing,” he said.
Over four and a half years into the full-scale invasion, Moscow has shown no signs of abating its relentless aggression. This is abundantly clear with non-stop aerial attacks battering Kyiv and other civilian areas, with the country lacking appropriate air defences to air attacks, such as deadly jet-powered drones.
Efforts by the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas to convince countries to pledge interceptor missiles to help defend against Ukraine have also failed.
Shifting tides: Complicating the matter on the ground is US President Donald Trump’s shifting alliances, manifesting recently through a controversial diesel deal catching Zelenskyy and European allies off guard. Sudden restrictions to Starlink technology, owned by Trump ally Elon Musk, also demonstrates fraying support from Washington.
Should we be surprised? Retired US Army Lieutenant General Ben Hodges recently told Euronews that Trump would always support Russia and that “he was never going to support Ukraine.”
How can Europe step in? Officials in Brussels are examining possible solutions for a widening funding gap of roughly €70 billion for 2027 to continue supporting the ally to the east.
Commission news: The European Commission will unveil new climate rules on Tuesday requiring EU governments to clarify who is responsible for protecting citizens from climate disasters, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews.
In an interview with EU news editor Maria Tadeo, Hoekstra warned that the world is heading towards a temporary or potentially prolonged overshoot of the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming limit, making it essential for governments to prepare for more extreme heat and climate disasters, even if efforts to cut emissions succeed.
“It is up to member states to decide where they want to put that responsibility. But what we do make mandatory is that they do have to appoint and articulate where the responsibility is going to lie,” Hoekstra said. Marta Pacheco has more on that important story.
One more thing: The EU executive will also propose new rules today beefing up the bloc’s border security. As part of the pitch, Frontex will be allowed to transfer migrants between third countries, expanding its operations beyond Europe and facilitating deportations from return hubs. Read more of that must-read reporting by Vincenzo Genovese.
Ukraine’s €70 billion shortfall could make or break the next EU budget
The fight over the European Union's next seven-year budget has taken a new twist, one that could very well make it or break it. In an explosive mix, the fraught negotiations have overlapped with the effort to fill Ukraine's €70 billion shortfall for 2027.
The vast scale of the deficit prompted a change of agenda in next month's special summit, which was originally planned to focus exclusively on the draft budget. The meeting has now been expanded to last two days, 26 and 27 November, to allow time for the discussion on Ukraine. New proposals on both fronts are expected.
Technically, the two issues remain separate. But politically, diplomats and officials say, they are becoming rapidly intertwined. Both are about money and both come with a pressing deadline before the French elections in April.
“We need a structural solution for financing Ukraine. We can’t keep scrambling at the end of every year under pressure,” an official said. “It’s good that these discussions are coming together in November.”
