Harry Kane is first Bundesliga player since Matthias Sammer to win Ballon d'Or
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:24:50 UTC
16:24:50 KST

The Bayern Munich striker's award ends a decades-long wait for a Bundesliga player or Englishman to receive the prestigious trophy.
Just ten kilometres from Brisbane Road, where he scored his first professional goal in England’s third tier, Harry Kane collected the biggest individual prize in men’s football on Monday night at the star-studded London Palladium Theatre.
The Bayern Munich striker becomes the first England player to win the Ballon d’Or since 2001, and English fans were quick to celebrate. Kane could hardly believe it himself.
“Not many people would have thought that, and maybe even I wouldn’t have thought that I could get this far,” he told streaming service DAZN.
He added that he was never the sort of player expected to become a superstar.
Seventy-three goals in 65 matches for Bayern and the England national team was, in the view of the journalists' jury, unsurpassed last season: not by Kylian Mbappé, Lionel Messi, Lamine Yamal or Rodri.
Kane's award also ended a long barren spell for the Bundesliga. The last time a player active in Germany was honoured with the Ballon d'Or was in 1996, when Matthias Sammer won it. For Bayern, Kane is the first recipient since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, who took the prize in 1981.
Bayern president Herbert Hainer called it a proud day for the club. “Harry Kane can do everything, and he scores goals, goals, goals,” he said, adding that Kane now stands alongside Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Müller and Rummenigge.
The atmosphere turned emotional when Kane thanked his family. He addressed his words to his in-laws, his parents, his brother Charlie and his wife Katie, who was sitting in the hall.
He also thought of his children at home and sent them a loving greeting.
He also thanked the people who have supported him in recent years. They include Bayern coach Vincent Kompany, who could not travel after collapsing on Friday, and Thomas Tuchel, his former Bayern coach and now England manager.
Tuchel said he ran out of superlatives for Kane’s performances long ago, but was delighted to see the football world recognise them officially.
**"**I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I am very happy to see that you have now also been officially recognised by the football world," said German coach Thomas Tuchel.
Even Prince Harry sent his congratulations. "What a fantastic achievement and so richly deserved. A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans around the world so many unforgettable moments."
Alexia Putellas Wins Third Ballon d’Or
Meanwhile, in the women's category, Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or féminin. The Spaniard prevailed in the vote for women's footballer of the year ahead of compatriot Clàudia Pina and England's Alessia Russo.
The 32-year-old Barcelona midfielder previously won in 2021 and 2022. She then suffered an ACL injury, and Bonmatí rose to stardom in her absence. Bonmatí completed her hat-trick of wins in 2025 but was left off this year’s shortlist after breaking her leg in December.
The women’s Ballon d’Or only dates back to 2018, when Ada Hegerberg became its first winner. Putellas used her moment to encourage young players to play with “love and passion".
Putellas joined Barcelona in 2012 and described her time at the Catalan club as “something special".
“I’m really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player (at Barcelona),” she said. “What I experienced last year was like a perfect story.”

SC seeks Centre’s response to media body’s plea challenging data protection act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:13:53 UTC
16:13:53 KST

SC asks for Centre's reply against Data Protection Act
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday issued notice to the Centre on a petition filed by the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) challenging provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and its accompanying rules. The association had alleged that the act infringe press freedom and the right to information.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued the notice after hearing senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the DNPA. The matter will be heard next on November 17 along with pending petitions.The plea seeks to strike down several provisions of the law, arguing that the absence of an exemption for journalistic activities could impede reporting, undermine investigative journalism and compromise the confidentiality of sources.Describing the petition as a comprehensive challenge by traditional news organisations, Divan told the bench, “This is perhaps the first comprehensive petition by what we call legacy media. There has been some debate over citizen journalists. We are the traditional, conventional legacy media.”She sought an interim stay on the challenged provisions, arguing that consent requirements could make routine and time-sensitive reporting difficult.
“If I am left to the mercy of the data principal as to whether he or she will give consent, how will news be reported?” she asked.Divan also warned that the provisions could affect live television coverage and restrict newsrooms from reporting without prior permission.
“What is the point if I have to ask for permission and consent,” she asked.According to Reuters, media groups told the court that the law amounted to pre-censorship and could force newsrooms to shut down. The challenge involves 21 news publishers.
RTI amendment also challenged
The DNPA has also challenged the amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, arguing that it restricts access to information and limits public scrutiny.“Section 8(1)(j), the deletion, is changing the whole concept of news,” Divan submitted according to news agency PTI.The petition further questions the Centre’s powers to requisition information under the DPDP Act, claiming they could affect news organisations’ ability to report on matters of public interest.The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear the matter on November 17 alongside pending cases.

Britain issues costliest five-year debt since 2008
Britain has successfully sold more government debt this morning, but at the highest price since the financial crisis almost two decades ago.
The Debt Management Office sold £4.5bn of 5-year debt at an average yield of 5.036%, the highest since 2008, Reuters reports.
There was plenty of interest in the gilts – perhaps not surprising, given the lucrative yields the DMO was prepared to pay. Investors bid for 3.51 times as much debt as was available, allowing the DMO to pick the best offers (ie, the investors offering to accept lower yields).
If Chancellor Healey can deliver the dull budget the market expects on Wednesday then the UK will be rewarded with lower gilt yields, says Matthew Amis, investment director, rates management at Aberdeen Investments:
“It’s been a year of negative gilt headlines. The rise in oil and gas has put pressure on gilt yields, which has impacted everything from Government borrowing to mortgages. In all this negativity what hasn’t been reported is that gilt yields have surprisingly held up okay. When we look at gilt yield moves we don’t simply view them in isolation. We have to view them vs our US and European peers. If UK yields move in isolation, the UK has a problem. If yields move in line, yes the yield move is a negative but it’s a global story.
Since the political volatility of May, gilt yields have been relatively well behaved. Against both Germany and US, gilts have remained in recent historic ranges. The big move has been against France. If Chancellor Healey needs any reminder of what can happen to gilt yields if you lose control of the fiscal message then the French OAT move is exactly that. In May, UK 10 year yields were approximately 1.30% higher than French yields, going into the budget they now trade only 0.30% higher; a huge move.
London’s stock market has been marking the 40th anniversary of the Big Bang – the sweeping, Thatcherite deregulation of the London Stock Exchange.
The Big Bang brought several fundamental changes to the City, including the end of fixed fees for share trading, allowing firms to operates as both brokers and market-makers, and bringing in electronic trading.
It also allowed foreign firms to buy UK stockbrokers, paving the way for the takeover of UK banks by (largely) American rivals.
To mark the occasion, this morning’s opening ceremony at the London Stock Exchange rang its new bell for the first time. This bell, the LSE says, is “a symbol of its heritage, ambition and the market community.”
This morning’s expensive sale of five-year UK bonds underlines how little room for error the Chancellor has, says Ion Jauregui, analyst at ActivTrades.
“I think the market will want a relatively dull budget with credible fiscal control, sensible spending commitments and greater breathing space. There is very little room for error here. With gilts yielding 5.35% 10-year, inflation proving sticky and the Bank of England remaining concerned about inflation, the market will not look kindly at any sign of slippage. I don’t think we should get too excited by the yield fall recently. It appears to be being done more as a precaution.
“Investors will want crystal-clear transparency. The extra £20.4 billion of funding proposal for the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank could help to boost long-term growth, but as borrowing is not expected to begin until 2028-29, this should not cause any issues for gilts. Investors will still want to know what borrowing needs are going forward, the credit risk and if the investments actually give value for money. As long as this is properly accounted for and is financially credible, then the markets should be comfortable. However, if it is seen as an exploit or abuse of accounting rules to disguise fiscal risks, gild yields may rise high again.”
UK borrowing costs could come under more pressure if bond investors are unimpressed by tomorrow’s budget.
The City is expecting a “low-key, low-vol event”, to quote MorganStanley analysts this morning.
Investors are expecting a drop in the UK’s fiscal headroom (the margin to keep within the borrowing targets), to around £15bn to £20bn, down from £23.6bn in March.
To achieve that, Healey will have to demonstrate spending restraint kicking in towards the end of this parliament, but the big questions about government spending will probably have to wait until next year’s Spending Review.
Berenberg say investors expect this Wednesday’s budget to keep the government’s fiscal consolidation plans on course, warning there is “a risk of a jump in yields if Chancellor Healey announces more borrowing than investors expect on 28 October.”

Book of Wills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:09:55 UTC
16:09:55 KST

“In Gaza, where the world wavers between silence and forgetting, the written word becomes a final sanctuary – a fragile, luminous act of survival,” Reem Ghanayem writes in the Editor’s Note to the bilingual edition of Book of Wills (Akoya Publishing, 2026). Both erasure and preservation are recorded in this collection of brief writings from Gaza during the genocide. As the writers in this anthology address various people, including the readers themselves, there is no escaping the importance of language.
“Language is a feeble tool,” Alberto Manguel writes in the foreword. “And yet, despite the impossibility of finding language adequate to address a victim’s suffering, when confronted with that suffering, our human condition impels us to speak.”
The book opens with a strong denunciation by Saleem al-Naffar, killed in December 2023 by an Israeli airstrike. Al-Naffar’s contribution is written just 25 days into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and his words are directed at the Arabs who failed to stand with Palestinians: “They and their leaders are part of the conspiracy that aims to exterminate us.”
In most of the writings in this anthology, extermination becomes a personal reckoning imparted to various audiences. Several contributions impart the final wishes of a person expecting death, because death became an inescapable reality during Israel’s genocide in Gaza, rather than a natural termination of life. However, the book also forces the world outside Gaza to a reckoning with its own oblivion, as Amal Abu Assi al-Yazji writes of the aftermath of genocide: “Tear Palestine out of the notebook of your memory, since you’ll have no need for it.” The reader cannot help but contemplate the various levels of oblivion, and al-Yazji’s use of language is particularly striking when she writes, “That worry of yours is gone for good.” How much did all the people outside Gaza worry about Gaza, and what form did that worry take from a sheltered distance? This is perhaps one of the book’s deepest moments, as no one outside of Gaza can truly comprehend the imminent threat of erasure Palestinians have experienced. What would the Palestinian people’s erasure mean, from a distance?
What significance does a will have when military power supports erasure? As the writers in this anthology ponder their last wishes, some create ambivalence through imaginings of survival, even as forced displacement and airstrikes limit areas of safety. Others ponder a will and testament from the hypocritical lens of the humanitarian paradigm, such as Hussein Hazrallah who writes, “I’m nearly certain that the world has seen nothing but a tiny fraction of what’s happening in Gaza, less than the trickle of crumbs that have reached the people here under the label of ‘humanitarian aid’.” The same humanitarian aid also carries death with it, as the author remembers “the death we carried away in sacks marked with United Nations logos, or with the propaganda of the Arab and Islamic nations.”
BOOK REVIEW: Every Moment Is a Life: Gaza in the Time of Genocide
Hazrallah also connects the past to the present when he notes of Palestinians’ ancestors, “They died after escaping death previously, and we were born to them in an attempt to restore the rights that are now slipping through our fingers.” Colonialism, however, made sure that rights and Palestinians are separated by the coloniser’s violence.
Layan Osama Abu al-Qumsan narrates the story of her family’s death by an Israeli airstrike, reflecting upon the fact that her father, a doctor, was unable to live up to his promises of keeping her safe: “I realise that the doctor, with his medicine and medical knowledge, couldn’t avert the disaster that had come upon us.”
Ni’mah Hassan also reflects on her inability to keep her children safe from Israel’s genocide. “I keep trying to put off writing my will,” she writes, while she imagines futures in Gaza despite the absence of futures. Turning to the present scenario, she writes of looking at her children’s fingers: “I never thought of writing their names on them, to prevent death from noticing them. May death leave their limbs intact.”
Other writings take a completely opposite direction – the normalcy in the abnormal life during genocide also speak of having abandoned the fear of death. “Death no longer concerns us as much as the question of how to get a bag of flour or a gas cylinder the next morning,” Nasser Rabah writes. Yet death also occurred during the search for necessities such as flour or gas. The mind filters out the fear of death to accommodate the human instinct to survive.
Writing provides testimony in the face of annihilation. The imagined audiences for each testament in this book vary – from loved ones to the global population away from Gaza. It is through reading from the point of view of the latter that the pain sears through in a different way. Language testifies not only to the lived experiences of the writers, but also as to how much all those not living in Gaza do not know. Under the threat of erasure, language is a tool of preservation.

Scientists uncover new clues to the actual night sky behind Van Gogh’s The Starry Night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
07:07:52 UTC
16:07:52 KST

Researchers led by South Korean scientist Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim argue that Vincent van Gogh's painting may show the Taurus constellation rather than Aries, challenging the accepted timeline of the impressionist masterpiece.
More than a century after Vincent van Gogh painted one of the most recognisable night skies in art history, scientists believe they may have pinpointed the real celestial scene that inspired it - and the answer could change the accepted date of his masterpiece.
Their findings indicate that rather than being a product of Van Gogh’s imagination, The Starry Night may have been inspired by what he saw as he gazed heavenward from his French asylum 137 years ago.
A South Korean team recently reported that after years of forensic astronomy and research into the Dutch artist, they have matched his masterpiece to a predawn sky over France’s Saint-Remy de Provence right around 22 July 1889.
That’s a month later than the long-accepted time frame for the post-impressionist painting which depicts a sky with swirling ribbons of blue, blazing stars and luminous crescent moon, with a village nestled below and cypress trees looming on one side.
Art historians have long dated the painting to June 1889, soon after Van Gogh checked into the asylum. He'd cut off his left ear several months earlier during an argument with painter Paul Gauguin.
A team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of a Seoul telescope maker, is now disputing that date in a study appearing in the journal Scientific Reports.
"No two skies are the same. Something always changes. I believe Vincent noticed those changes and put them into the painting," Kim said in an email. He added: "I am confident that July 22 is the better date. I will bet on this date."
The latest study addresses "a real puzzle" that in mid-June 1889, the moon was not the thin crescent painted by van Gogh, said Jose Luis Aragon at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. He has studied The Starry Night as a physicist, but did not take part in the new research.
"Still, I would see the July date as an intriguing hypothesis rather than a settled answer," Aragon said in an email to AP.
Kim and his team discovered that around 22 July 1889, the shape of the moon before dawn appeared like the one in the painting, with the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus rising in the east alongside Venus. The sky should have been clear enough for Van Gogh to see all this, based on their weather analyses.
The researchers tested and verified their methods on night skies in other paintings, making for what Aragon considers "a careful and genuinely interdisciplinary study."
There is another important complication: Van Gogh did not simply stand at his window and reproduce the sky exactly as he saw it. He worked on The Starry Night in a studio at the asylum, drawing on sketches and memory to construct its extraordinary landscape.
That means the painting’s celestial elements may not correspond to a single night at all, and that "the sky is likely a composite of many nights as the authors themselves acknowledge," Aragon said.

AI generated
LONDON – King Charles heads to the Caribbean this week on a tour that comes against the backdrop of increasingly vocal demands from the region that Britain pays reparations for its role in the slave trade.
Charles and his wife, Queen Camilla, will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana before heading to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), the biennial get-together of the international organisation the king heads. The tour runs from Oct 27 to Nov 4.
At a previous meeting in 2022 of the leaders of the Commonwealth – a group of 56 nations that were mainly former British colonies – Charles expressed deep personal sorrow over slavery, and the issue is certain to be prominent once again.
In September, the Caribbean Community (Caricom), a group of 23 member and associate member states that includes the Bahamas, Barbados and Jamaica, said it would push for reparations to be on the CHOGM agenda.
“The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” Caricom’s secretary-general Carla Barnett said in a speech in September.
“It is about recognition, accountability and transformation, and about building a just and equitable future for the descendants of those who, as the chattel of colonial owners, endured untold suffering, loss of life and freedom,” she said.
While Buckingham Palace has said the monarch would not shy away from Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade during his tour, he would not formally apologise for it as some have wanted, in keeping with British government policy that also excludes making any financial reparations.
“It is important to note here the work his majesty himself has done over many years both to acknowledge the wrongs of the past and to find creative ways to right inequalities that endure,” a palace spokesman said.
Shirley Botchwey, secretary-general of the Commonwealth that encompasses some 2.7 billion people, said last week the time has come for discussions about reparations, be they financial or in some other form such as the return of artefacts.
As for an apology from the king, who remains the head of state of a number of Caribbean nations, including both the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, she told Sky News: “It wouldn’t hurt to have that.”
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants, with Britain responsible for transporting an estimated 3.2 million people, making it the second most active European nation after Portugal. REUTERS

London’s most famous shopping street is now pedestrianised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:57:37 UTC
15:57:37 KST

Ahead of the holiday season, cars, buses and bikes are banned from nearly a kilometre of Oxford Street.
For first-time visitors to London, there are certain addresses you need to tick off, like Leicester Square, Brick Lane, or Abbey Road.
And while the latter is most famous for its zebra crossing – thanks to The Beatles, whose album cover of the same name was shot here – one popular tourist location is making sure marked crosswalks are no longer necessary: Oxford Street.
That’s because the world-famous shopping street is now closed to cars, buses and bicycles as of 26 October.
Nearly a kilometre of Oxford Street, between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street, is now traffic-free, with vehicles diverted onto surrounding roads.
The move is the first step in a makeover of the storied shopping precinct, with plans to plant trees, install seating and add two new public squares.
Oxford Street still sees about half a million visitors a day, with shoppers bustling between retailers such as Selfridges, Zara and John Lewis.
But city officials say pedestrianising the street will put it back into the league of top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla.
“This is a momentous day for London, a momentous day for Oxford Street,” London Mayor Sadiq Khan told the BBC. “It’s a new era.”
Why now?
While local officials began discussing the idea of pedestrianising Oxford Street more than a decade ago, momentum began to build over the last two years when the mayor’s office created the Oxford Street Development Corporation to shepherd the project.
That helped overcome opposition from local residents who complained that diverting vehicles from Oxford Street would clog their neighbourhoods with traffic.
A public consultation later determined that removing traffic would attract new shops and visitors to Oxford Street, making it “an iconic destination”.
The project also got a boost from the new Elizabeth Line, which runs through the heart of the city, with a stop on Oxford Street.
Further work on the makeover will begin in the new year, with city officials refining their plans based on feedback from visitors, Khan told reporters.
“In advance of Christmas, you know, I want people to come here and shop and enjoy the experience,” he added.
Oxford Street’s famed lights
As hinted at by Khan, one of the best times to visit (or worst, if you hate crowds) is during the holiday season when lights line Oxford Street, a tradition first started in 1959.
According to the official website, this year the Christmas lights will be Harry Potter themed to mark the opening of the UK’s largest official Harry Potter store as well as the launch of the controversial new HBO series.
Previous years have seen the street lit up with 5,000 stars glowing thanks to the help of 300,000 LED bulbs.

US, EU and 30 countries warn of famine risk in Sudan, call for aid

US, EU and 30 countries warn of famine risk in Sudan, call for aid
Countries also urge Sudan’s warring parties to ‘lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance’.
The United States, the European Union and 30 countries have warned of an “alarming deterioration” in food security in Sudan, calling for “urgent action” to prevent famine in the African country.
In a joint statement released by the US State Department on Monday, the signatories called on the groups fighting Sudan’s civil war “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance”.
The signatories included Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and the European Commissioner for equality, preparedness and crisis management.
“Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action,” the statement said. “The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people.”
Sudan’s army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when a dispute over how to integrate the two forces erupted into clashes in the capital, Khartoum. The war has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 13 million, and created the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises.
In June, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a United Nations-backed hunger monitor known as the IPC, said 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.
Farmers have struggled to harvest crops since the war began, and the IPC said a drought linked to El Nino had driven up food prices and reduced supplies this year.
Without immediate action, the joint statement warned, “the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000.”
The signatories urged the warring parties to allow humanitarian operations through all routes across front lines and borders, including air access to the region of Darfur. They also called on the parties to “sustain presence and protection of humanitarian personnel” throughout Sudan and to refrain from hitting civilian infrastructure.
“In the face of a potential famine, we call on all members of the international community to urgently scale up funding in response to increased needs and support efforts to ensure assistance reaches those most in need,” the statement said.
Besides the US, Australia and Canada, the statement was signed by 28 European countries.
Last month, the State Department said that neither the Sudanese army nor the RSF “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan”.

New fee added to packages sent from outside EU from November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:55:00 UTC
15:55:00 KST

New fee added to packages sent from outside EU from November
From November 1, a handling fee of €2 will be added for each item of goods contained in a shipment ordered from online stores outside the European Union, regardless of the shipment's value.
"The calculation logic for the handling fee is indeed the same or similar to that of the customs duty on small consignments. The amount of the fee depends on the number of goods lines listed on the declaration. If we take the example of 100 pairs of jeans, which are identical goods, they can be entered on a single goods line on the customs declaration," Kaari Lainevool, service manager at the Tax and Customs Board's customs administration department, explained to ERR.
A customs duty of €3 applies to shipments worth up to €150. If the contents of a package has to be declared on three goods lines, for example, the total customs duty is €9 and the new handling fee is €6.
Customs duty on more expensive shipments depends on the goods, but the €2 handling fee will also be added for each goods line in these shipments.
Tõnu Väät, executive director of the Estonian E-Commerce Association, said the additional cost may discourage buyers from ordering cheap goods: "The same product that I used to order and that cost, for example, €6 – if I add €3 to that and another €2 from November, then it is no longer worth ordering."
He added that some Estonian retailers have already noticed an increase in sales figures following the introduction of the customs duty in July.
"For example, several electronics retailers selling phone chargers, headphones, phone cases, screen protectors and other similar products have said that their sales have increased by 10-20 percent in recent months," Väät explained.
However, customs statistics do not show how much people in Estonia have reduced their orders from outside the European Union.
The Tax and Customs Board said the volume of small consignments declared in Estonia fell by 80 percent in July and August. However, some packages are cleared through customs in other European Union member states and arrive in Estonia as intra-EU shipments. As a result, they are not reflected in Estonian customs statistics.
The new handling fee will cover the costs of checking shipments, including risk analysis and package inspections.
Depending on the online store, buyers may pay the handling fee either when completing their purchase or only when importing the goods. The decisive factor is the date of declaration: the fee will also apply to packages ordered or arriving in Estonia before November if the customs declaration is submitted on November 1 or later.

Olpha introduce a new diabetes medicine in the Baltics in partnership with international pharmaceutical company Adalvo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:52:23 UTC
15:52:23 KST

Latvian pharmaceutical manufacturer Olpha has signed a cooperation agreement with Switzerland-based international pharmaceutical company Adalvo to introduce a new medicine for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and weight management in the Baltic markets. The partnership will expand Olpha’s diabetes treatment portfolio.
The agreement was signed at the CPHI Milan pharmaceutical industry exhibition in early October this year, and the new medicine is expected to become available to patients soon. The partnership combines Adalvo’s expertise in pharmaceutical product development and supply with Olpha’s sales infrastructure, market knowledge and presence in all three Baltic countries.
New treatment options are particularly important in Latvia, where more than 100,000 people are registered as living with diabetes. According to the Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 105,608 people in Latvia were registered as having diabetes at the end of 2025, an increase of 2.1% compared with the previous year. Approximately 7,000 people were newly diagnosed with diabetes during the year.[1]
Timely diagnosis, appropriate treatment and regular health monitoring can help prevent or delay the development of complications. Broader treatment options, alongside a healthy diet and physical activity, therefore, play an essential role in patient care.
“This agreement is a significant strategic step in the company’s development as we actively expand both our presence in Europe and our product portfolio. Our partnership with Adalvo strengthens our offering in the strategically important field of diabetes and obesity treatment and lays the foundation for long-term growth in the Baltic countries. By combining our regional expertise and sales infrastructure with Adalvo’s product development capabilities, we aim to improve access to treatment options and deliver long-term benefits for patients and healthcare professionals in Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia,” says Juris Hmeļņickis, Chairman of the Management Board of JSC Olpha.
The partnership aligns with both companies’ growth strategies. For Latvian pharmaceutical manufacturer Olpha, it offers an opportunity to expand its product portfolio and strengthen its position in the Baltics while pursuing broader development plans in Europe. For Adalvo, the partnership strengthens its position in the GLP-1 receptor agonist segment and supports the strategic objectives of its dedicated GLP-1 business unit. GLP-1 receptor agonists are prescription medicines that mimic the action of the naturally occurring hormone GLP-1 and help regulate blood glucose levels.
“Adalvo is committed to building strong partnerships to accelerate access to innovative treatment options in key markets. Olpha’s well-established presence in the Baltics makes it an ideal partner, and we are pleased to begin working together to realise the full potential of this collaboration,” says Anil Okay, CEO of Adalvo.
This is not the first collaboration between the two companies. In March 2025, a generic antibacterial medicine for the treatment of urinary tract infections, jointly developed by Olpha and Adalvo, was launched in the Baltic markets.
The companies will announce the trade name and availability of the new diabetes medicine in the Baltic countries separately.

Ukraine has asked five European partners to provide 10% of their existing stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot and IRIS-T air defense systems to help protect the country against Russian attacks, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said.
The request was directed to the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland. Khmara said Ukraine had already signed contracts for future deliveries of interceptor missiles and proposed an exchange that would allow Kyiv to receive ammunition immediately.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukraine already has contracts in place for future deliveries of interceptor missiles, so it is proposing an exchange: partners would provide a portion of their current stocks now, in return for the shipments that are scheduled to arrive in Ukraine later,” he said on Telegram.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces (AFU) also urgently need additional man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), he added.
“Ukraine is counting on funding for new acquisitions, as well as the transfer of systems from the existing stockpiles of its partners,” Khmara said.
The minister added Ukraine could double its drone production by 2027 if funding arrived on time. Kyiv is proposing not only to increase procurement but also to expand joint production of Ukrainian drones abroad.
“We are proposing not only to increase procurement but also to scale up the joint production of Ukrainian drones in other countries,” Khmara said. He added that the approach would help Ukraine obtain the drones it needs while strengthening the defensive capabilities of partner countries.

European allies prepare winter aid
Following a meeting in Paris with defense ministers from the UK, France, Italy and Poland, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the participating countries had already prepared winter aid packages for Ukraine.
“Moreover, we will do everything in our power to ensure that the United States continues to support Ukraine – through its own shipments, and, above all, by providing intelligence and satellite data,” Pistorius said.
He added that European countries were working with Kyiv to develop an air defense system.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia was preparing to intensify attacks on major Ukrainian cities.
Senior Ukrainian officials told The Economist that Moscow planned to paralyze Kyiv before the onset of colder weather in an effort to destabilize the political situation. According to the officials, Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered attacks on civilian infrastructure across the capital.
Separately, Ukrainian officials told the Financial Times (FT) that Moscow intended to increase pressure on Kyiv in hopes of forcing Ukraine to accept Russian demands, including surrendering territory in the Donbas, by early 2027.
Ukraine has waited nearly a month for Patriot missiles
Ukraine will again raise the issue of delayed air defense missile deliveries with the US, as Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, Zelensky said on Monday.
Zelensky added that he had instructed his team to raise the issue with Washington again. Ukraine is also seeking PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors from EU countries and other partners holding existing stocks.
The shortage comes as Ukraine struggles to secure enough ammunition to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelensky previously said Ukraine had received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite requiring around 350 per month.
He has also asked European partners to provide 300 interceptors for the winter, but efforts to obtain missiles from existing stockpiles have faced resistance, including from Greece.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian Air Force official Yuriy Ihnat said that missiles expended in the Middle East could have sustained Ukraine’s Patriot systems for several years.
He said Ukrainian crews had developed more efficient tactics, typically using one interceptor per target and employing ambushes before quickly relocating systems. By contrast, air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight interceptors at a single target, including relatively cheap Shahed drones.
Zelensky also called for faster implementation of decisions expected to support Ukraine’s air defense, as officials prepare for the next Ramstein-format meeting in November. “Every support package is an opportunity to protect people’s lives,” he said.

Lula win triggers investor jitters in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:35:04 UTC
15:35:04 KST

The BOVESPA stock index is displayed on an electronic board at the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange (B3) in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 26, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The reelection of Brazilian leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva rattled markets as investors, who had expected a win for his conservative rival, worried about fiscal discipline.
Sao Paulo's stock exchange, which had soared to new highs after Flavio Bolsonaro received the most first-round votes earlier this month, plunged 17 percent on Oct. 26 before slightly recovering to end the session down almost 14 percent.
The sharp decline in the benchmark Ibovespa index at one point triggered the first 30-minute halt to trading since the COVID pandemic in 2020.
"No one had this result on their radar," Leandro Gabiati, of the political consultancy firm Dominium in Brasilia, told AFP.
Against a backdrop of mounting fiscal pressures, Bolsonaro had promised to slash government spending and shrink the state.
However, he never gave details on where the cuts would come from, and vowed to maintain social programs.
The Brazilian state spends more than it collects, public debt exceeds 80 percent of GDP.
In the final stretch of his campaign, Lula rolled out costly measures, such as increasing the value of cash transfers to the poor or debt forgiveness for micro-entrepreneurs.
"Lula made several spending promises, and those need to be priced in," said Andre Perfeito, chief economist at the financial firm Garantia Capital.
"Sound fiscal reform is the price Lula 4.0 must pay to regain market confidence," said Mariano Machado, Americas Principal Analyst at global risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft.

Laos Expected to Scuttle ASEAN’s South China Sea Code of Conduct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:34:00 UTC
15:34:00 KST

Throughout its year as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Philippines has aggressively sought to push the China-ASEAN Code of Conduct (CoC) for the South China Sea to the top of the regional agenda and end the long and drawn out diplomatic saga, which dates back more than two decades.
The CoC is part of a long (and thus far inconclusive) quest to find peaceful resolutions to the many maritime and territorial disputes that persistently plague the sea lines of communications across a waterway that accounts for almost a quarter of world trade. A CoC would enable ASEAN to negotiate with China as a united entity, and after all that is what ASEAN is supposed to be all about: a centrist political and trade bloc that can represent the interests of 11 Southeast Asian states on the world stage through a rules based order.
It’s a process that does not suit China, which has done its best to belittle and intimidate Manila and specifically Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, who has demanded respect for international law while juggling heated diplomatic tensions and the ASEAN chair. Publicly, Beijing maintains its policy of non-interference and at times even espouses the virtues of potentially resolving maritime issues with Southeast Asian states through ASEAN. But behind the public spotlight, China has persistently used its proxies to obstruct and scuttle the CoC.
Cambodia was particularly useful in this regard. At the 2012 ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, hosted by Phnom Penh, Prime Minister Hun Sen was signaling a significant shift in foreign policy toward China and the CoC was topping the agenda. The Philippines and Vietnam pushed to explicitly mention the ongoing Scarborough Shoal standoff and Chinese maritime encroachment in their Exclusive Economic Zones, but Hun Sen and his Foreign Minister Hor Namhong balked and declared that such disputes should be handled bilaterally.
For the first time in ASEAN history, no joint communique was issued at the end of the meeting. It was a major embarrassment for the Cambodians.
The CoC was effectively frozen, delays amid the COVID-19 pandemic followed, and whenever necessary Cambodia could be relied upon to do China’s bidding and scuttle the process.
That is what China wants; bilateral negotiations between individual states that enable it to reject international verdicts like the 2016 arbitral ruling on the South China Sea while protecting its expansive unilateral claims and military bases on artificial reefs.
China has also secured its state, military, and civilian investments along Cambodia’s limited coastline, but times have changed with the roaring days of the Belt and Road Initiative disappearing into the vacuum of history.
Given the colossal damage caused by online scam compounds, Beijing would prefer to exact penance out of Phnom Penh than scout for new investments, and the Cambodians, sources in ASEAN are saying, are not prepared to weather the diplomatic heat from blocking another effort to resolve the CoC.
Thus Beijing has considered and pressed its alternatives ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit, to be held in Manila on November 16–18 and chaired by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Myanmar could work, but it remains barred from ASEAN summits in retaliation for the ousting of Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government in early 2021 by a junta led by current regime president Min Aung Hlaing. That could change next year.
Timor-Leste, ASEAN sources say, is moving rapidly into China’s orbit, but as the newest member remains unwilling to upset Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, or Singapore on the CoC, nor to offend Cambodia after it shepherded Dili into the trade bloc.
That leaves landlocked Laos, an economic basket case in a region struggling for growth, and an absolute dependent on Chinese largesse. There are shades of the Khmer-Sino relationship from a decade ago now emerging between Vientiane and Beijing.
Late last month, China and Laos announced the opening of a Military Joint Support and Training base north of Vientiane, which has already earned comparisons with China’s development of the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia. Joint military exercises known as “Peace Train 2026” were held in September.
“Cambodia does not have the appetite for this,” said a Western source privy to CoC negotiations between ASEAN states over the last 12 months.
“It’s overwhelmed by the mess created by organized crime, the scam compounds and the conflict with Thailand. Phnom Penh is now moving closer to the United States and it just can’t deal with any more pressure. Myanmar, not yet; Timor-Leste, watch this space.
“Laos? Laos has been tapped by China and will have to defend its interests, and it’s the only country in ASEAN that Beijing can lean on, and it has been doing precisely that. Laos is going to shatter the Philippine dream of using the chair to pass the Code of Conduct. It’s as simple as that.”

The bank said domestic demand was strengthening broadly, prompting it to revise its monetary policy outlook from an expectation that rates would remain unchanged to a forecast of a rate-hiking cycle beginning in December.
Goldman Sachs now expects the policy rate to reach 2.125% by the end of 2026 and 2.375% by the end of 2027, compared with its previous forecast of 2% for both years.
The bank also maintained its bullish outlook for the New Taiwan dollar, citing stronger economic growth, a large current account surplus, the AI boom, and its assessment that the currency remains undervalued.
The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 11.05% in August, citing stronger-than-expected exports, investment, and consumption. The estimate was 1.41 percentage points higher than its previous projection, per a press release.
The Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research also raised its forecast for this year to 12.16% on Oct. 16, marking its third upward revision and the highest estimate among major forecasting institutions cited in its report. CIER attributed the outlook to robust AI-related demand and stronger domestic investment and consumption.
The think tank expects Taiwan's economy to grow 5.97% in 2027, compared with Goldman Sachs' projection of 3.3%. Forecasts vary because institutions use different assumptions about trade, investment, domestic demand, and the AI boom.
DGBAS is scheduled to release its preliminary estimate of third-quarter GDP growth this week. Its latest official forecast put full-year 2026 growth at 11.05%, while the Central Bank's September projection was reported at 11.48%.
The third-quarter release will provide a fresh indication of whether economic activity is running ahead of official expectations, per CNA.

Former US official says Taiwan’s value goes beyond strategic location
Unknown

2026-10-27
06:31:27 UTC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Thomas J. Christensen warned that emphasizing Taiwan's strategic location could weaken efforts to deter a Chinese attack.
In an essay published Wednesday by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Christensen said Washington should focus on Taiwan's democracy, economic importance, and regional security rather than geography alone. He argued that focusing on Taiwan's location could imply unconditional US support for its defense, increasing tensions with China.
Taiwan sits at the center of the first island chain, which stretches from Japan to the Philippines. Christensen acknowledged its military importance but said preventing a Chinese attack matters more than denying Beijing control of a strategic location.
He said an attack on Taiwan would damage US credibility among Asian allies, regardless of any military advantage China might gain. A successful invasion could also encourage Beijing to use force in future disputes with neighboring countries.
Christensen noted that the Trump administration's 2025 National Security Strategy highlighted Taiwan's location as a key US defense concern. However, citing US Naval War College scholar Jonathan Caverley, he questioned how much additional military advantage China would gain from controlling Taiwan, given its growing military capabilities.
He warned that placing too much emphasis on geography could undermine Washington's policy of strategic ambiguity. Under this policy, the US does not explicitly state the circumstances under which it would intervene militarily to defend Taiwan.
Christensen argued that an unconditional US defense commitment could weaken support for peaceful unification within Chinese policy circles, increasing the risk of conflict. He also warned that stronger US guarantees could encourage Taiwanese politicians to pursue formal independence, further raising tensions with China.
Taiwanese officials have emphasized the country's strategic position as they seek stronger regional security cooperation. Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) has warned about China's expanding military reach, while National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) has said Beijing's military activities threaten countries beyond Taiwan.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) has also called for closer security cooperation with Japan and the Philippines to counter Chinese threats. Christensen said Taiwan's emphasis on the first island chain reflects efforts to secure stronger defense support from Washington and Tokyo.
Christensen said strategic ambiguity has helped prevent major conflict in the Taiwan Strait for decades. He cited the Taiwan Relations Act and the Six Assurances as key parts of US policy that support Taiwan's security without guaranteeing military intervention.
He urged Washington to maintain its current approach and continue helping Taiwan deter a Chinese attack. He argued that protecting Taiwan's democracy and preserving regional peace offer stronger reasons for US support than geography alone.

India’s privacy law could shut down newsrooms, media groups tell court
Italy

07:30:46 CET
15:30:46 KST

By Aditya Kalra
NEW DELHI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounted to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups told the Supreme Court on Tuesday, starting the most high-profile challenge against the legislation.
The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Prime Minister Narendra Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have not done enough to scrutinise Modi’s government, which has denied such allegations and says it respects press freedom.
A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged the privacy law, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow New Delhi to identify journalists’ sources, Reuters reported on Monday.
“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) told the judges.
“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission…it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”
The lawsuit is the most high-profile challenge to Modi’s privacy law. Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had challenged it.
The Supreme Court posted the case for next month.
BIG MEDIA GROUPS VS MODI
Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.
The publishers are demanding that most of the law’s contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, should be quashed. They say the law could also force publishers to erase stories and give powers to government to demand information from publishers that could expose reporters’ sources.
DNPA, the group which has challenged Modi’s government, counts as members Ambani’s Network18, Adani’s NDTV and other marquee media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.
Divan said during the hearing that earlier versions of the law excluded journalists, but the final one did not.

North Korean artillery pointed south stirs concern at border observatory

By Hyun Young Yi and Brenda Goh
GIMPO, South Korea, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Visitors to a South Korean observatory that overlooks North Korea said on Tuesday that the appearance of artillery pieces with their barrels pointed south on the border was worrying, as tensions between the two countries intensify.
The two Koreas have traded barbs and strengthened their postures along the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) separating them since September, after a mine blast there wounded three South Korean soldiers. South Korea has demanded that North Korea apologise, while Pyongyang has accused Seoul of fabricating the incident.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, said last Thursday that Pyongyang would place loudspeakers that can blast anti-South Korean propaganda on standby along the entire border within days and had put unspecified new countermeasures on alert.
On Friday, South Korean media photographed an armoured vehicle in clear view near the frontier. By Monday, there were three with their gun barrels pointed south, according to a Reuters witness.
“I’d only seen on TV that North Korea had deployed 122-mm artillery, but seeing the area in person makes me realise just how real the danger is,” Jang Gil-seong, an 83-year-old war veteran who fought in the Vietnam War, said outside the Aegibong observatory, which overlooks North Korea’s Kaephung county from about 1.4 km away.
“I’m really concerned about how much South Korea will need to do to prepare for and respond to this threat in the future.”
The DMZ remains a draw for foreign and local tourists despite periodic flare-ups in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war.
Hannah Robbins, a 28-year-old tourist from Canada, said her tour group had only found out about the artillery pieces after their guide told them about the weapons at the observatory.
“We’re a bit scared obviously,” she said. “The tour guide was like ‘don’t worry, they won’t shoot’ but then it’s a bit of a worry that we have right now.”
Analysts identified the weapons as M-1981 122-mm self-propelled howitzers, an older North Korean artillery system believed to have entered service in the late 1970s.
They have a maximum range of about 24 km (15 miles), putting areas such as the South Korean town of Gimpo where the observatory is located within reach, although they are less powerful than newer artillery systems, said Yang Uk, a military expert at Seoul’s Asan Institute for Policy Studies.
“I would view this more as a display of firepower than a meaningful increase in combat capability,” Yang said.
“The fact that it was positioned where it can be easily seen suggests it was deployed to be noticed.”
South Korea’s military also described the weapons as an older system.
“While North Korea has mentioned new weapons systems in its recent statements, we believe that this cannot be considered as such,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesperson Jang Do-young told a briefing on Tuesday.

Europe must prepare for a 3°C warmer world, EU climate chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:30:44 UTC
15:30:44 KST

As Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, new EU rules will require governments to clarify who is responsible for climate preparedness – but no new funding is being offered to help households adapt.
The European Commission will unveil new climate rules on Tuesday requiring EU governments to clarify who is responsible for protecting citizens from climate disasters, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews.
The move comes as Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, including scenarios involving 3°C of global warming by 2100.
Hoekstra warned that the world is heading towards a temporary or potentially prolonged overshoot of the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming limit, making it essential for governments to prepare for more extreme heat and climate disasters, even if efforts to cut emissions succeed.
“It is up to member states to decide where they want to put that responsibility. But what we do make mandatory is that they do have to appoint and articulate where the responsibility is going to lie,” Hoekstra said.
While the EU continues to pursue emissions reductions, the costs of adapting to a hotter world are becoming harder to ignore, from rebuilding after wildfires and floods to protecting homes, roads and public infrastructure.
The Dutch Commissioner estimated the economic damage from this summer's extreme weather at more than €100 billion.
Asked what a 3°C rise above pre-industrial temperatures could mean for Europeans, Hoekstra pointed to heat plans for cities and the need to prepare infrastructure for a hotter future, rather than relying on historical weather patterns.
The reference trajectory is based on scientific research, including work by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and advanced European climate modeling, he said.
The Commission's projections envisage 2°C of global warming by 2050 and 3°C by 2100 for Europe, reflecting Brussels' assessment that Europe is warming roughly twice as fast as the global average.
The trajectory is intended to be translated into national and local risk assessments, taking account of the uneven distribution of climate impacts.
“Even if we get all of this right, we have no way to avoid more summers than the one we saw last year,” the Commissioner said, arguing that readiness, resilience and preparedness must become the priority alongside emissions cuts.
The proposed legislation would require EU countries to specify whether national, regional or local authorities are responsible for preparing for climate disasters.
Governments would retain flexibility over how they allocate responsibilities, but would have to specify who is accountable — an attempt to prevent political disputes over who failed to prepare when floods or wildfires destroy homes.
The Commission also wants climate scenarios to be considered when planning new roads, bridges and neighbourhoods, recognising that infrastructure designed for past weather conditions may no longer be fit for purpose.
"We want to introduce a culture of preparedness and resilience by design, rather than dealing with the damages in the aftermath, which is often very ad hoc and doesn't always build back better," a senior Commission official said on Monday on condition of anonymity.
No new money
However, the question of how to pay for climate adaptation remains unresolved.
No new financial commitment to household support is expected from the Commission's climate resilience strategy, despite concerns that ordinary citizens may struggle to afford the investments needed to adapt.
Hoekstra pointed to the Commission's proposal to devote 35% of the EU budget to climate and nature.
But the strategy's effectiveness will depend partly on the outcome of ongoing negotiations over the EU's next multiannual budget, with climate spending competing against priorities such as defence, security, competitiveness and agricultural support.
The Commission is also counting on the recently announced €30 billion from the European Investment Bank for climate adaptation through 2030.
Nonetheless, the lack of new funding is a potential weakness in the Commission's ambition.
The Commissioner argued that preventive investment is economically worth it but did not announce a new household support scheme or explain how the EU would ensure that lower-income households could afford necessary improvements.
In an attempt to fill the bloc's climate protection gap, Brussels wants to work with the insurance sector, as Commissioner Hoekstra pointed out that many areas in Europe are underinsured against climate disasters.
According to the senior Commission official, only around 25% of assets exposed to climate impacts are insured, leaving governments and property owners vulnerable to substantial losses.
“The fact that so many areas are underinsured” is one of the issues the Commission will examine, Hoekstra said.
The strategy could therefore expose another fault line between Brussels' climate ambitions and the cost-of-living pressures facing European voters.

Even before the exit poll results of today's elections are known, the Finance Ministry has already prepared a plan that includes a series of harsh economic measures, intended, among other things, to finance the defense budget and prevent an increase in the deficit and the debt-to-GDP ratio.
Some of the measures were planned in cooperation with the Bank of Israel. The next government will be responsible for implementing the policy.
In addition, after Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich subsidized gasoline prices by NIS 1 per liter over the past two months to prevent price increases, the subsidy, which has cost more than half a billion shekels, will end Saturday night. As a result, gasoline prices will surge by at least NIS 1 per liter at midnight on Saturday, and may rise further as global fuel prices climb.
The price of a liter of self-service 95-octane gasoline is expected to reach NIS 8.90. However, the dollar's roughly 1% decline against the shekel yesterday will help moderate the increase.
Higher fuel prices are expected to trigger price increases across a range of other goods and services whose rates have so far been frozen at the government's initiative, including electricity, water, and public transportation. This is expected to drive up the Consumer Price Index.
The freeze on adjustments to income tax brackets, tax credit points, and National Insurance contributions, along with the current VAT rate, will remain in place in 2027 under existing automatic budgetary provisions.
Revenue from these measures is estimated at NIS 10 billion. In addition to ending the gasoline subsidy, further tax measures will be proposed to boost state revenue.
These include mandatory reporting of income from residential property rentals and taxation of rental income from the first shekel earned. Currently, rental income of up to NIS 5,654 per month is exempt from tax. Some of these legislative initiatives have been held up in the Knesset Finance Committee.
Another proposal would impose a tax on international content providers operating in Israel, commonly referred to as the "Netflix tax." Another measure expected to be implemented is a reduction in tax benefits on pension contributions, along with a recommendation to eliminate VAT exemptions for sectors that currently benefit from them.
Economic measures aim to fund increased defense budget
Broader macroeconomic measures are aimed at finding sources of funding for the required increase in the defense budget, which is expected to reach NIS 187 billion.
One almost certain source of funding will be sharp cuts to coalition funds, alongside sweeping efficiency measures across government ministry budgets.
The main challenge facing the coalition forming the next government will be the immediate need to pass a 2027 budget, or potentially a two-year budget covering 2027 and 2028. The budget must include comprehensive reforms under the Economic Arrangements Law.
As a result, the Finance Ministry is unlikely to secure approval by the end of 2027, so it will need to prepare a continuing budget.
The timetable for implementing these measures is tight, and the parties that make up the new coalition will have to begin taking action even before the next government is formed.

Palestinian citizens of Israel fear they’re next target if far-right wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:12:04 UTC
15:12:04 KST

Palestinian citizens of Israel fear they’re next target if far-right wins
Majd al-Krum’s peaceful protests have forced settlers to withdraw, but fears of further provocations loom after elections.
Majd al-Krum, Israel – The police closed the road to al-Rus, so the villagers found other ways up there.
Beginning on September 13, local Palestinian citizens of Israel made the steep climb to the pine-covered hilltop above Majd al-Krum using horses, off-road vehicles and on foot. A couple of weeks earlier, settlers from the occupied West Bank had begun building an outpost there, on village land – one of the first such attempts on this side of the Green Line, the name used for the boundary between Israel and the occupied West Bank.
The young Israeli settlers said they were there to graze livestock with a Jewish National Fund (JNF) permit. But there was no livestock, noted Hussein Mannaa, 50, a lawyer and member of the town’s Popular Committee. Within a week, the camp had grown from a handful of people to between 25 and 30, according to villagers, with a kitchen, a toilet, a water line and electricity.
Villagers rushed to the scene, so police closed the road to the site. Yet local Palestinians came in droves nonetheless.
Anas Sgaier, a 21-year-old law student and youth organiser, made the nearly hour-long climb up the mountain. “I remember one moment: I’m going up and it’s hard for me to breathe,” he said. “And to my right, I saw an older woman, in her 80s, with her husband … walking up 50 minutes, just to show her presence.”
After almost a week of peaceful protests that saw hundreds of Palestinians from Majd al-Krum and across the region come every day, the JNF ordered the settler tents removed. By September 16, the site was cleared out.
The village had won, for now.
A ‘pilot’ experiment
A little more than a month later, Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday, and Palestinian villagers fear al-Rus was a prelude to what may come next. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is campaigning on a promise to “Judaise” the Galilee, where Palestinian citizens of Israel make up a large proportion of the population, and says he will repeat there “the revolution we carried out in [the occupied West Bank]”.
“The al-Rus experiment is like a pilot … experiment: ‘come on, let’s see the reaction’,” said Husein Khalaily, 50, an economic consultant, while sitting at his home in Majd al-Krum.
Reaction was swift: the village’s Popular Committee met as soon as the rumours of the settler outpost were confirmed and, with the local council, called daily demonstrations. “The popular struggle alongside the legal track is what bore fruit,” said Mannaa, a mainstay at the weeklong demonstrations at the site.
It was young people who drove the protests, villagers said. “Bring your coffee and come,” beckoned Sgaier in Instagram posts alongside his cousin. “We’re only going up to drink coffee, because that’s our land.”
“Not only the people of Majd al-Krum: Deir al-Asad, al-Bi’na, Sakhnin, Arrabeh … from the Naqab they came,” recalled Mannaa. Some left-leaning residents of nearby Jewish communities also turned up. “There was this incredible solidarity,” said Khalaily.
Hanan, a Palestinian Christian from a nearby village, said the outposts she read about in the occupied West Bank had felt far away – until Majd al-Krum. “I never saw the Arab community so united and really fighting for their lands,” she said.
Smotrich came to Majd al-Krum, a village long known for its political activism, to campaign with a police force and a water cannon. “The young people were hot-blooded and wanted to go out and confront him,” Khalaily said, but the local committees and political parties talked them down.
But the targeting continued. On September 18, police announced the arrest of a 32-year-old Majd al-Krum resident over alleged contact with a Lebanese agent. Smotrich seized on it, saying Galilee residents were “in the atmosphere of October 6”, a reference to the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.
‘The language is clear’
On August 27, Smotrich posted a plan promising one million more Jews and 40 new Jewish communities in the Galilee and al-Naqab, another area of Israel where many of the residents are Palestinian. His party then released an AI-generated video in which a West Bank Palestinian frantically warns a relative in the Galilee that “the Jews are coming” to “do to you what they did to us”.
Sgaier said he and his friends laughed at the absurdity of the video. Then they watched it come to life at al-Rus.
“He came here and said it clearly: ‘I want to Judaise the Galilee,’” said Khalaily. “Back in the day, they used to say, ‘we want to develop the Galilee.’ Today – the language is clear.”
Villagers believe the recent provocations are intended to create a pretext for making that happen, where Palestinian citizens hold rights that Palestinians under military occupation in the West Bank do not, making dispossession a harder proposition. “Building the outposts, they wanted to lead the people into a confrontation,” said Mannaa. “They want to impose a state of chaos because chaos benefits them.”
The settlers pointed to a grazing permit granted on the land of al-Rus from the quasi-governmental JNF. But according to Khalaily, the plot, about 8.4 dunams (roughly two acres), is half privately owned by his cousin, and half administered by the Israel Land Authority, which has long refused to partition it so the owner can tell which part is his.
“They chose Majd al-Krum because it’s hard to break,” said Mannaa, pointing to the village’s history of defiance since the Nakba in 1948, when many villagers were expelled from their homes. “If they break Majd al-Krum,” said Khaled Kewan, 27, a singer from the village, “[it’s] going to happen all over the Galilee”.
The JNF later said the “grazing” initiative would move to another plot about 500 metres away on land villagers consider theirs. But the village rejects any relocation, “even one tent”, Mannaa said.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the JNF, the Israeli police and the Israeli Finance Ministry for comment, but has yet to receive a response.
‘Coming not just for Majd al-Krum’
Whether Smotrich remains in power depends on the election results on Tuesday – where the Palestinian vote will likely figure prominently. Polls suggest neither of the main Zionist blocs can reach 61 seats without support from the Arab parties.
Turnout by Palestinian citizens of Israel has hovered between 45 and 65 percent in recent years. However, organisers believe the demographic’s turnout may hit 70 to 75 percent, a level last seen in 1999.
After the settlers’ attempts and provocations in Majd al-Krum, Mannaa boldly predicted the town “will go past 80 percent”.
Khalaily, a longtime boycotter who has only ever voted once, now urges turnout at every talk he gives. “These prominent racists who are there now have to be removed, even if just for a stage,” he said. He sees little difference between Netanyahu’s government and its likely replacement, “except that Smotrich and [far-right National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir won’t be in it”.
After October 7, fear kept Palestinian citizens away from demonstrating. “People got busy with other things,” said Khalaily. “Busy with fear, with making a living.” Crime in the town made it worse. “I’ll be sitting here at night and I hear the sound of shooting,” said Khalaily, who has children who witnessed three men murdered. “Nothing moves. It’s become normal.”
Palestinian citizens have more rights than those in the West Bank, leaving them caught between a system they oppose but must live in. “We here have the most to lose,” he said, “because we’re settled on our land and we stayed on it.”
As a result, many stayed quiet in recent years. “We left Gaza alone, left the West Bank alone, left Lebanon alone,” said Sgaier. “I said after that our time is coming.”
“I just didn’t expect it to come this early.”
However, after Smotrich’s rhetoric and the settlers’ local incursions, “the people who were indifferent about the elections, who didn’t want to take part or vote: the matter provoked them,” said Mannaa. “They know well what awaits us if this government returns to power.”
Some, like Sgaier, will still boycott. “What happened in Majd al-Krum, we solve it by going out [to] the street – not through the Knesset [parliament] and the laws,” said Sgaier, who sees little difference between the two Zionist political blocs. “They don’t want Palestinians here.”
Sgaier believes there was a real change where it counts: on the streets. During the protests at al-Rus, he saw people he never expected. “They are not politically engaged,” he said, “but they came, too”.
The settlers’ tents are gone, leaving only sparse remains and Hebrew graffiti proclaiming “the nation of Israel lives”. Nonetheless, villagers keep trekking up the mountain every day. Families barbecue there, and schoolchildren draw and play music.
During the weeklong protests, Khaled Kewan would leave al-Rus in the evenings to go to a recording studio. He and fellow musicians from the town made the song “Ibn Bladi”:
“Oh, land of mine, land of my ancestors!” he sings. “No matter how many walls they build across my country … I am a son of this land, a son of my own country.”
The inspiration was clear, but Kewan deliberately chose not to name Majd al-Krum explicitly. “Haifa’s my town too, Akka’s my town too, Sakhnin’s my town too, Arraba’s my town too … I love the whole homeland,” he said.
The settlers’ “Judaisation” efforts, he said, “are coming not just for Majd al-Krum, but for the whole Galilee.”

Centre to train 10,000 healthcare workers in drug de-addiction by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:08:41 UTC
15:08:41 KST

The programme will be implemented through six central government institutions under the Drug De-addiction Programme (Representative Image)
NEW DELHI: With the Centre targeting a drug-free India by 2029, the health ministry has launched a nationwide capacity-building programme to train 10,000 healthcare professionals in the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of substance use disorders, including addiction to alcohol, opioids and other drugs.Union health minister J P Nadda launched the programme on Monday under the Vision Document on Narcotic Control 2026-2029, stressing that tackling substance abuse requires coordinated action by healthcare, social welfare and law enforcement agencies. The ministry aims to train 2,000 personnel in the current financial year, followed by 3,000 in 2027-28 and 5,000 in 2028-29.The programme will be implemented through six central government institutions under the Drug De-addiction Programme, with the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC), AIIMS, serving as the coordinating centre. The other institutions are NIMHANS, Bengaluru; PGIMER, Chandigarh; Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi; Dr Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, Delhi; and AIIMS Bhubaneswar.The training will combine live online sessions, self-paced courses and in-person programmes. Doctors and medical officers will undergo a 12-week online training course featuring lectures and clinical case discussions, while nurses, community health officers, auxiliary nurse midwives, counsellors and psychologists will have access to specialised modules.
The curriculum will cover substances ranging from alcohol and cannabis to opioids, sleeping tablets and inhalants, as well as addiction among vulnerable groups, including women and adolescents.More than 800 nominations have already been received through the health ministry and the National Health Mission for online and offline training. Around 150 personnel from de-addiction centres supported by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment are also expected to undergo in-person training over the next two months.Nadda said fragmented efforts among government departments had created gaps in coordination and service delivery. Effective implementation of the narcotic control strategy, he said, would require clearly defined responsibilities, sustained inter-ministerial coordination and collective accountability. He also stressed the need to strengthen de-addiction centres through training, institutional support and adequate resources.
At the launch, Nadda released the second edition of Substance Use Disorder: Manual for Physicians (Management of Addictive Disorders). First published in 2005, the revised manual incorporates advances in the understanding and treatment of addiction and is intended to help doctors manage substance use disorders in both specialised facilities and general healthcare settings.The initiative follows the Vision Document on Narcotic Control unveiled by Union home minister Amit Shah in June 2026. Besides enforcement against drug trafficking, the strategy assigns the health ministry the task of expanding access to evidence-based addiction treatment by strengthening the skills of medical and allied healthcare personnel.Officials said the programme would draw on the clinical expertise and training infrastructure of the six institutions to improve the availability and quality of addiction care across states and Union territories.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.
