Russia's assault on Ukraine's energy grid is a war crime, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:05:16 UTC
15:05:16 KST

The United Nations has determined that Russia's frequent and intentional attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure constitute a war crime, a U.N. inquiry report said on Oct. 26.
In recent months, Russian forces have strategically escalated attacks on Ukraine's energy grid in the lead up to the freezing winter months to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure, despite U.S. President Donald Trump having called for an energy ceasefire.
"Russian commanders ordering the attacks had the knowledge that the heating facilities they targeted in large civilian agglomerations were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter," a report from the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine concludes.
Last winter, the Kremlin also focused its attacks on energy sources, leaving millions of Ukrainians without power in temperatures as low as minus 21°C.
Based on interviews with 255 people who endured these conditions across Ukraine, the commission concluded that "Russian authorities have committed the crimes against humanity of other inhumane acts."
One interviewed man described how, during winter, he would attempt remain awake through the night out of fear of falling asleep and dying from the cold. "The scariest thing was to fall asleep and not to wake up; it was like torture to be scared of dying from cold," he said.
"The waves of attacks by Russian authorities against Ukraine's energy infrastructure were carried out with intent and pursuant to a state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering," the report outlines.
In addition, the report outlines how Russia's recruitment of soldiers from third countries also violates human rights law. Recruitment from 29 other countries through lies and coercion counts as human trafficking, the report finds.

‘Learning the language is hard’: Adewuyi on life in Lithuania, racism and missing Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

When Olugbenga Adewuyi decided to move from Nigeria to Lithuania, he did not speak Lithuanian and knew almost nothing about the country. Over the past seven years, he has reached A2 level in the language, obtained a permanent residence permit and grown accustomed to life there. But when discussing integration, he says language is not the only challenge.
For a non-white foreigner trying to become part of Lithuanian society, avoiding racism can be difficult – from offensive comments online to situations in which you feel unwelcome.
First shock: the weather
Adewuyi was given the opportunity to take part in an EU project for IT specialists and arrived in Kaunas in October 2019. At the time, he did not know he would settle in the country for the long term.
“I had lived in Nigeria all my life and really wanted to try something new. Many of my colleagues had found jobs in various European countries, so I started looking for an opportunity to do the same,” Adewuyi told LRT.lt.
His first impressions of Lithuania had less to do with a new city or a different culture than with the weather. On the day he arrived, the temperature was just 4C.
“Where I come from, the temperature almost never drops below 20C. I went outside wearing just a T-shirt because I wanted to find out what a Lithuanian autumn was like. I quickly realised it was not a good idea,” he says with a laugh.
Today, he works as a software developer and says he is satisfied with his standard of living in Lithuania.
“IT specialists are paid well here. Of course, I considered opportunities to move to another country, but for now, things have worked out in such a way that I am staying in Lithuania,” he says.
After living in the country for several years, Adewuyi has obtained a permanent residence permit. However, he admits that he is seriously considering spending part of his time in Africa.
“I miss Africa. Here, I always stand out from the crowd. Sometimes you just want to be among people who look like you,” he says.
‘I thought I would never learn Lithuanian’
One of the biggest challenges Adewuyi has faced in Lithuania is the language. His native languages are English and Yoruba, spoken by one of Nigeria’s largest ethnic groups.
Lithuanian seemed completely unlike any language he knew.
“When I first heard Lithuanian, I thought I would never learn it. The hardest part is the grammatical cases. In English, everything is much simpler: we use prepositions, whereas here you have to change word endings. For someone who speaks English, that is very unusual,” he says.
He began learning Lithuanian almost as soon as he arrived. His employer paid for his first language courses.
Adewuyi says his progress really took off when he began studying independently in preparation for the state Lithuanian language examination.
“I passed the A2-level exam. That is enough for everyday life – I can find my way around the city and deal with daily practical matters. But, for example, visiting a doctor and communicating in Lithuanian is still a difficult task,” he admits.
Adewuyi’s circle of friends now includes Lithuanians, Belarusians and people from other countries. One Lithuanian friend helped him prepare for the exam by speaking to him exclusively in Lithuanian and correcting his mistakes.
“Even now, when I write to him in English, he replies in Lithuanian. I still find grammatical cases particularly difficult to understand,” Adewuyi says.
He has noticed that many migrants are in no hurry to learn Lithuanian because they are unsure whether they will stay in the country for long.
“Most foreigners think they will live here for a while and then leave. So they are not always motivated to learn the language. But when they need to obtain a permanent residence permit, their attitude changes,” he says.
Adewuyi identifies the changing seasons, the way public institutions operate and the sense of security as the main advantages of living in Lithuania.
He says that when you approach a government institution, you generally get what you need “without unnecessary formalities or having to know the right people”. He has also grown quite fond of Lithuanian cuisine.
“I like variety. I often visit different cafes and restaurants and try new dishes. The food here suits me perfectly,” he says.
Nevertheless, Adewuyi believes cultural differences are one of the most challenging aspects of living abroad.
“Where I come from, people are generally very open and welcoming. Lithuanians are more reserved, so it takes time to make friends. Being a foreigner is probably difficult in any country, but here you feel it particularly strongly,” he says.
Racism and difficulties finding accommodation
Speaking about attitudes towards people with a different skin colour, Adewuyi acknowledges that during his seven years in Lithuania, he has experienced both positive encounters and unpleasant situations.
He says discrimination is far from always being obvious.
“The thing about discrimination is that it is often impossible to say for certain whether it has taken place. You cannot always prove that you were treated differently specifically because of your skin colour,” he says.
The most painful experience for Adewuyi has been looking for accommodation. This year, while searching for a new flat, he became acutely aware that, in his view, foreign nationals with a different skin colour have to make considerably more effort than local residents.
“If your skin colour is different from that of the majority of the population, you automatically find yourself at the bottom of the list of potential tenants. That was probably the most unpleasant experience I have had recently,” he says.
Nevertheless, Adewuyi says he has experienced few instances of overt aggression during his years in Lithuania. He recalls hearing racist insults on several occasions, but says such incidents have been rare.
“Yes, I have been called the N-word, but those incidents were very rare. In general, I cannot say that I constantly encounter this kind of attitude,” he says.
According to Adewuyi, he feels safe in everyday life. In public places, at events and in clubs, people tend to show curiosity and friendliness rather than hostility.
“When I go out, people are usually friendly and interested in where I come from. I do not feel that I am in danger, and I am not afraid to walk around the city,” he says.
Online comments cause concern
Speaking about religion, Adewuyi says he grew up in a religious family but now describes himself as an agnostic.
“I grew up first in a Muslim environment and later in a Christian one. But I am not religious now. I am an agnostic,” he says.
He says that over the past year or two, he has found some public debates in Lithuania particularly difficult to watch, especially those concerning religion and attitudes towards people from different cultural and religious backgrounds.
In particular, he is referring to the debate surrounding the burning of the Quran. Online comments and public discussions about migrants have had a significant impact on his emotional wellbeing.
Further reading
“The past year or two have been quite difficult. Sometimes you open the news or social media and see a huge number of negative comments. This is especially true when the discussion concerns events attended by Black people. Posts like these almost always trigger a wave of hatred,” he says.
He believes such rhetoric also influences how people perceive others in real life.
“After reading comments like these, you start wondering: if someone looks at you in the street, what are they really thinking? Perhaps the person is simply looking at you, but you have already started to doubt yourself. It really does have an impact,” he says.
One incident at a city fair has stayed in Adewuyi’s memory. He says he was standing in a queue at a market stall when the vendor, having served other customers, simply walked to the back of the stall without acknowledging him.
“To this day, I cannot explain it any other way. After that incident, I found it much harder to attend similar events. Perhaps someone will say it was a trivial matter, but when you live far from home and do not have the support of your family nearby, such seemingly small things hurt much more,” the Nigerian says candidly.
Despite these experiences, Adewuyi stresses that he does not consider Lithuania a dangerous country for foreign nationals.
However, he admits that he sometimes feels tired of standing out.
“Sometimes you just want to be among people who are similar to you. There are many foreigners, Ukrainians and Belarusians living in Vilnius, but I still stand out very clearly. Over time, you begin to understand how important it is sometimes to feel like part of the majority rather than an exception,” he says.

AFL abandons Opening Round for season 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:59:59 UTC
14:59:59 KST

The AFL has abandoned Opening Round for 2027 with all 18 teams now drawn to play in Round One.
Opening Round was played in the prior two seasons but was widely criticised for compromising the competition.
The AFL's first game in 2027 will be delayed by one week due to the 150th anniversary Test cricket match.
The AFL has abandoned the Opening Round fixture from the past two seasons, with all 18 clubs now set to play in Round One in 2027.
The previous seasons saw the four teams based in New South Wales and Queensland play home games, while this year's draw also included one game at the MCG.
The split fixture meant each of the teams that played in the Opening Round — also referred to as round zero — subsequently had an early season bye.
Critics say the fixturing caused distortions in the draw, giving an advantage to the teams that played in Opening Round.
"We have listened to feedback and are pleased to be able to deliver a Round One for all our 18 clubs and fans as we bring back a traditional nine-game opening weekend across the country," AFL chief Andrew Dillon said in a statement.
Former premiership coach with West Coast and Collingwood and now ABC analyst, Mick Malthouse, said Opening Round compromised the fixture.
"We don't need it and it's a blessing now that we don't have it," he told ABC Sport.
"Let me say that 'zero round' was appropriately named.
"It had zero impact on the public; in fact, I'll go in the reverse and say it had a completely negative impact."
Malthouse said the early season byes caused by the Opening Round meant the ladder was not meaningful until all teams had played the same number of games, which in the season just passed did not happen until the end of Round 4.
"All round zero did was compromise the ability of sides to be ready for the next game," Malthouse said.
"If you've got a game tucked under your belt, you're ready; you're miles in front of the next side.
"And don't worry about the results of those games; it's more important about the long-term effect on players.
The president of the AFL Fans' Association, Ron Issko, welcomed the move to reinstate a full Round One.
"Credit to the AFL for listening," he told ABC Sport.
"When you start a season after waiting six months for the season to start and not all teams are playing, it's sort of like a soft launch.
"It just didn't have that energy.
"We're a national competition and what's better than having all teams playing on Round One."
The AFL's move to highlight games in NSW and Queensland was seen as a response to the National Rugby League's move to stage that competition's opening games in Las Vegas.
"We've looked over the border and so seeing that there's games played in Las Vegas, [said] 'Wow, if that's the way they operate, let us do something similar,'" Malthouse said.
"Forget about what's happening over the border and in fact embrace what's over the border and applaud them," he said.
Round One of the 2027 season will be played from March 17-21, with matches in NSW, Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria.
It has been delayed one week from the usual season start time by the test cricket 150th anniversary match between Australia and England at the MCG.
The season will kick off with a match between the Sydney Swans and Geelong at the SCG on Wednesday, March 17.
The following night, losing grand finalist Fremantle will play the Western Bulldogs at home.
Three-time reigning premiers Brisbane will play on the Friday night against Hawthorn at the MCG.

UN experts disappointed shackling and strip-searching bills blocked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:59:39 UTC
14:59:39 KST

UN experts criticise parliament for blocking shackling and strip-searching bills
In short:
United Nations experts have rebuked the Australian parliament for failing to vote on bills banning the shackling of incarcerated women during childbirth and strip-searching children.
Advocates say the shackling of women during and immediately after childbirth can harm a mother and child.
What's next?
The UN experts are urging the federal government to ensure the treatment of women and children in custody is consistent with international human rights law.
United Nations special rapporteurs have expressed disappointment that the Australian parliament failed to vote on two bills banning the shackling of prisoners during childbirth and the strip-searching of children.
It comes after reports this month of a WA teen girl being shackled in hospital after being detained, and an Indigenous woman in a Queensland hospital allegedly shackled after giving birth.
In a statement, special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, Reem Alsalem, and special rapporteur on contemporary forms of racism, Ashwini K.P., said the bills were in line with international standards.
"It is disappointing that parliament was not given the opportunity to formally decide on reforms aimed at protecting the dignity, bodily integrity and rights of women and children deprived of liberty," they said.
"We encourage Australian authorities and parliamentarians to continue pursuing reforms that prohibit shackling during childbirth and protect children from invasive strip-searching practices."
The two bills were brought by senator Lidia Thorpe and debated in the Senate earlier this month.
They had support from the Senate crossbench, but the government and the opposition joined forces to block a vote on the legislation.
Senator Thorpe said she had thought the legislation would be an "easy win" after consulting senators on it.
"I thought that the Labor government would want to end shackling of women giving birth and strip searching of children," she said.
"Every senator I spoke to was horrified, so I thought we could have a chance here. But no, the political will is not there."
Shackling 'psychological and physical abuse'
The shackling bill would have banned restraints at "at any time" during the child birthing process, including immediately after giving birth.
The ABC last week reported Queensland Corrective Services officers allegedly restrained a prisoner at Townsville hospital after she gave birth via C-section earlier this month.
A spokesperson says the woman's care is under review and restraints on pregnant prisoners are only used as a last resort.
Chief executive of advocacy organisation Sisters Inside, Debbie Kilroy, said the woman was giving birth while debate on the bills was underway in the Senate.
"This was an opportunity for them to make a stance against violence against women, which is shackling women during birth [and] after birth, and they actually let us down," she said.
As a UN member state, Australia has endorsed the Bangkok rules, a UN resolution that sets out minimum standards for the treatment of women in prison.
They specifically outlaw the use of restraints on women during labour, birth or immediately after birth.
Ms Kilroy, who was part of initial meetings to develop the Bangkok rules, said Australia's failure to ensure those standards were met was an "embarrassment".
"It's psychological abuse and also physical abuse that not only harms mum, but can harm the child medically," she said.
"When they know that they were born in shackles, it can cause harm for them psychologically as well as the child grows older."
The bills remain in the Senate, but it could be months before they can come up for a vote again.
"Sadly, it means that they [women and children] will continue to be violated," Senator Thorpe said.
"I'll continue to ramp up a campaign to put a vote to the Senate once again to get the support and end the harm against women and children in this country."
A Labor-led Senate inquiry this month recommended the federal government "engage with states and territories" on shackling practices, which Ms Kilroy said was just pushing the issue back on the states.
"We're going to see more people die, more black deaths in custody, more women shackled, more babies harmed, unless the federal government intervenes. They have an opportunity and they can intervene, but they choose not to," she said.
"They need some courage and to step up and intervene into what's happening in states and territories."
The federal government and WA Department of Justice have been contacted for comment.

Israel election: Turnout at record levels at halfway stage
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026
What you need to know

- Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces a staunch challenge to his grip on power

Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:
Turnout reaches highest level on record at halfway point
Turnout in Israel's election keeps rising. It reached a record 44.9% by 2 p.m. (1200 UTC), the Central Elections Commission said.
Some 3.29 million Israelis had cast their ballots by that point, commission head Dean Livne said.
It was the highest turnout recorded at that hour since the commission began collecting comparable statistics in 1973.
Eisenkot promises 'change' after casting his vote
Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, urged voters on Tuesday to oust what he called the "worst government" in Israel's history and promised a more responsible style of leadership.
"There is a wind of change blowing in Israel, and this change will come into effect tonight at 10 p.m.," at which point polls close, he said after casting his own vote at a polling station in Holon, just south of Tel-Aviv.
"We will not lead Israel through division and scaremongering, but through unity and true love," he said. "We will win!"
Ahead of election day, Israeli pollsters had predicted a close race between Netanyahu's right-wing conservatives and Eisenkot's opposition bloc, with neither expected to win an outright majority.
"I call on all citizens of Israel to vote, not to buckle under the heat or the disruptions, to stick to the mission," said Eisenkot. "To replace tonight the worst government since the state was established."
WATCH: How Israel's PM Netanyahu holds on to power
Three years after the Hamas-led October 7 attacks exposed major flaws in Israeli security, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains the dominant figure in Israel's political landscape. DW examines how many Israeli voters judge him more on his response to the crisis than on the failures that preceded it.
Experts point to security concerns, fear, Israel's conflicts on multiple fronts, and the absence of a clear challenger as key factors behind Netanyahu's resilience. The report also explores why international criticism can strengthen his support ahead of Israel's upcoming Knesset election.
Netanyahu casts ballot, while accusing Arab-Israeli parties of fraud
Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday that "there are currently no indications of systematic tampering with ballot slips" after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arab-Israeli parties of "trying to steal the election."
Netanyahu made the allegation after casting his own ballot in Jerusalem while urging voters to choose his Likud party.
"We know what is at stake ... We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," he said.
Netanyahu has used Arab-Israeli parties throughout the election to stoke fears of a Palestinian state and mobilize voters for Likud.
"So no barbecues, don't go to the beach — go to the polling station and vote Likud."
Netanyahu had said that three senior officials from the opposition Ra'am party, which has an Arab Muslim voter base, had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes full of cash.
The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, referred to the "unusual" incident with the envelopes in a press conference Tuesday morning but said that "police, even before people arrived at the polling stations, caught individuals who tried to bribe voters."
He said the unidentified suspects were not actually at polling stations and were caught near their homes, adding the matter was under investigation.
"There are no similar incidents of this kind across the country," he concluded. "This was a localized case."
Opposition parties, including that of Netanyahu's main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, have also complained that ballot papers were being defaced and stolen at polling stations.
Early Israel election turnout highest in decades
Voter turnout in the first three hours of the Israeli general election was the highest in decades, Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday.
According to the committee, nationwide turnout by mid-morning was already at 16.68%, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981 and up from 15.9% at the same time in the 2022 election.
"By 10 a.m., more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted," said the committee's acting director general, Dean Livne.
Total voter turnout in Israeli general elections approached 80% the 1990s but hasn't been higher than 72.3% since the turn of the century. Turnout at the last general election in 2022 was 70.6%.
Turnout among Arab Israelis is expected to be particularly important given the role Arab parties could play as potential kingmakers in coalition talks.
"Our vote will change the government," predicted Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party as he cast his vote, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.
Arabs in Israel make up about 18% of the electorate, and pre-election surveys have suggested a sharp increase in voter participation.
Data from the Midgam Research Institute cited by the Qatar-owned The New Arab indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in previous elections. The National, based in the United Arab Emirates, said its sources were predicting an "astronomical" Arab turnout.
How does Israel's election work?
Who is eligible to vote?
Around 7.3 million Israelis (including around 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel) are eligible to vote on Tuesday.
More than 640,000 young Israelis will be eligible to vote in a general election for the first time.
Around 3.1 million Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank do not have the right to vote in Israeli elections, but 500,000 illegal settlers in those territories do.
A further 350,000 Palestinians live in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and also cannot vote, whereas around 230,000 Israelis living there can.
The US-based non-profit America-Israel Democracy Coalition (AID Coalition) has organized a "Fly&Vote" initiative, with as many as 67,000 voters returning to Israel to participate in the election, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data.
The coalition said half are coming from the US, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Israel does not have postal voting.
How does the voting system work?
Israel is a parliamentary democracy and voters elect a legislature rather than choosing their prime minister directly. Voters choose a party "list."
Israel uses a proportional representation system under which 120 parliamentary seats are distributed roughly in proportion to a party's share of the vote.
To enter parliament (known as the Knesset), parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes, which is equivalent to roughly four seats.
The party which can command a majority of at least 61 seats is called upon to form a government. No single party has ever won an outright majority, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Polls suggest this year will be no different.
Unlike many other democracies around the world, Israel is not divided up into geographic electoral districts.
Rather than electing individual lawmakers to represent local areas, voters in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and Haifa all choose from the same party lists in one, single, nationwide constituency.
When polling stations close at 10 p.m. local time (9 p.m. CET), broadcasters will publish their first exit polls, offering an initial indication of the results. Official results are scheduled to be published on November 4.
Arab-Israeli parties: Potential kingmakers in Israel's future ruling coalition?
While the main competition for the largest number of seats is between Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the Arab parties are projected to play a key role in determining Israel's next ruling coalition.
For a party or coalition to rule, it needs to secure 61 seats in the Knesset.
As per a recent Channel 12 poll, Eisenkot's bloc is hovering around 55 seats, while Netanyahu's bloc is trailing behind with some 51 seats. This means that either bloc would need to form coalitions in order to rule, should the election results come out similar to the polls.
The most likely parties to tip the scales are the Joint List (projected to win around 9 seats) and the Ra'am (projected to win around 5 seats). The Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by nationality, make up around a fifth of Israel's eligible voters. Polls suggest a higher turnout rate for the Arab voters than seen in previous elections.
Netanyahu's Likud and Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudi parties attempted last month to ban the Joint List and Ra'am from running in the race, but Israel's Supreme Court reversed the parties' disqualification earlier in October.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties. But analysts suggest such stances are not set in stone and can shift amid coalition talks, a move Netanyahu himself has resorted to in the past.
Gadi Eisenkot: Who is Netanyahu's main opponent?
The Israeli general election is considered by many to be a verdict on the country's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
But who is the opposition, and what do they stand for?
The main opposition force is a so-called "change bloc," a mixed group of center-right and some left-wing parties led by the newly formed Yashar (honesty) party and its leader Gadi Eisenkot.
A relative political newcomer, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to become the chief of the staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) between 2015 and 2019.
Eisenkot has positioned himself squarely in opposition to Netanyahu in terms of his personality — an unpolished man of the people in contrast to the highly stylized and controlling prime minister.
Campaigning on accountability, political reform, and national unity, Eisenkot has sharply criticized Netanyahu's leadership before and after the October 7 Hamas attacks.
But his politics don't differ massively and, although he has emphasized equal rights for all Israeli citizens, he has been ambiguous on the idea of a two-state solution since October 7.
While backing Israel's military operations, he argues the government lacks a clear strategy and has called for an independent inquiry into the failures surrounding the attacks. His military record and the death of his son in the Gaza war have strengthened his standing among many voters
The parties in Eisenkot's bloc all have ideological differences but are united by their goal of removing Netanyahu from power.
Polls open in Israel election
Voting began in Israel at 7 a.m. local time (6 a.m. CET) on Tuesday in the first general election since the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the devastating war in Gaza unleashed by Israel in response.
Some 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote, with polls showing a bloc led by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving premier, neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot's centrist opposition alliance.
Most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. local time (8 p.m. UTC).
WATCH: Netanyahu's final campaign? — Israel heads to the polls
There's a lot at stake in this election: The fallout and questions of political accountability for the attacks of October 7, 2023; mandatory military service for ultra-Orthodox men and sharing the burden of national defense; along with Israel's standing in the international community.
Nowhere can the division within Israeli society be more felt than in debate over Benjamin Netanyahu.
For the past four years, Israel's long-standing prime minister has led what has been described as the most right-wing government in the country's history. He broke with political convention by forming an alliance with ultranationalist politician Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Many Israelis want to see an end to this government. They blame it for the failures surrounding Hamas' terror attack and for the country's growing isolation internationally. Many are placing their hopes in Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as a leading opposition figure to challenge Netanyahu.
Security fears and domestic divides define Israel's election battle
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his top challenger Gadi Eisenkot are both against the creation of an independent Palestinian state, meaning the election is not expected to lead to major policy changes that could revive the long-stalled peace process.
Here are some of the other major campaign issues:
- Security and the War: Voters are focused on the management of the Israel-Hamas war, the future of Gaza, and handling threats from Iran and Hezbollah.
- Military Service: There is an intense debate over whether the exemption for ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) men should be extended or whether they should be required to serve in the military like other Jewish citizens.
- The Justice System: There are deep disagreements over proposed judicial reforms that would change the balance of power between elected politicians and the Supreme Court.
- The Economy: Voters are highly concerned about the cost of living, housing prices, inflation, and war-related spending, although these are not the primary campaign issues.
Welcome to our coverage
Israelis head to the polls today to elect a new Knesset in what is expected to be a tightly contested race.
Incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, is fighting to stay in power, with several court cases awaiting him if he loses office.
Polls suggest his opponent, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is in the lead.
Stay tuned as we closely follow the election, its results and the wider implications for the region.

What are double envelopes and how might they affect the election results?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:57:49 UTC
14:57:49 KST

While millions of Israelis vote in Tuesday’s elections for the 26th Knesset, hundreds of thousands of ballots are expected to be counted only after preliminary results are published, potentially changing the distribution of seats in the coming days.
According to a report by ynet, Israel’s Central Elections Committee expects between 600,000 and 650,000 people to vote using double envelopes, an unprecedented number in the country’s election history.
By comparison, around 463,000 voters used the method in the 2022 elections.
The expected increase is mainly attributed to the large number of reservists and residents evacuated from their homes due to the war, many of whom are unable to vote at the polling stations where they are registered.
The Elections Committee estimates that these ballots could amount to the equivalent of roughly 15 Knesset seats, potentially affecting the final allocation after the regular vote count.
The double-envelope method allows citizens who cannot reach their registered polling station to vote while preventing double voting and preserving ballot secrecy.
Under the system, voters place their ballot slips in regular envelopes, which are then inserted into outer envelopes bearing their personal details.
The envelopes are sent to the Central Elections Committee, which checks whether the voter has also cast a ballot at their registered polling station. Once verification is complete, the inner envelopes are separated from identifying details and sent for counting.
The method is also used by hospital inpatients, prisoners, police officers, foreign service personnel and people with disabilities who meet the legal requirements, in addition to soldiers and reservists.

World’s climate pledges would cut emissions a tenth of what’s needed: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:33:00 UTC
14:33:00 KST

World’s climate pledges would cut emissions a tenth of what’s needed: UN
- The UN said current climate pledges would cut global emissions by only 6% by 2035, far below the 60% needed to keep warming near 1.5 deg C.
- The report covered 154 countries’ NDCs and said even full delivery, including conditional targets, would cut emissions by just 9%.
- UN climate chief Simon Stiell said COP31 in Turkey can help close gaps, while climate finance rose to US$1.9 trillion a year but still falls short.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The latest climate pledges put forth by nations will cut global greenhouse gas emissions by just 6% by 2035, a UN report said on Oct 27, weeks before COP31 talks in Turkey.
That is a tenth of the roughly 60% reduction from 2019 levels that scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5 deg C, significantly down from the estimate in 2025 after the US withdrew from the Paris Agreement.
The report by UN Climate Change is a synthesis of 154 countries’ nationally determined contributions – obligatory submissions under the 2015 Paris deal – received between January 2024 and August 2026, covering 71% of global emissions.
It found that if the countries fully implemented their plans and also met conditional targets, emissions cuts would still amount to just 9%.
The UN in 2025 estimated a 10% cut by 2035, but that was before a large number of nationally determined contributions had come in, leaving it to model the missing pledges, and before the US was taken out of the equation.
Under President Donald Trump, the US left the Paris Agreement for a second time and is pursuing policies that heavily favour fossil fuels.
Last week, the UN Environment Programme found that global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions put the world on course for 2.6 deg C warming this century.
“With its focus on practical measures to support greater implementation”, the COP31 meeting in Turkey “can help address some of the key gaps”, UN climate chief Simon Stiell said in a statement.
To have a reasonable chance of limiting warming to 1.5 deg C by 2100, compared with pre-industrial levels, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates that global greenhouse gas emissions need to fall by 60% from 2019 levels by 2035.
For pathways to limiting warming to below 2 deg C – the Paris Agreement’s fallback goal – emissions would need to fall by 37% by 2035.
Scientists warn that every extra fraction of a degree above 1.5 deg C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.
The world has already warmed by roughly 1.4 deg C relative to pre-industrial times, and crossing 1.5 deg C is expected in a matter of years.
In another report released on Oct 27, the UN found that progress has been made in increasing financing to curb warming, but it still falls far short of what is required.
Global climate finance flows reached an average of US$1.9 trillion (S$2.4 trillion) a year in 2023 and 2024 – a 32% increase compared with 2021 and 2022 – driven largely by private investment in low-emission technology, including renewable electricity generation, and private household investment in electric vehicles and heat pumps. AFP

From Asbestos to Fungi: Eight New Materials Made from Waste and Living Matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Architecture is, above all, a material reality. The materials that surround us are the result of a chain of constructive, economic, aesthetic and, in more contemporary examples, environmental considerations. Decisions are shaped by available technology, manageable technique, time-related expectations and regulatory frameworks. To face the pressures on our built environment, those multidimensional conditions must change through what we call innovation: the tangible creation of new products and strategies with problem-solving capabilities. Matter is the general term for physical substance that has mass and takes up space. When matter is given a specific type, form, or useful application, it becomes material. Material transformation therefore requires going beyond recycling and reuse: combining existing matter to create new materials that open up new possibilities for construction. The research presented below suggests that demonizing existing materials is unnecessary as long as this capacity for innovation exists.
Transforming Existing Matter
Materials can be rendered obsolete when they are no longer usable under conventional methods, thereby becoming disposable. This is the case with asbestos, a mineral used mostly in finishes, cement and insulation, which has been gradually banned around the world since the 1970s due to its toxicity. With the ambitious aim of making up for that waste, the Australian architecture studio Besley & Spresser, in collaboration with Asbeter and Benedetta Pompili Studio, reinterpreted asbestos as a byproduct that the studio describes as harmless and carbon-negative, with architectural potential. According to the studio, asbestos can be recrystallized to form new, human-safe products, and waste building materials that contain it can likewise be safely recycled into non-hazardous materials. The studio presented a test installation at the 2025 Lisbon Architecture Triennale as an example of "radical repair" and the rediscovery of urban materials.
In a different example of reuse, researchers at the Kyiv National University of Construction and Architecture (KNUBA) are working with debris from war-damaged buildings. The solution under investigation combines this debris with industrial and agricultural waste to produce printable concrete suitable for additive manufacturing. The project, financed by the United States and international organizations, aims to add new options for large-scale housing reconstruction in the country. On another note, researchers from ETH Zurich and Empa are developing a new fire-resistant material made from sawdust. Sawdust is the powder, small grains and tiny wood chips produced while processing wood, most of which is burned to generate energy, releasing carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. Combining sawdust with the mineral struvite, made possible by controlling the struvite's crystallization with an enzyme extracted from watermelon seeds, would turn the material into a new fire-resistant composite that is easy to recycle.
New Materials Developed as an Alternative to Concrete
At the other end of the spectrum, cement-bonded materials such as concrete are harder to break down for reuse. Cement accounts for around 8% of global CO2 emissions and is an essential component of concrete, a composite commonly criticized for its environmental impact. It is therefore not surprising that numerous research projects are turning their attention to finding alternatives to this widespread material. From recycling biological byproducts from sugarcane to using the underground root system of fungi, researchers are testing components to emulate concrete's moldability, strength, and mass-production capabilities. Material research studio Matter at Hand and ceramic manufacturer Darwen Terracotta are transforming clay into a fluid, concrete-like material by combining it with recycled aggregates, sand and natural fibers. The result is Poured Earth, a castable material that uses sodium silicate or tannins to increase fluidity without adding extra water.
Mexican research and production studio MANUFACTURA, which specializes in sustainable construction materials and digital fabrication, was named one of the 20 honorees of the ArchDaily 2026 Next Practices Awards for transforming waste into circular architectural materials using robotic 3D printing and creating biocomposites that draw on pre-Hispanic Mexican construction techniques. As an alternative to concrete, they propose Corncretl, a new material composed of limestone derivatives, corn, and recycled nejayote, a calcium-rich byproduct of the processing of dried corn in Mexico. Another initiative using organic components for concrete alternatives is being developed by Montana State University. Researchers are using mycelium, the underground root network of fungi, to design load-bearing materials. The challenging process of transforming living matter into a durable material is achieved by letting the mycelium act as a "scaffold" to which microorganisms adhere and harden through a process called calcification.
Effect-driven Material Research
Research can also be driven by a kind of magical effect: the ambition that a single new element can change the experience of an entire system. Researchers from Nanyang Technological University (NTU) in Singapore, in collaboration with the ecology and biomimicry design firm bioSEA, are developing new tiles that cool buildings without consuming energy. The tiles are made from mycelium and bamboo shavings, combining the materials' insulating properties with a texture that mimics elephant skin, whose wrinkles and crevices help elephants regulate temperature. On a more magical note, researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science (CEMS) in Japan are developing a plastic that dissolves in seawater. Intended to prevent microplastics from further harming ocean life, the new material is a supramolecular plastic composed of two ionic monomers that can be consumed by bacteria and are quickly destabilized by salt water.
Other material and sustainability-related initiatives are being developed worldwide. In New York, London and Brussels, city governments are transforming former industrial infrastructure into circular construction hubs: sites that collect, store and redistribute building materials and demolition waste so they can be reused or repurposed rather than sent to landfill. Architecture firm HENN recently launched CarbonBudget, a digital tool that calculates project-specific CO2 budgets for buildings. The tool is designed to calculate whether the emissions of a building project located in Europe are compatible with the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C target, based on specific inputs such as location and building area. A new open-air laboratory and research site dedicated to sustainable living and advanced architectural 3D printing recently opened in Italy. The site, called Shamballa, hosts research and development centers that form an experimental "ecosystem" for developing new ideas in bio-construction and sustainable living.

Tracking the money: The biggest donors in the 2026 US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:29:24 UTC
14:29:24 KST

Tracking the money: The biggest donors in the 2026 US midterm elections
The 50 biggest contributors have poured $2.77bn into the race, led by Elon Musk’s $446m for Republican-aligned groups.
The 2026 US midterms are on track to be the most expensive in the country’s history. Spending on political advertising alone is projected to reach $11.6bn, more than in any previous election cycle, including the 2024 presidential race, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
Much of that money comes from wealthy donors, political nonprofits and businesses seeking to shape Washington’s priorities, and some of it passes through networks of organisations before it is spent.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera uses Federal Election Commission data to trace the billionaires, financiers and companies behind the largest contributions ahead of the November 3 vote.
The 50 largest donors contributed $2.77bn
The 50 largest donors and organisations have so far contributed a combined $2.77bn during the 2026 midterm election cycle.
Republican-aligned contributors accounted for $1.67bn, or about 60 percent of donations, double the $832m (30 percent) from Democratic-aligned contributors.
The remaining $264m, about 10 percent, came from contributors classified as bipartisan or special interest, including groups backing sports betting and cryptocurrency.
Individuals can donate up to $3,500 per election to a US federal candidate’s campaign in the 2025–26 election cycle. Yet some of the people on this list have given hundreds of millions of dollars.
That is legal because most of the money went not to candidates but to super political action committees, or super PACs, which can accept donations of any size.
What is a super PAC?
A super PAC is a group that can raise and spend unlimited sums to support or oppose candidates, mainly through advertising. The main condition is that it must not coordinate its spending with candidates or their campaigns.
They emerged in 2010 after two court rulings paved the way for unlimited spending on elections by groups independent of candidates.
Super PACs must report their donors to the Federal Election Commission (FEC), the US agency that oversees federal elections. But some major contributors, including One Nation and Majority Forward, are nonprofit groups that do not have to disclose their own donors.
This can hide where political money originally comes from, a practice known as “dark money”.
But Lawrence Lessig, a professor of law and leadership at Harvard Law School and a campaign finance reform advocate, argues that the money is hidden only from voters.
“It’s not dark to the politicians. It’s dark to us,” he told Josh Rushing on Al Jazeera’s Let’s Focus, in a debate on money in US elections with Bradley Smith, a former chairman of the Federal Election Commission. “Nobody’s confused from the politician’s side about where this money is coming from, and they know what they need to do.”
Who are the biggest individual donors?
Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and head of Tesla and SpaceX, is the largest individual contributor of the cycle, with $446m, according to Federal Election Commission data.
He is followed by Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein, founders of the shipping supplies company Uline, and Jeff and Janine Yass. Jeff Yass cofounded the trading firm Susquehanna International Group.
All three have given to Republican-aligned groups.
Republican-aligned top donors:
- Elon Musk: $446 million
- Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein: $150 million
- Jeff and Janine Yass: $110 million
The largest Democratic-aligned donors are George Soros, the billionaire investor and founder of the Open Society Foundations; Mike Bloomberg, the former New York City mayor and founder of the financial data company Bloomberg; and LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and his wife, Michelle Yee.
Democratic-aligned top donors:
- George Soros: $102 million
- Mike Bloomberg: $84 million
- Reid Hoffman and Michelle Yee: $41 million
Four individual donors have each given more than $100m. For Lessig, that concentration, not the overall cost of elections, is the real concern.
“The problem isn’t the spending. The problem is the concentration of donors,” he said. “If you don’t have $100 million to put on the table, you’re not going to matter in the way that we think that people ought to matter in a democracy.”
Which organisations contributed the most?
Political nonprofits led the organisational rankings, alongside cryptocurrency firms and an industrial conglomerate.
On the Republican side, the largest was One Nation, a nonprofit aligned with Senate Republican leadership, followed by American Action Network, which is linked to House Republican leadership. On the Democratic side, Majority Forward and House Majority Forward, nonprofits allied with the party’s Senate and House leadership, led the way.
Republican-aligned organisations:
- One Nation: $133 million
- American Action Network: $64.3 million
- American Prosperity Alliance: $50.7 million
Democratic-aligned organisations:
- Majority Forward: $102 million
- House Majority Forward: $93.7 million
- Economic Opportunity Fund: $41.5 million
Cryptocurrency companies also featured prominently. Coinbase, the largest US crypto exchange, gave $57.8m, followed by Ripple, the blockchain payments company, with $49.6m, and Foris DAX, the company behind Crypto.com, with $39m.
The industrial conglomerate Koch gave $46.8m, while the sports betting company DraftKings contributed $40.4m.

The 'growing' health threat now responsible for one in 10 Australian deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:29:18 UTC
14:29:18 KST

In Brief
- Dementia caused more than 10 per cent of deaths in Australia last year.
- The figure increased by almost 40 per cent in the past decade, while deaths due to heart diseases decreased.
Dementia now accounts for more than one in 10 Australian deaths for the first time as advocates warn of a continued surge in the condition as the population ages.
More than 19,000 people (10.1 per cent) died from dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, in 2025, according to analysis released on Tuesday as part of the Australian Bureau of Statistics' (ABS) Causes of Death report.
Dementia has been the leading cause of death for women in Australia since 2016, and in 2024 it overtook cancer and heart disease to become Australia's leading killer nationally.
This is the first time dementia deaths have exceeded 10 per cent, more than double the rates reported in 2006, when dementia was the fourth-leading cause of death nationally.
Dementia Australia's chief executive officer, professor Tanya Buchanan, said the new data reinforced the urgent need to raise awareness of the condition as a leading public health issue affecting Australians.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"The data underlines the critical need for more recognition and funding to support people living with dementia, their families and carers," Buchanan said in a statement.
"Despite the growing impact of dementia, investment in specific services, supports and prevention has not kept the same pace, and the stigma that surrounds dementia continues. This needs to change."
Buchanan said that with nearly 500,000 Australians living with dementia, without "significant intervention", the figure was expected to increase to more than one million by 2065.
A gendered killer
In 2025, women accounted for more than 60 per cent of all deaths attributed to dementia in Australia.
The report found that there were almost twice as many deaths from dementia as from ischaemic heart diseases, which is the second leading cause of death for women.
The ABS said that in 2025, there were just 2,791 deaths separating the top two leading causes of death, with that gap continuing to widen as dementia deaths increase over time, and deaths from ischaemic heart disease continued to decline.
Between 2016 and 2025, the number of deaths due to dementia increased by 37 per cent, while deaths due to ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases decreased by 16.2 per cent and 12.1 per cent, respectively.
The mortality rate for ischaemic heart diseases was the lowest on record since its peak in 1968.
After ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases, lung cancer and chronic lower respiratory diseases rounded the top five leading causes of death, which in 2025 represented more than 30 per cent of all registered deaths.

Israelis head to polls as voting begins in pivotal Knesset election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:05:50 UTC
14:05:50 KST

Polls opened across Israel on Tuesday morning as eligible voters head to the polls to elect the country's next Knesset in a pivotal race pitting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his sitting coalition against the opposition bloc seeking to replace him.
Within the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has taken the lead ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud in the majority of recent polling, though neither bloc still appears able to secure a 61-seat Knesset majority.
Polling stations opened at 7:00 a.m., and exit polls are expected at 10:00 p.m., offering preliminary projections of the election results. The official results will be finalized in the coming days, following the completion of the vote count.
Voting at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad concluded on October 16, while voting at some military bases began last week.
The fateful elections will be the first to take place since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, with the political landscape and the issues at the forefront of voters’ minds having shifted significantly since the previous vote in 2022.
IDF manpower crisis, haredi draft, Oct. 7 commission central issues for Israeli voters
Some of the central issues include the IDF’s severe manpower crisis after three years of war, contentious haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription legislation, and calls for a state commission of inquiry into the government’s failures surrounding the attack.
Meanwhile, traditional election issues, such as the establishment of a Palestinian state, have moved further to the background as Israel’s security outlook has changed, and most parties stand in agreement against Palestinian statehood.
Another major issue is the fate of long-serving Netanyahu, who has led Israel for 19 non-consecutive years.
Following the October 7 massacre and the ensuing war, the opposition bloc has called for Netanyahu to be held accountable for the attacks, arguing that he should no longer serve as prime minister.
There appears to be no clear outcome for the elections, as neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc has been projected as being able to secure a 61-seat majority without the support of the Arab parties.
According to the final Channel 12 poll released on Friday before the election, Netanyahu’s bloc stood at 50 seats, while the opposition bloc was projected to win 56 seats.
The Arab parties, meanwhile, were projected to win a combined 16 seats. Most opposition party leaders have pledged not to form a government with the Arab parties, arguing that such a coalition would not be viable following the October 7 attacks.
Netanyahu’s Likud party was projected to win 19 seats in the poll, down from the 32 seats it currently holds in the outgoing Knesset.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party projected to win greatest number of Knesset seats
Meanwhile, Eisenkot’s Yashar party was projected to win 22 seats, ahead of both Likud and B’Yachad, led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett, which was projected to receive 14 seats.
Voter turnout throughout the day will have a significant impact on the results of the elections. With the electoral threshold set at 3.25% of valid votes, the number of votes a party needs depends on how many people turn out on election day.
The Taub Center's updated calculations, prepared by Prof. Alex Weinreb, head of its Demography Area and research director, estimate that at a 70% turnout rate, similar to the 2022 election, a party would need 165,635 votes to cross the threshold.
The required vote count rises as turnout increases, meaning smaller parties could face a tougher challenge if more Israelis head to the polls.
Several parties are fighting to secure enough votes to enter the Knesset and clear the threshold, including Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel’s the Reservists-Economics party.
Whether these parties cross the threshold is expected to significantly affect both blocs' ability to form a coalition.
For these small parties, even a slight shift in voter support could determine whether they enter the next Knesset or leave their supporters without representation.
Meanwhile, police have prepared for the possibility of clashes and public order disruptions on Election Day, particularly in the hours following the release of exit polls.
Police announced on Monday that as part of special preparations, approximately 20,000 police officers, Border Police officers, and volunteers would carry out a range of actions throughout the country on Election Day.
Forces are expected to be deployed at thousands of polling stations nationwide and in surrounding areas to maintain public order and protect public safety and security, the police stated.
This will be done to “safeguard the integrity of the elections, and ensure that the democratic process is conducted properly and in accordance with the law,” the police added.
Alex Winston contributed to this report.

Election Day: A complete guide to Israel’s political parties and what they stand for

Unknown Publisher

Israelis head to the polls today to elect the country's next Knesset, with parties competing for votes and a chance to shape the country's future.
But what does each party stand for, who leads it, and what are its key policies and priorities?
The Jerusalem Post has prepared a series of explainers breaking down the platforms, leaders, and main positions of all the main parties running in the election.
Explore our guides below to learn what each party stands for before casting your vote.
What does Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar stand for?
Led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, Yashar is a centrist party focused on national security, government reform, and replacing Benjamin Netanyahu. Yashar is part of the opposition bloc.
Ballot letters: דרך | Explore Yashar’s policies and platform
What does Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud stand for?
Led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Likud is a right-wing party that emphasizes national security, Jewish nationalism, and a strong stance against Palestinian statehood. The Likud heads the right-wing bloc and Netanyahu's sitting coalition.
Ballot letters: מחל | Explore Likud’s policies and platform
What does Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad stand for?
Led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett, B’Yachad is a centrist party focused on government reform, economic growth, and the enlistment of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men into the IDF. B'Yachad is part of the opposition bloc.
Ballot letters: רק | Explore B’Yachad’s policies and platform
What does Yair Golan’s Democrats stand for?
Led by Yair Golan, the Democrats is a left-wing, Zionist party that emphasizes liberal democracy, civil rights, education reform, and a greater equality in military service. The Democrats is part of the opposition bloc.
Ballot letters: אמת | Explore the Democrats’ policies and platform
What does Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu stand for?
Led by Avigdor Liberman, Yisrael Beytenu is a right-wing, secular nationalist party focused on national security, a tougher stance against Hamas, and reducing the influence of religious parties in government. Yisrael Beytenu is part of the opposition bloc.
Ballot letter: ל | Explore Yisrael Beytenu’s policies and platform
What does Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit stand for?
Led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Otzma Yehudit is a far-right nationalist party that advocates a hardline approach to security threats, expanded Jewish settlement, and tougher law enforcement. Otzma Yehudit is part of the Netanyahu bloc and the sitting coalition.
Ballot letter: ב | Explore Otzma Yehudit’s policies and platform
What do the Joint List and Ra’am stand for?
The Joint List and Ra’am represent different strands of Arab Israeli politics. The Joint List is generally left-wing and emphasizes equality, civil rights, and Palestinian national rights, while Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am takes a more pragmatic approach focused on tackling crime, securing funding, and improving living conditions in Arab communities.
Ballot letters: ודם (Joint List); עמ (Ra'am) | Explore the Joint List and Ra’am’s policies and platform
What do Shas and United Torah Judaism stand for?
Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) are ultra-Orthodox (haredi) parties that prioritize protecting the status of religious institutions in Israel and maintaining broad exemptions from IDF service for yeshiva students.
Shas primarily represents Sephardi and Mizrahi haredi and religious Jews, while UTJ represents Ashkenazi haredi communities. Both parties are part of the Netanyahu bloc and were part of the sitting coalition.
Ballot letters: שס (Shas); ג (UTJ) | Explore Shas and United Torah Judaism’s policies and platform
What does Bezalel Smotrich’s RZP-Zehut stand for?
Led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Zehut leader Moshe Feiglin, Religious Zionist Party-Zehut is a far-right, religious-nationalist party that supports expanding West Bank settlements, applying Israeli sovereignty over the territory, and advancing judicial reform. RZP is part of the Netanyahu bloc and the sitting coalition.
Ballot letter: ט | Explore Religious Zionist Party’s policies and platform
What about the parties hovering above - or below - the electoral threshold?
Several parties are fighting to secure enough votes to enter the Knesset, with the 3.25% electoral threshold determining which lists win parliamentary representation. For these parties, even a small shift in voter support could determine whether they enter the next Knesset or leave their supporters without representation.
Recent polls have placed the People of Israel party and the Reservists-Economic Party near the threshold, with their standings varying between surveys. Their results could have a significant impact on the balance between the political blocs.
Led by former IDF general Ofer Winter, People of Israel is a right-wing party that supports Benjamin Netanyahu for prime minister and calls for new leadership outside the political establishment.
It makes haredi enlistment a condition for joining a government, rejects blanket exemptions for yeshiva students, and advocates a hardline security policy, including voluntary emigration from Gaza.
The Reservists-Economic Party, led by former minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha, combines a right-leaning Zionist and security agenda with an emphasis on economic reform. The party says it will join only a Zionist government and demands that a universal conscription law be passed before a government is formed.
Led by Moti Leitner, the Haredi Public Party seeks to offer an alternative to the established ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism. It supports broader haredi military or national service, core-curriculum studies including math and English, and greater accountability from haredi political leadership.
Ballot letters: ך (People of Israel); די (Reservists-Economic Party); זך (Haredi Public) | Explore these parties’ policies and platforms

A fire that broke out on Sept. 14 near a state-owned arms company in Romania was coordinated by a Russian network, Romanian officials said on Oct. 26.
The fire erupted in Brasov, in central Romania, near CARFIL SA, a subsidiary of the national company ROMARM.
The arson attack is "part of a larger campaign of sabotage operations attributed to the Russian Federation in Europe," according to a news release from Romania's Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, known as DIICOT, and the Romanian Intelligence Service.
Romanian officials identified three perpetrators who they said were coerced by Russian operatives into carrying out the attack. Two suspects are said to be from Belarus and one from Ukraine.
Two have been arrested, allegedly while preparing to carry out similar attacks in Germany, according to DIICOT.
The third suspect remains at large and is believed to be in Poland. European authorities issued a warrant for his arrest on Monday.
Romanian investigators believe that prior to the Brasov fire, the suspects instigated similar incidents which were also coordinated by Russia.
According to the Romanian Intelligence Service, the sabotage operations aim to intimidate and undermine the defense capabilities of affected states, and weaken their contributions to European and regional security.
The attacks join a string of similar incidents across Europe that authorities believe were instigated by Russian operatives.
Lithuanian forces thwarted Russian attempts to burn down Starlink satellite communications equipment on Oct. 18. A similar incident happened in Poland less than a month prior. In August, an arson attack against a defense contractor in Tallinn was likely caused by Russian sabotage operations, Estonian officials said.
Experts warn that the increase in Russian hybrid attacks is a way for Russia to test how far it can push NATO and Europe — probing the limits of NATO security and sowing chaos without triggering all-out war.
Romania, which borders Ukraine, has also been affected directly by Russia's full-scale invasion, particularly by drone activity in the Black Sea. A civilian cargo ship sank on Oct. 23 after a series of Russian strikes.

Israel election live: polls open in most consequential vote in country’s history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:01:26 UTC
14:01:26 KST

Voter turn-out for first half of day highest on record
We’ve reported on how many Israelis are viewing this election as one of the most important of their lifetime, and politicians across the spectrum have characterised it as “existential” for the future of the Israeli state.
That urgency does appear to be translating into record turn-out at the polls according to latest figures from the Central Elections Committee.
As of 2pm local time, 44.9% of voters had cast their ballot. This is the highest turn-out since record keeping began in the 1970s.
The voting level at this hour is also about 6% higher than the last election in 2022, where Netanyahu was ultimately able to scrape together a slim majority coalition with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
The queues are so long today that the electoral authority has also issued fresh guidance on how to ease congestion; advising polling staff to start verifying voters’ IDs while they’re still in line.
Voting is open until 10pm local time and any eligible Israeli who arrives by a polling station by then can cast their vote. As we’ve reported, many eligible voters have also flown back into the country for the sole purpose of making their ballot count today.
Robo calls and a socials onslaught: The Israeli right's racist scare tactics on election day
Emma Graham-Harrison
Amid the highest voter turnout in decades, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies resorted to racist scare tactics, including unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud, to urge their own voters to the polls.
“We’re in a war for our home,” Netanyahu said in a social media post in the early afternoon, with unsourced claims of low voter turnouts in strongholds of his Likud party. “Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections. Go out and vote, recover it!”
In 2015, Netanyahu claimed that “Arab voters are coming out in droves to the polls” in a bid to motivate his party’s base. The comments drew a rebuke from then-US President Barack Obama and Netanyahu apologised for them soon after winning another mandate.
A decade later he is doubling down on that political tactic. A robo-call to voters purporting to come from the prime minister made groundless accusations that Palestinian citizens of Israel were trying to “steal the election”. A spokesman for Netanyahu did not respond to questions about the call.
In the call, a man who sounds like the prime minister falsely claims that three leaders of the Ra’am party had been caught with envelopes full of cash. He also says that left wing women were driving Palestinian women to polling stations, which is not illegal under Israeli law.
He finishes by urging his own voters to turn out. Polling day is a holiday for most Israelis, who often use it to go to the beach, hiking or other activities with their family.
“You need to go to the polling stations. Everyone needs to vote. There is no beach. No barbecue, there is nothing (else) now,” it says. “Everyone must go out to vote to ensure the victory of the right against the left.”
Earlier he shared photos that purported to show empty polling stations in Likud-supporting areas, and long lines in opposition strongholds. The Guardian saw long queues on Tuesday morning in areas with high support for Netanyahu and his allies, including parts of Jerusalem and the settlement of Efrat.
After casting his own ballot, far right Jewish supremacist Itamar Ben Gvirwent to a Palestinian- majority town to make similar claims. “Now in Kfar Qasim. Don’t let them win”, he posted above a social media video filmed on the outskirts of the town, the site of a notorious massacre by Israeli border police in 1956.
“Voter turnout in the Arab sector is off the charts, unprecedented.” he says. “If you want this country to remain Jewish and Zionist...then get out and vote.”
US ambassador clarifies 'Arabs vote same as Israelis' post
The US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has just issued a clarification on his election day tweet this morning which prompted a few raised eyebrows. Earlier he’d written on X:
Today is election day in Israel, which is a national holiday. All voting is in person, ID required. No mail-in or absentee ballots. Arabs vote same as Israelis. Contentious process, but it’s a democracy-not many of those in this region!
The “Arabs vote same as Israelis” phrasing was perceived by some as appearing to imply that Arab voters in Israel aren’t Israeli or due the same vote.

"Correct and I should have stated it that way!” said Huckabee.
10 million ppl in 8m Jews, 2m Arabs. ALL are Israeli citizens-Jew, Muslim, or Christian. All vote, serve in IDF, in Knesset, & proudly have Israeli passports. Women equal to men. All have free speech.
As we reported earlier though, there are serious concerns about voter intimidation of Palestinian citizens in Israel - who represent about 21% of the population – and suppression of Arab parties.
So far today, Ra’am, the party headed by Mansour Abbas, has filed a complaint to the Central Elections Committee, saying their activists were detained by police this morning before voting began and there weren’t enough Arab language ballot papers being distributed, according to Haaretz reporting.
Huckabee’s comments were also likely only referring to the roughly 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel who live within the country’s pre-1967 borders and have full voting rights.
Of the 15 million people who live in areas under Israeli control, more than 5.5 million Palestinians have no vote including 3.1 million Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, 350,000 Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem and 2 million Palestinians in Gaza.
Voter turn-out for first half of day highest on record
We’ve reported on how many Israelis are viewing this election as one of the most important of their lifetime, and politicians across the spectrum have characterised it as “existential” for the future of the Israeli state.
That urgency does appear to be translating into record turn-out at the polls according to latest figures from the Central Elections Committee.
As of 2pm local time, 44.9% of voters had cast their ballot. This is the highest turn-out since record keeping began in the 1970s.
The voting level at this hour is also about 6% higher than the last election in 2022, where Netanyahu was ultimately able to scrape together a slim majority coalition with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
The queues are so long today that the electoral authority has also issued fresh guidance on how to ease congestion; advising polling staff to start verifying voters’ IDs while they’re still in line.
Voting is open until 10pm local time and any eligible Israeli who arrives by a polling station by then can cast their vote. As we’ve reported, many eligible voters have also flown back into the country for the sole purpose of making their ballot count today.
It has just gone past 3pm in Tel Aviv and 1pm in London, where we are currently blogging from. Here is a summary of where things stand:
Turnout is at its highest so far in decades as Israelis vote in what is widely considered to be one of the most consequential elections in the country’s history.
Polls have opened in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, Israel’s subsequent destruction of Gaza, and the launch of its war with the US against Iran.
Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad have flown in for the elections, according to Aid Coalition.

In the settlement of Efrat near Jerusalem, Shani, 19, had come to the polling station with her parents, to cast her vote for the far-right party of finance minister Bezalel Smotrich.
She is part of a large cohort of first-time voters who are more rightwing than older generations, and may help bolster support for Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners.
More than 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the last election in 2022, and three-quarters of first-time Jewish voters define themselves as right or centre-right, a recent poll for Channel 12 television found (it did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel).
Shani said she chose Smotrich, a settler himself, for his promises to expand Israel’s footprint in occupied Palestine. “Smotrich is pushing forward with settlement expansion and improving security,” she said.

Software engineer, Yitzchak Schwarz, 36 is an activist for far-right libertarian Moshe Feiglin, running on a joint slate with Smotrich for this election. “If there are sanctions, it’s going to hurt a bit, but we have to think about our own survival and our own national rights,” he said.
Sue and Tom Rosenfelt, who have lived in Efrat for over 30 years and have three sons in the reserves, said national unity and the unequal burden of military service are their main concerns. “I think that at this point getting another foothold and another hilltop isn’t the thing that’s going to strengthen the country as a whole,” Tom said. “We need to work more on unity.”
In an election which many Israelis describe as critical, turnout was so high at their polling station at a school in Efrat that they had left the long lines, and planned to come back later.
Both plan to vote for the party of Naftali Bennett, a rightwing settler and tech multimillionaire, who joined forces with centrist Yair Lapid. “I feel like this is a time when we need to come together,” Sue Rosenfeld said. “You know, Bennett and Lapid are on different sides of the spectrum, but they’ve come together and that’s something I want to support.”
