While the media attention has been focusing on the country’s parliamentary elections, Israel’s assault on Gaza has continued, a year after the signing of a so-called ‘ceasefire’ with Hamas.
A UN commission said yesterday that Israel was continuing to commit genocide in Gaza despite the signing of the US-brokered ceasefire last October.
The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, rejected a claim in May by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace that the truce had “largely held”.
It said Israeli authorities had kept committing “genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza”. The report said:
The perception of Palestinians and a possible Palestinian state as a threat to Israel and the desire to reduce the Palestinian population contribute to a permissive military culture where Israeli soldiers, with or without directives from commanders, directly target Palestinians whether or not they pose a real or immediate threat.
Testimonies by Israeli soldiers in Gaza display a disregard for Palestinian lives and a military culture where Palestinians are dehumanized, equated with “terrorists”, trivializing the killing of civilians.
The report noted that between the 10 October ceasefire in 2025 and 30 September 2026, Israeli attacks killed at least 1,431 Palestinian people in Gaza, including 300 children and 130 women.
In its latest update, Gaza’s health ministry said that 74,561 Palestinian people have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza since October 2023, when Isreal launched its assault on the territory following the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.
The report also accused Israeli forces of having committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank. It lists extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence. Israel has dismissed the findings of the report and has denied committing genocide in Gaza.
Netanyahu casts his ballot and urges his supporters to vote, saying 'this is an emergency hour'
Benjamin Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political survival, has just cast his ballot in Jerusalem.
In a post on X this morning, the Israeli prime minister wrote “right-wing voters, this is an emergency hour” as he urged them to get out and vote to counter any left electoral gains.
“Higher-than-usual turnout rates in the left’s strongholds. Right or Palestine, for real,” Netanyahu wrote.
Police believe the arrest of three people in southern Israel who are suspected of being involved in voting bribe attempts was a single incident and not part of a larger campaign, according to Dean Livne, acting director-general of the Elections Committee.
Early voting figures show highest turnout in decades
Citing figures released by the Central Elections Committee, the Israeli newspaper Ynet is reporting that voter turnout in the election reached 16.68% by 10am local time (8am GMT), the highest level recorded at that hour since 1981.
Over 1.2m Israelis had cast their ballots by 10am, according to the data, a rise of 0.78 percentage points compared with the same stage of the previous election in 2022.
In Sanhedria cemetery in north Jerusalem, ultra-orthodox voters came to the tombs of revered rabbis before they cast their ballots. There was no question of which way they were going to vote: for the parties representing Ashkenazi and Sephardic ultra-orthodox. But some at the Sanhedria cemetery, the young especially, made clear they only would do so reluctantly.
Yair Shuker, aged 19, said only one issue was important to him. “The election is about whether we will live by the Torah, or there will be no Torah. There will be a Jewish state or there will be no Jewish state,” he said.
And for him - as with almost all Israel’s ultra-orthodox (the Haredim) - the critical measure of the state’s level of observance is whether the Haredim would continue have exemption from military service.
“There are some who study the Torah, and some who stand and defend the land,” Shuker said.
The exemption for ultra-orthodox religious students dates back to the founding the state, but has long been a sort of tension among Israeli Jews, all the more so since the 7 October attack in 2023 and the start of the Gaza war. Israel’s supreme court ruled in 2024 that the blanket exemption for haredi men had no basis in law.
In return for their support in keeping him in power, Benjamin Netanyahu promised the ultra-orthodox parties (the Sephardic party Shas and the Ashkenazi United Torah Judaism) new legislation that would perpetuate the exemption, but has failed to deliver on that promise due to splits in his coalition. As a result both parties left the government, though Shas remained part of the coalition.
Whatever their feelings about Netanyahu, both would vote against a secular-led government led by the current opposition parties, which have pledged to end the exemption once and for all, and enforce military service if necessary.
Shuker said he did not trust either coalition, but would vote because he had been told to. “The rabbi has asked us to vote for Shas, so I will vote,” he said. A 23-year-old Ashkenazi ultra-orthodox, who identified himself as Yaacov K, expressed the same sense of disillusion mixed with duty. He said:
I’ll tell you the truth. To me and most of the people around me, we don’t believe in anyone.
If you’re asking me, I’ll never go and vote. But I have a rabbi and the rabbi told me listen, you have to go and vote. And if he says you have to go and vote, then that’s what I do. I don’t even start thinking if it’s worth it for me or not worth it for me.
The open distrust and contempt for Netanyahu, coupled with obedience and party discipline, could be one reason that the prime minister’s bloc has over-performed by a seat or two in past elections, compared to his poll numbers. That could be crucial if the pattern is repeated.
Azriel Zadok, a rabbi who had come for morning prayers at the Sanhedria cemetery, argued that the mass ultra-orthodox vote was essential to preserve Israel’s Jewish identity from “the left”.
“We have no problem with the secular. We pray for them, and we pray for the soldiers,” Zadok said. “Our problem is with the leftists we are trying to decide for us how we should live.” “They want us to go to the beach on Saturday and they want us to marry outside our faith. We want to remain Jews,” the rabbi added.
The centre left is only a small part of the opposition bloc, and it does not propose to change the ultra-orthodox lifestyle. But the bloc is united on the insistence that the Haredim should do their part in the defence of the nation. It is the most divisive issue among Israeli Jews voting today.
According to Israel’s Hareetz newspaper, United Arab List (Ra’am), an Islamist party headed by Mansour Abbas, has filed a complaint to the Central Elections Committee, alleging that a systematic campaign has been launched to disrupt voting for the party.
In a statement, the party said police arrested several of its leading activists in southern Israel’s Negev region before dawn with no clear justification, according to Hareetz.
The party also said there is a widespread shortage of its Arabic-language ballot slips in several areas, including the cities of Nazareth and Shfaram in northern Israel. We have not yet been able to independently verify these claims.
About 15 million people live in areas under Israeli control. Just over 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel live within the country’s pre-1967 borders, known as the “green line”, and have full voting rights.
In the occupied West Bank, more than 500,000 Israeli settlers can vote. They live among 3.1 million Palestinians who are subject to military rule and do not have the right to vote.
In occupied East Jerusalem more than 230,000 Israelis with voting rights live among 350,000 Palestinians who cannot vote.
Two million Palestinians in Gaza, who live under Israeli military occupation, according to the international court of justice, also have no vote.
How does the system work and when might we get results/a new government?
Emma Graham-Harrison
The Knesset, the Israeli parliament, has 120 seats, with lawmakers voted in through a system of proportional representation. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.
When the results are in, the president invites the party with the largest number of seats to try to agree a governing coalition. Exit polls are released at 10pm Israeli time (8pm GMT), and the first indication of actual voting counts usually emerges in the early hours of the morning.
Getting full results could take much longer, with the outcome potentially hanging on the electoral fortunes of two small parties, which need to win 3.25% of the overall vote to take up seats in the Knesset. Polling puts both around this threshold. If they cross it, they each get four seats, which would have a significant impact on coalition building options.
The far-right Amcha Yisrael is led by the former general Ofer Winter, who has pledged to back Netanyahu for prime minister if he gets into the Knesset. The Reservists is a rightwing Zionist party focused on ensuring universal conscription whose leaders sit between the two blocs.
They have ruled out joining any government supported by either the ultra-Orthodox – key Netanyahu allies – or Palestinian parties whose backing Gadi Eisenkot is likely to need. If it goes down to the wire, counting could take more than a day.
Palestinians with Israeli citizenship constitute about a fifth of the population but are consistently under-represented in the parliament.
Benjamin Netanyahu and most of his chief rivals have said they won’t form a coalition with parties (broadly) representing Palestinian citizens of Israel - even if that means political gridlock.
But after the votes are counted these parties could hold a critical balance of power, as my colleagues Emma Graham-Harrisonand Quique Kierszenbaum highlight in this story. Here is an extract from their report:
Palestinian citizens of Israel are forecast to secure between 12 and 15 seats, divided between the Islamist Ra’am and the Joint List alliance of three smaller parties, Hadash, Balad and Ta’al.
The mathematics of power are clear, even though most of the Jewish Israeli opposition has ruled out a coalition with Arab politicians, and Netanyahu and his allies have been doing everything they can to make such an alliance politically toxic.
There is recent precedent for breaking promises not to work with Palestinians, however. The Ra’am leader, Mansour Abbas, in 2021 took his party into a historic coalition government with Naftali Bennett, now part of the opposition bloc, and Netanyahu himself had previously started coalition negotiations with Abbas.
One prospective voter, Mohammed, works at a hi-tech company, managing both Jewish and Arab employees, which he sees as a template for a different future for Israel.
Although disappointed that most Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out a coalition with Palestinian parties, he understands the political logic, and he expects their position to shift once results are in.
“At the end of the day, everything is mathematics, right? One plus one is two. They cannot do anything without [those seats]. So they must do [some kind of deal] and they will do it.”
Who are Netanayhu's main opponents in the general election?
A consistent majority of Israeli polls show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition bloc with the ultra-Orthodox and the far right will fall below the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government.
But even though there is a clear anti-Netanyahu majority, polls indicate that the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc will also fall short of the required seats, meaning weeks or even months of political wrangling may be in store as parties make deals and trade concessions.
So who are Netanyahu’s leading rivals in the race?
As we have mentioned in a previous post, the man leading the field to potentially replace Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot, is a former head of the Israeli military who formulated the notorious Dahiya doctrine of using “disproportionate force” to cause damage and destruction.
Naftali Bennett is a former prime minister and former chair of the settler council, who supports annexing much of the West Bank.
Avigdor Lieberman wants to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and replace it with an Israeli-Jordanian confederation (though apparently he did not consult the Jordanians about this plan).
The Democrats, the only remaining political home for Israel’s Zionist left, are led by Yair Golan, a former general and deputy head of Israel’s military.

AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says

AI makes discoveries in mathematics, computer science, physics, OpenAI says
OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.
OpenAI has announced that its AI models have made several scientific discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics.
The AI giant said on Monday that the three new discoveries concerned the fields of harmonic analysis, complexity theory and quantum field theory.
Among the discoveries, AI models proved the local smoothing conjecture, one of the central propositions of harmonic analysis, in every spatial dimension for the first time, according to OpenAI.
Researchers in harmonic analysis, a branch of mathematics that studies how complex signals and functions can be broken down into elementary waves, had previously only proved the theory in three dimensions.
‘Historic development’
Alex Iosevich, a professor of mathematics at the University of Rochester who specialises in harmonic analysis, said OpenAI appeared to have “cracked” the conjecture in a “historic development”.
“The conjecture was formulated by my PhD adviser, Chris Sogge, so it is near and dear to my heart, and the news was a shock at first,” Iosevich told Al Jazeera.
“Now I am filled with joy and optimism, because the scientific enterprise as a whole is going to make giant leaps as a result of the AI revolution, and we have the chance to be a part of this historic development.”
Iosevich said he expected the field of theoretical mathematics to “change drastically” due to AI.
“I feel a twinge of sadness as a result,” Iosevich said.
“Many theoretical mathematicians I know feel the same way, but I firmly believe that these feelings will soon give way to the realisation that there is so much we can now accomplish.”
“Problems in pure mathematics did not arise in a vacuum,” he added. “Many of them came out of concrete physical considerations, and these connections can now be explored rapidly and decisively.”
According to OpenAI’s announcement, its models also disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which relates to the time it takes to solve complex computational problems, and provided “mathematically rigorous” proof of quantum chromodynamics, which studies the interaction of quarks and gluons.
Ryan Williams, an expert in computational complexity theory at MIT, said a confirmed refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis would be a major development.
“The ETH has been widely believed true since the late 1990s and a great deal of theoretical computer science was built on it being true,” Williams told Al Jazeera.
“We are working to verify and examine their proof and determine if it holds up,” Williams said.
“Their proof proposes a mysterious new method to more efficiently solve a variety of fundamental problems that have a wide range of potential applications.”
Williams said that while the development would not have real-world applications in the short-term, it could potentially lead to many “future real-world benefits for society”.
“It is hard to predict what will be possible next, because it’s a shocking development,” he said.
The ChatGPT creator said it had reached out to scientists outside the company to turn its “raw research data into scientific understanding”.
The San Francisco-based company said it decided on several different methods for releasing the findings based on consultations with three expert groups chosen to act as “shepherds”.
While the groups collaborating on the mathematics and computer science problems opted to make the AI-produced data public immediately, the physics group decided to defer the release in order to write up their own interpretation of the findings, OpenAI said.
“All of these approaches involve tradeoffs,” OpenAI said.
“On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community,” the $852bn start-up said.
“On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.”
OpenAI’s announcement is the latest in a series of claimed scientific breakthroughs credited to AI.
Last month, Claude creator Anthropic announced the discovery of a new enzyme said to resemble CRISPR, the groundbreaking gene editing mechanism used in treating conditions such as cancer and sickle cell disease.
Anthropic’s announcement drew mixed reactions among scientists.
While some researchers hailed the finding as an exciting development, others suggested that the AI company had exaggerated its significance.

A leaderless revolution has swept Serbia. The world should be watching | Aleksandar Matkovic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
05:00:04 UTC
14:00:04 KST

More than a decade ago, the WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange told an interviewer in Belgrade that Serbia was “a country where the future happens first”. The phrase circulated widely on Serbian social media in the weeks before Sunday’s election, but in a way that could not have seemed possible 10 years ago. Who would then have imagined that Serbia today could be at the forefront of global democratic change?
The images from Belgrade on Sunday night – people dancing and crying in the streets, while in Novi Sad, the city that sparked the student movement, a flag bearing the image of the convicted war criminal Vojislav Šešelj, which had hung from a building since the 1990s, was torn down – reinforced the feeling that the future had truly arrived.
Watching my home country from abroad, I found it hard not to share in the excitement and emotion. I became involved with the student movement behind this electoral earthquake and was an election candidate for it, for about six months before moving abroad. My involvement began while lecturing in Belgrade at the university’s blockaded faculties in 2024 and 2025. During these extraordinary blockades, something happened that was not widely discussed in the western media: the emergence of a collective sharing of intelligence and a process of shaping opinion that would become key to Sunday’s outcome.
For almost two years, students debated almost every aspect of Serbia’s economy and society – from lithium mining and resource exploitation to the economic power of local oligarchs, as well as issues such as healthcare and education. Sometimes discussions lasted six hours. All of this happened before the students developed any joint programme or formed an organisation capable of outmatching the traditional liberal parties. In a sense, knowledge came first, and organisation followed.
Sunday’s election victory for what became the Student List, therefore, emerged from a novel political culture: a leaderless movement based on collective self-governance and political education, unseen in the Serbian political arena since the collapse of Yugoslavia.
Given Serbia’s recent history, how was this remarkable democratic experiment even possible? One answer lies in the movement’s ability to rally a wide range of people who, despite different political convictions, wanted to counter the perceived corruption of Aleksandar Vučić, the authoritarian president. With the economy dependent on foreign direct investment after the destruction of Yugoslavia, the political leadership formed close ties with foreign-owned corporations. Vučić’s name was often intertwined with the activities of multinationals such as Rio Tinto, the Anglo-Australian mining giant that sought to extract the country’s lithium.
In this context I received death threats following the publication of a critical scientific paper on the contested lithium issue; many of my colleagues faced similar intimidation. But the mistreatment of Serbian citizens who challenged large-scale investment projects also began to shape public consciousness in Serbia. Vučić’s party was accused of standing by and even participating, while opposition parties offered only lacklustre responses.
From the students’ standpoint, party leaders were seen as easy to corrupt when confronted with the financial power of international projects. And so, to change the system, you had to start by changing the political structures that enabled it.
In this sense, this was not just another election; it was a monumental struggle between the old, which was dying, and the new, which was struggling to be born – to paraphrase Antonio Gramsci. In Serbia, the new movement has arisen out of the old: it began with faculty occupations, blockades and plenary assemblies, before evolving today into the largest political force in the country.
By winning the parliamentary election, the Student List has broken the monopoly of political parties. It has become more popular than both the rightwing government and virtually all the opposition parties across the spectrum, most of which did not even win enough votes to meet the electoral threshold. Thus, the “old”, in Serbia’s case, at least, is confirmed as dead.
And what the Serbian people chose was not another party but a list of 250 candidates, 134 of whom hold PhDs, 44% of whom are women, and 135–140 of whom are now projected to enter parliament. Behind them stood an organisation unlike anything seen in traditional, leader-based political parties. In this way, “a bunch of students”, as the Economist described them, has created something that should be studied as it goes beyond the traditional ways of doing politics.
Will a leaderless movement be able to govern? This is where things get tricky. In the context of what the historian Adam Tooze calls the world’s “polycrisis”, a collective intelligence based on self-organisation may be a tempting answer. After all, the student protests in France, Italy and Belgium, along with protests in Spain and Albania, have emerged in response to interlocking crises of housing, education and environmental destruction. For these crises elsewhere in Europe, so evidently mismanaged by governments, the lessons of the Serbian experiment may become crucial.
On the other hand, one should not idealise the situation. The list comprises ideologically opposed blocs, from rightwing adherents to leftwingers and liberals. Most of those elected have never before held political office, and the parliamentary system will require them to nominate a prime minister and, in future presidential elections, a presidential candidate. Will the Student List bring the same energy to the national assembly without jeopardising the very method that made it so strong? Moreover, for Vučić, losing the election does not necessarily mean losing the system. On the contrary, his concession of defeat may also have been a strategic move, allowing him to keep the party apparatus intact for a comeback.
Whatever happens, one question has been put on the table: to what extent are self-organisation and decentralised decision-making a basis for government? For the time being, people are celebrating on the streets of Belgrade, Novi Sad and many other cities and towns across Serbia. But the real fight has only just begun. The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics.
- Aleksandar Matković is a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Environmental Science and Technology in Barcelona and a fellow at the Transnational Institute in Amsterdam. He works on environmental history, political economy and the history of Yugoslavia

Lake Balkhash receives 40 billion of cubic meters of water as Kazakhstan steps up conservation efforts
Nearly 40 billion cubic meters of water have flowed into Lake Balkhash over the past three years, helping stabilize the lake’s water level, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, around 15.9 billion cubic meters of water were directed into the lake in 2024, followed by around 13.9 billion cubic meters in 2025. Since the beginning of 2026, more than 9.7 billion cubic meters of water have flowed into the lake.
Water is released into Lake Balkhash from the Kapshagay Reservoir, which is fed by the transboundary Ili River. The reservoir reached 98% of its capacity this year, compared with 100% in each of the previous two years.
“The inflow of water from the Ili River remains at its long-term average level. This helps maintain Lake Balkhash’s water level at the optimal elevation of 341 meters according to the Baltic height system,” said Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Nurzhan Nurzhigitov.
He added that work is underway with French experts to develop a master plan for the conservation of Lake Balkhash through 2040. Field studies have been completed, and the results are currently being analyzed.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kazakhstan attracted more than 192 billion tenge in water sector investments.

Israel heads to the polls as shift to the right dominates critical election

Israel heads to the polls as shift to the right dominates critical election
Netanyahu seeks to extend rule at helm of far right alliance facing off against predominantly right-wing bloc.
Israel is heading to the polls on Tuesday in a closely contested election that is being described as one of the most important in its history.
The vote is the first since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, as well as a wider conflict that has seen Israel carry out attacks on Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Syria and Qatar.
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to extend his tenure after leading the country’s most right-wing governing coalition which brought together far-right ultranationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
Wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza and faced with a long-running corruption trial, he is fighting for his political survival against a self-styled Zionist opposition bloc that has fundamentally embraced a right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges. Questions over accountability for alleged security failures, disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab-led parties dominated the campaign.
This has further dampened already low expectations that the vote would offer any meaningful improvement to the lives of Palestinians, as deadly attacks continue almost daily in Gaza despite a yearlong “ceasefire”, while settler pogroms and Israeli army raids have intensified in the occupied West Bank.
“The entire Israeli political system operates within the racist framework of Jewish supremacy,” Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani, a noted Israeli sociologist, told Al Jazeera.
“None of the leaders who present themselves as an alternative to Netanyahu can genuinely be described as left-wing. The horrifying reality we are witnessing is not simply the product of Netanyahu or the far right. It is rooted in Zionist political thought itself, which is structured around the principle of Jewish supremacy. There is no way around this fundamental fact,” he said.
Democracy?
Israel’s shift to the right did not begin with the establishment of Netanyahu’s most recent government in 2022, or what polls show to have been the rightward lurch that took place across Israel following the Hamas-led attack of 2023. Rather, the collapse of the peace process with the Palestinians and repeated security crises over the past few decades have combined to systematically erode the political centre and left, giving rise to landmark legislative milestones such as the 2018 Nation-State Law, which formally enshrined Jewish supremacy and the continued and violent expansion of illegal Israeli settlements into occupied Palestinian territory with little or no government restraint.
However, if the drift to the right was there beforehand, most analysts agree that its speed has accelerated to unprecedented heights under the latest Netanyahu government, which faced accusations of seeking to reshape the country in its own image.
They point to attempts to strip the Supreme Court of its power to review government actions and the flouting of its rulings on conscripting the ultra-Orthodox minority whose political support helped sustain the governing coalition, as well as the presence of figures such as far-right provocateur and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and religious Zionist Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s finance minister.
Together, in return for their seat at the table, both ministers offered crucial support to the controversial judicial overhaul that Netanyahu – himself on trial for bribery, fraud and breach of trust, charges he denies – launched in the early months of 2023 and which continues to this day. Similarly, both ministers have provided encouragement and cover for the surge in violence across the West Bank, while deflecting attempts to hold the coalition accountable for the alleged security failures that preceded the Hamas-led attack.
“If Netanyahu loses the election and, say, [Gadi] Eisenkot becomes the new prime minister, the main initial change will be the atmosphere, the vibe, as Netanyahu stirs deep emotions domestically,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
“Those who admire him, and there are many in Israel, regard him as God. Those who hate him, and there are many in Israel, hate him deeply,” said Bregman. “He’s a very divisive figure. A new prime minister is likely to calm things down.”
With the vote closely watched across the region and beyond, analysts also say the stakes go beyond the names on the ballot and cut through to the very nature of the character and future of Israel.
“The decision facing Israel of whether to retain a Netanyahu-led government or not is ultimately the decision on whether to live in a functioning democracy or a democracy in name only,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.
“It’s the choice between maintaining the occupation of the West Bank or annexing it entirely and the population’s ‘voluntary migration’ from there, as figures within the government have actually suggested.”
A respect for process and the rule of law would likely return to government in the event of an opposition win, added Bregman, a sharp contrast with what he described as Netanyahu’s approach to government. However, to expect too great a change in the overall direction of policy would be to miss the point.
“Don’t be mistaken,” he cautioned. “Israel, particularly after 7 October, turned sharply to the right, and any new government will reflect and mirror this reality.”
Peace?
What will not be on the ballot, analysts and observers say, is any opportunity to challenge a foreign and security policy that has underpinned the killing of more than 74,000 people in Gaza, the increased violence across the West Bank and the launching of multiple wars, including one on Iran that has seen key energy routes choked and has left global markets reeling.
None of the mainstream candidates for office in October have talked about including Arab-led parties in any potential coalition. In Israel’s popular media, references to the leaders of Ra’am or the Joint List are typically used by rival candidates to denounce each other for considering a future coalition with Palestinian politicians, now or in the past.
Shenhav-Shahrabani, the sociologist, said the ultra-Orthodox parties would still be welcome in government after the vote by either coalition, while the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel – one-fifth of the total population – would be excluded by a system built upon prejudice.
“The distinction is not between democratic and anti-democratic forces, but between Jews and Palestinians. As long as there is no genuine binational political vision, racism and the systematic restriction of Palestinian rights will remain fundamental features of Israeli society,” he said.
If that framework shapes who is allowed into government, it also shapes what the campaign is about. Netanyahu’s challengers largely framed their disagreements with him as questions of competence, timing and accountability for the alleged failures that preceded October 7, rather than challenges to the way Palestinians are treated.
For critics, that omission is not an oversight but a reflection of where the Israeli mainstream now sits: among the issues at stake in the election, none amounted to a referendum on the genocide in Gaza. “How can it be a referendum on genocide, or anything to do with the treatment of Palestinians in Gaza?” asked Daniel Levy, a former Israeli government adviser.
“You would have to have one side arguing it was a good thing and the other arguing it was a bad thing, let alone acknowledging that it was a genocide. So, no, obviously none of that is on the ballot,” he said.
“The treatment of Palestinians by the Israeli state and military is a consensus among Zionist parties,” added Levy, with differences among them primarily resting on “whether it’s the state’s job to oppress Palestinians, or if the settler militias also have a role – a significant role – to play”.

Dammed Between Energy and Water Scarcity: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the Nile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Every large dam divides as much as it connects, and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is no exception. A monumental feat of architecture and engineering, the mega-dam has brought everyone together, for better or worse, to interrogate who gets to declare sovereignty over the riches of the river, be it water or momentum, and to challenge colonial-era Nile treaties.
Inaugurated in September 2025, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, or GERD, is a grand concrete structure on the Blue Nile in western Ethiopia within the Benishangul-Gumuz region, just 30 kilometers upstream along the river and east of the border with Sudan. It is built as a major source of hydroelectric power, being consistently ranked in the top 3-30 globally, and symbolizes Ethiopia's national sovereignty, rise to exponential economic development, and technological self-determination. So, why has it become the center of a protracted dispute over regional water security and international law between Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt?
The Architecture of the Dam
Related Article
Ecologies of Repair: Reconciling Our Relationship with Water
To understand the debate, the architecture must first be outlined. The GERD, a gravity mega-dam built under the management of civil engineering company Webuild (née Salini Impregilo) for the Ethiopian Electric Power, is comprised of a roller-compacted concrete (RCC) main dam, a concrete-faced rockfill saddle dam, and a system of spillways and hydroelectric power stations at the base. Designed for a 6,000 MW capacity, documented as 5,150 MW in recent literature, and meant to double the country's electricity generation, the dam is 1.8 kilometers long and rises to a 175-meter height. The main dam, located only 14 kilometers from Sudan, holds back a reservoir that can contain 74 billion cubic meters of water — named Lake Nigat — that is 3.5 times the surface area of Addis Ababa.
Moreover, the 5-kilometer-long, 50-meter-high saddle dam crescents a lower area of the surrounding reservoir basin for passive water retention, where the average annual outflow of the entire reservoir amounts to approximately 50 billion cubic meters of water. The two hydroelectric power stations, flanking the river bank on both sides and consisting of 13 Francis turbines, produce an average of 15,700 GWh/year.
The system of spillways provides safety for the dam by discharging floodwater without causing damage as well as maintaining the reservoir level below the designated threshold. They include a main service-gated spillway, a free-flow crest spillway, and an emergency side-channel ungated spillway capable of handling severe flooding.
Webuild's internal laboratories tested and manufactured the materials for long-term structural stability and mechanical performance. This was achieved through an advanced, internally and internationally researched RCC mix designed with a low cement, low water content, and extended setting times. In addition, an integrated network of galleries in the main dam accommodates high-sensitivity precision instruments including vertical pendula, to monitor hydrostatic pressure, structural shifts, joint integrity, and turbine performance in real-time. This continuous operational data is channeled directly into a centralized database at the right bank control center, allowing engineers to conduct proactive maintenance and ensure maximum structural reliability.
The structural resistance of its reservoir allows the GERD to alter seasonal water patterns, manage floods, and generate hydropower. However, considering its location on an international and transboundary river system, filling the reservoir raises questions regarding water requirements and storage timelines. The project's multi-stage filling cycles have proceeded unilaterally, without transparency between the upstream country and its downstream neighbors, fueling geopolitical tensions. Operating the GERD depends on hydrological regulation, as lack of coordination in operations and transparent data-sharing could disrupt existing downstream infrastructure — a prime example being Sudan's Roseires Dam, due to its proximity to the GERD.
Egypt argues that Ethiopia's unilateral operations can cut down water flow, which is a national threat to its people and economy. It also supports its claims by addressing Ethiopia's "unilateral exploitation" of its transboundary waters in the Omo, Jubba and Shebelle basins, and the harm it causes its neighbors, Somalia and Kenya.
Resolving this issue peacefully would foster vital regional cooperation on the White Nile too, where uncoordinated dam releases from Uganda have triggered downstream flooding in South Sudan, increasing people's displacement and disease outbreaks.
But how did we get here, anyway?
Historical Hegemony
During the initial survey for the GERD, carried out in the 1960s, Ethiopia lacked the internal stability to progress with it. It was kept discreet until sufficient work was done because it was known that its development would carry a heavy geopolitical weight, especially on downstream countries in the basin.
This weight is amplified, considering the Nile Basin countries are 11, some of which are upstream, downstream, or both in relation to other countries. The solely upstream nations include Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, Eritrea, and Ethiopia, while the sole downstream nation is Egypt. Sudan and South Sudan are both upstream and downstream, with South Sudan being upstream relative to Sudan and Egypt, and downstream relative to Uganda, since the White Nile is sourced by rivers flowing into Lake Victoria. The Blue Nile, supplying 85% of the Nile River, originates at Lake Tana in the Ethiopian Highlands, where it flows into Sudan and finally converges with the White Nile at Khartoum to form the main Nile River flowing through Egypt into the Mediterranean Sea.
Historically, Nile Basin hydropolitics have been shaped by Egypt's hydrohegemony, a legal history formed from a century of colonial-era 'treaties' — the Nile Treaties — towards a multilateral agreement that still conflicts with water rights. The 1902 Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement originally secured Egypt's control of the Nile by restricting Ethiopia from modifying the Blue Nile without British consent. This was further amplified by the 1929 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty — an exchange of notes more than a treaty, which essentially allowed Egypt to veto upstream projects or embark on unilateral development — and the subsequent 1959 Nile Water Agreement, which granted exclusive annual allocations of 55.5 billion cubic meters to Egypt and 18.5 billion cubic meters to Sudan. Reality, however, is more nuanced: while these inequitable, colonial-era treaties should be abolished or reassessed, Egypt remains a water-scarce nation, where the Nile supplies more than 90% of its freshwater needs, and approximately 95% of its population lives along its course.
Also, unlike other riparian nations in the basin — excluding Eritrea, an observer in the Nile Basin Initiative, due to its minimal hydrological footprint, and Sudan, facing severe infrastructure collapse — Egypt relies on the Nile as an existential lifeline. Since the GERD sits on the Blue Nile, which supplies the vast majority of the Nile's total flow, it signifies a major shift in regional power that ends the 'monopoly' of the river and creates a threat to downstream countries' agriculture and water security, especially during multi-year droughts. To challenge asymmetric control, the Nile Basin Initiative (NBI) was launched in 1999, with the Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) following soon after in 2010, one year before the Renaissance Dam's groundbreaking in 2011.
Preoccupied with the internal politics of the Arab Spring, Egypt was unable to effectively oppose or block the project. Its isolation deepened when Sudan softened its earlier objections into a moderate neutrality. Sudan's position has since shifted repeatedly, from rejection to neutrality or support and back again, driven largely by internal fragmentation and domestic politics. The debate over the dam's benefits and drawbacks has also shaped these shifts. On the one hand, the dam promises more stable irrigation, lower dredging costs, and better flood management. On the other, it carries serious long-term risks: floodplains depleted as sediment builds up in the reservoir basin, disrupted local ecosystems, and a lack of cooperation between the three countries.
The pressure culminated in the 2015 Declaration of Principles on GERD, which remains the primary trilateral framework between Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt. In it, the three countries acknowledged the dam and committed to the principles of international water law. They have still not reached a binding agreement on how the reservoir is filled or on how to manage droughts.
Divisions persist on a wider scale too. When the Nile Basin Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) came into force in October 2024, Egypt and Sudan refused to sign it. Both want to protect their access to a vital resource and the veto rights they claim under colonial-era treaties.
The Architecture of Geopolitics
Concrete structures can control physical water flows, but they rarely can resolve political friction. Ethiopia positions GERD as a shared resource built for its people and neighbors, vowing to export surplus to promote its own economy as well as support the continent, but hydrological uncertainty remains the biggest issue in the absence of a clear, definitive binding agreement meant to operate the dam. An exemplar model for sustainable and equitable transboundary water governance can be found in the Senegal River Basin Development Authority (OMVS) — Organisation pour la mise en valeur du fleuve Sénégal — that utilizes a framework of collaborative benefit-sharing and joint infrastructure ownership.
Ultimately, unlocking the GERD's true potential as a driver of East African economic integration hinges on overcoming impasses to secure its downstream neighbors and provide a new example of equitable water governance, environmental safety and sustained trilateral cooperation. Otherwise, how can shared river basins foster a nation's right to build its economic future against the security of its neighbors?
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Taiwan rebuffs China’s commemorations for post-World War Two ‘restoration’ of island
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
04:59:31 CET
12:59:31 KST

TAIPEI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Taiwan’s defence minister on Tuesday said China was waging “cognitive warfare” after Beijing marked the anniversary of Japan’s handover of the island to Chinese rule with satellite images of Taipei and a military propaganda poster.
Japan took over Taiwan from China’s Qing Dynasty in 1895 and ruled it until 1945, when it transferred the island to the Republic of China government. Both Beijing and Taipei commemorate the event, now in its 81st year.
On Sunday’s anniversary of the handover, China released high-resolution satellite pictures of Taipei, including the train station and the National Palace Museum. The museum holds a vast collection of treasures brought to Taiwan in 1949, when the Republic of China government fled there after losing a civil war to the communists.
The Chinese military’s Eastern Theatre Command also published a poster with a map of Taiwan superimposed on images of fighter jets and warships, with the title “Remember the history of the restoration”.
Speaking to reporters at parliament in Taipei, Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said China was using the anniversary to carry out “cognitive warfare”.
“We must stress that the People’s Republic of China was established in 1949. The War of Resistance has absolutely nothing to do with the People’s Republic of China — this is a clear, objective fact,” he added, referring to World War Two and the Japanese invasion of China which began in 1931.
Taiwan’s military marked a different anniversary, the start of an unsuccessful late-October 1949 invasion attempt by the People’s Liberation Army of Kinmen, islands which sit next to the Chinese coast and remain under Taiwan control to this day.
Koo said that was a date much more worthy of remembering.
“This reminds us once again that China’s determination to annex the Republic of China and Taiwan by force has never changed. We should be even more vigilant,” he added.
Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control. The democratically elected government in Taipei rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims.
Neither government formally recognises the other, and their shared World War Two history is a frequent source of tension.
(Reporting by Ben Blanchard; Editing by Saad Sayeed)

Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year Ballon d’Or wait

The Bayern Munich striker accepted the prize at a ceremony at the London Palladium on Monday, following a prolific season for club and country.
According to England Football, Kane scored 73 goals in 65 matches during the season, including 61 for Bayern and 12 for England.
He becomes the fifth Englishman to win the award, following Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen.

“It was the best season of my career without a doubt,” Kane said, thanking his Bayern and England teammates and coaches for their contribution.
England head coach Thomas Tuchel congratulated Kane, calling the award deserved and praising his performances.
Kane is the first player representing a Bundesliga club to win the Ballon d’Or since Borussia Dortmund’s Matthias Sammer in 1996, according to the Bundesliga.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha had been nominated for the 2026 Men’s Goalkeeper of the Year award following his standout performance at the FIFA World Cup.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Wei Chuan Dragons defeated the CTBC Brothers 6-0 in Game 6 of the Taiwan Series at the Taipei Dome on Monday, securing their sixth Chinese Professional Baseball League championship with a 4-2 series victory.
Starting pitcher Cristopher Mercedes delivered a dominant performance, throwing eight scoreless innings, striking out six, walking two, and surrendering just two hits. Relievers Lin Tzu-yu (林子昱) and Lin Kai-wei (林凱威) combined to finish the shutout in the ninth inning, per CNA.
The Dragons won the first three games of the best-of-seven series before the Brothers rallied to win the next two, forcing a sixth game. The Dragons broke open a 1-0 game with five runs in the bottom of the eighth, including a two-run home run by catcher Jiang Shao-hong (蔣少宏).
The victory marked the Dragons’ sixth Taiwan Series title overall and their second since returning to top-flight competition in 2021. The team previously won championships in 1990, 1997, 1998, and 1999 before disbanding, then claimed its fifth title in 2023.
Manager Yeh Chun-chang (葉君璋) secured his third championship as a manager and his second with the Dragons since their return. His championship record also includes titles won during his playing career.
Yeh became emotional while speaking to reporters after the game, saying the team’s success stemmed from everyone’s efforts to improve the club.
“This team has achieved good results because everyone worked together. Everyone and every aspect of the team tried to make this team better,” he said. “Thinking about all of this, it’s impossible not to be emotional.”
Mercedes was named Taiwan Series Most Valuable Player after winning Games 2 and 6. Across his two starts, he pitched 14 innings and allowed one earned run, finishing with a 0.64 earned run average.
The Dominican pitcher did not allow a hit until the sixth inning of Game 6. After previously pitching for Japan’s Yomiuri Giants and Taiwan’s Uni-Lions, he achieved his championship goal with the Dragons.
“This game was the best I have ever pitched in my career,” Mercedes said. “I am so excited. I have never won a championship like this before.”
Dragons center fielder Kuo Tien-hsin (郭天信) said the experience of winning the 2023 championship had changed how he approached this year’s title run. He hoped to help younger teammates manage their nerves and learn from the experience, per CNA.
“Last time (2023), I just blindly fought hard and eventually won the championship. This time is different,” Kuo said.
“There are quite a few players younger than me on the team, and I hope they can learn something and be less nervous on the field. I am also someone who thinks a lot, and I hope to help them as much as possible.”
This year’s Taiwan Series, dubbed the “Dragon-Elephant showdown,” was the first championship series between the Dragons and Brothers. All six games were held at the Taipei Dome, with the schedule disrupted by a typhoon.
The six games drew a combined attendance of 230,615, setting a record for a single Taiwan Series. Games 1, 4, and 5 each drew 40,000 spectators, per UDN.

New report tracks how Russia helps China build better drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:54:05 UTC
12:54:05 KST

Russia's defense cooperation with China extends far beyond imports of dual-use goods, with evidence pointing to sharing drone design technology, providing testing services, and joint research, according to a new report from U.S. think tank C4ADS.
The report adds to earlier findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China's military collaboration with Russia throughout the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit that investigates security threats, released a report in October that maps lesser-known layers of cooperation between the two countries' defense industries, drawing on Russian trade records, corporate filings, leaked documents, and academic papers.
The investigation found that Russian designs for rocket-launched drones likely helped shape weapons China unveiled in 2025 and that Russian wind tunnels kept testing aircraft models for China's top arms maker after the invasion of Ukraine.
The report also documents how researchers from the two countries are jointly developing algorithms that could underpin combat drone swarms. Moreover, it shows that some suppliers to Russia's defense industry are moving production to China.
Beyond China’s well-documented supplies of components, raw materials and machine tools to the Russian defense industry, and Russia's recently revealed sales of airborne combat vehicles and munitions to China, the two industries increasingly work together further upstream, sharing designs, testing services and research.
read also
Joint drone development
A notable example involves the Science and Production Association SPLAV, Russia's leading maker of multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS). SPLAV is subject to multiple international sanctions and export controls.
Trade records show SPLAV sent Chinese arms giant Norinco technical documents for a "reconnaissance rocket" in 2014–2015, and apparently again in April 2022, less than two months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The rocket is most likely SPLAV's 9M534, which releases a reconnaissance drone in mid-flight.
In March 2025, China unveiled the Feilong 60A, a loitering drone launched from Norinco's SR-5 rocket system and reportedly capable of operating in swarms. Three months later, Norinco tested Sky Eye, a drone fired from a cannon. Both drones are similar to the Russian 9M534.
C4ADS believes the Russian technical documents helped speed up Norinco's work on both systems, though it notes that this conclusion rests mainly on how closely the Chinese and Russian systems resemble each other.
Russia's aerospace testing base is also working for Norinco, which now faces U.S. sanctions and Japanese and Taiwanese export controls.
The Russian state-owned Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI), which is under multiple Western sanctions, tested Chinese scale aircraft models in its wind tunnels and returned them to Norinco with the test data at least nine times between 2022 and 2024. The work comes as Norinco has been expanding into military drones over the past decade.
read also
The cooperation also extends to universities and research institutes. Drones have become a growing focus of joint research by Chinese and Russian scientists, according to C4ADS.
Researchers from the two countries co-authored 86 academic papers on drones and other unmanned systems between 2022 and 2026, an average of about 17 a year. In the dozen years from 2009 to 2021, they produced only 36 such papers, or about three a year.
Evgeny Neretin, a department head at the Moscow Aviation Institute, has co-authored multiple papers with researchers tied to Chinese defense laboratories — labs that also funded the work. The papers deal with algorithms for autonomous drone combat and, more recently, for keeping several drones in formation while they track targets, a likely building block for drone swarms.
In June 2025, the Chinese government approved the creation of a joint educational institute between the Moscow Aviation Institute (sanctioned by the U.S. and EU), and China's military-linked Northwestern Polytechnical University (subject to U.S. and Japanese export controls).
read also
Russian weapons, made in China
The C4ADS report also indicates that some Russian makers of machine tools and chips are moving production to China.
Stankomashstroy, a sanctioned Russian machine-tool maker, plans to move production of advanced five-axis machine tools to an industrial park in China's Shaanxi province.
In 2025, the company sold equipment to the Votkinsk Plant, which builds ballistic missiles, and to Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol, a producer of air defense systems and long-range attack drones.
Illustrating Moscow's reliance on Beijing for chips, Russia's sanctioned state-owned chipmaker Element set up at least four subsidiaries in China in 2025 and began assembling chipsets there. In 2026, Element also bought power electronics intellectual property from the Chinese defense contractor Shijiazhuang Tonhe Electronics.
According to C4ADS, these moves would likely help Element produce military-grade microelectronics despite Western sanctions and export controls. They also fit a recent Kremlin initiative to build up Russia's chip industry.
A deepening alliance
The C4ADS report adds fresh details to previous findings by the Kyiv Independent regarding China and Russia's military partnership.
While China officially claims neutrality in Russia's war against Ukraine, Beijing remains Moscow's key trading partner, economic supporter, oil buyer, and provider of dual-use equipment.
According to leaked Rostec documents, China bought Russian airborne combat vehicles, ammunition, and parachute systems after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dozens of Chinese officers and arms industry staff visited Russia during the war to negotiate the deals.
Separate Kyiv Independent investigations found that Chinese suppliers have helped keep Russia's missile and drone production pipelines running.
Machine tools shipped mostly from China fueled the expansion of the Votkinsk Plant, which makes ballistic missiles — including intercontinental ones.
Chinese and Hong Kong companies also supplied parts to the maker of Russia's Lancet attack drones and remain the main channel for Western chips used in Russian weapons.

Meta merges apps and device accounts under one system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
03:53:47 UTC
12:53:47 KST

Did you wake up to an email from Meta recently about your new Meta Account?
Or maybe you received a pop-up message on your Facebook or Instagram account?
Well you're not alone.
In April, Meta announced it would be unifying access to its accounts across the company's apps with some Australians already seeing the changes.
Here's a rundown of what's changed and how it affects you.
What's changing and why?
Meta is changing its current Accounts Centre with an updated system called Meta Account.
The idea of the new system is to bring account management for the company's various apps and devices under one system.
These include:
- Messenger
- Threads
- Meta AI
- AI glasses
- Meta Quest headsets
Meta says WhatsApp will not be added to a Meta Account by default. It will only be in your Meta Account if you choose to add it or you've previously added it to your Accounts Centre.
The switch should not change your profiles or how you use these apps.
Meta says it's designed to make "signing in and managing your settings easier".
Here are a few updates you can expect, according to Meta:
- One password
- Easy set up for new apps and devices
- Boosted security with passkeys
- 24/7 protection
- Personalised security recommendations
Can you opt out?
No.
The change is automatic and being rolled out gradually.
You should receive a notification on your social media platform and email when your account is updated.
But Meta says you can still control and choose which profiles are in your Meta Account at any time.
For example, you can have a Meta Account for your Facebook and another Meta Account for your Instagram profile.
Settings that are specific to each app will also remain independent.
"For example, who can see your Facebook posts is a Facebook setting," Meta's website says.
"Similarly, whether someone can tag you in a photo on Instagram is an Instagram setting."
So how can I keep my apps separate?
Here's a step-by-step guide to create separate Meta Accounts for each of your apps:
- Click your profile picture in the top right of Facebook
- Select Settings & privacy, then click Settings
- Click Meta Account, then click Manage account
- Click Manage on your app of choice
- Click Move out of this Meta Account
When it comes to your passwords, Meta should use the same login info you use currently. It's up to you if you want to create a single password or passkey to use across all apps and devices.
Is it safe to put all your apps under the same Meta Account?
Macquarie University cyber security lecturer Jennifer Williams says while the new account system is likely no more or less secure than the old one, a breach of the new system would have a greater impact.
"An attacker would be able to gain access to all of your private messages on Instagram, Facebook, and, for those who have connected it to their Meta account, WhatsApp," Dr Williams says.
"They could use information from those messages to blackmail the user, impersonate them and send messages to their friends and family, or make posts on their behalf."
But Dr Williams says in the end, security comes down to the user's practices.
"If they do not use strong, unique passwords or two-factor authentication, then there is a greater risk of a breach of their account."
Ryan Ko, director of the Cyber Research Centre at the University of Queensland, says the more significant question is privacy.
"A unified identity makes it easier for Meta to track and profile its users, which then enables them to sell on to their clients," Professor Ko says.
"When Meta Account users' profiles connect activity across services, it creates a richer and more comprehensive profile of the user.
"The security risk is concentrated access; the privacy risk is concentrated knowledge of the user."

S. Korea's real GDP grows 1.0 pct on quarter in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
11:26:01 CST
12:26:01 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's economy delivered a better-than-expected performance in the third quarter, driven by a semiconductor export boom, strong facility investments and significant growth in government spending, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP), adjusted for inflation, expanded 1.0 percent in the July-September quarter compared to the previous quarter, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
It was more than three times higher than the 0.3 percent growth forecast estimated in August by the central bank, which projected an annual growth outlook of 3.3 percent for 2026.
The quarterly growth rate rebounded sharply from negative 0.1 percent in the fourth quarter last year to 1.8 percent in the first quarter this year, before maintaining positive momentum with an increase of 0.6 percent in the second quarter and 1.0 percent in the third quarter.
Outbound shipments of the export-driven economy mounted 2.3 percent quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter thanks to strong demand for semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment.
Soaring demand for locally-made semiconductors was led by expanding global investments in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Imports gained 2.4 percent due to higher inflows of crude oil and semiconductor manufacturing machinery.
Facility investments jumped 4.1 percent on the back of robust demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, while construction investments added 0.7 percent in the third quarter after falling 0.1 percent in the previous quarter.
Investments in intellectual property products grew 2.3 percent due to increased spending on software and research and development (R&D).
Private consumption, another growth engine of the Asian economy, showed a slight setback with a decrease of 0.2 percent amid lower expenditure on both goods and services.
Fiscal spending climbed 1.9 percent, affected by higher government spending on health insurance benefits.
Amid the better-than-expected economic increase and the still high inflationary pressure, the BOK delivered a back-to-back rate hike in July and August, raising its benchmark interest rate to 3.00 percent.
By industry, the seasonally adjusted production among manufacturers swelled 2.0 percent in the third quarter on a quarterly basis, spearheaded by computers, electronic and optical devices.
Output in the service industry rose 0.2 percent, and production in the construction sector advanced 2.0 percent on an expansion in civil engineering projects.
Those in the agriculture, forestry and fishing, and the electricity, gas and water supply sectors increased 5.9 percent and 3.7 percent, respectively.
Real gross domestic income (GDI), which measures the actual purchasing power of income generated from domestic production activities, expanded 3.4 percent in the third quarter compared to the previous quarter.
From a year earlier, the real GDI surged 18.8 percent in the July-September quarter, representing the fastest growth in nearly 49 years since the fourth quarter of 1977.
It was powered by soaring global prices of locally-made semiconductors that improved the country's terms of trade. ■

UNITED NATIONS, October 27. /TASS/. Russia does not recognize the mandate of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine and rejects its findings as being based on fabricated data, Moscow’s permanent mission to the United Nations said in a statement, commenting on a report presented to the UN General Assembly.
"Russia does not recognize the mandate of the commission, which was established by a resolution adopted by the politicized UN Human Rights Council. The commission's conclusions are based on fabricated data provided by the Ukrainian authorities through the Kiev mission of the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights," the statement reads.
"The mission has long lost its neutrality, effectively turning into an agency seeking to legitimize allegations against Russia while failing to notice crimes committed by the Ukrainian armed forces," Russian diplomats said. In their view, the very existence and activities of the commission on Ukraine expose a crisis in the United Nations’ work that needs to be addressed.

Truce begins in wartorn Ukraine city after it was announced by Melania Trump
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:58:48 GMT
11:58:48 KST

Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive
- Published
A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents have been trapped without food, water and electricity.
Ukrainian officials and Russia's defence ministry say the limited ceasefire is being respected. The truce, which the White House said was secured by US First Lady Melania Trump, is meant to allow aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation on Friday.
Oleshky, along the front line in the Kherson region, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and on the other by Russian forces.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.
There are concerns that the truce will not hold, with one resident saying: "I don't believe in Russia's humanity."
Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, remain in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, Kyiv believes, with only 1,700 still living in the city itself.
Before the war it was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escape is highly dangerous because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water for three years.
Pope Leo XIV appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
The current truce is supposed to allow supplies in and enable roads to be cleared of mines to allow people safe passage out in an evacuation planned to take place on Friday.
One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a land mine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations.
"I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.
Many told the BBC last month there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
It is hard to make contact with people in Oleshky as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians, making it difficult to verify reports the ceasefire is being implemented.
Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, initially including how and where to register for it. Some people want to know if they can bring their pets. Others are questioning what future they will have if they opt to leave their homes.
"It is critically important that this mission to rescue our people proceeds successfully and safely," Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Zelensky's office, said on Tuesday.
Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".
While people are optimistic about leaving, there are also fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could see them be taken away and tortured.
Someone who has been speaking to family in Oleshky said they fear shooting could restart during evacuations and Ukraine will somehow be blamed for not upholding the truce.
Last month, the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
In response to the situation, the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (03:00 in Ukraine; 01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.
The truce is due to be in place until 23:59 local time on 1 November, according to Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament.
Ukrainian officials say parliament's commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has travelled to the areas to co-ordinate the operation.
"This is part of a humanitarian mission being carried out with the mediation and co-ordination of US First Lady Melania Trump, in co-operation with Yana Lantratova, Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights," Lubinets wrote on social media.
Ukraine's military general staff said that silence was being observed over the operation for humanitarian purposes, and urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there". However, he said some would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.
The White House said last week that "non-military, civilian leaders from both countries would work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require".
While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".
While a truce is under way in Oleshky, elsewhere strikes continue.
On Monday evening, attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv hit a university and a bridge, killing one person and injuring 14 others.
In Russia, one person was killed and six others were injured after a Ukrainian drone strike on Bryansk.
Additional reporting by Paul Kirby, Hafsa Khalil and Sareen Habeshian

The temporary halt in fighting is meant to allow an aid mission into the city in southern Ukraine later this week. Fighting is supposed to remain frozen until at least Saturday, according to the Associated Press.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," Lubinets said. He added that the agreements were reached in negotiations with Yana Lantratova, head of the Russian negotiating team.
Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, confirmed a "bilateral ceasefire" has begun in the embattled Ukrainian city of Oleshky, in a later statement on social media on Oct. 27.
The ceasefire will last until Nov. 1, David Arakhamia, the parliamentary leader of the president's Servant of the People party, said in a later post on social media.
The Russian Defense Ministry also announced that Russian forces had stopped fighting the area in preparation for the humanitarian mission.
The ceasefire, credited to the mediation of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, covers Oleshky and surrounding areas in Kherson Oblast. It is meant to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of humanitarian aid.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson, it has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering.
Residents face severe shortages of food, water and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
The move comes as the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city has drawn international attention in recent weeks, including from Pope Leo XIV.
Within minutes of the Oleshky ceasefire beginning, Russian forces launched a wave of ballistic missiles at other parts of Ukraine, including Kyiv.

Prediction markets open new front for US election misinformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:55:00 UTC
11:55:00 KST

Prediction markets open new front for US election misinformation
WASHINGTON – The US midterms are playing out against a controversial new scoreboard as the nation votes in its first major elections since prediction markets went mainstream.
With hundreds of millions of dollars on the line, experts are warning that the proliferation of live odds into news coverage and on social media could sow confusion – and provide fodder for misinformation.
Concerns range from motivated actors taking extreme measures to sway markets, to voters overtrusting the odds and baselessly blaming fraud where election results differ.
US President Donald Trump has already made unsubstantiated allegations of fraud central to his political movement ahead of the Nov 3 vote.
Polymarket and Kalshi are allowing users to buy and sell contracts on thousands of outcomes related to the midterms, despite surveys showing most Americans oppose betting on elections.
The companies have also partnered with prominent news organisations.
“They’re more and more becoming part of how Americans understand elections,” said Davina Hurt, government ethics director at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics.
“Elections are not games,” she told AFP. “My concern is that we’ve reached a point where financial market expectations carry more weight in the public’s mind than the votes themselves.”
‘Not a promise’
Prediction market trading has surged amid legal battles over whether they should be regulated as federal commodities or under state gambling laws.
Kalshi said its markets offer unique data distinct from polling, that probabilities do not guarantee outcomes, and that efforts to manipulate the odds are cancelled out by other buyers.
“Kalshi should be seen as a complement to traditional polling,” head of communications Elisabeth Diana told AFP.
“On prediction markets, you trade what you think will happen. On polls, you say what you want to have happen.”
Yet, experts expressed fears over markets being misconstrued, especially as Polymarket and Kalshi issue race “projections” on social media.
A high probability “is not a promise”, Hurt said. “When the prediction fails, that’s not evidence that elections fail. But people are going to read that in.”
Los Angeles
When Republican Spencer Pratt lost the Los Angeles mayoral primary in June, right-wing influencers pointed to prediction market odds which showed him favoured to advance to the general election as evidence of fraud.
Some X posts spreading misinformation carried “paid partnership” tags, prompting backlash and action from Polymarket and Kalshi.
“The June primary reinforced how quickly expectations about election outcomes can become confused with actual election results,” said Michael Sanchez, spokesman for the Los Angeles County’s registrar’s office.
In a recent memo shared exclusively with AFP, Kalshi told its paid partners they “shall not call into question the integrity or accuracy of any official vote tally result, legal ruling, or other official or formal determination in connection with the election”.
Partnerships will be terminated with those who post without evidence “that an election result has been corrupted, rigged, compromised, or otherwise improperly administered”, it said.
Polymarket did not respond to requests for comment.
Bracing for confusion
For the first time, researchers who monitor election misinformation at University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public are tracking how prediction markets are misrepresented online.
“There’s more reason to create these rumors because there’s that sort of financial element tied to it,” senior research scientist Rachel Moran told AFP.
“It’s becoming a significant part of our work.”
Jared DeMarinis, elections chief of Maryland, has asked the state to investigate whether election betting via prediction markets is legal under local law.
He told AFP he is prohibiting poll workers from placing election-related bets.
He still worries lopsided odds could depress turnout and inspire false claims that wear down his team, already facing pressure from Trump’s administration.
“Election administrations are all under attack,” he said. “Now you’ve just put more gasoline on this by having money involved.”
“You just don’t want to have the legitimacy of the outcome in question.” AFP
