US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:50:31 UTC
11:50:31 KST

One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will take part in the Eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit in Moscow.
The event is scheduled to begin at 12:45 p.m. Moscow time (9:45 a.m. GMT) at the International Trade Center. According to the Kremlin, the Russian leader will welcome the guests before a group photo. The plenary session, chaired by Putin, is set to begin at 1:00 p.m.
The Russian president will deliver the opening address, highlighting the importance of natural gas as a source of energy that supports economic growth. He will also discuss problems facing the gas industry and outline priorities for solving them.
Putin will then give the floor to GECF Secretary General Philip Mshelbila and the heads of delegations from member states. Representatives of several observer countries, including Mozambique, Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia and Senegal, are also expected to address the forum.
The Russian president is also expected to hold five bilateral meetings during the day, including with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Qatari Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Mozambican President Daniel Chapo, Equatorial Guinean President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo and Libyan Presidential Council Chairman Mohammad al-Menfi.
Gas Exporting Countries Forum
The Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) is an intergovernmental organization that aims to strengthen cooperation and dialogue among gas-producing and exporting countries and promote stability and safety in the global gas market. The forum’s first ministerial meeting took place in Tehran in 2001.
The GECF member states are Russia, Iran, Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru and Senegal participate as observer countries.
GECF member states account for about 70% of the world’s proven gas reserves, 38% of global gas production, 42% of global gas exports and 47% of liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday became the latest right-wing critic to accuse former President Barack Obama of elitism for mockingly comparing President Donald Trump's ostentatious White House renovations to the Cheesecake Factory.

"This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader's tomb," Bessent told a Fox Business reporter who asked about Obama's remark as he left the restaurant near the White House. "I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try," Bessent said. Obama vacationed on Martha's Vineyard as president, and he and his wife Michelle now own an estate on the exclusive island.

That's a "Charbroiled Cheeseburger Served on a Toasted Brioche Roll with Grilled Onions, Sriracha Mayo and Au Jus for Dipping," one of the "Glamburgers" on Cheesecake Factory's famously sprawling menu. The burger, which comes with french fries or a green salad, currently costs $22.95 at the restaurant's downtown Washington location.
"I recommend the Cheeseburger Spring Rolls," Bessent added in a follow-up post on X directed at Obama.
Bessent's biting comment followed those of other Trump allies who claim Obama sneered at working-class Americans when he tore into Trump over his extensive White House construction and decoration projects.
"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV!" Obama said of Trump during a speech at an Ohio rally for gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown on Saturday.

He has also built a White House helipad, the still-under-construction White House ballroom and an array of other projects.
Trump on Monday afternoon defended his White House redesign at length while claiming Obama had failed to address needed repairs.
"We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly," Trump said as he headed to Mississippi for a campaign rally. "Guys like Obama don't see it. You don't see dirt. He doesn't see filth. He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building."
"It has to be clean," Trump continued. "The columns can't be broken. The bricks can't be falling off from under the plaster. And for you to say it's a cheesecake factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president." 
Detractors insisted Obama's use of the Cheesecake Factory as an example of cheap, gaudy decor amounted to no less than class warfare.
"Classic Obama snobbery," Republican commentator Matt Whitlock wrote on X. "Cheesecake Factory is a great option for people who can't afford a private chef at their Martha's Vineyard estate."
GOP pundit Scott Jennings called Obama "undefeated at condescending to regular folks," while claiming the former president "has never been in a Cheesecake Factory."
That backlash quickly sparked its own backlash.

But even we understood that the White House should not look like the inside of a Red Lobster," Guy wrote. The food fight is taking place just days before the Nov. 3 midterm election, where most polls and analyst projections indicate Democrats are poised to make significant gains in Congress.
The election cycle has been defined by Americans' widespread unhappiness with high costs, which has dragged Trump's approval ratings to new lows and imperiled Republicans' majorities in the House and Senate.

This could be the biggest investment bet in the history of global capitalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:22:26 UTC
11:22:26 KST

analysis
Anthropic eyes biggest ever IPO as AI funding starts drying up
Anthropic is the next cab off the rank for mega-tech initial public offerings (IPO), and is slated to surpass SpaceX as the biggest capital markets fundraising in history.
An IPO involves a company asking big financial institutions and "mum and dad" investors for cash via the stock exchange.
Elon Musk's SpaceX played this game in June, raising $US85.7 billion ($121 billion), with a listing price of $US135.
It hit the boards of the Nasdaq and subsequently shot up to $US161, with unprecedented investor interest pushing the company to a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.
Prominent US analyst Dan Ives, in an interview from New York, said history was about to repeat itself with the listing of Anthropic.
"If you think about SpaceX obviously being the biggest IPO that we've seen this year, and this is, it's groundbreaking," the partner at Yorkville Ives said.
"It's a watershed event, not just for tech, but the AI revolution in terms of the role Anthropic plays."
Anthropic is a self-described AI safety and research company. Many Australians would be familiar with its Claude AI assistant product.
Locally, there's some healthy scepticism.
"Anthropic is trying to pull off a historic IPO right as the AI funding well is completely running dry," fund manager Roger Montgomery said.
On a wing and a prayer
When consumers spend on credit, it's often due to a lack of cash flow.
Companies are no different. They ask share investors (equity) and lenders (debt) for cash to operate.
The big difference is that firms will look to finance investments for future growth.
Investors, naturally, want to know they will not just get their money back but also have their investment grow over time.
This usually means the company needs to be generating a profit.
SpaceX was risky in that it was operating at a significant loss when it asked share investors for cash.
But it didn't matter. Elon Musk sold investors a dream, and the tech giant's Starlink operation acted as a much-needed cash cow for investors.
Anthropic is in a similar position, but its CEO Dario Amodei wants even more money.
The company is looking to raise about $US100 billion.
Analysts valued Anthropic earlier this year at $US2 trillion, but a recent financial results update showed the company revalued downwards to $US1.5 trillion.
There's no problem generating revenue — the company's third quarter revenue rose to $US16 billion.
"Anthropic's growth puts it in rarefied air," Betashares's head of investment strategy, Cameron Gleeson, said.
"Its annualised revenue run rate reportedly topped $US65 billion at the end of July, around seven times its level at the end of 2025, and many expect it to approach $US100 billion by year-end.
"It has overtaken OpenAI in business adoption, where much of the potential to monetise AI lies, and achieved this with a workforce of around 5,300."
Spending bonanza
Anthropic's costs are damaging its bottom line.
Like many big tech companies, Anthropic is building its business rapidly to meet expected demand.
It means building cloud computing infrastructure, AI training chips, and data centre capacity.
In the second quarter alone, it spent $US5.6 billion on computing power to run its Claude models.
Adding salt to a wound, the cost of debt, which big tech companies are increasingly chasing, is becoming more expensive as inflation affects the global economy and interest rates rise.
The fundamental problem is that if, for example, the demand for SpaceX and Anthropic's products does not justify the spending being undertaken by these companies, the entire artificial intelligence trade is at risk of collapsing.
Loading...
"[It's] basically playing chicken with a market where Elon Musk is warning that debt is impossible to get, over 200 over-leveraged neoclouds are going belly up, and [the failed] Firmus IPO," Roger Montgomery said.
In other words, the fund manager believes investors who want the huge artificial intelligence trade to keep going will invest in Anthropic or risk a Wall Street crash.
"I think they're trying to get ahead of the bubble possibly bursting,"
he said.
And while Ives is confident the IPO will be a success, he says the company has not yet produced the sort of numbers that would justify its current valuation.
"For investors, they're going to basically need to look past this year," he said.
"I think Anthropic, being that they're the centrepiece of the AI revolution, you're going to see probably a strong appetite for this offering."
Loading
Australia at the table
As with the SpaceX IPO, Australians will be able to apply for shares in Anthropic.
Macquarie Capital will act as sub-underwriter and Australian coordinator for the listing.
Ives says it's up to investors to weigh up the risks.
"We're all going into it. Whether it's here in the US, Australia, wherever we are … we're all going into this fourth industrial revolution together,"
he said.
"And there's a lot of opportunity and growth, but there's also risk."
You could argue this is modern capitalism's biggest ever test.
Massive AI tech companies have a spending addiction. They need the cash to invest to hyper-scale, to try and produce the amount of product or service necessary to meet forecast demand.
Now, having largely exhausted debt markets, they're looking to raise equity.
Simply put, if something disrupts this trade, there is no government on the planet, nor central bank, that could clean up the damage caused without major disruption to the global economy.

Kane became the fifth English player to win the award, joining Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen, who last claimed the prize in 2001.
He succeeded Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembele, who won the award in 2025.
Meanwhile, Putellas, 32, claimed her third Women's Ballon d'Or after winning in 2021 and 2022, matching former Barcelona teammate Aitana Bonmati's record.
The Spanish midfielder captained Barcelona to a quadruple in the 2025-26 season, winning Liga F, Copa de la Reina, the Spanish Super Cup, and the Women's Champions League.
She was also named the Champions League Player of the Season and helped Spain win the Women's Nations League.
Putellas joined London City Lionesses in July after her trophy-laden spell with Barcelona.
Other award winners
Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal won Men's Young Talent of the Year for the third consecutive year, while Barcelona forward Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second successive year.
Spain's World Cup-winning coach Luis de la Fuente was named Men's Coach of the Year, while Barcelona's Pere Romeu received the women's coaching award.
Athletic Bilbao's Unai Simon won Men's Goalkeeper of the Year, with Barcelona's Cata Coll claiming the women's honour.
Bayern Munich's Kane also received the Men's Striker of the Year award following his prolific campaign, while Mexican forward Charlyn Corral became the first Mexican to win the Women's Striker of the Year award.
Barcelona were named Women's Club of the Year, while Paris Saint-Germain claimed the men's club award.
Arsenal and England winger Bukayo Saka received the Socrates Award for his humanitarian work, including funding 120 medical operations for children in Kano, Nigeria through a partnership with charity BigShoe in 2022.

A tariff truce between the European Union and United States is potentially at risk due to a multibillion-dollar loan approved by the bloc's investment bank for Airbus this summer, President Donald Trump's top trade official said Monday.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer expressed concern that his office had received "no details about this loan" and pressed for the situation to be "resolved as soon as possible".

‘Russian breakfast’ could soon be on the menu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:17:04 UTC
11:17:04 KST

‘Russian breakfast’ could soon be on the menu
A ‘Russian breakfast’ featuring traditional national dishes could soon appear on menus at hotels, cafes, and restaurants across the country, under a proposal by Moscow’s Industry and Trade Ministry.
In a document published on Monday, the ministry noted that hotels and restaurants typically offer international options, such as full English, continental, and French breakfasts, while largely overlooking local culinary traditions.
As a result, domestic tourists are often deprived of familiar morning meals, while foreign visitors have no opportunity to experience the country’s cuisine, the ministry said.
“This situation has a negative impact on tourism: Research shows that interest in local cuisine is one of the key factors people consider when choosing a country or region to visit,” it said.
“As a cultural and gastronomic phenomenon, the Russian breakfast does not merely exist – it is genuinely authentic and possesses clearly recognizable characteristics.”
The proposed menu could feature blini (thin pancakes), syrniki (pan-fried cottage cheese cakes), porridge, meat and fish dishes, and caviar. Suggested drinks include herbal teas, berry-based fruit beverages, and kvass, a fizzy fermented drink traditionally made from rye bread.
Participation would be voluntary, with establishments encouraged to expand their existing offerings rather than replacing international favorites.
The ministry also suggested creating a special ‘Russian breakfast’ emblem to help hotels, cafes, and restaurants identify and promote traditional dishes.
The initiative aims to showcase the country’s culinary heritage, attract tourists, and support domestic food producers.

Taiwanese chef awarded France’s Order of Agricultural Merit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
02:16:00 UTC
11:16:00 KST

TAICHUNG (Taiwan News) — Chef Justine Li (黎俞君), founder and executive chef of Fleur de Sel in Taichung, has been named a knight in the Order of Agricultural Merit by the French government.
Frederic Laplanche, director of the French Office in Taipei, presented the medal during a ceremony at his residence.
Established in 1883, the honor recognizes distinguished contributions to agriculture, gastronomy, and food culture.
Li is the first Taiwanese chef and restaurant owner to receive the award.
Founded in 2004, Fleur de Sel has served French fine dining in Taiwan for more than two decades.
Early in her career, Li traveled to France to study at culinary academies and language schools and train alongside Michelin-starred chefs.
She continues to lead her team on annual trips to France to exchange techniques and explore regional cuisines.
Laplanche praised Li for spending two decades introducing French culinary culture to Taiwan by blending classical technique with local ingredients, while inspiring young Taiwanese chefs to train abroad.
Delivering her acceptance speech entirely in French, Li expressed gratitude for the recognition, noting that French cuisine had taught her so much and continues to inspire her today.
Over time, she incorporated her Taiwanese roots, home flavors, and Taiwan’s seasonal ingredients, finding her own style and voice at the intersection of two cultures.
Known as the “Godmother of Western Cuisine in Taiwan,” Li has kitchen staff who have worked with her for more than 15 years.
To maintain the physical stamina required for daily prep work and menu development, Li has followed a weight-training routine for more than a decade.
To mark the honor, Fleur de Sel launched its autumn tasting menu, highlighting seasonal produce, wild game, and mushrooms.
The new menu features sweet autumn crab balanced with yuzu and fennel, as well as tuna and Wagyu tartare combining land and sea ingredients with precise knife work, accented with caviar and perilla flowers.
A slow-caramelized French onion soup built on a beef consomme base recreates a recipe from Li’s student days in France.
For the main course, roasted pigeon is infused with subtle longan wood smoke, served with burdock root and autumn persimmon.
The meal concludes with a dessert pairing seasonal lotus seeds with sweet osmanthus honey, a reimagining of the classic Mont Blanc inspired by memories of Li’s grandmother.
Fleur de Sel launches autumn menu. (Taiwan News, Lyla Liu video)

All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are on the ballot, with public opinion polls suggesting the Democrats will regain control of the House and have a chance to retake the Senate.
A Republican victory would preserve Republican control of Congress, which Trump has enjoyed since returning to the White House after the 2024 election, while a Democratic victory could impede the president and trigger congressional investigations into his administration.
In Mississippi, an unexpectedly competitive US Senate race has given Democrats a rare opening ahead of next week's congressional elections.

Democrats are contesting all three Republican-held House seats in Mississippi, but none is viewed as a likely pickup opportunity. A fourth seat, represented by US Representative Bennie Thompson in a heavily Black district, is considered safe for the Democrats. REUTERS

US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:39:00 UTC
10:39:00 KST

US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
October 27, 2026
The US Justice Department has launched a third attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of illegally disclosing national defense information in 2016.
Court documents unsealed on Monday reveal allegations that Comey directed a subordinate to share classified information with a journalist.
The case marks another escalation in President Donald Trump's long-running conflict with the former FBI chief, who has denied wrongdoing.
What are the latest allegations against James Comey?
The case centers on an October 2016 New York Times article about a secret US surveillance order involving internet company Yahoo.
The order reportedly required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. It had been issued by a secret intelligence court.
Prosecutors allege that Comey instructed a staff member to contact a New York Times journalist to correct inaccurate information published by news agency Reuters the previous day.
According to the Justice Department, this resulted in the illegal transfer of classified national defense information to an unauthorized person.
However, the allegations have already been investigated twice.
Federal authorities began examining the disclosure in 2017. Prosecutor John Durham recommended against bringing criminal charges in December 2018, according to Comey's lawyers.
A second investigation, launched in 2019 under the code name "Tropical Vortex," was also closed without charges in February 2020.
How are Comey's lawyers fighting the new charges?
The Justice Department filed a legal document known as a "criminal information" in early October, shortly before the 10-year deadline for prosecuting the alleged offense.
Unlike an indictment, a criminal information does not require approval from a grand jury or judge.
Prosecutors say the filing allows them to extend the statute of limitations, which determines how long authorities have to bring criminal charges.
Comey's lawyers dispute that interpretation. They argue that federal law explicitly requires an indictment within 10 years and that the government's filing does not meet that requirement.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case. A ruling is still pending.
Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, also pointed to the two earlier investigations.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
Responding to the latest allegations in a video posted on Substack, Comey condemned the prosecution.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," he said.
"I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
What other criminal cases does James Comey face?
The latest case is the third criminal proceeding brought against Comey since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
In September 2025, prosecutors charged him with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding.
A federal judge dismissed the case after finding that the Trump-appointed prosecutor who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.
In April 2026, Comey was indicted again, this time over an Instagram photograph showing seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
The Justice Department interpreted the numbers as a threat against Trump, arguing that "86" referred to killing someone and "47" identified Trump as the 47th US president.
Comey denied threatening Trump's life and has sought to have that case dismissed.
Why has Trump targeted former FBI director Comey?
Comey was appointed FBI director in 2013 by Democratic President Barack Obama.
His relationship with Trump deteriorated shortly after the president took office in 2017.
Comey resisted Trump's request to pledge personal loyalty during a private dinner.
Trump fired him in May 2017 while the FBI was investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and possible connections to Trump's campaign.
The investigation was subsequently taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller. It established that Russia had interfered in the election but found insufficient evidence to prove criminal coordination between Moscow and Trump's campaign.
The two men have remained bitter political opponents. Trump has repeatedly accused Comey of treason, while Comey compared the president to a mafia boss in his 2018 memoir.

Source: European Pravda, citing a statement by the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI)
Details: Investigators established that three citizens of post-Soviet states who were legally residing in European Union countries had been involved in the sabotage attempt.
According to Digi24, the suspects are two Belarusian citizens and one Ukrainian. Two were detained by law enforcement in Germany, where they were preparing similar crimes. The third suspect was arrested in Poland. The Bucharest Court of Appeal has issued European arrest warrants for all three, and the Romanian authorities have begun extradition proceedings.
The intelligence service said the group's activities were not limited to Romania. Russian handlers had assigned it a number of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturers as well as other sites of military and industrial importance.
The case forms part of a wider campaign of sabotage operations coordinated by Russia across Europe, according to the service. Investigations conducted this year have uncovered other attempts targeting facilities in Romania, including international military sites and facilities used to train Ukraine's Armed Forces.
The service warned that these actions are intended to intimidate, undermine defence capabilities and weaken countries' contributions to European and regional security.
Romanian intelligence also highlighted that recruitment for sabotage operations typically takes place through social media. Recruits are initially offered money for individual tasks, such as monitoring or photographing specific sites. The assignments then become increasingly serious and may escalate to acts of destruction, arson or even murder. If recruits refuse, their handlers may resort to pressure and blackmail.
These networks exploit financial vulnerability, addiction or criminal records. To conceal their identities and movements, members often use transport, accommodation and payment methods registered in other people's names. They also communicate using SIM cards from third countries and encrypted messaging apps.
"The Intelligence Service, together with the Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism, General Directorate for Defence Intelligence and the Ministry of Internal Affairs, is continuing to investigate sabotage operations detected within the country," the statement said.
Background:
- Romanian President Nicușor Dan recently pointed to an increase in Russian provocations across the European Union.
- Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said there was intelligence indicating the possibility of a certain escalation of Russia's hybrid war against Europe before Christmas.

1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:35:08 UTC
10:35:08 KST

1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
- Summary:
- New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
- Share:
An archaeological site in the Jordan Valley is rewriting the timeline of early human migration. New research shows that 'Ubeidiya is at least 1.9 million years old, placing humans in the region hundreds of thousands of years earlier than previously believed. The revised dating makes 'Ubeidiya, alongside Dmanisi in Georgia, one of the oldest known sites of early human activity outside Africa. The findings suggest that ancient human populations, using different types of stone tools, had already spread into the Levant during a crucial early period of human expansion beyond Africa.
The research was led by Prof. Ari Matmon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Prof. Omry Barzilai of the University of Haifa, and Prof. Miriam Belmaker of the University of Tulsa. By combining three advanced dating methods, the team established a more reliable timeline for 'Ubeidiya, a site that has played an important role in research on human evolution.
Their findings indicate that the site is at least 1.9 million years old, making it one of the earliest known locations where ancient humans lived outside their African homeland.
Ancient Stone Tools Reveal Early Human Activity
The 'Ubeidiya Formation has attracted scientific attention for decades because of its early evidence of the Acheulean stone tool tradition. This technology is known for large tools shaped on both sides, including hand axes. The site also contains a rich collection of animal fossils, representing species originally associated with Africa and Asia, including several that are now extinct.
Despite its importance, researchers have struggled to establish exactly when early humans occupied the area. Previous estimates generally placed 'Ubeidiya between 1.2 million and 1.6 million years old, but those dates relied on comparisons with other archaeological and geological evidence rather than direct measurements.
To resolve the uncertainty, the researchers collected new samples from the site and analyzed them using three complementary dating techniques. Each provided an independent source of evidence about the age of the ancient deposits.
The first technique, called cosmogenic isotope burial dating, uses rare isotopes that form when cosmic rays interact with rocks exposed at Earth's surface. After the rocks become buried, these isotopes decay at known rates. Measuring what remains allows scientists to estimate how long the rocks have been underground.
The researchers also investigated evidence of Earth's ancient magnetic field recorded in sediments deposited at the bottom of a lake. As these sediments accumulated, they preserved the orientation of the magnetic field at the time. Comparing these records with known magnetic reversals showed that the deposits formed during the Matuyama Chron, a period that began more than two million years ago.
A third technique involved fossilized shells from Melanopsis, a genus of freshwater snails found within the sediment. Using uranium-lead dating, the team was able to establish a minimum age for the geological layers containing the ancient stone tools.
Together, the three approaches pointed to a much older age than earlier estimates.
A 1.9-Million-Year-Old Discovery Changes the Human Migration Timeline
The combined evidence indicates that 'Ubeidiya dates back at least 1.9 million years, significantly changing the timeline of early human settlement beyond Africa.
This places the Jordan Valley site at approximately the same age as Dmanisi in Georgia, another major location for understanding early human migration. The similarity in age suggests that ancient human populations were expanding into different regions around the same time.
The findings also raise intriguing questions about how these early migrations unfolded. Evidence from the two sites suggests that different groups of ancient humans may have carried distinct stone tool technologies out of Africa during overlapping periods.
These included the Oldowan tradition, associated with relatively simple stone tools, and the more sophisticated Acheulean tradition, known for carefully shaped tools such as hand axes. Rather than spreading in a single technological sequence, these different approaches to toolmaking may have traveled beyond Africa at roughly the same time as separate groups of early humans entered new environments.
Solving a Three-Million-Year-Old Dating Puzzle
The researchers also had to explain an unexpected complication in their results. Initial measurements of cosmogenic isotopes suggested that some rocks were approximately three million years old, considerably older than indicated by the site's magnetic, fossil, geological, and archaeological evidence.
Further investigation revealed why the measurements appeared to conflict.
The sediments had undergone a complicated history of repeated deposition, burial, exposure, and movement within the Dead Sea rift and the surrounding landscape. Some of the material had been buried long before it was eventually transported and deposited again near the ancient lake at 'Ubeidiya.
This recycling meant that the geological history recorded by certain rocks extended much farther into the past than the formation of the archaeological layers themselves.
As the researchers explained:
"The exposure-burial history that emerges from the model implies recycling of sediments previously deposited and buried in the rift valley... and then redeposited along the 'Ubeidiya paleo lake shoreline."
By accounting for this complex sediment history, the team reconciled the conflicting measurements and strengthened the evidence for the site's revised age.
The results establish 'Ubeidiya as one of the oldest known centers of early human activity outside Africa. They also suggest that the movement of our ancient relatives into new territories was already underway 1.9 million years ago, potentially involving multiple populations with different toolmaking traditions.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- A. Matmon, A. Kuzmenko, R. Shaar, P. Nuriel, A. Hidy, M. Guillong, R. Blevis, N. Wieler, S. Vainer, Y. Asscher, M. Belmaker, O. Barzilai. Complex exposure-burial history and Pleistocene sediment recycling in the dead sea rift with implications for the age of the Acheulean site of ‘Ubeidiya. Quaternary Science Reviews, 2026; 378: 109871 DOI: 10.1016/j.quascirev.2026.109871

Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in Oleshky brokered by US first lady takes effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:33:54 UTC
10:33:54 KST

Kanyshai Butun
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
A ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky brokered by US first lady Melania Trump took effect at 0100GMT on Tuesday to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
An official press release was issued Friday by the White House confirming that the first lady had served as the "Exclusive Intermediary" to secure the localized agreement.
The development came amid worsening shortages of food, medicine and clean water in Oleshky, a frontline town located on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine's southern Kherson region. Residents must also contend with limited access to electricity, mined roads and recurring military attacks, according to the White House.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster,” Melania Trump said. “It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”
Russian Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov said Moscow would implement a “regime of silence” in the Kherson direction from 4 am Moscow time on Oct. 27 to facilitate humanitarian operations.
“To ensure the safety of the population and the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be conducted, and the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy to the settlement of Oleshky, Kherson Region, will be facilitated,” the Russian Defense Ministry quoted him as saying.
Ukraine’s General Staff said it would implement a localized ceasefire from 3 am Kyiv time the same day to deliver humanitarian aid to Oleshky’s residents and ensure the safe, unhindered evacuation of civilians.
Under the arrangement, civilian representatives from Russia and Ukraine will assess residents’ needs. Those wishing to leave will receive coordinated transportation to destinations in either country, while a US media organization will accompany the teams to document the process, according to the White House.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the duration of the operation remained uncertain but noted that it could last several days.
The truce comes as Moscow and Kyiv trade blame for the worsening humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, a city that Russian forces captured in 2022.
Oleshky had a prewar population of around 24,000, but estimates suggest that only 1,700-2,000 people remain, many of them older residents unable to leave.
The collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in southern Ukraine in June 2023 triggered massive flooding in nearby communities, including Oleshky, that destroyed homes and forced thousands of people to flee, with Ukraine and Russia each accusing the other of deliberately destroying the dam.

Bolsonaro’s party accepts Brazil election after Trump calls vote ‘rigged’

Bolsonaro’s party accepts Brazil election after Trump calls vote ‘rigged’
Trump pushes unsubstantiated claims about Brazil’s presidential vote but says he ‘didn’t take sides’ in the race.
The political party of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has acknowledged the result of Brazil’s presidential run-off, despite the right-wing candidate pledging to annul the outcome.
On Monday, Valdemar Costa Neto, the leader of the right-wing Liberal Party, issued a statement saying his political group had accepted the outcome of the vote.
Still, he echoed Bolsonaro’s concerns about the circumstances surrounding the election.
“We recognise the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
On Sunday, Bolsonaro was defeated by left-wing incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by a margin of more than 4.4 million votes.
Bolsonaro has yet to formally concede. In a post-election speech, he called the election results “unacceptable”, citing a last-minute extension to voting hours.
“We will take legal action,” he told supporters. “I will request that these elections be annulled.”
In a video posted on social media on Monday, Bolsonaro also announced that federal police asked him to hand over his passports amid speculation that he could leave the country following his loss.
He said that he would comply with the order and had no plans to leave.
He said the decision came from a Supreme Court justice, and was based on a comment by his US-based brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who told a US podcast two days before the election that “if my brother does not win, I am in favor that he would leave the country.”
Eduardo cited investigations against his brother.
Brazilian police are probing Flavio Bolsonaro over alleged corruption linked to the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.
“I never had any intention of leaving the country. I will surrender my passports and defend myself against this travesty,” Flavio Bolsonaro said.
The right-wing candidate also took up the mantle as “leadership of the opposition” in a separate statement.
Extended voting
An extension to Sunday’s vote had been sought by the campaigns of both candidates — but for different reasons.
Bolsonaro’s camp had pointed to inclement weather that impeded some voters from reaching polling stations. Parts of southern Brazil, considered a right-wing stronghold, had experienced heavy rains on Sunday.
Lula’s campaign, meanwhile, pushed for longer voting hours after it accused some cities of limiting public transportation on election day.
The left-wing leader’s allies framed those reductions in service as an attempt at election interference, aimed at preventing Lula’s working-class base from voting.
Media reports indicated that Pablo Souza, a transportation official in the city of Salvador, was arrested on Sunday over the matter.
In response to the petitions, Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin agreed to extend voting by two hours.
Whereas polls across the country had been slated to close at 5pm Brasilia time (20:00 GMT), Zanin’s order allowed those that had not already closed to remain open until 7pm (22:00 GMT).
Following his loss, Bolsonaro cried foul, saying that the justice’s decision had disadvantaged his voters.
He pointed to Zanin’s relationship with Lula as support: Lula had appointed Zanin to the high court in 2023, and Zanin had formerly served as the left-wing politician’s personal lawyer.
“With a simple stroke of a pen, at the request of a former partner, [Zanin] changed the rules of the game mid-match,” Bolsonaro said in his address on Sunday night.
But experts signalled they were sceptical of Bolsonaro’s claims of malfeasance.
An analysis by Pedro Burgos, a professor at the Brazilian educational institute Insper, found that the extension resulted in 35,000 additional votes across the country, less than 0.03 percent of the total.
That amount was far short of Lula’s 4.4 million vote advantage. The incumbent won more than 64.25 million votes, compared with Bolsonaro’s 59.83 million.
Still, some right-wing allies rallied to Bolsonaro’s support. US President Donald Trump, who has clashed with Lula in the past, told reporters that the vote seemed “rigged”.
“Elections have to be indisputable and it looked very bad to me,” Trump said on Monday. “It looked like another rigged election, frankly.”
Still, Trump stopped short of suggesting that he would get involved on behalf of Bolsonaro, saying instead he “did not take sides” in the election.
Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept his loss has raised concerns about whether he will abide by the democratic process or follow in the footsteps of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who served as Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2023.
After his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election, the ex-president refused to acknowledge the outcome.
Instead, he and his allies sought to overturn the results, including through a legal challenge, and prosecutors accused him of plotting a coup to prevent the legal transfer of power.
Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence on coup-related charges.
Separately, he was also barred from serving in public office for eight years, after a court found he had misused his public office to spread misinformation about the election.
Flavio Bolsonaro, along with his siblings, has sought to have his father released. The family has denounced the elder Bolsonaro’s trial as a case of political persecution.
Still, it is unclear whether Flavio Bolsonaro will continue with his legal challenge over Sunday’s election.
The Brazilian news outlet Folha de S Paulo reported on Monday that legal advisers and political allies have convinced Bolsonaro to abandon his quest to have his loss annulled, citing the large margin of Lula’s victory and its validation by the Supreme Court and election authorities.

The joint statement urged parties in the conflict to authorise humanitarian operations through all cross-line and cross-border routes, including air access into Darfur.
It also called on them to “sustain presence and protection of humanitarian personnel” throughout Sudan and refrain from strikes on civilian infrastructure.
The statement was signed by the US, Australia, Britain, France, Germany and the European Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, among others.
The State Department said in September that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the RSF nor either of their respective leaders “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan”.
The war has displaced more than 14 million people and unleashed waves of ethnically driven killings.
A UN probe said in July that RSF forces had carried out mass killings, rapes and forced starvation in a city they besieged and captured in 2025, as part of an intentional policy amounting to genocide.

The United States has revealed the first nuclear submarine that will deploy to Australia under the AUKUS agreement, five years after the $386 billion defence pact was signed.
The USS Colorado, a 10-year-old Virginia-class submarine, will make its new home at Western Australia's HMAS Stirling from late 2027, Defence Minister Richard Marles revealed in a joint statement with his US and British counterparts on Tuesday.
It's the first of up to four US submarines, and one from the UK, set to rotate through the base while Australian Defence Force personnel get to grips with owning and operating nuclear submarines.
But Colorado's arrival in Australia will be controversial because of outrage sparked in late May over revelations that the US would deliver lesser equipment than first promised.
The original AUKUS plans were for Australia to receive two used vessels and a new Virginia-class submarine before building one of its own in Adelaide.

The fact the US would now be sending second-hand vessels was described as "trash" by Tasmanian independent senator and army veteran Jacqui Lambie, but ministers and top military brass at the time insisted used subs were the best option.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the time assured the public AUKUS was going "full-steam ahead" despite tweaks being made to the mega-money deal, which US defence secretary Pete Hegseth reiterated on Tuesday along with Marles and UK defence secretary Wes Streeting.
Colorado is a "fast-attack" submarine, reaching speeds of more than 46km/h, compared with Australia's Collins-class subs' underwater top speed of 37km/h.
While second-hand, the Virginia class is the US' most advanced line of attack submersibles.
The higher-speed, longer-range vessels are needed to help Australia defend its sea trade, Marles has said.
"The selection of USS Colorado ... is a decisive step in strengthening collective deterrence in the Pacific," the joint statement read.
Australia's own nuclear subs will be conventionally armed, but the US has maintained a policy of ambiguity about whether or not assets rotating through the country are carrying nuclear weapons.
Being nuclear-powered means its range is effectively limited only by its crew's need for food and water.
Tuesday's statement says the AUKUS rotation arrangement will abide by all relevant non-proliferation treaties.

Addressing the Real AI Challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:18:18 UTC
09:18:18 KST

Adaptive feedback at scale. Conversational practice before high-stakes human interactions. Exposure to dialectal and pragmatic variation that a single instructor could never provide. Robust analytics for many learners. Each is just one example of the ways in which AI is transforming how language is understood, taught, and learned. To shape this transformation, we must move past the familiar debates around AI toward bigger questions. Drawing from years of working as an academic researching second-language acquisition and pragmatics, as a director of a grant-funded, national research center, and as a CEO of a company building responsible learning technology, I am confident we cannot answer any of these questions alone.
The real AI challenge is not technical. It is structural. Education and industry have long been trying to solve shared problems on parallel tracks. This parallel work is further heightened by the pressures AI is placing on all areas. The opportunity in front of us is to bring those tracks together by pairing the energy and speed of industry with depth of learning and teaching expertise. My hope is that our next phase merges historically parallel work into something that genuinely inspires and transforms how we learn language.
Three Key Areas for Collaboration
Collaboration is the answer, and it is well within our reach. Three areas of focus have the potential to facilitate the kind of teamwork that produces real, lasting outcomes:
- Sustainable funding models
- Research-driven decision-making
- Technological expertise
Here are ideas and examples on each area designed to catalyze future models.
Sustainable Funding Models
Meaningful collaboration cannot run on goodwill and unpaid evenings. Research that informs product development takes time, infrastructure, and people. Furthermore, the timelines of grant cycles rarely match the timelines of a release schedule. Sustainable funding models enable researchers and builders to work in genuine partnership over the long term, rather than treating academic input as a one-time consultation or occasional opportunity. Examples include:
- Funding models that utilize both commercial funding and grant dollars in parallel instead of creating contexts that compete with one another (e.g., OER developers partnering with commercial systems for low-cost materials development and scalability instead of an OER versus publisher model)
- Reward structures that promote collaborative work (e.g., guidelines that account for transformational research work in tenure and promotion cases; bonuses to incentivize innovative academic collaboration)
Research-Driven Decision-Making
Going forward, research must shape what is built commercially, even when it complicates the development road map. That means striking a clear balance between what the research tells us is best practice and what is commercially viable. I have seen these two priorities come into conflict many times. Despite what some believe, this is not because all commercial companies want to cut corners and maximize profit, but rather because what works in language-learning research does not always lead to a commercially viable product. Central to moving forward is a shared perspective on what questions to ask and how to utilize the key data. This could happen in any number of ways, including:
- Research time during which commercial companies share current problems they are attempting to solve with the research teams in the position to investigate them, along with commitment by both to answer those questions (e.g., a weekly research challenge meeting with a stable team investigating key problems)
- Shared values and parameters for making decisions collaboratively when timeline, best practices, and cost are in conflict (e.g., a list that a commercial development team always consults when making decisions about tech and development timelines)
Technical Expertise
Researchers cannot guide what they do not understand. Building real fluency with the capabilities, limits, and fail states of core technologies is now part of the job for anyone serious about language education. Industry has the responsibility to ensure any systems are legible enough to be studied, questioned, and improved. This requires curiosity, detailed documentation, and support for expertise to be shared among developers, academic partners, and learners themselves. Some of my favorite problems have even been solved by student interns with the technical expertise necessary to try a different approach to a development problem we face.
A Shared Responsibility
Focusing on these three areas requires rethinking some things we have treated as settled. For example, it means reconsidering how products are developed, with educators and researchers in the room from the first design decision rather than brought in to validate the last one. It means rethinking how time for educators and researchers can be reallocated and valued to ensure there is an opportunity to prioritize collaborative industry work. Moreover, it means accepting a model of shared responsibility, where neither sector gets to point at the other when things go wrong.
The future of language education will not be decided by AI. It will be decided by the choices we make about how to build, study, and deploy it and whether we are willing to make those choices together.
Julie M. Sykes, PhD, is the CEO of Lingro Learning (https://lingrolearning.com) and a professor of Linguistics at the University of Oregon. Her work bridges industry and academic partnerships, responsible and ethical AI, content development, and games with research in second language acquisition, specifically intercultural pragmatics and technological innovation for teaching and learning.

Details
According to Tofan, Moldova could become an important logistics corridor for Ukrainian exporters seeking to expand their presence in European markets.
He emphasized that Romania's economy exceeds $480 billion, while Moldova itself already directs about 30% of its exports to that country. In his view, Ukrainian enterprises could also make more active use of similar routes.
How the new export route will operate
The Moldovan prime minister acknowledged that the decision to cut tariffs on the rail transit of Ukrainian cargo by 50% was not easy.
Among the main difficulties, he cited the limited capacity of the state budget, the interests of local farmers, and the unsatisfactory condition of certain sections of the railway infrastructure.
Despite this, Chișinău is ready to work with Kyiv to modernize transport routes, simplify border crossings, and develop new routes for transporting goods.
Such cooperation is expected to help Ukrainian producers gain additional opportunities to supply products to Romania and other European countries.

The disclosure came a day after Machado returned to Venezuela, and amid U.S.-backed efforts for an overhaul of the country's judicial and electoral institutions that Rubio argued are required before credible presidential elections can be held.
Machado snuck out of Venezuela in late 2025 to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, after spending nearly a year in hiding. Roughly one month after she departed the country, U.S. military forces captured Maduro and left his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, in control. No election date has been announced, but Rubio insisted that the interim government was adhering to agreed-upon deadlines for replacing the country's Supreme Court and electoral council, institutions long used by Maduro's government to control political competition.

Rubio cited what he described as compliance with U.S. national security demands to diminish Iranian and Cuban influence, pursue criminal organizations and extradite individuals wanted by American authorities, including former Maduro associate Alex Saab.

Israel election: What happens after polls close?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:06:05 UTC
09:06:05 KST

Israel election: What happens after polls close?
- Israel votes on Oct 27 in its first election since the Hamas attack on 7 October 2023, with Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power under pressure.
- Exit polls are due when voting ends at 10pm, but the result may take days or weeks because seats are shared by proportional representation.
- After results, President Isaac Herzog will pick a prime ministerial nominee, who has 42 days to build a coalition or face another election.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Israel is holding a parliamentary election on Oct 27, its first since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but it might take time before clear results are known.
When will we know who won?
It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear.
Voting starts at 7am local time (1pm Singapore time) and ends at 10pm, when Israeli TV channels will air exit polls giving the first indications of the outcome. The election results will then start coming in.
A clear picture may emerge quickly, but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer.
The final tally is expected by Oct 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on Nov 4.
Why is it so complicated?
Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be held every four years, but early elections have been frequent.
The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
What happens after the results are published?
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present Cabinet staying on as a caretaker government. REUTERS

Netanyahu’s political survival on the line as Israel votes

Fastest turnout in 45 years as Israelis pass wartime judgment on Netanyahu
JERUSALEM - Israelis surged to the polls at the fastest rate in 45 years on Oct 27, passing wartime judgment on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in what voters described as the most consequential election in their history.
In the first election since the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks, voters are passionately engaged over the trauma of the country’s deadliest day, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and have deepened Israel’s international isolation, but he has defended his record as the only leader with the mettle to face Israel’s foes.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, is an unmatched political survivor, and his nationalist politics are increasingly entrenched.
Israel’s fragmented system makes it difficult for an array of opponents to force out his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
His main rival Gadi Eisenkot, a military ex-chief of staff and security hawk, aims to unseat him with thesupport of parties on the right and centre, as well as the rump of an increasingly marginalised left.
Opinion polls show a close race, with neither leader facing an easy path to power.
Voters began casting ballots after polling stations opened at 7am (1pm Singapore time). The polls close at 10pm (4pm Singapore time on Oct 28).
The Central Elections Committee reported that 16.7% of eligible voters had already cast their ballots within the first three hours, the fastest early turnout rate since 1981.
“I think these elections are the most important of all the ones I’ve known,” said Ruth Epstein, an 81-year-old longtime left-wing voter in Ramat Gan near Tel Aviv, who voted for the opposition Democrats.
“I’m really scared about what will be here.”
Netanyahu supporter Louis Lipsky of Jerusalem said he was voting to keep the prime minister in power, crediting him with normalising relations with several Arab states under the Abraham Accords of 2020.
Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and an endorsement from US President Donald Trump, his ally in war against Iran, who has said they should “finish the job”.
If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held.
His opponents have managed to wrest him from the premiership only once since 2009, and that took four inconclusive elections in two years. He was back 18 months later.
Eisenkot sees ‘new spirit’
For many of Netanyahu’s opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of Oct 7, Israel’s deadliest day.
Opposition groups have promised to hold a national inquiry, which Netanyahu’s government has resisted.
“I am convinced that by the end of today, we will see a change – a new spirit for the State of Israel – that will serve as a rectification for the past three years and for that terrible day,” Eisenkot said during a visit to kibbutz Nir Oz in southern Israel, targeted in the Oct 7 attacks.
He walked to the polls with Gadi Mozes, one of 251 people kidnapped by Hamas and taken to Gaza during the attack that killed 1,200 people.
Eisenkot says Israel’s response – a war which health authorities say killed more than 74,000 Palestinians – was a failure because Hamas remains in charge.
He repeated his commitment to dismantle or destroy Hamas’ military and governing power in Gaza within 18 months of forming a government.
In his first public commentary on election day, Netanyahu shared an article on X about an incident in which police said three people were arrested over an election bribery attempt.
“Right-wing voters, dear Likud voters, in the face of attempts to undermine the integrity of the elections, we must go out and vote en masse, vote Likud for the sake of our country,” he said.
Netanyahu’s critics have said the prime minister may try to cast doubt on the integrity of the voting process, which his office rejects.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of a far-right party in Netanyahu’s coalition, cast his vote in the Kiryat Arba settlement in the occupied West Bank early on Oct 27.
He predicted Netanyahu would return as prime minister and his own party would serve as the right-wing anchor of the government.
Arab turnout could be key
Voters from Israel’s Arab minority – Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage – were voting in “unprecedented” numbers, Palestinian candidate Ahmed Tibi said.
Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, although some experts envision them propping up a minority government to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.
“My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide,” said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute.
The wartime record
Eisenkot joined Netanyahu’s war cabinet after the Oct 7 attacks but quit after eight months, criticising his leadership.
Israel flattened much of Gaza in the offensive launched after Oct 7, and now occupies around two-thirds of the enclave under a year-old US-brokered ceasefire.
Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and traded strikes with Iran before a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and the joint US-Israeli war in 2026.
Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.
But he has criticised Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel’s ties with Western states, and opposes Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners Ben-Gvir and Smotrich. REUTERS

AI generated
HOUSTON – Americans have paid more for their petrol and diesel at the pump on average during US President Donald Trump’s second term than they did under his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
Surging fuel prices are a major thorn in Trump’s side as midterm elections loom and the Republican Party looks to defend narrow majorities in both legislative chambers on Nov 3.
The price of a gallon of regular petrol has averaged US$3.472 (S$4.45) since Trump took office almost two years ago, edging out the US$3.471-per-gallon average for Biden’s term, according to data from the AAA.
Russia’s war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, as well as the US-Israeli war with Iran, almost in its ninth month, have both squeezed global crude and fuel supplies and forced emergency oil releases in the US and Europe.
The war in Iran has spilt out across the Middle East, with much of the conflict centred around the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of global oil and gas supplies flowed before the war broke out in February.
“Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically... Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers.
The seven-day moving average for Middle East oil exports including Hormuz flows and Gulf of Oman shipments as well as Red Sea shipments reached 24.6 million barrels per day in the week to Oct 18, according to Kpler, its highest level since the war broke out in late February, and surpassing pre-war levels.
Sticky inflation
Sticky inflation makes nominal price comparisons misleading, analysts said, with consumer expectations for inflation over the next year nudged up to 4.7% from 4.6% in September, a survey showed in October.
Twelve-month inflation expectations have surged from 3.4% in February before the US-Israeli war with Iran started.
“Adjusting for inflation puts this into context as the value of the dollar continues to impact prices over the longer run. Americans are still not paying record amounts of their income on filling up their tanks,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, on average fuel prices under Trump surpassing those under Biden.
Trump’s approval rating fell to a record low in October as Americans worried about high petrol prices, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Oct 19.
Some 31% of Americans approve of Trump’s performance in office, down a percentage point from two weeks earlier and the lowest level in either of his presidential terms, the four-day poll showed.
Just 23% of adults polled nationwide approve of his handling of the economy.
Prices for diesel, the fuel that powers the global economy from agriculture and heavy industry to shipping, have also surpassed Biden’s national average under Trump, at US$4.343 a gallon compared with US$4.078 a gallon.

Trump administration loses push to block California votes from alleged non-citizens

Trump administration loses push to block California votes from alleged non-citizens
- A US appeals court blocked Trump’s bid to stop California counting mail ballots from over 20,000 registered voters the government says may be non-citizens.
- The 9th Circuit said federal action would upset state election powers and risk “disorder and confusion” before the Nov 3 midterms.
- California called the case a “reckless political stunt” that could “disenfranchise thousands”, while evidence says non-citizen voting is very rare.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – A US appeals court on Oct 26 ruled against President Donald Trump’s administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely non-citizens.
The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump’s efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the Nov 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in.
The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Oct 27 in the case.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government “asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged non-citizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election.
The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent votes from being counted by a state, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people allegedly registered to vote in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.
Justice Department officials said on Oct 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting.
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives – 52 – than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump’s fellow Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its so-called “sanctuary state” policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has long asserted that California’s immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including non-citizen voting, is exceedingly rare.
A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which non-citizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration’s list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.
The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
California says the state’s safeguards against non-citizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data”.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing.
“At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration’s methods for scrutinising state voter lists to identify non-citizens risk wrongly flagging naturalised US citizens for removal from the rolls.
The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed non-citizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots.
It has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters’ sensitive personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one.
“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy,” said California Attorney-General Rob Bonta, a Democrat. REUTERS

US Justice Department charges former FBI Director James Comey again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
23:40:50 UTC
08:40:50 KST

Rabia Iclal Turan
27 October 2026•Update: 27 October 2026
The US Justice Department has filed criminal charges against former FBI Director James Comey for the third time, accusing him of leaking national defense information in October 2016, according to court records unsealed Monday.
 
The two-count criminal information, filed under seal on Oct. 5 in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges that Comey “knowingly and willfully communicated, delivered, transmitted and caused that information to be communicated, delivered and transmitted to a person not entitled to receive it.”
 
Prosecutors allege that on Oct. 5, 2016, Comey, “through one and more co-conspirators directed Individual #1 to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication.”
 
The information ended up in a New York Times article, according to The Wall Street Journal.
 
The filing was signed by Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter.
 
The department said the filing, made exactly 10 years after the alleged disclosure, was meant to preserve the case before the statute of limitations expired while it seeks a grand jury indictment.
 
Comey has moved to dismiss the case in sealed proceedings, arguing that an indictment is required within 10 years and the filing does not suffice.
 
“An indictment fundamentally differs from an information,” his lawyers said in a court filing.
 
In a video posted on social media, Comey said: “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.”
 
“Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary,” he said.
 
Asked about the charges as he arrived at Joint Base Andrews after a rally in Mississippi, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know too much about it. I just heard about it.”
 
“I think he’s a dirty cop, James Comey, but I know nothing about it,” he said.

US rapper Macklemore launches 'Free Palestine Tour' after Ed Sheeran fallout

Sheeran has said tour promoters, not he, made the decision to drop Macklemore, provoking outrage among musicians and pro-Palestinian activists.
"The USA is supposed to be the country of free speech, and instead people are being shut down. (Sheeran) should have stood up for what Macklemore was doing," said Grainne Healy, a 60-year-old retiree who had come to the Dublin concert with a former schoolfriend.
Four other supporting artists, including American singer Finneas, also pulled out of Sheeran's tour in solidarity with Macklemore, and Sheeran later broke his silence on the situation in Gaza at a concert in Philadelphia, calling it "unjustifiable and disproportionate".
Last month Macklemore announced his Free Palestine Tour, with shows in London and Paris in late October and US dates also planned, saying all proceeds would benefit pro-Palestinian organisations.
