05:00:09 KST

A US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) contractor with Top Secret security clearance was arrested by the FBI on Friday for allegedly leaking classified defense and Middle East-related information to an individual who published the information online, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ).
The contractor, 42-year-old Ian Brinksman, worked for a US government agency based in Virginia since 2020 before being hired by a contractor to the same agency in 2022. Throughout his employment, Brinksman held the Top Secret security clearance with access to Sensitive Compartmented Information.
In a statement about the arrest, CIA Director John Ratcliffe confirmed that Brinksman provided services to the CIA as a contractor.
Brinksman accused of leaking information for use in publication
The criminal complaint against Brinksman alleged that he had an ongoing personal relationship with a person the DOJ identified as “Individual 1,” who claimed to have published reporting based on classified government intelligence assessments.
An affidavit for the arrest included an email Brinksman sent to a friend in which he stated that he had recently begun seeing “a lady” who worked as a journalist and wrote articles on the online publishing platform Substack.
Brinksman told the friend that the lady’s work focused on foreign policy and that he was “helping her get that off the ground.”
Brinksman’s workplace, a facility that stores and processes classified information, does not allow employees to bring cellphones or personal electronics into the facility for security reasons.
According to the DOJ, Brinksman was documented on multiple occasions entering his workplace, accessing specific Top Secret reports, then exiting the facility and speaking to Individual 1 on the phone.
Shortly after speaking with Brinksman, Individual 1 posted Substack articles containing classified information related to the Top Secret reports Brinksman accessed.
According to the affidavit, Brinksman is accused of sharing information from at least five Top Secret intelligence reports, including material that “reasonably could be expected to cause exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the US if leaked. None of the reports Brinksman allegedly leaked fell within the scope of his work.
Affidavit details align with Substack articles published by American journalist
The DOJ and FBI did not identify Individual 1 or her Substack, but The Jerusalem Post’s analysis of the details of the affidavit found that the information may align with American journalist Aida Chavez and articles written by her for Substack publication Capital & Empire.
Reports from both Ynet and the New York Post also connected Chavez to the information released by the DOJ, but Chavez has not been charged with any offenses related to the investigation into Brinksman or officially linked to the case.
The affidavit notes multiple dates on which Individual 1 is alleged to have published articles containing classified information leaked by Brinksman.
Articles published by Chavez on corresponding dates cite sources including a “confidential US intelligence assessment,” a “classified CIA assessment,” and a “classified CIA analysis.”
Many of the articles alleged to contain leaked confidential information discussed Israel, US-Israel relations, and the ongoing war with Iran.

The package included €1 billion of investment in university campuses; a move to increase student grants with inflation; and the opening up of a further 15,000 higher education places for students.
"It's clear we have to ease the pressure being felt in the education system," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told a press conference.
There was no overall figure for how much funding the package would require. High borrowing needs are already complicating efforts to agree a budget for next year.

Over 1,400 arrested during protests on Saturday

"We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses," he said. "In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organized formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A selloff in French government bonds paused on Monday after rating agency Moody's on Friday refrained from downgrading the country's sovereign debt.
But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage.
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding this had led to sharp falls in sales.
"We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralized, and we are killing local commerce," he told Radio Classique.

'We do whatever they say': Yeshiva students defer to rabbis over response to IDF draft enforcement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:59:57 UTC
04:59:57 KST

Yeshiva students attending a massive United Torah Judaism election rally in Bnei Brak on Sunday told The Jerusalem Post that whether they would leave Israel, stay in the country, or enlist in the IDF if the next government stepped up draft enforcement would depend on their rabbis’ instructions.
The rally, held two days before Israel’s election, drew tens of thousands of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Jews under the slogan “Gather and Stand Up for Our Lives.” Central to the gathering was military conscription for haredi yeshiva students, regarded as a red line by much of the haredi community but widely supported among Jewish Israelis. An October Israel Democracy Institute survey found that 72% of Jewish respondents supported legislation requiring young haredi men to enlist.
Speaking at the rally, Rabbi Dov Landau, a leading haredi rabbinic authority, urged supporters to defend Torah study.
“Never have yeshiva students and kollel scholars been persecuted as they are being persecuted now,” Landau said.
The yeshiva students interviewed by the Post likewise described deferring to their own rabbis when asked how they would respond to draft enforcement.
“If my rabbi says to leave (the country), I’m going to leave,” Reuven, one of the students attending the rally, told the Post. When asked whether he would stay or enlist if his rabbi instructed him to do so, he replied that “of course” he would.
‘We would go through fire and water’ for our rabbis, yeshiva student says
Dovid, another young haredi man at the rally, said that he and others like him would “go through fire and water” for their rabbis.
“In our culture, we listen to whatever our rabbis say. If our rabbis will tell us to go, then we’ll listen to them,” he said. “We’re going to listen to them until the end.”
Shmuel, a fellow yeshiva student, emphasized that Torah study was his highest priority and that he would leave Israel if staying meant he could no longer continue his studies.
“If I need (to leave), that’s what I’ll do,” he said. “What’s more important for us is that we need to learn. And, if we can’t learn here, then we’ll learn in a different place. We’re not going to serve in the IDF because this learning is the most important thing in the world.”
Chaim, another of the students interviewed, also expressed a commitment to rabbinic authority, but argued that “the Jews doing Torah and mitzvot, to them, God gave Israel.” If the government enforced the draft, he believed the response should be to “fight it.”
Student emphasizes desire to stay despite saying he will obey rabbi if instructed to leave
Avi, another young man at the event, emphasized his desire to remain in Israel.
“We will stay (in Israel) because we believe it’s our country and Hashem will help us,” he said. Still, if his rabbi instructed him to leave, he would comply, “because he’s our rabbi, and we do whatever he says.”
Despite broad agreement about following their rabbis, the students appeared to hold differing personal views about military service.
When a group of young men was asked whether some yeshiva students wanted to enlist but refrained because their rabbis forbade it, several agreed, with one answering, “of course.”
One of the students, speaking anonymously, expressed frustration over the situation. He feared arrest at the airport over his draft status if he tried to travel abroad, and questioned why young yeshiva students were being targeted for draft evasion rather than the rabbis whose directives they were following.

Romania’s Intelligence Service has uncovered a sabotage network coordinated by Russian intelligence services that allegedly targeted the Carfil arms factory in Brașov and other military and industrial sites across the region, Romanian media reported.
The Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) is investigating three foreign nationals, one Ukrainian and two Belarusians, over the planned sabotage operations. Two suspects were arrested in Germany, where they were preparing similar actions, while the third was located in Poland.
The network allegedly planned to set fire to the Carfil arms factory in Brașov in the middle of last month. According to information released by the Romanian Intelligence Service, the group was also responsible for a fire at an industrial site in Central Romania near the state-owned defense enterprise in September.
The intelligence service said the network was uncovered in cooperation with domestic and foreign partners. Evidence collected so far suggests its activities extended beyond Romania, as coordinators in Russia assigned the group targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturers and other sites of military and industrial interest.
“Coordinators in the Russian Federation assigned [the group] a wide range of targets in the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as other sites of military and industrial interest,” the Romanian Intelligence Service said in a statement published on its website.
The Bucharest Court of Appeal has issued European Arrest Warrants for all three suspects, with the ruling made in their absence. Romanian authorities have requested their extradition and are taking steps to bring them to Romania, BTA reported.
Investigations conducted this year have also uncovered other attempted attacks against sites in Romania, including international military facilities and locations used to train the Ukrainian Armed Forces. The operations were intended to intimidate, damage defense capabilities and undermine the contribution of targeted countries to European and regional security, Digi24 reported.
Russia has repeatedly denied allegations that it carries out sabotage operations in Europe, Reuters reported.

Digital News Publishers Association is set to move the Supreme Court challenging provisions of the DPDP Act and Rules, alleging they violate free speech and threaten journalistic activity. (file photo)
NEW DELHI: Challenging the constitutional validity of various provisions of Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and subsequent rules framed by govt, Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) is likely to move Supreme Court, alleging that they were violative of the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression and threatened the full spectrum of journalistic activity.“It is prayed that sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37, 44(3) of DPDP Act and Rules 16, 17, and 23 of DPDP Rules framed under Section 40 be declared void to the extent they are in contravention of fundamental rights of the Constitution,” said the petition of the association, representing 21 of India’s leading media organisations.“The sections mentioned above fail to provide any exemption in favour of journalistic activity as a distinct class of processing, entitled to constitutional protection under Article 14 and 19(l)(a) of the Constitution and threaten the full spectrum of journalistic activity carried out by journalists, ground reporters, citizens, whistleblowers, RTI activists, and other stakeholders, and strikes at the core of our democratic framework and runs contrary to the basic tenets of the Constitution.”It said publishers, editors, reporters and correspondents will be brought within a regime of notice and prior consent, compelled erasure and verifiable consent, obligations that cannot be reconciled with the ordinary functioning of the press. Questioning the validity of Section 44(3) of the Act, which places every category of “personal information” beyond the reach of disclosure, without regard to whether it relates to a public activity, the petition said it dismantled the balancing mechanism between right to privacy and right to information that operated for two decades.
“These provisions, taken collectively, constitute a disproportionate and excessive curtailment of the fundamental right to free speech and expression and the implicit right to know and access information as recognised under Article 19(l)(a). DPDP Act creates restrictions on the fundamental right to free speech and expression in relation to the dissemination of news,” the petition added.

US designates first nuclear-powered submarine for rotational deployment to Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:13:53 UTC
04:13:53 KST

Diyar Guldogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The US has designated the USS Colorado, a Virginia-class nuclear-powered attack submarine, as the first American vessel to join a rotational submarine force based in Australia beginning in late 2027, the Pentagon announced Monday.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles, and British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting announced the designation ahead of a submarine maintenance period scheduled to begin later this week, the Pentagon said.
The maintenance activities are expected to demonstrate Australia's growing ability to service US and British nuclear-powered attack submarines under the three countries' AUKUS security partnership.
Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West) will operate from HMAS Stirling, a Royal Australian Navy base in Western Australia.
The base is expected to host up to four US attack submarines and one British attack submarine on a rotational basis.
The initiative is part of AUKUS Pillar I, which aims to help Australia acquire conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines.
The rotational force will allow Australia to develop the technical expertise, infrastructure and regulatory capabilities needed to operate and maintain its future submarine fleet.
It will also expand regional maintenance capacity and support submarine deployments by the three partner countries.
"The selection of USS Colorado (SSN 788) as the first submarine assigned to SRF-West in 2027 marks a significant milestone for AUKUS Pillar I and is a decisive step in strengthening collective deterrence in the Pacific," the Pentagon statement said.

UN calls Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure crimes against humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:13:00 UTC
04:13:00 KST

UN calls Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure crimes against humanity
According to Ukrinform, this information is posted on the Commission’s website.
“The Russian authorities have committed war crimes by deliberately targeting civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts, by carrying out continuous attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure,” stated the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine in its new report to the UN General Assembly.
The Commission investigated the impact of large-scale attacks by Russian armed forces on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure on the civilian population, particularly during the difficult winter of 2025–2026, as well as the cumulative effects of these attacks since the fall of 2022. The report notes that systematic waves of Russian attacks, during which hundreds of drones and missiles were deployed simultaneously, became increasingly frequent and intense and covered an ever-wider area, causing significant damage to Ukraine’s energy sector.
Last winter, when temperatures dropped to -21 °C, millions of people in Ukraine faced prolonged disruptions in the supply of heat, electricity, water, and gas and were forced to live in unbearable conditions.
“As winter approaches, the attacks have intensified again, raising serious concerns given the threats to the lives and health of the civilian population,” said Commission Chair Erik Møse.
The report emphasizes that prolonged exposure to the cold, lack of access to basic utilities, and the constant need to find ways to survive have significantly affected the physical and mental health of Ukraine’s civilian population.
Due to the risk of getting stuck in an elevator in the event of a sudden power outage, they were unable to go down to the shelter during an air raid alert and were forced to remain in unheated homes without electricity or water, without access to life-support equipment or basic services.
Due to the prolonged closure of schools during the acute energy crisis, children were unable to receive a full education. The lack of heating in their homes led to children falling ill and created additional hardships for their families.
The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately targeting civilian objects. The evidence gathered indicates that the attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure were carried out in a targeted manner, in accordance with a state policy aimed at depriving the civilian population of electricity and other vital services dependent on energy supply and causing them suffering. The Commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts. The Commission relied on the testimony of 255 individuals who survived the winter under the conditions described above in the Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Poltava, Zaporizhzhia, and Zhytomyr regions, as well as on information provided by Ukrainian authorities, doctors, and nongovernmental organizations.
According to the Commission’s assessment, the Russian commanders who issued orders to carry out the attacks were aware that the heating facilities they targeted in large population centers were vital to the civilian population, especially in winter. Russian authorities officially stated their intention to continue the attacks and referred to plans for their implementation.
The Commission also examined attacks by the Ukrainian armed forces on energy facilities in the Russian Federation and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. It is noted that the Commission was unable to investigate the consequences of these attacks in detail, as the Russian Federation did not grant it access to the relevant territories and did not respond to the Commission’s requests for information.
The Commission also concluded that Russian authorities recruited men who had been victims of human trafficking in various countries into their armed forces, which constitutes a violation of international human rights. In particular, compelling evidence was found that Russian authorities engaged in human trafficking involving individuals from 29 countries.
Human trafficking was carried out through deception and coercion in collaboration with agents and agencies operating in various countries around the world. The agents and agencies that recruited men in various countries presented themselves as legitimate companies or government-backed enterprises. They arranged visas and travel documents for groups of recruits and, in some cases, accompanied them during the trip. However, shortly after their arrival, they were forced to sign contracts with the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation, written in Russian.
The Commission noted a high level of coordination between agents operating in various countries around the world and the Russian authorities.
As a result, the men were sent to the front lines in Ukraine and assigned dangerous tasks. Many of them were killed or went missing; others voluntarily surrendered or were captured by the Ukrainian armed forces and were granted prisoner-of-war status.
The Commission reiterates that international law prohibits attacks on the civilian population and civilian objects and calls for an end to such attacks. The Commission also calls for the release from the Russian armed forces of all individuals who have been victims of human trafficking.
As previously reported, as of April 2026, Russian troops had attacked Ukrainian power substations—which are critical to nuclear safety—a total of 155 times since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Since October 19, 2026, alone, Russian troops have carried out approximately 60
targeted strikes, damaging energy and oil and gas infrastructure in a number of regions (including Rivne, Volyn, Khmelnytskyi, and Vinnytsia), as well as the Kyiv power coal depot.
As of May 2026, 80 repeat strikes on infrastructure facilities had been recorded at the very moment when State Emergency Service rescuers and law enforcement officers were arriving at the scene.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in the second round of Brazil’s presidential election safeguards the country’s path towards determining its own destiny and contributing to the construction of a less unequal international order.
For me, his victory over Flávio Bolsonaro also represents a defeat for the project of subordinating Brazilian foreign policy to the priorities of the United States and Israel. The ballot box has renewed the responsibility to translate diplomatic independence into development, solidarity and the defence of peace.
According to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Lula secured 64,256,232 votes, representing 51.79 per cent of valid ballots, against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 59,826,041 votes, or 48.21 per cent — a margin of 4,430,191 votes. In the first round, Lula had trailed his opponent, receiving 45.16 per cent compared with Bolsonaro’s 47.03 per cent.
Overturning this deficit demonstrated the campaign’s ability to mobilise society once again, increasing its vote by more than ten million between the two rounds.
Lula’s victory strengthens the prospects for a foreign policy committed to the Global South, expanding economic, scientific and cultural partnerships while advocating international institutions that better represent developing countries.
Strengthening BRICS is central to this strategy. During Brazil’s presidency of the grouping in 2025, cooperation among Global South countries and reform of international governance were among its priorities. Lula’s renewed mandate provides an opportunity to deepen this agenda, expand alternative sources of development finance and promote technological cooperation.
Among Brazilian citizens voting in BRICS countries, Lula won in mainland China with 73.67 per cent and Russia with 64.52 per cent. He also secured majorities in India, Iran and Egypt, where he received 78.95 per cent. The results were not uniform across the bloc: Flávio Bolsonaro won among Brazilian voters in South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. These figures reflect the choices of Brazilian voters abroad, not the political preferences of the populations or governments of those countries.
In Palestine, the election result carried particular political significance. Lula received 1,000 votes, equivalent to 95.60 per cent, compared with just 46 for Flávio Bolsonaro. Although voting decisions are shaped by multiple factors, I see this overwhelming preference as reflecting an affinity with Lula’s defence of Palestinian rights.
In Israel, by contrast, Flávio Bolsonaro, who advocates alignment with Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, which I regard as responsible for genocide, received 699 votes (80.8 per cent), compared with Lula’s 166 votes (19.2 per cent). The figures reveal a striking contrast between the two groups of Brazilian voters.
READ: Pro-Palestine protests sweep Latin America as Brazil’s presidential race intensifies
Lula’s relationship with Palestine has deep historical roots. In 2010, his government recognised the State of Palestine within the 1967 borders. As I examine in my book, Palestine: From the Myth of the Promised Land to the Land of Resistance, recognising Palestinian self-determination means acknowledging Palestinians as a people entitled to rights and sovereignty.
Faced with the devastation of Gaza, Lula denounced the genocide of the Palestinian people, condemned the complicity of Western powers and demanded an international response. In challenging Israel’s impunity, he reaffirmed that no state stands above international law.
Lula’s new mandate must reinforce this position and translate it into more effective diplomatic, commercial and military initiatives. Solidarity must have tangible political consequences, confronting the impunity of the Zionist regime that enables the continuation of violence and upholding the Palestinian people’s right to freedom and sovereignty.
Mercosur is another indispensable pillar. Brazil will have greater negotiating power internationally if it strengthens integration with its neighbours, develops regional production chains and expands the infrastructure connecting South American countries.
This approach also enables Brazil to contribute to conflict mediation. Our diplomatic strength depends on the credibility to engage with opposing parties, put forward proposals and uphold international law. Peace requires initiatives that reduce tensions and protect populations affected by war.
Brazil’s diplomatic efforts concerning Iran’s nuclear programme illustrate this potential. On 17 May 2010, Brazil, Turkiye and Iran signed the Tehran Declaration. The proposal envisaged transferring 1,200 kilograms of Iranian low-enriched uranium to Turkiye in exchange for 120 kilograms of nuclear fuel for the Tehran Research Reactor, used for medical purposes. The agreement sought to build confidence and open the way towards a negotiated settlement.
Although the declaration did not resolve the dispute and was separate from the 2015 nuclear agreement, it demonstrated that countries of the Global South can formulate diplomatic alternatives to international deadlocks. This experience should inspire renewed efforts towards negotiation, non-proliferation and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
Lula’s victory should usher in a new phase of sovereign national assertion. It offers an opportunity to strengthen BRICS and Mercosur, expand cooperation with the Global South and transform solidarity with Palestine into concrete political action.
Solidarity with Palestine and dialogue with Iran are integral to a foreign policy that must serve Brazilian sovereignty and the pursuit of peace. Lula’s renewed mandate must turn this opportunity into action.

‘Autonomy, not flesh’: RAF chief outlines AI drone-powered future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:09:51 UTC
04:09:51 KST

A future Royal Air Force will rely on “autonomy not flesh”, its chief said on Monday as he described plans in which Typhoon fighters are accompanied by four AI-enabled drones capable of patrolling hundreds of miles in the distance.
The technological shift would revolutionise warfare, limit the role of military personnel “towards the outside” and ease the pressure on recruitment, Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth said in a speech in London.
The senior military officer was setting out a strategy for the RAF, which has been told it must be ready to fight against Russia by 2030, at a time when the use of artificial intelligence by the US, Israel, Russia and Ukraine has made warfare more deadly.
“AI will enable warfare that speeds well beyond human comprehension, meaning that our role will shift towards the outside, and it will shift towards controlling the activity and setting the guardrails,” Smyth said.
The aim, he added, was to mirror the Anglo-American second world war model of “steel, not flesh” – relying on tanks and combat aircraft rather than infantry – to avoid the bloody trench warfare that had led to millions of deaths in the first world war.
“Given today’s changing character of war, I would argue strongly that the modern paradigm must now become autonomy, not flesh,” the chief of air staff said in a lecture at the Royal United Services Institute.
Few examples were given about the future use of AI by the air force, but Smyth did point to the £300m Storm Fighter programme of “loyal wingman” drones announced in July as part of the delayed defence investment plan. “Crewed platforms are no longer enough,” Smyth said.
Four armed, AI-enabled uncrewed craft would work alongside every RAF Typhoon, with the first tests to be conducted next year. The aim is for the drones to be in service by the end of the decade, in line with a Nato directive for the UK and other alliance members to be ready to fight Russia if necessary by 2030.
Over the weekend Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the UK had “a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win”.
The drones would “provide force multiplier function and the affordable mass we so definitely require” and, Smyth added, would be “placing sensors, weapons, and united warfare capabilities well within contested airspace”.
One possibility would be to use the drones to track Russian aircraft seeking to cross the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap into the north Atlantic, controlling them from a cockpit of a Typhoon flying over Scotland, several hundred miles away.
AI has been used by the Israeli and US military to dramatically increase the pace of target selection in the wars in Gaza and Iran, allowing them to run more bombing missions.
The IDF used two databases, Lavender and Habsora (or the Gospel), to increase the pace at which it could attack people and buildings during the war in Gaza. The US’s Maven Smart System, developed in conjunction with Palantir, was used to identify and strike 1,000 targets in Iran in the first 24 hours of the war this spring.
Russia and Ukraine have begun to use AI to identify and strike targets on the ground, eliminating the need for satellite or radio communication as they descend on their bombing mission. In July, Ukrainian investigators concluded that a drone that killed a person near a Zaporizhzhia gas station in July was relying on AI for its attack.
“Autonomous air systems penetrate Russia’s perceived sense of sanctuary on a routine basis,” Smyth said, describing how Ukrainian drones conduct long-range strikes against targets inside Russia, such as oil refineries.
Drones would allow the RAF to increase its ability to strike at a time when recruitment has been challenging. The RAF’s fully trained personnel numbers have fallen from 29,800 in 2020 to 27,850 today, and the total has only begun to increase over the last 18 months.

Civic responsibility and philanthropy strengthen Israeli society - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:52:45 UTC
03:52:45 KST

In the months prior to election day, public debate naturally focused on politics, parties, and the future direction of the country. Elections matter. They are one of the most important ways citizens shape the character and priorities of their nation. But democracy does not begin and end with voting.
If the events following October 7 taught us anything, it is that a healthy society depends not only on governments and elected officials, but also on ordinary people who choose to take responsibility for one another.
In those difficult days and months, countless volunteers, non-profits, and community initiatives stepped forward to support vulnerable populations and strengthen the country’s social fabric. They demonstrated that while governments govern, citizens build society.
Every one of us has opportunities to shape the world around us, not only through the choices we make at the ballot box, but through the causes we support and the people we help. Volunteerism and philanthropy allow us to transform our values into action.
However, we must not forget that government action alone is generally not enough. Reimbursements and public budgets often cover only part of what is truly needed to sustain essential human services, nurture community health, and support vulnerable groups.
Philanthropy and civic participation make it possible to bridge that gap, sustain essential care, and create opportunities where none existed before.
This spirit is embodied whenever dedicated volunteers and community partners give their time, energy, and financial resources – not for personal gain, but to ensure that members of our society facing extraordinary challenges receive the support they deserve.
These initiatives show what becomes possible when people refuse to be mere passive observers, and instead choose to become active participants in building their community.
For many active citizens, grassroots engagement represents an Israel they are proud to support: an Israel that respects the dignity of every human being, harnesses cooperation for the benefit of society, and builds shared resilience.
A clear reflection of this commitment can be seen in the upcoming Alyn Hospital Ride – “Wheels of Love.” The hospital’s annual event will take place from November 8 to 12 and includes hundreds of cyclists, hikers, and volunteers from Israel and around the world.
Former Alyn patients ride for others
All of them devote months to training and fundraising to ensure that children facing extraordinary challenges receive the care and opportunities they deserve. Among the most inspiring participants are members of The Swift & The Bold, a cycling team made up of former Alyn patients.
These children and teens are not merely beneficiaries of rehabilitation services; they are active participants in the ride itself as riders and fundraisers – a powerful demonstration of how civic action fosters independence and shared solidarity.
With election day behind us, dedicated volunteers, donors, and grassroots initiatives remind us that democracy is about far more than choosing leaders. It is about actively choosing values, taking mutual responsibility, and standing alongside one another.
A ballot may help shape the political direction of a nation, but it is our daily commitment to volunteerism, civic responsibility, and caring for others that truly defines its soul.
To learn more about the Alyn Hospital Ride or support its participants and the children of Alyn Hospital, visit www.Alynride.org
The writer is deputy director of resource development for Alyn Hospital Friends. Alyn Hospital Pediatric & Adolescent Rehabilitation Center in Jerusalem is a global leader in the active and intensive rehabilitation of children and adolescents with congenital and acquired conditions. Alyn Hospital Friends supports Alyn’s mission to maximize their abilities, foster their independence, and open the door to a life full of possibilities.

Legendary Jewish actor Walter Koenig, 'Star Trek's' plucky Chekov, dies at 90
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:52:26 UTC
03:52:26 KST

Walter Koenig, who brought humor and grit to the role of starship navigator Pavel Chekov on the classic 1960s sci-fi TV series "Star Trek" and seven subsequent feature films, has died at the age of 90.
"My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today," George Takei, who starred alongside Koenig in the show and was a long-time friend, wrote on Facebook on Monday. Koenig died at his home in Los Angeles, the AP reported, citing his talent agent.
"Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry picked Koenig, who had played only a few prior roles on television, when he decided to add a Russian character to the crew of the fictional Starship Enterprise. The introduction of a Russian officer who worked harmoniously with a racially and culturally diverse crew came amid the real-world Cold War tensions of the era.
"We were stating tacitly that peoples of all races and creeds, nationalities could not only co-exist but care for each other deeply, and in doing so we were heralding a future that was very optimistic," Koenig once told a BBC interviewer.
While Koenig was the son of Russian Jewish immigrants, he used an inauthentic Russian accent that was sometimes played for laughs.
Walter Koenig's career as Pavel Chekov on Star Trek
The original TV series ran for three seasons, from 1966 to 1969. Koenig appeared on 36 episodes, and then in seven movies from 1979 to 1994.
"I was informed while I was still there at my audition that I had the role," Koenig told the Joplin Globe in 2008. "It seemed like an engagement that might work out over several episodes, but I had no idea that it would totally shape my career and my life."
The show remained popular in syndicated reruns and inspired several later TV series and a succession of films. It attracted a devoted worldwide fan base and earned an enduring place in pop culture.
Koenig's "Star Trek" fame was a blessing and a curse, as it was for cast mates such as William Shatner (Captain Kirk), Leonard Nimoy (Spock), DeForest Kelley (Dr. McCoy), Nichelle Nichols (Uhura), James Doohan (Scotty) and Takei, who played Lieutenant Sulu.
They were often typecast because they were so closely associated with "Star Trek."
"Most of the '70s, I didn't work at all, and I blamed it on typecasting," Koenig told the St. Petersburg Times in 1998.
Walter Koenig's life and career beyond Star Trek
He later landed a regular role on the 1990s sci-fi series "Babylon 5" and was an author, script writer and occasional director.
Koenig was born on September 14, 1936, raised in New York City and attended the University of California, Los Angeles, before beginning his professional acting career. He suffered a personal tragedy in 2010 when his son, actor Andrew Koenig, took his own life. Koenig married his wife Judy in 1965. They also had a daughter, actress Danielle Koenig.

'Lack of Jews hasn't meant lack of antisemitism,' Expert on Jews in Wales tells 'Post' - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:52:25 UTC
03:52:25 KST

"The absence of Jews in Wales hasn't meant the absence of antisemitism; it's actually the opposite," Bangor University Professor and expert in Welsh Jewry, Professor Nathan Abrams, told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
Abrams was born into a Jewish family in North London but has lived in Wales for twenty years and speaks Welsh fluently.
He recently published a book, Jews in the Welsh Imagination: Medieval Times to the Present, which explores the nation's attitudes towards Jews over the centuries.
“For most of Wales’s existence as an entity – for 15 centuries – there have been no Jews here. The fascination the Welsh have with Jews is inversely proportional to the numbers," he said. "So the absence of Jews hasn't meant the absence of antisemitism or similar attitudes. It's actually the opposite."
According to the 2021 UK Census, 2,044 people in Wales identified as Jewish by religion, representing approximately 0.07% of Wales's population of 3.1 million.
Most of Wales' Jews are located in Cardiff, where there are two synagogues: a Reform synagogue and an Orthodox synagogue. A Chabad synagogue also serves Llandudno, and small community-organized groups or individual Jews exist in other cities.
Antisemitism in Wales often overshadowed by wider UK statistics
Jews in Wales are not a commonly discussed topic in Jewish media, and reporting on antisemitism in the nation is often swallowed by wider UK statistics, which do not typically show breakdowns by country.
The latest Welsh policing figures show 6,157 police-recorded hate crimes across Wales between April 2025 and March 2026, including 4,098 motivated by race and 325 motivated by religion.
Of those, 325 had a religious motivation, down from 451; however, there is no breakdown of which religion was targeted, so it is not possible from these figures to determine the number of anti-Jewish crimes.
The UK's Community Security Trust, however, separately recorded 25 antisemitic incidents geographically associated with Wales during calendar year 2025, including 13 in North Wales, 8 in South Wales, 2 in Dyfed-Powys and 2 in Gwent.
Separately, a Freedom of Information disclosure from Dyfed-Powys Police shows the force recorded 17 crimes classified as anti-Jewish in 2025, up from 12 in 2024, an increase of about 42%.
The figures are for the Dyfed-Powys policing area, not all Wales. They also do not necessarily capture every antisemitic offense recorded under other categories. It also, of course, differs from the CST reporting, suggesting that on-the-ground figures may far exceed those ultimately reported to CST.
While the available national police statistics do not establish how many anti-Jewish crimes occurred specifically in Wales, the number is clearly high enough to be deemed serious, as the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) recently met with Jewish community representatives from across Wales to discuss tackling antisemitism.
During the meeting, Jewish community representatives spoke about growing anxiety about antisemitism, including routine verbal abuse, concerns about children in schools and people changing their behavior to avoid identifying as Jewish in public.
The South Wales Jewish Representative Council said: “The Welsh Jewish community is long-established and deeply rooted."
"We are a resilient community, but there is no doubt that the rise in antisemitism in recent years has left many people shaken and concerned."
Forms, sources of antisemitism in Wales
What forms does antisemitism take in Wales, and who does it come from?
"In a sense, it's a microcosm of England, and similarly a lot of the antisemitism is on social media," Abrams told the Post. "Obviously, a lot of it coalesces around the Israel-Palestine conflict."
Abrams referenced the phenomenon known as "ambient antisemitism," which speaks to the impact demonstrations, ripping down posters, putting up stickers, ripping down stickers, and the like have on creating an environment that is hostile to Jews.
"It's not specifically hurting Jews, physically, but it creates an environment in which Jews are not comfortable being themselves. And I think that's quite a good way to describe it here."
Abrams' experience of antisemitism, he continued, is shaped by living in the northwest of Wales, which is highly nationalist, Welsh-speaking and supportive of Plaid Cymru, the left-leaning Welsh nationalist political party.
Plaid Cymru's official stance is critical of Israel and very supportive of Palestine. It has long campaigned for Palestinian State recognition, and deems Israel's actions to be genocide. In September 2025, the party leader called for "harsh sanctions against the Israeli Government" in light of its actions in Gaza.
"Wales has always been a place where there's been eyes on Palestine. It fits in with the narrative that the Welsh Nationalists have of themselves. The first colony of the British Empire was the Welsh, so [they see themselves as] the Palestinians of the British."
"Because of this, the antisemitism here is kind of an obsession with Israel," Abrams continued. "You'll get the antisemitism that's expressed by people who don't think they're being antisemitic."
"The position I would take [in Wales] is that many people are well-meaning but cross the line into antisemitism through repetition of age-old tropes. They won't know that this emphasis on killing babies has been used throughout history."
Abrams also noted a class difference in Wales regarding who cares about Israel-Palestine and who does not.
"If you're working class, you probably don't care; you probably hate the demonstrators more. Whereas the middle-class protesters are kind of indistinguishable from the academic antisemitism."
"A lot of it is not expressed in front of Jews, because Welsh society is polite. Older, middle-class Brits, right, aren't so vulgar as to be openly racist."
"So I would say across Wales, outside of the metropolises, it's older white people, do-gooders, right thinking, wrong application."
As discussed in his book, Welsh attitudes towards Jews started with Israel and now, 1600 years later, have returned full circle.
"The complexity of Jewishness is still reduced to the Middle East conflict," Abrams concluded.

France: Lawmakers must reject regressive “Rioters Pay” bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:50:43 UTC
03:50:43 KST

France’s proposed bill to make demonstrators pay for damage caused to property by acts of violence in street protests, even if they did not directly cause it themselves, will have a chilling effect on freedom of peaceful assembly and must be rejected by lawmakers, Amnesty International said ahead of a two-day debate in the Senate.
This bill threatens to further deter people from exercising their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly
Nathalie Godard, Amnesty International France
If passed, the legislation commonly referred to as the “Rioters Pay” bill, could hold individuals liable for acts they did not personally commit, provided they ‘knowingly’ participated in a gathering where acts of violence, theft, destruction, or property damage took place. A protester could be liable to pay up to 10,000 euros; in addition, social benefits could be seized if compensation is not paid, which risks plunging already marginalised families further into poverty. Parents may also be held civilly liable for acts that their children did not commit.
“This bill, coming on the back of a series of legal amendments to restrict the right of protest in France, threatens to further deter people from taking to the streets to exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly,” said Nathalie Godard, Director of the Action Department at Amnesty International France.
“Holding protesters responsible – and making them pay – for acts committed by others creates a risk of arbitrary punishment and would be contrary to France’s international obligations. If passed, this bill would be a deeply regressive step, and it must be categorially rejected by lawmakers.”
Under international law, those participating in demonstrations may only be held responsible for their own conduct and any such responsibility must be based on evidence of individual culpability.
If passed, this bill would be a deeply regressive step, and it must be categorially rejected by lawmakers
Natalie Goddard, Amnesty International France
Under current French law, family social security allowances and housing benefits are generally protected from seizure to recover debts. The bill introduces additional exceptions to this protection, allowing these benefits to be seized to recover compensation. This would include where damage is caused by children and would reduce the financial support available to families to meet their essential needs and costs. The bill further allows for the possibility of seizing payments from the Active Solidarity Income (Revenu de Solidarité Active), a benefit designed to provide a minimum income for people who would otherwise have no or very low income.
“Seizing family allowances, housing assistance, or the active solidarity income could have disastrous consequences for some of the most vulnerable people, impacting their ability to access an adequate standard of living for themselves and their families,” said Natalie Goddard.
The proposed bill also expands the scope of the penalty of exclusion from French territory for people who are ‘foreign nationals’ and who have been found guilty of certain serious offences committed during public gatherings. These include attacks against the physical integrity of others, serious damage to property, such as arson, and aggravated theft or looting.
Amnesty International calls on the lawmakers to ensure that in no case should the penalty of expulsion from French territory result in the violation of the principle of non-refoulement, which is absolute and prohibits the expulsion of anyone, regardless of status, to a place where they would be at real risk of persecution or human rights violations.
“Existing law already allows for the penalty of expulsion from French territory. We are therefore deeply concerned that this amendment may introduce xenophobic rhetoric into the legislative debate, and further fuel the scapegoating of refugees, migrants, asylum seekers and minorities,” said Nathalie Godard.
Background
The bill is due to be debated by the French Senate on 27 and 28 October.
The French government announced the proposed bill titled “Compensation for damage resulting from violence or property damage in public spaces and the recovery of damages” in the summer of 2026, following the incidents of violence and property damage during the UEFA Champions League final in May 2026. The French authorities put this bill on the parliamentary agenda and initiated an accelerated procedure for its consideration in the context of the ongoing protests in France, which started on 31 August 2026 in the overseas territories and from 18 September in Metropolitan France.

Anthropic warns the risk of AI-created weapons could slow frontier models down

As artificial intelligence pioneer Anthropic prepares to go public, the company has warned users—including scientists—on Monday that advanced models may be delayed because of cybersecurity and safety threats that risk eclipsing the models’ benefits.
In documents filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission ahead of Anthropic’s expected initial public offering, the AI lab vowed to weigh the effects of its models on the public good before issuing any new products.
“Moving quickly brings AI’s benefits sooner, but moving too quickly could outrun the world’s ability to make AI systems safe,” the company wrote.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In the filing, Anthropic acknowledged that its future relies on outpacing its competition in developing increasingly capable and complex large language models. But it also raised the risk of its AI being used for harmful purposes, such as developing biological or chemical weapons.
“We deploy technical safeguards, including automated classifiers, specifically intended to detect and block these categories of misuse,” the company warned. “But such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented.” The comments reflect a debate among AI experts over what adequate safety testing looks like in light of repeated AI breaches and hacks.
Still, Anthropic highlighted the potential for new discoveries in biology and medical sciences as a key pathway to profitability—the company currently runs at a loss in the billions of dollars. Anthropic cited its life sciences laboratory, which recently discovered a segment of DNA that bears some resemblance to CRISPR, as an example of how it could access new markets. Even that expansion presents dangers, the company acknowledged, because more traditional science and research is outside its current area of expertise.
“These activities expose us to categories of liability, including for workplace injury and environmental contamination, that differ from those associated with our core business,” the company acknowledged.
Anthropic also warned investors that the company will like make investments into compute power that could appear “irresponsibly large at first glance.” Those vast sums of money are part of a bet that AI will have “wild exponential” growth.
“In order to fully capture the opportunity in front of us, we need to invest more aggressively than would a business that operates in a more slowly changing technological regime,” the company wrote.

Google Fitbit Edge Review: I Still Prefer the Air (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:49:49 UTC
03:49:49 KST

The Edge brings Fitbit’s screen-equipped offerings up to speed with better health tracking, a brighter display, and improved durability. After testing it, I’m still not ready to give up my Fitbit Air.
Google’s first repairable tracker. A bigger screen with adjustable brightness. More advanced health metrics and workout tracking.
TIRED
Band fastening can be finicky. Auto-pause can be overly sensitive. No Google Wallet.
Earlier this year, the Google Fitbit Air won me over and made me wonder why I ever wanted a display on my fitness tracker in the first place. Of course, not everyone is ready to quit the screen cold turkey, especially if your wearable doubles as your everyday smartwatch. Google Fitbit hasn’t introduced a new tracker with a screen since 2023, and the older models are starting to fall behind on health features and hardware. That deters both newcomers who want a screen and longtime users who have to choose among aging models.
At $180, the new Google Fitbit Edge costs $20 more than Fitbit's Charge 6 ($160) and $80 more than the screenless Air ($100), but far less than Google's Pixel Watch 5 ($400). After 12 days of testing, I’d recommend it to Fitbit owners looking to upgrade. Personally, though, the Edge hasn’t given me enough reasons to give up my Fitbit Air.
A Screen Has Its Perks
The Edge is comfortable enough to wear throughout the day and overnight. Its dimensions are slightly larger than the Charge 6’s (39.2 x 25.5 x 11.5 mm versus 36.73 x 23.09 x 11.20 mm), but I found the capsule shape sat more naturally on my wrist than its predecessor’s rectangular build. It feels like a better option for people with slimmer wrists and those who might find the Pixel Watch or Apple Watch too bulky to sleep with.
As with any smartwatch, comfort also depends on the band. The Edge comes with Google’s Active Band, which is fine for workouts but isn’t my favorite of the available options. Google also offers the HNBR (high-performance synthetic elastomer) Active Sport, the breathable Performance Loop, the silicone Magnet band, and the Metal Links band.
I found myself alternating between the Metal Links and Performance Loop. I love the look of the former for a night out or a more formal setting, and the latter is best for everyday wear. The Performance Loop’s micro-adjustable fit makes it easy to get a precise fit, but it's just as easy to pull it a little too tight. I also noticed that the band occasionally popped loose while I was adjusting it. The tracker was still attached from one side, so I wasn’t worried about losing it, but the fastening mechanism didn’t feel as secure as it should. I eventually noticed that the locking button was stuck and had to fiddle with the mechanism to fix the issue.
The 1.34-inch display is the Edge’s obvious advantage over the screenless Air. I noticed the difference most during workouts. On outdoor runs, I could check my metrics and control my music without slowing down. The display also reaches roughly twice the Charge’s maximum brightness, making it easier to read in direct sunlight. With Google Maps integration, I could follow turn-by-turn directions from my wrist while running or cycling, without having to pull out my phone.
I do prefer Wear OS’s more colorful interface; Fitbit’s watch faces also feel a little elementary by comparison. But Fitbit’s software offers up to seven days of battery life, which is a feature the Pixel Watch can’t match. The Edge is also compatible with both iOS and Android, unlike the Pixel Watch. Plus, in a first for Fitbit, the Edge is Google’s first repairable fitness tracker, with modular construction including a replaceable battery, matching the Pixel Watch. This is likely due to battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union, which will require removable and replaceable batteries in smartphones, smartwatches, and similar devices starting February 18, 2027.
Two Steps Forward, One Step Back
The Edge is a significant upgrade over the Charge 6 when it comes to health and fitness capabilities. Google has added more detailed workout metrics and a few hardware upgrades that make the Edge a more capable fitness tracker.
Some of the additions are aimed at long-term health tracking. Like the Pixel Watch 5 and the Air, the Edge offers monthly blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Its SpO2 readings now include nightly averages, ranges, and changes over time. There’s also 24/7 heart rate tracking, cardio load metrics, and an updated ECG app with atrial fibrillation (AFib) detection. Alongside nutrition logging, if you use a continuous glucose monitor (CGM), you can view glucose insights.
Like any Google wearable, most features are locked behind Google Health Premium, which costs $10 per month or $100 annually. Without the subscription, you still get the core metrics and scores, but the deeper analysis and AI coaching are inaccessible. In other words, the Google Health Premium membership is essential to the experience. (Buying any new device gets you a three-month trial.)
The hardware has also caught up to Google’s latest models. A barometric altimeter measures elevation changes and floors climbed. The Edge also finally gets an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. Its display brings more of these metrics to your watch face, including live workout data and visual guidance.
Google adds a gyroscope that improves automatic activity recognition, but it may have overcorrected a little. During outdoor runs, the Edge auto-paused when I stopped and resumed when I started moving again. At times, it was too sensitive; even taking a single step forward while catching my breath sometimes restarted my workout. It’s not a major downside, but worth noting that I sometimes had to correct the Edge’s decisions.
The Charge 6 supports contactless payments, but the Edge doesn’t, which feels like a regression for a newer model. If you want to use the Edge as a smartwatch, the lack of NFC technology is disappointing. I didn’t miss it much myself because I rarely leave home without my phone, but it’s a beloved feature that shouldn’t have disappeared without good reason.
The Fitbit Edge is a robust smartwatch, and Charge 6 owners will be happy with the improvements. I’m less convinced it’ll win over newcomers. The Fitbit Air remains the most appealing value in Google’s lineup, and the Edge doesn’t offer much more to change that. Without NFC for contactless payment, it feels like a smartwatch with one too many compromises.
Boutayna Chokrane is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering consumer wearables, wellness tech, and online trends. She specializes in smartwatches, fitness trackers, beauty tech, and more. Before joining the Gear team, she was a music editorial fellow at Pitchfork. She also worked as a freelance journalist, covering fashion, ... Read More

U.S. Air Force F-16 fighter jet to get hypersonic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:47:46 UTC
03:47:46 KST

- Castelion received a contract modification from the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin integrating its Blackbeard hypersonic missile onto the F-16.
- The company did not disclose the value or timeline, and the U.S. Navy has already ordered 444 Blackbeard missiles for production.
Hypersonic missile startup Castelion has received a contract modification from the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin integrating its Blackbeard hypersonic weapon onto the F-16 fighter jet, the company announced on Oct. 26, bringing the missile one step closer to the U.S. Air Force after earlier work for the U.S. Navy and U.S. Army.
Castelion did not disclose the value of the modification, how long the integration work will take, or when the first test launch from an F-16 could happen, and the U.S. Air Force has not commented on the award.
“Castelion has been awarded a contract modification to its existing work with the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin Blackbeard integration activities with the F-16. We are grateful to the Air Force for their trust,” the company wrote on X.
Blackbeard is designed to fly faster than Mach 5 while maneuvering inside the atmosphere, which makes it harder to intercept than a ballistic missile on a predictable arc, and Castelion has built the program around producing it cheaply and in large numbers. The company, founded in 2022 by former SpaceX engineers and based in Torrance, California, is building a factory campus in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, aimed at turning out 500 weapons a year.
The Air Force Research Laboratory added $16.4 million to an existing Castelion contract in September, raising its total value to $37.2 million, for work on a low-cost, mass-producible long-range strike weapon running through June 2028. Castelion described the F-16 award as a modification to its existing work with the laboratory, though it did not say whether it falls under that same contract.
The U.S. Navy is furthest along with the weapon. It awarded $105 million in April to integrate Blackbeard onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and carry out live-fire testing in the Indo-Pacific, ordered 50 early operational capability weapons in June, and in August awarded nearly $90 million to move Blackbeard toward a formal program of record, including features meant to speed sales to allies. In September, the Navy placed a first production order worth up to $200 million for 444 missiles. The U.S. Army received an integration award in October 2025 for a ground-launched version compatible with the HIMARS rocket launcher.
Putting Blackbeard on the F-16 would give it a launch platform far more common than the Super Hornet. The F-16 remains the most numerous fighter in the U.S. Air Force and flies with more than two dozen other countries, although Castelion has not said whether the integration work covers export versions of the jet.

Ukraine Extends Martial Law and Mobilization Until Jan. 29
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:47:02 UTC
03:47:02 KST

Ukraine has extended martial law and general mobilization for another 90 days, until Jan. 29, 2027, as Russia’s full-scale invasion continues in its fifth year.
Since February 2022, both measures have been renewed every three months. On Monday, Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky signed laws No. 5029-IX on martial law and No. 5030-IX on mobilization after they were approved by the parliament on the same day.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Both laws take effect on Oct. 31, when the current extension expires, Ukrinform reported.
Decrees cite ongoing Russian aggression
The laws Zelensky signed approve two presidential decrees; No. 1060/2026 on extending martial law and No. 1061/2026 on extending general mobilization, which required parliament’s consent to take effect.
The martial law decree points to Russia’s continuing large-scale armed aggression against Ukraine as the reason for the extensions.
It was issued on a proposal from the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC), under Article 106 of Ukraine’s Constitution and the law on the legal regime of martial law. The decree amends Article 1 of Decree No. 64/2022 of Feb. 24, 2022, which first introduced martial law nationwide.
Parliament backs extension
According to Ukrinform, lawmakers approved both measures earlier on Monday, after parliament’s committee on national security, defense and intelligence had endorsed them.
Bill No. 16182, approving the martial law decree, received 293 votes, while Bill No. 16183, covering mobilization, passed with 281 in favor.
Trump’s Diesel Scam Backfires
Speaking in parliament ahead of the vote, NSDC Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine Ihor Klymenko said the extension would help Ukraine take “adequate measures to counter armed aggression.” The move would also safeguard the country’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, he argued.
According to Klymenko, the extension also keeps in force the special powers held by state authorities, the military command, military administrations and local governments, which they need to repel the invasion.
Deferment rules tightened days earlier
The extension comes days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretsky’s government finalized an overhaul of Ukraine’s worker deferment system on Oct. 23, effectively ending automatic exemptions from mobilization for defense and energy companies.
Unless they qualify for a deferment due to health-related issues or work, Ukrainian law requires men aged 25 to 60 to serve in the military. Under the previous rules, most critical companies could defer up to 50% of their draft-age employees, while defense and energy firms have been allowed to defer up to 100%.
The latest overhaul ends automatic 100% protection and aims to create fair rules for those working away from the front, and, above all, for soldiers who have been fighting for nearly five years and need a realistic chance to return home.
“Unconditional full deferment is unfair to those who serve and opens the door to misuse,” Koretskyi said earlier, adding that some companies had been set up purely to obtain deferments and that “it became a business.”
The new approach makes full protection conditional – companies can keep their entire workforce only in case they contribute to the military on a rotating basis.
“The ultimate goal is that no one has to search for anyone on the streets,” Koretskyi said, in an apparent reference to recruiters forcibly detaining men in public.
Defense manufacturers have already lobbied against the new measures, noting that lowering the quota, even to 85%, could halt production lines, delay weapons deliveries and expose companies to penalties for missing state contract lines.
Speaking at the Kyiv International Economic Forum on Monday, Koretskyi reiterated that Russia could mobilize another 300,000 to 500,000 people. Without planning ahead, he argued, Kyiv could again be forced into unpopular emergency decisions.
On Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree No. 700, increasing the size of Russia’s armed forces to 2.4 million, including 1.5 million active-duty military personnel, marking the fourth time such a decree was signed in 2026 alone.
Around the same time, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia had already begun additional mobilization, including the expansion of foreign troops, with over 8,000 already in Russia and up to 50,000 more planned.

An independent review has been launched into the murder of 18-year-old Henry Nowak, with an initial report expected by March 2027, UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced.
The review will be led by former Conservative Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC and will examine the circumstances surrounding Nowak’s death, including potential missed opportunities to prevent the attack and the treatment of his family by criminal justice agencies.

Feed recommendations are the most common way teens encounter self-harm content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:48 UTC
03:00:48 KST

An analysis of data from the 2025 OxWell Student Survey found that about a third of 11- to 18-year-old students in England had come across self-harm content online in the past month. Most of these encounters were unintentional, and about two-thirds of exposed students said the content had appeared in their social media feeds or been suggested while they were browsing. Students who were lonelier, had experienced other online harms, or had poorer mental health were more likely to report exposure. The paper was published in Nature Mental Health.
Social media has become an integral part of young people’s everyday lives. It provides wide opportunities for communication, entertainment, self-expression, and social connection. Platforms such as TikTok and Instagram offer an almost endless stream of content, much of which is selected by recommendation algorithms that personalize what users see based on their interests and online behavior.
While this personalization can help users discover content they enjoy, it can also expose them to potentially harmful material. One particular concern is content related to self-harm, which can range from personal stories of recovery and supportive discussions to graphic images and videos that portray self-injury in a positive or encouraging way.
Research suggests that repeated exposure to such content may increase emotional distress and the risk of self-harming thoughts and behaviors, particularly among vulnerable adolescents. However, the effects are not always negative, as some online communities that discuss self-harm also provide emotional support and encourage young people to seek help.
Adolescents also do not need to search for self-harm content to encounter it, as recommendation algorithms may place it in their feeds without them seeking it out. Their interactions with such content may then lead algorithms to recommend more similar material, potentially creating a cycle of repeated exposure.
Study author Holly Bear of the University of Oxford and colleagues examined how often adolescents in England reported coming across self-harm content online in the past month and the routes through which this happened. They were particularly interested in whether exposure was passive (unintentional) or active, such as searching for the content or having it shared with them, and how these different routes related to students’ demographic characteristics, social experiences, and mental health.
The researchers analyzed data from the 2025 OxWell Student Survey, a school-based survey of young people in England run by researchers at the University of Oxford. The analysis drew on 32,102 students in school years 7 through 13 (ages 11 to 18) at 49 secondary schools and further education colleges, mainly in Liverpool and Oxfordshire, who completed the survey between February and May 2025.
Students were asked whether they had come across content about self-harm on online platforms in the past month and, if so, how. They also answered questions about loneliness, bullying, online aggression and coercion, and symptoms of anxiety and depression. A total of 28,797 students answered the question about exposure, 14,083 of whom were girls.
Of these students, 9,940 (34.5%) reported encountering self-harm content online in the past month. Most of them (55%) had seen it once or twice, while 26.5% had seen it a few times and 18.5% several times.
Among exposed students who described how they came across the content, 66% said it had appeared in their feed or been suggested while they were browsing, and 24% said it was embedded within other, unrelated content. Fewer said they had accidentally encountered it (12%), searched for it (8%), or had it shared with them by someone else (8%), and 15% reported some other route.
Based on these answers, the researchers sorted students into groups. Nearly three-quarters (73%) had been exposed only through passive routes, 12% through a mix of routes, 9% only through “other” routes, 3% only by having the content shared with them, and 3% only by searching for it.
How often students saw the content depended on how they encountered it. Most students exposed only passively (59%) or only through content shared by others (62%) had seen it just once or twice in the past month, compared with about 30% of those who had only searched for it or who were exposed through a mix of routes. The authors note this is consistent with a feedback loop in which actively engaging with self-harm content leads algorithms to show more of it.
Each exposure route was associated with higher levels of loneliness, online harms, anxiety, and depression compared with students who reported no exposure, though the patterns differed across groups. Girls had higher odds than boys of passive-only exposure but lower odds of having content shared with them, and trans and gender-diverse students had elevated odds across most routes, particularly searching for the content.
Black students and students from mixed ethnic backgrounds were more likely than white students to have only searched for the content, as were students who often went to bed hungry compared with those who rarely did. Searching was most strongly linked to depression, while having content shared by others was more closely tied to receiving aggressive or threatening messages online. Students exposed through a mix of routes had some of the most pronounced risk profiles, with especially strong links to online aggression and coercion.
“Exposure to online self-harm content is widespread and shaped by distinct pathways that differ according to adolescents’ wider vulnerabilities, social environments and digital behaviors. Around one-third of our large community sample reported recent exposure, underscoring the need for interventions that account for diverse exposure experiences, from passive, algorithmically driven delivery to more intentional searches and peer sharing,” study authors concluded.
The authors call for a public health approach that combines regulation to reduce self-harm content in feeds, efforts to direct young people who search for it toward supportive resources, and digital literacy education for adolescents and their parents.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of how adolescents encounter self-harm content online. However, it should be noted that the survey was cross-sectional, so it cannot show whether loneliness, online harms, and mental health difficulties make exposure more likely, result from exposure, or both. The researchers also did not ask what kind of self-harm content students saw, which could range from graphic material to recovery stories and peer support.
In an earlier wave of the survey, about two-thirds of students who had actively sought out self-harm content cited potentially positive motivations, such as finding support or connecting with others with similar experiences. The data were self-reported and came mainly from two regions of England, and the wording of the exposure question, which asked whether students had “come across” such content, may have led some who sought it out to underreport.
The paper, “Algorithmically driven exposure to online self-harm content and its association with broader psychosocial risk in 32,000 adolescents,” was authored by Holly Bear, Emma Soneson, Galit Geulayov, and Mina Fazel.
