US midterm elections 2026 in maps and charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:07 UTC
03:00:07 KST

US midterms 2026: All you need to know in maps and charts
On November 3, Americans decide which party controls the US Congress for the second half of Donald Trump’s presidency.
On November 3, about 210 million registered voters will decide how much power Donald Trump has for the rest of his US presidency.
Trump is not on the ballot, but control of the United States Congress is. Made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate, Congress writes the country’s laws and controls federal spending.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera breaks down how the elections work, which races matter and what the results could mean for either party.
What happens in the midterm elections?
Held halfway through a US president’s four-year term, midterm elections decide the makeup of Congress.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested, including special elections in the states of Florida and Ohio to fill the seats vacated by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance. Voters in 36 states will also elect governors.
House members represent one congressional district each and serve two-year terms, while senators serve six-year terms.
Midterm elections are also widely considered a referendum on the sitting president’s performance.
Since 1946, the president’s party has lost an average of 26.5 seats in the House and a handful in the Senate in midterm elections, according to Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University.
Beyond Congress and governors, voters will also elect state legislators and local officials.
Nadia Brown, a professor of government at Georgetown University, said that while national elections get most of the attention, “It is important to remember that local politics is where most Americans interact with government.”
She added that “It is the local propositions or referendums on ballots [that] will impact the everyday lives of people.”
What is at stake in the House and Senate?
Republicans hold majorities in both chambers. Losing either would give Democrats the power to block legislation and launch investigations into Trump’s administration.
Democrats need to gain three seats in the House and four in the Senate to take control. A 50-50 split in the Senate would leave Republicans in control, because Vance can cast tie-breaking votes.
Belt said a Democratic victory could significantly limit Trump’s ability to pursue his domestic agenda.
“If Democrats take one chamber, all non-government funding legislation will grind to a halt,” he told Al Jazeera.
How do House elections work?
The House of Representatives is the lower house of the US Congress.
Its 435 members each represent one local district and serve two-year terms, so every seat is contested every two years.
Seats are divided among the states by population, based on the US Census conducted every 10 years. California, the most populous state, has 52 seats, while the least populous, such as Wyoming and Vermont, have one each.
A party needs 218 seats for a majority.
Republicans currently control the House, with 218 seats to the Democrats’ 214, and one independent sits with the Republicans. Two seats are vacant, one last held by each party.
The new House will be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
The House races to watch
Each district elects its own representative, and the party that wins 218 seats takes control, so a few narrow wins in close districts can decide the majority.
Belt estimates that about 35 House races could decide the majority. He predicts Democrats could gain about 15 seats, despite Republican redistricting that he says has given the party an advantage in nine additional districts.
“People generally vote straight ticket, meaning they will vote for all the candidates of one party, so this is likely to affect down-ballot races [as well],” he said.
A battleground district is a seat either party could realistically win. The graphic below highlights 12 of these key races to watch.
How do Senate elections work?
The Senate is the upper house of the US Congress.
Its 100 members, two from each state regardless of population, are elected statewide and serve six-year terms, with about a third of seats contested every two years.
This year, 33 seats are being contested in regular elections, alongside special elections in Florida and Ohio. Those two contests will fill the remaining two years of terms previously held by Marco Rubio and JD Vance.
Of the 35 seats being contested, Republicans hold 22, and Democrats hold 13.
Republicans currently have 53 senators. Democrats have 45, and two independents sit with them, giving the Democratic bloc 47 seats.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 and take control. Republicans can keep control with 50 because Vice President Vance can break tied votes.
The new Senate will be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
The Senate races to watch
To win the Senate, Democrats must hold the 13 seats they are defending and flip Republican-held ones.
In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff faces Republican Mike Collins. Michigan’s open seat pits Democrat Abdul El-Sayed against Republican Mike Rogers, while Democrat Chris Pappas faces Republican John Sununu for an open seat in New Hampshire.
Republican-held seats offer Democrats opportunities elsewhere. In Maine, Senator Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson, who replaced primary winner Graham Platner after he withdrew in July. North Carolina’s open seat pits Democrat Roy Cooper against Republican Michael Whatley.
Ohio, Alaska and Iowa are also competitive, while Texas and Kansas have drawn growing attention as Democrats look for more routes to a majority.
Although Democrats face a more difficult path to a Senate majority than to control of the House, the growing number of competitive races has increased their chances of winning the chamber, according to election analysts.
What are the key election issues?
The cost of living tops voters’ concerns, with rising petrol prices, housing costs and healthcare coverage squeezing household budgets.
Reproductive rights remain a major issue, while immigration and the state of US democracy are also on the ballot.
The US-Israel war on Iran and the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI)` and data centres have raised further questions about security, jobs and energy costs.
Who votes in the midterms?
About 210 million Americans are registered to vote, nearly eight in 10 US residents aged 18 or older, according to USAFacts, a nonpartisan organisation that compiles government data.
California has the most registered voters, with 23.2 million, followed by Texas (17.4 million) and Florida (13.6 million). Together, they account for about 26 percent of all registered voters.
Wyoming (278,468), Vermont (459,455) and Alaska (603,310) have the fewest.
How different groups plan to vote
A Pew Research Center survey conducted from September 28 to October 4 found that 44 percent of registered voters backed the Democratic candidate in their district, compared with 36 percent for the Republican. Five percent support another candidate, and 15 percent are unsure.
Men are evenly split, with 42 percent backing each party, while women favour Democrats by 45 percent to 31 percent.
The graphic below shows how voting preferences differ by gender, race, age, education and party affiliation.
US election voter turnout
Fewer Americans vote in midterms than in presidential elections. Since 1944, average turnout has been about 42 percent in midterms, compared with 58 percent in presidential races.
What happens if Republicans lose the House?
A Democratic House could block Republican legislation and use its committees to investigate the Trump administration. It would also hold the power to impeach the president, which only the House can do.
Control would also give Democrats leverage over government funding. Every bill needs approval from both chambers, so a Republican Senate could not pass laws on its own.
Belt expects a Democratic-controlled House to lead to more confrontations over federal spending, including the 12 annual bills needed to fund federal agencies. That raises the possibility of further government shutdowns, when funding lapses and many federal services stop.
Belt also believes that Trump could turn increasingly to foreign policy if his domestic agenda faces opposition in Congress.
“Traditionally, presidents facing divided government in their last two years pivot to foreign policy almost exclusively. I think the same will be true for Trump,” he said.
What happens if Republicans lose the Senate?
A Democratic Senate could block legislation and reject presidential nominees, including federal judges, Supreme Court justices, cabinet officials and ambassadors.
That makes Senate control consequential beyond the next two years. Federal judges serve for life, shaping rulings long after a presidency ends.
The Senate also holds the trial if the House impeaches a president. Removing a president from office requires a two-thirds majority, a threshold neither party is likely to reach.
Would winning both chambers give Democrats full control?
No. Trump would remain president and could veto legislation, and overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber.
Senate rules also require 60 votes to end debate on most legislation, though some budget bills can pass with a simple majority. A narrow majority therefore does not guarantee a party can pass its programme.
A Democratic House could open impeachment proceedings against Trump, who has already been impeached twice. However, removing a president from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate.
Belt considers another impeachment unlikely.
“There will definitely be investigations,” he told Al Jazeera, but added, “There will not likely be another impeachment because Democrats tried that twice and Republicans rallied behind Trump.”
When will we know the results?
Results will begin emerging after the first polls close at 6pm Eastern time (23:00 GMT) on November 3, but some close races could take days to resolve.
Election night results are preliminary. Final tallies can take days or sometimes weeks as officials count mail-in, provisional and other outstanding ballots before certifying the results, and the pace varies by state.
“In some states, it may take up to a week or more,” Belt said.
Some contests may go further. In Georgia, if no Senate candidate wins a majority, the race goes to a run-off election on December 1.
Belt warned that early results could give a misleading picture of the outcome. Because Republicans have historically been less likely than Democrats to vote by mail, some states could initially appear to favour Republican candidates before later-counted ballots narrow or reverse their leads. This is known as the “red mirage”. In states that count mail ballots first, the reverse can happen.
A delay in counting or a change in which candidate is leading does not, by itself, indicate electoral fraud.
The vote will decide who writes legislation, scrutinises the administration and controls federal spending, setting the balance of power for the rest of Trump’s term.

Volcanoes lurk behind the scenes of human history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Volcanoes lurk behind the scenes of human history
Cold spells after eruptions may have spurred famine, disease, revolt and religious changes
“The bright sun was extinguish’d … and the icy earth swung blind and blackening in the moonless air.” These words from Lord Byron’s 1816 poem Darkness evoke a hellish apocalypse. But Byron may have been inspired by the fallout of a real cataclysm — one that happened half a world away.
Mount Tambora, in present-day Indonesia, blew its top in 1815. More than 71,000 people in the vicinity died. And climate-cooling aerosols from the eruption ushered in extreme weather the following years in far-flung places. Cold weather in the summer of 1816, sometimes with frosts and snow, destroyed corn in New England, rice and buckwheat in China and wheat, oats and potatoes in Ireland. In some places, the rising cost of bread sparked protests and riots. The circumstances may have helped spread typhus. Some called 1816 “the year without a summer,” others “the year of the beggars.”
Like Tambora, volcanoes, and the cooling they cause, may be an underappreciated geologic force at times moving behind the scenes of human history.
“These climatic impacts of the Tambora eruption were recorded without any knowledge that this had anything to do with an eruption,” says Clive Oppenheimer, a volcanologist at the University of Cambridge.
While Tambora is the most well-studied eruption in history, others have also rattled the planet. Oppenheimer and his colleagues analyzed 38 large eruptions in the 2026 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences. Their work pulled together studies linking the geologic events and their effects on climate with their potential societal fallout in food systems, the economy, unrest, culture and religion. The locations and exact timing of the eruptions that spurred some notable cold spurts aren’t known. But understanding how the events impacted the climate, environment and society can offer clues to the past, including how people coped with climate stress.
“Volcanic eruptions, they are kind of this like hammer blow to the climate system,” says Heli Huhtamaa, a climate and environmental historian at the University of Bern in Switzerland. Volcanoes may offer lessons about resilience for modern societies in a warming world, she says.
Volcanic gases create a chilling effect
Volcanoes spew sulfur-containing gases. Over weeks, those gases react in the atmosphere to form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. Paintings from years after eruptions show bloodred sunsets or landscapes shrouded by hazy skies.
Because no two eruptions are exactly alike, it takes work to grasp each one’s impacts on weather and climate. “If we understand the climate response of one [eruption], that does not mean that we understand the climate response of another,” says Ulf Büntgen, a paleoclimatologist at the University of Cambridge.
Up in the air
A volcano’s explosivity impacts how high it shoots its gases and where they travel. Over time, those gases form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. In this computer model of a 1991 eruption, colors represent how high particles are in the atmosphere. Red is high and blue is closer to Earth’s surface.
Researchers find the traces of past eruptions in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. Scientists try to nail down the date on a sulfur-loaded ice core layer and compare it with tree ring data, a logbook of sorts for summer growing conditions since temperatures impact how trees lay down their wood each year. Scientists can pull together tree ring records from far-flung places and use statistics to work out annual temperatures in a hemisphere.
Cold spells sometimes jump out from tree ring records. For years when cool summers impeded the final stages of wood formation, a chemical method used to estimate temperatures turns wood layers blue. Büntgen and colleagues saw two blue rings around 1345. “And that is very rare. We never saw that two years in a row,” he says. The rings coincided with the timing of the Black Death’s spread in Europe, the team reported in 2025 in Communications Earth & Environment. The researchers traced the connections between chilly summers, poor grain harvests in the Mediterranean and shipping records showing how Italian city states imported flea-ridden grain from the Caucasus.
Oppenheimer, Büntgen and their colleagues broadened the detective work for their 2026 review. The team studied Northern Hemisphere temperature responses to the 38 largest eruptions between A.D. 1 and 1900. On average, each volcano caused about 0.5 degrees Celsius of cooling in the year after the eruption. Recovery to normal temperatures was slower for eruptions that occurred in times that were already colder on average, Büntgen says. In some periods, large or successive eruptions may lead to an elevated amounts of particles in the atmosphere for a long time. The team’s calculations show that high aerosol levels concur with some of the past two millennia’s coldest spells, such as the one preceding the Black Death.
Human agency factors into eruptions’ outcomes
Those cold snaps often had dire consequences. Out of 17 large-scale famines in Europe from 1300 to 1800, 11 followed major eruptions. In addition to faltering crops and famines, the most frequently societal responses described in studies collected by the review authors were disease outbreaks, political turmoil and migration.
The societal circumstances surrounding eruptions are as important as the amount of cooling, Huhtamaa says. She and her colleagues studied crop failures and farmstead desertion in three different volcanic eruptions that impacted Ostrobothnia, in what is now Finland. During the 17th century, Ostrobothnia experienced cooling from three sets of eruptions at different time periods.
Although the latest eruption event, in 1695, was the coldest of all, peasants fared better than they had after eruptions earlier in the century, Huhtamaa and colleagues reported in 2022 in Climate of the Past. Though people still starved, only around 7 percent of peasants lost their farmland, compared with 20 percent in the other periods. This was because the crown provided tax relief, Huhtamaa says. This wasn’t humanitarian aid, as it was meant to preserve the tax base and prevent possibly decades of lost revenue.
“When there is a climatic shock, it doesn’t matter if it’s 0.5 or 1.5 degrees cooler, because what really matters is the societal vulnerability,” Huhtamaa says.
Studies like Huhtamaa’s reveal how societies can tick on in spite of climate disasters. But historians haven’t always been keen to look to climate for clues to explain history. Human agency has often been considered the only reasonable explanation for human affairs, Huhtamaa says. “And climate explanations sounded lazy.”
Investigating societies’ preconditions and responses to the climate change caused by volcanoes could help people prepare for a now warming world. A recent report from the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, noted that not enough research had been done on responses, Huhtamaa says. Researchers could examine one place’s response to different events, as in Huhtamaa’s work on Ostrobothnia, or parse different locales’ responses to the same event. Meanwhile, greater use of insights from ecology, agronomy and economics, for instance, can help with this detective work that reveals how humans respond to climatic events beyond their control.
Those responses appear in religion, too. For instance, lines in the famed 10th century poem Vǫluspá seem to reference the 939 eruption of Iceland’s Eldgjá volcano, with high-flying flames and blackened sun beams. “It’s like an eyewitness description of a phenomenal lava flood,” Oppenheimer says. The poem foretells a fiery end to pagan gods, such as Odin, who are replaced by one god. Vǫluspá, which explained the eruption in terms of divine displeasure,may have contributed to the island’s Christianization around 1000, Oppenheimer and colleagues suggest.
Famines, riots, disease, migration. The widespread climatic effects of volcanoes across the ages may be subtler than the hellscapes conjured by poets but more tangible in the marks they’ve left on history.

Top cyber spy braces for more AI-powered hacking attacks

Disruptions 'inevitable' as AI-powered cyber threats grow, Australian Signals Directorate says
In short:
The Australian Signals Directorate says more disruptions to essential services are likely as AI increases the risk of cyber attacks.
AI is turbocharging the number and potency of cyber threats Australia faces from criminal networks and state-aligned operators, the agency says.
The ASD has also revealed previously secret details of its offensive operations, including the targeting of criminals hoarding and selling personal data on the dark web.
Australia's top cyber spy is warning the country to prepare for more frequent disruptions to everyday services amid a surge of AI-powered cyber attacks.
Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) director-general Abigail Bradshaw said artificial intelligence frontier models had "redefined" the threat facing Australia.
"What is inevitable is that with each capability increase, we are likely to see more disruption," she said.
"Disruption can look like what we've seen over the last few weeks, with websites that require patching having to be taken down in order to be secured.
"Disruption could look like data breaches. Disruption could look like service disruption.
"Virtually any service that you rely on in your life today is enabled in some respect by a digital network."
The warning comes just days after a number of government websites, including the ASD's, were brought partially offline after vulnerabilities were found.
Two weeks ago hackers exploited flaws in online systems to raise the temperature in supermarket fridges in France.
Today the ASD is publishing its annual cyber threat report, which details a 20 per cent jump in cybersecurity incidents the agency was required to respond to last financial year.
But Ms Bradshaw said the defining event of the past year was the release of frontier models such as Anthropic's Mythos.
Models such as Mythos were touted as being too dangerous to release publicly due to their capability to find vulnerabilities in cyber defence systems.
A swarm of AI agents was responsible for breaching Australian health data security, in what was described as the first autonomous hack of a government website.
Ms Bradshaw said that incident led to a reworking of the relationship between agencies such as the ASD and the massive American companies at the forefront of the technology.
She said the ASD had worked "very quickly" to set up protocols to act as an "early warning system" with AI companies, including OpenAI.
"These protocols have been shared with all of the labs, and all of the Five Eyes [intelligence agencies]," she said.
"We now have an equal expectation about the sorts of things that agencies like ASD need to be engaged on ahead of model testing."
Dismantling dark web operators
Responding to cyber incidents makes up a large portion of the ASD's work, but the agency is also keen to talk up the success of its offensive operations.
It revealed details of a recent effort to take down criminal groups selling and operating a piece of malware known as Amadey.
Hidden inside free software, Amadey steals the personal data or login details of its victims and transmits it back to criminal groups, where it is then sold on the dark web.
The ASD said in one case, it was found hidden in a free, illegitimate version of Photoshop editing software.
It also found evidence of the software being sold on the dark web for about $US500 ($712).
ASD operators were able to access the back end of Amadey's operation and found the criminal network had access to 180,000 computers across the globe, including in Australia.
"The next steps that we took were to disconnect that Amadey controller from all those victims," ASD acting deputy director-general of intelligence Tauri Gregory said.
"And so, effectively, that cyber criminal can no longer access those 180,000 computers and no longer steal data from all those people.
"If ASD had not acted here, you'd have 180,000 businesses or individuals whose data was being stolen and be either sold on the dark web or monetised in other ways, or used to inform follow-on crimes such as fraud and identity theft."
In another case, the ASD was tipped off to the sale of 5 terabytes of data stolen from a business that was unaware it had been hacked.
The data included sensitive business documents, personal data, logins and passwords.
Mr Gregory said the agency was able to break in and destroy the data before it could be sold.
"To give some context, we think there are about 4.8 million files which were stolen from Australians, which we destroyed in that operation, as well as hundreds of thousands of files from other victims around the world," he said.
Mr Gregory said AI was increasing the scope and scale of attacks, but it was also an enormous asset to those trying to defend against them.
"We are using AI to generate software capabilities much more quickly, and so we use it to support our software engineering and development of new tools and capabilities directly," he said.
An accelerating threat
The agency has previously joined international partners in warning of Chinese-aligned actors building hidden networks of hijacked devices that can be used for espionage or offensive operations.
It has also warned that some state actors want to maintain access to essential services and infrastructure that could be disrupted if conflict were to break out.
Ms Bradshaw said strategic tensions in the region would increase that threat.
"The natural progression of this is, as the world becomes uncertain, of course nation states will try to reduce that uncertainty by obtaining more information," she said.
"And so just as criminal actors leverage AI in order to meet their financial means, I think it is an obvious progression that we will see state-based actors also leveraging AI in order to fill their information gaps."
Ms Bradshaw said there was a huge amount of work to do in both corporate and government systems to better prepare for and defend against cyber threats, particularly in replacing vulnerable "legacy" systems.
She said it also meant learning how to best use AI as a defensive tool.
"There is much more that we need to do and, in the current context, that is now a matter of urgency," Ms Bradshaw said.

What's next?
MPs are demanding tech giants do more to tackle online abuse and threats.
Almost 5,000 threats and violent comments have been flagged on the social media accounts of 22 Labor politicians in just three months as MPs have turned to technology to combat online abuse.

Senior public servants have also warned that social media clips of various parliamentary committee hearings were fuelling abuse towards bureaucrats.
Abuse has 'chilling effect' on community
A few female Labor members began experimenting with Areto, which uses AI to identify and hide abusive and threatening comments, earlier this year before a trial was then extended to others in the caucus.
Analysis of the results for 22 parliamentarians using the tool in the past three months found high-profile accounts typically received more attacks, with one MP recording 57,522 abusive comments.
Facebook carried about 94 per cent of all comments, of which 51 per cent were abusive, compared with 42 per cent of the small number of comments on Instagram and 21 per cent of the comments on TikTok.
Finance and Women's Minister Katy Gallagher, who has started using Areto, said the volume of abuse online was "extraordinary".
"It is having a chilling effect on genuine community engagement," she said.
"For women, the abuse is usually sexualised, a lot about physical harm that will be done to you or your children."
Senator Gallagher said the automated AI tool was not filtering critical comments about the government or policy, but was giving her staff and others "respite" from abusive content.
"It's not a perfect solution, and I don't think anyone expects it to be, but the platforms themselves are not dealing with this," she said.
Minister told 'you're next' after Haines attack
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said the behaviour of the social media platforms was "pitiful", accusing them of prioritising profits over safety.
"These platforms are profiting off people treating each other with disrespect, anger, aggression and abuse. Then they play dumb at the devastating social effects that are happening across the country," she said.
Ms O'Neil said the fact that Areto existed was a "tragedy", but it was essential in helping to manage the mental health of her team.
"Female MPs shouldn't have to have a program that screens for death and rape threats, but that's where we are,"
she said.
Ms O'Neil said the majority of public interactions she had as an MP were respectful, but she sensed the "online environment is seeping into the way people behave in real life".
"No-one should feel sorry for us; that's not what this is about," she said.
"Politicians just happen to be in the public conversation right now, but it doesn't matter if you're an AFL footballer or a nurse working in a hospital, or a retail worker … Anyone who interfaces with the public is feeling this declining respect."
Ms O'Neil said the abuse directed at politicians went beyond the "democratic process" of "people being upset with government and wanting to convey that".
"I don't see a straight line between that and, 'You're next s**t,' being written on my social media wall two days after Helen Haines [was attacked]."
MP's children the target of racist abuse
Bonner MP Kara Cook has been trialling Areto for the past six months. She said as someone who did most of her own social media, she had noticed a vast improvement.
"For me, having a safe space for people locally to be able to genuinely express their views has been positive because I want to hear those," she said.
Areto has hidden 15,244 comments, mostly on Ms Cook's Facebook page, which were identified as "abusive", with racism, gender microaggression and transphobia the most common categories of attack.
Ms Cook, who has three First Nations children, said posts about her family often attracted "overwhelmingly racist comments".
"I've never hidden who I am as a person from my community … and I don't want that to change, but I also want to protect my family from that abuse," she said.
The first-term MP, who was a domestic violence lawyer and has previously served as a local councillor, said the day after she was elected to federal parliament, her home address and pictures of her house were published online.
"From that moment it was very clear to me that I'd entered a very different environment to any other workplace I'd ever been in," she said.
Ms Cook also said tech companies had an "obligation" to stop threatening and racist abuse appearing on their platforms.
She said the attack on Ms Haines needed to be a "pivotal moment" when Australia changed its approach to the safety of everyone, particularly women.
Public service hits out at 'ridicule' and 'vile abuse' of officials
At a Senate estimates hearing on Monday, top public servant Steven Kennedy said officials were also subject to increasing abuse online, and that parliamentarians were partly to blame for sharing "misleading" clips.
Those concerns were first aired in September when a senior defence official told a committee she did not want her answers clipped up for social media.
That request was rejected, with opposition and crossbench parliamentarians outraged by the idea.
But Mr Kennedy, who heads the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, said while he did not propose censoring footage, the "health and safety" of officials was a concern.
"Conduct that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets witnesses is inconsistent with the behaviour code for parliamentarians," he said.
"Evidence has been edited [for social media] in ways that invite ridicule, hostility or abuse directed at individual public servants … Unfortunately, some public servants have been the subjects of vile abuse."
Mr Kennedy urged parliamentarians to moderate comments on their social media posts and to delete abuse directed at officials.

Russian Spy Network Exposed in Alleged Scheme to Stage Fake Pro-Nuclear Rally in Budapest
Russian intelligence-linked operatives allegedly attempted to stage a paid demonstration outside Hungary’s parliament in Budapest to promote a nuclear power project backed by Russia’s state-owned Rosatom, according to a new investigation based on leaked intelligence documents.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The alleged operation was uncovered by InformNapalm and Ukrainian Militant, which published their findings on October 26 after examining correspondence, internal documents, and digital records obtained by the hacker group 256 Cyber Assault Division.
Investigators identified Russian Colonel Timur Sirtlanov and Lieutenant Colonel Irina Parman, both linked to military unit 33949, previously identified in open-source investigations as a structure associated with Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
A leaked email dated September 16 reportedly showed Sirtlanov asking Parman to conduct psychological profiling ahead of a postponed operation in Budapest. The correspondence referred to an “active measure,” a term used by Russian intelligence services for covert influence operations targeting foreign governments and public opinion.
The planned demonstration was intended to generate public support for Paks II, a nuclear power plant expansion project involving Russia’s Rosatom.
Organizers reportedly recruited Russian-speaking residents through Facebook advertisements and coordinated preparations in a private Telegram group called “Friendship of Peoples,” which had 106 members.
Participants were instructed to prepare banners and promotional materials supporting the nuclear project. Organizers also offered additional financial compensation, although investigators found no evidence that payments were actually made.
InformNapalm further traced promotional materials to Parman after discovering that a PDF file contained the author name “Irina Larina,” matching a surname she had previously used online.
The rally was initially scheduled for September 20 outside Hungary’s parliament before being postponed to September 26. However, organizers canceled the demonstration approximately 30 minutes before it was due to begin.
The alleged Russian influence operation emerged amid worsening relations between Moscow and Budapest. On September 8, Hungary expelled ten Russian diplomats over activities incompatible with their diplomatic status.
Meanwhile, the Paks II project has faced increasing scrutiny. Hungarian authorities launched an investigation into financial transactions associated with the project in August, following a European Union court ruling in 2025 overturning the European Commission’s approval of state aid for its construction.
Earlier, in May 2026, Hungary expelled a Russian diplomat identified as an undercover officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. According to VSquare, the diplomat had allegedly spent years cultivating contacts within Hungarian institutions and gathering intelligence on government officials and the Paks II nuclear power project.

You’ll Never Guess What Ukraine Uses to Keep Drones Flying at −20°C

- Category

You’ll Never Guess What Ukraine Uses to Keep Drones Flying at −20°C
Ukraine’s defense industry builds drones capable of reaching deep inside Russia and cruise missiles carrying massive warheads—but when temperatures plunge to −20°C (−4°F), one surprisingly effective engineering solution is considerably less sophisticated: salo .
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point on October 26 revealed that extreme cold can cause frost to form on drone cameras and cables while batteries discharge significantly faster, threatening the reliability of unmanned systems operating through the winter.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One workaround is a simple layer of salo used to help shield vulnerable components from freezing conditions.
It is an unusually low-tech solution from a company responsible for some of Ukraine’s most advanced long-range weapons.
Fire Point manufactures the FP-1 deep-strike UAV and FP-2 strike drone, as well as the FP-5 Flamingo ground-launched cruise missile. The company is also developing the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles, with the latter designed for strikes at ranges of up to 850 kilometers.
Its FP-1 and FP-2 drones are already used extensively for strikes deep inside Russia, while the Flamingo has become another component of Ukraine’s expanding domestic long-range arsenal.
Yet battlefield engineering is not always about finding the most technologically sophisticated answer.
At around −20°C, preventing a camera, cable, or other exposed component from freezing can matter just as much as advanced guidance software or propulsion.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine and Norway were accelerating development of the Fire Point FP-5.x FREYJA anti-ballistic missile defense program, with initial components already showing progress and the first tests targeted for the end of 2026.

Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Iran have agreed to continue talks aimed at strengthening cooperation on regional issues, including peace and security, according to a joint statement issued after a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran.

What Israel's election could mean for the West Bank's future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:51:28 UTC
02:51:28 KST

Breadcrumb
Beyond the ballot: The West Bank's future after Israel's election
Ramallah - Driving in the occupied West Bank, motorists are confronted with a barrage of campaign billboards for the Israeli elections.
The messages are geared towards Israeli settlers in the territory, not the Palestinians barred from voting.
Many of the posters express support for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s far-right Jewish Power party, as he draws his core voter base from settlers.
But there are also numerous posters for Prime Minister Netanyahu’s Likud party, including an ominous ad along the road to Jerusalem featuring Zohran Mamdani and Ayatollah Khomeini, warning against the power of Palestinian allies.
Against this radicalised backdrop, Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday in an election that many hope will spell the end of Netanyahu’s 19-year non-consecutive rule as prime minister.
The election comes in the wake of growing domestic resentment against Netanyahu over reports of his advanced knowledge of the 7 October attacks.
Netanyahu’s Likud is seemingly facing an uphill battle against a bloc of four Jewish opposition parties that have joined forces to defeat him: the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beitenu party, and the Together alliance.
After the bloc’s establishment, the parties announced their goal was to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.
The elections are projected to be a near deadlock with no bloc winning an absolute majority. That outcome would trigger a period of negotiations and coalition building, where different parties must agree to come together to form a government.
But as settler violence reaches record levels in the West Bank, many Palestinians are left wondering: will any electoral outcome change the facts on the ground?
West Bank violence surges ahead of election
Approximately 750,000 Israelis live in settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem today, illegal under international law.
The settlers comprise a disproportionately powerful bloc in Israeli politics, despite accounting for around 7-8% of the total Israeli population.
Under Netanyahu’s current administration, which has brought settlers from the far-right fringes into a governing coalition, the settlers’ political influence has coincided with a rapid acceleration of settlement expansion.
But it’s unlikely that another government would slow the pace of settlement building.
“In order to ameliorate pressure from the settler lobby, the left often are tempted to expand settlements even more than the right,” Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, a political commentator and former Israeli diplomat, tells The New Arab.
“It [the opposition winning] might even lead to an increase in settlement construction in order to pay them off for concessions.”
As settlements expand, so does the pressure on Palestinians living nearby. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded an average of six settler attacks per day this year thus far.
Those numbers were released before the autumnal olive harvest commenced, when violence dramatically escalates as settlers launch coordinated attacks against Palestinian farmers in their olive groves.
And after two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on an Israeli checkpoint on 23 October, Ben-Gvir suggested that Palestinians should be barred from driving on the roads in the West Bank - or the land of Judea and Samaria, as he refers to it.
The Israeli army subsequently launched a collective punishment operation and began home demolitions across the neighbourhood where the shooters hailed from, displacing 400 families thus far.
Netanyahu has promised the biggest military occupation in the West Bank since 1967, though many experts say he may be bluffing to bolster support for Likud ahead of the elections.
The election will now take place against a backdrop of expanding settlements, escalating settler violence, and increasingly severe restrictions on Palestinian movement, fuelling fears that tensions across the West Bank are near boiling point.
“There are a lot of people in the Israeli security forces who want Palestinians to have a better quality of life, just so that the West Bank doesn't explode into another Intifada,” says Ben-Ephraim.
Projected electoral outcomes
Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot of Yashar!, is seen as the leading centrist alternative for Prime Minister.
Eisenkot has promised to rein in settler violence while firmly opposing a two-state solution. Once the Israeli army Chief of Staff, Eisenkot was the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine in 2006, which advocates "disproportionate force” against Israel’s perceived enemies.
“None of the Israeli governments that would come is going to give a Palestinian state to the Palestinians, but change may come, depending on how you define change,” Muhanned Qafesha, a Palestinian journalist from Hebron, tells The New Arab.
An Eisenkot government could mean greater restrictions on settler violence and a slight change in settlement policy, without fundamentally interfering with the settler project.
Alternatively, if Netanyahu secures another term or temporarily heads a caretaker government if a stalemate arises, the settlers in his administration may feel their time is limited and accelerate their existing plans for the annexation of the West Bank.
As it stands, neither major political bloc is projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
While the opposition bloc has sworn not to form a coalition with either of the Palestinian parties on the ballot - the left-leaning Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) - that pledge may not hold, as they could be a potential lifeline to forming a government.
“The two Arab parties can maybe win like 15 seats or something, and this will make a huge difference because if they can make a coalition with the opposition, they can kick out Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir,” Qafesha tells The New Arab.
“I do believe that the opposition in Israel is saying they won’t form a coalition with the Arabs because they want to get as many votes from the Jewish community as possible. But if they need the Arab parties to form a coalition to kick out Netanyahu, they might do it,” he adds.
But any coalition will also depend on parties that oppose Palestinian statehood, and thus a fundamental shift in Israel’s approach to the occupation is virtually impossible.
Even if Eisenkot eventually forms a government, his fragile coalition across the ideological spectrum would struggle to agree on significant changes towards settlement policy in the West Bank.
Will the opposition improve life in the West Bank?
The 3.4 million Palestinians living in the West Bank under military occupation cannot vote in Israeli elections, but Palestinian citizens of Israel can.
Arab voters have long boycotted Israeli elections, but there has been a recent push for their participation - with a record turnout for the group anticipated.
The vast majority of Palestinians in the West Bank want Palestinian citizens of Israel to vote in the elections to improve their daily lives, explains Qafesha, who himself cannot vote.
He believes an administration without settlers at the helm may alleviate some of the daily struggles in the West Bank.
“We live in hell. We just want to breathe,” Qafesha says.
But if Netanyahu finally goes down, some Palestinians believe Western governments may attempt to rehabilitate Israel’s image under a new administration - and lift the recent round of European sanctions against settlements that were years in the making.
“The upcoming election is between fascists and ultra-fascists. If Netanyahu loses the chance to lead the next government, his loss can be used to alleviate the pressure that is just starting to build from the international community,” Mazin Qumsiyeh, Director of Palestine’s Natural History Museum in Bethlehem, tells The New Arab.
Yet Qafesha remains adamant that the reality on the ground is more important than the views of the international community, which could promote a new government as an example of Israel’s return to democracy.
“Over the past three years, Israel has killed more than 100,000 Palestinians in Gaza. What has the world done for us? Has anything changed in our life? I don't want the view of the world to change at the expense of the blood of Palestinian children, whether it's in Gaza, West Bank, or Jerusalem,” says Qafesha.
An opposition government less reliant on far-right parties could potentially curb some of the policies driving unchecked violence and forced displacement, ameliorating a few of the numerous obstacles to a dignified life under occupation. But any improvement would likely be limited in scope.
“If the opposition wins, the intensity of the ethnic cleansing will probably somewhat lessen, but it's only temporary,” concludes Ben-Ephraim.
“I think that the Israeli public opinion has turned so far in favour of genocide and ethnic cleansing that it will just be a respite at best.”
Kate McMahon is a freelance journalist and foreign correspondent focused on the Middle East and South Asia. She reports on environmental change, human rights, and geopolitical conflicts

A jury at Winchester crown court will this week begin hearing the trial of four other men charged with sexually assaulting Joanne Young.

Polish city of Przemyśl suspends cooperation with Lviv over Year of UPA decision
Councillors in the Polish city of Przemyśl agreed on Monday 26 October to suspend cooperation with Lviv following a recent decision by the Lviv Oblast Council to designate 2027 as the Year of the UPA The UPA, or Ukrainian Insurgent Army, was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. and Roman Shukhevych, one of its commanders-in-chief.
Source: Przemyśl Mayor Wojciech Bakun on Facebook, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Twenty-one councillors voted in favour of the resolution to suspend the partnership with Lviv. No one voted against or abstained.
According to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), Przemyśl councillors said the decision adopted by the Lviv Oblast Council on 20 October "insulted" the memory of Polish victims of crimes committed by the UPA and ran counter to efforts to build relations based on historical truth and mutual respect.
The resolution requires Przemyśl Mayor Wojciech Bakun to take legal steps to terminate the 1995 cooperation agreement.
However, it also provides for cooperation between the cities to resume if the Lviv Oblast Council definitively repeals or formally withdraws the resolution and Lviv's city authorities clearly distance themselves from initiatives that "glorify structures responsible for crimes against civilians".
The mayor must inform Lviv's city authorities of this position and report to Przemyśl councillors on the measures taken and the date on which the agreement will cease to be in force.
"After a lengthy discussion on the matter, all councillors unanimously decided that we would suspend all joint activities until Lviv's authorities clearly state their position on the promotion of ideologies directed against Poland and the Polish people. I would like to thank the councillors for taking this position and demonstrating that we will not remain indifferent to provocative and anti-Polish actions," Bakun wrote.
Background:
- On 20 October, the Lviv Oblast Council voted to declare 2027 the "year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army and Oleh Olzhych". The decision immediately drew criticism from Polish officials.
- Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk later said that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had made it clear that he would not support further steps by the Lviv Oblast Council to declare 2027 the year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych.
- The city council of Wrocław, Poland, unanimously condemned the decision by the Lviv Oblast Council to declare 2027 the year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army.
- Meanwhile, Kraków's new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, has proposed suspending the city's partnership with Lviv in response to the Lviv Oblast Council's decision to declare 2027 the year of the UPA.

Tax service advises gas producers to report export volumes of gas injected into storage for royalty administration
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:47:56 EET
02:47:56 KST

The State Tax Service (STS) recommends that gas-producing companies notify it in writing of the volumes of domestically produced gas exported after being injected into underground gas storage facilities (UGS).
According to a statement on the agency's Telegram channel, the information should be submitted together with monthly acts documenting the movement of natural gas in storage facilities. This will allow tax authorities to administer subsoil-use royalty payments without making additional requests to taxpayers.
The STS recalled that certain provisions of Ukraine's Tax Code exempt companies from paying royalties on extracted gas injected into UGS facilities until it is sold. The obligation to pay royalties resumes in the reporting period in which the gas is sold, with the amount due calculated based on the actual volume sold.
The procedure for exporting domestically produced gas was approved by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 1251 of October 7, 2026.

Pope cleared for South America trip after lung cancer surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:19:58 UTC
02:19:58 KST

Pope Leo cleared to make his trip to South America after successful lung cancer surgery
Only two weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV has been given the medical green light to embark on an ambitious 12-day tour of South America next month.
"Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey to Latin America as planned," the Vatican said in a statement on Monday. "The Pope is following medical recommendations with great care and diligence, and with a deep determination to continue serving the Church."
The trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, set for Nov. 6 to 17, is particularly grueling. The 71-year-old pontiff plans to travel to 10 cities, board 14 flights, and attend many public appearances and religious ceremonies.
The Vatican also confirmed that the trip would proceed "according to the program previously published," which means that a visit to the Peruvian city of Cuzco, Peru, situated at more than 11,000 feet above sea level, remains on the schedule. The thinner air there could pose difficulties for someone recovering from lung surgery.
Doubts about the pope's ability to undergo the South American trip surfaced again last week, when, on the advice of his doctors, Leo canceled a visit by helicopter to Assisi for an international peace gathering to take place Tuesday. Doctors said they advised him to do so preventively, because of the unpressurized air on the helicopter journey.
The upcoming journey carries particular personal significance for the first American-born pope, who spent more than two decades working as a missionary and bishop in Peru.
"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a statement Monday. "May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy."
Leo was operated on Oct. 13, when doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after discovering a malignant tumor. The cancer, identified as a lung adenocarcinoma, was discovered accidentally during a routine abdominal examination, his doctors said. The operation was successful, without complications, and Leo was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 17.
Since leaving the hospital, Leo has gradually resumed his public duties, including his weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square and meetings with visiting church leaders.

Iran says Europe has yet to offer concrete proposal for negotiations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran says Europe has yet to offer concrete proposal for negotiations
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that Tehran had received no concrete proposal from European countries for negotiations, questioning whether recent European calls for diplomacy reflected a genuine change in policy.
Speaking at his weekly press conference in Tehran, Baqaei described the statements as potentially no more than a political gesture, criticizing France, Germany and the United Kingdom for failing to explicitly condemn the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran over the past two years.
He also criticized Europe's role in efforts to reinstate UN sanctions on Iran through the snapback mechanism, urging European governments to adopt a more independent and constructive approach to developments in West Asia.
Baqaei criticized the 'selective application of human rights principles' by European governments and institutions, citing police actions against protesters in France and Belgium.
He said Iran had summoned the French ambassador and, more recently, the Italian ambassador to convey its concerns over reported human rights violations during protests in Europe. He also criticized European officials for attributing domestic unrest to foreign interference rather than addressing underlying grievances.
Regarding protests in Albania, Baqaei said public opposition to corruption and the transfer of land to foreign business interests was an internal matter. He argued that allegations of foreign interference failed to address the reasons behind the demonstrations.
Iran reaffirms position on nuclear program
Addressing US allegations about Iran's nuclear program, Baqaei reiterated that Iran had never possessed or sought to acquire nuclear weapons.
Referring to former US President Barack Obama's remarks on diplomacy and Iran's nuclear program, he said Tehran had entered the 2015 nuclear agreement in good faith, while Washington withdrew from the deal three years later.
Baqaei argued that allegations about Iran's nuclear intentions had been used to justify military action, pointing to a 'contradiction between US assertions' that Iran's nuclear program had been destroyed and subsequent military threats and attacks.
He stressed that Iran remained prepared to defend itself against threats. Asked about potential threats to submarine communications cables and digital infrastructure, he said decisions on any response rested with the competent authorities and would not be disclosed in advance.
Regional diplomacy and security
Baqaei said a visit by a Qatari delegation to Tehran formed part of ongoing regional consultations on bilateral cooperation and Qatar's mediation role amid heightened tensions.
He also said the cancellation of a meeting in Salalah would not change Iran's position that regional countries should establish collective security arrangements based on their own capabilities. Tehran had advanced similar proposals at meetings in Baghdad and within the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, he added.
On Yemen, Baqaei called for the dispute between Yemen and Saudi Arabia to be resolved through dialogue, warning that sanctions and military action harmed the Yemeni people and their rights.
Pezeshkian's Russia visit to focus on energy cooperation
Baqaei said President Masoud Pezeshkian's planned visit to Russia for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit on Tuesday would provide an opportunity for major energy suppliers to consult on shared challenges and priorities.
He highlighted longstanding energy cooperation between Iran and Russia, particularly efforts to increase investment, facilitate technology transfer and diversify natural gas export routes. Pezeshkian was also expected to hold bilateral meetings with other leaders attending the summit.
Iran questions US commitment to negotiations
Baqaei said Iran remained open to diplomacy but questioned Washington's commitment to a genuine negotiating process, citing its withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement and 'its failure' to honor the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
He stressed that meaningful negotiations required reciprocal commitments rather than demands for unilateral concessions while sanctions and military threats continued.
Iran's foreign policy decisions, including those concerning possible negotiations with the United States, were guided by national interests and a broader diplomatic process, he added, rather than short-term fluctuations in global oil prices.
Iran monitoring border and security developments
On border issues with Pakistan, Baqaei said consultations were continuing over technical matters involving system upgrades and security concerns, describing the process as positive.
Regarding Iran-Iraq border issues, he said Iran's embassy in Baghdad and its consulates were pursuing a resolution, stressing the importance of protecting the interests of both countries. He also noted that US sanctions had consequences for the Iraqi people.
Baqaei added that Iranian authorities were monitoring reports concerning drone bases near Iran and Ukrainian movements in Iraq, saying the relevant institutions would take necessary measures to counter threats.

Pentagon preparing for ‘major war’ – Fox News
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:19:20 UTC
02:19:20 KST

Pentagon preparing for ‘major war’ – Fox News
Major military bases in the continental US will be expected to sustain essential operations for at least 90 days without external support under a new Pentagon strategy, Fox News has reported.
The autonomy target was set out in FORTRESS documents reviewed by the network, it said on Sunday. Critical military supplies would also require at least two qualified supply or production routes to guard against disruption.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the initiative last month. The US military has faced serious logistical disruption in the Middle East following Iranian strikes on American facilities and other sites used by US forces in retaliation for the US-Israeli attack on Iran.
Fox News, which is generally supportive of President Donald Trump’s agenda, wrote that the US needed to be prepared for a contingency in which military action would “cripple power grids, disrupt supply chains and threaten critical infrastructure on American soil.”
FORTRESS stands for Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply and Survivability. A founding memorandum signed by Hegseth last month identifies five pillars: energy independence, supply-chain resilience, strategic reserves, physical protection and cybersecurity, and resilience in space and the electromagnetic spectrum.
Pentagon planners aim to reduce reliance on civilian infrastructure that could be severely damaged in a major armed conflict. Proposed options include small nuclear reactors and large battery banks to support base microgrids if external electricity supplies are cut. The program also envisages preparing civilian factories to switch to defense production in an emergency, alongside other measures.
The report comes less than two weeks before midterm elections in which polls suggest the ruling Republican Party could suffer significant losses. The Iran war and the resulting surge in fuel prices are major factors bolstering opposition candidates.
Trump’s rhetoric has fueled widespread expectations that the US could escalate the war with Iran shortly after the election, or even before it. According to NBC News, Washington has withdrawn some personnel from its Middle Eastern bases ahead of a possible renewed airstrike campaign.

Pezeshkian to Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi officials: Iran seeks cooperation, will defend rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

Pezeshkian to Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi officials: Iran seeks cooperation, will defend rights
TEHRAN – Senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — the three countries that recently signed the Mecca defense pact — traveled to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met with President Masoud Pezeshkian and with Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
Speaking at a joint meeting with the three visiting officials, President Pezeshkian welcomed dialogue among Islamic countries and stressed the failure of enemies to achieve their objectives against Iran.
"They imagined they could bring the Islamic Republic of Iran to collapse through pressure and aggression; but the result of these actions was the strengthening of internal unity and cohesion and increased solidarity of the Iranian nation," Pezeshkian said.
"Our people, despite the imposed losses and hardships, defended their land with power and steadfastness. The notion that the Iranian nation can be forced into surrender is a false and void notion," he added.
The president said the Islamic Republic of Iran pursues its legal rights within the principles and rules of international law, and relying on those very principles, will firmly defend the legitimate rights and interests of the Iranian nation.
Call for united front against Israel
Pezeshkian expressed hope that the presence of major and influential Islamic countries could play an effective role in strengthening regional stability and unity.
"We should not allow the Zionist regime to commit terror and aggression against any individual or country whenever it wishes. I am confident that if Islamic countries stand together and adopt a coordinated position, such actions cannot be repeated," he said.
"I believe that if we manage our differences and emphasize commonalities and shared interests instead of focusing on divisive issues, we can overcome regional problems more easily and effectively," he added.
He warned against interventionist and divisive policies, saying one of the objectives pursued in the policies of the US and the Zionist regime is to weaken regional countries, create rifts among Muslim nations and gradually weaken major Islamic states.
"We must, by strengthening mutual cooperation and supporting one another, prevent the realization of such objectives and not allow regional countries to be exposed separately to pressure and threats," Pezeshkian said.
He added that Islamic countries should move to meet each other's needs through constructive engagement, economic cooperation and the use of mutual capacities. "The notion that nations can be forced into surrender through pressure and sanctions is a void notion. The deeper and broader cooperation among regional countries becomes, the greater their ability to manage problems and confront external pressures will be."
Pezeshkian stressed that Iran, relying on domestic efforts, the support of the nation and the guidance of the Leader, will successfully pass through difficulties, adding that Islamic countries must understand the interconnectedness of their security and interests. Weakening any major regional country, he said, could pave the way for increased pressure and threats against other Islamic countries as well.
From words to joint action
Emphasizing the need for consistency between words and deeds in regional relations, Pezeshkian said: "We should not say what we do not believe in or fail to uphold in practice. We must, hand in hand, provide the ground for flourishing the region's scientific, economic, cultural, political and security capacities; develop communication routes, facilitate travel, turn borders into opportunities for cooperation and link the universities, scientific centers, traders and merchants of Islamic countries to one another."
He said expanding multilateral cooperation lays the ground for sustainable security, noting: "When science, culture, trade and economy cross borders and communications among nations expand, the ground for the spread of terrorism and insecurity will disappear. Therefore, strengthening scientific, cultural and economic bonds not only helps the development and welfare of nations, but is one of the most effective ways to consolidate collective security in the region."
Pezeshkian said any understanding reached in such meetings that leads to stronger regional unity, cohesion and cooperation will enjoy Iran's serious and all-out support, adding that focus must be placed on common ground and areas of cooperation and differences must not be allowed to hinder shared interests.
Nuclear rights and double standards
In another part of his remarks, Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran's principled position on nuclear activities, saying the Islamic Republic is not seeking nuclear weapons and, as a member of the NPT, wants to continue its nuclear activities within the framework of international rights and obligations.
"Iran accordingly reserves the right to benefit from peaceful nuclear activities and expects these rights to be respected within the framework of international regulations," he said.
He criticized dual approaches toward Iran, saying: "Using the nuclear issue as a pretext for exerting pressure, threats, attacks on nuclear facilities, and claiming readiness for talks and dialogue simultaneously with attacking Iran is a contradictory and unconstructive approach that has undermined public trust and increased distrust among Iranian officials and people."
Pezeshkian said Islamic countries must, by strengthening their interactions and coordination, not allow such approaches to become a routine for dealing with regional nations. Safeguarding nations' rights, respecting countries' sovereignty, countering aggression and strengthening regional cooperation require common will and coordinated action, he added.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran is also ready, relying on religious commonalities, mutual interests and respect for nations' rights, to expand its cooperation with Islamic countries in this path," he said.
The officials of the three neighboring countries also held separate meetings with SNSC Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. At the end of the meetings, the four countries issued a joint press statement, stressing: "The participants agreed to continue talks to strengthen cooperation among the four regional countries, including in the field of peace and security in the region."

British PM Burnham says he wants UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime
LONDON – Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted Britain to rejoin the European Union during his lifetime, calling for an “honest” discussion about the impact of Brexit.
“I don’t think things have worked out as people said they would,” Burnham told ITV of his country’s 2016 decision to leave the bloc, adding that he wasn’t proposing any changes during this Parliament. “I’m going to lead a discussion on how we make it better.”
Reshaping Britain’s relationship with the European Union has become one of Burnham’s key pledges since he became prime minister three months ago, as he gambles on revisiting a divisive issue that dominated British politics over the last decade.
The 56-year-old prime minister opened the door to rejoining the EU at his party’s annual conference in September, saying he would set out options for a new relationship later in 2026.
Burnham said he wouldn’t seek to re-run the 2016 referendum nor break Labour’s 2024 election pledge not to join the EU’s single market or Customs union.
He was speaking ahead of a UK-EU summit which is due to take place on Nov 20, when the premier has said he wants to make progress on boosting economic growth and tackling illegal immigration into the UK.
Burnham said he’s seeking a deal that aims “to support our farmers, our food manufacturers, but also to increase collaboration on immigration because we lost that and we need to get it back”, he told Sky News later on Oct 26. “I’m talking about practical steps to deal with the things that matter to people.”
He said Britain had stronger return agreements for the arrival of people in small boats when it was in the EU, and that immigrants have now become more likely to settle in the country permanently, rather than leaving after a few years.
He added that he’ll “never move ahead” of public opinion on the issue of Brexit, though it’s unclear how he intends to achieve that. Asked whether Burnham would use a referendum or a general election to gain a mandate for his new EU position, his deputy official spokeswoman, Cat Simmons, declined to comment.
“We’re not at that stage yet,” Simmons said to reporters at a briefing on Oct 26. “The first step here is the substance rather than the process.”
Burnham also used the ITV interview to rule out an early election, saying it’s not something he’s thinking about.
“There is no election coming any time soon,” he said. “Britain is starting to regain its momentum.” BLOOMBERG

Zelenskyy calls out monthlong wait for Hegseth to sign off on Patriot missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:07:20 UTC
02:07:20 KST

Kyiv has repeatedly pressed the need for more interceptors to be delivered to its forces as Ukraine continues to defend against deadly Russian missile attacks and jet-powered drone strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on much coveted Patriot interceptor missiles.
In an update on weapons supplies shared on social media, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been awaiting approval to receive missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
"We are working on several tracks – with the United States, Europe, and other partners that have stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles," he wrote.
"In particular, we have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS," Zelenskyy continued, adding that he had instructed his team to raise the issue with Washington once again.
"Conversations with other countries are also ongoing," he said.
Kyiv has repeatedly pressed the need for more interceptors to be delivered to its forces as Ukraine continues to defend against deadly Russian missile attacks and jet-powered drone strikes.
On Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russian forces had fired 48 missiles - including ballistic missiles - at Ukraine over the past week, as well as around 1,600 guided aerial bombs and close to 2,300 attack drones.
"Unfortunately, almost every day, these brutal strikes leave people killed and injured," he wrote on X. "We need to unblock the deliveries of Patriot interceptors already approved by European countries."
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriot missiles through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.
Munitions stockpiles under strain
Global munitions stocks have come under significant pressure in recent months amid the US' war in Iran.
A report from the US Department of Defence's inspector general, published in September, said American forces had fired $22.3 billion worth of munitions from the start of Operation Epic Fury in late February to the end of June.
Yurii Ihnat, a colonel in the Ukrainian military, said in an interview published on Monday that the number of Patriot missiles used in the Middle East could have supported several years of combat operations in Ukraine.
It is unclear how many of the missiles Ukraine is waiting for Hegseth to sign off on, although Ukrainian media reports suggest that it is a sizeable figure.

Source: 63rd Separate Mechanised Brigade on Facebook

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Dominican Republic President Luis Abinader is scheduled to address the security situation along the border with Haiti on Monday after ordering additional military deployments, local newspaper Hoy reported.
Abinader is anticipated to address the border situation on Monday during his weekly program, La Agenda Semanal, which will air at 3 pm local time (1900GMT).
He will be accompanied by Defense Minister Carlos Antonio Fernandez Onofre, Foreign Minister Victor Bisono and senior military officials.
Abinader ordered two additional battalions, heavy equipment and artillery to reinforce the southern border sector on Sunday, Hoy reported.
The Dominican Republic already had around 11,000 troops deployed along the border before the latest reinforcements.
“We are in permanent session,” Abinader said, adding that authorities were monitoring the situation in Haiti, according to the Dominican Presidency.
He also said he had been in contact with Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and maintained communication with the Gang Suppression Force operating in Haiti.
The Dominican government has also been monitoring the kidnapping of four Salvadoran military technicians in Haiti.
Bukele announced the deployment of a team to help rescue the technicians, according to the Dominican Presidency.
The Dominican Republic has tightened border controls in response to the crisis, including building a border wall aimed at curbing irregular migration, smuggling and other cross-border activities.
Authorities have also stepped up migration enforcement and deportations of undocumented Haitians amid escalating violence in the neighboring country.
Haiti has been grappling with a prolonged security crisis, with armed gangs controlling large parts of the country, including the capital, Port-au-Prince.

Beyza Binnur Donmez

Russian authorities committed “war crimes” and “crimes against humanity” through systematic attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, deliberately depriving civilians of essential services, UN investigators said Monday.
In a report submitted to the UN General Assembly, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine concluded that Russian forces intentionally targeted civilian facilities, causing widespread suffering, particularly during the winter of 2025-2026.
Millions of people in Ukraine faced “lengthy outages of heating, electricity, water, and gas, and had to cope with intolerable living conditions,” the commission said.
“As the cold season approaches, the attacks have intensified once again, raising serious concerns about the threats to civilians’ lives and health,” commission chair Erik Mose warned.
Investigators found that the attacks were carried out under a “state policy” intended to “deprive civilians of essential services,” constituting crimes against humanity.
The commission also uncovered evidence that Russian authorities trafficked men from 29 countries into military service through deception and coercion, according to the report.
Recruits were “forced to sign Russian-language military contracts” before being deployed to frontline positions in Ukraine.
The commission called for an immediate end to attacks on civilian infrastructure and the discharge of all trafficked recruits from Russian forces.
