Beijing is boosting ‘Ocean Wave’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:26 UTC
01:49:26 KST

Since last month, the most eye-catching phenomenon in Taipei’s politics has been the “Ocean Wave” (洋流) — officially called “Taipei Current” — stirred up by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) and his supporters. However, if we only attribute this political wave to innovative campaign tactics or social media mobilization, we might overlook another key variable that is secretly fueling the situation behind the scenes — the “Chinese factor.”
Shen’s rise in politics has always been intertwined with the “Chinese factor.” Even before he announced his mayoral bid, Beijing listed him as a “die-hard Taiwanese independence separatist” and imposed sanctions against him in 2024.
Fundamentally, the reason Beijing dreads and loathes Shen is not because he has proposed a highly systematic “Taiwan independence” doctrine, but because his research on prevention and coping with “gray zone” conflicts in the past few years has struck at the weakness of China’s infiltration and information manipulation efforts.
Traditional political criticism often remains stuck in a war of words, but Shen’s defense theory directly addresses social resilience and the construction of civil defense systems. His attempt to institutionalize and popularize the concept of defense naturally is seen by Beijing as a difficult institutional obstacle.
Beijing’s crackdown on Shen includes its Taiwan Affairs Office issuing the sanctions, the Chongqing Municipal Public Security Bureau filing a case for his “crime of secession,” as well as the extension of the sanctions to his family and affiliated enterprises. A case filed by the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office further confirms that some Hong Kongers hired a detective agency to secretly monitor Shen’s Taipei residence. Shen was also tracked by China when traveling overseas.
More recently, Taiwanese entertainer Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) was boycotted by Chinese Internet users after he attended the opening of Shen’s campaign office. Tsai’s deals with Chinese brands were cut.
This series of maneuvers of “transnational repression” and a “chilling effect” by Beijing have a clear intention.
Despite this deterrence logic being part of authoritarian rule, when it fell into the democratic soil of Taiwan, it generated a huge counterforce.
Strong external threats often fail to achieve internal deterrence due to the “rally round the flag effect” and negative participation theory, according to political science. Instead, they might quickly transform into the political defense legitimacy of the oppressed. When an external power oppresses a Taiwanese politician, voters are likely to develop a defensive group mentality.
When the Chinese side condemned Shen harshly and filed a criminal case, its actions not only failed to isolate him, but also pasted an “anti-China, pro-Taiwan” label on him. This has laid an irreplaceable symbolic position in the eyes of the pro-independence camp and even the center-green voters. In other words, Beijing’s overwhelming oppression has become the best catalyst for the “Ocean Wave” to flood out of the green camp’s bubbles.
If Beijing continues to fail to understand the true logic of voter psychology and power operation under a democratic system, and further intensifies its criticism of Shen during the critical campaign period, it might allow the “Chinese factor” to boost the wave and repeat its mistakes.

Wearing her trademark white T-shirt and blue jeans, she leaned through the sunroof of a vehicle to wave to the crowds and shake hands with her supporters. In Guacara earlier, reporters witnessed Machado singing the national anthem as supporters packed out a plaza, waving flags and cheering her return.
Photo: AFP
A woman shouted “Maria, if you come back, my daughter has to come back,” referring to one of the millions of Venezuelans who have fled repression and a moribund economy.
Her return puts Venezuela’s most influential opposition figure back at the center of the nation’s tumultuous politics.
Machado slipped out of the country in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending nearly a year in hiding. Since then the 59-year-old had made at least seven unsuccessful attempts to return to Venezuela, according to sources in her party. She finally reappeared pm Sunday at the Santa Rosa church in the western city of Barquisimeto, where supporters greeted her with chants of “Viva Maria Corina!”
Two Venezuelan exiles said she had entered the country from Colombia, although Colombian authorities did not immediately confirm that account.
She returns to a country much changed — nine months ago her nemesis president, Nicolas Maduro, was captured in a US military operation and jailed in the US. However, to the democratic opposition’s dismay, his deputy, Delcy Rodriguez, took over as interim president, with Washington’s blessing.
Since then, the Nobel laureate had been forced to watch from exile in Panama as US-backed talks on a political transition took place without her. The interim government has promised elections, but so far has not set a date.
Machado has repeatedly praised US President Donald Trump for launching the risky operation, and even gifted him the Nobel medal she received.
Trump has repeatedly expressed satisfaction with Rodriguez as she fulfills key US demands, particularly on granting access to Venezuelan oil.
Trump said he was not aware of Machado’s return, adding: “but I think she’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?”
“We’re doing very well in Venezuela,” he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Machado’s return had been made possible by the Washington-backed talks — and he urged her to support them going forward.
“We expect all political actors to support these talks, which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in 30 years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election, but an enduring democracy,” he said.
Last week, thousands demonstrated in Caracas and other cities, demanding Machado’s return and elections.
Many leaders from her Vente Venezuela party have recently returned from exile that was prompted by a post-election purge that left 28 dead and resulted in more than 2,400 arrests, including dozens of Machado’s associates.
Her party wants elections next year and for her to be allowed to run, unlike the last presidential vote.

Critical PHP flaw forces Web sites worldwide offline, sparks cyberattack fears PHP爆重大資安漏洞　全球網站緊急下線防駭客攻擊
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:23 UTC
01:49:23 KST

Web sites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the World Wide Web.
Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70 percent of Web sites.
The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday last week, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of Web sites will need to be fixed. One Internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organized criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks.
Photo: Reuters 照片：路透
WordPress, one of the most common Web site systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and — at least historically — much of Facebook. The Wikimedia Foundation said it had taken down several systems on Wednesday last week as a precautionary measure until they could be patched.
The organization behind the language issued a patch on Wednesday last week after researchers testing cyberdefences discovered the flaw. The US National Security Agency told all organizations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. It said the vulnerability could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database.”
Because a fix is now public and AI tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates.
Photo: EPA 照片：歐新社
AI was powering a “race to exploit,” said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the “mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the Internet.”
OpenAI said it led a coalition of researchers that discovered the flaw and claimed “frontier AI” had been key. The researcher who found the weakness, however, said they used models available to the public.
Cybersecurity company Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on Aug. 1 and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.
Photo: AFP 照片：法新社
The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz’s post said.
Michal Wozniak, an Internet infrastructure expert, said: “There’s going to be a lot of automatic exploitation of this.” The bug might allow cryptocurrency miners to exploit vulnerable servers at other people’s expense, he said.
He also said large crime organizations and Russian state actors could use the vulnerable sites as a launching pad from which to conduct distributed denial of service (DDoS) and other cyber-attacks.
The issue highlighted the poor state of Internet infrastructure, Wozniak said, something that was being brought to light by advancing AI models but that had been a long-developing problem. The underlying vulnerabilities the researcher found were decades old.
“This is an environmental problem in an industry where there’s an incentive to move fast and make changes,” he said. “There’s an incentive to deploy a thing and then never update it and not think about maintenance.”(The Guardian)
由於廣泛用於架設全球資訊網的程式語言發現嚴重安全漏洞，全球多地網站紛紛暫時關閉。
比利時、荷蘭、芬蘭、法國及德國等國的部分網站，都因政府緊急修補PHP程式語言的重大安全漏洞而暫時下線。PHP是全球近七成網站使用的程式語言。
PHP程式語言的漏洞上週二曝光後，美國華府與英國倫敦的國家安全機構紛紛發出警示，意味全球數百萬個網站都必須進行修補。一名網路基礎設施專家表示，俄羅斯國家級駭客或組織犯罪集團可能會利用這個漏洞發動網路攻擊。
全球最普遍使用的網站建置系統之一WordPress採用PHP，維基百科（Wikipedia）、通訊軟體Slack，以及Facebook過去的大部分系統，也都使用PHP語言。維基媒體基金會（Wikimedia Foundation）表示，已於上週三預防性關閉數個系統，直到完成漏洞修補為止。
研究人員在測試網路防禦系統時發現這個漏洞後，PHP開發團隊於上週三發布修補程式。美國國家安全局（NSA）呼籲所有使用PHP的機構，若無法立即修補漏洞，就應將相關系統暫時下線。NSA指出，這項漏洞可能「讓攻擊者直接存取伺服器的檔案系統或資料庫」。
由於修補程式已經公開，加上人工智慧（AI）工具能夠輕易逆向分析漏洞，專家表示，正準備因應可能接踵而來的大規模入侵行動，因為駭客正爭相在系統更新完成前發動攻擊。
網路安全研究與事件應變公司TLP:Black共同創辦人科斯汀．拉尤表示，AI正在推動一場「漏洞利用競賽」。他說，接下來可能出現的情況，是「網際網路上所有存在漏洞的網頁伺服器遭到大規模入侵」。
OpenAI表示，由該公司領導的研究團隊聯盟發現了這項漏洞，並聲稱「前沿AI」（FrontierAI）對於漏洞的發現扮演了關鍵角色。不過，實際發現漏洞的研究人員表示，他們使用的是一般大眾也能取得的AI模型。
網路安全公司Calif在部落格文章中表示，該公司8月1日在大型語言模型的協助下發現這些漏洞，接著便持續投入修補工作。Alphabet旗下的網路安全公司Wiz也在部落格文章中表示，該公司同樣發現了這些漏洞，所使用的是旗下自主式AI漏洞研究工具Wiz Atlas，以及Google的Gemini 4 Argon和OpenAI的GPT-5.6 Sol。
Wiz指出，這些漏洞隱藏在PHP程式碼中超過10年，人類駭客若要利用它來攻擊，技術難度將極高。
網路基礎設施專家米哈烏．沃茲尼亞克表示：「這項漏洞將引發大量自動化攻擊」。他指出，此漏洞可能讓加密貨幣挖礦業者利用有安全弱點的伺服器，在未經授權的情況下使用他人的運算資源進行挖礦。
他也表示，大型犯罪組織及俄羅斯國家級駭客可能利用這些有漏洞的網站作為跳板，發動分散式阻斷服務攻擊（DDoS）及其他網路攻擊。
沃茲尼亞克指出，這起事件凸顯網際網路基礎設施長久以來狀況很差。隨著AI模型能力不斷提升，這些問題逐漸浮上檯面，但實際上早已存在多年。研究人員發現的底層安全漏洞，甚至已有數十年歷史。
他說：「這是整個產業環境的問題，因為業界有強烈誘因追求快速開發與修改」。「企業有誘因迅速部署系統，之後卻再也不更新，也不考慮維護問題」。

Group proposes AI system to predict, prevent roadkill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:22 UTC
01:49:22 KST

The Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network (TaiRON) has proposed using artificial intelligence (AI) to simulate and predict road sections at high risk of wildlife-vehicle collisions, along with an early warning network to help prevent roadkill and other traffic accidents.
Over the past eight years, an average of 3,000 traffic incidents per year involving animals have been reported, TaiRON said, citing government statistics.
Motorcycles accounted for 95 percent of the cases, while the accidents caused a total of 25,345 injuries over the period, it said.
Photo: Screen grab from Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network’s Web site
Authorities estimated that the incidents have resulted in NT$800 million to NT$6.4 billion (US$24.61 million to US$196.9 million) in economic losses per year, it added.
The actual number of traffic accidents involving animals is likely much higher, as available data cover only major cases, TaiRON said.
It estimated that 500,000 to 1 million collisions involving medium-to-large mammals occur annually.
The AI proposal aims to identify high-risk road sections to create warning systems rather than waiting to put up signs after an animal has been killed, the group said.
To do so, TaiRON proposed integrating existing datasets, including its own records of animal deaths, wildlife activity data from the Taiwan Biodiversity Network, reports of injured or dead wild animals made through hotlines and Ministry of Transportation and Communications data on traffic accidents involving animals.
These data would be cross-referenced with road maps, speed limit and traffic volume information, gridded microclimate data from the Central Weather Administration and Google Street View images to identify conditions associated with frequent roadkill.
AI would then be used to simulate and predict high-risk areas, according to the proposal.
TaiRON also proposed installing a network of electronic signs linked to a real-time warning system equipped with heat and light sensors to alert drivers to animals crossing or approaching roads.
The prediction system would initially focus on pangolins as a pilot species, with plans to expand it to other wildlife such as leopard cats, endangered land crabs and frogs.
The group has also developed a low-cost, solar-powered warning device that works in low light and uses infrared sensors to detect passing warm-blooded animals and light sensors to detect vehicles.
The device would be tested on roads managed by the New Taipei City Government before potentially being deployed nationwide, TaiRON said.
The proposal was submitted to the Presidential Hackathon and is among 20 proposals advancing to the final round next month.
Winners would receive government support to implement their proposals, the Ministry of Digital Affairs said.
TaiRON is a citizen science initiative launched by the Ministry of Agriculture’s Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute in 2011 to document wildlife deaths associated with roads, with the aim of reducing threats to wildlife, improving road safety and preventing collisions.
More than 36,000 people have contributed over 330,000 records of animal deaths involving more than 600 terrestrial vertebrate species to the network, its official Web site says.

ETF gains split as stock picks face fresh test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:22 UTC
01:49:22 KST

Taiwan’s fast-growing actively managed exchange-traded fund (ETF) market is facing a test of managers’ stock-picking skills as volatility and closer scrutiny of artificial intelligence (AI) investments widen performance gaps across the sector.
The 20 Taiwan-focused active ETFs in the latest performance rankings posted an average return of just 0.60 percent over the past three months, with fewer than half generating gains.
The gap between the best and worst performers reached 17.61 percentage points, according to the Securities Investment Trust and Consulting Association. Cathay Taiwan High Dividend Momentum Active ETF (00400A) topped the rankings with a 7.91 percent return, outperforming the category average by 7.31 percentage points, the association’s data showed.
Photo: EPA/Ritchie B. Tongo
The divergence comes as investors increasingly demand evidence that heavy spending on AI infrastructure can translate into sustainable revenue and earnings growth. Even within the same supply chain, differences in order quality, profit margins and earnings prospects can lead to sharply divergent share-price performance.
Taiwan’s active ETF market has expanded rapidly, with 40 funds managing a combined NT$988.6 billion (US$30.41 billion) at the end of last month, nearing the NT$1 trillion milestone. Together, the funds had more than 4.25 million beneficiary accounts, association data showed.
Despite overlapping portfolio holdings, active ETFs have delivered widely differing returns, as performance depends not only on which stocks managers select, but also on when they buy, how much they invest and when they adjust their positions.
Cathay fund manager Liang En-yi (梁恩溢) said recent volatility reflected investors’ reassessment of corporate prospects as the AI investment theme entered a phase in which earnings must justify expectations.
Although AI-related stocks have propelled Taiwan’s equity market to new highs this year, investors are looking beyond the hype to determine which companies can turn AI demand into sustainable profits, he said.
The supply chain spans semiconductors, servers, cooling systems and power infrastructure, with demand and earnings growth varying across segments, he added.
Rapid shifts in investor preferences make it increasingly critical for fund managers to adjust their portfolios as industry conditions change, Liang said.
A market correction does not necessarily mean growth opportunities have disappeared, but it can expose differences in companies’ earnings prospects and valuations, he said.
For active managers, the challenge is to identify companies whose earnings can justify their valuations while managing the risks of concentrated positions in a volatile market, Liang said.

Flu season came early; your vaccination is overdue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:18 UTC
01:49:18 KST

This fall, like every other, I tried to game the flu season. My goal, always, is to get my vaccine at just the right moment: before the first cases pop up, yet late enough so that its protective effects last beyond the holidays and well into January or February, when infections tend to peak. That typically means scheduling my appointment for sometime in mid-to-late October.
This year, the virus snuck up on me. Earlier this month, I started hearing from friends with sick kids — weeks before my own teen and I had gotten vaccinated. Drat.
The US is experiencing an unusually early flu season, one that, in another twist, started to pick up steam on the West Coast rather than following its more typical path from southern states north. Not only is that leaving many people unprepared, but early indications suggest it could be another year when our vaccines are not an ideal match against the circulating virus.
It has been a humbling reminder that the flu has a way of thwarting even the best-laid plans.
Infectious disease experts like to say, “You’ve seen one flu season, you’ve seen one season,” says Melissa Stockwell, professor of pediatrics and of population and family health at Columbia University Irving Medical Center. Because it is so hard to predict when it’ll hit, she recommends skipping my game-the-system strategy and trying to get vaccinated by the end of September or early October.
What is behind this early takeoff for the flu? Nobody can say for sure, but the virus’s infuriating ability to stay one step ahead of humans could take some of the blame. Influenza is constantly undergoing tiny genetic changes (and in very rare instances, abrupt, major ones) to the pieces of the virus targeted by vaccines. Global health authorities and infectious disease experts closely track those shifts with the goal of choosing the most protective composition for annual vaccines.
It is hard to get that recipe exactly right. The WHO’s flu team typically picks the strains in February so that vaccine manufacturers can have the shots ready for the fall — a long enough lag for the flu to surprise us. The world was reminded of the challenge last year, when a new strain called subclade K, a mutant of H3N2, was able to circumvent both the flu shot and our preexisting immunity (protection acquired from past infections and vaccinations).
This year, preliminary evidence suggests the culprit behind the West Coast’s unexpectedly early flu cases is a mutation in H1N1 called G155E, says Alex Greninger, a virologist who leads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington. About 80 percent of the patient samples sequenced by Greninger’s lab in August and September carried the mutation, which he says was also prevalent in cases during flu season in the Southern Hemisphere and Southeast Asia.
To be clear, existing vaccines, while not a perfect match, are still worthwhile. Last year’s shots offer a good case for that: though subclade K rendered them less effective than in prior years, they still lowered the risk of doctors’ visits and hospitalizations for the flu. And they seemed to work best at protecting kids, who in recent years have been hit hard by the virus.
So even though the G155E mutation is not present in this fall’s flu shots, lab studies suggest the vaccines should still offer some level of protection. Moreover, anyone who did not get the flu last year will want the updated shot, as it protects against subclade K, which is still hanging around, as well as against influenza B, a strain that tends to circulate later in the season.
Another piece of good news: We are moving closer to a world where flu shots can be better matched to the circulating virus. In August, the US Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna’s flu vaccine for older adults, making it the first mRNA-based shot against the virus to reach the market. Studies suggest the technology can elicit a broader and longer-lasting antibody response than conventional shots, and it takes far less time to manufacture. That in theory suggests a future where the vaccine composition could be chosen much closer to the actual flu season.
For now, though, anyone feeling behind on the crucial task of getting their flu vaccine should take some comfort in the fact that there are more options out there than ever before — whether that is conventional shots, Moderna’s mRNA-based product, or even an intranasal spray that this year can be mailed directly to the majority of Americans.
And remember that there are no bad choices — so long as you follow through and get vaccinated.

Web site fined for illegally posting payment QR codes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:16 UTC
01:49:16 KST

New Taipei City has fined a Web site operator for posting QR codes that link to a parking payment service beneath public parking signs in Tamsui District (淡水), a practice that could expose users’ personal data.
Residents reportedly found suspicious parking payment signs at several locations in Tamsui, where an additional QR code had been hung beneath official public parking signs.
The signs could mislead people into thinking the QR code payments were part of an official government service. People reported it to the borough warden, who reported it to police.
Photo: Hsu Sheng-lun, Taipei Times
An investigation by police and the city’s Transportation Department found that the QR code linked to a legitimate Web site for paying parking fees.
However, as private companies are prohibited from placing advertisements on public signs, the operator was fined for contravening the Waste Disposal Act (廢棄物清理法), police said on Saturday.
Under Article 27 of the act, posting advertisements without approval carries a fine of N$1,200 to NT$100,000, the department said.
People should not trust unfamiliar QR code links posted on public signs, as criminals could exploit them to steal money or personal information, police said.
People should verify links with government agencies or call 110 for assistance, they said.
Parking meters are public facilities and not places for private advertising, the transportation department said, adding that it would step up enforcement in collaboration with police and the Taipei Department of Environmental Protection.
The only platforms offering self-service roadside parking payment options are the Parking Loudspeaker (停車大聲公) and Space4Car (易停網) apps, the transportation department said.
People should follow the information on their parking tickets and pay through legitimate channels, such as the city’s roadside parking fee Web site or convenience stores, it said.

Democracy makes its own waves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:15 UTC
01:49:15 KST

A simple orange ribbon has become one of Taiwan’s most unexpected political fashion statements. Supporters of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) have transformed “The Taipei Current” campaign ribbons into roses, stars, accessories and imaginative designs. What began as a campaign symbol has taken on a creative life of its own in Shen’s “Ocean Wave” (洋流).
Who knew an election campaign could inspire a fashion movement?
The phenomenon is more interesting than a passing campaign trend. Citizens are not merely consuming political messages; they are producing and reshaping them. In communication theory, this reflects participatory culture, in which audiences become creators rather than passive recipients.
Taiwan’s politicians are also showing their less conventional sides. Shen plays the clarinet, while the DPP’s New Taipei City mayoral candidate, Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), has demonstrated her piano skills. These performances say little about administrative competence, but they narrow the symbolic distance between politicians and members of the public.
Imagine China’s top leaders inviting similar public playfulness — including jokes at their own expense.
The contrast reveals an important distinction between democratic and authoritarian political aesthetics.
Beijing has devoted considerable resources to cultivating emotional identification with China among Taiwanese audiences. Its cross-strait cultural initiatives increasingly employ documentaries, animation, artificial intelligence-generated films and exhibitions to portray family reunions, shared ancestry and historical belonging.
That approach can be understood as the aestheticization of peace: translating political objectives into visually attractive and emotionally reassuring narratives.
Three mechanisms are particularly revealing. Emotional domestication transforms political separation into stories of family longing. Aesthetic normalization presents closer cross-strait relations through appealing images of everyday life. Cultural depoliticization embeds political messages within apparently nonpolitical artistic and cultural experiences.
Productions such as the documentary Letters Across the Strait (兩岸家書) and the animated short The Reunion Journey (團圓令) illustrate these approaches. Despite their different artistic forms, their institutional presentation repeatedly returns to familiar themes of separation, shared identity and reunion.
The problem is not the authenticity of emotions or the creativity of Chinese artists. It is the predetermined political framework surrounding these narratives. When the preferred conclusion is established before the story begins, even sophisticated imagery risks becoming predictable.
However, cultural appreciation should not be confused with political consent. Taiwanese audiences can enjoy Chinese artistic traditions without accepting Beijing’s political claims.
The limits of this approach become particularly apparent when humor challenges political authority.
Taiwanese comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪), known for satirizing Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), was last month injured in a vehicle collision. Taiwanese prosecutors have indicted five suspects, alleging that a China-based suspect financed a staged collision to prevent his performance.
The case highlights the tension between cultural attraction and political intimidation. Soft power depends on credibility and voluntary identification; coercion can undermine both.
An authoritarian political system restricting independent expression faces a structural dilemma: It seeks the emotional appeal of cultural creativity while limiting the freedom from which much of that appeal emerges.
Taiwan’s democracy is noisy, polarized and far from perfect. Nor does a fashionable ribbon make a good mayor. Yet its political culture allows Taiwanese to improvise, parody, disagree and transform public symbols in ways that no campaign headquarters can fully control.
That is a form of democratic soft power rarely captured by official publicity campaigns.
The beauty of The Taipei Current is not that everyone follows the same direction. It is that, in Taiwan, everyone is free to make their own waves.
Bonnie Yushih Liao is an assistant professor in Tamkang University’s Department of Diplomacy and International Relations.

Japanese companies are moving to pay compensation to users following waves of cyberattacks that have disrupted Internet services and raised concerns about economic stability.
GMO Internet Group Inc, a leading provider of online financial services, said customers would be compensated for losses stemming from unauthorized access following a cyberattack on its foreign exchange trading service, and all customers would receive ￥5,000 (US$32) as a gesture of goodwill, CEO Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post on Sunday.
“The Internet itself is now starting to break down,” said Kumagai, whose sprawling group includes Internet infrastructure and cryptocurrency trading.
Photo: Reuters
Japan said on Friday it would set up a team to simulate cyberattacks using artificial intelligence (AI) to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organizations scrambled to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the Internet.
More broadly, Japanese companies are being roiled by attacks with experts saying AI is helping automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect.
“The Internet is increasingly being transformed into a tool that malicious actors use to threaten and rob people,” Kumagai said.
Government and company Web sites in Japan, Europe and elsewhere went offline last week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts.
Kumagai has urged the Japanese government to apply cyberdefense measures in response to the cyberattack, after the introduction of a cyberdefense system this month.
The system could involve steps such as attacking hostile servers to neutralize threats.
“Now is the time for the public and private sectors to work together to protect Japan,” Kumagai wrote.
GMO said it received a demand for money from a party believed to be behind the attack, along with a threat to disclose company and customer information if it did not comply.
GMO said it would not comply with the demand and would respond to the incident in coordination with police and other authorities. It did not mention any connection to PHP flaws.
The company, which will provide a free alternative service to its customers for six months, said it could not currently calculate the impact on earnings from the goodwill payments and compensation for losses.
White-hat hackers working for the company had identified security issues but the depth and speed of the response were insufficient, Kumagai wrote.
Meanwhile, Park24, which operates the Times car-sharing service, said on Friday it would make ￥3,000 payments to customers following a personal data breach last month.
The company said it would no longer retain identity document images after completing registration verification and expects to book an extraordinary loss of ￥5.5 billion due to responses to the attack and compensation payments.

Cheng Li-wun hits ground in Changhua
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:49:13 UTC
01:49:13 KST

With fewer than 50 days to go before election day, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) has finally appointed a director-general of the campaign headquarters for Changhua County commissioner candidate Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政). KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) on Oct. 12 announced that she would be taking on the role.
The KMT’s incumbent Changhua County Commissioner Wang Hui-mei (王惠美) has enjoyed strong support in the county, but has distanced herself from Cheng’s handpicked successor candidate, Wei. The party had originally hoped that Wang herself would chair Wei’s campaign, but to no avail. The waiting dragged on so long that it became hard to watch, and Changhua voters have long grown weary of Wei. Wang is ostensibly worried about being scapegoated if the KMT were to lose the race.
After Wang’s refusals and Cheng’s announcement that she would lead the campaign, pan-blue newspapers jumped on Wang for being a turncoat and for biting the hand that feeds. One editorial resorted to old-fashioned emotional blackmail, emphasizing how Wang had been nurtured by the KMT throughout her 30-year political career from councilor to township chief, legislator and county commissioner, but now, because of a nomination dispute over her successor, she is willing to let power fall into the opposition’s hands rather than work with Cheng. It denounced Wang’s “unprecedentedly hardline stance.” With such impassioned criticism, the editorial made the KMT resemble a scorned lover: If it could not have Wang for itself, it must destroy her.
Since becoming KMT chairwoman, Cheng’s parachuting of Wei into the Changhua race has been one of the few major nominations she has directed. With Wei’s campaign showing unmistakable signs of weakness and his chances of winning appearing slim, Cheng is the obvious first target for blame. Plenty of eyes are watching to see her stumble. Remaining tied to Wei might be more of a political liability than an asset, but allowing the standoff to continue would expose the party to ridicule. With few alternatives, Cheng chose to wade in personally to clean up the mess.
It is notable that her role as party chairwoman has become increasingly marginal to this year’s election campaigns.
Candidates in other administrative regions have repeatedly asked her to stay away; Changhua has become one of the few stages on which she can still appear. Her frequent visits only underscore how unwelcome she has become at the local level.
Cheng’s opening move was to assemble a group of former KMT technocrats to act as policy advisers to Wei’s campaign. Convenor for agricultural economics Lin Hsiang-nung (林享能), a former Council of Agriculture chairman, is a nonagenarian. Convener for transport George Chen (陳世圯), a former acting transport minister, is 88. Convenor for science, technology and economics Hsueh Hsiang-chuan (薛香川), a former secretary-general of the Executive Yuan, is a comparatively sprightly 81. All three held public offices two or three decades ago and have long since fallen out of step with rapidly changing policy developments; none are particularly familiar with Changhua. Cheng has brought the advisory team to lend Wei their support, but at best has achieved a half-day excursion for retired officials whose ability to rally voters remains negligible.
By taking over as director-general of Wei’s campaign headquarters, Cheng has further cemented the impression that a vote for Wei is a vote for herself. As for whether Cheng proves to be a burden or an asset at the ballot box, that is up to Changhua voters to decide.
Cheng Yung-chang is a freelance writer.

Protesters kill longtime nurse treating Ebola patients in Congo
KINSHASA, Oct 26 - Youths killed a longtime nurse treating Ebola patients in eastern Congo and other health workers were sheltering under police guard, health officials said on Monday, in the latest in a series of attacks that have been fuelled by misinformation.
The nurse worked at the general hospital in the town of Bafwasende in Tshopo province, where he sought to help residents understand and protect themselves from Ebola. He was attacked and killed on Friday.
"We are shocked at how the population turned against this nurse. It is impossible to believe that he was mistaken for a stranger," a local health official told Reuters.
A colleague survived the attack and was recovering in hospital, the official said. Other health workers were sheltering at the general hospital under police guard, too afraid to go home, while the army also briefly deployed to the area, he said.
"None of the nurses have slept at their homes because they fear for their security," the official added.
Tshopo is among eight provinces in Congo that are battling a fast-spreading outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus. Congo's public health institute on Friday reported 9,964 total confirmed cases with around a 48.6% fatality rate since the outbreak was declared in May
Attacks on health workers have targeted hospitals, vehicles and staff involved in the Ebola response, underscoring the challenge of building trust among the population.
The local health official said that youths in the area had previously attacked another colleague, setting his house on fire, without providing a date for that incident.
Reuters has previously reported how the rapid spread of health misinformation posed a threat to health workers in eastern Congo even before Ebola began to spread, with multiple health workers killed in Tshopo after they were accused of spreading an imaginary disease that caused male genitals to atrophy.
"The killing of a nurse yesterday in Bafwasende is a loss to the Ebola response and an even greater loss to patients," Julien Harneis, the senior United Nations Ebola coordinator, said in a post on X on Sunday. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Analysis: No Elon Musk, Russian soldiers in Ukraine are not 'kids' who have 'no choice but to fight and die'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:40 UTC
01:24:40 KST

Analysis: No, Elon Musk, Russian soldiers in Ukraine are not 'kids' who have 'no choice but to fight and die'
"We should (have) some sympathy for the poor Russian conscripts too. Those kids have no choice but to fight and die in drone strikes."
For anyone watching and understanding Ukraine's years-long struggle for survival, the words of SpaceX founder and world's richest man Elon Musk ring with deep moral bankruptcy.
But more importantly, Musk's post on Oct. 25 — made in the middle of a hurricane scandal around the near-trillionaire's throttling of Starlink internet terminals used by the Ukrainian military — badly misrepresents the reality of how Russia staffs its wartime military.
The misconception that Russian soldiers are forced to fight against their will in Ukraine is one that has consistently reached the most powerful men in the United States.
Earlier this year, U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly lamented the deaths of soldiers on both sides, seemingly equating their suffering and the circumstances under which they found themselves in the trenches.
"Every day people are dying. Young handsome soldiers are being killed. Young men, like my sons. On both sides. All over the battlefield," he said in February.
"Young, young, beautiful people. They’re like your kids, two million of them — and for no reason."
But this sentiment ignores one important fact — Russian soldiers are not young men forced to fight in Ukraine against their will.
Most Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine chose to do so voluntarily, and did so not for values, but for cold, hard cash.
“Many think that the Russians are forced to fight. In fact, the Kremlin is afraid of mobilizing its people,” Kateryna Stepanenko, Russia research fellow at the Institute for the Study of War, told the Kyiv Independent.
Instead, Russian President Vladimir Putin relies on paying vast sums of money in order to entice people to sign up voluntarily, which they continue to do in droves — up to 40,000 a month according to NATO estimates from August.
"The moral equivalence of these two armies is impossible," Pavel Luzin, an independent Russian military analyst, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russia’s side is completely immoral, and the vast majority of its soldiers went to war voluntarily — driven by financial and psychological interests, not by coercion.
“One side is an occupying force trying to subjugate another country and its people. The other is fighting for its freedom. These are fundamentally different causes."
How does the average Russian soldier die on the front?
Russia effectively operates with two armies — a conscript army and a contract army.
The conscript army is the standing force used to defend Russia itself. The Kremlin conducts conscription twice a year, in spring and fall, requiring eligible men to serve for one year. By law, conscripts cannot be sent abroad to fight.
Instead, the Kremlin has relied on its contract army, which consists of paid volunteers and soldiers who sign short-term contracts with the Defense Ministry.
The way Moscow wages its war dictates that the Russian army fighting in Ukraine requires a constant inflow of warm bodies.
Since the Battle of Bakhmut in 2022-23, Russia's offensive tactics have relied mainly on a near-endless stream of dismounted infantry assaults.
As the war has transformed over time, so have these attacks, with assault squads shrinking first from 6-10 infantrymen around 2023, to the small infiltration teams of two soldiers — sometimes just one at a time — sent to seep through Ukrainian lines.
What has stayed consistent is the fact that these men for years are treated by their command as single-use soldiers.
Interviews with Russian POWs consistently tell a story of the assault soldier's mission being nothing more than to advance to a given point on the map, often past enemy lines, and wait for more orders.
While some may pierce through and survive to be reinforced and later sent out again, many are killed or wounded before reaching their assigned objectives, eliminated by a Ukrainian drone, shell, or mine.
But amazingly, despite this grim everyday reality of Moscow's war machine, Russia is able to continue without resorting to forced mobilization, as tens of thousands of Russians continue to sign up voluntarily every month.
"Money remains central to how the Kremlin sustains its forces."
Motivation and coercion
Money remains the main motivator for Russian soldiers signing up to fight in Ukraine.
Recruits are offered sign-up bonuses and monthly salaries several times higher than the national average. Federal-level sign-up bonuses from the Defense Ministry are complemented by bonuses paid out by Russian regions, operating under strict recruitment quotas imposed by Moscow.
For many from poorer regions, joining the army means solving years of financial hardship in a single decision.
"They’re incentivized not only by finances but also by numerous social benefits. These include free education, housing subsidies, discounts on cars, and other privileges that make service more attractive," Stepanenko said.
Some also enlist to resolve personal or legal problems.
"There’s recruitment among prisoners and people facing financial or legal issues, like those with unpaid loans or minor criminal charges. For them, signing a contract can mean avoiding debt or punishment," Stepanenko said.
This supply of recruits is complemented by men from Russia's prison system, as well as foreigners, an important exception to the largely financially driven domestic recruitment system.
Migrants from Central Asia and other countries are another target group. Many are pressured to enlist through the threat of deportation or the loss of Russian citizenship.
Russia has also recruited smaller groups of foreign nationals from countries such as Cuba, Syria, Nepal, and sub-Saharan Africa, through local intermediaries or misleading job offers that later turned into military contracts.
"There’s a lot of coercion. Recruitment sometimes involves abuse, manipulation, or pressure in workplaces to meet quotas. But there’s also a large number of people who willingly sign contracts to fight in Ukraine because of the financial rewards. Money remains central to how the Kremlin sustains its forces," Stepanenko said.
Putin's social contract
Well into the fifth year of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia continues to sustain a large army without declaring general mobilization or facing mass protests.
"Putin has two overriding priorities — to subjugate Ukraine and to stay in power. When he announced partial mobilization in the fall of 2022, his popularity dropped the most," Max Bergmann, director of the Europe, Russia, and Eurasia program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), told The Kyiv Independent.
"Another mobilization risks provoking backlash not only against the war, but against his rule itself."
To avoid that, the Kremlin promotes the idea that participation in the war is voluntary. It presents those who fight as contract soldiers, rewarded with high pay and other benefits.
"There’s a kind of social contract between Putin and Russian society. Putin will not mobilize the broader Russian society and will pay those who serve, as long as people do not oppose the war," Stepanenko said.
“So far, it has worked — there have been no large-scale protests across Russia."
Mobilization around the corner?
Even though recruitment numbers remain steady, Russia's military has performed poorly on the battlefield over 2026 compared to years past — taking far less territory despite high losses, failing to capture the Donbas region, and even losing ground to Ukrainian counteroffensives.
According to Kyiv, the Kremlin is planning a so-called "peripheral mobilization" of 300,000 people before the end of 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027.
The term "peripheral" refers to Kremlin's alleged intention of drafting large numbers of people without announcing it publicly, and focusing efforts on more remote, disadvantaged regions — the same areas that have provided most of the volunteer recruits.
The new forced draft was expected to come after United Russia's planned victory in Russian State Duma elections in September, but five weeks later, it hasn't, with only a few reports of ramped up coercive recruitment.
If large-scale mobilization is eventually announced again in Russia, the experience of 2022 would suggest a likely exodus of military-aged men and other forms of day-to-day avoidance.
But even then nowhere in that picture is any expression among ordinary Russians — especially those invading a neighbor with weapon in hand — that their country's war against Ukraine is inherently wrong.

Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:37 UTC
01:24:37 KST

A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing last year of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was unlawful.
Judge Jesse Furman, in his ruling, also granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay as an assistant U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York from her termination on July 16, 2025, through Dec. 20, 2025, when the judge inferred she accepted another job.
The DOJ said it would appeal Furman's ruling in which the judge rejected the department's arguments that the attorney general had authority to dismiss Comey without cause. The case is in in U.S. District Court in Manhattan.
Comey's lawyers, in a statement, said, "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
"As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system,'" the lawyers said. "This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."
Before her termination, Comey was involved in a series of high-profile federal prosecutions, including ones against the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean "Diddy" Combs.
Her lawsuit against the DOJ argued that her termination violated federal law and the Constitution and stemmed from President Donald Trump's longstanding animus toward her father, whom Trump had fired as FBI director in 2017.
James Comey is currently under federal indictment that accuses him of threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells forming the number "86 47." His attorneys are seeking to have that case tossed out.
James Comey, who denies any wrongdoing, previously had another federal indictment against him filed by the DOJ under Trump dismissed.
Maurene Comey's suit said the DOJ did not give "any explanation whatsoever for terminating Ms. Comey," and, "In truth, there is no legitimate explanation."
"Rather, Defendants fired Ms. Comey solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B. Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both," the suit said.
Furman, in his ruling for Comey, referenced that claim, but his decision was based on other grounds.
The judge rejected the DOJ's arguments that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi could remove a federal prosecutor "at will" and without cause and that current Attorney General Todd Blanche could ratify that act after the fact as he did in May as acting attorney general.
Furman also rejected the DOJ's argument that even if the Civil Service Reform Act requires removal of a prosecutor for cause, an attorney general's firing of her constituted an implicit determination that she was removed "for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service."
"The Court need not dwell long on Defendants' second statutory argument justifying Comey's removal," Furman said, referring to that claim.
"That is because the argument borders on frivolous."
The judge noted that Comey was fired despite having had excellent performance reviews.
"Comey's supervisors and peers consistently lauded her work, describing her as a 'brilliant lawyer and a gifted supervisor,' 'the lawyer the office turns to when legal excellence is a must,' and 'an outstanding AUSA in every respect' with 'judgment, work product, and courtroom advocacy [that are] among the finest in the country,'" Furman wrote.
The DOJ admitted that Comey's termination "was not 'for cause' and was not based on her
performance," Furman noted.
In addition, the judge said, the DOJ's argument that Comey's termination was lawful ignored parts of the Civil Service Reform Act, which "required that Comey be given advance written notice (subject to certain exceptions not relevant here); 'a reasonable time' to respond orally and in writing; representation; and 'a written decision and the specific reasons therefor at the earliest practicable date.'"
"Defendants concede, as they must, that Comey was not afforded these procedural protections," the judge said.
Furman also said the DOJ all but admitted that its argument that the attorney general had power to fire Comey under Article II of the U.S. Constitution — which establishes the executive branch of government — sought "to overturn nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."
"This Court, however, is bound to follow the Supreme Court's precedents unless and until the Supreme Court overturns them," Furman wrote.
The DOJ, in a statement, said, "The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."
That appeal would happen after Furman issues a final judgment in the case.
The judge reserved judgment on Comey's claim that her firing violated her First Amendment rights. Furman gave her until Nov. 9 to file arguments on why that claim should not be dismissed as moot given his order in her favor on other grounds.
The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to a post by the DOJ's Rapid Response account on X, which said, "The Department disagrees with this decision, which obstructs President Trump's constitutional authority to fire individuals who wield executive power on his behalf. We intend to appeal the decision in due course.
Comey, in a note to colleagues at the U.S. Attorney's Office after she was fired, wrote, "If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decisions of those who remain."
"Fear is the tool of a tyrant, wielded to suppress independent thought. Instead of fear, let this moment fuel the fire that already burns in the heart of this place," she wrote. "A fire of righteous indignation at abuses of power. Of commitment to seek justice for victims."

‘Everything destroyed’: Hebron businesses count cost of Israeli assault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:24 UTC
01:24:24 KST

‘Everything destroyed’: Hebron businesses count cost of Israeli assault
Israeli demolitions and road closures have devastated businesses in Hebron, leaving owners facing millions in losses.
Hebron, occupied West Bank – Sufyan al-Qawasmi stood near the rubble of his factories in the Farsh al-Hawa area of Hebron, lamenting the business he watched vanish beneath the debris.
Israeli bulldozers demolished the factories on Friday without any prior warning or notice, following a shooting attack carried out by two Palestinians that morning near Hebron’s western entrance. The attack killed two Israeli soldiers, as well as the two Palestinian gunmen, and prompted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to announce a large-scale military operation across Hebron and order preparations for a wider closure of the illegally occupied West Bank.
Demolitions are regularly used by Israel to punish Palestinians, typically the family members of attackers, but in al-Qawasmi’s case, for the misfortune of being close to the site of an attack. Human rights groups decry the practice, which is regarded as collective punishment.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich justified the demolitions as “establishing deterrence and exacting a price”.
The Israeli bulldozers destroyed a business that al-Qawasmi’s family had built up for his whole life, and provided a livelihood for more than 70 people. The first factory, which produced ceramics, is the same age as he is – it was established 50 years ago. Fifteen years later, the family opened a marble factory.
Their business flourished, becoming one of the most significant industrial operations in the West Bank, with goods exported to Israel.
In the space of a few hours on Friday, the ceramic factory and marble factory were gone, as well as several neighbouring buildings, including a three-storey house and various commercial facilities. Simultaneously, the city faced an Israeli military incursion that included the closure of all entrances, raids, arrests, and the forced evacuation of more than 3,000 Palestinians from their homes, severely disrupting the lives of residents and the city’s commercial activity.
The message was clear: the whole city would be punished for the actions of the attackers.
A devastating loss
Al-Qawasmi says he was given no chance to retrieve goods from the family businesses’ warehouses and factories before the demolitions began, leaving the stock buried under the rubble, where it remains.
“We managed to retrieve some marble slabs and store them in facilities belonging to friends nearby, but most of the stock was destroyed,” he told Al Jazeera.
Al-Qawasmi says that 1,300 square metres of their business’ property was destroyed, including the family’s offices. He estimates the losses at no less than 60 million shekels ($19m).
Those losses are devastating for al-Qawasmi’s family, but also for the wider economy in Hebron and the Palestinian economy as a whole.
According to the Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Hebron serves as a primary pillar of the Palestinian economy, contributing approximately 42 percent of the Palestinian gross domestic product (GDP). It is home to more than 23,000 economic establishments, including more than 5,000 industrial and artisanal facilities that employ approximately 40,000 workers.
Hebron’s economy is notably diverse, encompassing sectors such as stone and marble, plastics, metals, food production, leather and footwear, and glass, alongside robust commercial and agricultural activity.
Adnan al-Natsha, vice president of the Hebron Chamber of Commerce, told Al Jazeera that there are no precise figures yet regarding the total losses resulting from the Israeli military operation so far. He noted that work is currently under way to compile statistics on the damage inflicted on businesses and homes, losses estimated to be in the millions of dollars.
Al-Natsha explained that the extensive Israeli measures, including closing off areas of the city, displacing residents from their homes, demolishing buildings and shutting down commercial shops, have exacerbated the already difficult economic situation in Hebron – which already has an illegal Israeli settlement in its commercial centre that severely disrupts Palestinian movement and trade there.
“Business owners have been unable to operate their facilities because workers couldn’t reach their workplaces, and employees have been unable to get to their jobs. The impact of these measures is not limited to Hebron; it extends to the Palestinian economy as a whole,” he stated, adding that work was ongoing to assess the losses and damages of the ongoing Israeli operation so far.
Paralysed commerce
The Israeli military continues to lock down Hebron, including the installation of checkpoints, earthen berms, and concrete blocks across the city, as it conducts raids. As a consequence, economic activity has been severely disrupted.
Ibrahim Ahmaro, who owns a vegetable shop in the al-Jalada neighbourhood, one of the areas targeted by the Israeli operation, told Al Jazeera that he had been arranging his stock on Friday, preparing for Saturday, which is typically the busiest day for commerce due to the arrival of buses carrying Palestinian citizens of Israel shopping for cheaper produce.
Military vehicles suddenly stormed the area, and soldiers forced Ahmaro to leave his shop immediately. He says that he wasn’t given an opportunity to turn on the refrigeration units, which would have kept his goods from spoiling, nor allowed to retrieve his vehicle, which remained parked in front of the shop.
“My brother, the staff and I all left, thinking it would only be for a few hours. Instead, we were met with a total lockdown of the area, and we were unable to reach our shops, meaning everything inside was lost after being left unattended for days,” he added.
On Sunday morning, Ahmaro was able to return to check on his stock, despite the heavy military presence in the area. As soon as he entered, he said soldiers attacked him inside the shop and forced him out. He pleaded with them to let him remove at least a few crates; they granted him a few minutes to do so.
“I placed the crates 400 metres away from the shops so that local residents, facing the lockdown, could take whatever they needed. My losses on these goods alone exceed 50,000 shekels [$16,200],” he said with a sigh.
Economic expert Ali Oweiwi said that the Israeli military’s restrictions and lockdowns imposed on Hebron have created significant challenges for commercial and industrial establishments, which rely on road access to transport production supplies and distribute their products.
He explained that the impact of the closure is not limited to retail shops but extends to companies, factories, suppliers, and the transport and logistics sector, not to mention the workers who are forced to take alternative routes to reach their workplaces, all of which ultimately affect consumers.
Oweiwi said that if the Israeli operation concludes within a day or two, the economy might recover relatively quickly. However, if it persists for more than 10 days, it could lead to significant problems, including the accumulation of goods, disruptions to transport and a decline in productivity due to the difficulty of moving both workers and merchandise.
Israel – which will vote for a new parliament in pivotal elections on Tuesday – has not announced an end date for the lockdown in Hebron.
“The destruction of facilities specialising in vehicle dismantling, spare parts, and tile shops has resulted in losses estimated at 70 to 80 million shekels ($22.7m to $26m), in addition to the seizure of dozens or perhaps hundreds of vehicles belonging to the owners of these establishments,” Oweiwi said.

Italy flotilla torture case against IDF officials even broader than ICC war crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:23:43 UTC
01:23:43 KST

Italy’s criminal probe of flotilla activists’ torture claims against Israel impacts far more IDF officials than even the pending file before the International Criminal Court (ICC), multiple Israeli officials with knowledge of the case have confirmed to The Jerusalem Post.
Since 2007, flotilla activists have periodically sought to block Israel’s blockade to prevent weapons smuggling to Hamas in Gaza.
Although the activists claim they are seeking to bring Gazans humanitarian aid, Gazans have been receiving over 600 trucks of aid per day since the October 2025 ceasefire – almost triple what they were receiving pre-war.
Gazans’ overall situation is still far worse because the Strip is years away from being rebuilt, but there is no actual food shortage.
ICC seeks to arrest Netanyahu, Gallant, may target other Israeli officials
Currently, the ICC is confirmed to be seeking to arrest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant, with reports that it is also seeking to arrest minister Betzalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, and possibly also Defense Minister Israel Katz, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, and former IDF chief Herzi Halevi.
That is still a short list, and most of the officials are government officials because Israel has not probed its government officials.
In contrast, the Italian criminal probe relating to Israel’s treatment of arrested activists from the September-October 2025 and April-May 2026 flotillas not only includes many of the same ministers, but it also implicates a long list of IDF and prison service officials, of around a dozen.
In fact, the IDF officials being targeted are even more noteworthy than the prison service officials, given that there is some cloud of impropriety hanging over the prison service since it has been managed in recent years by Ben-Gvir.
Ben-Gvir himself was condemned by the entire Israeli government for various actions he undertook and statements he made relating to the flotilla activists.
But the IDF officials include completely apolitical and generally highly regarded officials, such as: former navy chief David Saar Salame, current Navy Chief Eyal Harel, each of their top advisers Tal Politis and Guy Levy, Ashdod Naval Base Chief Eitan Paz, and the Shayetet 13 Naval Commander.
While none of the activists’ claims against Israeli officials have been proven, there have been Israeli officials concerned that police and prison guard officials, who are under Ben-Gvir’s command, may have roughed up some of the activists.
Put differently, even if some of the most sensational charges might be untrue or exaggerated, some officials recognize that some of the lesser claims against officials under Ben-Gvir may be true.
Yet, there are no Israeli officials who believe that the navy’s conduct was anything other than highly professional, leaving many mystified as to what prosecutors from Italy – a country which has been one of Israel’s stronger allies even after October 7- could really be trying to get after going after IDF and naval officials.
The Post understands from officials with knowledge of the case that the prosecution is being run by a local Italian prosecutor, who is not coordinating with the Italian federal government.
Italian prosecutor rogue prosecutor, Israeli officials tell 'Post'
In other words, Israeli officials speaking to the Post portrayed the prosecutor as a rogue prosecutor who is using an Italian law for universal jurisdiction that the government would not have intended or expected to use against an ally like Israel, as much as it may have been passed to go after a traveling warlord from a more broken non-democratic country.
Further, the case has been a major domestic politics issue within Italy, such that some officials may see it as advantageous internally to make noise about such a case, without necessarily moving it forward to the end, something which could take many years in any event.
Around the time of the flotillas, Italy suspended certain defense cooperation arrangements with Israel, and the sides have sparred publicly over the treatment of some activists who were recently detained in the West Bank while assisting Palestinians with the olive harvest.
However, Israeli officials still view this criminal proceeding as being in conflict with overall Italian government policy, which has not sought to inflame relations.
Rather, multiple sources with knowledge of the case said that the long list of IDF officials who are considered highly professional simply indicated how politicized and disjointed the specific prosecutor likely was.
Moreover, they indicated that once a criminal probe is opened, it is always easier to add other suspects into the probe, even if they have less of a true connection to the heart of the issue.
The Israeli minister, IDF officials, police, and prison officials were all put under official investigation in Italy on October 16.
The move expanded an investigation that was previously focused on Ben-Gvir.
The case concerns alleged torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of boats headed towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026, the Rome prosecutors’ office said in a statement.
Probe opened after activists launched complaints
Investigators opened the probe after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions in September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.
Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission had reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism.
Notably, being insulted and being accused of terrorism might be problematic or fully justified, but would usually not be criminally probed.
Activists involved in the second mission alleged even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark, the use of rubber bullets, and tasers, a statement said.
Once again, some of these actions would clearly be criminal, but using a non-lethal taser to subdue a person resisting arrest is standard even in the West.
Investigators had identified various individuals forming the military and police chains of command involved in the operations, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors said they had sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information needed to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility. They did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
Questioned about their response, multiple Israeli authorities declined to address the issue, signaling that Israel may view the request as invalid if it is not endorsed by the Italian federal government or may choose to deal with it through diplomatic channels as opposed to strictly technical channels.
An interesting question would be whether Israel might comply more if the requests were more limited to Ben-Gvir and some of his officials, who took videos of themselves at minimum verbally harassing detainees.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
Being placed under investigation in Italy does not imply guilt and does not automatically lead to a trial. However, if the probe determines that charges are warranted, prosecutors could lodge a formal request for trial.
Reuters contributed to this report.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan hold rare Iran talks as Houthis strike again

Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday in an unusual diplomatic effort to ease tensions across the Middle East, even as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved military assistance to help defend the kingdom. Reuters reported that the meeting marked the first high-level talks between Iran and the three countries since the regional war expanded to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the visit, initiated by Pakistan, was intended to prevent further escalation. Saudi Arabia was represented by Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, the younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, also attended. Reuters reported Sunday that Qatari mediators had arrived in Tehran as part of the broader diplomatic effort.
The meeting brought together Iran and the three members of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all three. Iran has previously been mentioned as a possible future participant in the pact, but the arrangement is facing a significant test as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continue despite the mutual defense commitments.
Iran rules out nuclear talks as threat of US strikes grows
An Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran's nuclear program was not discussed at the meeting and would remain off the agenda until Iran's conditions for ending the war were met. Those demands include lifting the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and removing sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Iranian reports said the discussions instead focused on regional security and assistance to people in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon.
Pezeshkian expressed support for greater cooperation among Muslim-majority countries, saying Iran was prepared to deepen regional ties, resolve disagreements and strengthen collective security. He urged countries in the region to stand together against common threats and accused Israel, with U.S. support, of committing atrocities while accusing others of terrorism. According to Iranian reports, participants agreed to continue discussions aimed at strengthening cooperation among the four countries, particularly on regional peace and security.
The diplomatic initiative comes amid renewed threats of military confrontation between Washington and Tehran. Reuters reported that Iran had prepared detailed plans to attack undersea cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel launched another offensive. CNN, meanwhile, reported that U.S. forces already deployed in the Middle East could begin major military operations against Iran within 96 hours of receiving an order from President Donald Trump.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei during the Tehran talks, where Iran's nuclear program was reportedly not discussed
According to two U.S. officials cited by CNN, sufficient forces are positioned in the region to carry out an operation potentially broader than previous limited strikes against Iranian radar systems, missile launchers and other military assets that could be quickly rebuilt. Trump has not issued an order to launch such an operation.
Egypt approves military assistance as Houthis target Saudi oil lifeline
Meanwhile, Egypt's parliament approved defensive military assistance for Saudi Arabia in a closed-door session Monday, following an earlier postponement of the vote. The authorization allows President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to take the necessary measures to help Riyadh defend its territory and sovereignty against external aggression. The parliament did not disclose a detailed breakdown of the vote or specify the scope of the assistance.
A regional official familiar with the plans said Egypt would deploy air defense systems to help intercept missiles and drones launched toward Saudi Arabia. The official emphasized that Cairo's involvement would be strictly defensive and would not include ground forces. "Egypt will not send ground troops," the official said.
At the same time, the Houthis claimed to have launched new attacks on pumping stations along Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline and on Riyadh's airport, where two terminals had resumed operations only a day earlier after previous attacks forced their closure. Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed the latest Houthi claims.
The East-West pipeline has become a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, allowing Saudi Arabia to transport oil across the kingdom to the Red Sea port of Yanbu without relying on the strategic waterway. A pumping station strike disrupted the route about a month ago, highlighting its vulnerability to further attacks.
According to an earlier report by The Guardian, the pipeline played a critical role in protecting Saudi oil exports during the war with Iran, when shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was severely disrupted. Saudi Arabia used the route to divert approximately 4 million barrels of oil per day, equivalent to roughly 4% of global supply, to Yanbu. The renewed attacks threaten an energy lifeline that has helped the kingdom withstand one of the most serious disruptions to Gulf oil exports in recent years.

Pope Leo's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru to go ahead, Vatican says

Unknown Publisher

Pope fit enough to make Latin America trip next month, Vatican says
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo’s trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru will go ahead, the Vatican said on Oct 26, indicating that his recovery from lung cancer surgery was on track and that he was fit enough to make the Nov 6-17 journey.
The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering from an Oct 13 surgery in which doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung and diagnosed him with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
“The Holy Father’s recovery after the surgery continues, and the latest medical examinations attest to his good health and favorable clinical condition,” the Vatican said in a statement, citing the Pope’s personal physician Luigi Carbone.
“Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey,” the statement said.
Pope returning to familiar region
The Pope’s South America tour is set to be one of the most intense foreign trips taken by a Catholic leader in decades. He is scheduled to travel some 31,000km over the 10-city tour and give 36 speeches.
The Vatican said the trip would proceed with no changes to the previously published agenda.
The Pope had spent decades as a missionary in Peru before his predecessor Francis called him back to Rome in 2023 and promoted him to Vatican positions, so the trip will mark a homecoming of sorts for the first US pontiff.
“I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I’ve experienced so many moments of my life,” he said in the Vatican message.
“May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy,” Leo said.
In its statement, the Vatican said the Pope was “adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritise his recovery while continuing to fulfil the responsibilities of his ministry”.
On Oct 25, the Pope addressed the faithful in St Peter’s Square, but on doctors’ advice he cancelled a day visit to the central Italian town of Assisi, which had been scheduled for Oct 27. REUTERS
