‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:51:18 UTC
00:51:18 KST

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return to Brazil after winning a historic fourth term in power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro.
“This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.
A few hours earlier, Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from a first-round defeat in early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff.
“Today is a historic day,” Lula declared, before telling a sea of elated supporters: “Democracy always, dictatorship never again. Democracy always, fascism never again.”
Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.
But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo and cities all across Brazil. He won with 64.2m votes to Bolsonaro’s 59.8m, a 51.79% to 48.21% victory. It was at least 10m more votes than Lula secured in the first round.
While Bolsonaro initially refused to concede, his party acknowledged the election results on Monday, nearly a full day after Lula’s win.
“We recognize the presidential election results,” the Liberal party head, Valdemar Costa Neto, said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.“
Lula’s health minister, Alexandre Padilha, told the Guardian shortly after the result was confirmed: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defence of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme-right candidate entailed.
“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha said at the hotel where the president’s team was following the count in São Paulo.
Bolsonaro rejected the result, following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.
The US administration had been rooting for a Bolsonaro victory that would have seen the pro-Donald Trump so-called “orange wave” continue its sweep across the region into Latin America’s largest democracy. Trump took almost 24 hours to comment and, on Monday, appeared to endorse Bolsonaro’s claim when asked about Brazil’s election.
“It looked terrible to me. I thought it was a terrible look. I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election, frankly,” the US president said.
When asked if he intended to do anything in response, Trump said: “Well, I’m not running Brazil. I’m running the USA. And I just thought that the election was – I like Lula. I get along with him very well. I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated. The extension given was very strange.”
Other leaders and governments from across the political spectrum were quicker to recognise Lula’s victory. Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum, tweeted: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, wrote: “The global progressive resurgence has just begun.”
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called Lula’s victory “a historic win for the global progressive movement” and said his government looked forward to continuing to collaborate on “shared values of democracy, social justice and climate action”.
Rightwing South American leaders also recognised Lula’s victory, with Chile’s president, José Antonio Kast, calling Lula to offer congratulations and Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, saluting “the Brazilian people for this democratic day”.
Even Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella – who had publicly backed Bolsonaro and appeared in a recent live broadcast with him on social media – acknowledged Lula’s win, tweeting: “When the people decide at the ballot box, their will is respected because it is sacred. That’s what democracy is all about!”
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.”
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said: “China respects the choice of the Brazilian people.”
Besides Trump, one of the few powerful international voices of dissent was Elon Musk, who claimed the “math doesn’t add up” for Lula’s comeback, ignoring the fact that it did because of the historically low level of abstention in the second round.
In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the US had been accused of seeking to influence the result through a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure. Erika Hilton, a transgender lawmaker who recently became the most voted-for woman in Brazil’s congress, said those efforts had failed. “We have defeated the interference of the US government, which thought it could turn our country into its back yard. Brazil and the Brazilians are too gigantic to be anybody’s back yard,” she said.
Lula’s victory will also have profound consequences for the environment and the Amazon rainforest in what is the world’s most biodiverse nation. On the eve of the vote, the former environment minister Marina Silva had warned that Bolsonaro, if elected, would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rainforest destruction started by his father, whose 2019-22 administration coincided with a surge in deforestation.
On Sunday night, Silva was in a buoyant mood, telling the Guardian: “My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people.”
She said: “The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations.”
For Flávio Bolsonaro, the future looks bleak. As the scale of Lula’s victory became clear on Sunday night, the mood at the Brasília mansion where Bolsonaro was watching the count soured, with what had initially resembled a lively birthday party turning into something closer to a wake. Like football supporters heading for the exits midway through the second half because their team was being thrashed, crestfallen guests began heading home.
One of them approached the dozens of journalists waiting for Bolsonaro’s speech to shout that it was the “north-east’s fault”, insulting the region where Lula has historically won most of his votes.
One photograph circulated by Lula supporters showed a dejected Bolsonaro in tears, although it had been taken on the eve of the vote. Another image showed a red-faced Bolsonaro flanked by visibly mortified allies as they came to terms with their defeat. São Paulo’s pro-Bolsonaro governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, sat next to him covering his face with his hand.
On Paulista Avenue, where huge crowds had gathered to hear Lula speak, one reveller wore a costume of Flávio Bolsonaro behind bars. Some suspect the senator is likely to flee the country to the US once his term runs out in February and he loses parliamentary immunity. Bolsonaro is facing a series of federal police investigations over suspected misdeeds including money laundering, although he maintains he is innocent.
Lula supporters delighted in the idea that the far-right politician may soon join his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his coup attempt, in jail.
“Oh, how awful! Poor little thing!” João Maluf, a 27-year-old psychologist, shouted sarcastically as he held up his mobile phone to the crowd to show them a photograph of a visibly distraught Bolsonaro. “We want rid of these fucking Bolsonaros,” Maluf said.

Digital Communications and Video Frequency Selection: TAF Industries Unveils Upgraded Kolibri 13” FR1 Repeater Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:50:34 UTC
00:50:34 KST

Ukrainian company TAF Industries has released an upgraded version of the Kolibri 13″ FR1 relay carrier.
Viktor Tymoshenko, the company’s Brand Manager, told Militarnyi more about the modifications during the Future Forces Forum in the Czech Republic.
The main change is switching to digital communication between the operator and the carrier. Control commands and video transmission from the carrier now use a single digital channel. This improves the safety of the carrier’s crew, as the digital video feed cannot be intercepted to determine the pilots’ location.
The upgrades also include changes to the signal relay system for strike drones. The module transmits control commands to FPV drones during combat missions.
The repeater is available in several configurations with different video communication frequency bands for long and short ranges. These include the 6000–7200 MHz and 7000–8000 MHz bands for long ranges.
The link between the relay and the strike drone is analog. However, the developers are already working on a fully digital version.
“To receive video from the strike drone, a horn antenna is installed in the nose of the carrier. Its advantage is that it effectively filters out external radio noise, allowing it to receive a clean video signal,” Viktor Tymoshenko shared.
The carrier has a modular design, with the repeater installed as a separate unit.
The military selects the required frequency configuration when placing an order. The upgraded platform has already been codified, making it eligible for purchase using e-Points.
However, demand for the upgraded Kolibri 13″ FR1 is currently high, with orders booked two months in advance.
“This is the result of continuous iterations in collaboration with the military. They tell us what they need, we develop a product that we believe will meet those needs, test it together, and make adjustments,” the company representative concluded.
In July, The Fourth Law and TAF Industries codified the Kolibri 10″ Advance FPV drone with Level 1 autonomy.

EXPLAINER - Serbia's students won the election, but who will govern?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:50:14 UTC
00:50:14 KST

A student-led movement that emerged after a deadly railway station collapse has won Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, challenging the political camp led by President Aleksandar Vucic, which has been in power for more than a decade.
Vucic conceded defeat following Sunday’s snap election, putting the Student List, a slate of candidates selected by student assemblies, on course to form the next government.
The movement has brought together academics, doctors, artists, farmers and activists under a campaign promising to tackle corruption and restore public trust in state institutions.
But while students organized the campaign and selected its candidates, none stood for parliament themselves.
And despite its electoral victory, the movement has yet to announce who will lead the next government.
The protests erupted after a concrete canopy collapsed at Novi Sad railway station on Nov. 1, 2024, ultimately killing 16 people.
The disaster, at a recently renovated station, sparked accusations of corruption, poor oversight, and failures in public procurement.
Tensions escalated after students and lecturers holding a vigil in Belgrade were attacked weeks later.
Four days later, students at the Faculty of Dramatic Arts began a blockade, demanding accountability for the attacks. Other universities soon joined.
The students organized through plenums, assemblies where participants debated and voted on decisions, rather than appointing a single leader.
Their initial demands included the release of documents relating to the station's reconstruction, prosecution of those who attacked protesters, dismissal of charges against detained students and increased university funding.
The movement soon spread beyond campuses, drawing support from teachers, farmers, professionals and other citizens.
Months of demonstrations contributed to the resignation of Prime Minister Milos Vucevic in January 2025, although the protests continued after Djuro Macut formed a new government in April.
One of the largest demonstrations took place in Belgrade on March 15, 2025, drawing an estimated 275,000 to 325,000 people, according to the independent Archive of Public Gatherings, and between 88,000 and 107,000, according to official estimates.
The movement also had support beyond those attending rallies. A CRTA survey published in January 2025 found that 61% of respondents supported the protests and blockades, including some people closer to governing parties.
By May 2025, students were demanding early parliamentary elections.
Rather than establish a conventional political party, the movement formed a citizens' group and selected candidates through more than a year of assemblies, discussions and collective work.
Its electoral slate, known as "Student List - Students Win," featured 250 candidates from different professions and regions.
Students themselves were excluded from the list, as were former members of governing coalition parties and former officials of parliamentary opposition parties. The candidates include doctors, university staff, artists, entrepreneurs and activists from different parts of Serbia.
The campaign relied heavily on volunteers traveling across Serbia, meeting voters and presenting the election as an opportunity to challenge entrenched political power.
With almost 99% of votes counted, the Student List had secured 52.7% of the vote, compared with 39.2% for the alliance led by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party, according to preliminary election commission figures. That would give the Student List 139 seats in the 250-member parliament.
The Student List has not publicly named a candidate for prime minister.
However, two prominent figures have attracted the most attention: cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, who heads the parliamentary list, and former central bank governor Dejan Soskic.
Srdanovic is a professor at the University of Novi Sad's Faculty of Medicine and has worked at the Institute for Cardiovascular Diseases of Vojvodina since 1997.
A prominent supporter of the protests, he has advocated improvements to Serbia's healthcare system, particularly primary and secondary care.
During the campaign, he emphasized direct engagement with voters. Following the election, he also called for better relations with neighboring countries and the international community.
Soskic, an economics professor at the University of Belgrade, served as governor of the National Bank of Serbia from 2010 to 2012.
He resigned after proposed legislative changes that he argued threatened the central bank's independence.
His economic background has made him a prominent figure in discussions about the direction of a future government.
Vucic claimed during the campaign that Soskic was the students' preferred candidate for prime minister, but the movement has not confirmed that.
Radomir Saicic, another candidate, has said lawmakers would decide on a prime minister in consultation with the student movement.
The Student List brings together figures from academia, sports, culture and grassroots activism.
Dejan Bodiroga, a former basketball star and current Euroleague Basketball president, is among its most recognizable names.
A three-time EuroLeague champion who played for clubs including Real Madrid, Barcelona and Panathinaikos, Bodiroga is 24th on the list.
Saicic, ranked 91st, is a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade and a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts.
An outspoken supporter of the protests, he has also criticized the authorities' handling of Kosovo.
Sociologist Jovo Bakic, 76th on the list, is known for his criticism of Vucic's administration.
A professor at the University of Belgrade, Bakic has researched nationalism, political sociology and Europe's far right.
After Vucic conceded, Bakic told N1 that he had expected a decisive student victory but had not expected Vucic to acknowledge defeat. He called for action against organized crime.
Farmer Zlatko Kokanovic, 17th on the list, is a leading opponent of Rio Tinto's proposed Jadar lithium and boron mining project.
He has pledged to seek a permanent ban on lithium and boron exploration and extraction, bringing environmental concerns into the movement's political agenda.
Playwright Zeljko Hubac, third on the list, and actor Tihomir Stanic, eighth, are also prominent figures from the cultural sphere.
Hubac helped establish the citizens' group through which the movement contested the election, while Stanic publicly supported its campaign.
Other candidates include Mirjana Nikolic, rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade, civil engineering academic Sanja Fric, geological engineer Zoran Djajic and lawyer Sarah El Sarag.
Their varied backgrounds reflect the movement's attempt to build a political alternative far beyond Serbia's established parties.
The Student List's 11-point program focuses on fighting corruption, strengthening institutions and improving living standards.
Its proposals include protecting courts and prosecutors from political interference, investigating officials' assets and confiscating illegally acquired property.
It also promises greater transparency in public procurement, audits of infrastructure projects and reforms to public broadcasters and media regulators.
Appointments to state-owned enterprises would be based on professional qualifications rather than political connections, the plan adds.
The program also includes free school textbooks, affordable housing, greater support for farmers and domestic businesses, and improved access to medicines and healthcare in rural areas.
On employment, it proposes reducing the maximum duration of fixed-term contracts from 24 to 12 months.
Many of these pledges address grievances that fueled the protests, particularly corruption, weak institutions and declining trust in public services.
Winning the election does not automatically give the Student List control of the government.
Under Serbia's Constitution, the president nominates a prime minister after consulting representatives of the parties and lists elected to parliament.
The nominee then presents a proposed Cabinet and government program to the 250-member National Assembly. At least 126 lawmakers must vote in favor for the government to take office.
Election-night projections suggested the Student List had secured enough seats to reach that threshold on its own, although the final allocation depends on certified results.
The new parliament must convene within 30 days of the official declaration of results. If lawmakers fail to elect a government within 90 days of the assembly's formation, parliament is dissolved.
The process is complicated by Vucic's resignation as president on Sept. 27 to pursue the premiership.
Parliamentary Speaker Ana Brnabic, a close Vucic ally, is serving as acting president pending a separate presidential election due before the end of the year.
The Student List’s parliamentary victory now puts the movement in a strong position to challenge Vucic’s camp for the presidency as well.

Cabinet under pressure from both sides as budget talks resume

Cabinet under pressure from both sides as budget talks resume
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet is resuming talks with seven opposition parties this week as it tries to secure the votes it needs to steer its budget for next year through parliament.
Prime minister Rob Jetten and finance minister Eelco Heinen still hope they can win support from both sides for a broad deal, despite warnings from party leaders that their demands are irreconcilable.
The largest opposition party, the left-wing Pro, is calling for the coalition parties to scrap plans to raise income tax to fill the gap created after it abandoned its welfare cuts, under pressure from Pro and the trade unions.
Pro and the pro-European party Volt say the money should be raised instead through higher taxes on savings and investments, but Heinen’s party, the liberal-conservative VVD, want to replace the wealth tax system with a capital gains tax.
The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA needs the support of at least two opposition parties to secure its legislation through parliament.
Pro and Volt have enough seats in the two houses of parliament to guarantee a majority, but the VVD fear that making too many concessions on the left will damage their already precarious standing in the opinion polls.
Asylum and nitrogen
Many VVD voters were dismayed by Heinen’s proposed reforms to the “box 3” wealth tax, which would have led to people with modest investment portfolios paying more, prompting the finance minister to go back to the drawing board.
Opposition parties on the right, such as JA21, are pressing the cabinet to tighten the rules on asylum further as the price for their support.
JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans wants the status of all 70,000 Syrian refugees in the Netherlands to be reviewed and asylum claims to be processed outside the EU. The party also wants to water down the so-called “spreading law” so that the government in The Hague cannot force municipalities to take in minimum numbers of asylum seekers.
Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen is also expected to take part in the talks, suggesting the cabinet is prepared to compromise on its plans to cut nitrogen pollution, even though Pro has warned the reforms “must not be weakened”.
Another pivotal issue is likely to be the proposed surrogacy law, which the orthodox Protestant party SGP wants the cabinet to withdraw.
The bill was put in the spotlight last week when Jetten and his partner Nicolás Keenan announced they were having a baby next year with the help of a surrogate mother.
At the moment there is no law regulating surrogacy in the Netherlands. Couples who make their own arrangements must have the child adopted before they are legally recognised as parents.
The SGP have said they will not support the cabinet unless it withdraws a bill that would recognise the rights of parents who have children born through surrogacy immediately.
The party also wants the government to intervene to stop hospitals offering to perform abortions after 22 weeks without a compelling medical reason.

Kenya releases first Ebola contacts from quarantine, milestone in containment efforts
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:16:23 CET
00:16:23 KST

NAIROBI, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Kenya on Monday released from quarantine the first group of people who came into contact with its index Ebola patient, a milestone in its efforts to contain cases to a single infection cluster.
The 20 people released completed 21 days of monitoring without developing Ebola symptoms and are in good health, the director-general in Kenya’s health ministry, Patrick Amoth, said in a statement.
Kenya has reported nine Ebola cases so far, two of whom have died. The remaining seven patients are stable and receiving treatment, Amoth said, adding that 98 others still in quarantine would be released in four waves beginning on November 3.
“This is a milestone worth celebrating,” Amoth said. “It is also a reminder that the work is not yet done.”
Kenya’s first case died in a hospital in Nairobi on October 5, after which eight others fell ill while in quarantine. It announced on Friday that a second person had died.
Ebola’s spread from Congo, where the outbreak was declared in mid-May, to Kenya has raised concerns about lapses in border screening.
Nigeria has said its first Ebola case in more than a decade, which it reported last week, appears to be closely related to Kenya’s index case, citing genomic analysis. The two cases both flew out of Uganda’s Entebbe airport on the same day in early October.
Amoth said those leaving quarantine posed no risk to their families or communities where they live and urged Kenyans to welcome them home. “We cannot afford to drop our vigilance,” he said.
(Reporting by Vincent Mumo Nzilani and Ammu Kannampilly;Editing by Alexander Winning and David Holmes)

‘No fuel to keep babies warm’: shortages push hospitals in Yemen’s Taiz to brink
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:16:18 CET
00:16:18 KST

By Olivia Le Poidevin
GENEVA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Fuel shortages in Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz have forced one hospital to cut the number of incubators it can operate from 40 to 10, putting newborn babies at risk as weeks of fighting choke off vital supplies and deepen a humanitarian crisis affecting hundreds of thousands of people.
“There’s no oxygen, there’s no fuel to run the incubators, to keep the babies warm,” said Nada Ahmed, a nurse in the neonatal unit of the Yemeni-Swedish Hospital for Maternity and Childhood.
Nawal Najeeb, a supervisor in the neonatal unit, warned the facility could be forced to halt operations if fuel supplies do not arrive.
“It will be a catastrophe for the babies, a catastrophe of deaths and disabilities.”
Taiz has been largely isolated since October 3, with fighting preventing humanitarian supplies from entering and civilians from leaving, following an escalation in clashes between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
FUEL PRICES SURGE
Key supply routes, including the Taiz-Aden corridor, have been blocked by Houthi forces, worsening shortages of water, food and fuel. The city hosts nearly half of the 250,000 people displaced by the latest fighting, according to the United Nations.
In Taiz city, 42 health facilities are reporting acute shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said.
Fuel prices have surged to 2,000 Yemeni rials per litre, driver Abdullah al-Radfani told Reuters.
Oxfam Yemen’s policy, advocacy and media manager, Fatma Jaffar Shotah, described one dialysis patient who has to spend two nights at a healthcare centre rather than travelling home between sessions because regular journeys have become unaffordable, the cost rising from half a dollar to around $10.
“Fuel shortage inside the city is having catastrophic impacts on people’s lives,” she said.
The strain is being felt beyond Taiz. Aid group Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said fuel shortages were causing power outages at hospitals and primary healthcare centres in the southern governorates of Aden and Lahj, affecting operating theatres and intensive care units.
HUNGER AND MALNUTRITION
UN agencies and aid groups also warned of worsening hunger and malnutrition. The World Food Programme says that more than 800,000 people have been cut off from food assistance in Taiz and surrounding areas.
UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said 52,000 of the 168,000 children screened in Taiz so far this year are acutely malnourished, including more than 11,500 suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
Although UNICEF has put in place nearly 8,000 cartons of life-saving therapeutic food, enough to sustain treatment services for around three months, Pires warned that worsening insecurity and movement restrictions could hamper future deliveries and prevent families from reaching treatment centres.
MSF said growing displacement was aggravating child malnutrition in southern Yemen, an area which has already faced a long-standing hunger crisis, as families flee fighting in the north and along the west coast.
Between September 15 and October 22, MSF screened 299 children under 5 at its mobile clinics in Aden and Lahj. Forty-four children, or 14.7%, were suffering from moderate acute malnutrition, while 28 children, or 9.4%, were severely malnourished and in need of hospital care.
“In each location we go, on a daily basis, we see at least one or two children who are in severe acute malnutrition,” said MSF’s mobile health activity manager, Sara Ghanem.
(Reporting by Olivia Le PoidevinEditing by Keith Weir)

MEXICO CITY, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The head of Mexico’s National Electoral Institute will resign amid allegations of corruption, a decision President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Monday that she supports.
INE chief Guadalupe Taddei’s resignation is the most high-profile departure tied to alleged corruption in Sheinbaum’s two-year-old presidency.
The move raises fresh questions over the credibility and leadership of the autonomous electoral authority as it prepares for the 2027 midterms and after lawmakers rejected Sheinbaum’s broader attempt to reform Mexico’s electoral system earlier this year. Lawmakers later supported a narrower package of electoral changes.
“There couldn’t be this shadow of a conflict of interest. It’s good that she made the decision to step aside,” Sheinbaum said at her daily press conference, while rejecting the notion that the resignation pointed to a political crisis.
Mexico’s Superior Audit Office is investigating alleged irregularities involving INE contracts, including possible conflicts of interest and the triangulation of public funds. Taddei, in local news outlets, has been accused of favoring an INE contractor, with whom she has a personal relationship, with contracts worth millions of dollars.
“Over the past few days, rumors, fabricated material, leaks, and versions of events have spread through the media and social networks, and as in all such cases, their authenticity, context, and purpose must be verified and corroborated,” Taddei said in a Sunday statement announcing her planned resignation.
Taddei said her resignation aimed to protect the INE and allow it to fulfill its constitutional mission.
The 2027 elections are expected to be hotly contested, and the INE’s credibility is essential to avoid conflict, said Antonio Ocaranza, a consultant who was a spokesman for former President Ernesto Zedillo. He called Taddei’s exit “a necessary and timely correction.”
Ocaranza said the case also poses a broader test for Sheinbaum, as there are already many cases of political families close to her political party, Morena, accused by local news outlets, and “the government has shown little desire to investigate and punish them.”
Authorities are also investigating potential fraud linked to several contracts signed by other INE officials in which there may have been conflicts of interest.
Opposition party PRI’s President Alejandro Moreno said Taddei’s resignation should not be used to “impose another person close to Morena.”
“Mexico cannot go into the 2027 elections with an electoral authority whose impartiality is in serious question,” he added.

Swiss city's unique council for francophone affairs celebrates 20 years

Swiss city’s unique council for francophone affairs celebrates 20 years
The Council for Francophone Affairs of the Biel/Bienne district (CAF), an institution established by the Canton of Bern to represent the interests of the French-speaking population, is celebrating its 20th anniversary. It is the only political body of its kind in multilingual Switzerland.
Until November 26, the public can visit the City of Biel library to see a bilingual exhibition on 20 years of the CAF. Seven themed panels showcase this political council, which represents the voice of the region’s French-speaking community and promotes bilingualism.
“This exhibition aims to raise the profile of the CAF’s activities,” said its president, Renaud Lieberherr, on Monday, adding that the body is a key partner in dealings with the Canton of Bern concerning French-speaking residents of Biel and its neighbouring municipalities. Recently, he has expressed concern about developments in Biel’s media landscape and voiced his opposition to the late introduction of French-language teaching.
More
Why bilingual schools are few and far between in multilingual Switzerland
Among the key issues for the next four-year legislative term that also affect the CAF is the cantonal law on languages and bilingualism. “We will be putting forward proposals for the law,” said Lieberherr.
Culture, education and health
The CAF is involved in the cultural sector, providing advice on cantonal grants, and in the education sector, ensuring that apprenticeship places are available for French-speakers.
“The CAF is also committed to ensuring that French speakers can access healthcare services in their own language,” said its president.
The body, comprising 18 members – representatives from Biel and Evilard as well as from the 17 German-speaking municipalities in the bilingual Biel/Bienne district – appoints representatives from the bilingual region to councils, commissions and committees at cantonal, regional and local levels.

What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:16:00 UTC
00:16:00 KST

What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump
October 26, 2026
1. What is Audi's $4 billion US investment plan?
US President Donald Trump announced the investment on Saturday, during a campaign rally in Georgia, a key battleground state for his Republican Party in the midterm elections next week.
Audi quickly confirmed the plan, saying it would build its first US factory near Macon, Georgia, costing around $4 billion (€3.6 billion) and creating some 4,500 jobs.
The German automaker said construction would begin next year, with a planned annual production of up to 200,000 vehicles due to start in the early 2030s.
The firm plans to build premium SUVs for the US market at the plant, marking a "long-term commitment" to what it said was "one of the world's most important premium markets."
The US investment comes as German automakers face unprecedented pressure from China, rising costs and two conflicts.
Backed by huge government subsidies, Chinese rivals have stolen a march in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), scaling up production of new models that are fast gaining market share in a crowded global auto market.
BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi's parent company, Volkswagen— the world's second-largest automaker — have all issued profit warnings in recent months as margins come under pressure.
They've also announced major cost-cutting. VW is preparing to axe up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, while Audi's factory in Neckarsulm, which has around 15,000 staff, is one of four plants at risk of closure.
2. Why is Audi investing in US car production?
Trump credited his 15% tariffs on European-made vehicles for Audi's investment, saying it "would not have happened without tariffs."
While the commitment does feed into Trump's plan to bring manufacturing back to the United States from abroad, Audi said it was making the huge outlay for growth and resilience.
“We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America," said the carmaker's CEO Gernot Döllner, who appeared alongside Trump at the Republican's campaign rally.
"The United States is one of the world's most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that ... This is about building a stronger Audi business in America — not only about building a factory," he said.
However, Trump's tariffs have undoubtedly added to the automaker's woes.
Audi, which currently exports to the US market from Europe and Mexico, said the additional costs amounted to about €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) last year.
With more than 160,000 vehicles sold, Audi's US sales last year fell 16%, amid intense competition and after Trump scrapped subsidies on electric vehicles in its second-biggest market.
By building a US factory, Audi should be able to avoid or reduce Trump's tariffs, industry analysts say.
3. What is the reaction in Germany amid huge cuts in the domestic auto sector?
There's been fierce criticism of the deal due to the severe pressure facing German automakers and because the new US investment could mean further job losses at home.
Much of the criticism focused on Döllner's rally appearance alongside Trump.
The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)'s transport policy spokesperson Isabel Cademartori described it as campaign assistance for an autocrat who is waging a trade war against Germany.
"This is a disgrace, especially considering the history of the Volkswagen Group," she stated, referring to the company's links with Adolf Hitler's Nazi party during World War II.
Christiane Benner, president of the powerful IG Metall union, labeled the rally appearance as "extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and not worthy of the company."
VW works council chief Daniela Cavallo went further, saying Döllner had let himself be turned "into a puppet in [Trump's] propaganda show."
Cavallo, however, noted that the US plant could make sense from a business perspective, as VW needs to grow its market share there.
An Audi spokesperson defended the US investment, saying it was "not a decision against Germany, but rather a step toward strengthening our global competitiveness."
Manfred Döss, chairman of Audi's supervisory board, insisted the automaker's future cannot be secured by cost-cutting and efficiency alone.
"We need the courage to invest, to seize new opportunities and to make decisions that will shape our company for decades to come," he added.
4. Will Audi's investment help Trump in the US midterms?
The announcement certainly appears timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on November 3.
Voters will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats hold the balance of power in Congress during Trump's last two years in office.
Holding the announcement in the key battleground state of Georgia is seen as a strategic move to boost the fortunes of local Republican candidates.
Since he returned to the White House last year, Trump has used tariffs and political pressure to force global automakers to relocate their factories to American soil.
Audi's investment follows moves by Stellantis and Japan's Toyota to expand US production, while Honda is in talks to build a new US plant.
US auto giants General Motors and Ford have also promised to increase domestic production.
While one investment announcement may not be enough to sway many voters, it serves one of Trump's main election promises — to revive industrial production in the US.
Edited by: Rob Mudge

Ukraine’s Air Force Is Going Fully Western—F-16 Wings, Gripen-Ready Bases and New Upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:15:16 UTC
00:15:16 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Air Force Is Going Fully Western—F-16 Wings, Gripen-Ready Bases and New Upgrades
Ukraine is restructuring its combat aviation around Western-style fighter wings, has already established the 107th F-16 Aviation Wing, and is preparing airbases capable of supporting multiple aircraft types—including Sweden’s Gripen—as part of a long-term Air Force transformation through 2035.
Yurii Ihnat, head of communications for Ukraine’s Air Force Command, told RBC-Ukraine on October 26 that the reform is intended to move Ukrainian aviation away from a structure built around individual Soviet-era aircraft types and toward more flexible bases and formations capable of operating Western fighters.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine is also counting on cooperation with US defense giant Lockheed Martin to repair, modernize, and improve the performance of its existing F-16 fleet.
For Ukrainian pilots, Ihnat said, the ultimate goal would be newer F-16 Block 70/72 aircraft.
“The dream of our pilots regarding the F-16 is to receive them in the newest modifications—Block 70/72. They would already allow us to confront Russian Su-35s with considerable confidence,” Ihnat said.
Gripen is also attracting significant attention inside the Ukrainian Air Force because of its relatively low operating costs and ability to function from less demanding infrastructure.
“Many of our pilots are discussing the Gripen because it is undemanding and one of the cheapest aircraft to operate,” Ihnat said.
Ukraine could initially receive older Gripen C/D variants already in service, he added, while manufacturer Saab is continuing work on the newer Gripen E.
“At first, we could receive aircraft that have already been in use—the C/D versions, Charlie and Delta. But the Swedish company Saab is already working on the new E—Echo—modification, which has very good characteristics,” Ihnat said.
Ukraine’s aviation plans extend well beyond wartime deliveries.
“We already have to think about the strategy for developing the Air Force after the war. It has already been laid out through 2035, including what the Air Force model will look like, what types of weapons we will have, and what the organizational structure will be,” Ihnat said.
For combat aviation specifically, that means transitioning toward wing-based formations.
“If we are talking specifically about aviation, this involves creating aviation units of the ‘wing’ type. For example, yesterday we already presented the Facebook page of the 107th F-16 Aviation Wing, which may publish some materials about its work,” he said.
At the same time, Ukraine is preparing what Ihnat described as universal airbases rather than facilities tied to a single fighter model. The goal is for the same infrastructure to be capable of supporting F-16s, Gripens, and potentially other Western aircraft.
Previously, reports emerged that US defense manufacturer Lockheed Martin is considering a specialized version of the F-16 fighter jet for Ukraine, featuring extended flight range, upgraded radar systems, and improved capabilities to intercept Russian drones and cruise missiles.

Norwegian MP Smuggled Thermal Drones to Ukraine—Then Helped Change the Law

Norwegian MP Smuggled Thermal Drones to Ukraine—Then Helped Change the Law
Norwegian lawmaker Peter Frølich knowingly broke his country’s export rules in 2023 to get civilian drones equipped with thermal cameras into Ukraine, arguing that bureaucratic delays were putting Ukrainian soldiers’ lives at risk. He revealed the episode in his book Om krigen kommer and later discussed it with Norwegian broadcaster NRK on October 21.
Frølich, a member of Norway’s Conservative Party, sent drones through Fritt Ukraina, an organization he founded with a group of volunteers to support Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The group initially attempted to ship several thermal-imaging drones aboard the Kiel ferry, but Norwegian customs officials stopped the shipment. At the time, a decades-old regulation dating back to the 1950s made the export illegal.
Fritt Ukraina then appealed to the Norwegian government but received no immediate response. Frølich wrote that the situation was urgent and that delays could cost Ukrainian troops their lives.
The organization ultimately went ahead with the transfer despite the restriction.
Frølich said he does not encourage others to routinely break the law, but still believes the decision was justified.
“This is not something one should make a habit of. But sometimes you have to follow your gut and do what is obviously right, and show decisiveness,” he said.
The morning after the drones had been sent, the organization was informed that the government would fast-track consideration of the issue.
The rules were later changed, allowing civilian commercial drones to be legally sent to Ukraine.
Frølich has said he does not regret the decision, arguing that the episode exposed how outdated regulations were slowing assistance at a time when thermal-equipped drones had become critical tools for Ukrainian forces on the battlefield.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine and Norway were accelerating development of the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile defense program, with initial components already showing progress and the first tests targeted for the end of 2026.

Ukraine's steel production fell by 80% in September
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

00:14:00 KST

Ukraine's steel production fell by 80% in September
Ukraine's steel production fell by 80% in September following Russian attacks that hit seven blast furnaces: five at Metinvest facilities and two at ArcelorMittal.
Source: a study by the Centre for Economic Strategy (CES)
Details: In addition, the value of metal exports fell by 48% in August compared with August 2025 due to logistical difficulties.
"Ukraine still has the potential to export ore, but the blockade of ports has effectively made it impossible to ship it along traditional maritime routes. Switching to alternative routes is too expensive," the study said.
Even before the attacks, steelmakers had faced the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). On 1 July 2026, the European Union also introduced stricter restrictions and reduced duty-free quotas for imports of Ukrainian steel products.
In addition, steelmakers suffered from electricity supply disruptions during the winter.
Ukraine's metallurgical industry, along with related sectors, contributed more than 5% of GDP last year. In an October forecast, investment company Dragon Capital estimated that the suspension of steel production and a decline in ore mining would reduce GDP by 1.5%. It has since revised its outlook and now expects the Ukrainian economy to contract in both 2026 and 2027.
If steel plants remain idle throughout 2027 and other sectors fail to make up for the lost output, the economic contraction could be even deeper, CES noted.
Background: Following Russian attacks, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih began the process of placing the plant into cold shutdown mode. The plant will not resume operations until the war ends.

How Zelensky's team sent Brussels scrambling over a meeting that never was
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:04:30 UTC
00:04:30 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky's planned Oct. 26 trip to Brussels descended into a diplomatic guessing game, with conflicting signals from his own team leaving EU and NATO officials scrambling to establish whether he was coming — and who was supposed to meet him.
At the center of the confusion was a proposed four-way meeting between Ukraine, the U.S., the EU, and NATO on efforts to end Russia’s war. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were expected to join the talks and brief European officials on their recent meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
But the meeting was never officially confirmed. An official from Zelensky's office leaked word to the press that the president would come anyway, setting off a scramble among European officials to prepare for a visit that remained uncertain.
The result was a rare public breakdown in coordination: Ukrainian officials gave reporters one account, European officials prepared to travel to Brussels, and Kyiv ultimately pointed to a change in U.S. plans to explain the confusion.
As a result, European officials began the day scrambling to answer the most basic question: Was the meeting even happening?
A trip announced, then thrown into doubt
The first indication that something might be in the works came from Zelensky himself.
In an interview with Ukrainian state television on Oct. 25, the Ukrainian president said a meeting was expected in Brussels "this week."
"We had a briefing from the Americans, and now they no longer want just a briefing — they want to have a broad discussion about security, guarantees, the EU, and participation," he said. "And they want a meeting this week in Brussels."
Yet the plans appeared to change almost as quickly as they emerged. A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent late on Oct. 25 that Zelensky had planned to visit Brussels but that the trip had since been called off.
By the morning of Oct. 26, the story appeared to have changed again.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing unnamed sources in Zelensky's team, reported that the Ukrainian leader was going to Brussels.
Ukrainian and European journalists began reporting the visit, while EU and NATO officials appeared to be hearing about it at roughly the same time as everyone else.
Even after it became clear there would be no meeting in Brussels, European media reported it was canceled, even though it had never been confirmed in the first place.
The European Commission offered little clarity, saying it continued to participate in talks and efforts with allies and partners to achieve a just and lasting peace for Ukraine, but had "no further information to share." Behind the scenes, European officials were trying to work out whether the reports were real.
One senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent they had no idea Zelensky was coming.
"Now we are in fact trying to assess if they are surprise visiting," the official said. "We are leaving for Canada and do not currently expect to have such a meeting."
"We are traveling to Canada and not expecting visitors."
The timing made the confusion particularly awkward.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa were preparing to travel to Montreal for the Canada-EU Summit — hardly the ideal moment to improvise a high-level meeting with the Ukrainian president.
Washington's plans may have changed
Part of the confusion appears to have stemmed from uncertainty over the U.S. delegation. Witkoff and Kushner had been expected to join the meeting, but Kyiv learned that Trump had decided to keep them in Washington around the time of Israel's Oct. 27 elections.
"Donald wants those two to be in Washington with him," a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
Without the two envoys, the meeting seemed pointless.
When Ukrainian reporters pressed Zelensky's office for confirmation that the Ukrainian president would travel to Brussels, presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said Kyiv could not confirm the meeting "due to a change in plans on the part of the U.S."
That explanation helped clarify why the plans might have shifted, but it did little to explain why European officials had been left trying to determine whether the Ukrainian president was arriving in the first place and who was responsible for the false leak.
A communications breakdown
The conflicting accounts sparked a heated exchange among senior members of Zelensky's communications team over why reporters had received different information about the trip, the Kyiv Independent can reveal.
One Ukrainian official suggested the confusion may have stemmed from a simple problem: not everyone on the team is "on the same page."
A senior EU official offered a more diplomatic — if pointed — assessment of the recurring coordination challenges.
"We love (Ukrainians), but (they are) sometimes a bit chaotic."
The episode came as Kyiv and its partners were trying to coordinate the next stages of talks to end Russia's war. On Oct. 23, Zelensky said Ukrainian, Russian, and U.S. negotiating teams would meet in Abu Dhabi in November to begin peace talks.
An EU official told the Kyiv Independent that European partners still expected another round of discussions on the continent before those multilateral talks.
"We do expect a session of talks in Europe in the coming weeks before the expected Abu Dhabi multilateral talks," the official said.
Whether that meeting will take place remains uncertain.
"That may or may not happen given the temperaments of all involved."

Ukraine will demand the cancellation of the permit for the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships in Moscow
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is preparing an appeal to the IWF and the IOC demanding a review of the decision to hold the 2030 World Championships in Moscow. Matvii Bidnyi called on partners to prevent the competition from taking place in Russia.
Ukraine is preparing an appeal to the International Weightlifting Federation and the International Olympic Committee regarding the decision to grant Russia the right to host the 2030 World Championships. Youth and Sports Minister Matvii Bidnyi stated this on social media on October 26, UNN reports.
Details
"We are preparing official appeals to the International Weightlifting Federation and the International Olympic Committee regarding the shameful decision to grant Russia the right to host the 2030 World Championships. We call for this decision to be reviewed and for a new, transparent selection process to be held to determine the country that will host the championships," Bidnyi wrote.
He noted that he would raise this issue with international partners, in particular at upcoming official events with the sports ministers of the countries of the Council of Europe and the EU.
"We seek to consolidate the international position—we call on the international sports community to publicly oppose holding the championships in Russia. As long as Russia continues its war against Ukraine, holding international competitions on its territory is unacceptable. This decision is especially cynical now, when, on the eve of winter, Russia is intensifying its strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, killing people and threatening Europe. Against this backdrop, the international federation is inviting the global sports community to gather in Moscow, from where orders for these crimes are issued. In effect, it is asking them to turn a blind eye. For the Kremlin, such a championship would become an instrument of propaganda and Putin’s political rehabilitation. This is a dangerous signal that a country can continue waging war while simultaneously returning to international sport. It encourages impunity and shows contempt for the principles that global sport should protect," the minister added.
Bidnyi emphasized that Ukraine "will use all available mechanisms and will continue working with international partners to call for this championship not to be held in Russia."
As a reminder
The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) granted Russia the right to host the 2030 Senior World Championships. The competition will be held in Moscow. This is the first case since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in which an international federation of an Olympic sport has entrusted Russia with hosting a World Championships event of this level.

SBU: Head of Russian occupation administration in Kherson region, Saldo, notified of suspicion regarding illegal transfer of Ukrainian children
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:04:26 EET
00:04:26 KST

The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) has documented further crimes committed by Vladimir Saldo, the head of the Russian occupation administration on the left bank of Kherson region. According to the SBU, he and two accomplices were involved in the illegal transfer of Ukrainian children following the seizure of the regional center.
"The investigation established that on October 7, 2022, the individuals in question organized the illegal removal of students from Kherson Vocational Shipbuilding Lyceum to so-called 'sanatoriums' in temporarily occupied Crimea," the SBU stated on its Telegram channel on Monday.
It was determined that the students were first transported by bus to a river port, and from there, taken by boat to the left bank, where further transport awaited to carry them to the peninsula.
"To facilitate this illegal removal, Saldo enlisted the help of Viktor Loginov, former Russian military serviceman who, at the time of the crime, held the position of 'deputy director of the lyceum,'" the agency specified.
According to investigators, in order to conceal the illegal transfer of the children, Loginov personally entered fictitious information into the educational institution's official records.
"A second accomplice, Nikolai Dolzhenko, a teacher at the lyceum, which had been seized by that time, accompanied the students along the entire route to Crimea," the message notes.
The message emphasizes that, through these actions, the individuals involved violated Article 49 of the Geneva Convention (IV) relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War, which prohibits the forcible transfer of protected persons from occupied territory.
Based on the evidence gathered, investigators from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) have notified Saldo and two of his accomplices in absentia that they are suspected of committing crimes under Part 2 of Article 28 and Part 1 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (war crimes committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy).
"As the perpetrators are currently hiding in a temporarily occupied part of Ukrainian territory, comprehensive measures are underway to bring them to justice," the SBU noted.
The Ukrainian security service also pointed out that, in a separate criminal proceeding based on evidence provided by the SBU, Saldo has already been sentenced in absentia to 15 years in prison.
The investigation was conducted by investigators from the Main Investigative Directorate under the procedural guidance of the the Prosecutor General’s Office.

WASHINGTON, October 26. /TASS/. US Congress representatives are threatening businesses, demanding that they refuse to participate in agreements to supply Russian diesel fuel to the US market, Axios reported.
According to the news outlet, Democratic members of the Senate and House of Representatives, along with one Republican who joined them, sent a letter to that effect to major US banks, as well as to several of the country’s ports.
Should the Democrats win next month’s midterm elections, these politicians will head the Senate’s key committees: Foreign Relations, Banking, Finance and Judiciary. In addition, Democratic Congressman Greg Meeks, who signed the letter, is poised to become the chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee if the Republicans lose in November. The lawmakers pointed out that the agreements may also become the subject of "congressional oversight," clearly adopting an anti-Russian stance in the letter. The politicians urged American businesses to refrain from "purchasing, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing, or distribution" of Russian diesel in the US or the financing of its acquisition. At the same time, the lawmakers required the business community to "preserve a wide range of potential records and communications related to ‘proposed or actual’ transactions" of this kind, including correspondence with "suppliers, intermediaries and US government officials." Finally, the authors of the letter also ordered them to identify all other companies and contractors involved in such transactions. Businesses are required to report on their completed work by October 28.
The letter was sent to J.P. Morgan, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley. The document was also sent to the ports of Houston, Beaumont, and Corpus Christi in Texas, as well as to ports in New York and New Jersey.

Most Ukrainians see anti-corruption progress despite scandals, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

15:04:05 UTC
00:04:05 KST

Around 55% of Ukrainians believe genuine efforts are being made to fight corruption and that progress is being achieved, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) published on Oct. 26.
The findings come amid persistent public concern over corruption, which remains one of Ukraine's most pressing issues even as the country nears the fifth year of Russia's full-scale invasion. A string of high-profile scandals has implicated top officials and allies of President Volodymyr Zelensky over the past year.
KIIS asked respondents how they viewed the media reports on corruption scandals. While 55% said the reports pointed to genuine efforts to tackle corruption and positive developments, 41% said Ukraine was "hopelessly corrupt," seeing no signs of progress.
The remaining 4% were undecided.
The share of respondents who saw progress fell slightly from 57% in December 2025, while the share who viewed Ukraine as "hopelessly corrupt" rose from 35%.
The recent survey was conducted among a representative sample of 1,031 adults across all regions of Ukraine except for areas under Russian occupation, between Oct. 8 and 26.
A separate KIIS poll published earlier this fall found that 72% of Ukrainians believe the level of corruption has increased since Russia launched its all-out war. Only 6% said it has decreased.
Corruption was also the most frequently cited concern, named by 50% of respondents, followed by Russia's mass missile and drone attacks at 40%.
The same poll found that 72% of Ukrainians believe Zelensky bears personal political responsibility for corruption among his associates.

Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:42:27 UTC
23:42:27 KST

The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.
Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.
Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.
She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.
Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference to VW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.
A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.
Döllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday that Audi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the US and create 4,500 jobs, even as VW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plants in Germany.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.
He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.
Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.
The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.
She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.
She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.
Volkswagen is locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.
Its German factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.
“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.
Trump is deeply unpopular in Germany and has riled its political mainstream by vocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party, according to polls, and has actively courted Trump’s support.
The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive in the Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.
Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports are helping the US economy.

====================================================================================================

Serbia’s student victory raises hopes of an EU reset
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:42:21 UTC
23:42:21 KST

The Student List’s election win ends Vučić’s 14-year rule and raises hopes of an EU reset, but its stance on Russia sanctions and Kosovo leaves Brussels cautious.
The Student List’s landslide victory in Sunday’s parliamentary elections has raised hopes that Serbia will mend ties with Brussels and relaunch its EU accession bid, but whether Belgrade will actually change its foreign policy remains unclear.
The movement born from months of student protest has secured an absolute majority in parliament, ending the 14-year rule of Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and fuelling expectations that the new government might seek closer ties with the EU.
“We are at the very beginning of the new path. But at least it’s a new path. We have no guarantees of anything. There’s just one guarantee that now we have the possibility, we have hope. And this is a huge achievement,” MEP Matjaž Nemec (Slovenia/S&D) told Euronews.
Protest movement
The Student List is the electoral arm of a student-led movement that grew out of a deadly disaster at a recently renovated railway station in November 2024, which raised questions about government accountability and corruption.
After nearly two years, the protests became a nationwide challenge to Serbia’s political establishment, demanding institutional reform and democratic accountability and marking a historic rupture with the SNS’s 14 years in power.
The movement has elected a mix of figures from outside the traditional political class, including students, professors, doctors, artists and businesspeople.
For Brussels, the new political class’s roots in a pro-democratic, anti-corruption movement are an encouraging sign that Belgrade could align with EU values and push through much-needed rule of law reforms.
At the same time, the student movement is also very heterogeneous, at times harbouring opposing views, meaning that, beyond opposing Vučić, it is still unclear exactly what it stands for.
"Ousting Vučić from power was the pre-requisite for Serbia's European future," Jelena Vasiljević, a senior research associate at the University of Belgrade, told Euronews. "Now I hope we will be able to have an open, democratic discussion on the EU accession path."
Democratic change
The movement’s door-to-door campaign centred on corruption and accountability, drawing parallels between Vučić’s defeat and the ousting of Viktor Orbán in Hungary after 16 years. Hungary’s new Prime Minister Péter Magyar ran on a similar platform.
Magyar was the first foreign leader to call the Student List to congratulate it on its result. “I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle,” he wrote on X.
The fair, competitive vote and the peaceful transfer of power, after Vučić conceded defeat, are seen as proof that Serbia’s democratic process is working.
Still, whether the change of government will translate into a broader realignment with Brussels, and into progress on EU accession, remains to be seen.
“It is not exactly clear what their take on foreign policy is. Many EU countries will be watching very closely,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, pointing to Serbia’s weak alignment with the bloc on foreign policy. “It remains to be seen if that will change.”
EU accession
Senior EU officials have welcomed the result. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos went as far as saying that “the door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together.”
In July, the European Commission pushed to open Cluster 3 of Serbia’s accession talks, which have been stalled for years, but eight member states blocked the move citing democratic backsliding concerns and lack of alignment on foreign policy.
The programme the Student List published last month, however, focuses solely on domestic governance: public procurement, education, media freedom, judicial independence and health care.
Bojan Vranić, a political science professor at the University of Belgrade, cautioned EU officials against excessive enthusiasm, saying the change of government would hardly lead to a breakthrough in European integration.
“So far, the Student List has been very conservative when it comes to the European Union. They aim to, firstly, improve the system within. And once they, as they said, become a credible partner in a negotiation, then the European Union will be their partner,” Vranić said.
Proceed with caution
Optimism in Brussels is tempered by history. In 2003, Serbian Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić was murdered by former members of the country’s security apparatus for pursuing a pro-Western agenda of closer ties with Europe, economic reforms and a crackdown on organised crime.
The EU executive is due to publish its enlargement package next week, an annual report on the state of play in candidate countries that will offer a first sign of whether the bloc’s approach to Serbia is shifting, though the new Serbian government is unlikely to be in place before the reporting period ends.
Perhaps more telling will be the conclusions the Council of the European Union adopts on the package, which will show where member states stand and whether they want to encourage Belgrade.
A key test may be how the Student List-led government treats Montenegro, the frontrunner to join the EU. Vučić and the SNS tried to undermine its accession by sowing divisions based on identity politics.
“I firmly believe that a new chapter lies ahead for Montenegro and Serbia, based on respect and open dialogue, without unnecessary escalation of tensions,” Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić wrote on X.
Foreign policy
Russia sanctions are among the main sticking points between Brussels and Belgrade, which has refused to align with the measures the EU imposed after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“The Republic of Serbia will retain its principled stance on not introducing restrictive measures toward the Russian Federation,” the student movement wrote on X in September, citing Serbia’s historical experience with sanctions.
Beyond its heavy dependence on Russian gas, Belgrade relies on Moscow’s diplomatic backing to prevent international recognition of Kosovo’s independence, which the student movement openly rejected in a memorandum published in May.
The Student List itself is split between staunchly pro-European figures and others who back a traditional Serbian nationalist agenda. Which camp prevails will shape the country’s foreign policy.
“There are strong nationalist voices in Studentska lista who would want to keep Russia onside because of Kosovo. Energy ties will persist as well. China ties might be downgraded a bit, but foreign direct investments and economic links are already there,” said Dimitar Bechev, a senior fellow at the think tank Carnegie Europe.
Vincenzo Genovese contributed to the reporting.

Russia ready for further cooperation with Slovakia on nuclear energy — minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:38:50 UTC
23:38:50 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia is ready for further cooperation with Slovakia in the area of nuclear energy, including both large-and small-scale power generation, Russian Minister of Science and Higher Education Valery Falkov said at the 22nd meeting of the Russian-Slovak inter-governmental commission for economic, science and technical cooperation.
"We attach particular importance to nuclear energy. Russian enterprises have been supplying nuclear fuel to Slovakia’s nuclear power plants for many years, conscientiously fulfilling their obligations. We are ready to discuss future projects, including those involving both large-and small-scale nuclear power generation," said Falkov who serves as Russia’s co-chair of the commission.
In addition to the energy sector, the minister pointed to the importance of further cooperation in agriculture, including genetics and plant breeding, as well as in environmental matters, specifically regarding air quality and waste management. In the humanitarian sphere, he expressed readiness for cooperation regarding the education of Slovak students at Russian universities, the study of the Russian and Slovak languages, and in the fields of sports and tourism. Moscow is prepared for a substantive dialogue that takes mutual interests into account, Falkov emphasized. "We are prepared to work toward gradually bringing other areas back to the agenda of the intergovernmental commission, including industry, finance, transport, healthcare, standardization, and metrology," he said.
The commission reconvened after a five-year hiatus, with contacts between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico playing a key role in the resumption of its activities, Falkov stressed. "Despite the challenging international situation, Russia and Slovakia managed to maintain cooperation in a number of key areas," he said. Among these areas he mentioned energy, both nuclear and oil and gas sectors, as the primary focus.
Following the meeting, a ceremony was held to sign the final protocol. The document was signed by Falkov and Slovakia’s Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Juraj Blanar.

Viktoria Angelova becomes first Bulgarian to win European Rising Star award

News
Viktoria Angelova becomes first Bulgarian to win European Rising Star award
Monday 26 October 2026 15:16
Monday, 26 October 2026, 15:16
PHOTO facebook.com/bfla.official
Font size
Bulgarian triple jumper Viktoria Angelova, 17, has become the first woman from her country to win the European Athletics Rising Star award, the Bulgarian Athletics Federation announced on Facebook.
The world and European junior champion received the award at the annual Golden Tracks ceremony in Lausanne, Switzerland.
Angelova beat two other finalists: Czech hurdler Linda Botkova, the European under-18 champion in the 400 metres hurdles, and Slovenia's Živa Remič, who won the European under-18 and world under-20 titles in the 800 metres this season.
PHOTO facebook.com/bfla.official
The award follows a remarkable season for Angelova, who is coached by Georgi Pomashki. In July, she won the European under-18 triple jump title in Rieti, Italy, with a leap of 13.98 metres, setting a championship record and recording the world's best under-18 mark of the season.
Less than a month later, she won the world under-20 title in Eugene, United States, with a jump of 13.91 metres, claiming gold in an older age group at just 17.
Previous winners of the women's European Athletics Rising Star award include Olympic and world champions Nafissatou Thiam, Yaroslava Mahuchikh, Femke Bol and Jessica Ennis-Hill.

“Strasbourg Calling” Daphne Caruana Galizia’s son calls for a retrial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:17:12 UTC
23:17:12 KST

Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
The European Pariament Prize for Independent Journalism is named after Daphne Caruana Galizia
“Strasbourg Calling” Daphne Caruana Galizia’s son calls for a retrial
Impunity for attacks on journalists in Europe is a worrying sign
Interview with Interview with Matthew Caruana Galizia
Monday 26 October 2026 15:32
Monday, 26 October 2026, 15:32
Matthew Caruana Galizia
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
October brings back two names that Europe must not reduce to mere anniversaries: Anna Politkovskaya, the Russian journalist murdered in Moscow 20 years ago, in October, and Daphne Caruana Galizia, the Maltese investigative journalist killed in Malta nine years ago, also in October.
This year, the European Parliament’s commemoration of Daphne Caruana Galizia has been overshadowed by a new twist in the legal proceedings. On 2 September, a jury acquitted Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech of charges of complicity in her murder and criminal conspiracy. On 22 September, the Attorney General appealed the verdict, while an investigation into possible misconduct by jury members has further undermined confidence in the trial.
What remains of justice when people have been convicted of carrying out the murder itself, but responsibility for commissioning it continues to be contested in court? And what does this case tell us about the protection of journalists in Europe?
Matthew Caruana Galizia is the son of the Maltese investigative journalist and chairs the foundation established in her memory. Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed when a bomb planted in her car exploded.
“Our top priority at the moment is to fight for a retrial, because there were serious problems with the trial over the summer, particularly with the selection of the jury. So this is the most important issue for us right now. I see no reason why there should not be a retrial,” he told the BNR on the live "Strasbourg Calling" programme from the European Parliament in Strasbourg. He added:
Matthew Caruana Galizia and Irina Nedeva in Radio Studio 3 at the European Parliament on “Strasbourg Calling”, 21 October 2026
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova
“One of the most troubling aspects of our justice system is that jurors are not required to explain why they reached a particular verdict. This means they can base their decisions on corruption or prejudice without facing any consequences.”
According to him, Malta’s institutions remain crippled and unable to provide society with the democracy and freedom it needs.
“It is not enough for the Attorney General simply to bring charges. The justice system itself must deliver fair outcomes,” Matthew Caruana Galizia stressed, adding:
“And if we cannot obtain fair outcomes, then Parliament and the government should step in and amend the legislation so that fair outcomes become possible.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with Matthew Caruana Galizia was aired on the BNR's Horizon channel and can be heard HERE.
