US President Donald Trump disparaged Jewish voters who support Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, at a rally in Port Huron on Sunday.
“Any Jewish person that supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” Trump told some 4,000 supporters in the city north of Detroit, where he stumped for Republican nominee Mike Rogers. “You should never speak to them again.”
Hundreds of Michigan Jews have pledged to vote for El-Sayed, who polls indicate is narrowly leading Rogers in a race key to determining control of the Senate. Another subset of Jews has pressured El-Sayed, a staunch critic of Israel, to defend “Jewish safety - including for Zionist Jews” and “Jewish sovereignty in Israel.” Still others have urged their community members to reject El-Sayed outright and back Rogers.
El-Sayed opposes US military aid to Israel, saying the country has committed genocide in Gaza and is “not an ally.” Those positions divided the Democratic Party during his primary campaign against pro-Israel US Rep. Haley Stevens, whom he narrowly bested in August.
A former public health official, El-Sayed has also emphasized affordable healthcare, housing, and education. He has made a concentrated push to reach undecided Jewish voters in the homestretch before the Nov. 3 midterm election, hiring a Jewish outreach director last week.
Trump previously disparaged Jewish Democrat voters as 'disloyal' to other Jews, Israel
Trump has in the past accused Jews who vote for Democrats of being “disloyal to Jewish people” and “disloyal to Israel.”
At the Port Huron rally, he said he is “polling at 99% in Israel,” which will hold national elections on Tuesday.
Trump did not cite evidence for the claim, and no publicly available surveys support it. While he has historically been popular among Israelis, a June poll by the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) found the Israeli public’s trust in him was declining. The poll said 12% of Israelis reported having a great deal of trust in Trump, down from 21% in May, while the share of Israelis who completely distrust him rose from 32% to 37%.
Trump joined his comments about Jews and Israel with anti-Muslim rhetoric about El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim in the Senate if he is elected.
El-Sayed 'on the side of the terrorists,' Trump says
Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” who was “on the side of the terrorists,” adding that he would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”
He threatened that “if Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”
Trump claimed that El-Sayed’s half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, celebrated the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. On the first anniversary of the attack, Abdelhadi posted a video that said, “no matter how great the brutality, the oppression, the intensity of what we’re going through, the horizon of justice is just around the corner,” according to The New York Times. She did not directly mention or celebrate the violence.
Trump also said that El-Sayed’s mother had “worked for an organization that gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda.” A Times investigation reported that El-Sayed’s mother worked as a nurse in Missouri for a Muslim aid group that was later designated by the US government as a supporter of terrorist groups. She was never accused of wrongdoing.
El-Sayed’s campaign has said that he “disagrees” with his sister on “a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use, including on foreign policy.” He was raised by his father and stepmother and has said that he had little relationship with his biological mother while growing up.
Former US president Barack Obama campaigned with El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday, praising his potential partnership with Democratic Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who has endorsed El-Sayed.
“Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa,” said Obama. “You got a Muslim man, you got a Jewish woman, fighting for you in the United States Senate. That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of.”

Russian Intelligence Services Tried to Organize Rally in Support of Paks II Nuclear Plant in Budapest — InformNapalm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:16:29 UTC
23:16:29 KST

Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) organized a provocative rally in Budapest in support of Rosatom’s Paks II nuclear power plant construction project, aiming to influence Hungary’s political situation.
The international intelligence community InformNapalm reported this in cooperation with the Ukrainian Militant analytical group, based on an analysis of leaked CYBINT data.
The 256 Cyber Assault Division group uncovered the Russian intelligence operation after intercepting correspondence in which Russian Colonel Timur Sirtlanov instructed SVR Lieutenant Colonel Irina Parman to prepare an “active measure” in Budapest.
In Russian intelligence terminology, “active measures” refer to information campaigns, covert operations, and manipulations designed to influence public opinion and the policies of foreign states.
Both subjects of the investigation are linked to military unit 33949, which open sources and analytical reports identify as an official structure of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
Irina Parman specializes in profiling and the use of psychological methods in operational activities, as evidenced by the courses she took at the SVR Academy.
To organize the rally, anonymous Facebook posts were published on September 16, calling on Budapest’s Russian-speaking community to attend an event in support of the energy sector.
Participants were coordinated through a private Telegram group called ‘DRUZHBA NARODOV’ (eng. ‘FRIENDSHIP OF PEOPLES’), where people were offered monetary rewards to attend the rally outside the Hungarian Parliament.
Analysis of the metadata of campaign PDF files featuring slogans in Hungarian confirmed that Irina Parman authored them, using her maiden name, Larina.
The attempt to stage a manipulative rally came amid worsening relations between Hungary and Russia following the expulsion of ten Russian diplomats over espionage activities.
The organizers canceled the planned rally at the last minute, so it never took place.
Earlier, Hungary launched an official investigation into former Minister of Foreign Affairs Péter Szijjártó over suspected treason linked to his ties with Russia.

No winner in first round: Bulgaria sets presidential runoff for Nov. 1
The Iotova-Valchev ticket has secured 34.76% of the vote, while Gurov-Kandev has received 31.95%, with 99.95% of tally sheets processed by the district election commissions. The figures are as of 10 a.m. on Monday, according to data published on the Central Election Commission's (CEC) website.
Under the Constitution, a presidential candidate can be elected in the first round only if they receive more than half of the valid votes cast and more than half of all eligible voters take part in the election. If no candidate is elected, a new vote is held within seven days, with the two candidates who received the most votes taking part.
The results of the presidential and vice-presidential election show the following distribution:
Ilana Iotova/Kiril Valchev - 34.76%
Andrey Gurov/Georgi Kandev - 31.95%
Kostadin Kostadinov/Petar Volgin - 12.54%
Radostin Vasilev/Krasimir Manov - 4.61%
Ivelin Mihaylov/Yuliana Mateeva - 3.79%
Ivan Hristanov/Stoyanka Cherkezova - 2.39%
The “I do not support any candidate” option was chosen by 4.43% of voters.
A total of 6,637,238 voters were eligible to take part in Sunday's election, in which 27 presidential and vice-presidential tickets competed. Some 46,001 people were eligible to vote for the first time.
As previously reported, Bulgarian citizens were voting Sunday to elect the country's seventh president.

How will growing US-Ukraine tensions shape the course of the war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:16:07 UTC
23:16:07 KST

Growing tensions between Washington and Kiev are exposing differences that extend beyond the personal rivalry between US President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as the White House pursues closer ties with Moscow.
The latest signs of a US-Russia rapprochement emerged last week when US mediator Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg, with both sides issuing positive statements about renewing peace talks and ending the war in Ukraine.
Yet just hours after the statements, Russia and Ukraine exchanged a deadly barrage of attacks, underscoring the challenges facing efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict.
The growing US-Russia rapprochement, marked by Washington brokering a diesel deal with the Kremlin and lifting most US sanctions on Moscow, has frustrated Zelenskyy, who has recently publicly opposed Washington's softer approach toward Moscow.
Trump has also demanded that Zelenskyy stop targeting Russian refineries.
The disagreements mark a further deterioration in relations that have remained strained since a heated White House meeting in March, when Trump and Zelenskyy engaged in a public shouting match.
Although Zelenskyy subsequently sought common ground with Trump through European mediation, their latest exchanges suggest that the divisions between Washington and Kiev run deeper than disagreements over how to end the war, reflecting increasingly divergent geopolitical priorities and international alignments.
“I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” the US president said in a speech last week, underscoring his affinity for the Russian leader, who recently proposed a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump to address the war in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy has shown less hesitation in confronting the US administration, which has long provided Ukraine with weapons, funding and essential intelligence in its war against Russia.
“How can Trump be friends with him? I think that it’s a mistake. It’s his choice again and again,” Zelenskyy said in a recent Financial Times interview, referring to the political rapprochement between Russia and the US.
Rapprochement disrupts Ukrainian resistance
Growing differences between Washington and Kiev, coupled with Trump's rapprochement with Putin, could strengthen Moscow's position both on the battlefield and at the negotiating table, according to experts.
The deepening tensions between the US and Ukraine are “exerting a disruptive influence on the dynamics of the war in Ukraine, affecting both military operations on the ground and the parameters of a potential peace settlement,” Ozgur Korpe, an academic at National Defence University, tells TRT World.
“On the battlefield, uncertainty regarding US aid—compounded by political conditionality—is compelling Ukraine to adopt a more defensive, resource-conserving strategy, while simultaneously granting Russia greater latitude to maintain its offensive tempo and intensify pressure,” he says.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has faced disruptions to US intelligence sharing and Starlink satellite connections, which Kiev believes contributed to its vulnerability during recent deadly Russian missile attacks on the capital.
Shortages of missile interceptors, compounded by delays in US supplies, have further strained Ukraine's air defences.
According to Korpe, Ukraine's predicament reflects a well-documented phenomenon in international relations: when a weaker partner depends heavily on a stronger ally for security, declining support or growing uncertainty over assistance can undermine its willingness and ability to continue fighting.
Since the war began, Kiev has relied heavily on American political, economic, military and intelligence assistance.
Under the Trump administration, however, that support has declined, while the US president has increasingly portrayed Zelenskyy as an obstacle to a potential peace settlement.
Ukraine has sought to offset shortages of American weapons and disruptions to intelligence sharing with support from Europe.
But questions remain over whether countries such as France, the UK and Germany have the military capabilities to replace US assistance.
Domestic priorities
Trump and Zelenskyy have different pledges to their respective national audiences, making compromise increasingly difficult.
While Trump has long pledged to Americans to bring immediate peace to the Russia-Ukraine war, Zelenskyy aims to minimise any territorial concessions to Moscow to keep national support for his presidency strong.
The tensions between Washington and Kiev are “largely a product of US domestic political factors, with the Trump administration facing pressure due to rising energy costs amid prolonged wars in both the Middle East and the Russia/Ukraine conflict,” says Eugene Chausovsky, senior director of analytical development and training at the New Lines Institute.
With the US midterm elections approaching, Trump is seeking ways to ease economic pressures, particularly rising diesel prices and their wider impact on inflation.
“This frames the US agreement with Russia on allowing diesel shipments, as well as Trump’s frustration with Zelensky for Ukraine continuing to target Russian energy and refinery infrastructure at a politically sensitive time,” Chausovsky tells TRT World.
However, experts warn that the diesel deal is unlikely to immediately affect US fuel prices, as European countries continue to enforce their own sanctions on Russia.
Trump’s declaration of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia also failed, as both sides said they did not sign the agreement.
“Trump frames Ukraine not so much as a front line for the defence of liberal democratic norms, but rather as a costly foreign burden in the context of US domestic politics and a bargaining chip to be used at the negotiating table when striking a ‘grand deal’ with Russia,” Korpe says.
By contrast, Zelenskyy views Ukraine's struggle as existential and closely tied to the country's aspirations to join Western political and military institutions, according to Korpe.
Will Ukraine and the US break up?
Ukraine has long sought closer integration with Western political and military institutions, including NATO and the EU. But deteriorating relations with Washington have raised questions about whether Kiev can keep relying on American support.
Oleg Ignatov, a senior analyst on Russia at the International Crisis Group, says the Trump administration has recently changed its approach to negotiations aimed at ending the war.
“Previously, Washington tried to reach an understanding with Moscow first, then took its proposals to Ukraine and its allies, who rejected them.
“Now the United States is trying to secure support from Ukraine and its European allies first and find out what they are prepared to accept. It would then take those proposals to Putin,” Ignatov tells TRT World.
Last week, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, met Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo before Witkoff travelled to Saint Petersburg for further talks with Putin.
“This approach requires Zelenskyy to be clearer about the compromises Ukraine might accept. That is likely to cause friction between Kiev and Washington because their approaches still differ,” Ignatov tells TRT World.
If the US continues to push Zelenskyy to make further concessions to Russia, this approach could “lead to further friction or even conflict between Kiev and Washington,” Ignatov says.
Zelenskyy has insisted that any potential ceasefire must be backed by Western security guarantees without territorial concessions to Russia.
In a recent CNN interview, Zelenskyy maintained that Ukraine “will survive” and “will stay strong” despite tensions with Washington, while rejecting territorial concessions to Russia.
Although some analysts attribute the tensions partly to personal animosity between Trump and Zelenskyy, Korpe argues that the differences run deeper.
“The rift between the two leaders is not merely personal; rather, it is rooted in deeper disagreements regarding the objectives of the war and the vision for a final settlement.”
Korpe says institutions such as the US Congress and the Pentagon, alongside NATO, have helped prevent American support for Ukraine from collapsing entirely.
Nevertheless, “it is fair to say that the crisis of trust between the two leaders is moving distinctly toward a complete ‘break’,” he adds.
Chausovsky, however, offers a different assessment.
While Zelenskyy and the Trump administration remain at odds, he says, “these tensions should not be seen as a sign of a breakup” between Washington and Kiev.
Instead, Chausovsky describes the current friction as “rather a down period in the ebb and flow of their ties amid the protracted conflict with Russia.”
“Greater diplomatic activity can be expected as a result, though any sustainable ceasefire or peace agreement is unlikely to materialise in the short term,” he tells TRT World.

Syria arrests Assad's cousin and senior former regime officers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:16:04 UTC
23:16:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria arrests Assad's cousin and senior former regime officers
Syrian authorities have arrested several senior officers from Bashar al-Assad's former regime, including his cousin, as part of an ongoing crackdown on suspects accused of atrocities during the country's 14-year-long civil war.
Syrian Interior Ministry spokesperson Nour al-Din al-Baba announced the arrests on Monday, saying those detained included senior military and intelligence officials, former air force pilots and individuals suspected of involvement in massacres and attacks on civilians.
Among those arrested was Yahya al-Assad, a cousin of ousted president Bashar al-Assad who held the rank of colonel in Branch 105, a unit of the former regime's security apparatus.
Al-Baba said the detainees also included a major general who had commanded the 24th Division and the Air Defence Directorate, as well as senior officials from the Air Force Intelligence Directorate.
Another suspect was allegedly involved in the Tadamon massacre, one of the most notorious atrocities committed by Assad's forces during the Syrian uprising.
The arrests also included a fighter pilot accused of bombing Syrian cities, a brigadier general from the Political Security Directorate, the head of investigations at Air Force Intelligence and a judge who served in the former regime's Counterterrorism Court.
Other detainees included two brigadier generals from the Republican Guard, a senior officer at Tishreen Military Hospital, a military doctor, a helicopter pilot and another fighter pilot accused of taking part in attacks on civilian areas.
The arrests are part of efforts by Syria's new authorities to pursue former military and security officials suspected of committing abuses during the uprising against Assad, including aerial bombardments, arbitrary detention, torture and massacres.
Former regime pilots targeted
Syrian authorities have stepped up arrests of former air force personnel in recent weeks, targeting officers suspected of involvement in bombing campaigns against opposition-held areas.
In September, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of nine former regime pilots in Latakia province.
According to the ministry, preliminary investigations indicated that the pilots had participated in combat missions and airstrikes targeting several areas, including Eastern Ghouta, Aleppo and its countryside, Deir ez-Zor and rural Hama.
On 18 September, authorities detained five former air force officers and commanders in Tartous province, including pilots and officials who had held operational and field responsibilities.
Two days later, security forces arrested Brigadier General Zakaria Mohammed Sannoun, who served as head of operations in the 22nd Division between 2012 and 2020.
Authorities accused Sannoun of overseeing operations at the Hama, Tiyas (T4) and Shayrat military airbases during the conflict.
On 28 September, internal security forces arrested Colonel Khaldoun Hussein Mubarak in the Jableh countryside of Latakia province.
He was accused of participating in combat sorties against Syrian areas during the uprising.
The Interior Ministry has described the arrests as part of continuing investigations into former officers and military personnel suspected of war crimes and other violations, with judicial proceedings expected to follow.
Suspect in 2013 massacres arrested
The latest arrests come less than two weeks after Syrian authorities announced the detention of Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural and nicknamed the "Butcher of Baniyas".
Kayali was arrested on 15 October over his alleged role in the 2013 massacres in Baniyas and al-Bayda, in the Tartous countryside.
Syrian authorities accuse him of responsibility for the killings, which took place during the early years of the uprising against Assad.
The successive arrests mark a widening effort to track down former regime figures accused of involvement in atrocities committed during the conflict.
Authorities have said investigations will continue and that suspects will face further judicial proceedings over their alleged roles in abuses against Syrians.

This Tuesday, millions of Israelis will enter the voting booth with mixed emotions – feelings of trauma and pride.
Trauma from the invasion and a sense of pride in the military actions that followed. During an ongoing existential war on seven fronts, Israel needs proven, clear, and decisive leadership.
That’s why in that quiet, sacred cubicle – I will be voting for victory.
Yes, I am still living through the trauma of October 7, which needs to be thoroughly investigated through a cross-party inquiry that will question current and former IDF chiefs of staff, prime ministers, and defense ministers on both sides of the aisle – but that doesn’t change the current challenges on the horizon.
In the past three years, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rewritten our national defense doctrine and delivered some of the greatest military feats in the history of warfare.
Every step of the way, he faced immense pressure from home and abroad, including from those who seek to replace him in this election.
Had he capitulated and ended the war when Gadi Eisenkot had suggested, we would have never entered Rafah. We would have potentially left countless hostages in the hands of Hamas. Not to mention the beeper attacks on Hezbollah and actions against the Houthis and Iran.
Instead, we now control over 60% of Gaza.
All the hostages were returned to Israel.
Hezbollah is crushed.
And the Islamic Republic of Iran is on its last legs.
The current government has many naysayers, but nobody can deny that what they have achieved on the battlefield thus far is historic; however, much of the progress could unravel if the missions are not completed.
Voting for victory
Voters need to ask themselves who is more likely to bring down the Iranian Regime, end the nuclear threat, and usher in a new era of regional peace and stability.
Those with a proven track record in war and peace who have committed to Iranian regime change or a newly formed amalgamation of parties who agree on few things beyond their disdain for Netanyahu.
There is no path for Eisenkot to reach a Knesset majority without joining forces with the far-left, Arab and Islamist parties, which would render his government impotent.
Imagine we are on the eve of a joint American Israeli attack against the remnants of the Iranian nuclear program, and the Pentagon is waiting to hear if Israel is on board, pending a decision from the Islamist Ra’am movement’s Shura Council of elders.
This isn’t a joke; it’s a dangerous possibility.
In contrast, Netanyahu has a much clearer path to a majority and has already stated that once he joins with his natural allies, he will reach out to others to bolster the national consensus.
This comes alongside an unprecedented endorsement by US President Donald Trump, who clearly wants to keep the winning team together to finish the job.

====================================================================================================

Lizard's secret of defense preserved in 100-million-year-old amber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:05:13 UTC
23:05:13 KST

Almost 100 million years ago, a lizard in what is now Myanmar was in mortal danger.
We know this because the presumably terrified reptile did exactly what lizards do today in similar situations: It "voluntarily" shed its tail and the rest of it scuttled off.
The tail would have remained on the ground wriggling madly, which the lizard would have hoped would distract the hunter. How this scenario panned out and whether the lizard survived, we do not know.
But we do know that the tail did exactly what it shouldn't have: It survived – the decay process at least – and became embedded in tree resin. Over millions of years, the resin fossilized into amber and now, according to researchers at Tel Aviv University, we have the earliest known proof of the reptilian defensive mechanism known as autotomy – voluntarily shedding one's tail.
Theoretically it's possible that the lizard wasn't being hunted but some creature stepped on its tail, which it promptly shed. But close analysis of the tissue shows the hallmarks of voluntary discard, which is important, because it's no great defensive trick for the tail to simply get stomped.
The wonder is that now we know that the real defensive trick existed in lizards at least 100 million years ago, explain doctoral candidate Dolev Fabrikant and his supervisor, Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou, of Tel Aviv University's School of Zoology and its Steinhardt Museum of Natural History. They worked in collaboration with researchers from the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and Israel's Volcani Institute, publishing in Palaeontologia Electronica.
Until now, we could only speculate that ancient lizards living with dinosaurs had this defensive ability, Davranoglou notes. Now we know they did because the paleontological team observed a clean ring of tissue resembling the structure seen in tails shed by living lizards – absent trauma damage.
In fact, the small piece of cloudy amber had been found years ago but only now did Fabrikant examine it, using micro-CT scanning, and realize that what looked like a twig or insect fragment was covered in scales.
"Micro-CT… allowed us to examine structures hidden by the amber without needing to cut this one-of-a-kind piece open," says Ahmed Nasser, head of the Volcani Institute's Inter-Institutional Analytical Unit.
Which lizard it was, we do not know because this amber contained only its tail, not its head. Could have been almost anything.
"Possible affinities include the groups containing today's wall lizards or, alternatively, slow worms and monitor lizards," says Apostolos Christopoulos, a student at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.
Note that snakes aren't lizards, they're snakes, and almost none in travail shed tail. They can't regenerate it. But likely, the ability goes back an insanely long way – tuataras can defensively shed their tail, and they split from other reptiles a quarter billion years ago, in the Jurassic.
There is one other option beside being stepped on or attacked. The lizard may have been climbing a seeping tree, its tail got stuck in the sticky resin and it shed it and moved on. If that's so, the little reptile may have regrown its tail. That's a nice thought.

26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Anthropic, the San Francisco-based developer behind AI chatbot Claude, has officially unveiled its initial public offering (IPO) prospectus, setting the stage for one of the largest market debuts in history.
The company expects to target a market valuation between $1.5 trillion and $1.75 trillion, according to its regulatory filing.
The nearly 240,000-word prospectus showed that the firm recently told backers its third-quarter revenue surged nearly 50% from the previous quarter to $16.8 billion, reaching profitability on an adjusted basis.

Investment bank Goldman Sachs secured the lead advisory role for the public offering alongside Morgan Stanley.
The filing also detailed a multi-class corporate governance structure with five distinct share tiers.
Under the proposed framework, Anthropic's seven founders will retain 50.1% of the total voting power through Class F shares, while its Long-Term Benefit Trust will hold Class T shares granting it the authority to appoint the majority of the board of directors.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former researchers and executives from OpenAI, including Chief Executive Dario Amodei.
The listing is scheduled to take place after the US midterm elections in November but before the Thanksgiving holiday.

The architectural heritage of Greece's Kea island: Vibrant colours, stone houses and watermills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:03:18 UTC
23:03:18 KST

Kea has around 2,500 permanent residents, and despite the growth of tourism, the island has managed to retain its traditional character.
Every summer, Greece's Cyclades islands attract countless visitors from all over the world.
In recent years, the Cyclades have become increasingly popular with tourists looking for more than just the sun and the sea, with many also choosing to make the trip in autumn or spring to go hiking and take in the local archaeological sites and architecture.
Kea, also known as Tzia, is an island in the western Cyclades known for its history and natural beauty.
It is described as the "gateway to the Cyclades" due to its proximity to Athens. It is just 16 nautical miles from the port of Lavrio.
Ioulida is the island's capital and one of its four historic towns. It is the only one situated inland, having once been the commercial centre of Kea. The architecture of Ioulida differs from typical Cycladic styles, as it incorporates elements of urban and neoclassical construction.
"We see the narrow streets, the arches and the stone buildings, and we also see colour on the walls. In fact, Tzia has always been a colourful place. During the Metaxas regime (1936–1940), white and blue were imposed, with white mainly for reasons of hygiene," Rena Velissaropoulou, the mayor of Kea since 2019, said.
"But Tzia has colour, and we see this every time we come across an old building where we can see the plasterwork. There, we almost always find colour," Velissaropoulou added.
Kea has around 2,500 permanent residents, and despite the growth of tourism, the island has managed to retain its traditional character.
Ioulida is built in an amphitheatre-like layout on the slopes of two hills (Kastro and Mylos). In 1978, it was granted the status of a protected traditional settlement.
Its distinctive architectural identity is also due to a distinctive type of rock found on the island.
"There was also miltos, a type of stone that was quarried in the cave-like pits of an exceptional cave in the Otzia area. This colour is a shade of greyish red, like the colour we see at Knossos, and in the past this stone was exported to Athens,” Velissaropoulou said.
As you leave Ioulida and drive up the island’s hills, you will also come across a number of traditional stone buildings. Most of them are uninhabited. Some have undergone minor alterations, whilst others have been converted into tourist accommodation.
Preserving them is vital for safeguarding Kea’s cultural heritage and history.
"The farmstead is the home, the base of the island’s farmers and livestock breeders, which used to be situated in the countryside. Because their main home was in Ioulida. All farmers who owned farmhouses also had a home in the capital. Usually, the home was the wife’s dowry, and the farmhouse belonged to the husband,” livestock farmer Dinos Vrettos told Euronews.
As a rule, farmers did not build on hilltops so as to avoid the strong northerly winds. However, they did not build low down in the ravines either, so as not to suffer from the summer heat.
For 25 years, Vrettos he worked as a stonemason, whilst for five years he was part of the excavation team at the ancient theatre of Karthia.
With his help, we were introduced to one of the traditional houses which, although no longer in use, retains all the characteristic features of the "Tziotiki dwelling."
"They used stones from ancient structures to build the houses. Over the years, the craft passed from one generation to the next, so I learnt it too. Unfortunately, the house in this condition has changed hands; it has been sold. Usually, the houses are bought by foreigners, not Greeks – mainly foreigners who, however, try to preserve them as they found them,” Dinos Vrettos told Euronews.
In the Mylopotamos area, along the stream and near the Flea spring, there were also once 11 watermills. Of these, one is now used as a residence, whilst another operates solely for visitors to the island.
The watermills likely date back to the period of Ottoman rule. They remained in operation until the Second World War and were gradually abandoned by the 1980s. Savvas Michael, a retired aviation worker, feels he has a duty to keep the island’s history alive.
"Technology has advanced enormously. Young people and children being born today have no idea what life was like in the past. So we’re trying to bring young people closer to tradition so that they know what we’ve inherited. Even if we don’t use them anymore, it’s important to keep at least one of them ‘alive’,” Michael said.
White and blue dominate most of the Cyclades islands. On Ioulida, however, one encounters vibrant colours, such as yellow and, of course, the red miltos of Kea, a mineral-based red dye that was highly prized in antiquity.
When you visit the island, look out for the "kathikies," the traditional stone houses that have stood the test of time.

High-level delegation in Iran in push to avert flare-up of conflict with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:03:06 UTC
23:03:06 KST

The Middle East’s ability to solve its problems has been held back by America’s 50-year insistence that the Gulf states should view Iran as a security threat, Oman’s foreign minister said on Monday in a significant speech designed to break the deadlock over the region’s future.
Badr Albusaidi called for a non-aggression security pact involving all six Gulf states as well as Iran and Iraq. The US would in future no longer be the primary provider of security, he said.
He was speaking on the day high-level defence and intelligence officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent a renewed outbreak of fighting between the US and Iran.
Tehran said the meeting also explored future security arrangements in the region. The high stakes were underlined by the sight of the Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, in Tehran weeks after Iran had struck Saudi infrastructure and as Iran-backed Houthis continue to send missiles towards Riyadh.
Albusaidi is the first Gulf leader to break ranks so explicitly by calling for the mainly Sunni Gulf states to form a security alliance with Iran, a long-term aspiration of Tehran’s.
Speaking at Girton College, Cambridge, he said the talks might be difficult and the proposal appeared counterintuitive, but “issues such as the strait of Hormuz have become impossible to resolve because external powers continue to define the terms of engagement, while regional powers are unable to take collective responsibility for making their own security arrangements and reach a consensus on them”.
He added: “What holds us back is that issues which ought to be handled at a regional level by the states of the Gulf themselves, are made more complex, more intractable and sometimes simply impossible to resolve because the region’s security arrangements are insufficiently developed.
“And they are insufficiently developed because they have relied for too long on the involvement of external powers.”
He said that for half a century Iran “had been systematically excluded from playing any meaningful role in the security arrangements of the region”. This had led to “profoundly negative consequences, not just for Iran, but for the region as a whole”, including the imposition of priorities on the region by external powers such as “the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf”.
He added: “Perhaps the most damaging of the priorities imposed on the region from the outside has been the requirement that Iran be excluded. Not just excluded. Worse. Positioned as the threat against which regional security had to be organised.”
Oman is on the southern side of the strait of Hormuz, with Iran on the northern shores. The two countries have reached a temporary agreement on how shipping traffic should be managed in the strait, but the plan is on hold until the US and Iran lift their respective blockades of the waterway.
Albusaidi also indirectly challenged Donald Trump’s case for a further attack on Iran by saying he believed the previous round of talks between the US and Iran in February, which Oman mediated, were “making significant progress, and that an agreement was within reach. We still stand by that judgment today.”
The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role. The US-Iran conflict may have reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.
No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attacks on Iran last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.
The meeting in Tehran was taking place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Israeli media reports claimed that the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that the US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity.
The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners increasingly say Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb.
A pact that is likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

KAMPALA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- One person was killed and 25 others rescued after a building under construction at a church collapsed Monday in Uganda's central district of Wakiso, police said Tuesday.
Rachael Kawala, spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan Police, told Xinhua that one body had been retrieved from the rubble of the collapsed structure, an extension of the main church building in Bwerenga, Katabi Town Council.

Preliminary findings indicate the structure reached the fourth floor when it collapsed, according to an earlier police report.

Afghan gov't seeks international support to fight illicit drugs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:55:20 CST
22:55:20 KST

KABUL, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Afghanistan's Foreign Minister Mawlawi Amir Khan Muttaqi on Tuesday described illicit drugs as an international problem, calling on the international community to help Afghanistan overcome the challenge.
Illicit crop cultivation and drug production are not confined to a specific geographical area, and the fight against this menace is a shared responsibility of Afghanistan and the international community, Muttaqi said at a gathering attended by Kabul-based diplomats and government officials.
As part of efforts to combat the drug menace in Afghanistan, Muttaqi urged the international community to help farmers switch to alternative crops, cooperate in providing treatment for drug addicts, and assist in combating drug trafficking networks.
Although Afghanistan has made significant progress in combating illicit drugs in the post-war period, sharply reducing poppy cultivation, drug production and processing, and trafficking, the country still needs more time to become drug-free. ■

Mongolia warns of widespread extreme winter weather risk
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:55:16 CST
22:55:16 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- At least 83 percent of Mongolia's territory is at some level of risk of experiencing dzud, an extreme winter weather phenomenon, this winter, the country's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change said Tuesday.
Dzud is a Mongolian term for severe winter conditions that can cause large numbers of livestock to die because of frozen ground, deep snow or a lack of accessible pasture.
"A recent dzud risk assessment showed that 26 percent of the country's total territory faces a very high or high risk of experiencing dzud this winter," the ministry said in a statement.
The areas at very high or high risk include the western provinces of Bayan-Ulgii, Uvs, Zavkhan and Khovd; the southern provinces of Umnugovi and Dundgovi; and the central provinces of Arkhangai and Uvurkhangai.
Mongolia is known for its harsh continental climate, characterized by long, bitterly cold winters and short summers. ■

TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- The navy of Iran's army said Tuesday a "violating" oil tanker that sought to cross the "forbidden region" east of the Strait of Hormuz caught fire after hitting naval mines.
In a statement published on the army's website, the navy said the oil tanker, which had turned off its tracking systems, suffered damage after colliding with the mines in the "unsafe region" east of the waterway.
The navy reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and unsafe for violating vessels attempting to cross it, stressing ships must ensure necessary coordination with the Iranian armed forces.
Iran tightened its grip on the strait on Feb. 28, barring safe passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States, following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iranian territory. ■

Uganda Airlines launches direct flights between Entebbe, Ghana's Accra
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:55:13 CST
22:55:13 KST

KAMPALA, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Uganda Airlines, the country's national carrier, has launched scheduled flights between Entebbe and Accra, Ghana, establishing a new air link between East and West Africa to facilitate trade, tourism and investment.
The service operates four times a week, offering passengers more convenient travel options and connections to destinations across the airline's international network.
Uganda's Minister of Works and Transport Fred Byamukama said the new route would facilitate business engagement, promote tourism and strengthen ties between Uganda and Ghana.
"The Entebbe-Accra service will offer travelers a direct connection between two important commercial centers, facilitate business engagement, support tourism and strengthen people-to-people relations," Byamukama said on Tuesday before flagging off the inaugural flight.
He commended Ghana for its visa-free entry policy for holders of all categories of Ugandan passports, saying improved air connectivity should be accompanied by policies that facilitate cross-border movement.
"As we implement continental initiatives such as the Single African Air Transport Market and the African Continental Free Trade Area, improved connectivity must go hand in hand with policies that make it easier for Africans to travel, trade and invest across borders," he said.
Byamukama said Uganda had placed a firm order for eight Boeing aircraft. The country is also pursuing the acquisition of additional freighter aircraft to strengthen cargo operations.
Uganda Airlines currently serves several African destinations, including Nairobi, Dar es Salaam, Juba, Johannesburg, Lagos and Abuja, as well as international destinations such as Dubai, Mumbai and London. ■

Nordic leaders call for overhaul of digital platforms to protect children
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:55:08 CST
22:55:08 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Nordic leaders on Tuesday called for fundamental changes to the design of social media and other digital platforms to better protect children and young people's health and development.
At a meeting in Helsinki hosted by Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo and attended by representatives from Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Greenland, the Faroe Islands and the Aland Islands, a joint declaration was adopted stressing the urgent need to strengthen online protection for minors.
The declaration warned that smartphones, social media and artificial intelligence pose significant risks to children's and young people's wellbeing, mental health, learning and development. The full extent of their impact remains unclear.
Children are gaining access to digital platforms too early and too extensively, and the platforms are not designed to support healthy growth and learning, according to the declaration.
Several Nordic countries are currently preparing legislation and recommendations on age limits for social media platforms.
Meanwhile, leaders also held discussions on Tuesday with students aged 12 to 14 and young politicians on the protection of children and young people in digital environments.
The meeting took place on the sidelines of the 78th Session of the Nordic Council, held in Helsinki from Monday to Thursday.
Finland holds the presidency of the Nordic Council in 2026, while Denmark and the Faroe Islands jointly hold the presidency of the Nordic Council of Ministers. ■

====================================================================================================

Riga considers postponing Vanšu Bridge repairs as plans for temporary bridge remain uncertain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
13:48:51 UTC
22:48:51 KST

The reconstruction of Riga's Vanšu Bridge could be postponed by three to six months, from the fourth quarter of 2027 to mid-2028, unless effective traffic management solutions are developed and implemented, Riga Mayor Viesturs Kleinbergs of the Progressives said on Tuesday during a discussion organised by the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI).
The mayor explained that several solutions are currently being assessed simultaneously, including redesigning intersections to increase traffic capacity and constructing a temporary bridge to partially alleviate congestion during the reconstruction.
"If we see that certain preparations cannot be completed by the deadline, we will postpone the start of the repair works," Kleinbergs said.
Kristaps Kauliņš, Director of Riga City Council's Department of Outdoor Space and Mobility, said the current plan envisages reconstruction beginning in late 2027 and continuing until 2030.
The first two stages are not expected to involve significant traffic restrictions, as they will focus on reconstructing the Daugava river embankment and Krišjāņa Valdemāra Street.
During the third stage, when the bridge itself undergoes major repairs, traffic will be reduced to one lane in each direction. Exceptions will apply during the replacement of the bridge's suspension cables, which is planned for nights and weekends.
Kauliņš explained that there are 20 signal-controlled intersections around Vanšu Bridge. The municipality is examining ways to increase their capacity and redirect traffic away from the bridge.
Possible measures include additional traffic lanes, redesigned turning arrangements and adjustments to traffic light timings.
Kauliņš also said that the start of the bridge's main reconstruction works could be postponed until the second quarter of 2028 without significant difficulties.
The overall project has been divided into three separate construction projects, each with its own building permit, allowing the stages to begin independently.
Mārtiņš Lazdovskis, Chairman of the Board of Latvian State Roads (LVC), explained that the government has begun replenishing its strategic material reserves and has signed a contract to purchase temporary bridge structures, as the existing bridges in state reserves have reached the end of their service life.
Two years ago, LVC launched the procurement of modern bridge spans and signed an agreement with an Austrian company to purchase single-lane bridge sections measuring 45 metres in length and capable of supporting loads of 100 tonnes.
Initially, deliveries were scheduled to take place gradually until 2029.
However, Lazdovskis explained that if the government decides to bring forward the funding allocated for 2028 and 2029 to 2027, the Austrian manufacturer could produce and deliver the required bridge components within eight months.
"At the same time, we must remember that these are only Lego blocks from which the bridge is assembled. Temporary supports or pontoons are also needed, along with access roads," Lazdovskis said.
Guntars Vītols of the United List, an adviser to Finance Minister Māris Kučinskis, stressed that funding for the temporary bridge could be found because the economic losses caused by severe congestion should be avoided.
However, the Ministry of Finance is concerned that planning for the temporary bridge may have started too late.
Vītols added that a political decision is needed to simplify procurement and design procedures.
Guntis Āboltiņš-Āboliņš, Chairman of the LCCI Construction and Real Estate Development Committee, recalled that a temporary bridge design originally developed for Rail Baltica is already available.
He suggested that a temporary bridge could therefore become operational within a year.
"It is urgently necessary to examine the riverbed, determine what should be installed where, and establish which supports are required," Āboltiņš-Āboliņš said.
Riga Deputy Mayor Māris Sprindžuks of the United List argued that approximately 80% of the solution would depend on reorganising traffic.
In his view, the priority is to avoid delays in launching accelerated design-and-build procurements for intersections that would allow traffic flows to be redirected.
Sprindžuks believes a temporary bridge could realistically be installed in 2028, but traffic arrangements must be redesigned before then.
Kauliņš explained that Riga City Council favours placing the temporary bridge alongside Vanšu Bridge on the Old Riga side.
Under this option, vehicles on the left bank would access the temporary bridge via the existing Ķīpsala exit near the Saules akmens office building.
On the right bank, a temporary intersection would need to be constructed connecting the bridge to 13. novembra krastmala.
However, LCCI representatives, including road engineer and entrepreneur Jānis Vasaraudzis, argued that the temporary bridge should connect to Muitas Street, on the side of Riga Passenger Port.
Kauliņš said the final decision would be made by engineers and designers.
He pointed out that the Daugava riverbank near the port is privately owned and that the river is considerably deeper there than on the Old Riga side.
Kleinbergs added that both fixed-support and pontoon-based bridge solutions remain under consideration.
Dace Zīle, a researcher at the University of Latvia's LV PEAK research institute, said Vanšu Bridge is crossed daily by between 55,000 and 60,000 vehicles.
In addition, 759 Riga public transport services cross the bridge each day, carrying approximately 20,000 passengers.
According to LV PEAK research, if daily travel times increased by 30 minutes, the resulting losses would amount to 1.2 million person-hours per month, equivalent to 12.5 million euros.
The additional congestion would also generate 222.6 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.
Zīle explained that the economic impact of an additional 30 minutes of congestion on Vanšu Bridge would correspond to 23.3% of Latvia's gross domestic product generated during a 30-minute period.
LETA previously reported that the most significant reconstruction works on Vanšu Bridge were scheduled to begin in 2027.
To manage traffic during the reconstruction, Riga City Council has proposed installing a temporary bridge.
Earlier plans envisaged one traffic lane in each direction, with construction costs estimated at approximately 20 million euros.
Officials have previously suggested that such a bridge could also serve national civil and military purposes, rather than being used exclusively by the municipality.
However, there has been no definitive agreement on how the temporary bridge would be provided.
The mayor previously promised to discuss potential cost-sharing arrangements with the finance minister and prime minister.
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs of the United List described the proposal for a temporary bridge during the reconstruction as an "outside-the-box" idea.
However, he stressed that state participation in financing the project would depend on several factors.
"It is good that solutions are being considered from a national perspective," Kulbergs said.
He acknowledged that, at first glance, the possibility of reusing the temporary bridge elsewhere in the future appeared reasonable, provided it was technically feasible.
The tender for the reconstruction of Vanšu Bridge was won by the Vanšu tilts consortium, which offered to complete the works for 69.8 million euros excluding value-added tax.
The consortium comprises Hanza Construction Group, Tilts and Baltijas mākslīgo būvju projektēšanas birojs Vektors T.
The reconstruction is expected to require up to 6.7 million euros in 2026, up to 42 million euros in 2027 and up to 35.76 million euros in 2028.
Vanšu Bridge has a total length of 593.6 metres, while its main pylon reaches a height of 108.7 metres.
The project includes resurfacing the roadway and creating separate pedestrian and cycling infrastructure.
The pedestrian pavements will measure 1.7 metres wide on one side of the bridge and 1.9 metres on the other.
The bridge railings will be restored to their original height of 1.3 metres.
The reconstruction will also include replacing the suspension cables, which will have a combined weight of 385.5 tonnes.
New protective coverings will be installed along 3,084 metres of existing and replacement cables to ensure long-term durability and protection against environmental conditions.
The reconstruction will be carried out using the design-and-build approach, under which a single contractor is responsible for both preparing the construction design and completing the works.
This approach is intended to ensure consistent planning, coordination and accountability throughout the contract.
